### Book I. Section I. Chapter II.

...and the earth was called, which owes its name to its drying and its production <note>The author is likely making an etymological link between the drying out of the land in Genesis and the Latin word for earth/dry land.</note>. Our earth, however, which we treat in this chapter, stands as the principle of the world and has its origin in the first creation. 
<margin>N. 2.</margin>
For as has been demonstrated from the preceding pages, only two principles of the world exist: one **Hyperphysical** <note>Meaning "beyond the physical" or supernatural, referring to the heavens</note>, the other **Physical**. From the latter, all physical bodies take their origin, just as from the former the hyperphysical qualities of physical things are derived. The first relates to the second—namely, the heaven to the earth—as **form to matter** <note>A classic Aristotelian concept where "matter" is the raw potential and "form" is the active principle that gives it specific identity</note>. We assign to the heaven the **efficient cause of all forms**, and to the earth the **prime matter** of all things. We do this not for frivolous reasons, but for many causes which we will share in due time, should anyone dare to treat us too harshly for this opinion. We ask the reader, however—so that he may properly and sufficiently understand us, especially in these first three chapters—that when we speak of *heaven* or *earth*, he understands nothing other than the heaven and the earth of which Moses says: *In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth, etc.* For if our opinion were understood to refer to the *other* heaven and earth mentioned later in the same chapter, it would surely be absurd, nor would it correspond to the present theory or subsequent practice.
<margin>N. 3.</margin>
Furthermore, we wish the reader to be advised that in this place, under the name of "earth," we always understand the **earth-water-air globe**. For although Sacred Scripture, in the history of creation, makes no mention of the creation or production of water or air, but immediately adds to the text: *The earth was without form and void, and the Spirit of the Lord moved over the waters*, I nevertheless hope no one will be so inexperienced as to understand *the waters* to be anything other than those in which the earth was enveloped. Nor should the *Spirit of the Lord* be interpreted as anything other than the **air** <note>The author argues for a naturalistic interpretation of "Spiritus," which in Latin can mean breath, wind, or spirit</note> by which the entire mass of earth and water was surrounded. Indeed, not a few commentators interpret the *Spirit of the Lord* as the *Holy Spirit*; but these are either little-skilled in physical matters, or they do not sufficiently understand the style and customary speech of Sacred Scripture. For the aforementioned Scripture is often accustomed to call not only *air*, but even the winds, the *Spirit of the Lord*. They get stuck on words and imagine mysteries where there are none; for this, they are not undeservedly mocked by the **Arians** <note>A theological sect that denied the Trinity; the author suggests that weak physical interpretations of the Bible give ammunition to heretics</note>, because their adversaries resort to such frivolous interpretations while abandoning more solid ones.
<margin>N. 4.</margin>
In a single moment, as it were, and in an instant—namely at that very point when time first began to be, that is, in the **beginning of time**—this earth-water-air globe was created with that general threefold division which still exists, yet of a **Harmonic Nature**, and indeed of **earth**. For we shall demonstrate elsewhere that *water and air are a fluid earth*. This globe differs within itself by three diverse degrees; this difference does not consist in *rarefaction and density* alone (otherwise *air and water* could have been *produced from earth* by way of production, like other things). Rather, it differs by a **difference of creation** which the Creator impressed upon it at the first moment. Hence it happens that *Air, Water, and Earth* can indeed be confused and mixed among themselves, but never can one be truly **transmuted** into the nature of another.
<margin>N. 5.</margin>
In the creation itself, even if the earth-water-air globe was one and the same regarding its coherence and connection, it existed in no way in a state of **confusion**. For every Element, without any motion or re-

Furthermore, it is most certain that God, in the creation of this universe, preserved that same order which we still call the *course of Nature*; for it was a natural consequence 
<margin>N. 6.</margin>
that the place exist before the thing placed within it—namely, the heaven before the earth—and motion before the thing to be moved. From this it appears, as sacred Scripture also testifies was done, that it was necessary for the heaven, as the *containing space* <note>original: "locans"</note> and *moving cause*, as the container of this universe, to be created before all things, so that it might both provide a place and contain, *move the contents*, and mix those things that were moved. Since, however, a single and simple thing cannot be mixed except numerically, it was necessary that for a 
<margin>N. 7.</margin>
physical mixture, the primordial earth be *diverse*. Hence, divided into three classes by the creation itself, as has been said, the earth-water-air globe was made: so that it might indeed be *mixed*, but could not be *transmuted* <note>Alchemical term for changing one substance into another, such as lead into gold</note> against the will of the Creator. Moreover, air was necessary as the most subtle portion of the earth, so that it could be moved most closely by the heaven; and water was required so that a *medium* of acting upon the thick earth might be given to the air; while the Earth was the densest part, so that it might provide the **Subject** <note>The underlying material or "substrate" that undergoes change</note> to be dissolved. From all of which it follows that the earth-water-air globe was entirely *trinal* <note>Consisting of three parts</note> and was not confused during creation. It also follows that 
<margin>N. 8.</margin>
all mixtures ought to be reduced *into three classes*, namely, as they exist in their final degree as *earthy, watery, or airy*. I do not think this should be overlooked, however: that the name is taken from the earth in sacred Scripture as the more important part, while no mention is made of water and air. For the earth provides the underlying substance <note>original: "hypostasin"</note> to the two remaining elements, acting as the subject upon which the other two act. Whence in all of sacred Scripture, the earth always holds the first place. So regarding man, the text says: *earth you are, and to earth you shall return* <note>Genesis 3:19; originally "dust," but translated as "terra" in the Latin Vulgate</note>; for even if in the mixture of man there is much water and air besides earth, the name is taken from the earth as the more powerful ingredient. Nor does man alone come from the earth, but whatever we see comes from there. Thus, the earth is not only the mother, source, and origin of all things, but also the receptacle and end of all bodies. For the final reduction and annihilation of all things is *earth*; nor do only sublunary things <note>Things below the moon, i.e., on Earth</note> consist of earth, but superlunary things <note>Celestial objects or things above the moon</note> also consist of earth, as will be shown in the following chapter. From what has been 
<margin>N. 9.</margin>
said so far, it necessarily follows that in creation, the heaven occupied *less* space because of its density, while the earth occupied *more*, because the *material substance* of all super- and sublunary bodies still lay hidden within it. Hence it is beyond doubt that the earth at that time was far different and distinct from our modern earth, being mixed in various ways and containing many other substances within itself; for the substances and seeds of all things and bodies lay hidden in it, whence 
<margin>N. 10.</margin>
it could rightly and deservedly be called the virgin earth or **Panspermia** <note>From Greek, meaning "all-seeding" or containing the seeds of everything</note>. From this, as if from a fertile womb, all things would obtain their *being* through successive production. # Book I. Section I. Chapter II.

...mutation <note>original: "transmutationem", continuing from the previous page's discussion on the movement and change of elements</note>. Mention of this latter state will be made in the following section. In this place, however, we shall treat the earth insofar as it existed before its production as the first material of all things and a **universal seed-bed** <note>original: "Panspermia", a philosophical term suggesting that the "seeds" or blueprints of all things were present in the initial matter</note>, existing in a state of confusion as **Chaos**; a mixture confused in five ways, and indeed this occurred immediately in the very first creation, as the Creator willed. Therefore, these five divisions or types of earths which are in the Chaos can never be either radically mixed or *transmuted* into one another. They were indeed mixed in the Chaos, but not in such a way that they did not preserve the nature of their place or gravity; for the lighter things clung to the circumference, and the heavier things remained at the center. Yet they were mixed insofar as their nature desired a mutual cohesion, for *nature delights in nature* <note>original: "natura enim naturae gaudet", a common alchemical and philosophical maxim suggesting that like substances are drawn to one another</note>, as we still see today. For the stars participate much in sublunary <note>things beneath the moon; i.e., the Earthly realm</note> things, sublunary things not a little in superlunary <note>things above the moon; i.e., the heavens</note> things, animals in vegetables, and some things in others. This confusion is not accidental but primordial and essential, from which the proverb arises: *In Nature, anything is in anything, and that which is below is similar to that which is above* <note>original: "in Natura quidlibet esse quodlibet, & quod inferius est, ei simile esse, quod superius est"; a variation of the famous Hermetic principle from the Emerald Tablet</note>. For by this confusion, all of Nature clings together like a chain or magnetism.

It now remains to explain what those five types of earths were, which we have mentioned so far. The first type of earth is the noblest of all and provided the material for the planets and stars; the *second* is the mother of various *Meteors* <note>In the 17th century, "meteors" referred to any atmospheric phenomenon, including rain, wind, and lightning, not just falling stars</note>; *from the third, animals were made*; the *fourth* was the origin of *vegetables* <margin>N. 11.</margin> <note>plants</note>; and the *last* was the origin of *minerals*. Therefore, the diversity of bodies, whether super- or sublunary, does not arise from water or air, but from the difference of the earths. For the confusion or Chaos took place in the earth, not in water or air; for however much the Elements are confused, they return again to their triple number <note>The three elements: earth, water, air</note>. However, to what extent water and air allow themselves to be separated from the earth will be clear from what is said below. In this place, however, it could be asked whether such a confused primordial Chaos still exists in the nature of things—namely, a mass of the aforementioned five earths? For this was called Chaos in respect to the various mixed earths; not because in creation the terrestrial globe, although surrounded by water, was drenched by or mixed with the same, as will be clear from the following chapter.

<margin>N. 12.</margin>
To return to the question, I answer by denying it; for just as before the actual production from Chaos, no specific body existed *actually*, but only *potentially* within it, so after the actual production, such a fivefold mass or Chaos no longer exists except separately in diverse bodies, nor is it any longer so confused, except as much as the first kind of confusion impressed in the creation itself permits, and even now it exists in fact—that is, *potentially*. By this decision, those are also refuted who call the *fifth essence of things* <term>Fifth Essence: often called the "quintessence," this was believed to be a pure, celestial substance distinct from the four earthly elements</term> something that still survives in the world as "virgin"—that is, entirely simple and without production.

<margin>N. 13.</margin>
Because of the fivefold difference of the earth, I will not deny that the first Chaos could be called the *fifth of all things*. But who would doubt that the Chaos—since after the production of the six days of creation it exists only in *specific* bodies and in a certain way—contains this simple fifth essence in another way than it was in creation, once bodies were produced from it? From the aforementioned, therefore, it is concluded that this virgin and first earth, before the act of production, was entirely earthy and dry,

->T E X T.<-

<margin>N. 1.</margin> Thus far we have dealt with the state of heaven and earth as they were in the act of creation; now it remains for us to explain what their state was before "production" <note>the process by which organized things were formed out of the initial raw matter</note>. The text says: *the earth was without form and void, etc.* <note>original: "terra autem erat inanis & vacua," quoting Genesis 1:2</note> from which it follows that it was pure, and not yet mixed with water or air. For since neither *fire* nor any other moving force was yet present to rarefy the heaven, it was necessary for it to have existed in a most dense state, as if it were crystalline. It is necessary that air, water, and earth were dense in the same way, like ice; and this common density was the cause of the darkness and the greatest cold at that time. It also prevented the Elements from being able to mix with one another. For since the earth, on account of its most narrow and dense pores, had no entry point, neither could water act upon it, nor air upon water, and consequently nothing could be *mixed*. For the medium of mixture
<margin>N. 2.</margin> is rarefaction, which we said above was still lacking. Therefore, the state of our heaven and the earth-water-air globe in the first creation, before production, was like an **egg**...

...to have had <note>original: "buisse," the conclusion of the catchword "habuisse" from the previous page</note>, let us imagine for ourselves; whose yolk signifies the *earth*, the white the *water*, the membrane the *air*, and the shell the *heaven*, while the surrounding place or the container of the egg indicates the Deity.
<margin>N. 3.</margin>
As for the fact that the text uses the words *void* and *empty* <note>original: "inane & vacuum," referring to Genesis 1:2</note>, this is not taken in the way some of the Moderns <note>referring to "Neoterics," the new scientists or philosophers of the 17th century</note> accept it—namely, as a *physical* vacuum. Instead, it ought to be understood in terms of *production*: specifically, that the earth, though fertile through the mixing that occurred during the subsequent *production* (which we will discuss in this chapter), was still empty—that is, it was not yet full of any specific, distinct bodies. For the Sacred Text describes the earth here as it existed in creation, not as it existed in *production*. Now that the creation of heaven and earth has been explained—which was made by God out of nothing and led from a state of non-existence into essential being—it will not be out of place to offer a few remarks on the *production* that followed. This will allow us to move, as if by steps, from general concepts to more specific ones, and toward our goal: the *origin* <term>genesis: the process of coming into being</term> of underground things.

Before all else, the difference between the words *to create*, *to be made*, and *to produce* must be explained, for the Sacred Text uses these in the history of creation: 
<margin>N. 4.</margin>
namely, *he created*, *let it be made*, and *let it bring forth*. We have already spoken of the word *to create* in the preceding pages. The term *let it be made* <note>Latin: "fiat"</note> differs from the word *let it bring forth* <note>Latin: "producat"</note> in this: that the latter refers to *mixture*, while the former refers to *motion*. For *let it be made* is the voice of one commanding, which is directed toward an intelligent being. We maintain that the first motion in the world was caused by *Angels*, to whom the word *let it be made* was directed by God. Thus, when the Sacred Text says, *let there be light*, etc., it is to be understood that the light was fashioned by Angels. And when the same text says, *let the waters bring forth creeping things*, etc., it should be understood as referring to the water or the earth, just as with the sprouting of plants, all of which were done by the help of a secondary *mixture*.
<margin>N. 5.</margin>
Therefore, all things are either *made* or *produced* from heaven and earth—heaven acting as the moving cause, and the earth (under which we also include water and air) providing the matter. All these things occurred not through further creation, but through the successive production that followed, which, as will now be shown, was achieved by the help of *mixture*. For this universal and primordial *mixture*, *motion* was required, and motion does not occur without *rarefaction* <note>the process of a substance becoming less dense or expanding</note>. Therefore, the subject of the rare and the dense, which we have said is heaven, had to be moved before all else—specifically at the first moment when creation ended and the act of 
<margin>N. 6.</margin>
production began.
<margin>N. 7.</margin>
And since *light* was not yet present, nor the effect of light, namely *heat* (which would rarefy things and, by rarefying them, move them), it was necessary for heaven to be moved by another *external* moving cause. Through this motion it would be rarefied, and through that rarefaction, the mixture of all things would occur. This first *moving cause* of the world is ascribed to angelic power—specifically to the *Angel* as the prime mover, to whom, as we said before, the word *let it be made* was directed. Nor does this opinion of ours contradict the Metaphysicians. Whether there was one or several moving Angels, we shall not dwell upon, although (as we will later cite from the words of Job <note>original: "Hiob"</note>) the more curious might defend the idea of a plurality of Angels occupied with this duty.
<margin>N. 8.</margin>
To return to the point: the first duty of the moving Angel was to *rarefy* heaven (that heaven which we mentioned in the first chapter). Once rarefied, it was extended more widely, just as all the atoms of air, water, and earth began to extend, as if from heaven, being the subject of the rare...

From this progression, it followed that an entry was opened for the Elements into one another, by which they could act upon themselves and mix together. And this operation is the first foundation of universal production and mixture. *The second effect of this angelic rarefaction* 
<margin>N. 9.</margin> *was that, due to the excessive thinness of the heaven in that place where it was moved by the Angel, the air also became more rarefied; by being rarefied, it was driven forward, and this impulse provided the winds:* from which *the motion of the air into the water (which was already rare to certain degrees) and the entry of water into the expanded and rare earth was granted.* From all these things, the first mixture and confusion of air with water, and water with earth, followed. *The third effect of this angelic rarefaction is*

Truly, since the *earthy* particles, which were elevated and rarefied along with the water, were most strongly agitated by the first mover, they finally began to conceive *fire*, which the Sacred Text calls the first *light*. This first appeared in the place where the strongest rarefaction occurred—namely, where the direct motion was made by the Angel—and where, consequently, by the strong rarefaction, a great part of the water and earth was lifted up, rendering the earth-water globe directly below the light lighter in that part. Therefore, the earth-water globe, now unequal in its own weight, began to turn itself gradually toward the *light*, and from this conversion the first *day and night* arose. For that part of the globe which stood directly below the *light* was illuminated by it, which *illumination is called day*; the other part of the globe, however, diametrically opposite the first and removed from the light, suffered *night*—that is, it was not illuminated by the light. In one part of the earth-water globe, therefore, there was day, and in the other, night, which the Sacred Text expressed when it said: *Let there be light, and light was made, and he divided the light from the darkness, and called the light day, and the darkness night, and the evening and the morning were one day, etc.* <note>Genesis 1:3-5</note> For every single *turning of the globe constituted a day and a night*; although these primordial days stood as far greater and longer than our modern ones, due to the slower turning of the globe, which occurred because of its greater *mass*: for in it, all the stars and meteors were still contained materially and before their production. 
<margin>N. 11.</margin> From these aforementioned things, it follows that the mixture of air, water, and earth was the first step of production, while the manifestation of *light* was the second. This density of the air did not permit those aforementioned celestial waters to fall back. For the earth-water globe at that time was not yet dry, but was watery on its surface in every direction, even if it was no longer overwhelmed by such vast and copious waters, since a great part of the waters had been removed to construct the clouds. Therefore, the production of the firmament was the separation of waters from waters—namely, the lifting of a certain portion of water from the earth-water globe. And this construction of the firmament occurred again through a single *rotation* <note>original: "conversione"</note> of the globe, which we have said always constitutes a day and a night.

It was then able to divide it more easily, to strip the earth of its waters, and thus to work upon the earth itself. # Book I. Section I. Chap. III.

...all these were the effects and duties of the *first-produced light*: namely, to rotate the earth, to illuminate it, and by the rotations of the globe, to create day and night. <margin>N. 17.</margin> For the purpose of lifting the immense and vast mass of waters—partly into clouds, partly into the stars, and turning them into winds—an extreme rarefaction <term>rarefaction: the process of making a substance thinner or less dense, which early scientists believed allowed matter to rise and transform</term> was required, and to achieve it, a *most powerful fire* was needed, which the *Sacred text* in the history of creation calls light. But once the Earth was already dried, the clouds lifted, the stars and meteors produced, and the plants also perfected, such a great quantity of fire was no longer necessary. Therefore, it is rational and consistent that once the stars, and especially the *sun*, were produced, the moving Angel <note>referring to the "motive intelligence" or angelic force scholastic philosophers believed moved the celestial spheres</note> ceased the rarefaction, and consequently, that *primordial* light came to an end.

In the place, role, and duty of the ceasing light, the *sun* succeeded. It was far more moderate and weaker in its rarefaction than the previous light, yet it was sufficient for the remaining things that were still to be produced—namely *animals* and various *insects*—and for preserving and nourishing the plants already brought forth. For these and similar duties of nature to be fulfilled, the sun was far more suitable than that *most vehement primordial fire*. Therefore, once the sun was produced, the first motor—and thus the first light—ceased; and newly born nature began to perfect itself, *namely by the work and help of the sun.* <margin>N. 18.</margin> From these and similar points, we can easily conclude that those who still insist on the existence of the aforementioned *primordial light* in some unknown *Empyrean Sphere or heaven* <note>The Empyrean was traditionally the highest, most fire-filled heaven in medieval cosmology</note> without any cause or logic are thrusting non-existent things upon us.

We could also, at this point, propose and debate the *incombustible matter* of the stars—especially the *Sun*—namely concerning the transparency and perpetuity of the stellar earth, as well as its analogy with a certain type of earth still existing on our terrestrial globe. However, since we strive for brevity, and we are treating these things which we have written so far concerning creation for no other purpose than to demonstrate the *origin of subterranean things*, we shall rightly hasten toward the end of our goal, and therefore to the *fifth day*, which follows the fourth.

These *dregs*, after they had been precipitated (just like those in the firmament from which we said the stars proceeded), were of a very moist and muddy nature. Consequently, they would easily *putrefy* <note>original: "putrescerent." In early modern science, "putrefaction" or rotting was viewed as a creative, fermenting process that sparked spontaneous generation</note>, and by putrefying, they provided various new species. From these dregs, various *aquatic creatures* were produced according to the diversity of the sediment, such as *fish and great whales*, and so on.

Therefore, two things followed from this deposition of dregs: first, that by depositing the dregs, the sea water was rendered *purer* and *clearer*, just as the firmament was made clearer by the gathering of the stars. Thus, once the *sun* was produced, the *first motor* and the first light ceased; and the newly born nature began to perfect itself, specifically by the power and help of the sun.

<margin>No. 18.</margin> From these and similar points, we can easily gather that those who still thrust upon us the existence of the aforementioned primordial light—placing it in some "Empyrean Sphere" or heaven without any cause or logical necessity—are presenting us with non-existent things. <meta>This page transitions from the general history of creation (the six days) to a systematic classification of matter. The author moves from a theological/historical narrative to a physical and chemical analysis of how "mixed bodies"—specifically minerals and subterranean substances—are formed from the primary elements. Book 1, Section 1, Chapter 4.

->## S Y N O P S I S.<-

*No. 1. The primary elemental principles of things are air, water, and earth. No. 2. How air enters into mixtures. No. 3. Three universal mixtures. No. 4. Mixtures that consist of water and earth. No. 5. Mixtures that consist of water and water. No. 6. Mixtures that consist of earth and earth. No. 7. The difference between metals and stones. No. 8. Why the Sacred Text, in the history of creation, makes no mention of subterranean things, especially metals and stones.*

->## T E X T U S.<-

<margin>No. 1.</margin>Having finished the history of universal production, order requires us to discuss the differences and general distinctions of produced bodies. This is so that we are not confused by their great multitude in the following sections, but rather move forward with an orderly arrangement: from the more general to the general, and from the more specific to the specific—namely, from the genus to the species—until we arrive at the specific origin, location, and type of subterranean things among the other mixtures. Although there are many bodies that, upon external inspection, appear entirely different from one another, the origin, source, and principle of them all is grounded in earth and water. We have demonstrated at length in the preceding pages that all bodies consist of and are produced from these two, acting as the principles of the entire universe. From this, it is clear that *earth* is the foundation of all things and, when mixed with *water*, has produced diverse bodies. Although it cannot be denied that *air* is found in mixtures, it is most certain that it enters them as an *instrument* <note>The author distinguishes between the "matter" of a thing (earth/water) and the "agent" or tool that helps form it (air/fire)</note> rather than a primary ingredient.

<margin>No. 2.</margin>Just as *water* is the immediate *vehicle* for the kneading and mixing of the *earth*, so *air* is the immediate *instrument* by which water can be moved and driven toward motion and mixing. In this way, motion and mixing happen gradually from the more subtle elements to the thicker ones. For *heaven* <note>In this context, "heaven" refers to the celestial influences or heat from the stars and sun</note> acts upon *air*, *air* acts upon *water*, and *water* acts upon *earth*, as is sufficiently known from the preceding history of production. Therefore, only *earth* and *water* are *miscible* <term>miscibilia: substances capable of being blended together into a new compound</term> and are the principles of all mixed things. *Air*, *heaven*, and *fire*, however, are the *mixers*, or the *causes* of the mixtures; depending on the diversity of the mixing process, they produce different mixed bodies.

<margin>No. 3.</margin>The first class of these is the mixing of *water* with *earth*. This is the universal mixing that occurred at the very beginning of the first production of all things, the likeness and appearance of which we still see, in part, in *salty sea water*. Furthermore, every mixture is of two types: *superficial* mixture, when water is mixed with earth not as a substance to be permanently combined, but as an *instrument* of the mixing. Such a mixture can be separated again without the destruction of the substance, as we see in *flour* <note>referring to dough</note> and in *mud* used for *fired bricks*. In both cases, the subject is turned into a paste by water so that it can be mixed and the parts of the earth can cling together; once this coagulation has occurred, the water evaporates again with the help of heat, leaving the mixture behind. A *central* mixture, however, is when water is so thoroughly mixed with the earth that it cannot be separated without the total destruction of the mixture—as when it enters into the composition of a *cucumber*, an *apple*, or other such mixtures. For the water cannot be separated from the compound except by the *disruption of the mixture*. Various degrees exist in this cohesion, in which—

...for in certain mixtures, earth clings more stubbornly to water than in others; and this indeed happens according to the axioms that we will propose in the following pages of Section 4, Chapter 3. Furthermore, there are *three general kinds of mixtures* in existence, corresponding to the universal triple mixing that occurred during the first production <note>The "first production" refers to the Creation described in Genesis.</note>. For there, as is clear from what has been said, three mixings were made, from which three kinds of mixtures emerged:

<margin>No. 4.</margin>
*The first kind of mixture is when water was thoroughly mixed with earth*; and from this mixture—with water as the more dominant part—not only the *stars, but also animals, vegetables, and a great part of minerals* (namely those whose composition water enters into, such as gums and solidified juices) consist.

<margin>No. 5.</margin>
*The second mixing is where water was mixed with water*; for although "water" is understood generically under a single name, it is not at all to be doubted that there are various *species of water*. Whether these differ by their own nature, or by the greater or lesser amount of earth mixed in, does not concern us much here, provided they cause the diversity of waters. Therefore, when different waters are mixed together, different *aqueous mixtures* must necessarily emerge, as we see in *snow, frost, dew, hail, and ice*, and other meteors <note>In 17th-century science, "meteors" referred to any atmospheric phenomena, including rain and snow, not just falling stars.</note>. Everyone sees that these, although they are aqueous products, are of a different nature than ordinary water. We could also demonstrate this with an elegant mathematical experiment, if we did not have a greater concern for *subterranean things* than for *meteors* in this place: where, in our desire for brevity, even if we avoid all detours, we can hardly prevent ourselves from being accused of wordiness by some.

<margin>No. 6.</margin>
*The third kind of mixture consists of earth, namely when earth is mixed with earth*; for although "earth" is called an Element under one generic name, it is known even to "the blind and the barbers" <note>original: "lippis & tonforibus"; a Latin idiom meaning it is common knowledge or obvious to everyone.</note> that various *species of earth* exist. These, when mixed, produce new compounds which ought to be called *earthy*, because nothing but earth enters into their composition. To this class of mixtures, *metals and stones* are numbered; for it is most certain that they consist of *earth*, as we will prove at length in Section 3. Just as in the aforementioned three classes of mixtures, various species and subdivisions are found, so among *earthy mixtures*, there is again a great difference. Since we are only reviewing general matters here and will treat specifics in the following sections, we will mention no distinction except that which is between

<margin>No. 7.</margin>
*stones and metals.* For both are earthy compounds, and both contain *three earths*—as we will prove in Section 3—as their principles. Both have *two earths in common*, but they differ in the *third earth*, which gives *metallicity and malleability* <note>term: malleability (the quality of being able to be hammered or pressed into shape without breaking)</note>. Thus *metals are malleable, while stones are friable* <note>term: friable (easily crumbled or broken into chalky fragments)</note>: all of which we will prove in Section 3 almost to the point of sufficiency and exhaustion. The benevolent reader will find the *specific* differences of metals and stones in Section 6 of this book; here it was only pleasing to draw out the general difference of mixtures from the first sources of production, so that the specific correlation of subterranean things with the rest comes more clearly before the eyes. If we consider this more accurately, we will find that the class of *metals and stones* stands diametrically opposite to that of *meteors*; for just as those consist of *water and water*, so *stones and metals* consist of *earth and earth*. Both are *more simply mixed and more homogeneous in their mixture* than the first...

<meta>This page continues the author’s systematic classification of the "three general kinds of mixtures." **Book 1, Section 1, Chapter 4.**

...the third class of mixtures, which consists of water and earth, and involves animals and vegetables, as well as a part of the mineral juices <note>original: "succorum mineralium"; in 17th-century science, minerals were often thought to form from "juices" or "vapors" that solidified over time</note>. Because of this connection of subterranean things with meteors <note>In this context, "meteors" refers to any atmospheric phenomenon (rain, wind, lightning), not just shooting stars</note>, I think some have emerged who seized the opportunity to imagine not only a great harmony between subterranean things and meteors, but even to attribute to meteors—and especially to the planets—an influence, or even a productive cause, over them. 

But truly, whatever the case may be, I place the harmony and affinity of both mixtures—namely, the meteors and the subterranean things—in nothing other than a bare correlation. Specifically, just as those things which are aqueous mixtures are called "meteors," so those things which exist as earthy mixtures can be called *terrestrial meteors*: they are related to the former by name alone. And I believe this is the proper reason why some Physicists <note>The author uses "Physici" to refer to natural philosophers or scientists of his time</note> have always treated the doctrine of subterranean things under the title of *meteors*. 

Now, for the conclusion, it remains for us to consider why the Sacred text, in the history of production <note>The creation story in the Book of Genesis</note>, makes no mention of subterranean things? But we will not wonder at this if we consider that Holy Scripture speaks only of those products that have physical motion and consist of dissimilar parts. For the production of these things, because of the diversity, offices, and functions of their parts, is more *miraculous*; therefore, the Sacred text chose to mention them so that we might perceive from them the omnipotence of the Creator and Producer. 

For even if, as we will demonstrate later, subterranean things also grow and are generated daily, and undergo reactions and various physical motions, there is nonetheless a great disparity in their genesis compared to other bodies. As has been said, the structure of subterranean things is more simply mixed and more homogeneous <note>Meaning it consists of similar parts throughout, unlike an animal which has distinct organs and limbs</note>. For this reason, in Holy Scripture, they are included under the single and general name of *earth*. 

*For the Sacred text seems to have taken more account of the things produced from the earth than of the earth itself*, since it makes a long mention of the products, but embraces the creation of the *earth* in only a few words: namely, *In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth* <note>original: "In principio creavit Deus cælum & terram"; Genesis 1:1</note>. 

In the text, however, there is a long mention of the production of all things from the earth; namely, by what means the earth was mixed with waters in various ways, and then freed from them again, boiled down, and in part made dry: *therefore God called the dry land earth*, from which various animals and vegetables were produced. What then remained of the earth was attributed to the subterranean things under a silent name, as being the driest and thickest part, which Holy Scripture not infrequently calls *earth*. For thus Esdras <note>Referring to the book of 2 Esdras (or 4 Ezra), an ancient Jewish work often included in Bibles of this period</note> says: *the earth gives much matter for shaping earthenware vessels, but little dust from which gold is made* <note>original: "terram multum materiæ pro fingendis vasis fictilibus, paucum autem pulverem dare, unde aurum fit"; 2 Esdras 8:2</note>. From all of which we conclude that the matter and principle of subterranean things is the *thickest earth*; which stands in opposition to the most subtle "earth" of the stars, and varies no less than the stars and planets differ in their clarity and brightness.

## Book One, Section Two
# On the state and physical motion of the terraqueous globe after the universal production, in relation to the origin of subterranean things, where the wonderful construction of the terraqueous globe is treated, as well as the specific motion of water and earth above and below ground.
### Chapter One

<margin>N. I.</margin> In the preceding Section, we discussed the *Universal* rise, creation, and production of all things, as if they were the most remote principles and causes of matter. Now, order demands that we turn away from other things and hasten toward the *more specific origin of subterranean things*. Primarily, we must teach how the principles of *subterranean things*, which we said consist of earth, come together and move toward that end and order, so that they may constitute a mineral mixture and compound. 

And since it was said in the previous pages that *water* is the cause and vehicle of all mixing—even of those bodies where it enters the composition only *superficiality*—and secondly, that there are many subterranean *compounds* which consist of *earth and water*, where water constitutes the mixture somewhat more *intimately*: it will not be unpleasant or useless to the reader if, in this Section, I first offer a few things regarding the *motion of water*. Specifically, I will address how it serves the mixture and origin of subterranean things, or how it acts as the *Instrument* and vehicle of subterranean mixing. 

Regarding mineral *earth*, as the mixable *subject* <note>In 17th-century logic, the "subject" is the underlying material that receives a form or quality</note> of subterranean things, we will deal with that sufficiently in the following third Section. In <margin>N. 2.</margin> this place, however, we shall speak of water as the mixing and moving cause. By *physical motion*, we mean the *intrinsic physical power of the principles*, by which nature always intends to act toward its end; this action consists in mixing <note>original: "mixtione"; the chemical union of elements into a new substance</note>, which we will discuss specifically in the fourth Section. In this place, however, we will consider only the *motion* of the principles...

[...we] treat, insofar as they tend toward mixture. We shall proceed from the universal to the particular, namely from remote matter to proximate [matter]; therefore, in this place we will consider the motion of *water* and *earth*; first, as it is universal, like the most remote principle of subterranean things: then, as it is particular, like a derived principle <term>principiatum: a principle that is itself produced from a prior cause</term>, or matter proximate to the genesis <note>original: "genesin"</note> of subterranean things—namely, how it is disposed and moves within those three earths which we will discuss in the following Section. In order to begin from a more evident demonstration, we will first consider the *common features* that occur regarding the mixture of water and mineral earth.

<margin>N. 3.</margin>
For it is manifest that common *water* enters into the mixtures of *Vitriol, Alum, Borax, Nitre, Salt*, and other subterranean juices; and experience daily confirms that this happens in *acidic and thermal springs* <note>"acidulae" refers to cold mineral-rich springs, while "thermae" refers to hot springs</note>. Since water is not like this by its own nature, it follows that it is imbued and colored by *mineral* earths; namely, when it runs through *veins of minerals*, it is tainted. We shall treat this mixture now in a preliminary way, and then provide more specific details on how mineral *earths* are *produced and moved* by means of water in the order of subterranean genesis. As far as acidic and thermal springs are concerned—namely, *common waters colored by mineral earths*—we have already briefly described their mixture and soaking: specifically, that common water runs through *mineral veins* and, in its course, dissolves something of the mineral earths. This opinion is indeed common and seems irrefragable <note>undeniable</note>.

<margin>N. 4.</margin>
But in truth, if it is examined more accurately, it holds much doubt; for we know that some acidic springs have flowed most copiously for *many centuries*. If their earthy contents were thickened <note>original: "inspissata"; concentrated or solidified by evaporation</note> in one place together, I believe they would equal the mass of vast *mountains*. No subterranean channel would be so capacious, nor any vein so rich, that it would not be exhausted <term>elixaretur: literally "boiled out" or "extracted"; a term from alchemy and cooking for drawing out substances by liquid</term> over the course of time. We see this in salt mines <note>original: "salinis"</note>, where vast spaces are completely exhausted of salt by a single inflow of fresh water, so that by a second inflow of water, the area remains tasteless. On the contrary, that *acidic and thermal springs* have flowed for so many centuries and have always remained equal in their mineral content is clearly proven by the *tests* of the salt-works from year to year. Two difficulties are therefore proposed regarding the resolution of this question: First, from where does such a great *abundance and perpetuity* of thermal and acidic springs come? Second, from where does such a great *quantity of contents*—namely, the *mineral juices and earths* with which the waters are tainted—arise?

<margin>N. 5.</margin>
Regarding the first difficulty—namely, from where such a great abundance of subterranean water comes—it could be easily resolved if thermal and acidic springs were always *below the horizon* of a nearby river or *sea* or pond; for from there, the water would hurry by natural propensity and descent. But since we often find acidic and thermal springs on the *highest* peaks of mountains, we are rightly forced to place their origin far *above the horizon* and to flee to other reasons, specifically those which are commonly discussed regarding *springs* <note>original: "scaturiginibus"</note>.

<margin>N. 6.</margin>
Although, to speak frankly, none of these satisfy me, of which the Reverend Father *Schott* <note>Gaspar Schott (1608–1666) was a German Jesuit scientist who wrote extensively on hydraulics and mechanical marvels</note> makes mention in a special treatise on the origin of springs. He collected the opinions of almost all authors on this matter; finally, he concludes that the origin of all springs must be attributed to the *sea*, which he believes to be far *higher* than the land. But that long-standing claim...

On the contrary, it is well-attested from year to year in salt-works, and is manifest, that *acidic springs and hot baths* have flowed for so many centuries and have always been equal in their mineral content. Second, from where does such a vast quantity of contents—namely, *mineral juices and earths* with which the waters are infected—arise?

<margin>N. 5.</margin>

is far too long and distant; for how great a distance is required so that the level of the sea's surface might correspond to the horizon of the highest *springs* <note>original: "scaturiginum," meaning gushing springs or fountain-heads</note>? Then, how great are the intervals and distances often involved? Since we see islands in the sea itself, mountains on those islands, and on the highest peaks of mountains there are *springs*, which accurately correspond to the ebb and flow of the neighboring sea in terms of their increase and decrease. We have also noticed this in the region of the *Rhine*; where we observed copious *springs* at a height of at least a hundred feet above the horizon of the nearby *Rhine*, which accurately undergo changes in rhythm with the rise and fall of the *Rhine*. From this it is manifest that springs of this kind proceed from the *Rhine*. Yet, when we took observations of this matter at *Mainz* <note>Moguntiæ</note> on *St. Michael’s* mountain, it would follow—since the ascent of that mountain's spring proceeds from the horizon of the lower *Rhine*—that the aforementioned spring, according to the opinion of *Father Schott* <note>P. Schotti: Kaspar Schott (1608–1666), a Jesuit physicist and mathematician famous for his works on hydraulics and mechanical "miracles"</note>, must take its origin in that part of the *Rhine* which, as far as horizontal height is concerned, would match and balance the surface of the aforementioned mountain. This would have to happen many miles away, at least fifty, from *Mainz*. For I hardly believe, due to the slow flow of the *Rhine*, that two miles downstream would be steeper than *one foot*. But if, according to *Father Schott’s* opinion, the origin of this spring is to be attributed to the ocean, one must certainly go over a thousand miles before reaching a horizontal line where the sea and this mountain are in equilibrium. For the beginning of this process cannot be sought from the *Dutch sea* <note>The North Sea off the coast of Holland</note>, since it is lower than the *Rhine*; because the *Rhine*, by natural gravity, is carried there as if to a lower place. Next, granted but not conceded, that the origin of this spring, or of all *springs*, proceeds from the sea—and indeed at such a distance, as we have already given an example, so that the sea's horizon and the spring's horizon (and thus the beginning and the end of the spring) would balance—yet I see no path, or evident subterranean duct, by means of which the seawater is led from beginning to end, namely from the sea to the spring. For we must not propose some solitary and naked imaginary path, but rather recur to practice, and consider nature practically in its ducts. For as we notice in common water ducts through channels or *lead pipes*, great solidity, accurate connection, and integrity are required, if even at the smallest height or distance some quantity of water is to be contained in them and led from one place to another. And, although such channels are made solid by the greatest industry of hydraulic engineers, there is nonetheless often a danger that they might burst. Very small and barely sensible holes also open up and reveal themselves, especially if the lead, when it is cast for the channels, becomes somewhat porous due to excessive heat. As we have an example among many others in the castle of *Würzburg* <note>Herbipolensi</note>, where from the *Main* <note>Mœno</note> river, by means of a common pressure machine, through a mill, water is pushed through lead pipes to the castle for a distance of 800 feet in a *hypotenuse* line, with such power and force that, although the water in the pipe contains barely *two inches* or thumb-widths in diameter—and thus the whole pipe contains only a few hundredweights of water—it nonetheless not rarely bursts. From this it can be gathered what would happen if water had to be elevated in a diameter of a *foot*, as

### Book I, Section I, Chapter II.

...as we see happening daily in many **springs** <note>original: "scaturiginibus," referring to bubbling or gushing water sources</note>. And lest anyone think that this immense force of the aforementioned machine proceeds from the pressure of *lines* <note>likely referring to geometric or linear force paths in a diagram</note>, to which it might perhaps be attributed by the unskilled, I shall bring forward another example where no pressure is added, but water is directed from one mountain to another solely by its own *equilibrium* <note>the principle that water in connected containers seeks the same level</note> through a continuous pipe. This does not even involve such a great height, distance, or volume of water; and we observed this at **Bratislava** <note>original: "Posonii," the Latin name for modern-day Bratislava, Slovakia</note> in the garden of the Archbishop. There, water is led from a nearby mountain through pipes into certain hydraulic works, and indeed it is nowhere near the height from which it first falls. Nevertheless, a great deal of labor is required in framing and cementing the pipes, since the water seeks an exit with the greatest diligence, force, and penetration.

What, then, would happen if—to account for a vast quantity of water—such a pipe had to be manufactured to a distance of *a thousand miles* from one immense height to another, and required to be perfectly continuous? I maintain, certainly, that such a thing is possible neither by *nature* nor by *art*, nor can it be put into practice. For how many valleys, mountains, and rivers lie in between? Furthermore, for springs on islands in the middle of the sea, such as on the island of **St. Helena**, etc., a pipe would be required beneath the floor of the sea for a very long distance—namely, a distance across the sea that would balance the horizon of the spring—which in the sea would extend for *a thousand miles*. If we consider such a stupendous length of pipe and the need for the most exacting solidity, we must utterly doubt its existence. For unless such a subterranean channel were perfectly solid, or if it had even the smallest crack, the water contained within would immediately leak out and be mixed with the surrounding salt water of the sea.

From what material and substance does the kind reader imagine this subterranean channel to be made? It is *impossible* for it to consist of *sand* or *mud*; and the very nature of seawater argues against *stone* pipes of such number and size being manufactured in the first creation. Since *fresh water* <note>original: "dulcis aqua," literally sweet water</note> leaps forth from these springs, it must be that either such water was never *salty*, or it was once *salty*. The latter is probable if the water of the springs takes its origin from the *sea*; but if that is assumed, it follows that this salty water must have deposited its saltiness. Where could it deposit it without obstructing the channels? One would have to account for the rejected **grit** <note>original: "saburra," usually meaning ballast or dregs; here referring to the salt residue</note> from a perpetual flow over so many centuries, even until today. 

Indeed, we see that if fresh *fountain* water, even the *clearest* kind, runs through pipes to this or that place for a long time, the pipes eventually fill with various impurities and, unless they are cleaned, become blocked. It makes no difference whether we say these dregs come from the water or from the pipe (part of which is likely to be dissolved by the water over time, especially salt water), provided they do appear and cause harm. This is precisely what we wish to infer: that for so many centuries, subterranean pipes could not have consisted of any material that would not be either dissolved or obstructed by the internal water and the external salty seawater. From these and similar points, therefore, we can conclude that it is easier to conceive of such *pipes* and *subterranean channels in the brain* than to demonstrate them in practice. Whichever way a perceptive man turns, he will not find satisfaction in the opinion of Father Schott regarding the origin of springs; and it is a wonder that the aforementioned Father Schott, who was otherwise not ignorant of hydraulics and especially mechanics, did not foresee these difficulties before reaching his conclusion. # Subterranean Physics

<margin>N. 7.</margin>
I am surprised that he judges **Helmont** <note>Jan Baptist van Helmont (1580–1644), a chemist and physician who believed water was the primary element of all things</note> so freely, even going so far as to say he "deliriously raves" regarding this subject; and yet **Helmont** provides far more solid foundations for this matter. For even if, as the saying goes, he did not "touch the needle to the point" <note>An idiom meaning to hit the mark exactly or solve a problem perfectly</note> of this most difficult question concerning the origin of springs, he should have been praised rather than accused of madness without sufficient reason, simply because he wished to reach the goal. This is especially true since he puts forward ideas on this subject that are more consistent than those of Father Schott. For Helmont explains the motion of subterranean water in a **natural** <note>original: "Physico"</note> way, rather than a crude mechanical way as Father Schott does. He attributes a certain **vital spirit** to subterranean spring water, by whose help it tends upward by its own nature. However, he asserts that as soon as it leaves the sphere of its "subterranean-ness," it is deprived of such a spirit and acquires the nature of gravity. He offers the example of **blood in a living versus a dead body**; for in a living human, the blood by its nature moves **upward**, but in a dead one, it moves **downward**. In this way, he distinguishes between "living" and "dead" water. And certainly, experience teaches us that spring water possesses a bit of a warm **spirit**, because it does not freeze in winter; we also see **steaming vapors** evaporating from the springs; and we find that as soon as it comes from the source, if held in the mouth, it sends certain spirits to the head. Yet, whether the entirety of spring water—and in such great quantity—is carried into the **heights** by its own nature and because of these spirits, is rightly called into doubt.

<margin>N. 8.</margin>
Lest we bother the kind reader by examining the opinions of others at too great a length, let us return to our own matters and set forth our opinion. We believe a distinction must be made between **above-ground** <note>original: "superterraneas"</note> and **subterranean** waters. I call "above-ground" those which are on the surface of the earth, such as **seas, rivers, lakes**, etc. I call "subterranean" those which are within the earth, such as **springs, water-channels, reservoirs of water in mountains, caves, and dens, and various other water-stores** <note>original: "hydro-phylacia," a term used by scholars like Kircher to describe massive underground water chambers</note>. With this distinction established (which even miners observe, as they distinguish between surface waters, which they call **day-water** <note>German: "Tagwasser"</note>, and central waters, which they call **ground-water** <note>German: "Grundwasser"</note>), I proceed further. I say it is manifest that **all rivers return to the sea**, namely on the surface of the earth; and nowhere is it observed that even the smallest **stream** comes out of any **sea** on the surface of the earth. Rather, it is evident that all rivers draw their origin from springs and sources, and afterwards flow down into the seas—and all these things happen with above-ground waters on the surface of the earth. Now we must demonstrate the method and order by which **subterranean** waters are exchanged and moved. I say, therefore, that **the motion of such subterranean waters is the opposite of above-ground waters**; for just as all rivers above the earth tend from springs toward the sea, so within the earth, sea waters hasten upward toward the springs. The consequence is this: **just as within the earth the sea is the origin of springs, so above the earth, springs constitute the origin of the seas.**

> *All rivers enter the sea, yet the sea is not full; to the place from which the rivers come, there they return, to flow again*, etc.

For what they fable concerning subterranean *conduits* and *pipes*, as well as the *height of the sea* above the earth—from which they defend the origin of springs according to the common laws of *hydrostatics* <note>The study of fluids at rest and the pressure they exert</note>—is entirely alien to our opinion. We are more skilled in natural philosophy <note>original: "Physicis"</note>, and better acquainted with the nature of the dissolving water which continually *licks* the surrounding objects, than to join Father Schott in his book *The Anatomy of Springs*, book 4, page **242.** There, we would either have to imagine subterranean conduits for ourselves, or construct them out of unsuitable materials once imagined, or—not without a mark of rashness—dare to measure those constructed conduits geometrically and place them before the reader’s eyes as if we had handled them with our own hands.

For in this way, that "new Argus of springs" <note>A sarcastic reference to Argus Panoptes, the hundred-eyed giant of myth; the author implies Schott claims to see things hidden deep underground</note> whom you would swear was most sharp-sighted, speaks in the cited passage from the mouth of *Arias Montanus* <note>Benito Arias Montano (1527–1598), a Spanish scholar and editor of the Polyglot Bible</note>: *Through the middle of the earth’s innards, God led certain channels like veins, fortified either with stone, or lime, or another bitumen; some wider, others narrower, and sometimes having the quality of a sponge; they are intended to sometimes strain out the moisture sent through tuff or sand, and sometimes to contain the moisture received in abundance, allowing it to flow forth through continuous paths.* The beginnings of these channels are connected to the *abyss* <note>A vast, ancient reservoir of water believed to exist deep within the earth</note>, and their furthest ends reach all the way to the surface of the earth. The first openings are wider, so that the liquid received can enter in abundance, but the furthest ends are generally narrower. The intermediate parts vary, now wide, now narrow, according to the nature and opportunity of the soil, rock, sand, clay, or tuff. And by the *spirit of Elohim* <note>original: "spiritu Elohim"; the Hebrew name for God, referencing the "Spirit of God moving over the face of the waters" in Genesis</note>, perpetually moving and agitating the face of the waters, the liquid moves into the neighboring channels. Once it enters the channels, it is unable to turn back or flow away, partly because of the great mass of the surrounding abyss, and partly because of the force of the liquid following behind it, pushed by the *Spirit of Elohim* or otherwise by the wind. Yielding to this force, it rushes through the continuous channels, whether it finds them sloping downwards or gradually rising, until it finds a door through which to break out, either on the ridge of a high mountain or in the depression of a valley or field, etc.

Father Schott cites these and similar ideas from *Arias Montanus* in the aforementioned place, asserting that he has philosophized both learnedly and elegantly. We, however, having stripped away all bias and respect, judge that the title of *delirium* should be granted to this philosophy rather than to Helmont’s opinion. For whatever Father Schott may toss about, distinguish, and doubt in his whole treatise on the origin of springs—namely, whether the sea is higher than the land, and whether springs proceed from the seas—we do not dwell on. For as long as our question is about the *most common* origin of springs, which we also attribute to the sea, we utterly deny that the seas are carried into springs through subterranean *channels* and *pipes*, as Father Schott defends.

Since our opinion is that sea water seeks the *center of the earth* by way of *transcolation* <note>The process of filtering or straining through a porous substance</note>; there it is resolved into vapor; the vapor tends from the center toward the circumference; and there finally it is *thickened* into water, as Father Schott also agrees with us in the cited work, book 5, page 344. ...we will explain our opinion. Lest the reader think that our view is merely borrowed from the aforementioned Father Schott, we have chosen to add those few words which the often-cited Father Schott has regarding this matter in the previously mentioned place, and so conclude this chapter. *Sea water*, he says, *ascends to the sources of certain springs through evaporation and a kind of distillation. This is proven because, once filtered from the sea into subterranean reservoirs, the water is heated by subterranean fires located beneath or around it. Once heated, it is resolved into vapors; these ascend into the heights and cling to the vaults of caverns. There, by the force of external cold, they thicken into water and drip down, and having found an exit, they form into springs.* Thus far Father Schott. 

In this, two things please us: first, his proposal that sea water gathers in subterranean reservoirs and is filtered there; and second, that it is turned into vapor, carried upward, and resolved back into water. However, two things also displease us. *First*, his proposal that subterranean water is thinned and turned into vapor by heat or—as he calls them—subterranean fires. For it is certain, as we shall demonstrate elsewhere, that no burning fire exists in the depths of the earth. This is due to the weight of the air above, by which all fire is extinguished. We see this in deeper mines and in <term>diving bells</term> <note>original: "vasis urinatoriis"; these were early underwater chambers used by divers (urinatores)</note> which, even if they have sufficient air through tubes, nevertheless have their flames extinguished immediately when they are sent into the depths. 

From these and other experiments, the non-existence of subterranean <term>fire-chambers</term> <note>original: "Pyrophylaciorum"; a term popularized by Athanasius Kircher to describe massive central storehouses of fire within the Earth</note> near the depths and center of the earth is easily demonstrated. We do not deny, however, that near the surface of the earth, sulfurous breaths may ignite and turn into flame; but this contradicts Father Schott's assertion, where the fire heating the water would have to lie in the deepest reservoirs of the earth in order to push the water vapor to the outer edges. It could not do this if it were already at the edge and surface of the earth; nor could water be said to be pushed to the edge if it were already hiding at the edge. 

*Secondly*, we are displeased by the same reasoning: his claim that the heated waters cling to the vaults of caverns, thicken into water there, drip down, and form into springs. For it would follow from this that the vaults of the caverns must always be higher than the springs, so that the water could fall from them into the springs. Anyone can see how absurd this is, and <term>direct observation</term> <note>original: "autopsia"</note> itself cries out to the contrary; for the horizon of many springs is sometimes higher than all the surrounding mountains and hills. In these matters, therefore, and in similar points, we differ from Father Schott's assertion.

At the beginning of this chapter, lest the kind reader become confused, it should be known that we do not deny all subterranean **passages**; rather, we first call into question whether such passages function like tubes and canals, and secondly, whether they are carried across such a vast distance. We must therefore distinguish between subterranean passages that are beneath the earth but not so **deep**, through which seas and rivers are **joined**. We see this in many places, even here in **Bavaria**, roughly halfway between **Munich** and **Wasserburg**, where an entire river is suddenly swallowed by the earth and proceeds through a subterranean passage until it emerges again into the light after some miles. Likewise, the Reverend Father <term>Kircher</term> <note>Athanasius Kircher (1602–1680), a famous Jesuit polymath who wrote "Mundus Subterraneus."</note> *testifies that the Caspian Sea, the Black Sea, the Red Sea, and the Indian Ocean meet through subterranean passages.* We shall make no mention of such **passages** here; for we shall hasten to the deeper channels by which springs are advanced and originate. By these **channels**, we do not mean "ducts," but rather **fissures** in the rocks and the **pores** of subterranean gravel. For our opinion is that sea water tends toward the center of the Earth and is there reduced to vapor; this vapor is expelled in every direction and finally **condenses** into water upon the surface of the earth. Therefore, in this chapter, we shall deal with the **motion of sea water toward the center of the Earth**; in the following chapter, we shall deal with the motion of water from the center of the Earth to the surface. We assert that the latter motion occurs by **physical gravity**, while the former occurs by **mathematical** gravity. <note>In the 17th century, "mathematical gravity" often referred to the geometric tendency of heavy objects to seek the center of the universe/Earth, whereas "physical gravity" here refers to the actual physical forces—like heat or pressure—that drive the water back up.</note> However, so that our demonstration may be understood more accurately, it must be considered above all else that water, by the nature of its own weight, presses directly and perpendicularly against the bottom; it weighs much less against the sides. We see this in **Holland**, where the entire sea is held back by certain small dikes. But the truth of these words can also be placed before one's eyes by a mechanical experiment. ### Subterranean Physics

...of size and capacity; in the middle of its bottom let a *hole* be made, as *round* as possible and one foot in diameter. Through this, a *wooden tube*, whether solid or hollow, should be directed: it should be of such *length* that it projects several feet both below and above the tub. Its width, however, should be such that it fits the sides of the aforementioned hole precisely, like a stopper, yet in such a way that it can be moved up and down within the hole. Therefore, it must not block the hole too tightly, nor too loosely. Then, let the upper part of the tube be suspended from the end of a balance scale; on the opposite side—namely, at the other end of the scale—let a *weight* also be attached, which balances the aforementioned wooden tube. Thus, the tube and the opposing weight should establish a perfect equilibrium. The tub, with the tube inside, should be placed upright in a perpendicular position. Once these things are así arranged, you shall fill the tub entirely with water. When it is full, you will see that the original *equilibrium* between the tube and the counter-weight is not changed at all. This, however, could not happen if the water weighed upon or pressed against the sides of the tube with even the slightest movement. The mathematical hypothesis, therefore, is that water does not exert pressure unless it touches a body from above or below. From this I conclude that the sea presses and weighs down more upon the *bottom* than upon the *shores*, which is most evident. Furthermore, it is also certain that the more bodies are pressed by water, the more frequently they are *moistened*; especially since bodies are by their nature *porous*. A body is properly called *porous* when it consists of smaller, *disjointed* particles. We see this in sand and other very fine powders, which for this purpose are reduced in the chemical art to a very fine powder and <term>Alcohol</term> <note>In early modern chemistry, "alcohol" referred to any substance ground into an impalpable, fine powder, not specifically to spirits.</note> so that they can be penetrated more quickly by solvents.

<margin>N. 2.</margin>
Since, therefore, the bottom of the sea consists of very fine sediment, *sand and gravel*—that is, of infinite particles that are minimal in their division—upon which an immense mass of water meanwhile rests: it follows that the aforementioned bottom of the sea is very strongly and deeply penetrated and moistened by the waters; specifically in those places where there is a greater abundance of water, namely in the seas. And since, by the common consensus of all learned men, the bottom of the sea is entirely *similar to itself* <note>Meaning it is consistent in its composition across the globe.</note>; it follows that the same is penetrated by the waters all the way to the end, namely as far as the *center of the earth*. By the *center of the earth*, however, I do not mean some imaginary *geometric point* that is divided and measured in respect to the *whole globe*; but I take it to mean a certain cavity in the heart of the earth, *which hereafter we shall call the center of the earth*. And we establish that this cavity is of *vast capacity* and convexity. For since the *diameter of the earth* contains more than 700 <term>miles</term> <note>The "mile" used here likely refers to a German mile or league, which was significantly longer than a modern English mile.</note>, if we set only 20 miles for the diameter of the central cavity, how great will the area of the contents be? And how great a quantity of water would it be capable of holding? I propose, therefore, that the center of the earth is a certain space, not so very small, filled with waters which *drip* there continuously through the bottom of the sea. Indeed, they cannot break through in a single rush, since it is probable that the *inner bottom* of the sea around the curve of the center consists of a more tenacious *mud*: just as we see in any part of the earth when we come deeper to the foundation, where a certain *solid and firm* mud is found. Moreover, the closer we come to the depths, the more water is found, even in places that are very dry on the surface; which mani- <note>Catchword: mani- (likely "manifestum" or "manifestly").</note>

### Book I, Section II, Chapter II

...it is a clear sign that the earth around the bottom is watery, yet not entirely permeable.

<margin>No. 3</margin> Although there are many who affirm that there are unfathomable **abysses** <term>abyss: from the Greek *abyssos*, meaning bottomless; historically used to describe the deepest parts of the ocean believed to be connected to the interior</term> in the sea, the matter is actually quite different. For since the **semidiameter of the earth** <note>radius</note> **contains about sixty miles**, ten of which we attribute to the center: it is not surprising if the **upper depth of the sea** extends to at least **thirty** miles. If its limit cannot be explored in any way, it is therefore regarded as an **abyss** by those trying to measure it, since there is no means of testing its bottom. For who could provide a rope or cord extending thirty miles? Or what ship could carry it? Or stay motionless in one place until the measurement was completed? I conclude, therefore, that the sea, by its own depth, never immediately reaches the center of the earth, except by **distillation** <note>original: *destillatorie*; the process of water seeping or filtering through the porous crust of the earth</note>.

<margin>No. 4</margin> Regarding why I call the **center of the earth a convex space**, and indeed one that is not so small, I have many reasons and causes. The **first of these is that God and Nature have made nothing in vain**; but I ask you, of what use would such an immense mass of subterranean earth be if nothing were at work there? And what could be at work in it if it were solid, continuous, and impermeable for so many miles? According to our view, however, it follows that the space we have called the center is **no less fertile and necessary** than the outer surface of the earth itself. The **second argument** is that in all products of nature, even in apples, pears, and other fruits, we see the interiors are **hollow and refined**; why then would we want to exclude the **Macrocosm** <term>Macrocosm: the "great world" or the universe as a whole, often compared to the "microcosm" of the human body or small fruits</term> from the common course of nature?

<margin>No. 5</margin> The **third argument** is that **Holy Scripture** itself often calls the **base of the earth**—namely the **center—watery**; indeed, it describes it in such a way that many theologians have been moved to locate the **seat of hell** there. And truly, if we consider more diligently from what follows how much confusion, silt, mixing, rot, stench, vapor, darkness, anguish, drippings, sweatings, estuaries, and various movements and actions exist and occur in the aforementioned center of the waters (even from a physical perspective); certainly no greater punishment, except for the deprivation of the vision of God, could affect the damned than for their souls to be banished into such a **Chaos** and place so far removed from the living. There, they are placed beneath the feet of all mortals as the most abject of beings. No more worthy place could be assigned to them than to be enclosed within the earth—those who, in this world, were devoted entirely to earthly wealth and riches coming from the center of the earth, and who thirsted for nothing but gold. It is fitting, I say, that such people should enjoy the earth to satiety after this life, and be covered by such an immense mass of earth, so that like moles digging in the ground, they may be thrust into its innermost bowels. Moved by this reasoning, certain people have also determined that various **subterranean spirits** dwell in the hidden parts of the earth; and if any credit is to be given to miners and divers, spirits are not infrequently seen and heard in subterranean places and those closer to the center of the earth. Furthermore, **below, the etymology of "Infernus" <note>Hell</note> explains that the place is "infra nos" <note>below us</note>, namely within the earth.** From these and many other points, it will not be so absurd to conclude: **the center of the earth is a great convex space, into which waters from the foundation of the sea distill, and are gathered as if into a universal receptacle of nature, or a hydrophylacium.** <term>hydrophylacium: a water-storehouse; Kircher’s specific term for massive underground reservoirs that feed the world's springs and oceans</term> For what need is there for many [arguments] of this kind...
