# Subterranean Physics

<meta>catchword: mani-</meta>

...of size and capacity; in the middle of its bottom, let a **hole** be made, as round as possible, one foot in diameter. Through this, a wooden **tube**, whether solid or hollow, should be directed. It should be of such **length** that it protrudes several feet below and above the barrel. Its width should be such that it fits the sides of the hole snugly, like a stopper; yet in such a way that it can move up and down in the hole, it should not obstruct the aforementioned hole too tightly nor too loosely. Then, let the **upper** part of the tube be suspended by a rope from the end of a balance; on the opposite side, namely at the other end of the scale, let a **weight** also be tied, balancing the aforementioned wooden tube. Thus, the tube and the opposite weight should establish a perfect equilibrium. Let the barrel be placed upright with the tube in a vertical position. Once these things are so arranged, you shall fill the barrel entirely with water. When it is full, you will see that the original equilibrium between the tube and the **counterweight** <term>counterweight: referred to in the original as *antifacoma*, a Greek-derived term used in early physics for a balancing weight</term> is not changed at all. This could not happen if the water weighed upon and pressed the **sides** of the tube with even the slightest motion. Therefore, the mathematical hypothesis is that **water does not press except where it touches a body from above or below.** From this, I conclude that the sea presses and weighs down more near the **bottom** than near the **shores**, which is most evident.

Next, it is also certain that the more bodies are pressed by water, the more they are moistened; especially since bodies are by their nature **porous**. A body is properly called **porous** when it consists of smaller, **separated** corpuscles, as we see in sand and other very fine powders. For this purpose, in the chemical art, materials are reduced to a very fine powder and **Alcohol** <note>original: *Alcohol*; in 17th-century chemistry, this referred to any substance ground into an impalpable, extremely fine powder, not specifically a liquid spirit</note> so that they can be penetrated more quickly by solvents. Since, therefore, the floor of the sea consists of very fine **gravel, sand, and grit**, consisting of infinite corpuscles that are the smallest in terms of division, upon which an immense mass of water meanwhile rests:

<margin>No. 2</margin> it follows that the aforementioned seabed is very strongly and deeply penetrated and moistened by the waters—namely in those places where there is a greater abundance of water, specifically in the seas. And since, by the common consensus of all learned men, the floor of the sea is essentially **similar to itself** throughout; it follows that the same floor is penetrated by the waters all the way to the end, namely to the **center of the earth**. 

However, I do not mean by the **center of the earth** some imaginary **geometric point**, which is divided and measured in respect to the **entire globe**; but I take it to mean a certain cavity in the very **middle of the earth**, **which hereafter we shall call the center of the earth**. And we establish that this cavity is of **immense capacity** and convexity. For since the diameter of the **earth** contains more than 700 miles <note>The author likely refers to German miles, which were much longer than modern English miles</note>, if we set only 20 miles for the diameter of the central cavity, how great will the area of its contents be? And how much water would it be capable of holding? I propose, therefore, that the center of the earth is a certain **space**, not at all small, filled with waters which continually **drip** <note>original: *instillant*; literally "distill" or "drip in drop by drop"</note> there through the floor of the sea. They cannot break through in a single rush because it is probable that the **inner floor** of the sea near the curve of the center consists of a more tenacious **mud**, just as we see in any land when we come deeper to the foundation, where a certain **solid and firm mud** is found. Furthermore, the closer we come to the depths, the more water is found, even in places that are very dry on the surface; which...

### Book I. Section II. Chapter II.

...it is a clear sign that the earth near the bottom is watery, yet not entirely permeable.
<margin>Note 3.</margin>
For although there are many who assert that there are unfathomable abysses in the sea, the matter is far different in reality. Since the semi-diameter of the earth contains about sixty miles <note>The "mile" used here refers to an archaic geographic league; the author is calculating the Earth's radius according to seventeenth-century estimates</note>, of which we attribute ten to the center, it is no wonder if the upper depth of the sea extends at least thirty miles. If its limit cannot be explored by any means, it is therefore regarded as an "abyss" by those who investigate it, as there is no medium for testing its bottom. For who could provide a rope or cord extending thirty miles? Or what ship could carry it? Or stay motionless in one spot until the measurement was completed? I conclude, therefore, that the sea, by its own depth, never immediately reaches the center of the earth, except by a process of distillation <note>original: "destillatorie"; here meaning water seeping or dripping through porous rock like a chemical still</note>. As for why I call the center of the earth a **convex space**, and a rather large one at that, I have many reasons and causes.

<margin>Note 4.</margin>
The first of these is that *God and Nature have made nothing in vain*; but I ask you, of what use would such a massive bulk of subterranean earth be if nothing were at work there? And what could work within it if it were solid, continuous, and impermeable for so many miles? In our model, however, it follows that the space we have called the center is no less fertile and necessary than the exterior surface of the earth itself. The second argument is that in all produced things—even in apples, pears, and other fruits—we see the interiors are hollowed and intricately fashioned; why then should we wish to exempt the **Macrocosm** <term>Macrocosm: the Earth or Universe viewed as a large-scale reflection of smaller biological systems</term> from the common course of nature? The third argument is that Holy Scripture itself not infrequently calls the base of the earth—namely, the center—watery; indeed, it describes it in such a way that many theologians have been moved to locate the **seat of Hell** there.

<margin>Note 5.</margin>
And truly, if we consider more diligently from what follows how much confusion, refuse, mixing, rot, stench, vapor, darkness, anguish, drippings, sweatings, estuaries, and various motions and actions exist and occur in the aforementioned center of waters (even from a physical perspective), certainly no greater punishment could afflict the damned—except for the loss of the sight of God—than for their souls to be banished to such a **Chaos**, a place so far removed from the living. There, they are placed beneath the feet of all mortals as the most abject of beings. No more fitting place could be assigned to them than to be enclosed within the earth, for those who in this world were entirely devoted to earthly wealth and riches coming from the center of the earth, thirsting for nothing but gold. It is appropriate, I say, that such people should enjoy the earth to satiety after this life, and be covered by such an immense mass of earth, so that like moles digging in the ground, they are thrust into its innermost bowels. For this reason also, some have been moved to establish that various **subterranean spirits** dwell in the hidden parts of the earth; and if any credit is to be given to certain **miners** <term>original: "metallocolae"; literally "metal-dwellers"</term> and **divers** <term>original: "urinatores"; an old term for breath-hold divers</term>, spirits are not infrequently seen and heard in subterranean places and those closer to the center of the earth. Furthermore, the etymology of *Infernus* <note>The Latin word for Hell, meaning "the place below"</note> explains the place to be beneath us, namely within the earth. From these and many other points, it will not be so absurd to conclude: *The center of the earth is a great convex space, into which waters distill from the foundation of the sea, and are collected as if into a universal receptacle of nature or a **hydrophylacium**.* <term>Hydrophylacium: a "water-storehouse" or massive subterranean reservoir believed by early modern scientists to feed the world's springs and oceans</term> For what need is there for many things of this sort...

### Subterranean Physics.

...to establish reservoirs? And thus to multiply entities without necessity, when *one* suffices; since with this single repository of Nature, all those things which, according to the minds of some, are usually attributed to many such reservoirs, can be explained more sufficiently and solidly than if we were to imagine infinite reservoirs of that kind. I do not deny, indeed, that subterranean pools and marshes exist; but not for the purpose of producing springs and making the subterranean regions fertile: as we shall demonstrate in what follows, this is the proper function and purpose of our universal reservoir. Therefore, this central reservoir of waters differs from the rest of the particular <term>hydrophylacia: a term coined by Athanasius Kircher for massive subterranean water-storage chambers</term> for the reasons we have just stated.

As for the cavity of the earth's center (to come to its structure), it is probable that it was fashioned during the first creation of the earth, not by a secondary *production*. For as certain distinguished theologians believe, that place—namely the *sulphurous and pitchy swamp*—was prepared for the Devil from the beginning of the world, specifically during the very creation of heaven and earth. For since he foresaw the future creation and the entire history of the human race, and opposed God through pride, he was cast down from heaven; therefore, a place was necessarily required into which he might be thrown, since before the creation of heaven and earth no place or "where" existed. It is probable, then, that immediately after the creation of heaven, the Devil was cast into the center of the earth; specifically so that he would not be present for that universal production of all things from the earth, nor envy such a noble operation, toward which the rest of the Angels hastened with such joy that they all exulted for gladness, according to that passage in Job: *Where were you when the morning stars sang together, or while they all exulted, and at the same time all the sons of God sounded with trumpets, etc.* <note>original: "Ubi eras, dum ovarent stellæ matutinæ..." - This is a Latin translation of Job 38:7, used here to show the angels' joy at creation while the Devil was excluded.</note>

### Book I. Section II. Chapter II.

...namely, that two walls might be whitened with a single bucket of lime <note>original: "una nempe fidelia duo parietes dealbarentur"; a Latin proverb similar to 'killing two birds with one stone'</note>; specifically, that the sediment of the water—the sand—is separated from the water through the bottom, acting as a filter <term>transcolatorium: a strainer or filtering device</term>. This sand indeed serves to preserve the seabed and to strengthen the convex center of the earth, constituting a kind of new material. This ensures that both the saltiness of the seawater and the stability of the earth's foundation are maintained, and the seas might daily have material to overflow, cast out, and deposit upon the shores.

<margin>Note 10.</margin> Therefore, it is not to be doubted that the central waters are of a different nature than the marine waters; for marine waters are *clear and salty*, whereas central waters are *muddy and bituminous*. They have less salt, but more earthiness, sulfur, and bitumen. This arises both from the nature of the saline water itself (*for sea salt contains within it living sulfur*, as we shall demonstrate in Book 2) and from the nature of the seabed itself. For experience teaches that filters and strainers impart much of their own nature to the things filtered and strained; which one can experience if you filter a certain wine through merchant's paper <note>paper used for wrapping or filtering</note>, for you will find it to be of a far different nature than it was before. Therefore, from this so long and deep filtration of sea water, we have said before—not without reason, nor without experience—that it is altered, turning from *saline to sulfurous and bituminous*, as we will specifically prove in Book 2, in the chapter on common salt. From these things it can easily be gathered that, due to its sulfurous and bituminous nature, a certain innate heat exists in this central water. For experience proves that salt consists of *water and sulfur*, and that from common salt, *common burning sulfur* can be prepared. We shall also prove elsewhere, especially in Book 2, in the chapter on "Zoo-minerals" <note>minerals derived from or resembling living things</note>, that another *astral sulfur* or earth—analogous to the *stellar matter* mentioned in Chapter 3 of the preceding Section—is present in *sea water*; this is the substance that provides the silver color and semi-transparent luster to pearls, shells, and other testaceans <note>shell-covered sea creatures</note>. Therefore, it will not be doubted at all that, due to the extraction of the watery parts, the remaining parts become thicker and more *sulfurous*: namely, through filtration and the distillation of sea waters through the floor of the earth. We can thus state without rashness that *an innate heat exists in these*, and reason suggests, as does practical experience, that from this heat various alterations are caused in the central waters. For since the convex firmament is, as it were, closed on all sides in the center of the earth, and permeable only through pores, there must necessarily be great warmth and vapor there. Consequently, the enclosed water, having been warmed and placed as if in "digestion" <note>an alchemical term for prolonged heating</note>, undergoes a separation of its parts aided by its own internal fermentation, by which the earthy particles are resolved from the watery ones.

<margin>Note 11.</margin> It follows naturally that the greatest heat arises from this, and is daily before our eyes in other operations of nature; as can be seen in cellars where *new wines ferment*, or indeed in *sweat-rooms and baths*. But the very nature of central water, through its own change, promotes this heat in no small way; for it is changeable *and prone to putrefaction*, which should be a wonder to no one: since saline water itself, and even more so, the very strong *spirit of salt* <term>spiritus salis: an early name for hydrochloric acid</term>, when handled with the proper operation, can be led into the highest *putridity*, so that it rots in color like ink and stinks like a corpse, as we shall further examine in Book 2. From all these things, therefore, I conclude that *the central water is warm and vaporous, filled with sulfurous particles, and by its own heat always exists in action and motion*. Thus far, then, we have lurked in the center of the earth, and...

-># Subterranean Physics<-

...we have labored as if in a boiling tide; indeed, we have followed the waters on a tedious journey from their springs through rivers into the seas, and from there to the center of the earth—the ultimate end and simultaneously the beginning of the waters. Now time and order require that, having finished with the mathematical motion of the waters, we consider their **Physical** motion—namely, having explained the distillation of the waters to the center of the earth, we now look at their return and ascent to the springs and sources.

<margin>Note 12.</margin> It is clear, moreover, that vapors tend upward and from the center toward the circumference—that is, from a hot place to a cold one—as all distillation processes demonstrate. It will not, therefore, be a paradox if we establish that the central water (which we have shown to be vaporous) tends from the center to the circumference **by its own nature** and because of its innate heat.

<margin>Note 13.</margin> These aforementioned vapors will travel toward those places that are permeable, specifically those parts of the central foundation that are not pressed upon by any external seawater, but instead have land and mountains above them. For those parts of the central foundation upon which the **seas** rest are muddy and more compact, specifically so that the waters do not break through with a single violent force. Furthermore, so that the aforementioned filtration and distillation might better succeed, it is both probable and natural that the central vapors would not seek those convex parts of the center through which the seawater **drips** <note>original: "instillant"</note> by powerful distillation; this is due both to the solidity of that place and to the immense mass of the sea lying upon it. Therefore, the vapors leave those parts and penetrate the convex sections that are more penetrable. These, as we have said, are the parts upon which the **mountains** and the rest of the land rest, which is entirely fitting and natural.

<margin>Note 14.</margin> Those parts are indeed more porous than the others for two reasons: First, because no water lies upon them which could break through and push them back; second, because by the will of the Creator, they were made porous during their very production so that the lower vapors could breathe through. I call it "porous," however, not because it behaves like a **sponge**, but because **fissures** are found even in the most compact stones and rocks. Miners call these <term>Klüfften</term> <note>German for "clefts" or "fissures"</note> and consider them a good sign; they observe that fertile **mineral** vapors pass through them, from which experience proves metals are generated. Yet, if we approach closer to the center of the earth, it is probable that all rocks, stones, mountains, and the **hardness** of the earth cease. From this it seems, as we taught in Section 1, Chapter 3 of this book, that due to various boilings, withdrawals, and extractions during the first **creation**, the earth became dense and encrusted only around its surface, while it remained more humid and soft near its heart. We remember reading in the <term>Chronologia minerali</term> <note>original: "Mineral Chronology"</note>, commonly called the <term>Berg-Cronick</term> <note>German for "Mining Chronicle"</note>, that miners working at a vast depth in a certain mountain went below the Earth's horizon. They found that the rocks gradually became more manageable and softer, until finally they ceased altogether and turned into gravel so fine it could have been used for hourglasses <note>original: "clepsydris"; literally water-clocks, but here referring to sand-timers</note>. This was, however, mixed with infinite springs of water—so much so that if anyone had fallen in, they would have been submerged in such sand no differently than in water. It was so divided, subtle, porous, and yielding. The miners explored the bottom of it with a very long pole, but could find no end to it. We support this story based on our own experience. Therefore, **Helmont** <note>Jan Baptist van Helmont (1580–1644), a famous Flemish chemist and physician</note> is not raving when he speaks of such gravel, which he calls **living**; certainly, it swells with living springs, and if—

->### Book I, Section I, Chapter II.<-

...nor are any springs found in that depth. But to return to the matter at hand, it is in every way probable that the earth around the bottom and the foundation of the earth's center is not entirely of one nature, but of a diverse constitution. At the bottom of the sea, where water filters down toward the center, the earth is muddy; but in other parts of the earth, and in the mountains resting upon the earth’s foundation, through which the **central water** <note>Latin: "aqua centralis"; Kircher’s term for the reservoir of water he believes exists at the core of the globe.</note> rises again and spreads like a vapor, the earth is porous. Furthermore, regarding our statement that the aforementioned water in the center of the earth is reduced into vapor, I would prefer to attribute this to the internal heat and activity of the waters rather than to some unknown intelligence or an angel assigned to that duty by certain authors. For it seems to me that natural things should always be explained naturally, especially if evident natural causes are at hand.

Moreover, lest anyone think that our opinion—in which we establish that the central water is carried upward in the form of vapor and resolved into springs—is new or absurd, we shall not merely cite the consensus of various Physicists such as Fromondus, Cabeus, Maurus, and Descartes <note>Libert Froidmont, Niccolò Cabeo, Sylvester Mauro, and René Descartes: prominent 17th-century natural philosophers.</note>; the first of whom expressly supports us in the following words, when he says:

<margin>Note 15.</margin>
*The mountain is like the head of an **alembic** <term>alembic: an alchemical still used for distillation</term> in the distillations of the Alchemists; in it, vapors driven upward from a slow fire placed beneath are cooled, and by both the internal form of the water and the coldness of the surrounding rocks, they reduce themselves to their natural density: at first drop by drop, but then many flowing together like a rain into a single torrent, and gathering increases through a longer circuit, they finally bubble forth in a full vein.*

From this, it is clear that the generation of springs is plainly related to rains, etc. I say we shall not bring forward these and many other testimonies; instead, we shall fly to the testimony of Holy Scripture itself, for the Sacred Text holds thus: *For the Lord God had not rained upon the earth, and there was no man to work it, but a **fountain** <note>original: "fons"</note> ascended from the earth, watering the entire surface of the earth, etc.* Here it must be noted that the original text uses the word "vapor" in place of "fountain"; it then adds that the entire surface of the earth was irrigated, meaning that the central vapor transpired from all permeable parts. 

But why was the earth first irrigated by the subterranean vapor of the earth, and not by super-terrestrial rain, and thus stimulated to its first fertility? We shall discuss this later, when we treat the fertility of the central vapor. In this place, however, if we consider why some versions of Holy Scripture put "vapor" and others "fountain," we can easily reconcile them; for vapors, when they are cooled, are resolved into waters and fountains, as all Alchemical distillations testify. Nor is it contradictory that the earth, in this primordial fertilization, was irrigated in some places by watery vapor, and in others by a fountain or a **river** flowing therefrom; since we see this happen daily even now. For experience teaches us that watery vapors moisten the earth, and the Nile also performs this by its flooding. 

Therefore, this passage of Holy Scripture does much for our demonstration: *firstly*, because it expressly says that vapors came forth from the earth, the presence of which is even now a manifest sign of mountains according to Vitruvius <note>A famous Roman architect and engineer who wrote on finding hidden sources of water.</note>, though they must be observed in the morning; for when the seas swell at night, the distillations toward the center also become more copious, and hence the central evaporations are stronger again around daybreak. *Secondly*, it is because the *Sacred Text treats vapors and fountains as synonyms*, namely that the central vapors were resolved into gushings and fountains, and this last point now falls to us to demonstrate.

### Section Two, Chapter Three
# On the movement of water from the center to the circumference of the earth, where springs and fountains are specifically discussed.

### S Y N O P S I S.

*N. 1. On the cause of the diversity of subterranean vapors. N. 2. On central effluvia, pestilential air, and earthquakes. N. 3. Central-earthly aqueous effluvia are twofold: namely, fresh and mineral. N. 4. On the cause of fresh water, as well as the Spirit that is within the water. N. 5. The cause of abundant spring water. N. 6. How aqueous vapor is resolved into the liquid which we call water. N. 7. The path and effect of the mud that is usually found around springs.*

### T E X T.

<margin>N. 1.</margin> To successfully complete our account of the physical motion of central subterranean water, which we began in the preceding chapter, and to consider the changes and conditions the central vapors undergo in their ascent: above all, it must be known that subterranean water, while it is carried upward, is altered no less than when it was tending downward and distilling from the seabed to the center. For just as it laid aside some of its saltiness there <note>Kircher argues that seawater is "desalinated" as it filters through the earth toward the central heat</note>, and dripped into the center in various ways from different parts of the seas; so while it ascends, it not only deposits much sediment and dregs near the beginning of its ascent, but also rises from the center in different ways depending on the condition of the earth and is altered on its path, as is evident from the effect. However it may be altered, at the end of its motion—namely, when it reaches the surface of the earth—it is thickened and congealed, or to speak more accurately, condensed, as will appear more clearly from what follows. Moreover, there are three types of subterranean effluvia <term>effluvia: flowing vapors or microscopic particles emitted from a body</term>, corresponding to the three elements of the earth-water-air globe: hence we perceive subterranean effluvia of air, water, and earth.

<margin>N. 2.</margin> We shall not dwell long upon the aerial ones; for from these arise *mineral* and *sulphurous* exhalations, which miners call *Witterungen* <note>original German: "Witterungen"; in a mining context, this refers to the "weather" or vapors found in the shafts, often signaling the presence of ores</note>. When these reach the surface of the earth, they are not infrequently so strong that they burn trees, herbs, and sods, and indeed even stones themselves, as if by lightning; these are consequently called *Ausbränd* <note>original German: "Ausbränd"; literally "burn-outs," referring to scorched or barren patches of earth that miners believed sat atop rich mineral veins</note> by miners. Such mineral exhalations sometimes strike the nostrils of travelers from several miles away; and if they are driven by contrary qualities, they become *pestilential*. When they are blocked on their path, they eventually break out with force, and from this *earthquakes* arise. For there is no doubt that a great amount of air is stirred up in the center of the earth due to the vast and flatulent abundance of vapors; if its exit is blocked by various chances, it must necessarily break out by force, sometimes with such great power that it occasionally overturns entire cities, as we recently had a sad experience of in Epidaurus <note>Kircher likely refers to the devastating earthquake of 1667 in Ragusa (modern Dubrovnik), which was historically associated with the site of ancient Epidaurus</note>. Therefore, the trapped vapor returns to the open air with such vehemence, carrying various earthy effluvia with it,

And this is the reason why <margin>N. 3.</margin> mostly after earthquakes, plague and other contagious diseases follow. 

Concerning the aqueous effluvia <term>effluvia: the vapors or outflows of a substance</term>, about which we will speak more specifically in this chapter, direct observation teaches us that they come forth into the light or onto the earth's surface in a twofold quality; *firstly*, as fresh spring water; then, the aforementioned subterranean aqueous effluvia present themselves to our eyes in the guise of *mineral* water. However, the central water is fresh when, near the beginning of the curve or the firmament of the earth's center, that which pours through encounters slime or mud, which they commonly call *clay-loam* <note>original: "Thon-Letten," a German term for clay-rich soil</note> <margin>N. 4.</margin> etc. For water passing through mud of this kind is, as it were, filtered and strained, and deposits its dregs; the same thing happens in its ascent when it is purified through various stones, sands, and clays. 

Therefore, this aqueous vapor, which at the start of its journey was very hot and *sulfurous*, as well as foul, is gradually purified and thickened by cold until it is resolved into water near the surface of the earth and passes into springs: in the form of clear and fresh spring water, perfectly purified by straining, and imbued with no *mineral* juices in its path and ascent. In this, spring water really differs from mineral waters, which we will discuss later.

Now two things occur to be considered concerning the nature of *spring* waters. *First*, that although fresh spring water appears sweet and tasteless to the sense of taste, it actually contains a subtle *spirit* <note>In this context, "spirit" refers to dissolved gases or "vital" properties that were thought to give water its freshness and life-sustaining qualities.</note> within itself; which chemical analysis and the very nature of springs teaches, by which they steam in the morning and freeze more slowly than other waters. Furthermore, they manifest singular qualities above other stagnant waters regarding the arts of *papermaking, brewing, and dyeing* <margin>N. 5.</margin> <note>original: "papyro-pœiam, zytho-pœiam, & tinctoriam"</note>. Hence they are commonly called *Hard-Water* <note>original: "Hart-Waffer"</note> and are notably distinguished from soft waters, commonly called *Soft-Water* <note>original: "Weich-Waffer"</note>.

*Next*, the resolution of the central subterranean vapor into water might be suspect to many because it flows so copiously and continuously; but it will not be surprising that in different subterranean channels, because of the different nature of the straining, different spring waters also come forth with respect to health—being useful or useless for this or that temperament, art, craft, or use.

Then, since in the bowels of the earth the central vapors have *prepared* various channels and exits for themselves, and have enlarged them by penetrating through so many centuries; what wonder is it if they are now carried there continuously, with new vapor always succeeding, and flow incessantly? So much so that, if a spring is blocked near the surface of the earth, it immediately seeks new channels for itself and breaks out elsewhere. If someone also adds a *tube* to the opening of a spring, he will find the spring water *rises* in it to such a height as the *lateral earth of the springs is capable of bearing*: For when that gives way, the spring is diverted elsewhere and falls in the tube. This does not happen, as some wish, from the principles of the *Horizon* and the *equilibrium of the spring*; but from the causes we have already given, namely from the *yielding sides of the springs*. Moreover, in passing, it must not be passed over in silence what we have observed diligently and with great pleasure in the aforementioned tube adapted to the opening of a spring; namely, that at night the water rises an entire foot *higher* in it, but in the day it is diminished: which certainly con-

In the body, the humors, when they have by error opened subcutaneous channels to this or that limb, flow toward them continuously, but more abundantly around the morning hour. They do this even more when a path is opened for them by unskilled physicians through **fontanelles** <term>fontanelles: small surgical incisions or "issues" kept open to drain supposed "bad humors" from the body</term>, which afterwards cannot be closed without the dangerous regurgitation of humors back into the body; instead, if one hole is covered, they seek a new one elsewhere, and thus render the afflicted body like a place full of springs.

Now we must return to the third difficulty: namely, by what means such a great abundance of springs can arise from the mere condensation of subterranean vapor. But let no one wonder that copious vapor provides copious water: for a rain-shower proceeds from rain, and this from the resolved vapor of clouds falling drop by drop, producing in a few hours an immense quantity of water. We also notice, in certain subterranean caves, drops sweating from the vaults, which in a short interval produced a spring three inches in diameter in size. In the distillation of **spirit of wine** <note>original: "spiritus vini," an early term for ethanol or high-proof alcohol</note>, which they prepare from dregs and grain, we clearly see that a few subtle vapors, by means of an **alembic** <term>alembic: an early chemical apparatus used for distillation, consisting of two vessels connected by a tube</term> and cooling coils, are condensed almost instantly so that they flow continuously and copiously in the form of water, like a vein. Jonstonius <note>John Jonston (1603–1675), a famous naturalist and physician of Scottish descent who lived in Poland.</note> reports in his *Dendrographia* <note>A "treatise on trees."</note>, under the title of "admirable trees," book 10, chapter 4, page 459, section 6: *“In one of the Canary Islands, commonly called Ferro, a tree is found that pours out water in such abundance that it suffices for the inhabitants, the herds, and the ships that call there for watering.”* <note>This refers to the "Garoé" or Rain Tree of El Hierro (Ferro), which captured moisture from the mists to provide water on the arid island.</note>

<margin>N. 6.</margin>
But we must consider whether subterranean vapors are condensed by cold alone and resolved into water. To this I respond that cold is indeed the more powerful cause. No one is ignorant of the fact that the earth is cold beneath its surface, and indeed more so in the summer time; for in the winter it is somewhat warmer, which is why spring water freezes less than other stagnant waters. Furthermore, experience teaches that great cold is contained within the earth, by which soldiers, when they stay in the field, cool their flasks full of drink almost in a moment; they do this by placing them in a pit, around which they build a fire, and in this way they repel the cold that is in the earth toward the flask, which consequently becomes cold immediately. 

But leaving all these things in their place, those who assign the cause of the condensation of subterranean vapors to *cold alone* do not entirely satisfy me; for other reasons seem to underlie it, which we will point out by narrating the following story. Previously, I applied myself much to hydraulic study, both theoretical and practical; hence I sought various springs and made various water conduits, which I also demonstrated at **Mainz** <note>original: "Moguntiæ"</note> in the **Carthusian monastery** at Saint Michael’s Mount. This place is situated on a fairly high hill near the Rhine, which we mentioned previously. Meanwhile, they had no water nor springs in the monastery, except what they drew with exhausting labor from a certain deep well; so much so, that they had almost more wine than water in the Carthusian house. Because of the friendship that existed between me and the **Father Prior** of that place, I frequented the location often, and the aforementioned Father...

### Book 1, Section 1, Chapter 3

When he had frequently complained of this inconvenience, I began to search for and investigate the springs on the mountain more accurately. Having found certain signs and indications, I began to promise that I would find a spring level with the **horizon** <term>horizon: here referring to the topographical elevation or "water level" relative to the monastery</term> of the Carthusian monastery, and that I would lead spring water so that it would perpetually flow into the monastery's kitchen—which is exactly what I did. I found a spring about 2,000 feet from the Carthusian monastery on another hill, but it was outside the territory of the aforementioned monastery, although it was scarcely ten paces away. This indeed pleased the Father Prior, yet he wished that he might have a spring within his own territory and in the monastery’s vineyard. For the other one I had found was located by a public road; at the same time, there was a common rumor that the **Archbishop of Mainz** <note>original: Archi Episcopum Moguntinum. The Electorate of Mainz was a powerful ecclesiastical state in the Holy Roman Empire.</note> was going to abolish that road entirely, because it seemed it might provide an opportunity for the retreat and concealment of enemies. Thus, our aforementioned Father Prior feared lest—to say nothing of the monastery itself—that road where I found the spring might also be covered over with earth. Therefore, he wanted to have either no spring at all, or one within his own power.

So, searching anew for springs in the Carthusian vineyard, I finally found a most pleasant one about five feet below the ground level. For having dug through the superficial garden soil, I came upon *bluish-gray clay*, and once this was reached, the spring itself was immediately present. For it is a general axiom and experimental fact: *no spring is found without such clay*; on the contrary, the presence of said clay is a most certain sign of a forthcoming spring. And although some springs flow out of the hardest mountains and rocks, nevertheless, if one inquires more deeply into them, such *clay* will not be absent. 

Therefore, in the aforementioned vineyard, as soon as I hit similar clay, the spring immediately began to seep through; but since I hoped it would be more abundant if I dug the clay out deeper, I had the digging continue until finally all the clay was dug out, and I hit *sand*. For three types of earth were found in that place: the first was the superficial black garden soil; the second was the *clay* of which we have just treated. The former extended to about five feet, the latter to ten. The sand, however, which I set down as the third type of earth, certainly extended to a great depth; there was no need to investigate its bottom, nor would it have suited our purpose. 

For we had already proceeded deeper in digging out the *clay* than was conducive or necessary; and from this, a contrary effect followed: while we hoped we would have a more copious spring at depth, on the contrary, we had a smaller one, and finally none at all. For all the springing water vanished as soon as we reached the end of the *clay* and the beginning of the *sand*. 

Since this troubled me greatly, I began to speculate more accurately on all the circumstances, and I could find no reason other than the excavated *clay*; for the underlying sand was clear and porous, and obstructed by nothing. I also went there at dawn and found the entire pit full of *vapors*, as if covered by a cloud. By this sign, my spirit began to return somewhat; for I attributed the denial of this vapor to the excavated clay, which I therefore ordered to be thrown back into the pit and solidified somewhat with a **rammer** <term>fistuca: a heavy tool, often a wooden log with handles, used for tamping or packing earth down firmly</term>. The next morning, when I approached the pit with a mix of hope and fear, yet with great desire, I observed with the greatest admiration and joy that my spring had returned and had become even more abundant. This event provided a firm foundation for my speculation—

### Physicæ Subterraneæ

...laid the foundation [of his argument], namely that subterranean vapors are thickened and reduced into a body not only by cold, but especially by such clay. And since this case, which we have reviewed, happened in such a short time in so little clay, what wonder is it if we often find copious **springs** <term>springs: original *scaturigines*, referring to bubbling or gushing sources of water</term> near the surface on the highest mountains? While, on the contrary, no wateriness appears near the bottom of the mountains or in their very center, because of the lack of the aforementioned thickening clay. 

In this, it is certainly wonderful that two contrary qualities are found in one subject at one and the same time; for the same aforementioned clay resists physical and **thickened water** <note>original: *densata aqua*</note>, as we see in dikes, where such clay is usually employed against the breaking in of waters as a unique remedy, obstacle, and fortification. But our experiment and other observations teach that watery vapors, or rarefied water, are **thickened** <note>original: *densari*</note> into a body through the aforementioned clay and made liquid. 

Justly, therefore, this clay should be called the **tinder of water** <term>tinder of water: original *fomes aquæ*. In early chemistry, a "fomes" refers to a substance that "catches" or harbors a specific quality or element</term>, or its receptacle, in which watery vapors come together and lay aside their **spirituality** <note>In the alchemy of the 17th century, "spirituality" refers to the gaseous, volatile, or vaporous state of a substance before it condenses.</note>. Accordingly, this clay also possesses no small power in Physics. For if you take that **blue variety** <note>original: *cæruleam... speciem*</note> of the aforementioned clay, which is **the only one I mean** in this place, and distill it through a **gourd** <term>gourd: a *cucurbit*, the glass vessel forming the lower part of a distillation apparatus</term> with an **alembic** fitted to it, even using the **slowest** fire, immediately a most subtle spirit will heat the alembic so much that it cannot be touched by hand. It will sometimes make **streaks** <note>original: *strias*. These are the visible "veins" or oily swirls seen on the glass during distillation, often called "tears."</note> exactly like spirit of wine <term>spirit of wine: ethanol or high-proof alcohol</term>; although nothing but **tasteless water** <note>original: *insipida aqua*</note> comes forth into the receiving vessel. 

This water would be regarded by the **Galenists** <note>Galenists: followers of the traditional Greek medical system of Galen, who focused on balancing four humors and often rejected the new "chemical" medicine of Becher's era.</note> as useless **phlegm** <term>phlegm: in early chemistry, the watery, tasteless, and supposedly inactive portion of a distilled substance</term>; but it is of the greatest power, both regarding metallic operations and **medical** ones—indeed, regarding the **growth** of vegetables, I think there is scarcely anything in the world that can snatch the palm of victory from this water. For it is truly the **Mercury** of vegetables, or to use the **Helmontian term** <note>Refers to Jan Baptist van Helmont (1580–1644), a famous chemist who coined the word "gas."</note>, their primary **Gas**. 

We see this clearly in wine, with which this liquor has such an affinity that when mixed with it, the wine is **preserved** and **strengthened** to a miraculous degree. It is that vapor, or spirit of the earth, which is released during the **fermentation** of **must** <term>must: freshly crushed grape juice that has not yet finished fermenting into wine</term>, and which strikes the brain so sharply; and which some people, by closing off the fermentation, drive back into the wine and fix there, whereby the wines are made **very strong** but slow, commonly called **Mute Wine** <note>original German: *Stumme Wein*. This refers to wine where fermentation has been stopped early, often resulting in a very sweet, heavy, and potent liquid.</note>. Although the business succeeds much better if this Mercury is added to wine that has already been fermented; for in this way it is not thickened, but remains supremely Mercurial, which is why such wines are usually called **airy** <note>original German: *lufftig*. This implies a sparkling, lively, or "spirituous" quality.</note>, as we shall discuss more fully in Section 5, in the chapter on Fermentation. 

Great power, therefore, resides in this liquor; so much, indeed, that in the universal **production** of things, it came forth from the earth like a **vapor** and fertilized the whole earth, as we have previously cited from Holy Scripture. Truly, in this place I reveal a great **secret** <term>secret: original *arcanum*, a hidden principle or powerful chemical remedy</term> to the worthy and unworthy alike; but it will be esteemed as vile because it comes from a vile material, and because these things are revealed by me, a man of humble standing before the world. But let these things be: **the truth of the Lord shall remain forever** <note>A reference to Psalm 117:2.</note>, who has placed this vapor for the fertility of the earth from the beginning of the world until now: **one drop of which fertilizes more than a wagonload of manure**. 

Let those who care for nothing but **gold** wait for something more profitable; He fills the hungry with the good things of knowledge and sends the rich away empty <note>Alluding to the Magnificat, Luke 1:53.</note>—not indeed of temporal riches, but of the good things of science, experiences, and reasons, by which one approaches the Creator more and more closely than by any other way...

## Section Two, Chapter Four
# On mineral waters, acidic springs, saline waters, and hot springs.

->S Y N O P S I S.<-

**N. 1.** *The origin of mineral waters arises from insufficient filtration.* **N. 2.** *Central waters in the center of the earth are imbued with a singular earth, from which they become acidic and acquire a universal quality of dissolving, by means of which various minerals and stones of the earth are dissolved; hence the difference in **acidic springs** <term>acidic springs: original *acidulae*, referring to naturally carbonated or tart mineral waters</term>.* **N. 3.** *The origin of saline waters.* **N. 4.** *The difference between acidic and saline waters.* **N. 5.** *A universal acid dissolves various mineral species, resulting in various compounds.* **N. 6.** *The origin of mineral juices and compounds.* **N. 7.** *The perpetual flow of acidic springs.* **N. 8.** *On liquid earthy mineral effluvia.* **N. 9.** *On fire-vomiting mountains, caves, and caverns.* **N. 10.** *On the origin and nature of hot springs.*

->T E X T U S.<-

<margin>N. 1.</margin>
Thus far we have treated the Origin of Springs; namely, of that kind of subterranean vapor which, being pure and without admixture, is resolved into spring water. Now, according to our previous division, we shall treat of that vapor which, in its resolution, is mixed with other *mineral* species: as we see in *acidic springs* and other mineral waters commonly called **Wild-Mountain-Water** <note>original: *Wild-Berg-Wasser*</note>. It is not to be thought, however, that mineral waters of this kind arise only because certain mineral juices are dissolved by spring water flowing through them. For as experience teaches, if such a thing happened, in a very short time—as we said above—the vast subterranean places full of minerals would be washed out by such continuous dissolution,

<meta>This page continues Becher's explanation of how the earth's internal heat creates "central vapors." ### Subterranean Physics

...otherwise they would be scattered and soon fail. Therefore, it must be established—just as chemical practice demonstrates—that the central vapor <note>original: *vaporem centralem*; the hot gas rising from the earth's core</note> which breathes through the base of the "firmament" of the earth's center, is not of the same nature in all places. This is due to the diversity of that firmament, which acts like a filter <note>original: *transcolatorii*; literally a strainer or percolator</note>, and its further progress through the earth. Since there is no doubt that such places differ in their solidity and porosity, it necessarily follows that the subterranean vapors passing through are filtered and altered to a greater or lesser degree according to the condition of the filter. It is quite evident that through a solid filter, vapors are purified more (becoming spring water), whereas through a porous one, they are purified less (becoming mineral water).

Since we dealt with the strict filtering of springs in the preceding chapter, we shall now proceed in this chapter to the looser filtering. If a free passage is given to the central vapors, it will not be surprising at all that they carry away and elevate much terrestrial and sulfurous substance with them from the center. We see this in all distillations of plant matter, where the evaporating moisture usually carries oil—a sulfurous and terrestrial substance—along with it. We are also familiar with a liquor which, by the same principle, lifts the heaviest and most compact gold with it, a subject we shall discuss in the second book.

<margin>N. 2.</margin> Therefore, since the central water is sulfurous, bituminous, and saline, it easily seizes these sulfurous, saline, and earthy substances when it is resolved into vapor, unless it is purified by filtering. The "hungry spirit" refers to a powerful mineral acid capable of "eating" or dissolving metals.</note>. This is indeed the most remote source of the subterranean juices, as we shall later cite from Rupecissa <note>John of Rupescissa (c. 1310–1366), a Franciscan friar and alchemist famous for his work on the "quintessence."</note>. For by this mineral acidic vapor, subterranean places are filled with mineral juices, rather than being deprived of them by the boiling process mediated by this mineral water. For it is manifest that salt mines, commonly called *Saltz-Berg* <note>German: Salt Mountain</note> or *Stein-Saltz* <note>German: Rock Salt</note>, when they are completely cut out and washed away by the introduction of fresh water, are refilled and grow again after some interval of time. This is an evident sign that it proceeds from a subterranean saline vapor. Furthermore, the great abundance of salt water which flows for so long from salt springs, commonly called *Saltz-brunnen* <note>German: Salt Springs</note>, comes from nowhere else but the center of the earth, acting as the universal Steward and Storehouse <note>original: *Promocondo*; a Latin term for a cellarer or one who manages a pantry.</note> of nature. For it is entirely impossible for it to proceed from the **sea** through Mediterranean channels to such distant places, since we proved above that no channel can be so continuous over such a distance without rupture, mixing, or leaking away.

<margin>N. 3.</margin> We therefore establish that the perpetual flow of salty waters from salt springs proceeds from the central vapor as it runs through porous places and deposits that earth, through whose presence and mixing the **universal acid** is caused, which we discussed before and will discuss more at length later. ### Book I. Section II. Chapter IV.

...what are commonly called *Salt Spring Waters*. However, this saline water differs from "gem salt," commonly called *Rock Salt*, in that it is found in liquid form and on the surface of the earth, mixed with a great quantity of water; *whereas rock salt is found without water, in solid form, within the bowels of the earth, like a hardened juice.* Indeed, a central and saline vapor easily condenses near the bottom of the earth, especially if it carries few watery vapors with it; on the other hand, watery vapors that carry saline ones are easily resolved into liquid near the earth's *surface*. Furthermore, *boiled* spring salt differs from *rock salt* in that the latter contains more "earthiness" and the former less, and thus the spring salt is finer. Both of these, however—both *spring salt* and *mountain salt*—differ from *sea salt* in that sea salt is *bituminous* <note>original: *bituminosum*; oily or waxy in texture</note>, more *sulfurous*, and stronger; this is because it has not been filtered, strained, and purified by the firmament of the earth's center, neither during its first or second passage, nor in its descent through the seabed, nor in its ascent through the floor of the earth.

Let no one be surprised that we determine common salt to draw its origin from the aforementioned universal acid <note>original: *acido universali*; a theoretical primary acid in alchemy believed to be the source of all salts</note>, and indeed *once a certain earth is set aside, from which the acidity and base of the predicted acid follows*; which is true in every way. For when this earth is *rejected* <note>original: *rejecta*; cast off or separated during a process</note>, though through certain stages, the remainder is changed into salt. If this earth is added back, the best saline water can again become *mineral water*, commonly called *Wild Water* <note>original: *Wildwasser*</note>; indeed, *if this is added beyond measure, a completely new species of mineral juice leaps forth*: and *if this earth is thoroughly separated*, even the strongest saline water can be resolved into *tasteless* elemental water, as all these things will be demonstrated to the eye by various experiments in Book 2 under the appropriate sections. 

Therefore, much must be considered regarding this *earth* of the universal acid; for this acid is, as it were, the *first matter of all mineral juices*. Hence, it is not without merit that *Rupecissa* <note>John of Rupescissa, a 14th-century Franciscan alchemist</note> says: *Vitriol or salt is the first principle for generating all minerals, as a most remote principle, etc.* Although *Rupecissa* means neither *Vitriol* nor *common salt* specifically, he proposed both as examples because *earth* is found in both, which often constitutes the mentioned acid.

<margin>N. 4.</margin> For although the "earth of salt" is very closely related to the *earth of our acid*, it also differs from it greatly; for the earth of salt renders all bodies *volatile* and fluid. On the other hand, the earth of *vitriol* <note>original: *vitrioli*; iron or copper sulfates</note>, or the universal acid, *fixes* all things and binds them together. We see this by a clear experiment when iron or copper is dissolved in *spirit of salt* <note>original: *spiritu salis*; hydrochloric acid</note>; once thickening has occurred, we indeed receive a vitriol, but it flows in the air like "salt of tartar" <note>potassium carbonate, which absorbs moisture from the air and turns liquid</note>. Conversely, if these same metals are dissolved in the spirit of *Sulfur* or *Vitriol* <note>sulfuric acid</note>, a vitriol will be produced that is similar in all ways to the *natural* kind. And this comparison holds a place in the preparation of *alum* and many other mineral juices for the purpose of drawing out many differences. It is most certain that this diversity proceeds from the earth of our acid, as we shall prove in Book 2, in the chapter on the anatomy of the Spirit of Vitriol and *sulfur*, and we shall place this *whitest earth of the universal acid* before your eyes. Indeed, it is of the greatest importance, since without it, hardly anything can be successfully accomplished in metallic operations. This *virgin* earth of the acid is *prepared* in the vaults of the earth's center, or in its convex firmament; there, having undergone a reaction within itself from the central water, it rises to the circumference as a *sulfurous and bituminous Gas*...

### Subterranean Physics

...[would be consumed], and would soon fail. This is due to the diversity of the aforementioned firmament, which acts as a filter <note>original: *transcolatorii*; literally a strainer or colander</note>, and its further progress into the earth. Since there is no doubt that such places differ in **solidity and porosity**, it necessarily follows that the subterranean vapors passing through are more or less filtered and altered according to the condition of the filter. For it is entirely evident that through a solid filter, vapors are purified more to become **spring water**, whereas through a **porous** one, they are purified less to become **mineral** water. 

Since, therefore, in the preceding chapter we dealt with the **strict** filtering of springs, in this chapter we shall proceed **to the looser** filtering. This is indeed the most remote principle of subterranean juices, as we shall later cite from Rupescissa <note>Johannes de Rupescissa, a 14th-century alchemist known for his work on the 'quintessence'</note>. Furthermore, such an abundance of **salt water**, which has flowed for so long from salt springs—commonly called **Salt-Springs** <note>original: *Saltzbrunnen*</note>—comes from nowhere else but the center of the earth, acting as the **steward of universal nature** <note>original: *naturæ universali Promocondo*; a 'promocondus' is a household manager or butler who brings forth supplies</note>. 

For it is entirely impossible for it to proceed from the **sea** through inland conduits to such distant places, since we have proved above <margin>No. 3</margin> that no conduit could be so continuous and over such a distance without rupture, mixing, or leakage. That is to say, the greater part of this decomposed mineral water consists of the **universal acid, namely the hungry earth** <note>original: *terra esurina*—a term Becher uses for a highly reactive, acidic mineral principle that "devours" metals</note>, while only the smallest part consists of some added and dissolved mineral species, whether metal, earth, or stone.

The entire remaining substance of the increase comes from the distilled vinegar. The dissolved corpuscles of copper adhere to the solvent saline corpuscles of that vinegar; though they are small in quantity, they provide great extension and coloration, thickening the mixture and binding it into a certain form, namely a saline and angular one. Experience proves this when the same mixture is distilled: the **saline** parts are torn away from the copper parts and carry some of the copper qualities with them, whereby they acquire a singular quality. The **earthier** parts of the **acidic** portions, however, remain behind with the copper corpuscles in the residue, from which the copper parts also acquire **other** qualities. Thus, by frequent dissolution of new copper in the **aforementioned** torn-away spirit, eventually all the **earth**—from which vinegar gets its sourness—is fixed with the copper, and the vinegar turns into **elemental water**. 

Exactly the same thing happens in the vitriolization of metals through the spirit of **sulfur or vitriol**, where the greater part of the vitriol and its increase is to be attributed to the **spirits** <note>volatile acids</note>. The whole mixture, in **analysis**, agrees with the preceding experiment.

# Subterranean Physics

...pushed out from the convexity <note>The "convexity" refers to the outer curve of the earth's internal central core or vault</note>, it is digested and successively extracted through transuding vapors, and carried into the subterranean parts. There, in various *caverns*, as the aqueous vapors evaporate, it sometimes congeals and settles upon the vaults and sides in the form of *streaks* <note>original: *Striarum*; refers to the fluted or ridged patterns found in mineral deposits like stalactites</note>; for the most part, however, it is disguised in the form of *water*, into which it impresses dissolving and astringent qualities. From this, *acidity* arises, and the first disposition of this acidic water is varied in its passage by its ability to *dissolve*, and through such a solution, to produce new *composites* <note>original: *decomposita*; in early chemistry, this refers to substances formed by the combination/re-arrangement of simpler parts</note>.

<margin>N. 5.</margin>
For when it *flows and lingers* above mineral veins, *earths, and stones*, it dissolves some particles of such subjects; and, according to the nature of the gravity of the dissolved corpuscles, it constitutes a mixture, and is formed into various *streaked, square, foliated, and angular* shapes, etc.: as we see in common salt, nitre, alum, borax, and other juices. Namely, as has been said, according to the diverse gravity of the corpuscles, concerning all of which we shall speak specifically in Book 2. However, I would not want the reader to think at this point that the primary cause of mineral waters consists only in this: that certain solid mineral juices are dissolved in the subterranean *spring* waters flowing past them. That would be absurd; for fountain water, even if boiled over *iron* for a very long time, will acquire no *vitriol-like quality* <note>original: *vitriolitatem*; the characteristics of vitriol or metallic sulfates</note> from it; and *common salt* itself—for I exclude the Spirit <note>The "Spirit of Salt" or hydrochloric acid</note>—hardly dissolves metals even if it boils *with them* in liquid form. And although it may wear away a little through longer boiling, it produces far more imperfect composites, as we said a little while ago regarding the vitriolization of metals through the spirit of salt.

<margin>N. 6.</margin>
Therefore, mineral juices, whether solid or liquid, which are produced by this universal acid of ours, ought to be considered regarding their Genesis in such a way that we presuppose that only the smallest part of the external species lies *dissolved* in those mineral waters and acidic springs that we see daily. That is, the greater part of this composite mineral water consists in the universal acid—namely, in the *hungry earth* <term>terra esurina; Becher’s term for the acidic, active principle that "hungers" to consume or dissolve metals</term>—while the smallest part consists in some joined and *dissolved* mineral species, whether metal, earth, or stone. It behaves no differently than the mixture which they call *distilled verdigris* <note>original: *viride aeris destillatum*; copper acetate</note>; where in a hundred pounds there is scarcely a *thirtieth* part of copper, and the entire remaining substance of the increase comes from the distilled *vinegar*. To its dissolving saline corpuscles, the dissolved copper corpuscles—though in the smallest quantity—adhere with the greatest extension and coloration, thickening the mixture and binding it to a certain form, namely saline and angular. Experience proves this when the same mixture is distilled: the *saline* parts are torn away from the copper ones and carry some copper parts with them, from which they acquire a unique quality. The more *earthy* parts of the acidic portions, however, remain with the copper corpuscles in the residue, from which the copper parts also acquire other qualities. Thus, by frequent solution of new copper in the *aforementioned* torn-away spirit, all the earth from which vinegar gets its sourness is finally fixed with the copper, and the vinegar turns into *elemental water*. Plainly the same thing happens in the vitriolization of metals through the spirit of *sulfur or vitriol*, where the greater part of the vitriol and the increase must be attributed to the spirits; and the whole mixture in its *analysis* agrees with the preceding experiment.

# Subterranean Physics

Even if the cause and origin of these subjects are attributed to other things—as we shall teach later in Section 6—nevertheless, a <term>burning fatness<gloss>an oily or flammable quality, often associated with the 'sulfur' principle in alchemy</gloss></term> lies hidden in the very nature of *sea salt*, as we shall demonstrate in Book 2 in the specific chapter on salt. Moreover, just as <term>aqueous outflows<gloss>effluvia; invisible watery vapors or particles emitted by a substance</gloss></term> were shown to be twofold—namely, pure (such as spring water) and mixed (such as mineral waters)—the same distinction must also be observed regarding *earthy outflows*. Specifically, one part of them is more general, which we have dealt with until now, and the other is more specific, which we are about to discuss. We shall consider those earthy outflows that are the *proximate principles of metals* <note>the "immediate building blocks" or primary components from which metals are formed</note>, which we will discuss at length in the following Section at 
<margin>N. 2.</margin> because it is for the sake of these that we are writing this entire treatise, so that we might sufficiently prove their genealogy from head to heel. For there is no doubt that *diverse earths* are produced in the sea, and from there through the central waters—some more perfect than others—since experience teaches that one sulfur is *purer* than another. Therefore, the earthy outflows are twofold, even though they proceed from one source, namely *sea-earth*; which is therefore called the *first matter of all things*, and the *split mother* <note>original: "mater bifida"</note> of this aforementioned twofold earth, or the *hermaphrodite*. Hence Albertus Magnus <note>a 13th-century philosopher and alchemist</note> says: 
> All men agree on one [source], which is split in two. <note>original: "Omnes concordant in uno, qui est bifidus."</note>

We have already said that two kinds of earths proceed from the center of the earth; the first produces all subterranean mixed sulfurous and fatty things, and the *latter* produces saline things. For we shall prove in the "anatomy" of each substance in Book 2 that *sulfur* and *salt* consist of earth. Since these two earths differ in both <term>digestion<gloss>the process of refining or maturing a substance through heat over time</gloss></term> and purity, it is no wonder if *imperfect* sulfurs and salts are produced, especially in mixtures where water is present, as we see in common salt. But where these two earths are entirely *simple* and not transformed into any composite, then, I say, the true and *proximate principles of metals* exist, of the nature and condition that we shall explain in the following section. And this happens when these earthy outflows exist *without water* and without being decomposed into sulfurs and salts. Meanwhile, they are purified and more *digested*, by which they are distinguished from the preceding *sulfurous*, earthy, thick, and bituminous outflows. For the former are crude and mixed with various things; but these latter exist as the 
<margin>N. 3. +</margin> *pure, subtle, compressed, and penetrating principles of minerals*. Nevertheless, there is a great harmony, connection, and affinity between these imperfect and perfect earthy outflows; for they are rarely found *separately*, and they are found such that one is never without the other. Hence sulfurs and bitumens usually carry *minerals* with them, and a mineral is hardly ever found that is free of common *sulfur*. And just as the *perfect* earthy outflows are mixed with the imperfect ones, as we have said, so those perfect outflows are also mixed *among themselves*. Thus, almost no *ore of metal* is found that is not also fertile in and a *partaker* of other metals. For although we have said that the aforementioned earthy outflows are *perfect*, this is to be understood not so much in respect to themselves as in respect to the preceding impure and less-digested outflows, namely the salts and sulfurs. For the mineral outflows themselves, though they may be more digested and perfect in respect to the others (as has been said), still differ greatly among themselves both in digestion and in perfection. Anyone can see this in *antimony, lead, and silver*, and likewise in <term>marcasite<gloss>a term used at the time for various shiny mineral ores, often iron pyrite</gloss></term>, *copper, and gold*. Although these proceed from one foundation, they differ by "the whole heaven" <note>a Latin idiom meaning "entirely" or "diametrically opposed"</note> regarding the two extremes and the middle points, in terms of their perfection and digestion. <meta>This page continues the author’s explanation of how "earthy outflows" (effluvia) from the Earth's center transform into solid minerals. While the previous page discussed the generic nature of these vapors and their relationship to sea salt, this page focuses on the specific process of metallic maturation—how volatile vapors become "fixed" into rich ore veins—and introduces the German mining terminology used to describe these subterranean "breaths" or exhalations.</meta>

This is the specific reason for the diversity of *metals and minerals*. Furthermore, these <term>earthy mineral outflows<gloss>effluvia; invisible mineral-bearing vapors or particles emitted from the Earth's core</gloss></term> share this in common: at the beginning of their movement—namely, when they are preparing metals—they are volatile and penetrating; but at the end, once they have passed into metallic solidity, they become thick, heavy, and solid. We will provide the reasons for this in Section 7 of this book, in the chapter on solidity and fluidity. 

It must also be observed that the aforementioned mineral outflows are subtler near the surface of the earth than at the bottom; for reason dictates that through that long process of straining <note>percolation or filtering through rock</note>, the vapors are finally rendered more refined. On the other hand, because the thicker parts are deposited near the bottom, that very bottom abounds with metallic matter and <term>dregs<gloss>feculentia; the heavy, solid sediment of the mineral process</gloss></term> that are pleasing to mortals <note>meaning profitable or valuable to humans because they contain more concentrated ore</note>. 

And this is the reason why, near the base of mines, the ores are generally more abundant and richer; as the common saying goes, *the ore veins are mightier in the depths than at the surface* <note>original German: *die Ertzgänge seynd mächtiger in der Tieffe als an dem Tag*</note>. This is because near the bottom of the earth, or in its depths, the "primary earth"—which will be mentioned in Chapter 2 of the following section—namely the stones commonly called *quartz* <note>original: *Quertz*</note>, in which metals are usually generated and conceived, are found more abundantly. These stones are penetrated and softened by these kinds of inhaling vapors; the vapors, conversely, are strained through them like filters, thickened, and *fixed* <note>the alchemical process of turning a volatile vapor into a stable solid</note>. 

However, I believe it should not be overlooked that these vapors observe a certain order in their movement from the center to the circumference of the earth, which movements miners call *exhalations* <note>original German: *Witterungen*; literally "weatherings," referring to the subterranean vapors thought to grow metals</note>. Therefore, when these central mineral outflows inhale into the aforementioned stones from the depths, inhalations occur which miners generally call *in-weathering* <note>original German: *Einwitterungen*</note>. They use this name as long as the vapors are arranging and preparing the metal—commonly called "the stuff" <note>original German: *den Zeug*</note>, that is, the material for metals. 

When the metal is afterwards *perfected*, it is called "resting"; commonly, *a resting, sleeping ore* <note>original German: *ein ruhend, schlaffend Ertz*</note>. If the aforementioned earthy, central, mineral outflows come upon and reach it even after its perfection—and *more than is right*—the metal *revives* again and is, as it were, *resuscitated*. From this, the fixed metal is drawn out once more, made volatile, and *exhales*; this is what miners call *weathering out* <note>original German: *auswittern*</note>, and they call the exhaling metal *a living metal* <note>original German: *ein lebendig Metall*</note>. Just like grain, it occasionally revives and flies away <note>volatilizes</note>; however, they call the remaining empty and extracted stone *a dead metal* <note>original German: *ein todt Metall*</note>. But we shall deal with these matters more extensively in Section 4; at this point, we shall conclude the discussion on central outflows of fire, air, water, and earth.

Thus far, we have explained—sufficiently, I trust, and almost to the point of exhaustion, yet not without great labor and study—those things which pertain to the origin and movement of subterranean principles and <term>outflows<gloss>effluvia; the invisible mineral-bearing vapors discussed on previous pages</gloss></term>. Now, let us conclude this section under "good birds" <note>original: *bonis avibus*; a Latin idiom meaning "under good omens"</note> as they say—unless certain owls screech at us or harpies fly by, creatures that tear apart everything that does not belong to them. But first, let us illustrate that admirable circulation of nature—which we have tracked in the preceding pages as if following Ariadne's thread—with one or two examples for the better understanding of the reader.

<margin>No. 1.</margin>
In truth, this perpetual circulation can be compared to <term>chemical distillation<gloss>destillationi Chymicæ; the process of purifying a liquid by heating it into vapor and cooling it back into liquid</gloss></term>. In this process, a liquid enclosed in a <term>cucurbit<gloss>a gourd-shaped glass vessel used in a still</gloss></term> is warmed by heat and resolved into vapor. This vapor passes through the <term>beak of the alembic<gloss>the "nose" or tube of the still</gloss></term> and various coils or cooling vessels where it thickens and flows out again in the form of a liquid. If this liquid is then channeled back into the bottom of the cucurbit through a small tube—as is usually done in "circulatory" vessels or "blind" alembics—it will once again be resolved into vapor by the continued heat, ascend through the coolers, and condense back into water.

<margin>No. 2.</margin>
In this way, it establishes a perpetual circulation, just as we have put into practice in a certain <term>thermoscope<gloss>an early instrument for showing changes in temperature, a precursor to the thermometer</gloss></term>. We "animated" this device with constant heat and cold, establishing a perpetual circulation of liquid in such a way that its motion could turn a mechanical clock—a not-inelegant imitation of that great physical circulation of the Earth. And it was this imitated circulation of the aforementioned thermoscope that we intended in our **physico-mechanical perpetual motion machine**, which features the image of a serpent with the inscription: *The perpetual circulation of nature*. However, against our will and intention, Father [Gaspar] Schott <note>a famous Jesuit mathematician and physicist (1608–1666)</note> included and explained this machine in his book *Curious Technology* <note>original title: *Technica Curiosa*, 1664</note> on page 732. He falsely persuaded the reader that this "perpetual circulation of nature" referred to rainwater, and he added many other things without my knowledge. I wish Father Schott had either written his own material and left the labors of others untouched, or had shown himself to be a fair judge and critic.

<margin>No. 3.</margin>
If he had done so, he would not have—without any reason—accused me of a <term>false syllogism<gloss>paralogismum; an unintended error in reasoning</gloss></term> regarding "Pipe V" and "Capsule X" in the passage cited. It is known even to "the half-blind and the barbers" <note>original: *lippis & tonsoribus*; a Latin idiom meaning "common knowledge known to everyone"</note> that an empty pipe can be raised back up by the <term>counterweight X<gloss>antifacoma; likely a specific mechanical component in his diagram</gloss></term>, and that an empty pipe can never be as heavy as one filled with water. He imputed to us an error made by the engraver <note>the person who carved the copper plates for the book's illustrations</note> regarding the wheel of "Drum O" and "Weight M," where a change-gear was omitted near "Drum R." He acted as if, in a machine so complex (which he himself admits is ingenious), we were so inconsiderate or ignorant as to not know that the motion of "Globe M" ought to be directed upward! It is certain that Father Schott was "looking for a knot in a bulrush" <note>original: *nodum in scirpo*; an idiom for finding a problem where none exists</note> for the sake of other malevolent people, especially a certain third party. From this, such a copious harvest came forth that the peasant, along with all his neighbors, was seized with <margin>N.</margin> admiration, as the aforementioned author recounts more at length in the place cited. It was not, therefore, without reason that the Ancients placed the goddess *Venus* <note>In classical mythology, Venus (Aphrodite) was said to be born from the sea foam, symbolizing fertility and generation.</note> in charge of the sea; she acquires this fecundity partly from the stars and partly because she flows around the shores on all sides, steeping them and impregnating them with various substances. <margin>N. 6.</margin> Thus, the fertile sea penetrates the bottom of the earth; hence even in Holy Scripture, the *seas* are called the *ends of the earth* <note>original: "maria finis terræ"</note>.
