Kircher is mocking a linguistic corruption where the Latin "Maria" (seas) was confused with "Maria" (The Virgin Mary), and "finis terrae" (end of the earth) was mangled into the German "finster Stern" (dark star).</note>. There, they contracted *maria* for *Mary*, and *finis terrae* into *finster Stern*, and thus, not without laughter, they attributed improper and stolen praises to the Blessed Virgin. But let us return from this obscure etymology to our subject; where we assert that the seas constitute the end of the earth. For those things which are situated toward the center or across the surface can be said to be outside and at the end of the earth; for the shores can rather be called the beginnings of the earth than the end.

<margin>N. 7.</margin> We assert, therefore, that the sea penetrates into the center of the earth, there turning into vapor; that this vapor tends upward *through the earth*, and on its way fertilizes the subterranean earth; then, having been cooled near the surface, it is resolved back into *water*. This water is gathered into brooks and rivers and flows back again into the sea. Thus, it completes a perpetual circulation and a truly physical perpetual motion, <margin>N.</margin> as I hope we have sufficiently proved from what was said before. Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure to whom many alchemical and philosophical works were attributed.</note> supports this in the <term>Emerald Tablet<gloss>A brief, foundational alchemical text that describes the relationship between the celestial and terrestrial worlds.</gloss></term>, where he says: <margin>8.</margin> > *it ascends from the earth to the heaven, and again it descends from the heaven to the earth, and thus it receives the power of the higher and lower things into itself, which is perfect, or which attains its end, when it is changed into earth:* 
namely, when it deposits its qualities into the earth. For in such a way, not only minerals, but also the sweetest vegetables—namely the strongest wines and most fragrant balms—are produced and nourished from there. Thus the Creator willed it, so that the vapors, after they have deposited their gifts in the bowels of the earth, having been purified and, as it were, <term>rectified<gloss>a chemical term for being purified or refined through distillation</gloss></term>, might finally serve the plants and mankind.

Book I. Section III. Chapter I.

## Chapter One of the Third Section
# On the Definition and Nature of Subterranean 
# Principles.

### S Y N O P S I S .

*No. 1. The definition of principles. No. 2. The difference between the most general, the more general, and the general principles of things. No. 3. Concerning the most general principles of things. No. 4. Concerning the principles of the Aristotelians regarding general and proximate things. No. 5. Concerning the principles of the Paracelsians* <note>Followers of Paracelsus (1493–1541), a Swiss physician and alchemist who established the use of chemicals and minerals in medicine.</note> *and others regarding the same. No. 6. Paracelsus’s three principles are improperly called "principles," as they are actually composite substances. No. 7. The shameless lies of certain Chemists regarding these matters. No. 8. In what way salt, sulfur, and Mercury are said to be "non-beings." No. 9. Concerning the "dead head"* <note>original: "capite mortuo"; a term used by alchemists to describe the useless residue left after distillation or sublimation.</note> *of the Chemists. No. 10. How Paracelsus’s opinion might be defended. No. 11. Concerning the most specific principles of subterranean things, where it is proven that subterranean bodies, as mixed things, consist of parts which must be considered their principles. No. 12. It is difficult to reduce metals back into their principles without a new decomposition. No. 13. The method for extracting subterranean principles and investigating their genuine and proper constitution.*

### T E X T .

<margin>N. 1.</margin>
There is no need to set forth the definition of "principles" as it is commonly given, since it is known to everyone that *a principle is considered to be that from which something takes its beginning* <note>original: "id pro principio haberi, ex quo aliquid initium sumit"</note>; and because in this place we are aiming for practical application, and therefore we wrap all theoretical subtleties regarding the definitions of things in silence, we shall approach the series of the matter itself as it is in reality. Since, therefore, our discourse concerns *subterranean* things—which are mixed bodies and consist of parts—it necessarily follows that such parts, since they constitute a thoroughly *homogeneous* <term>homogeneous</term><note>Meaning a substance that is uniform in character and composition throughout.</note> mixture, must be most simple before that mixing occurs. For this is the common definition of principles: that they are, namely, *simple, pure, and unmixed*.

<margin>N. 2.</margin>
However, we do not mean this in relation to that general mixture which we discussed in Section 1; where even the primary parts of subterranean things, although they appear most simple, will be somewhat mixed, as we explained in that same Section. For if we carefully consider the word *principle*, it can be applied to the bodies of things in different respects. *First*, God can be called the principle of all things; then *nature*, which I define as *the physical motion that preserves all things in that disposition in which they were created and produced by God*. <margin>N. 3.</margin> *Third, Fire* can be called a principle of things, specifically insofar as it mixes and nourishes all visible things with its heat. *Fourth*, those things which constitute the "mixable parts" are rightly to be called principles; and these in turn are to be considered *most generally* in relation to the universe, and then *proximately*, according to how they are already disposed and "principled" <note>By "principled" (principiatæ), Kircher means substances that have already begun to take on a specific form or character but still serve as the basis for something else.</note> so as to be convertible into one thing or another. Subterranean Physics

<meta>catchword: considered</meta>

...are generated, Sacred Scripture says of man, *that he is earth, and to earth he must be returned.*

<margin>No. 4.</margin>
Finally, those things should also be called principles, and held as the most specific origins of things, which have been reduced from proximate matter into a specific form. In this way, the *seed of a man, an ox, an apple, a bean, gold, or silver* is truly to be called the principle of those bodies, such as are produced from them: for a kite <note>A type of hawk or bird of prey.</note> does not give birth to a dove. I think a distinction must therefore be made between *material and formal principles*; I call *material* those which provide the matter and the subject, but *formal* those which move, act, and mix: which we will deal with in both the preceding and subsequent sections.

<margin>No. 5.</margin>
Regarding material principles, they are again *most remote*, such as *water and earth*; and *most specific*, such as any specific *seed* of things; and *intermediates*, such as the *first mixtures* from which *seeds* arise. Aristotle explains this whole concept through form and matter; understanding "form" as the *agent* <note>The active force or "doer."</note> and "matter" as the *sufferer* <note>original: "patiens"; the passive element that receives the action or shape.</note>. Although his followers have explained this opinion of their Leader with infinite words, terms, and entanglements, yet there is none of them who, beyond words and empty names, can truly explain himself. For if, as they explain it, Aristotle understands "form" and "matter"—especially "prime matter"—then surely both will be nothing but a non-existent Chimera: in short, a "non-being" that merely teases the wits of idle men. 

For if you look at the prime matter of all things, they will be earth and water; if you look at the proximate matter, they will be the *first mixtures* produced from these; if the most specific, they will be the special *seeds* of things. But if you desire that *immaterial matter* of the modern philosophers, you will find no place for it here; you must seek it among those who, amid royal riches, fill the minds of idle men with immaterial nullities of this sort, so that they strip them of material faculties, losing their reason along with their time and expense. 

It is believable, therefore, that Aristotle understood something else by his "form" and "matter"; and indeed, if we consider the first and common *cause of forms* more accurately, reason persuades us it should be attributed to the heavens, because we proved in Section 1, Chapter 1 of this book that the heavens are the unique subject of rarity and density. It can be demonstrated with little effort that all forms proceed from rarity and density, if we consider—as we shall demonstrate in the following fourth section, in the chapter on the generation of animals—that the *forms of things consist of the particles of matter, and the weight and position of the particles*, toward which they are carried by the nature of their gravity: and this happens when the particles are "rare" <note>Spaced out or less dense.</note>, so that by natural propensity, any small body can be carried freely here or there according to the proportion of its weight. For without rarefaction, as we have proven elsewhere, nothing can be physically moved. 

Regarding *matter*, in whatever way we consider it, it must be something *material*, and indeed that from which all things consist: otherwise the very definition of prime matter would be false, if for instance something *immaterial* were understood by the word *matter*. Aristotle proposed the *proximate principles of subterranean things* a bit more successfully when he said they are subterranean, fat, oily, and sticky vapors and breaths, but everyone sees how general all these are. St. Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the influential medieval theologian who wrote extensive commentaries on Aristotle.</note> interpreted Aristotle much more skillfully when, in his commentary on the third book of Aristotle's *Meteorology*, he discourses on the principles of subterranean things as follows: *It must be considered...*

### Book I. Section III. Chapter I.

We must consider the material principles of metals, which exist in two different forms. Some are **remote matter**, such as the vapor trapped in the stony places of the earth. Others are **proximate matter**, and these are **sulfur** and **mercury**. Thus, in the aforementioned stony places of the earth, **sulfur** and **mercury** are generated through a mineral power; then, from these, various metals are generated according to their different mixtures. For this reason, even the **Alchemists** themselves—through the true art of **Alchemy**, using the aforementioned principles, or rather the things derived from those principles—sometimes achieve a true generation of metals. Thus far, we follow **St. Thomas** <note>St. Thomas Aquinas, a 13th-century theologian who also wrote on the nature of minerals.</note>, whose words weigh heavily in our favor.

<margin>No. 6.</margin>
Yet some, not yet content with these explanations, have fled to other speculations; especially from the time when **Paracelsus** <note>The famous and controversial Swiss physician and alchemist (1493–1541) who rejected traditional medicine.</note> began to become known. He attacked physicians so severely that, without shame, he did not blush to treat them as if they were buffoons on a platform. After him, there followed a very fertile age of **Chemists**. They gave themselves such license, not only to rage against anyone at their own whim, but also to bring forth into the world I know not what kind of tangled and almost infinite new opinions.

But let us turn ourselves toward these **philosophasters** <note>A derogatory term for pretend philosophers or charlatans.</note>. A vast number of **Chemical** books opens up to us immediately at the start; among them, there is no consensus, no harmony, and finally, almost no one agrees with another regarding the origin and principles of subterranean things. It could move someone to laughter if they were to read through their foolish speculations, in which neither sense nor consensus is found; as if, indeed, it were better to write what no one—not even the writer himself—understands, so that you would believe them to be fanatics rather than philosophers.

The leader of them all, **Paracelsus**, so tormented himself regarding the principles of subterranean things that he did not know which way to turn. At last, he broke forth into those famous three principles: **salt**, **sulfur**, and **mercury** <note>Known as the *Tria Prima*, the three primary components of matter in Paracelsian theory.</note>. How empty these are, we shall prove in the following pages; but even **Paracelsus** is not believed to have been the inventor of these. Indeed, **Bernard Penotus** <note>A French alchemist and physician who eventually became a critic of Paracelsus.</note> accuses him of the greatest plagiarism in his work *The Medical Denarius*:

> *These three principles of Mercury, Sulfur, and Salt,* he says, *Paracelsus took word-for-word from the "Vegetable Work" of Isaac Hollandus <note>A 15th-century Dutch alchemist.</note>. So too the doctrine of the separation of the four elements. He took the gradations of medicines from Arnold <note>Arnaldus de Villa Nova, a 13th-century physician.</note>; the "Archidoxa" from Raymond Lull <note>Ramon Llull, a Majorcan philosopher and mystic.</note> out of his "Operational Art"; and the "Secrets" from Rupescissa <note>John of Rupescissa, a 14th-century Franciscan chemist.</note>. He added absolutely nothing of his own except for vices and curses. He holds the synonyms he uses from the most learned Master Garland the Englishman. Various things from Trithemius. If anyone reads Arnold and Raymond's "Operational Art" attentively, they will notice that Paracelsus cut pieces from the writings of those men and claimed them for himself. Read Lanfranc <note>A 13th-century surgeon.</note>, and you will notice Paracelsus took his surgery from the same. Why does he not cite Arnold in the chapter on Paralysis, or regarding his "Galbanetum," or the book written on "Tartaric Diseases"? There are many other things which I leave to learned men to investigate. Weary of the present life, I open the way for you students by which you can arrive at better and easier things, and do not expect another "Elias the Artist" <note>A legendary figure in alchemy predicted to reveal all secrets.</note> beyond the works of Isaac Hollandus.*

Thus far **Penotus**. How these things please the **Paracelsians**, they themselves shall see. Not a few learned men testify that **Paracelsus** does not satisfy many, and consequently, they have fled to other ideas. Among these, the leader of our time is **Helmontius** <note>Jan Baptist van Helmont (1580–1644), a Flemish chemist and physician who bridges the gap between alchemy and modern chemistry.</note>, who, fashioning more solid principles for himself, conceived of I know not what **Archaeus** <note>An internal "master-workman" or vital force that Helmont believed governed the functions of the body and minerals.</note> or **Chimeras**; and thus, he did not so much change his insanity as change the *type* of insanity. # Subterranean Physics

...the schools of nullities, while in the meantime he <note>Likely referring to Van Helmont or a similar theorist.</note> imposes upon us with those kinds of **masked Archei** <note>original: "larvatis Archæis"; the Archeus was envisioned by Van Helmont as an internal "master workman" or vital spirit that governs the formation of matter.</note> and brings forth non-entities. However, since the three aforementioned principles of either **Isaac Hollandus** <note>A 15th-century alchemist whose works influenced Paracelsus.</note> or **Paracelsus** are more widely accepted than the **Helmontian Archeus**, we shall return to them and examine them more specifically.

<margin>No. 7.</margin>
I hope, however, that no one will be so absurd as to understand the three aforementioned principles as anything other than **proximate** and **derived** <note>original: "propinqua & principiata"; meaning they are products of a process, not the ultimate "first" building blocks of nature.</note>; namely, as matter already very nearly disposed toward action. And even if they are considered in this way, nevertheless, however they are explained, they are called **Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury** **metaphorically** <note>original: "impropre"; literally "improperly" or "inaccurately."</note>. For if you understand common sulfur, or any kind of sulfur, it will be a **mixture**; and this must also be understood regarding **Mercury** and common **Salt**, all of which are **mixed** and consist of parts. This is contrary to the nature of "principles," which are defined by the requirement that they must be **simple**. These Paracelsian principles, however, are not only mixed, but are even **complex compounds** <note>original: "decomposita"; in 17th-century chemistry, this referred to substances made of multiple components, rather than primary elements.</note>, as laboratory practice teaches.

For no salt, sulfur, or mercury can be drawn out of any metallic body unless certain things are added, which constitute a new compound—namely, some "third thing"—which they then call a "principle." But by the same reasoning, **vitriols**, and **glass-pastes** <note>original: "amausa"; imitation gems or enamels.</note>, and **metallic oxides** <note>original: "croci"; literally "saffrons," referring to the reddish-orange color of certain calcined metals.</note>, and **sublimates** <note>original: "flores"; literally "flowers," the fine powders that form when a substance is heated and then condenses.</note>, and **chemical butters** <note>original: "butyra"; thick, oily substances like Butter of Antimony.</note>, and finally everything that is prepared from metals, could be established as the "principles" of metals. This is because they are prepared from them; and although the things that are added seem to be utterly lacking in all **Sulfur, Salt, and Mercury**, and such subjects are not found in them **actually** <note>original: "actu"; meaning currently present in their manifest form.</note>, it is nonetheless not surprising if the compound does not exist before the decomposition, but rather arises first **as a third thing, from the decomposition**.

We see an example of this in **vitriolization** <note>The process of turning a metal into a vitriol (a sulfate).</note>; where **actually** neither the metal nor the **acid spirit** is the vitriol: yet meanwhile, when they are mixed, a "third thing" is produced which was in neither of them, namely, actual vitriol. The same is to be understood regarding **Sugar of Lead** <note>original: "saccharo Saturni"; lead acetate, which has a sweet taste but is highly toxic.</note> and many other things. For even those most skilled in the mixing of things and the quality of subjects are deceived, since the natures of things are wonderfully masked. For who would believe that **bodily earths lie hidden** in certain **most subtle spirits**? Who would look for the **burning spirit of wine** <note>Ethanol.</note> in the **spirit of vinegar**? Who would look for **red earth** in **salt of tartar**? Who would look for the **most bitter sulfur** in **common salt**? Who would look for **living sulfur** <note>original: "sulphur vivum"; native or virgin sulfur.</note>—solid, burning, and combustible in a **sufficiently large quantity**—in the acid **spirit of sulfur**, even though it was prepared through the burning of sulfur? Meanwhile, experience proves that not only these, but far different subjects lie hidden within, which places these and similar things before our eyes when the nature of things is more diligently weighed.

It is therefore no wonder if such subjects in decomposition deceive even the most learned men; especially **Sulfur, Salt, and Mercury**. These subjects, however they are taken, must be understood metaphorically if they are established as the principles of things; and however they are prepared from bodies, they are mixed and complex, and are not to be held as the **simple principles** of things.

<margin>No. 8.</margin>
I cannot, therefore, sufficiently marvel at the boldness of certain **Chemists** <note>original: "Chymicorum."</note> who are so brazen that they do not blush to publicly deceive the world with the densest lies when they profess that they can extract Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury from all bodies—even from animals and vegetables—and in that very form which is found in common **quicksilver** <note>original: "argentum vivum"; mercury.</note>, **sulfur**, and **salt**. Yet, laboratory analysis shows to the eye that **quicksilver is a complex compound, made of metal and fluid earth; sulfur...**

# Book 1. Section III. Chapter I.

...while truly sulfur <note>original: "sulphur vero vivum"</note> is composed of an acidic salt and the bitumen of the earth; and common salt consists of that universal water and marine earth, as we shall demonstrate specifically in Book 2 under the chemical analysis <note>original: "anatomia"; here meaning the structural breakdown or decomposition.</note> of any given subject.

<margin>No. 9.</margin>
For this reason, there were not a few, especially the **enemies of chemistry** <note>original: "misochymici"; those who opposed or disparaged the study of alchemy and chemistry.</note>, who not only utterly denied the existence of the three preceding principles, but also called into doubt whether they could be **produced** from metals through decomposition. A singular little book exists on this matter, titled *The Non-Entities of Chemists* <note>original: "non entium Chymicorum"</note>. In this, the author intends to demonstrate expressly that such principles cannot be elicited from any body unless they are added from the outside; and **Angelus Sala** <note>A 17th-century physician and chemist known for his skeptical and empirical approach.</note> strongly denies, for these reasons, that **Mercury** <note>Referring here to "living" or liquid quicksilver.</note> can be made from any metal without the addition of Mercury. 

This, however, is false; for since living mercury is a certain decomposed mineral in its own substance (as we shall prove in Book 2), what wonder is it if, from the parts that constitute such a composite, that very composite is made which we call **living mercury**, without the addition of living mercury? And indeed, experience teaches that by means of **common salt alone, from lead or antimony**, true living, running mercury can be produced, as we have often experienced in practice. From this, however, I do not yet wish to infer that the aforementioned Mercury is a **principle** of lead or antimony any more than any other composite that can be produced from such bodies—such as **sugar of Saturn** <note>original: "saccharum Saturni"; lead acetate, named for Saturn, the planetary symbol for lead.</note>, **butter of antimony** <note>original: "butyrum antimonii"; antimony trichloride, a thick, oily substance.</note>, and many others. For it does not follow that "Living mercury is not a principle of metals, therefore living mercury is a non-entity of metallic bodies and can only be produced from metals by the addition of Mercury"—which production, in such a manner, ought rather to be called an addition and a deception. Just as it also does not follow that "Mercury can be prepared from metals without the addition of Mercury, therefore Mercury is the principle of metals."

Two axioms must be observed in the study of Chemistry: first, that we should not easily establish or reject anything rashly and without firm reason and experience; for **if one person is ignorant of something, why should everyone be ignorant?** <note>original: "quæ enim unus nescit, cur omnes nescirent?"</note> Second, Chemistry is accustomed to putting on many masks, so that things which appear most simple are actually composites; and hence one should not easily establish anything as a principle whose temperament and nature are unknown. If modern Chemists had weighed these things, many things which they concluded to be **non-entities** would have been found to be **entities**; and what they held as **entities** would have been found to be **non-entities**. And this is the reason why they have regarded those decomposed mixtures—salt, sulfur, and mercury—as the simplest **principles**, while rejecting and condemning earth and water as useless matter, calling them **dead head** <note>original: "capite mortuo"; the inert residue left after distillation or sublimation.</note> and **phlegm** <note>original: "phlegmate"; the tasteless, watery distillate.</note>.

<margin>No. 10.</margin>
Yet it clearly appears that earth and water are the simple principles of all things, into which all bodies can ultimately be resolved, and which exist as the unique principles of **new mixing and generation**.

<margin>No. 11.</margin>
One must conclude, therefore, unless we wish to impute the crudest ignorance to Paracelsus and his followers regarding the doctrine of the three principles, that **something else is understood by the three principles** than what the common crowd thinks. We have attempted in our *Chemical Oedipus* <note>original: "Oedipo Chymico"; referring to Becher's 1664 work which sought to solve the "riddles" of alchemy.</note> to defend and reconcile the opinion of Paracelsus. This, however, must be added here: that **by sulfur, earth** should be understood, and **by salt, water**; earth and water, therefore, when they are in a more subtle degree, can be called **mercurial** <note>original: "mercurialia"</note> on account of their fluidity and penetra-

### Book 1. Section III. Chapter I.

...native sulfur <note>original: "sulphur vero vivum"</note> is produced from acid salt and bitumen of the earth; common salt, however, consists of that universal water and sea-earth, as we shall demonstrate specifically in Book 2 under the chemical analysis <note>original: "anatomia," literally "anatomy," but used here to mean the breaking down of substances into their parts</note> of each subject. 

<margin>No. 9.</margin> 
For this reason, not a few—especially the **misochymists** <note>From the Greek, meaning "haters of chemistry." These were scholars who rejected the chemical theories of the time in favor of traditional Aristotelian philosophy.</note>—have not only utterly denied the existence of the three preceding principles, but have also called into question whether they can be **produced** from metals through decomposition. A particular small book exists on this subject titled *On Chemical Non-Entities*. In it, the author intends to demonstrate expressly that such principles cannot be drawn out of any body unless they are added from the outside. **Angelo Sala** <note>An early 17th-century chemist and physician who was a pioneer in laboratory-based chemistry and skeptical of some alchemical claims.</note> strongly denies for these reasons that **Mercury** can be made from any metal without the addition of existing Mercury. 

This, however, is false. For since native Mercury <note>original: "Mercurius vivus," literally "living mercury," referring to liquid quicksilver.</note> is a certain mineral decomposition in its own substance (as we shall prove in Book 2), what wonder is it if that very compound we call **native Mercury** is formed from the parts that constitute such a compound, even without the addition of native Mercury? Indeed, experience teaches that by means of **common salt alone, a true, living, running Mercury** can be produced from **lead or antimony**; we have experienced this very thing many times in our own practice. 

From this, however, I do not yet wish to infer that the aforementioned Mercury is a "principle" of lead or antimony any differently than any other compound that can be produced from such bodies—such as **sugar of lead** <note>Lead acetate, a sweet-tasting but highly toxic white crystalline compound.</note>, **butter of antimony** <note>Antimony trichloride, a chemical compound that had a thick, buttery consistency.</note>, and many others. For it does not follow that "Native Mercury is not a principle of metals, therefore native Mercury is a non-entity of metallic bodies and cannot be produced from metals except by adding Mercury." Such a production would better be called addition and deception. Just as it also does not follow that "Mercury can be prepared from metals without adding Mercury, therefore Mercury is a principle of metals." 

Two axioms must be observed in chemical study: first, let us not easily establish or reject anything rashly and without firm reason and experience; for if one man does not know a thing, why should everyone be ignorant of it? Second, **Chemistry** is often accustomed to putting on many masks, so that things which appear most simple are actually compounds. Hence, one should not easily establish anything as a principle whose constitution <note>original: "crasis"</note> and nature are unknown. If modern chemists had weighed these things, many things which they concluded were "non-entities" would have been found to be entities, and what they held as entities would have been found to be non-entities. 

<margin>No. 10.</margin> 
And this is the reason why they have regarded those compounds—salt, sulfur, and Mercury—as the simplest **principles**, while rejecting earth and water as useless matter, condemned as **dead head** <term>caput mortuum: the useless solid residue remaining after a substance has been distilled or heated to exhaustion</term> and **phlegm** <term>phlegma: the watery, tasteless distillate that was often thrown away by early chemists</term>, as they call them. 

Yet it clearly appears that earth and water are the simple principles of all things, into which all bodies can ultimately be resolved, and which exist as the sole principles of new **mixture** and **generation**. 

<margin>No. 11.</margin> 
Therefore, it must be concluded in every way—unless we wish to impute the densest ignorance to Paracelsus and his followers regarding the doctrine of the three principles—that **by the three principles, something other is understood than what the common crowd thinks**. We have attempted in our work *The Chemical Oedipus* <note>A reference to Becher's own book, *Oedipus Chymicus* (1664), where he "solves the riddles" of alchemical language.</note> to defend and reconcile the opinion of Paracelsus. It must be added in this place, however, that by **sulfur**, "earth" should be understood, and by **salt**, "water." Earth and water, when they are in a more subtle degree, can therefore be called **mercurial**, on account of their fluidity and penetration...

### Underground Physics
<note>original: "Physicæ Subterraneæ"</note>

...substance: not that they are Mercury, but that they borrow the name from Mercury because of certain common properties. And this is to be understood when water and earth exist in a coarse and bodily state; for there they seek their name from the nature of fixed salt, which they emulate. In a similar case, when water and earth are placed in a **middle** state, neither too rare nor too dense, they derive their naming <note>original: "etymologiam," literally etymology</note> from common **sulfur**; for that is neither too volatile nor too fixed. Hence, if the term **sulfur** appears, you should understand it as **earth**; but if it is called **mercurial sulfur** or **mercurial salt**, then **subtle earth** or **subtle water** is to be understood, as we have explained more extensively 
<margin>No. 12.</margin> in our **Chemical Oedipus** <note>original: "Oedipo Chymico," a work by Becher published in 1664 where he attempts to "solve the riddles" of alchemical language.</note>. It would have been desirable, however, if **Paracelsus** <note>Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim (1493–1541), the influential Swiss physician who popularized the "Tria Prima" theory of Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury.</note> had explained himself, for with this new doctrine of his, he introduced into the world not only many absurdities, but also many doubts. Indeed, the doctrine of principles can be explained far more easily, clearly, and solidly if we begin from practice: **for those are the true and genuine primary principles of things from which bodies consist, and out of which they are daily mixed and prepared.**

In order that the reader may sufficiently understand my opinion, I will set it forth candidly and in few words: **The universal and catholic principles of the world are earth and water, as far as matter is concerned; as far as form, they are heaven and the instruments of rarefaction, which are fire and air; these universal principles (from which the whole world was produced, as we taught in Section 1) were eventually mixed in various ways and became the principles and specific elements and nutrients of bodies: from which comes that threefold class and kingdom of animals, vegetables, and minerals.** 

In each kingdom there are specific seeds as principled principles <note>original: "principia principiata," a scholastic term referring to principles that are themselves derived from higher, more fundamental principles.</note> and most singular principles; and **thus the most remote principle of all things is earth and water,** as they existed in the act of creation: **the proximate principle is the same earth and water, but after production, according as they are variously mixed: while the most specific principle is that from which any body begins its actual generation, as from a principled principle.** And this is the specific seed of any body, namely earth and water, insofar as they are disposed and changed from proximate principles into the most specific—namely, the seeds of things. Thus all things came forth from earth and water, and all things can eventually be reduced back into earth and water. 

Just as we made a distinction between mixtures in Section 1, Chapter 4, and proved that some consist of **earth and water**, others of **various species of water**, and others of **various earths**; so in this place we will consider the principles only of those bodies which are purely earthy, or which consist only of earths. We demonstrated in that same cited place that there are several such subterranean bodies. For some subterranean things are more imperfectly mixed, namely decomposed; such as salts, mineral juices, etc., into whose decomposition water enters, as we demonstrated in the preceding section; we will not say much about these here since, with the exception of water, they have the same origin as metals and stones. Others, however, are perfectly mixed, and these consist only of earth; such as minerals and stones. For although these subjects are not infrequently generated in waters, no one who has investigated their nature even slightly will think that waters **essentially enter into their mixture**; for the first glance demonstrates them to be earthy, especially under the **anatomy of fire** <note>original: "ignis anatomia," referring to chemical analysis or decomposition performed through heating in a furnace.</note>. Let the general axiom therefore be: **the substance of metals and stones**...

### Book I. Section III. Chapter I.

...of stones is earthy. Now indeed a second question arises concerning the **principles of subterranean bodies**; whether, since their substance is earthy, **at least one or several earths concur?** Certainly the diversity of mixtures **demonstrates** that there are different earths in different mixtures; for there is a different earth in a **diamond** <note>original: "adamante"</note> than in **marble**, and again a different one in **gold** than in **copper**, which everyone sees. Nor do we dwell on whether these earths **differ in perfection**, purity, or **in whatever way**; although they are understood under the one generic name of "earth," provided they **differ** and constitute different species, which the very nature and diversity of subterranean things confirms. This truly is the most disputed point: whether in **each species** (suppose any subterranean mixture, metallic or stony) **more than one earth comes together**, is required, and is mixed? We therefore set aside the earth and heterogeneous matter which enter the composition of minerals by chance, such as the **stones and earths** mixed in minerals, commonly called **ore** <note>original: "Ertz"</note>; and in stones the chaff, **coverings, envelopes, veins**, and other things. For in this place we speak only of a mixture that is entirely homogeneous; namely, whether in **copper, gold, diamond, and ruby**, and other bodies either metallic or stony, there are different ingredients, and how many? Or **whether and how many different earths enter such mixtures**, and **essentially constitute them?** <margin>No. 12.</margin> This question is difficult, both because it has been treated by no one until now, and because it cannot be decided except through the **anatomy of bodies** <note>original: "anatomiam." Becher uses this term to mean the chemical decomposition or "taking apart" of a substance to see its components.</note>. These bodies, indeed, since they are entirely homogeneous and **of the strongest mixture**, most tenaciously resist all elements and resolutions into their primary parts: <margin>No. 13.</margin> So much so that subjects of this kind cannot be reduced into their principles by themselves; but if they are dissolved by additives, new decompositions immediately occur, which obscure and confound the genuine truth of the **simple primary parts**, so that composite things rather than simple principles come before the eyes. From this come those infinite errors of practitioners <note>original: "artistarum," referring to alchemists and laboratory workers</note>; from this comes the great and, for so many centuries, vast ignorance concerning this matter; finally, from this it happens that no one until now has decided the aforementioned question, or arrived at a solid knowledge of the subterranean principles as they actually exist in bodies. By some fate, I know not what, I have stumbled upon this matter and undertaken to examine it; whether I shall satisfy the reader, the outcome will prove. <margin>✓</margin> Should some indulgence be given to one trying for the first time? But some authority should also be granted to one who is the first to experience and who writes from practice. Regarding the **question**, therefore, as to **what kind of principles subterranean things have?** It has already been said that they are earthy; but it is probable that metals and stones, because they are different, also consist of **different earths**, as far as their species is concerned. But also, **any metallic species contains not one but several earths within itself; that is, it consists not of one but of several principles.** This latter point it now falls upon us to prove. We conclude, however, that any mixture from the number of those of which we are now dealing—namely, homogeneous ones, specifically metals and stones—consists not of one but of several earths; for common reason dictates this. For a thing single in number cannot be mixed, yet metals are mixtures; therefore they do not consist of one, but of several. Furthermore, it is manifest from experience that stones and metals can be entirely deprived of their color; which, contrary to the **followers of Aristotle** <note>original: "Aristotelicos." Aristotle believed color was an accidental quality, but Becher argues it is a physical substance.</note>, is not some imaginary non-entity and accident, but in truth is a **certain subtle earth**. This, I say, can be separated, and nevertheless a mixture...

# Subterranean Physics

...some part remains; which is a clear sign that mineral mixtures consist of *different* parts. If this were not so, no specific reaction could occur in such mixtures without the total destruction and alteration of the whole. For if mineral mixtures consisted entirely of only *one* matter, they would be subject to only one type of condition; however, practice demonstrates the opposite. Such subjects can be rendered *malleable, brittle, heavy, light, compact, porous, solid, fluid, volatile, or fixed*, <note>These are the "physical properties" that Becher argues cannot come from a single, simple substance.</note> and so on. These alterations arise not only through additions from the outside, but from the internal nature of the essential parts of the mixture itself. It is not believable that so many different changes could proceed from a single simple subject. But setting aside such things, which are evident in themselves, this **Gordian knot** <note>A metaphor for an intricate or unsolvable problem; Becher intends to "cut" the problem using experimental evidence.</note> must be untied by the sword of practice. 

I say therefore as a conclusion: *stones and metals consist of three earths*; the *first* of which provides the **foundation** <note>original: "hypostasin," referring to the underlying fundamental substance.</note>, substance, or base for such mixtures; the *second* provides the color; and the *third* provides the form, **metallicity** <note>original: "metalleitatem," the quality that makes a metal a metal.</note>, or **stoniness**. We shall defend these claims in the following chapters of this section, not based on some abstract theory, but through *practice*. I say *practice*, for when these three earths are mixed, they produce both metals and stones *even through artifice*—creating mixtures that are in every way similar to natural ones. This occurs according to the diversity of the *third earth*, as we shall teach in the following chapters. 

Indeed, the difference between *stones and metals* consists in that third earth. In metals, there is an earth that gives them their metallic nature, while in stones there is another earth that gives them their *stoniness*; the reader should observe this distinction well. In the other two *earths*, both metals and stones agree—namely, in their substance and color. I believe this is the strongest argument: when substances are established as "principles" <note>In 17th-century chemistry, a "principle" was a fundamental constituent of matter.</note> that, when mixed together, constitute a perfect metallic or stony composition, they must be the true origin; *for from whatever a thing is made, that is believed to be its true principle.*

Among the true Chemical Philosophers, many are found who constantly affirm that those are the true principles of metals which, when joined to metals without a new breakdown of the external appearance, provide a real and uniform increase to the metal to which they are added. For as **Geber** <note>The Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, an influential 8th-century alchemist often cited by early modern scientists.</note> says: "where you find even the smallest metallic increase, there we say you are before the doors of the Philosophers." 

<margin>Note 14.</margin>

And truly it is a fitting judgment; *for that through which a body receives a uniform increase is the very thing that can be held as the principle of that body.* To place the foundations of this entire theory and practice concerning subterranean principles before the eyes of the curious reader in a few candid words without any ambiguity, I say that *three different earths exist in metals and stones: the first is found outside of its mixture in stones or in alkali salt; the second in nitre; and the third in common salt.* 

These three earths, when mixed without any other addition, constitute a true and genuine metal, or, by varying the practice, a stone. From this I conclude that both metals and stones naturally consist of these ingredients, as we shall demonstrate specifically in the following chapters of this section and in Book 2. This is our particular opinion, confirmed by practice: that metals and stones consist of three simple earths. Their evidence is seen not just after the fact (when they are already mixed and exist within the mineral), but from the beginning, insofar as they are able to be mixed and, once mixed, actually form the body of which they are the principle. Thus, in this kind of philosophy, moving from the beginning to...

It is called *Schist* <note>original: "Schifer," referring to shale or schistose rock</note>: without which no mineral is good, nor does it promise fertility. Indeed, this stone is so necessary to minerals that even when it exists in the mountains plainly and without any metal, it is an infallible sign of future metal; relying on this sign, seekers of minerals search for it, sometimes at no small expense. Therefore, not without pregnant causes, we establish and recognize this earth or stone as the *first principle* <term>principium primum</term> of all metals, minerals, stones, and gems. We rely on certain experiments, as we shall demonstrate in the
<margin>N. 4.</margin>
following pages: by which we can prove that the aforementioned earth exists *actually* in all metals and minerals, as well as in stones and gems, and enters their mixture as a base and foundation. From this, they obtain their *substance* <note>original: "hypostasin," a Greek term for the underlying reality or essence of a thing</note>, opacity, *translucency*, and flux <note>the ability to melt or flow</note>. Consequently, the diversity of these properties proceeds from the different grades of this
<margin>N. 5.</margin>
earth, consisting in its quantity and purity, as will be explained more extensively later. Therefore, this earth is an infallible sign of metal being present not only when it is *present*, as has been said, but its *absence* serves as the same sign that metal will be lacking. For even if the other two principles—namely the earths of which we shall treat later, which are not rarely seen in the *form of smoke* <note>referring to the volatile/mercurial and combustible/sulfurous principles</note>—are present in sufficient abundance, they cannot take on a metallic form due to the lack of the first earth, which acts as the matrix, receptacle, and seal. Instead, adhering to the walls, they produce various kinds of metallic *flowers, tufas, fluxes, and colors*; these are *sterile and poisonous*, unless they are corrected by art. Not without merit, then, does Mary the Prophetess <note>an legendary alchemical authority, often identified as Miriam, sister of Moses</note> call this kind of stone the *white herb*, when she says: *smoke embraces smoke, and the white herb, growing on the little hills, captures both.* By this saying, she points to this earth in the clearest words. Therefore, the lack of this earth stands as the most immediate and frequent cause of *sterile* minerals, which happens for various reasons. Either it is because the Creator willed it so, and it does not exist in all places, having been so placed at the first production; or it is because, through the ignorance of miners, it is cut away in great quantities to prepare paths in the mountains or for the sake of a slight profit from the metal they sometimes notice contained within it. From this come those massive subterranean caves, commonly called *hollows* or *recesses* <note>original: "Kübren, Zäcken"</note>, in which we do not see new metals being regenerated, except for some *metallic fluxes*. The reason is obvious: because of a *defect of the matrix*. Yet they could remedy this evil by art, if they were willing to follow good counsel; for in this way they would have a double utility. First, the mineral smokes wandering here and there, and luxuriously spreading to no use, would be fixed by their matrix, producing metals and being of use. Second, because once captured in this way, they would cease to wander in the form of *poisonous smokes* and harm people. For they are already a great inconvenience to miners in the mines, and are sucked out with great labor by bellows, which they call *driving out the bad weather* <note>original: "daß böß Wetter austreiben," referring to ventilating foul air or "damps" from the mine</note>. Truly, the error in cutting away this earth arises from this cause: when miners are cutting paths to the minerals—either perpendicular ones, which they call *Shafts* <note>original: "Schächt"</note>, or horizontal ones, which they name *Adits* <note>original: "Stollen"</note>—and they fall upon this kind of earth (which leads them to the minerals like Ariadne's thread), they cut it away more willingly than the side-rock. This is because it is much milder, softer, and more manageable than the other rocks, which are sometimes so hard that they not rarely require half a year to excavate a distance of five feet; whereas, on the contrary, in one day of our earth or

Specifically, they call our particular earth or stone "a tender Quartz" <note>original German: "ein zarten Quartz"</note>.

<margin>N. 6.</margin>
For it is somewhat transparent, white, and interspersed as if with silvery leaves, and it melts easily in fire. Two things regarding this stone, which I sometimes call "earth," should be noted in particular. First, it is not always found so pure, but is discovered in many forms mixed with various substances. It is found mixed with common stone, yet it keeps its veins separate from the rest of the stone—which they call the "solid rock" <note>original German: "Bergveſte," referring to the stable, non-mineralized country rock</note>—making them easily recognizable. Since our stone is softer, it pleased the Creator to produce columns of harder stone to support the mines, which are not infrequently interspersed with our stone. Therefore, miners should take care that, in their excessive hope for profit, they do not extract a great quantity of such support rocks simply because of the small amount of metal sometimes present in them; if these are removed, the entire foundation of the mountains is endangered. I could demonstrate this with specific examples of many rich mines that can no longer be worked without peril to life because of this single error. 

But we must return to the varieties of our stone, which is frequently found mixed not only with various stones but also with different types of earths. In this latter way—namely, according to the different mixtures of earths—it is designated by miners with various names, such as *Spathblende* <note>original: "Spathblenthen," likely a type of spar or sphalerite</note>, *Mica* <note>original: "Katzenſilber," literally "cat-silver"</note>, *Talc* <note>original: "Talch"</note>, etc. It is very well established that metals are generated in all of these, and indeed in such abundance that letters written to me from Norway <note>original: "Norvvegia"</note> testify that a single hundredweight of talc contained thirty-two lots <note>a historical unit of weight, roughly 1/32 of a pound</note> of pure gold. Not even content with this, the <term>Assayers</term> <gloss>specialists who test the purity of ores; original: "Docimaſtæ"</gloss> suspected more was present, if only they knew how to separate it, which is why they consulted me. For the types of earth that mix with our stone are not of the same nature; that is, they are not the "principles" <note>the fundamental building blocks</note> of metals, which is why they cannot enter into their radical mixture, but only adhere superficially. Yet they cling most tenaciously, often causing great labor for those who separate metals. It is easier to separate <term>Antimony</term> or <term>Arsenic</term> and any other mineral from metals than to free them from this most tenacious earth, by which not only their flow <note>ability to melt</note> but also their cohesion and malleability are hindered. Hence, such minerals are called "smothered metals" <note>original German: "Underkhüttete Metallen"</note> by the smelters.

<margin>N. 7.</margin>
The *second* thing that should be noted regarding the nature of our stone is that it is found neither as abundant nor as fertile in metal on the surface of the mountains. For as will be demonstrated later when we treat mineral vapors, metals are generated by a process of <term>percolation</term> <gloss>filtering through a porous substance; original: "tranſcolationis"</gloss> and are pushed from the base of the mines toward the surface. Thus, it is necessary that they are found more abundantly near the bottom. It follows that their <term>matrix</term> <gloss>the "mother" stone or container in which minerals grow</gloss> is found there more than anywhere else, which experience also proves. 

However, before I conclude this first principle of minerals, one question remains for us to decide: namely, whether metals are conceived in this stone only as in a "matrix"—the matrix itself not entering into the essential nature and mixture of the metal—
<margin>N. 8.</margin>
or whether metals are generated in this stone as in their necessary "principle," which enters their mixture as a foundation and truly exists within them?

# Subterranean Physics

How is this question decided? I decide it thus: The stone, which we have discussed so far, is required for the generation of metals not only as a **matrix** <note>original: matrix, meaning the "womb" or geological mold in which minerals form</note>, but also as an **ingredient and a principle**. Not that it is transmuted in its own nature into metal, in the way that blood turns into flesh; but rather that, when the remaining two principles (which we are about to discuss) are added and **mixed** with it, it acquires new qualities. These new qualities arise from the nature of this mixture, and these qualities are called **metal**, serving as a third distinct product. Therefore, it is natural that this stone—to the extent that it exists within the mixture of metals—can no longer retain its original qualities. Instead, due to the addition of the others, it becomes heavy, opaque, and **malleable**. By its **own nature, it remains fusible and liquefiable**; this quality does not change in it, even though new ones are superimposed. 

Thus, we should not think that when we find **pure ore**, which they call *gediegen* <note>original German: "gediegen," a term still used today for "native" metals like gold or silver found in their pure metallic state</note>, our stone has vanished. Rather, we must conclude that through the mixing of the other principles, it has taken on new qualities and become a new mixture. It still exists within that mixture truly and as a **principle**. Experience teaches this, proving that the nature of **fusibility**—which is proper and essential to fossils <note>In the 17th century, "fossils" referred to anything dug out of the earth, including minerals and stones</note>—flows from this stone.

<margin>N. 9.</margin> Another question of no small importance regarding this **principal stone** must be discussed: namely, whether it always exists in the nature of a **stone** and suffers no increase or decrease—that is, whether it remains without any natural movement or change, just as it was ordered by the Creator in the first production? This is a serious question, for it touches upon the **universal origin of stones**. Primarily, it involves the question: **are rocks and stones still being generated in the world today?** Do "petrifying juices" <note>original: *succi lapidifici*, fluids believed to have the power to turn substances into stone</note> and similar things exist? We shall treat these in their proper place.

<margin>N. 10.</margin> For although **our stone**, mentioned here, shares much with other stones (since it is a stone in its entire nature), it nevertheless has certain unique characteristics **not shared** by other stones: namely, that it is the parent and **principle** of all stones, producing different species because of the different earths joined to it, as we will discuss later at length. Furthermore, it is not rarely found in the form of **earth, water, and smoke**. For when the stone is of such a nature as we have described so far, and insofar as it is the first principle of metals and is called **Quartz**; insofar as it exists in that form, it is a "principled principle" <note>original: *principium principiatum*, a philosophical term for a substance that acts as a foundation but was itself created from something else</note>—that is, matter closely prepared for the generation of minerals. 

<margin>N. 11.</margin> Conversely, in the form of earth, water, and the resulting exhalation and vapor, the principle is somewhat **more remote and universal**. What, then, prevents this second form from being **nourished** and produced even now? It is no different from how butter is made from milk. It is therefore entirely certain that <term>stone-making matter</term> <note>original: *materia lapidifica*</note> exists; for we see stones and rocks growing and increasing daily. However, the **matter** of stones cannot be an **actual stone**, but only a potential one. For if it were already a stone in actuality and form, stones would only be made by placing things next to each other, joining them together, or by external growth, which is absurd. For two stones placed next to each other do not merge; otherwise, all sand would become a single stone. Furthermore, all things that are brought from potentiality into actuality pass from one state to another; but in that way, they would pass from one thing to the same thing, from like to like, which is again absurd. But **experience** ends this whole dispute, teaching us that stones are **mixtures**. Since they are mixtures, they consist of parts; but

Through a specific experiment, using the aid of *only fire and common water*, I resolved even the hardest stones into a pulp <note>original: "mucorem," a moldy or slimy substance</note>, which, when distilled, yields a subtle *spirit* and an *oil* that cannot be sufficiently praised. From these and many other experiments, it will not be difficult to conclude that our stone is not always contained in the form of a stone, but sometimes under the mask of *water, smoke, and earth*; and when it is mixed with others, it *increases* substantially, as will be discussed more broadly below in the history of stones. I cannot, however,
<margin>N. 14.</margin>

By this, our stone is wrapped as if in an envelope and an amnion <note>the inner membrane surrounding an embryo</note>, and in truth is nourished and increased by it. A wonderful *spirit* can also be drawn from it, not unlike that which we prepared from stones, and which we mentioned a little earlier regarding the silt of springs. From this it is clear that it is not impossible for this stone to be masked under the form of *earth*; indeed, even under the idea of a most subtle and penetrating *spirit*, which spirit is most abundantly present in the aforementioned earth, as practice teaches, and as we explained more fully in the preceding Section on the history of *earth, silt, and mud*. It is most certain that by this stone-forming and all-penetrating vapor, the

Specifically, it is the earth that remains after the roasting <term>calcination: heating a substance to high temperatures to remove volatile components</term> of vegetables and the washing <term>elixation: the process of boiling or leaching to extract soluble salts</term> of their ashes. However, as soon as the aforementioned earth from ashes is cast in, not only is the entire paste of glass immediately rendered more fluid, but it also takes on a great increase and growth therefrom, often by more than half. *This proves not only the great affinity of vegetable earth with mineral earth, but indeed a very great similarity, harmony, and analogy. This is because this earth can also be turned into glass by itself, as happened to us once in Poland with the dregs of wormwood* <note>original: "absynthium"</note>*. Furthermore, this earth is so compatible with mineral glasses prepared from sand and flints that it can be distinguished by nothing other than its color, which is green or somewhat bluish; it preserves an indelible mark of its own kingdom, expressing a vegetable greenness. This, however, is a great inconvenience to glassmakers, who desire clear glass rather than colored. This, therefore, is what I wish to infer: that there exists in vegetables a fusible earth which is their basis, just as there is in minerals.* 

But who would believe—to prove this threefold analogy—that such an earth is also given in animals? *A fusible earth, I say, capable of being turned into glass, and indeed the most noble of all, so much so that even the entire array of Chinese vessels* <note>A reference to porcelain, which was highly prized and its composition a secret in the 17th century</note> *cannot be compared with it.* Deeper mysteries lie within the animal earth, which it would be a sin and a sacrilege to publish indiscriminately in this place; let it suffice to have said that *there is a great analogy in man with the two aforementioned earths, and indeed, it is their fulfillment.* 

Oh, if only it were the custom, and if I had friends who would one day perform this last small service for my own dry bones, exhausted by many labors! Those, I say, who would reduce them into that transparent substance, incorruptible by any dregs, presenting a most pleasant color of its own kind—not indeed the greenness of vegetables, but rather representing the milky appearance of a trembling narcissus. This could be done in a few hours, so that they might become a proof of divine omnipotence on the day of resurrection and clarification <note>original: "clarificationis," referring to the theological concept of the "glorified body" after death</note> that is to come to us. Would it not be better for them than to rot under the earth now, and be exposed in public places in a semi-putrid state—a terrifying spectacle to passersby, especially pregnant women and children—with gaping eye sockets, teeth not yet consumed, and various cavities and abscesses of the face, rendering death more terrible than lovely? 

This is what I wish to conclude: *man is glass, and can be reduced to glass, just like all animals; a transparent glass, the most noble of all glasses, fusible, and tinted with a color of its own kind, being in all ways homogeneous with the former mineral and vegetable glasses.* By what manipulation it may be prepared, however, is not my purpose to reveal here, because of various abuses. With how much labor the ancients burned <note>original: "combuserint"</note> the bones of mortals...

<margin>No. 3.</margin>
Therefore, from the aforementioned *harmony* of the three kingdoms, it must be concluded that the first principle—namely the fusible, liquefiable, and vitrescible earth—exists in all things as their foundation <term>hypostasis: the underlying substance or essence</term> and base. From this, it will not be so absurd to deduce that nature, since it preserves such harmony in one principle, also maintains it in the others. And so far, we have argued from mineral earth to vegetables and animals to demonstrate its truth and constitution; now indeed we shall proceed from the opposite direction, and from animals and vegetables, we shall deduce the *second* earth, the *second* principle of minerals, which is the *fatty earth* <margin>No. 4.</margin> <note>original: "pinguis terra"; Becher's second principle of matter, which would later influence the theory of phlogiston</note>. For since we find fatness <note>pinguetudo</note> in all animals and vegetables, which our modern thinkers call *oil*, who can doubt that it is also present in *fossils* <note>in the 17th century, "fossils" referred to anything dug out of the ground, including minerals and ores</note>? For it is established that some mineral things can burn, blaze, and be reduced to ashes—even the metals themselves, and indeed *gold* and *silver*, can be reduced to flames and consumed, as we shall prove in the second book, in the chapter on *Sulfur*. 

In order to arrive at a more specific origin <note>Genesis</note> of this earth, it must be known that it differs from the first one only by the degree of *humidity*; for whereas the first earth, which we discussed just before, is *extremely dry*, this one is more humid. 
<margin>No. 5.</margin>
It was brought to such a state and distinction in its very first production. For since, as we proved above regarding the production of things, the entire production and drawing-forth from the first earth-water-air globe was nothing other than the *mixing of earth and water*, the thinning <term>rarefaction: the process of making a substance less dense</term> of the mixed parts, and the abstraction and separation of those thinned parts; it necessarily follows that the entire work of production was nothing other than a boiling <term>elixation: the process of long boiling or digestion to extract substances</term>. The difference in the remaining earth consisted only in a duality, namely being different either in *density* <note>original: "raritate"</note> or *humidity*. 
<margin>No. 6.</margin>
And in this respect, animals and vegetables are not only far superior to *metals in their lightness*, but they also excel in *humidity*. Subterranean things, on the contrary, are more *fixed* and less humid; therefore, they are more enduring of *fire*. Just as in the *stars and celestial phenomena* <term>meteoris: referring to all atmospheric phenomena, such as clouds and lightning, not just shooting stars</term>, as well as in animals and vegetables, various degrees of these qualities are given, from which different species arise; so too, who would doubt that similar diversities exist in subterranean things? For experience alone and eyewitness observation <term>autopsia: seeing for oneself</term> lead us to this and convince us. 

Why then would this class of products have any other reason for its different species than the other two kingdoms—namely, by differing in density and humidity? But there is also much difference within the very principles of the mixtures themselves, though from the same cause. For that which serves as the base is *drier*; that which thickens and binds is *more humid*; and that which shapes is *more subtle*. This we see exactly in the generation of man and animals. For in the seed, when it begins its action in the womb, before all else, the first part settles and forms a clot; this is the driest part, namely that substance which provides the material for the *bones*, to which the remaining parts for the nerves, flesh, and blood are bound. Meanwhile, a more subtle part remains and operates, which is so delicate that if it is agitated by the mother’s imagination <note>original: "phantasia matris"; the early modern medical belief that a mother's thoughts or fears could physically mark the fetus</note> alone and thinned out beyond its proper order, it immediately errs in its operation and imprints various birthmarks <note>original: "nævos"</note> upon the offspring. We see the same in vegetables, where above all the *root and the stalk* grow...

He explains that all matter originates from a primal mixture through a process of boiling and separation, with differences between species determined by their varying levels of density and humidity.</summary>

# Book I. Section III. Chapter III.

...then the fruit, and finally the seed, specifically when the entire product matures. From this, it necessarily follows that there are distinct parts of the seed: one drier, another more moist; one more fixed, another more volatile—just as effects (that is, physical bodies) teach us. For some of their parts are colder, others drier; some hotter, others more moist, porous, dense, fixed, or volatile. For in animals, flesh is moister than bones; and in vegetables, fruits are generally more succulent than wood. Who, then, would deny that the same occurs in fossils <note>In the 17th century, "fossils" referred to anything dug out of the ground, including minerals and ores</note>, as we learn from experience? For lead has more *moisture than copper; tin has more fluidity than silver.* It is therefore entirely rational and probable that in the very first mixture of minerals—namely, in their *principles*—there are various mixtures, degrees of these mixtures, and different arrangements of these degrees. Moreover, it is absurd to suggest that so many diverse operations could arise from a single subject without some change or addition occurring. Hence, we must rightly conclude that the 

<margin>No. 7.</margin>
principles and parts of mixtures do not proceed from one thing, but from various ingredients. And since there are three physical constitutions of all bodies—namely, having a *hypostasis* <term>hypostasis: the underlying substance or essence</term>, a *covering of the hypostasis*, and a *form of the covering*—who can deny that such things also apply to minerals? The *hypostasis* of animals contains the *bones*, and of vegetables, the *wood*; the *covering of the hypostasis* in animals is the *flesh and blood*, and in vegetables, the *pulp and fruit*; the *form of the covering* in animals and vegetables consists of their various *shapes* as well as their qualities. Likewise, the *hypostasis* of minerals is the *fluid earth* <note>original: "terra fluida"; Becher's first principle, associated with weight and density</note>; the *covering of the hypostasis* is the *coalescing fatty earth* <note>original: "pinguis terra"; Becher's second principle, the source of inflammability</note>; and the *form of the hypostasis* is *gravity and malleability*, or the *mercurial earth* <note>original: "terra mercurialis"; Becher's third principle, providing metallic luster and fluidity</note>, which provides the "metallic-ness" <note>original: "metalleitatem"</note>. I know indeed, that I do 

<margin>No. 8.</margin>
not philosophize according to the mind of Aristotle or Paracelsus. The former <note>Aristotle</note> thrust upon us some unknown *form and matter* in name only, attributing the essence of all things to them; yet that which truly is and exists, he calls "mere accidents," contrary to all reason and experience. The latter <note>Paracelsus</note> persuades the world of three principles of things <note>Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury</note>, which are actually bodies—not simple ones, but decomposed—as we demonstrated more fully at the beginning of this Section regarding the certainty of metallic principles. It is enough for us, even if we do not speak or write through the mouths of others like a "wooden puppet moved by another's sinews" <note>original: "nervis alienis mobile lignum"; a reference to Horace, describing one who lacks independent thought</note>, and do not swear by the words of a Master, that we have nevertheless philosophized according to experience and truth. He who delights in words may seek words and chimeras; we write *practically and for practitioners*. In this method, one must heed the proverb: *it is one thing to say, another to do*, as the truth of the matter itself proves. For the entire Philosophy of Aristotle, along with its author and all his supporting Philosophasters <note>pretenders to philosophy</note>, could never, through a priori reasoning or speculation, have discovered *that silver is dissolved in strong water* <term>aqua forti: nitric acid</term>; *that it is precipitated by copper, common salt, salt of tartar, or urine—and indeed that it achieves different operations in different ways due to the diversity of these precipitants; and that the precipitated lime of silver* <note>original: "calx argenti"; the residue left after heating or chemical treatment</note>*, if not yet reduced back into a metallic body, can no longer be dissolved in strong water, etc.* On the other hand, it would have been desirable either for Paracelsus to have remained entirely silent, or to have explained his doctrine of principles more infallibly, so that by raging against everyone else while demonstrating nothing, he might not have branded the whole of Chemistry <note>original: "Chymiæ"</note> with a damnable stigma. But to return to our circle,

<margin>No. 16.</margin>
There is a city where, for reasons I do not know, the Master of the Mint was entangled in many various debts, owing several thousand florins, so that he was reduced to utter desperation and narrowly escaped imprisonment. Placed in these hardships, he anxiously prayed to God that He might deign to help him by some extraordinary means, since no hope remained in ordinary ones. He then began to dissolve silver <note>original: "lunam solvere"; alchemists used "Luna" (the Moon) to represent silver</note> in the aqua fortis, and an *eighth part* fell out as a black powder. Suspecting that the aqua fortis had not been sufficiently purified, he tested it again with new silver, but the same thing happened. He tried another batch of aqua fortis not made with this specific vitriol, and an entire mark <note>a unit of weight, about 250 grams</note> of silver contained scarcely *half a drachm* of gold. Thus entangled in new worries, he feared the entire batch of aqua fortis was ruined and worthless. He suspected the black powder was merely *dregs*, for he did not dare hope for such great fortune. At last, as is the custom, after the aqua fortis was poured off and the residue was washed and heated to a glow, he found it to be *pure gold*. Giving thanks to God and keeping silent, he did nothing but dissolve silver with that aqua fortis. He confessed to a private friend that from the aforementioned ten hundredweights of vitriol and the aqua fortis prepared from it, he had gained 10,000 ducats <note>gold coins</note>. With these, he not only paid all his debts but returned to his former prosperity. However, once that vitriol ran out, he could never replicate the result, even though he traveled to Hungary specifically to find what species of vitriol it had been.

For when it exists as the most remote principle of metals, it is a **vapor** <note>original: "fumus"; literally "smoke," but in 17th-century chemistry, it refers to a subtle, gaseous substance or exhalation</note>, as we shall teach later. But when it is a secondary principle, even most closely disposed and formed into a beginning, it is not infrequently found beneath the earth in the guise of sulfur, arsenic, realgar, silt, and other subterranean substances. For this reason, it is called by some the **first being** <note>original: "primum ens"; the primordial or essential state of a substance before it becomes a specific metal</note>, specifically of a metal.

<margin>No. 19.</margin>
Nor does it exist only in an earthy form; it is also found abundantly in waters. These are sometimes tinted by a thin film of various colors, which some call **foliated earth** <note>original: "terram foliatam"; referring to its appearance in thin, leaf-like layers or scales</note> due to its appearance; above all, the **first being of Mars** <note>original: "primum ens Martis"; Mars is the alchemical name for iron</note> is found in this way. We have also seen films of silver, tin, and gold, either in waters prepared by art for the purpose of **mercurification** <note>the process of reducing a metal to its essential liquid "mercury"</note>, yet with such elegance, variety, and patterns that no painter could imitate them. Indeed, they possess such power of extension that a single drop of our **oil** (for metals must be reduced to oil for this operation) tinted a three-foot diameter of the water's surface and covered it as if with a **single leaf** <note>original: "uno folio"</note>. Thus, one might believe the entire water to be pure tincture, or gold and silver. It is truly a more pleasant sight than if one were to drink a thousand cups.

<margin>No. 20.</margin>
Therefore, when our earth is drenched in much water, it liquefies and dissipates; but when it contains a small amount of moisture, it flows like wax, especially in the older crevices of mines, commonly called **Zäcken** <note>a German mining term for mineral-filled veins or cavities</note>. For since (as was demonstrated before) the **former earth**—namely the matrix of minerals—has been cut away, the remaining two vapors or earths cannot be received and fixed. Nevertheless, whether individually or joined together, they seek various locations, and having nothing to which they may adhere, they persist as **fluores** <note>original: "fluores"; minerals that flow or melt easily, the root of the modern "fluorspar"</note>. It is certain, and experience teaches, that these are sometimes coagulated when a stone-making vapor (the **first earth**) arrives. This metallic flow of ours, or **unctuous earth**, now disposed very closely to the generation of metals, the miners call **mountain guhr** <note>original: "die Bergguhr"; a gelatinous, white mineral substance found in damp mines, once thought to be the "embryo" of metals</note>, as if they were saying the **ferment of metals**. Indeed, concerning this unctuous liquor which sweats and drips in older caves and from the stones themselves, we have examples and experiences of it dripping onto the wooden beams (which support the subterranean caverns and are called **Stämpfel** <note>mine props or timbers</note> by miners) and there becoming pure, refined **branching silver** <note>original: "argentum ramosum"; native silver that grows in moss-like or tree-like structures</note>, as direct observation proves. This is a demonstration by no means to be looked down upon. Our earth performs no less wonderful operations when it wanders in the form of a vapor, which some miners call **inhalations** <note>original: "Einwitterungen"; referring to the "weathering" or gaseous influence within a mine</note>.

<margin>No. 21.</margin>
For when it is alone, it is especially healthy for the lungs; but where it is mixed with the following vapor, its companion, it is poisonous and is called **choke-damp** <note>original: "Schwaden"; dangerous, suffocating gases encountered in mining</note>, as will be said shortly. In this place, we shall treat it insofar as it is found alone; there, it sometimes spontaneously causes the sweetest flames in the mines; indeed, it sometimes heats the caves so much that they seem like steam-baths, driving out the miners. Above all, it is worthy of consideration that this vapor penetrates all stones, even the densest, with their substance unharmed but not unchanged; and there, in their midst, it is found as metal or sulfur (for no metal is without sulfur,

<margin>No. 22.</margin>
and nothing is more associated with metals and acts upon them than sulfur, as [will be shown] later...
