### Subterranean Physics

(as will be demonstrated more extensively where we deal specifically with sulfur.) We said a little earlier that stony substance is altered by this earth; for it is tinted and penetrated by it, as has already been stated. No one should wonder at this; for although it may seem marvelous that a magnet penetrates glass even while their substance remains unharmed, such wonder will easily cease if we consider that the most compact metals, even gold itself, do the same. For we know of an experiment, which we have performed more than once, by which we rendered gold—by means of this earth—so penetrating that 

<margin>No. 23.</margin>
*it penetrated a thick glass retort, and created a reddish, transparent film* <note>original: "cuticulam"; literally a "little skin" or thin layer</note> *on the outside around the entire retort*, while the retort itself remained completely intact, not tinted at all on the inside, but similar to itself in every way. We still keep fragments of this retort with us. For we melted down the greater part of the retort to see what could be expected from the union and mixture; we received, however, a *semi-opaque blue glass, like an opal*, marked here and there with *blood-red and intensely dark-red streaks*. We noticed no reduction of the gold <note>meaning the gold did not return to its metallic form after the glass was melted</note>. We then entered into the same process with silver and copper, and saw the same effect, though with different colors. From this, not only is the penetrating power of *this earth* defended, but also its great **magnetism** <note>In 17th-century chemistry, "magnetism" refers to a natural attraction or affinity between different substances</note> with stones and glass is proven.

<margin>No. 24.</margin>
This is also proven by all metals that easily pass into glasses. Although there are some who ascribe this glassiness not to the metals, but to the **crucibles** <note>original: "tigillis"; the heat-resistant pots used for melting metals</note>, a part of which joins with the metal and turns to glass, it is nevertheless irrefutable that metals—even in this way—willingly turn to stone and can hide in great quantity under the mask of stone or glass, as we see in the **glass of Saturn** <note>original: "vitro Saturni"; Saturn is the alchemical name for lead. Lead glass (crystal) was a major technological discovery of this era</note>. The **expansion** of this earth, and of the metals themselves, within glass is also astounding. For we have observed that *one grain of metal notably tints five hundred grains of glass.* Even if we do not deny that lead glass scrapes off something from the crucible and turns to glass in this way (which is sufficient for us to defend the "magnetism" and compatibility of metal and glass), we have nonetheless observed that **tin** <note>original: "stannum"</note> *turns entirely into glass by its own substance, with nothing added, not even the scraping of the crucible.* For just as the glass of lead penetrates and perforates crucibles by dissolving them, so this *glass of tin*, since it scrapes nothing from the crucible but acquires its glassiness from its own nature, never dissolves or perforates the crucibles in which it sits. It can be kept in flux and in the fire for a long time without harming the vessels that contain it. By this experiment, those are also confounded who deny that *ashes of tin* <note>tin calx or oxide</note> *can be reduced back into a metallic body.* But let us return to our goal, where it seems this also should not be passed over: that *this fatty earth of ours (the mineral principle)*, besides its fatness, flammability, oiliness, and many other properties 

<margin>No. 25.</margin>
which it holds in common with the oils of **animals and vegetables**, also has this **analogy** with them: just as our mineral earth tints the former [glass], so the other two in animals and vegetables have the same operation as ours. For it is most certain that the **sulfur of coals tints glass**, and indeed so strongly that the color can hardly be expelled even by a great fire. We once made an elegant **Emerald** by the help of prepared **human blood**. From these things it is clear that there is a great analogy between these three earths <note>mineral, vegetable, and animal</note>, and each one proves the certainty and qualities of the other;

### Book I, Section III, Chapter III. 75

<margin>No. 26.</margin> Now let us come to the second class of differences of this our earth, which we said consists in *rarity and density*. From these, in the first place, various *effects of colors* follow, especially according to the diversity of the substances mixed in. For gold, when dissolved in aqua regis <note>original: "aqua regis," or "royal water," a mixture of nitric and hydrochloric acids capable of dissolving gold</note>, produces a red color, yet it tints *glass green*. Conversely, silver in aqua fortis <note>original: "aqua forti," or nitric acid</note> exhibits a *blue* color, but shows a *yellow* color in glass. Indeed, many colors arise from refraction, as we see in *spirit of urine* <note>ammonia solution</note>, which, when poured over aqua fortis, exhibits the color of amethyst. Copper in its own substance is red, but it *turns green* in vinegar, and when spirit of urine is poured over it, it is tinted with a *cyan* <note>original: "Cyaneo," a deep blue-green</note> color, which entirely vanishes when spirit of salt <note>original: "spiritu salis," or hydrochloric acid</note> is added. Likewise, spirit of turpentine always undergoes a reaction of *a single color* when placed over metals. Spirit of wine <note>alcohol</note> turns red over any alkali. I say nothing of many other colors that arise from chemical reactions. For the purpose of establishing our thesis, let it suffice that the *colors of metals proceed from the aforementioned earth* <note>the "second earth" or terra pinguis</note>; and they differ only by reaction, dilution, rarity, and refraction. For if this were not so, no transmutation of colors would be possible, which is contrary to experience. Indeed, metals can be *essentially tinted* so that they cannot recover their original color. We must distinguish, however, between colors that arise from simple mixing—such as when *red lead* <note>original: "minium"</note> is mixed with *chalk*—and colors that proceed from rarefaction and condensation. We see this happen in fire, where many things turn red by the action of the flame <note>original: "reverberatione"</note> alone. We see such colors imprinted by the help of fire not only upon *lead, iron, and tin*, but there is also no doubt that the colors of flowers among vegetables are altered and perfected by the power of the *Sun*, as was sufficiently demonstrated in the third part of our *Metallurgy* cited above.

These things are indeed to be understood regarding that rarefaction which occurs through heat, to which all metals and fossils are subject. However, the primordial rarefaction of our earth into various colors—as seen in gold, silver, sapphire, copper, emerald, and other <margin>No. 27.</margin> subterranean things—does not proceed from heat, but from the admixture of the *third earth*. This is the third principle of minerals, which was mixed with the second earth in a certain degree during the first order of production. By this third earth, the substance is diluted or saturated, and reduced to transparency or opacity, as we see in stones and metals. Although I do not deny that transparency is to be attributed to the *first* earth <note>the "stony" or "vitrifiable" earth</note>, by which the second is diluted, I nevertheless maintain that opacity arises from the *third* earth, which we are now about to discuss. And although we will later conclude that this following *third* earth is not present in stones (even though we often see them as opaque), our words should not be taken so strictly as to deny that stones possess *something analogous* to the third earth. We conclude here, therefore, the *second principle of subterranean things*, about which more will be said in the following pages; and we shall hasten to the *third and final mineral principle*, which we shall also briefly explain.

For the sake of establishing this thesis, let it suffice for us that *the colors of metals proceed from the aforementioned earth*; and they differ only by reaction, dilution, rarity, and refraction. For unless this were the case, no transmutation of colors would be possible, which is contrary to experience. For metals can be *essentially tinted*; so that they cannot recover their former color. However, a distinction must be made between colors that arise from mixture—as when <term>red lead</term> <note>original: "minium"</note> is mixed with <term>chalk</term> <note>original: "cretae"</note>—and between colors that proceed from rarefaction and condensation, as we see happen in fire, where many things turn red by <term>reverberation</term> <note>The process of reflecting heat or flame onto a substance in a furnace.</note> alone. And it is not only colors that we see imprinted by the help of fire upon lead, iron, and tin; but there is no doubt that the colors of flowers among vegetables are altered and perfected by the help of the *Sun*, as was sufficiently demonstrated in the third part of our *Metallurgy* cited above. And these things are indeed to be understood concerning that rarefaction which occurs through heat, to which all metals and <term>minerals</term> <note>original: "fossilia"; in this period, the term referred to anything "dug up" from the earth.</note> are subject. But the primordial rarefaction of our earth into various colors—as in gold, ruby, silver, sapphire, copper, emerald, and other

<margin>No. 27</margin>
subterranean things—does not proceed from heat, but from the admixed *third earth*, namely the third principle of minerals: which is mixed into the second earth in a certain degree, by the order of the first production, by which it is as if diluted or saturated, and reduced into transparency or opacity, as we see in stones and metals. Although I do not deny that transparency is to be attributed to the *first earth*, by which the second is diluted; I nevertheless maintain that opacity arises from the *third earth*, which we are now about to discuss. And although we shall later conclude that the following *third earth* is not present in stones, though we meanwhile not infrequently see them as opaque; yet our words are not to be taken so strictly that they do not grant to stones *something analogous* to the third earth. Therefore, we conclude in this place the *second principle of subterranean things*, about which more will be said in what follows; and we shall hasten to the *third and final principle of minerals*, which we shall also explain in a few words.

### Section Three, Chapter Four
# Concerning the third principle of minerals, which is fluid earth, improperly called Mercury.

->S Y N O P S I S.<-

*No. 1. The probability of a third earth. No. 2. An analogous earth in vegetables and animals. No. 3. The existence of this earth in stones, and specifically in Jasper. No. 4. It is improperly called Mercury. No. 5. It renders metals fluid and mercurial. No. 6. This same earth is fixed along with the two prior principles. No. 7. <margin>No. 1.</margin> That there exists a certain third thing, which intermingles itself with the two prior principles and from which they obtain their specific form, is not only likely but most certain. For as we proceed to the origin of subterranean things—as will be demonstrated below—stones, and especially all transparent ones, consist of the first and second earth; but in the opaque ones, a certain third earth is intermixed, from which comes the "idea" <note>The essential formative principle or blueprint of a substance.</note> of their species, namely *stoniness*. It cannot be denied, therefore, that a similar principle is given in metals, yet one *different* from the former; for the being of metals is distinct from the substance of stones; namely, being of a malleable and extensible nature—in short, that in which "metallicity" consists. This property specifically arises from this third principle, as we shall demonstrate more extensively hereafter.

<margin>No. 2.</margin> Furthermore, we find a substance analogous to this in *vegetables and animals*. In vegetables, indeed, which when they are <term>calcined</term> <note>Burned to ash or reduced to powder by heat.</note>, not only exhibit salts of different shapes, but their <term>volatile salts</term> <note>Salts that evaporate or sublimate easily, such as ammonium carbonate.</note> sometimes express the original "idea" of the plant: as can be seen in *wormwood* and *fir* wood. But above all, it would be desirable if <term>Quercetanus</term> <note>Joseph Duchesne (c. 1544–1609), a prominent Paracelsian physician and chemist.</note> and others, who profess to know the mystery of resurrection—that is, the regeneration of flowers <note>Referencing "palingenesis," the alchemical attempt to make a plant's ghost-like image appear from its ashes.</note>—had more clearly explained this noble manual operation to the world; for the reasons for many things could then be resolved and traced back. In *animals*, their volatile salts come before our eyes more frequently, especially from *hartshorn*, which exhibits its "idea" most clearly. We also read in the dissertation of the most noble <term>Digby</term> <note>Sir Kenelm Digby (1603–1665), an English courtier and natural philosopher.</note> concerning vegetables, that he burned crabs, and from the ashes, with their own liquor...

<margin>No. 3.</margin>
It was my intention to melt **Jasper** <note>A dense, opaque variety of silica, usually red, yellow, or brown.</note> in a crucible for a certain purpose, which I indeed achieved by applying the necessary requirements and a **most powerful fire**. However, so that the pieces would not fall into the embers of the hearth, I covered the crucible—which was filled about halfway with jasper—with a lid, sealing the joints somewhat with clay. When the melting was finished and the crucible had cooled, I opened it, and behold, a sight truly incredible: for at the bottom, the jasper had united through melting into one solid mass, preserving its original hardness, but entirely **milky** in color and semi-opaque, resembling the most natural **white agate**. Yet the upper parts, which had been empty in the small crucible—namely the lid and the sides of the vessel (which the jasper could in no way have touched during the melting process)—were so tinted with the natural color of jasper that, if they had possessed the hardness and if the color had not been merely superficial, these fragments of the crucible could have been sold as the most elegant and polished **Jasper**. Indeed, they were scattered here and there with greenish streaks and spots, while the rest appeared red and yellow, with these colors so pleasantly mixed that a painter could hardly have imitated them; they even turned out more beautiful than the Jasper I had originally used. I keep these fragments in my Chemical Archive as a **chemical miracle**. Therefore, let no one doubt that these upper parts were tinted by the "soul" of the **Jasper**, which was driven out of its lower body by the powerful fire and adhered to the body of the crucible; especially one who sees the pieces of the crucible tinted in this way with their own eyes. For they could not be prepared this way by any dye, deception, or art, unless Nature herself had worked so. Convinced by this argument, I necessarily conclude that there lies hidden in things a certain immortal **form** that preserves its own characteristic; and that this is a **subtle earth** will be proven shortly.

<margin>No. 4.</margin>
For although some of the Chemists call it **Mercury**, if you understand this literally, it is false—either that **Mercury** <note>In this context, the author refers to "Quick-silver" or the metal mercury.</note> actually exists within bodies (as will be proven later), or, if it does exist, that it is a "principle," since a mixture is a mere **composite**, which contradicts the simplicity and unity of a **principle**, the definition of which is to be a simple, homogeneous, and unique thing. It is more appropriate, therefore, to conclude that this earth is called **Mercury** because of its **mercurial quality**—namely, its volatility—as we have proven in our *Chemical Oedipus* <note>original: "Oedipo Chymico"; referring to Becher's own 1663 work, *Oedipus Chymicus*, which sought to "solve the riddles" of alchemy.</note>.

<margin>No. 5.</margin>
Furthermore, it is because it enters into the mixture of common **Mercury**, as will be proven later: namely, that if this earth enters into metals beyond the proper proportion, they become entirely fluid and volatile. This happened to us once when we mixed more of this earth than was right with a portion of **Luna** <note>The alchemical name for silver.</note> (refined silver). When we were about to separate it again by means of distillation through a gourd and an alembic <note>A two-part distilling apparatus; the gourd (cucurbit) holds the liquid, and the alembic is the cap with a "beak" for runoff.</note>, the earth adhered to the silver so firmly that it carried some part of the silver with it through the alembic and the beak of the alembic into the receiving vessel—which was also a small gourd (commonly called a **separating flask** <note>original: "Scheidkoelbel"; a German term for a glass vessel used in the separation of substances.</note>). In all its qualities, it became a living and running silver, no longer changeable back into silver in any way, nor separable from its earth, except by fixation and the help of heat. We learned this because, owing to the shortness of the alembic’s beak, we moved the aforementioned receiving vessel closer to the furnace...

<margin>No. 6.</margin>
But regarding **Mercurifications** <note>Processes used to extract or create the "mercurial" essence of a substance.</note> and the **differences between Mercuries**, we shall treat these more particularly below, in a special chapter on Mercury. In this place, however, it must not be overlooked that the aforementioned earth **essentially grows into metals**; for it adheres when fixed and provides an increase that withstands fire, and it passes all tests according to the diversity of the metal with which it is joined: as we have learned this specifically in **gold** and **silver**. But a small amount of earth gives only a small amount of increase; and it is small indeed, since from a hundred pounds of the subject matter from which it is prepared, I believe scarcely a few ounces can be elicited. Thus, that saying of **Esdras** <note>Referring to the apocryphal book 2 Esdras 8:2, which uses the analogy of many seeds but little gold-dust.</note> fits it well: *a little dust, from which gold is made* <note>original: "parvum pulverem, unde aurum fit"</note>. Truly, enough concerning this earth for now. Now we must return to our circle and consider by what different degrees of rarity and density this earth differs, and what various qualities follow from this difference; for it is one thing in **animals**, another in **vegetables**, another in **stones**, and yet another in **metals**.

But even in these it is diverse, both in purity and perfection, and is more thoroughly cooked by digestion, as will be seen more widely in the below-cited chapter on Mercury.

<margin>N. 7.</margin>
It must also be considered that there is a great diversity within this earth; for insofar as it is either a remote or a proximate principle—that is, matter already disposed to the act of growth and mixing—in short, it undergoes the same vicissitudes as the previous two earths. However it is disposed, it is **far more volatile than the former ones**.

<margin>N. 8.</margin>
For, since its office is to form and penetrate, and to impose upon things a sort of leaf-like quality and metallicity, and to make them opaque, it is necessary that it be highly penetrable.

Accordingly, also, insofar as it was disposed by the Creator for the mixture of subterranean things, it exists as a most penetrating force; for it penetrates stones, rocks, and all the hardest bodies. Sometimes it does so with such violence that it thins and dilates the very flames of lamps; which is a sign to the miners that, unless they withdraw as quickly as they can, they will all be suffocated by this smoke. This is indeed to be understood when, having already joined with the "second earth," it pervades the channels of the ores; for then it is sulfurous and is called **mine-damp** <note>original: "Bergſchwaden"—a German mining term for窒息 choke-damp or toxic vapors found in mines.</note>. But when left in its own purity, it is not indeed so violent, but much more dangerous and poisonous. For from this come the diseases of miners, namely **wasting** <note>original: "tabes"</note>, **hectic fever** <note>original: "hectica"</note>, **consumption** <note>original: "phthiſis"</note>, and **paralysis**: for it dissolves most powerfully, which we see even in common Mercury, in which not even a **thousandth** part of this earth is present (the rest consisting of metal); nevertheless, it affects not only the nerves in animals, but even the hard...

### Book 1. Section III. Chapter IV. 79

it resolves and penetrates the hardest woods, the most compact metals, and glass. So much so that **Mercury of Antimony**, as *Digby* <note>original: "Dygbæo"; referring to Sir Kenelm Digby (1603–1665), an English diplomat and natural philosopher.</note> testifies (for although we prepared the same Mercury ourselves, and during its preparation we suffered a dangerous, corrosive <term>catarrh: historically, an inflammation of the mucus membranes, here caused by inhaling toxic fumes</term>, we did not perform the following experiment because it did not occur to us at the time, and we had meanwhile used the Mercury for other purposes), it is said to be so penetrating that a gold coin—commonly called a ducat—held in the mouth will be whitened as if it were coated with mercury, simply by dipping one's **big toe** into the Mercury of Antimony. From this, it can easily be gathered how penetrating the *earth* itself must be if it exists in a pure state, since the compounds derived from it are so piercing. For this reason, it is by no means to be 

<margin>No. 9.</margin>
doubted that the liquor **Alkaest** <note>The universal solvent, a substance theorized by Paracelsus and Van Helmont capable of reducing all bodies to their "prime matter."</note>, which is *such a pure earth*, easily penetrates all things and is the most penetrating of all; a fact we experienced once, not without danger to life and loss of health, when we rather incautiously moved the aforementioned liquor toward our nostrils: for we nearly died of a sudden death, with all our senses abolished as if in a moment. How much damage it also brings to the **chest and eyes** cannot be put into words. For this reason, we cannot comprehend how *Paracelsus* could recommend this liquor for the liver, since, as it is, it simply cannot be taken into the human body. It is therefore credible that if *Paracelsus* wrote the truth, he dissolved a certain **stegnotic** <note>original: "stegnoticum"; a medicine that is astringent or "binding," used to stop discharges.</note> in the aforementioned liquor, and then administered the dissolved substance, *not the solvent*, to people. For the aforementioned liquor is of incredible penetration, and can be driven to such an excellence of piercing that it penetrates all vessels, even glass itself, **without any rupture or injury**, like a leaf that passes through glass yet does not harm it. 

<margin>No. 10.</margin>
This liquor therefore has a great analogy with **spirit of wine** <note>ethanol or concentrated alcohol</note> and **aqua fortis** <note>nitric acid</note>; in which **solvents** <note>original: "menstruis"</note> various bodies are dissolved into the thinnest substances. However, our liquor differs from all other solvents in that these other solvents dissolve by creating a **reaction and association** of the solute with the solvent; hence, the dissolved substance must be separated from the solvent by precipitants, which create a new **reaction** in the non-solvents. But our liquor dissolves in no other way than by 

<margin>No. 11.</margin>
**penetrating** and reducing bodies into the thinnest atoms; which, since they are affected by our liquor with no **reaction**, sink down once penetrated, being torn into the various substances of which the mixture consists. No **foreign** substances are added, which usually happen in common solutions due to a **reaction**. Hence, all things dissolved in the liquor **Alkaest** retain their entire powers and qualities; this settling, however, differs from precipitation in that the latter, as we said, proceeds through reagents, while the former proceeds of its own accord and from the **nature of its own weight**: with the thinner parts staying above and the thicker ones below. It is no different than if liquors of different weights were mixed together, and each were to occupy the place of its own weight: or if **oil, flour, and sand** were mixed and dissolved in water; for each of these would keep the natural place of its own weight. Therefore, the solution that is made by the liquor **Alkaest** is nothing other than the penetration of a body and its reduction into the finest atoms, without any **reaction** or communication with the solute, so that its parts can settle freely, while their mass remains intact. Hence, from this solution—namely from the effect and the parts of the body dissolved in this liquor—not a few things can be learned. It is therefore a wonder why some have compared this liquor with fire; since all things that are dissolved by fire are not only into diverse...

substances are carried away, altered in their temperament, even transformed. Secondly, fire—as we shall prove later in the chapter on sulfur—acts only superficially on physical bodies; our liquor, however, penetrates the finest pores, leaving everything unchanged except regarding its continuity. For the solution that is made by the liquor **Alkaest** is nothing other than a **dissolution of continuity** <note>original: "solutio continui"; a term in physics and alchemy referring to the breaking down of a solid substance into its constituent parts without changing its chemical nature.</note>, or a species of continuous solution, which we treated in our *Chymical Oedipus* <note>original: "Oedipo Chymico"; referring to Becher’s own work, *Oedipus Chymicus* (1664), which attempted to "solve the riddles" of chemistry.</note>. It is unable to be combined with any mixture, and thus remains always **immutable**. For since, as was said before, it consists of the "third earth" of the mineral kingdom, it follows that this earth is far stronger and more penetrating than the other two earths (namely those of the animal and vegetable kingdoms), even if they are analogous to it. Because of its incredible thinness and its greater degree of digestion, it cannot be combined with those aforementioned analogous earths. Just as **spirit of wine** <term>spirit of wine: archaic term for concentrated ethanol or alcohol</term> does not truly combine with **water**, because they can be separated from each other again. 

However, just as **spirit of wine** poured into a large quantity of water is deprived of its thinness and becomes thickened, so it happens to our liquor: **for it is overcome by its own match.** For by common **water**, it is itself **resolved into tasteless water**. Since **it is not corrosive at all**—because it is not a salt or a mixture, even if it is the <gloss>first being</gloss> of salts—its sole power lies in this: that its most penetrating earthy atoms act as if united, not by burning or corroding. It follows, then, that all the energy of this liquor perishes when its particles are **diffused**, and by that very diffusion they are rendered tasteless and useless. I know of **no means at all** to separate them from the water again; they adhere most powerfully to the atoms of water because of their great similarity. 

Nor should the reader wonder that this liquor of ours is overcome by common water and remains as tasteless water. We could show the preparation of a certain water which is altogether **tasteless**, yet meanwhile of astounding operation; were it not that communicating it (which could do much good) would simultaneously carry the greatest disadvantages, because of the most dangerous and almost inevitable **poison** that can be prepared from it, which would give wicked men an opportunity for doing harm. I must therefore remain silent, lest, while wishing to benefit the good, I aid the wicked. 

Furthermore, as has been said, our liquor does not combine with animal or vegetable mixtures; so, on the other hand, it must be admitted that as the principle of minerals, it adheres somewhat more tenaciously to their mixtures, namely metals, specifically **gold** and **silver**—and indeed, more to **perfect** metals than to those that are less perfect. For since imperfect metals (which are indeed perfectly complete according to their own mixture and temperament, and are only called "imperfect" in relation to **gold and silver**) contain much of that earth from which this very liquor is made, it follows that they are not torn apart into such diverse substances, being of a more porous framework that is more easily penetrated. But **gold**, since it consists (as we shall later demonstrate) of a triple earth in equal parts and is most compact, gives our liquor much work, and hence the liquor adheres to it more tenaciously: so much so, in fact, that it carries the gold up with it during distillation in the form of a **scarlet liquor**.

This earth is prepared from **spirit of wine**, once the sulfurous parts have been separated, just as our mineral earth is...

Book I. Section III. Chapter IV. 81

about which we are now speaking, or (if you wish to begin from the end <note>original: "a posteriori"; reasoning from effects back to causes.</note>) it may be obtained from common mercury—namely, by separating the **quicksilver** <note>original: "argentum vivum"</note> in such a way that the metallic parts are set aside, and the earth, through which the aforementioned parts were held in a fluid state, is drawn away. Or (if you begin the process from the beginning <note>original: "a priori"; reasoning from causes to effects.</note>), it must be taken from that principle which abounds in ores, and which creates "mercuries" out of metals, entirely without any artifice, and indeed in great abundance. We have an example of this in certain places in the form of **virgin mercury** <note>original: "Mercurio virgineo"; mercury found in its pure, liquid state in nature, rather than smelted from ore.</note>, which flows spontaneously from the mines. <margin>N. 13.</margin> This earth, however, is masked under the appearance of either water or smoke; it sometimes clings to the walls of the mines like thin filaments, or like snow, or the "flowers" of saltpeter <note>original: "nitri florum"; referring to the crusty, crystalline efflorescence found on damp walls.</note>, possessing the luster of pearls. It is believed by some to be the principle of arsenic. I myself have seen it in the mines, but I have forgotten the name by which the **miners** <note>original: "Metallicolæ"</note> commonly call it in their local tongue. Furthermore, what need is there to seek it in the mines, when there are mineral waters in which it is contained? Indeed, as will be proven later in the second book, in the chapter on **Salt**, the entire sea is full of it, for it is the **first essence of salt** <note>original: "primum ens salis"</note>, or that earth from which salt is made. You should know that it is more easily and abundantly separable from one subject than from another. 

A distinction must also be made between the liquor **Alkaest** <term>Alkaest: a hypothetical universal solvent capable of reducing any body to its primary matter.</term> and the **Mercury of the Philosophers**; lest, while you seek the one, you accidentally create the other. Although such an error might not be unpleasant, it would nevertheless be harmful with respect to your goal; for when I am traveling toward Rome, I must leave Venice behind, even if both cities are beautiful. <margin>N. 14.</margin> Therefore, the **Mercury of the Philosophers** differs from the liquor **Alkaest** (or this, our "third earth") in this: the Mercury of the Philosophers consists of this third earth of ours combined with the second earth <note>The "second earth" in Becher's system is the "fatty earth" (terra pinguis), associated with sulfur and inflammability.</note>, as if from two principles of minerals already prepared for the act of mixing. Namely, it is made from the earth of sulfur and the earth of mercury of the purest quality, which is why it is usually called **doubled Mercury**: "doubled" because of the two earths, and "Mercury" because of the volatility of both. This must be fixed by the operation of fire and afterward fermented with **gold**, which serves as the "first earth" or the **womb** <note>original: "matrice"</note>—that is, the stone—of which we spoke in the second chapter. The **Alkaest**, however, consists of only a single earth, specifically the one we have just discussed; for this reason, it does not possess a primordial and essential transformative power over metals on its own, except that it softens them, "mercurifies" them <note>Turns them into a mercury-like liquid state.</note>, and, if too much is used, tears them apart into various different substances. <margin>N. 15.</margin> But due to the lack of the second principle—namely, the second earth, from which the aforementioned Mercury of the Philosophers is also composed—it cannot induce new metamorphoses in metals; though it may sometimes separate a significant amount of gold and silver from them. 

For since, as was said above, it reduces metals into the smallest atoms, the heavier ones (which are mostly gold and silver) easily settle to the bottom. Consequently, this improvement of metals should be called nothing other than **subsidence** <note>original: "subsidentia"; a physical settling or precipitation.</note> resulting from the solution; because the atoms of the metals have been penetrated and thinned more powerfully than by any other solvent. Because of this, a metal dissolved in this manner is reduced back to its solid state only with great difficulty. We see almost the same effects, though not of such excellence, in **nitric acid** <note>original: "aqua forti"</note>; metals dissolved in it always yield more gold than when tested by fire or common assaying. Indeed, silver digested in nitric acid daily casts down a small amount of gold **calx** <note>original: "calcis auri"; a powdered residue or oxide.</note>, which comes from the finer solution of the mixture. Furthermore, there are solvents which carry metals over an **alembic** <term>alembic: a type of still used for distillation.</term> like **spirit of wine** <note>original: "spiritus vini"; concentrated alcohol.</note>, which can hardly be precipitated except with great labor. <margin>N. 16.</margin> All of which...

# Subterranean Physics

### Book I, Section III, Chapter IV (Continued)

...prove the truth of the **Alkaest** <note>original: "liquoris Alkaest"; the hypothetical universal solvent sought by alchemists, capable of reducing any body to its primary matter.</note> liquor. At this point, we could also substitute an analogous and very closely related **solvent** <note>original: "menstruum"; a term used in alchemy for a substance that dissolves others.</note> in place of the **Alkaest**, which is easier to prepare—just as it could also take the place of the "Solvent of the Philosophers" in several instances. However, we fear that we might overtax the reader's patience.

<margin>N. 17.</margin>
Nevertheless, I believe it should not be overlooked that there are earths from which—indeed, from the **air** itself, through rain, snow, and dew—a **burning spirit, by far the most penetrating, can be drawn out**. This spirit, when digested by itself, is reduced into a salt and a "celestial balsam" of almost infinite praises. When separated from its **sulfur** <note>In this context, sulfur refers to the principle of inflammability or the "soul" of the substance.</note>, it bears a great analogy to our "earth" which we are currently discussing; indeed, it is almost equal, if not superior, in its medicinal power. We recently lost nearly half a pound of this most noble treasure—the labor of two years—when a vial broke because a fire was applied more strongly than intended by an assistant. It is absolutely certain that such an immortal substance lies hidden in the air, from which all **animals live and are preserved**; this substance has a great analogy with our **mineral** earth, as well as with the **vegetable** kingdom. While our mineral earth is poisonous in its first state, this arises from its **most penetrating** and yet excessively **earthy nature**, which is required for the formation of minerals. By contrast, the nature of **vegetables** and **animals** is far more subtle and, if we look at its use and purpose, more noble.

<margin>N. 18.</margin>
For it is from this that all vegetables grow and animals draw their spirit; without it, neither the **heat of the heart** would be maintained, nor the **balsam of life** preserved. Indeed, that this **balsam** is the seat of blood and life, and that the **air** is its nourishment, is not to be doubted at all if we consider the movements that follow from the alteration and diversity of the air. This can be seen in the **plague**, where the atoms of the air—which we proved above, in the section on the creation of the world, consist of earth—especially those atoms closer to the ground that arise from various exhalations of the earth, are agitated **into confusion and out of their state of natural arrangement**, causing horrendous changes and alterations in bodies, **especially human ones**.

<margin>N. 19.</margin>
For when such particles are **agitated out of order**, their entire substance becomes hostile to the human body and to all **living things**. Since they are chased away, as it were, from individual bodies by the various expansions and inhalations of the lungs, it necessarily follows that such particles, being harmful, inflict the greatest and most contrary offense upon a living body. Thus, it is not surprising that bodies are killed by the plague in a very short time. We see this in other bodily afflictions as well, namely in wounds, fevers, and others, where the disease immediately increases from contrary particles. The entire power of medicine, therefore, consists in this: that we learn to recognize particles that cling together and are "friendly" to one another. From this knowledge, medicines—or the **worsening** of diseases—arise; for from this come **sympathy and antipathy**, and the growth and decay of things. These particles are the **effluvia of bodies** <note>Tiny, invisible particles flowing out from a substance.</note> which breathe even out of the most **compact** bodies. For **tin and copper** give off a noticeable **odor**, as does the **magnet**; we also see the marvelous transpiration of **cats**, which is so heavy to some people that they can smell them even if they haven't seen them, or even if they are shut inside boxes. Such particles are agitated in various ways: sometimes by imagination alone, by touch, or by the slightest inhalation, as we see in the plague and contagious diseases.

...where in the space of a few hours, such a great agitation of these tiny bodies can be caused that there is danger to life. But with whatever force they invade a person, they can be restored to rest with equal ease, and indeed more so at the *beginning* than at the end, of which I will give a memorable example. About four years ago, an *epidemic petechial fever* <note>original: "febris epidemica petechialis"; likely typhus, a bacterial disease often spread by lice, characterized by purple spots on the skin and high fever.</note>, very malignant, was spreading through the region of Mainz <note>original: "Moguntino"; Mainz is a historic archbishopric and city in Germany.</note>. Not far from Mainz is a town called Groß-Winternheim, where the aforementioned epidemic fever was ruling ruinously, so much so that it wiped out the greater part of the town. Due to religious freedom, many noble families live there, among whom is a nobleman named *de Gambs*, who has a son-in-law, another nobleman, named *Jaxthausen*. This son-in-law, along with his entire household, was infected by this evil and was lying very ill. Even though his regular physician had been *Dr. Horst*, he could not be summoned, perhaps because of the distance of the journey or for other reasons. Therefore, I was called—at that time teaching theoretical medicine at Mainz as an *Ordinary Professor* and also practicing (for at that time I had devoted myself entirely to medical practice).

Having been called at cock-crow, I came to the aforementioned town by night. Upon entering the house, I encountered a dead man upon the straw; some were in their death throes in the *heated room* <note>original: "hypocausto"; in early modern German houses, this was the main living area heated by a stove, often where the sick were cared for.</note>. But the master of the house stayed on the second floor. Priority had to be given to him before all others, as I had been called by him; for as soon as it became known in the town that a Doctor was present, everyone flocked to me as if to some God. They lacked a Doctor, and no one could be persuaded to come because they knew that the barbers <note>Barber-surgeons often performed minor surgeries and treated the sick.</note> and some others who dealt with the sick had died from the infection. And this was the reason that our Nobleman, of whom we are about to speak, could not even have a Minister, for he was *Evangelical* <note>original: "Evangelicus"; at this time, this term specifically referred to a Lutheran.</note>. Finally, however, a *Reformed* <note>original: "Reformatus"; a term referring to the Calvinist tradition.</note> minister had come.

When, therefore, after seeing this miserable spectacle, I climbed to the upper *heated room*, I found the nobleman utterly furious and rabid; naked upon the bed, his shirt, linens, and bedding scattered and torn; meanwhile, he was so terribly driven by epileptic-like convulsions, and continuously so, that the *grinding of his teeth* could be heard outside. There was also a massive purging of the bowels—liquid and black feces. Being so miserably disposed in this state and already almost next to death, he made everyone lose hope of recovering his health; a set of linens was being prepared on the table for one who was just about to die, to wrap the corpse. To tell the truth, if I had known beforehand the danger of the times, the infection of this house, and the miserable state of the patient, I could not have been induced to come myself, even for a large sum of money; for I myself despaired for the Nobleman. For who would not despair when he saw nature acting against itself in every way, raging and wandering?

Lest I should seem to have arrived in vain, I tried what I could. Above all, I saw to it that an *enema* <note>A liquid injection used to clear the bowels.</note> was administered so that the bitterness of the intestines might be halted, from which I suspected the convulsions originated. Then I applied very powerful *blistering agents* <note>original: "vesicatoria"; substances applied to the skin to cause blisters, a common medical practice intended to "draw out" bad humors or toxins from the head and vital organs.</note> behind the neck to pull the malignancy away from the head. Once these things were done, though the patient was no better, I turned to the ultimate remedy, namely my **celestial salt** <note>original: "salem meum cælestem"; a proprietary chemical medicine developed by Becher, likely based on his alchemical research into "celestial" principles in the air.</note>; *three grains* of which I administered to him in a cordial emulsion, and his whole nature returned to its former quiet within a few days, with no other medicine applied. <margin>No. 21.</margin>
By way of conclusion, I will set down one more experiment: a servant girl in Frankfurt suffered so vehemently in her right arm from a type of arthritis that she would frequently fall into a fainting fit. Furthermore, there was no visible alteration, swelling, or wasting of the arm. She spent two years consumed by such pain, and since she could perform no service, she was reduced almost to beggary; yet she was restored to health by us within the space of a single week, and the ailment never flared up again <note>original: "redincruduit"; literally "became raw again"</note> afterward. From this, it is certain that what *Paracelsus, Helmontius, Digby*, and our dearest *Emerich of Stahl, the Hermit* <note>Johann Emerich von Stahl, an alchemist and associate of Becher</note> write and testify is true: that plasters work through the *transpiration of corpuscles*. Since these particles are contrary to other harmful influences flowing in, the latter are necessarily expelled by the former. We could bring forward many other points here regarding the nature and excellence of medical applications <note>original: "epithematum"; topically applied medicines</note>, if we had proposed to write about medicine rather than the *Genesis of subterranean things*. For now, let these points suffice for proving our *third earth* <term>tertia terra: the "stony" or vitrifiable earth, one of Becher's three fundamental principles of matter</term>, about which we will bring more to light in the following chapter. Now we shall conclude regarding the three *subterranean principles*.

### TEXTUS.

<margin>N. 1.</margin>
Thus far we have treated the three earths which we have established as the principles of minerals, and which the ancients encompassed under the names of *salt, sulfur, and Mercury*. This is not because common salt, sulfur, and Mercury are the pure principles themselves, but because a certain part of these "decomposed" <term>decompositorum: substances made of multiple simpler components</term> substances must be considered the principles of subterranean things. Thus, they took the whole for the part, naming the substance after its most dominant quality. For salt, sulfur, and Mercury are composite things, and are called such; however, when that part which constitutes *our earth* is separated from them—which is a truly *simple* principle of subterranean things—it can no longer be called salt, sulfur, or Mercury except in an improper sense. Why the Ancients encompassed the first earth—namely, *fusible stone* <term>lapidem fusilem: a type of earth that melts into glass</term>—under the name of *fixed salt* may perhaps be obscure to someone who does not know that in every *alkali salt* <note>original: "sale alcali"</note> there lies hidden a fusible and glass-making earth, *which is the first principle of minerals*. This we shall demonstrate in the fifth section, in the chapter on fermentation, paragraphs 48, 49, and 50.

<margin>N. 2.</margin>
By the same reasoning, in common *sulfur* the *second earth* lies hidden; and in *Mercury*, the *third*, as we shall teach further below regarding "Mercurifications," and in the second specialized book in the chapter on Mercury. Therefore, these earths or Principles are called salt, sulfur, and mercury by the *Philosophers* <note>original: "Philosophorum"; here meaning alchemists</note> (albeit improperly); conversely, they are called *vulgar* or common when they exist as composite substances, such as in common salt, sulfur, and mercury.

<margin>N. 3.</margin>
Before they arrive at this state of decomposition, however, other purer and more homogeneous things constitute *simpler* mixtures. For instance, when the *second earth* (of sulfur) and the *third* (of mercury) are mixed, a compound arises. This is not a perfect metal, due to the lack of the *first earth*, but it is nonetheless a mineral—namely, *realgar* <term>realgar: a bright red arsenic sulfide mineral</term>. If this is freed from its sulfurous dregs, it yields the *Mercury of the Philosophers* with little effort. For it is *volatile, fusible, and tints silver in flux* <note>original: "argentum in fluxu tingens"; a property where a substance changes the color or quality of molten silver</note>. It is found not infrequently in mines, *transparent* like a ruby. But it errs in that it contains too much of the *fertile* <note>original: "fecunda"; also called terra pinguis or "fatty earth," Becher's second principle of matter</note> earth, and consequently the mixture is rendered more solid. It must, therefore, be deprived of this so that it may be rendered more *fluid*; for then it will be *our* and the *Philosophical arsenic*. But regarding this, we shall speak elsewhere in what follows. It is also found in a state where the *third earth* predominates; but such a mixture is neither named nor shown, except by a friend, for unique and serious reasons. Just as the *third earth* is mixed with the *second* to constitute a compound, so the *fertile earth* is very often mixed with the *first*. From this come stones that vary in color according to the difference and "tincture" of the *fertile earth*; and in these again there are various differences, depending on the quantity of the former or the *fertile earth*. ...of things simple, composite, and doubly-composite, in the following order, which we shall consistently maintain throughout this entire treatise.

<margin>No. 4.</margin>
First, we must consider the principles themselves—namely, the three aforementioned earths—insofar as they exist on their own and constitute the "seeds" and foundations of all subterranean things. Second, it must be understood that these principles mix in two ways: first among themselves, and then with other foreign <note>original: "heterogeneis"; referring to substances of a different nature, like water</note> materials. When they mix among themselves, they do so either imperfectly or perfectly. They mix **imperfectly** when the three earths do not all come together, but one of them is missing (as we see in stones, various crystal fluxes, and metallic earths, as was mentioned previously). They mix **perfectly** when all three earths combine to form a metal. This metallic mixture is again of two types: equal or unequal. 

An **equal mixture** occurs when the three earths are mixed in such a proportion that they form a malleable metal. This category is threefold: in two metals, such as **lead and tin**, the third earth predominates; therefore, they melt before they glow red-hot. In **copper and iron**, the second earth exceeds the others; hence they glow red-hot before they melt. In **gold and silver**, there is an equal mixture of the three earths; thus, as soon as they glow, they melt. 

An **unequal mixture** of principles occurs when the principles are mixed in a false proportion and produce "spurious" <note>often called "bastard" metals in early chemistry</note> metals, which fail due to their volatility, fixity, or brittleness because of the uneven mixing. Examples include *Antimony, Bismuth, Zinc, Cobalt, and Marcasite* <note>a term then used for various metallic sulfides like pyrite</note>. 

So much for the principles as they mix among themselves; next follows how they mix with foreign substances, which happens in two ways. First, when they take water into the mixture; from this come **salt, nitre, alum, and borax**. Second, when they take earth into the mixture, whether it be a simple earth—giving rise to *sulfur, bitumen, and stone-coal* <note>original: "lithanthraces"</note>—or a mixed metallic and simple earth—giving rise to *arsenic, quicksilver, and cinnabar*—or a simple mineral, stony, and variously mixed earth—from which come the ores commonly called *specimens* <note>original: "Stuffen"</note> and *ore-stone* <note>original: "Aertzstein"</note>, or the mineral byproducts commonly called *calamine, mountain green, smalt, red ochre, and bole* <note>original: "Gallmay, Berggrien, Schmalten, Rötel, Bolus"</note>. Indeed, innumerable mixtures can arise if we take into account the variations of composites and double-composites, as we shall demonstrate in the fourth section, second chapter.

<margin>No. 5.</margin>
For since Arithmetic teaches that eight numbers can be transposed 40,320 times <note>The author is calculating 8 factorial (8!), showing the vast possibilities of combinations</note>, is it any wonder if far more species are found in the mineral kingdom than in the vegetable kingdom? The reason we are unable to set them before our eyes as clearly as **Botanists** do with their illustrated figures is that the difference between minerals lies not so much in their external shape as in their internal structure; furthermore, because of the depth of this science, there are few who truly master it.

<margin>No. 6.</margin>
For although the **Galenists** <note>followers of the ancient Greek physician Galen, often criticized by "modern" chemists for their old-fashioned theories</note> have written about *acidic mineral waters* <note>original: "acidulis"</note> as if they were just one type of composite mineral, claiming they consist of this or that specific mineral, their claims are false because they did not know the correct method of investigation. By using evaporation <note>original: "inspissatione"</note>, the species are altered, as we shall demonstrate in the fifth section, in the chapter on fermentation, specifically the paragraph on **Glauber’s concentration** <note>referring to Johann Rudolf Glauber, a famous 17th-century chemist known for his salts and distillation methods</note>. It is impossible to discover the quality of waters solely by weighing them, as they do in salt-works. Although the weight might be revealed, and although every body has a different weight, the quality cannot be found from the quantity; to this day, the proportion of quantity to quality remains unknown to us—unless the nature of the subject is already known to us in a general way, as in the case of the metallic crown whose quality **Archimedes** discovered from its weight. Even though the more skilled **Physicists and Chemists** test waters and mineral species through reagents...

...prove them; for **common salt** <note>original: "sal commune"; sodium chloride</note> precipitates a solution of **silver** <note>original: "luna"; the alchemical name for silver</note>; if **vitriol** <note>original: "vitriolum"; a term for metallic sulfates</note> is hidden in the water, **oak gall** <note>original: "galla"; used historically to test for the presence of iron</note> will be blackened; if **sulfur** is present, the lye rejects it, and so on. These tests are indeed more certain than common ones, yet they are still not sufficient; for the ingredients themselves frequently cause new reactions among one another that are in no way able to be precipitated, or even recognizable through precipitation. It is no wonder, therefore, that we are, in fact, mostly ignorant of the specific diversity of subterranean mixtures. From this arise infinite errors in the descriptions of mineral species; from this come the various and different results in experiments; where sometimes one species is taken for another because it matches in outward appearance, while in its intrinsic quality it differs by a whole heaven <note>a common idiom meaning "entirely different"</note>: but we shall deal with these matters to your heart's content in the following section.

<margin>No. 7.</margin>
At this point, it was pleasing to set down only the general system from which the practice of the aforementioned mixtures can easily be drawn. For what concerns specific mixtures, we shall explain that in the following three sections; in this section, we do nothing else than demonstrate that **metallic mixtures** are **earthy**, and have the **threefold earth** <term>threefold earth: Becher’s theory that all matter is composed of three types of earth: the "stony," the "fatty/combustible," and the "mercurial/fluid" earth</term> as their principle. For I do not think anyone will exist who believes that clear, common **water** enters into the **mixture of metals** as an **actual principle**; nor can water be prepared **from metals** in any way, whether by art or by force <note>original: "arte aut Marte"; literally "by art or by Mars," a phrase meaning by chemistry or by violent mechanical means</note>, although some small amount may be drawn **from ores**. But however small that amount is, we demonstrated in Section Five, in the chapter on fermentation, paragraph 162, that it proceeds from **sulfur**. And in this step, we are entirely in agreement with **Angelo Sala** <note>a 17th-century chemist and physician who was a pioneer in transitioning from alchemy to chemistry</note>; who consistently denies that the **aqueous liquidity of potable gold** <note>original: "auri potabilis"; a sought-after alchemical medicine</note> originates from the inherent nature of gold itself.

<margin>No. 8.</margin>
For just as it is folly to hope for flowing **Mercury** <note>quicksilver</note> from animals, so it is ignorance to desire it from metals: for neither enters into their composition, as we shall better prove in Section Five, in the chapter on liquefaction. Moreover, we are speaking here of **homogeneous, subterranean mixtures**—metallic and mineral—not **heterogeneous** ones, of which we said above that water enters into a part, as in **salt, nitre, alum, and borax**. The remaining mixtures, however, which consist of earth, are entirely **homogeneous and earthy**; nor is it enough to attribute the origin of all things to water by words alone, or by the experiment of **Helmont** regarding the growth of a tree, which **Robert Boyle** cites in *The Sceptical Chymist*. **Water** will certainly never become **earth**, except insofar as it carries earthy corpuscles along with it.

<margin>No. 9.</margin>
But lest we wander into mazes, we must return to our task <note>original: "ad Spartam nostram"; literally "to our Sparta," an idiom meaning to return to the business at hand</note>, and prove that **metals consist of earth**—namely, that they **are earthy**—which their first appearance demonstrates; then their treatment in fire: and finally, their harmony and sympathy with various kinds of earths in the smelting flow: where **metals**, both **noble** and **base**, take on increases **from various earths**. Finally, in whatever way metals may be resolved—whether by fire into smoke and "flowers" <note>fine powders produced by sublimation</note>, or by waters into "calx" <note>a powdery metallic oxide</note>: when and in whatever way, I say, they are dissolved point by point, they appear **earthy** and **dry**: and they take an **increase** from the solvents, and even from the fire itself, as we shall further demonstrate in section five, the chapter on liquefaction. And lest anyone think that the powdery earthiness, when metals are treated in fire, proceeds from fiery corpuscles; we tested this with **tin** and **lead** in a glass retort, and converted the whole into powder, even exceeding its original weight. Which notable **excess of weight** from the corpuscles [of] the glass <note>original: "vitream"; catchword for the next page</note>...

He references contemporary scientists like Robert Boyle and Angelo Sala to challenge the idea that water is the universal building block of matter, pointing to the increase in weight of metals when heated as evidence of their earthy nature.</summary>

...it is scarcely credible that it proceeded from things *penetrating* the glass <note>original: "vitream penetrantibus"; likely referring to the alchemical belief that fire or external spirits could pass through glass vessels</note>; and if it should happen so, it nevertheless proves a great harmony between metals and earth. Therefore, with the reader's kind permission and nature’s approval, we shall conclude that mixed metals are earthy. But are there truly three earths, which we mentioned toward the end of the first chapter of this section, that alone constitute a metallic mixture? And are they hidden in *salt, sulfur,* and *alkali*? As we said in the place cited, this seems to require more accurate and solid proof: lest we commit the very thing we condemn in others, namely, *empty words without experience* <note>original: "vacua sine experientia verba"</note>.

<margin>No. 10.</margin>
Therefore, to come to the matter at hand, let us recall what we have said: namely, that there are three earths which, when mixed, create a *true metallic substance*. By "earths," however, I do not mean those that are *actually* <note>original: "actu"</note> mineral and metallic, but only *potentially* <note>original: "potentia"</note> so. To the *first* earth, I attributed stoniness; to the *second*, color; and to the *third*, the quality of being metallic <note>original: "metalleitatem"</note>. I said the *first* is a stone and is hidden in any alkaline salt; the *second* in saltpeter or sulfur; the *third* in common salt. I was led to this by various experiments, which I deal with in the second book under the specific "anatomy" of each subject. For it is certain that through the medium of *common salt*, *liquid mercury* <note>original: "Mercurium currentem"; literally "running mercury"</note> is produced from metals; through the medium of the *earth of saltpeter*, metals are *tinged* <note>original: "tingi"; referring to the change of color or "exaltation" in alchemical transformation</note>; and through the medium of *alkaline earth*, metals are notably altered in their flow and consistency. Again, I have mixed the *earths of alkali, saltpeter* (or *common sulfur*), and *common salt*, and treated them in the proper way; and I found, saw, and handled with my own hands a true metallic nature, as I shall demonstrate in the second book. From these experiments, I began to conclude that the principles of metals are earths which we step upon almost daily with our feet; it would be an easy task, if God willed to open someone’s eyes, so that *they could be prepared by art in the greatest abundance*, so that what we have proven on a small scale might be done on a large one, and with which we have been content to defend the truth of our opinion.

<margin>No. 11</margin>
But we would easily give the prize to the *younger Mr. Helmont* <note>Francis Mercurius van Helmont (1614–1698), a famous alchemist and philosopher</note>, if he would deign to communicate for the public good that experiment which he mentioned to me two years ago at Sulzbach <note>A town in Bavaria known for its intellectual and alchemical circles</note>; *namely, that he knows how to make true iron from any common mud and sulfur*, and indeed not in a small but a large quantity. This experiment would, with one stroke, resolve the Gordian knots of infinite questions regarding the principles of minerals. But we could obtain this through no prayers, except that the author promised he would soon send his chemical experiments into the light. We, however, moved by curiosity about the matter, took the opportunity to conduct various experiments regarding it; for although the title of the experiment seems impossible at first glance, nevertheless, having seen many incredible things in nature beyond hope and belief, I am not accustomed to lose heart in any matter. And supported by this constancy,

<margin>No. 12.</margin>
I know not by what chance I dissolved *Red Chalk* <note>original: "Rubiam vulgo Rötelstein"; likely a form of hematite or red ochre</note> in *spirit of salt* <note>original: "spiritu salis"; what we now call hydrochloric acid</note>; I repeated the solution, and finally, when all the color was extracted, the red chalk was changed into *common white mud*. From this transformed material, I had a little pot made, so that I might investigate the truth of the *mud*; even in the kiln, it remained *true mud*, having all the qualities of mud. But the extracted substance was a *Tincture of Mars* <note>original: "tinctura Martialis"; an iron-based solution, "Mars" being the alchemical name for iron</note>. From this, I began to argue that it is not so absurd that *mud can be converted into iron*; which we may also see in fact, that *iron is generated most abundantly in mud*, in the form of kidneys, commonly called *Iron-Kidneys* <note>original: "Eyffen-Nieren"; likely siderite or hematite nodules found in clay or bog deposits</note>: especially if sulfur is added. For we have learned through a singular experiment that the metallic nature is hidden in sulfur, by which common *antimony* in...

...we converted it entirely into common sulfur in great quantity, and we do not know how to reduce it back into antimony in practice, as will be discussed more extensively in the second book under the history of antimony. My very dear friend and diligent investigator of nature, Mr. Krafft <note>Johann Daniel Kraft (1624–1697), a famous German chemist and merchant</note>, also reported that there is still a certain Patrician in Augsburg <note>original: "Augustæ Vindelicorum"</note> who can extract true running Mercury from common sulfur in such quantities that he could, if he wished, even sell it at a profit for the price of common Mercury. Although these things may seem incredible, they will nevertheless deserve some credit if we bring back to the anvil <note>original: "sub incudem revocemus"; an idiom meaning to examine or reconsider something closely</note> those things which we reviewed in the history of sulfur in the third chapter of this section. Moreover, once Mercury is obtained, it is probable and evident that metals can easily be generated. I only wish that the two aforementioned gentlemen would expose their experiments for the public good and set aside their envy <note>in this context, "envy" or *invidia* refers to the common alchemical practice of keeping secrets to prevent others from benefiting</note>; then we might finally arrive at a clear understanding of the origin of subterranean things <note>original: "subterraneorum genesin"</note>, with no harmful consequences. For the things we have attempted regarding such matters were neither done in such great quantity nor so established that they could be communicated to the worthy and unworthy alike, since they prepare the way for higher secrets.

<margin>No. 14.</margin>
In the meantime, however, it is certain that metals—even silver itself—are generated from a slime which miners call <term>Bergmilch</term> <note>literally "mountain milk"; a soft, white, milky precipitate of calcium carbonate found in limestone caves</note>. For this substance, when it is entirely liquid like a thick water and frequently drips over stones in caves commonly called <term>Zächen</term> <note>German *Zechen*, meaning mine workings or pits</note>, is initially completely slimy and liquid. If it is distilled by art, it yields a spirit, an oil, and an earth that is in no way reducible to metal; for it is entirely volatile and in every way similar to common slime, as we have also proven in the anatomy of fire (subsequently, we also produced such a liquor from metals by art). Yet, in a short space of time, it solidifies most elegantly, rising up into little branches and growths, and becomes pure, refined silver without any loss of its substance; it is commonly called <term>gediegen</term> <note>meaning "native," referring to metal found in its pure metallic state in nature</note> or <term>fein stahlgantz</term> <note>literally "fine steel-glance," referring to the bright, metallic luster of the mineral</note>. This observation clearly proves to the eye that metals are generated from earth and are therefore earthy mixtures, as we shall further demonstrate in the second book and in the following sections of this book: especially how metals are changed back into earth, how they take their growth from the earth, and how they arise from the earth. I remember reading in <term>Tabernaemontanus</term> <note>Jacob Theodor von Bergzabern (c. 1520–1590), a famous physician and botanist</note>, if I am not mistaken, that he changed gold into an irreducible "sealed earth" <note>original: "terra sigillata"; a term for medicinal clays, but here used for a chemical state of gold</note>. A similar experiment is known to us as well, as we shall explain later in the second book in a special chapter on gold.

<margin>No. 15.</margin>
But we shall understand all these things more solidly if we carefully consider the manner in which metals are mixed from their principles. Therefore, having explained the "earths" as the three principles of minerals, order requires that we discuss something of their mixture; afterward, we shall consider the mixture in solution, and finally in its own consistency. We shall complete all these things in the following sections, and hurrying toward them, we now conclude the present section.

## Section Four, Chapter One
# On the Necessity and Obscurity of Physics regarding Mixture.

### S Y N O P S I S.

*N.1. Knowledge of the mixing of subterranean substances is obscure and difficult. N.2. Aristotle's lack of clarity regarding the doctrine of mixing. N.3. In what way the spagyric <note>the art of alchemy, specifically the separation and recombination of natural substances</note> science differs from the Aristotelian. N.4. The ignorance and falsehood of the Chemists <note>referring to contemporary alchemists</note> regarding the study of subterranean mixing. N.5. The cause of ignorance in spagyric study. N.6. The "mixtures" of the Galenists <note>followers of the ancient Greek physician Galen, typically focused on herbal medicine and the four humors</note>. N.7. A critique of certain Chemists. N.8. The term "spagyric" is explained. N.9. The necessity of spagyric study. N.10. The sign of a perfect spagyricist. N.11. Without the knowledge of how subterranean things mix, the nature of minerals cannot be perfectly known.*

### T E X T.

Hitherto, we have drawn the origin of subterranean things from the very springs of creation and production; we have scrutinized the principles, demonstrated the certainty of those principles, and followed their movement from beginning to end, from the circumference to the center, as if guided by a thread of Ariadne <note>a classical reference to the mythological thread used to navigate the Labyrinth; here it means a logical guide through a complex subject</note>. Now it remains for us to explain what the aforementioned principles do during their progress and when they come together.
<margin>No. 1.</margin>
We stated in the title of this chapter that their action is "mixture"; namely, that while they are being mixed, the various subterranean species are produced. But how are they mixed? And which species are produced, and from what causes? These things must be explained in this place. This is a truly difficult business, upon which the entire hinge of our *Philosophy* turns. For since these are subterranean bodies, and all bodies are "mixed"—especially subterranean ones, which for the most part consist of the strongest homogeneous mixing—it follows that these mixtures consist of "mixable" parts which, by means of the process of mixing, produce the compound bodies. And this is what we shall shell <note>original: "enucleabimus," meaning to take the kernel out of a nut</note> in this place with a laborious *nut-cracker* <note>original: "nucifrangibulo"</note>; for if, according to the proverb, "a hard knot requires a hard wedge," then the strongest arguments must be sought so that we may loosen the incredibly strong structure and mixture of subterranean things and reduce them back to their principles. This is especially necessary because this material has been left untouched by everyone, both the ancients and the moderns, the Aristotelians as well as the Chemists; and therefore it remains entirely raw, not even peeled of its first layer of bark.
<margin>No. 2.</margin>
For if we take the doctrine of the Aristotelians <note>the traditional university scholars who followed Aristotle's natural philosophy</note> regarding the mixing of subterranean things, what else does it teach but generalities? Or rather, it provides "little boxes" <note>original: "capsulas"</note> and names that could be placed upon things once they have already been explained. For no one is ignorant of the fact that subterranean things are mixed, that they consist of elements, and that they have their own temperaments and qualities. But from where these mixtures arise, and how so many diverse species of subterranean things proceed from those mixtures—"there is the work, there is the labor" <note>original: "hic opus hic labor," a quote from Virgil's Aeneid</note>. It is here that the empty cares of the craftsmen are exercised. Why *tin can be mixed with lead, and yet not with silver* without resulting in brittleness, they will easily give a reason: namely, that they are contrary substances of a different temperament. But in which parts...

<summary>Becher introduces the concept of "Mixture" as the fundamental process that creates minerals and metals, arguing that previous scholars like Aristotle have only provided vague labels rather than explaining the actual chemical mechanics.</summary>
