where this diversity and temperament <note>referring to the specific "balance" or ratio of elements in a mixture</note> resides, here we fall utterly silent. These pseudo-philosophers will say that *aqua fortis* <note>Nitric acid, literally "strong water," used to dissolve metals</note> dissolves metals because of its "resolutive quality" <note>original: "qualitate resolutiva"</note>—that is, "insofar as it is" <note>original: "quantum est"</note> the means by which something is said to be "how much" <note>original: "quantum"</note>. This is clearly a "begging of the question" <note>original: "petitio principii"; a logical fallacy where the conclusion is assumed in the premise</note>. But as for where this resolutive quality comes from, and why it dissolves all metals except for gold alone, here all philosophy fails, as does the diligence of all the Peripatetics <note>followers of Aristotle, known for theoretical rather than experimental science</note>, if they were required to discover *aqua fortis* "from prior principles" <note>original: "ex antecedenti"</note>.

<margin>No. 3.</margin>
Therefore, that most noble spagyric <term>Spagyric: the alchemical art of separating substances into their components and then recombining them</term> science is far different. It extracts the solid causes and reasons for mixtures from practical foundations and experiments, treating them as established theses; and consequently, it always discovers new combinations of nature. Of this most sagacious, subtle, and curious study, you will not find a single letter in all the books of the [Aristotelian] philosophers; since they are content with mere "ideas, abstractions, and chimeras" <note>original: "ideis abstractionibus & chimæris"</note>, they remain stuck only on names. They are happy in this one thing: that they do not know how much they do not know. Nor is it a wonder that the Peripatetics are strangers to this study, since the Chemists <note>referring here to traditional alchemists</note> themselves, whose sole profession is chemistry, are also entirely alienated from the truth.

<margin>No. 4.</margin>
Indeed, all of them—as many as have written books—can be reduced "into two classes" <note>original: "in duas classes"</note>. For they either set down "processes" <note>experimental recipes</note> or the "theory of their Stone" <note>the Philosopher's Stone</note>. Regarding the processes, who does not know that they are all set down in the manner of some "Recipe," without cause, reason, order, or effect? They describe such incongruous mixtures that, at times, they could not be dreamed up even by the most foolish of men. This is the reason why, until now, very few have been able to discern the process before putting it into practice. Furthermore, whether they succeeded or failed, the causes remained unknown. From this, infinite errors arose; for since even the smallest circumstance can sometimes hinder and alter a mixture—and was omitted through ignorance of the "causing cause" <note>original: "causae causantis"</note>—truths were proclaimed as false, and falsehoods as true. From these mixtures, various decomposed substances resulted, which the ignorant immediately concluded were "principles and new entities" <note>original: "pro principiis & novis entibus"</note>.

<margin>No. 5.</margin>
From all this, a great lack of knowledge followed, which stems from greed: because everyone immediately pants for gold, and without sufficient learning, they put into practice any "gold-bearing processes" they find. They read "alchemical books" <note>original: "alchymisticos"</note> more willingly than true "spagyric" <note>scientific/experimental</note> works on physics. But since very few of those who wrote processes about the Stone actually possessed it, those who believe them are rightly deceived. What I say regarding the ignorance of Chemists about the study of mixture, I also affirm regarding the "Metal-workers" <note>original: "Metallicolis"; those who mine or assay metals</note> themselves. For although those types of "probatory" or "docimastic" <term>Docimastic: the art of testing or assaying the purity of metals and ores</term> books teach how to purify metals, and how to separate or fuse them together, they are still far from explaining the "intrinsic" temperaments and mixtures of minerals from which the qualities of metals arise. There is, therefore, a great blindness and ignorance in the world regarding this fact, in this one kingdom of nature—namely, the "subterranean" <note>original: "subterranea"</note>. Regarding the other two kingdoms—namely, "animals and vegetables" <note>original: "animalium & vegetabilium"</note>—and especially the mixtures of the Galenists <note>followers of the physician Galen, who used herbal remedies based on the four humors</note> concerning them, I shall not linger much, unless I were to undertake the "cleansing of the Augean stables" <note>a Greek mythological reference to a nearly impossible task of cleaning massive, filthy stables in a single day</note>. It is therefore to be hoped that this study of Mixture, and the true physical causes of mixture regarding subterranean things, had been stripped of its outer bark and better treated; then, surely, we could have been spared a great deal of labor.

<margin>No. 6.</margin>
Glauber <note>Johann Rudolf Glauber (1604–1670), a famous German-Dutch alchemist and apothecary</note> especially attempted this before all others; but in many things, he was himself deceived and deceived others, or perhaps by his study he intentionally wished to deceive, and placed a different mask upon things than that which is appropriate. Ludovicus... <note>likely referring to Ludovicus de Comitibus</note>

**Ludovicus de Comitibus** <note>A 17th-century Italian alchemist and author</note> was a theorist alone, and a student of gemstones, who never accomplished anything in practice. I would grant the prize above all others in our century to **Robert Boyle**, if he had set aside his *elater* <note>original: "elaterio"; referring to Boyle’s work on the "spring" or elasticity of air</note> and continued his **Chemical** experiments further; and if, in explaining them, he had not set out to treat them as more matter for doubting rather than as a basis for reaching a conclusion in each case. **Werner Rolfinck of Jena**, flown on I know not what Aristotelian wings outside of his own office, also flew into Chemistry and wished to reduce it to a form of art—specifically, an Aristotelian one. But just as Theology is shamefully masked when it is personified in the mask of Aristotle, so too does it fit very poorly with Hermes <note>referring to Hermeticism or the alchemical tradition</note>. Furthermore, in his aforementioned "form of art," I see no reasoning other than a new way to order the descriptions of processes; and by smearing certain Greek terms over things, he established many falsehoods as truths, and truths as falsehoods, not without proving his own lack of experience. Some of these **Theorists** would be good if they wrote the theories and reasons for **practices**; but by philosophizing in the shadows in this way, they run into that warning of **Chrysostom**: <note>John Chrysostom, an early Church Father known for his eloquence</note> *a foreign doctrine, boasting of many trifles and detaining listeners with much talkativeness, finally dismisses them with empty hands, having gained neither great nor small benefit.* For the saying of **Gellius** <note>Aulus Gellius, a 2nd-century Roman author</note> must be observed: *he who wishes to speak what no one understands performs a great service if he remains silent.* Therefore, many books abound with such useless theory and talkativeness, whose authors have philosophized without experience. Regarding **Faber of Montpellier** <note>Pierre-Jean Fabre, a French physician and alchemist</note>, I cannot wonder enough that he was not ashamed to write such blatant **lies**. The Reverend Lord Charles Bendegin tells me that, drawn by the same fame and love for this science, he traveled from Italy to France to meet the man, but he saw not even a single furnace, nor noticed the slightest practical skill in the man. It is a wonder that he did not meet the same fate as **Agricola** <note>Georgius Agricola, the "father of mineralogy"</note> regarding **Poppius** <note>Johann Poppius, a chemist criticized for his lack of practical knowledge</note>, who, having been refuted by a **Pharmacist** and publicly convicted of many lies, was put to shame. Regarding the elder **Helmont** <note>Jan Baptist van Helmont, a foundational figure in chemistry and medicine</note>, I know not what to say; some report that he could not even cure a simple fever, and that he died of a burning fever <note>original: "causone"</note> because, out of shame, he would not implore the Physicians (whom he had held in such excessive contempt) but preferred to die without help. Certainly, the often-mentioned **Mr. Krafft** <note>Johann Daniel Krafft, a famous chemist and associate of Becher</note> related to us that in Brussels, at the house of the elder Helmont, he questioned the neighbors and old men in the very street where Helmont lived for many years, but his name was entirely unknown. This seems almost impossible—that a Physician who supposedly cured so many sick people so successfully, like a second **Aesculapius** <note>The Greek god of healing</note>, and to whom there should have been a great influx of people, was not even known by his neighbors after living in one place for so many years. But many also complain about his **theory**, that it clearly does not correspond to practice; whence not only many sick people, but also Physicians have died. This happened recently during the plague on the Rhine, where a certain little monk and his brother happened upon Helmont’s treatise on the plague, which he read so thoroughly that he knew it by heart, believing it impossible for practice not to follow the theory. Coming from Belgium to the Rhine, he asked to be given the power to cure those infected with the plague; as soon as this was granted to him, he perished with his brother in a short time. Therefore, many plausible things can be written with a subtle style and talkativeness, but few can be practiced: and rarely is solid theory joined with practice, as we said in the preamble of this book. I do not value all the remaining writers of **processes** <note>chemical recipes or procedures</note> in the least, for their method of writing a process differs little from that by which words inscribed on various dice are thrown together—without order,

...manner, method, reason, and end. For no one should profess himself a true spagyric <note>The term "spagyric" refers to alchemical pharmacy, specifically the process of separating and then recombining the components of a substance to purify it. The word comes from the Greek *spao* (to tear apart) and *ageiro* (to gather).</note> who does not immediately recognize any process or mixture presented to him, noting and foreseeing either its failure or success. For experienced spagyrics, having established their foundations and theses, work upon either written or printed processes only to detect errors; 
<margin>N. 7.</margin>
since they can produce infinite true, genuine, and nature-conforming processes from their own wit and experience. In this, therefore, lies the difference between true spagyrics and Pseudochymists <note>False chemists or charlatans</note>; the latter are "smoke-sellers" <note>original: "fumivenduli"; a derogatory term for fraudsters who sell empty promises or "smoke."</note> and ignoramuses; the former interrogate and search through nature, certain of their matters, doing nothing against the order of nature. 
<margin>N. 8.</margin>
To gain knowledge of every mixture, especially of subterranean things <note>Minerals and metals found underground</note>, an accurate spagyric knowledge is required. For although the subject of this science is the knowledge of mixture and mixed things—and thus spagyrics ought rather to be called the "art of mixing" than the "art of separating"—the ancients nevertheless took its name from the latter, namely from separation, as the more powerful and necessary part; especially regarding the mixture of subterranean things. For since no one can be present at their original subterranean mixing—partly due to the discomfort of the location, and partly due to the long duration of the time and operation—but our entire study of subterranean things consists of their separation and analysis above ground through art, it is necessary that we begin from the dissolution and separation of parts, and from there learn the structure of the whole and its parts. Therefore, separation should rightly be called the beginning and more important part of this study. Hence, not without reason, the term spagyric also received its name. For even if it treats the mixture of things, it nevertheless obtained its name from the *instrument* used to arrive at the nature of the mixture—namely, from *dissolution*, or because the dissolved parts are the first principles of mixture, since, as will be taught later, *all mixture comes from dissolution*. 
<margin>N. 9.</margin>
Therefore, spagyric study is highly necessary, for without it, neither can medicines be skillfully prepared, nor can Physics <note>Natural Philosophy or the study of nature</note> be sufficiently taught, or the nature of things be known; specifically, mixed subterranean things would be left entirely unknown, except regarding their external shape, which even oxen and donkeys can distinguish. And although many works on metallurgy <note>original: "metallurgiæ"</note> have been written about subterranean mixtures, they have all accomplished nothing because they began from the mixtures themselves, and not from the *process* of their mixing. For, to use *Wine* as an example: it will be obvious to anyone who has tasted it that people get drunk from it, that it is sweet or tart, red or white; but unless they have seen it grow on the vine, what would they know of its nature? And if they should happen to see that too, what else would they say but that it grows in such and such a way, it needs these things for its growth, and it shuns others. Such a person differs much in knowledge from the first group, who only saw the effect—namely, the wine already prepared. But meanwhile, both are far from knowing the intrinsic nature of wine: how, for instance, from the acidic matter of grapes, sweet must <note>unfermented grape juice</note> is prepared by nature, why it ferments, why it transforms into the nature of wine, and why wine is eventually reduced to vinegar, stale wine, and dregs? These things, I say, and many others, are unknown even by those who have written entire books about wine; as **Löwenheim** <note>Christian Schütz of Löwenheim, a contemporary author who wrote a compendium on wine.</note> recently did, who collected in his treatise whatever has been written about wine by everyone; but meanwhile he only wrote *about wine*, not about *its nature*; because [he lacked] the essential parts of wine and the mixture of these parts, due to a lack of [co-gnition]...

<summary>Becher argues that true chemical knowledge (spagyrics) comes from the ability to analyze and separate substances into their parts to understand their internal "mixture." He uses wine as a metaphor, explaining that observing the final product or even its growth is insufficient to understand its intrinsic chemical nature.</summary>

knowledge of the spagyric art <note>The art of alchemical separation and recombination</note>, has been ignorant of it, and has not put it into practice. *Subterranean things* <note>original: "Subterranea"; referring to minerals, ores, and metals found beneath the earth</note> follow exactly the same pattern; for although we know many things about their external qualities, about which entire books have been written, we remain ignorant of the causes, differences, and successions of these qualities. This is because we do not know the essential parts, or the "essentially mixed" components that constitute subterranean bodies, nor do we understand the specific way these parts are mixed together.

<margin>N. 10.</margin>
For even if we know the component parts, if we are ignorant of the *way* in which those parts are mixed, we will immediately fail to understand the whole. A person does not perfectly and clearly understand the mixture of subterranean things—especially of metals—if, after obtaining their principles and other requirements, they cannot also produce metals through art above ground. This is no different than a gardener who, having the principles of a tulip, produces that same flower above the ground before a window.

<margin>N. 11.</margin>
Since, therefore, as is clear from what was said before, the most important knowledge of subterranean things consists in the *mixture* of subterranean principles, it will be necessary—before we deal with the subterranean mixtures themselves and their types in the sixth section of this book—to examine and discuss the doctrine of subterranean mixture here in a slightly more detailed manner.

### On the method of acquiring the science of mixture.

### Book I, Section IV, Chapter I.

...proceeds. Since mixing is a *conjunction* of two or more things, or a *combination* of subterranean bodies, of which many types exist and from which many combinations arise—given that only *eight* bodies can be combined in 40,320 different ways <note>Becher is referencing the mathematical principle of factorials; 8! (8x7x6x5x4x3x2x1) equals 40,320</note>—it follows that nearly innumerable and infinite mixtures arise. No mortal could ever perform all these combinations, nor see them all once made, especially if no *order* is observed and everything is confused and mixed together indiscriminately. In such a state of mixing, no logic, cause, *effect*, or *use* can be assigned. From this arises an inextricable labyrinth of infinite processes and books, all of which could be reduced to a few if only *order and logic* were maintained in both theory and practice.

<margin>No. 2.</margin>
In this latter practice, above all else, one needs extreme caution and a guiding thread—like that of Ariadne <note>In Greek mythology, Ariadne’s thread allowed Theseus to navigate the Labyrinth; Becher uses it as a metaphor for a logical method</note>—so that the work may be established skillfully and with *fruitful results*. Therefore, let the apprentice of Chemistry and the Spagyric art <note>The "Spagyric art" refers to the alchemical process of separating and recombining substances</note> first learn and experience the *principal and cardinal* combinations of subterranean bodies, whether they are natural or artificial, simple or complex, and whether they are parts or principles. Although this might normally require the years of a Nestor <note>A legendary Greek king known for his great age and wisdom</note> and immense expense, all of this can be condensed into a manual if the reader is willing to follow the method that I use, and which I have found to be of great benefit.

<margin>No. 3.</margin>
First, one should procure the necessary subterranean bodies, both simple and compound, and arrange them into certain classes, placing each in its own small container; one or two pounds of each, or a smaller quantity for the more precious items. Let him maintain *order, such that in the first place he puts the metals*: gold, silver, copper, iron, tin, lead—both pure and in their ore. *Secondly, let him place the minerals*: Antimony, Bismuth, Zinc, Marcasite, Cobalt, Zaffre, Manganese <note>original: "Braunstein"</note>, magnesia, arsenic, realgar, Mercury, and orpiment <note>original: "auripigmentum"; a yellow arsenic sulfide</note>—again, both pure and in their ore. *Thirdly, he should arrange the "decomposed" <note>In this context, Becher means processed or chemically altered</note> minerals*: such as "fulminating gold" <note>an explosive gold compound</note> from *gold*; horn silver <note>original: "luna cornua"; silver chloride</note>, calx <note>a powdery metallic oxide</note>, and ultramarine from *silver*; verdigris and burnt brass from *copper*; "saffron" <note>original: "crocus"; a term for various metal oxides, often iron</note> from *iron*; ashes from *Tin* <note>original: "Jove"; alchemical shorthand using the planet Jupiter for tin</note>; and from *Lead* <note>original: "Saturno"; using the planet Saturn for lead</note>, sugar of lead, cadmia, tutty, graphite, minium <note>red lead</note>, glass, and litharge. From *Antimony*, he should have the regulus <note>the metallic part of the ore</note> on its own, the "Martial" regulus <note>antimony reduced with iron</note>, flowers of antimony, glass of antimony, cinnabar, and saffron of antimony. From *Mercury*, he should have cinnabar, sublimate, and precipitate. *Fourthly, let the salts be presented*: such as common salt, nitre <note>saltpeter</note>, vitriol, ashes, Tartar, Soda, borax, chrysocolla <note>a term used here for borax or a copper glue</note>, vitriol, alum, sulfur, and tartar. *Fifthly, the gums*: such as wax, pitch, camphor, coral, amber, sugar, and turpentine. *Sixthly, the earths*: such as quicklime, "Passau sealed earth" <note>a medicinal clay from Passau</note>, mud, clay, Armenian bole <note>a red medicinal clay</note>, sand, and chalk. *Seventhly, the stones*: such as flint, crystal, talc, and both precious and common stones. *Eighthly, various spirits and oils*: such as aqua fortis <note>nitric acid</note>, Aqua Regia <note>a mixture of nitric and hydrochloric acids</note>, spirit of salt <note>hydrochloric acid</note>, spirits of nitre, vitriol, sulfur, alum, vinegar, wine, urine, tartar, "May dew," and turpentine; also common lye, "fetid" oil of tartar, oil of tartar made by "deliquium" <note>allowing a substance to melt by absorbing atmospheric moisture</note>, oil of vitriol, oil of salt, oil of wine, butter of antimony, linseed oil, olive oil, oil of sweet almonds, etc. In these eight classes, the principal subjects are included, through which the most important combinations can be completed. For here you have the principal *letters of nature*, and as it were, the entire *Alphabet*—for though there are few letters, a great many combinations arise from them. Indeed, nearly infinite *syllables* can be produced from them, and *words*—that is, mixtures and compounds—can emerge. Study this *Alphabet* diligently, and...

# Subterranean Physics

<margin>No. 4.</margin>
Maintain the same method that Nature exhibits to us in reading. First, so that you may know the letters—that is, the aforementioned subjects, whether they are simple or complex—gaze upon them diligently and consider them according to all circumstances; let them not be fake or substituted, which might cause you to stumble in your combinations, as often happens. It would therefore be wise for you to extract natural materials yourself from the very places where they are generated; for in this way, you will acquire an eye-witness knowledge of minerals. As for complex things, such as sublimates, prepared items, and *spirits* <note>In 17th-century chemistry, "spirits" referred to volatile substances obtained by distillation, such as "spirit of salt" (hydrochloric acid)</note>, prepare them yourself from simple substances. For in this way you will have a double benefit: first, that in such a manner you may learn the **manipulations** <margin>No. 5.</margin> and understand the nature of the mixture more accurately; and second, that you may be certain of the integrity and purity of the subject, **which is a great thing**. For even the most sagacious men sometimes stumble in their mixtures because they have employed foreign substances. From this arise those infinite complaints and cases where these or those processes succeed now **happily**, and then **unhappily**. For as the Jurists say, *the smallest circumstance changes the law* <note>original: "minimam circumstantiam jus variare"</note>, so, as will appear later, the smallest circumstance—time, order, or inadvertence—sometimes overturns the entire operation. Moreover, a very skillful and sufficient preparation of subjects <margin>No. 6.</margin> is necessary, and it brings much utility if it is always at the ready; for many combinations are hindered by a lack of subjects. For before you run to the pharmacy for every single subject—where it is either falsely kept or not kept at all—many processes and concepts are neglected and not brought into practice. Furthermore, even if you have the subjects, if you are either too **stingy** or too **prodigal** in applying them, it will again be detrimental; therefore, you will go most safely by the middle path. For just as it would be foolishness to pour out the aforementioned subjects uselessly and without reason, so it would be useless to keep them only for appearance and sight. Let this **alphabet of Nature** therefore stand ready, so that whatever occurs, you can immediately reduce it to practice. <margin>No. 7.</margin> It cannot be said with how little expense, how light a labor, and how great a delight and utility **many**, even the **weightiest** experiments can be undertaken, if everything is thus at hand. I have sometimes performed fifty experiments in the space of **one day**; indeed, if sometimes during the writing itself a difficulty arose regarding this or that experiment, I then immediately undertook the experience: since the Alphabet of Nature stood in the aforementioned order to the right of my desk, so that I was as ready for experimenting as for writing. I cannot, therefore, wonder enough at those who spend so much and such great sums of money on Chemical labors <margin>No. 8.</margin> and proceed I know not how, when they ought to throw away their money if they wish; but scoundrels and impostors gape for gold and silver, they turn away from nature, they waste money on delicacies, they steal gold, they hate concise combinations, and they love long, rambling processes, so that they may fatten their gullets in the meantime. I would believe in such a way that a great sum of money could be poured away, if someone wished to pour it away studiously and give credit to such scoundrels. <margin>No. 9.</margin> Within two years I have made over 3,000 combinations, and indeed not in such a small quantity **by which the truth of the experiment is not infrequently hindered**; nevertheless, as far as materials are concerned, I have spent barely more than **one hundred ducats** <note>A gold coin used across Europe; Becher is emphasizing that real science is cheaper than the fraudulent "get rich quick" schemes of pretenders</note>: excepting, however, the charcoal and vessels, which are absolutely required: especially glass and earthenware, the catalog <margin>No. 10.</margin> of which we have set forth in our *Chemical Oedipus* <note>Reference to Becher's work *Oedipus Chymicus* (1664), a guide to chemical terminology and equipment</note>. It is not indeed hidden from me that there are certain...

### Book I, Section IV, Chapter II

(As Sir **Oswald** <note>original: "Oswaldus"; referring to Oswald Croll, a famous 17th-century Paracelsian chemist</note> says) there are those who boast that they *have spent so many thousands*; as if it were a glory to *waste money and know nothing*. Once these matters of rank are set aside, you must now prepare yourself for "syllables"—namely, the practical experience of the principal combinations, mixtures, solutions, and reactions—so that you may know the nature of bodies as exactly as possible. For just as one never arrives at a perfect *reading* without a knowledge of the *syllables*, so too without a knowledge of the sympathy and antipathy, the joining and dissolving of bodies, and their actions and reactions, one never arrives at a complete understanding of a compound's Nature or a sufficient knowledge of it. Our "puffers" <note>original: "ciniflones"; a derogatory term for amateur alchemists who spent their time blowing at charcoal fires without theoretical knowledge</note> do not pay attention to this; instead, gaping only for gold, *they wish to read the most difficult script* while remaining ignorant of the simple knowledge of the letters.

<margin>No. 11.</margin>
For this reason, it happens that among countless chemical writers, you will not find even one who has written so much as a page about these combinations—these "first syllables," as it were, of compound bodies. Consequently, nothing of the **Spagyric** <note>Spagyric refers to the alchemical art of separating substances into their components and then recombining them for medicinal use</note> study is known to us except the name. To come closer to the matter, however, certain things must be observed above all regarding such combinations.

<margin>No. 12.</margin>
I pay very little attention to *Time* when I wish to experiment with anything of this kind. For just as noble human beings are generated at all times, and as vegetables in the Indies proceed in their growth at any time of planting due to the perpetual heat, so it is certain that subterranean things are also generated at all times. Therefore, I have absolutely no esteem for the conjunctions and constellations of planets or celestial houses and similar trifles, which *the astrologers make necessary to us so that they themselves may seem necessary*; nor have I ever observed anything contrary to happen because of them, or a different effect to be produced. What they babble about regarding glass and the **regulus of Antimony** <note>The "regulus" is the metallic form of antimony, often cast into a star-shaped crystal</note>—that they turn out more beautiful under a clear sky—is utterly false, since I have made them most successfully even in cloudy and rainy weather. However, it is entirely necessary to observe *Time* with respect to the operator; namely, that there be a *sober, serene, composed, wise, perceptive mind, attentive to all circumstances, not distracted, diligent, pure, and tireless*. For what **Ovid** says about writing poems—that *they require the seclusion and leisure of the writer* <note>original: "secessum scribentis, & otia quaerant"</note>—applies very well to such chemical combinations, so that they are not done in vain, do not cause harm, but are instead beneficial.

<margin>No. 13.</margin>
As I have said, the smallest circumstance sometimes stands in the way, which is why everything must be diligently observed: *material, vessels, weights*, and especially *order*. For the same subjects, taken in the same weight, will nevertheless have a vastly different effect if they are mixed without order, even if it is believed that there is no difficulty in this. The following mixture will serve as an example. Take **spirit of salt** <note>hydrochloric acid</note>, **oil of tartar** <note>a concentrated solution of potassium carbonate</note>, and **sal ammoniac** <note>ammonium chloride</note> in equal parts, and mix them. If you proceed according to the order of this process and mix the spirit of salt with the oil of tartar first, a reaction of both will occur and a new mixture will form; if the sal ammoniac is then added and the whole mixture is driven by fire, you will receive a **sublimate** <note>a solid substance produced by heating and then cooling, bypassing the liquid phase</note>. On the other hand, if you err in the order and mix the sal ammoniac with the oil of tartar first, before you pour in the spirit of salt, you will receive **spirit of urine** <note>ammonia gas or solution</note>, and a mixture far different from the first. From this it is clearly evident that the order and method of mixing must be observed.

<margin>No. 14.</margin>
But what is greatest of all is that *everything which happens must be diligently noted, including what can help or hinder the mixture*; therefore, pay attention to the *residues* <note>original: "faeces"</note>, to those things which evaporate,

# Subterranean Physics

...boil, or distill; you must accurately attend to the color, the thinning, and the weight of what remains, and examine each detail. For often *we have thrown away the kernel among the dregs and kept the shells for their outward shine* <note>original: "nucleum in facibus abjecimus, & putamina in splendore servavimus"; a metaphor for missing the essential substance while focusing on worthless byproducts</note>. Since the Author of Nature is inscrutable, who could doubt that his daughter, Nature, can never be sufficiently known?

<margin>No. 15.</margin> Lastly—though I truly ought to have placed this in the *first* position—**reason** must be applied above all else. You must know what you desire to test and what your goal is, lest, lacking this guiding star <note>original: "Cynosura"; the Greek name for the constellation Ursa Minor, used here as a metaphor for a guiding principle</note>, you are swept away into a vast sea of uncertainties. For there are many who have consumed their entire lives in experiments; but because they did not organize them into certain principles and categories, nor consider them according to their efficient causes and effects, it profited them as much as if they had done nothing at all. For any thing, when deprived of its use, belongs to the realm of non-being rather than being.

Therefore, certain axioms and boundaries must be established for you to follow. And since the end and scope of this work is *to perceive the simpler mixtures, decompositions, solutions, and reactions of subterranean things*, this is the path you must follow: the one that leads you most directly there. Specifically, you must mix one thing with another and see whether the things being mixed are compatible or contrary.

For example: mix metal with metal, salts with salts, and spirits with spirits; then, once you know the properties of each class, mix those as well. Treat *metals with salts or spirits; mix spirits with salts*: and let your whole study persist in asking questions. For example: what will **nitric acid** <term>aqua fortis</term> do with gold? What will it do with silver, what with iron, what with tin, what with **antimony** <term>antimonio</term>? What will happen if you pour in a solution of **distilled vinegar** <term>spiritus aceti</term>, or **ammonia** <term>spiritus urinæ</term>, or **hydrochloric acid** <term>spiritum salis</term>, or **potassium carbonate** <term>oleo tartari</term>? How are oily, salty, urinous, metallic, earthy, and shelly substances dissolved and **precipitated** <note>precipitated: the process of a solid settling out of a liquid solution during a chemical reaction</note>? Why and how does a compound of **sal ammoniac** <term>salis armeniaci</term>, **mercuric chloride** <term>sublimati</term>, and **cinnabar** <term>cinabrii</term> <note>cinnabar: a bright red mineral consisting of mercury sulfide, the primary ore of mercury</note> coalesce and then get torn apart again? In this way, you should pose many questions which you will then decide through practice; and you should always move from the complex decompositions back to the simpler elements by performing an "anatomy" <note>anatomy: here meaning the chemical analysis or breaking down of a substance into its component parts</note> of every subject.

<margin>No. 16.</margin> It is true, however, that it is easier to put these things into practice than it is to show the way to that practice—namely, how to pre-establish similar questions, various concepts, and inventions. Therefore, it would have been greatly desired that someone, studying for the public good, had published a *synopsis of such questions and resolutions—if not all of them, then at least the principal ones*. How convenient that would be, and how much praise that person would deserve! For truly, they would discover an entirely new field of doing good, which no one until now has even entered.

<margin>No. 17.</margin> For in common works of Physics, you will not find even a word about these things. The **Galenists** <note>Galenists: followers of the traditional medical system of Galen (2nd century AD), which relied on the four humors rather than chemical analysis</note> know nothing besides the inspection of urine; but they do not even know the "anatomy" or the chemical mixture of that. Where would they have learned it, since neither Aristotle nor Galen mentions these matters by so much as a word? Indeed, in the Universities, there is no one to teach these things. Even the **pharmacists** <term>Pharmacopolæ</term>, if they do know anything, know it from experience without the guidance of reason. As for our "little new doctors" in the Universities, they devote more effort to *carnal mixture* <note>original: "mixtioni carnali"; a biting pun by Becher, suggesting the students are more interested in sex/worldly pleasures than chemical mixtures</note> than to this; they consider themselves learned enough if they can force "occult qualities" <note>occult qualities: a traditional philosophical catch-all term used to explain phenomena that couldn't be understood through the five senses</note> upon people and kill the sick methodically. They think of nothing less than the hidden secrets of nature, even though no medicine can be skillfully prepared without this science, the virtues of no subject can be clearly known, and no disease can be fundamentally diagnosed or...

# Book I. Section IV. Chapter II.

...can be cured. For just as Spagyric <term>Spagyric: A term for alchemical medicine, from the Greek words meaning "to separate and to combine."</term> physics is by far the most excellent of all, so Galen himself and all his followers are worthless compared to Spagyric medicine—that is, the method of understanding and curing diseases based on Spagyric foundations. This is because the Spagyrics provide both evident reasons and solid cures, while the Galenists, bound only by the limits of their vocabulary, attempt to restore the sick with fantastical and imaginary powers and qualities. Meanwhile, they flatter themselves marvelously and, in their pride, despise all others.

Wretched owls! <note>original: "Miseræ noctuæ!"; Becher uses the owl as a metaphor for those who are blind to the light of truth and prefer the "darkness" of old, incorrect theories.</note> Though you are granted the privilege to fly into the homes of the great and nest there, you truly possess no happiness except for the fact that you do not know how much you do not know; in this alone are you blessed—especially if others are as ignorant of your ignorance as you are. Believe me, however, that you will one day give an exact account before God for your pride, ignorance, envy, and indeed your slander. For it would be your duty, you who receive many thousands annually from Princes, to apply yourselves to the restoration of medicine; instead, you take the money and leave the care of patients to the pharmacists, satisfied only with the inspection of urine <note>original: "solo lotio contenti"; a critique of uroscopy, the common practice of diagnosing all ailments by merely looking at a flask of urine.</note> so that you do not appear to be doing nothing. 

Furthermore, with your insuperable greed, you ward off all others with deceits and lies, lest others should do what you ought to be doing. Thus, miserable patients are deprived of all help—both your own (which is non-existent or meager) and that of outsiders—because of your trifles. It is not enough for you to kill the sick, unless you first impoverish them with your superfluous and most foolish Galenic mixtures, which are utterly inconsistent and long-winded; it is as if it does not satisfy you to kill them unless you also reduce the patients to extreme expense at the same time. Meanwhile, when a patient might sometimes be restored at very little cost and time by Spagyric means, you lying Harpies <note>original: "Harpyiæ"; mythological monsters with the faces of women and the bodies of birds, known for stealing food and leaving a foul stench.</note> screech nothing but "poisons" from your filthy mouths to deter the patient from the offered help. 

O, "conscientious" Physicians, to whom a trivial little gift is more dear to the heart than the truth, or the honor and life of their neighbor! I would rather hear pigs grunting in a pen than be present at your councils, wickednesses, and follies. What good fruit is to be expected from you in the refinement of studies and sciences, you who are so filthy and ignorant in practice that the most "skilled" among you—unless he does so by chemical means—cannot even discern Salt of Tartar from Cream of Tartar? <note>Salt of Tartar (potassium carbonate) and Cream of Tartar (potassium bitartrate) were common chemical substances; Becher is mocking the physicians' lack of basic laboratory knowledge.</note> O, expert "chief physicians," you are worthy only of feeding Salt of Tartar to pigs about to be slaughtered so they do not need a knife, and worthy of being raised to the ranks of Nobility and Barony for it—even if you reward those thoughtless "ennoblers" with that same "coin" and tyranny, which is the only thing in you worthy of praise.

<margin>No. 18.</margin> I return, therefore, to the Chemists. It should have been their duty to omit those fabulous writings and bring to light the desired practical combinations; but they too gape for gold and seek gold day and night. Indeed, what is stupider, they seek books that might teach them how to make it; they study them, read them through, and spare no expense or time in experimenting with them. In this one thing alone are they more honest than the aforementioned Galenists: they harm their own purses, not the lives of their neighbors. 

Therefore, those most noble Spagyric combinations are far exiled from this place, and where, I ask, shall they be found, if they are not found even where they ought to be found in their own place? I know, curious reader, what you are about to say: that it is easy to command, but hard to execute. But know that both to command and to execute are very easy for me; for with the same effort by which I have woven the web of this writing...

# Subterranean Physics

### Book I. Section IV. Chapter II.

...I have woven, and performed experiments; I have, I say, written down these same combinations and <margin>No. 19.</margin> organized them into certain classes. It was my intention to commit these to print under the title *A Thousand Chemical Hypotheses on Subterranean Matters*, but hindered by other business, I was unable to read through them after they were transcribed by my secretary. In the meantime, the book fairs <note>Becher refers to the great trade fairs in Frankfurt and Leipzig, which were the primary venues for announcing and distributing new scholarly books in the 17th century.</note> have passed, but if it pleases God, they will perhaps be added to this writing in place of an index in the future, or if it seems best, they will be printed separately. These include the *primary combinations, propositions, and practical resolutions*, with their attached *causes and reasons*. This writing will serve as a sort of handbook <term>handbook: Original Latin "manuductio," literally a "leading by the hand" or an introductory guide.</term> to the rest, which are infinite, and which I leave to others.

For no age will suffice to experiment with every combination; there will always be something remaining. If, from that time when that wretched itch for writing <note>original: "pessimum illud scribendi cacoëthes"; a reference to the Roman satirist Juvenal’s phrase for an uncontrollable, often pathological, urge to write.</note> broke out among the chemists, labor had been spent on these combinations and honestly brought to light instead of fables and false processes, what a treasure of experiments and combinations would we now possess? And how deeply would we have penetrated into the secrets of Nature? On the contrary, what a shame, what proof of our ignorance and negligence! That among so many chemical writers and such a vast supply of books over so much time, not even one can be found who has written even a page on this matter—*on which, nevertheless, the entire hinge of the spagyric study depends.*

Let us therefore be the first to break the ice; we will open the field to you, but we will not fill it. We will show the way, but in such a way that you follow, not only in theory but in practice. For it is not enough for you to read the aforementioned *thousand Hypotheses*; it is required that you apply your hand and gain experience, relying on this as a guiding thread <note>original: "filo ariadneo"; a reference to Ariadne's thread in Greek mythology, used by Theseus to navigate the Labyrinth. Becher views his method as the only way to escape the "maze" of false alchemy.</note> as your leader. You must know which combinations to work with at the beginning and how you ought to operate, until finally, having become accustomed to it, you may create new ones from your own mind. Indeed, while you reduce these prescriptions of mine to practice, new observations will occur to you, which you will be able to record alongside mine as if in <margin>No. 20.</margin> commonplaces <term>commonplaces: From the Latin "loci communes," notebooks where scholars categorized and stored useful information and observations under thematic headings for easy reference.</term>.

With these "conjunctions of syllables" having been put forward, a third task remains: namely, that you learn to read and to combine whole "words"—that is, that you now work out entire processes. I do not mean those foolish and false ones, whose emptiness you will easily recognize at first glance when you read them, supported as you are by your previous experiments. From these, you will easily be able to gather whether this or that combination is suitable and fitting, or what will come of it. For just as words consist of syllables, so do chemical processes consist of various combinations.

I would wish, therefore, that you work out those processes which you have made for yourself, which will lead you to a further knowledge of nature. Above all, however, undertake an "anatomy" of subterranean subjects. Once this is known, purify the impure, fix the volatile, take away what is in abundance, add what is lacking, fashion new mixtures, and in a word, strive for this: that you provide a remedy for diseases and for the household economy. This will indeed be easy, since Nature is most wealthy and, in chemical matters, she has no middle ground; she gives either <margin>No. 21.</margin> nothing or everything. For the smallest medicine that certainly cures some disease is more precious than all gold and gems; furthermore, the smallest improvement of metals—even if it yields no more than a single ducat <term>ducat: A gold coin used as a standard of currency across Europe; Becher is arguing that even minor successful transmutations are revolutionary.</term> at one time—is more powerful than the treasury <note>original: "gazophylazio"; a term of Greek origin meaning a treasury or storehouse, often used in a royal or biblical context.</note> of the Emperor himself. For who among Kings or Princes is there who can assert that he possesses even a single ducat, which [every time...]

...as often as one wishes, one can multiply these results in every place, state, and condition, without external help, the burdening of subjects <note>Becher is likely referring to the heavy taxation of citizens to fund state projects or wars.</note>, or the intervention of other uncertain matters. This is the genuine way; it requires no arms, no deceptions or tricks, nor miracles to make you rich—indeed, more powerful than all Kings. Nature uses a simple path; indeed, in a moment the cataracts of the dark mind are sometimes dissolved so that one can see how wonderful, rich, and powerful nature is. Aim for this goal, so that, as *our Majorcan Philosopher* <note>Ramon Llull (c. 1232–1315), a famous polymath and alchemist from Mallorca whose "Art" attempted to organize all knowledge through combinations of symbols.</note> says, *you may reach such a temperament that you become worthy to be seated at the table of the twelve peers* <note>original: "ad mensam duodecim parium"; a reference to the legendary paladins of Charlemagne, symbolizing the highest rank of nobility and excellence.</note>. This could easily happen if you join even one suitable syllable. 

And so we have put forward these few things concerning the method to be established, by which a solid knowledge of nature and the <margin>No. 22.</margin> mixture of things is reached; I hope they will not be unpleasant to the reader. Now, in accordance with our plan and the title of this Section, we shall deal with some things concerning the mixture itself, albeit *theoretically*, so that the reader may more easily follow those things which we shall demonstrate *practically* in the second book. For all practice without theory is uncertain, and theory without practice suffers from the same disease; yet theory must precede practice. For before you do anything, it is necessary that you know what you are doing; the will precedes the act, and reason precedes the will. Since, therefore, in the second book we undertake the anatomy of subterranean subjects <note>That is, the chemical analysis of minerals, metals, and earths found underground.</note>, in which we shall often appeal to theory, we have deemed it necessary to put forth the theory here, as far as is required. Especially since in the sixth section of this book we shall deal with the *practical* difference of mixtures, it was required above all that we derive it from the intrinsic nature of the mixture. We must seek this mixture not from elsewhere but from the very principles of mixture themselves, wherefore we shall now begin with them in this place.

<margin>N. 1.</margin> If you read what the <term>Peripatetics</term><note>Followers of Aristotle's philosophy, dominant in medieval and early modern universities, whom Becher often critiques for being too theoretical.</note> have written regarding mixture, you will indeed find many terms, but all are established in such a way that they are entirely useless in practice. For that entire school of philosophy aims only at imposing names on things, and thereafter brawling and arguing about them; hence it happens that no practical application can be drawn from such study. Yet when things are actually discovered and reduced to practice, they immediately add an innumerable heap of terms. Thus, they have many terms for mixture which they force upon children; these students learn such names without knowing what they signify. Thus, under pretentious titles such as *the action, passion, and mixture of the Elements, the generation and destruction of natural bodies, temperament and decoction*, and others, they treat many empty things. They use various terms, such as *virtual contact of magnitudes, physical contact, primary action, secondary action, primary and secondary qualities, activity, similarities, dissimilarities, incipient action, imperfect and perfect action, the remaining of elements in a mixture, the refracted forms of elements, intensity, remission, etc.* Finally, there are infinite others, from all of which they could not provide a single reason why <term>salt of tartar</term><note>Potassium carbonate, which absorbs moisture from the air (deliquesces).</note> *flows easily in air and fire, yet if it is precipitated with <term>spirit of salt</term>,<note>Hydrochloric acid.</note> it does so no longer, neither in air nor in fire.* They will say, of course, that the qualities have been changed—which everyone knows—but as to *why* they are changed, and *how*, here there is deep silence. Nor could they assign evident reasons even if they were to sweat for eternity alongside their master Aristotle. Therefore, the doctrine of mixture must be investigated more closely and clearly if it is to serve practice, for nature holds the rule in practice. Whatever the most subtle wit might speculate upon for a whole year and set forth in the most refined terms—if it contradicts nature when it comes to practice—it is nothing; it appears as mere trifles, and the whole <margin>N. 2.</margin> speculation collapses in a moment. Therefore, those terms are true, and 그 speculation good, with which practice and nature agree. From this foundation, we shall draw forth certain things which serve our purpose; for it is not our intention to explain the entire doctrine of mixture, since we have undertaken only to discourse on the mixture of subterranean things. We set aside, *firstly*, the mixture of quantity, such as when three or four pounds are mixed together (which some call the mixture of the continuous), since the mixture we are <margin>N. 3.</margin> to treat in this place is *Physical mixture*. This is twofold: namely, *superficial* and *central*. I call it *superficial* when things are mixed, but in such a way that they can be separated again; that is, when <term>spirit of wine</term><note>Ethanol or high-proof alcohol.</note> is poured over wormwood and mixed with its parts. For when it is distilled off, the extract of wormwood remains in its own <gloss>constitution</gloss> <note>original: "crasi"</note> and the spirit of wine in its own. But I call it *central* when things are mixed so that they cohere and constitute whole bodies. As when rain-<margin>N. 4.</margin>water *is mixed with a seed of millet, and is altered into the mixture of the millet.* The basis of *superficial* mixture is *rarefaction*; for dense and coarse things are penetrated, resolved, and mixed by rare and subtle things, so that they are scattered into the smallest particles which cling within the rare substance. From this come various solutions and precipitations, according to the thinness and density of the solvent and the solute. Thus silver...

He introduces a distinction between "superficial mixture" (reversible combinations like tinctures) and "central mixture" (irreversible transformations like biological growth).</summary>

<meta>On the previous page, Becher critiqued the theoretical jargon of the "Peripatetic" (Aristotelian) philosophers, arguing that their definitions of "mixture" were useless for practical chemistry. Here, he begins to define his own mechanics of how substances combine, distinguishing between temporary physical mixtures and permanent chemical bonds.</meta>

Book I. Section IV. Chapter III.

is dissolved in <term>aqua fortis</term><note>original: *aqua forti*; literally "strong water," the historical name for nitric acid.</note>, copper is precipitated by iron, and copper by iron; this occurs because one is more subtle and penetrable than the other. In this way, many solutions and mixtures are made which appear "central" <note>Deeply or chemically bonded.</note>, but in truth are only "superficial" <note>Surface-level or physical mixtures that are easily reversed.</note>. <margin>N. 5.</margin> Truly, the basis of a central mixture is the **appetite for the dry and the moist**. For those things which are mixed based on this foundation are strongly combined and become new "decompounds" <note>Becher’s term for a compound made of other compounds.</note>. For all bodies are composed of principles; but even these compounds, when mixed among themselves, create **new mixtures**, which are called **decompounds**. For example, when **native sulfur** <note>original: *sulphur vivum*.</note> and **quicksilver** <note>original: *argentum vivum*; mercury.</note> are mixed and sublimated, **cinnabar** <note>Mercury sulfide, a bright red mineral.</note> is produced; this is a **decompound** made from two compounds, namely sulfur and quicksilver. For both sulfur and quicksilver are themselves compounds and consist of parts, as we shall prove later.

<margin>N. 6.</margin> To explain what we have said so far with an example: if **oil of vitriol** <note>Concentrated sulfuric acid.</note> is poured over filings of either copper or iron, it will not dissolve them because it is too dense; on the other hand, when it is poured with a portion of water and thinned out, it dissolves them immediately. From this we clearly see that "rarity" <note>Low density or thinness.</note> and "density" are the governing rules of a superficial solution. Therefore, from this solution—if it is freed from dregs through filtration (which relates to the mixture of quantity, for it separates the part of the quantity, since the dregs, or that which is not dissolved, is of the same nature as that which is dissolved, differing only in that not all of it could be dissolved by the solvent due to a lack of quantity)—through the evaporation of the water, a **new mixture** comes forth, namely **vitriol** <note>Metallic sulfates, such as copper sulfate or iron sulfate.</note>. This is a certain **decompound** made from oil of vitriol and metal, but it is **superficial**. For when treated with fire, the subtler parts are resolved again, while the fixed parts remain.

<margin>N. 7.</margin> On the contrary, let **oil of tartar by deliquescence** <note>A liquid form of potassium carbonate formed when the salt absorbs moisture from the air.</note> be precipitated with **spirit of salt** <note>Hydrochloric acid.</note>; the dry earth which is in the salt of tartar—which is extremely hot and caustic when treated with great fire—will seize the humidity from the spirit of salt. If it is then thickened, it will make a **new mixture**, which can no longer be dissipated by any art, for it arose from the "appetite for the moist and the dry." Therefore, the **Magnetism of Nature** has two poles: **the rare seek the dense, and the dry desire the moist**; and from these two foundations, whatever joins together in the nature of things is mixed, even though heat may intervene as an instrument.

For since heat thins the parts, it opens the ways for both superficial and central mixture. <margin>N. 8.</margin> Various effects arise from these proposed foundations; for the rare seek the dense in proportion to their own rarity. Hence, **highly rectified spirit of wine** <note>High-proof, distilled alcohol/ethanol.</note> dissolves and extracts more than a less rectified spirit; but when it reaches the degree of temperament <note>The point of saturation or balance.</note>, it stops. <margin>N. 9.</margin> For **water** dissolves only as much **salt** as its degree of rarity permits; the rest sinks to the bottom. For the same reason, **Wine** does not dissolve more from **glass of antimony** <note>A glass-like form of antimony oxide used as an emetic.</note> than it can hold. For the extremely rare and the extremely dense do not agree. Hence, **highly rectified spirit of wine** does not unite with a **highly fixed alkali** unless water intercedes. It must be added that various colors, smells, and tastes arise from superficial mixture. <margin>N. 10.</margin> For example, if you dissolve copper in *aqua fortis* and add **spirit of salt** to the solution, it will turn green; if you add **spirit of urine** <note>Ammonia solution.</note>, it will turn violet; but in *aqua fortis* alone, it will be blue. These colors do not come from the solvent, nor from the thing dissolved, but arise according to the diversity of the "rarities" of the solvents. If you dissolve **silver** in *aqua fortis* and add **spirit of urine**, the smell will vary according to the digestion; soon it will breathe out the artificial scents of peaches, oranges, and other fruits. **Vinegar** <note>original: *acetum*.</note> becomes sweet over lead; and over shells and

### TEXT.

In the preceding chapter, we said that the appetite of the moist and the dry, or the magnetism of earth and water, through the mediation of rarefaction and condensation, exists as the primary cause of mixture; that this is so is certain in every way, and it agrees with our prior theory on the creation of heaven and earth: where we proved that the first mixture occurred with earth and water, through the mediation of the rarity of heaven.

<margin>N. 1.</margin>
Earth, therefore, behaves in mixture as the male, and water as the female; hence Adam was created from earth, and Eve from Adam, which is why males are of a drier nature than females. Earth, therefore, is rightly called by Trismegistus <note>original: "Trismegistus"; referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Egyptian sage and father of alchemy.</note> the mother of all perfection, as if the foundation of all mixture. And since it is our intention in this place to consider the diversity of mixed things and mixtures in the relation they have with one another, so that the nature of the mixture and the specific difference of the mixed things may become clearer; before all else, we must turn to certain distinctions, according to the saying: *he who distinguishes well, teaches well.* We said, however, in the third section of this book, first chapter, that all mixed things are reduced to three classes; for they are mixed either from water with water, or from earth with earth, or from water with earth.

<margin>N. 2.</margin>
In this place, however, we shall make a division of the more specific two latter mixtures, and we shall establish that it is threefold: namely, animal, vegetable, and mineral. In which three kingdoms not only are the mixed things diverse, but also the mixtures are diverse...

Rightly, then, does Trismegistus <note>Hermes Trismegistus, a legendary Hellenistic figure to whom many foundational alchemical and philosophical texts were attributed</note> call the Earth the mother of all perfection, as it is the foundation of every mixture.* And since it is our intention in this place to consider the diversity of mixtures and mixed things in the relation they have to one another—so that the nature of the mixture and the specific difference of the mixed things may become clearer—we must first turn to certain distinctions, according to the proverb: "he who distinguishes well, teaches well." <margin>No. 4.</margin> Yet many things vary regarding the method, the subject matter, and the time required. *For minerals, since they have a form that is entirely uniform, simple, and composed of similar tiny particles, and is complete in itself, are mixed more quickly; they achieve their mixture through growth alone. From this it follows—as we shall later prove—that they are perfected in an instant, provided all the necessary requirements are present. Vegetables, on the contrary, have parts that are far more dissimilar; for their perfection, growth alone is not enough, but there must also be alteration and digestion—namely, the preparation of the parts, which is called "vegetation."* Animal mixtures are far more intricately crafted;
<margin>No. 5.</margin> *for, because they possess the faculty of motion, they require many vessels, channels, and organs. Hence, they are completed neither by growth alone, nor by vegetation—that is, the digestion and preparation of parts—but by the implantation of the animal spirit. For since the basis of the animal body consists of bones, these had to be clothed and moved: it was necessary for them to be joined by ligaments, moved by nerves, and for the nerves to be supported by muscles and nourished by blood. This blood had to be contained in veins, prepared by the heart and liver, and find its origin in the stomach and intestines, arising from food and drink. The whole was to be covered by skin. Truly, the movement of the nerves proceeds from the thinning and thickening <note>original: "raritate & densitate"</note> of the implanted spirit. Thus it was necessary to place something in animals that could, at will and in whichever part of the body it pleased, thin out or compress the aforementioned spirit or "nervous air." This thing certainly had to be of such a nature that it was "all in the whole"—that is, a most simple essence. Some call this the "fifth essence" of the stellar essence, others "the number that moves itself," others "the spirit congealed to the animal body," others the "fifth element," others "Entelechy" <note>An Aristotelian term for the "realization" or "vital force" of a living thing</note>, and we call it the*
<margin>No. 6.</margin> *Soul.* Whether this soul be rational or irrational, it is discerned and recognized by this certain and specific sign: that it moves. It does not only move the completed body, but it also perfects the body itself during the process of generation. For this perfection and preparation, which proceeds from the soul, must be called "generation," which shapes its own species according to the qualities of the underlying seed. I shall not define here whether the soul moves through the brain or in any other specific part of the body, nor whether the soul of a fox is different from the soul of a wolf; but I wish to conclude this one thing: that the soul concurs in the formation of the fetus and exists as the moving cause
<margin>No. 7.</margin> of that formation. *Therefore, animals require a unique workshop—namely, the maternal womb—and a slow heat, which is suitable for thinning and facilitates the operation of the soul.* For although the "form" <note>The blueprint or organizing principle</note> of the body to be produced lies hidden in the seed or male sperm (as is not doubted), yet without the help of the soul, it could not be brought from potentiality into reality, just as nerves could not move themselves. However, how the "form" is said to be within the sperm is hardly clear if we only stick to words; yet we see clearly that it is present, because the sons of a father
<margin>No. 8.</margin> are sometimes extremely similar to him, not only in body but even in the defects and diseases of the body. In what way it is present, "this is the task, this the labor" <note>original: "hic opus, hic labor," a famous quote from Virgil’s Aeneid referring to a difficult struggle</note>. ...to be, but are produced into action by the help of the soul; moreover, the soul works by means of **rarefaction** <note>original: "rarefactionis"; the process of making a substance less dense or expanding it, often through heat</note>, a movement which also belongs to it regarding the movement of the nerves. Nor is this so controversial in Metaphysics, since it is established that Angels and souls act by means of rarefaction, and it was believed so by the most ancient Philosophers. <margin>No. 9.</margin> *Therefore, the material form consists in the **seed** <note>original: "semine"</note>;* I call it material, not imaginary or verbal, but real and truly corporeal, which, through the addition <note>original: "accretionem"</note> of the female seed, comes into the first disposition of an actually formed body: which is then nourished by the uterine blood, and from a state of addition it passes into the stage of **vegetation** <note>the plant-like stage of growth and nutrition</note>, and from that into the genus of **animality** <note>the stage of sentient life and motion</note>. For all these things, not only a long time but also a *quiet and warm* place is required, entirely secure, safe, and immune from external mixtures. <margin>No. 10.</margin> *For the whole seed is the very and pure form,* which consists of the various particles of the entire animal body, varying by different weights <note>original: "gravitate"; here meaning density or specific gravity</note>, in which weight the entire *formation* consists—which is a *placement* <note>original: "locatio"</note>, or the relation of one place to another in a different position. <margin>No. 11.</margin> For every *image and form* consists in this: that various particles—some in this figure, others in another—varying by line, point, and place, all differ in weight. Hence quantity has always been considered the first and most natural attribute of a body. And although the particles of the lungs, liver, and heart are believed to be of a different substance than the bones, they are of a different substance precisely because they are of a different weight. For by that very fact, if they were altered in weight, they would necessarily also be changed in substance. For it is manifest from many other experiments that *quality arises from quantity*. But let us set these things aside and return to the seed, in which it suffices for us that particles of its own kind lie hidden from the universal animal form (as if in an **extract** or **essence** of a man); although these are mixed together, they nevertheless have a tendency, according to the weight of the members from which they proceeded, to arrange themselves in different positions and places if they are expanded <note>rarefied</note>, to which they are carried by their natural weight. No differently than if you were to mix tiny bodies of feathers, wood, and lead, and by adding mud reduce them to a paste; as soon as it is dissolved, whether in air or in water, each of these tiny bodies will seek that place to which it is carried by its natural weight. a principle and one total cause emerges: from which a single motion toward the production of offspring proceeds, maintaining a specific order. Once the seeds are conceived in the womb, they are nourished by the innate force of the uterus, and the latent power within the seed is awakened; the expression of the organs begins, and conception is said to have occurred. At this stage, the conceptus is called a <term>knema</term> <note>original: "knema"; from the Greek κύημα, referring to the product of conception before it is fully formed</note>. First, the spermatic parts are formed, and indeed all at once. Or, if the woman is not pregnant, this blood is sent to the uterus every month and purged through it, so that it does not burden the woman or become corrupt.

Since the fetus receives everything it needs from the mother after the first outline from the seed, the umbilical vessels were made—namely, a vein, two arteries, and the <term>urachus</term>—which all meet at the navel. The vein is an offshoot of the portal vein, to which it is continuous, acting as the infant’s nourisher; the two arteries are branches of the iliac branches of the descending aorta, through which arterial blood and spirit are communicated to the infant, and through which the infant draws spirit. The <term>urachus</term> <note>a duct connecting the fetal bladder to the umbilical cord</note> is carried from the base of the bladder to the navel. Once the infant is brought forth into the light, and there is no longer a need for this service, these vessels close up and function in the place of ligaments.

Physicians divide the entire time from conception to birth into two parts: the time of *formation*, from conception until the time the infant begins to move; and the time of *perfection*, which is from movement until birth. Others, however, divide it into three parts: namely, the *time of formation*, which *Hippocrates* (in *On the Nature of the Child*) defines as *forty* days for females and *thirty* days for males; the *time of movement*, which is commonly said to occur in the third month for males and the fourth for females; and the third, which is *birth*. Regarding the time of birth, it is *variable* in humans; however, experience teaches that a viable offspring is not delivered before half a year. One who is born in the seventh month is already viable. But according to Hippocrates, no one born in the eighth month ever lives; though some nevertheless maintain that even such a child is sometimes viable. The most legitimate and frequent time for giving birth is the *ninth month*; and most births occur from the fifteenth day of the ninth month until the fifteenth day of the tenth month. Although births in the eleventh month, and even after the eleventh month, have been noted by physicians, such births are to be referred to among those things that rarely happen. ...given to the white <note>original: "albi"; referring to the white of the egg</note>, since I have no quarrel with it. Furthermore, certain animals are found that give birth not only frequently, but even to many offspring at once, and moreover, more rarely. In most cases, all these things occur through the mediation of both sexes; in no kind of animal are the sexes confused, such that a female becomes a male, or a male a female—though some do not hesitate to affirm this regarding hares, although it could perhaps be conceded that <term>hermaphrodites</term> <note>individuals possessing both male and female reproductive organs</note> occur here more frequently than in other species. Thus far Sennertus <note>Daniel Sennert (1572–1637), an influential German physician and chemist</note>. Those who have written more clearly on these matters may also be consulted, such as the author of *On the Formed Fetus*, *Fienus on the Power of Imagination*, and *Sir Kenelm Digby on Sympathy and Antipathy*.

<margin>No. 24.</margin>
From the aforementioned points, we shall conclude nothing else but this: we prove that the method of **animal mixture is accretion and vegetation, occurring by the concurrence of the soul.** We attribute the entire animal form, which consists of <term>similar and dissimilar parts</term> <note>In Galenic medicine, "similar" parts are uniform tissues like bone or flesh, while "dissimilar" parts are complex organs like the hand or eye</note>, to the seed. Consequently, if you look at the internal mixture, it is mixed unequally, because it contains particles from every part of the human body, of different weight and quantity. These, through the mediation of <term>rarefaction</term> <note>the process of becoming less dense or expanding</note> by the soul, are carried spontaneously to their proper places, toward which they incline by a natural propensity. They begin with the particles of bone, which are the very first to be separated; then, as the superfluous moisture of the seed is expelled through evaporation (moisture which was required accidentally in the seed for the mixture of the seminal parts), they form into clumps. Upon these, the remaining parts are layered, they grow, they are altered, and finally, they are brought into being together.

<margin>No. 25.</margin>
Hence comes the long delay of this generation, and the corruptibility of the mixture. For since it consists of diverse parts—indeed, almost infinite ones—it follows that both the seed itself and that which is produced from the animal seed are easily dissolved, altered by any cause, and driven into different parts. From this arise various putrefactions and "boilings" <note>original: "exæstuationes"; internal heat or fermentations</note> in the animal body, and "ebullitions" <note>original: "ebullitiones"; eruptions or bubblings up</note> in the newborn, such as in **measles and smallpox.** Furthermore, human bodies rot in water as they do in earth; in fire, they are most easily destroyed. Although plants are also subject to these changes, animals suffer far more because of the powers and qualities of the soul, and the resulting **motion and imagination.** For from these arise **mental madness, corruption of the imagination, convulsion of the nerves,** and many other impediments.

<margin>No. 26.</margin>
Therefore, the animal mixture is by far the most **laborious and perilous** of all; the animal mixture is also the most corruptible of all mixtures, yet it consists in a unity of parts. Thus, the animal mixture shall be called **union**; the mixture of plants is **coagulation**; but that of minerals is **fixation**, as we shall now teach.

<margin>No. 27.</margin>
Indeed, although the animal mixture is the lightest and most corruptible of all mixtures—and this on account of the **infinite and diverse** particles of which it consists, due to the very diverse parts and shapes of the animal body—yet, because of those same things, it is the most miraculous and noble mixture of all. From this, above all, the omnipotence of the Creator can be gathered, who produced so many different animals, such diverse parts, instruments, vessels, nerves, veins, ducts, glands, valves, ventricles, intestines, bones, coverings, excrements, and many other things from earth alone. If we now look at the functions, motions, faculties, duties, and uses of such products and parts, and consider the harmony and admirable structure of the whole animal mixture—

## Section Four, Chapter Five
# On Vegetable Mixture.

->S Y N O P S I S.<-

*No. 1. The difference between animal and vegetable mixture. No. 2. <margin>No. 1.</margin>
Now the order of things calls us to Vegetables and their mixture; their mixture differs from the former <note>animal mixture</note> because it lacks animal spirit, and it occurs in the open, subject to the various changes and alterations of the air. For the parts capable of growth are not prepared beforehand, as blood is in the womb of animals; rather, they are prepared, digested, and "cooked" <note>original: "coquuntur"; early science often viewed biological ripening as a form of heat-driven cooking or "concoction"</note> within the plant itself. For this reason, it is acid or bitter at the beginning, and sometimes sweet toward the end. <margin>No. 2.</margin> This alteration occurs by way of confinement; wherein the effluvia of the earth and air flow in by means of water, and
