By the heat of the sun, and by the extraction and evaporation of watery parts, the earths are dried, digested, and thickened. Whence by day, plants are rendered arid and dry, and at night they attract moisture; which by day is again evaporated, and leaves behind in the plant the earthy substance it brought with it. Therefore, rain is called *fertile* because of the contents by which the plant is nourished and increased. This *astral substance* <note>In early modern science, "astral substance" referred to a celestial influence or "spirit" believed to descend with rain and dew to animate matter</note> flowing into the plant, and being cooked and digested by the sun, is altered into a pleasant substance—watery, oily, solid, and moist, subtle and gross—according to the diversity of the inflowing particles and the property of the seed,

<margin>N. 3.</margin>
which *already contains the parts of its own idea within itself* <note>original: "partes suæ ideæ"; the "idea" refers to the formative blueprint or internal design of the species</note>. By the same reasoning, when it putrefies in the earth through moistening, or rather is resolved and rarefied *according to the limits of weight and quantity*, just as happens in the animal seed, it exhibits the first "idea" of its plant. This is then increased by the inflowing and accruable parts until it reaches its absolute form. However, vegetables can be *hindered and promoted* in their growth in many ways.

<margin>N. 4.</margin>
They are hindered by *harsh wind, cold, and excessive heat*; they are promoted by the *strengthened power of the seed*, diligent cultivation, and the breathing <note>aeration</note> of the earth commonly called *stirring* <note>original: "gerürt"; a German term for tilling or turning the soil</note>, as well as by adding stakes for support against winds, coverings for winter, and moistening for drought.

<margin>N. 5.</margin>
Furthermore, they are altered by various *transplantations*; various *transmutations* and alterations are caused by art, both for the sake of form and for color, scent, and taste. Above all, the *fertility of the seed* can be promoted either by the strengthening of the earth into which it is inserted, or by the *imbibition* <note>soaking or steeping seeds in nutrient-rich liquids before planting</note> of the seed before it is committed to the ground. The most noble man Digby <note>Sir Kenelm Digby, 1603–1665</note> reports in his dissertation on the vegetation of plants that *the Fathers of Christian Doctrine in Paris, as a kind of monument, perpetually preserve a certain barley plant containing 249 stalks or stems, all of which take their origin from a single root or grain, and in which they themselves counted over 18,000 grains or seeds of barley*.

<margin>N. 6.</margin>
While we have not seen one quite so large, a not insignificant *imbibition* of this kind is known to us, by which any grain sometimes brings forth *twenty*, but ordinarily *eight stalks*, of such thickness that they had to be supported by sticks like carnations <note>original: "caryophyllorum"; can mean cloves or carnations, here likely referring to the garden flower</note>. But let us return to the goal and consider in what ways the *vegetable mixture agrees with the animal*. It is certain that it agrees greatly in *corruptibility* <note>propensity to decay</note>, and this because of the various particles constituting the whole mixture, which are easily altered. Though some mixtures decay faster than others—namely, those that have more *water* and less *earth*. Thus the *cypress* rarely or never putrefies; *apples* contract rot in the space of a single night. Therefore, the "mixture" is stronger in certain vegetables than in animals, as in the *oak*, and weaker in others, as in *flowers*, which wither in a single night. Just as among animals themselves, some are stronger than others according to the power and nature of the seed. Thus *Stags* live longer than men, the cause of which is that they live more moderately and are free from all cares; furthermore, they feed on vegetables, whereas men on the contrary feed on meat, *even though men eat no carnivorous animal*

<margin>N. 7.</margin>
*themselves*, because we believe their meat to be unhealthy, while we ourselves are meanwhile carnivorous in the highest degree. But let us return to plants; they also agree with animals in that they attract nourishment from one part and transmute it into substance from the other;

...just as a fetus is nourished through the umbilical cord and converts nutrients into flesh and blood. <margin>N. 8.</margin> For as I have accurately observed in a grain of barley, four days after it has been sown in the earth, it begins to break out from its sharper end and push out two tips—one tending upward and the other toward the bottom. Meanwhile, the matter within the grain liquefies and becomes milky, flowing into both tips. But as the grain withers from this gradual emptying, it contracts and finally falls away once all the seminal matter has flowed into the two tips. Then, these two tips grow together at the start of the point where the seed was flowing in. This is not unlike how the womb is closed once it has received the seed, which, once formed into an embryo, is afterwards nourished by the umbilical cord. For through the lower tip, which is called the stalk or the root, the new vegetable embryo is nourished by the earth; whereas before, it drank the "seminal milk" <note>original: "lac feminale"; a term for the nutrient-rich fluid found in a germinating seed</note> from the grain and received the power to convert the nourishment it attracts through the root (the umbilical cord) into itself. I have noted this with great zeal and through many diligent experiments.

<margin>N. 9.</margin> Nor does it agree with the animal mixture only regarding the umbilical cord and the root, but also in the formation of many parts, which are even named after their similarity to the parts of animals. These include solid and simple parts: flesh, pulp, nerve <note>original: "nervus"; in this context, it refers to the tough fibers or "sinews" of a plant</note>, vein, membrane, skin, root, stalk, stem, trunk, stalk, straw, shoot, trunk, bark, coat, inner bark, hide, wood, bones, pulps, tubers, the matrix <note>original: "matrix"; often used to describe the womb or the formative part of a plant</note>, the heart, marrow <note>original: "medulla"; the pith of a plant</note>, knots, branches, layers, the little fork, the shoot, the reed, the branch, the foliage, runners, the vertex, the cross, the eye <note>original: "oculus"; a common term for a plant bud</note>, wings, folds, joints, knees <note>original: "genicula"; nodes or joints on a stem</note>, internodes, vertebrae, sides, filaments, tendrils, sprouts, "heads of hair" <note>original: "comae"; refers to the foliage or tufts of a plant</note>, clusters, and leaves—in which one may observe flaps, notches, furrows, teeth, feathers, little ears, ribs, stalks, styles, and petioles. There are also flowers, fruits, seeds, and the almost innumerable parts, forms, and figures of all these. If any studious person wishes to consider these and combine them with the animal mixture, they will find a great similarity and analogy between the parts of both.

<margin>N. 10.</margin> And just as the mixture of an animal is considered the most wonderful of all because it happens in darkness, and so many operations are completed without the hand of any artisan being applied, and such varied organs are produced and perfected; certainly, the mixture of vegetables should be held in no less admiration. It should not be considered second to the former just because it happens before everyone's eyes. We see that it has progressed, but how it has progressed, even if *Argus* <note>In Greek mythology, Argus Panoptes was a giant with a hundred eyes, making him the ultimate observer</note> himself were standing by, he would still not be able to grasp it—so much does it deceive the sight and all the senses. 

<margin>N. 11.</margin> Nevertheless, it does not escape reason; for where the external senses fail, reason calls upon the internal ones and brings the mind into focus. The *most Noble and equally Learned Digby* <note>Sir Kenelm Digby (1603–1665), an English courtier and philosopher who wrote extensively on the "vegetation" of plants</note> provided us with an example of this in his description of the bean. There, he clearly shows us that we are utterly ignorant of those things we see daily; we stare at them like cows, or play with empty terms regarding them so as not to seem silent, as if it were better to speak words that signify nothing. He explains the bean to us, writing about it not in the manner of *Galen* <note>original: "Galenice"; referring to the traditional medical theories of the Greek physician Galen</note> or the *Peripatetics* <note>original: "Peripatetice"; referring to the followers of Aristotle, often criticized by early modern scientists for relying on abstract logic rather than observation</note>, but *Physically* <note>original: "Physice"; meaning according to the laws of nature and physical observation</note>—namely, concerning its *mixture, vegetation, and production*. Although it grows in everyone's gardens, its production is known to the minds and brains of only a few. And since the mixture and production of almost all vegetables is contained within his description of the bean, such that it might serve as an example for the rest, I believed my labor would not be unwelcome to the curious reader...

### Book I, Section IV, Chapter V. 115

<margin>N. 8.</margin>
*...just as a fetus is nourished through the umbilical cord, and converts nutrients into flesh and blood.* For as I have accurately observed in a grain of barley <note>original: "grano hordei"</note>, after it has been set in the earth for four days, it first begins to break out from beneath its sharper extremity and protrude two tips, one tending upward and the other toward the bottom; meanwhile, the material in the grain liquefies and turns milky <note>original: "lactescente"; referring to the conversion of starch to sugars/fluids during germination</note>, flowing into both tips. For through the lower tip, which is called the pedicle or the root, the new vegetable embryo is nourished from the earth; whereas previously it drank in the seminal milk from the grain and received the power of converting into itself the nourishment which it attracts through the root (the umbilical cord). This I have diligently noted through great study and many experiments.

<margin>N. 9.</margin>
*And it is not only in the matter of the umbilical cord and the root that it agrees with the animal composition,* but also in the formation of many parts, which are even named for their similarity to parts in animals; such as solid parts, simple parts, flesh, pulp, nerve, vein, membrane, skin, root, scape <note>a leafless flower stalk</note>, trunk, stem, stalk, straw, shoot, trunk, bark, tunic, inner-bark <note>original: "liber"</note>, hide, wood, bones, pulps, tubers, matrix <note>the womb or life-giving source</note>, heart, marrow <note>or pith</note>, nodes, branches, benches <note>structural supports</note>, little-forks, tendrils, reeds, spadices <note>flower spikes</note>, foliage, runners, the crown, the cross, the eye <note>original: "oculus"; a common term for a bud</note>, wings, folds, joints, little-knees, the internode, vertebrae, sides, filaments, curls, sprouts, tufts, clusters, and leaves, in which one may observe shreds, notches, furrows, teeth, feathers, little-ears, ribs, pedicles, styles, and petioles. There are also flowers, fruits, seeds, and of all these things the parts, forms, and figures are almost innumerable. If anyone wishes to consider these more studiously and combine them with the animal composition, he will find a great similarity and analogy between the parts of both.

<margin>N. 10.</margin>
*And just as the animal composition is judged to be the most wonderful of all,* because it takes place in darkness, and so many operations are completed without the hand of any craftsman being applied, and such varied organs are produced and perfected; certainly the composition of vegetables is to be held in no less wonder, nor ranked behind the former, for the fact that it happens before the eyes of all. <margin>No. 9.</margin>
Nor does the plant agree with the animal "mixture" <note>original: "mixtione"; the internal physiological composition</note> only regarding the *umbilicus and root*, but also in the formation of many parts which are even named after their similarity to parts in animals. These include solid and simple parts: flesh, pulp, nerve <note>original: "nervus"; in early botany, this referred to tough fibers or tendons</note>, vein, membrane, skin, root, scape, trunk, stalk, stem, stalk-pipe, straw, hillock, trunk-proper, bark, coat, inner bark <note>term: <term>liber</term> (the living inner bark of a tree that carries nutrients)</note>, hide, wood, bones, pulps, tubers, matrix <note>womb or formative layer</note>, heart, marrow <note>original: "medulla"; the pith of a plant</note>, nodes, branches, benches <note>original: "scamna"; likely referring to the tiered levels of growth</note>, shoots, sprouts, reeds, flower-stems, fronds, stolons, the crown, the cross, the eye <note>original: "oculus"; a common term for a budding node</note>, wings, folds, joints, knee-nodes, the space between nodes, vertebrae, sides, filaments, tendrils, young shoots, foliage, flower-clusters, and leaves. In these leaves, one may observe fringes, notches, streaks, teeth, feathers, ears, ribs, stalks, styles, and petioles. There are also flowers, fruits, seeds, and the almost innumerable parts, forms, and figures of all these. If any studious person wishes to consider these and combine them with the animal mixture, they will find a great similarity and analogy between the parts of both.

<margin>No. 10.</margin>
And just as the animal mixture is judged to be the most wonderful of all because it happens in darkness, and so many operations are completed without the hand of a craftsman being applied, and such varied organs are produced and perfected; certainly the mixture of vegetables should be held in no less admiration, and not placed second to the former. This is because plant growth happens before the eyes of everyone, and it can be seen to have progressed—yet how it progressed, even if Argus himself <note>Argus Panoptes, the hundred-eyed giant of Greek myth</note> were standing by, he could not perceive; thus it eludes sight and all *senses*. However, it does not escape reason; for where the external senses leave off, reason summons the internal ones,

<margin>No. 11.</margin>
and calls the mind into sharp focus. The *most Noble and equally Learned Digby* <note>Sir Kenelm Digby (1603–1665), an English courtier and natural philosopher who famously described the germination of a bean in his "Two Treatises" (1644)</note> provided us an example of this in his description of the bean. There, he clearly shows us that we are entirely ignorant of those things we see every day; we gaze at them like cows, or play with them using empty terms so as not to appear silent, as if it were better to speak words that signify nothing. He explains the bean to us, therefore, writing of it not in a Galenic or Peripatetic <note>referring to traditional medical or Aristotelian Scholastic philosophy</note> manner, but *Physically* <note>original: "Physice"; meaning according to the laws of nature and experimental observation</note>—namely, concerning its *mixture, vegetation, and production*. Although it grows in everyone's garden, its production is known to the minds and brains of very few. And since the mixture and production of almost all vegetables is contained within his description of it, such that it can serve as an example for the rest, I believed I would be performing a not unwelcome labor for the curious...

# Subterranean Physics
### [Page 116]

I believe I will be doing a service to the reader if I set down in this place, where it fits so well, a few points concerning the aforementioned **bean**, taken from Sir Digby’s <note>Sir Kenelm Digby (1603–1665), an English courtier and natural philosopher</note> dissertation on the growth of plants. I do this so that the benevolent Reader may see what we have discussed thus far applied in practice, and so that, by providing Sir Digby’s own words, we might satisfy those who perhaps do not have his aforementioned dissertation at hand (as it is not for sale everywhere and is difficult to obtain). It would be an inconvenience to them if they were merely held back by a simple citation. Therefore, in that most learned dissertation on the *growth of plants*, which that illustrious and now-blessed Hero delivered at Gresham College on January 23, 1660, in London, he provides an example of the bean and its growth on page 8. Although he occasionally makes digressions into other matters, we shall intentionally omit those for the sake of brevity and remain solely and continuously with the description of our bean.

<margin>No. 12.</margin>
"From this **Bean**, then," he says, "let us take the beginning of our observation. This dry, wrinkled, and compact substance is committed to the moist soil only at that time of year when the approaching Sun (that great <term>Archaeus</term><note>A vital force or "internal chemist" that Paracelsus and his followers believed governed the processes of life and nature</note> and the fire of Nature) begins to dilate and sublimate the surface of the earth. The Sun stirs up within the earth that volatile and <term>balsamic salt</term><note>A term for a nourishing, life-giving mineral principle thought to be essential for growth</note> which, during the winter, had been constricted, condensed, and driven back toward the center of the earth by the Sun's absence."

<margin>No. 13.</margin>
"Within its own substance, therefore, the bean must necessarily receive that saline moisture which surrounds it, lies adjacent to it, and makes an incursion into it from every side. The immediate effect following this moistening of the bean or acorn must necessarily be a swelling and an increase in size of the body. For as the substance of the water enters the substance of the grain itself (which lies in the water so that it may soak), these two substances necessarily require more space than either of them required previously on its own. From this it follows that the skin <note>original: "cortex"</note> which involves and contains the substance of the bean must necessarily crack and burst asunder to grant a path and freedom for the dilation of the swelling body. Once it has secured a place for itself in this manner, it proceeds to perform such actions as are natural and necessary for it in these circumstances."

<margin>No. 14.</margin>
"For previously, it was enclosed and hindered by a certain cold, dry, and hard external shell; now it immediately follows its own proper impulse. It will happen, therefore, to this swelling bean—now that its prison has been broken—that its fiery parts will attempt to overcome the watery ones. These fiery parts, calling upon certain cold and dry elements for assistance, will effect a certain violent agitation throughout the whole mass, shaking and driving one into the other. From this, an internal motion <note>original: "intestinus motus"</note> will excite a much greater dilation of the body in such a 'combustion' than was excited by its first moistening. For since the natural action of fire consists in flowing out from its center in every direction in the form of a continuous army of highly rarefied atoms, and since these atoms carry away with them a certain continuous trail of moist and viscous atoms, it follows necessarily that they require a larger field than they possessed at their first emergence to complete the intended work."

<margin>No. 15.</margin>
"Even though the swelling and the breaking forth <note>original: "eruptio"</note> of its fiery and viscous parts extend themselves here and there in every direction, according to the nature of fire, which flows from the center everywhere toward the circumference, this eruption will nonetheless be..."

### Book I, Section IV, Chapter V.

the eruption, which tends upward toward the air, is most effective because it traverses this path with less resistance than any other. For below the bean, the earth is more compacted than it is above; the soil above the bean has been moved and crumbled so that the ground is made loose and porous. Furthermore, lying beneath the bean is a vast quantity of earth which becomes less penetrable the deeper one goes. In contrast, the path from the bean to the surface of the earth is very short, and no obstacles are encountered there, because the Sun, air, dew, and rain perpetually strike the surface and exert their power to keep it light and spongy. Therefore, there must be a very swift and great convergence of these tiny bodies—the warm and sticky effluvia <note>In 17th-century science, "effluvia" were thought to be invisible flows of particles that carried physical properties or forces</note>—upward toward the air. When these encounter the cold air, which attacks them from every side, they contract themselves into a shape most suited to resisting the assaults of such an enemy, and this is the **circular** figure. For, speaking physically, the surrounding air presses these effluvia from every side, forcing them into the narrowest space (yet large enough to be useful to them); and since the **circular** figure is the most capacious of all shapes, the cold air, by condensing them, contracts them into such a form so that the greatest number of particles can be contained in the smallest space.

<margin>No. 16.</margin> Meanwhile, the effluvia that flow downward and toward the sides from the decaying husk of the bean are not entirely ineffective, though they are not as vigorous as those that ascend toward the air. The ascending and descending (or lateral) parts, which flow out from the **fermenting** mass, differ in this: the ascending parts are **warm, moist, airy, and consequently green and tender**; but the descending and lateral parts are drier, cold, and earthy, and thus **hairy, hard, and white**. The hardness and hairiness of these parts are further increased by being pressed and constrained by the earth.

<margin>No. 17.</margin> In this manner, then, the **root** is formed. Since it continually draws new sap from the moist earth surrounding it and abounds in heat—which continuously digests and **sublimates** <note>original: "sublimat" — In this context, to refine or lift a substance upward through heat, similar to the alchemical process of purification</note> the moisture it has attracted—and since the agents from the earth (that is, the **Sun and air**) also play their parts, it follows that a new, digested, and spiritual juice will be sublimated into that round, green, and tender part which broke out from the earth toward the air, and which we may now call the **stem**.

<margin>No. 18.</margin> And so, both heats—namely the internal and the external—concur to bring growth to this plant while both parts, the root as well as the stem, are continually filled with its new moisture. One of these, the stem, being exposed to the sun and winds, must necessarily become hard and hairy on its outer side to defend the internal part—which remains tender and succulent—against the external injuries of the air; otherwise, it would have been suppressed and constricted in its ascent.

<margin>No. 19.</margin> The other part, the **root**, continually thrusts its hard parts deeper into the earth, which renders it firm and fit for resisting the shaking of the winds so that it cannot easily be uprooted. Now, the same thing happens to the plant as happens to a burning wooden pyre: for the greater the quantity of wood added, the more intense the heat becomes. The same occurs here, for the growth of new **balsamic** <note>referring to "balsam," a life-preserving or healing resinous substance thought to be the vital principle of plants</note> juice, which occurs every day and hour, increases the heat inherent in the plant itself. It follows from this that a larger and larger quantity of juice is continually carried upward, and in this way, the stem becomes taller. But the further...

### Subterranean Physics

<margin>No. 22.</margin>
As the sap rises here from its common center, from which it is sublimated upward <note>Sublimation in this context refers to the early scientific theory that internal heat turns liquid sap into a vapor, allowing it to rise through the plant's channels</note>, it becomes softer, weaker, or more delicate, and less capable of resisting the attacks of the cold air. Consequently, when it can no longer ascend, it comes to a halt. Nevertheless, the innate heat <note>original: *Calor innatus*; a vital heat believed by early modern scientists to be the driving force of life and growth</note> continuously sublimates the moisture more and more. Since this moisture is not strong enough to pierce through the bark which it meets at the end of its journey, it swells into a certain **Bud** (*gemma*). This bud grows larger and larger until the bark covering this rising and daily "digested" <note>Digestion here refers to the process of maturation and chemical change brought about by heat</note> sap can no longer sustain its volume and activity, and it bursts open. From this ruptured bud or node, a new sap ascends in the same manner and progression as before, until,

<margin>No. 23.</margin>
at a **certain just distance** <note>original: *justam quandam distantiam*</note> appropriate to the causes that produce it, a new and fresh bud is formed. In this way, growth proceeds **from one bud to another**, each one surpassing the last, until finally the sap fails to raise the plant any higher. At the same time, the heat that sublimates this sap becomes weaker at such a distance, and the Sun begins to exert less influence upon it.

<margin>No. 24.</margin>
In a word, the entire **Economy of Nature** <note>The "Economy of Nature" refers to the organized, efficient system of laws governing the natural world</note> conspires to set a limit on the expansion of this plant. Some plants only grow upward, but in others, the bud is pressed in various directions by the ascending sap. This sap is pushed out toward the sides no less than upward, and in this way, a **branch** is created, bursting forth from the larger trunk.

<margin>No. 25.</margin>
It happens that as many branches burst forth as there are concurring circumstances and accidents (such as those we have mentioned) present to create them. But **when nature has placed a certain limit**

<margin>No. 26.</margin>
**on the expansion of her growing plant, and she grows tired**, as it were, of struggling longer with such robust and sinewy parts—that is, when the innate heat, the Sun, and the sap begin to fail in their operations (for the reasons I have touched upon)—Nature does not wish to remain idle or cease all operation. Instead, she applies herself to **actions of less strength and virtue**. By refining the sap more and more through light sublimations and the purification of the sap she has carried to such a height, she ensures that the thicker parts of the sap are continually cast out. These parts are neither fit to ascend higher, nor subtle enough to pass through those narrow channels which permit an easy passage to the purified and refined spirits. Thus, they remain in that place. However, these thick parts are not idle or without function (I call them "thick" only in comparison to the former spirits, for otherwise they are much more subtle and "cooked" than those remaining in the stalk, trunk, or cavity of the plant). It is true that they are not capable of accompanying the **ethereal spirit** <note>original: *æthereum spiritum*; the most refined and volatile portion of the plant's fluids</note>, which ascends much higher, as you will soon hear. Nevertheless, they are continuously increased by hourly additions of similar thick or subtle parts (for in truth they are either one or both: they are subtle compared to the thicker sap from which they were extracted by sublimation and which remains below in the body or trunk of the plant, and they are thick compared to the **fiery Spirit and balsamic oil** <note>original: *ardentis Spiritus, & balsamini olei*</note> that has been extracted from them by rectification). This perpetual and new flow of this fresh matter, or its gathering at the branches, fills them so much that they can no longer contain it. This is therefore the cause of their splitting in various places where this sap...

Its harder part often contains another part which is very dry but not so hard; the reason for this is that the outer surface of this earthy substance has been made remarkably hard by the concurrent causes that make it so, such that no moisture (or at least no significant quantity) can penetrate through it. ...[sublimated] and made accessible, and mortals might easily penetrate into its innermost recesses, if only a suitable and convenient method is maintained in its dissection and contemplation. From what has been said so far, it will not be difficult to satisfy those questions and doubts concerning this matter, which at first sight might seem full of difficulty and almost inextricable;

<margin>No. 35.</margin>
as, for example, for what reason the material of any tree would affect such or such a position and inclination with respect to the great universe. This is something that several not-very-wise "little scholars" wish to classify among the hidden mysteries of nature that exceed human understanding; furthermore, these same people contend that there is a certain secret instinct and sympathy between plants and the North Star. However, this is nothing other than this: a tender plant, in its first production, is constricted by the surrounding air and dissolved by its life-giving heat, but it is primarily restricted by cold and earthy **atoms** <note>original: *atomos*; here referring to minute particles or corpuscles, a key concept in 17th-century natural philosophy.</note> which, by the force of the Sun, are drawn from the poles toward the equator. For since there is a constant and perpetual course of these atoms between the equator and the poles, everything in their path must be affected by their continuous and repeated turns. And that side which is exposed to their immediate strikes must be most affected by them. On the other side, the Sun—which embraces the opposite part of the plant with its crowd of warm and moist atoms—must necessarily produce an effect contrary to the first. Thus you see a plain and evident reason why one side of a plant, compared to the other, cannot help but be dense, hard, and heavy, tending toward a sharp rather than an exact roundness. The other side, by contrast, will be spongy, tender, light, and extended or dilated, with a shape exceeding external roundness. Since this first impression serves as a rule for what follows—and the external casing or cavity of the plant is like a **mold** <note>original: *typi*; literally a "type" or "stamp," used here to mean a physical template that dictates future growth.</note> into which the succeeding sap is placed—it follows necessarily that in any year, month, or week (depending on the nature of the plant), as new sap is **sublimated** <note>original: *sublimatur*; the process of a substance being raised or refined through heat.</note> into the hardened cavity, it expands the casing to find a place for itself. It will acquire the same form and shape—pointed toward one side and blunt toward the other—that the casing already has and is capable of yielding. This will be repeated every year in trees and such plants as do not die annually. Through these circles or spirals of matter, you will not only know how the tree grew and increased according to how it was planted with respect to the North and South, but also how many years old it is. If you wish to transplant it to another location, you must take the greatest care to place it in the same orientation in which it previously grew. Otherwise, by exposing the tender, soft, and southern side of the tree to the sharp and dire "wedges" of the northern air, they will split it and harass it with their blows so that in a short time, it will breathe out its spirits and finally die. For the same reason, it happens that any piece of wood—even after it is deprived of life and cut—possesses the nature of a magnet and the poles that correspond to the universe.

<margin>No. 36.</margin>
*Thus far the most illustrious Sir Digby <note>Sir Kenelm Digby (1603–1665), an English courtier and natural philosopher whose works on the "Vegetation of Plants" are cited here.</note>, who in the place cited, discourses more fully on the remaining qualities of plants; it is not our purpose to bring all his words here,*

### T E X T U S.

<margin>No. 1.</margin> It remains for us to come to the mixture of minerals, for the sake of which we have provided the two preceding mixtures [animal and vegetable], so that we might indeed make a comparison of this third one with the previous ones, whereby its nature may come before our eyes more exactly and solidly. However, this mineral mixture differs first from the animal and vegetable because it consists of the simplest parts, which are homogeneous <note>Of the same kind or nature throughout.</note> to themselves; whereas those others coalesce from many corruptible particles, sticking together only by coagulation and union. For this reason, mineral mixture is most fixed <note>original: *fixissima*; in chemistry, "fixed" refers to a substance's resistance to change or evaporation when heated.</note>, and carries off the prize from the other three regarding its stability, the simplicity of its mixture, and its structure. Whence also mineral mixtures are far more indissoluble and less corruptible than animals and vegetables. For just as we wrote in the section on the production of all things, especially animals and vegetables: that the mixture of animals consists of a more subtle earth, and that of vegetables from a moderate one; for which reason they also very easily [dissolve] into [sub-]stance...

<margin>No. 2.</margin> For as we shall now demonstrate, in all perfectly mixed subterranean things, **there is only one and the same form**; but there is a diverse addition of nourishment. To prove this, we must recall from what was said before regarding animal mixture that the **form lies hidden in the seed**, and is nothing other than parts of the seed having different weights, and hence different inclinations and positions, and from this, various resulting shapes, according to the nature and diversity of each body as it was endowed by God at its first production. From this it follows that the "form" is that to which the remaining locatable parts adhere; the diversity of the form appears from the shape and location of these parts, as if from a presiding architect. Since, therefore, it is established that metals have an altogether **simplest**, everywhere homogeneous, and indeed **round** form in their smallest particles; it follows that the **seed of minerals is altogether one**, and consists not of diverse particles but of **one most simple subject**. For although it is most evident that there are diverse parts in the mixture of minerals, we are nevertheless speaking of that part acting as the **form and seed**, to which the rest cohere and from which they receive their shape. We have stated, however—and proved in the entire third section of this book—that **three** diverse things enter into a mineral mixture; which indeed also occurs in animal and vegetable mixture. 

In the animal, indeed, the *sperm* <note>original: *sperma*; used here in the sense of the vital "forming" agent.</note> holds the first place as the **former**; then the female seed <note>early modern embryology often posited two "seeds" or "semens" that combined to create life.</note> acts as the prior part, and is thus more easily inclined toward the first sticking-together; then the menstrual blood serves as nourishment to feed the Embryo already formed: the idea of which is also found in the process of making blood. In the vegetable mixture, you will also find three ingredients: first, the **forming seed**; second, a certain subtle moisture of the earth by which the seed is diluted and forms as if a first Embryo, namely the stalk; third, the rainwater and the remaining cruder juice of the earth by which the already formed plant is nourished. So in the mixture of Minerals, there is a **seed**, to which a certain unctuous <note>oily or fatty in texture</note> moisture **first** adheres, which is then increased and nourished by a certain **Mercurial** moisture <note>Refers to the alchemical principle of "Mercury," associated with liquidity and the metallic essence.</note>.

<margin>No. 3.</margin> However, just as a great deal depends on the female seed (which is first mixed with the male seed) and on the moisture of the earth (which is also first united with the seeds of plants); for according to its diversity, different mixtures and products arise, sometimes entirely foreign to the nature of the male seed, even clearly putting it to sleep or overcoming it: just as we see in the production of females, where the female seed predominates and erases the principal part of the seed—namely masculinity—which it changes into femininity. And we see this in the seeds of vegetables: for even if they are brought from the best places, yet when the juice of the earth is acidic (which comes together in the first mixture), the entire plant will be changed; even if nothing is lacking in heat or rain, and it is nourished perfectly. But to return to the point: that first forming element, to which the rest adhere, can be called that in which the rest are caught and *shaped*—that is, from which they take their form. ### Book 1. Section IV. Chapter VI.

...[resulting from] decomposed substances and precipitations, as we see; where in a single moment they are either united or separated. We must therefore distinguish between the **mineral matter that is flowing in** and the **matter that has already flowed**, which is what we are discussing now.
<margin>No. 11.</margin>
For we do not deny that the "inflowing" matter is digested and prepared along its very path; nor are we so reckless or bold <note>original: *perfrictæ frontis*, literally "with a rubbed forehead," a Latin idiom for being shameless or brazen</note> as to dare to measure and define the time of its movement and influence with a water-clock <note>original: *clepsydra*</note>; heaven forbid. But meanwhile, let it be certain that the mixable parts of minerals, when they come together, are mixed in a moment, and the mineral mixture is perfected in an instant: this is what both reason and experience dictate. Reason indeed, as Lullius <note>Ramon Llull (c. 1232–1316), a Majorcan philosopher and polymath whose name was frequently attached to influential alchemical texts</note> himself brings forward in his book *On the Fifth Essence*, in the third distinction, in the final part concerning questions, where he writes thus:

> *If in Alchemy there were gold or silver and a "vegetative" substance <note>meaning an active, life-like principle of growth and change</note>, and it did not produce gold or silver, nor transmute the primary essence through the primary location, science would be false; for this reason: because the gold and silver and the vegetative power would exist in something actually, in a place where it would be proper for them to produce gold and silver and to transmute—yet they would not do so. This would be against the course of nature, because it would then follow that there could be some place in nature where principles could naturally be "empty" <note>meaning inactive or failing to fulfill their potential</note>, which nature could not suffer; for it would be against its own definition, since nature is that through which every natural thing becomes full,* thus far Lullius.

If therefore, based on this valid and solid foundation, it is granted to Art <note>referring to human alchemy and chemistry</note> that it must operate in a moment once the principles and requirements are present, who will deny the same to Nature, which is much more diligent, and is indeed the Mistress, not the servant? As for the fact that some object to **fixation** <note>The chemical process of making a volatile or liquid substance stable, solid, and resistant to heat</note>; I respond to them that they do not know what is understood by fixation, or else they contradict themselves. They claim that a gold-making tincture fixes Mercury in a moment into the strongest mixture of gold, even before it has felt the heat of the fire—from which it would otherwise flee before being "tinged" <note>transformed by the alchemical tincture</note>. No one will say that the heat of an external fire is the cause of this fixation; it must therefore be attributed to the tincture, which completes the work in a natural operation; otherwise, the science would be preternatural, which would be absurd to claim. If metals can be fixed in a moment by human art, why should we not grant the same to natural principles? Especially since, as will be taught in what follows, the causes of volatility and fixity will be sufficiently weighed. For to come to experience, it is well known that by a single extraction of **oil of vitriol** <note>concentrated sulfuric acid</note>, the most volatile bodies are rendered the most fixed; indeed, they obtain entirely different virtues—to say nothing of the other principles of fixation, which we shall discuss in their proper place.
<margin>No. 12.</margin>
There is therefore no reason why the principles should not work continuously if they are joined in the proper way and place. The reason why the mixing of Minerals is completed in a single action is that a mineral mixture is far different from an animal or vegetable mixture; namely, it is a very simple mixture, not shaped by various features or distinguished by different organs, but entirely **homogeneous**.
<margin>No. 13.</margin>

And to come to natural experience, stones of the hardest mixture are certainly generated in a man in a very short time,

For just as animals are generated and conceived at any hour, and just as in Eastern lands where there is little alteration of the air and Sun, plants grow at all times—indeed, as Barlæus <note>Caspar Barlaeus (1584–1648), a Dutch polymath who wrote an account of the Dutch expedition to Brazil</note> reports regarding Prince Maurice’s expedition to Brazil, one can sometimes see mature, immature, flowering, and falling fruit all on a single tree at once—why should metals not also be produced at all times, provided the mixable parts are present? We maintain that minerals, even those of the most perfect mixture, are produced **in an instant**, provided the principles and requirements are present.

### Book I. Section IV. Chapter VI.

...we see in decomposed substances and *precipitations*; where in a moment they are either united or separated. Therefore, a distinction must be made between the *incoming* matter of minerals and the *infused* matter, of which we are now speaking.

<margin>No. 11.</margin>
For we do not deny that the *incoming* matter is digested and *prepared* along the way; nor are we so reckless and bold-faced <note>original: *perfrictæ frontis*, a Latin idiom for "shameless" or "impudent"</note> as to dare to measure and define its *motion* and the time of its influence with a water-clock, heaven forbid. But meanwhile, let it be certain that the mixable parts of minerals, *when they come together*, are mixed in a moment, and the mineral mixture is perfected *instantly*: which both reason and experience dictate.

Reason indeed is what [Ramon] Llull <note>Ramon Llull (c. 1232–1316) was a Majorcan philosopher and polymath whose works were central to later alchemical theory.</note> himself brings forward in his *Book on the Fifth Essence, third distinction, in the final part on questions, where he writes thus: "If in Alchemy there were gold or silver and a vegetative substance, and it did not produce gold or silver, and did not transmute the first essence through the first location, science would be false. This is because gold and silver, and the vegetative power, would be in something actually present where it would properly belong to them to produce gold and silver and to transmute—yet they would not do so. This would be against the course of nature, because it would follow that there could be a place in nature where principles could naturally be empty [of action], which nature could not suffer. For it would be against its own definition, since nature is that through which every natural thing becomes full."* Thus far Llull.

If, therefore, from this valid and good foundation, it is granted to Art [alchemy] that once the *principles and requirements* are held, it must work in a moment; who will deny the same to *Nature*, who is much more diligent, and indeed the Mistress, not the servant? As for those who object regarding *fixation* <note>the process of making a substance resistant to heat so it does not evaporate</note>; I respond to them that they do not know what is meant by fixation, or such people contradict themselves. They claim that the gold-making tincture <note>The "tincture" is often synonymous with the Philosopher's Stone or the agent of transformation.</note> fixes Mercury <note>Quicksilver</note> into a *most strong gold mixture* in a moment—even before it has felt the heat of the fire, which it would otherwise flee before it was tinged. No one will say that the heat of external fire is the cause of this fixation; it must therefore be attributed to the *tincture*, which completes the task in natural operation. Otherwise, the science would be supernatural, which would be absurd to profess. If things *made by art* can fix metals in a moment, why shall we not grant the same to *natural* principles? This is especially true as will be taught later in the following sections, where the causes of volatility and fixity will be sufficiently weighed.

For to come to experience, it is known that by a *single distillation of oil of vitriol* <note>sulfuric acid</note>, the most volatile bodies are rendered *most fixed*; indeed, they obtain entirely other virtues—to say nothing of the remaining principles of fixation, which we will discuss in their proper place.

<margin>No. 12.</margin>
There is, therefore, no reason why the principles should not work *continually* [immediately] if they are joined in the proper way and place. The reason that the mixing of Minerals is completed in a single action is that a mineral mixture is far different from an animal or vegetable mixture. It is the *most simple mixture*, distinguished by no shaping or various *organs*, but is entirely homogeneous [uniform in substance].

<margin>No. 13.</margin>
Because of this, it can be completed in a single period of action, as smoothly and quickly as a magnet attracts iron, or *lime attracts water*, or *silver dissolved in nitric acid* <note>original: *aqua forti*</note> and *precipitated with spirit of salt* <note>hydrochloric acid</note>, or *oil of tartar* poured over with *spirit of salt*. From these, a mixture comes forth in a moment that is not again dissolvable by any violence of fire, or any art that I know of. And to come to natural experience, it is certain that in a very short time, stones of the hardest mixture are generated within a human being <note>likely referring to the rapid formation of kidney or bladder stones as a natural proof of "instant" mineral growth</note>,

### Subterranean Physics

...it is found that they are generated; and we have seen water dripping from a cave, scarcely touching the earth, and already petrifying into hard stone. No one will judge the diamond to be anything other than a more fixed, perfect, and strong mixture than gold itself; meanwhile, those skilled in Indian affairs testify that every three years they are generated in the same gravel and found where they had been dug out before; and examples testify that metals in suitable locations of mines sometimes regenerate in a short time where they were previously dug out. And we read in the *Mineral Chronicle* <note>Likely referring to a collection of mining histories or a specific mining journal of the period.</note> that a certain miner left his **iron nail** in a cave; when he had forgotten it and returned after a month's time, that tool had meanwhile grown into the rock, while on one side, an elegant **branching growth of silver** had grown onto the iron nail: which, when he freed it from the rock, he gave to the overseer of the mines of that place as a unique curiosity. Various mineral decompositions of the **strongest mixture** are also known to us, which proceed as if in a moment: yet let no one think that I posit such an instantaneous mixture of subterranean things so as to admit no exception.

<margin>No. 14.</margin> For it is also well known to me that the mixable parts—namely the principles of minerals—do not always flow in at a single instant, but sequentially; whence, since they fail either by excess or defect, or even by the quality of refinement and purity, various species of minerals are born (and more abundantly the imperfect than the perfect ones), not because of the influx itself, but because of the nature of the influence. Indeed, as the most famous Digby <note>Sir Kenelm Digby (1603–1665), an English courtier and natural philosopher known for his "powder of sympathy" and early chemical experiments.</note> says in the previous citations regarding the growth of vegetables: if anyone considers all the circumstances required for such a mixture, they would scarcely believe that one in a thousand mixtures is perfected; when on the contrary Nature is most fertile in the slightest and calmest way, and produces a huge abundance of subterranean things unceasingly: and she holds our subtle speculations, cares, and precautions in mockery.

<margin>No. 15.</margin> For without vessels, glassware, distillations, degrees of heat, or finally any fire or lamp, she performs all these operations: more successfully and frugally than the alchemists, who cooked their "phoenix" <note>An alchemical metaphor for the Philosopher's Stone or the final stage of the Great Work.</note> for nine years.

<margin>No. 16.</margin> In this, however—that subterranean Nature performs its business in darkness and in confinement—it agrees with the animal "workshop"; so that it holds the extreme with it. For just as animals are the most subtly mixed, so on the opposite side minerals are the strongest and coarsest; both, however, are perfected in darkness. But the mixture of vegetables is midway between the animal and the mineral, whence it is, as it were, **hermaphroditic**, completing one part **outside** the earth and another part **inside** it, and thus inclines toward both mixtures, both the animal and the mineral.

<margin>No. 17.</margin> It is necessary, however, for the mineral principles to be mixed in their own matrix, namely **their own seed and receptacle**; but where they meet, and in what place they are surrounded, matters little. For experience testifies that subterranean things, especially metals, are mixed and produced **outside of mines**, provided the requirements are met. The story of the Silesian boy with the innate golden tooth <note>A famous 16th-century medical curiosity where a child in Silesia allegedly grew a gold molar; it was later revealed to be a clever gold leaf covering.</note> is still in controversy; the *Mineral Chronicle* testifies that **fragments of lead** were found near the front part of the brain of a certain miner: and our former colleague Dr. Rapp, physician to the Elector of Mainz <note>original: *Electoris Moguntini*</note>, related to us with the greatest faith that he, from **wings of Spanish flies** <note>original: *cantharidum alis*; these beetles were frequently used in early medicine and alchemy.</note>, dried and powdered, and soaked in **lead melted in a cupel** <note>original: *plumbo in capella*; a cupel is a shallow porous dish used in assaying to separate precious metals from lead.</note>...

Book I. Section IV. Chapter VI.

...that they have sometimes received pure gold in the quantity of a large pea, even though the lead otherwise contained not even a tiny bit of it. Some testify that gold is occasionally found in the heads of **"gilded ones,"** commonly called **trout** <note>original: *Forellen*</note>. It is certain that metal-bearing herbs exist, especially if they grow above mineral veins. The author **Borellus** <note>Pierre Borel (c. 1620–1671), a French physician and chemist who wrote on the "doubling" of metals.</note> claims that **lead increases and becomes heavier in the air**. That metals are found in water is a daily occurrence, nor is it possible that all of it is carried there through subterranean channels, since some testify that gold is regenerated in gold-bearing sand even after washing, and indeed even out of water.

Nor do I see it as so complicated if one says that the principles of minerals, if they meet, produce their own kind even in water itself, and are not hindered in their mixing by the water; for we daily see stones and even precious gems generated in water, and not hindered by it, since water does not enter into their composition. It is certain that metals are produced in water within the mines themselves. Father **Athanasius Kircher** <note>A famous Jesuit polymath known for his theories on the "subterranean world."</note> reports in his *Great Art of Light and Shadow* of a plant that grows in the middle of the water, which we ourselves have seen in the Baltic Sea, resembling a species of **water lily** <note>original: *Nymphaeae*</note>. 

Furthermore, **Averroes** <note>A medieval Andalusian polymath; here cited for a common but medically inaccurate folktale regarding spontaneous generation.</note> writes that he knew a woman living nearby, of good character and upright faith, who confirmed by oath that she had conceived an infant from seed drawn from a bath, which a wanton **masturbator** had spilled. I also remember that my grandmother in **Speyer** <note>A historic city in southwest Germany.</note> had a servant girl who at night drank water from a vessel in which frogs had deposited their seed. After some time, she suffered the most atrocious pains, and with a swelling belly, she finally threw up six live frogs through vomiting. In my own time, this happened with snakes to a certain nobleman of Franconia.

If, therefore, the "seeds" <note>The author uses "seed" (semina) to mean the vital organizing principle of a thing, whether it is a plant, animal, or mineral.</note> of both animals and vegetables are not hindered or destroyed in water, but rather retain their seminal power, why is it surprising that the principles of minerals—far stronger than the former—do not lose their potency in water, but also complete their mixing within it? There is no doubt, then, that metal and minerals can be produced everywhere if the necessary requirements are present, though primarily in the accustomed places within mines. Yet even there, miners testify that they maintain a certain location and orientation, which they observe with a mineral horoscope, commonly called a **mining compass** <note>original: *Berg-Compaß*</note>, namely according to a certain direction of the pole. And what wonder is it that Nature preserves certain fertile paths in all mixtures, when we see the same in animals, where one part of the body is more fruitful and fertile than another? 

The remaining things that can be said about subterranean matters—namely, regarding the special mode of mixing, their form, and specific qualities—we shall treat in the following chapters. We will now conclude this chapter by briefly establishing the diversity of subterranean species and their analogy with the other mixtures and differences of the two remaining kingdoms <note>The "three kingdoms" refers to animal, vegetable, and mineral.</note>, so that we omit nothing pertaining to a full knowledge of the aforementioned subjects.

## T E X T.

<margin>N. 1.</margin>
**F**irst, it is certain that *sperm and seeds* are provided in animals and vegetables; we see this also in the mineral kingdom, especially in their *principles* <note>The fundamental "starting materials" of matter</note>, which we discussed in the third Section.

<margin>N. 2.</margin>
*Secondly*, *nutrition* is provided in the animal and vegetable kingdoms; in the animal it is *blood*, in the vegetable it is *rain*: so also in the mineral kingdom there is no doubt that they are nourished by mineral vapor, as we taught in the fourth chapter of the third Section when we dealt with Mercurial earth <note>One of Becher’s three theoretical "earths" that make up matter; Mercurial earth was thought to provide liquidity and metallic properties.</note>.

<margin>N. 3.</margin>
*Thirdly*, in animals and vegetables there are also *excrements* <note>The author uses "excrement" in the broader sense of "waste products" or "byproducts" of growth.</note>, both those in which they are generated and those which they reject after being generated; such as in animals the amnion <note>The membrane surrounding a fetus</note>, the umbilical cord, sweat, urine, etc.; in vegetables the husks, receptacles, cases, pods, tendrils, small vessels, compartments, etc. We see that such things are also provided in minerals, in various *earths, gravels, tufa, spars*, and dross, such as *scales, slag, chaff, flowers* <note>A term for powdery chemical precipitates</note>, and others.

<margin>N. 4.</margin>
*Fourthly*, both animals and vegetables produce *perfect bodies*, but of a dual species, namely male and female; likewise in the subterranean world, metals and stones are *perfect* species, but *metals hold the place of the male, and stones the female*: this is because stones completely lack the "third earth" <note>The "Glassy Earth" in Becher's theory, which provides solidity</note> for perfection, which gives "metallicity" and a kind of virility, as we noted in the place cited above, and will note further in the following section.

<margin>N. 5.</margin>
*Fifthly*, in animals Nature sometimes produces *imperfect offspring*, failing either through an abundance or a lack of limbs; thus we see men who have six fingers on each hand, others only two; some are clearly footless <note>original: "apodes"</note>, others are many-footed <note>original: "polypodes"</note>. In the vegetable kingdom, nature also wanders very far at times; hence fruits are either fewer or more numerous than is right, larger, smaller, without skin or a pit, or soon abounding in both. This also happens in greatness and smallness of size; hence we have seen pygmy trees which nonetheless bring forth larger fruits. Likewise, the *younger Helmont* <note>Franciscus Mercurius van Helmont (1614–1698), a Flemish chemist and philosopher.</note> *is the author of the Alphabet of Nature*, where he claims that if *shoots of Medlars are grafted onto their own trunk in reverse order* <note>Upside down</note>, at the part where they are thinnest, when they sprout—having been cut off from their natural place and thus stretched out with their "feet" as if toward the heights—and the sap is drawn through the "head," they bring forth fruit lacking their natural seed and pits. Such *imperfect* mixtures are therefore also given in minerals, when the principles come together in an unequal proportion; hence various products arise, such as *Antimony, Bismuth, Zinc, Marcasite, Magnesia <note>Likely manganese or magnesite in this context</note>, Cobalt*, which differ in no way from *metals*, since they have common principles with them, but are mixed unequally. Hence some are fluid, others too dry; some porous, others compact,

<margin>No. 6.</margin> are called monsters <note>In a historical context, "monsters" (monstra) were unusual births or hybrids that seemed to defy the natural order.</note>, such as when a donkey mates with a mare and a mule comes forth; and when either beasts mate with humans, or humans with beasts, diverse monsters are produced. It is certain, therefore, that among minerals various composites are also found, which are of two kinds: some are more natural, such as sulfur, arsenic, realgar <note>A ruby-red arsenic sulfide mineral</note>, cinnabar, and quicksilver <note>Mercury</note>; others are further removed from the natural state of minerals, such as *vitriol, alum, borax*, and the like. Seventh, just as among animals there are amphibians, 
<margin>No. 7.</margin> and among vegetables there are plant-animals <note>original: "Zoophyta"; organisms like sponges or corals that seem to share traits of both kingdoms</note>; so among subterranean things there are animal-minerals <note>original: "Zoomineralia"</note>, such as *pearls, shells, and all shellfish*, and there are plant-minerals <note>original: "phytomineralia"</note>, such as *amber, coral*, and petrified wood. Eighth and finally, just as every species in the animal and vegetable kingdom has innumerable degrees of its own perfection, so in minerals every species varies according to the accidents of its mixture and the quality and purity of its principles; for even *gold* 
<margin>No. 8.</margin> *and diamond* are found in various types, one of which always exists as more perfect than another. And so we conclude the analogy which minerals have with animals and vegetables, which we hope will not be unpleasing to the reader. Now order would require that we discuss something of the order of subterranean mixture and production; however, since we have dealt with that much in the section on their principles, and the section on the motion of principles, it would be superfluous to repeat what has already been said. We only wished to add this one thing to persuade the reader that the entire mixture and production of subterranean things occurs gently, 
<margin>No. 9.</margin> mildly, and simply—indeed, continuously. Metals are indeed generated in stones, which we discussed above; mineral fumes (which were discussed in the third and fourth chapters of the same section) fly into and penetrate these stones, which the miners call *weathering-in* <note>original German: "einwittern"; the process by which a rock becomes impregnated with mineral vapors</note>. As soon as they attempt to penetrate the stone and take themselves into it, then the stone is tinted with *various colors like a painter's*, according to the nature of the inflowing smoke; and the stone breathes out a *sulfurous odor*. Finally, when the proportion of the penetrating fumes reaches the right temperament, the stone is covered in certain parts—indeed sometimes entirely—with a *metallic leaf*, which the miners call *native ore* <note>original German: "gediegen Aertz"; ore found in its pure metallic state</note>. Furthermore, just as a metal is generated by flowing in, so when it is mature, unless it is cut out, if any fumes continue flowing in, they draw out the metal that had flowed in and carry it away with them, leaving a vacuum and a porous stone, which the miners call *dead metal* <note>original German: "eintodt Metall"</note>. However, these fumes do not fly in with only one quality, but with many; hence in one stone, metals of various kinds are mostly found. Stones are generated both inside and outside the earth from the two primary fumes mentioned previously; these, when resolved into a liquid, first *become moldy* <note>original: "mucesctunt"; likely referring to a gelatinous or mucilaginous state</note>, then are slowly dried 
<margin>No. 10.</margin> by their own nature, so that they can be handled almost like wax; at length they harden, and finally they become extremely hard, so that they can be dissolved by no liquid except their own, and whatever foreign material comes into that mixture turns to stone <note>original: "lapidescit"</note> along with it. The transparency of stones comes from the purity of the liquids; opacity comes from the mixed *earth of lime* <note>original: "calcis terra"</note> that enters the mixture. These, when mixed in turn, produce new compositions, though they are far more imperfect than the previous ones and more easily dissolved. For the further a substance is removed from its natural state, the more it is altered and liable to corruption. We see this in these complex mixtures, which are dissolved by distillation alone; whereas, by contrast, the mixtures and compositions of metals and stones are the strongest. So much for the mixture of minerals; more will follow in the subsequent pages.

<margin>No. 11.</margin> regarding the second principle, they are of the same nature as metals. *Imperfect* minerals, such as *Antimony*, etc., are generated in the same way as metals, except that their principles are mixed unequally. <margin>No. 12.</margin> **Decomposed substances** <note>original: "Decomposita"; in this context, it refers to substances formed by the secondary mixing of already compounded materials</note>, such as sulfur, arsenic, cinnabar, and mercury, are made from metals and from both perfect and imperfect minerals. This is also to be understood regarding more remote decomposed substances like vitriol <note>metallic sulfates</note>, alum, and Borax. These involve a mixture of water, an acid solvent, and earth (whether metallic or stony); when mixed together, these produce new compositions, although they are far more imperfect than the primary ones and are more easily dissolved. For the further something is removed from its natural state, the more it is altered and prone to decay. We see this in these decomposed substances, which are dissolved by distillation alone; whereas, by contrast, the compounds and mixtures of metals and stones are very strong. So much for the mixture of minerals; more will be said in the following pages.

### Subterranean Physics

...of animals and vegetables, so that we might explain the nature, analogy, agreement, and diversity of one by relating it to and contrasting it with the others. All of this, as has been said, was done with the goal of making the nature of minerals better known to us, which could be made clear above all else from their structure and mixture.

<margin>N. 2.</margin> For just as for a perfect understanding and science of clocks, it is required first—but not only—that one dismantle a combined, constructed, and finished clock and consider each individual part more exactly, and then combine them again. For just as no one who has never seen a clock could join and combine its disconnected parts, so too no one can dismantle its joined parts and know them exactly unless he himself dismantles and reunites the clock from head to heel <note>original: "a capite ad calcem," an idiom meaning from beginning to end or top to bottom.</note>, as the saying goes.

<margin>N. 3.</margin> Since we have dealt with the mixture and *conjunction* of bodies up to this point, it will not be without use if we discuss their *solution* <note>In this context, "solution" refers to the process of dissolving or breaking a substance down into its component parts.</note> here, along with the relation, analogy, and discrepancy of that solution. We shall consider the solutions of bodies insofar as they are opposed to mixtures and cohesions. For it is in this area that the more powerful part of Chemistry and Physics is found—namely, the most noble *study of Spagyrics* <note>Spagyrics is an early term for alchemy, specifically the art of separating substances into their elements and then recombining them for medicinal or scientific purposes.</note>. In treating this, so far as it serves our purpose, we will maintain the *order* we held in the preceding chapters: namely, proceeding *from the more subtle to the more fixed*, from the remote to the near, from the more common and well-known to the more secret—in short, from animals and vegetables to minerals and their solutions, proceeding as if by steps and solid logic.

<margin>N. 4.</margin> In this chapter, therefore, we shall begin with the *solution* of animals, albeit succinctly and briefly, and not as a full profession except so far as it fits the fabric of our undertaking. Just as we established three mixtures for the triple kingdom—calling the mixture of Animals *generation*, the mixture of Vegetables *vegetation*, and the mixture of minerals *union* (also called *coagulation* or *fixation*)—so too we propose here three *solutions*: namely, *putrefaction, fermentation, and liquefaction*. We attribute the first to animals, the second to vegetables, and the third to minerals. These solutions, however, arise from the same cause as the mixtures, but in reverse. Meanwhile, *rarefaction and condensation* <note>Rarefaction is the thinning or lessening of density; condensation is the thickening or increasing of density.</note> are the instruments, and the "resolution of the moist and the dry"—or the separation of earth and water—is their foundation, as was discussed above under the title of "Axioms." And since mixture draws its origin from these, it follows that solutions arise from the same source.

<margin>N. 5.</margin> That is to say, some things are dissolved in the "continuous," and others in the "whole." <margin>N. 6.</margin> Things are said to be *dissolved in the continuous*, or in quantity, when they are reduced to a different weight and change their state or figure—as when a half-part is separated from a mark of silver, or an arm is cut from a body. For just as in bodies where the parts are dissimilar, those parts together with similar ones constitute a whole; so when a body consists of purely similar parts, any particle of it will be considered as a whole in every respect. For an ounce of lead, or even the smallest atom of lead, can just as easily be called a "whole" as a hundredweight of lead. When such particles are divided, they are then said to be dissolved in the continuous—not in respect to themselves, but in respect to us and the

<margin>N.</margin> proposed quantity. Truly, concerning this solution of the continuous, we have dealt sufficiently in our *Oedipus Chymicus* <note>original: "Oedipo Chymico," a reference to one of the author's other books, titled after Oedipus, the mythical riddle-solver, implying the work "solves" the riddles of chemistry.</note>.
Chymi-

### Book I, Section V, Chapter I.

We have already dealt with the Chemical aspect, to which we refer the reader. In this place, we speak of those solutions which physically dissolve bodies and simultaneously change their state in both quantity and quality. <margin>N. 8.</margin> We shall therefore begin with **putrefaction**, which we attribute to animals and consider their characteristic process; not because vegetables do not putrefy just as much as animals, but because in the natural course of things, the *beginning* and the *end* of animals is to so rot, or be putrefied. Vegetables, however, usually undergo **fermentation** and turn sour before they reach putrefaction. Furthermore, *animal* putridity is far more potent than that of vegetables, on account of their <margin>M</margin> subtler spirits. Properly speaking, therefore, it is called putrefaction in animals, while in vegetables it is called so *improperly* or is considered a less perfect form; it is rather a certain corruption, yet analogous to putrefaction. For just as fermentation occurs in animals too, especially in the blood—which should nevertheless be called an ebullition <note>original: "ebullitio," a bubbling or boiling up</note> or a rarefaction of the same, rather than a formal fermentation—so it is with the *corruption* of vegetables when compared with the *putrefaction* of animals. Since, therefore, a designation should always be taken *from the more powerful instance* <note>original: "a potiori," a logical principle where a thing is named after its most prominent characteristic</note>, in this chapter we shall treat the *putrefaction* of animals, to which we shall relate the corruption of vegetables, and in the following chapter, we shall speak of *fermentation*; but in such a way that we also draw the ebullition of animals, which is analogous to fermentation, into that discussion.

<margin>N. 9.</margin> As far as *Putrefaction* is concerned, it must be known that it is indeed an action *outside* of, or *against Nature*, because it leads the body away from its natural state and changes it; yet, if it is considered in respect to other supernatural solutions, it will be found to be *entirely natural*. For combustion or calcination by a strong fire, which usually happens to bodies, although it is a species of *putrefaction* and analogous to it, is nevertheless a thing of art and is violent. By contrast, 그 calcination which occurs through *putrefaction* is not only gentler but results in a far different state. *In both*, however, bodies are eventually resolved to their furthest limit, and the energy and temperament <note>original: "crasis," the healthy mixture of humors or elements in a body</note> of the whole *mixture* is dissolved. Furthermore, all things burned and putrefied are found in the end to be *dry* and *earthy*; though in the beginning they differ from one another by the whole heaven <note>original: "toto coelo," an idiom meaning they are poles apart or completely different</note>, as they also do in the middle stage. 

For *Combustion* in the beginning, by means of fire, *rarefies* the parts of the body and carries the *subtler* parts away from the body with it; *putrefaction*, on the contrary, in the beginning *moistens* the body and attracts the neighboring air and *humidity*. *Combustion* in the middle produces *soot* and *coals*, as well as *flame* and *smoke*, but all of a fiery nature; *putrefaction* in the middle of its operation procreates <term>sanies</term> <note>a thin, watery discharge from a wound or sore</note>, *pus*, *worms*, and a *stench* from the exhaling rarefied and putrefied atoms, all of which are of a *moist* temperament. *Combustion* in the end reduces all things to *ashes*, which are of a *most dry* and *fiery* nature—indeed, if you look at the <term>alkali salt</term> <note>Potassium carbonate or similar salts derived from plant ashes</note> elicited therefrom, they are of a caustic nature. The end of *putrefaction*, however, is *earth*, and indeed a *fertile* one. Toward this earth we are inclined by nature, by divine mandate: *you are earth, and to earth you shall return* <note>original: "terra es, & in terram reverteris," a reference to Genesis 3:19, traditionally "dust thou art..."</note>. From this it clearly appears that the reduction into earth, which happens by the help of putrefaction, is a *natural action* and *inclination*; whence it also happens that, unless it is utterly hindered, it begins *even in living* bodies: as we see daily in *gangrene*, <term>sphacelus</term> <note>the death of soft tissues; a more advanced stage of gangrene</note>, <term>scurvy</term> <note>original: "scorbutus"</note>, <term>the French disease</term> <note>original: "lues gallica," a historical name for syphilis</note>, *putrid fevers*, the *plague*, and other enemies of the human race. It will not, therefore, be useless if we discuss putrefaction a little more fully in this place, and by what causes and impediments it is promoted or hindered.
