### Subterranean Physics

...so that we may teach the unlearned; since not only Physicists <note>In this era, "Physicists" refers to natural philosophers who study the physical laws of nature.</note>, but also Physicians and Surgeons, may draw quite a few fundamental principles from this study. <margin>N. 10.</margin> *The effect of putrefaction, therefore, is the resolution <note>original: "resolutio," the breaking down of a substance into its component parts</note> of the body; to which is opposed its conservation in its natural mixture and cohesion:* which we said in the preceding pages arose from the seed. Now, the quality of the animal seed has a great analogy with the vegetable seed, which we have demonstrated in the previous sections to be like an extract from all the substantial parts of the plant, so that <margin>N. 11.</margin> it may rightly be called its *being* or *essence*. *Since this consists of an unctuous moisture <term>unctuous moisture: an oily, fatty substance believed to be the fuel for the "vital flame" of life</term> or radical moisture <term>radical moisture: the fundamental life-sustaining fluid within an organism</term>, in which a certain innate warm balsam is present; it follows that the state and conservation of this unctuous moisture consists in a degree suitable to its nature: and consequently, it is a preservation from rot.* For we clearly see this in plants, whose seed is unctuous and fatty (as are all seeds of vegetables), which attracts only as much moisture from the earth—and is united and mixed with it—as is conducive to the right proportion for conserving and producing its particular species from such a mixture. And in this mixture, before it reaches the required proportion, it is not hindered by any moisture, even the greatest and continuous rain, as it is a material friendly and compatible to itself. However, when the right mixture has been reached, if it rains more than is right even for a single night, it immediately begins to reverse; and the moisture, which previously served as nourishment and was passive in respect to the seed, now begins to be the active agent, and starts to spread and dissolve <note>original: "colliquefacere," to melt or make liquid</note> the substance of the unctuous seed. This happens because the unctuous substance of the seed cannot resist a superfluous and preternatural quantity of water, whereby it is overcome and resolved. But, just as in this "mortification" <note>The death or breakdown of the original form</note> every particle of moisture was imbibed and tinted by the unctuous seed—so that every part or the whole form of the unctuous seed lay hidden, shapeless, within every particle of moisture, though dead, buried, ineffective, and diluted—likewise, when the moist parts (those in excess of what is right) are again drawn away by the heat and help of the Sun, their earthy parts, being thicker and heavier, adhere to the parts of the unctuous seed which are now also being concentrated again. They multiply them, and thus joined together, in the course of time they begin to react against the water, and are able to overcome and coagulate a greater quantity of it than before; from this arises a seemingly infinite multiplication and growth of vegetables and their seeds. And this is indeed the continuous process of nature, by which she brings forth from putrefaction and such struggle a new **regeneration, with multiplication and profit.** <margin>N. 12.</margin> From this it must be concluded in every way that the entire energy and conservation of a mixture depends on the unctuous moisture of the seed; and that the mixture is altered according to the seed's own alteration. Therefore, the more the temperament <term>crasis: the specific internal balance or "mixture" of qualities in a body</term> of the seed is subject to change, the more changeable and prone to rot those bodies also exist. However, the alteration of the seed arises from the first principles of mixture (which we dealt with in Section 4, Chapter 3), namely extrinsically through rarefaction and condensation, and intrinsically through the dry or the moist—that is, through earthy or watery particles—if they flow in beyond the proper proportion and the temperament of the mixture. For while it is most certain that bodies and **radical moisture are nourished and conserved** by their continuous influx, it is also not to be doubted...

Many changes are forced upon the entire **mixed animal** <note>original: "animali mixto"; this refers to a living creature composed of a mixture of different elements and humors, such as a human or animal.</note>, specifically according to the nature and state of the *inflowing* particles. For either these particles are thin to the highest degree, from which arise the greatest fevers of the whole body; or they are entirely thick, constricting the blood, as we have seen not infrequently in our practice during the plague and petechial fevers <note>Fever characterized by small purple spots (petechiae) on the skin, often associated with typhus.</note>, as well as in malignant smallpox and measles. In these cases, despite great effort and testing many parts of the body, *we were unable to draw any blood by bloodletting.* <note>original: "venæ sectione"; the practice of opening a vein to treat illness.</note> Furthermore, when particles are too *earthy or moist*, they impress many harmful alterations upon the body, as we see in *scurvy, the venereal disease <note>syphilis</note>*, and other contagious diseases, especially the *plague*. In these instances, before such particles can be digested or expelled, or in any way reconciled with nature, many patients occasionally die. This is especially true when such particles are, in their entire substance, contrary to nature; they flow in such great abundance that they destroy the fountain of life, unless they are overcome with the greatest industry, strength, and caution.

<margin>No. 14.</margin> For this reason, in such malignant diseases, **antidotes** <term>alexipharmaca: medicines used to ward off or neutralize poison or infection</term> are ordinarily mixed with **sweat-inducers** <term>diaphoretica: substances that promote perspiration</term>. Indeed, *diaphoretics* are necessary so that if the blood becomes thick, or is filled with a narcotic, poisonous, or sleep-inducing spirit (which mostly happens in the plague, and indeed in its worst form, which first puts the patients to sleep and then kills them), then, I say, such unnatural vapors may be thinned out and thus can be *expelled*. If, however, the blood is infested with particles that are already too thin, they are expelled even more quickly through the opened *pores of the skin*, which happens quickly in this state. *Antidotes*, however, are added so that nature may be strengthened; for in my opinion, no antidote drives out poison except by tempering it. This is because antidotes contain particles that are entirely homogeneous and equal to those of the "mixed animal" when it is in a good state; therefore, they assist by increasing the good particles and overcome the malignant ones by tempering them. This is the reason why more antidotes are found in the animal kingdom than in the vegetable or mineral kingdoms; *for nature delights more in nature.* <note>original: "natura namque magis naturæ gaudet"; a classic alchemical and medical axiom suggesting that like-substances have a natural affinity and healing power over one another.</note>

<margin>No. 15.</margin> Therefore, when the seminal particles or the oily *radical moisture* <term>radical moisture: the fundamental life-sustaining fluid of an organism</term> are increased by their own homogeneous particles, it necessarily follows that the moisture itself is strengthened. Thus aided by *sweat-inducing medicines*, it can more easily expel foreign particles, or thrust them out to the less vital parts of the body's surface, or even entirely *alter and mix* them. For since such particles proceed from and offend either the sources of thinness and thickness, or the nature and imbalance of earth and water, who could doubt that they can be tempered? They can be led back through opposites into a natural state suitable to the mixed animal. For it is well known that from any flesh, through an imbalance caused by art, a lethal poison can be prepared; yet, by performing the opposite operation, it can be reduced back into a medicine and a balanced state. The method is also known to us for *converting all poisonous animals and their venoms into good medicine* in a moment.

<margin>No. 16.</margin> Therefore, there is no doubt that just as in moral matters great benefits come from persecutions, so also great medicines can be prepared from poisons. And this is the correct and natural method of healing: namely, that the "sinning matter" <note>original: "materia peccans"; the harmful or diseased substance in the body.</note> is *converted* into nourishing matter. That which otherwise had to be *thrown out* because of the harm it caused is instead retained for its benefit, so that what was once poison is *converted into nourishment*. This will not be so difficult in practice if we consider how...

# Book 1, Section V, Chapter 1

[with greater] speed than oil itself, or spirit of wine <note>original: "vini spiritus"; an early term for distilled alcohol or ethanol</note>. In this **balsamic spirit and fire**, the entire power and goodness of the blood consists; once it is corrupted or altered, the body’s entire constitution <note>original: "crasis"; a term from Galenic medicine referring to the unique blending or temperament of the four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) that maintains health</note> is changed. Therefore, when this spirit is cut off so that it cannot flow, its absence causes putrefaction; for all parts, whether of flesh, blood, or the rest of the body, immediately rot when they are deprived of it. We might rightly call this balsamic spirit the **innate heat** that perpetually flows into all parts—indeed, a fiery entity and the essence of the stars—or the "Fire of Nature," as it has been named by some. 

Where it draws its origin, however, and how it acquires its nourishment and preservation from the air, would be too lengthy to explain here; since we are not writing a universal physics, but a particular one, and specifically a <margin>No. 21.</margin> *mineral* physics. Yet it serves our present purpose to consider briefly how this spirit is intercepted, and what follows from its interception, exclusion, or total absence, extinction, and suffocation. 

It is intercepted in various ways. First, by internal causes, when the paths and passages through which it flows are obstructed; namely, the blood itself is rendered thick, sticky, and sluggish, which we have said happens in the plague, scurvy, the French disease <note>original: "lue gallica"; a historical term for syphilis</note>, and other illnesses. Second, when the blood is called back and pulled away <note>original: "revellitur"; refers to "revulsion," a medical theory where fluids are diverted from one part of the body to another</note> from one limb or another by overly strong evacuations. In this way, parts are deprived of blood and its inherent spirit, and they die. 

Not long ago here in **Munich**, we had an example of this in the Illustrious and Noble **Lord von Preysing**. Having been purged with more-than-just violence, he suffered a mortification of one foot—or rather a drawing away of the blood from it—so that the foot began to die after a few days, eventually turning into gangrene, and the patient began his journey to heaven. 

Such interception also happens through many external causes; namely, when the flesh is compressed too forcefully, whether by the fingers (which is called *pinching* <note>original: "pfetzen"; a German dialect term for pinching or nipping the skin</note>), or by tight bandages, especially garters around the knees. Experience testifies that from such things, parts often die and gangrene <margin>No. 22.</margin> follows. 

Above all, however, it is intercepted by wounding and the "solution of continuity" <note>original: "partium solutione"; a surgical term for any break in the skin or bone, such as a cut or fracture</note>. When parts are injured and forced apart by any instrument—as by a cut, a puncture, a blow, a crushing, or a burn—the fibers from which the flesh is entirely composed (if examined accurately) and through which the aforementioned animal spirit flows, are damaged. Thus, the flowing spirit is hindered in its order and intercepted, so that it cannot flow into the wound and the parts within the wound in the right order. Therefore, such intermediate or cut-off parts of blood, bone, or flesh rightly die and rot, as they exist separated from the healthy parts and the aforementioned balsamic spirit. They are resolved into discharge <note>original: "saniem"; a thin, greenish-yellow fluid from a wound, distinct from thick pus</note> and pus until they fall away, and the healthy parts can be reunited by means of an **intrinsic glue**, namely that balsamic spirit. For we see that there is a great power of coalescing in the blood during bloodletting, where the vein closes and reunites by itself.

It happens that parts deprived of the vital balsamic spirit—which previously defended and preserved them from every external cause—now suffer the influence and action of the surrounding air and other circumstances. ### Book I. Section V. Chapter I.

...volatile is nothing other than rarefied sulfur: it follows that volatile or oily salts, when refined into the form and penetrative power of salt, greatly preserve against rot. They do this by strengthening the **innate balsam** <note>The body's natural internal preservative or life force</note> and penetrating the tissues. When the edges of wounds are usually in pain, fluids flow toward them because of that pain, and the pores are blocked by this influx. It follows necessarily that the vital balsamic spirit is less able to flow into the area. However, when the aforementioned medications change the corrupted matter and prevent putrefaction with their own heat, they offer great help by necessity, because their penetrative nature opens the pores of the surrounding parts so the vital spirits can flow in more freely. Therefore, all **thick** and **sticky** oils are harmful in this regard, unless they are either highly fragrant—meaning they contain much volatile salt—or are artfully refined into the nature of volatile salts.

This is why **spirits of human dung** <note>original: "stercoris humani spiritus"; distilled substances from organic waste were a common, albeit pungent, part of 17th-century pharmacology</note>, which are entirely volatile oily salts, and other **burnt oils** <term>empyreumata: chemical substances produced by high heat that have a smoky or "burnt" smell</term> are of great importance. I will not even mention the volatile salts artfully prepared from balsams; these heal burns and almost all wounds nearly instantly. (In cases of burns, oily substances are otherwise avoided because their dense nature blocks the pores; indeed, burned parts are often placed near a fire to rarefy the pores so fresh blood can flow, or the influx is caused by various incisions). This also explains the great power of Indian Balsam and other volatile oils.

<margin>No. 29.</margin>
The often-mentioned **Dr. Krafft** related to us that there was a man in the Indies whose hand was sliced through the palm by a sword. A European surgeon testified that the **man would necessarily lose the use of his fingers**. Yet, the man smeared the edges of the wound with a certain oil, placing nothing—neither a dressing nor a linen plug—inside the wound. Within a few days, he returned from his people with full use of his hand and showed himself to the Dutch surgeon. It was wise to smear the edges of the wound with an oil that opens and protects; as for why he did not bind the wound with any bandage, I believe the reason is that the Indians, knowing the healthfulness of their air, do not wish to block it out. Since the air there is found to be balsamic, it does not cause rot but promotes healing and restoration.

This would not succeed in these regions [Europe], where the air is filled with thick and sharp atoms, causing great harm to wounds unless they are protected from it. Thus, due to the diversity of the air, wounds are cured in different ways and times in various regions, according to the healthfulness of the environment—though **diet and lifestyle** also contribute much. 

<margin>No. 30.</margin>

### Subterranean Physics

<margin>N. 24.</margin> ...known [parts] of severed or dead tissues, it moderately thins and moistens them, overcoming the inherent oily parts. As a result, these parts must inevitably break down. This causes a great release of foul-smelling, decaying particles that have been freed from their structural bonds. Consequently, in this process, they acquire entirely different qualities; they are thinned out beyond the natural state appropriate for their body, which results in the heavy and piercing stench of rotting things.

<margin>N. 25.</margin> I have said that warm, moist air is the greatest contributor to decay; this should also be understood regarding warm, moist bodies, whose temperament is more subject to putrefaction than all others. For the watery parts already present are easily increased if new moisture is added. Conversely, for this very reason, **cold and dry** bodies—and especially **hot and dry** ones—rot with difficulty, or some not at all. Such preserved bodies were consequently regarded as **Holy** by the unlearned <note>The author refers to "incorruptible" saints; he argues their preservation is a result of natural chemistry (dehydration) rather than a miracle</note>. Thus, **cold and dry** air, and especially **hot and dry** air, also preserves against decay. We see this in Spain and other hot regions endowed with **dry**, hot air, where bodies **do not rot or break down**. It is certain that corpses in the East <note>The "Orient" or Levant</note> are dried in the sand, and even here among us, they can be dried by art in ovens, and thus preserved from rot until the end of the world. **Intense cold** also preserves against rot; for this reason, we noticed bodies in Stockholm hanging on the gallows the entire winter **without rotting**, as we saw when one happened to fall down.

<margin>N. 26.</margin> Excessive **moisture** also hinders decay, just as excessive **heat** does. Experience teaches us that bodies in water are **consumed** <note>slowly dissolved or washed away</note> rather than **rotted**, provided there is a constant flow of new water. Thus, we have seen entire bodies submerged for a long time that remained completely immune to putrefaction. Indeed, it once occurred to us to speculate whether cadavers intended for anatomy should be treated in such a way so they might remain free from stench and rot for a longer time. This is also the reason why corpses among Christians are placed in the earth; and specifically here in Munich (Monachium), they use a split or latticed lid so that the bodies may break down and rot more quickly due to the slow moisture of the earth.

<margin>N. 27.</margin> Therefore, the primary cause of decay is the lack of the vital balsamic spirit; the secondary cause is the surrounding external air. As we demonstrated above regarding the plague, the air is sometimes so putrefying and warm-moist that it overcomes the remaining balsamic spirit even in living bodies, unless that spirit is strengthened and increased. From this, it can be gathered that **preservatives** against rot **must be subtle, fiery, oily, and balsamic**. Experience, medical practice, and the method of healing all teach this. For even setting aside the plague, anything that resists rot must be thinning and subtle; therefore, they must be fragrant, so that they may open the paths through which the balsamic spirit can flow. Furthermore, they must be fiery, balsamic, and oily, so that in corpses they may take the place of the vital fire, and in the living, they may strengthen it.

<margin>N. 28.</margin> Upon this foundation, the essence of **sulfur** (which we mentioned above) works so miraculously. In cases of **gangrene** and other **putrefactions** occurring in the living body, we see great help in **spirit of wine** <note>High-proof alcohol/ethanol</note> in which fragrant balsams have been dissolved. From this comes the great importance of the **spirit of human dung** <note>original: "stercoris humani spiritus"; this was a common substance in 17th-century alchemy, believed to contain highly refined salts of the human body</note>, which consists entirely of oily volatile salt, as well as other distilled oils. <margin>Note 29.</margin> The frequently mentioned **Mr. Krafft** related to us that there was a certain **Indian** in the East Indies who was injured by a sword drawn across the palm of his hand. I believe the reason he used no bandages was that the Indians, knowing the healthfulness of their air, do not wish to block its access. Since that air is found to be balsamic, it not only prevents decay but also promotes healing and restoration. 

Yet, this would not succeed in these regions <note>referring to Europe</note>, where the air is filled with thick and sharp atoms, bringing great harm to wounds unless they are protected from it. This is why wounds are treated differently and take different amounts of time to heal in various regions, according to the healthfulness of the air—though diet and lifestyle also contribute much. 

<margin>Note 30.</margin> It is certain that food in some lands is healthier than in others. Experience teaches that the nourishment used to sustain the blood matters greatly for wounds. If even the slightest error is committed in diet, an alteration is immediately felt in the wound because the blood, originating from that nourishment, flows continuously to the injured parts.

Because of this, it seizes the bodies it is mixed with and joins itself to them. 

This is the reason we are accustomed to eating salt in daily use: specifically so that thicker foods may be digested and broken down. But when we use it to excess, the sharpness of the salt necessarily dissolves and corrupts the structure of the animal's composition; indeed, at this stage, if moisture is added, it leads to a horrific rot. For as will be demonstrated below in the second book under the "anatomy of Mercury," something **Mercurial** lies hidden in salt which is caustic and eroding by nature. Hence, those who eat too much salt are eventually plagued by salty catarrhs, scabies, scurvy, and leprosy; for the excessive use of salt makes the body rot, just as a moderate amount preserves it from rot. 

We see the proof of this in sea voyages, where the long use of salted foods induces scurvy. And certainly here in **Bavaria**, where because of the abundance and low price of salt, the common people salt their food very heavily—believing they are thus preserved from rot—they instead fall into dangerous diseases, especially **leprosy** <note>In the 17th century, "leprosy" often served as a general term for various severe skin afflictions, including those caused by poor diet</note>, of which there is a great number of infected people throughout Bavaria. Although some ascribe this to the pork which the inhabitants eat frequently, I assign it to the excessive use of salt; for in other places men eat pork frequently and are nonetheless immune to leprosy. 

Salt, therefore, brings great utility, but also great harm if it turns into decay. This decay is not simple; because of the added corrosion, it imprints a ferment upon the entire blood, causing all **microcosmic salt** <note>salts found naturally within the human body (the "microcosm")</note> to become corrosive and rage against its own body. The preceding facts therefore teach that there is a great power in sugar to resist decay. Indeed, experience demonstrates that sugar preserves against rot far better and more strongly than salt; for though you may preserve fruit, apples, and similar things with plenty of salt, they will still rot, while on the contrary, those coated with sugar—a craft in which the **Genoese** excel—persist for a very long time.

They regard Europeans as fools for taking such a bitter substance into their bodies; for they call sugar **sweet salt**. These people, because they use sugar instead of salt, are never found to suffer from **scurvy**.

to become rarefied. This is not indeed by way of *fermentation;* where the whole mixture, or its equal parts, are rarefied and together produce a new mixture that is useful for other purposes. And although bodies suffer many alterations even when this spirit is present (as we shall see later in the chapter on fermentation), nevertheless its absence causes the greatest of all alterations: namely, *putrefaction:* which is the disturbance of the entire *mixture*, and is diametrically opposed to *generation*. For just as in generation parts are *coagulated* and formed into a body, so in putrefaction the parts are *resolved and become, as it were, formless.* For some parts contract *mold* <note>original: "situm"</note> when moist air approaches; others are resolved into *sanies*, namely by the mixing of external humidity with internal; others, dissolved and thinned, exhale into the air with a great *stench*. These putrid emanations from a corpse are thoroughly *pestilential*, for the particles have been driven outside their natural constitution <note>original: "crasin"; the healthy balance of elements in a living body</note>. ### Book I. Section V. Chapter 1.

...the waters are overcome and melt away; the same thing happens with animals, but more intensely, since it occurs not in their seed but in their body—the seed itself being weaker and containing more moisture. Next, in vegetable seed there is another difference: namely, that it is still endowed with its <term>balsamic spirit</term> <note>original: "spiritu balsamino"; a vital preservative force in early chemistry believed to prevent rot</note>, which is the cause of vegetation, or what <term>Lullius</term> <note>referring to Ramon Llull (c. 1232–1316), a Majorcan philosopher and alchemist</note> calls the "vegetable substantive." By means of this spirit, the seed overcomes humidity and brings forth a new generation. In an animal carcass, however, such a spirit is now exiled and absent. Hence, the animal mixture indeed suffers an alteration of its parts due to humidity, just as the vegetable seed does; but because of a lack of <term>vital fire</term>, it is unable to react and overcome the moisture as we described regarding the vegetable seed. Therefore, no new regeneration follows—as we demonstrated in that section—but rather a disturbance and breakdown of the entire mixture. 

First, an alteration of the "oiliness" or the "glue" of the blood occurs; for since these oily parts are those upon which humidity acts first (being the primary subject of putrefaction), it necessarily follows that they are changed before the rest. 

<margin>No. 42.</margin>
Hence experience teaches that *fatty things, especially blood, and bloody carcasses, as well as corpulent fats, putrefy most easily.* And since putrefaction is a species of <term>rarefaction</term> <note>the process of a substance becoming less dense or more "airy"</note>, and rarefaction is a species of combustion (as we demonstrated previously), it follows that from such putrefaction of oily parts, the same new entities emerge as from burning: namely, vapors, soot, and especially <term>volatile salt</term> <note>original: "sal volatile"; a salt that evaporates easily, often associated with the essence of a substance</note>. 

For as we shall demonstrate in the preceding and following chapters—especially in the specific chapter on liquefaction—all things, when they are burned, exhibit either an *acid or a urinous spirit*. In this spirit is the volatile salt, which consists of rarefied oil, or in which oily parts exist, but in an "inverted" state. Although these parts do not then burn or flame, they can nevertheless be reduced back into flammable matter by simple manipulation, as we clearly see in <term>oil of sulfur</term> <note>original: "oleo sulphuris"; sulfuric acid produced by burning sulfur under a bell jar</note>. 

Thus, while the more "fixed" parts are reduced to earth by putrefaction (just as they are reduced to ashes by combustion), the lighter and subtler parts are reduced to the nature of volatile salt, whether in a dry or liquid form. Because these parts are now outside their former shape and solidity, and because of their greater rarefaction and the mixing of moisture, they are completely reduced to a different temperament. The remaining parts are rendered "attractive," meaning they draw in more moisture. 

<margin>No. 43.</margin>
We see this in the *spirit of sulfur or vitriol* <note>vitriol refers to sulfate minerals or sulfuric acid</note>, whose oil, when exposed to the air, attracts it copiously and resolves it into a liquid. Indeed, this even happens during its distillation. For no one would be so unrefined as to believe that the *wateriness in oil of sulfur comes from the sulfur itself*; rather, in the very act of burning, as soon as it is thinned, it attracts the surrounding air and resolves it into the water with which it clothes itself. 

We also see that when arsenic or <term>orpiment</term> <note>original: "auripigmentum"; a deep-orange or yellow arsenic sulfide mineral</note> is soaked in oil of vitriol and, after the moisture is drawn off, is dried again and exposed to air, it immediately attracts the air and resolves itself into an oil, as will be more clearly explained below. At this point, I only wished to infer from what has been said that the parts made more volatile through the breakdown of putrefaction behave like a foul-smelling or <term>empyreumatic</term> <note>smelling of burnt organic matter</note> volatile salt; these oily parts are "inverted" and attract air like oil of sulfur, resolving it into a flowing <term>sanies</term> <note>a thin, greenish-foul discharge from a wound or decaying flesh</note>. 

<margin>No. 44.</margin>
Since they do this over a long time, and because a certain "animal and seminal chaos" lies hidden in the air—which is attracted by such an "animal magnet"—it necessarily follows that this new attracted seminal object operates within the putrid animal subject, and [new] spe-

# Subterranean Physics

...to bring forth species, from which arises the generation of **insects** and all things that spring from putrid matter. Now, the reason why oil of sulfur does not attract such seminal power—and why no small worms are generated within it—is that this "magnetism" or attraction operates according to the nature of the subject doing the attracting. 

**Borellus** <note>Pierre Borel (c. 1620–1671), a French scientist and physician</note> is our authority for the fact that minerals attract a "mineral virtue" from the air; he asserts that lead exposed to the air for a long time *increases* notably in weight. It is also certain that earth which has been dried, thoroughly boiled, and thus cleared of vegetable seeds, will nevertheless produce grass and other herbs when exposed to the air, because it attracts their seed from the atmosphere. By an infallible consequence, therefore, we conclude that **animal** subjects also attract something similar to themselves from the air; namely, a certain animal virtue. However, this virtue is imperfect because of the corruption of the "vessel" (the decaying body). Hence, it is inevitable that only insects emerge. Nature wills it so: when one subject dies, another is born; when one vital balsam ceases and flows out, another balsam from the air begins to flow in. From this comes the saying: *the corruption of one is the generation of another* <note>original: "corruptio unius, est generatio alterius"; a fundamental principle in Aristotelian natural philosophy</note>, though not of the same species, for the reasons already stated. 

We conclude, then, that the **animation of insects comes from the air**. We rely, among other reasons, on the **Würzburg experiment**, 

<margin>No. 45.</margin>
which the Most Eminent Elector of Mainz <note>Johann Philipp von Schönborn (1605–1673), a patron of the sciences</note> ordered to be performed in the citadel at Würzburg to disprove Father **Valerian’s** <note>Valeriano Magni (1586–1661), who debated the existence of a vacuum</note> theory of the vacuum. For if a vacuum truly existed, no putrefaction or corruption could occur within it. Therefore, using a receiving vessel—evacuated by a pneumatic pump according to the instructions of a certain citizen of Magdeburg, **Guericke** <note>Otto von Guericke (1602–1686), inventor of the air pump</note>—meat was placed inside and the vessel was perfectly sealed with luting <note>a clay or cement seal</note>. Within a few days, the meat began to putrefy, and eventually worms began to grow—but they were not alive, nor did they move. When the vessel was finally opened, they immediately 

<margin>No. 46.</margin>
began to live and move. **Glauber** <note>Johann Rudolf Glauber (1604–1670), a famous alchemist and chemist</note> also affirms this: namely, that putrid things *do not turn into living animalcules unless they feel the open air*. From this it is clearly established that "vivacity" (the spark of life) comes from the air, which acts as a common nursery and a reservoir of <term>panspermia</term> <note>original: "panspermiæ"; the theory that "seeds" of all things are scattered throughout the atmosphere</note>. 

We see this also in the process of turning into vinegar; which, as will be taught in the following chapter, is a species of corruption—specifically, a slow resolution and "exaltation" of salt. Thus, experience teaches that when vinegar is at its strength and exposed to the open air (yet kept warm and moist), countless 

<margin>No. 47.</margin>
flies grow from the vinegar or its emanations. Indeed, those who have more accurately observed the use of **microscopes** show us a huge abundance of worms both in vinegar and in the blood of those suffering from fevers. 

It is certain, moreover, that oily and **fatty** substances are more liable to this alteration than **lean** and **watery** ones; hence, in lean cheese, worms do not arise as quickly or in such great numbers as in fat cheese. But fatness alone does not cause putrefaction; rather, it resists it, unless it is watery and has taken on a sort of "soapy" nature. Otherwise, it could not be affected by external moisture—as we see in trees and other sulfurous things, which are free from all rot. On the contrary, in bacon, lard, fat, and tallow, corruptions are felt immediately. Once these substances are raised to the state of a volatile salt, they begin to more powerfully attract the seminal virtue of the air and are brought to life. 

Since we have thus far followed the process of putrefaction from the loss of the vital balsam to its reduction into foul and corrupt matter, and finally to the "revivification" of insects, worms, and animalcules, it remains for us to look at the end—specifically, the end of the worms and moths...

### Book I. Section V. Chapter I.

...the end, namely the resolution of insects back into the earth. For although a new mixture is produced from the discharge <note>original: "sanie"; often referring to the fluid from a wound or decaying matter</note> or putrefied matter through the attraction of the air, it is nevertheless less perfect and, for this very reason, less stable; this is because it arises only by accident and clings to foreign emanations. Since these are always evaporating, and eventually the nourishment and matter fail, it is inevitable that such tiny creatures quickly die.

<margin>No. 48.</margin>
At this point, we must consider: why are different creatures produced? This surely comes from the diversity of the surrounding air acting as the "object," and the alteration of the decaying matter acting as the "subject." For from putrefied ducks, owls <note>original: "bubones"; this reflects early modern folk beliefs in spontaneous generation where specific animals were thought to transform into others</note> arise; from spinal marrow, snakes; from certain putrid waters, worms; from others, serpents; and from others, gnats—called *Mußkitten* <note>original: "Mußkitten," a phonetic rendering of "mosquitoes"</note> in India—and a great variety of insects. If anyone wished to explain the specific and particular cause of each, they would be eaten by worms themselves before they could finish the task.

<margin>No. 49.</margin>
Various arguments could also be brought forward concerning the indivisibility and permanence of **forms**; but since the entire quarrel surrounding these things consists only of names and words, we shall omit making words about words and instead deal with things and realities. For what prevents us from stating that **forms** perish—or rather, emerge—through the imposition of others? Here we are speaking of the *external and superficial form*. 

Certainly, a piece of wood, whether rough or turned on a lathe, exists in a different form; but if you look at its intrinsic nature, and reduce both pieces of wood to ashes and oil, the form will again be different, according to the diversity of the process and the temperament into which it is led by the preparation. It is always new and new again, and entirely different from the previous one, just as one and the same form can be superficially shaped into many figures by the lathe. Would the world then perish if we established that *forms perish*? Certainly, it would not perish, if we concluded that another world emerges from the destruction of the old; just as we demonstrate that from the corruption of one form, another is produced.

<margin>No. 50.</margin>
Meanwhile, whatever certain people scrupulously discuss regarding that *inherent universal form* of Aristotle, and other word-battles <note>original: "logomachiis"</note> of that sort, matters little to us. We believe that such pseudo-philosophers <note>original: "Philosophastros"</note> contend with sublime words because they are ignorant of things and realities; and lest they be quickly accused of ignorance by the common people, they torture the minds of the idle with idle speculations, terms, and words. They would be spared all this labor if they dealt with real things, where a single practical experiment <note>original: "praxis"</note> sometimes proves an entire philosophy (of that sort, anyway) to be false.

But let us return from these "learned worms" to the physical worms born from putrefaction, and let us teach what happens when they too have passed away into the earth.

<margin>No. 51.</margin>
We said previously that such earth is **nitrous**; this must necessarily happen if we consider that the particles of the fiery, life-giving atoms of such insects partly evaporate upon death, and partly cling to the volatile saline (or rather, the inverted oily) parts, constituting a new mixture which we call **Nitre** <note>saltpeter</note>. 

<margin>No. 52.</margin>
The truth of what has been said is demonstrated by a clear experiment: if earthworms are taken, placed in a glass, and resolved into water, and this is thickened to a third of its volume, flammable crystals of **Nitre** will grow together, as we shall explain more specifically in the second book in the history of Nitre. But even **nitre** itself is not yet the ultimate end of putrefaction; for when its fiery parts are separated, the remainder is converted into earth that is entirely *pure and tasteless*, but endowed with a singular magnetism...

### Subterranean Physics

...of attracting a new aerial spirit and becoming nitre <note>original: "nitrum"; refers to saltpeter, which early modern scientists believed was a vital salt that circulated between the air and the earth</note> once again. Such earth also remains in great quantity after putrefaction—specifically from the more fixed parts of the body, which could not be so quickly dissolved or turned into vapor, and therefore could not be brought back to life or turned into nitre by the world's aerial spirit. Thus, when this spirit is absent or driven away, the nitre itself is converted back into earth; Helmontius <note>Jan Baptista van Helmont (1580–1644), a pioneering chemist who bridged the gap between alchemy and modern science</note> writes that he knows how to turn all nitre into entirely elemental earth. Therefore, this nitrous earth—whether left over from the process of making nitre or from decay—is indeed elemental, but as I have said, it is not a simple earth. For it attracts new spirit, and is therefore fertile and very conducive to the growth of plants, to which it communicates the attracted spirit, and is thus rendered fruitful. By always attracting new spirit and becoming nitre, and then losing that spirit and dying away—I say that in such an operation, as the spirit departs, certain earthy particles also depart. In this way, all the remaining earth, which may be called **dead earth**, is gradually consumed until it entirely vanishes into the empty air and mixes with other bodies.

<margin>Note §4.</margin> For this reason, if you set aside the soul, the ancient idea of the transformation of bodies into various species is not so absurd; for unless one thing were made into another, it would follow that the whole world would be filled with corpses, the contrary of which is demonstrated by experience. For we see cemeteries used for several centuries, yet they always maintain the same location, size, and mass. This could not happen if bodies were only changed into earth and that earth did not evaporate and be carried away with the air.

<margin>Note §5.</margin> To bring the doctrine of putrefaction to a conclusion, we shall also add this: nature maintains nearly the same *time and manner in putrefaction* as it observed in generation. Just as it gradually solidifies in the latter, it *slowly dissolves* in the former. For as soon as a human dies, their corpse immediately breathes out a mortal and *cadaverous vapor*, which is very subtle; when this has lasted for five *days*, it begins to *grow sour*. Finally, after ten or twelve days, it *breathes out a sulfurous odor, like human dung*. Meanwhile, around the *thirtieth* day (though all these things happen sooner or later depending on the variety of the corpse and the place, the constitution, and the type of death), the skin is usually covered with a kind of downy fuzz and first *turns yellow*; then *green* spots are seen here and there, which finally become *livid* and *turn black*. Having reached this final state, they are covered with a *thick mold*; finally, they begin to *sink in*, and holes are formed, from which *putrid discharge and water* sometimes flow. Meanwhile, the spots also run together and create streaks and marks across the whole face, as if a finger had been drawn through it. Thus they gradually turn into *worms*, and the entire face is destroyed, so that nothing remains except the *skull* <note>original: "calvariem"</note>. It was not possible to observe how the putrefaction proceeded in the rest of the body. We observed these things accurately in a boy <note>The author is likely referring to a controlled observation of a child's corpse to document the stages of decomposition</note> over the course of a year, with which Mantuanus <note>Baptista Mantuanus (1447–1516), a famous Neo-Latin poet</note> beautifully agrees in his second book on Alfonso, when he describes death—or rather putrefaction—in the following lines:

> *A huge monster, whose brow is bereft of twisting snakes:*
> *And whose face is deformed by a truncated nose,*
> *Two caves of a hollow head show shameful pits,*
> *The back of the head lacks an ear, but on both sides twin caverns*
> *Always gape open, and breathe foul gore into the breast,*

<note>This poem is a vivid *memento mori*, describing the gruesome physical reality of a decomposing body as a residence for vermin and a court for personified death.</note>

<margin>Note § 6.</margin>
Furthermore, not every putrefaction <note>the biological process of rotting</note> reaches such an end or follows such an order; for this reason, it is threefold. One is properly called "putrefaction," which we have discussed until now; the other is merely "corruption," where bodies are spoiled without maintaining the preceding order, such as when they are altered in their natural mixture <note>original: "crasi," referring to the specific balance of elements in a substance</note> by excessive heat, water, fire, or other causes. <margin>Note § 7.</margin> For by the name "corruption" in this context, we understand every alteration by which bodies are driven out of their natural state. This consists not only in the internal destruction of the parts but also in their extreme and even superficial confusion. For a grain of wheat, or any vegetable seed, if it is crushed and reduced to flour <note>original: "pollinem"</note> and then committed to the earth, it will never grow. Likewise, a magnet <note>original: "magnes"</note> if crushed and pulverized will never again attract iron. This is a certain sign that the existence of bodies consists not only in their internal essence, but also in their external form; according to the alteration of that form, the body is either perfected or corrupted, as we shall teach below in the chapter *on configuration*. <margin>Note § 8.</margin> Subterranean things are immune to this specific type of corruption, as their form is entirely homogeneous <note>uniform throughout</note> and similar to itself in even its smallest points and particles; therefore, in terms of its arrangement or location, it remains one and the same. Intrinsically, however, metals can hardly be corrupted by themselves into a completely new subject or leave their natural mixture, unless something is added. For they can be so confused and mixed into a heterogeneous substance <note>a substance made of unrelated parts</note> that their entire nature is corrupted. <margin>Note § 9.</margin> Although it is against nature to proceed in this way—since whatever nature does, she always tends toward producing another mixture where the parts agree and cohere intrinsically. But things mixed in such a way that there is no order, end, or use to the mixture are rightly said to be corrupted, confused, and led into an unnatural state. In this way, I will easily grant that such heterogeneous corruption occurs in subterranean things, especially minerals; where by inexperienced spagyrics <note>early chemists or alchemists who practiced "the art of separating and recombining"</note> and sellers of *Processes* <note>itinerant alchemists who sold fraudulent recipes for making gold</note>, they are sometimes so foolishly mixed and handled that these men can boast of being able to "corrupt" bodies—something Philosophers <note>the "True Philosophers" or genuine alchemists</note> so greatly desire. However, their corruption is far removed from this "sophistical" <note>deceptive or false</note> version, as we shall explain immediately. <margin>Note § 10.</margin> Furthermore, it is most certain that metals, especially the more imperfect ones, are corrupted in air, fire, water, and earth, if we look at such corruption externally—that is, in respect to the body, status, and *former figure*. But except for the corruption of metals occurring in mines (which we dealt with at the end of the preceding chapter under the term "dead metal" <note>original German: "ein todt Metall"</note>) and what follows now, no corruption is specific to metals; rather, however they are altered, they become decomposed rather than new...

### Subterranean Physics

...compounds, easily reducible to their former state.

<margin>N. 61.</margin>
Indeed, we do not deny that stones consisting of a less stable mixture can be corrupted; for they are dissolved by *rains*, stained by *grease*, and covered by a *crust* or *film* <note>original: "cute vel ungue," literally "skin or nail," referring to surface encrustations or patinas</note>: and to put it briefly, their perfection depends on us—that is, according to how we value them. In this respect, various qualities in transparency and opacity, color, hardness, and other accidental properties can be found wanting. This should also be understood regarding juices, bitumens, and other decomposed minerals.

<margin>N. 62.</margin>
For nothing is *imperfect*, as we shall later teach under the heading of "perfection," except by comparison or relation; and when something is corrupted, it is said to be corrupted in respect to its prior state, not by reason of its own essence or existence: for nothing exists, or is found, that can be reduced to nothing, but, as it is said, *the corruption of one is the generation of another* <note>original: "corruptio unius est generatio alterius," a fundamental principle in Aristotelian physics suggesting that matter is never destroyed, only transformed</note>.

<margin>N. 63.</margin>
Now we come to the final and third species of putrefaction, which is called *mortification*; it is the best of all, for this leads to *new production and the generation of its own species*; whereas *formal putrefaction produces a mixture of another species and loses its own original idea* <note>original: "ideam," referring to the formal blueprint or essential character of a substance</note>. *Mortification*, therefore, differs from putrefaction in this: it *causes the seminal power to die only for a time*; yet, in the course of time, it *rises again gloriously with interest and profit*: as we explained more fully using the example of vegetables at the beginning of this chapter. It is called "mortification" because, due to a slow corruption, the seed seems, as it were, to die; thus animal seeds in the first days in the womb are slowly corrupted: which also happens to the seeds of vegetables, which lie hidden, as it were, and are overcome and "killed" by the radical moisture of the earth: until, aided by the help of both internal and external fire <note>natural heat and environmental warmth</note>, they revive, and complete their regeneration with increase and profit. This profit is the only honest "interest" <note>original: "fœnus," a term for financial interest or usury, here used metaphorically for the natural bounty of a harvest</note> granted by nature, and it proceeds from mortification, as we have just said. Both theory and experience defend the idea that *subterranean things*, especially the purer compounds like metals, are subject to this mortification;

<margin>N. 64.</margin>
for although we have often said that their structure consists of a mixture—and indeed a sudden one—mortification is not thereby excluded, as it can happen both instantly and successively. *Instantly*, indeed, since according to Holy Scripture we ourselves who survive at the end of the world are to be changed in a moment; and experience teaches that *metals are transmuted immediately by means of a tincture* <note>an alchemical agent or "philosopher's stone" capable of changing the properties of a metal</note>; which certainly cannot happen without some reaction and mortification.

<margin>N. 65.</margin>
Regarding *successive* mortification, which occurs in the mixing of metals, whether natural or artificial, we shall discuss a few things to conclude this chapter. We said at the end of the previous chapter that *when metals in the mines reach the completion of their mixing, if some principle continues to flow into them—especially the third principle, which we discussed in section three, chapter 4—the whole mixture is resolved again, and the metal flies away, just as rotten grain, changed into an insect, revives and flies away* <note>Becher refers here to the theory of spontaneous generation, where decaying matter "revives" as a new life form like a fly or beetle</note>: such a metal is therefore called *dead*. This does not refer to the part that has fled and been resuscitated (for that is *living*), but to that which remains: namely, the empty husks. From these, therefore, we have begun—working backward from the result—so that we may properly understand the preceding stages of metallic mortification, for the sake of which we have written this entire chapter and labored until now.

<margin>N. 66.</margin>
Metals, however, cannot putrefy, especially formally, as in the first species of putrefaction...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the nature of "mortification" (alchemical death) versus common putrefaction. The previous page established that while common corruption destroys, "mortification" in the mineral kingdom is a necessary step toward the generation of a more perfect substance, like a seed dying to sprout.</meta>

<header>Book I. Section V. Chapter V.</header>

...as we explained in the preceding sections and demonstrated to occur in animals. For minerals, because they possess homogeneous parts that are either all equally fixed or all volatile, do not admit such a separation. Furthermore, they can only be thinned <term>rarefied: the process of making a substance less dense</term> by fire; this thinning is contrary to the thinning of putrefaction, which is caused by moisture. Common putrefaction occurs through moisture, by which the "glue" or balsamic viscosity in a mixture is overcome and dissolved. This is impossible in metals, as common moisture does not penetrate the metallic mixture, and therefore is not intimately united with it, nor does it act upon it—especially not in a way that would dissolve the sulfurous glue, the active agent, and the "gum" of the metals, which are of an extremely strong composition.

<margin>N. 67.</margin> Therefore, another mode of putrefaction and another putrefying agent is required to make metals die away and to "mortify" them. This agent is their own **radical moisture** <note>original: "humidum radicale," the fundamental fluid believed to sustain the existence of a substance</note>, which is a **liquefying earth**, as we shall explain in Section Three, Chapter Four; in Chapter Three of this Section; and in Book Two, in the specific chapter on Mercury. Indeed, when the metallic "glue" is over-saturated with this **dry moisture** <note>original: "sicco humido," a classic alchemical paradox describing a substance that behaves like a liquid but does not wet the hands, often associated with Mercury</note> as its own internal principle, it is dissolved and mimics vegetable mortification in all respects. For it is overcome by an excess of its own moisture; and although this moisture was its "life" at the beginning of the mixture as a component, when it arrives in excessive quantity, it becomes the death and destruction of that very mixture—namely, the dissolution of the compound. In this state, due to the retreat and liquefaction of the sulfur, **various colors are seen** <note>This refers to the "Peacock's Tail" (cauda pavonis), a stage in alchemy where the matter changes colors as it decomposes and rearranges</note>, until it gradually overcomes the moisture again and forms a new mixture with an increase in quality.

This mortification of metals and "improper" putrefaction is observed not only in the mines (nature's workshop) but also in the work of the **Philosophical Art** <note>Alchemy</note>, where the professors of said art anxiously desire such a fertile mortification and putrefaction as the very principle of their craft. For as **Plato the Chemist** <note>A pseudonym used by medieval alchemical authors, not the Greek philosopher</note> says: *the egg first putrefies, then the chick is born*; and **Philippus de Ravilasco** states: *through putrefaction the corporeal dies, and through a new vegetation the spiritual rises*; and **Arda**, a disciple of Aristotle: *the grain is nourished by its own connatural moisture until it grows and is animated*; and **Rachaidibi**: *everything that is nourished is nourished by reason of the diminished; that which is vivified is vivified by reason of the two.* And the *Book of the Saturn of the Philosophers*: *it is mortified for so long until it is dead to the metallic form, which is the leper's shadow of the stone* <note>original: "lapidis leprosa umbra," referring to the idea that base metals are "leperous" or imperfect versions of gold</note>. And **Bernhard of Gravia**: *Our dead son lives.* And **Cardinal Melchior** says: *one must kill him wisely, because death will bring him back to life.* And the author of the *Table of the Elder*: *let us do it many times until it dies and is softened.* And the *Allegory of Arisleus*: *conception and betrothal occur in rot, and the generation of things generated occurs in the air.* And the author of the *Twelve Chapters on the Philosopher’s Stone*: *that which was the cause of your life was also the cause of death.*

# S Y N O P S I S.

*N. 1. Many things have been written about fermentation by many authors, yet our own findings, which we shall present, will be new and untouched by anyone until now. N. 2. # Subterranean Physics
### Page 156

...visible and tangible examples of animals and vegetables, we are able to place before our eyes the deeper and more obscure conditions <note>original: "pathemata"</note> of subterranean things. <margin>N. 3.</margin> Thus, **fermentation** differs from **putrefaction** <note>decay or rotting</note> in that, while the parts are indeed thinned out <note>rarefied</note> in fermentation just as in putrefaction, and while some resolution and alteration of the small bodies within the mixture follows from this thinning, this resolution is not a destruction of the mixture. Rather, it is a perfection, a refinement <note>original: "subtilisatio"</note>, and a thinning. In this way, it is diametrically opposed to **putrefaction**, which totally alters and disturbs the mixture in its basic constitution <note>original: "crasi," referring to the specific balance of elements</note>. For **putrefaction**, during the thinning process, takes in moisture or humid particles, by which it is dissolved; and the oily parts of the mixture, as was said in the preceding chapter, are washed away. But **fermentation**, during the thinning process, intercepts aerial particles <note>gas or air atoms</note>, by which the substance is expanded, thinned, and refined, while the essential "seed" or constitution remains whole and is even exalted into a more perfect state. Therefore, **putrefaction** differs from **fermentation** in reality because in the former, the thinned parts are pulled apart, while in the latter they remain continuous. In both, however, the parts are thinned and altered through the intake of external particles—**putrefaction** tending toward a worse state, and **fermentation** tending toward a better.

<margin>N. 4.</margin> As for why I have made **fermentation** specific to vegetables <note>plants</note>, the reason is that we see it suits them more due to more frequent use. Since the mixture of vegetables is a middle ground between animal and mineral mixtures, it also holds the middle place in terms of dissolution: namely, **fermentation**. For between **putrefaction** and **liquefaction** <note>melting</note>—the latter of which belongs to minerals and the former to animals—**fermentation** is the middle path. Animals, due to their diverse and numerous particles, suffer a reaction from any external cause; from this follows **putrefaction**, an internal resolution and alteration of the whole mixture. Mineral mixtures, however, since they are entirely homogeneous <note>of the same kind throughout</note>, do indeed thin out; but because of their perfect mixture, the particles cling together, and from this arises **liquefaction**, which is proper to minerals. Vegetables are also composed of various particles, but because there is less diversity among their parts, they cling together more than animal mixtures, yet less than mineral ones. Hence, when treated with fire, their parts do not stick together or melt like metals, nor are they resolved as quickly as animals. For this reason, they are said to **ferment**, which is an action halfway between **putrefaction** and **liquefaction**.

<margin>N. 5.</margin> For **putrefaction**, **fermentation**, and **liquefaction** all require a thinning of the substance and resolve it point by point in a continuous flow; but as I have said, **putrefaction** takes in watery particles during its thinning, **fermentation** takes in aerial particles, and **liquefaction** takes in fiery particles. Therefore, they differ both by the reason of this intake and by the resulting effect, as we shall further teach in the following chapter concerning **liquefaction**. In this place, we shall deal with **fermentation**, of which three species exist: one is **swelling** <note>original: "intumefactio"</note>, or **boiling** <note>original: "ebullitio"</note>, or internal heating; another is **fermentation** properly speaking; and the third is **acidification** <note>original: "acetificatio"</note> or becoming sour.

<margin>N. 6.</margin> As pertains to the first species, namely **boiling**, we see that it happens in animals if they have taken in poisons; for they immediately swell up. This also frequently happens to bodies after death if they have been killed by a malignant disease. Even in the living, we see **buboes** <note>swollen lymph nodes</note>, **carbuncles** <note>original: "anthraces," or infected sores</note>, **mumps** <note>original: "parotides"</note>, and other malignant tumors. Specifically in malignant fevers, as well as in measles and smallpox, the blood is said to **ferment**, though the word **boil** would be more appropriate. For **boiling** blood thins out and separates its parts, which we shall discuss later regarding the **fermentation** of blood. In...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the internal transformation of matter, transitioning from the theoretical differences between fermentation and putrefaction to specific physical observations of swelling and heating in plants, minerals, and grain.</meta>

# Book I. Section V. Chapter II.

In vegetables, a certain boiling <note>original: "ebullitio," refers to bubbling or effervescence</note> is observed, especially in flatulent foods which swell up when cooked, such as pottage. This swelling properly comes from the air trapped inside becoming thinned out <note>rarefied</note>, and from the moist and viscid <note>sticky or thick</note> parts of the mixture. However, in metals and subterranean substances, various types of swelling are also found. *As when you pour oil of tartar <note>a solution of potassium carbonate</note> over alum, it creates a great foam and swelling. Johann Rudolf Glauber <note>a famous 17th-century chemist</note> is the authority for the fact that metals dissolved in aqua fortis <note>nitric acid</note>, then dried out, will immediately swell and grow into little branches* <margin>N. 7.</margin> *if a small piece is placed in oil of tartar or liquid flint <note>potassium silicate</note>.* But setting aside swelling, let us consider heating <note>original: "incalescentiam"</note>; for we see that horse manure heats up by itself; and leather handled by tanners heats up so violently that, unless it is removed in time, it is burned. Among vegetables, hay also heats up greatly if it is placed in a pile and becomes a little damp; and grain soaked in water and then piled up heats up so much that it sprouts. In metals, one could also include the heating of iron during its dissolution and swelling; *which, although not identical to the previous type of heating in all respects, is nonetheless analogous.* Such heating occurs in subjects that are dry, oily, viscous, or glutinous; when moisture is added, their thickness is somewhat thinned out. Once this happens, the particles—which are now somewhat free and released, and which we have said are of a hot nature—begin to act upon the added moisture: *Like the example of ungrateful men who do harm to those by whom they are set free, and repay them first with evil deeds.* This heating <margin>N. 8.</margin> therefore, and the swelling that follows it, is like a preparatory handmaid to putrefaction and fermentation. *It is mostly employed and caused so that very sticky substances may be somewhat loosened in this way, so that they might afterward be better able to ferment.* We see this clearly in wheat; for although it may be broken by a mill (*commonly called malting* <note>original: "gemaltzet"</note>), unless it first heats up and sprouts (*commonly called germinating or growing out* <note>original: "kaimen, auswachsen"</note>), even if <margin>N. 9.</margin> you drench it with water and cook it, it will never ferment when cooked, because the substance of the wheat is entirely glutinous. *For, as you will hear later concerning fermentation, things that are too thick do not ferment; for fermentation is a thinning out, and the first cause of thinning is the widening of the pores. If these pores are too tightly compressed and glued together, they cannot be opened, and for that reason no fermentation can follow.* Therefore, wheat and other glutinous fruits are drenched with water so that they become moist; then they are placed in a pile so that the inner parts are protected from the cold surrounding air, allowing them to act and heat up. Thus, the natural fire is awakened, and being thinned by the water, it begins to act upon it to create a new mixture, naturally and according to the natural order, namely toward the process of vegetation. *Hence it produces those sprouting tips as the foundation of growth, which we discussed in the chapter on vegetation. For the added moisture serves in place of the moisture it would otherwise draw from the earth; but since this added moisture is neither sufficient nor continuous, such growth cannot proceed further. Nor is it desired that it should proceed, since Art begins in this place where Nature ends.* The wheat that has sprouted is therefore dried, both so that the growth may die and so that the more subtle spirits released by such growth—which some call "wild spirits" <note>original: "spiritus sylvestres," a term used by early chemists like Van Helmont to describe gases or volatile substances produced during fermentation</note>—may be expelled. *For since they are very subtle, they strike the head <note>cause intoxication or headaches</note> if they remain and are mixed into the drink through fermentation; and this is the reason for...*

->### Subterranean Physics<-

<margin>N. 3.</margin> So that we might place before our eyes visible, tangible, and well-known examples from the animal and plant kingdoms to explain the deeper and more obscure conditions <note>original: "pathemata," meaning the states or "passions" matter undergoes</note> of subterranean things: *Fermentation* therefore differs from *putrefaction* in that, while in both processes the parts are thinned out <note>rarefied</note> and some degree of breakdown and alteration of the chemical mixture follows, this breakdown in fermentation is not a destruction of the mixture. Rather, it is a perfection, a refining, and a thinning. In this, it is diametrically opposed to putrefaction, which totally alters and disturbs the mixture in its fundamental constitution <note>original: "crasi," referring to the specific temperament or "crasis" of a substance</note>. For *putrefaction*, during this thinning process, takes in moisture or humid particles, through which it is dissolved, and the oily parts of the mixture are washed away, as was said in the preceding chapter. But *Fermentation*, during its thinning, intercepts aerial particles, by which it is expanded, thinned, and refined, while the essential "seed" of its constitution remains intact and is even raised to a more perfect state. Therefore, putrefaction really differs from fermentation in that the thinned parts are pulled apart in the former, but remain connected in the latter; yet in both, the parts are made thin and are altered by the taking in of external particles—putrefaction tending toward a worse state, and fermentation toward a better one.

<margin>N. 4.</margin> The reason why I have assigned *fermentation* specifically to plants is because we see it suits them more appropriately due to more frequent occurrence. Since the composition of plants sits in the middle between animal and mineral compositions, it also holds the middle place in terms of how it breaks down—namely, fermentation. For *fermentation* is the middle ground between *putrefaction* and *liquefaction* <note>melting</note>, the latter of which belongs to minerals and the former to animals. For animals, because of their many and diverse particles, suffer a reaction from any external cause; from this follows putrefaction and the internal dissolution and alteration of the whole mixture. Mineral mixtures, however, since they are entirely uniform <note>homogeneous</note>, do indeed thin out; but because of their perfect mixing, the particles stick together, and from this arises liquefaction, which is proper to minerals. Plants, truly, also consist of various particles, but because there is less diversity among their parts, they cling together more than animal mixtures, but less than minerals. Hence, when treated with fire, they do not hold together nor do their parts melt like metals, yet they are not dissolved as quickly as animal matter. For this reason, they are said to ferment, which is an action halfway between putrefying and melting. For just as *putrefaction*, so too *fermentation* and *liquefaction* require a thinning out, and they break down the substance point by point in a continuous way; but as I said, putrefaction takes in watery particles, fermentation takes in aerial particles, and liquefaction takes in fiery particles during their thinning. Therefore, they differ both by the nature of what they take in and by the resulting effect, as we shall further teach in the following chapter on liquefaction. In this place, we shall treat fermentation, of which three species exist: one is *swelling* <note>original: "intumefactio"</note>, or boiling, or internal heating; another is fermentation properly speaking; and the third is *acetification*, or the turning to vinegar.

<margin>N. 5.</margin> As for the first species—namely, boiling <note>ebullition</note>—we see that it happens in animals if they have taken in poisons, for they swell up immediately. This also frequently happens to bodies after death if they died of a malignant disease. Even in the living, we see *bubos* <note>swollen lymph nodes</note>, *carbuncles* <note>original: "anthraces," or infected boils</note>, *parotids* <note>swellings of the salivary glands</note>, and other malignant tumors. Specifically in *malignant fevers*, *measles*, and *smallpox*, the blood is said to ferment, although the word "boil" <note>ebullire</note> would be more appropriate. For boiling blood thins out and separates its parts, which we will discuss later regarding the fermentation of blood. In
<margin>N. 6.</margin>

### Book I, Section V, Chapter II.

In the world of plants, a certain bubbling <note>original: "ebullitio"</note> occurs, especially in *flatulent foods* <note>such as beans or legumes</note> which swell up when they are cooked, like pottage. This swelling properly comes from the thinning of the air trapped inside, and from the moist and sticky parts of the mixture. However, in metals and minerals found underground, various types of swelling are observed. For instance, if you pour oil of tartar <note>a solution of potassium carbonate</note> over alum, it creates a great foam and swelling. Glauber <note>Johann Rudolf Glauber (1604–1670) was a famous chemist known for his work on salts</note> is our authority for the fact that if metals are dissolved in aqua forti <note>nitric acid</note>, then dried out, and the resulting pieces are placed in oil of tartar or "liquid of flints" <note>potassium silicate</note>, they immediately swell up and grow into little branches <note>a chemical phenomenon now known as a "chemical garden"</note>.

<margin>Number 7.</margin>
But leaving aside swelling, let us consider "heating" <note>original: "incalescentiam"</note>; for we see that horse manure heats up by itself. Likewise, leather handled by tanners heats up so violently that it would be burned up unless it were removed in time. Among plants, hay also heats up greatly if it is placed in a pile and becomes slightly damp. Even grain, if soaked in water and then placed in a pile, heats up until it begins to sprout. Among metals, we could also mention the heating of iron during its dissolution and swelling; although this is not exactly the same as the heating mentioned before, it is analogous. Such heating occurs in subjects that are dry or fatty, and *viscous* or *sticky*. When moisture is added, their stickiness is somewhat thinned and expanded. Once this happens, the particles—now somewhat free and released—begin to act upon the added moisture, since we have said they possess a hot nature. They behave like ungrateful men who do harm to those who set them free, repaying them first and foremost with ill deeds.

<margin>Number 8.</margin>
Therefore, this heating, and the swelling that follows it, is like a preparatory handmaiden to putrefaction and fermentation. It is usually employed and triggered so that very sticky substances can be broken down in this way, so that they may afterwards be better able to ferment.

<margin>Number 9.</margin>
We see this clearly in wheat. Even if it is broken by a mill (commonly called *malted* <gloss>original: "gemaltzet"</gloss>), unless it first heats up and sprouts (commonly called *germinating* <gloss>original: "kaimen"</gloss> or *growing out* <gloss>original: "auswachsen"</gloss>), it will never ferment after being cooked, even if you drench it with water and boil it. This is because the substance of wheat is entirely sticky. For, as you will hear later concerning fermentation, things that are too thick do not ferment. Fermentation is a thinning <note>rarefaction</note>, and the primary cause of thinning is the widening of the pores. If these pores are too tightly compressed and glued together, they cannot be opened, and therefore no fermentation can follow. For this reason, wheat and other sticky fruits are drenched with water to become moist; then they are placed in a pile so that the inner parts are shielded from the cold surrounding air, allowing them to act and heat up. Thus, the "fire of nature" is resuscitated, and being thinned by the water, it begins to act upon the grain to create a new mixture—naturally and according to the natural order of growth. From this, it produces those sprouting tips as the foundation of growth, which we discussed in the chapter on vegetation. The added moisture serves in place of the moisture it would otherwise draw from the earth. But because this added moisture is neither sufficient nor continuous, such growth cannot proceed further. Nor is it desired that it should proceed further, since art <note>human skill or technology</note> begins here where nature ends. The wheat that has thus sprouted is then dried, both so that the growth might die off, and so that the <term>wild spirits</term> <note>original: "spiritus sylvestres," a term used by early chemists for gases like carbon dioxide</note>—which are thinned and released by such growth—might be expelled. For since they are extremely subtle, they strike the head <note>causing intoxication or headaches</note> if they remain and are mixed into the drink through fermentation; and this is the reason for the heat—
