# Subterranean Physics

...the heating of wheat; which, when it is sown in the earth, heats up in the same way as was stated previously regarding the process of vegetation. <margin>N. 10.</margin> Having therefore sent this "heating" ahead as a handmaid, let us proceed to the Mistress herself: namely, fermentation. *Fermentation is therefore defined as the thinning <note>original: "rarefactio"</note> of a denser body and the placing of air particles in between its own.*

<margin>N. 11.</margin> From this it is concluded that fermentation must take place *in the air, though not in air that is too hot, lest the parts capable of thinning be driven out; yet it must be in an open vessel, or in a space empty enough that the parts are able to thin out: for a tight seal and the filling of a vessel to the brim completely prevents fermentation.* Frequent movement is also an impediment; for the thinning parts are shaken and cease their action; hence the concussions caused by *thunder, cannons*, and other such things are harmful. <margin>N. 12.</margin> This is to be understood regarding the very beginning of fermentation, when the tender parts easily cease fermenting; but toward the end of fermentation, a moderate stirring helps, as it rouses the parts to ferment. This is why fresh *beers* <note>original: "cerevisiæ"</note>, when they are transported by wagon and shaken, become stronger and better.

<margin>N. 13.</margin> Furthermore, a distinction is made between *open and closed* fermentation; in *open* fermentation, the fermented drink is healthier but *weaker*; in *closed* fermentation, it is not as healthy but *stronger*. The reason is that the thinned, evaporating little bodies—especially a great abundance of "wild spirits" <note>original: "sylvestrium spirituum"; a term used by early chemists like Van Helmont to describe gases produced during chemical reactions</note> which we discussed before—are retained and cast themselves back into the drink itself. This makes it very strong.

<margin>N. 14.</margin> Moreover, to explain fermentation briefly and yet sufficiently, we must recall what we said in the chapter on vegetation, or the mixing of vegetable matter; namely, that it happens by way of *restraint, digestion*, and through a slow thickening <note>original: "incrassationem"</note>; by which the mixable parts are coiled together, thickened, and condensed in a sweet and tight union. To take an example from wine: while the liquid is still in the *grape*, it does not ferment, but enjoys its sweet union; however, as soon as it is pressed out so that the *air* has access to it, it begins to ferment. If, however, the *must* <note>unfermented grape juice</note> is cooked before it begins to ferment and is thickened into a juice, that sweet union of parts will appear: for they cohere so strongly that they permit nothing but pure and tasteless water to evaporate, while the parts remain together in the substance of a kind of syrup.

<margin>N. 15.</margin> Indeed, to prove expressly that this union, cohesion, and mixture occur and are increased through the boiling of salt and the removal of watery parts, I have learned by experience that must cooked to the consistency of a syrup—even if it is mixed and dissolved again with the original amount of water that was removed—is nevertheless *first found to be wonderfully exalted in color;* so much so that it can now tint ten times more water to its original color than it could before. <margin>N. 16.</margin> For it turns reddish in a marvelous way, which is an evident sign that by cooking alone, a tincture can be exalted infinitely. *Second*, this syrup, even if diluted with the proper amount of water, *barely ferments a tenth as much as it did before it was cooked; indeed, by no art can it be led to fermentation anymore, but it remains a weak and foul-tasting drink.* This happens because of the cooking: by which the parts capable of thinning and fermenting are more strongly thickened and established so that they cannot be separated. Indeed, if you thicken common *ink* <note>original: "atramentum"</note> and dissolve it again, it will no longer yield true *ink*; which also happens in the opposite case with thinning.

<margin>N. 17.</margin> For if you take a measure of noble wine and distill the *spirit* from it, then pour the distillate back in, the mixture of the *wine will immediately be disturbed*, and established outside its natural flavor...

# Book I, Section V, Chapter II.

...established, for this reason: because some particles of wine are thinned <note>original: "rarefactæ"; referring to the expansion of particles into a gas or spirituous state</note> more than is proper through distillation than they were otherwise thinned in nature through fermentation. <margin>N. 18.</margin> For parts that are excessively thinned strike the tongue and nose more sharply than others, and thus reveal themselves. This happens even if you pour the smallest amount of **flaming spirit** <note>original: "spiritus ardentis"; high-proof alcohol or ethanol</note> into a large quantity of drink. And certainly, just as it is difficult and scarcely possible to condense the thinned **flaming spirit of wine** again so that it can be mixed into a drink without an unnatural or foreign taste; so it is hard, and almost impossible, to "re-animate" such **thickened syrups, condensed by cooking**, through thinning so that they might **ferment** in their original manner. For just as the flaming spirit errs through **thinning** <note>original: "rarefactione"</note> which it received through even a single **distillation**, and must be thickened again by as many degrees as it was thinned by distillation if it is to return to its natural state; so this cooked substance errs through **thickening** <note>original: "condensatione"</note> which it received by even a single boiling, and must be thinned again by as many degrees if it is to return to its natural state and **fermentable potential**. How difficult this is in practice—not to say impossible—no one believes except he who has tried it in practice. Having spent an entire year in this study, I immediately pledge one hundred, or even two hundred ducats <note>a gold coin used for trade across Europe</note>—and I will keep this promise in good faith—if anyone can successfully teach me one or the other of these two proposals; for it is of greater importance than I am able to write in this place.

<margin>N. 19.</margin> If **Glauber** <note>Johann Rudolf Glauber (1604–1670), a famous German-Dutch alchemist and apothecary</note> had considered these things and tested them in practice, he would have written so much less about the **concentration of must and beer** which he wrote so shamelessly in his *The Prosperity of Germany* <note>original: "prosperitate Germaniæ"</note>! He makes the matter so light that he does not blush to impose it upon the whole world; whereas I estimate it to be as difficult as the Philosopher's Stone itself. However, I do not deny that **wines can be fully fermented** if they are concentrated only moderately and slightly; as we see in **cooked wines**, commonly called *fired wines* <note>original: "gefeuerten Weinen"</note>, which by such an operation are rendered not only sweeter, but also stronger.

<margin>N. 20.</margin> But let us return to **Fermentation**; where it is established from what has been related that fermentable matter **must not be too thick or dense**. This is the reason that **oil does not ferment**, even though it is a **pure and subtle flaming spirit**, and differs in nothing from a flaming spirit except that a flaming spirit is thinned oil, and oil is condensed flaming spirit. However, we consider **oil to be fermentable**, relying on experience but requiring previous preparation; for it is not as thick as a syrup. Indeed, a certain great secret lies hidden in the **fermentation of oils**, as well as in the effect—namely, in fermented oils. For not only could **various kinds of very sweet and strong drinks** be prepared from them at a low price, but from those same drinks, **flaming spirits** (namely the thinned parts of the oils) are prepared. These are highly medicinal, penetrating, pleasant, fragrant, and cordial <note>invigorating to the heart</note>, such that they ought only to be taken by Kings and princes. For it cannot be told, except by one who has tasted and smelled it, how much fragrance a **flaming spirit** possesses which is prepared from nutmeg, cinnamon, or mace oil, rosemary, or any other thinned and fermented oil. From this, the **restoration of the vital spirits** is felt immediately—an effect in the sick that differs widely from the use of pearl-water <note>a medicinal tonic made from crushed pearls and lemon juice or vinegar</note>, even though pearl-water is far more expensive than this spirit. <margin>No. 33.</margin>
The third substance of a fermented liquid is entirely new, which few until now have observed, namely the *mother of the preceding double spirit*. To explain this clearly, we will place before the eyes of the reader any fermented drink, especially a *noble* and *clarified* wine—one that is old—in which we will demonstrate that there are *three diverse substances*; differing only in *rarity, density, and digestion* <note>original: "coctione"; literally "cooking," referring to the internal chemical maturation</note>: for as far as the two-fold substance is concerned, namely the *sulfurous* and *saline*, or the *earthy and aqueous*, they are one: to demonstrate this accurately to the eye, the following *experiment* is necessary. 

<margin>No. 34.</margin>
Take as much noble wine as you wish; distill from it the *spirit* in the usual manner, which you should then rectify <note>purify by repeated distillation</note> and set aside; thicken the remainder in a cucurbit <note>original: "cucurbita"; a gourd-shaped glass distillation vessel</note> to the consistency of a *syrup*, and precipitate it with the previously mentioned *spirit* of wine: immediately all the tartar <note>original: "tartarus"; potassium bitartrate crystals</note> will separate, appearing very white: and the *spirit* of wine will be tinged with a very deep red color; separate this from the tartar either by decanting or by filtration, and distill it again in a cucurbit to the consistency of a syrup: you will have the *spirit* of wine; then in the cucurbit, a *sub-acid syrup*, and separately, as I said before, the *tartar*. 

In this way, you will receive three different *substances* from the wine. Concerning the nature of the *spirit* of wine, which has already been discussed in the preceding pages, we will call it in this place the *highest* or *volatile Mercurial* substance of the wine; the *syrup* of the wine we will call the *middle* substance, or improperly the *sulfurous* part of the wine: and the *tartar* we will call the *lowest* substance, or, because of its *fixity*, the *saline* part of the wine. First, however, we will examine where these three substances originate; then we will teach their affinity and quality. 

<margin>No. 35.</margin>

Hence, when must is treated with a violent fire, the whole is burned and reduced to an *acid spirit*, *not a burning one*; and a *foul-smelling oil*: leaving behind very few dregs. But when it has been *fermented*, it exhibits the aforementioned three *diverse* substances; of which the *first is the most subtle* and *most volatile*, and the last is the *thickest* and *most fixed*, as we see in the Tartar. 

And although in the must there is only one substance, while in fermentation and violent distillation three different substances appear; nevertheless, they are neither one, nor are they many or diverse substances, but they all proceed from a single split root, as we will now demonstrate. <margin>N. 38.</margin> secondly, because once drawn into the *vine or plant* itself, it is not sufficiently prepared due to the surrounding air and the restriction of the sun. For it is manifest that by a lack of sun, *acidic wine* is generated; for the substance drawn from the earth cannot be cooked, digested, and altered: regarding this restriction, and the pleasant thickening and influence, we have treated more fully above in the chapter on vegetation. <margin>N. 40.</margin> Hence those *strongest* wines, which are *more spirituous*, have little *gross and middle* substance: yet they always retain something of it, the Creator so willing it that one substance might be enfolded in another. <margin>N. 41.</margin> This middle substance provides us with extracts; and in *purgatives*, the purging power consists in that alone. In fermentation, when the "thin-able" parts have been thinned, and thus the whole liquor exists in a refined state, the heterogeneous parts are separated by *natural gravity*.

<margin>N. 62.</margin> For just as we said in the chapter on the generation of animals, that the *weight and quantity of accreting parts* is the proximate cause of growth, mixing, and *formation*; so too does unsuitable weight exist as the cause of heterogeneity and separation.

<margin>N. 63.</margin> Hence, once a drink is brought back to its natural state and a balance of thinness and density through thinning—this state being the middle degree between density and thinness (for an extremely *dense* liquor is *must* <term>unfermented grape juice</term>, and an extremely *thin* one is *vinegar*)—once this liquor is thinned, I say, the heterogeneous parts, if they are lighter, like feathers, leaves, or spiders' webs, seek the surface of the liquor. If they are heavier, they tend toward the bottom. From this comes the *sediment or dregs*, which nature casts down as superfluous and thicker parts; for they can no longer remain within the thinned liquor, but sink by their own weight. The types of *must* that are not sufficient...

...thrice rarefied, nor sufficiently cooked out so that it might be further rarefied; nevertheless, you will find in it everything that is present in a fermented drink: for it contains an abundance of *spirit of wine* <term>alcohol</term>; much *salt*, from which it easily turns sour; and a great deal of drinkable substance, if it were to be pressed out. Even the "middle substance" lies hidden within the drinkable part: *you will find a great quantity of tartar, but a very great abundance of earth, from which* <margin>No. 64.</margin> *alkali salt is prepared.* Therefore, provident mother Nature gave this sediment to the *wine*, so that if many small particles evaporate during fermentation, they might be replenished by the sediment. Hence, this sediment is like the mother, nurse, or the "milk" of the wine, or indeed of any drink. For this reason, it should not be drawn off immediately in the early stages; otherwise, wines—unless they are very strong—easily degenerate (commonly called *falling off* <note>original: *abfallen*</note>). Eventually, however, it is drawn off, lest this "mother," no longer being idle, causes sourness, toward which she naturally inclines due to the abundance of salt and middle substance.

<margin>No. 65.</margin> And so, we have described *Fermentation* with a simple sketch, insofar as it suits our purpose; for it is not our intention to treat these and similar matters in specific detail, except in how they serve the knowledge and better explanation of *subterranean* things. We could otherwise write a massive volume on fermentation alone. And although, as has been said, it is not our intention to present the entire doctrine of fermentation at this time, we nevertheless hope that in these few remarks we have handed down many rare and hidden things regarding the matter of fermentation which are found in no other books, even those written expressly about fermentation. The Reader will easily understand the truth of this if he reads other authors on fermentation and compares them with these observations of mine. Having therefore established the preceding foundations of fermentation,

<margin>No. 66.</margin> we shall build some examples upon them, so that we may illustrate more clearly what we have hitherto outlined with a rough and simple brush and pen. Before all else, *sugar* comes to view, which could be called *dried and condensed must* <note>"Must" is the freshly crushed fruit juice, usually grape juice, that contains the skins, seeds, and stems.</note>; in which the most sweet and balsamic *juice of the earth* is revealed. After this juice is drawn from the moist earth into canes, cooked by the surrounding air, digested, and thickened, the canes are finally cut; the juice is <margin>No. 67.</margin> pressed out through mills and thickened. Once thickened, it is dissolved and coagulated again. It is cast into a pyramidal shape <note>This refers to the "sugar loaf," the traditional form in which refined sugar was sold until the late 19th century.</note> covered with clay, which draws out the more liquid parts of the sugar, so that the remainder becomes drier and harder. *The extracted liquid sugar,* <margin>No. 68.</margin> *they call syrup*; and in truth, it is the *middle* substance of sugar, or the juice of the earth not sufficiently cooked and exalted by nature. Consequently, it is not very healthy, for he who enjoys it too much suffers from dysentery <note>original: *dysenteria laborat*; historically known as the "bloody flux."</note>. A similar liquid middle substance still lies hidden within the sugar itself, which the following "anatomy" of sugar will demonstrate, which we shall now begin.

<margin>No. 69.</margin> We have called sugar "condensed must," and not without merit; for in all things it is similar to must, if you distill it before fermentation. You will receive *spirit, urinous tartar, and a stinking oil*, just as from must. But if you mix one pound of sugar with six or eight pounds of water, adding one spoonful of fresh beer yeast, and mix it and expose it to gentle heat; in a few hours it will begin to ferment with great violence <margin>No. 70.</margin> and the emission of Gas <note>The author uses the term *Gas*, a word coined by Jan Baptist van Helmont in the early 17th century to describe the "wild spirit" or carbon dioxide released during fermentation.</note>, where the odor of common smoke will appear, which became mixed in during the drying of the sugar. If you allow it to ferment for four weeks in a vessel that is somewhat empty but closed (for it ferments for a long time due to the abundance of spirituous parts), you will receive a *very strong drink*, not unlike Spanish wine <note>likely referring to fortified wines like Sack or Sherry</note>, in which *all the parts of naturally fermented wine* are found.

This cannot be said of unfermented sugar—otherwise the same logic would apply to *must* <term>unfermented grape juice</term> as to *wine*, though their qualities are contrary, as daily experience testifies. I say this because I know that certain ignorant asses—though they be chief physicians <note>original: *protomedicos*</note>—despise this saccharine drink among the common people and the sick on that account, even though what they say about the "sliminess" <note>original: *Schleimen*</note> of this drink actually applies to their own syrups. Furthermore, these *sweet things increase bile, provoke thirst, take away appetite, upset the stomach, and obstruct the viscera*; whereas on the contrary, fermented sugar—with its *spirit* <note>alcohol</note> removed in *hot diseases* through extraction—is, in short, a sub-acid middle substance of sugar with a most pleasant taste: it diminishes bile, sufficiently settles thirst, provokes appetite, preserves the stomach, opens the viscera, relaxes the bowels, and prompts urine and sweat. Finally, just as Physicians are never more poorly spoken of by the sick than for an unpalatable drink, so for this reason alone—the most sweet and healthy drink—a Physician could and should recommend himself, if he wished to care more for the patient than for the pharmacist and the Purse <note>original: *Marſupio*, referring to financial greed</note>. It cannot be said how sweet a drink is made if this middle substance of sugar is mixed with the middle substance of wine as desired. Then, besides *medical use*, there is another civil use; for I could, if I wished, show travelers a way they could carry a dry drink with them, yielding to none, even the strongest and most expensive: whether in the form of wine or beer: which they could reduce to liquid in a short time, provided they have any fresh water. This is a great comfort for those who travel in hot and exotic regions; where usually the first cause of diseases comes from unusual and foul drink. Especially for *sailors* would this art be useful, who on whatever island or place, provided they find water...

# Subterranean Physics

<margin>No. 74.</margin> ...they might have a sweet taste, and be able to prepare wine or beer. But let us return to our purpose; although we pass over many economic and useful things that arise from fermentation, we shall not omit those which are necessary for the knowledge of fermentation and its nature. Even though we do not write about this matter as a primary profession, we cannot fail to serve the public good, especially in a subject so well known to us; for we have spent several years in the practice of fermentation, so that all things might come accurately before our eyes. Indeed, we do not write from the works of *Angelo Sala* <note>Angelo Sala (1576–1637) was a pioneer in chemistry who famously analyzed the composition of sugar.</note> and other compilers. This, therefore, must be noted regarding the fermentation of sugar and of all fermented liquids: that when it is halfway finished (or even from the beginning), it can be very easily stopped, either by vigorous shaking, or—what
<margin>No. 75.</margin> succeeds more happily—by *adding new material*. For example, if you cast pulverized *sugar* into fermenting sugar, you will immediately notice a reaction with a great deal of foam; when this has finished, add more again until the reaction ceases, then mix it: and immediately all fermentation will stop, so much so that with all the diligence applied, I could never again *lead it back into fermentation*. The reason for this is that the *spirituous* parts, and especially the rarefied *saline* parts, act upon the newly added sugar and constitute a *new mixture* by thickening its pores in the meantime, not unlike *oxymel* <term>oxymel: a medicinal mixture of honey and vinegar</term>: and that is enough *in passing regarding Sugar*.

<margin>No. 76.</margin> Now we shall proceed from vegetables to *animals*. First to *honey*, which is a species of *manna* <note>In this context, a sweet substance gathered from plants, often thought to fall like dew.</note>, or *flowery dew*, collected and digested by bees, and thus easily separable; for in fermentation, there is a general axiom: the more the subjects are endowed with sweetness, *fatness, and dense salt*,
<margin>No. 77.</margin> the more fermentable they are. On the contrary, the more acidic, *saline, and thin* they are, the more they tend toward acidity <note>sourness or vinegar-making</note>, as we see in sugar and *common salt*; the former of which ferments easily, while the latter leads to *souring*. *Honey*, therefore, since it is very sweet and
<margin>No. 78.</margin> fatty, ferments easily; but it has much of a *middle substance* <note>The author uses "middle substance" to describe the parts of a material that are neither volatile spirits nor solid dregs.</note> which cannot ferment to the end. This must therefore be drawn off, so that first the honey is boiled several times and *skimmed*, by which the *wild spirits* <note>original: *sylvestres spiritus*; likely referring to volatile gases or impurities.</note> may partly evaporate: then, with the proper moisture added, it is fermented, and the superfluous middle substances are precipitated. At this point, I could, in a single word, open a secret to the Honey-masters <note>Mellariis: professional mead-makers</note> by which they could prepare a *very strong and very pleasant* thin drink from honey, without an unpleasant taste, and not yielding to *Spanish wine* in quality. But let us finish with

<margin>No. 79.</margin> the nature of *honey*, which is varied according to the quality of the dew that the bees suck. Furthermore, it varies by the diversity of the bees. Hence there is domestic and *wild* honey. And it is a wonder that in cold places, such as *Poland* and *Muscovy* <note>An early name for Russia.</note>, the bees, the dew, and the honey are of a stronger and more digested quality than in *Germany* or elsewhere. For the honey among us has much *middle substance* and little *spirituous* part; hence weak drinks are made from honey here. In contrast, *Polish Mead* <note>original: *Hydromellia*</note>, especially *Lithuanian* mead, yields to no wine in strength. In the *Indies*, I have not noticed that bees are found; if they were, they would certainly produce a noble honey: but I fear lest the great heat dries up the dew, so that the bees would have no nourishment. Now, from a substance that is almost hermaphroditic—namely *honey*, which is an intermediate between animals and
<margin>No. 80.</margin> vegetables, produced from the nature and help of both—let us proceed to *animals*. History records that the *Tartars* and *Scythians* <note>Nomadic peoples of Central and Northern Asia.</note> make a drink from meat, but they will not ferment it unless other things are added, such as *Rice* and similar items; and in this way, we have fermented *dried blood*.

From these, it can easily be gathered which parts in man are more fermentable, and which, as practice teaches, can actually be fermented.

We shall therefore pass from the **natural fermentation** of animals to their **preternatural** <note>original: "praeternaturalem" — meaning "outside of nature" or "pathological"</note> fermentation, namely the **fermentation of Fevers**. And since **Willis** <note>Thomas Willis (1621–1675), a famous English physician who wrote extensively on the "fermentation" of blood as a cause of disease.</note> has written accurately about these, we shall repeat nothing from him, but only add our own observations. This comes especially from foods that are too viscous or hot, such as strong wines and heavily seasoned foods, particularly those that are sticky and ingested in large quantities. This **saburra** is cooked, digested, and restrained like **must** <note>original: "mustum" — young, unfermented wine</note> on the vine, so that this must-like substance swells with sulfur and salt. It is viscous and thick, and therefore difficult to dissolve, and much less permeable. When it reaches a sufficient mass, and as it is dried and essentially "toasted" day by day by the continuing heat, it increases greatly in heat (though a digested and fixed heat), and therefore becomes

<margin>No. 84.</margin>
**attractive** and hungry for moisture, which it **attracts** in great quantities. The internal heat follows the attracted moisture, as it **intends** to overcome such a large quantity of liquid. Hence the heat gathers there from all the limbs; as a result, the other parts, now deprived of such heat, feel **cold**, from the cold comes **shivering** <note>original: "horror" — the medical term for the chills or rigors preceding a fever</note>, and from the shivering comes **shaking**. While these things are happening in the **external** parts and they are freezing, the **internal** parts meanwhile are **burning**—specifically in the place where this primary action occurs. For the **moisture**, flowing in to dilute the febrile ferment, grows hot and becomes thin due to the heat flowing in at the same time; this makes it more suitable for partially dissolving this saburra, as much as it can take into itself. And while it is so "tinted" and imbued with the small particles of the febrile ferment, the internal heat of these particles of saburra is also excited by the surrounding external heat. Thus, the now-thinned particles begin to **ferment**, which can happen quickly, as we see in the fermentation of sugar, which begins to ferment within the space of an hour. Therefore, the **resolution of this febrile matter** lasts as long as the shivering and cold persist; for when they begin to ferment, the heat that had flowed in ceases (because the moisture now grows hot on its own from the mixed-in particles) and returns to the limbs. The moisture, heated and imbued with the fermenting particles, follows this heat...

# Physica Subterranea

...[it results in], from which comes a great agitation <note>original: *fervor*</note>, and from that agitation, heat, which lasts only until the fermentation is completed. Moreover, in febrile fermentation, three stages <note>original: *tempora*</note> and three effects must be noted:

<margin>No. 85.</margin>
First, the period of flowing moisture is observed; this is proportioned according to the quantity and stubbornness of the **digested waste** <term>saburra: a medical term for the accumulation of undigested matter or foul humors in the stomach or intestines</term>, and the febrile ferment. Thus, it flows sufficiently sometimes on one day, sometimes on the second, and sometimes on the third, also depending on the quality of the diet, especially drink. For things that rarefy, like wines, dissolve the material more quickly and powerfully; hence **paroxysms** <term>paroxysm: a sudden attack or increase of symptoms, like a fever spike or "fit"</term> are increased, delayed, or anticipated. They are **delayed** if the moisture flows little and slowly; they are **anticipated** if it flows excessively. 

<margin>No. 86.</margin>
Now, any period involving the influx of moisture, absorption, the dissolving of the waste matter, its fermentation, and the resulting shivering <note>original: *horroris*</note> and heat, is called a **paroxysm**. A **period** or **crisis**, however, is when such a febrile ferment is totally dissolved through several paroxysms and is expelled in the aforementioned manner. This **sometimes happens at one time** and in a single paroxysm due to a lack of material, as in **ephemeral fevers** <note>original: *ephemeris* — fevers lasting only one day</note>; sometimes in seven, sometimes in twenty paroxysms. Sometimes, if the material is stubborn, as in a **quartan fever** <note>original: *quartana* — a fever recurring every third day, typically associated with malaria</note>, it is barely finished in a whole year. All these things occur and vary according to the **quantity and quality of the febrile material**; for various effects arise based on that. 

Hence come cold fevers—or **spurious** ones—and hot ones—or **exquisite**, putrid, or malignant ones. We have spoken of the **cold** ones so far; these happen when the material or febrile ferment is too **viscous and thick**, and therefore requires much moisture to be dissolved. From this copious influx, an influx of heat also follows, and thus the cold follows <note>The author is describing the sequence where a chill precedes the fever</note>. 

<margin>No. 87.</margin>
**Hot** fevers, however, occur when the material is not so sluggish, viscous, and insoluble, but is more refined; for it is thus more soluble, needing less moisture, which the external heat does not follow and flow into so strongly, but does so only imperceptibly. Therefore, the difference between cold and hot fevers consists only in the **subtlety of the material**; for there is no febrile shivering that heat does not follow, nor is there any heat that a slow, though imperceptible, shivering does not precede. Since nothing can **ferment** that is not dissolved, nor can anything be dissolved unless a solvent is present. What we have said so far about fevers is to be understood regarding **intermittent** fevers.

<margin>No. 88.</margin>
I call them **intermittent**, not because the material and cause of the fever ceases, but because it lies hidden; just as when it is first prepared, digested, and cooked, as I said above. Then, through successive paroxysms and attacks, the material is diluted and scattered. For when the moisture flows, it is not felt until it has flowed sufficiently; and that time during which it is not felt is called the **intermission**. This is not by reason of the biological action, but with respect to our senses. 

It is possible, however, even though some paroxysms have preceded, for the febrile material to be **lulled to sleep**, so that it remains unresolved for a time and moisture does not flow to dissolve it. But such a remedy is **dangerous**, and is only called a **palliative cure** <note>A "palliative" cure in this context means one that masks symptoms without removing the underlying cause</note>. 

<margin>No. 89.</margin>
Hence, whatever surplus is left behind in fevers tends to cause **relapses** <note>original: *recidivas*</note>. Accordingly, this method of suppression should not be admitted except in highly weakened bodies where strength is lacking to endure the paroxysms; otherwise, intermittent fevers must be cured from their foundation. Namely, by the resolution and dispersal of the febrile material, and its expulsion once resolved—either through vomiting if the material is in the stomach, or through the bowels if in the intestines. 

<margin>No. 90.</margin>
In this matter, **incisive** medicines <term>incidentia: medicines traditionally thought to "cut through" or break up thick, viscous humors or phlegm</term> take the prize over others. To us, such a thing is known, which in pra—

### Book I, Section V, Chapter II

...through our practice, praises be to God, we have restored over a hundred people in the space of a single quarter of a year; so much so that we dare to make a pledge—helped primarily by divine blessing and provided no notable error is committed by the patient or by the present dangerous symptom—that we will cure any intermittent fever within the interval of three **paroxysms** <term>paroxysm: a sudden attack or increase of symptoms, such as the shivering and heat of a fever</term>. We do this not **empirically** <note>original: *empirice*—referring to medical practice based on trial and error rather than theory</note>, but from a scientific foundation: by dispersing and expelling the material through the proper channels without violence. We have even administered this to pregnant women, and it appears to be clearly the same medicine that *Kerger describes in his book on fermentation, section 3, chapter 3, where he says:*

<margin>91.</margin> *From the year 1649 to this very day, through 14 full years, I have cured over a thousand feverish patients without bloodletting, without purging, without sweat-inducing drugs, without diuretics, without altering drugs, without strengthening tonics, without topical applications, or anything else, using almost a single medicine. I did not consider whether the fever was intermittent, or continuous, or daily, or a third-day or fourth-day fever; I did not wait for the "cooking" <note>original: *coctione*—the traditional medical idea that humors had to "ripen" before being expelled</note> of the humors, nor did I have respect for sex (not even exempting women who had just given birth), age, the year, the season, or other circumstances. Indeed, I cured them in the space of a few days, without a relapse or any notable discomfort, except where the patient himself provoked new paroxysms through lack of self-control. Hence I have come to know that what Helmont says is true (regarding time, n. 53, p. m. 509): that there is never a crisis where a Physician, skilled in his art, has removed the disease before the expectation of the crisis.*

<margin>N.</margin> Thus far *Kerger*, with whose medicine ours entirely agrees, except that ours works through **evacuation and resolution** <note>original: *evacuationem & resolutionem*—thinning the fluids and then removing them</note>; whereas *Kerger* says his medicine works by **precipitation**.

<margin>92.</margin> This seems a harsh way to put it, unless he is merely playing with terms. For to "precipitate" denotes separating one thing from another, which cannot happen in such a febrile ferment. If the ferment is still obstructed and thick, it is perfectly mixed within itself, and no parts can be separated in it through precipitation—just as it cannot happen in any other ferment. For example, take **sapa** <term>sapa: a syrup made by boiling down grape juice (must) until it is very thick</term> of must or beer; you will not be able to cause precipitation even with the strongest precipitating agents. However, if it is thinned by adding water and fermented, certain earthy parts will precipitate on their own; but meanwhile the fermentation will not be hindered, but rather accelerated by such precipitation, as the parts are made thinner in this way.

Above all, therefore, the **resolution** (dissolving) of the febrile ferment is required, and the evacuation of what has been resolved. Meanwhile, I do not deny that an **alteration** can occur through reacting agents, both in thick and thin ferment; but it should be called a reaction and alteration, not precipitation. For if you pour **oil of tartar** <term>oil of tartar: a concentrated solution of potassium carbonate, used in early chemistry as a strong alkaline reagent</term> over sapa or the must itself, it will never ferment again; and wine fermenting most strongly, if mixed with oil of tartar, will immediately cease from fermentation. **Quicklime** <note>original: *calx viva*</note> does the same thing. 

But these are not to be called precipitants, but rather **alterants**, which come from condensation, based on the fundamental appetite of the "dry" and the "moist." Thus experience teaches that in cases of **anorexia** (lack of appetite), **dyspepsia** (indigestion), **nidorosa** (foul belching), and **acida** (acid reflux), and likewise in **pica** <note>strange cravings for non-food items</note>, great results are achieved by **magisteries** <term>magistery: a chemical precipitate or refined extract of a substance</term>, corals, pearls, shells, and especially **sealed earth** <term>terra sigillata: medicinal clay stamped with a seal, used as an antitoxin and astringent</term>; for such things have the nature of lime and are astringent. In the same way, the **powder of Crollius and Cornachius** <note>famous 17th-century chemical medicinal formulas</note>, the latter of which *Kerger* himself cites, work as alterants for the same reason. Here it should be noted that *Kerger* attributes a precipitating power to this powder of *Cornachius* in addition to its purging power, which is manifestly false: since nothing that precipitates is able to purge. Otherwise, **spirit of wine** (alcohol) would purge, or common water, which are the best precipitants of all. And even though from the reaction of the rarefied and the dense...

# Subterranean Physics

precipitations also occur; just as when **aqua fortis** <term>aqua fortis: nitric acid, a powerful corrosive used by alchemists to dissolve metals</term> is precipitated with **oil of tartar** <term>oil of tartar: a concentrated solution of potassium carbonate</term>. However, such precipitation is not to be attributed to the oil of tartar or the aqua fortis except by accident. This is because the rarefied aqua fortis seizes the dense parts of the oil of tartar, unites them to itself, and leaves the heavy, heterogeneous parts of the dissolved metal to sink to the bottom. This is also how we should understand copper, by which silver is precipitated for the aforementioned reasons, and not at all from the "nature" of the copper, for that has no intrinsic precipitating power. 

Even if the aforementioned **Cornachini's powder** <note>original: *Cornachii pulvis* — a famous 17th-century purgative consisting of scammony, cream of tartar, and antimony</note> were to precipitate, or to use the words of **Kerger** <note>Martin Kerger, a physician who wrote on fermentation</note>, "leaves a precipitation behind after purging," such a method of purging would still be preposterous and harmful. For it can leave behind the precipitation of nothing but the thickest parts after the thinner ones have been evacuated; hence the remaining parts must necessarily become thicker and less able to be evacuated, which is contrary to the method of healing. Furthermore, the ingredients of Cornachini’s powder themselves are, besides being purgatives, "alteratives" <note>medicines that gradually restore healthy functions</note> and not precipitants. I am confident, therefore, that there is an error in the terminology used, if the other things the author writes are true. 

We do not, however, doubt the truth of his results, since we ourselves are acquainted with a certain simple composition of water—made without any distillation, at little expense, and almost tasteless—which <margin>No. 93.</margin> cures fevers of every kind without purging or vomiting, solely through **insensible alteration** <note>original: *insensibilem alterationem* — a healing process that happens without obvious bodily evacuations like sweating or diarrhea</note>. Moreover, it stands as a divine medicine in cases of scurvy, hectic fever, internal inflammations, and even attacks of gout. We generally use this medicine as a preliminary "incisive" treatment <note>a medicine intended to break up thick humors</note>. 

We therefore maintain in every way that the febrile matter can be altered, tempered, and moved out of the state of fermentation; <margin>No. 94.</margin> especially if it still lingers in the **first ways** <term>first ways: the stomach and intestinal tract</term>. For this reason, we administer the drink even during the "shivering" stage <note>original: *horrore* — the initial cold stage of a fever</note>, where it alters the condition notably, for no heat will follow that paroxysm. 

If, however, a certain portion of the febrile matter has already fermented and been carried into the blood, the operation certainly proceeds more slowly. There is then no better help than to allow those things that are in flux to be left to nature, so that during that time and paroxysm, the heat may be allowed to end by itself, and <margin>No. 95.</margin> nature may afterward be assisted by a light sweat. By this means, she can expel the more "spirituous" febrile substance that was carried into the blood by fermentation. 

For this reason, sweating is more pleasing in this state than **phlebotomy** <term>phlebotomy: the surgical opening of a vein to withdraw blood</term>. Indeed, unless a "plethora" <note>an actual excess of blood volume</note> is present, bloodletting does not seem admissible, since the entire blood has been infected by the febrile ferment with a hot and bilious quality; you would therefore have to extract all of it. 

Furthermore, what such bloodletters call **making space** <margin>No. 96.</margin> <note>original: *luftmachen* — a German term meaning "to create air or room"</note> is entirely harmful, since it promotes fermentation. We see this in filled and closed vessels, which do not ferment at all, but if they are opened, they begin to ferment most vigorously. Beyond this, frequent bloodletting exhausts the **vital spirits** <term>vital spirits: the subtle substances believed to flow through the body to sustain life and heat</term>, which are required for the "cooking" <note>coction: the body’s process of processing or "ripening" disease-causing fluids</note> of the crude matter. The result is crude blood and the weakening of the entire nature of the person. This is why such bloodletters exhaust strength, blood, and money all at once. 

A certain jovial physician known to me related that during the time of the German wars, he was called to a certain Colonel in **Frankfurt am Main**. He persuaded the Colonel to have a bloodletting. Once the vein was cut, the Colonel gave **12 imperial thalers** to the physician and **6** to the surgeon. After a few days, the physician said to the surgeon that on account of the "good payment," the Colonel’s vein should be opened again, even though it was not necessary. When the vein was let, the Colonel paid **6** to the doctor and **3** to the surgeon. A third time the vein was tried, and he paid the doctor **3**...

They bind its sharper parts and carry them out through the bowels. # Physica Subterranea

...that the spiritual, heterogeneous particles may be expelled, and those remaining may be tightened and altered. There is also a middle substance in the blood, comprised of scorched parts, which nature tries to expel through various crises. Furthermore, before we finish this, it is pleasing to add that the modes of fermentation differ according to density. For when wine ferments, it ejects medium-sized bubbles; *sugar* smaller ones; *beer* larger ones; the *blood* becomes foamy and ejects elongated bubbles, yet very thin and barely visible. ...observed these streaks, which they declared to be *worms*. <margin>N. 104.</margin> But now order calls for us to proceed from vegetable and animal fermentation to *mineral* fermentation; for this reason, we have previously set forth all the preceding information about fermentation. However, *minerals* are said to ferment *improperly* <note>original: *improprie* — meaning not in the strict or literal sense, but by analogy</note>; since, due to their very uniform parts, they can hardly be torn apart into different substances or altered from their own nature. 

Yet when they are made thinner <term>rarefied</term> by additives, we shall call this thinning *improper* fermentation, because in many—and indeed the most important—points, it agrees with true and properly named fermentation. By additives, we mean those things which must be subtle and able to be mixed, whereas metals and minerals are coarse; <margin>N. 105.</margin> therefore, subtle additives and coarse metals do act upon each other, and the latter move from their coarseness to a middle state of thinness, while the former move from their thinness to a middle state of density, and they are mixed: solution, action, and reaction arise, not unlike vegetable fermentation. For it also throws off infinite pores and *bubbles*, and the metals are dissolved point by point, making a *new mixture and compound* of another and third kind of nature. 

This action and solution happen based on the foundations we laid above; namely, from the *appetite of the thin and the dense*, and likewise of the *moist and the dry*. From these foundations, all the causes and reasons for *corrosive solutions and mixtures* can be derived and explained. <margin>N. 106.</margin> For to begin with *spirit of nitre* <term>nitric acid</term>, or *aqua fortis* <term>literally "strong water," another name for nitric acid used as a solvent</term>, which two differ little from each other; it is certain that *nitre and vitriol* <term>sulfate minerals</term> in their natural dense form never dissolve silver, no matter what *Glauber* <note>Johann Rudolf Glauber (1604–1670), a famous chemist and apothecary known for his work with salts</note> says. Therefore, the *thinness* of these subjects is the sole cause. The sole cause, I say; for when *spirit of nitre* is distilled, if the *nitre* is pure, you will receive a pound of *spirit* from a pound of nitre, leaving no "dead head" <term>caput mortuum, the useless residue left in the flask after distillation</term> behind. This also happens in the preparation of *aqua fortis*; where you will receive as much *aqua fortis* as you added nitre, nor will you lose anything of the vitriol. The liquidity and moisture of the distillate come from the watery parts, previously frozen within the subject due to density, and now, due to thinness, liquefied and reduced into a fluid form. No one should wonder at this, since even the driest subjects, if thinned by fire, are rendered *fluid*; as we shall demonstrate in the following chapter on liquefaction, where this matter belongs and will be discussed. 

Therefore, with such subjects thinned and by repeated distillation—so that they are exalted by thinning (I say *exalted* by distillation, not *rectification* <term>the process of purifying a liquid by repeated distillation</term>; for only by *frequent distillation* are liquids rendered so corrosive throughout—even common water—that they can hardly be kept in a vessel. Once the *spirit of urine* is poured back in, it will regain its original color. So also do the *tastes* vary; for *copper* provides a *bitter taste* and *lead* a *sweet taste* in solution. For **Ripley** <note>George Ripley, a famous 15th-century English alchemist</note> said well: *every spirit is fixed by the calces* <term>calx</term> <note>A "calx" is the powdery residue—typically a metallic oxide—left after a metal has been burned or dissolved and precipitated.</note> *of its own kind*; if you observe this well, you will reap the fruit of it.

<margin>N. 111.</margin>
That the aforementioned subjects and corrosive solvents impress new qualities upon the things they dissolve is apparent from these calces. For from the **calx of gold**, if it is precipitated with *salt of tartar* <note>potassium carbonate</note>, **fulminating gold** <note>an explosive gold compound</note> is made; from **silver**, if it is precipitated with common salt, **horn silver** <note>silver chloride, which looks waxy or horn-like</note> is made, which is very volatile. Indeed, silver dissolved in strong water and precipitated into a calx is no longer dissolved in strong water unless it is first reduced back into a metallic body. **Spirit of salt** <note>hydrochloric acid</note> joins with **lead** and makes crystals that are entirely volatile; but **spirit of vinegar** <note>acetic acid</note> reduces lead into an **oil** <note>lead acetate solution, often called "sugar of lead"</note>. I am silent about **mercury, which is precipitated by various spirits**; it is discovered that it always strongly retains certain particles of the solvent within its own nature.

<margin>N. 113.</margin>
For moister bodies require hotter solvents, and hotter bodies require moist ones; as we see visually in the dissolution of gold, silver, and iron. Therefore, corrosive solution does not proceed from **rarity** <note>porosity or thinness</note> alone; for many rare things can be made which nevertheless do not dissolve metals. And although **spirit of wine, spirit of turpentine, and various oils** may act upon metals, nevertheless rarity or density alone is not the cause; rather, a **hidden and rarefied salt** will perform that work.

<margin>N. 114.</margin>
Therefore, **metallic fermentation** agrees in this with animal and vegetable fermentation: it ferments not by rarefaction alone, but also by an intrinsic quality and **sympathetic action**. For just as without air, no vegetable can ferment—nor could air, or even water, act toward fermentation—unless a certain **occult harmony** and likeness with the fermentable parts lay hidden within them.

<margin>N. 115.</margin>
(On account of the diversity of these things, in various places, one and the same drink ferments differently—slower, faster, stronger, or weaker—due to the diversity of both the air and the water. So too in the **fermentation of minerals**, it is not rarity alone, but the internal and **seminal sympathetic force** of the rarefying agents that works with the metals.

<margin>N. 116.</margin>

<margin>N. 127.</margin> **saline** parts, a slightly greater and more prolonged heat is required. If a fermented drink is subjected to this, it *turns sour*, and this is what we call *acetification* <note>the process of turning into vinegar (acetum)</note>. Furthermore, there is a 

<margin>N. 128.</margin> great difference among the *saline* parts themselves: for if they are well "digested" <note>matured or chemically refined through heat</note> and mixed, they will yield not only a *strong* vinegar but a *stable* one. If they are *weakly* mixed, however, they easily resolve back into their basic elements through a form of *putrefaction* after turning sour. Hence, vinegar becomes flat and dissolves into mold and *mustiness*, as we shall hear later. This is the reason why the better the wines are, the more noble, excellent, and durable the *vinegars* they produce; for it is a sign that they abound in much well-refined salt.

<margin>N. 129.</margin> Because of this, such vinegar can even withstand transport over water, whereas others would be ruined. Furthermore, the sourness of vinegar differs from salt and corrosive sourness: the former binds, while the latter dissolves and *erodes*. Saline acidity thus differs from the acidity of *vinegar*, and the acidity of vinegar differs from the acidity of wine. ...of wine, and of great profit in hot climates and for sweet drinks, which in this manner could be tempered and brought to a pleasant vinous acidity; for in both the **Indies** <note>Referring to the East and West Indies; the author notes a lack of natural vinegar-like acidity in the local beverages there</note> there is no vinous acidity. But it must also be understood in what way and how these acidities differ from one another; it is most certain that they differ in rarity <note>In 17th-century physics, "rarity" refers to how spread out or "thinned" the particles of a substance are</note> and digestion <note>original: *coctione*; the process of "cooking" or chemical ripening through heat</note>. For the acidity of wine arises when the **sulphurous parts** <note>The flammable, oily components</note> are thinned, ferment, and carry away, mix, and thin the finer **saline parts** with them. When later, with the addition of further heat, the remaining saline parts are also thinned, **vinegar** <note>original: *acetum*</note> is produced; but those saline parts are not as subtle and light as those that came forth in the first thinning. Consequently, they accompany the sulphurous parts, and not only equal them in quantity but also surpass them. Thus, the sulphurous parts

<margin>N. 131.</margin>
are entirely buried and hidden; hence it is called **vinegar**. For although in **spirit of wine** <note>original: *spiritu vini*; ethanol</note> there are also saline parts, they are far fewer and leave the precedence to the sulphurous spirit; hence in the distillation of wine, the **spirit of wine**, on account of its lightness, precedes all **phlegm** <note>original: *phlegma*; the watery, inactive part of a distillate</note>; but in the distillation of vinegar, the **phlegm** precedes the **spirit**. The spirit becomes heavier due to the mixed, activated, and predominant saline parts, which cling to the sulphurous spirit and make it like a subtle soap or alkali. The truth of this clearly

For when the pores of the thinned saline parts are satisfied and constricted by the insertion of the lead particles, they change from a liquid state into the consistency of salt, and from sharpness into sweetness—since we shall demonstrate below that flavor arises from the thinning of particles. Meanwhile, with the saline particles partially constricted and thickened in this way, the hidden sulphurous particles are freed again.

<margin>N. 133.</margin>
From this it happens that if spirit of vinegar is digested with lead in a closed vessel for a time and sweetened, and then distilled, it no longer comes out as spirit of **vinegar**, but again as **flaming spirit of wine** <note>original: *spiritus vini ardens*; alcohol</note>. It has cast off its previous saline mask, by which it was called **spirit of vinegar** and appeared as such in practice and effect. For the spirit of **wine** has a far different nature than the spirit of **vinegar**; since, because of its rarity, **spirit of wine** heats, whereas the spirit of vinegar, because of its density and constriction, **cools**. It follows that the elevated saline substance, separated from the sulphurous parts and now existing by itself, is that second principle of **salt of Tartar**, volatilized by the help of nature during acidification, and then prepared by the art of chemistry through separation. ### Subterranean Physics

...is not to be despised; as the sugar of Lead <note>original: *saccharum Saturni*; lead acetate, known for its sweet taste but high toxicity</note> alone demonstrates, which possesses many powers. From this, the process for acquiring volatile salt of Tartar <note>original: *sal Tartari*; potassium carbonate derived from wine lees</note> is clear: namely, by turning Tartar into vinegar with the help of nature, and separating the volatile acid salt. This labor—should anyone attempt it out of curiosity using common salt of Tartar—is superfluous, since it is already found in abundance in vinegar itself. <margin>N. 135.</margin> But for the most part, in chemistry we seek and value such things where they are found in the smallest amounts, or where they are produced with the greatest effort. Now order requires that we explain how common salt differs from the salt of vinegar; and we maintain that they differ only by **rarefaction** <note>In 17th-century physics, "rarefaction" refers to the thinning or expansion of a substance's particles</note>. For the same earth and intrinsic sulfur belong to common salt as to the salt of vinegar, but it is not so elevated. <margin>N. 136.</margin> This is the reason why common salt—unless it is moderately putrefied and transformed so that it takes on the nature of sal ammoniac <note>original: *salis armeniaci*; ammonium chloride</note>, as sea salt does—does not fertilize well; as if it were not so easily transmutable into the constituent parts of vegetables. But lest we fall into further digressions, we shall complete the whole history of vinegar in a few lines by narrating its preparation and providing the reasons for that preparation.

*First, therefore, wine (for we shall take that as an example), once the fermentation is finished and the dregs have settled, is cooked; but only until a small amount is consumed, namely until the spirit of wine <note>original: *spiritus vini*; ethanol/alcohol</note> evaporates. This is done so that what remains may turn sour more quickly: for just as fermentation makes a drink thinner and lighter, so acetification* <margin>N. 137.</margin> *renders the same drink heavier and denser.* But whatever fermentation accomplishes, it does so through the elevation and rarefaction of the **sulphurous parts** <note>The oily, flammable components</note>; this is opposed to acetification <note>The process of turning into vinegar</note>, which is like the condensation of the parts. Therefore, when these sulphurous parts are present—since their effect is to rarefy—acetification is completed with difficulty and slowly. For this reason, they are evaporated through slow cooking; and at this stage of **vinegar-making** <note>original: *acetopœiæ*</note>, using large bronze kettles and distillation vessels, they could capture the precious spirit of wine, which they currently allow to escape into the air. <margin>N. 138.</margin>

Next, there is a question not to be despised: *whether vinegar could be made from wine if no spirits were evaporated? To which we answer in the affirmative;* and we maintain *that those who drive off the spirit of wine by such cooking do poorly.* For they strive for brevity, while in the meantime producing a weak and imperfect vinegar. For since vinegar is a mixture consisting not only of saline parts but also of sulphurous ones, it is a mistake if the more powerful parts of the vinegar are kept away. From this it happens that in common vinegar, those same effects are lacking which the ancients ascribed to it; namely, that it thins [the humors] while simultaneously warming moderately, and that it behaves like an alkali or soap and a cleansing agent. I believe that some, deceived by such weak vinegar deprived of its sulphurous part, have been led to utterly deny the existence of a **burning spirit** <note>Flammable alcohol</note> in sugar of Lead, and have placed it among the **chemical non-entities** <note>original: *non-entia Chymica*; things that do not exist in reality or are theoretical errors</note>.

In order that we might know these things accurately, we filled a glass vial with wine, sealed its opening by melting the glass <note>A process called hermetic sealing</note>, and exposed it to digestion <note>Gentle, continuous heat</note>. We received a most potent and stable vinegar, even though no parts had evaporated; however, the acetification proceeded more slowly than if it had been done in the common manner, even though the vinegar was stronger. *It proceeds slowly, I say;* for since the internal saline particles must be rarefied by external heat and must surround—indeed, overcome—the sulphurous parts, a longer time is required. For the sulphurous parts of wine cause much thinning; and until the saline parts reach such a state that they overcome the sulphurous ones, a long and continuous heat is required. ### Book I. Section V. Chapter II.

...they swell with much ardent spirit <note>original: *spiritu*; here referring to the high alcohol content</note>, they turn sour slowly and with difficulty, unless a long and continuous heat is applied. For this reason, spirit of wine <note>original: *spiritus vini*; ethanol or high-proof alcohol</note> also serves as an excellent medicine in putrid regions and against scurvy <note>original: *scorbuto*</note>, where the blood becomes acidic from excessive salty air and food; thus, its consumption is great during sea expeditions.

<margin>N. 139.</margin>
For spirit of wine preserves against acidity due to its extreme "tenuity" <note>In 17th-century physics, "tenuity" refers to the thinness or subtleness of a substance's particles</note>; likewise, fixed alkalis <note>original: *acalia fixa*; likely a typo for *alkalia fixa*, such as potassium carbonate</note> also hinder acidity because of their excessive fixity and astringency. Hence, when drinks begin to sour, common folk—to prevent further acidification—throw in ashes, glowing flints, or even quicklime <note>original: *calcem vivam*; calcium oxide</note> itself. However, this is of little or no use, since alkalis, due to their extreme fixity, do not act upon the "acid spirit," but rather upon the "medium substance," as we have demonstrated above.

<margin>N. 140.</margin>
Instead, shells <note>original: *testacea*; such as ground oyster or snail shells</note> and other similar things should be added, upon which the volatile acid salt acts, rather than the medium substance. For if this medium substance is changed, the drink easily becomes flat and spoiled. Meanwhile, when the volatile salt—whether it is beginning to sour or is already acidic—is bound by these astringent reagents, a new mixture arises which remains mixed into the liquid form of the drink and is not healthy for those drinking it. Therefore, one should use such astringents that constrict the acid spirit and, once constricted, fall to the bottom as a new mixture. But since it is not our purpose here to write about those things which hinder the making of vinegar, we shall instead proceed to those things which promote it and follow our process of vinegar-making <note>original: *acetificationis*</note>.

<margin>N. 141.</margin>
To the cooked wine, therefore, they add a vinegar ferment <note>original: *fermentum aceti*</note>, which is of two kinds: one used when vinegar is being prepared from scratch, and another when ready-made vinegar is already on hand. The first is called the **vinegar-set** <note>original: *der Essig-Satz*</note>, and the other the **mother of vinegar** <note>original: *die Essig-Mutter*</note>; we shall treat both. However, we will first put forward the general difference between the ferment of *wine* and that of *vinegar*. The former is commonly called **yeast** or **barm** <note>original: *Hefen oder Gäst*</note>, while the latter is called **sour-leaven** <note>original: *Saurtaig*</note>. In the former, "unctuous," fatty, and oily particles predominate; hence fermented drinks foam, for foam proceeds from oiliness, though it differs according to the type of oiliness. In wine, a *thinner* foam appears; in beer, a *thicker* foam; because the oiliness of the former is more subtle, while the latter is coarser. In vinegar, by contrast, *foam* is not praised, because the saline parts ought to predominate; for it is an infallible test that vinegar that **foams a lot is not good**. This is how wine vinegar is distinguished from beer vinegar. Therefore, for the fermentation of wines or any fermentable drink, a ferment is required that has more abundant *unctuous* particles so that it can excite the sulfurous particles. But for **vinegar-making**, a ferment is required in which saline particles abound, so that it can elevate the saline particles of the wine. For although any drink may sour by itself, and any drink—if it is strong enough—may ferment by itself, nevertheless both fermentation and acidification are aided by their own proper ferment. In this, therefore, the ferments differ from each other: in the former, the *unctuous* parts predominate, and in the latter, the *saline* parts; and if the ferment is deprived of these parts through evaporation, it will be useless. Furthermore, when either ferment begins to act more violently due to the abundance of concentrated particles, it easily causes the whole substance in which it resides to ferment, sending infinite little bubbles and small bodies into its parts, as we see in practice and have said previously.

<margin>N. 142.</margin>
Having explained this general difference, we shall proceed to the specific nature of each ferment. First, indeed, a distinction is made between fresh and old wine ferment—that is, between that which is first added for fermentation, and that which...

# Subterranean Physics

...which comes through fermentation, namely between *froth* <note>original: *Gäscht*; the foam or barm on fermenting beer</note> and *yeast* <note>original: *Hefen*; the settled dregs</note>, of which the former is more **spirituous** <note>richer in alcohol/spirit</note> and the latter more **cooked** <note>original: *coctius*; meaning more matured or chemically "digested"</note>, and consequently works more slowly; in short, they differ in their stage of development.

<margin>N. 143.</margin>
Secondly, there is also a distinction between vinegar ferments, as we mentioned above; namely between **sourdough** <note>original: *Sauertaig*</note> and **mother of vinegar** <note>original: *Essig-Mutter*</note>. The first makes things sour, or rather aids, promotes, and accelerates the souring process. The second arises from the acidification itself—it is a sediment, analogous to the sediment of wine <note>original: *fæcibus vini*; the lees</note>. It is also similar in that, just as the wine lees which settle on their own after fermentation are more "cooked" than fresh yeast, so too the sediment of vinegar is more "cooked" and "digested" <note>processed by heat or chemical action</note> than the first ferment itself, commonly called **sourdough**. We shall now explain the nature of both, as promised.

<margin>N. 144.</margin>
The ferment commonly called **sourdough** consists of flour sprinkled with a little salt. From this, saline parts analogous to common salt—though rarer—are excited, and the whole paste begins to sour. Flour contains much <term>volatile salt</term> <note>an early chemical term for salts that vaporize easily, often associated with life or fermentation</note>, as the distillation of flour teaches us. Hence, flour is considered more suitable than all other substances for an acidic ferment. We use this acidic paste in anything that needs to be turned into vinegar, but especially in the making of **bread**: it is mixed in so that it may both ferment and acidify at the same time. For bread begins to swell from this ferment and slowly ferments within itself. In this fermentation, certain sulfurous and acidic particles are raised and thinned <note>original: *rarefiunt*</note>, which makes the bread **porous** and more **digestible** in the stomach <note>original: *nicht so taigig*; not so doughy or raw</note>, and more easily dissolved due to the expanded pores. Because of the oily and well-digested parts of the flour, it is otherwise difficult to dissolve and digest; therefore, in daily use, it would be insoluble without this prior fermentation. This moderate **fermentation** is therefore analogous to the "mortification" or sprouting of wheat in beer-making, which we discussed previously, so that it may be more quickly **dissolved**: thus the flour is fermented so that the bread may be better digested in the stomach. When the bread is baked in the oven, part of the resolved **spirits** vanishes into the air; these could be captured with little effort, but they are lost, though they refresh the noses of passers-by with a cordial <note>heart-strengthening</note> scent. Indeed, in this glowing **spirit of bread** that vanishes uselessly into the air, more comfort lies hidden than in all the "pearl water" <note>a costly medicinal tonic made from ground pearls</note>; but because it is simple and inexpensive, it is not valued. Let us return to vinegar: so that it may be prepared and sour more quickly, it is aided by this saline ferment, commonly called **sourdough**.

<margin>N. 145.</margin>
Others increase the souring power of vinegar by adding **pepper, ginger, cinnamon, sugar, raw tartar, and honey**. From these they make a paste and bake it like bread, calling it a **vinegar starter** <note>original: *Essigsatz*</note>, particles of which they throw into the drink to be soured. Such substances are added to promote acidification; for since all such substances swell with copious <term>volatile salt</term> that is easily thinned, it necessarily follows that the whole drink into which they are thrown is gradually infected by these copious saline particles. The drink's own similar particles are then excited, thinned, and increased. From these and similar foundations, we have found a way to arrange any **musty** <note>freshly pressed juice</note> drink during its first fermentation of sulfurous parts so that, once the first wine-like fermentation is finished, it begins a second **acidic** fermentation on its own and finishes fermenting in a short time—namely, until the saline parts are "exalted" <note>raised to a higher chemical state</note>. This elevation of parts is most powerful, for it excites even the smallest saline particles, even in **rainwater**, from which a **strong and thin** vinegar can be made. In the same way, frequent distillation alone can change any **spirit**...

### Book I. Section V. Chapter II.

...the **burning** quality <note>original: *ardentem*</note> is increased in a wonderful way, so that it can later endure more water. For we have said in the preceding sections that the more forcefully particles are thinned out <note>original: *rarefiunt*; rarefaction or the expansion of matter</note>, the sharper they become and the more powerfully they strike the tongue. Indeed, it matters little whether, according to **Descartes**, these sorts of tiny bodies are needle-like or toothed, round or oblong; certainly, unless they are thinned out, they will not strike the tongue. We have therefore set forth our opinion regarding **winy, vinegary, and saline acidity, as well as those that are astringent, dissolving, and corroding.**

<margin>N. 146.</margin>
To return to the subject of water, it must be understood that such vinegar made from water, or any thin drink, must be handled with total caution and kept sealed; for since in such substances there are few **saline** parts, which evaporate easily, the vinegar is also very liable to go flat <note>original: *vappescere* / *wird schahl*; to lose its potency or become vapid</note>. This is to be understood for any vinegar, which becomes flat if left open for a long time. 

<margin>N. 147.</margin>
Nothing contributes more to the preservation of vinegar than that it be sealed slowly, exposed to a gentle heat, and not moved or disturbed at all. For just as we said previously that movement hinders fermentation, for the same reason we prohibit it in acidification, which is a much more subtle and slower process. It is impossible for many people to make vinegar because they proceed with it too impetuously; they then blame the cause on luck, menstruating women, and I know not what else. But certainly, other very small and light circumstances are often the cause; for everything regarding the ferments, the heat, the vessels, and the drink itself must be attended to—especially the **filling**. 

Hence, some more careful practitioners, when they fill the vessels, do so through a **siphon** <note>original: *syphonem*</note>, which they dip slowly below the horizontal line or the surface, and thus pour in the warm supplement so that they do not disturb the whole liquor with one sudden rush. For acidification requires **constant** heat, both slow and equal; otherwise, the particles might be thickened by too much cold, or thinned out and driven off into the air by too much heat, causing the drink to go flat. Therefore, a moderate heat is required so that the saline particles may be thinned; and this thinning of the particles is properly called the **action of acidification**.

From this, two consequences arise. First, that certain subtler particles exhale, as in the <margin>N. 148.</margin> fermentation of wine; these shall henceforth be called the **Gas of vinegar** <note>original: *Gas aceti*; Van Helmont's term for the vapors released during chemical reactions</note>. But they are not so spirited and subtle, being more earthy; consequently, they are dissolved by the surrounding air and, with the addition of heat, they slowly putrefy and come to life in the very path of their exhalation in the air. This is why an immense multitude of flies arises around vinegar-making vessels, as we said above in the chapter on putrefaction <note>a reference to the theory of spontaneous generation, where life was thought to arise from decaying matter</note>.

The second consequence is that the **tartar of wine** <note>original: *tartarus vini*; cream of tartar or potassium bitartrate</note> is thickened by <margin>N. 149.</margin> this slow digestion. Many thinned, acidic saline parts adhere to it, forming a sort of harmful paste; by its own weight, this seeks the bottom and there produces a sediment. This is another species of ferment and is called the **mother of vinegar**. It holds the same relationship to the first vinegar paste—commonly called **vinegar-starter** <note>original: *Essigsatz*</note> or **sourdough** <note>original: *Sauertaig*</note>—as the dregs of wine hold to new yeast, commonly called **froth** <note>original: *Cäst* or *Gäscht*</note>. And just as good and winy dregs—commonly called **wine lees** <note>original: *Weinläger*</note>—strengthen and preserve wine, acting as a mother to it, so this vinegar sediment preserves and strengthens the vinegar, and is called its mother. It is highly valued because it is generated slowly, since we have said it comes from slow digestion; such a "mother" is a superior and nobler substance of the vinegar. We see this also in distilled waters; if they stand for a long time, they also deposit a mother (sediment) of this kind; namely, the **spirituous and...**
