<meta>This page continues the investigation into the chemical transformation of liquids, moving from the physical stabilization of vinegar to a broader theory of fermentation as a form of "internal combustion" or thinning of matter.</meta>

->Physica Subterranea<-

The *saline* <note>original: *salinæ*; referring to the salt-like mineral components</note> parts, through internal heat, digest themselves, and they fix and condense (just as *tartar* <note>cream of tartar or potassium bitartrate sediment</note> does in old wine). From this, a specific sediment follows, which they call the *mother*: in which the primary power of the distilled water resides. Thus, when waters deposit such sediments or "mothers," they easily go flat <note>original: *vappescunt*; to lose flavor or potency</note>; this is because the remaining parts of the water are deprived of their spirits. Once deprived, they are easily corrupted, turning into rot and mold. Moreover, the *mother* of a great vinegar is highly valued for this reason: that once the previous liquid has been acidified and poured off—namely, the stored vinegar being moved to vessels—if new wine or another liquid to be acidified is poured over the surviving *mother* of vinegar, it is changed in a very short time into good and strong vinegar. (For this reason, vinegar vessels are highly esteemed because they swell with acidic spirits.) There is no longer any need for a "first paste" (commonly called *sourdough* or *vinegar-starter* <note>original German: *Sauertaig, oder Essigsatz*</note>). For the saline parts of the wine are excited by similar parts of the mother of vinegar, just as light is kindled from light. This perpetual kindling also occurs in
<margin>*N. 150.*</margin>
fermentation. For one fermenting vessel sets another "on fire"; and this "fire" in turn sets another; and so on to infinity, while the virtue and power of the substance is not weakened in the meantime.

This might seem wonderful and impossible if we were to conclude that this kindling happens through the mere communication and exhalation of parts. We do not, of course, deny that a ferment—whether winy or vinegary—imprints its own "little bodies" <note>atoms or corpuscles</note> upon the drink when mixed with it; thus, according to the specific quality of the ferment, every drink acquires a special flavor. But we maintain that this mixture is only superficial and accidental, and serves no purpose except to thin out <note>rarefy</note> the substance and cause the trapped air to swell—that is, to dispose the substance toward its own nature. Once this is done, the whole ferment sinks back down again, and is found at the bottom not only in its original quantity but in a greater amount, since the thicker dregs sink down at the same time the drink is thinned. Therefore, the strength and faculty of the ferment is not lost or diminished, but rather 
<margin>*N. 151.*</margin>
increased, for the reasons already stated. We see this clearly in light, which kindles light only by thinning; for the burning of a candle is entirely a fermentation—namely, a thinning out from point to point, and an elevation of the moderately densified parts. These parts are fatty, yet mixed with salt, as we see in oil, tallow, and other substances. Even in the 
<margin>*N. 152.*</margin>
burning of wood—which no one will deny happens through thinning and the manner of fermentation—this holds true for anyone who has properly considered the analogy between the two. For from burning, all things proceed that occur in fermentation: first, the fire acts as a ferment, which thins out and kindles that which is to be burned. That which is flammable must be capable of being thinned; hence it must be porous, sulfurous, and saline. By burning, or rather by the thinning out of the parts, a separation occurs. Indeed, the first and most subtle of all parts turn into flame, just like the *Gas* <note>A term coined by Van Helmont to describe the elusive, "wild" spirit of life or chemistry that cannot be easily contained</note> in wine, which can never be condensed again. Then a subtle spirit comes forth, sulfurous and saline; if captured, this is resolved into a liquid, as we see in the distillation of wood. Even charcoal, if it is distilled skillfully so that it cannot catch fire or flame, yet the smoke is captured regardless, is changed into a spirit. This spirit is of two types: sometimes it is flammable, like *spirit of wine* <note>alcohol</note>, specifically if the sulfurous parts predominate in the burned material; sometimes it behaves like *spirit of vinegar or urine* <note>acidic or alkaline/ammoniacal spirits</note>,
<margin>*N. 153.*</margin>
specifically if the saline parts are more powerful in the burned material. We see this in the burning of sulfur and in the *acid spirit of sulfur*, which behaves much like vinegar, and in which the saline parts

### Book I. Section V. Chapter II.

...predominate: although the sulfurous <note>In alchemy, "sulfur" refers to the combustible, oily principle of a substance.</note> parts are not observed and lie hidden, they are nevertheless revealed through practice and with little effort, appearing once again as combustible and flammable; but more on these in the second book concerning sulfur, and further toward the end of this first book. Therefore, having first established this substance—which is analogous to the **spirit of wine** <note>original: *spiritui vini*; ethanol or alcohol</note> and the highest substance in wine—there follows that which has a comparison with the "middle" substance; namely, neither the highest nor the lowest, such as soot, which is of an intermediate quality. The ashes, however, being more "cooked" and digested by the very flame and heat, liken themselves to the **tartar and dregs of wine** <note>original: *tartaro & fecibus vini*</note>.

<margin>N. 154.</margin>
And lest the reader think this comparison is flawed, we shall prove it by experience. First, just as **salt of Tartar** <note>potassium carbonate derived from wine lees</note> seizes the middle substance and creates a certain intermediate mixture, almost like an

<margin>N. 155.</margin>
**oxymel** <note>original: *oxymelleum*; a traditional medicinal mixture of honey and vinegar, used here to describe a balanced chemical compound</note>, as we taught above; so do ashes (or the fixed salt of ashes, as their purer substance) when joined to soot, especially in the form of **lye** <note>original: *lixivii*</note> (that is, when ashes are reduced to the form of lye), they constitute a new mixture and strongly seize one another. They form a composite that can be compared to **soap** <note>original: *saponi*</note>, which is entirely analogous to the previous mixture (mentioned above) of the middle substance of wine and salt of tartar; except that it possesses an **empyreuma** <note>a "burnt" or charred smell and quality resulting from the action of fire</note> that comes from combustion—whereas the former action is natural, while this one is fiery, preternatural, artificial, and violent. Next, just as the **spirits of wine and vinegar** (which two differ from each other in that the former, as has been said often, contains more sulfurous parts and fewer saline parts, while the latter contains more saline and fewer sulfurous parts) seize and seek out the *middle* substance of wine or vinegar, freely uniting with it and resolving it; so also that **urinous spirit** <note>original: *urinosus ille spiritus*; likely referring to ammonia or similar volatile alkaline vapors</note> which seeks the air during the combustion of things, stinging the eyes and twitching the nostrils, freely resolves soot. Furthermore, just as fermentation requires free and **open** air, so does combustion;

<margin>N. 156.</margin>
for just as in **closed** fermentation, a certain part of the rarefied spirit is, as it were, fixed again and changed into a middle substance, which consequently becomes **oilier** and fattier; so in **closed** combustion, certain sulfurous parts are fixed and concentrate themselves into **charcoal**, fixing and receiving themselves. This charcoal, when later exposed to open fire and ignited, thins out and rarefies its concentrated sulfur again, much like a **subtle and very penetrating spirit** that strikes the head. We have occasionally **condensed** <note>original: *condensavimus*; the author claims to have captured the vapors of burning charcoal as a liquid</note> this spirit and received a not-insignificant liquor, analogous in all respects to the **spirit of wine**. To finish in a few words: we could run off into immense digressions on this occasion if we wished to bring forth everything that should be said about combustion; for even metals, and even **gold** itself, can be burnt with very little effort and reduced into most sweetly glowing flames. Many other things proceed around, in, and from the foundations of combustion which would be superfluous to recount here, as we shall deal with them in their proper places. For what we have said thus far concerning combustion was done for no other purpose than to show a certain analogous operation of fermentations, so that we might omit nothing pertaining to the doctrine of fermentation. Now, therefore, we must return to our **acetification** <note>the process of turning into vinegar</note>. We said previously that three things are required for it: namely rest, heat, and moderate closure. We have dealt with the first two at length; now we come to closure.

# Subterranean Physics

...the elevated particles might evaporate too much; through their evaporation, the vinegar would fail and become stale <note>original: *schahl werden*</note> and corrupted. However, since we have so far scrutinized the secrets of fermentation from head to toe, as the saying goes, we shall not bypass the end, the reason for which must be sought from the beginning. For just as we stated in the chapter on the generation of animals, three things are required for any generation and new production: namely, the **agent**, the **patient** <note>The "patient" refers to the passive matter acted upon by the active agent.</note>, and **nourishment**. In plants especially, **water** serves as nourishment, the **oily** particle serves as the seed, and the **saline** (whether nitrous or urinous) serves as the patient and, as it were, the female seed. 

To return to the simplest principles, there are three earths according to our doctrine in Section 3, Chapters 2, 3, and 4: the first is of a **limy** and **lean** nature; the second is of a **sulfurous** and **fatty** nature; the third is the nourishment of both, mixed from the former two and thus **soapy**. These, therefore, as the simplest of all things, also exist as the primordial principles of vegetables. Indeed, we demonstrated in the first section that all things consist of earth, and water is only an accessory principle. 

Into these principles, therefore, all vegetable bodies are ultimately resolved. Indeed, experience teaches that the most subtle and flammable **spirit of wine** <note>original: *spiritum vini*; ethanol</note> is finally resolved into elemental earth, albeit highly refined and purified. Even the strongest **spirit of vinegar** <note>original: *aceti spiritus*; concentrated acetic acid</note>, when reduced to **sugar of Saturn** <note>original: *saccharum Saturni*; lead acetate, produced by dissolving lead in vinegar</note> and that sugar distilled into an **oil**, can easily and with brief manipulation be resolved into **elemental earth**, analogous to quicklime.

<margin>N. 158.</margin>
Lest anyone should think these chemical operations <note>original: *enchyrisies*; from the Greek for "hand-handling" or manual manipulation</note> are impossible, let them consider that this very thing happens naturally in the process we are about to explain: namely, in the "flatness" <note>original: *vappescentia*; the process of wine turning into *vappa*, or stale, lifeless liquid</note> or **degeneration** of **wine**, **vinegar**, or any **drink**, and its resolution into its final parts, namely **mold, mustiness, and earth**. This happens quite often—in fact, whenever the more subtle, **mercurial** parts of the wine (the highest substance, both **sulfurous and saline**) evaporate. In this state, the "middle" substance—which by this stage is usually also deprived of the "lowest" substance due to continuous settling—is left to its own devices. Lacking internal heat due to the failure of fermentation, acidification, and digestion, the watery parts it still contains (which until now were strongly mixed and blended with the water) exhibit themselves in their original **earthy** form. 

And so that very tight union is dissolved—the union which until now had been cooked by Mother Nature in the vine, digested, and united into a sweet **juice** <note>original: *glykeia*; a Greek term for sweetness or sweet must</note>, moderately thinned by fermentation, further elevated and perfected by acidification, and coupled by the **spirituous** parts as if by a strong bond. This union of the mixture, I say, begins to dissolve when the **spirituous** parts fail (just as we spoke in the preceding chapter on putrefaction regarding the hindered and extinguished vital balsam). No differently than in animals when the heat of life fails, it begins to return to its first elements: namely, into **dry, light earth**, floating upon the water to which it was once united. Therefore, the former color, odor, taste, and common qualities perish—those which once flourished when the mixture was in a good state. All now lie hidden in tasteless water (which we commonly call **stale** <note>original: *abgestanden*</note>) and earth, which we commonly call **film and mold** <note>original: *Kahnen, Schimmel*</note>. Nor does this putrefaction and final resolution occur only when the drink passes through all the stages already listed (becoming wine-like, then acidic, then stale); it happens even in good wine that is still in an intact state.

->Lib. I. Sect. V. Cap. II. 191<-

...especially around the internal orifice and the external stoppers, at those parts where air easily passes through due to frequent opening and the sticking of wine. This causes the hidden parts there to **turn sour** <note>original: *acescere*</note>, the spirituous parts <note>The volatile, alcohol-rich components of the liquid.</note> to evaporate, and the remaining parts to **become flat** <note>original: *vappescere*; to lose flavor and potency</note>; hence, having been reduced to a state of decay, they float upon the wine. This happens especially when the barrels reach the end of their liquor, for there, in the empty space of the barrel, the spirituous parts can wander more freely and evaporate away from the rest. Hence, when the drink tends toward the end—or as it is said, **reaching the dregs** <note>original: *auff die Naig gehet*</note>—the things we have described mostly occur. This happens particularly when vessels are left **open** for a long time. In such cases, skilled wine-cellarers and coopers use **sulfur smoke** (though the process works better with **burning spirit of wine** <note>High-proof alcohol or brandy used to fortify the wine.</note>), and in this way they strengthen and **preserve** the wine; just as we preserve bodies from the corruption of the plague using **sulfur smoke**.

These things occur naturally, often, and quickly in wine and any fermented or acidified drink, where it degenerates into **mold**, **decay**, and **flatness**. For mixed vegetable substances, as we stated in the section on their composition and growth, consist of many particles, which is why they are easily dissolved; and the more subtle they are, the more they "transpire" or breathe away. We see this in flowers and all strongly scented things. In weak drinks, these things happen more quickly than in strong ones, for reasons we have already sufficiently provided.

And although all these things are most clearly before our eyes every day, we shall nonetheless demonstrate our claims through chemical experience. <margin>N. 159.</margin> If the middle substance—whether of wine or any other fermented liquor—is taken and mixed with water, within a few days it will contract decay and mold. Even **Tartar** <note>The potassium bitartrate crystals that settle in wine casks.</note> itself, when mixed with enough water, **putrefies**.

Furthermore, although this putrefaction, mortification, and final resolution happens quickly, it nonetheless occurs slowly and not without internal action. It is, as it were, a chemical analysis; from this, there is an emission and emanation of certain subtle "little bodies" <note>corpuscles or atoms</note>, just as we showed happens in **putrefaction** in the preceding chapter. <margin>N. 160.</margin> If you allow the middle substance of wine, or **tartar**, to become flat in the aforementioned way and pass into decay and mold (even with a slow sealing of the vessel), and afterward you distill it, you will receive a powerful and penetrating **spirit**, about which much could be said.

As for the "earth"—commonly called **Mold** <note>original: *Schimmel*</note>—if it is thoroughly dry and powdery, and reduced to its ultimate end, it is entirely dried out and behaves like a **dead head** <note>original: *capitis mortui*; the useless solid residue left after distillation or extreme heating.</note>, just as we observed in bread changed into mold. For the claim that bees are generated from putrefied bread is false; if you consider the ultimate mold, it is extremely dry, and both reason and experience teach that nothing is generated within it.

But, lest we abuse the reader's patience too much, we shall hasten to the end of this subject. As a conclusion, we shall make a digression from the **acidification of vegetables** to the **acidification of minerals**, just as <margin>N. 161.</margin> we did at the end of the section on fermentation. We set aside the souring of **bitumens**, **sulfurs**, **salts**, and other subterranean juices; for their acidity behaves either like the common souring of vinegar (if treated naturally), or like the acid **spirit** <note>acidic vapor or liquid</note> that comes from the burning of wood. Therefore, we refer these and similar cases to what has been said before. <margin>N. 162.</margin> As for what is handed down regarding the **vinegar of minerals**—especially the **Ore of Antimony**—this seems to be ascribed to the **common combustible sulfur** mixed within the ores, as experience confirms. For once the flammable sulfur <note>original: *sulphure phlogisto*</note> has been burned away and the ore has been melted once, no more "vinegar" will be produced. Vinegars...

# Subterranean Physics

...that in such things there is a **spirit of sulfur** <note>original: *spiritum sulphuris*; an early chemical name for sulfuric acid</note>, no one will deny; since they differ either not at all or very little from it, except that they occasionally carry some metal with them. Therefore, acidity comes not from the metal, but from the sulfur, the acidity of which we have treated in the preceding pages.

<margin>N. 163.</margin>
The Philosophers, therefore, definitely do not mean this when they speak of their own **Philosophers' vinegar** <note>original: *acetum Philosophi*; a symbolic solvent in alchemy, not common vinegar</note>, namely the "rooted" vinegar, which *holds itself as the principle and root of minerals*. For the **Vinegar of the Philosophers**, their solvent and radical liquid **menstruum** <note>term: *menstruum* — a solvent used to extract the essence of a substance</note>, is actually **Mercury**, **Lathon**, and **Azoth** <note>alchemical names for the primary fluid or universal solvent</note>; it is not the common precipitated Mercury, as certain pretenders <note>original: *Sophistæ*; "Sophists" or false alchemists</note> believe. Rather, it is the more subtle substance of Mercury, namely the **essence of common salt**, which in the Ores (even *by artifice*) mixes itself with metals and creates a decomposition with them, so that they appear before our eyes in the form of **running Mercury** <note>original: *Mercurii currentis*; liquid quicksilver</note>. Therefore, when metals are Philosophically separated from this noble essence, or precipitated in whatever way, that substance is acquired which revivifies metals and makes them flow; this is the essential substance of salt, behaving like vinegar, but of a more digested and more easily "fixed" disposition: yet possessing a great analogy with vinegar.

<margin>N. 164.</margin>
For this substance also creates new decomposed forms from metals; and when it is driven from them again by the power of fire, it carries the purer particles of those metals away with it, as **practice in the oil of Saturn** <note>original: *oleo Saturni*; a solution of lead acetate, often called "sugar of lead"</note> **teaches**: in which certain *evidences of the truth regarding the correct Philosophical vinegar shine forth*. Just as we said that the earth—or saline particles—cloaks, binds, and fixes the sulfurous parts of wine; so the **Philosophical vinegar**, namely the earth, the saline or **third (mercurial) earth** <note>Becher’s system relied on three "earths": stony, sulfurous, and mercurial</note> (which we discussed in Section 3, Chapter 4), embraces, loves, binds, overcomes,

<margin>N. 165.</margin>
volatilizes, and finally fixes and is fixed by the second (namely sulfurous) earth (which we treated in Chapter 3 of the same section). Thus, the **Philosophical spirit of wine and vinegar** comes into the light: namely, a **soapy mixture** <note>original: *mixtum saponatum*; a stable, unified chemical compound</note>, the most wonderful of all wonders. Because of the "fixity" of its particles, it never evaporates; and because of the homogeneity of its parts, it can never be resolved into flatness, mold, musty residue, dross, or hard crust <note>original: *stomoma*; likely referring to a metallic scale or impurity</note>.

<margin>N. 166.</margin>

## Chapter Three of the Fifth Section.
# On the dissolution of metals, which is liquefaction.

---

->S Y N O P S I S.<-

*N. 1. A digression to the third type of dissolution, namely liquefaction, primarily of minerals. N. 2. The liquidity of minerals is threefold: earthy, watery, and fiery. N. 3. Solidity is contrasted with liquidity, and the types of solidity are enumerated. N. 4. The author considers only metallic fluidity in this place. N. 5. It is false that animals and vegetables provide running **Mercury** <note>original: *Mercurium currentem*; quicksilver or liquid mercury</note>, and much less do they flow in fire like metals. N. 6. ...it follows that the **Mercury of the Moon** <note>original: *Mercurium lunæ*; silver was associated with the Moon in alchemical theory</note> is sophisticated <note>meaning artificial or deceptive rather than natural</note>, as de Comitibus contends, because it can be reduced back into silver. **N. 36.** A pleasant story is interspersed regarding the **malleable glass** <note>original: *vitro malleabili*; a legendary ancient material said to be as durable as metal</note> of the ancients. **N. 37.** Ludovicus de Comitibus <note>a 17th-century Italian alchemist and physician</note> defends the idea that common Mercury can in no way be converted into silver except through a **tincture** <note>an alchemical agent capable of transforming the properties of a substance</note>, from which it is inferred that the Mercury of silver is sophisticated. **N. 38.** Why is the Mercury of the common people called "common"? **N. 39.** From what subjects does it consist? **N. 40.** Some Mercuries of the metallic bodies are irreducible to their original bodies; the cause of this difference from common Mercury is explained at the same time. **N. 41.** Common Mercury consists of various mineral subjects, where the true **mineral electrum** <note>a natural alloy of gold and silver, often discussed as a primary mineral state</note> is treated as the occasion arises. **N. 42.** Common Mercury is partially reduced into gold and silver in the same manner that Ludovicus de Comitibus reduces the Mercury of silver. **N. 43.** The cited author [de Comitibus] clearly contradicts himself when he proposes a method for converting common Mercury into a fixed metal without a tincture, using only the **alcaest** <note>original: *alcaest*; the theoretical "universal solvent" that could reduce all bodies to their primary matter</note>, which he nevertheless denied could be done in paragraph 37. **N. 44.** The doctrine of the aforementioned author is defended, claiming that all common Mercury is actually the Mercury of silver. **N. 45.** From where does mercurial fluidity arise? **N. 46.** What is properly called the **radical moisture** <note>original: *humidum radicale*; the fundamental fluid essence that provides life or flexibility to a substance</note> of metals? **N. 47.** In which subjects does the **mercurifying earth** <note>the specific component responsible for turning a solid into a liquid mercury</note> lie hidden? **N. 48.** The Mercuries of the bodies leave a red spot behind them during evaporation. **N. 49.** A great secret is opened. **N. 50.** The song of Orpheus concerning the riches of Mercury. **N. 51.** Neptune’s trident denotes the triple liquidity of things. **N. 52.** Concerning oily and watery moisture. **N. 53.** Water is a solid body, or rather, a fluid earth. **N. 54.** Air consists of earthy particles; <meta>This page continues the transition from discussing the fermentation of organic substances (vegetables and animals) to the unique properties of minerals and metals. *...of the liquidity of subterranean bodies. N. 131. Three seas must be sailed through before the desired port is reached.* <note>original: "tria maria trananda sunt"; a common alchemical metaphor suggesting that a practitioner must master three distinct stages or "seas" of knowledge—usually the vegetable, animal, and mineral kingdoms—before achieving the final goal.</note>

## T E X T

<margin>N. 1.</margin> Until now, we hope, we have lingered in a rich vintage, not without pleasure pressing various grapes and extracting various sweet juices. When we committed these to fermentation, we were so nearly intoxicated by the penetrating vapors that we could hardly leave the cellar. Now, with a cleared mind, we shall hasten from **Bacchus** <note>The Roman god of wine, representing the vegetable kingdom and fermentation.</note> to **Vulcan** <note>The Roman god of fire and metalworking, representing the mineral kingdom and the forge.</note>; from wine to gold, and from vegetables to metals. In short, we move from *fermentation* to *liquefaction*, which is the proper characteristic of metals. However, because we shall deal more extensively with the causes of liquefaction and fluidity in the seventh section of this book, and in the second book under the chapters on the *anatomy of stones and Mercury*, we will (rightly, so as not to repeat the same thing in various places and incur a wordiness which we naturally hate) present here only some preliminaries concerning minerals in general and their fluidity,

<margin>N. 2.</margin> which in the following pages we shall always call *liquefaction*. This is threefold: first, some minerals *receive earthy particles into themselves*, whereby they are continuously dissolved, liquefied, and flow; this flow is called *mercurial*. The bodies that flow in this way are called *quicksilver* <note>original: "argentum vivum," literally "living silver."</note>, though improperly, for if *lead* were to flow in this way, it should be called *living lead*, not silver. It is called *living* <note>original: "vivum"</note> because it moves itself by running, as if it were alive. Second, some minerals *receive water* into their pores, by which they are dissolved and reduced into an *aqueous* flow; these are called *mineral waters*. Third, certain minerals admit *air and fiery particles* into their pores, whereby they are dilated, disunited, and liquefied, flowing in the fire. To this threefold liquidity or fluidity, we oppose a single term:

<margin>N. 3.</margin> solidity, from whatever cause it may proceed. Its lowest degree is *consistency*, as when bodies consist like a *gelatin* <note>original: "gelatinæ"</note>, so that they do not flow. The second degree of solidity is *coagulation*, namely when the particles *cohere*, but in such a way that they easily allow for dissolution. The third degree is *fixation*, when bodies are *most compactly* united, such as *stones and metals*. From this, it is clear why I have placed *liquefaction* among the types of *dissolution*, because it is indeed the opposite of *solidity*. Since, therefore, in the preceding section we considered the *solidity, consistency, coagulation, structure, and fixation* of bodies; and in the first and second chapters of this section, we investigated the *opposite* of mixture, namely the *dissolution* of animals and vegetables; it would be unjust and contrary to our intention if we left *minerals* untouched in this place. Therefore, we shall now also explain, though in few words, what changes they undergo in their dissolution. And although we shall remain focused on the aforementioned *threefold flow*, we shall nevertheless take only *minerals* as examples, as this property 

<margin>N. 4.</margin> properly belongs to them. Accordingly, we shall take their naming and demonstration from them, as the superior subjects; for neither *animals* nor *vegetables* can be reduced 

<margin>N. 5.</margin> into the form of a running metallic fluid, or *Mercury*. Although in *Stockholm*, in an opened tomb, we once saw matter that was fluid and did not moisten the earth, we believed it to be grease, or tallow, or something of that sort. For true *Mercury*...

### Book I. Section V. Chapter III.

...mercury is a decomposed mineral, as will be clear from what follows. Therefore, it is utterly false what certain imposters and sycophants claim: that they can create metallic Mercuries <note>In this context, "Mercuries" refers to the liquid metallic state or "quicksilver" extracted from a substance.</note> from animals and vegetables. Furthermore, animals and vegetables—because they follow the aforementioned species of liquidity—are dissolved in *caustic waters* <note>original: "in aquis causticis"; likely referring to strong acids or alkaline solutions used in early chemistry.</note> in a different manner than minerals, even if they agree with minerals in this middle stage of "watery flux" more than other things. However, they are completely excluded from the third flux, since neither animals nor vegetables can flow in fire so as to be poured, except *through additives*. 

Indeed, we have seen wood and bones liquefied and cast into molds in this way; but this is rather a certain simulation of liquefaction, namely *impastation* <note>term: <term>impastation</term> (Latin: *impastatio*); the process of turning a solid into a thick, dough-like paste rather than a true liquid melt.</note>, which proceeds by a slow fire and utterly rejects incandescence; and when it cools, it solidifies into a consistency not by "fixation" (which belongs to those metals liquefied after a *fiery flux*), but by drying. We shall therefore rightly set aside animals and vegetables in this chapter, as hardly anything *analogous* to mineral fluxes is found within them. What can be brought forward regarding their *solidity and liquidity* has been said partly in the preceding chapters, and will be explained partly in the seventh section of this book, in a specific chapter on solidity and fluidity. 

Now we shall hasten specifically to the *fluidity of minerals*, insofar as it pertains to the "solution" of minerals; for the discussion here concerns how minerals are *properly* 
<margin>N. 6.</margin>
dissolved, and what changes they acquire from that solution: namely, *fluidity* and *liquidity*, whether they be *earthy, watery, or fiery*. 

The first of these, the *earthy*, we shall now approach. We stated at the beginning of this chapter that it is called *mercurial* because it *flows like mercury*; *not wetting* that over which it flows, but cohering to itself in a homogeneous 
<margin>N. 7.</margin>
unity. For this is how *mercurial* liquidity is defined and distinguished from the others. We assign the cause of this flux to *earthy* particles that have been thrust into the pores of the metals more than is natural; whereby the solid bodies are pulled apart and rendered fluid. Nonetheless, they preserve their metallic homogeneity, even though they are *volatile*. 

For these interspersed earthy particles, being volatile by their very nature, easily evaporate due to the separation of the metallic particles; not only do they evaporate themselves, but they also carry the *joined* particles away with them. We see this happening daily when we mix *volatiles with fixed things* in too great a proportion: *for the greater dominate the fewer, both in the political forum and in the physical* <note>original: "potiora enim paucioribus dominantur, & in foro politico, & in Physico"; a common early modern analogy suggesting that the laws of nature and the laws of human society follow the same hierarchical principles.</note>. 

There is also a ready reason why 
<margin>N. 8.</margin>
no bodies except minerals (and not even all of those) can be reduced into such a *mercurial flux*. Because this flux preserves a *roundness* in its smallest particles, it follows that the components which enter into it must cohere "amicably"; they must not be heterogeneous (different in kind) but homogeneous and "sympathetic" <note>The principle of "sympathy" in alchemy refers to the natural attraction between substances of a similar essence or "inner nature."</note>. That is, they must be things which, by the order of nature, contain something of this mercurifying and fluidifying earth as a *principle* in their primary mixture. This allows the substance to seize this new and superfluous earth amicably and, as if *sympathetically*, unite with it. 

Otherwise, no entry would be granted to this incoming earth. Therefore, all those subjects that lack this specific earth—such as *stones, juices, resins, animals, and vegetables*—even if they are mixed with a great quantity of this "earth of mercurification," will nonetheless *not be changed into running Mercury*; this is also because such subjects are unequally mixed and contain heterogeneous ingredients. Therefore, nothing can become *Mercury* unless it is homogeneously mixed; namely the metals, which are the only things that enjoy this first mercurial flux.

# Subterranean Physics

...independent. Not that it is necessary for all metals, *before* they become metals, to flow in such a way as some people claim; those who establish *Mercury* as the primary principle of metals. But we have already responded to these people in the third section, chapters four and five: namely, that common Mercury is a *compound* <note>original: "decompositum"; in 17th-century chemistry, this refers to a substance made of multiple components that can be separated, rather than a simple element.</note>, where by a figure of speech a part is understood as the whole—specifically, *mercurifying earth* <note>term: <term>mercurifying earth</term> (Latin: *terra mercurificans*); Becher’s principle of "fluidity" or "metallicity," also known as *terra lapidea*.</note> is mistaken for the mercurified substance itself. In this substance, besides this earth, there is also metal, which cannot be the principle of another metal.

<margin>No. 9</margin> I say, therefore, it is not necessary for all metals in their creation to exist in such a liquid state; although it is necessary that all metals—if it pleases the craftsman—can be reduced into such a mercurial flow, that is, into a compound of *true Mercury*. This also happens not infrequently by nature in mines, where *certain tracts of mercurifying earth* from central locations and materials (which were discussed in the second section of this book) 
<margin>No. 10</margin> reach the *metallic veins*, dissolve them, and rarefy the contained metals so that they flow spontaneously in the form of *true running Mercury* within the mines themselves. However, it often happens that when sulfurous particles are introduced, a new compound is made from such a mixture—namely, a *complex substance* <note>original: "decompositum"</note> which they call *cinnabar* <note>term: <term>cinnabar</term>; the bright red mineral form of mercury sulfide (HgS), the primary ore of mercury.</note>. Yet, once its *sulfurous particles* 
<margin>No. 11</margin> are removed, the *fluid composition of Mercury* appears before the eyes once more. Likewise, when the *mercurifying earthy parts* are removed, the metal is also revealed, which previously lay hidden in the fluid mercurial compound. Indeed, it is clear from the opposite that it is the *earthy* particles that "mercurify" or liquefy; because it is the *earthy* ones that halt such a flow. We see this in *sulfur* and the *fume of Saturn* <note>Saturn is the alchemical name for Lead.</note>. For just as a metal becomes fluid and running when it receives too much *mercurifying earth*—even though the same earth, albeit in smaller proportion, enters the composition of all metals as a principle (as we demonstrated in section three, chapter four)—so too when other earths enter this *fluid mixture* of Mercury in excess, they halt the fluidity and coagulate the mixture, even if they are principles of metals themselves, especially the *fecund* earth <note>original: "fecunda"; likely referring to Becher's second earth, *terra pinguis* or fatty/inflammable earth.</note> (concerning which see section three, chapter three). We clearly see these extremes of *fluidity* and *solidity* in *common Mercury*; 
<margin>No. 12</margin> which, when it is mixed with other metals (an operation they call *amalgamation*), seizes and softens as much of them as it exceeds in *fluid earth*. For if too much metal is added, the amalgam hardens because the fluid parts are overwhelmed. Moreover, this connection of Mercury and metal is not so superficial or to be passed over lightly; for if you make such an amalgam from *Mercury* and *lead*, and draw the Mercury off again through a retort with a strong fire so that the lead *flows* in the retort, you will receive your Mercury back, but it will be notably not only heavier, but also altered. For it unites some portion of the lead to itself in such a way that it leads it through the retort and carries it with it through the leather <note>Mercury was commonly purified by squeezing it through chamois leather; Becher notes that some lead remains so tightly bound that it passes through the pores of the leather with the mercury.</note>, separable from it by no art that I know of, except by slow digestion. Consequently, it also runs more slowly in its flow and forms a skin. From this it is clearly evident that in the compound of common Mercury, the *fluidifying earth* is in excess; which, lest it be idle, seizes particles of lead, mixes them with itself, and leads them into fluidity. But if indeed metals are added to Mercury in excess, then the amalgam is coagulated because the fluidifying parts are overcome by the 
<margin>No. 13</margin> *dry terrestrial parts*. By the frequent extraction of *Mercury* from gold, it happens that the *Mercury* in amalgamation *no longer* seeks that *same gold*, nor assumes it, or is joined to it by way of...

### Book I, Section V, Chapter III

...until it is joined by amalgamation. The reason for this is that a certain amount of *Mercury*, through such amalgamations and abstractions <note>original: "abstractiones"; refers to the process of drawing off or distilling the mercury away from the gold.</note>, clings to the gold and becomes fixed within it. From this, such a "calx" of gold <note>term: <term>calx</term> (Latin: *calx*); a powder produced by heating a metal, which alchemists believed was the metal's true essence stripped of its "greasiness."</note> acquires a singular medicinal quality, not unlike a precipitate, which it retains even if it is strongly heated or washed many times. Mercury, however, through such frequent amalgamation and abstraction, has mixed some of the gold into itself, which it has taken into its innermost constitution; this is demonstrated by the digestion of such *animated Mercury*, in which it reveals its golden nature.

From all of this, it follows that *Mercury* softens metals in proportion to the abundance of its fluidifying earth; and that *common Mercury* itself is nothing other than a fluid amalgam—that is, a mixture of fluidifying earth with a certain metal. Thus, as many *Mercuries* exist as there are metals that can be mixed with fluidifying earth. Six of these are "perfect" metals: *gold*, *silver*, *copper*, *iron*, *tin*, and *lead*; and some are "imperfect," such as *antimony*, *bismuth*, *zinc*, and *marcasite* <note>A term often used for iron pyrites or other shiny minerals that resemble ores.</note>; amalgams can be made from all of these.

<margin>No. 14</margin>
These differ from common *Mercury* in nothing except that they do not contain sufficient fluidifying earth; when that is added, they become true *Mercuries*, which are called *Mercuries of the bodies*. Yet even *common Mercury* itself is derived from some metallic body, and therefore it ought to be called a *Mercury of a body*. There are, then, six metals, not seven; for *Mercury* is a compound <note>original: "decompositum"; in 17th-century chemistry, this refers to a substance made of multiple components rather than a simple element.</note> of the others. Indeed, no *common Mercury* is found that does not consist of metal, though this is manifested with difficulty because of the abundance of fluidifying earth. This is not surprising if we consider that *animated solar or Saturnine Mercury* <note>Mercury that has been processed with gold (Sol) or lead (Saturn).</note>, which was mentioned above, gives up its mixed metal only with great difficulty; its fluidifying earth seizes the particles of the metal into its innermost constitution, so that the earth itself often coagulates with the metal it has taken up rather than allowing it to be torn away.

<margin>No. 15</margin>
And truly, in this wonderful sympathy of fluidifying earth with metals lies the whole secret of the Philosophers. This secret consists in obtaining the fluidifying earth in its pure state—that is, in its condition before it is mixed with any metal. Indeed, the *Mercury of the Philosophers* differs from common mercury in this: in the common variety, the fluidifying earth has already formed a compound by taking up a certain metal; but in the Philosophical variety, the earth is still "virginal," unstained by any mineral, and therefore capable of receiving the perfect *sulfur of the sun* <note>The alchemical essence or "soul" of gold.</note>. *Raymond Lully* <note>A 13th-century Majorcan philosopher and polymath to whom many later alchemical works were attributed.</note> learnedly explains this in the following words:

> *We remember,* he says, *that we said in our Testament that no quicksilver is more readily converted into the substance of sulfur than that in which the qualities of sulfur are sufficiently introduced by dissolution; nor does any sulfur more quickly congeal quicksilver than that in whose nature the substance of the quicksilver itself already exists, having been converted by the skill of art. The power of the transmuting quicksilver possesses the parts of the transmuted sulfur, so that within itself, before its own transformation, its own non-burning sulfur—whether white or red—is mixed through its smallest parts. For such quicksilver will then possess its own proper matter, and then nature embraces its own nature, and rejoices in it more amicably than in something foreign.*

Thus far *Lully*.
<margin>No. 16</margin>
In these few words, he has revealed the greatest mystery; but we, casting aside all secrecy, will add the key in even fewer words. Namely, that the fluidifying earth, upon which the whole matter hinges, is found in common salt...

# Subterranean Physics

...proceed. that all metals in their genesis consist of such a flow; although it is necessary that all metals, if it pleases the craftsman, can be reduced into such a mercurial flow—that is, into a *compound of true Mercury*.

This also happens not rarely in nature within mines, where *certain tracts of mercurifying earth* from central locations and materials (which were discussed in the second section of this book) reach *metallic veins*, dissolve them, and rarefy the contained metals so much that they flow of their own accord in the form of *running true Mercury* even within the mines themselves. However, it is not rare that when sulfurous particles happen upon them, a new compound is made from such a compound—namely, a *doubly-compounded substance*—which they call *cinnabar* <note>The bright red ore of mercury (mercury sulfide).</note>. Yet, when its *sulfurous* particles
<margin>No. 11</margin>
are removed, the *fluid composition of Mercury* again appears before the eyes. So also, when the mercurifying earthy parts are removed, the metal is also manifested, which previously lay hidden in the fluid Mercurial compound. That it is indeed the *earthy* particles that mercurify or liquefy is evident from the opposite: for it is *earthy* things that stop such a flow. As we see in *sulfur* and the *smoke of Saturn* <note>Saturn is the alchemical name for Lead; "smoke of Saturn" refers to lead vapors or oxides.</note>. For just as a metal becomes *fluid and running* when it receives too much *mercurifying earth*; although the same earth—even in a smaller proportion—enters into every composition of metals as a principle (as we demonstrated in section three, chapter four): so when other earths, although they exist as principles of metals, especially the *second* <note>Becher’s "second earth" is the fluid or mercurial earth (*terra fluida*).</note> (concerning which see section three, chapter three), enter this *fluid mixture* of Mercury more than is proper, they stop the fluidity and
<margin>No. 12</margin>
coagulate the mixture. We see these *extremes of fluidity and solidity* clearly in common Mercury; which, when it is mixed with other metals (an operation they call *amalgamation*), seizes and softens as much of them as it exceeds in *fluid earth*. For if too much metal is added, the *amalgam hardens*, because the fluid parts are overcome. Moreover, this connection of Mercury and metal is not so superficial as to be passed over with a light foot; for if you make such an amalgam from *Mercury and lead*, and draw off the Mercury again through a retort with a strong fire so that the lead flows in the retort, you will receive your Mercury back—but it will be notably not only heavier, but also *altered*. For it unites some portion of lead to itself in such a way that it carries it through the retort and takes it with it through the leather <note>Mercury was commonly purified by squeezing it through chamois leather; Becher is noting that the Mercury has "swallowed" some lead so thoroughly it passes through the pores of the leather.</note>, separable from it by no *art* that I know of, except by slow *digestion* <note>The process of exposing a substance to gentle, continuous heat.</note>. Consequently, it also runs more slowly in its flow and forms a skin. From which it clearly appears that in the compound of common Mercury, the fluidifying earth is in excess; which, lest it be idle, seizes particles of lead, mixes them with itself, and leads them into fluidity. But if indeed metals are added to Mercury in excess, then the amalgam is coagulated, because the fluidifying parts are overcome by

### Book I, Section V, Chapter III.

...until it is united by amalgamation. The reason for this is that a certain amount of *Mercury* <note>original: *Mercurio*</note>—through these kinds of amalgamations and abstractions—adheres to the gold and is fixed within it. Consequently, such a calx <note>A "calx" is the powdery residue left after a metal has been roasted or "calcined"; it was considered the metallic earth.</note> of gold acquires a unique medicinal quality, *not unlike a precipitate*, which it retains even if it is strongly heated or boiled many times. But through such frequent amalgamation and abstraction, the *Mercury* has mixed some of the gold into itself, which it has taken into its innermost constitutive parts; as the digestion of such *animated Mercury* <note>original: *Mercurii animati*; mercury that has been "vitalized" or "soul-filled" by the addition of gold.</note> shows, in which it reveals its golden nature. From all this, it follows that Mercury softens metals according to the abundance of its fluidifying earth; and that common Mercury itself is nothing other than a *fluid amalgam*, that is, a mixture of fluidifying earth with a certain metal. Thus, there are as many *Mercuries* as there are metals that can be mixed with the fluidifying earth: six of which are perfect, such as gold, silver, copper, iron, tin, and lead; and some are imperfect, such as antimony, bismuth, zinc, and marcasite: from all of which amalgams can be made.

<margin>No. 14.</margin>
These do not differ at all from common Mercury, except that they do not contain enough fluidifying earth; when this is added, they become true Mercuries, which are called *Mercuries of the bodies*; although common Mercury itself is also derived from some metallic body, and therefore ought to be called a "Mercury of a body." *There are therefore six metals, not seven*; for Mercury is a composite of the others. Nor indeed is any common Mercury found that does not consist of metal, although this is revealed with difficulty due to the abundance of fluidifying earth. This is not surprising if we consider that the animated solar or Saturnine Mercury <note>Mercury joined with Gold or Lead.</note> mentioned above returns the mixed metal with great difficulty; because its fluidifying earth seizes the particles of the metal in its innermost constituents: so that eventually it coagulates with the substance it has taken up more quickly than it allows it to be torn away. And indeed, in this wonderful *sympathy of the fluidifying earth with metals*, the entire *Secret of the Philosophers* lies hidden.

<margin>No. 15.</margin>
This secret consists in this: that the fluidifying earth is held in its pure state—that is, in a state before its mixture with any metal. It is in this that the *Mercury of the Philosophers* <note>The theoretical "First Matter" of the alchemists, as opposed to the common liquid metal found in shops.</note> differs from common mercury; in common mercury, the fluidifying earth has already formed some *compound* <note>original: *decompositum*</note> by taking up a certain metal. In the *Philosophical* Mercury, however, it remains virginal, stained by no mineral, and therefore capable of receiving the perfect sulfur of the sun <note>The "sulfur of the sun" refers to the essential, combustible, and coloring principle of gold.</note>. *Raymond Lully* <note>A famous 13th-century Majorcan philosopher and alchemist to whom many texts were attributed.</note> learnedly explains this in the following words:

> *We remember,* he says, *having said in our testament, that no quicksilver is more promptly converted into the substance of sulfur than that in which the qualities of sulfur have been sufficiently introduced through dissolution; nor does any sulfur congeal quicksilver more promptly than that in whose natural substance the quicksilver itself exists, having already been converted by the ingenuity of art: and let the power of the transmuting quicksilver hold the parts of the transmuted sulfur in their entirety, so that within it, before its own transmutation, a proper, non-burning sulfur, white or red, may be mixed at the most minute level. For such quicksilver will then have its own proper matter, and then nature embraces its own nature, and rejoices in it more amicably than in something foreign.*

Thus far Lully.

<margin>No. 16.</margin>
In these few words, he has uncovered a great mystery; but we, setting aside all professional jealousy, shall add the key in even fewer words. Namely, the fluidifying earth, on which the whole matter hinges, is in common salt...

<margin>No. 17.</margin>

One is *mercurial*, the other is *sulphurous*: the former constitutes running Mercury from metals, the latter constitutes volatile *arsenic* or *sulfur* from them. And the *latter is more powerful than the former*; hence there is great labor in knowing and discerning these kinds of earths: *for only the former earth works for mercurification*. The latter is the essence of all sulfurs and salts, and it constitutes the arsenical decomposites, as we have said, toward which metals are naturally prone. It is believable, therefore, that this arsenical mask has been imposed on many; indeed, it seems probable to me, if I wished to correct the errors of others, where I could demonstrate that by a single manipulation, even the most brilliant men have erred in this business. ### Book I, Section V, Chapter III

...thinking that with an idle brain—as is done in the **Peripatetic Philosophy** <note>The school of philosophy following Aristotle, often criticized by early modern scientists for prioritizing abstract logic over physical experimentation.</note>, in a mere game of words—the **Mercury of bodies** <note>The essential "mercurial" component that alchemists believed could be extracted from solid metals.</note> should be numbered among **non-entities**. I am easily convinced that because I so frankly profess the reality of **mercurification**, a heavy indictment will be written against me by these men; but I do not care in the least. For, relying on experience, I laugh at the foolish theory of such idle speculators, and at their foolish **temerity**. For what an absurdity it is to conclude that things are **non-entities** simply because they did not succeed for this or that person! It is just as if I were to say that the art of painting is a non-entity because I am not skilled in it; or if I were to say, "I do not believe you have a thousand Imperial coins <note>original: *Imperiales*; referring to the Reichsthaler, the standard silver coin of the Holy Roman Empire.</note> unless you share them with me." All these things, though they consist of absurd conclusions, are nevertheless taken up by learned men—as they seem to themselves—as arguments against the **Chemists**. 

And lest I seem to say things that I cannot prove, leaving aside many other examples, let us consider that other **Aesculapius of Jena, Werner Rolfinck, Doctor of Philosophy and Medicine**, 
<margin>Note</margin>
practitioner, and **public Professor of Chemistry**, a distinguished **anatomist**, and indeed, among the unlearned 
<margin>19.</margin> 
commoners, a **Hermes** <note>A reference to Hermes Trismegistus, the mythical founder of alchemy; here used sarcastically to describe Rolfinck's god-like reputation among the public.</note>, who is believed to be as incapable of erring in his speech and writings as **Luther** himself. This man, I say, who is approved by so many, we shall nevertheless examine in the ash-test under the cupel <note>original: *in cineritio sub capella*; Becher uses a metallurgical metaphor here—a cupel is a tool used to test the purity of gold or silver—to mean he will put Rolfinck’s theories to a rigorous practical test.</note>, since we do not trust every outward splendor. 

We will not examine his entire book, which he calls ***Chemistry, Reduced to the Form of the Galenic Art*** <note>original: *Chymiam, in artis, scilicet Galenisticae, formam redactam*; referring to Rolfinck's attempt to reconcile new chemistry with traditional ancient Greek medicine.</note>; but we will only bring forward those things which he thrusts upon the reader concerning the **Mercuries of bodies** on pages 428, 429, 430, and 431. There, without any reason or **experience**, he places them among the **Chemical Non-entities**, and thus expressly testifies that the experience of such operations is, to him, a great 
<margin>Note</margin>
**non-entity**. Lest he escape through **Aristotelian** quibbles, distinctions, and empty verbal 
<margin>20.</margin> 
limitations and exceptions, we will briefly repeat as a preliminary what we proposed in the third section, fifth chapter of this book, against the unskilled **Aristotelians** and **Chemists** regarding the definition and real existence of **Chemical principles** and **entities**. 

Namely: First, we do not establish **salt, sulfur, and Mercury** as the "first principles" <note>The most basic building blocks of matter.</note> of metals, but as "common subjects." Second, these subjects are **decomposed** and consist of parts. Third, the parts themselves, before decomposition and mixing, do not constitute the **formal** <note>The "form" or essential nature of a thing in Aristotelian/Scholastic logic.</note> decomposed thing, which arises only after decomposition. That is to say, the parts that enter into the mixture of **salt, sulfur, or Mercury** do not constitute the subject itself before they enter it and while they are still **divided**. Just as the parts belonging to a clock, before their combination—and especially each particle **by itself**—cannot be called a whole clock. 

Now, having sent ahead this triple caution and warning, I will not fight with **Rolfinck** over whether common **salt, sulfur, and Mercury** are "remote principles" or "proximate principles" of metals. We have sufficiently explained our mind in the place cited; nor will **Rolfinck** deny the second point, that the aforementioned three subjects are not **simple mixtures** but are **composite** and consist of parts; nor will he oppose the third, that divided parts do not constitute the whole before the act of mixing. This alone, therefore, is the question: **whether all the parts constituting the mixture of salt, or sulfur, or Mercury, lie hidden in metals; so that by themselves, without any addition, such subjects and mixtures can be elicited from them?** This, I say, is the question; and not **whether the things elicited** are such...

# Subterranean Physics

...that such subjects are the principles of the things from which they are elicited; for I set aside that question here, as I have addressed it in the place cited. Nor does **Rolfinck** <note>Werner Rolfinck (1599–1673), a German physician and chemist who was often skeptical of more extreme alchemical claims.</note> discuss it in the passages mentioned.

<margin>No. 21</margin>
Returning, therefore, to the point of the question, I say that there is no **Chemist**, nor any chemical book, that promises to prepare **salt, sulfur, and Mercury** from metals without any addition; the controversy is actually whether the parts that are added are effectively such that they constitute the aforementioned mixtures *by themselves*. If that were the case, those subjects would be added rather than elicited, and the **Chemists** would be practicing a deception. Or, rather, the question is whether all the parts required for the perfect constitution and composition of the aforementioned subjects are added, so that some are lacking from the metals for the completion and perfection of the mixture—which, when the former are added, associate themselves and make an absolute mixture. Without this, neither the added parts nor the metal by itself could constitute that third mixture; instead, the conjunction of both the *added material and the metal* is required. 

<margin>No. 22</margin>
The question, therefore, concerns this operation: namely, whether from a metal (which in itself has no sulfur) and a material (which is added and is also free of all actual sulfur), true sulfur is produced if they are joined. This is also to be understood regarding **salt and Mercury**. This is the core of the case. For if **Rolfinck** denies that **Chemists** can elicit **salts, sulfurs, and Mercuries** from metals without the addition of any thing, then he denies what all **Chemists** deny; his negation, therefore, does not harm the **Chemists**, but only himself, for he ascribes non-entities to them. If, however, **Rolfinck** says that **Chemists** add **salts, sulfurs, and Mercuries** to metals and then extract the same things from them again (namely, the very things they added), then he is dealing with deceivers and idiots; for prudent **Chemists** are wise enough to be able to discern newly produced things from the additions. They are not so dull as to be treated in such a crude manner. **Dr. Robert Boyle** <note>Robert Boyle (1627–1691), the famous Irish natural philosopher; Becher refers here to his 1661 work "The Sceptical Chymist," which challenged the traditional Tria Prima theory.</note> dealt with **Chemists** more subtly in his *Sceptical Chymist*. Yet I would not entirely concede to **Rolfinck** that, even if **salt, sulfur, and Mercury** are added to metals, the additions do not take on an increase—not a heterogeneous one, but a homogeneous one. Indeed, this increase is such that **Rolfinck**, with all his experience, could no longer reduce it back to its original form, as I gave an example above regarding **animated Mercury** <note>Mercury that has been "quickened" or processed with other substances to give it new chemical properties.</note> and in the third section, 

<margin>No. 23</margin>
third chapter, in various accounts regarding **sulfur**. Finally, if **Rolfinck** denies that anything can be produced unless the things added to the metals are already effectively the same subjects that later emerge, then he denies all mineral **decomposition** <note>The process of breaking a complex substance down into its simpler chemical components.</note>. This is so evident that one must be blinder than a mole not to see it. For metals enter into the decomposition of **salts, sulfurs, and Mercuries** not merely accidentally, but necessarily and essentially as constituent parts. This is also true for the decompositions of **vitriol, arsenic**, and many other mixtures. Nor will anyone deny (who has even the slightest experience in practice) that from **spirit of vinegar** <note>original: *spiritu aceti*; a concentrated acetic acid produced by distilling vinegar.</note> by itself, without addition, a sweet, white, bodily salt can in no way be elicited; just as it cannot be from lead. Meanwhile, however, when they come together, a composite emerges in the form of a very sweet salt, which we therefore call **Sugar of Lead** <note>original: *Saccharum Saturni*; Lead(II) acetate. It is sweet-tasting but highly toxic.</note>, analogous in every way to common salt except for the taste. **Oil of sulfur** <note>original: *Oleum sulphuris*; sulfuric acid, often produced by burning/deflagrating sulfur under a glass bell.</note>, prepared by burning, is certainly devoid of all bodily sulfur; nor by itself can even a grain of living sulfur

can be elicited: **molten antimony**, though treated many times by fire, is devoid of **living sulfur** <note>original: "sulphuris vivi"; refers to native or "active" sulfur</note> on its own, and will provide no living sulfur by itself; but when these two are joined, they provide a great quantity of true, living, solid **burning sulfur**, as we shall demonstrate through practice in the second book, in the special chapter on antimony. What does

These matters concern us little, for we do not take it upon ourselves to patronize or **defend every absurd opinion**; rather, we wish to infer nothing other than what Rolfinck has dared to brand as a **stigma upon all Chemistry**, using only words and no demonstrations: namely, his claim that **salt, sulfur, and Mercury from metals are non-entities, except by analogy, or except through such additions**. Perhaps he feared that if he established the truth and reality of such entities, he would be forced to demonstrate them to his students and those frequenting his Chemical colleges (in which there are more words than practice) in exchange for the quite large sums of money they paid him. We do this for free, seeking our profit in the truth. For just as in the third section, fifth chapter, we reclaimed the truth against certain Chemists themselves who establish such **decomposites as principles**, so in this place we must convict those who deny such compositions, and who change the state of the question in order to **blacken Chemistry**, even though they write themselves down as its **Professors**. I conclude, 
<margin>No. 25.</margin>
therefore, that **metals essentially enter into a mixture of salt, sulfur, and Mercury as parts**; since from salt, sulfur, and Mercury certain parts enter **essentially** into metals and constitute various decomposites <note>complex mixtures</note>, which could not exist or be made without them. Especially **Mercury**; which we are dealing with specifically in this chapter, and for the sake of which we have digressed into the preceding points, and whose **non-entity** Rolfinck specifically attacks in the place cited. But let us hear 
<margin>No. 26.</margin>
his absurd conclusion: *Ambitious men,* he says in the cited place, *chatter about this craftsmanship; but when it comes down to the thing itself, they appear more silent than a fish. They do not add their secret modes of preparation,* 
<margin>Rolfinck</margin>
*fearing criticism; but if one moves the hand closer, the brooms are fallen apart* <note>An idiom meaning the whole thing falls to pieces or is revealed as nonsense</note>, *thus far* Rolfinck. Here he rightly advises that Chemists do not publish this noble *enchirisin* <note>from Greek "encheiresis": manual operation or handling</note> indiscriminately; but he errs in this: that he says it happens out of fear of criticism—whose criticism? Rolfinck’s perhaps, or that of some other **Chemist-hater** <note>original: "Misochymici"</note>? Surely we do not fear him or any other; let it suffice that Chemists say it is true that **Mercury can be elicited from metals**. Rolfinck now [demands] the practice...

The precipitated lime is called ***horned Saturn*** <note>original: "Saturnus cornuus"; a historical name for lead chloride</note>: mix this with an **equal** <note>original: "anatico"; from the Greek "ana," meaning in equal parts</note> weight of **common salt**: and again with an **equal** weight (as much as the whole total weighs) of some **non-melting earth**, such as **Passau earth** <note>a heat-resistant clay from Passau used for making laboratory crucibles</note>: once the mixture is very well blended, distill it by degrees through a retort, and no small part of the Saturn [lead] will pass over into the receiving vessel like metallic leaves, such as we use in mirrors, which are entirely fluid, so that for their full **mercurification** <note>the process of turning a solid metal into a liquid mercury-like state</note> nothing is lacking except a brief manipulation, which it would be a sin to expose indiscriminately to the light. If the adversaries are not yet satisfied by this evidence, let them study the treatise by **Glauber** <note>Johann Rudolph Glauber (1604–1670), a famous chemist known for "Glauber's Salt"</note> which he wrote concerning **Mercuries**, and they will find the truth, though in very few drops. It is a natural and sound conclusion: if metals can be softened in part so that they flow, they can also be softened so that they flow more liquidly **in their entirety**; since the former is true, so also is the latter.

<margin>No. 30.</margin>

Therefore, if you look at the title, he is of the greatest authority; now dead, while he lived he was devoted to speculations, deprived of both lights [eyes] and blind. He attempted hardly anything **in practice**, as I understand from those who knew him more accurately. He also wrote a *metallurgy*, but of no great importance, nor based on any experiment. However, his *Disputation on Manual Practice, regarding the two miracles of art and nature*, seems to have more weight; although it contains many things **contrary to practice itself**. In the aforementioned little work, he raises a question and a doubt: whether, even if metals are liquefied and brought into a mercurial flow, they are to be regarded as **true Mercuries**? This the author denies; we will set down his own words, for on page 80 of the Frankfurt edition in duodecimo <note>original: "in 12."; a book size where the printed sheet is folded to create twelve leaves</note>, he states the following:

> *Silver, he says, having been reduced into a lime by **parting water** <note>original: "separationis aquam"; nitric acid used to separate silver from gold</note>, and mixed very well with a triple amount of sal ammoniac, I add oil of tartar; after five or more repeated soakings and dryings over a light fire, the silver is sublimated and rendered so volatile and fluid that it was thought to be true quicksilver not only by the unskilled, but even by the more experienced, since it is found to have obtained many of its properties from this operation. Yet they wander blindly here; for while it indeed appears to be quicksilver, it is by no means anything but false and **sophistical** <note>counterfeit or artificial in a deceptive way</note>, for it easily returns to silver as before if it is cast upon other silver melted in the fire; the **solvent** <note>original: "menstruum"</note>, through which it was held in liquidity and which is otherwise not easily separable, thus flies away, and it recovers its previously lost form. This happens by no means to common quicksilver, for it will never be possible to change it into silver—unless it be adulterated—without the application of the silver-making stone <note>the Philosopher's Stone specifically prepared for silver transmutation</note>.*

Thus far the cited author.

could. Regarding the first point—namely, whether the *process* of making *mercury* out of silver <note>original: "luna"</note>, whether it be true or sophisticated, is *true* according to the author’s cited description? I answer in a few words that the process in practice, however it is set up, *is false and completely fails to succeed.*

<margin>No. 32.</margin> For with great zeal and diligence, I have attempted it many times. From this I gather that the author himself never tried it, but either heard of it or received it by word of mouth from someone; or, if he did know the whole truth, he omitted certain things and thus intentionally deceived the reader. I took care through a friend to have the author in Venice warned about this matter, but the author died before he could be informed of it. The reason why this process does not succeed according to the description is twofold: *first*, because the **silver calx** <term>calx: the powdery residue left after a metal has been "burnt" or dissolved in acid</term> prepared by **aqua fortis** <term>nitric acid</term> is not sufficiently prepared, and therefore it is not dissolved by **sal ammoniac** <term>ammonium chloride</term>; hence there is no connection between the two. Then, he adds **oil of tartar** <term>a concentrated solution of potassium carbonate</term>, by which the **spirit of sal ammoniac** (or of urine) is released; and because it is subtle, and the author orders the material to be dried slowly, it evaporates easily and does not act upon the silver calx—even though the whole power of the process consists in this. Thus, when the **spirit of sal ammoniac** has been driven off, the remainder is **sublimated** <note>heated until it turns to vapor and then solidifies again</note>, and the silver calx is **fixed** <note>made resistant to heat</note> by the oil of tartar (which has formed a *new mixture with the sal ammoniac*) rather than being made **volatile** <note>capable of being vaporized</note>. Consequently, little or nothing of the silver is sublimated. For these reasons, and as experience witnesses, the process does not succeed. It would otherwise be desirable if the **mercury of silver** could be prepared with such light effort.

<margin>No. 33.</margin> I now approach the *second* point: namely, *if the mercury of silver were possessed or given, and it were cast upon molten silver, would it be reduced into a solid body by the loss of the solvent <note>original: "menstrui"</note> through which it was held in a liquid state?* Since the prescribed process is false, it is believable that the author of this description never possessed so much as a grain of the *mercury of silver* in this way, and consequently never performed a proper test, but rather—according to his custom—merely performed it within his own mind. I, however, supported by practice, will grant the author that *mercury of silver by itself* evaporates entirely in the manner of common *mercury*; *but when cast into liquid silver, some of it (though a tiny part) is reduced, and there exists silver of another quality. However, the greater part evaporates*, not as **De Comitibus** <note>Ludovicus de Comitibus, a prominent alchemical author of the period</note> thinks, by the *loss of the solvent, but by the loss of the entire body.* For from an ounce of properly volatile and prepared mercury of silver, you will not receive even a **drachm** <note>a small unit of weight, about 1/8th of an ounce</note> in the reduction; the rest evaporates in mercurial form, and if captured again, it is mercury.

<margin>No. 34.</margin> Here again the author stumbles when he says that silver is freed from its **solvent** <term>menstruum: any liquid used to dissolve a solid, though here referring to the chemical "agent" holding the metal in liquid form</term>—which is otherwise not easily separable—in this way. Would that he had written the truth! Then with light effort and great savings we would have that longed-for **mercurifying earth in virgin form** <term>terra mercurificans: the theoretical "earthy" principle that alchemists believed could turn metals into mercury</term>, without which all labor is in vain. But just as silver is not "fished out" of that mercurifying earth from sal ammoniac and urine with such light effort as **De Comitibus** posits, so once it has been grasped, the silver does not lose it so lightly; rather, it retains it most tightly and fixes it with itself into a truly metallic body.

<margin>No. 35.</margin> From the aforementioned, the explanation of the *third* point follows: namely, that the author is wrong to call the mercury of silver **sophistical** <note>meaning "fake" or "deceptive" in an alchemical context</note> just because part of it is reduced back into silver. Indeed, I would pronounce it *sophistical* if it did *not* do this! For where else would it show evidence of its origin? Would a seed of wheat be "sophistical"...

Did he then require of the *Mercury of the moon* <note>mercury supposedly extracted from silver</note> according to *De Comitibus*, that it be reducible into *Saturn* <term>lead</term> or *Jupiter* <term>tin</term>? Or that it be as crude and volatile as common mercury? If it possessed those properties, it should not be called *Mercury of the moon*, but *common mercury*. Where would that "fixability" <term>the ability of a substance to resist the heat of fire without evaporating</term> remain, which is so greatly desired and praised by *Philosophers* <note>Becher refers here to alchemists or natural philosophers</note> in the *Mercury of the Sun and Moon*? We often create unnecessary subtleties where they only cause harm, and we interpret the teachings of the ancients and nature poorly. For who ever required of *Mercury of the moon* that it should either completely lose or lack its lunar temperament and intrinsic fixability? Such a request is impossible and contains a contradiction in terms: namely, to call it *Mercury of the moon* and yet expect it to be *Common or vulgar Mercury*.

<margin>No. 36.</margin> A certain "know-it-all" <note>original: "sciolus," a person with superficial knowledge</note> was lingering in my laboratory <term>ustrina: literally a place for burning or smelting</term>, who knew how to talk much about the lost and dreamed-of sciences and experiences of the ancients; among other things, he lamented the lost malleability and ductility of glass. I immediately promised to show him such a feat; I grabbed a piece of glass and threw it into the fire. When it was glowing brilliantly, I stretched it out with a hot hammer. The other man smirked and said that the ancients were able to stretch cold glass. To which I replied: are you so simple—not to say foolish—that you have convinced yourself that when the ancients wanted to draw out and extend iron, a much more manageable subject, they committed it to the fire; yet when they wanted to extend glass, the most brittle subject of all, they would have handled it cold against all reason? But we are so constituted by nature that we always aspire to the impossible and value those things which smell of impossibility, while we neglect those things which are true and easy, and proceed by the straight path of nature.

But let us hurry to the fourth and last difficulty, where the author seems to cut through all objections with one blow, like a sword, when he says: <margin>No. 37.</margin> *Common mercury can in no way be changed into silver except through a tincture.* From this it clearly appears that the author groups and draws *common mercury and Mercury of the moon* into one single category. Because *common mercury*, when cast into liquid silver in the fire, is not partially reduced into silver like *Mercury of the moon*; therefore, *Mercury of the moon* is not *common mercury*. I concede all of this; but to say that because *Mercury of the moon* is not *common mercury*, it is therefore "Sophistical"—this I deny, for there is no logical consequence.

For something is not "Sophistical," adulterated, or a substitute if it preserves the essential temperament of its subject. But *Mercury of the moon*, by preserving its potential fixity, does exactly this: therefore it is not Sophistical, but natural. For it is known even to "the bleary-eyed and the barbers" <note>A Latin idiom, "lippis et tonsoribus," meaning something is common knowledge known to everyone</note> that wheat and barley are of different species and nature. Since *De Comitibus* admits that *Mercury* can be made *from silver*, he must simultaneously admit that *Mercury* can be prepared *from lead, or from gold, or from antimony*; and by consequence, he will admit that *Mercury of the Sun* is of a different nature than *Mercury of the moon, or of Saturn, or of Antimony*. Indeed, the only point I wish to conclude is that *Mercury of the Sun or moon* must be of a different nature than Mercury...

It is called *common*, however, because it is generated in the mines by nature alone, without the intervention of art.
