In the case of the *Mercury of the Sun* <note>gold</note> and the *Mercury of the Moon* <note>silver</note>, we do not deny it, nor in the *Mercury of Venus* <note>copper</note> and the *Mercury of Mars* <note>iron</note>; but in the *Mercury of Saturn* <note>lead</note> and the *Mercury of Jupiter* <note>tin</note>, we deny it entirely. This is because bodies of that kind are rendered so volatile that they can in no way be reduced to their original body anymore, unless Sun or Moon is added. This is to be understood only regarding the Mercuries of bodies made by art, where the metals, during preparation, do not attract more of the fluidifying earth than is required for their fluidity. In the *Genesis of common Mercury*, however, the "mercurification" does not happen by way of attraction, but by *conjunction*: here the metals do not need to attract the fluidifying earth from other coverings and subjects; instead, nature adds it—already *prepared and free*—in the greatest abundance and at will. Thus, the metals are rendered extremely volatile, and in the *common manner*, they are not "fixable" <term>able to withstand fire</term> by themselves, even though they retain a *potential for fixability*. If Art likewise possessed this fluidifying and mercurifying earth separately and in its bare form, so that it could add it to and join it with metals *at will*, then it would produce a Mercury of bodies—even if made by art from the most "fixed" <note>fire-resistant</note> metals—that would be in every way similar to the common type, and not "fixable" in the common manner.

For this reason, it is also called *electrum* <note>usually a gold-silver alloy, but here meaning a complex mixture</note>, because it is a confusion of different metals. In the same way, different metals are usually mixed in a fire, and that paste is afterward called *electrum*, but a solid one; to which this mercurial liquid is the opposite. We shall prove that *common* Mercury, if it is *solar* <term>gold-like</term> or *lunar* <term>silver-like</term> (and nearly all of it is, though one more than the other), is fixed in the same way that Ludovicus de Comitibus fixes the *Mercury of the moon*; namely, by injecting it into *liquid silver*.

Consequently, the aforementioned author calls this mercury *Sophistical* <note>original: "Sophisticum"; meaning an imitation or a chemical "cheat" rather than a true transmutation</note>. From this, it would follow that common Mercury would also be Sophistical, because it is fixed in the same manner. For if, under a vaulted tile, a portion of *living Mercury* <term>liquid quicksilver</term> is injected into *silver* in a liquid cupel <note>original: "cineritio"; a vessel made of bone-ash used to refine precious metals</note> just as it is flashing <note>original: "coruscato"; the "blick," a sudden brightening of molten silver at the moment it becomes pure</note> and finally forming small flower-like patterns, and the silver is afterwards tested, it will provide a clear proof of *gold*; and this happens as often as you do it. 

There is also another way of demonstrating this, but it must not be shared with the common people. From this, it is clearly evident that only as much of common Mercury is fixed in this way as it contains *solar Mercury* within itself. For no reason can be assigned as to how Mercury, in this rapid operation, separates the aforementioned *gold* from the body of the *moon* <term>silver</term>, and not from *its own* body. On the contrary, once the Mercury is captured and treated this way a few times, it *no longer* performs the same feat, as it has been deprived of its *solar Mercury* through abstraction. 

It will therefore not be surprising, nor difficult, to judge the various cases that occasionally happen to Chemists in the fixation of *Mercuries*; namely, according to the diversity of common Mercury. If it contains much *solar* part, it will yield much *gold*, and so on for the others. It is therefore possible for a part of common Mercury, entirely *without a tincture*, to be fixed and reduced in the same way as the Mercury of silver. Therefore, neither this one nor that one is *Sophistical*. However, the remaining part of common Mercury—or the Mercury of imperfect bodies—cannot be changed *into silver*; nor can the imperfect metals <note>such as lead, tin, or copper</note> themselves, from which such Mercuries arise, be changed *without a tincture*. 

I do not deny that this is the easiest way to convert them, but it is not the only one. For, as I shall demonstrate toward the end of this chapter, *metals can be really transmuted, entirely without any tincture*; therefore, their *Mercuries* can be as well, which are only decomposed metallic substances. And indeed, as far as the fixation of common Mercury is concerned—whatever kind it may be—which occurs without a tincture, the aforementioned author seems to contradict himself in the cited booklet on page 75,

<margin>No. 43.</margin>
where he says that *Mercury* is fixed by means of the *Alkaest* <term>the hypothetical universal solvent</term> liquor. We will set down the author’s words:

> *Indeed, some of the metals, such as Mercury, are so far removed from their natural state after the extraction (perhaps it should read abstraction) of the aforementioned solvent from it, that they acquire properties far different from their previous ones; for it is fixed in such a way that it is not destroyed in the lead assay.*

Thus far the cited author. Here it should be noted that the lead assay <note>cupellation</note> is only applicable to *gold* and *silver*; therefore, common Mercury acquires this primary fixation and quality of gold or silver by means of the Alkaest liquor. Yet the author himself contends at length in the cited booklet that this liquor is neither the *Mercury of the Philosophers*, and much less a *tincture*. It will therefore be possible to bring common Mercury to a *silvery* quality and fixation *without a tincture*; which the author proves here but denies there, and thus contradicts himself. It should be noted, however, that the author uses the word *extraction*, for which perhaps...

# Subterranean Physics
## Page 210

Perhaps it should be read as *abstraction*; but let us allow the term "extraction," from which it follows that the *Alkaest <note>A hypothetical universal solvent sought by alchemists, capable of reducing any body to its first liquid matter</note> is prepared from common Mercury by the separation of parts—namely, the fluidifying or "mercurifying" parts—as we demonstrated in the third section, chapter four.* However, two arguments against the author arise from this operation. First, if the "mercurifying earth" is separated from the mixture of Mercury, what remains will be the *metal* from which the mixture was originally composed. <margin>No. 44.</margin> Once the cause of its volatility and fluidity is removed (that is, once the mercurifying earth is extracted from it), the author asserts that this substance can withstand the cupel <note>A shallow porous container used in refining gold or silver; if a substance "withstands" it, it is considered a "fixed" or precious metal</note>. Therefore, it is necessary that such a metal was, in its original nature, "fixed," and consequently was either *gold* <term>the Sun</term> or *silver* <term>the Moon</term>. Thus, common Mercury would actually be the Mercury of gold or silver; and since, in the author's own opinion, this is "true Mercury," it cannot be *Sophistical* <note>original: "Sophisticus"; a fake or deceptive substance</note>, even if it is reduced back into a metallic body.

Secondly, regarding the author’s assertion that the liquor Alkaest consists of mercurifying earth, and yet is not the *Mercury of the Philosophers*—as he strongly contends—he seems either to be playing with terms or to be mistaken about the materials. He falls into the very trap about which we warned the reader at the beginning of this chapter: namely, taking *arsenical* earth for the *Mercury of the Philosophers*, and *Mercurial* earth for the *liquor Alkaest*. In doing so, he provides "this for that," or as he himself notes in his trouble, he puts the cart before the horse <note>original: "hysteron proteron"; a Greek rhetorical term for reversing the logical or natural order</note>. For the *Alkaest consists of arsenical earth, whereas the Mercury of the Philosophers consists of Mercurial earth*. Both are found in Mercury, and both contribute to *fluidity*, but with different ends and respects. Therefore, both must be handled and distinguished with the greatest caution and wisdom. 

But lest we run out into a vast sea of observations, we must pull in our sails and seek the harbor. For two skiffs still remain to be sent into the *aqueous* and *igneous* <term>fiery</term> fluid seas. <margin>No. 45.</margin> We therefore conclude and establish that the mercurial flow proceeds from metals when they are resolved, softened, and liquefied with "mercurifying earth." This earth is related to them and is their principle; it enters into their mixture, though in the proper proportion. <margin>No. 46.</margin> It is not without merit, therefore, that it is called the *radical moisture of metals* <term>humidum radicale</term>. For just as common water is the radical moisture of vegetables, uniting with their seeds, resolving them, and again coagulating with them during growth, so too does this *dry* mineral water—which does not wet the hands—resolve metals and is fixed with them again. This resolution and fixation is the first and most common characteristic of metals, belonging to nothing else except *metals and their moisture*. For as Count Bernard <note>Bernard of Trevisan (1406–1490), a famous Italian alchemist</note> testifies, *no substance or water is suitable for metals in solution which does not remain with them in matter and form during coagulation*. 

As to where this mercurifying earth draws its origin, we have sufficiently demonstrated in the second section; <margin>No. 47.</margin> for it is the most subtle essence of *salts*. It is not arsenical but mercurial; it is found not only in common salt, but also in sea salt, nitre, vinegar, urine, and finally in the air itself. From this, it will not be difficult to explain what the Ancients said about the "Philosophical matter": that all men live by it, that the rich and poor alike possess this matter, and that Adam carried it out of Paradise—*namely, urine*. Many other parabolic sayings can be easily explained from this foundation. Lest anyone wonder that I assert the mercurifying earth lies hidden in the air itself, I shall add some testimonies and examples as a finishing touch. Let those things be read which Glauber <note>Johann Rudolf Glauber (1604–1670), a significant German chemist and apothecary</note> wrote in the fourth part of his *Spagyric Pharmacopoeia*, page 44, and concerning the [nature] of Saturn...

On the subject of Mercury specifically, on pages 47 and 48, he writes about the *Mercury of the Sun* <term>Mercury supposedly extracted from gold</term>; where he explicitly attributes the conversion of gold into mercury to the air, or to the earth *which the wind carried in its belly* <note>original: "quam ventus in utero portavit"; a famous alchemical maxim from the Emerald Tablet, suggesting the air contains a life-giving or transformative principle</note>. Master Rapp reported to me that in common *Vitriol* <term>metallic sulfates</term> exposed to the air, he found running, liquid *Mercury* after some time. And I hear that even now in Erfurt there is a craftsman who, having exposed the *caput mortuum* <term>the "dead head" or useless dregs left after distillation</term> to the air and distilled the spirit from it, elicits true *Mercury* from *Antimony*. In a certain tower, I had constructed a clock, to which I hung various leaden counterweights <note>original: "antisacomata"; weights used to balance a mechanism</note> constantly exposed to the air; the lead began to contract a very white downy film, which, when scraped off, was converted with little effort into running *Mercury*.

<margin>No. 48.</margin> Such an earth, therefore, lies hidden not only in the sea and in various salts, but also in the air itself: hence all the *Mercuries* of bodies, when they evaporate, leave a red spot on silver, thereby attesting to the immortal soul of nitre <note>original: "nitri anima"; saltpeter was often thought by 17th-century chemists to be the "clue" to the life-force found in the atmosphere</note>. We could reveal a great secret at this point; indeed, in the preceding chapters, we have already stated the whole method and everything else, so that nothing remains but to point out where we said it. But it will not benefit the wicked, and the good will find fault with me for throwing bread to swine <note>A biblical reference suggesting that holy or deep truths should not be shared with those who would disrespect them</note>, I who have written so clearly that I believe no other mortal has done the same.

<margin>No. 51.</margin> We have said that Neptune holds a trident in his hand, by which it is probable the Ancients very aptly indicated the three fluidities or liquidities of things. Having overcome one tine—namely the mercurial fluidity—we shall now consider the second tine: the aqueous liquidity. Thus, we shall set sail from the terrestrial sea into the aqueous one.

<margin>No. 52.</margin> Moist liquidity is of two types: *oily and aqueous*; although if you consider it accurately, oily liquidity is nothing other than water filled with fatty terrestrial atoms, as practice shows: for if you draw off the oil, you will find a middle part of water; and varnish, if burned in a retort <term>a glass vessel with a long neck used for distillation</term>, will be largely resolved into *spirit*, so that very little charcoal remains; all the rest can be reduced to *elemental water*, which is entirely *liquid and moist*.

<margin>No. 53.</margin> Common water itself is a *solid body, or earth*, with air mixed into its smallest atoms, which is why it flows and liquefies, as experience teaches; for when the air contained in the water is withdrawn or constricted by cold, the aqueous parts immediately come together and become a solid body, *namely ice*: from which it follows that water is composed of *transparent earth* and air. *Oil*, however, consists of *air, water, and earth*, and is therefore a *composite* <note>original: "decompositum"; Becher uses this to mean a substance made of several layers of elements</note>.

### Subterranean Physics
->Page 212<-

<margin>No. 55.</margin> ...maintaining its nature and, so to speak, homogeneity. From which it follows that aqueous fluidity is nothing other than the interposition of air atoms; the truth of this definition is evident from practical operation <note>original: "enchirisi"; from the Greek for "handling" or manual manipulation</note>. For **Nitre** <term>saltpeter, a key ingredient in gunpowder and a focus of early chemistry</term> **(to say nothing of other salt-like substances)**, when treated in a retort with the fire closed off and distilled, is entirely resolved into water; so much so that a pound of nitre yields a pound of *spirit* if you proceed correctly. Certainly, no one would call *nitre* ice, or water coagulated in the manner of ice; rather, one must believe that its liquid state comes from elsewhere: namely, from the hot *air* that is mixed in. Similarly, **common Mercury** <term>quicksilver</term>, by the power of **fire alone** in a closed vessel, is totally converted into a clear and *moist* water that wets the hands, provided great heat is used during the preparation and nothing else is added. I do not mean to establish that *moist* liquidity proceeds from the external hot air itself, but rather I conclude that there are certain substances whose atoms take in air, and in this way are rendered fluid, like clear water. This is no different from what was said before, that metals take in "mercurifying" earth and are reduced to a *mercurial* flow. Indeed, the pneumatic experiments of **Mr. Boyle** <note>Robert Boyle (1627–1691), the famous Anglo-Irish chemist known for Boyle's Law</note> testify that the proportion of air contributes much to the relationship between *solvents* and the *substances to be dissolved*.

<margin>No. 56.</margin> However, exactly how, in what proportion, and into which substances air enters to liquefy them and make them moist, we can hardly reveal in this location—given the brevity of our current project—in a way that would satisfy the Reader in all things. For it is a long and obscure science, and as far as I know, hardly treated by anyone, or even touched upon in the slightest. It is certain that air can be changed by either heat or cold so that it no longer maintains its natural state, as we have observed in *thermoscopes* <term>early instruments for showing changes in temperature</term> and the melting of glass.

<margin>No. 57.</margin> By what reasoning, however, air is so excluded from the water of **crystal** and other substances that it can hardly be forced in even by the greatest power of *fire*, while on the contrary it acts so readily upon *salts* that it dissolves and changes them into *water* with little effort: this is difficult to explain. The reason cannot be attributed to heat or cold alone, since it is false to claim that *crystals* are generated from ice; after all, they are generated even in places where neither great nor continuous ice is observed. Meanwhile, it is certain that *crystals and stones are not resolved into moist water* even by the most intense heat. Therefore, the changeability of air must be attributed to the quality and internal structure of the substances; hence air dominates in some, while in others it is, as it were, exiled: as we see in the **diamond, crystal**, and other **stones**, which reject not only this second, aqueous flow, but also the third. **Helmontius** <note>Jean Baptiste van Helmont (1580–1644), a pioneer of pneumatic chemistry</note> indeed writes on page 409: *I know how to reduce rock and all stones into a pure salt weighing the same as its original rock or stone*; but that is not the same as resolving it into water by air alone, nor does it happen without the addition of several other things.

<margin>No. 58.</margin> **Sendivogius** <note>Michael Sendivogius (1566–1636), a famous Polish alchemist</note> says that one can, with little effort, prepare precious real stones that can so constitute *air* that it does not admit rarefaction; this is easy to say, but impossible to do. We must believe, therefore, that stones arise from water indeed, but water that is very *compact*; which consequently expels air when it is coagulated, nor does it easily receive the same in such great quantity. Even if air is taken in and thinned out, it cannot split apart the heavy and material compact atoms of the substance so as to penetrate them entirely and render them clear—that is, moist. For we are now speaking of a moist flow: for air, having taken to its aid...

We see this clearly in **aqua fortis** <term>literally "strong water," the historical name for nitric acid</term>, where a pound of **aqua fortis** dissolves almost an entire pound of silver. Just as in **mercurification** <term>the process of turning a substance into a mercury-like liquid</term>, by means of a "fluidizing" earth, entry was given to the air into the body of the metal (which was totally reduced into the liquidity of Mercury); so in this second "aqueous-moist flow," entry is granted to the air into the metal by means of water (or the earth that constitutes water). Consequently, the metal is dissolved and takes in the liquidity of the transparent,
<margin>No. 61.</margin> water-making earth, just as it had previously put on the liquidity of the **mercury-making earth**. And indeed, as we said in the preceding pages, once a metal is properly united to the mercury-making earth and made fluid—that is, reduced into the liquidity of **Mercury**—it can only be separated from such earth with great difficulty. Likewise, when a metal is sufficiently dissolved and thinned in a "menstruum" <term>a solvent</term> or aqueous solvent, it is again separated from it with the greatest difficulty—so much so that in liquid form, they even transcend the highest **alembics** <term>distillation apparatus</term> under the gentlest heat. They cannot be precipitated again **except by the help of the most highly rectified spirit of wine** <term>concentrated ethanol</term>; the spirit of wine fills the pores of the solvent, and the atoms of the metal fall away like a very light sponge, as we see in the process of **Polemann** <note>Joachim Polemann, a 17th-century chemist and follower of Van Helmont</note> **concerning the sulphur of the Philosophers**, in the solution of **Venus** <term>the alchemical name for copper</term> performed by **spirit of salt** <term>hydrochloric acid</term>. The industry of mortals has even reached the point where gold, the heaviest of all metals, can be attached to the most subtle and volatile
<margin>No. 62.</margin> spirit of wine, so that they evaporate, distill, and flame up together, and can no longer be precipitated in any way; since nothing more subtle than spirit of wine is found, nothing exists that can force it to precipitate. This, therefore, they call **potable gold** <note>original: "aurum potabile"; a legendary medicinal oil made from gold</note>; not so by its own nature, but by circumstance, yet possessing powers not to be despised. For since it can be precipitated neither by **acids** nor by **urinous substances** <term>alkaline substances like ammonia</term>, there is no doubt that in the human body, along with its own most subtle spirit of wine, it is raised to the heart and the blood. Here a question arises: since we have proven that metals, by means of such solvents, can be reduced in various ways into a **moist aqueous flow**, can they also take on the **mask of an oil**?
<margin>No. 64.</margin>
To this I answer in the affirmative; for there are various oils that dissolve metals and mix with them most intimately. There are also subjects that are entirely saline and aqueous (as we see in **oil of vitriol** <term>concentrated sulfuric acid</term>, **spirit of vinegar**, and other substances) which dissolve metals—especially **Iron (Mars), Lead (Saturn), orpiment** <note>a yellow arsenic mineral</note>, and others, whether they be "perfect" or "imperfect" minerals. Finally, after the solvent is drawn off, they appear under the mask of an oil, though they do not float upon water; the oil of **orpiment** is an exception, as it is similar to common oil in almost every respect. Such metallic oils, however, do not come from the metals or their inherent nature, but from the additives, which are sulfurous (participating much in the **fertile earth** <note>referring to *terra fecunda*, the second of Becher's three types of earth</note>, of which we made mention in section three, chapter three), even if they are masked under a saline form and thus deceive us. 

Nonetheless, metals brought to a true state of "oiliness" are not to be looked down upon; especially if they first reached the state of **Mercury**, and thus passed from that "first flow" into this "second flow," and were increased and animated in a double principle. But these things I say will scarcely reach—as the Philosopher says—men of **stiff necks** <note>a biblical idiom for the stubborn or prideful</note>. 
<margin>No. 65.</margin>
I say they will scarcely be understood, since many most excellent craftsmen have erred no less in this **oil-making** <note>original: "oleificatione"</note> than in the preceding **mercury-making**. 
<margin>No. 66.</margin>
Among these, the aforementioned **Polemann** <note>Joachim Polemann, a 17th-century chymist and follower of van Helmont</note> must be considered, in his treatise written *On the Sulfur of the Philosophers*. In the preparation of the **element of the fire of Venus** (or **Venereal sulfur**), he dissolves copper in a singular **spirit of sal ammoniac**, volatilizes it, precipitates it with **spirit of wine** <term>ethanol</term>, and the powder prepared in this way he calls **Crocus** <note>literally "saffron," referring here to a reddish-yellow powder</note>, which is to be extracted by a **subtle alkali**; namely, for the extraction of the sulfurous substance of Copper (Venus). 

Here two things must be noted in which the author leads himself and the reader into error. First, that the entire **preliminary preparation of Copper** is directed toward "mercury-making" rather than "sulfur-making"; for with little effort, a true running **Mercury** of the same can be produced from such a Crocus of Copper. Second, he proposes an extraction from such a Crocus by means of a certain subtle alkali. 
<margin>No. 67.</margin>
On this point, it must be known that by no art or "Mars" <note>a play on words meaning "by no force"</note>—as we have often proven and said—can even the smallest solution of the **essential** parts be made from metals, because of their homogeneous and most powerful mixture. For whatever is extracted, whether by **color** or in any other way and under whatever mask, can be reduced back into the original, whole, homogeneous body. 
<margin>No. 68.</margin>
Therefore, metals (whose principles cannot be pulled apart) can receive into their mixture and constitution principles that are homogeneous to them; according to the quality and quantity of these, they are altered in their essential constitution <note>original: "crasi"</note>, so that they can be said to be truly changed. For when metals receive **mercurifying earth** into themselves, they become **Mercury**—namely, a new compound. And when they receive **alkaline earth** or **glass** into themselves, they again become another compound, which takes its name from the additive as the more powerful part. This is not because some "extraction" of the metal occurs, or a separation of parts; for the whole metal can be reduced to its original form from **glass, sulfur, and Mercury**, and the whole metal can be converted into **Mercury, sulfur, and salt** (or glass). Therefore, those who believe that only some part of a metal is mercurial and must be extracted from the rest are mistaken; just as they defend...

### Book 1. Section V. Chapter III.

<margin>No. 69.</margin>
...they present the trinity of decomposed Paracelsian principles <note>the *Tria Prima*: Sulfur, Mercury, and Salt, which Paracelsus believed were the building blocks of all matter</note>: so also do those err who maintain that something sulfurous can be extracted from metals which is not already entirely present, or which does not vary except by the addition of the solvent. For if the solvent is mercurial, the dissolved substance becomes mercurial; if it is sulfurous, the dissolved substance likewise appears sulfurous; if saline, it turns out saline. Thus, when Polemann <note>Joachim Polemann, a 17th-century chymist and follower of van Helmont</note> says that the "Sulfur of Venus" <note>Venus is the alchemical name for Copper</note> must be extracted, it is the same as if he said that a sulfurous solvent—or one containing the **first essence of sulfur**—must be added to the dissolved **Saffron of Venus** <term>crocus Veneris; a reddish copper oxide produced by calcination</term>, so that the dissolved metal appears in a sulfurous form, just as the preceding example appeared in a mercurial form.

<margin>No. 70.</margin>
Therefore, nothing will remain of the substance to be dissolved if the quantity of the solvent is sufficient; because the whole will be converted into a sulfurous substance, by the same logic that an entire metal becomes **Mercury** if a sufficient "mercurifying earth" is present.

<margin>No. 71.</margin>
I cannot sufficiently wonder at Ludovicus de Comitibus <note>Luigi de' Conti, an Italian physician and alchemist</note>, who says in his short works, in the *Practical Manual Dispute*, pages 75 and 76: *Copper turned into vitriol is divided into two substances; one of which is oily or sulfurous, which is the Tincture of Venus, the other is the body of Venus turned to whiteness, which will never grow green again.* He repeats the same in his *Metallurgy* on page 188 and following: *The coloring part of copper is judged to be superficial, not contained in the depths, coming from a wonderful hidden liquor which has plucked away all the liveliness from the vitriol of copper; the residue of this is changed into a white metal, never to be revived thereafter, which will be none of the seven metals, but a new one, rising from the corruption of the copper.* By these words, the author clearly testifies that he believes in the solution and separation of **parts**; which we pronounce to be impossible.

<margin>No. 72.</margin>
For that "extracted greenness" which he imagines—or the "Oil of Venus" as he calls it in the previous citation—can be reduced back into copper with very little effort. Furthermore, the residual metal, which he calls white, received its whiteness from the nature of the solvent. Since this solvent is not as volatile as arsenic, it does not evaporate, but clings to the copper and prevents it from turning green. The **dead earth of tartar** <note>the residue left after the combustion of cream of tartar, primarily potassium carbonate</note> impresses almost this same quality upon gold when melted with it. Indeed, there are many solvents, even very volatile ones, which precipitate white calxes <note>powdery metallic oxides</note> when they dissolve metals; these calxes then mix with the metals, making them white, but they are driven off by the **cupel** <term>a shallow, porous ceramic tray used in refining to separate precious metals from base metals</term>, whereupon the original color returns. From this come infinite deceptions and "sophistications" in the solutions of gold, where the solvents acquire a color and precipitate white dross, so that the gold becomes white upon reduction; thus it is judged to be extracted and deprived of its sulfur. But truly, when it is treated in the fire, the color returns as the tinting calx evaporates. Let such "white copper" be cemented with common sulfur and reduced again, and the original color will return.

<margin>No. 73.</margin>
For it is a most certain axiom: *Metals, after their first mixture in the mines, can be reduced into their diverse principles with the same impossibility that a man, after birth, can be reduced to sperm, or a tree, after growth, can be reduced into a nut or a seed.* Therefore, whatever can naturally happen to metals consists in this one thing: that **homogeneous principles** can be essentially added to them; not unlike how moisture is added to a grain of wheat, whereby it is softened and rots. Thus the "three" can be added to metals, which alter them fundamentally; we have spoken of "mercurification" previously, and in this place we deal with "sulfurization" or "oleification" <note>the process of making something oily</note>. For just as...

He uses a biological analogy to state that once a metal is formed, it cannot be reverted to its "seeds" or "first principles."</summary>

# Subterranean Physics

<header>Subterranean Physics</header>

...is strong water <note>original: "aqua forti"; nitric acid</note>, but concerning any solvent whatsoever: urinous, acidic, saline, or oily. Here a question arises: since we have proved that metals, by means of such solvents, can be reduced in various ways into a *watery flow* that wets things, might they also take on the **mask of an oil**? 

<margin>No. 64.</margin>
To which I respond in the affirmative; since various oils exist which dissolve metals and mix with them most closely. Even subjects that are entirely saline and watery (as we see in *oil of vitriol* <note>sulfuric acid</note>, *spirit of vinegar* <note>acetic acid</note>, and other substances) dissolve metals—especially *Mars* <note>Iron</note>, *Saturn* <note>Lead</note>, *orpiment* <note>auripigmentum; an arsenic sulfide mineral</note>, and other minerals, whether perfect or imperfect. And finally, in the process of abstraction, they are seen under the **mask of an oil**, though it is not an oil that floats on water; except for the *oil of orpiment*, which is similar to common oil in almost every way. Such metallic oils, however, do not come from the metals or their nature, but from the additives, which are sulfurous (participating much in the "fertile earth" <note>terra fecunda; one of Becher's three primary "earths" which provides the principle of inflammability or sulfur</note>, which we mentioned in section three, chapter three), even though they are masked under a saline form and deceive us. 

<margin>No. 65.</margin>
Nevertheless, metals reduced to a true state of **oiliness** are not to be despised; especially if they first reached the state of **Mercury**, and thus passed from that "first flow" into this second one, and were increased and animated in a double principle. But these things I say will hardly reach men of "stiff necks" <note>an idiom for the stubborn or proud</note>, as the Philosopher says. I say they will hardly be understood, since many most illustrious craftsmen have erred *no less in this "oil-making" than in the preceding "mercury-making"* <note>mercurificatione</note>.

<margin>No. 66.</margin>
Among whom the aforementioned *Polemann* <note>Joachim Polemann, a 17th-century chemist and follower of van Helmont</note>, in his treatise written *On the Sulfur of the Philosophers*, must be reckoned. In the preparation of the *element of the fire of Venus* <note>Venus is the alchemical name for Copper</note>, or *Venereal sulfur*, he dissolves copper in a unique *spirit of sal ammoniac* <note>ammonium chloride</note>, volatilizes it, precipitates it with *spirit of wine* <note>ethanol</note>, and calls the powder thus prepared **saffron** <term>crocus; a term for a fine metal oxide powder, usually reddish</term>, which is to be extracted by a *subtle alkali*; namely, for the extraction of the *sulfurous substance of Venus*. Here two things must be noted, in which the author leads himself and the reader into error: first, that the entire *preliminary preparation of Venus* is directed toward **mercury-making** rather than **sulfur-making**. 

<margin>No. 67.</margin>
For with little effort, from such a *Saffron of Venus*, its true running **Mercury** can be produced. Second, he proposes an extraction from such saffron by means of a certain subtle **alkali**. Here it must be known that by no art or "Mars" <note>here meaning "force" or "labor," playing on the name of the metal iron</note>, as we have often proved and said, can even the smallest solution of the *essential* parts be made from metals, because of their homogeneous and very strong mixture. 

<margin>No. 68.</margin>
For whatever is extracted, *whether in color or in any way, and under whatever mask, can be reduced back into the original, whole, homogeneous body*. Therefore, metals (whose *principles* cannot be dissolved) can receive principles homogeneous to themselves into their mixture and constitution. According to the quality and quantity of these added principles, the metals are altered in their essential temperament <note>crasi; a Greek-derived term for the specific "blend" of qualities in a substance</note>, so that they can truly be said to have **been changed**. For when metals receive **mercurifying earth** <note>terra mercurialis; the principle of fluidity and density</note> into themselves, they become **Mercury**, namely, a new compound; and when they receive the earth of **alkali** or **glass** into themselves, they again become another compound, which takes its name from the additive as the more powerful part. Not that some extraction of the metal occurs, or a *separation of parts*; for the *whole metal, from glass, sulfur, and Mercury*, can be reduced to its original form: and the *entire metal can be converted into Mercury, sulfur, and salt (or glass)*. Therefore, those stumble who believe that only some part of the metal is *mercurial* and must be extracted from the rest; so that they defend...

# Book 1, Section V, Chapter III.

<margin>No. 69.</margin>
They present a trinity of decomposed **Paracelsian** <term>Paracelsicorum; followers of the Swiss physician Paracelsus who believed all matter was composed of Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury</term> principles: thus, those people are in error who maintain that something sulfurous can be extracted from metals. In truth, this "sulfur" does not exist within the metal in that form, nor does it change except by the addition of the solvent. For if the solvent is mercurial, the dissolved substance becomes mercurial; if it is sulfurous, the dissolved substance also appears sulfurous; if it is saline, it turns out saline when dissolved. Therefore, when **Polemann** <note>Joachim Polemann, a 17th-century alchemical writer</note> says that the **sulfur of Venus** <term>sulphur Veneris; "Venus" is the alchemical name for copper</term> must be extracted, it is the same as if he said that a sulfurous solvent—or one containing the "prime essence" of sulfur—must be added to the dissolved **saffron of Venus** <term>croco Veneris; a red or orange oxide of copper</term>, so that the dissolved metal appears in a sulfurous form. This is no different than how the previous example appeared in a mercurial form.

<margin>No. 70.</margin>
Nothing, therefore, will remain of the substance to be dissolved if the quantity of the solvent is sufficient; because the whole will be converted into a sulfurous substance, by the same logic that the entire metal becomes **Mercury** if a sufficient "mercurifying earth" is present.

<margin>No. 71.</margin>
I cannot wonder enough, therefore, at **Ludovicus de Comitibus** <note>Ludovico de' Conti, an Italian alchemist and physician</note>, who says in his short works (*On Practical Manual Disputation*, pages 75 and 76): *Venus <note>copper</note> turned into vitriol <note>metallic sulfate</note> is divided into two substances; one of which is oily or sulfurous, which is the tincture <note>color-giving essence</note> of Venus; the other is the body of Venus turned into whiteness, which will never grow green again.* He repeats the same in his *Metallurgy* on pages 188 and following: *The coloring part of copper is judged to be superficial, not contained in its depths, arising from a hidden, admirable liquor which plucks away all greenness from the vitriol of copper; the residue is changed into a white metal, never turning green thereafter, which is none of the seven known metals, but a new one rising from the corruption of copper.* By these words, the author clearly testifies that he supports the solution and separation of *parts*; a feat which we pronounce to be impossible.

<margin>No. 72.</margin>
For the extracted "greenness" which he imagines—or the **oil of Venus** as he calls it in the preceding citation—can be reduced back into copper with very little effort. Furthermore, the residual metal, which he calls white, received its whiteness from the nature of the solvent. Since this solvent is not as volatile as **arsenic**, it does not evaporate but clings to the copper and prevents it from turning green. The **dead earth of tartar** <note>potassium carbonate residue</note>, when melted with gold, imprints almost this same quality upon it. Indeed, there are many solvents, even very volatile ones, which precipitate white powders <note>original: "calces"</note> when they dissolve things; these powders then mix with the metals, causing them to whiten. However, they are driven off by the **cupel** <term>capellam; a porous ceramic bowl used in high-heat refining to separate noble metals from base metals</term>, whereupon the original color returns. From this come infinite deceptions and sophistications in the solutions of gold, where the solvents acquire a color and precipitate white dregs, so that the gold becomes white upon reduction; thus it is judged to be extracted and deprived of its sulfur. But truly, when it is treated in the fire, the color returns as the tinting powder evaporates. Let such "white Venus" be cemented with common sulfur and reduced again, and the original color will return.

<margin>No. 73.</margin>
For it is a most certain axiom: *metals cannot be reduced back into their diverse principles after their first mixing in the ores, by the same impossibility that a man, after birth, cannot be reduced to sperm, or a tree, after growth, be reduced to a nut or a seed.* Therefore, whatever can happen naturally to metals consists solely in this: that homogeneous principles can be essentially added to them. This is no different than how moisture is added to a grain of wheat, by which it is softened and rots. Thus, three things can be added to metals which alter them fundamentally; we have spoken of **mercurification** <note>turning to mercury</note> in the preceding pages, and in this place we treat **sulphurification** or **oleification** <note>turning to oil</note>. For just as...

# Underground Physics
### Book 1, Section V, Chapter III.

<margin>N. 75.</margin> ...for while the prior operation happens through *mercurifying* <note>original: "mercurificantem"</note> earth, so this second one happens through the first essence of sulfur, which is so closely related to metals that nothing is more similar, as we also see in *common sulfur*. Therefore, such a *sulfurous essence* must be added to metals, and then 
<margin>N. 76.</margin> they will be soaked in and strengthened by their *own principle*, so that they can no longer appear in their *former shape*, and even become irreducible. We see this in gold: when it is reduced to an "oil" by means of this sulfurous essence, it cannot be turned back into a *physical body* by any force, except through the *form of a tincture* <term>tincturae; in alchemy, a substance capable of transforming or "dyeing" other materials</term>. **Basil Valentine** <note>Basilius Valentinus; a legendary 15th-century alchemist and Benedictine monk</note> emphasizes this operation so strongly that he testifies in express words, and many times, that *gold cannot transform unless it is itself transformed, and fed with its own blood*. This must be understood entirely as referring to the first essence, or the *earth of sulfur*. For that is the *principle of metals*, which I discussed sufficiently in the third section, third chapter.

<margin>N. 77.</margin> When metals are saturated with this principle, they are no longer common metals, but *transformative and animated*. But whoever he may be—whether an impostor, as some claim, or a Philosopher—regarding **Monte-Snyder** <note>Johann de Monte-Snyder, a 17th-century writer on the "Universal Medicine"</note>, if I consider his theory and his practical methods in his booklet on potable gold, he certainly satisfies me more than **Polemann**, **de Comitibus**, **Glauber**, and all the others. It may be, however, that he is like Caiaphas <note>A biblical reference to the High Priest who unknowingly prophesied the truth; the author suggests Monte-Snyder might write truths he does not fully understand</note>, divining and writing true things that he himself does not comprehend. What he wrote is good, and we hope the writer himself is also good; we care as little about the private lives of writers as we do about preachers, provided that what they write and preach is sound.

<margin>N. 78.</margin> Now we shall move our raft forward and consider whether, according to Polemann’s mind, such a subtle *sulfurous* essence is found in *subtilized Alkali*, as the author calls it? What he means by *volatile alkali* is obscure. If we look at his argument, he stubbornly defends the idea that fixed alkali consists of fixed sulfur. We refuted this before your very eyes in the preceding section on fermentation, in the paragraph on **salt of tartar** <term>sale tartari; potassium carbonate, often derived from wine lees</term>. For a *stony and glass-like* earth is the only foundation in every alkali; and this earth is not the essence of *sulfur* (the second principle), but the *first principle* of metals, discussed in section three, chapter three. But you will say that **Polemann** requires a *volatilized alkali*. To this I respond: volatilization does not change the substance of a thing so that saline things become sulfurous; it only lifts and *thins* <note>original: "rarefacit"</note> them so they dissolve more quickly. Furthermore, that he presents the volatilization of *alkali* as such a great secret is ridiculous rather than a mystery, since—as shown in Book Two, in the chapter on the anatomy of Alkali Salt—any corrosive spirit can become a volatile alkali.

<margin>N. 79.</margin> The truth of this is clear from the following: if you dissolve *common sublimate* <term>mercuric chloride</term> *in common water and precipitate it with oil of tartar* <term>a concentrated solution of potassium carbonate</term>, you will instantly have a *red precipitate*. Dry this, and heat it under a clay dish until all the **Mercury** <note>original: "Mercurius"</note> departs: there will remain an insoluble **calx** <term>a powdery metallic oxide remaining after heating</term>, very dry, very white, and very fixed. Now, dissolve common Mercury in **aqua fortis** <term>nitric acid</term>, and precipitate it by drawing off the liquid: heat it in the same way, and you will receive the same calx. You certainly cannot attribute this residue to the *Mercury* for reasons obvious to anyone; therefore, it must be attributed to the solvent. Now, is it not a wonder that such a fixed *calx* lies hidden in such a *volatile water*? It is no wonder, then, if the substance of salt of tartar, which is such a calx, can be lifted and volatilized. Therefore, its volatilization is not so secret, nor is it an effect of great importance.

# Underground Physics
## Book I, Section V, Chapter III.

...he provides a manual discussion on the **volatilization of tartar** <term>volatilisatio tartari; the process of turning solid potassium carbonate into a vaporous or "spirit" form</term>, which he himself never tested in practice. As he sets it up, it cannot succeed according to the course of nature, since he orders the precipitation and separation of the **earth of the salt of tartar**, which is the very substance one is working to volatilize. The author's words on page 71 of the cited book are these:

<margin>N. 81.</margin>
*Therefore, a saline body can by no means be reduced to a volatile form by the addition of water; it will therefore be necessary to proceed by another method, namely, that some of the earth itself be taken away, so that the remainder may be rendered more moist or watery, and acquire the nature of a mercurial property. This is indeed permitted to art, for art can destroy most things subject to nature, though it cannot construct them. This transmutation, therefore, is a certain destruction performed by art through the violence of fire as an instrument. By the same token, given the opportunity of another suitable body, the internal seminal spirit—which was violently led away from the saline body into a mercurial mixture—easily reassumes from a foreign body the corporeality it had previously lost from its own. Thus, by dissolving many simple things, it is itself re-coagulated.* Up to here are the author's words. Wherein the reader will notice that what I noted is true: namely, that by the abstraction of the earth, that which ought to be volatilized is removed. Hence **Polemann** <note>Joachim Polemann, a 17th-century chemist known for his work on the "Novum Lumen Medicum"</note> himself rejects this method and says it is a *spirit weakened by having undergone a reaction*.

<margin>N. 82.</margin>
But as for why he defends [De Comitibus] the idea that nothing watery can be added to a saline body, while on the contrary much earth must be removed, the reason is what he subjoins—or rather, what he puts forward at length on page 70 in these words:

<margin>N. 83.</margin>
*For it is not granted to art that anything can be added to the primordial constituents by means of fire, so that one permanent thing is made with them; otherwise, new mixtures and species could be produced by art through fire, which is known by experiment and reason to be impossible.* Up to here the author. Since he denies such mixtures to fire, he will even more easily deny them to water, as it is a weaker element. But both claims, by the testimony of common experience, are most false. For it is known even to the "bleary-eyed and barbers" <note>original: "lippis & tonsoribus"; a Latin idiom meaning "everyone knows it"</note> that **glass**—the strongest and most indestructible of all mixtures—is produced by fire. That water can be added to primordial constituents, such that it cannot be driven out from the mixture again, is shown by the following experiment, among others: Pour **spirit of salt** <term>spiritus salis; hydrochloric acid</term> into **oil of tartar** <term>oleum tartari; a concentrated solution of potassium carbonate</term> until it no longer hisses. Certain earthy dregs will be precipitated (indeed, the **lime** <note>calx</note> we have discussed until now) like a white earth; separate this. Thicken the remainder until it crystallizes; you will find elegant, oblong, angular crystals like true **nitre** <note>potassium nitrate, though here likely referring to the shape of the resulting potassium chloride</note>, which you should separate from the rest and dry. These crystals, born from the *spirit of salt* and *oil of tartar*, you will not be able to drive out of the mixture by any fire, any precipitant, nor any force or power; for they are so fixed in the fire that they are in no way dissolved or separated into parts. It is therefore entirely possible for things to be added to the primordial constituents of bodies which then enter into their mixture; otherwise, no **mercurification**, no **sulfurification**, or **oilification of metals** <note>original: "mercurificatio, sulphurificatio, aut oleificatio metallorum"; alchemical processes for breaking metals down into their primary "principles"</note> would be possible.

<margin>N. 84.</margin>
Furthermore, the fact that even if a volatile alkali is obtained, the effect desired by **Polemann** does not follow—indeed, as I hear, it did not succeed for the author himself in England, despite having all requirements and being given the best promises—the reason is ready at hand: because in alkali, whether fixed or volatile, only the **first earth** (of which I spoke in Section Three, Chapter Three) is found,

The words of the author <note>referring to the author of the cited book, likely Monte-Snyder or a similar contemporary</note> on page 71 of the cited book are these: 
<margin>N. 81.</margin> *Therefore, a saline body can by no means be reduced into a volatile form through the addition of water; one must therefore proceed by another method, namely, that some earth be taken away from it, so that the remainder is made more moist or watery, and acquires the nature of a mercurial property. This is indeed permitted to art, for nature itself can at least destroy most subjects, but not construct them; this transmutation, therefore, is a certain destruction achieved by art through the violence of fire as an instrument. By this means, given the opportunity of another suitable body, the internal seminal spirit—which has been violently drawn out from a saline body into a mercurial mixture—easily resumes the lost corporeality from an external source, which it had previously lost from its own; wherefore, by dissolving many simples, it is itself recoagulated.* <note>original Latin: "Salinosum ergo corpus per aquae additionem... ipse recoagulatur;"</note>

Thus far the words of the author. Here the reader will notice that what I have noted is true: namely, that by the removal of the earth, that very thing which ought to be volatilized is taken away. Hence **Polemann** <note>Joachim Polemann, a 17th-century alchemist and follower of van Helmont</note> himself rejects this 
<margin>N. 82.</margin> method, saying that the spirit is weakened because it has undergone a reaction. But why does **De Comitibus** <note>likely referring to an alchemical writer of the period</note> defend the idea that nothing watery can be added to a saline body, but on the contrary, much earth must be removed? The reason is what he adds—or rather, what he sets forth at length on page 70 in these words: 
<margin>N. 83.</margin> *For it is not granted to art that anything can be added to the primordial constituents <term>the fundamental building blocks of matter</term> through fire, so that it might be permanently made one with them; otherwise, mixtures and species could be produced anew by art through fire, which is known by experiment and reason to be impossible.* <note>original Latin: "Non enim arti conceditur... ratione impossibile esse;"</note>

Thus far the author. Since he denies such mixtures to fire, he will even more easily deny them to water, as it is a weaker element. But both claims, by the witness of common experience, are utterly false. For it is known to "the bleary-eyed and the barbers" <note>original: "lippis et tonsoribus"; a Latin idiom meaning "everyone knows" or "it is common knowledge"</note> that **glass**—the strongest and most indestructible of all mixtures—is produced by fire. Furthermore, the following experiment teaches that water can indeed be added to primordial constituents so that it can never again be removed from the mixture. Pour **spirit of salt** <term>hydrochloric acid</term> into **oil of tartar** <term>a concentrated solution of potassium carbonate</term> until it no longer hisses. Certain earthy dregs will precipitate (indeed, the lime <note>calx</note> of which we have treated until now) like a white earth; separate this. Thicken the remaining liquid until it crystallizes, and you will find elegant, oblong, angular crystals like true nitre <note>saltpeter</note>; separate and dry these. These crystals, born from the spirit of salt and oil of tartar, you will be able to remove from the mixture by no fire, no precipitating agent—in short, by no force or power. For they are so fixed in the fire that they are in no way dissolved or separated into parts. 

It is therefore entirely possible that certain things can be added to the primordial constituents of bodies which then enter into their mixture. Otherwise, no **mercurification** <term>transformation into a metallic liquid or "mercury"</term>, no **sulphurification**, or **oleification** <term>transformation into an oil</term> of metals would be possible. Furthermore, although one may possess a **volatile alkali**, the effect that Polemann desires does not follow. Indeed, I hear that the author himself in England—despite having all the requirements and being given the best promises—did not succeed. 
<margin>N. 84.</margin> The reason is ready at hand: since in an alkali, whether fixed or volatile, *only the first earth is found* (concerning which, see Section Three, Chapter Three)...

For that essence exists as the principle of metals, concerning which I have written sufficiently in section three, chapter three.

<margin>N. 77.</margin> Since, therefore, metals exceed in this principle, they are no longer common metals, but are *tinging and animated*. But whoever he may be—whether an impostor, as some wish, or a Philosopher—*Monte-Snyder* <note>Johannes de Monte-Snyder, a 17th-century alchemist known for his "Treatise on the Universal Medicine"</note>, if you look at his theory and practice in his booklet on potable gold <note>original: "auro potabili"</note>, he certainly satisfies me more than *Polemann*, *de Comitibus*, *Glauber*, and all the others. Yet it may be that he is like Caiaphas <note>a biblical reference to the High Priest who unknowingly prophesied correctly; Becher suggests Snyder might speak truth without understanding it</note>, divining and writing truths which he himself does not understand. What he has written is good; we hope the writer himself is also of such quality; and we care as little for the lives of writers as we do for those of preachers, provided that what they write and what they preach is good.

For a *stony and glass-making* earth is the sole foundation in every alkali; and this earth is not the essence of *sulfur* (acting as the second principle), but is the *first principle* of metals, as discussed in section three, chapter three. But you will say, *Polemann desires a volatilized alkali;* to which I respond that volatilization does not change the substance of a thing, turning saline things into sulfurous ones: it only elevates and thins them so that they dissolve more quickly.

<margin>N. 79.</margin> Furthermore, that he puts forward the *volatilization of alkali* as such a great secret is more ridiculous than it is an arcane mystery, since—as shown in the second book, in the chapter on the anatomy of Alkali salt—any corrosive spirit is a volatile alkali. The truth of this matter is clear from this: *if you dissolve common sublimate in common water and precipitate it with oil of tartar <term>a concentrated solution of potassium carbonate</term>, you will instantly have a red precipitate; dry this, and heat it in an earthenware dish until it glows, so that all the Mercury departs. An insoluble, very dry, very white, and very fixed calx <term>a powdery metallic residue</term> will remain. Now dissolve common Mercury in aqua fortis <term>nitric acid</term> and precipitate it by drawing off the liquid: heat it in the same way, and you will receive the same calx.* Surely you cannot attribute this calx to the *Mercury*, for reasons obvious to anyone; it must therefore be attributed to the solvent. But is it not strange that in such *volatile water, such a fixed calx lies hidden?* It will not be strange, then, if the substance of the salt of tartar, which is such a calx, can be elevated and volatilized. Therefore, its volatilization is not so secret, nor is it an effect of great importance. From this, liquid metals occupy **more space** than solids; for they swell with rarefied fiery particles; hence, when the pores are thickened by cold, the small bodies are constricted, and pass into a continuous and solid substance, occupying **less space**—commonly called **shrinking** <note>original: "Schwinden"; a German term used here to describe the contraction of metal as it cools</note>. <margin>N. 88.</margin>

As we see, if metals are dissolved in **corrosive solvents** <note>original: "menstruis corrosivis"</note>, and paper is soaked in the solution and dried, then committed to flames; the metals immediately tinge the flames with a pleasant color and simultaneously vanish into the air, though they be heavy and fixed.

We speak in this place of *actual* fire, not potential <note>Actual fire is the active state of flaming, while potential fire refers to the heat or energy stored within a substance before it is ignited</note>. Although fire consists of various *subjects* <note>original: "subjectis"; here meaning the source material or fuel that sustains the fire</note>; such as *the sun, earth, stones, wood*, burning waters <note>referring to flammable spirits or alcohols</note>, oils, sulfurs, and various fats, suet, and grease; and one fire is drawn from all of them according to external appearance: nevertheless in reality, in effect, <margin>N. 93.</margin> according to the variety of the *subject* from which it consists, it is different: *of another virtue and operation, not only according to quantity, or according to remission and intensity, but according to quality and mode of application.* For although in a water bath, ashes, sand, and open fire, one degree of heat is maintained, one *subject* is placed in, and it is digested for a similar time; yet according to the different application of fire, different effects will follow. For those things placed in a water bath become moist; in sand they are dried, and so with others. Indeed some *subjects* seek the sand and reject the water bath; some, though very volatile, wish to be distilled from a water bath, and in no way can be distilled from sand, as among others *Polemann, in his treatise on the sulfur of the Philosophers, page 53*, testifies, whose words we will set down here:

> *Take then the spirit of wine <note>ethanol</note>, into which you have thrown sublimated sal ammoniac <note>original: "sal armeniacum"; ammonium chloride</note> mixed with golden flowers <note>likely ferric chloride, used in alchemical preparations</note>, decant it, then draw it off from a water bath; and you will note that you do this from a water bath, for it is driven neither from ashes nor from sand, nor does it pass through the distilling head <note>original: "alembicum"</note> if pushed by those, which consider, etc.*

Thus far the author. It is therefore evident that there are different qualities in fire, according to the *subject* from which it consists and the medium by which it is applied; and it is known even to the "blind and the barbers" <note>a Latin idiom meaning "everyone knows this"</note> that fir-wood flames are of another nature than oak ones: which is observed in the refining of metals, and in the *reverberatory* fire <note>a furnace that reflects heat onto the material from the roof</note>, as well as by smiths using *mineral coal* <note>original: "lithanthracibus"</note> and various charcoals. For as we shall demonstrate later in the discourse *on the effect of fire*, when *subjects* are treated with fire, they begin to take in and fix some part of the fiery atoms. It will therefore follow that, according to the variety of the nature of the fiery *subject*, such atoms also vary; and in the bodies to which they are united, they cause various and diverse effects. Hence in the *Philosophical* work <note>referring to alchemy</note>, <margin>N. 94.</margin> not so much the knowledge of materials as the knowledge of the *subject of the fire to be administered* is required; without which all labor is superfluous. For unless you know the matter from which the Philosophers prepare their fire, which they apply to the work, you will achieve nothing, even if you have the materials to be digested perfectly prepared; for fire, as it passes with its atoms into the matter or receptacle or matrix in which it is fixed, must necessarily destroy the matter or fill it with incongruous atoms, if it consists of an incongruous *subject* from which it draws its nourishment. Therefore, the Philosophical matter is not inappropriately called the *Salamander* <note>a mythical creature believed to live in and eat fire</note>, which is nourished by fire; <margin>N. 95.</margin> but not *common* fire, except as to external form. *For the fire of the Philosophers, because of the subtle subject* from which it is prepared, *is purer and more penetrating than any fire*, not to say the Sun itself. For the rays of the Sun, if they are reduced into a body, vanish into dust. Nor do I delay over whether, according to the Peripatetics <note>followers of Aristotle</note>, the bare word "fire" in the abstract, or the rays and accompanying atoms (which nevertheless in reality alone constitute fire or heat) generate this new product; let it suffice that corpuscles of this kind, the subtlest, penetrating glass and all bodies, are not Aristotelian Chimeras but real entities, palpable...

No fraud could underlie this operation, for nothing was contained in the vessels before they were arranged; it also had to be carried out in the warmer season of the year so that the effect itself would follow. Both of these, as far as external form is concerned, are analogous to common fire in all respects, though intrinsically purer and more penetrating, because they consist of a purer and more spiritual subject: *for according to the substance of the fire, its effect will vary—namely, the corpuscles that evaporate from it and adhere to other bodies.* And so much for the subject of fire, from which fire itself consists as a liquefying cause. ### Book I, Section V, Chapter III.

It must therefore be noted that **Bernard** <note>likely referring to Bernard of Trevisan, a famous 15th-century alchemist</note>, in the manner of the **Peripatetics** <note>original: "Peripateticorum"; followers of Aristotle's philosophy who focused on abstract qualities like "hot" and "cold" rather than physical particles</note>, speaks of fire in the abstract and not of the atoms that accompany fire. For Bernard himself, in another place which he also cites from **Natalis Conti** <note>original: "de Comitibus"; a 16th-century mythologist and scholar</note>, confesses that internal fire is excited by external fire. But how shall this be done without the communication of particles or corpuscles? For there is no "action at a distance" without the medium being affected, and the imaginary actions and qualities of the Peripatetics fail at this point—this point, I say, where there is a need for practice and one is not playing with empty terms. Therefore, let those who delight in terms read those who have written about light, namely **Vossius** and **Kircher** <note>Gerard Vossius and Athanasius Kircher were famous 17th-century scholars known for their massive theoretical works</note>; but let those who seek the reality of things read **Artephius**, **Empedocles**, and others.

Indeed, there is a famous saying of **Empedocles**: *we can assist nature with fire, for besides this we have no other help.*
<margin>N. 99.</margin>
That is to say, for the purpose of thinning, resolving, penetrating, and altering things, there is no help besides heat. And certainly, if we consider what wonderful transformations solar heat alone accomplishes in animals, plants, and minerals, I scarcely believe a prudent man could doubt anything regarding the necessity and cooperation of heat in the alteration of all things—unless he is someone who willfully wishes to see spots on the bright Sun. 

To say that all these mutations proceed from heat, and yet that heat is not communicated to the things heated except through "excitation," is foolish. For no one—except perhaps a foolish Peripatetic—can explain with empty words what the "excitation" of internal fire by external fire consists of, if he does not admit the meeting and union of the external or internal fire through physical particles. But they may play with words, on which they consume their whole lives and write entire books; meanwhile, by elegantly applying empty words to real operations, they incur public censure. This is like a certain recent author in his *Mathematical Lexicon*, who says that **pearls** <note>original: "uniones"</note>
<margin>N. 100.</margin>
are not dissolved in **strong water** <term>strong water: "aqua fortis" or nitric acid</term>, but rather in vinegar. It is certain that pearls are dissolved in both vinegar and strong water, and it is certain that the author had experience of neither. But just as readers who are "jubilant"—or rather "clouded"—and itching for such public writing are bound to believe any impostor due to their own lack of practice, so it is necessary for such authors to write false things as if they were true.

It would therefore be desirable that they write about theoretical terms, whose emptiness hardly anyone will notice in practice, and that they stay away from practical matters 
<margin>N. 101.</margin>
of which they are ignorant. For practical matters belong to practitioners, and theoretical matters to theorists; therefore, let them not "put their sickle into another man's harvest" <note>a Latin idiom meaning to meddle in someone else's business</note>. 

I recall a certain monk, Father G., a man otherwise (it seemed to him) not a little experienced in the world (for he was at Rome, where he believed all arts were taught in excellence). This man, I say, promised me a certain great secret: namely, of making **strong water** or caustic water in a pig’s or ox’s bladder by the method of **deliquescence** <term>deliquescence: the process by which a substance absorbs moisture from the atmosphere until it dissolves in the absorbed water and forms a solution</term>, which he himself had discovered. He claimed that if the ingredients usually used for common strong water were placed in a bladder, and the bladder were closed up and lowered into a cellar or a well, then these substances would dissolve and be changed into a true, very strong water. 

Do you see the man's vain speculation, so contrary to all practice? For even assuming that it were strong water (which is just as impossible as saying that a Peripatetic could become a Father Provincial of his order), the author of this invention should have been mindful of his lie—namely, that the acid would corrode the bladder as its container. It is a total paradox that strong water could be contained in a bladder, let alone prepared in one, while that bladder remained...

As if **Moses** could grant authority to **Aristotle**, or Aristotle to **Hermes** <note>referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy</note>.

<margin>No. 102.</margin>
But let us return to the matter at hand, and consider the second point of our proposal concerning the *matter* that causes liquefaction; namely, the **cause of fire, or ignification** <note>the process of turning into fire</note>. (The preceding point will be more fully completed in the following sections). Regarding the cause of light or ignification, we have stated in our discourse on **fermentation** <note>the author views fire as a type of rapid chemical fermentation</note> that it is a **rarefaction** <note>the process of a substance becoming less dense or more "thin"</note> arising through ignition. This ignition acts like a fermenting agent that thins the substance out. How it happens that once a single ignition is made, the whole thing then continually follows and blazes, will not be so difficult to explain if we properly consider fermentation—and the fact that the burning proceeds in the manner of a continuous stream of smoke. Just as if the **tap** <note>original: "epistomium"</note> of a barrel is opened, all the liquid flows out unless hindered; so, once a single ignition is made, a continuous dissolution occurs. The flammable material is thinned and resolved from point to point, as we sufficiently demonstrated in the preceding section on fermentation and combustion. From this it is clearly evident that nothing can burn which is not highly capable of being thinned; and everything that burns must rarefy and be resolved into **atoms** <note>tiny, indivisible particles</note> which can never again be compressed into their original density. It is no different than **must** <note>unfermented grape juice</note> which, once fermented and thinned, cannot be turned back into must. Therefore, those who dream of **perpetual light** <note>original: "lumen perpetuum"; a legendary lamp that burns forever without consuming fuel</note> are deservedly confounded when they presume to produce it from gold or other **incombustible** matter.

<margin>No. 103.</margin>
For by the very fact that they choose *incombustible materials*, they contradict themselves. That which is incombustible is that which is **extremely dense**; and which, therefore, cannot be thinned, and consequently cannot blaze. If, however, they choose a *combustible* matter, it is impossible for it to burn without rarefaction, or for the thinned atoms not to be dispersed, unless they are caught again and fixed. Without this **circulation** <note>a cycle where the fuel is consumed and then reconstituted</note>, there will be no perpetuity, except by a continuous and new flow of material—but then it will not be a "perpetual light" except by coincidence.

<margin>No. 104.</margin>
This is what the Reverend Father **Kircher** proposes in his *Subterranean World* <note>original: "Mundo subterraneo"; a massive 1664 work on geology and science by the Jesuit scholar Athanasius Kircher</note>, in the chapter on perpetual light. There, in places where **oil** flows perpetually, he applies a wick made of **asbestos** <note>original: "asbesto"; a mineral known for being fire-resistant</note> and thus constructs a perpetual lamp due to the continuous inflow of new oil. But even this will not succeed, since experience teaches that asbestos is corrupted and extinguished in a short time, whether by its own nature or due to adhering soot. Others have therefore fled to threads of gold, iron, or silk, but all these things were attempted in vain.

<margin>No. 105.</margin>
Regarding the claim made by some that they have found **sealed jars** <note>original: "occlusas ollulas"</note> from which fires leaped out as soon as they were opened, but were immediately extinguished once they took in air—this I could easily believe. But that such a fire had been burning in that *sealed jar* for so many centuries before the opening, and was destroyed because the vessel was opened, is simply not credible or possible. We must conclude, therefore, that a **potential fire** <note>original: "ignem potentialem"; energy that has the capacity to become fire but is not yet burning</note> lay hidden in such vessels, which, upon receiving air, immediately burst into flame, and was consumed a little later due to the scarcity of matter. This could even happen mechanically: if someone were to place a **fire-lock** <note>original: "Feur-Schloß"; a flint-lock mechanism</note>—prepared with such craftsmanship that it strikes fire from a flint by means of a spring, as they are now commonly made—into a small vessel, so adapted that when the lid is opened, the fire is struck at the same moment...

### Book I, Section V, Chapter III

Certainly, after a vast amount of time, if someone were to open a vessel unexpectedly, they might find a fire within. However, it would be foolish to conclude that such a fire had always been burning in the vessel in the same way it blazes the moment it is lit—even if the ignorant might easily be persuaded of such a thing. <margin>No. 106.</margin> But let us return to **potential fire** <term>potential fire: the internal capacity of a substance to ignite or produce heat when triggered, though it is not currently burning</term>. Here the question is: *Can a matter be produced which, upon receiving air or water, conceives a flame?* Although almost all books are full of such descriptions, very few of these processes actually succeed in practice. This led **Father Kircher** <note>Athanasius Kircher (1602–1680), a celebrated Jesuit polymath and author of *The Great Art of Light and Shadow*</note> to totally deny the possibility and to state that it is impossible for **actual fire** to be drawn from any subject by either air or water alone.

While this is difficult, it is not impossible, as practical experience shows the opposite. We occasionally see various substances mixed together that not only grow intensely hot but actually catch fire. We see this daily in the pouring of **spirit of nitre** <term>spirit of nitre: nitric acid</term> and **butter of antimony** <term>butter of antimony: antimony trichloride, a chemical used in alchemy and medicine</term> into a solution of **Iron** <note>original: "Martis" — Mars was the alchemical name for iron</note>, and in other reactions. 

Most notably, **iron** grows so powerfully hot in **aqua fortis** <term>aqua fortis: "strong water," another name for nitric acid</term> that unless it finds room to expand, it will burst any container. An example of this can be observed in the iron fire-pot, commonly called an **iron grenade** <note>original: "eiserne Granat"</note>. If a small glass vial full of *aqua fortis* is placed inside it but left open, and the grenade is then sealed and turned upside down so the acid flows out and acts upon the iron interior, it will do so with such power that it will shatter the thick iron grenade with a massive crash. 

Even if no "fire" is yet visible in these examples, a clear demonstration is found in **spirit of wine** <term>spirit of wine: concentrated ethanol or alcohol</term> and **oil of Vitriol** <term>oil of Vitriol: concentrated sulfuric acid</term>, provided both are properly purified. As soon as they are mixed, they **catch fire**; the flame is extinguished if the vessel is blocked, but ignites again when opened. Furthermore, a paste made of **iron, zinc ore, tartar, and saltpeter** <note>original: "ferro, cadmia, tartaro & nitro"</note> subjected to a strong fire creates a substance of the most powerful potential heat and caustic ability; as soon as it feels water or even saliva, it ejects **fiery flames and sparks**. Regarding these and similar matters, one should read **Glauber** <note>Johann Rudolf Glauber (1604–1670), a famous German-Dutch alchemist and chemist</note> in his *Little Book of Fires*. 

We conclude here that the cause of "fire-making" or ignition is everything that **rarefies** <note>thins out or expands the density of a substance</note> and extremely attenuates a material. Hence, shaking, friction, the concentration of light rays, and finally all intense thinnings can ignite thin and **combustible** materials.

<margin>No. 107.</margin> Now we shall proceed to the **effect of fire**. Although in a general sense this consists of thinning, dilating, and rarefying bodies, its specific effects are fourfold. First, fire **dissolves and disunites** all things that consist of different parts. For things that are not perfectly mixed are not only dissolved in their physical continuity but are separated into their parts; fire raises the volatile parts and leaves the heavy ones behind. 

<margin>No. 108.</margin> However, in things that are strongly bonded, such as metals, fire certainly thins their pores; but because the metallic **mixture** holds together, the introduction of abundant air and "fire-particles" renders the metal **fluid**. This is the true **fiery cause of fluidity**. It behaves much like ice; when the pores are thinned, solution and liquefaction follow. This, however, only happens in metals that are thoroughly mixed; in those imperfectly mixed, the more volatile part is driven off by the fire. 

<margin>No. 109.</margin> The same is to be understood regarding stones. Some do **not flow** in the fire, but through the expulsion of certain particles and the taking in of other fiery ones, they are reduced to what is called **quicklime** <note>original: "calcem vivam"</note>. Others flow and turn **into glass**. Still others neither turn to lime nor glass but remain immune to the fire—indeed, they are highly...
