# Book I. Section V. Chapter III.

Certainly, after a very long time, if someone unexpectedly opens a small vessel, they will find fire: yet it would be foolish to conclude that such an excited fire had always been burning in the vessel in that way; it blazed at the moment it was kindled, although those who are ignorant might perhaps be convinced otherwise.

<margin>No. 106.</margin>
But let us return to **potential fire** <term>potential fire: the capacity of a substance to ignite or produce heat when triggered by another substance, like water or air, even if it is not currently burning</term>; where the question is, *can a matter be given which, upon receiving air or water, conceives a flame?* Although nearly all books are full of such descriptions, very few processes succeed in practice. This was so much the case that the **Reverend Father Kircher** <note>Athanasius Kircher (1602–1680), a famous Jesuit scholar and polymath</note> was moved, in his work *The Great Art of Light and Shadow*, to totally deny the possibility; he stated that it is impossible for actual fire to be drawn out of any subject by either air or water. While this is difficult, it is not impossible, since practice shows the contrary. We see various things sometimes mixed together which not only grow extremely hot but actually catch fire: as we see daily in the pouring of **spirit of nitre** <note>nitric acid</note> and **butter of antimony** <note>antimony trichloride</note> into a **solution of Mars** <note>a solution containing iron; alchemists used "Mars" to represent iron</note>, and other things. Especially, however, **iron in aqua fortis** <note>literally "strong water," a term for nitric acid</note> heats up most powerfully, so that if it does not find space to expand, it bursts every container. An example of this can be observed in the iron pear, commonly called an **iron grenade** <note>original German: "eiserne Granat"</note>: into which, if a small glass vial full of *aqua fortis* is placed but left open, and the "pear" is later closed up, and then, being properly closed, is turned upside down so that the acid contained within pours out and acts upon the iron casing: it will do this with such power that it bursts the pear—even though it is iron and thick—with a massive crash. Although no *fire* is yet seen in all these examples, there is nonetheless an evident demonstration in **spirit of wine** <note>ethanol or high-proof alcohol</note> and **oil of Vitriol** <note>concentrated sulfuric acid</note>, provided both are properly **rectified** <term>rectified: purified or concentrated through repeated distillation</term>. For as soon as they are mixed, they **catch fire**; the flame is extinguished when the vessel is blocked and kindled again when opened. In particular, from **iron, calamine** <note>original: "cadmia" — an ore of zinc</note>, **tartar, and nitre**, a paste is made by a strong fire, possessing a most powerful potential and caustic heat; for as soon as it feels water, or even spit, it **ejects fiery flames and little sparks**. But concerning these and similar things, let **Glauber** <note>Johann Rudolph Glauber (1604–1670), a prominent chemist known for his work on salts</note> be read in his *Little Book of Fires*. We conclude in this place that the cause of ignification or kindling is everything that **rarefies** <term>rarefies: the process of making a substance thinner or less dense</term> and highly breaks down a substance. Hence concussions, frictions, concentrations of rays [through a lens], and finally all intense rarefactions can ignite materials that are prone to thinning and **combustible**.

<margin>No. 107.</margin>
Now we shall proceed to the **effect** of fire; which, although in general it consists in the fact that it thins, expands, and rarefies bodies: in specific cases, however, its effect is varied, primarily fourfold. First, fire **dissolves and disunites** all things that consist of **heterogeneous** <term>heterogeneous: made of different, unrelated types of parts or substances</term> parts. For things that are not perfectly mixed, fire not only dissolves their continuity but also separates them into their parts; it lifts up the volatile parts and leaves the heavy parts behind.

<margin>No. 108.</margin>

This, however, only happens in properly mixed metals; for in those that are imperfectly mixed, the more volatile part is driven out by the fire.

# Subterranean Physics

...when heated to a white glow, even if they are extinguished in cold water, they do not break: as we observe in the ruby, the garnet, the diamond, and others. Indeed, this is a necessary and natural consequence of what preceded;
<margin>No. 110.</margin>
for those things which are so compact that they do not admit the expansion <note>original: "rarefactionem"</note> of fire and its tiny particles <note>original: "corpuscula"</note>, will also necessarily not let water in. Thus, they are not shattered when they are cast into it. Glass, on the contrary, because it is *more porous* (for it flows <note>meaning it melts/liquefies</note>), when heated and then doused with water, breaks immediately; for it takes the water into itself. Indeed, metals themselves do this; hence they are granulated <note>the process of turning molten metal into small grains by pouring it into water</note>. At this point, I dismiss the Peripatetics' <term>antiperistasis: an Aristotelian theory that a quality is intensified when surrounded by its opposite, such as heat becoming more concentrated when surrounded by cold</term>,
<margin>No. 111.</margin>
to which they assign these effects. For if it were true, why would a diamond, heated to the highest degree of whiteness and thrown into cold water—or even ice—not break? This useless term shall therefore cease; the cause of this effect must be attributed to the **structure** <note>original: "compagi"</note>. For the **diamond** is the most compact of all stones—indeed, of all things under the sun—which is why it is the *hardest*, though *not the heaviest*.
<margin>No. 112.</margin>
From this, it follows that structure alone is not the sufficient and sole cause of weight <note>original: "gravitatis"</note>, as some wish to believe. Furthermore, regarding the fact that **earthenware** vessels bear heat better than **glass** ones; such as porcelain, which can be safely placed over a fire without danger of breaking, even if it contains cold liquid, whereas glass would break: certainly, "antiperistasis" is again not the cause, otherwise the porcelain
<margin>No. 113.</margin>
would also break. From this it is clear that both *porous and extremely dense* things can endure being extinguished in cold water without breaking; thus, glass will be *midway between precious stones and earthenware*, for it cannot be heated or cooled without the danger of shattering. We see a delightful demonstration <note>original: "enchirisin"</note> of this matter in the small glass pieces recently invented called **Prince Rupert's Drops** <note>original: "Spring-Glaeſer"; glass droplets with long tails that remain solid unless the tail is nipped, at which point they explode</note>. Although these are *most solid*, as soon as they are broken at one part—where they end in the form of a thin thread—they are immediately dissolved into the smallest parts and dust with a loud bang. They are prepared in glassworks, where drops of fluid glass are cast into *cold water*; many indeed break, but
<margin>No. 114.</margin>
those which remain unharmed exhibit the aforementioned effect. The reason for this is that, because of the surrounding cold water into which the drops are cast during preparation, the expanded air constricts and condenses itself primarily around the surface, while the glass body follows into the highest state of compaction out of the greatest "dread of a vacuum" <note>original: "metum loci vacui"; the Aristotelian idea that nature abhors a vacuum</note>. Therefore, when a part of the thickened outer skin is broken, the air enters immediately and expands and scatters all the atoms of the glass, however solid, so that they appear like crushed powder. But let us return to our purpose,
<margin>No. 115.</margin>
and having finished with the *first* effect of fire—namely, the pulling apart of continuity—let us proceed to the *second*, namely the **alteration of weight**, which follows closely upon continuity or quantity. That weight is altered by fire is most evident and certain; for **tin** <note>original: "stannum"</note>, although it is reduced to ashes by itself, nevertheless becomes *heavier*: and **antimony** calcined by a burning-mirror <note>original: "speculo caustico"</note>, although it evaporates many particles, nevertheless becomes *heavier*. And if you carefully weigh **cupels** <term>cupel: a shallow, porous bowl used in assaying to separate precious metals from base metals like lead</term> with the metal placed in them, although much of the metal seems to evaporate, if you weigh them afterward, you will find them to be notably heavier than they were before in total, including the metal and all additions. The **Nominalists** or **Peripatetics** <note>followers of scholastic and Aristotelian philosophy</note> do not like to hear of this weight caused by fire; they attribute the power of fire only to imaginary qualities and empty words, and they deny that it is a *substance*. But if it is not a substance, how can it make bodies *heavier*? You will say by **calcination** <note>original: "coctione"; literally "cooking," but here referring to alchemical heat treatment</note>; and this is acceptable, although this solution...

### Book 1, Section 5, Chapter 3

...[it is shown what] of the false might be in this place. It will therefore be clear that metals treated with fire, without any other addition, are rendered **heavier**; that is, they are changed in their weight. To claim that this happens by the sole word of "cooking" <note>original: "coctio," an early chemical term for the ripening or processing of a substance by heat</note>, without the entry and intervention of *tiny particles* <note>original: "corpusculorum"</note>, is absurd and difficult to accept. <margin>No. 116.</margin> For since weight is a consequence of *quantity* <note>meaning the amount of matter present</note>, and quantity is the first and most common property of bodies, those things which are changed in their *essential* weight must be said to be changed in their whole substance and *essence*. For example, if *gold* were to acquire the weight of *tin*—suppose in the same container, as they test tin in rounded, convex molds—even if it kept its color and stability, it could no longer be called *gold*. Consequently, it will not be sufficient to ascribe such a change to "cooking" alone. It must therefore be established that *particles go forth from the fire* which act upon bodies and, depending on the variety of the subject, are *fixed* in them; hence the greater weight. Moreover, we shall explain in the seventh section regarding transparency whether and when such fiery corpuscles *shine*. <margin>No. 117.</margin> Now we shall return to the proposal where *fire not only makes bodies heavier, but also lighter*; this latter effect, however, it performs "by accident" <note>an Aristotelian term meaning an indirect or non-essential result</note>, namely in bodies *joined by a heterogeneous mixture* <note>a mixture of different types of matter</note>, where it drives away the imbalanced parts; but we shall deal with these things more extensively in what follows. <margin>No. 118.</margin> Now it remains for us to proceed to the *third* effect of fire, namely regarding the "accidents" of bodies, as the Peripatetics <note>followers of Aristotle</note> call them. Here, experience proves first of all that *color is changed by fire*, as we see in the preparation of *minium* <note>red lead, used as a pigment</note>, especially in a *reverberatory furnace* <term>reverberio: a furnace where the flame is reflected or "reverberated" off the roof onto the material being heated</term>; where it should be noted that unless the bodies of the *flames* directly touch the material, it is not colored; but if they are committed to an open fire, most things *turn reddish*. Because we shall deal with *smell, taste, sound*, and their other "accidents" insofar as they are altered in fire—partly in the third part of our *Metallurgy* and partly in the following seventh section of this book—we rightly refrain from further treatment here, lest we *serve up "twice-cooked cabbage"* <note>original: "cramben bis coctam obtrudamus," a Latin idiom for a boring or stale repetition</note> to the reader; since it is well known to practitioners that flames contribute much to heat in *vitrification* <note>the process of turning a substance into glass</note>. Indeed, the variety of *subjects* from which such *flames* consist is usually noted. Nor is there need for many demonstrations, since in the preceding sections, especially concerning *fermentation*, we have sufficiently proven that by heat alone, vegetables are altered in *taste, smell, and heat*. Now we shall hasten to the *fourth effect of fire*, namely *alteration in the total substance*. For it is certain that *heat and fire totally alter subjects*, which we see daily in vegetables and in animals; in which *bitter and acid juice is changed into sweet, chyle into blood* <note>chyle is the milky fluid produced during digestion</note>, and finally one thing into another: as we see above all in the *hatching of chicks*. For of fire it can be said what is usually said of time: *fire takes away or alters everything*; whence *Empedocles* <note>a Greek Pre-Socratic philosopher who proposed the four elements</note> wisely and practically said: *We can assist Nature with fire, for besides that we have no other help*. <margin>No. 119.</margin> However, it is not only as has been said thus far, that fire and the consequent heat dominate the continuity, structure, quantity, weight, and *accidents* of bodies; but in truth, it turns the whole *seminal substances* <note>the internal "seeds" or essential blueprints that determine what a thing is</note> of things upside down, as is obvious to anyone who has even the slightest experience with fire and has observed the mutation of animals and vegetables which happens by means of heat. I believe there will hardly be anyone, unless he be of a hardened brow <note>shameless</note> and of no experience, who would deny it. *But that stones and metals are changed in substance and species through fire, might perhaps seem hard to someone...*

### Subterranean Physics

...as it might seem to some; but we shall see, and we shall break open this nut, though I confess it is a hard one. <margin>No. 120.</margin> Regarding stones, no experienced person will deny that their "specific form," quality, and distinction consist in transparency or opacity, color or tint, and softness or hardness. Yet, as the saying goes, even "bleary-eyed men and barbers" <note>original: "lippis & tonforibus," a Latin idiom meaning something is common knowledge or obvious to everyone</note> know that *fire, regarding these specific markers and qualities, changes any stones that are alterable and workable by fire;* and thus in their whole being and specific substance, they are altered so that they are no longer the species they were before. *For they mostly lose their hardness and color.* Indeed, who would believe a sapphire is still a sapphire if it has lost all its color? Experience teaches that a sapphire can be deprived of these two necessary and essential requirements by fire alone. Therefore, fire truly changes stones in their whole species and substance. I will pass over the fact that from certain stones, fire makes glass; no one is ignorant that glass is of a different species than stones, a point which perhaps will not be much contested. But that metallic species are transformed from one into another by fire alone might seem a paradox to many.

<margin>No. 121.</margin> But we shall dissolve every difficulty that arises with two infallible experiments. The first is *steel-making* <term>chalybificatio: the process of transforming iron into steel</term>; which, if considered accurately, will clearly demonstrate that fire alone makes steel from iron. The process of *steel-making* happens in the following way: They take a large mass of good iron, several hundred pounds; having thrown this into the fire, they press it with a strong heat until the outer parts gradually flow away, roughly until the middle part is reached. Then they take out what remains and, as they call it, draw it out into bars using a large hammer driven by a water-powered machine. After they have thrown the white-hot bars into water to cool them, they sell them. They are entirely hard and brittle—in a word, *steel*. Now the question is: whence arises this change of iron into *steel*? Since nothing but fire is added (I set aside the *steel* which is found naturally in ore veins). You might say, *it comes from the heating and the immersion in water;* but this is absurd, for though you might heat iron a hundred times and cool it again with water, it will still not be steel. Therefore, it must be established that it proceeds from iron, which before such preparation is not steel; otherwise, this superfluous preparation would be foolish. By fire, therefore, iron is changed into steel; for the reason that while the aforementioned parts of the large mass suffer the strongest fire, the internal parts are meanwhile "digested" <note>original: "digerantur," an early chemical term for using heat to mature, soften, or refine a substance over time</note> and reach maturity. And lest you believe this reasoning is weak, throw pieces of iron into an empty crucible without any other material, and having closed it very well with clay, commit it to a continuous and strong fire for 48 hours. Afterward, open the crucible, and you will find the iron particles (unless the fire was too intense so that they melted, which would be harmful) intact, but for the most part—indeed, if you proceeded correctly, entirely—changed into good steel, without losing a grain of weight. Conversely, if the crucible is left open, the whole iron will be converted into *iron-scale* <term>stomoma: the hard outer crust or scale of iron</term>, or slag, or rust, commonly called *Sinter* <note>original: "Sinter," a German term for the mineral or metallic scales that flake off hot iron</note>. But in the closed one, you will not find a grain of this, but the whole will be converted into steel. From this, two things follow: subjects *closed and open* are affected by fire in different ways; and secondly, iron in the fire is altered, if not in its whole species, certainly for the most part. But regarding steel-making, in Book Two, in the [special] chapter...

<margin>No. 122.</margin>
how by fire alone, from silver, lead, tin, *bone ash, and potash* (commonly called *Pottäsch*), true copper may be made, with no other subjects added (except those mentioned). This experiment is of no small importance, communicated to us by the most illustrious Mr. Dr. Gerbardus Thilenus, formerly a physician in Frankfurt, now taken by the plague raging there—a man most worthy of trust, who spent his whole life in experiments concerning the melting and treatment of bodies in strong fire, leaving behind experiments that are not to be despised. This one, which he shared with us and which we have found to be *true* in practice, we shall faithfully share with the curious reader; although it is a tedious labor and requires a good smelter, it is nonetheless curious and brings many consequences in its wake, not unwelcome to curious researchers. The process is as follows. Take *half an ounce of lead*, and when it begins to boil (or "drive") in a scorifier <term>Treibscherben: a shallow ceramic dish used in assaying</term> under a muffle furnace <term>muffel: a semi-cylindrical ceramic cover used to protect samples from direct flame while allowing airflow</term>, add *one dram of tin*. After adding two or three grains of *silver*, leave them until they have been reduced together into dross. If you reduce this dross in a strong crucible, you will have a *regulus* <term>regulus: the metallic lump that settles at the bottom of a crucible after melting</term> and a portion of the metals lying upon it, not yet reduced, which you should save. From the *regulus*, just as you did before, produce dross under the muffle; and the remaining metal that stays in the dish (segregation lead) examine in a cupel <term>cupella: a small, porous bowl made of bone ash used to refine precious metals</term>. This *cupel*, together with the dross remaining from the reduction (which I ordered you to save earlier in the first operation) and with those drosses produced by the scorifier the second time, grind all together. To this powder, add also the grain of *silver* which the cupel produced, and reduce it again in a crucible with the strongest fire. Reduce the *regulus* again into dross as described, and then proceed with the Regulus and dross as before. If you repeat this labor several times—three or four—make a powder from the dross and the metal-heavy cupel, and with three or four parts of potash in a strong crucible, reduce it with the *strongest fire*, and you will have *pure grains of copper*. Thus far the process. Regarding its practice, various

<margin>No. 123.</margin>
things must be noted; first, that you should do this in a larger quantity, for then the proof is more evident; second, that you must examine whatever subjects you use very well, so that they contain no copper within themselves; third, that in the reduction, which requires a strong fire, you must be accurate and diligent. Regarding the theory and reason of the process itself, it was even obscure to the author himself where this effect followed from; though in other matters and manipulations he was sufficiently circumspect and cautious, he could scarcely grasp where the copper originated. At last, he ascribed it to the *sulfur of Jupiter* <note>In alchemy, "Jupiter" refers to Tin. He believed tin's "essential sulfur" caused the change.</note>, in which he believed a transmuting power resided. But in truth, all circumstances considered, it is most certain that this entire effect proceeds from the fire. For *tin and lead* are moist subjects and attract the fire; for by fire alone lead is changed into minium <note>red lead</note> and a most reddish color; and we have demonstrated above that the *ashes of Jupiter* <note>tin ash or tin oxide</note> become heavier by fire alone. For *lead* is *heavy, soft, white, fluid*, and flows before it glows; whereas *copper* is a *lighter, hard, red, and flowing* metal after it glows; in no respect, therefore, does it agree with *lead*, as it does in many respects with *gold*. It should not be thought, therefore, that *copper and lead* are so related that one is easily transmuted into the other, or that one lies hidden in the other. We also know a way to transmute *copper into iron by fire alone*; but since there is no profit in it, just as in the preceding process, we did not wish to detain the reader with useless things, although no demonstration is useless to a philosopher: and therefore we hope that what we have said thus far will not be unwelcome to the curious reader. Now we shall pull in the sails, and according to the division made at the beginning of this discourse concerning liquidity, we shall cross from the liquefying cause to the *liquefiable subject*, soon to return to the desired port.

<margin>No. 124.</margin> All things, however, that are liquefied, can be reduced to *three classes*: for they flow either as *salts*, or as *metals*, or as *glasses*.

<margin>No. 125.</margin> Regarding the flow of *salts and sulfurs*, various things must be considered; for some flame and flow, and thus evaporate in the flow, such as *salts, saltpeter* <note>original: "nitrum"</note>, *common salt, and sublimated arsenic*: others are rendered more liquid in the flow, such as *wax, common butter, and butter of antimony* <note>original: "antimonii," referring to antimony trichloride, an oily chemical compound</note>; others become more constricted <note>i.e., they thicken or solidify</note> through the flow, such as *Vitriol, alum, sugar of Saturn* <note>original: "saccharum Saturni," or lead acetate, known for its sweet taste despite its toxicity</note>, etc. Some flow *before they glow red*, like watery salts and sulfurs; but others flow when they also glow, like saltpeter, salt of tartar, and common salt. But the *tincture* alone is the completion of all such flows, for it flows and does not flame, nor smoke, nor become more liquid or more constricted, nor is it altered, whether in gentle heat or when it glows. He who, therefore, leads his subject to such a temperament in his operation, will be worthy to be seated at the table of the twelve peers, as Lullus <note>Ramon Llull, a 13th-century scholar and reputed alchemist</note> says in the *Theory of the Testament*. Specifically, let the tincture not flame; for whatever flames is still capable of being made rare and is unequally mixed. Second, let it not smoke, for those things which smoke suffer a loosening and separation of parts, which proceed from an unequal mixture. Third, let it not become more liquid through fire, like *butter of antimony*, which the first and second time stays with the consistency of *butter* in the cold; but if it stands longer in flow, or is distilled several times, it stays like a *liquid oil* not only in heat but in the cold: the cause of which is unequal mixture, the taking in of air, and the separation of earthy parts. <margin>N.</margin>Regarding how their liquefaction occurs—namely, by means of **rarefaction** <note>Rarefaction is the process by which a substance becomes less dense; here, the author suggests heat expands trapped air to push metallic particles apart</note>—it has been discussed in the preceding pages. Since the physical penetration of bodies is not granted—that is, that various equal contents cannot be in one container at one and the same time—it follows necessarily that metallic particles must be disunited because of the abundant, trapped, rarefied air; not unlike how dry wood is broken and creates a fissure because of trapped rarefied air. In this, however, metals differ from that kind of cracking: because of their round and globular homogeneity in every atom, such rarefactions, distensions, and fissures occur so that they are disunited in every atom; yet, due to their homogeneity, they cohere as much as possible. Whence they are able to be poured, and this is properly called being liquefied in fire.

<margin>126.</margin>For we do not dwell here on liquefactions that occur through "impastations" <note>Mixing substances into a paste or dough-like consistency</note> and are finished with a light heat, for these are improperly said to be liquefied. In this way, gypsum, horns, and even the "rust" <note>original: "ferrago," likely referring here to sawdust or wood shavings</note> of wood itself can be cast into a pasted shape; but setting aside such heterogeneous liquefactions, we shall return to our igneous one. Once the cause of liquefaction has been explained, its method and differences must be considered.

For some metals and minerals flow before they glow with heat, such as **lead** and **tin**; others flow after a long period of glowing, such as **copper** and **iron**; others flow at the same time they are white-hot, such as **gold and silver** <note>original: "aurum & argentum"</note>. Some persist unchanging in the fire while in flux, such as the aforementioned metals **Gold and Silver** <note>original: "sol & luna," literally "the Sun and the Moon," the standard alchemical symbols for gold and silver</note>; others evaporate, such as copper; others are reduced to ashes, glass, and slag, such as tin, lead, and iron. 

In liquefaction, therefore, one must take care that those things which are easily corrupted are treated with a sudden fire, so that they flow before they are reduced to slag. We have a manifest example of this in **copper**: if you wish to liquefy it and treat it with a long and slow fire, it will be changed into a saffron-colored powder <note>original: "crocum," referring to a chemical oxide</note> (**copper ash** <note>original German: "Kupferäsch"</note>), and even if you then apply the greatest fire, you will not liquefy it, but rather you will burn the entire body. If, however, you first heat the crucible itself excellently, then throw in the copper and apply a sudden strong fire, it will flow immediately. And this is the reason why there have been few who knew how to liquefy copper by itself. ## On Mixed Bodies.
### Chapter One
# On Mixed Bodies in General.

->S Y N O P S I S.<-

**N. 1.** *A digression from the act of mixing to the mixed bodies themselves.* **N. 2.** *How mixed bodies are considered in this place.* **N. 3.** *The most general division of mixed bodies.* **N. 4.** *A general consideration of animal mixed bodies.* **N. 5.** *An exposition of vegetable mixed bodies.* **N. 6.** *The general arrangement of subterranean mixed bodies.*

<margin>N. 1.</margin>
In the preceding two Sections, we treated the *Instruments* by which bodies are resolved into their principles and combined once again; namely, **mixture**, and its opposite, the **solution** of things. We placed these before the eyes of the reader not without labor and industry, yet, I hope, not without fruit and utility. Now it remains for us to consider the *mixed bodies* <note>original: "mixta"; in 17th-century science, "mixed bodies" refers to any substance composed of the basic elements or principles, encompassing all physical matter.</note> themselves, the parts of which, and the nature and affections of those parts—namely their origin and destruction—we have explained at length in the preceding sections, and which we shall explain specifically in the final section of this book, as well as in the second book. <margin>N. 2.</margin> Indeed, in this section, we shall review the mixed bodies only according to their external difference, namely according to genus and species, by name alone and according to their order; with a small description and the identification and definition of each mixed body added. For as far as the internal nature and difference of mixed bodies is concerned, we shall explain it accurately in the second book under the "anatomy" of each mixed body. In this place, however, we shall provide only a sort of *Catalog* beforehand, so that the curious reader may see the subjects at first glance which are to be subjected to anatomy in the second book...

### Subterranean Physics

[sul]phurs, which hinder the flow, and to free the metals from them. However, if the metals are deficient in the **first earth** <note>In the author's theory, the "first earth" is the principle of saltiness and solidity.</note> (as discussed in Section 3, Chapter 2), borax is rightly employed to supply this deficiency from its own substance for the reasons mentioned above. This is the reason why skilled smelters add **vitrifiable stones** <note>Stones capable of being turned into glass, such as quartz or sand.</note> to ores if they are resistant to melting; this is done so that the flow may be promoted, and the **styptic sulphurs** <note>original: "stiptica sulphura"; refers to harsh or binding sulfurous impurities that prevent metal from flowing smoothly.</note> may be gathered into the glass and fixed there. On the other hand, when metals are too fluid and "mercurial," they add **quicklime** or **iron scale** <term>stomoma ferri: literally "the mouth of iron," referring to hard iron scales or iron essence used to "dry" a mixture</term>; this is so that, by the added dryness, the moisture may be partially removed and tempered. This is also the reason why some people, in small-scale operations, add salt of tartar or alkali instead of **borax**; namely, because within such fixed salts lies hidden a **vitrifiable** earth which performs the role of **borax**, even if it requires a stronger heat to flow. If the smelters of ores were to properly consider these and similar things, they could—not without profit—melt many **intractable** ores and bring them into use. But we shall explain these matters more fully in the seventh section of this book, where we will discuss the testing of metals, especially the explanation of **cupellation** <term>cineritii: the process of refining gold or silver by melting it in a "cupel" made of bone ash</term> and what is required for the melting of metals.

<margin>N. 127.</margin>
Now we shall proceed to the third type of liquefaction, namely to vitrification, or the flow of glass. How glass differs from metals has been sufficiently taught and demonstrated in the preceding sections: namely, that in place of the **third** principle (the third earth, discussed in Section 3, Chapter 4) of the metallic **Mercurial**, they possess another imperfect analogue. This analogue is of a different, primarily **dual** nature: in some stones, it tends toward fusibility, or glassiness and **transparency**; in others, however, it tends toward **opacity** and **infusibility**—in short, toward **quicklime**. For as was said previously, stones that produce **quicklime** cannot be changed into anything except **quicklime**; the most wise Creator of the world ordained it so, so that nothing would be lacking for human needs. It is also impossible for quicklime to be changed into glass; for if it were to flow before it was calcined, it would become **glass** and not **quicklime**. This must also be understood regarding glass: if it did not flow, it could not become glass. Since, however, we will deal specifically with vitrification in the seventh section, we will not further expand this chapter—already lengthy beyond our intention—but will conclude it. We advise the Philosophical reader not to forget this glassy flow in the **Philosophical work** <note>The "Philosophical work" or "Great Work" refers to the alchemical process of creating the Philosophers' Stone.</note>; for one must acquire the **Philosophers' Borax**, which is called the **Seal of Hermes** <note>original: "sigillum Hermetis"; a method of sealing a glass vessel airtight, but here also referring to a specific alchemical substance or stage.</note>, to imbue the tincture. And this is fixed in our white or red crystal, where the Philosophical spirit is to be summoned and fixed by **lawful and honest magic**.

<margin>N. 128.</margin>
And so we shall finish the teaching on the **dissolution** of things (which is the opposite of mixture) with this section. Although it is lengthy and may perhaps seem to many to be irrelevant, let the kind reader know that we have set down nothing that does not have either a hidden or open use and application regarding **mineral** knowledge; as the chemistry-loving reader will notice if they study it a little. In a few words, **much has been said**, from which certain "polygraphs" <note>A dismissive term for overly wordy authors who write much but say little.</note> could write immense volumes. We, striving for brevity in our words, writings, and deeds, love the succinct truth; which, specifically in this latter

<margin>N. 129.</margin>
chapter on liquefaction, we have exposed more clearly than the sun: so that one would have to be as [blind] as a mole, or deprived of both eyes...

<header>Book I. Section VI. Chapter I.</header>

[no one] ought to be [so ignorant] who does not understand how many things occur to be investigated regarding the nature of minerals: and that the **spagyric art** <note>original: "spagyrica"; the alchemical art of separating and recombining substances.</note> is occupied not only with *raw coals*, but certainly also with *subtle speculations and reasoning*. Above all, I wish the reader to consider (so that he may reap the fruit of all these things treated in this chapter) that the *triple* enumerated *liquefaction—Mercurial, aqueous, and igneous*—is necessary in every way, not only for the knowledge of minerals, their treatment, and civil use, but in the work of the Philosophers <note>Referring to alchemists, often called "Philosophers" in this period.</note>. For this is the unique *key* for opening, resolving, vivifying, calcining, killing, and changing metals, as we have sufficiently proved up to this point. <margin>N. 30.</margin> Therefore, make Mercuries out of **Silver and Gold** <note>original: "Luna & Sole"; the alchemical planetary names for these metals.</note>, which you must precipitate with the "First Being" of sulfur; thin the precipitate with the *Philosophers' fire*, exalt it, and liquefy and fix it with the salt of the *Philosophers' borax* <note>A specific alchemical flux, distinct from common borax.</note> until it flows without smoke. Although these things are briefly stated, they are acquired through long labor and a long journey: for one must travel from the sandy, terrestrial Arabic sea into the *aqueous* Red Sea, and from this into the bituminous, burning Dead Sea—not without danger of rocks and whirlpools. We, thanks be to God, have already arrived at the port.

### Book One, Section Six
## Concerning Mixed Bodies.
### Chapter One
# Concerning Mixed Bodies in General.

->S Y N O P S I S.<-
N. 1. *A digression on mixing as it leads toward mixed bodies.* N. 2. *How are mixed bodies considered in this place?* N. 3. *The most general division of mixed bodies.* N. 4. *A general consideration of animal mixed bodies.* N. 5. *An exposition of vegetable mixed bodies.* N. 6. *The general arrangement of subterranean mixed bodies.*

->T E X T U S.<-

<margin>N. 1.</margin> In the **p**receding two Sections, we dealt with the *Instruments* by which bodies are resolved into their principles and combined again; namely, *mixing* <note>original: "mixtio"</note> and its opposite, the *solution of things*. These we have placed before the reader's eyes not without labor and industry, yet, as I hope, not without fruit and utility. Now it remains for us to consider the *mixed bodies themselves*, whose parts and the nature and affections of those parts—namely, their origin and destruction—we have explained at length in the preceding pages, and which we shall explain in the final section of this book, as well as specifically in the second book. <margin>N. 2.</margin> In this section, however, we shall review the mixed bodies only according to their external difference—namely, according to *genus and species*—by name and according to order; adding a small description and a recognition and definition of each mixed body. For as far as the internal nature and difference of mixed bodies is concerned, we shall explain it accurately in the second book under the "anatomy" of each mixed body. In this place, however, we shall only provide a sort of *Catalog* in advance, so that the curious reader may see at first glance the subjects to be subjected to anatomy in the second book...

# Subterranean Physics

[...to be studied] so that the student should perceive and know how to name [these things]. Since it is not within our power to impose diverse and new names on so many mixed things, we are therefore bound to follow the **Ancients** and consequently to borrow the greatest part of this entire section from others, and thus speak with another's mouth; but in the following seventh section, we shall return to our own thoughts. Since in the preceding sections we have always proposed to the curious reader an analogy with the remaining two kingdoms—namely the **animal** and the **vegetable**—we shall not fail in this place either. Instead, we shall move step by step from the *most general* to the *general*, and from the *general* to the *specific*. Therefore, we will speak about some things that are excluded from the circle of subterranean things, but which nevertheless have a great relationship with subterranean things in the *triangles* <note>Referring to the tripartite division or "trinity" of creation common in 17th-century philosophy.</note> of created beings: *their nature and existence are proved through the other two kingdoms.*

<margin>No. 3.</margin>
Now we shall approach more closely the natural and genuine location, situation, and relationship of subterranean things, and their analogy with other created things. It must be known, however, that this entire universe consists in some *being* <note>original: "esse"; the state of existence</note>; this *being* is something, and this *something* is either uncreated or created. The only uncreated being is **God**, in whom there is a **Trinity**, which we have explained elsewhere in our theological writings. Whatever exists besides or outside of God was created by Him: and *this created world is again threefold: either spiritual, or corporeal, or a medium between these.* In *spiritual* creations, there is again a Trinity; for there are *good spirits, evil spirits, and, as some would have it, indifferent spirits.* In *Intermediate* creations, which are neither *pure spirits nor pure bodies*, you will again find a trinity: of *souls, powers, and hidden qualities* <note>original: "qualitatum occultarum"; properties that cannot be directly observed but are known by their effects.</note> according to the opinion of some. In *corporeal* creations, there is also a Trinity: for some are supremely *simple*, like the elements; others are *somewhat mixed*, like the planets and meteors; others are *more mixed, such as bodies*. And these are again threefold: either *animals, vegetables, or minerals*, which are the subject of our discourse. In these too, the *Trinity* is not hidden, for a part of them is *Earth*, a part *stone*, and a part *metal*. Finally,

<margin>No. 4.</margin>
we have proved in the preceding pages that the metals themselves consist of three principles or earths. Therefore, wherever you turn, you will observe the *Trinity* of created things with their Creator and among *themselves*; we leave this for your further consideration and approach a closer analogy of the *three kingdoms*. The first of these is the *animal kingdom*, in which, by reason of *place*, one may also observe a certain Trinity; for some animals live in the *air*, others upon the *earth*, and others in the *water*. Some live in *only one*, others in *two*, and others in *three* elements: for *it is false that animals live in fire.* <note>The author here dismisses the medieval belief that the salamander lived in fire.</note> There is a great variety of *birds*; for some birds are *terrestrial*, and others are *aquatic*. Of the *terrestrial* ones, some are *carnivorous, plant-eating, grain-eating, or berry-eating*, and of these some are *large, small, songbirds, non-songbirds, dust-bathing, or non-dust-bathing*. Of the *aquatic* birds, some are *domestic* and others are *exotic*; of the domestic, some are *web-footed* <term>web-footed (palmipedes): birds with skin between their toes for swimming</term>, others are *split-footed* <term>split-footed (fissipedes): birds with separate toes</term>. The *exotic* birds—whether terrestrial or aquatic—that resemble ours are often fabulous. To the birds, one may add the genus of *insects* as a sort of decomposed class. Some of these are *aquatic, with feet or without feet*; others are *terrestrial*. These again are either without feet or with feet: and some of these are *few-footed or many-footed; wingless or winged*, whether they have *sheathed wings* <note>original: "vaginipennia"; insects like beetles where the front wings form a hard case.</note> or *exposed wings, two-winged, four-winged, mealy-winged* <note>original: "farinacea"; referring to the scales on the wings of butterflies and moths.</note>, *membrane-winged, honeycomb-making, or not honeycomb-making.*

### Book 1. Section VI. Chapter 1.

Following those that *fly* and *creep* come those that *walk* and *run, namely the terrestrial animals*; some of which are *two-footed*, and others *four-footed*; and among these, some are *hoofed* <note>original: "fulcata," likely a variation of "sulcata" meaning furrowed or hoofed</note>, others *fingered* <note>animals with distinct toes or digits, like cats or dogs</note>. Among the *hoofed* animals, both *single-hoofed* and *cloven-hoofed* are found: some of which are *ruminants* <note>animals that chew the cud</note> and some *non-ruminants*, some *horn-bearing*, and others *not horn-bearing*; the *fingered* animals, moreover, are distinguished into *viviparous* <note>giving birth to live young</note> and *oviparous* <note>egg-laying</note>; the latter being covered by skin or a shell, while the former are *wild, semi-wild*, or *domestic*. Now the *fishes*, which live in the water, present themselves; some of these are *exotic, lake-dwelling, rock-dwelling, fossil* <note>In the 17th century, "fossil" often referred to anything "dug up," including fish found in subterranean waters or dried-up beds</note>, *river-dwelling, coastal*, or *deep-sea* fish. And of these, again, some are *scaly, cartilaginous, smooth, long*, or *flat*. Among the *aquatic creatures*, one may also count the *bloodless* animals, of which some are *zoophytes* <note>organisms like corals or anemones that appear to be midway between plants and animals</note> and others are *aquatic*; and of these, several are *soft-bodied, crustacean, long*, or *round*: some are *shelled* or *spiral-shaped* in a *winding* or *circular* form, and there are *shellfish* with *many* or *few spirals*. To these, add the *Amphibians*.

<margin>No. 5.</margin>
The differences between animals having been considered, the *composite* and bodily *vegetables* come forward; which are either *trees* or *herbs*. The *trees* are *pome-bearing* <note>like apples</note>, *stone-fruit-bearing*, *nut-bearing, aromatic, acorn-bearing, berry-bearing, resin-bearing* <note>original: "lacrymiferæ," or tear-bearing, referring to sap or resin</note>, *pod-bearing, rose-flowered*, and *miscellaneous*. *Herbs* also exist in various forms, such as *bulbous* or *long-stalked and leafy*; and of these, some are *grain-bearing*, some *not grain-bearing, nerve-leafed, round-leafed, thick-leafed, rough-leafed, leaf-less, star-shaped, hair-like, cluster-flowered, crowning, umbel-bearing* <note>with umbrella-like flower clusters</note>, *headed, pod-bearing, climbing*, or *harmful garden plants*. You have there the second kingdom of nature; now the third

<margin>No. 6.</margin>
follows, namely that of the *minerals*, which we treat specifically in this book; but in this chapter, we shall consider its differences in a general way, in the same manner as the preceding kingdoms. As far as the composite *minerals* are concerned, they exist in three types: namely *simple, composite*, and *de-composite* mixtures. The *simple* are called *principles*; from which the *composite* and *de-composite* are formed, about which we will speak at length in the third section. The *most remote* <note>the most basic underlying elements</note> are *earth* and *water*: the proximate ones are the *three earths*, discussed in the third section. From these *subtle earths, three composites* arise—specifically when they are mixed with one another; which *composites*, although they are related to each other, are nevertheless generally varied according to the quality and quantity of the earths: just as in animals the flesh varies, and in vegetables the pulp varies, even though in a general sense flesh is flesh and pulp is pulp. Hence, in this mineral division, *three composites* exist: namely *earth, stones*, and *metals*; which, although they are related to one another, nevertheless differ specifically—not only in this general three-fold division, but within every genus. For various *earths* are given, which are distinguished into *common, middling*, and *noble*; and which are *fat, lean, salty*, or *oily*. Various *stones* also exist, which are either without a fixed shape, or with a fixed shape, or are *miscellaneous*. *Stones of uncertain shape* are either *transparent, semi-transparent*, or *opaque*; and these again are noble or ignoble, larger or smaller. *Stones that exhibit fixed shapes* present the likenesses of either natural or artificial things; the *miscellaneous* ones are either *animal-like* <note>likely referring to fossils of shells or bones</note> or doubtful and not sufficiently known. Stones also differ in *hardness, weight, flammability, color*, and *luster*. The third type of composites encompasses *metals*; which consist of mineral principles mixed either equally or unequally, homogeneously or heterogeneously. Whence some are called *ores* <note>original: "mineræ (Ertz)"</note>, being still mixed with heterogeneous things such as earths and stones; others are properly called *minerals*, such as *Antimony* and *Bismuth* <note>original: "Bis-muthum"</note>.

<summary>The author classifies the three kingdoms of nature—animal, vegetable, and mineral—detailing the various sub-categories of each to demonstrate a universal taxonomic order. He introduces the mineral kingdom as being composed of simple principles that combine to form earths, stones, and metals.</summary>

All these differ by various **physical** properties, such as *volatilitate* <note>volatility: the tendency to evaporate</note>, *fixitate* <note>fixity: the ability to withstand heat without changing</note>, *malleabilitate* <note>malleability: the ability to be hammered thin</note>, *friabilitate* <note>brittleness</note>, *gravitate* <note>heaviness</note>, *levitate* <note>lightness</note>, *porositate* <note>porosity</note>, *compactione* <note>density</note>, *colore* <note>color</note>, *fluxu* <note>flow or melting point</note>, and *sono* <note>sound or resonance</note>. After the "composites" come the "doubly-compounded" or **decomposites** (I do not mean artificial ones, for we are not discussing those here, since we deal only with natural things). These again exist in **three types: namely, earthy, stony, and metallic.** Among all these, they are either dry or liquid, hard or soft. As for the **earthy decomposites**, they are of two kinds: **dry, such as bitumens, sulfurs, and salts; and liquid, such as oils and salt waters.** The **stony decomposites** are **dry, such as [petrified] animals and wood**; also metals that have become stony, such as various **fluors and tuffs** <note>original: "fluores & tophi"</note>, or salts like **alum and borax**; or **liquid, such as petrifying and stone-forming waters.** The **metallic decomposites** are either **dry, such as Mercury, cinnabar, arsenic, realgar, and orpiment** <note>original: "auripigmentum," a yellow arsenic mineral</note>; or **saline, such as vitriols and mineral waters, like hot springs and acidic springs.** Into the mixture of all these decomposites, either water or earth enters, of varying quality or quantity; hence, decomposites turn out to be **homogeneous, heterogeneous**, or of a strong or weak mixture. By "decomposites," I mean that the three aforementioned composites—whether **Earths, stones, or metals**—enter into further combinations; from which a new and doubled mixture, or a "composite of a composite," arises. And so in this chapter, we have descended from the most universal series, difference, and division of things and products, to the most specific division of subterranean things; we have done so in such a summary that it has caused us more labor than if we had written a long book on such matters. Now we return to our designated task <note>original: "spartam," a reference to the proverb 'Spartam nactus es, hanc exorna'—meaning to do one's duty in the lot they have been given</note>, namely the naming and explanation of subterranean things, according to the proposed scheme we have set for ourselves. Therefore, in the following chapter—the second—we will tackle the first type of subterranean composites by explaining the various earths; in the third chapter, stones; in the fourth, metals. In the fifth, we will explain the first type of mineral decomposites, the **earthy type**; in the sixth, the **stony**; and in the seventh, the **metallic**. And thus we conclude this sixth section, and indeed this chapter.

### Chapter Two of the Sixth Section,
## The First Subterranean Composite,
### *namely the various earths, explained in general and specific types.*

<meta>This page continues the classification of the mineral kingdom, moving from the general overview of "composites" into a specific taxonomy of Earths. It establishes the physical qualities that distinguish different types of soils and clays used in industry, art, and medicine.</meta>

<header>Book I. Section VI. Chapter II.</header>

## T E X T .

<margin>N. 1. N. 2.</margin>
By "earth" I do not mean that *primordial* <note>original: "primordialem"; the fundamental element existing at the beginning of the world's creation</note> earth which existed at the start of the world, of which we spoke in the first section; nor do I mean that which we discussed in the third section, namely as it constitutes the *principles* <note>the basic chemical components</note> of subterranean things. Rather, I mean that which is already *composite* <note>original: "composita"; a mixture formed from various distinct earths</note>. For although all earth is earth in a general sense, there can be various qualities of *earths*—mixtures of mixtures—varying in quantity, purity, and other degrees of physical properties. From these, different earthy compounds arise. All of these, however, are conveniently reduced into *three classes*, according to their threefold origin and the *three principal earths* discussed in the third section above.

<margin>N. 3.</margin>
That which possesses much of the *first* earth is called *gravel, grit, or sand* <note>original: "glarea, sabulum, arena"</note>. That in which the *second* earth dominates is named *mud or silt* <note>original: "lutum, limus"; in German: "clay, loam, mud"</note>. However, that in which the *third* earth predominates is usually called *common garden soil* <note>original: "terra communis hortensis"</note>. All earths that can be found can be reduced to these three classes.

<margin>N. 4.</margin>
Furthermore, each class differs within itself. For *sand* is varied: some is changed in fire into *glass* <note>original: "vitrum"</note>, some into *lime* <note>original: "calcem"</note>, while others remain *unchangeable* and semi-transparent, such as *Porcelain*. How this is prepared and treated is taught by *Heinrich Neuhoff* <note>Jan Nieuhof (1618–1672), a Dutch traveler whose account of the Dutch embassy to China was widely read</note> in his account of the embassy to the Emperor of the Chinese, on page 105. There, he asserts that a massive tower was constructed out of porcelain. *Mud* <note>clay</note> is also varied according to its degrees of "fatness" <note>viscosity or richness</note>; it may be *white or blue*. Some *melts easily in fire*, while others *resist it most powerfully*, such as *Passau earth* <note>original: "terra Passaviensis"; a heat-resistant clay from Passau, Germany, famous for making chemical crucibles</note>. There is also no small difference in *garden soil*; for it may be *salty, nitrous, urinous, sterile*, or *fertile*, depending on its nature and what is mostly generated from it.

<margin>N. 5.</margin>
These three classes are also usually *mixed* with one another for various uses. Potters mix *silt* with *sand*; gardeners mix *garden soil* with *silt*. Indeed, wonderful effects come from this mixing, as we shall teach in the second book, in the chapter on *Alkali*. There we shall prove how the *acids* and *alkalis* *lying hidden* in these earths act upon one another, and what new qualities arise from them.

Earths are also commonly distinguished into *lean* and *fat*, and into common, middle, and noble varieties.

<margin>N. 6.</margin>
Among the *common* earths, farmers use *Marl* <note>original: "Marga"; a lime-rich mudstone used as fertilizer</note> and *Marrow* <note>original: "Medulla"; a soft, fatty mineral substance</note>. Potters and cleaners use *Potter's Clay* <note>original: "Argilla"</note>, *Samian earth* <note>from the island of Samos</note>, *Cretan earth*, *Cimolian earth*, *Eretrian earth*, *Chian earth*, and *Selinusian earth*. The *Middle* earths are used by painters, such as *Paraetonium* <note>a white pigment</note>, *Melian earth*, *Ochre*, *Cadmia* <note>an oxide of zinc</note>, *Red Chalk* <note>original: "Rubrica"</note>, and *pignitis* earth. The *Noble* earths are used primarily by doctors, such as *sealed earth* <note>original: "terra sigillata"; medicinal clay pressed into cakes and stamped with a seal of authenticity</note> and *Armenian Bole* <note>a reddish clay used as an astringent and for cleaning wounds</note>. Now we shall consider each according to its external appearance and differences.

<margin>N. 7.</margin>
**1.** *Marl* is a certain fatness of the earth, much like a gland in the body, which thickens into a core of fat at the joints. The white variety is *Leucargillon* <note>original: "Leucargillon"; from Greek for "white clay"</note>; the reddish is *Capnomarga* <note>literally "smoke-marl"</note>. It is so easily dissolved by the sun and frost that it forms very thin flakes. The variety called *Columbina* <note>"dove-colored marl"</note> is said to be more fertile for fodder than for crops; another is *gliśchromarga* <note>a "sticky" or "tenacious" marl</note>. *Moonmilk* <note>original: "Lac Lunae"; a soft, white, milky carbonate deposit found in limestone caves</note> in the Swiss mountains, *Balma* which is crumbly, and the Indian *cotton stone* <note>original: "lapis gossypii"; likely a form of asbestos</note>, which is bright white and grows on the crags of rocks, belong here. **2.** *Marrow of stones* <note>original: "Medulla saxorum"</note>, if white, is fluid or fat; if metallic, it hardens immediately in the air. **3.** *Clay* of a snowy color is Pliny’s *Tasconium* <note>a white clay from Spain</note>, from which *crucibles* <note>original: "Catini"</note> are made for melting metals. Similar to this is the earth dug from Mount Carlo near Pisa, from which vessels are made to hold molten glass in furnaces. There is also the sulfur-smelling *Majellana*, and the thin, red *sigillaria* <note>used for making figurines or seals</note>, which is like wax...

<meta>This page continues the specific taxonomy of "Composite Earths," providing a detailed catalog of various clays and soils known in the 17th century. ...like a flexible substance, from the **Fields of Damascus** <note>original: "Campi Damasceni"</note>; the most sticky is the **Portuguese** <note>original: "Lusitanica"</note>, which is thick, fatty, and tenacious. From this are made the very rare **Waldenburg vessels** <note>original: "Valpurgensia vasa"; famous stoneware from Saxony</note>. There is also the **Gisellan** earth, which is porous enough to allow liquid to seep through. From **Spain** near the town of **Massa**, there is a pumice-like and ash-colored earth. The **Ipsian** <note>original: "Ipsensis"; from Ybbs in Austria</note> earth is lead-colored and resists fire. The **Aretine** <note>original: "Aretina"; from Arezzo</note> is sprinkled with grit; a vessel made from it, when thrown into fire, bends like glass. Here, you should also include **Porcelain** <note>original: "Porcellanam"</note>. 

4. **Samian earth** <note>original: "terra Samia"; from the island of Samos</note> is white and fatty; it sticks to the tongue. It is used in eye-salves, where it is called **Collyrion** or **Syropicon**. A more clod-like and crusty variety is called **Aster** <note>meaning "star"</note> because it was traditionally marked with the image of a star. Among the "adopted" <note>imported or substitute</note> varieties are those from **Elba** <note>original: "Ilvensis"</note> and **Malta**. 

5. **Chalks** <note>original: "cretae"</note> come in various colors, the most common being white. The green variety is called **Theodotian** <note>original: "Theodotia"</note>, named after the estate of Theodotus. That which reflects the shine of silver with its mica is called **Argentaria** <note>silver-chalk</note>. The types used for ring-seals are called **Figillaria** <note>seal-chalk</note> or **Annularis** <note>ring-chalk</note>. Among the people of Fez, a gray-white earth is called the **Chalk of God** <note>original: "creta Dei"</note>, because it is used to wash the bodies of the dead. A rust-colored variety is used by the Moors in place of soap. In **Thuringia**, a blue variety is dug up, and at **Waldenburg**, a violet one. A lean, dry, rare, and light variety is called **Cretula** <note>little chalk</note>. 

6. **Cimolian earth** <note>original: "Cimoliae"; also known as **Fuller's earth** (Smectis)</note> includes varieties like **Sardinian** and **Umbrian**, which they call "rock" <note>original: "saxum"</note>; it expands when soaked. It is either white or inclining toward purple; it is very fatty and has a strong astringent quality. 

7. **Eretrian earth** <note>original: "Erethria"</note> turns a violet color if rubbed with bronze. A related fatty earth from **Hanover** is ash-colored with a slight blue tint. 

8. **Chian earth** <note>from Chios</note>, because it is very white and fatty like starch, is used for women's skin. **Ecludis** earth was sought for the same reason, as was its relative, **Vincentine earth**, called **Fioneto of Chios**.

9. **Selinusian earth** <note>original: "Selinusia"</note> is milky in color, shining like nitre, and dissolves very quickly in water; it is used to refresh the surfaces of plasterwork. The town of **Selinus in Sicily** gave it its name. 

10. **Paratonium** is named after a port in **Egypt** toward Cyrenaica. Theophrastus perhaps called it **Phalaris**, others call it **shore-chalk** <note>original: "creta littoralis"</note>. They say it is sea-foam solidified with mud, which is why shells are found in it. It is white, extremely fatty, and very tenacious for plasterwork because of its smoothness. 

11. **Melian earth** <note>original: "Terra Melia"</note>, called *Melina* by Theophrastus, comes from the island of **Melos**. It is rough and slightly aluminous <note>containing alum</note>. Pliny describes it as white, Dioscorides as ash-colored. A rival to it is the **Maltese earth**, both in its natural ash-colored state and when soaked in water, which then takes on a saffron color and is shaped into tablets <note>original: "pastillos"</note>. **Ochre** <note>original: "Ochra" or "Sil"</note> is yellow and somewhat pale; it is found mostly in lead mines. The best is the yellow, crumbly **Attic ochre**, which **Mycon** <note>an ancient Greek painter</note> was the first to use for painting. A marble-like variety is found in mines. There is also a "tubular" <note>original: "fistularis"</note> kind. A **synthetic** <note>original: "factitia"</note> variety is prepared from red ochre or from burnt and soaked lead. Among the "adopted" earths are **Indian earth**, used for dyes; **Tripoli earth**; earth from **Hildesheim**; and **Alanian earth**, which is ash-colored and pale. 

12. **Cadmian earth** <note>original: "Terra Cadmia"</note> is yellowish if hard, and sometimes white if softer; it is dug up between **Cologne** and **Aix-la-Chapelle** <note>original: "Aquisgranum"</note>. 

13. **Red Ochre** <note>original: "Rubrica", also known as "Minium" or "Sinopian earth" after its homeland</note> has its own color in clods, though spotted on the outside. The ancients used this for its luster. The **Egyptian** kind, called *cicerculum* <note>meaning "little chickpea"</note>, is most used in paintings. A darker, more compressed kind is found at **Annaberg**. Near **Karlsbad** <note>original: "Thermas Caroli"</note>, there is a red and very fatty variety. It is also made from yellow ochre burnt in new clay pots. Among its relatives are the **Persian Cambil**, which is penetrating if rubbed, and the **earth of Hebron**, which the inhabitants eat and sell throughout Egypt as a type of spice. 

14. **Pignite earth** <note>original: "Terra Pignitis"</note> is very similar to Eretrian earth: fatty, soft, and sticky. It chokes the person who swallows it <note>this may be a warning about its high clay content or toxicity</note>, hence the name; it comes from **Pigneus**, a village in Mareotis, Libya.

...shining, fatty like tallow <note>original: "sebi instar"; referring to the waxy or greasy texture of certain clays</note>. That which is marked with a seal of many signs and turns reddish, they call **Aromatic**, which was once sacred to the image of Diana. That which is shaped into small cakes <note>original: "pastillos"; medicinal lozenges</note>, and in which whiteness is mixed with redness, is called **Spotted**; that which served craftsmen is called **Workman’s**; and that used by fullers for cleaning clothes is called **Fuller's earth**. The earth of **Legnica** <note>original: "Lignicensis"; a city in Poland</note> is called **Lunar Fat** <note>original: "axungia lunæ"; so named because it was believed to be impregnated with the "sulfur of the Moon," often an alchemical reference to silver</note> and **Mineral Unicorn** <note>original: "unicornu minerale"</note> because of its medicinal efficacy. Other varieties include the **Blois** earth, the **Marsic**, the **Piedmontese**, and the **Yellowish**, which is reddish-white inside. The **Elban** earth is either bright white or white sprinkled with rusty spots, or pale yellow with white spots running through it. The earth of **Bologna** mimics wax and is associated with **Hercules of Saxony**; that of **Ljubljana** <note>original: "Labacensis"</note> strongly induces sweating. The **Ebusian**, **Balearic**, and **Galatian** earths, the latter of which kills serpents, are among its relatives. 16. **Armenian Earth** <note>original: "Terra Armena"; also known as **Armenian Bole** or "Armenian mud"</note> was brought from the mountains of Armenia, specifically from Baganosa, during the time of Galen; it tends toward the color of a snail shell <note>original: "cochræ colorem"</note> and, if of the best quality, melts in the mouth like butter when chewed. Other varieties of **Bole** <note>term: Bole (a medicinal earth/clay usually rich in iron oxide)</note> include the **Matarensian** (or Acheruntian) in Italy, the **Roman**, the **Cassinese**, the **Meldulensian**, the **Vesulensian**, and the **Elban**. Elsewhere, there is the **Oriental** bole; the **Julicensian**; the **Strigensian**, which is slippery and reflects the color of the "Bole of Theophrastus"; the **Tokay**; and the **Baetic**. The **Bohemian**, **Rose-colored**, **Saffron**, and **Fatty** boles, as well as the **Buda** and **Wurtemberg** varieties (which are reddish-white), can also be categorized here.

<meta>This page continues the transition from the study of "earths" (clays and boles) to the study of stones, beginning a systematic classification of minerals based on their physical properties and transparency. It marks the shift into Chapter Three, drawing heavily on the work of the naturalist Johannes Jonstonus.</meta>

<header>Subterranean Physics</header>

### TEXT.

<margin>
Note 1.
</margin>
Having explained the first type of subterranean compounds, namely the *earths*: we now proceed to the *second*; namely to the mixture and difference of *stones*. Stones, moreover, are considered more complex than *earths*; because they consist of two principles, with some *third* element interposed, as we demonstrated in the section on the principles of things <note>The author likely refers to the alchemical principles of Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury, or his own specific elemental theory where stones require a "binding" agent to solidify from earth and water</note>. Next, they are considered more complex because they are bound together by a stronger bond than earths, and are thus less dissolvable and more resistant to all alterations. However, how they are generated, where they vary, and for what causes they differ from one another, has been said partly in the preceding parts, and we shall say more in the following final section, where we shall deal with the "accidents" and attributes of things <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "accidents" are qualities (like color or smell) that do not change the essential nature of a substance</note>.

<margin>
Note 2.
</margin>
In this chapter only, we will investigate the nominal and specific differences of stones regarding external knowledge; we will explain their nature more specifically in the second book under the "anatomy of stones."

<margin>
Note 3.
</margin>
But to come to our purpose, it must be known; the difference is taken in various ways; that is, *stones can be considered and divided in their differences in various ways*: as they are changed either into *lime* or into *glass*; or they persist *red-hot* <note>original: "candefacti"</note> in fire, or are destroyed; or, when *quenched in water*, they break or remain unharmed. They are also divided by reason of hardness, color, transparency <note>original: "diaphaneitatis"</note>, *shape*, *weight*, *origin* <note>original: "ortus"</note>, and according to many other physical attributes, about which we will speak in the second book. In this chapter, we shall follow the most noble and famous, and the preeminent Naturalist of our time—not only a prolific writer <note>original: "Polygraphum"</note> but one of vast knowledge—the man *Mr. Jonston* <note>Johannes Jonstonus (1603–1675), a Polish-Scottish physician and naturalist whose "Thaumatographia Naturalis" was a standard reference</note>. By his leave, we shall extract certain things for this chapter from his *Mineral Knowledge* <note>original: "notitia minerali"</note> concerning the differences of stones. Indeed, that man (who, I hear, is most kind) will not take this ill, as he will frankly admit that he also took the principal things from *Boëtius de Boodt* <note>Anselmus Boëtius de Boodt (1550–1632), a Flemish mineralogist and physician</note> and others; he will therefore allow us the same right over his work that he took over the works of others. We allow the same right regarding our own writings, if there be anything that can bring light to subterranean matters; since we study not for ourselves, but for the public good and wish to be of service.

To come then to the purpose. The aforementioned author establishes *certain stones of definite shape, and others of indefinite shape*; some he considers *doubtful*: to these he adds those which are usually numbered among stones, namely *animal stones* <note>This refers to fossils or stones formed inside biological organisms, such as bezoars or pearls</note>. Under the category of indefinite shape, he includes transparent, semi-transparent, and opaque stones. Among the *Transparent* ones he lists: the "watery" stones, such as the *Diamond* <note>original: "Adamas"</note> and *Crystal*; the *Reddish* ones, such as the *Ruby*, *Garnet*, *Hyacinth*, *Sardonyx*, and *Carbuncle*. The *Blue* ones, such as the *Sapphire*, *Amethyst*, and the *Hyacinth* of Pliny; the *green* ones such as the *Emerald* <note>original: "Smaragdus"</note>, *Beryl*, and the *Topaz* of the ancients. The *Yellow* ones, such as the *Chrysolite* of the ancients, the *Topaz* of the moderns, and *Xanthium* <note>A yellow gemstone mentioned in classical texts</note>. The *Black* ones, such as *Pramnium* <note>A black gemstone, possibly a variety of morion or obsidian</note>. The *White* ones, such as the *Bologna stone* <note>A variety of barite known for its phosphorescence after being heated</note>. The *Various* colored ones, such as the *Opal*, *Panderos* <note>A rare gem described by Pliny as having many colors</note>, the *Whetstone* <note>original: "lapis Novacularum"</note>, the mineral *Bezoar*, and various *fluors* <note>Fluorspars</note>. Among the *semi-transparent* stones, he places two types: some known to the ancients, others unknown. Among the *known* ones he lists *Sard*, *Chalcedony*, *Onyx*, *Agate*, *Jasper*, and *Heliotrope* <note>Also known as bloodstone</note>. To the *lesser known* he ascribes the *Nephritic stone* <note>Jade, traditionally used to treat kidney ailments</note>, the *colic stone*, the "berry" of the *Paraguayans* <note>likely a reference to a mineral or stone-like seed used by indigenous peoples of South America</note>, and the hailstone of *Worm* <note>Ole Worm (1588–1654), a Danish physician and collector of curiosities</note>. He distinguishes *Opaque stones* into the lesser and the greater; among the former he lists the *nobler* ones, and among the latter the *common* ones of various kinds or the less noble. Of the *noble* ones, the green are *Malachite* <note>original: "Molochites"</note>, *Callais*, and *Turquoise*. The *blue* are the *Sapphire* of Pliny, and the stone *Cyanus*

<meta>This page continues the classification of stones, moving from general definitions to a specific catalog of "opaque" stones—those that light cannot pass through—and stones that resemble natural or man-made objects. The author relies heavily on the works of ancient authorities like Pliny the Elder and Dioscorides, as well as early modern naturalists like Conrad Gessner and Ole Worm.</meta>
