**Lapis lazuli**, **Armenian stone**; **Lipis stone**. *Those that are white* are **Amianthus** <note>original: "Amianthus"; a type of asbestos or "mountain flax" that could be woven into fireproof cloth</note>, **mineral Toadstone** <note>original: "Bufonites mineralis"; these were traditionally believed to be found in the heads of toads, but are actually the fossilized teeth of ancient fish</note>, and **Callaimus** <note>likely a type of turquoise</note>. *Those that have their own specific color* are **Bloodstone** <note>original: "lapis sanguinalis"</note>, **Hand-stone** <note>original: "manualis"</note>, **Hysteric-stone** <note>used in traditional medicine to treat "hysteria" or womb ailments</note>, the **Itzlihuilotli of the Mixtecs**, the **Toltec-Itzli** <note>these are Nahuatl names for varieties of obsidian from the New World</note>, **Garatronius** <note>a mythical stone supposedly found in the bellies of birds</note>, **Pliny's serpent egg**, **Gessner's snake stone**, the **snake stone of the Bohemians**, **Eagle-stone** <note>original: "Aetites"; a geode with a loose stone inside that rattles, believed to be found in eagles' nests</note>, and the **Eye of the World** <note>original: "oculus mundi"; a type of hydrophane opal that becomes transparent when soaked in water</note>. *Among the less noble stones, some are red*, such as **Hematite**, **Schist** <note>a stone that easily splits into layers</note>, **Vermilion-stone**, and **Gold-sand stone**. *Others are white, such as* **Samian stone**, **Galaicos**, **Mirror-stone** <note>original: "specularis"; likely mica or selenite used for windows</note>, **Tufa** or **Tuff**, **Elban stone**, **Phrygian stone**, **Ageratus**, **Arabian stone**, **Galaxia**, **Milk-stone** <note>original: "Galactites"; so named because it produces a milky liquid when rubbed</note>, **Spongestone**, **Sulfur-stone**, **Sand-stone**, the **Oldenburg stone**, and **fossil white coral**. *Those that are green are* **Morochtus** <note>a type of French chalk or leech-stone</note>; *those of a rust-color* are **Emery** and **Magores**; *those of various colors* are **Gypsum-stone** and **Memphis-stone**; *and of their own color* are **Talc**, **Pumice**, **Water-stone**, **Spromus**, **Sarcophagus-stone** <note>a limestone believed to consume the flesh of the dead</note>, and **Honey-stone** <note>original: "Melitites"</note>.

Now that the minor opaque stones, both noble and ignoble, have been explained, the cited author approaches the *major opaque stones*, which he reduces to **marble**, **rock**, **flint**, and **whetstone**. Finally, he proceeds to stones of *certain shapes*, some of which he asserts represent the images of natural things, others of artificial things. Of the natural shapes, some belong to the *sublunary* world <note>the region below the moon, i.e., the Earth</note>; several of these resemble plants, parts of animals, or even of man himself. *Displayers of celestial things* are the **Star-stone** <note>original: "Astroites"</note>, the **true Thunderstones of Pliny** <note>original: "Ceraunia"; often prehistoric stone axes believed to have fallen from the sky during storms</note>, the **Moonstone of Pliny and Dioscorides**, the **Astrios**, the **Hildesheim stone**, and **Tephrites**. *Those in the form of sublunary things* are **Stalactites**, **Stalagmites**, **Indian Sardonyx**, and the **Caiman-stone**. *Those representing plants* are **coral**, **Jews' stone** <note>original: "lapis Judaicus"; fossilized spines of sea urchins</note>, **Worm’s Mushroom-stone**, **Nut-shaped stone**, **Pipe-stone** <note>original: "Syringites"; fossilized reeds or wood</note>, **Worm’s Indian stone**, and **Millet-stone**. *Parts of animals* are represented by the **Hawk-stone**, **Crane-stone**, **Partridge-stone**, **Eagle-stone**, and **Pigeon-stone**. *Parts of fish* are shown by the **Scale-stone**, **Turbot-stone**, **Star-caster**, **Ammonite** <note>the "Horn of Ammon"</note>, **Pea-stone**, **Millet-stone**, and **Poppy-stone**. *Parts of bloodless creatures <note>invertebrates</note> are exhibited by* **Oyster-stone**, **Pot-stone**, **Shell-stone**, **Porphyroides**, **Conch-stone**, **Megarian stone**, **Comb-stone**, **Muscle-stone**, **Trumpet-shell stone**, **Onyx-stone**, **Crab-stone**, and **Centipede-stone**. *Members of quadrupeds are presented by* the **Cat’s eye**, **Belus' eye**, **Wolf’s eye**, **Three-eye stone**, **Tongue-stone** <note>original: "Glossopetra"; fossilized shark teeth</note>, **Kidney-stone** <note>original: "lapis Renalis" or Nephrite</note>, **Horn-stone**, **Cross-bearer**, **Ammon’s horn**, **Bone-breaker**, **Testicle-stone**, **Earth-stone**, **Tortoise-stone**, **Bull’s-heart**, **Ox-tongue**, and **Snake-shaped stone**. *The parts of man are approached by* **Onyx** <note>resembling a fingernail</note>, **Venus’s navel**, **Womb-stone** <note>original: "Hysterolithus"; fossilized brachiopods resembling female anatomy</note>, **Double-natured stone**, **Idea-stones**, **Finger-stones**, **Pock-marked stone**, and **Tongue-like stones**. Thus far regarding stones presenting the shapes of natural things; now we shall consider those that imitate artificial shapes, some of which are round, hemispherical, cylinder-shaped, wedge-shaped, or display the idea of **wheels**, **arrows**, **plates**, **bread**, **staffs**, **nails**, **hats**, or **keys**. Thus far regarding stones of uncertain and certain shape.

Now the cited author reviews certain *doubtful* stones, for which he establishes a threefold division: some bear the appearance and shape of other things, some bear none, and some are not sufficiently described. Of the *shaped ones* are the **Amphitane**, **Acorn-stone**, **Date-stone**, **Altizoe**, **Hail-stone**, **Crocallis**, **Blue-stone**, **Heart-stone**, **Eumeces**, **Bud-stone**, **Frankincense-colored stone**, **Nympharena**, **Flame-stone**, **Seaweed-stone**, **Prontea**, **Bladder-stone**, **Ivy-stone**, **Narcissus-stone**, **Laurel-stone**, **Oak-gall stone**, **Fawn-skin stone**, **Cluster-of-grapes stone**, **Soapstone**, and the **Ant-stone**, **Lyre-stone**, **Falcon-stone**, and **Man-tamer**. *Those not shaped are distinguished by color, and indeed the white ones*, such as the **Sallius**, **Cimilianthus**, **Sun-gem**, **Lysimachus**, **Onion-stone**, **Erystalis**, **Cynedia**, **Corsoites**, **Antipathos**, and **Emites**. *Ash-colored stones such as* the **Galaticides**, **Sysinus**, **Thelerrhizos**, and **Painless-stone** <note>original: "Acopis"</note>. *Pale stones* such as the **Successor-stone** <note>original: "Diadochus"</note> and the **Golden-lamp**. *Reddish-white stones* such as the **Aphrodisiaca**, *lion-skin colored* like the **Agapis**, *silvery stones* like **Agyrites**, and **Crystalline**...

# Subterranean Physics

...crystalline like the **Amber-stone** <note>original: "Kakabre"</note>; glassy like the **Wood-stone** <note>original: "Lignites"</note> and **Zingnites**; wine-colored like the **Orphan-stone** <note>original: "orphanus"; a legendary opal described by Pliny as being unique and having no equal</note>, which is a species of opal; the **Etindros** and **Cambaites** are numbered among these. Clearly black are the **Opposite-feeling stone** <note>original: "Antipathos"</note>, **Sagda**, **Horcus**, **Catemia**, **Opicardelos**, **Middle-black stone** <note>original: "Mesomela"</note>, and **Copper-sounding stone** <note>original: "Chalcophonos"</note>. Near-black stones include the **Milk-stone** <note>original: "Galachites"</note> and **Eurotias**. Iron-colored stones include the **Sword-stone** <note>original: "Machæra"</note> and **Asbestos**; lurid or yellowish like the **Jaundice-stone** <note>original: "icterias"</note>; smoky like the **Capnites**. Some are black derived from white, like the **Egyptian-stone** <note>original: "Ægyptilla"</note> and **Lynx-stone** <note>original: "Lince"</note>; black with reddish veins like the **Dionysius-stone**; with gold-colored veins like the **Medea-stone**; with reddish veins like the **Unspotted-stone** <note>original: "Astictos"</note>; with red streaks like the **Wormwood-stone** <note>original: "Absinthus"</note>; with bloody and white nodes like the **Baroptis**; with white and bloody foliage like the **Borficites**; and with a white border like the **Vejentana**. There are those where lightning rays run from the center across a white or dark blue ground, like the **Lightning-stone** <note>original: "Astrapia"</note>. Green stones include the **Meadow-stone** <note>original: "Limoniaces"</note>, **Golden-wing** <note>original: "Chrysopterus"</note>, **Copper-emerald** <note>original: "Chalcosmaragdus"</note>, **Many-hair** <note>original: "Polytrix"</note>, **Cholo**, and **Dotro**. Leek-green stones include **Eumetres** and **Sagda**. Herb-like stones include **Chlorites** and **Gold-leek stone** <note>original: "Chrysophrasus"</note>; those turning pale from green like the **Gallerica**; green and gold like the **Horminodes**; and those with a golden glow like the **Choaspides**. Blue stones include the **Sky-colored stone** <note>original: "Cœlicolor"</note>; violet ones include the **Violet-stone** <note>original: "Jon"</note> and **Proconnesus**. Red stones include **Epistites**, **Gaditane**, and **Yettus**. Stones with bloody black veins include the **Nasomonites**; air-colored stones like **Ottonna** and **Chalaites**. Fire-colored stones include **Hormesion** and **Aspilates**. Amber-colored stones include **Zanthene**, **Myrites**, and the **Aroma-stone** <note>original: "Aromatites"</note>. Saffron-colored stones include the **Saffron-stone** <note>original: "Crocias"</note> and **Syrtites**. Vermilion-colored like the **Coral-stone** <note>original: "Corallis"</note>; gold-like like the **Filatericus**; tawny like the **Perithe**. Some are whitish-tawny like the **Yellow-stone** <note>original: "Xanthos"</note>; honey-colored like the **Honey-flesh stone** <note>original: "Mellichrotus"</note>; and wax-like stones like the **Wax-stone** <note>original: "Cerites"</note>. Multicolored stones include the **Sixty-stone** <note>original: "Hexacontalithos"</note>. Those the color of a panther's skin include **Kaman**, **Dew-stone** <note>original: "Drosolithus"</note>, and **Good-leaf** <note>original: "Eupetalos"</note>, etc. Finally, there are those known neither by shape nor color and which are not sufficiently described, such as **Ananchitis**, **Synochites**, **Baptes**, etc. The **animal stones** conclude the entire group; these are taken partly from aquatic creatures, birds, quadrupeds, and partly from man himself. From aquatic creatures we have **Pearls**, **shark-stones** <note>fossilized shark teeth, often called 'tongue stones'</note>, **Manatee stones**, **sea-breams**, **little crows**, **raven-stones**, **shade-fish stones**, **Tooth-shells** <note>original: "Dentalis"</note>, **Perch**, **Carp stones**, **Tooth-together stones** <note>original: "Synodontides"</note>, and **crab eyes** <note>calcium deposits found in the stomachs of crayfish, used in early medicine</note>. From quadrupeds are extracted **Bezoar** <note>stony concretions from the stomachs of goats and other grazers</note>, **Toad-stones** <note>original: "Batrachites"</note>, **pig-stones**, **Malacca stones**, **Bulgolda**, **wild ass gallstones**, **bear stones**, **Beaver stones**, and **deer stones**. From birds are obtained the **Rooster-stone** <note>original: "Alectorius"</note>, **Swallow-stone** <note>original: "Chelidonius"</note>, and **Wood-pigeon stone**. From the rest are taken the **Dragon-stone** <note>original: "Dracontias"</note>, **Snail-stone** <note>original: "Limacites"</note>, and the **stone of Cenar**; and in the various limbs of man, **stones** <note>original: "calculi"</note> are generated. So much for the general differences of stones; now we shall consider each by name in their specific types.

1. The **Diamond** <note>original: "Adamas"</note> was once thought to grow only in gold; it is said to be perfected in two years. The **Indian variety**, having a certain kinship with **Crystal**, is twisted with a six-angled smoothness into a point. Its hardness is believed to be inexpressible, and its nature is such that it conquers fire and never grows hot. The millet-sized variety is called the **millet-stone** <note>original: "cenchros"</note>; it has the shine of iron. The **Iron-stone** <note>original: "Sideritis"</note> is the heaviest of all, while the **Cyprian stone** leans toward a copper color. 2. **Crystal**, which competes with frozen ice, has a very soft body <note>compared to the diamond</note>, and its hexagonal smoothness of sides is so perfect that it cannot be matched by any art. Pure and faultless ones are called **acenteta** <note>Greek for "without prick" or flawless</note>; transparent ones are **mountain crystals**; darker ones, and those that reflect colors when applied to the forehead, are **Rainbow-stones** <note>original: "Irides"</note>. Harder ones are called **false-diamonds**; some have a very hard and brittle center.

<margin>

5.
</margin>
3. The **Ruby** is first white in its rose-colored matrix, but soon, when it has matured, it reddens and appears with a tiny portion of blue. The **Balas-ruby** <note>original: "Ballassius seu Pallacius"</note> is the "mother of the ruby," tinted with a very diluted crimson. **Spinel** is redder. The final spark of the **Rubicells** <note>original: "Rubanorum seu Rubicellorum"</note> usually turns yellow, and its body is not sufficiently hardened against fire. 4. The **Garnet**, from its yellowness, is like fire...

### Book 1, Section 6, Chapter 2

4. If the redness of cinnabar is excessive, it is called **Soriana**; if it has the yellowish tint of the **Hyacinth** <note>original: "Hyacinthi"; likely referring here to a reddish-orange zircon or garnet</note>, it is considered a species of that stone. If it is streaked with the color of the **March Violet** <note>original: "Martiolæ Violæ"</note>, it is called **Rock Ruby** <note>original: "Rubino de la Roccha"</note>, perhaps an **Amethyst-like Carbuncle** <note>original: "Carbunculus Amethystizon"</note>. **Bohemian stones** <note>original: "Bohemici"; these are Bohemian garnets</note> are imbued with a deep redness, and unless they are hollowed out, they appear black. **Alabandic Almandines** <note>original: "Almandini Alabandici"</note> are carbuncles, as are **Troizenian Amandines** <note>original: "Amandini Troëzenii"</note>. 5. The **Hyacinth**—at least of the more recent variety—reflects the color of very bilious blood, which is considered the best; it turns yellowish with the redness of **saffron** <note>original: "croci"</note> in cheaper varieties; the yellow of **amber** <note>original: "succini"</note> is the cheapest of all, as it is not even translucent. 6. The **Sardonyx**, if it is the Indian variety, is understood to have the whiteness of the **Sard** <note>original: "Sarda"; carnelian</note>: that is, like a human fingernail placed over flesh, with both being translucent. The surface of the Sard is the root of the onyx, or vice-versa. "Blind" stones are those that are not translucent. In the **Arabic** variety, the root is black, or imitating dark blue, with the "nail" being a cinnabar-red mixed into a fatty white, not without a certain hint of Purple passing into the red. 7. The **Carbuncle** <note>original: "Carbunculus"; known as "anthrax" or "pyropus" meaning fire-stone</note> resembles fire and shines even in the dark. The **male** variety has a clearer flame, while the **female** has a more languid glow; they both cast their brilliance far outside themselves. The faint spark at the edge of the **Amethyst-like** <note>original: "Amethystizonton"</note> variety fades into the violet of an Amethyst. The **Sirtitæ** radiate with a feathery brilliance. The **Indian** stones are parched in appearance, and if any of them are more leaden, they are called **Stone-like** <note>original: "Lithizontes"</note>. The **Carthaginian** <note>original: "Carchedonii"</note> stones have a blacker appearance but are more sharply excited by a tilt of the stone. Of its relatives, the **Anthracite** <note>original: "Anthracites"</note> is girdled by a white vein; it is extinguished and "dies" in fire, but when soaked in water, it blazes up. In the **Sun-stone** <note>original: "Sandastro"</note>, golden sparkling drops inside imitate the **Hyades** stars in both number and position. The **Sandaresos** (also called **Sandasr** or **Sandaseros**) is of lower value than the former. The **Lamp-stone** <note>original: "Lychnitis"</note> is a milder carbuncle, particularly favored for its beauty when lamps are lit. The **Ionian** variety radiates with a certain purple, another with scarlet.

<margin>Note 6</margin>
8. The **Sapphire** <note>original: "Sapphirus"; also called "Thalassites" or sea-stone</note>—understand here the more recent variety—is either a very saturated dark blue or diluted and **Watery** <note>original: "Hydarestheros"</note>. Whitish and milk-colored stones, or those with only a little blue mixed in, are degenerate; their color is even removed by fire. 9. The **Amethyst** shines with a violet light, such that the **Indian** variety has the perfect color of royal purple and presents a gently charming appearance. A second type declines toward the hyacinth color, called **Sacodion** by the Indians; a third is more diluted, the **Sapinos** (also called **Paranites**); a fourth is the color of wine; a fifth descends toward the appearance of Crystal, with a whitish purple in its depths, called **Prederota** by some, **Anterotæ** by others, and the **Gem of Venus**. 10. In Pliny’s **Hyacinth**, the brilliance of the amethyst is diluted; it is pleasing at first sight but fades before it satisfies, and it does not "fill the eyes" so much as barely touch them, withering more quickly than the flower of its name. The **Sea-stone** <note>original: "Thalassites"</note> has the color of a wave. The **Rose-stone** <note>original: "Rhodenos"</note> imitates roses; the **Natibos** plays between rose and a more diluted tint; the **Watery** <note>original: "Hydarestheros"</note> variety (also called **Chaunaios** or **White-edged** <note>original: "perileukos"</note>) verges more toward whiteness.

<margin>Note 7</margin>
11. Of the **Emerald** <note>original: "Smaragdo"; also called "Prasinus", "Neronianus", or "Domitianus"</note>, nothing at all is greener when compared to anything else. Its appearance is amplified from a distance, tinting the reflected air around it; it always radiates gently due to its thickness and its easy translucency. None have greater sharpness than the **Scythian** variety; the **Cyprian** loses its color but takes a keen edge, sometimes appearing sea-gray. The **Herminean** stones swell with a rich oiliness. The **Persian** ones radiate but cannot be seen through. The **Attic** ones are more beautiful from a distance. The **Median** ones are wavy and contain images of things. The **Carthaginian** or **Chalcedony** stones are of uncertain color, veined and scaly. There is also a stone called **Cholos** or rather **Chloros** <note>original: "green"</note>, the **Copper-emerald** <note>original: "Chalcosmaragdus"</note>, which is clouded with bronze-colored veins, and the **False-emerald** from which spheres are made. That which is bound with white veins is called the **Milk-stone** <note>original: "Galactites"</note>. 12. **Beryls** imitate the greenness of the pure sea; unless their dull color is excited by the reflection of their angles, they grow faint, the paler ones turning toward a gold—

# Subterranean Physics

...with a brightness, they are **Chrysoberyls** <note>literally "golden beryls"</note>; those that are paler and perhaps of their own kind are **Chrysoprases** <note>a leek-green variety of chalcedony</note>, followed by the **Hyacinth-like** stones, the air-colored ones, the **Waxy** ones, the **Olive-colored** ones, and those resembling **Crystals**. 13. To the **Topaz** of the ancients belongs the greenness of fresh oil, retaining a golden brilliance; it is the largest of gems and the only noble one that feels the file <note>it is soft enough to be worked with metal tools</note> and is worn down by use. The whole appearance of the **Prasoid** 
<margin>N. 8.</margin> is directed toward the juice of a leek. In the **Chrysopter** <note>literally "golden-winged"</note>, the brightness issues forth into a color similar to gold. 14. The **Chrysolite** <note>literally "golden stone"</note> of the ancients, when compared to gold, forces it to appear white with a certain silver appearance. It inclines toward the color of amber when the **Chryselectrum** <note>literally "golden amber"</note> is present with a white vein. The **Leucochrysos** <note>literally "white gold"</note> appears as if pure honey is translucent through gold; the **Mellichrysos** <note>literally "honey gold"</note> is similar. There is also the **Capnias** <note>literally "smoky stone"</note>, and that which is similar to glass, shining like saffron. In the **Arabic** varieties, the brightness is interrupted by a cloud of spots. 15. The **Topaz** of the moderns, if Oriental, glows like the purest gold, less hard 
<margin>N. 9.</margin> only than the diamond; if from elsewhere <note>the text repeats 'orientalis' likely in error for 'occidentalis'</note>, it blackens slightly with gold and is softer than **Crystal**. 16. The **Xanthum** or **Xantha** 
<margin>N. 10.</margin> <note>literally "yellow stone"</note> is a common gem, pale yellow in color. 17. The **black** gem is the Indian **Morion**, which is called **Pramnian**, and specifically the **Alexandrian** kind; if the color of a carbuncle is mixed in, it is called **Sardium**, or if mixed with **Sard** <note>carnelian</note>. 18. **White** or bright is the **Bologna Stone** or **Lithophosphorus** 
<margin>N. 11.</margin> <note>literally "light-bearing stone"; a form of barite famous for its phosphorescence</note>, having a clarity almost like **Crystal**, the weight of lead, and containing white streaks radiating from the center to the circumference like a star. When calcined <note>heated to a high temperature</note> and exposed to the sun or a flame, it receives light without heat and gives it back to the sight in the dark. 19. In the **Opal** there is the thinner fire of the **Carbuncle**, the shining purple of the **Amethyst**, the green sea of the **Emerald**, and all these things shining equally in an incredible mixture. That which encloses a light like a star wandering within is the **Astroites** <note>star-stone</note>. That which is similar to the eyes of fish and shows a hint of blue like milk is the **Pseudopalus** <note>false opal</note>. 20. The **Paederos** (which the Indians call **Sangenon** and **Argenon**) mimics the grace of the eye, but more softly, and is rarely not rough. It lacks the supreme greenness of the **Emerald** derived from air and purple. 21. **Whetstones** (called **Ihli**) boast of blue, white, and black; they return the 
<margin>N. 12.</margin> images of things and are translucent in their white parts. 22. Mineral **Bezoar** <note>original: "pietra d'aventura"; likely aventurine glass or quartz</note>. 23. **Fluors** <note>Fluorites</note> are similar to gems, but yielding in hardness; they are red, or diluted purple, blue, yellow, ash-colored, or blackish; they melt in a metallic fire. 24. The **Sard** <note>original: "Sarda Carneolus"; carnelian</note> sometimes clings to the heart of a rock, resembling a small cloud like the washings of meat. The **males** shine more excitedly; the **females** are richer and shine more thickly. The **Red Indian** variety is called **Disemos** because of its size; it does not hold a piece of wax in a seal <note>it doesn't stick to the wax</note>. There is the **Polia** which brings a certain grayness to the Sard, and the **Spardopolios**, which is the same but rarer and black among its kin. 25. The **Chalcedony** turns from white to a diluted blue, so that if it is of the best quality, it shines with a truly dull paleness; it is distinguished by milky zones or covered by a smoky cloud if it is of inferior quality. 26. The **Onyx** was once defined as that which has many various veins with milky zones, with an inexpressible color in the transitions, returning to a single harmony with a pleasing sweetness. Now, it refers to those which show zones of various colors distinctly superimposed on one another, with the luster of a human fingernail in the underlying layer. When a white zone is carved with an image, or a black one is placed underneath, it is called **Memphites** or **Camahuia** <note>cameo</note>. 27. The **Agate** is marked by a numerous variety of lines and spots, which display forests, rivers, trees, and even men themselves. That which is marked like a small tree is the **Dendrachates** <note>tree agate</note>; that which is distinguished by golden drops is the **Coralloachates**; that which resembles a lion's skin is called the **Leonine** agate. There are also the **Phassachates**, **Cerachates**, **Sardachates**, **Hemachates**, and **Leucachates**...

# Book I. Section VI. Chapter III.

28. In **Jasper**, there is the same variety of colors as in other gems, but it is less intense, possessing a dusty roughness and a hardness that prevents it from being exactly polished. The variety girded by a transverse white line is the **Grammatias** <note>literally "lined stone" from the Greek *gramme*</note>; that with several lines is the **Polygrammos** <note>literally "many-lined"</note>. The **Onychipuncta** <note>nail-spotted</note> contains a cloud and imitates snow, while the **Jasponyx** <note>Jasper-Onyx</note> appears as if stained with smoke and is called **Capnias** <note>literally "smoky"</note>. The **Terebinthian**, **Airy**, and **Cross-bearing** jaspers also owe their names to their color and shape. 29. The **Heliotrope** <note>literally "sun-turner," commonly known as bloodstone</note> bears blood-red points on a dark green body.

<margin>N.</margin>
30. The **Nephritic stone** <note>Jade or Nephrite, traditionally used for kidney ailments</note> is truly a darker **Emerald**, but it sometimes varies with tiny white points and always has a surface that seems as if it were anointed with oil.

<margin>13.</margin>
31. The **Colic stone** is green without any points; when sprinkled with the "saliva of colic" <note>likely referring to its mottled pattern or its use in drawing out "colic" humors</note> and applied to the navel, it is a remedy. 32. The **Paraguayan Grain** (also called the **Crystalline Belly** or the **Gemmed Eagle-stone**) has the appearance of a thick sausage; on the outside, it is a mixture of impure red and white, but when polished, it is of the same color as the best **Chalcedony** and is hollow in its center. It bursts spontaneously when empty and emits a great cracking sound. 33. **Worm’s Hailstone** <note>Named for the Danish scholar Ole Worm (1588–1654), who described these stones as falling from the sky</note> falls during thunder and lightning along with hail of unusual size; it is snow-colored, similar to chalk but harder, and armored with a glassy crust.

<margin>N.</margin>
34. **Malachite** and **Callais** (also called **Callaina**): the former is a denser green like a fresh mallow plant, if it is of good quality. <margin>14.</margin> In poorer specimens, white veins run through it, sometimes with black spots, or a blue color is distinctly intermixed. The latter [Callais] is a pale green, closest to the **Emerald**; it bulges in the shape of an eye on inaccessible and icy cliffs and adheres lightly, not as if born from the rocks but as if placed upon them. 35. The **Turquoise** (known to some as **Turchesia**, **Turquesia**, **Turcosa**, or **Turchina**, and to some followers of Pliny as **Boreas**, **Callais**, or **Airy Jasper**) has the color of copper rust; however, in the Eastern variety, it tends toward blue rather than green, while in the Western variety, it is either whiter or greener. It preserves its color if taken from an old rock but loses it if from a new one. 36. The **Sapphire** rarely shines with purple and golden points; however, it is never transparent and is useless for carving; the "masculine" variety has crystalline centers running through it. The **Oriniscos** <note>literally "mountain-like"</note> scattered with golden points is the **Chrysopastos** <note>gold-sprinkled</note>. 37. In **Cyanus** <note>an azure stone, likely Lapis Lazuli</note>, golden dust is sometimes present. 38. In **Lapis Lazuli**, there are golden points and little flames; the Eastern variety is resistant to fire, while the Western variety yields and is resolved into powder. 39. In **Armenian stone** <note>Azurite</note>, there is a blue tint within the green, with no golden veins and no tolerance for fire. With age, it degenerates into green. 40. In **Lapis Lipis**, there are glinting sparks like silver, and it has a biting taste.

<margin>N.</margin>
41. **Amianth** (also called **Carystian stone**, **Asbestos**, **Bostrichites**, **Corsoides**, or **Iscultos**) is similar to alum; it is fibrous, soft, white, and greenish. <margin>15.</margin> It loses nothing in fire; it "blooms" when rubbed into downy feathers and is prepared into threads; when polished, it shines like ivory. It is also called **Entalium** and **Sweet Amentum**. 42. The **Mineral Toadstone** is the color of a medlar fruit, a whitish-gray, sometimes with the shape of an eye in the middle, or a very fine white or black circle. It grows on high rocks along shores and cliffs lashed by the sea. 43. In **Callaimus**, part is transparent like crystal and part is cloudy like **Sard**; it is sometimes found in a large geode, and even contains wonderful images.

<margin>N.</margin>
44. The **Bloodstone** is distinguished by blood-red spots. 45. The **Hand-stone** heals cracks in the hands and feet. <margin>16.</margin> 46. The **Hysteric stone** is black, heavy, and for the most part smooth and round; placed on the navel of the womb, it brings comfort. 47. The **Izlihuilotli of the Mixtecs** <note>A Nahuatl name for a stone from the Mixtec region of Mexico, likely obsidian</note> is very black and, when polished, serves as an ornament. 48. The **Toltec-Izli** is variegated with black and red points. 49. **Garatronio** has markings like Arabic characters, golden in color on a purple background. 50. The **Snake’s Egg** of Pliny, found in the great [lands] of the Gauls...

--- Page 333 ---
<meta>This page continues the catalog of stones and fossils, specifically completing the description of the "Gemmed Eagle-stone" or "Paraguayan Grain" before moving into the legendary snake eggs of the Druids and other curative or "living" stones.</meta>

...the fame of which <note>original: "rum fama," likely completing "Druidarum fama," the fame of the Druids</note>, though omitted by the Greeks, is that of a stone the size of a modest round apple, encased in a cartilaginous crust and covered in numerous little cups like the suckers on the arms of a polyp; it is the celebrated badge of a **Druid**. Innumerous snakes, coiled together in the summer, are said to be gathered into a mass by the skillful intertwining of their bodies and the froth of their mouths and jaws. This may perhaps be a turtle's egg hardened into stone. § 1. **Gesner's Snake Egg** <note>named for Conrad Gesner, the famous 16th-century naturalist</note> has a lenticular or hemispherical shape, of a whitish-brown color, but bright white inside; its outer crust is flinty, and from its flat base, it has "tails" like those of snakes or lizards. § 2. The **Bohemian Snake Stone** is actually glass; for this reason, women use it as a whorl for drawing out threads during spinning. § 3. The **Eagle-stone** <note>original: "Ætites," a stone traditionally believed to be found in eagle nests</note> is said to be found in the nests of eagles; it has a great reputation, based on the theory that it can either promote or delay childbirth. The variety from the East, called **Callimus**, is "pregnant" <note>containing a smaller stone that rattles inside</note>; the female variety is ashy, made of clay or marl, and both types are rough. The **Taphiusian** variety has a bright whiteness and a round face. The **Saxon** variety is marked by little cells on its surface. § 4. The **Eye of the World** <note>original: "Oculus Mundi," likely a variety of hydrophane opal</note> is the size of a pea and the color of ivory; when thrown into clear water, it immediately begins to turn translucent and shine, starting from the edge and moving to the center, until the whole stone glows. Once removed, it gradually loses its light.

<margin>No. 17.</margin>
55. **Hematite** <note>literally "Bloodstone"</note> is darker than blood, looking as if iron filings were mixed with native red lead. The **Androdamas** <note>literally "man-tamer"</note> is black and notably heavy, and it yields a blood-like juice. The **Elatites** is useful for burns as long as it is raw; when cooked, it is called **Miltites**. Once roasted, it imitates the color of red lead. 56. **Schiston** <note>Split-stone</note> is distinguished by reddish veins and is composed of transparent layers. While it is naturally blackish, the variety resembling saffron is more highly prized, for it shines with a peculiar brilliance. 57. The **Red-Lead Stone** or **Cinnabar** <note>the primary ore of mercury</note> declines from a purple hue toward red; it is remarkably heavy and is the host to "living silver" <note>quicksilver or mercury</note>. In its pure form, it has the luster of scarlet; the "secondary" variety's brilliance is sensitive to the dampness on walls. Obtaining the **Ephesian Cinnabar** from the **Cilbian** fields was a labor of great effort. The Spanish soil was known for it by the most ancient peoples.

<margin>No. 18.</margin>
58. **Ammochrysos** <note>literally "gold-sand"</note> or **Aurenius** has the color of native red lead, sometimes with a yellowish sandy substance that appears sprinkled with gold dust. 59. The **Samian Stone** is whiter and harder; a blackish variety of fossil ivory is called **Exhibenus**. 60. **Pliny’s Galaicos** is perhaps related and similar to **Argyrodamas** <note>silver-tamer</note>, but dirtier. 61. The **Mirror Stone** <note>original: "Specularis," likely Muscovite mica or Selenite</note> is transparent like crystal, flexible, and very easily split into the thinnest sheets; it is easily baked into gypsum. 62. **Porus** or **Tufa** (also called **Chernites**) is sometimes equal to Parian marble in color and hardness, yet it is rough and harsh, easily resolving into sand. There is also a soft, black, and "veber" variety. 63. **Pliny’s Elban Stone** is perhaps **Acapis**, similar to nitre, pumice-like, and starred with golden drops. 64. The **Phrygian Stone** is a pumiceous clod, pale and distinguished by white lines; it is considered the best of its kind but is unknown today. 65. **Ageratus** is not dissimilar to this and is used by tanners. 66. The **Arabian Stone** is very similar to spotted ivory, and would be mistaken for it if its hardness did not prove otherwise. 67. The **Galaxia** <note>Galaxy-stone</note> from the Nile is notable for its milky color, juice, and taste; it is also called **Leucogæa** <note>white-earth</note> and **Smectis**. 68. The **Galactites** <note>Milk-stone</note> is ashy but emits a sweet, milky juice. 69. The **Sponge-stone** <note>original: "Spongites"</note>, called by some **Terolithus**, is found inside sponges; it is white, crumbly, and resolves into a similar juice. 70. In the **Sulfur-stone**, certain particles radiate with a golden color; while burning, it shoots out sulfurous sparks. 71. **Sandstone** <note>original: "Sabuli"</note> is usually a dusty ash color but sometimes very white; it is easily ground into a very fine powder with an iron tool. 72. The **Aldenbergius** stone breathes the scent of violets, whether it is white on the outside and ashy within, or reddish.

<margin>No. 19.</margin>
73. **White Fossil Coral** is sometimes **branched** and juts out in various ways; sometimes it is jointed, with a branched surface, and sometimes...

### Book I. Section VI. Chapter III.

...rough and unformed. 74. **Morochtus** <note>original: "Morochtus," also known as *moroclis* or *leukographis*</note>, which is leek-green, shines, and "sweats" a milk-like liquid; and **Thyites** <note>original: "Thyites" or *Thoites*</note>, which is somewhat green with the appearance of Jasper and pours out a biting juice. 75. **Emery** <note>original: "Smyris"</note> and **Magnetite** <note>original: "Magores"</note>. The former is used for carving gems due to its hardness; the latter tends from a rusty color toward blue and is a wonder of the world for its attraction, its polarity <note>original: "verticitate," the ability to point North</note>, its inclination, and its noble variation. Iron is drawn by the magnet and takes on its character; that substance, the master of all things, runs toward some unknown void, and as it comes closer, it stops, is held, and clings in an embrace. There are both black and bright varieties; a white magnet <margin>N. 20.</margin> inscribed with black lines is called the **White Loadstone** <note>original: "Calamita alba"</note>. A stone that repels iron is called **Theamedes**, and one said to attract gold is called **Pantarbas**. 76. **Gypsum Stone** and **Memphite Stone**. From the former, lime is shaped and made, from which we get gypsum. The latter is fatty, about the size of pebbles; when smeared on, it numbs the limbs <note>Ancient authors claimed this stone could act as a local anesthetic during surgery</note>. 77. **Talc** <margin>N. 21.</margin> <note>original: "Talcum," also called "Star of the Earth," *Argyrodamas* or "Silver-tamer," and the *Selenitis* of Dioscorides</note> shines like the stars with a silvery luster; it is composed of very thin layers and is everlasting even in fire. 78. **Pumice** <note>original: "Pumex," also called the stone of Scyros, the Tyrrhenian stone of Vulcan, or rock-foam</note> is the dregs and froth of stones that have been melted and burnt; it is full of little tubes and floats on water. 79. **Water-stone** <note>original: "Hydrolithus"</note> usually grows in caves from dripping juices or in water-channels from sediment. 80. **Spromus Stone** is first yellowish and later ash-colored; it is spongy and soaks up water, which is then squeezed out drop by drop as if distilled. 81. **Sarcophagus** or **Assian Stone** is split along a flaky vein; it is known that the bodies of the dead are consumed in it within forty days, except for the teeth. 82. **Honey-stone** <note>original: "Melitites"</note> is the color of honey and gives off a sweet juice when used. 83. **Marble** <note>original: "Marmor"</note> is of a purer substance and is likewise <margin>N. 22.</margin> very hard; it takes on a shine if polished. It regrows in the mines once excavated and hardens over the passage of time. *If it is grainy or rough*, it shatters like flint while being carved. A hard spot like a nail-head is called the **center**; from this we also get the term "central shavings." The **Parian** variety shines, which as **Lychnites** <note>from the Greek *lychnos*, meaning lamp</note> radiates with luster, especially if it is translucent. This is Pliny’s **Phengites**, which sometimes has yellowish veins. **Coralliticum** is found in sizes no larger than two cubits; its whiteness is very close to ivory, sharing a certain likeness. **Alabaster** <note>original: "Alabastrites"</note> is a little softer than the others and is the first stage of marble's development. It is most prized when honey-colored, spotted at the top, and not translucent. **Augustan marble** is somewhat curled with waves at the top. **Tiberian marble** is scattered with greyish coils. **Basalt** <note>original: "Basalies" or "Basanites"</note> has the color and hardness of iron. **Obsidian stone** is sometimes translucent but with a denser vision, and in wall mirrors, it reflects shadows instead of a clear image. **Lydian stone** <note>original: "Lapis Lydius," also called *Basanus*, *Chrysitis*, or the *Coticula* (Touchstone)</note> is the color of iron or sometimes red; it is used to test gold and silver. The best kind is that which immediately "sweats" from a person's breath and then clears the cloud. **Porphyry** <note>original: "Porphyrites"</note> is red; if it has white spots or "bran" scattered through it, it is called **Leucostictos** <note>white-spotted</note>, or rather **Leptosephos**. If defiled with black spots, it is **Hyenites** or **Stygmites** and **Psaronium**. If it is sprinkled with golden drops, it is **Thebaic**; if its appearance inclines more toward purple, it is **Alabandic**. The green variety is of the most precious kind and more cheerful than all others, known as **Lacedaemonian** <note>Spartan</note> marble. That which is like the spots of serpents is **Ophites**; one spotted with an ash color is **Tephrias**. That which shows the appearance of eggs in its spots is **ovate**; that which mimics the shape of lice is called **Pediculate**; and that tinted with various colors is called **Maculose** <note>spotted</note>. You will sometimes find within these stones the image of a dog, a cat, birds, fish, a man, a Hermit, a Monk—indeed, even the Crucified One, the Mother of God, cities, and letters. 84. **Rock** <note>original: "Saxum"</note> differs from marble only in its more impure matter...

-># Subterranean Physics<-

...descends, and often contains shells and flints: the protrusions are called **ledges**. **Sandstone** <note>original: "Arenarium"</note> is composed of coarse and very fine sands. **Crusty** or **fissile stone** <note>original: "Crustosum seu scissile"; perhaps what was once called *Spinus*</note> splits into layers useful for tiles and roofs. **Mud-stone** <note>original: "Limosum"</note> is the **beginning** of future rock; it is easily dissolved back into mud. **Tufa** <note>original: "Tophaceum"</note> is sometimes so soft within the earth that it can be cut with a saw. **Limestone** <note>original: "Calcarium"</note>, when roasted, provides lime for cement. **Millstone** <note>original: "Molare"</note> consists of small flints and finer sand. **Como stone** <note>original: "Comense," also called "stone of Como," "pot-stone," or "serpent-stone"</note> is spongy, green, and sprinkled with white spots that radiate with silver glints; little vessels are turned from it with such thinness that they are almost flexible <note>original: "ductilia," suggesting they are as workable as metal</note>. **Pholas-stone** <note>original: "Pholadis"</note> is dusky-white in color, rough, and cavernous but not porous all the way through; it is also called **pholadion** or **pholetyrion** <note>These names refer to stones containing the remains or burrows of Pholas, a type of boring mollusk</note>. **Barnacle-stone** <note>original: "Balani"</note> is an intense ash-gray, smoothed, with no trace of a hole on the outside but filled with barnacle-shaped fossils within. **Lesser stone** <note>original: "Minus"</note> is properly the name for stone of more impure material, rough, porous, and capable of taking any color. **Soft stones** among these are entirely useless for buildings because of their "mortality of softness" <note>original: "mortalitate mollitiei," meaning they perish or crumble due to their lack of hardness</note>. They are worn away by the breath of the sea, rubbed by the wind, and beaten by rains. If any are workable in a project, they can only endure labor when kept under a roof. **Travertine** <note>original: "Tiburtini"</note>, though strong for other purposes, shatters when exposed to steam. **River-stones** always seem as if they are moist. **Round stones** are strong against injury but unreliable for structures unless bound together by many supports. The **Mushroom-bearer** <note>original: "Fungifer"</note> has a thick crust; when sprinkled with warm water, it yields mushrooms on the fourth day. 

85. **Flint** <note>original: "Silex"</note> is the hardest kind of stone and one that does not "drink" lime <note>it does not bond well with mortar</note>; it is tinted by nature with various but obscure colors. It is the material for glass and artificial gems; if it is translucent and white, it is generally meltable. **Fire-stone** <note>original: "Pyrimachus"</note>: if it is hard, it fosters a "silent liquid of fire" <note>sparks</note> within itself. **Pyrite** <note>original: "Pyrites"</note>: if it turns black but shows a silver smoothness in bands, it is called **Silver-black** <note>original: "Argyromelanos"</note>. 

86. **Whetstones** <note>original: "Cos"</note> among the working stones can be black, white, green, reddish, yellow, or variegated. Among the **water-whetstones**, which are also called **wheel-stones** or **rotating stones**, the highest praise was once given to those from Naxos. Stones have been found in Italy that sharpen an edge with the keenest effect when using water; there are also those they call *passernices*. **Laconian stones** require oil; **Flaminitan stones** require saliva. These are useful to men, and because they are moistened in barbershops, they are called **Salivary-stones** <note>original: "Salivariæ dies," likely a reference to the tools used for daily grooming</note>. For **Oil-stones**, which are also called "Crotic oil-stones," engravers use them to wear down chisels and gravers. **Eye-stones** are used to grind down **eye-salves** <note>original: "Collyria"</note>. 

87. <margin>N. 23.</margin> **Star-stone** <note>original: "Asterias" or "Astroites"</note> exactly represents stars, sometimes roses, or the swirls of worms and tails, though often these spots are confused. 

88. In the **true star-stone** or **stellar stone**, the layers are placed so that they can be separated from one another. The rays stand out with their own angles, there is a cavity in the middle, and the margins are furrowed with transverse streaks. 

89. **Pliny’s Star-stone** <note>original: "Asteria Plinii"</note> is nearly white; it contains an enclosed light like a pupil and pours it out when tilted, as if the light were walking inside, reappearing from one place to another. 

90. **Thunder-stone** <note>original: "Ceraunia"</note>, found among the white stones, catches the glow of the stars and has a star running around inside it. 

91. **Pliny’s Selenite** <note>original: "Selenites Plinii"</note> is translucent white and contains the image of the moon, which it renders daily according to the moon's increasing and decreasing phases. 

92. **Dioscorides’ Selenite** <note>original: "Selenites Dioscoridis," also called *kupholitos*, *Aphroselenus*, or by some, **Talc**</note> is white, hollow, and smooth; it is found to be fuller and more solid during the waxing of the moon. 

93. **Star-gem** <note>original: "Astros"</note> is close to Crystal; it shines from the center with the glow of a full moon. 

94. **Hildesheim Stone** <note>original: "Lapis Hildesheimensis"</note> bears the appearance of a new moon curved into horns; it is covered in a gold-colored armor and is sometimes streaked. 

95. **Ash-stone** <note>original: "Tephrites" or "Menois"</note> has the form of a crescent and horned moon. 

96. <margin>N. 24.</margin> **Stalactite** <note>original: "Stalactites"</note> is the progeny of water falling from on high, similar to icicles, shaped into a pyramid...

...ending in the same way, white and transparent. 97. **Stalagmite** <note>original: *Stalagmites*</note>, which is formed from round drops hardened in dense earth, the size of peas or coriander; often many are found in a single mass, enclosed as if in honeycombs. 98. **Indian Sardonyx** <note>original: *Sardonyci*</note> has a base like wax or horn, with white circles and a certain imitation of a rainbow; its surface resembles locusts <note>This likely refers to a speckled or segmented pattern</note> and is redder than the crusts of the sea. 99. **Caiman Stone** <note>original: *Lapis Caymanum*</note>, a rival to river pebbles and a ward against quartan fever <note>A form of malaria where fever recurs every fourth day</note>, is found in the stomachs of crocodiles. 100. **Coral** <note>original: *Corallum*; also called *Lithodendron* ("stone-tree"), *Dendritis* ("tree-like"), or *Gorgonius*</note> which has the appearance of a shrub and is often the height of a man; its color varies before it turns to stone, and its primary material is like wood. In the **Warty False-Coral** <note>original: *Pseudo-corallo verrucario*</note>, the surface is marked with lines and frequent warts that contain small blisters. 101. **Jew's Stone** <note>original: *Lapis Judacius*; also known as *Syrian*, *Aetio*, *Phœnician*, *Pyrene*, *Thecolithos*, *Eurhæus*, or *Cisteolithos*</note> is shaped like an olive, with stripes drawn along its length as if on a lathe; it is white and somewhat ash-colored. <note>These are actually the fossilized spines of sea urchins</note>. 102. **Worm's Mushroom-stone** <note>original: *Fungites Wormii*, named after the Danish naturalist Ole Worm</note>, in which the stripes are partly deep and partly prickly like a sea urchin, ending in a small scale; it has the shape of a mushroom. 103. **Nut-shaped Stone** <note>original: *Nuciformis*</note>, which resembles a nutmeg in substance, with the pulp inside variegated with yellow. 104. **Pipe-stone** <note>original: *Syringites*</note>, which is similar to the joint of a straw and is hollowed out by a continuous tube. 105. **Worm's Indian Stone** <note>original: *Indicus Wormii*</note> is categorized among the **Agates**. 106. **Millet-stone** <note>original: *Cenchrites*</note>, which displays what looks like scattered grains of millet; there are also stones that playfully mimic the shapes of **Eagle-wood**, **Sandalwood**, tree trunks, small gourds, melons, pinecones, peaches, chestnuts, cashews, wheat, peas, pepper, lentil seeds, and turnips. 107. Among those presenting the shapes of birds <margin>N.</margin> is the **Hawk-stone** <note>original: *Hieracites*</note>, which alternates between the feathers of a kite and black feathers. The **Crane-stone** <note>original: *Geranites*</note> mimics the eye of a crane. The **Partridge-stone** <note>original: *Perdicites*</note> expresses the feathers of partridges through its stripes and <margin>25.</margin> color. The **Eagle-stone** <note>original: *Aetites*; distinct from the one mentioned previously</note> has the color of an eagle with a white tail. The **Dove-stone** <note>original: *Peristerites*</note> resembles a dove in its head, beak, feet, breast, and tail, though it lacks the markings of wing feathers. 108. Among those resembling fish, <margin>N.</margin> there is the **Scaly-stone** <note>original: *Lepidotes*</note>, which imitates scales in various colors. The **Rhomb-stone** <note>original: *Rhombites*</note> is white and the size of a chestnut; it is full of small, oblique scales protruding on all sides. <margin>26.</margin> 109. The **Fish-eye Stone** <note>original: *Astrobotos* or *Astrolos*</note> is similar to the eyes of fish when set against a white ground. The **Ammonite** <note>original: *Ammonites* or *amites*</note>, which is composed of sands, is the size of a walnut and resembles fish eggs. That which consists of stones the size of a pea or vetch is called **Pea-stone** <note>original: *Pisolithos*</note>; that which resembles millet is **Millet-stone** <note>original: *Cenchrites*</note>; and that resembling poppy seeds is called **Poppy-stone** <note>original: *Meconites*</note>. 110. **Oyster-stone** <note>original: *Ostracites* or *lithostreos*</note> resembles oysters, being crusty and easy to split; <margin>N.</margin> it gives off the sound of a pot when struck. It is called **Pottery-stone** <note>original: *Ceramites*</note> because it has the color of a clay shard; <margin>27.</margin> it is called **Cheramite** <note>original: *Cheramites*</note> when it is encircled by dark blue spots. 111. **Purple-stone** <note>original: *Porphyroites*</note> is ash-colored and studded with spikes like a purple sea urchin, but without a spiral. 112. **Shell-stone** <note>original: *Conchites*</note> boasts curved lines returning to the "shoulders" and a golden-colored armor. 113. **Megarian Stone** <note>original: *Lapis Megaricus*</note>, in whose entire body marine shells are scattered. 114. **Comb-stone** <note>original: *Ctenites*</note> refers to scallops <note>original: *pectines*</note> and sometimes the shape of a whale's mouth; you may find six or seven in a single rock, ash-gray in color. 115. **Mussel-stone** <note>original: *Myites*</note> imitates mussels; it is oblong and round in the manner of a scallop. 116. **Spiral-stone** <note>original: *Strombus* or *strombites*</note> is similar to a water snail; it tapers from thick to thin like a whirlwind or a top, twisted into a spiral toward the right. 117. **Onyx-stone** <note>original: *Onychites*</note>, named for "scented nails" <note>original: *unguibus odoratis*; likely referring to the operculum of certain shells used in incense</note>, is similar to onyx in both color and shape. 118. **Crab-stone** <note>original: *Cancrinites*</note> resembles the breast of a crab turned to stone; white lines mimic the joints of the ribs and pervade the whole body. 119. **Centipede-stone** <note>original: *Scolopendrites*</note>, in which lines run almost in the path of waves, full of very short transverse stems,

...as do centipede worms. 120. **Cat’s Eye** <note>original: *Oculus cati* or *felis*</note>, also known as the **Sun’s Eye** <note>original: *oculus solis*</note>, the **Mithrax** of the Persians, or the **False Opal** <note>original: *Pseudopalus*</note>, which perfectly captures the appearance of this animal's eye. It is composed of milky and dark brown colors, separated in the middle as if by a parting line; if you turn it over, one side is always whiter and brighter. 121. **Bel’s Eye** <note>original: *Oculus Beli*, named after the Babylonian deity Bel</note>, which is whitish and depicts a black pupil shining from the center with a golden glow. 122. **Wolf-Eye** <note>original: *Lycophthalmos*</note>, which is blood-red and has a black center encircled by white, much like the eyes of wolves. 123. **White-Eye** <note>original: *Leucophthalmos*</note>, otherwise reddish, contains a white and black eye-like appearance. 124. **Three-Eye** <note>original: *Triophthalmos*</note>, which is born alongside onyx, displaying three "eyes" at once. 125. **Tongue-Stone** <note>original: *Glossopetra*; also called "witch's tooth" or *glottis* by Cardano</note>, which resembles the tongue of a serpent or, more likely, a woodpecker <note>original: *pici*</note>. The thick part is stony and pointed like horn; in both colors, it shines like the claw of a starling. It is also found with serrated edges. <note>These are actually fossilized shark teeth, though early naturalists often mistook them for petrified tongues.</note> 126. **Kidney Stone** <note>original: *Lapis renalis*</note>, which displays the shape of a kidney; it is reddish and covered with an iron-like crust. 127. **Horn-Stone** <note>original: *Ceratites* or "fossil horn"</note>, which is sometimes so large in its horn-like appearance that it can be attributed to no known animal; it is soft inside, white, light, and crumbly, the offspring of a marl-like juice that has been sprayed with petrifying liquid. 128. **Cross-Bearer** <note>original: *Crucifer*</note>, which easily resembles a bull's horn, and when cut transversely into small discs, it mimics a cross in a black color. 129. **Horn of Ammon** <note>original: *Cornu Ammonis*</note>, which renders the image of a ram's horn in a golden color, sometimes knotty as if held together by joints. <note>These are the spiral shells of extinct cephalopods, named after the Egyptian god Ammon, who was depicted with ram's horns.</note> 130. **Bone-Breaker** <note>original: *Ossifragus*; also known as *Osteites*, *Amosteos*, *Osteocolla*, *Osteolithus*, *Holosteus*, *Stelechites*, or "Sandy Stone"</note>, which resembles a bone; it is hollow with a crumbly marrow and dissolves into liquid. It sometimes sprouts from the earth and shows the shape of a mutilated trunk's branches. A variety is the **In-Bone Stone** <note>original: *Enostios*</note>, which looks like a broken bone. 131. **Testicle-Stone** <note>original: *Enorchis*</note>, which is the size of a pigeon's egg and, though dingy with dark colors, contains a stone inside shaped like testicles. According to Pliny, it is white, and when divided into fragments, it represents the image of testicles. 132. **Oblong Geode**, appearing like dog dung, white and pointed at both ends; some call it the **Fossil Bezoar of Egypt**, or Pliny’s **Female Eagle-Stone** <note>original: *Aetites foemina*</note>. 133. **Turtle-Stone** <note>original: *Chelonites*</note>, a representation of turtles recently hatched from eggs, which has a vaulted cover distinguished by various quadrangles; it often resembles a whole turtle, both face-down and face-up. That which is believed to have fallen with thunder and has large protrusions is the **Thunder-Stone** <note>original: *Brontias*</note>; that which falls with rain and has small protrusions is the **Rain-Stone** <note>original: *Ombrias*</note>; and that which has none and is hemispherical in shape is the **Lightning-Stone** <note>original: *Ceraunias*</note>. 134. **Bull-Heart** <note>original: *Biucardia*</note>, a rock similar to a bull's heart, coming from Babylon and around Naples. 135. **Ox-Tongue** <note>original: *Buglossus*</note>, shaped like an ox's tongue, with the weight of iron and having two holes in its thicker part. 136. **Snake-Stone** <note>original: *Ophiomorphites*</note>, which has the appearance of a serpent coiled into a spiral, with the tail occupying the center. 137. **Onyx**, which has a whiteness in its base like a human fingernail <note>The Greek word *onyx* literally means "fingernail" or "claw."</note>.

...is similar, the **Cevites**. 260. The **Hexacantalithus** <note>original: *Hexacantalithus*; literally "six-thorn stone"</note> is multicolored. 261. Those with the color of a panther's skin are the **Kaman**, the **Drosolithus** <note>Dew-stone</note>, the **Eupetalos** <note>Good-leaf stone</note>, the **Exolicetus**, the **Polyzonos** <note>Many-zoned stone</note>, the **Chitonites** <note>Tunic-stone</note>, the **Fongites** <note>Mushroom-stone</note>, the **Olea** <note>Olive-stone</note>, the **Orca** <note>Jar-stone</note>, the **Phanchrus**, the **Panthera**, the **Turti**, the **Ziazaa**, the **Demonius**, and the **Syderopaecilos** <note>Iron-variegated stone</note>, to which you may also add the **Pontic stone**. 262. <margin>N. 33.</margin> Neither the shape nor the color is known for those that are not sufficiently described, such as the **Amanchitis**, the **Synechites**, the **Baptes**, the **Cactonites**, the **Cadmites**, the **Colondronius**, the **Camascus**, the **Caratobates**, the **Catochites**, the **Catapyrites**, the **Cegolithes of Albertus** <note>referring to Albertus Magnus, a medieval scholar of minerals</note>, the **Chrysanterinus**, the **Clites**, the **Dorialtides**, the **Glossites**, and the **Erotylos**, along with the **Aphicome** and the **Hieromnemone** (which are the same), the **Eusebes**, the **Hyenia**, the **Kenne**, the **Kinocettus**, the **Lauraces**, the **Linurgus**, the **Liparis**, the **Nemesites**, etc. 263. <margin>N. 34.</margin> **Margarites** or **Pearls** (which, if they are large, are called **Uniones** <note>original: *uniones*; "unique ones," because no two large pearls were thought to be exactly alike</note>) are hard and round "warts," and are the grains of the Red Sea. They are the offspring of a viscous fluid, dissolved into tiny parts, which gradually dries and hardens; this fluid grows out of the shell of a tuberous and somewhat diseased oyster. They consist of multiple layers of skin; if the fluid is pure, a brilliant whiteness is seen; if it is turbid, the "offspring" is foul and dirty. The highest praise for their color is to be called **Exaluminatas** <note>resembling the clarity of alum</note>. They called those **Elenchi** <note>Teardrop-shaped</note> which end in a fuller orb from a tapered length. The **Physema** is an "abortion," a species that is hollow and without a body. Those that are **Tympania** <note>Drum-like</note> have only one round face, with a flat surface on the reverse. When preserved, they turn yellow and grow dull with wrinkles; that vigor which is sought after lasts only during their "youth." For poorer women in former times, a single large pearl served as their "lictor" <note>an official who cleared the way for Roman magistrates; here used metaphorically to mean a status symbol that commands respect</note> in public. 264. The **Shark Stone** <note>original: *Lapis tuberonum*</note>, found in the shark, is located above the eyes; it is very white, large, sometimes weighing two pounds, very soft and crumbly like dust, and tasteless; it is used against difficulty in urination. 265. The **Manatee Stone**, which also sticks in the head of this fish, is the size of a small playing ball, shaped like the bone that holds the taut string in a crossbow—it is bone rather than stone. The male is white; the female is like the color of diluted red blood. 266. The **Sea Bream Stone**, found in the head of the same fish, is white and split by a crack in the middle. 267. The **Corvulus Stone**, which is bumpy on the outside, and on the inside has a protruding tubercle with an appendix. 268. The **Corvinus Stone**, which is hollowed out by the "raven-fish" <note>likely the *Corvinus* or drum fish</note>; it is oval in shape and concave. 269. The **Umbra Stone**, which is split into two parts at the top. 270. The **Dentalis Stone**, which is serrated on the outside, cracked on the bumpy part, and scaly inside. 271. The **Perch Stone**, which is a double bone, oblong, white, flat, and seemingly toothed on one side. 272. The **Carp Stone**, or something bony, is found near the start of the dorsal spine, by whose aid the head is joined to the spine; it is triangular and yellowish. 273. <margin>N. 35.</margin> The **Synodotides** comes from the brain of the fish of the same name. 274. The **Crab's Eyes**, reviewed above. 275. The **Bezoar** or **Pazahar**, which grows in the stomach of a certain kind of goat in Persia; it is layered like an onion, shining or smooth, usually dark brown or chestnut-colored, rarely blackish-green, and has a fragment of straw or herb in its center. 276. The **Batrachites** or what is believed to be **Borax** <note>not the modern chemical, but the "Toadstone"</note>, which is produced in the head of the horned toad called Borax; it appears more like a bone than a stone, resembling the palate or tongue of a toad. The color is not the same for all: some are dark on white, others are black with livid spots; sometimes there is a blue "eye" in the middle, or a white spot on the top; its size is that of a medium bean. 277. The **Hog Stone**, which is found in the gall of a pig near Malacca; it is a diluted red, bitter like the touch of French soap, and rivals the Bezoar. 278. The **Malacca Hog Stone**, found by some in the gall of a porcupine, is of a clearer purple color, bitter, slippery, and fatty. Carried in the hand, it moves the menses and causes abortion. 279.

### Subterranean Physics

The **Bulgolda stone**, found in the head of an animal called the *Bulgoldulf*, is the size of a hazelnut and relates to the fear of venereal matters <note>original: *venereorum metus*; likely referring to a remedy for lust or sexual anxieties</note>. 280. The **gallstone**, also known as **Haraozi** and **Mazatius** according to Sylvaticus <note>referring to Matthaeus Silvaticus, a medieval medical lexicographer</note>, is found in the gall bladders of animals; it is ochre-colored and covered in layers. In certain cattle, it is called **Alcheron**. 281. The **stone of the wild ass** is oval, the size of a walnut, and ranges from white to a lemon-yellow color with certain cracks. 282. The **bear stone**, which lies hidden between the flesh and the skin of a bear, is solid, the size of a thumbnail, oval-shaped and hemispherical, and is ash-colored with yellow spots. 283. The **beaver stone**, found in the central part of the beaver, is round, nearly yellow, and of a gypsum-like substance. 284. **Stag stones**, which grow in the corners of the eyes of deer after they have thrown themselves into rivers after eating serpents <note>This refers to a classical myth that stags eat snakes to rejuvenate themselves, then stand in water to cool the resulting heat, which causes these "stones" to form</note>. 285. The **Alectorius** <note>Cock-stone</note>, which is found in the stomachs or livers of roosters, is similar to a dark crystal, sometimes brownish or marked with blood-red veins. The best kind is that which, when thrown into water, shows the appearance of a piece of grain. 286. The **Chelidonius** <note>Swallow-stone</note>, whose source is in the bellies of young swallows, is the size of a linseed and hemispherical in shape; the color on the convex side is a pale dark-brown, while the concave side is purple with black spots and boasts golden droplets in the most prized specimens. 287. The **stone of the wood-pigeons** is small and found in the stomachs of these birds; it is a very potent remedy against kidney stones.

<margin>N. 37.</margin>
288. The **Dracontias** or **Dracontides** <note>Dragon-stone</note> is imagined to be formed from the brains of dragons when they are cut off as they die; if cut from a living dragon, it never becomes a gemstone, due to the envy of the animal sensing its own death. 289. The **Limacites** <note>Snail-stone</note>, which is obtained from the head of a garden snail, is white and livid with some prominent lines.

<margin>N. 38.</margin>
290. The **Chinese Cenar stone** prevents wrinkles from arising on the body. 291. # Chapter Four of the Sixth Section,
## Explaining the Third Kind of Subterranean Compounds.
### Concerning Metals and Minerals.

---

->S Y N O P S I S<-

*No. 1. The term "mineral" is explained. No. 2. The twofold difference between minerals. No. 3. Less perfect minerals. No. 4. Perfect minerals.*

->T E X T<-

<margin>No. 1.</margin>
Now we approach the third kind of subterranean compounds, namely Minerals. The term *mineral* is quite broad. In common usage, it is applied to any fossil that is *dug out of the earth*; for the *origin* of the word from *Hebrew* indicates this, namely (*from the earth*) <note>The author suggests a Hebrew etymology for "mineral," though modern linguists trace it to the Medieval Latin *minera*, meaning "ore" or "mine"</note>. Specifically, however, only those substances that are metals or heavy with metals are called minerals. Thus, strictly speaking, when *metallic veins are mixed with stones*, such stones are called in German *Ertz* or *stuffen* <note>original: *Ertz (stuffen)*; referring to ore samples or mineral specimens</note>. *Antimony, Bismuth, Zinc*, and others are called minerals; however, *perfect* metals, such as *gold, silver*, and the rest, are called minerals only in a general sense, but they specifically keep the name *Metal*, which derives its origin from the Hebrew *Metil* <note>original: *Metil*; meaning to cast or hammer out</note>.

<margin>No. 2.</margin>
Having explained the term mineral, we shall now proceed to the *distinction* of minerals, which varies among authors. Some distinguish minerals into *true and perfect* metals, and *imperfect* ones, which are nonetheless related to the true and native ones. Then they consider certain parts of minerals, either made by nature or by art. However, since it is not our aim in this chapter to deal with either minerals or metallic compounds in general (since we shall do that in the seventh chapter of this section), we rightly return at this point to the *simpler* metallic compounds. These are of *two types*: some are *imperfectly mixed*, while others exist as *perfect*, and are therefore *malleable* <note>capable of being hammered or pressed into shape without breaking</note>; others are *imperfect*, and thus *friable* <note>easily crumbled or reduced to powder</note>. *Perfect* minerals are called metals; minerals have the same principles as metals, but of a less *perfect quality*, and of an *unequal quantity* in *respect* to metals. Among the *less perfect* are listed *Antimony, Bismuth, Zinc, and Marcasite*; for these are truly *metallic* bodies, though imperfect in comparison to other metals—that is, a certain *metallic nature* <note>original: *metalleitas*</note> is seen in these minerals, which is why I assign them to the class of compounds. For those which show no *metallic nature* but are earthy in existence are "de-compounds," such as *Calamine, Cobalt, Magnesia*, and what is commonly called by potters *Braunstein* <note>original: *Braunstein*; typically referring to manganese dioxide, used as a glaze or pigment</note>, of which we will speak in chapter 7 of this section.

<margin>No. 3.</margin>
Now I shall explain the aforementioned minerals, namely the *less perfect compounds*, among which *Antimony* holds the first place. This is *twofold*: the *ore*, where stone is mixed in, and the mineral itself or *melted Antimony*. This in turn is *twofold*: the purer substance, which yields the *regulus* <note>the metallic button or mass that settles at the bottom of a crucible during smelting</note>, and by reason of its form is commonly the...

The mass is distinguished by its streaks and tested by its brittleness; it is called *stimmi* by the Greeks, *Zadahab* <note>original: *Zadahab*; a Hebrew term associated with golden or shining substances</note> by the Hebrews, **Antimony** in common speech, and in German *Spißglas* <note>original: *Spießglas*; literally "pointed glass," referring to the needle-like crystals of stibnite</note>, named for its striated form resembling lances, and because it turns into glass when treated with fire. Concerning its use, parts, and origin, I shall not treat them specifically here, for these matters belong to the second book, where it will be examined by water and fire. It must not be overlooked that it is varied and included under various names; it is called **red**, **starred**, or **Saturnine Magnesia**, though improperly; for we shall treat Magnesia under the category of compounds. It is also called the **wolf**, because it "devours" gold <note>In alchemy, antimony was used to purify gold because it would react with and remove other metals (impurities), appearing to "eat" them</note>, although it vomits it back up once purified; for this reason, some call it the primary **Entity of Gold**.

Next in order is **2. Bismuth**. Miners call it the **roof of silver**, because it is found in silver mines and serves as an indicator of silver; it is volatile, yet heavy and closely related to lead, and they use it to adulterate tin. **Schröder** calls it *Marcasite* in the third book of his *Pharmacopoeia*, chapter 18, page 466, but incorrectly; for **marcasite** is a different mineral, which we will discuss later. He also calls it *Magnesia*, but again incorrectly; for *Magnesia* is another composite mineral, as we shall demonstrate in the seventh chapter of this section. 

Following Bismuth is a certain mineral they call **3. Zinc**, commonly known as **Spelter** <note>original: *Spiauter*; an early term for zinc or zinc alloys</note>, which is mostly brought from the **Indies**. It has the brittleness of Bismuth but is of the same nature, being a medium between **Antimony, Bismuth, Marcasite,** and **Calamine** <note>original: *cadmia*; an ore of zinc</note>. Copper is elegantly colored by this mineral into the nature of brass <note>original: *orichalci*; a golden-colored alloy, typically brass</note>, which we will discuss in the seventh chapter of this section under the title of artificial compounds. 

**4. Marcasite** is a yellow mineral, usually so accurately and curiously quadrangular <note>The author is likely describing the cubic crystals of pyrite (fool's gold)</note> that **they use them as weights in mineral balances**; it is an indicator of copper, under which immature mineral all species of copper are encompassed.

Now that the minerals have been explained, we shall approach the **Metals**. There are six of them (for quicksilver, which has until now been falsely numbered as the seventh among metals, is a **compound**, which we will discuss in the seventh chapter of this section). They are distinguished by a threefold division: two of them, **gold and silver**, flow in the fire when they are glowing white; two glow for a long time before they flow, namely **copper and iron**; and two flow before they even begin to glow, namely **tin and lead**. 

The most illustrious **Dr. Jonston** <note>Referring to John Jonston (1603–1675), a famous naturalist and physician</note> explains the differences of each. **Gold**, he says, or the *Sun*, owes itself to clear Mercury, white Sulfur, and mixed salt; hence it is tawny, the color of the stars. It endures in conflagrations and funeral pyres and is worn away very little by use. No other substance can be spread out more widely or divided more numerously while always maintaining its weight. It is **pure** <note>original: *apyron* (Greek) or *apepton*; meaning "unfired" or "un-cooked" because it is found pure in nature</note>, being perfect by itself without any labor; it is commonly called **Placer-gold**, **Wash-gold**, or **Refined** <note>original: *Obryzum*; gold that has been tested and refined by fire</note> (pure, cleaned by boiling, re-boiled, and tested by the touchstone); it is frequently skimmed of dross, and therefore radiates a similar color when tested by fire. It reaches up to 24 carats. Among the ancients, there was no mention of it under this name; for the purpose of the touchstone, it was called **silvery** if it was defiled by some portion of silver. **Arrugia** <note>A term from Pliny the Elder referring to gold mining via shafts and tunnels</note> is gold sought by digging and immediately recognizable; the Spaniards called masses found in this way **Palacras**, others **Palacranas**; that which is small is called **Baluca**. Gold collected in torrents was called **Ramentitium** or **Syrtos**. **Canal-gold** is that dug out of wells, which wanders through the stones in the channels of veins. **Raw gold** (pure) is that found in masses. A small lump of pure gold found in metals is called a **gold-knot** <note>original: *aurinodus*; Greek: *kentron adamas*, meaning "diamond center" or "hard point"</note>.
