Silver** <note>original: *Argentum*; associated with the Moon or *luna*</note> arises from perfected, pure, and clear mercury, white sulfur, and salt (according to the common opinion followed by **Doctor Feston**) with a more cheerful color, more similar to daylight. From a mixture of gold and silver, with a fifth part of the gold added, **Electrum** <note>original: *Electrum*</note> is made. **Oriental silver** <note>original: *Orientale*</note> adheres to the blue Sapphire stone and its own pyrite. Seek **scraping silver** <note>original: *Ramentosum*</note> in rivers and the heads of streams. **Raw silver** <note>original: *Rude* or *infectum*</note> is that which is still mixed in a mass with other metals and materials. **Pure-pure** <note>original: *Purum purum*</note> is that which is immediately in its natural state. **Refined silver** <note>original: *Pustulatum* or rather *Pusulatum*</note> is of the first rank. **Copper-mixed silver** <note>original: *Acrosum*</note> is that to which bronze was added; it is otherwise thin and smooth yet heavy, in which nothing but weight is valued. **Worked silver** <note>original: *Factum*</note> is found in vessels and statues; **Stamped silver** <note>original: *Signatum* or *Cælatum*</note> is that expressed in some artistic form. **Embossed work** <note>original: *Toreuma*</note>. **Plain silver** <note>original: *Purum*</note> is without ornaments. **Leaf silver** <note>original: *Foliatum*</note> is hammered into sheets. **Winter silver** <note>original: *Hibernum*</note> refers to refined silver, because Spain abounded in it; **Pellet silver** <note>original: *Pastillatum*</note> is gathered into masses and small cakes. **Table or service silver** <note>original: *Escarium* or *mensale*</note> consists of silver platters and furnishings; as it appears in the vein, it is **branching, forked, pointed, or curled** <note>original: *ramosum, furcatum, acuminatum, crispatum*</note>. **Hair-like silver** <note>original: *trichites*</note>. **Fine brass** <note>original: *chalkolibanon*; a biblical term for a glowing metal alloy</note> was brought from Mount Lebanon. **False silver** <note>original: *Pseudargyrum*; also called *sterile, Exter*, or *theatricum*</note> is that which, stretched into thin plates, was hung in theaters.

**3. Bronze** <note>original: *Æs*; associated with copper/*cuprum* or Venus</note> consists mostly of red and impure sulfur, a little Mercury, and a more impure salt (see my opinion regarding the principles of metals on page 20, paragraph 6, and elsewhere). It is mostly **red**, though sometimes violet, whitish, golden, purple, black, and variegated. Melting is better in great cold, and its value is closest to its practical use. **Liver-stone** <note>original: *Hepatizon*</note> tends toward the appearance of a liver. **Cyprian bronze** <note>original: *Cyprium*</note> is usually mixed with nitre for melting and is properly called **copper** <note>original: *cuprum*</note>. **Orichalcum** <note>original: *Orichalcum* or *aurichalcum*</note> has the hardness of bronze but the splendor of gold; it was formerly a source of great admiration but was not long-lived and quickly failed. **Campanian bronze** <note>original: *Campanum*</note> is that from which bronze pots and cauldrons are made. **Delian bronze** <note>original: *Deliacum*</note> had the most ancient fame in the market at Delos, celebrated by the whole world. **Aeginetic bronze** <note>original: *Ægineticum*</note> received the next praise; the island itself was famous for the tempering of its workshops. **Corinthian bronze** <note>original: *Corinthium*</note> is of the most precious grade, which was created by chance during the burning of that city, when veins of bronze, gold, and silver flowed together. **Cast bronze** <note>original: *Caldarium* or *fusile*</note> is that which is only poured, being fragile under hammers. **Wrought bronze** <note>original: *Regulate*, *ductile*, or *batutile*</note> is thinned into plates by a hammer. **Polished bronze** <note>original: *Extersum*</note> contracts rust more quickly than neglected bronze. **Crown bronze** <note>original: *coronarium*</note>, dyed with bull’s gall, took on the appearance of gold; it was called **Lucar** <note>original: *Lucar*</note> by the ancients. **Tinted bronze** <note>original: *Tinctum*</note> was painted by the Egyptians so that they might look upon their god **Anubis** <note>original: *Anubim*</note> on their vessels. **Collected** <note>original: *Collectaneum*</note>...

...bronze <note>original: "neum," likely the end of "Aeneum"</note> which is purchased for common use. It is dark when in cakes <note>original: "panibus"</note>, consisting of disks of soldered bronze bread.

4. **Iron** (**Mars**) contains a great deal of crude, earthy, and undigested sulfur, a little mercury, and impure salt; it is hard and slow to melt, and once heated in the fire, it is ruined unless it is hardened. It is the best and worst tool of life: so that death might reach men more swiftly, we have made it winged and given feathers to iron <note>A reference to iron-tipped arrows speeding the arrival of death</note>. Its core is **Steel** <note>original: *Chalybs*</note>, which is forged to further harden the blade. **Damascus steel** <note>original: *Damasci elaboratus*</note> is purchased for its weight in gold. That iron which, when rubbed, attracts and holds other iron to the magnet, they call **living iron** <note>original: *vivum*</note>. **Cast iron** <note>original: *fusile*</note> is that which is poured and is brittle; later, when moved to other furnaces, it turns from brittle to **ductile** <note>malleable</note> and can be bent. **Apalon** <note>original: *Apalon*; from the Greek for "soft"</note> is that which comes from a vein of softer composition; the more brittle kind is **thrypton** <note>original: *thrypton*; from the Greek for "broken/brittle"</note>. The masses of molten and glowing metal while being hammered in the furnace are called **strictures** <note>original: *stricturæ*; sparks or tightened masses</note>, a term not used for other metals. **Sponges** <note>original: *Spongiæ*</note> are the porous masses pulled from the furnace; in ancient times, no types of iron were tempered for blades except for **Chinese** <note>original: *Sericum*</note> and **Parthian** <note>original: *Parthicum*</note> iron.

5. **Lead** <note>original: *Plumbum*; specifically "black lead" or *plumbum nigrum*</note> was once called black lead; it shares much with impure mercury and a little with foul-smelling sulfur and salt; it is soft and bluish-gray. Sometimes it appears in great abundance in the very top layer of the earth, and it grows when buried in moist places, increasing in weight; it melts easily, and when melted, it floats upon silver <note>A reference to the separation of metals during smelting or cupellation</note>.

6. In **Tin** <note>original: *Stanno*; formerly called *plumbum candidum* or "white lead"</note> there is much less of the imperfect quicksilver, and a small amount of impure, poorly digested sulfur and salt. It has a habit of making other metals brittle, and it rots if left in water for a long time. It does not take on its white color unless it is corrected by fire; it gathers a white dross <note>original: *sordidiem candidam*</note> and cannot be joined to itself without the addition of "black" lead. In the past, it was mixed with a certain portion of silver to create **argentarium** <note>a 50/50 tin-lead alloy</note> and **tertiarium** <note>a 1:2 tin-lead alloy</note>, for it was useful for nothing without a mixture. But we shall speak of these more specifically in the second book.

## Section Six, Chapter Five,
# On Composite Earthy Substances: Dry and Liquid, Fat and Lean.

### S Y N O P S I S.
Note 1. What a "Composite" <note>original: *Decompositum*</note> substance is. Note 2. General division of Composites. Note 3. Specific division of earthy ones. Note 4. Earthy, dry, and fat Composites. Note 5. Lean Composites. Note 6. Oily ones. Note 7. Aqueous ones are explained.

Thus, when earths are mixed with metals, or stones with earths, composites are produced; indeed, even when different species of one genus are mixed, such as various metals among themselves, composites are also produced;

### Book I. Section VI. Chapter V.

Furthermore, such complex mixtures <note>original: "decomposita"; refers to substances made of multiple mineral components</note> can be categorized into three groups: the *first* contains earthy mixtures, the second stony ones, and the third metallic ones. Each class of these complex mixtures is further divided into two types: namely, the dry and the aqueous. Among the dry, some are classified as "fat" <note>oily or combustible</note> and others as "lean" <note>non-oily or salts</note>. Among the liquids, there are sometimes oily and sometimes watery types, though occasionally only watery ones are found. Since we have explained the simpler subterranean mixtures and their differences in the preceding chapters, we shall now direct our attention to the complex mixtures, following the established order for their explanation.

<margin>N. 3.</margin> Specifically, in this chapter, we shall begin with the *earthy* complex mixtures to maintain the order we have set for ourselves and the reader. Just as in the previous sections, where earthy substances stood at the head of the subterranean compounds, so too shall the earthy mixtures provide our starting point here. As we have said, these are of three kinds. Those earthy substances that are *less* complex (being more simple in nature) were mostly reviewed in the second chapter of this section under the title of "subterranean earthy compounds." Having explained those in their proper place, we shall now proceed to the *more* complex mixtures. 

Some of these have a distinct consistency, *either soft, such as mineral juices <note>original: "oposphalta"</note> and bitumens;* among which are *flower of salt* <note>original: "Halofanthos"</note>, *spermaceti*, *ambergris* <note>original: "ambra odorata"</note>, and *mineral pitch*; or they have a *hard consistency, such as sulfur, amber <note>original: "succinum"</note>, and jet <note>original: "Gagates"</note>.* All of these are *fat* <note>meaning they contain oils or resins</note> in nature. On the other hand, the *lean* substances are *salt* and *nitre* <note>saltpeter</note>, to which two "super-complex" substances can be added: *ammonium salt* <note>original: "sal armeniacus"</note> and *alkali salt*. 

The *liquids* are either oily—and these are the more refined types, *such as naphtha and petroleum*—or they are less refined, *such as mineral fat <note>original: "axungia"</note>, maltha bitumen <note>a thick, waxy mineral tar</note>, and ambergris.* Among the *aqueous* types, one must include *saline waters, nitrous waters, and all sulfurous waters*. Although the greatest part of these consists of water, no one should doubt that earth lies hidden within and enters the mixture as a compound. Therefore, let it not surprise anyone that *salt and nitre* themselves (as "lean" earthy mixtures) and sulfur and other "fat" substances are composed of various earths. We demonstrated this at the beginning of the discussion on *moist liquidity* in the final chapter of the previous section, and in the second section regarding *sea water*; we shall also sufficiently demonstrate it under the specific analysis of each substance. 

For now, however, we shall consider the aforementioned subjects according to their outward differences:

1. The *Halofanthos* <note>original: "flower of salt"</note> of the Ancients (called "flower of salt" by Pliny) is collected in the Nile. The top part, which is fatty, turns white; the middle part is tinged with saffron-yellow and smells of fermented fish sauce <note>original: "garum"</note>. The best kind has a fiery heat like salt and yields a fattiness like oil. It is often adulterated with red ochre or crushed pottery. The terms *emmiltron* <note>red-dyed salt</note> and *thrombus echon* <note>lumpy or clotted salt</note> refer to this faked variety.

<margin>N. 4.</margin> 2. Sometimes floating in vast expanses of the Northern Sea is *spermaceti* <note>original: "sperma Ceti"; also called whale seed, white amber, marine amber, purified amber, or flower of the sea</note>. It was perhaps unknown to the ancients. It is fatty, salty, and slightly acidic; when rubbed, it breaks into scaly little bodies that shine like mica. On hot coals, it gives off the scent of tallow, and because it is exceedingly thin, it penetrates through storage boxes. When fresh, it has the smell of fish sauce; when old, it smells of rancid almonds or spoiled oil. If washed, it loses the medicinal powers it derives from salt. They say a *red* variety, saturated with color, is extracted from the sea. A related fatty substance found around Luanda Island, perhaps flowing from wounded whales, does not even congeal in the cold.

3. *Ambergris* <note>original: "Ambræ"; also called "Aromatites" by Pliny or "Oriental Amber"</note> originates in the earth or the sea from a fatty and coagulable material; its scent comes from a most noble sulfur. When fibrous...

...folded tufts <note>original: "villi"; refers to fibrous textures</note> or ducts with white fibers and red dots. The **gritty** variety is formed as if from a powder with lemon-yellow and white spots. The **crusty** and **nipple-shaped** varieties grow together in the form of tears. The **armored** variety is covered with a leathery skin. **White Porambar** is very light and of great value. **Sechra** is brought from Sechria, a town in Arabia Felix <note>A historical name for the southern part of the Arabian Peninsula, modern-day Yemen</note>. The **gray** variety is the most common and most widely used, marked with white dots. **Sky-blue** amber, which Serapio <note>likely referring to the medieval physician Serapion the Younger</note> called blue, has a mucus-like efflorescence. There are also spots similar to sulfur. There is also a type that can be drawn into threads if pricked with a needle; if it pours out an oily liquid, it is considered the best. **Ceylonese** <note>original: "Zelainitica"</note> is found on the island of Ceylon; it is perhaps the same as the "Selachitica" or "Alzecheleti" of Ibn Sina <note>Avicenna</note>, or the "Zinguitana" of Serapio. The **whale-like** <note>original: "Cetacea"</note> variety is said to be found either in the belly of an animal or near the spine. The **golden** variety is hard and burns like sulfur. The **artificial** category includes several species.

**IV.** Under the heading of **mineral pitch** are categorized **asphalt**, **pissasphalt**, and **mummy**. **Asphalt** usually reaches a solid state near springs and outflows of liquid pitch and mortar <note>original: "maltha"; a thick, tar-like mineral</note>; it is mostly black, and when lit, it produces much black smoke, leaving behind a porous coal like pumice. The pure form is **Jew’s pitch** or **Sodom bitumen**. **Pissasphalt**, or pitch-bitumen, is a resident of Epidaurus; cast onto the banks by the heat of rivers, it hardens into a clod, shifting in color from black to gray. It is best when it floats on water while boiling. **Mummy** <note>original: "Mumia"</note> was once a thick and fragrant "honey-mead" found in the tombs of Egyptian Princes; now it is a mixture of human flesh seasoned with salt, bitumen, resins, and gums. In apothecary shops, it is available as the liquid that has flowed out from those buried in tombs, or as the medicated corpse itself.

**V.** **Sulfur** (known as *Scythian Comaris*, *Androdamas* <note>meaning "man-tamer"</note>, *oil of the earth*, *living metal*, or by the Greeks as ***Theion***) is born from a certain fatty material of the earth, thickened and hardened by a moderate boiling within the ground. That which has experienced no "torments of fire" <note>has not been processed by heat</note> is called ***living and unfired*** <note>original: "vivum & hapyron"</note>, and it is born around Mount Hecla. Near Naples, it is liquid and white. It naturally grows into hair-like filaments in the Vulcanian Field <note>the Solfatara crater</note> at Naples, and is used for dyes; otherwise, the pure form is called ***virgin*** sulfur. In places that burn spontaneously, it grows on high stones through sublimation and is called ***sublimated***. A blue-colored variety was known to Ausonius. A type called ***glow-worm*** <note>original: "lampyridon"</note> radiates like a firefly; it is found on the island of Melos, turning from green to yellowish. Among the ***artificial*** types, that which is common only in the workshops of fullers <note>laundry workers who cleaned cloth</note> is called a ***clod***. ***Egula*** is the type that provides whiteness and softness to wool through its fumes. ***Burnt*** sulfur <note>original: "Kauston"</note> is used to prepare sulfur matches for lighting lamps. ***Horse-sulfur*** <note>original: "Caballinum"</note>, which is made from iron scales and sulfur, cures the mange in horses. ***Stick-form*** sulfur refers to a smooth rod; others call it smooth and ***reed-like***. It is called ***long-bean-shaped*** <note>original: "Dolichoëides"</note> when individual drops are shaped to the size of a kidney bean; this same type, having experienced fire, is called ***perfect*** or ***common sulfur***. That which is dug out from mines, boiled in oil, and poured into iron tubes is called ***extinguished and dead***. Among the Chemists, you will find it classified as living, decocted, "clubbed," natural, artificial, fire-resistant, and so on.

**VI.** **Amber** (also called ***electrum***, ***gold-bearer***, ***wing-bearer***, ***snatcher*** <note>Greek: "harpax"; referring to its ability to attract light objects</note>, *glessum*, *sacrium*, *lynx-stone*, lemon or yellow Amber, *carabe*) floats out from the mud of certain mountains under the summer suns. It thickens in cold and grassy soil, is swept away by the swelling tide, and is pushed onto the shores like refuse, so buoyant that it seems to hang and then settle in the shallows. When the "soul of heat" is received by the rubbing of fingers, it draws straw and chaff to itself...

...and dry leaves. The valuation of these was once immense among luxury goods, and there was great confidence in keeping them in caskets, as their display or use pleased those with other vices. **Pure amber** <note>original: "Hololektron"</note> is clean and contains no foreign matter within it. **White amber** <note>original: "leucoelectrum"</note> is sometimes transparent like crystal. **Callistratus’s golden amber** <note>original: "Chrysoelectrum callistrati"; Callistratus was an ancient author who wrote on the properties of stones</note> has the most pleasing appearance of the morning sun; it is a greedy consumer of fire if any should be near it. **Falernian** is named for the color of the wine, transparent with a soft glow. **Fossil amber** is found in the trenches of Lesna <note>likely Leszno, Poland</note>; once reduced to ash, it can never be restored to its former size and splendor as things now stand, though it was found when the city was once being fortified with a rampart. Nothing is as pure as that without internal mixture: in the "pregnant" variety, butterflies, flies, and gnats, which stuck to the liquid sap, are enclosed and hardened. The name for the yellow variety is **amber** <note>original: "Flavo electri"</note>; the tawny is called **Sualternician**, while the white is counted among medicinal resources.

VII. **Jet** <note>original: "Gagati"; also called Gangotis, Gangitis, Eagle-stone, Thracian stone, Engangis rock, demon-stone [lithodæmon], obsidian stone, Thracian gem, black bitumen, black amber, or black succinum</note> has an exquisite blackness, smoothness, and polish; because it breathes out the scent of bitumen and pours it forth when melted, it easily attracts straws <note>referring to static electricity</note>. The **Pilegnian** variety is rarer, lighter, and similar to wood; the **Obsidian** variety is denser and becomes very light through polishing. **Urbinas** is a bright stone among rocks; the **Prussian** variety comes from the nearby sea under the title of "black amber." The **pumice-like** variety is sapless and catches fire with difficulty. Not much different are **Pliny's wood-stones** <note>original: "Dryites Plinii"</note>, which burn like wood; the "rusty wood" with blackish spots of **Aldrovandi** <note>Ulisse Aldrovandi, a 16th-century Italian naturalist</note>, which breathes the scent of bitumen when burning; the **Samothracian gem**, which is weightless, black, and wood-like from the island of Samothrace; and **fossil ebony**, which is fibrous like wood, bituminous, and can be carved, scraped, and polished. The **Doldian beech-stone** found at Altorf is very similar to beech-wood coals; **Thracian stone** consists of an earthy concretion of dry bitumen; **Aristotle's Spinus** is of a similar kind to the preceding; **Smarilus** is the ash of Vesuvius or Etna according to Libavius; and **Maritha** is a natural quicklime in Hainaut, which some say is usually dug out of the earth along with marbles and bitumen.

VIII. **Salt** <note>original: "Sal, hals & halas"; the Latin and Greek terms for salt</note> is produced from compressed and dried moisture; it is quarried from mountains of stone-pits, sometimes regenerating itself, and is cemented together by water. It is dug out of the earth in fields as a gem-like thickened soil; the grains are called "crumbs" <note>original: "micarum"</note>. In desolate places where the sand has been cleared away, **Ammoniac salt** is found, very light within its caves, but of almost incredible weight when brought into the light. It is collected in lakes that turn into salt. **Tattaean salt**, along with **Tritaean and Cantaean**, are perhaps the same, all being very fine. In rivers where the surface thickens into salt, it is called **river salt**; in sea waters, where the moisture is compressed by the summer sun, it is **sea salt**. **Tragasaean salt** does not crackle or jump in the fire. **Native salt** is sometimes transparent like a gemstone. There is a variety like crystal, square in shape, which melts like iron in the fire; sometimes it turns reddish, with the hardness of alabaster, and sometimes it is yellow and imitates a piece of quince fruit. **Saffron-colored salt** is found in Cappadocia. **Reddish-brown** is found near the Oxus river among the Bactrians. **Purple salt** in Spain turns white when it is ground. **Red salt** is sometimes found in Dacia. **Cologne salt** has the taste of a roasted egg. Among the **artificial salts**, the **Norwegian** is black and is boiled in iron pots. **Flower of salt** <note>original: "Flos salis"</note> is like its rust, of a moister nature; in mines it is very white, blooming like a whitening downy wool. **Foam** <note>original: "Spuma"</note> is the scrapings settled on the furthest rocks. Common salt is drawn from **brine** <note>original: "Muria"</note>. **Aspergo** is found in fields and meadows where salty streams flow, appearing like frost. **Brine or salt-liquor** <note>original: "Salfugo seu falsilago"</note> is the moisture in saltworks that is entirely liquid,

...saltier than sea water, and differing in its force. 9. **Nitre** <note>original: "Nitrum"; in this period, "nitrum" often referred to both naturally occurring sodium carbonate (natron) and potassium nitrate (saltpeter) used in gunpowder</note> is produced in earth of its own kind, or from coagulated moisture on walls and rocks. If the most deceitful **Glauber** <note>Johann Rudolf Glauber (1604–1670), a famous chemist and apothecary known for "Glauber's salt"</note> is to be believed, it can be extracted from any metal or wood; the best kind is very thin, tubed, and spongy. It is commonly known by the name **Saltpeter and nitre**. From this comes gunpowder. **Aphronitrum** <note>original: "Aphtonitrum"; literally "froth of nitre"</note> which distills in cave masses, is brittle and purple if of the best quality. The salty down that blooms on walls is called **flower of nitre**; if it is dissolved by fire, it is called **flower of the stone of Assos** <note>original: "flos petræ Assiæ"; Assos was a Greek city famed for a type of stone thought to consume bodies (sarcophagus stone)</note>. The variety in Media, where valleys turn white through dryness, is called **balmirrhage**; that which Maidens use in cosmetics and baths is called **Virginal nitre**, and that used by matrons is called **Matronal**. **Chalastrian nitre** comes forth around the rising of the Dog Star in the waters of Macedonia near the promontory of Chalastra. There is also a black and a red variety in Egypt. The **Volaterran rose-colored nitre** mentioned by Dioscorides, which is produced with inky juice, is yellow; the Puteolan variety is **yellowish** like a pigment. **Thoracic nitre** found at Philippi is in the surface skin of the earth, and because it is filthy, it is called **worthless** <note>original: "anreion"</note> by the inhabitants. Among its relatives are **Tartar** as well as **Sal** 10. **Alkali and 11. Sal Ammoniac**. Although these belong to artificial compounds, which we shall not deal with in this place, they will nevertheless be sufficiently explained by us in Book 2 under the same headings—namely, the "Anatomy" of lime and common salt—insofar as they pertain to the subjects from which they are prepared. 12. The white filtrate of Babylonian bitumen is **Naphtha** (the drug of Medea, with which she anointed the crown and robe of Creon’s daughter; also called Medea's oil). It has such an affinity for fire that flames leap into it from wherever it is seen. When sprinkled with water, it hisses and throws off sparks with a loud noise; much of it is overwhelmed by water, but when pure and ignited, it burns into a solid mass. When mixed, it leaves behind a residue like fatty grease. There are **Yellow and purple** varieties; if it comes out of a spring with salt water, "naphtha salt" either congeals of its own accord or is prepared by art. The deserts of the Arabs pour forth a black variety. 13. **Petroleum** <note>original: "petroleum"; literally "rock oil"</note> (also called oil-asphalt or fig-oil) is less easily ignited because it is thicker, but once refined, it can turn into naphtha; it changes its golden color according to the vessel. The pure kind comes closest to naphtha. When mixed with **Pissasphalt** <note>a mixture of pitch and asphalt</note>, it is fouled. The **Golden and transparent** kind does not take flame by itself, but when a wick is inserted, it burns like pitch. The **Violet** variety has the scent of **Violets**, and nothing can float in its spring. Other bitumens include **Cuban**, which has a heavy odor in Cuba, **Spanish**, and **Rhadinace**, which stinks; also **Corinthian oil**, which is thick, muddy, shimmering with red and yellow, and has a nitrous smell, found in marshy meadows. **Artificial** bitumen is drawn from **Dry Asphalt** <note>original: "Xerabalto"</note> through chemical resolution. When pure and thinned, it is pleasing with a crimson color. The **Brochdorpian** variety is found in the plains of Brunswick and is **heavy-smelling** <note>original: "baryosmos"</note> among its kind. 14. **Bituminous grease**, called **Pissasphalt** by Pliny, is a black filtrate of bitumen, usually found in the same matrix as black petroleum, and is sometimes sold as wheel grease when mixed with cooked tallow. **Zacynthian bitumen**, which smells of **Asphalt**, and **Asphaltic bitumen**, which is either more liquid or thicker—both being black and impure, though not smelling overly foul—are among its relatives. 15. A substance of a consistency between this and **Dry Asphalt**—unless it hardens—is **Maltha** <note>a mineral tar or cement</note>; it catches fire easily, congeals, and dries. When it touches anything solid, it sticks tenaciously, and follows those who try to flee its touch. In the past, soldiers' armor would catch fire when the city <note>Samosata</note> was defended against Lucullus <note>a Roman general who fought against Mithridates and Tigranes</note>. This is the **Samosatian** variety mentioned by Pliny. **Artificial maltha** is made either from natural pitch and other things, with which the walls of Babylon were cemented, or from quicklime extinguished with wine and pig

Wallachian bitumen smells of wax and is used for making candles. 17. Saline waters, both from the sea and from springs, which were discussed above. 18. Nitrated waters, such as those found in the East Indies; there, as the watery parts are evaporated by the continuous heat along the banks, nitrous substances crystallize like salt. 19. There are also sulfurous waters, such as those found in hot springs and acidic springs; however, because they are mostly mixed with minerals, we place them here only on the condition that they consist of sulfur alone. We shall deal with the other mineral waters in the seventh chapter, where metallic compounds will be reviewed. Now we shall proceed to the other class of compounds, namely the stony ones.

# Section Six, Chapter Six
## On dry and liquid stony compounds, both fatty and lean.

### S Y N O P S I S.
<margin>N. 7.</margin>
N. 1. What is called a stony compound. N. 2. The division of stony compounds. N. 3. Fatty stony compounds. N. 4. Marcasites <note>original: "marca"; likely a shorthand for marcasites or "lean" stony compounds mentioned in the text</note>. N. 5. Minerals. N. 6. Saline substances. N. 7. Aqueous substances.

### T E X T
<margin>N. 1. N. 2.</margin>
Having explained the earthy compounds, we shall hasten to the stony ones. Whether earth, salts, or water dissolve into a stony mixture, they create a new compound. Therefore, there are five types. First, "fatty" earth grows within stones, as shown to us by *ampelitis* <note>a bituminous, coal-like earth</note> and coal <note>original: "lithantrax"</note>. Second, "lean" earth constitutes another type of stony compound, as we see in slate <note>original: "lapis scissili"</note>, fossil ivory, and fossil horn, as well as in the belemnite <note>fossilized internal shells of extinct cephalopods</note>, coral, and petrified wood <note>original: "lithodendro"</note>. Third, there is another type of stony compound found in ores where stones are intermixed, commonly called *Ertzstein* <note>ore-stone</note>, *Stuffen* <note>mineral specimens</note>, *Quartz*, etc. Fourth, with the addition of a type of salt, alum, chrysocolla <note>at this time, the term could refer to malachite, borax, or a soldering agent</note>, and borax are produced. Fifth, petrifying and stone-dissolving waters, such as tufa <note>original: "tophi"</note>, fluorspars <note>original: "fluores"; used here to mean minerals that aid in melting</note>, etc., close out the list. We shall now explain each in detail. 1. *Ampelitis* earth is mixed with a silty quality; it cannot be resolved into mud by pouring water over it. It has the power of *pharmacitis* <note>a medicinal earth used in antiquity</note> against worms, is moderately crumbly, and is soluble in oil and easy to mix. *Selericia* is named from its homeland; in Belgian, it is called *Torvenacum* from the word for turf <note>peat</note>. It is black and serves as a substitute for wood. The Brabantine or "inland" variety has a less foul odor because it is less imbued with vitriolated saltiness. The Zeeland variety is corrupted by a similar saltiness due to the proximity of the sea. *Callaica* comes from Peru and "sweats" when placed on poles in the heat of the sun. The British variety, which is the sod of fatty meadow clods, is called *Mottenacum* <note>from "motte" or "moer," referring to peat-rich bog soil</note> from the bituminous concretion of earth and roots. The Cologne variety...

The **Altorf type** <note>referring to Altorf, a region known for its geological deposits</note> resembles charcoal made from birch or beech wood. Sometimes shining pyrites are present, and sometimes sulfur; often the internal particles are transformed into ochre. In the fire, the black color is persistent. **2.** **Stone-coal** <term>Lithanthrax; from the Greek for "stone-coal"</term>, being mixed with bitumen and a petrifying juice, possesses inflammability and stony hardness; it restores itself through a renewable "seed-bed" and becomes useful for hearths once more. <note>The author reflects a 17th-century belief that minerals grew back in mines like plants.</note> Its flame becomes fiercer when water is poured on it, but is smothered by oil and sand.

There are Belgian and Scottish varieties of this coal. The **softer variety** gapes open easily in the earth. The **lean** decomposed substances which we reviewed above—such as **shale** <note>original: "lapis scissilis"</note>, **fossil ivory and horn**, **Belemnites** <note>fossilized cephalopod shells</note>, **coral**, and the **stone-tree** <note>Lithodendrum</note>—we have already explained under the chapter on stones, and we shall further explain their nature in the Second Book. **3.** Now the order of things calls us to the ores, which consist of stones with metals interspersed throughout them; these are commonly called **Shale, Quartz, Hornstone, and Limestone** <note>original German terms: "Schiefer, Quartz, Horn, Kalchstein"</note>. In all of these, metals are generated, and they adhere so tenaciously that when they are cast back into liquefied stones, they constitute a new such compound, which is commonly called **enamel** <term>amausa; a glass-paste or imitation gem material</term>, as we 

<margin>N. 5.</margin>
sufficiently explained in the section on principles. Now we shall hasten to those compounds where stones are united with salts, as happens in **alum, chrysocolla, and borax**. In this entire exposition of compounds, we shall always observe this order: we will explain the compounding of any constituent first regarding earthy things, then stony things, then metallic, saline, and aqueous things, which is what we have observed up to this point. 

<margin>N. 6.</margin>
The order now calls us to **alum**. **3. Alum** <note>described as "halsugo terrae," or the saltiness of the earth</note> is gathered in the winter and ripened by the active sun. If it is liquid—such as **rock alum and Ligurian alum**—and milky, you might call it *phorimon*; if it is pale, rough, and dirty, it is called *paraphoron*. When solidified, if it resembles a knucklebone, it is *astragaloites*; if it resembles a brick, *plinthites*; and because it consists of crusts, it is called *palkontites*; it is called **sugar alum** <note>original: "saccharinum"</note> if it is shaped like a cone. **4. Bubbling alum** swells up like bubbles. **Fungus-shaped alum** is dissolved in the mouth most easily of all. **Pumice-like alum**, which is similar to the pipes and holes of a sponge and is born on the island of Melos, is called *melinum*. **Split alum** is the flower of the clod-like variety. **Hair-alum** <term>Trichites</term> splits into whitening filaments. **Iamenum** is brought from Babylonia. **Scagliola alum** <note>a type of gypsum-based plaster</note> is a more perfect part of gypsum, called **feathered alum** by some. Among the man-made varieties is **turnip-shaped or icy alum**, which is made in the Roman countryside from a very hard, whitish stone cut from a cliff and burnt. **Potash-alum** <note>original: "Catinum"</note> is prepared in a basin from the ash of the **Kali plant**; some call it "sparrow's dung." **5. Chrysocolla** <note>literally "gold-glue"</note> is like the solder of gold—the exudate of gold <note>original: "akestis"</note>. It is a fluid in wells that flows through a vein of gold as mud, which then hardens into the toughness of pumice during the winter frosts. Among copper metals, it is more highly praised when found near gold. Of the man-made varieties, that which is the color of vetch <note>a type of legume</note>, or formed like vetch seeds, is called *orobytes*. **6.** That which is prepared from the urine of a prepubescent boy, Cyprus copper-rust, and nitre, is called **Santerna**, which is nitrous in nature. **7. Borax.** This chapter concludes with petrifying waters, from which various kinds of **Tufa** and **spar** <note>original: "To-phorum & fluorum"</note> are produced in caverns like icicles. Among these, the principal 

<margin>N. 7.</margin>

From one of these, water flows that turns whatever is thrown into it into stone; the water of the other spring, however, dissolves again those things that were petrified in the first spring. If these things were true, we would have an easy way of dissolving the **stone** <note>calculus</note> in the human body; but regarding these things, see Book 2.

Book 1, Section VI, Chapter VII.

# Chapter Seven of the Sixth Section,
## On Metallic Compounds

->S Y N O P S I S<-

N. 1. Division of metallic compounds. N. 2. Dry, "fatty" <note>oily or combustible</note> metallic compounds.
N. 3. Intermediate compounds. N. 4. "Lean" <note>non-combustible or astringent</note> compounds. N. 5. Earthy, natural compounds. N. 6. Artificial compounds. N. 7. Liquid metallic compounds.

->T E X T<-

<margin>1.</margin> Now the order of our study calls us, in this final chapter, to close the section on compounds. We shall do this by considering metallic compounds <note>original: "decompoſitiones metallicas"; refers to substances formed by the combination of metals with other elements like sulfur or salts</note>, which are varied and produce different substances, whether dry or liquid. Among the dry substances, the **fatty** minerals hold a place; among these are **sulfur heavy with metals**—whether it be uncommon or mineral sulfur—**arsenic**, **realgar** <term>red arsenic sulfide</term>, and **orpiment** <note>original: "auripigmentum"</note>, also known as **Sandarac**. The **intermediate** substances include **quicksilver** <note>mercury</note> and its "super-compound," namely **cinnabar**. This may be **artificial**—made from sulfur and common mercury, or from sulfur and the "mercury of metals"—or it may be **native** <note>naturally occurring cinnabar</note>. To this group, one may also add the ore commonly called **red silver ore** <note>original: "Rothguldenertz"; pyrargyrite</note>. The **lean** compounds are the **vitriols** <term>metallic sulfates</term>, whether made by nature or by art. These include the vitriols of the **Sun** (gold), the **Moon** (silver), **Venus** (copper), **Mars** (iron), and **Saturn** (lead)—though the latter is improperly called **sugar of lead** <note>original: "ſaccharum Saturni"; lead acetate</note>. 

The **earthy** metallic compounds are also of two types: **natural**, such as **calamine** <note>original: "Cadmia"</note>, **cobalt**, and **manganese** (commonly called **brownstone** <note>original: "Braunſtein"</note>), to which may be added **brass-stone** <note>original: "Chalcitis"</note>, **yellow vitriol** <note>original: "Miſy"</note>, **ink-stone** <note>original: "Sori"</note>, **copperas** <note>original: "Melanteria"</note>, **galena**, **zinc ore** <note>original: "Calaminaris"</note>, and **metallic ash** <note>original: "Spodos"</note>; or **artificial**, produced by fire or by various "waters" <note>acids or solvents</note>. Those resulting from fire inside a furnace appear either in the **primary paths**—whether they rest on the floor, such as **slag** <note>original: "ſcorea"</note>, stone disks, and **furnace residue** <note>original: "diphryges"</note>, or whether they adhere to the walls, such as **artificial galena**, **furnace calamine**, **tutty of Alexandria**, **zinc oxide** <note>original: "Pompholyx"</note>, and **ash**—or in the **secondary paths**, when a metal is separated from another metal, such as **litharge** <term>lead monoxide</term> and **molybdenum** <note>here referring to a lead-like byproduct of refining</note>. They also arise when metals are melted together and new compounds emerge, such as **brass** <note>original: "Orichalcum"</note>, **black-wash** <note>original: "blachmal"</note>, and various metallic **alloys** <note>original: "ligaturæ"</note>. Outside the furnace, there break forth **rusts and scales**, such as **verdigris** (copper rust), **iron rust**, **minium** (red lead), **Spanish white** <note>original: "album Hispanicum"</note>, **ultramarine**, and **blue pigment**; some of these are prepared by fire, others by solvent waters. Among the scales may be included **copper scale**, the **flower or chaff of copper and iron**, and **hardened iron** <note>original: "ſtomoma"</note>. The **liquid** metallic compounds are various juices, **acidic mineral springs**, and **hot springs**. Now, following the proposed sequence, we shall consider each of the aforementioned subjects by name according to their external differences. 

<margin>N. 1.</margin> We have dealt with "living sulfur" <note>native sulfur</note> above; here, however, we mean **metallic sulfurs**. This is when an oily matter dissolves a metallic <margin>2.</margin> substance and causes a new compound, of which various types exist among the chemists, such as the **sulfur of antimony**, **sulfur of Venus** (copper), **sulfur of Mars** (iron), and so on, which we shall discuss in part in the second book. **2. Arsenic**: concerning its **lead** <note>original: "plumbo"; likely referring to its metallic form or "lead of the philosophers"</note> or its reduction, there is much dispute among the Philosophers. We could indeed decide this matter in a few hours by resolving the compound of arsenic into its principles and reducing it to its **metallicity**. This is done by the addition of nothing other than a certain **vegetable reagent**, by which the corrosive spirits are saturated, leaving behind some true metal or mineral.

Twice-roasted stone** <note>original: "Diphryges"</note> is roasted twice and consists of copper-bearing stone that has been parched, burned, or thoroughly smelted. **23. Gold and silver galena** usually adheres to the furnaces. **24. To these, add common arsenic**, also known as **smelter-smoke** <note>original: "Hüttenrauch"</note>, which is as multifaceted as the metals themselves, of which we spoke above. **25. Alexandrian Tutty** <note>original: "Tutia Alexandrina"</note> is ash-colored, similar to the bark of trees, grainy like a cluster of grapes on the outside, and is born from the "grape-stone" residue. **26. Zinc oxide** <note>original: "Pompholyx"</note> is the ash of copper and calamine, adhering to the ceiling of the roof, first appearing bubbly, then soon like tufts of wool; it is sometimes ashen on a white background, or copper-colored, also called **white nothing** <note>original: "nil album"</note>. **27. Cinders** <note>original: "Spodos"</note> (a little ash) is blacker and heavier, sometimes mixed with sparks and coals, and is found on the walls of the furnaces. **28. Litharge** <note>original: "Lithargyris"</note> (silver foam or lead stone) melts in lead furnaces like oil and, when cooled, usually hardens into the likeness of foam. **29. Molybdena** is made from lead, and when cooked in oil, it takes on the color of liver; it is a **manufactured graphite**. **30. Brass**, commonly called **bell-metal** <note>original: "Gloggenspeiß"</note>, or in Italian **bronzo**, consists of copper, tin, calamine, silver, and others, according to the nature of the mixture and its use. **31. There is also another kind** of composite mixture which smelters commonly call **matte** <note>original: "Plachmal"</note>, consisting of various metals not properly separated, to which one may add the composite commonly called **stone-slag** <note>original: "Schirstein"</note>. **32. There is yet another** species of composite made by art, commonly called **billon** <note>original: "Pagament"</note>, from which coins are made; it usually consists of copper, gold, or silver, or gold and silver together, and from this come the various assays and values of coins. **33. From rusts, Blue pigment** <note>original: "Cæruleum"</note> is drawn from silver by the vapor of vinegar. **34. Verdigris** (the flower of copper <note>original: "χαλκοῦ ἄνθος"</note>, or green of copper) comes from copper while it is being eroded in mines by a vehemently acid juice; it is sky-blue tending toward white in color, and sharp in taste. That which blooms around copper-bearing stones and is scraped off is called **scraped verdigris** <note>original: "Rasilis"</note>, which is drawn into the shape of little worms. **Worm-like verdigris** <note>original: "Scolecias"</note> was formed by the Rhodians into the likeness of a **round roll** <note>original: "του κόλλικος"</note>. The **artificial** kind that was scraped from copper is also called "scraped"; that which is formed into cakes is called **cake-shaped**. **The goldsmith's variety is prepared from the urine of a prepubescent boy** in a mortar with a pestle made of Cyprian copper. Painters and sculptors use the sublimated variety. **35. Iron rust or blight** <note>original: "Ferrugo seu Rubigo ferri"</note> is a defect caused by contact with moisture, its color being red mixed with blackness; it is rarely found within...

...is found in the earth. 36. **White lead** <note>original: "Cerussa plumbi"</note> is the rust of lead created when it is exposed to the vapor of vinegar. The ashy variety is called **lead-ash** <note>original: "cinis plumbarius"</note>. For the **minium of the ancients** <note>red lead or cinnabar</note>, look under the entry for the Minius stone. **Common minium**—which Pliny called **Sandyx**, others called **Phykos** (meaning a dye), and Vitruvius called **Sandaracha**—is made from white lead roasted in a pan over a fire. **Spanish White** <note>original: "Album Hispanicum"</note> is prepared from tin in the same way that white lead is made from black lead. 37. **Scales** <note>original: "Squamæ"</note> include **copper scale**, which is struck off from the copper bolts used in fabrication; the thick, yellow variety is called **Helites**. 38. **Flower of copper** <note>original: "Flos æris"</note>, or copper filings, is made from dark copper that has been quenched in water and moved to other furnaces; it falls off spontaneously like husks of millet. 39. **Iron scale** <note>original: "stomoma"</note> is more refined and is struck off from the very surface of the metal; it is commonly called **Sinter** <note>a term for the dross or scale produced during forging</note>. 40. Having finished the dry artificial metallic composites, liquid ones follow: these are the **thermal** <note>hot springs</note> and **acidulous** <note>carbonated or mineral-rich</note> waters, which were discussed in Section 2 regarding the state of the world above and below ground. At this point, we shall only consider their diversity according to their various locations. The principal thermal springs are in Italy: those of **Padua**, of which the most famous is the **Ebani Bath**, consisting of a mixture of sulfur, alum, nitre, salt, and lime; the **Porretta** springs, forty miles from Bologna; those of **Lucca**, the chief of which is called the **Bath of Corsena**; **Santa Maria in Bagno**, situated in Romagna; the **waters in the territory of Pisa**; the **Petriola** springs in the Duchy of Siena, which are swollen with alum; the **Grotina** springs in the territory of Viterbo, which consist of iron and copper; the **Perugian** springs, which contain a small amount of sulfur and asphalt; and those of **Montecatini**, all of which are salty, and so on. In Germany, the **Plombières** <note>original: "Plumbariæ"</note> are praised; they are so named in Lorraine because of their copious mixture of lead. The **Baden** springs in Switzerland consist of abundant sulfur and a little alum. The **Wildbad** <note>original: "Ferinæ"</note> springs in the Duchy of Württemberg; the **Zell** springs not far from the **Black Forest** <note>original: "Martiana Sylva"</note>; the **Ammendingen** <note>original: "Amenses"</note> springs situated near Rottenburg on the Neckar; the **Ems** springs on the borders of Lake Constance; the **Carlsbad** <note>original: "Carolinæ"</note> springs in Bohemia; the **Wiesbaden** springs located across the Rhine not far from Mainz; the **Gastein** springs in Bavaria, which, through a powerful astringency, bring about the ease of pregnancy; and the **Abudiacæ** springs <note>near Regensburg</note> above Regensburg, which recall the smell of fried eggs, etc. 41. After the thermal springs come the **acidulous waters**, of which various types exist, for there are many acidic springs in Europe. Among the principal ones in Germany are: the **Spa** <note>original: "Spadani"</note> springs, namely these four: **Geronstère, Pouhon, Sauvenière, and Tonnelet**, about which Henricus ab Heer wrote. The **Griesbach** spring, located at the entrance to the Hercynian Forest, is imbued with iron-vitriol <note>original: "ferro Chalcantho"</note>, crystalline salt, bitumen, and sulfur. The **Petersthal** <note>original: "Petrinus"</note> spring in Alsace, a quarter of a mile from Griesbach, possesses minerals similar to the former. The **Antogast** spring, which is imbued with alum, sulfur, and a moderate amount of vitriol. The **Rippoldsau** <note>original: "Ribelsfavienfis"</note> spring near the same forest in the County of Fürstenberg, which contains the spirited refinements of iron, nitre, vitriol, chalcitis <note>a copper-bearing mineral</note>, and bitumen. The **Guebwiller** <note>original: "Gebersveilenfis"</note> spring in Upper Alsace consists of alum, nitre, and iron. The **Schwalbach** spring; the **Eger** spring in Bohemia; the **Niedernau** spring near Rottenburg on the Neckar; the **Teinach** <note>original: "Deinachiensis"</note> spring in the Hercynian Forest; the **Pfäfers** <note>original: "Federanus"</note> spring in Rhaetia, which contains alum and copper with a tiny bit of sulfur. There are three springs at **Trier**, one of which flows past yellow earth and iron. I shall remain silent regarding the rest. And so I have completed the chapter on metallic composites, and at the same time this entire Sixth Section on mineral and subterranean subjects, as far as their external names and differences are concerned. In this section, although I have been forced at times to speak through the mouths of others contrary to my usual custom, nevertheless...

However, I wish the distribution, order, and direction of this same work to be kept entirely as I intended: for I have arranged it according to my own plan and not without reason, following the standards and laws of *nature. This arrangement did not proceed from some mere dichotomy* <note>original: "Dichotomia"; a method of classification by dividing things into two opposite parts.</note>*, but from the very nature of the subjects themselves, as the second book—which is entirely practical—* will show all these things. It will clearly demonstrate that our division was not made without sufficient reason. Now, having explained this labyrinth, we shall return to our own approach—that is, to our own findings—and in the following chapter, using the chemical method, we shall place the composition and decomposition of minerals (that is, everything proposed in this section) more clearly and, as it were, *in summary* before your eyes, and thus conclude this section.

# Exposing the Composition and Decomposition of
# Subterranean Substances Chemically.

N. 1. *The necessity and utility of this chapter.* N. 2. *The origin of the three principles.* N. 3. *Their simple progression for composing stones, earths, and metals.* N. 4. *Their variety, and the differences in stones, earths, and metals born from it.* N. 5. *The three great solvents from the aforementioned principles.* N. 6. *The decompositions of the universal acid.* N. 7. *The decompositions of the sulfurous solvent.* N. 8. *The decompositions of the mercurial solvent.* N. 9. *The imitation of art in the triple solvent* <note>original: "menstruo"; a solvent used in alchemy to dissolve solids.</note>. <margin>N. 1.</margin>
**A**lthough enough and more has been said in the preceding chapters regarding subterranean composites and decompositions, yet because of the multitude and variety of bodies, as well as the lengthy descriptions, the compositions of the bodies themselves do not come before the eyes in such a way that they are ready as a single idea or occur to the intellect. Even though in Section 3, chapters 5 and 6 of this book, I reviewed the compositions and decompositions of subterranean substances in a general way, those were too *general*, just as the *specific* details reviewed in this section were perhaps too numerous. Therefore, I wished to choose a middle path for the conclusion of this section, lest I omit anything that a curious reader might desire. For although much has been said in Section 4, chapters 6 and 7 regarding the mixture of subterranean substances, the things that will be said here were omitted there because they belong here—to that place, namely, where the entire genesis <note>original: "genesis"; the process of origin or formation.</note> of subterranean substances must be placed before the eyes in a single view, neither too generally nor too specifically.
<margin>N. 2.</margin>
In order to achieve this, we must return to the principles of Minerals, which we have proved above to be *three in number*: *the first is the mother of stones; the second, of earths; the third* [is the mother of metals] <note>The text continues on the next page with "metallorum" (of metals).</note>

of metals: yet in such a way that they concur in various ways, as we shall say later. We proved at the beginning of this book that the first has its natural seat in the earth; that the second and third proceed from the center of the earth and the sea; and we showed in Section 3, chapters 2, 3, and 4, that they are seen under the mask of water, earth, and vapors. *For the first earth is hidden in the Spirit of Vitriol* <note>original: "Spiritu Vitrioli"; a historical term for sulfuric acid</note> *or sulfur, indeed in any alkali; the second in spirit of nitre* <note>original: "spiritu nitri"; nitric acid</note>*, indeed in any oil; the third in spirit of salt* <note>original: "spiritu salis"; hydrochloric acid</note>*, vinegar, soot, and urine* (note these words). For all subjects, not only those beneath the earth but also those above it, consist of these three subjects or participate in them; therefore, *potentially the whole world is filled with metals*. But when these sorts of principles are disposed toward action—that is, in relation to subterranean things—they acquire various degrees of qualities and dispositions. For when they are pure and unmixed, they exist in the simplest form of mixture;

<margin>Note 4.</margin>
*the first is stone*; which is twofold regarding its *surface, either solid or sand*; regarding its *substance, either a stone of glass or of lime*, commonly called *glass or limestone* <note>original German: "Glas oder Kalchstein"</note>, that is, prepared for transparency or opacity: either pure or impure, soft or hard, clear or tinted by the second principle, and from here come so many genera and species of stones: *hard, soft, clear, opaque, watery, tinted, meltable, persistent, pure, impure*; *The second principle is earth*; which is twofold regarding its *surface, dry or liquid*; regarding its *substance, lean or fat, pure or impure*, variously tinted: *white, black, yellow, tawny, red, blue, green*: and from here come not only various genera and species of the earth itself, such as *garden earth, agricultural, potter’s, smelting, medicinal, and painters' earths*; but also mixed things, namely stones and metals, which these earths enter into; according to their diversity, they exist and vary differently. Hence stones and metals of various kinds, varying in color; indeed in substance, purity, and goodness. *For iron has a more impure earth than gold; silver possesses a white earth, copper a red one; the emerald is green, the ruby red, etc.* *the third principle is a viscous glue, coagulating, bonding, giving malleability and extensibility, as well as metallicity* <note>original: "metalleitatem"; the essential quality that makes a substance a metal</note> *or the metallic leaf.* Therefore if (for example) *the first principle is alone, we have Crystal; if the second is added, say a red earth, the Crystal is tinted into a ruby; if the third is added, it will become gold, and it will receive metallicity and extensibility*. The first earth, therefore, properly belongs to *stones*, the second to *earths*, and the third to *metals*. Stones, therefore, are the simplest mixtures; earths more so; metals are the most mixed of all. But to return to the *third* principle, in which the form of the metal lies hidden, it must be known that it also varies in purity and impurity; yet not as much as the first and second principles. Hence <term>metallicity</term> is nearly the same for all metals, but the variety arises partly from the first, and *mostly from the second* principle, as we have said: hence certain metals are *fluid, brittle, tenacious, resonant, light, or heavy*, as we shall explain in the following and final Section. *Fusibility and consistency, transparency and opacity belong to the first principle; color, odor, and taste to the second; and form to the third.* In metals there is *metallicity*, in earths *earthiness*, in stones *stoniness*. And in this triple form, the latter two forms are analogous with the metallic, yet not entirely the same. Therefore, this third principle varies by the aforementioned general trinity; for in its species, many forms of sto-

### Book 1, Section VI, Chapter VIII

<margin>Number 5.</margin>
For nature has produced three great component solvents, from which all decompositions arise; and these owe their origin to the trinity of principles. The first great solvent is called the *universal acid*, concerning which see *Section 2, chapter 4, paragraphs 2 and 5.* The second is *sulfurous*, and the third is *mercurial* or saline. The first owes its origin primarily to the first principle <note>the "vitrifiable" or stony earth</note>, the second to the second principle <note>the "inflammable" or oily earth</note>, and the third to the third principle <note>the "mercurial" or fluid earth</note>: yet in such a way that the remaining principles concur in each, although the name is usually taken from the dominant part.

<margin>Number 6.</margin>
*The first solvent, therefore*, whose primary ingredient is *lime, or an aluminous earth of lime*, and is thus *astringent and acidic*, produces three kinds of decompositions (I will not treat now the nature and cause of this solvent and solution, for I dealt with such matters in *Section 4, chapter 3*). The first *kind of decomposition is of stones*; for when the acid dissolves *limestone* <note>original: "lapidem calcis"</note> by permeating subterranean passages, it prepares alum; because alum consists of lime, as its chemical analysis <note>original: "anatomia"</note> testifies. If it dissolves the stone of glass—that is, a *fusible stone*—*Borax* is formed, for it consists of that, as experience testifies. *The second kind of decomposition from the acidic solvent is earthy*; for when the acid dissolves earths, if they are "lean" <note>low in combustible matter</note>, then *astringent earths of various kinds* are formed; or if they are "fatty"—that is, if it dissolves the pitch or grease of the earth—then *sulfurs* are produced, for *sulfur* consists of *fatty earth and acid*. *The third kind of decomposition from the acidic solvent is metallic*; namely, when the *universal acid* dissolves metals, creating *vitriols* <note>term: vitriola; historical name for metal sulfates like copperas or iron sulfate</note>: of which there are as many species as there are metals—indeed, even metallic decompositions exist. For I have composed Vitriol from Mercury itself, with nothing added but the *acid of sulfur*. Now that the decompositions by the *universal acid* have been explained, we shall proceed to the second decomposing agent, namely the *oily, fatty sulfurous solvent*.

<margin>Number 7.</margin>
This again makes threefold decompositions: the first kind is *earthy*, from which come all *bitumens* <note>natural flammable substances like asphalt or petroleum</note>; the *second is stony*, from which come *coals* <note>term: lithantraces; fossil stone-coal</note> and other things of that kind, as sufficiently explained in preceding chapters; the *third is metallic*, from which come *various metallic sulfurs and arsenics and realgars* <note>term: realgaria; a bright red arsenic sulfide mineral</note>, of which there are as many species as there are minerals.

<margin>Number 8.</margin>
*The third solvent is the Universal Mercurial, from which the decomposition of Mercury arises; which is as manifold as the metals that exist:* and if a species of the second earth is added, a "super-decomposition" occurs, which we call *cinnabar* <note>the bright red ore of mercury</note>. <margin>10</margin> But concerning this mixed and noble super-decomposition, see *Section 3, chapter 5, paragraph 3.* If the reader is wise, he will take this physical-historical narrative as the practical foundation for this whole book, and not disdain to read it through well; for I have written nothing in vain, but everything *from practice*, and so clearly that I must fear on account of envious philosophers, lest I be endangered for their sake, because I reveal those things which no mortal has hitherto disclosed.

<margin>Number 9.</margin>
But having cast off the mask of envy, I shall proceed to be of use, and just as in the preceding parts I have shown all things composed and decomposed from the *triple earth and triple solvent* <note>original: "menstruo"; a chemical solvent</note>...

# Subterranean Physics

I have said that they proceed from the decomposer; so here I assert that it is possible for art to imitate this sixfold group with greater perfection than nature itself. In this place, however, I will speak only of the decomposing solvents <note>original: "menstruis decomponentibus"; 'menstruum' is the standard alchemical term for a solvent</note> (for concerning the components themselves, namely the principles, more than enough has been treated in the preceding parts.) Therefore, in the art <note>the "art" of chemistry or alchemy</note>, there are three solvents, the great decomposers.

The first is the **great acid**, or the **Philosophers' spirit of Sulfur** (rather of their lime or **borax**) which Ripley <note>George Ripley (c. 1415–1490), a famous English alchemist and author of *The Compound of Alchymy*</note> calls superficial; the second is named **Alkaest** <note>a mythical "universal solvent" sought by alchemists</note>, and it is a subtle **oil**, properly owing its origin to the "fatty earth" <note>Becher's second principle, *terra pinguis*, responsible for flammability</note>, namely the fertile principle; with this, bodies are **naturally calcined** (or rather, reduced to powder.) The third is **Mercurial**, which, as Ripley says, is a **most permanent humidity, incombustible and unctuous in its nature**; with this, the revivifications of bodies are performed, whereas with the first, fixations are done, and with the second, **sublimations and incerations** <note>the process of softening a substance to a wax-like consistency</note> are carried out. 

Now, however, a great contradiction will appear from my sayings; for in section three, chapter 4 of this book, I said the **Alkaest** proceeds from the third principle, namely the "mercurifying earth" <note>the third principle, *terra mercurialis*</note>; and in section five, chapter three, paragraphs 17 and 44, I said it proceeds from the **second earth**, which are repugnant to each other. O, how pleasing it is to those who encounter such contradictions in authors' books, so that they may have something with which to pluck at good men and satisfy their envy! But behold the medicine; what if these contradictory things were written so that idiots and such proud asses might be confounded, and might confound their Aristotle, that he might grant them an Ariadne’s thread <note>a guiding clue to get through a labyrinth</note> for this crossroads: but in Philosophy, because of such scoundrels, good men ought not to suffer; therefore, a few words in the ear of our own people: **the beautiful form of women blinded both the strongest Samson and the wisest Solomon; why not me?** <note>Becher uses this biblical metaphor to excuse his human error in the face of nature's beauty and complexity</note> 

O, an error pleasing to the prudent. **"Happy is he who could know the causes of things"** <note>original Latin: "Felix qui potuit rerum cognoscere causas", a famous line from Virgil’s *Georgics*</note>, which is also to be understood regarding what is said of Venus <note>the alchemical name for copper</note> in Section 3, chapter 1, paragraph 13, page 59 and following, and Section 5, chapter 3, paragraphs 71 and 72. Experiments certainly deceive, not only when they do not succeed, but most especially when they do; for then they substitute one thing for another <note>original: "quid pro quo"</note> and blind the eyes. For human reason cannot be driven to believe in simple things, but it delights in subtleties, whence it is deceived. 

Thus this **extraction of Venus** <note>copper extraction</note>, which not only I, but also de Comitibus <note>likely referring to Natalis Comes</note>, Helmont <note>Jan Baptista van Helmont, a pioneer of pneumatic chemistry</note>, and Paracelsus himself believed in, was deceptive, not in practice but in knowledge; for the whiteness proceeds **from the mercurial solvent**, **and by this error I learned to make Mercuries, and to distinguish the arsenifying and mercurifying earth—that is, the Alkaest—from the Mercury of the Philosophers.** Therefore, lovers of chemistry will thank me for these contradictions and detected errors; for I write so freely and candidly, professing my error and uncovering the **truth**: for nature is inscrutable, and we learn every single hour. Pardon must also be given for such a subtle error, which consists almost more in the name than in the reality. 

But we shall hasten to the end of this chapter and section; where also everything is full of danger, lest we run into contradictions; for the Peripatetics <note>followers of Aristotle's philosophy</note> get stuck in words, but we in things, upon which we freely impose names at times, and various ones, according to the exigency of nature. Peripatetic terms differ from chemical ones; **no good Peripatetic is a good spagyrist <note>alchemist</note>, and vice versa**: for nature is repugnant to the fantasy upon which Peripatetic philosophy is chiefly supported. We have praised authors whom elsewhere we have blamed, **but in a different matter**; and that because of the truth...

He emphasizes that practical chemical experience is more valuable than the rigid word-play of Aristotelian (Peripatetic) philosophers.</summary>

->### Book I. Section VI. Chapter VIII. 271<-

...we have considered the nature of things more than the status of persons. Finally, and this is of the greatest importance, we are writing such things as have been read in no author until now; namely, definitions of subterranean mixtures <note>The term "mixtures" refers to minerals and ores composed of different elements.</note> derived not from their external form, but from their internal constitution, mixture, and **crasis** <term>crasis: the unique "temperament" or proportional blending of qualities in a substance</term>. These are few words; but to the reader, if he be wise, they will be more pleasing than all the preceding apparatus gathered from Jonston <note>John Jonston (1603–1675), a natural historian</note>, Boëtius <note>Anselmus de Boodt (1550–1632), author of a famous work on gems and stones</note>, and others. For my work rests upon experience. I hope, therefore, to satisfy the good, or at the very least to provide an occasion for further investigation; for the wicked and envious, I shall provide material for slander—which, however, as it has done until now, will only stimulate me daily toward greater virtue.

Therefore, with good courage, I shall gird myself for certain definitions of subterranean composites and de-composites, and I shall break through the ice in this field, which is quite stubborn and solid. To anyone whom these things do not please, **let him do it better** <note>original German: "der mache es besser"</note>; provided that he does not, like **Mayer** in his recently published *Philosophical Assemblies*, transcribe whole pages word-for-word from my *Metallurgy* without even citing the author, though he had cited many others. That poor little fellow <note>original: "homuncio"</note> feared, I suppose, that nothing would be left for him that could be called his own, for he had claimed mine for himself. This did not actually trouble me, nor did it change my friendship toward the man; indeed, I would have held out alms to him as if to a beggar. He would have been a luckier philosopher if he had been a charcoal-burner <note>A "carbonarius" or practical worker at the furnace</note> rather than a "bookshelf philosopher," and had not written until he had learned how to write—a pitiable youth. But now, as far as possible, I will append the **Physical Nomenclature** in a brief compendium, and thus close this section, which has been truly most laborious for me.

**Salt**, if it is taken as a principle of things, is a stone of either glass or lime, lurking in its own **mask** <note>original: "larva"; here meaning its outward appearance or "guise"</note>; thereafter it is found in **alkali**, and in any spirit of vitriol or sulfur. For **alkali** is defined as that which becomes lime dissolved in water. It differs from alum in that an **acid** intervenes there, whereas in alkali it is an **oil**; and **Spirit of vitriol and sulfur** is defined as what becomes volatile lime dissolved and volatilized through **acid**.

**Sulfur**, if it is established as a principle, is the earth of sulfur and of every fatness and flammable matter, even **spirit of nitre** <note>Nitric acid</note>; which is defined as what becomes **fatty earth** dissolved by **urinous salt** <note>Salt derived from organic sources, often ammoniacal</note> and volatilized.

**Mercury**, if it be established as a principle, is the **mercurificating earth of common salt**, findable in every **acid and urinous substance**, arising and prepared through the **separation of arsenical earth**.

**Aqueous Stone** is defined as that which becomes the **first pure principle**; if it is opaque, a **second earth** has been added, namely an opaque one; if it is **tinctured by the earth of sulfur**, it is threefold: either of lime, of glass, or an intermediate.

**Earth** is defined as that which becomes a principle. Namely, the second; if the **first** is mixed in, it **turns to stone**; if the **third**, it **turns to metal**, and becomes a "de-composite," concerning which we spoke before; it is lean, fatty, etc., as was said in the preceding parts.

**Metal** is either a mixture of just proportion, and then pertains to the six metals; or it is unequally mixed, and then pertains to **minerals**; it acquires its metallicity from **molten earth**, and receives various stones, earths, and salts into the mixture.

**Salt of Nitre** <note>Saltpeter</note> is fatty earth, dissolved by a volatile, urinous, and acidic salt.

*Common salt* is a mixture of water and a mercurial and arsenical earth.
*Alkali salt* is made of lime, fatty earth, and water.
*Salt of alum* is made of lime and the universal acid.
*Salt of Borax* is made from vitrifiable stone <note>Stone that can be turned into glass</note> and the universal acid; it is a rival to the **chrysocolla** <term>chrysocolla: a material used in soldering gold, often associated with borax in early chemistry</term> made by art.
*Salt of Vitriol* is from metal and the universal acid.
*Sal ammoniac* is an artificial salt, both urinous and saline.
*Sulfur* is from the bitumen of the earth and the universal acid; sometimes metals are added.
*Fatness* <note>original: *Pinguedo*</note> is fatty earth dissolved by volatile salt.
*Arsenic* consists of the sulfurous earth which is found in common salt, with metal intermixed.
*Orpiment* <note>original: *Auripigmentum*, a yellow arsenic sulfide mineral</note> is arsenic, except that common sulfurous earth is added.
*Quicksilver* <note>Mercury</note> is a metal, vivified through the fluidifying earth of salt.
*Cinnabar* is quicksilver with the earth of common sulfur intermixed.
*Mineral waters* consist of the aforementioned dry bodies placed within aqueous ones.
Art imitates all these de-composites; hence artificial gems <note>original: *amausa*, glass pastes used to mimic jewels</note>, flowers, crocuses <note>fine metallic powders</note>, salts, butters <note>thick, oily chemical precipitates</note>, horns <note>such as *Luna Cornea* or silver chloride</note>, mercuries, arsenics, vitriols, and sulfurs are made by art.
*Universal acid* is the spirit of salt, altered by the earth of lime.
*Alkahest* <note>The hypothesized "universal solvent" of alchemy</note> consists of subtle oil—that is, the arsenical sulfur-earth found in salt—which has been refined.
<margin>G</margin> *Mercury of the Philosophers* is the mercury-making earth lurking in salt; it is called "doubled" if it be animated by the Sulfur of the Philosophers.
*Sulfur of the Philosophers* is the second fatty earth, most pure, incombustible, present everywhere, yet known by few.
*Tincture* <note>The Elixir or Philosophers' Stone in liquid form</note> is the Mercury of the Philosophers, imbued with the aforementioned sulfur, and led to fixation and more than perfection.
*Earth* in general is dry; *water* is fluid earth; *air* is subtle earth; *fire* is rarefied earth.
*Heaven* is the element of the rare and the dense.
*Nature* is motion, preserving all things in that disposition in which they were created and produced by God.
*God* is the first and uncreated being, the sole cause and principle of movement.

You have here, kind reader, the entire Alphabet of Nature; see how modestly **Philosophy** dwells—what a great task it was to reduce her into a compendium from such many wanderings! The aforementioned definitions are practical, and therefore their truth will be defended in the second book under the specific "anatomy" of each subject; now we shall put an end to this Section and hasten to the last.

## T E X T U S.

Now that the subterranean bodies have been explained, it remains for us to discuss their *Physical* accidents and properties, and that *only in general terms*: since in the second book we will provide all these things most sufficiently in practice. In this place, however, we will provide the reasons and causes of these properties, so that it will not be necessary to involve many theoretical matters in the second book, which is entirely practical; and this is the reason why we have added this section to this first book, intending to add in its place, in the second book, *certain manipulations concerning the anatomy of subterranean things, such as the assaying of metals, salts, and stones, and their liquefactions and refinings.* 

But to come to our purpose, I had indeed decided to explain each paragraph in a lengthy chapter of its own; however, because much *practice* <note>experimental or laboratory work</note> would have to be mixed in, which would rather belong to the *second book*, I did not want to fill this first book, which is theoretical, with much *practice*, just as I did not want to fill the *second* with much *theory*. Furthermore, I remembered that I had explained these paragraphs for the most part in the *third part of my Metallurgy*; and so it would be useless to write the same thing twice. It pleased me, therefore, to reduce this entire teaching on the physical accidents and properties of subterranean things into a compendium, to include it in this single chapter, and to insert those things which were either omitted in my *Metallurgy*, or placed more obscurely, or have been better discovered by me until now. It will be your part, kind Reader, to look upon this labor with favor.

It should be known, then, to make a beginning, that every subterranean body is *mixed*, whether it be *composite* or *de-composite*. For the listed principles of subterranean things themselves are mixed in a certain *respect*;
<margin>N. 1.</margin> 
for there is nothing in the sublunary world <note>the region of Earth, as opposed to the unchanging heavens</note> that is not mixed: yet one more than another. Hence those things which are mixed in the positive degree are called *simple*; those in the comparative, *composite*; and those in the superlative, *de-composite and super-de-composite*. Which are simple, which composite, and which de-composite, I have explained enough and more, and almost to the point of nausea, in the preceding Section; hence I will spare you an unpleasant repetition. You will find the causes of composition and decomposition in various places in this book, especially in Section 4, Chapter 3. Now, we will explain what is *homogeneous* or *heterogeneous*.

<margin>N. 2.</margin> 
It should be known, however, that in nature nothing is heterogeneous, namely with respect to the symmetry of the whole; for all things cohere most sweetly and naturally, and all are perfect in their own way, and necessary with respect to the whole.
