## T E X T.
Now that we have explained the subterranean bodies, it remains for us to discuss their physical properties and characteristics, and to do so *only in general terms*; in the second book, we shall demonstrate all these things sufficiently in practice. In this place, however, we shall provide the *reasons and causes of these properties*, so that it will not be necessary to involve many theoretical matters in the second book, which is entirely practical. This is the reason why we have added this section to this first book, intending to add in its place in the second book certain manipulations regarding the <term>anatomy</term> <note>In 17th-century chemistry, "anatomy" referred to the chemical analysis or breaking down of a substance into its parts.</note> of subterranean things, such as the assaying of metals, salts, and stones, as well as their melting and refining.

To come to our purpose: I had indeed intended to explain each paragraph at length in its own chapter. However, because much practice would have had to be mixed in—which belongs more properly to the second book—I did not want to fill this first book (which is theoretical) with much practice, just as I did not want to fill the second with much theory. Furthermore, I remembered that I had explained these paragraphs for the most part in the third part of my *Metallurgy*; thus, it would be pointless to write the same thing twice. Therefore, it pleased me to reduce this entire doctrine of the physical properties and characteristics of subterranean things into a compendium, to comprehend them in this single chapter, and to insert those things which were either omitted from my *Metallurgy*, stated too obscurely, or which I have discovered more clearly until now. It will be your task, *Benevolent Reader*, to judge this labor fairly.

<margin>N. 1.</margin>
To begin, it must be known that every subterranean body is a mixture, whether <term>composite</term> or <term>decomposed</term> <note>Becher uses "decomposed" to mean a substance that has been combined multiple times, not "rotted" in the modern sense.</note>. For the very principles of subterranean things that we have reviewed are, in a certain respect, mixed; for there is nothing in the <term>sublunar world</term> <note>The Earthly realm below the sphere of the moon, subject to change and decay.</note> that is not mixed, though one thing may be more so than another. Hence, those things which are mixed in the "positive" degree are called simple; those in the "comparative" are called composite; and those in the "superlative" are called decomposed and super-decomposed. Which things are simple, which composite, and which decomposed, I have explained more than enough—almost to the point of boredom—in the preceding section; therefore, I shall spare you an unwelcome repetition. You will find the causes of composition and decomposition in various places in this book, especially in Section 4, Chapter 3.

<margin>N. 2.</margin>
Now, we shall explain what is homogeneous or heterogeneous. It must be known that in nature there is nothing heterogeneous with respect to the symmetry of the whole; for all things cohere most sweetly and naturally, and all are perfect in their own way and necessary with respect to the whole. But if we consider the mixture, those things are called heterogeneous which are of a different mixture—that is, those which, when mixed together, do not cohere; as...

...as if you were to mix wood with flesh, or an apple with gold. Thus, among subterranean things, there are heterogeneous substances <note>Substances of a different kind that do not naturally bond</note> which do not remain stable in a mixture; such is tin, which—except for lead—makes all metals with which it is mixed brittle. This is also to be understood regarding **brass** <note>original: "Orichalco"</note>, and among stones, the **vitrifiable** ones <note>Stones that can be turned into glass</note> do not mix with those from which **quicklime** <note>original: "calx viva"; a caustic substance produced by heating limestone</note> is prepared. For just as all stones are either opaque or transparent, so too are they all changed either into **glass** or into **lime**. For those stones which produce **lime** do not **vitrify**; if they were to turn into glass, they could not be reduced to lime, and thus **lime** would not exist in the nature of things. Conversely, stones that **vitrify** do not produce **lime**, because they are reduced to glass before they can be calcined <note>Reduced to powder by heat</note>; if they did not do so, **glass** would not exist in the nature of things. Therefore, the common axiom is: *Vitrifiable stones do not produce lime; and conversely, lime-stones do not produce glass.* Because of this difference, these two kinds of stones are mixed with great difficulty, and in their mixture, they are, as it were, **heterogeneous**. 

Furthermore, those things are called **heterogeneous** which do not cohere, especially in **metals**, which ought to be entirely **homogeneous** <note>Uniform in substance</note> to one another, so that every part of them preserves its roundness and **homogeneity**. Then again, many things seem to be **heterogeneous** which nevertheless truly enter into a **homogeneous** mixture with metals; such are their principles, namely **those three earths** about which I wrote in Section 3 of this book. From this foundation, various **earths and stones** enter into the mixture of metals. On the occasion of this "entry," I cannot help but recount to the reader a remarkable experiment, which proceeds as follows:

**Glauber** <note>Johann Rudolph Glauber (1604–1670), a famous apothecary and early chemist</note>, in the treatise he titled *Proserpina*, and in his other trifles, teaches how the tincture of **precious stones** can be extracted by means of **oil of Vitriol** <note>Sulfuric acid</note>. He concentrates the extracted tincture into a stone, with which he tints silver <note>original: "lunam" (the moon), the alchemical symbol for silver</note>. *But just as all his works are empty dreams, deceptions, and impostures—partly mere conjectures—so too does it go with this experiment, which is utterly false.* For the **oil of Vitriol** is indeed colored, but not from the stones; that coloration proceeds from the very nature of the oil of Vitriol itself. I sweated much to amend the process so that it might succeed, but everything was attempted in vain. 

I then took an entirely different path; for I observed that stones lack the **third principle**, namely **metallicity** <note>original: "metalleitatem"; the quality that makes a substance a metal</note>. Therefore, suspecting that stones have a great harmony with the principle of **Mercury**, I dissolved them easily by that means. Having taken a mineral subject which, more than others, was filled with a penetrating and abundant **Mercury**, I began to pulverize it and mix it in a certain proportion with crushed stones, and then to melt it. I found a **metallic mixture**; for the mineral of which I speak had totally absorbed the stone—which, in this case, was a garnet. In the melted mass, I observed nothing heterogeneous, neither glass nor slag; from which I firmly concluded (as the weight also demonstrated) that the entire quantity of the garnet had assumed **metallicity**. This is also shown by the **regulus** <note>The metallic heart or button found at the bottom of a crucible after smelting</note>, in which I discovered the true tincture of the garnets to be hidden. 

I was thus greatly rejoiced that I had found a way to resolve any stones with little effort. For I progressed further and treated **hematite** <note>Iron ore</note>, **red ochre** <note>original: "rubricam"</note>, and various other stones—even **earths** such as **emery** <note>original: "Smiridem"</note>, **Armenian bole** <note>A medicinal red clay</note>, etc.—in this way, and not without profit. If the reader is wise and understands what I write here, he will thank me greatly; for he will find a way to prepare not only the most excellent **medicines**, but **certain other things** as well. In this place...

### Book I. Section VII. & Final Single Chapter.

...I only wished to demonstrate that earths and stones, although they appear to be **heterogeneous** <note>composed of different kinds of substances</note> with metals, are nevertheless **homogeneous** <note>composed of the same kind of substance</note>, and essentially enter into the metallic mixture itself. Hence, it is most certain that metals consist of these types of principles—namely, from earths—which I have demonstrated at length in Section 3, Chapter 5, Paragraph 14, page 98.

<margin>N. 3.</margin> We have reviewed mixture and **solution** <note>the process of dissolving a solid into a liquid</note> at length in the preceding Sections, as well as in our *Chemical Oedipus*; specifically, what constitutes a **radical solution** <note>original: "radicalis solutio"; a deep dissolution that returns a substance to its primary "root" or elements</note>, which occurs through its own principles. And since the third principle, which is **Mercurial** <note>the volatile, fluid, or "spirit" principle in alchemy</note>, is generally more penetrating than the others, it is therefore more frequently used for dissolution. However, a distinction must be made between the solution proper to stones and that proper to metals; for to dissolve stones, a different dissolving earth is required than for metals. This is because the third principle varies in them, as we said in Chapter 6, Section 4. This is to be understood if the solution is established for the purpose of **natural augmentation** <note>the "growth" or transmutation of metals</note>, that is, so that the solvent is re-coagulated with the dissolved substance. In that case, the solvent belongs to metals if it gives and preserves **metalleity** <note>the essential quality of being a metal</note>, and to stones if it gives **stoniness**. All Philosophers <note>Referring to "natural philosophers" or alchemists</note> require this first in their solvent; hence **Count Bernard** <note>original: "Comes Bernardus"; likely Bernard of Trevisan, a famous 15th-century alchemist</note> says: <note>original: "Amen dico tibi, quod nulla aqua corporibus in solutione conveniat, quae non eis permanet in materia & forma, & quam metalla soluta recoagulare possunt, &c."</note> *Verily I say to you, that no water is suitable for the dissolution of bodies which does not remain with them in matter and form, and which the dissolved metals are able to re-coagulate, etc.* I have placed a rare and pleasing experiment concerning the dissolution of stones on page 71, paragraph 13 of this book, where the solvent passed into the nature of the dissolved stone; see the remaining points on mixture and solution in their proper places.

<margin>N. 4.</margin> **Perfection** and **deterioration** are to be understood such that nothing in nature is evil, for God created all things in perfection, and each thing persists in its own being. Deterioration, however, happens in respect to something else, or a prior state. For if **lead** were made from **gold**, it would certainly be deteriorated in respect to its prior existence. Meanwhile, insofar as it is lead, it would be perfect in its own kind. Perfection, therefore, consists in some relation according to those who value it; hence that proverb: <note>original: "Ein edler Stein ist so viel werth, als ein reicher Narr dafür giebt."</note> *A noble stone is worth as much as a rich fool pays for it.* If perfection is considered more specifically, it is the **natural state** of any body. For example, in a **diamond** <note>original: "adamante"</note>, transparency, clarity, and hardness cause perfection; if spots, impurity, or something similar are added, it is then called imperfect. In **gold**, **fixity, weight, malleability, and a yellow color** are desired; if one of these is missing, it will be imperfect. Therefore, that is said to deteriorate which changes for the worse from its natural state. But that is perfected which is either exalted in its own being or transmuted from one being into another that is more highly valued in civil relations; for in a **Physical relation**, all bodies are **perfect**. In a **feather**, lightness is of as much value as weight is in **gold**; and **softness** in **leather** is of as much praise as **hardness** is in a **diamond**.

<margin>N. 5.</margin> **Corruptibility** and **persistence** (which is opposed to corruptibility) were sufficiently explained in Sections 4 and 5, namely regarding mixture, solution, and their causes. There I proved that the fewer and simpler parts bodies have, the less they are subject to corruptibility. Hence, animals are the most corruptible of all things, while metals, on the contrary, are the most durable. Indeed, although nothing under the sun is constant and eternal, especially among **sublunary things** <note>things on Earth, below the moon, which were thought to be subject to change and decay</note>, nevertheless by means of art, **Glass** is prepared that will certainly last forever; yet it can still be resolved by art...

# Subterranean Physics

...can endure by force; and the **tincture**, or as they call it, the **Philosopher’s Stone** <note>original: "lapis Philosophorum"; the legendary substance capable of turning base metals into gold</note>, also cannot be corrupted by any Element, even though its generation proceeds from corruption—specifically, from the conjunction and **putrefaction** <note>original: "putrefactio"; in alchemy, a stage of breaking down substances to their primal state</note> of the **primal essence** <note>original: "primi entis"</note> of metals **with gold**. Some have called that primal essence **steel** <note>original: "chalybem"</note>, which is attracted by a magnet—that is, by **immature electrum** <note>original: "electrum immaturum"; here referring to a substance with attractive properties like amber or a specific metallic alloy</note>—and in this attraction the whole business consists. But to return to our purpose: that is said to be "corrupted" which departs from its natural state. However, the natural state is twofold: one **at rest**, the other **in motion**. **Stones and mixed metals** are fixed and exist **at rest**; but **those things which grow**, which are generated, and which **live** are in **continuous motion**. That motion consists of a perpetual **reaction**: thus the **action of fire upon oil** causes a reaction, from which comes flame; and the **soul** perpetually reacts upon the **body**, from which comes life, which behaves like a flame. But I have treated the subject of corruptibility sufficiently in the chapter on **putrefaction**.

<margin>N. 6.</margin>
The masks <note>original: "larva"; the outward appearance or "disguise" of an element</note> of subterranean **fire, air, water, and earth** are not rarely seen. The **earthy form** is their own property, and hence, as I said at the beginning of this book on page **21**, they are included under the name of "earth" in Holy Scripture. I treated **stony and metallic waters**, as well as **minerals**, in Section 2. If you make **distilled verdigris** <note>original: "viride æris destillatum"; a green pigment or salt of copper</note> from copper and dissolve it in **spirit of wine** <note>original: "spiritu Vini"; distilled alcohol</note>, soak a paper in the solution, and set it on fire, you will see an **elegant green flame**. In this, there is no doubt that copper atoms are present in a **masked flame** <note>original: "flamma larvari"</note>. Furthermore, the **flame** is resolved into air, to which it also communicates the copper atoms. Many things should be observed regarding this combustion, for the metal **so ignited** undergoes wondrous changes. Moreover, the **thunderstone** <note>original: "cerauneas lapis"; ancient term for meteorites or fossils believed to fall from the sky during storms</note> teaches us that **stony corpuscles** wander in the air, for it consists of such corpuscles **coagulated as if in a moment**.

<margin>N. 7.</margin>
**Heat and cold** exist within minerals. Heat is understood in two ways: **external and internal—namely, actual and potential.** Actually, metals are **cold**, and this is due to the constriction of their pores and the tight structure of their principles. However, they are capable of being heated; they receive fiery particles and communicate them to one another across a long sphere of activity. For instance, if you place a plate of iron, copper, or silver—even many feet long—into a fire at just one end and heat it, the heat will immediately extend all the way to the other end. But if metals are treated with **flames**, they feel no small **alteration**; for since flames are acidic, they gnaw away at metals, and from this come the **saffrons of metals** <note>original: "croci metallorum"; the colorful powders or oxides formed when metals are corroded by acids or heat</note>. I have treated these in the chapter on **liquefaction**. I said before that a perpetual **cold** exists in subterranean things, but experience teaches that a **potential heat** also lies hidden within. This is especially true in that **universal acid** which I discussed in Section 2, where I also treated **fire-vomiting mountains** <note>volcanoes</note> and **hot springs**. If **Oil of Vitriol** <note>original: "Oleum Vitrioli"; concentrated sulfuric acid</note> is properly rectified, it contains the **highest heat potentially**. You can test this if you suddenly pour a quantity of cold water into it; you will immediately notice the greatest heat and boiling, but more on this elsewhere.

<margin>N. 8.</margin>
**Humidity and dryness** exist in metals and stones: one is **accidental**, the other **essential**. Certain stones, such as **marble**, sweat almost perpetually; but that sweating does not come from the stone, but from the **surrounding air**. The air, condensed by the cold marble, is resolved into water; and this is also the reason for **oils produced by deliquescence** <note>original: "oleorum per deliquium"; the process where a salt absorbs so much moisture from the air that it turns into a liquid "oil"</note>. Truly **essential** humidity does not make the hands wet, nor is it properly "moist," but rather **viscous and mercurial**. The **humidity of stones**, however, is more **watery**, because it is usually mixed with water as the instrument of its composition. ### Book I. Section VII. & Last. Single Chapter.

...metals <note>original: "metalla"; completing the word from the previous page</note> also cannot be dissolved into any liquid state unless moisture is added; hence the things that not only **Glauber** <note>Johann Rudolf Glauber (1604–1670), a famous chemist known for "Glauber's salt" and his work on "potable gold"</note> but also others babble about regarding **potable metals** <note>original: "metallis potabilibus"; gold or other metals processed into a drinkable medicinal form</note> are trifles. This is true unless one wishes to play with definitions, for gold leaves are indeed drunk in common **aqua vitae** <note>literally "water of life"; high-proof distilled alcohol</note>, but they are drinkable not by their own nature, but by the help of the spirits of wine.

<margin>N. 9.</margin>
We have explained **solidity and fluidity** at length in the chapter on liquefaction (Section 5, page 196 and following), to which we refer the reader. Here we will repeat only a summary: all **fluidity proceeds through the internal reception of corpuscles—whether earthy, watery, airy, or fiery**: this is mediated by rarity and density, which are caused by heat or **cold** within the subject that we called **heaven** <note>original: "cælum"; here likely referring to the internal atmosphere or "space" within a substance</note> in the first chapter of this book.

<margin>N. 10.</margin>
**Hardness and softness** come from the rarity and density of the **pores**; but an internal **constitution of principles** is also required. For those things that possess much of the **first principle** are **hard**, as we see in bones; those that have much of the **second principle** are **soft**. We have sufficiently explained all these matters in the third part of our *Metallurgy*.

<margin>N. 11.</margin>
**Malleability and brittleness** <note>original: "friabilitas"</note> acknowledge **hardness and softness** as their mother, as it were. **Porosity and softness** create **malleability**; whereas **density and hardness** are required for **brittleness**. But these are not the only causes of malleability and brittleness; for malleability proceeds from the **second earth**—namely the fatty, viscous, and therefore extensible earth—while brittleness proceeds from the **first earth**. Tin abounds in this first earth, which is the source of its **crackling** <note>original: "stridor"; the "cry of tin," a distinct sound made when bending a bar of pure tin</note>; and if you mix tin with other metals, they are rendered brittle, which is the same effect that **lime** <note>original: "calx"; the powdery residue left after a metal or mineral is burned</note> produces.

<margin>N. 12.</margin>
**Porosity and compaction** come from rarefied or densified air which the body receives into its pores; the body varies according to the quantity and degree of this reception. This variation, however, comes from lightness and gravity; for the more or less light or heavy bodies are, the more or less they cohere to themselves, and they receive much or little air in proportion to this cohesion.

<margin>N. 13.</margin>
**Lightness and gravity** are the most common qualities of a body, although nothing in nature is truly light except in relation to something else, for everything light is heavy to a certain degree. Therefore, **gravity** is the most common and primary quality of a body. Every physical body must have quantity, and by the alteration of that quantity the whole body is essentially changed, as we proposed in the chapter on liquefaction (§ 126). Indeed, in Section 4, Chapter 4, § 11, we proved that **gravity is the essential cause of form**. Furthermore, **gravity** varies not only by the ratio of rarity and density, but proceeds from an internal cause, specifically the **third earth**. For the **diamond** <note>original: "Adamas"</note> is a most **compact** body, certainly much more compact than gold; yet it does not follow that it is the **heaviest**. Experience teaches that gold is much **heavier** than a diamond, but we dealt with these matters in the chapter on liquefaction (§ 112).

<margin>N. 14.</margin>
**Volatility and fixity** come from rarity and density; yet there is also an internal reason for these qualities which lies in the principles themselves. When subjects contain much of the **first and second** principle, they are **more fixed** than if they exceed in the **third** principle, and vice versa. It is from this foundation that **oil of Vitriol** <note>original: "oleum Vitrioli"; concentrated sulfuric acid</note> **fixes** substances so powerfully, because the **earth of lime** <note>original: "terra calcis"</note> lies hidden within it. Thus, just as I attributed the diverse gravity of earths to their diverse substances produced by the Creator, so I assign **fixity** to certain earths that were **specified** in this way during their very first production. You will find the remaining arguments on **fixity and volatility** in my *Metallurgy*.

...such things cannot be resolved into any liquid unless something is added; therefore, the stories told about **potable metals** <note>Metals in a drinkable, liquid form, often sought as a medicinal "elixir of life."</note>—not only by **Glauber** <note>Johann Rudolf Glauber (1604–1670), a famous chemist known for his work on salts and mineral acids.</note> but by others as well—are nonsense. This is true unless one wishes to play with words, for gold leaf is indeed drunk in common **water of life** <note>original: "aqua vitæ"; a strong alcoholic spirit or brandy</note>, though it is not drinkable by itself but only by the power of the **spirit of wine** <note>original: "spiritus Vini"; purified alcohol or ethanol</note>.

Based on the ratio of this cohesion, they take in more or less air.

<margin>No. 13.</margin>
**Lightness and heaviness** are the most common qualities of a body, although nothing in nature is truly light except in relation to something else; for everything light is heavy to a certain degree. # Subterranean Physics
### Page 278

<margin>No. 15.</margin> **Combustibility and incombustibility** <note>original: "Ustibilitas & incombustibilitas"</note> are also properties specific to subterranean things. A thing is said to be **combustible** <note>original: "ustile"</note> when it is thinned out and dissolved into flames, a process similar to **fermentation**, as I explained in the chapter on **fermentation**, section 151 and following. Indeed, nothing burns—even if it is oily or "fatty"—unless salt-like particles are present. These salt particles consist largely of water, which is required for burning so that it may be resolved into air and the air may be thinned. Therefore, those subterranean substances which are indeed fatty but not salty do not burn. Furthermore, things are said to be **consumed** <note>original: "comburi"</note> when they are used up by fire; however, properly speaking, fire consumes nothing, but rather alters it and causes the volatile parts to evaporate. In this way, everything in the fire is "consumed" that is not **fixed** <note>In alchemy and early chemistry, "fixed" refers to a substance that remains stable and solid when exposed to high heat, rather than evaporating or turning to gas.</note>. Nothing can be called fixed if it is altered by fire or driven into flames. Hence, stones that yield **lime** <note>Calcium oxide, produced by heating limestone.</note>, although they are extremely stable, should not properly be called fixed, since they are changed into lime and thus altered. On the other hand, the **diamond** and the **ruby** remain unchanged in the fire, and for this reason, they are called fixed. This is also to be understood regarding **gold and silver**, whose **incombustibility** consists in the fact that they are not only unconsumed by fire, but they remain unchanged in **cupellation** <note>original: "cineritio"; a refining process where ores are heated in a shallow hearth or "cupel" made of bone ash to separate precious metals from lead and impurities.</note>; they preserve their compact homogeneity. Thus, like fatty substances, they form "flowers" <note>likely referring to the bright, metallic surface or "bead" that forms during refining</note> in the cupellation hearth; meanwhile, **lead** and other metals are absorbed into the pores of the cupel, being of a thinner mixture. And so **gold and silver** remain in the cupellation hearth, as if filtered, appearing more compact, thicker, and richer. The remaining points concerning incombustibility were set forth previously, where we spoke of the **Incombustible Sulfur of the Philosophers**; this is nothing other than a "fatty earth" <note>original: "terra pinguis"; Becher's term for the principle of inflammability, later known as Phlogiston.</note> that is highly fixed, pure, mixed with no salt, but soaked and waxed with **mercurial earth** <note>original: "terra mercurialis"; the principle of fluidity and metallic luster.</note>.

<margin>No. 16.</margin> Account must also be taken of **transparency and opacity** <note>original: "diaphaneitatis & opacitatis"</note>. Here, it must be recalled what I have said quite often: namely, that from the beginning of creation, God produced various types of earths, some of which are transparent and others opaque. From the mixing of these, various species arise. **Metals would be transparent** if they lacked the "third earth" <note>original: "tertia terra"; also called "terra lapidea" or stony earth, which provides weight and solidity.</note>; but then they would not exist as metals. **Stones are transparent**, even if they are mixed with the "second earth"; but if the opaque "third earth" intervenes instead, the transparency ceases. This must also be considered: not every transparent thing is porous, despite how some define transparency and believe it consists in having pores. For a **sponge** is a most porous stone, yet it is nonetheless opaque. **Glass**, on the contrary, is a most compact body, yet it is entirely transparent. Therefore, those things should rather be called **transparent** which lean more toward "watery earth," and those will be **opaque** which tend more toward "earthy earth," if I may put it that way.

<margin>No. 17.</margin> The **sound of subterranean things, especially metals**, is attributed to rarity and density. In this regard, the subject acts **like a sieve** <note>original: "cribri instar"</note>, in whose pores the struck air is reverberated. Hence, red-hot metals give off a different sound than cold ones, as we have explained all these things at length with many observations and experiments in the third part of our **Metallurgy**.

<margin>No. 18.</margin> I attribute the **diverse figures and forms of things** to **gravity** <note>weight or heaviness</note>, by which particles are carried into different positions; and from this arrangement, the form of things essentially proceeds. Therefore, the fewer and simpler the particles that enter into a mixture, the simpler and more homogeneous the form is; we see this in metals, which preserve a rounded shape. Those...

# Book I. Section VII. & Last. Single Chapter.

Meanwhile, forms that constitute various figures, such as **vegetables** <note>In this context, "vegetables" refers to the entire plant kingdom.</note> and animals, must necessarily consist of particles of differing gravity. Because of this diversity, they cannot cohere as strongly as metals; thus, such **forms**, though beautiful to look upon, are easily altered by even a slight mishap.

<margin>No. 19.</margin> Among purely earthy subterranean substances, there is no **taste** <note>original: "Sapor"</note> except for **astringency** <note>A dry, puckering mouthfeel.</note>. However, in those mixtures where **water** and **salts** meet, various kinds of tastes emerge. We see this even in **artificial products** <note>original: "artefactis," referring to chemically prepared substances.</note>, such as in **Sugar of Saturn** <note>original: "saccharo Saturni"; this is lead acetate, a poisonous but sweet-tasting substance.</note> and others. We have proved above that all such taste is merely superficial, proceeding from the rarity or density of the substance, and varying according to the diversity of the solvent and the solute. Indeed, experience proves that various medicinal operations consist in this rarity and quality of taste. This also convinces those who deny that metals possess medical power, and those who contend that no medicine can be rightly prepared from a metal unless it is reduced to its **prime matter** <note>original: "primam materiam"; in alchemy, the formless base substance from which all things are made.</note>. But these people themselves do not know what they mean by "reduction into prime matter." In my book ***Chemical Oedipus*** <note>original: "Oedipo Chymico"; a work by the author, Johann Joachim Becher, published in 1664.</note>, I distinguished between the **solution** <note>The process of dissolving a solid into a liquid.</note> that serves for generation and that which serves for medical use. In the latter, various medicines can be given even without reduction to prime matter, as we see in Sugar of Saturn. The same is seen in **vitriol** <note>Sulfate minerals.</note>, **sublimate** <note>Likely mercuric chloride.</note>, **crystals of the moon** <note>original: "crystallis lunae"; silver nitrate.</note>, and other mixtures; in their simple state, these have none of the effects they achieve when they are changed by art into new decomposed forms. For neither silver nor **strong water** <note>original: "aqua fortis"; nitric acid.</note> by themselves drive out urine; yet when silver is dissolved in strong water and drawn off to a third, and then condensed into crystals in the cold, it acquires a very great **diuretic power** <note>The ability to promote the production of urine.</note>. Furthermore, how taste is produced on the tongue, and which nerves allow the tongue to taste, is not for me to explain here, nor shall I recount what the more curious observers have found so far with **microscopes** in this matter; for these things belong rather to the physics of the world above the earth. To this must still be added: that by means of a certain simple salt, a "vitriolated" taste can be drawn from gold, which possesses the greatest medical virtue. It is extremely helpful in the resolving of the internal organs, and more precious in its operation than all the reductions of gold into prime matter. But regarding this preparation, I shall speak in the second book.

<margin>No. 20.</margin> Common experience of the sense of **smell** <note>original: "olfactus"</note> teaches us that subtle atoms emanate from metals—especially copper, tin, and **brass** <note>original: "Orichalcum."</note>—which are perceived by the nose, especially if the metals are rubbed with a finger so that they heat up a little. However, it is not so obvious to everyone how they can transpire so perpetually without a loss of their virtues or a degradation of the subject. Yet it is credible that the surrounding air is indeed somewhat filled with metallic atoms, and that the air itself communicates new and perpetual atoms to the metal by some mutual communication and reaction; for metals, especially lead, are found to take an increase rather than a decrease from the air. Furthermore, if what they commonly say about the falling rod—popularly called the **dowsing rod** <note>original: "Wünſchel-Ruth."</note>—is true, namely that it inclines toward metals (*which, indeed, I have never seen with success*), certainly no other reason could be assigned than that metallic atoms of this sort exhale, commonly called **scenting** <note>original: "Wittern"; a mining term referring to the "exhalation" or "weathering" of ores.</note>, and this exhalation draws that rod toward itself.

<margin>No. 21.</margin> It now remains for me to explain the **color** that exists in subterranean things, about which I have handed down much in the third part of my *Metallurgy*. It is for the most part attributed to the rarity of the substance and the subjects in which it is diluted; although I do not deny that the essential cause and difference reside substantially in the **second principle** <note>In Becher's theory, the "second principle" is *terra pinguis* (fatty earth), which he associated with color and inflammability.</note>.

**Combustibility and incombustibility** <note>original: "Ustibilitas & incombustibilitas"</note> are also characteristic of subterranean things. A substance is called **combustible** <note>original: "ustile"</note> if it is rarefied and dissolved into flames through a type of **fermentation**, as I explained in the chapter on **fermentation** in section 151 and those following. Indeed, nothing **burns**, even if it is **fatty** <note>original: "pingue"; in 17th-century chemistry, "fatness" or "oiliness" was synonymous with the principle of inflammability, later known as Phlogiston.</note>, unless saline particles intervene. These saline particles consist largely of water, which is required for burning so that it may be resolved into air and the air may be rarefied. Therefore, those subterranean things which are indeed fatty but not saline do not **burn**. Furthermore, things are said to be **consumed** <note>original: "comburi"</note> which are **destroyed** by fire; although strictly speaking, fire consumes nothing, but rather alters it and causes volatile parts to evaporate. In this way, everything that is **not fixed** is burned in the fire. However, nothing can be called **fixed** <note>original: "fixum"; a term for substances that resist the transformative power of fire.</note> if it is altered by fire or driven into flames. Hence, stones that produce **lime**, though they are very fixed, should not strictly be called fixed because they are changed into lime and thus altered. The **diamond** <note>original: "Adamas"</note> and the **ruby**, on the other hand, remain unchanged in the fire, and for this reason they are called fixed. This must also be understood regarding **gold and silver**, whose **incombustibility** consists in the fact that not only are they not burned, but they remain unchanged in the **cupellation furnace** <note>original: "cineritio"; a refining process where metals are heated in a dish made of bone ash to separate noble metals from base ones.</note>. They preserve their **compact homogeneity**. Hence, like fatty substances, they produce **flowers** <note>original: "flores"; here referring to the bright, crystalline appearance or beads formed by pure metals at the end of the refining process.</note> in the cupellation; whereas, by contrast, **lead** and other metals are absorbed into the pores of the ash, being of a thinner mixture. Thus, **gold and silver** remain in the cupel as if filtered, becoming more compact, thicker, and fattier. The remaining points regarding incombustibility were explained previously, where we spoke of the **incombustible sulfur of the Philosophers** <note>An alchemical principle representing the perfectly refined, fire-resistant essence of matter.</note>, which is nothing other than a fatty earth—extremely fixed, extremely pure, mixed with no salt, but soaked and waxed with mercurial earth.

**Transparency and opacity** <note>original: "Diaphaneitatis & opacitatis"</note> must also be taken into account. Here we must recall what I have said quite often: namely, that from the beginning of creation, God produced various kinds of earths, some of which are transparent and others opaque. Various species arise from their mixing. **Metals would be transparent if they lacked the "third earth" <note>Becher's "terra pinguis" or fatty earth, which he believed gave metals their shine and solidity but also their opacity.</note>; but then they would not exist as metals.** Stones are transparent even if they are mixed with the **"second earth"** <note>Becher's "terra mercurialis," the principle of fluidity and weight.</note>; but if, in place of the third earth, an opaque one enters, then the transparency ceases. This must also be considered: **not every transparent thing is porous**, as some define transparency, thinking it consists of pores. For a sponge stone is very porous, yet meanwhile it is opaque. **Glass** <note>original: "Vitrum"</note>, on the other hand, is a **most compact** body, yet it is entirely transparent. **Therefore, those things should rather be called transparent which approach more closely to "watery earth"; and those will be opaque which tend more toward "earthy earth," if I may put it that way.**

# Book I. Section VII. & Final Chapter. Unique.

<meta>catchword: be,</meta>

Meanwhile, **forms** <note>original: "formæ"</note> that constitute various figures, such as **plants and animals** <note>original: "vegetabilia & animalia"</note>, must necessarily consist of particles of different weights. Because of this diversity, they cannot cling together as tightly as metals do; hence, such **forms**, though beautiful to look at, are easily altered by a slight accident.

<margin>No. 19.</margin>
Among subterranean things that are purely earthy, there is no taste except for a certain astringency. However, in those mixtures where water and salts meet, tastes of various kinds emerge. We see this even in artificial products, such as in **sugar of Saturn** <note>original: "saccharo Saturni"; lead acetate, which has a deceptively sweet taste but is highly toxic.</note> and others. I have proven above that all this taste is merely superficial, proceeding from the rarity or density of the substance, and varying according to the diversity of the solvent and the thing dissolved. Indeed, experience proves that various medicinal operations consist in this rarity and quality of taste. This also convinces those who deny that metals possess any medical power, and those who contend that no medicine can be properly prepared from a metal unless it is reduced back into its **prime matter** <note>original: "primam materiam"; the fundamental, undifferentiated substance from which all things were thought to be made.</note>. But these people themselves do not know what they mean by "reduction into prime matter." I distinguished in the **Chemical Oedipus** <note>original: "Oedipo Chymico"; a reference to the author's earlier work on chemical secrets</note> between a solution that serves generation and one that serves medical use. In the latter, even without reduction to prime matter, various medicines can be given, as we see in sugar of Saturn, in vitriol, sublimate, **crystals of the moon** <note>original: "crystallis lunæ"; silver nitrate</note>, and other mixtures. In their simple state, these have none of the effects they acquire when they are changed by art into new decompositions. For neither silver nor **strong water** <note>original: "aqua fortis"; nitric acid</note> by themselves drive out urine; yet when silver is dissolved in strong water, reduced by a third, and thickened into crystals in the cold, it acquires a very great diuretic power. Furthermore, how taste is produced on the tongue, and which nerves the tongue tastes with, is not for me to explain here, nor shall I recount what the more curious observers have discovered so far with microscopes; these matters belong rather to the study of the living body. One thing must yet be added: by means of a certain simple salt, a vitriolic taste can be drawn from gold, which possesses the greatest medical virtue. It is extremely helpful in the dissolving of obstructions in the internal organs, being more precious in its operation than all the reductions of gold into prime matter; but I shall discuss this preparation in the second book.

<margin>No. 20.</margin>
Common sense and the **sense of smell** <note>original: "olfactus"</note> teach us that subtle atoms emanate from metals—especially copper, tin, and brass—which can be perceived by the nose, particularly if the metals are rubbed with a finger so that they warm up a little. However, how they can perpetually breathe out in this way without losing their virtues or the subject degenerating is not so obvious to everyone. Yet it is credible that the surrounding air is indeed filled with metallic atoms, and that the air itself communicates new and perpetual atoms back to the metal through some mutual exchange and reaction; for metals, especially lead, are found to gain weight from the air rather than lose it. Furthermore, if what is commonly claimed about the **dowsing rod** <note>original: "Wünschel-Ruth"</note> is true—namely, that it inclines toward metals (a thing I have never seen with success)—certainly no other reason could be assigned than that metallic atoms of this sort exhale, commonly called **scenting** <note>original: "Wittern"; a German mining term for the "breathing" or exhalations of mineral veins</note>, and this exhalation draws the rod toward itself.

<margin>No. 21.</margin>
It now remains for me to explain the color found in subterranean things, about which I have handed down much in the third part of my *Metallurgy*. It is for the most part attributed to the rarity of the substance and the materials in which it is diluted; though I do not deny that the essential cause and difference reside substantially in the **second principle** <note>In the author's system, the "second principle" usually refers to the fatty, combustible earth or "Sulfur," which was believed to be the source of color and odor.</note>.

Subterranean Physics, Book I, Section VII.

...to be. How glass, *stones, and metals are tinted*, I have sufficiently explained in the preceding sections; the remaining things that can be said about colors are found in that most learned book titled *Experiments on Colors by the Illustrious Robert Boyle* <note>original: "Experimenta de coloribus Illustris Viri Roberti Boyle"; Boyle was a foundational figure in modern chemistry, and this 1664 work explored the physical nature of color.</note>, where among other things he recounts the immense extension of colors. The words of the Author on page 219 are these: *one grain of cochineal* <note>A red dye derived from crushed insects.</note>, *dissolved in a moderate quantity of spirit of urine* <note>An old term for an aqueous solution of ammonia.</note>, *and then gradually dissolved in clear water, imparted a perceptible color to about six glasses filled with water, each of which contained approximately 43 and a half ounces; this multiplies its own weight one hundred and twenty-five thousand times and more*, thus far the Author. If, therefore, *one simple vegetable* <note>Cochineal was often categorized with vegetable dyes, though it is insect-based.</note>, through such a simple preparation and in such a small quantity as *one grain*, can tint 125,000 parts, why should we doubt the "Great Magistery" <note>The "Magisterium" refers to the highest goal of alchemy: the creation of the Philosopher's Stone, capable of transmuting metals.</note> of the Philosophers regarding its tinting power? And what wonder is it—since, as we demonstrated in the chapter on fermentation, section 15, the *sapa* of wine <note>A thick syrup made by boiling down grape juice.</note> can be exalted into an immense color by a few hours of boiling—if the "earth of the tincture," which is pure and fixed by its own nature, is boiled for so many months, and is penetrated and waxed by the "third earth," and furthermore is tinted and exalted by the "fire of the Philosophers" for so long a time: what wonder, I say, if it then performs the same feat in the extension of its tincture over metals that the tincture of cochineal performed in water. We conclude, therefore, with the saying of the most wise and equally most pious Emperor of glorious memory, *Ferdinand III*, which he ordered to be engraved on a coin minted at *Prague* in the presence of His Majesty from transmuted metal, and which is cited in our *Chemical Oedipus*: "Let God be praised forever, who communicates a part of His infinite power to us, the lowliest of creatures."

## C O N C L U S I O N.

**O** Holy Mother Nature, eternal order of things! You know how many different mixtures I have entered from the world’s founding until this animal birth; how many masks I have worn. You know from what foods and nutrients my parents mixed me; you know under what forms I must travel in this little body of mine after death—that is, after the disruption of this animal mixture and its reduction to earth—until the end of the world. I remember or know none of these things. I know not what I was, I know not what I shall be; I pass from one potential state into another. This I know: at the present time I am a mixture, consisting of earth and water with vital air interspersed, which was drawn into a mixture by my parents; they call it a rational animal, that is, a human, to whom they gave the name *Becher*, so that I might be named by others, just as I am able to be distinguished by reason from the brutes and from other men who do not differ far from beasts. Toward this last goal alone do I keep watch: namely, that it may be established that I have been a man—that is, that I have investigated the principles of the mixture of things, so that I may give thanks to the Supreme Mixer for that degree of mixture in which He willed me to survive for thirty-three years. Thus I hope that I, who perform the duty of a true man in this way, shall one day obtain again from the Supreme Mixer a merciful mixture after death, and a certain "sweetness" <note>original: "glykeian" (Greek: γλυκείαν); meaning sweet or pleasant.</note> of parts, to whom be honor and praise forever, from every mixture, above and below the earth, Amen.

# JOHANN JOACHIM BECHER,
->Doctor of Medicine from Speyer, Counselor to His Sacred Imperial Majesty.<-

# SUPPLEMENT
## To the first book of his Subterranean Physics,
->In Which<-
->It is practically demonstrated what was theoretically stated in the aforementioned work regarding the generation of metals, namely<-

## That metals consist principally of earth.
->With the addition of experiments for proof, by which it is demonstratively shown,<-

1. That from common mud—specifically that from which bricks are fired—and any "fatness" <term>pinguetudo; in alchemical theory, a fatty or oily substance (often associated with sulfur) that was believed to give matter its combustible or metallic properties</term>, whether animal or vegetable (for example, linseed oil), without any other materials, in the space of four hours, by the simplest manipulation—with nature working and art assisting as a midwife—a true and genuine metal, such as iron or another, is produced in a quite notable quantity.
2. That with certain common and easily found earths, one can actually transmute all metals.
3. That with these same earths, one can "fix" all volatile sulfurs <note>original: "sulphura"; in this context, substances that easily evaporate or sublimate when heated</note>, such as common sulfur, arsenic, cinnabar, and even common mercury itself, so that they do not flee from the fire.

New Chymical Paradoxes, hitherto hidden from the world by envious Philosophers, but now shared with the "sons of doctrine" <note>a traditional alchemical term for dedicated students or initiates of the craft</note> for the defense of the most noble Chymistry and its foundation—namely, the Universal Matter of Metals, or the Clay of Wisdom <note>original: "Luti sapientiæ"</note>—all confirmed by infallible experiments and the sayings of the wise.

->*Albertus Magnus, Book on Transmutation, chapter 2.*<- <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280) was a Dominican friar and philosopher widely (though sometimes apocryphally) cited as an authority on alchemy.</note>
> The primary matter of metals is a subtle, oily moisture, which is incorporated into a subtle earth and strongly mixed; such that a great deal of each exists not only with a great deal of the other, but even within a great deal of the other. <note>original: "Prima materia metallorum, est humidum unctuosum subtile, quod est incorporatum terrestri subtili fortiter commixto; Ita quod plurimum utriusque, non tantum cum plurimo utriusque, sed etiam in plurimo utriusque fit."</note>

# Supplement to Subterranean Physics,

## CHAPTER I.

### The Proposition.

There is an ancient controversy among Natural Philosophers <note>original: "Physicos"; in the 17th century, a "physician" or "physicist" was someone who studied the laws of nature and the physical world</note>, *whether Alchemy is a true science (or if you prefer, an art) or whether it is merely a deceptive theory?* This controversy has grown all the more because the *Alchemists* themselves have perpetually fueled it. Since no controversy can be decided except by either theory or practice, and since the *Alchemists* avoid both, their adversaries easily hold the field. For the *Alchemists* say they cannot hand down their theory in clear words unless they wish to give occasion for the greatest crimes and disturbances; for what do you think would happen if everyone had an abundance of gold? A malicious man with wealth is like a madman holding a sword. Alchemy would even rage against itself, for it would never change its own persecution more than if it promulgated the art to the wicked without distinction. Certainly, as *Suidas* <note>a 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia that preserves many ancient historical details</note> records, there would be no lack of *Diocletians* <note>the Roman Emperor who allegedly ordered the burning of ancient Egyptian books on alchemy to prevent them from funding rebellions</note> who would consecrate not only the writings but the very bodies of the *Chymists* to *Vulcan* <note>the Roman god of fire; meaning they would be burned at the stake</note>. Indeed, they would justly rage against those who sought to liberate men from all servitude; for there is nothing that could more effectively reduce all people to the original state of nature and equality than the sufficient possession of goods. Therefore, the *Chymists* are to be excused because it is not permitted for them to defend themselves theoretically.

We must come, then, to practice—though that too is dangerous. For not a few of the Great Lords of our time gape for gold, and none but a fool, or one who wishes to be imprisoned by his own will, would demonstrate the truth of the art to them in practice. Thus, every way of defense, both theoretical and practical, is cut off from the *Chymists*. They have indeed published many books in which they taught their theory *hieroglyphically* and in a covered manner, and they have also secretly performed many *specimens of projection* <term>projectionis specimina; the act of casting a small amount of the "Philosopher's Stone" or powder onto a base metal to transmute it into gold</term> here and there. But many *spurious* books, as well as many *practical impostures* regarding *projection*, have intermingled themselves; so that this kind of demonstration has benefited the adversaries more than it has harmed them, and has brought more uncertainty than truth to *Chymistry*. *Unhappy Alchemy, which, if it defends itself clearly with both theoretical and practical truth, risks its life; if it does not do so, it risks its reputation!* It has come to the point that in this day and age, Alchemists and Scoundrels are almost synonyms; and not only Alchemists, but all Searchers of natural things who examine nature by *fire* or *distillation* are called such names.

And it is indeed for this reason that I have undertaken the defense of this "Sparta" <note>original: "hanc Spartam defendendam"; a classical idiom meaning to take up a difficult duty or lot in life that one has been assigned</note>, not of my own will, but *compelled*. For since I am carried toward the investigation of natural things by natural inclination and thus by divine calling, and have devoted my labor to them as if from the cradle, and have become known to the world through various chymical writings, I could not escape being branded with the stigma of *Alchemy* for the reasons mentioned above. Which mark, indeed, I could not undertake to erase in any other way than by...

# Chapter One.

...alchemical, can it assist nature? Regarding refining, of which we have already treated, there is no doubt; for from this comes the entire **art of assaying** <term>docimastica: the art of testing the purity of metals</term> and smelting, which is publicly practiced as a mechanical art in treasuries and mints. But as for the two extremes—namely the *generation and transmutation of metals—the question turns on whether it is possible for the alchemical art to imitate these through ingenuity outside of the mines, and thus assist nature.*

It does not escape me that human art is occupied in many ways concerning the *generation of animals*; for instance, eggs are hatched by art <note>A reference to early incubators</note>; the *metamorphosis of silkworms* is completed; pigeons and horses are varied in color; the mule is produced, as well as various monsters. Crabs are regenerated from the ash of crabs <note>This refers to "palingenesis," an early modern belief that organisms could be reconstituted from their chemical salts or ashes</note>; silkworms from putrefied veal; and other insects from other things. Concerning the genesis of vegetables, art notably alters their colors, flavors, and shapes; and in pots before windows, or in <term>hypocausts</term> <note>Rooms heated from below, like a greenhouse or laboratory stove</note> prepared and heated for this purpose, by applying natural principles, art quickly completes what nature takes a long time to work out in the earth and in distant places and provinces.

But I have never read, nor heard, that it is possible by art to generate a true metal in any place and time, outside of the mines, from things found everywhere—even non-mineral things—in the space of a few hours. This is certainly an experiment of great importance; for to transmute one metal into another is not so contrary to reason, nor is it difficult, since the species can easily be changed while the genus remains the same. # Chapter One.

...alchemy, *can it assist nature?* Regarding refining, which we have already discussed, there is no doubt; for from this comes the entire *docimastic* <term>the art of assaying or testing the purity of metals</term> and *smelting* arts, which are practiced as mechanical crafts here and there in public treasuries and mints. But as for the two extremes—namely the *generation and transmutation of metals*—the question is whether it is possible for the alchemical art to imitate these by human ingenuity outside of the mines and to assist nature.

It does not escape my notice that *various arts are occupied with the generation of animals*; thus, *eggs are hatched by art; the metamorphosis of silkworms is completed; the colors of pigeons and horses are varied; the mule and various monsters are produced; crabs are regenerated from the ash of crabs; silkworms from putrefied veal; and other insects from other things.* Regarding the *genesis of vegetables, art notably alters their colors, flavors, and shapes; and in clay pots before windows, as well as in heated rooms* <term>original: *hypocaustis*, rooms heated by underfloor systems</term> *prepared and heated for that purpose, it quickly accomplishes by applying natural principles what nature labors over in the earth in distant places and provinces.*

But I have never read, nor heard, *that a true metal can be generated by art outside of mines in any place and time from things found everywhere—even non-mineral things—within the span of a few hours*. In no chemist, I say, have I read this, except for *Saint Thomas* <note>St. Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274). These final words seem to indicate this artificial metallic genesis. For the preceding words show that *Saint Thomas* does not mean "transmutation" here by "generation."

*Borellus* <note>Pierre Borel (c. 1620–1671), a French scientist and physician.</note> in his observations, and *Andreas Solea* in his treatise on the increase and decrease of metals, certainly mention metallic growth; but regarding the *generation of metals from first principles, anew*, which *Saint Thomas* mentions here, no one has written even a little word. ...cannot be achieved if they are ignored by the craftsman; therefore, before all else, it is necessary that they be understood. Once known, these principles can either be brought to hand and possessed, or they cannot. If the latter is true, then all Alchemy is useless, for it would base its foundation upon things that cannot be obtained. But if they can be had, then it is necessary that once the metallic principles are possessed and joined, a metal may be generated in a single moment, even outside of the mines. This is because generation happens in an instant, according to the testimony of all the Philosophers—especially **Geber**, who says:

*“And if they say that perfection is granted in an instant, but our preparation is not done in an instant, and they conclude from this that it cannot be perfected by art, and therefore the art itself is void; we say their heads are foolish and empty of human reason, and they are to be likened more to beasts than to men. For they conclude from premises that have no relation to the conclusion reached; their argument holds as much weight as saying 'a donkey runs, therefore you are a goat.' This is because, even if the preparation does not happen in an instant, it does not prevent the form or perfection from being given to the prepared material in an instant. For the preparation is not the perfection itself, but rather the enabling of the matter to receive the form.”* <note>original: "non enim praeparatio est perfectio, sed habilitatio ad suscipiendam formam." Geber refers to Jabir ibn Hayyan, the legendary 8th-century Islamic alchemist whose Latinized works formed the core of European alchemy.</note>

Therefore, I have always been of the opinion that a craftsman cannot radically transmute metals if he cannot produce metals by art—that is, from natural principles, making a metal from things that are not already metallic. For this is the definition of "principles": they are the things from which something is made, not the thing that has already been made from them. Furthermore, **Democritus** <note>likely "Pseudo-Democritus," an early alchemical author</note> in Book 3 of the *Physics*, chapter 3, on meteors, expressly says: "Let the Alchemists boast and exult however they wish; unless they reduce metals into their first matter, they will not transmute them."

The reason for this axiom is evident and ready at hand: for the first matter of metals consists of the principles of metals. From the perfection or imperfection of these principles—namely their quality and quantity—the first metallic matter, and the metallic body produced from it, must necessarily be diversified and specified. This is because metallic specification happens not by accident, but by the very essence of the principles. Without altering these, the *crasis* <term>the specific temperament or constitution of a mixture</term> of the compound cannot be radically and essentially altered or transmuted.

Indeed, if in any conception—for example, a human one—the "first matter," which is both the masculine and feminine seed, could be so treated by art, purified, exalted <term>raised to a higher state of purity or potency</term>, and mixed according to the proportions that the nature of the human mixture requires in its highest degree, do you not think it would result in the generation of most perfect human beings? A certain Englishman wrote a curious treatise on this matter, which he once dedicated to **Christina, Queen of Sweden** <note>Christina (r. 1632–1654) was a famous patron of the arts and sciences who abdicated her throne and studied alchemy in Rome</note>; however, it has not been published in print, although it is very necessary for the perfection of human generation.

In the vegetable kingdom, the "imbibition" <term>the soaking of seeds in specialized solutions to accelerate growth</term> of seed grain is known to me. I shared this with the most illustrious Lord, **Baron de Perneii**, a most curious gentleman, who saw the success of it in practice—namely, an increase in the quantity and quality of the grain, resulting in great profit. The seeds of certain vegetables can also be so exalted that what they previously could scarcely achieve in a month, they might achieve in the space of an hour with the help of art, growing visibly from the earth on a table when the vessel is placed over a little heat. I am not speaking here of the resuscitation of flowers from their ashes <note>a reference to "palingenesis," a popular 17th-century claim that the "phantom" of a flower could be raised from its burnt remains</note>, but of the real vegetation of a seed. For example, a lettuce, sown at the start of a dinner, had grown so much by the end of the meal that it could be placed among the desserts <note>original: "bellaria," referring to sweetmeats or the final course</note> and eaten. # Chapter One.

...from an egg, if you proceed correctly, comes a chick. For if a diseased quality is introduced into human seed, the offspring will certainly be diseased; hence hereditary diseases. And if a plant seed is treated by soaking it in certain substances, the flowers and fruits produced from them will be altered in color and flavor. Likewise, if a good quality is introduced into the <term>metallic seed<note>original: "semen metallicum." Alchemists believed metals grew from "seeds" of mercury and sulfur within the earth, analogous to plants or animals.</note></term>, it will produce a good metal. Regarding this, the most learned **Lull** <note>Raymond Lull (c. 1232–1315), a Majorcan polymath and philosopher to whom many later alchemical works were attributed.</note> says in Chapter 32: *“We remember having said in our testament that no quicksilver is more readily converted into the substance of sulfur than that in which the qualities of sulfur have been sufficiently introduced through dissolution; nor does any sulfur more readily congeal quicksilver than that in whose nature the substance of the quicksilver itself already exists, having been converted by the ingenuity of the art; for then nature embraces its own nature, and rejoices in it more amiably than in something foreign.”* <note>original: "quia tunc natura naturam complectitur propriam, & amicabilius gaudet in ea quam extranea." This reflects the alchemical principle that "nature rejoices in nature."</note> These are truly the clearest and most golden words.

Therefore, keeping this theory intact—which no one can deny—we shall establish a firm, artificial metallic genesis in the following chapter. For once this foundation is laid, transmutation (as I demonstrated above) becomes evident by itself. For whatever *true metallic* principle you either *take away from or add to* a metal, it will essentially alter the metal within the mixture. *In this experiment, therefore, as I said at the beginning of this chapter, we shall commit ourselves.* For if it becomes clear through truth that art can generate a true metal from universal materials found everywhere, in any place, and in just a few hours—and produce a true metallic mixture—it will also be able to alter and transmute metals according to the diversity of those materials or principles. Hence that philosophical maxim: *“he who knows not how to construct metals is also ignorant of how to destroy them.”* For so says **Bernard**: <note>Likely Bernard of Trevisan, a 15th-century alchemist.</note> *“Whoever is ignorant of the roots of minerals, both the simple and the composite, is ignorant of the principles of nature, and therefore of the art; wherefore he is a Sophist rather than a Philosopher.”*

This alone, therefore, must be demonstrated by us, as the foundation of transmutation and the argument for alchemical truth. For as **Lull** learnedly says: *“If in Alchemy there were the principles of gold and silver, and after mixing they did not transmute the first essence through the first location <note>The author glosses this "first location" (localitatem) as "unless in an instant it became metal." In Aristotelian physics, "local motion" or change of place was the primary form of change.</note>, nature would be false; because it would follow that there could be some place in nature where principles could naturally be void (that is, not operating), which nature could not suffer, because it would be against her own definition—since nature is that through which every natural thing is made full.”*

This demonstration, therefore, does much for the truth of Alchemy, both theoretically and practically. It is so arranged as to provide everything desired by Alchemists at the start of this chapter: namely, that they might be able to defend the truth physically without political danger. <note>The author suggests that by proving alchemy through "natural philosophy" rather than "gold-making," one avoids the legal or social risks associated with counterfeiting or rogue alchemy.</note> For those whose intellect God illustrates, they will extract many useful things from these words. But those who seek gold while neglecting good intentions should know that nothing is written in this book except the poor and naked Truth. I propose iron as an example, not gold; for although the experiment may not be **profit-bringing**, it is nevertheless **light-bringing**. <note>original: "lucriferum... luciferum." A play on words: "lucriferum" means bringing wealth/gain, while "luciferum" means bringing light or enlightenment.</note> Truly, for those not content with the truth but who desire formal processes for making gold and wish to work with the hands of others, I will communicate three processes. The first is from **Avicenna**, <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), the Persian physician whose works were foundational to European alchemy, though he was famously skeptical of transmutation.</note> who says: *“He who takes what he should, and works as he should, proceeds from there as he should.”* The second is from **Isaac Hollandus**, <note>A name attributed to one or two legendary 15th-century Dutch alchemists.</note> who writes: *“You have known all the minerals that grow in mines; from them, choose that which...”*

## Supplement to Subterranean Physics
### CHAP. II.
# Experiment.

**W**hen I saw that the doctrine of the <term>principles<note>In this context, "principles" refers to the fundamental components of metals, usually thought to be sulfur and mercury.</note></term> of metals was necessary in every way, I applied myself day and night so that I might share in it; therefore, I reduced the state of the question into five parts, so that I could resolve it more clearly.

*First, it is asked: do metals have principles?*
*Second: if they have principles, how many are there?*
*Third: what is their substance and appearance according to external qualities?*
*Fourth: can they be drawn out from already existing metals?*
*Fifth: can they be obtained individually from ores or elsewhere, still in their first state without being mixed, and be treated by art?*

Regarding the *First Point*, it seems foolish to doubt whether metals have principles; but some modern, scrupulous critics, lest they seem to have nothing to say, bring this doubt forward. They say *the metal itself is the principle, produced thus by nature in an instant. So that the metal had no other potential state before its existence.* There are not a few who deny all metallic *composition*; asserting that whatever *metal is found in mines was placed there at the first creation.* <note>This refers to the "Creationist" view of minerals—that God put gold in the earth on the third day of creation exactly as it is found today, rather than it growing over time.</note> This was also the opinion of *St. Augustine*. But all these people are very much in error. First, those who assert that the metal *is its own principle*. For it would follow that metal could not be counted among <term>mixed things<note>original: "mixta." According to Aristotelian physics, everything in the "sublunary" world (below the moon) is a mixture of elements. If a metal were a single "principle," it wouldn't be a mixture.</note></term>; although every sublunary body is a *mixture*. However, it could not be called a *mixture* if it consisted of a single unit; since *mixture is defined as the joining of two or more things.* To this, it would follow that every metal was an *absolute* metal in an instant; but we already see *in mines that metals are generated successively, and over a period of time,* due to a delay in the joining of the principles. For when those principles are present, we grant that a metal is made in an instant. But now, very often, *one principle must wait for another;* which demonstrates the plurality of principles. Furthermore, if there were only one principle, there would be no *reaction* or *succession*; but the following authors prove that these occur in mineral genesis, also refuting those who deny that metals are generated after the first creation. *Albertus Magnus* <note>Albert the Great (c. 1200–1280), a scholar who wrote extensively on minerals and was believed to have discovered the element arsenic.</note> records that in his time it happened in <term>Slavonia<note>A historical region in modern-day Croatia.</note></term>, where when metal...

Mining histories testify to this. For if the digging was paused for a period of one hundred years and they returned there again, the miners found a massive amount of iron had been reborn. For the earth that is dug out while the vein is being excavated turns entirely into ore as time passes." 

And <term>Agricola<note>Georgius Agricola (1494–1555), known as the "Father of Mineralogy" for his work *De Re Metallica*.</note></term> writes that at the town of Saga in Germany, iron is dug up in the meadows; once they have dug to a depth of two feet, he adds, it is reborn in ten years and dug anew, just like the iron of Elba. <term>Boccaccio of Certaldo<note>Giovanni Boccaccio (1313–1375), the famous author, here cited for his observations on geography/minerals.</note></term> writes it is well-proven that the mountain of Fiesole in Tuscany, overlooking the city of Florence, contains lead stones; if these are cut out, they are restored by new growth in a short span of time. <term>Gerhard<note>Likely Johann Gerhard, a professor of medicine and chemistry.</note></term>, a Professor of Medicine, attests that "blue water" <note>original: "aquam caeruleam," likely referring to copper vitriol or a mineral-saturated solution.</note> was found at Annaberg while it was still in its <term>first being<note>original: "primo ente," referring to the "prime matter" or initial liquid state of a mineral before it solidifies.</note></term>; once coagulated, it was reduced into the <term>calx<note>A powder or residue left after heating a substance; here, a purified state.</note></term> of fixed and good silver. For wherever that single principle arrived, it would immediately be metal. I conclude, therefore, that metals consist of principles, and that such principles are not themselves metals in their current state; otherwise, they could not be called "principles" <note>The author argues that a "building block" cannot be the same thing as the finished "building."</note>.

I turn now to the second question: namely, how many principles are there? I said in the previous question that there are more than one. These all ascribe a dual number to the metallic principles. But <term>Theophrastus Paracelsus<note>Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim (1493–1541), who revolutionized medicine and alchemy.</note></term>, a more deceptive Philosopher, added a third—namely, the "sun"—which many and nearly all of the moderns agree with. Even <term>Hermes<note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure to whom the foundational texts of alchemy are attributed.</note></term> seems to approve of this Trinity when he says: "The Sun is the Father of this Marriage, and the white Moon is the Mother; a third succeeds as..."

The Governor of Fire, and *Mary the Prophetess* <note>An early alchemical authority, often identified as Miriam the sister of Moses, though likely a later Alexandrian figure.</note>, say: "Smoke embraces smoke, and the white herb on the small hills [contains] both heads." *Albertus Magnus* <note>Albert the Great (c. 1200–1280), a Dominican friar and polymath who wrote extensively on minerals.</note> explained this trinity of principles best of all when he said: *The primary matter of metals is a subtle oily moisture, which is incorporated into a subtle earth, strongly mixed together*, though more will be said about this statement later. I conclude, therefore, that there are two principles that behave like a male and a female, but the third is the Matrix—the vessel or nourishment, or that which grows upon the principles—and this indeed can be numbered among the principles because it is of the same nature as the principles.

*Thirdly*, of what substance and appearance, according to external accidents <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "accidents" are the outward qualities of a thing (color, texture, smell) as opposed to its internal essence.</note>, are the aforementioned principles before their mixing? The opinion of authors varies. Some call it smoke, like *Mary, the Sister of Moses*; some an *oily* vapor, like St. *Thomas* <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), to whom several alchemical treatises were traditionally attributed.</note>; some call it *water*, and some *earth*. *Albertus* names it *oily moisture*. *Aristotle* in Book 3, Chapter 6 [of *Meteorology*], calls the primary matter of metals a *moist breath*. But since a metallic mixture is entirely earthy, no *water* can *radically* <note>meaning "at its root" or fundamental level</note> enter into their composition. Therefore, when these authors speak of "humidity," there is no doubt they mean a *Mercurial* and *sulfurous* flow that does not wet the hands. Nor should we think that these principles appear in the form of common *mercury, sulfur, and salt*, even if they occasionally deceive us under these masks. For common sulfur, quicksilver, and salt are themselves mixtures and compounds; therefore, they cannot be the primary and plural principles of metals. *Petrus de Zelanto*, in his explanation of the word <term>Brumazar</term> <note>A term used in alchemy to describe the 'first matter' or the raw, unrefined spirit of metals.</note>, says regarding the generation of metals that the smokes of sulfur and quicksilver (that is, the vapors of white and red sulfur, and of water and earth) exhale from the depths of the earth and embrace each other. In their mutual embrace, through the action of continuous heat, a certain *oily* fatness is generated, which is called <term>Brumazar</term>. This is the substance that is not recognized in minerals even though it is seen, because it exists in such small quantities; yet it is the ferment of the whole work, without which no fermentation can take place. Regarding this <term>Brumazar</term>, the *Clangor Buccinae* <note>original: "Clangor Buccinae" (The Sound of the Trumpet), a well-known 16th-century alchemical text.</note> declares:
> *Leavened and baked bread is perfect in its state of being and has reached its final end; so it is with gold. Pure gold has been led through the trial of fire into a firm and fixed body, and it is impossible to ferment it further unless it has Brumazar—that is, the primary matter of metals—in which it is resolved into the primary matter and the miscible elements. Let us therefore take that matter from which gold will come, and by means of craftsmanship let it be led into the true philosophical ferment; let this be changed with ingenuity into the perfect matter, and only then let us begin the operation.*

Our local miners show a substance, resembling fat, which they call in German <term>Berg-guhr</term> <note>Literally "mountain-juice" or "rock-milk," a soft, white, creamy mineral deposit found in limestone caves or mine veins, believed by early miners to be the "embryo" of metals.</note>. Hence, regarding the aforementioned blue water of Annaberg <note>A famous mining town in the Ore Mountains of Saxony.</note>, it must be noted that it ought to have been coagulated by the evaporation of its wateriness, otherwise it would never have been changed into silver. Therefore, I conclude: the principles of metals are three earths—dry and not wetting the hands—resolvable into vapor; if they are joined into an oily substance, they later grow together into a metallic substance.
