I now proceed to the fourth question, and I say that these principles can only with the greatest difficulty be extracted from the metals themselves, while the seminal power <note>The "seminal power" refers to the inherent ability of a substance to grow or reproduce its own kind, a key concept in alchemical metallurgy.</note> of the metals remains intact. For *Fire* and the help of solvents alter them, and metals are dissolved into their principles by themselves only with great difficulty, because of their strong and homogeneous mixture. So much so, that I am forced to conclude that whether by themselves, or by the help of *fire* or solvents, *the principles cannot be obtained from metals*, except by the addition of *principles*, and the reduction of metals into their primary matter, as you heard before regarding *Brumazar* <note>An alchemical authority often cited in medieval Latin texts, possibly a corruption of an Arabic name.</note> and gold in the *Clangor* <note>original: "in clangore"; likely referring to the *Clangor Buccinae* (The Trumpet's Blast), a famous alchemical treatise.</note>. Last or fifth, whether these principles can be obtained from ores or from elsewhere, and handled by art? I respond that the principles are found in ores and in *minerals*; and that the mineral virtue or power is *universally disseminated*, and found everywhere. Therefore it is also called the philosophers' *universal elixir* <note>The "Universal Elixir" or "Philosopher's Stone" was believed to be a substance that could perfect all matter, whether by turning lead to gold or curing human illness.</note>; as if its matter could be prepared from all things. For thus says *Hermes* <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the mythical founder of alchemy.</note> in the "Sayings of the Wise": *That stone is the whole secret and the life of every thing, and every man needs it, and this is the water which is the grain in wheat, and the oil in the olive, and the gum in peaches, and the fruit in all trees, and the principle of the generation of man; and from it comes that which is living, which does not die as long as the world exists, because it is the head of the world—that is, the moisture.* And *Rozinus* <note>A common name in alchemical literature for an Arabic source, possibly Zosimos of Panopolis.</note> in the book to King Sarratanta [says]: *This stone is cast into the valleys and onto the mountains, and it dwells in the air, and feeds in the river, and rests on the peaks of mountains; it is in all waters, and both the rich and the poor possess it. How precious is it to everyone who knows it!* *Rhasis* <note>Muhammad ibn Zakariya al-Razi (c. 865–925), a Persian polymath and physician.</note> in the "Book of Divinity" says: *Know that the things of nature are so bound together by subtle artifice, that in any thing, any other thing exists in potentiality, though it may not be seen in actuality.*

All philosophers also agree in this *universality*, about which more will be said in a specific chapter later. This certainly seems impossible and difficult to grasp, which keeps many away from the art; indeed, for many, including myself for many years, it blinded my reason: so that, with *Geber*, I was forced to hide for a long time under the shadow of despair. These five points having thus been established, I then made a general conclusion, namely: *those are the first principles of metals which are most specifically mixed with metals in their essence, and nonetheless, according to the mind of all philosophers, agree most generally with this universe.* That is, so that their power is everywhere in all bodies, but in actuality nowhere except in *minerals*; or rather, they wander and lie hidden separately in all bodies, *but joined together, they immediately produce metal.* With this North Star <note>original: "Cynosura," the constellation Ursa Minor, used as a guiding principle for sailors.</note> set, I dared to swim across that vast sea of experiments. First of all, I observed that nothing affects, alters, or enters metals more than salt, sulfur, and mercury. For I know how to reduce all salts into earth; I know how to convert flints, by the weight of fire and water alone, into an alkali salt; and even quicklime into a fixed alkali oil <term>fixed oil of alkali: a concentrated, caustic liquid made from potash or lime, used as a powerful solvent</term>. Moreover, it will not escape anyone skilled in the art of smelting how much metals undergo metamorphosis during fusion by the addition of earths, stones, or lime. For these enter into their composition or mixture essentially; they transmute them into glass or slag; they thin them out wonderfully, and when altered, they are notably reduced. Thus, there is almost nothing that alters the metallic constitution <note>original: "crasin metallicam"</note> in such a way. We also see metals generated within earths and stones; for this reason, they are not without merit called by Mary the Prophetess <note>Mary the Prophetess: A legendary foundational figure in alchemy, traditionally associated with the invention of the water-bath (bain-marie).</note> "the white herb growing on the little hills, receiving both vapors" <note>original: "herba alba in monticulis crescens, utrosque fumos recipiens"</note>. I have observed various earths enter into metals in such a way that they form a homogeneous mixture with them, and produce a true increase in all tests. There is a known earth which, when cast into molten silver, enters its mixture and withstands the cupel <note>cupel: a porous ceramic vessel used in assaying to separate precious metals from lead and impurities</note>; yet when the silver is dissolved in *aqua fortis* <term>aqua fortis: literally "strong water," refers to nitric acid</term>, that same earth falls to the bottom in its original form, fixed as before and not reducible into metal like other "calx of gold" <note>calx: the powdery residue left after a metal or mineral has been roasted or "calcined."</note>. From all of this, I concluded that *Earth*—under which name I include the aforementioned species—is one of the metallic principles. Second, I observed in Sulfur that it penetrates all metals and essentially alters them; and when converted into earth (with its combustibility removed) and cast into metals, it truly increases them, from which I concluded that it, too, is one of the principles. Thirdly, I observed that common *Mercury* unites amicably and sympathetically with metallic bodies, and after frequent sublimation, extraction over the metals, and precipitation, it leaves behind a true alteration within them. From this, I concluded that there is an earth within Mercury that serves as a principle for metals. For I did not take the entire body of Mercury as a principle, since it is a composite thing; I wish the same to be understood regarding sulfur and salt (or earth). For thus Albertus <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280): A medieval scholar and bishop who wrote extensively on the "secrets of nature" and mineralogy.</note> says, as I noted before:

> *The first matter of metals is an unctuous, moist, subtle substance, incorporated with a subtle terrestrial matter strongly mixed, so that the greatest part of each is not only mixed with the greatest part of the other, but is actually within it.*

If Hobbes <note>Thomas Hobbes (1588–1679): The English philosopher. The author is referencing Hobbes's disdain for the complex, "absurd" language of Scholasticism and alchemy.</note> were to hear these words, he would judge them no less insane than those "sweet things" which he cites among the ravings in his *Leviathan* (Chapter 8, on Man). But we shall soon hear that they are most profound and clear. By *unctuous*, he understands the "earth of sulfur"; by *moist*, the "earth of mercury"; by *subtle*, he indicates that neither crude sulfur nor quicksilver, but rather their more subtle parts, are to be considered the metallic principles. By *incorporated with a subtle terrestrial matter strongly mixed*, he understands the purest species of earth or stone which, having been frequently refined and most evenly mixed, flows lightly in the fire; of this species are all those earths and stones in which good metals are usually generated. *Incorporated:* here he intends that the two principles of metals be incorporated into this third one—that is, that they take on a metallic body. Thus Hermes says: "Its power is perfect if it be changed into earth" <note>A famous line from the Emerald Tablet, the foundational text of Hermetic alchemy.</note>; likewise, "The earth is its nurse. The mother of all perfection." That earth indeed possesses the fixing power of all mineral spirits, you shall hear toward the end of this chapter. So much so, that this "subtle terrestrial" is not raw earth, but truly the *First Being of Earth* <note>original: "primum Ens terrae"</note>. Thus *the greatest part of each:* by this he understands that the matter does not consist of a large quantity of common sulfur and mercury coming together for metallic birth, but rather that the "most part" of the subtle essence of each concurs.

## Chapter Two.

For what is required is not the thick corporeality of sulfur and mercury, which consists of the decomposition of combustible and arsenical earth. Not only with *the most of both*: here, "the most" indicates the quantity or proportion of the mixture, just as in the previous mention of "the most," it indicates quality. It is natural that if *the most of both seeds* concur in generation, a strong offspring is produced. But also in *the most of both*: through this, he indicates the third principle, namely the Matrix <term>Matrix: in alchemy, the "womb" or environment—such as a specific type of rock—where minerals and metals are conceived and grow</term>, or the *subtle terrestrial matter*, which is of a hermaphroditic nature—namely sulfurous and mercurial—and thus shares the nature of both seeds. Then, it follows that it should not be of common earth or stone, but must consist of the greatest amount of its essence. For in truth, as you will hear in the following chapter, the quantity of metal acquired in this generation (both natural and artificial) depends on the quality of the matrix. And we see daily in mines <term>mines: original "mineris", referring both to the place of extraction and the ore itself</term> that a lack of good stones or earths is the cause of mineral sterility.

Therefore, having taken and joined these three earths according to the preceding doctrine of Albertus Magnus <note>Albertus Magnus: A 13th-century Dominican friar and philosopher whose works on alchemy and nature were highly influential in the Middle Ages.</note>, it was evident to me that metal must necessarily be generated. However, by what practice I could obtain the *most* of these earths and free them from their "wrappings" of various decompositions was still entirely hidden from me. Therefore, anxious about practical ease, I began to test whether these three earths might lie hidden in other things—and indeed, according to the opinion of the Philosophers, in all bodies. These would provide what I desired, not according to their external appearance (for they can be masked by the form of any of the elements) but according to their *effect*, and they could be laid bare with far less effort. 

To this end, and so that I might also examine the other part of my Cynosure <term>Cynosure: literally "dog's tail," referring to the North Star; metaphorically, a guiding principle or something that directs one's path</term> prefixed above, I observed *first* that in both the animal and vegetable kingdoms, *earth* acts as the foundation. I observed a certain terrestrial power that ossifies, hardens, and petrifies, wandering here and there in all bodies in the form of a spirit, or even a liquid. I have seen the rays of the Sun reduced into earthy atoms; and I myself saw the very flames of our material fire fixed into *earth*. And so, through the "microscope of reason," I discovered the entire world to be filled with earthy atoms. I also observed that the more subtle and rare the earth becomes, the more it is purified and ennobled. 

Having discovered the universality of earth, I hurried to the remaining two principles, namely *sulfur* and *quicksilver* <term>quicksilver: mercury</term>. I presuppose, however, that no one will read this supplement who has not first thoroughly read my *Subterranean Physics* and understood my mind regarding metallic principles; for once this foundation is laid, what I present here will be easily understood. I observed that for all generation, a double seed is required: male and female, active and passive, innate heat and radical moisture. *Each seed, however, contains the most of both*, and is of a sulfurous, fatty, gluing, and shaping nature—one prevailing in cold, the other in heat. For contrary agents are the principles of all generation; and I carefully observed that this occurs not only in generation, but in the action and reaction of this entire universe. I saw in the heavens two lights, of the Sun and Moon; I found in the earth two sulfurs: one hot, the other cold; one dry, the other moist; one red, the other white; one active, the other passive. And besides these two sulfurs, one of which receives its light from the other, I could find no other. Rather, these two are like examples of the two great universal lights, the *Sun* and *Moon*...

### Supplement to the Underground Physics

...and I discovered that these arguments lie hidden in all subjects of this world. For everything possesses a certain "fatness" <term>fatness: original "pinguedo," an alchemical term for the oily, combustible principle or "soul" of a substance</term>, and every fatness is twofold: one part blazes, the other smokes; one is consumed by fire, the other is not; one turns red, the other turns white; through combustion, one becomes volatile, while the other becomes fixed. I say in truth that the essence of mercury is just as sulfurous as the essence of sulfur; but the former is white, the latter red; the former is externally cold, the latter hot; the former is feminine, the latter masculine. 

Yet they proceed from a single source, which is universal; for I found in every fatness the essence of mercury—an essence, I say, that creates metal and turns things white, from which is prepared that "white water" with which the Philosopher orders us to whiten "Laton" <note>original: *Latonem Philosophus*; "Laton" or "Latten" is an alchemical term for an impure metal—often base copper or brass—that must be purified or "whitened" to reach the state of silver</note>, and to tear up all other books regarding the rest. 

Next, I found the essence of sulfur, which is the "form" <term>form: in the Aristotelian sense, the organizing principle that gives a thing its specific identity and properties</term> of things, according to whose nobility bodies themselves are ennobled. These two joined together produce that gum, or vapors, which must be "fixed" <term>fixed: to "fix" a substance in alchemy means to make a volatile or gaseous substance solid and resistant to fire</term> by the "white herb." I write clearly in this place because, being persecuted by wicked sophists and "philosopher-killers" <note>original: *Sophistis & Philosophicidis*; the author uses this harsh term to describe those who corrupt or destroy the true secrets of natural philosophy</note>, I am scarcely safe for an hour of my life; and I would hope that others might bring to completion those things for which I have laid the foundations here. Although I know there will be few who undertake this immense labor; for to make the mass manageable, and to free it from so many decompositions and wrappings—this is the work, this is the toil.

*When I was certain of this—that this double sulfur lay hidden in every fatness—I examined many subjects, both animal, vegetable, and mineral. Among other things, I greatly sought the reduction of oils into earth. Accordingly, among various manual operations <term>operations: original "enchirises," referring to laboratory techniques or handiwork</term>, I took common clay (from which bricks are fired and furnaces built), dried in the air so it could be sifted, and soaked it with linseed oil so that little balls could be formed from it, sized for the neck of a retort <term>retort: a glass or ceramic vessel with a long, downward-pointing neck used for distilling substances</term>. I did this so that, after distillation, the retort would not have to be broken to remove the "dead head" <term>dead head: original "caput mortuum," the useless solid residue remaining after all volatile spirits have been driven off</term> as they call it, but could be saved for another use. Then, so that the power of the fire could penetrate those small balls more vehemently than if they were in one mass, I filled the retort with such balls and distilled them by degrees over an open fire. Toward the end, I increased the fire strongly for an hour or two.*

*When the distillation was finished, I found in the receiving vessel an oil almost similar to that which they improperly call the "Oil of the Philosophers" <note>original: *oleum Philosophorum*; traditionally an oil made by distilling olive oil over bricks, used as a solvent or medicinal base</note>. Having cooled the retort, I took out the balls. Because they did not turn red even in a sufficiently strong fire, but instead turned very black, I suspected that this blackness proceeded from the oil, certain earthy parts of which—fixed and sequestered by the power of the clay—had assumed a physical body there. I had to test what kind of body this was. Therefore, having crushed and sifted these black balls, I placed them in a dish and poured common water over them and stirred. I gradually poured off the turbid water by tilting the dish, then added fresh clear water, always stirring the material. I did this until the poured-off water ran clear, and a heavy black sediment remained at the bottom of the dish.*

*Because of its weight and sudden settling, as well as its blackness in water, I joyfully suspected it was of a metallic and indeed of an iron-like nature. Having dried it, I placed it on paper, and—caught between hope and fear—I applied a magnet. When I moved the magnet here and there through the material, it extracted a fine iron powder (though not much) in one go. I repeated this and finally collected a copious amount of the extracted powder in proportion to the material, which I found in all tests to be the best iron. And so I found the end of my speculation, or rather the beginning of infinite ones. For when I perceived that the sulfurous spirits were fixed by clay as if by a matrix, I instituted the same method with all minerals, sulfurs, and even Mercury itself...*

...of your own, seeing new things in all things. However, because I did not include the experiment at that time, but reserved it for the second book of *Underground Physics*—and that book will hardly see the light of day so soon—many curious and distinguished men have asked me (some of whose letters I have placed at the end of this supplement) to publish this experiment, which could bring the greatest light to all Alchemy, and to stop the mouths of the "Miso-chemists" <term>Miso-chemists: from the Greek *misos* (hatred) and *chemeia*; those who despise or skeptically attack the study of chemistry</term> who snarl at this new opinion.

And so you have not only the history of the theory and practice, but also the reason for the discovery and publication of this experiment. There are those living who, by the occasion of this experiment, have experienced "rich Alchemy" in fact, and instead of thanks, have recommended my own *Underground Physics* back to me. Thus, by lighting a light for others, we ourselves are consumed and grow dim. For it is easier to *follow a thing already discovered* and add to it, than to discover it anew. So much for the experiment, of which a critic <note>original: *Zolius*; referring to Zoilus, a Greek grammarian known as a "scourge" for his harsh criticism of Homer</note> will say: *the mountains are in labor, and a ridiculous mouse is born* <note>original: *parturiunt montes, prodit ridiculus mus*; a famous Latin idiom from Horace suggesting a grand beginning that leads to a trivial result</note>. 

But in truth, even if this experiment be slight, it teaches how to make real *iron* from matter that is not even mineral, but in a short space of time; and so it confounds the subtleties of all those who assigned I-know-not-how-many centuries to the generation of metals. Where are the three principles of Paracelsus now? <term>Paracelsus's principles: the *Tria Prima*—Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury—which the famous physician Paracelsus claimed were the components of all matter</term> *Common silt and common linseed oil generate true iron.* You must therefore confess either that these principles of Paracelsus do not contribute to the generation of metals, or, if they are required, they lie hidden in the *silt and linseed oil*. If, having seen this truth, you still doubt the reality of Alchemy, I respond with the Count of Mirandola <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494), a famous Renaissance philosopher</note> that by the same doubt it can be doubted of you: whether you are *Genuine or Spurious, a changeling, born of a father or an incubus.*

# Supplement to the Underground Physics
## CHAPTER III.
### Physical Demonstration.

It now remains for us to examine the proposed experiment *physically* and assign physical causes to it. Above all, however, two things must be premised: *First*, whether this experiment is true; *Second*, whether the iron *produced* from it was not already hidden in the silt or oil, and thus practiced an imposition?

To the first, I respond that the experiment *is true* and successful; as it has been proven many times by me and others. It also succeeds with several *other oils*; but with *silt* <term>silt: original *limus*, specifically fertile river mud or sediment</term> alone, not with common mud <note>original: *luto*; distinguish between rich, mineralized silt and common garden dirt</note>. If you take ten parts of *native sulfur* <term>native sulfur: original *sulphuris vivi*, or "living sulfur," naturally occurring sulfur that hasn't been processed by fire</term> and a hundred parts of *silt*, and make a paste and bricks from them in the common manner, and bake them either in a brick-kiln or a potter’s oven, then crush the bricks and proceed by washing—as explained at the end of the preceding chapter—

...has been learned by experiment, and you will find iron there as well, though not of such good quality, nor in such quantity.

*To the second question I reply*, that the iron extracted from the powder by a magnet, if it is reduced <note>“Reduced” here refers to the chemical process of smelting or returning a substance to its metallic state</note>, *is true metal and iron*. Since, however, not everyone has the opportunity to reduce it into a solid mass, because such a reduction requires a large apparatus of fire, it is necessary that in the meantime they be content with that quality which *is the first, essential, and specific quality of iron*, namely, *to be drawn by a magnet*. For it has never been reported or observed that a magnet draws anything other than *iron*, or that *iron* is drawn from anywhere other than by a magnet. If, therefore, there are those who *deny that this fine powder is iron*, and yet admit—compelled by experience—that it is drawn by a magnet, I say that if they can prove this, they will be setting forth a new experiment for us, far more remarkable than our own.

*To the third objection I say*, that I have washed the silt with great diligence—commonly called *geschlemmt* <gloss>levigated or washed to separate fine particles from grit</gloss>—so that all mineral particles, if any were inside, might be separated. I then treated the silt by itself without linseed oil; as the experiment shows, I did not find even an atom of *iron*. Thus, there can be no deception in the *silt*. Next, I suspected that since linseed oil is usually sold by merchants who also sell iron, perhaps certain iron atoms had crept into the oil. Therefore, I bought that oil from the *restiariis* <note>original: *restiariis*; rope-makers or dealers in cordage who used oil for their trade</note>, but the effect was the same, even with other oils and certain *animal tallows*. I also took linseed oil and placed it alone in a retort, distilling it down to the consistency of varnish, and finally to a carbon residue, which I examined with a magnet and found nothing.

I conclude, therefore, that there is no *actual iron* in either the silt or the linseed oil. I will not dispute regarding the *potential* iron—especially the *universal mineral potential*—which I demonstrated in the preceding chapter to be present in all subjects; indeed, if it were not there in *potential*, it would never come into *actuality*. I wished to add this: I have observed that by too much extraction of this iron, the magnet is weakened, that is, *satiated*. Since this fine powder undoubtedly still contains many *spiritual atoms of iron* (and, as it were, its *first essence* <term>first essence: *primum ens*; the most basic, formative stage of a substance in alchemical theory</term>) which could not be fixed in so short a time, the magnet becomes filled with them. But after a few days, when they have evaporated, it returns to its former strength. Curious researchers might perhaps find an opportunity here to investigate the *direction* of the magnet toward the pole, if they correctly studied the motion of the "atom-sphere" from these things; but more on this elsewhere at another time.

Having premised these things, I come to the *physical examination* of this experiment, for which reason I specifically included this chapter, which I shall settle with two questions: *first*, what is the *metal-making cause in general* in this experiment; and *second*, what is the *iron-making cause specifically*?

*To the first question I reply*, that *true, corporeal iron* is effectively produced by this experiment, and thus it is necessary that the *causes of this iron’s production be natural*: and that this iron comes either from the silt, or from the oil, or from both. That it is not produced from *silt by itself*, or *from oil by itself*, I have demonstrated above. Therefore, it is certain that it arises from the *conjunction* of both. Nothing else is added but a moderate *heat* (of which more later), which contributes not so much to the substance as to the preparation of the iron, and acts as an *instrumental cause, not a material one*. *Therefore, everything that results comes from the silt and the oil.* It must then be considered how much each of the two contributes to this metallic *genesis* <gloss>origin or creation</gloss>. *It is a property of iron* that it does not flee the fire, but withstands it; it is a property of oil...

<header>Chapter Three.</header>

It is the nature of iron not to flee fire, but to endure it; it is the nature of oil to be set ablaze and to flee fire. If, therefore, oil is to be changed into iron, the first requirement is that it be fixed—that is, that it becomes dry, earthy, and capable of bearing fire. This can indeed happen in such a way that the oil, through slow distillation in a retort, is thickened into a varnish, and finally burned into a coal. For it is certain that all *sulfureity* <note>original: "sulphureitatem"; refers to the oily, combustible principle in a substance</note> or fatness, through slow digestion and the removal of the watery or thinner parts, is concentrated, thickened, and turned into earth; meanwhile, the oil is eventually reduced into *elemental water*. We see this in all wood; a part of it is driven into flames by fire, and once that is gone, the remainder of the fatness is changed into charcoal.

And it should be noted that any charcoal never *rots*, because of the highest concentrated *fire* within it which preserves it from putrefaction; and it is never consumed, even if it stands for a thousand years in a sealed, massive fire. However, in the open air, it rarefies <note>breaks apart or dissipates</note> because of the fire atoms penetrating it. And if ash remains, there is no small amount of *sulfur* in it, as we shall hear later. Therefore, lest this oil-charcoal—or the concentrated part of the sulfur—be able to rarefy even out in the open fire, *silt* is added to fill its pores. This silt, by its astringency, retains the volatile part, and by a mutual embrace, creates this admirable *marriage* <note>The "marriage" or "chemical wedding" refers to the binding of two substances into a new compound</note>. 

For it is notable that neither the oil-charcoal nor the silt is drawn by a magnet on its own; but *as soon as they are joined according to the laws of this experiment, they are greedily seized by the magnet. Therefore, something from the silt is added to the sulfureity of the flax [linseed oil], and by this addition, that magnetism is completed.* What the nature of this is, we shall hear later. Now we shall more fully examine the requirements of the linseed oil. 

It is certain that nothing is drawn by a magnet except *iron* (to which I add steel); and experience teaches that iron is a true metal. For thus says my *Geber* <note>Geber was the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, an influential 8th-century alchemist</note> concerning the nature of Mars <note>Mars is the alchemical name for iron</note> in chapter 8, book 2: *if indeed there be a fixed earthy sulfur, mixed in nature with a fixed earthy mercury, and these two be not pure but of a livid whiteness, and if the quantity of sulfur be greater, iron is generated from them, etc.* 

Therefore, that which possesses *sulfur* and *mercury* is defined as a metal. Since, then, the magnet draws iron, it draws it as a metal; and drawing it as a metal, it draws it for the reason that it possesses *sulfur* and *mercury*. For unless it had these principles, it would not be a metal, and consequently not iron. Therefore, by definition, the *attraction of the magnet happens to iron as a metal, consisting of mercury and sulfur*. This is what I wish to infer: for neither *mercury* nor the *sulfur of Mars*, each alone without the other, is drawn by a magnet, as is clear from experiment, since neither the *silt* nor the *oil* is drawn by a magnet. 

Now, this dispute having been contested, I proceed and ask: in which subject does the *sulfur* hide, and in which does the *Mercury of Mars* hide? If both were hidden in both, each subject—the silt and the linseed oil—would be drawn by the magnet on its own. But since this does not happen, it is necessary that the sulfur hides in one, and the mercury in the other. When these are joined, they produce a metal that is drawn by the magnet. 

I say, therefore, that in the linseed oil hides the *mercury*, and in the silt hides the *sulfur of Mars*. I pronounce something wondrous and great, and as I believe, unheard of until now, nor ever produced by any Philosopher: namely, that *Mercury* hides in linseed oil—but *take it as said* <note>original: "dictum puta"; a phrase asking the reader to accept the premise for the sake of the argument</note>. *Metalleity* <term>metalleity: the essential quality that makes a substance a metal, traditionally associated with mercury</term> has always been ascribed to Mercury by all the Philosophers; for that is what properly renders a metal malleable, which is the specific property of metals, and without which a substance cannot be called a metal. That which brings this metalleity to things—that, I say, is *mercurial*.

In a few words, I shall repeat the definition of common mercury, so that you may know how to distinguish the philosophical kind from it. Philosophical or "true" mercury, which is the metallic principle and provides the "metallicity" <note>original: "metalleitatem"; the essence that makes a substance a metal</note>, is a certain whitening genus of sulfur that produces metal. However, common mercury consists of a defective antimonial and arsenical earth joined with true mercury. Thus, true mercury is a simple earth and the principle of metals; common mercury, on the other hand (if I were to call it a "fluid arsenic," I would not be speaking improperly), is a composite. Because common mercury is a decomposed substance, its essence does not desire any sulfur other than what it already possesses in its decomposition; it will work no good unless that sulfur is separated. But the principle of mercury, if it be stripped bare, acts immediately as a principle if it is joined to its own sulfur, and it produces a metallic body according to the quantity, quality, purity, and impurity of itself and the added sulfur. Whence, learnedly and like a father, *Arnold of Villanova* <note>A famous 13th-century physician and alchemist</note> advises:

> Let your whole study be directed toward digesting and cooking the mercurial substance; for according to its dignity, bodies will be dignified, which exist as nothing other than a cooked mercurial substance.

Indeed, the mercury of metals differs from common mercury because our mercurial principle has taken up a metallic body in place of sulfur or other defective earth, has penetrated it, led it into a flowing state, and rendered it a fluid metal. With this, depending on the quality of the added metal, it is frozen <note>solidified</note> again. *Nicolas Barnaud of Crest* <note>A 16th-century French physician and alchemist</note> testifies to this with a memorable example in his short commentary on that famous enigmatic epitaph readable at Bologna: *Ælia Lælia, Crispis etc.* <note>The "Aelia Laelia Crispis" is a famous mysterious inscription that many alchemists tried to decode</note> (where on page 18 he narrates) that there was an English man of great authority, still living in the author’s time, who turned common gold into mercury using a liquid prepared for that purpose. From that mercury and the "earth of the sun" <note>refined gold</note>, he finally prepared a tincture. Of this, the Author says:

> While I was staying with Master Doctor Thaddeus Hagetius <note>Tadeáš Hájek, a noted astronomer and physician to Emperor Rudolf II</note> in Prague, I saw the golden fruits a hundred times and held them in my hands—namely, a small cake or mass of pure, refined gold weighing six ounces, made by the same Master Hagetius from common mercury by the "projection" <note>the act of casting a small amount of transmuting powder into a melt</note> of a single grain of red powder in a single moment.

The *Rosary* <note>The *Rosarium Philosophorum*, a seminal alchemical text</note> seems to agree with these things in the following:

> Quicksilver is worth nothing by itself; but when it is "mortified" <note>chemically altered or killed</note> with its hidden body, then it is worth something, and it lives with an incorruptible life. This body is of the nature of the Sun <note>Gold</note>; therefore it is necessary that all quicksilver be converted into the nature of the sun, just as leaven converts the whole dough into the nature of the ferment.

*Paracelsus* <note>The famous Swiss-German physician and occultist</note> agrees with this in Book 1 of *On the Nature of Things*:

> The regeneration and renewal of metals occurs just as man returns to the earth from which he was first taken, and so will be reborn again on the Last Day. In the same way, metals can return again into mercury (from which they were first born), be dissolved with it, and become mercury; and through fire (which shall also judge the world), they can be reborn and clarified. In this way, he says, stones and special tinctures of silver and gold are generated.

But concerning these matters, we shall speak in the final chapter of this supplement. Now let us come to the continuation of our mercury, reviewing in a few words the reasons that have driven me to believe that the mercurial entity—the "mercurifying" and "metallizing" essence—lurks in every fatness <note>oils or fats</note>. I shall explain this candidly, lest anyone suspect I have attempted something beyond reason. *First*, I am moved by the very harmful smoke of all burnt fats; this was confirmed for me by the vapor of coals, which has a thoroughly arsenical and mercurial effect. *Second*, I observed that coals [mix] them- <note>The page ends mid-sentence; the catchword "scere" suggests the Latin word "miscere," meaning to mix or combine</note>

### Chapter Three.

...to know it, and to change it into steel; likewise to impart various colors to iron and other metals. I proceeded further, taking soot and treating it with metals; I observed a wonderful alteration. I observed that coals in melting make metals volatile; likewise I found that copper ashes <note>cinders or burnt copper</note> whiten; the black residue of tartar <note>original: "caput mortuum nigrum tartari"</note>, which are the washed-out dregs of black tartar used by engravers for printing <note>original: "chalcotypi pro impressione utuntur"</note>, when melted with gold, whitens it and makes it brittle. I proceeded further, and in alkaline solvents, in volatile alkalis, I found such a masking, whitening earth, by means of which I made the mercury of bodies. 

Finally, I will set down a manifest experiment which convinced me. If you mix soap, tallow, oil, or any fatty substance with arsenic and distill it through a retort, it will sublimate into the neck under the force of fire as an arsenic significantly "metallicized" <note>endowed with the appearance or properties of a metal</note> like antimony. I first believed the arsenic had been reduced to a metal, the fat absorbing the corrosive saline spirits: but I found myself deceived. For when this metallicized arsenic was placed under a bell jar and heat was added, it began to flame; in that flame, the mercurial essence <note>original: "ens mercurii"</note> departed, and the arsenic sublimated back into the bell jar in its original form. 

Deinde & hoc notatu dignum, quod arsenicum taliter metallifatum, intra paucos dies etiam optime reconditum, nigrescat, concidat tandem, ac sua sponte pulverisetur; quod manifestum signum est, deesse huic mixto etiamnum aliquod principium, quod ex aere quaerat: *fortis enim inter mercurii & sulphuris ens, magnetismus est.* 

Furthermore, it is worth noting that arsenic metallicized in this way—even if kept perfectly sealed—turns black within a few days, eventually collapses, and spontaneously turns to powder; which is a clear sign that this mixture still lacks some principle that it seeks from the air: *for there is a strong magnetism between the essence of mercury and sulfur.* And so, I moved from one level of experience to another, until finally, I was forced to conclude—to my own astonishment—that *a metallic mercurial essence lies hidden in all sulfurous bodies of this world, and wanders most freely even in the air itself;* whence it was not undeservedly called *Steel* <note>original: "Chalybs"</note> by Sendivogius <note>Michael Sendivogius, a famous 17th-century alchemist who theorized that an invisible "food of life" existed in the air</note>, which is seized by magnetic sulfur. *I therefore attribute the "metallicizing" cause to Mercury, and the principle of mercury to the oil in this process, moved by the preceding causes.* 

Now we shall proceed to the second part of the mixture. I said that the principle of mercury is neither a metal by itself nor attracted by a magnet by itself; therefore, a second thing is required, which is sulfur, and whose home I assign to *slime* <note>original: "limo"; refers to a primordial or fertile earth</note>. Before I begin this demonstration, it is necessary to set forth the process of all generation in a few words. *For the joining of the masculine seed, a feminine one is required, and for these two, nourishment, which latter is of a feminine nature: for the female not only adds her own seed, but also gives that which causes both seeds to grow, namely nourishment or the "menstruum"* <note>In alchemy, a "menstruum" is a solvent or a nutritive fluid that fosters growth or transformation</note>. 

In vegetables, there is a seed, with which the moisture of the earth is joined, and finally a portion of the earth's sulfur grows into both, which is the nourishment. So in metallic birth <note>original: "genesi metallica"</note>, mercury and sulfur are like male and female; there is also, as our Albertus <note>Albertus Magnus, a 13th-century scholar and saint often cited as an authority in alchemy</note> says, *a subtle terrestrial nourishment strongly mixed in*, that is, not every earthy thing is the nourishment of metals; but that which is subtle, which is strongly worked: namely, that which has the most of both, *becomes sulfurous and mercurial.* Since I am treating "slime" in this place, I say that in it lies hidden not only sulfur, but also this subtle terrestrial growth or metallic nourishment; which, when joined with mercury, produces the mixture we call metal. Thus, in this birth, as much metal is made as there is mercurial essence in the oil, and sulfur and subtle terrestrial [nourishment] in the slime...

It is true that I maintain *sulfur* lies hidden in the mud <note>original: "limo"; refers to a fertile, silty earth or sediment</note>, yet I would not want anyone to understand this as common sulfur (which is a compound made of universal acid and bitumen). Rather, I mean the *principle* of sulfur. These two differ so much in their powers and nature that they are of entirely different kinds. However, I do not deny that by dissolving acids, a compound sulfur can be produced from mud or clay. Indeed, that very experiment led me to the study of mud, since a flaming sulfur can be produced even from *quicklime* <note>original: "calce viva"; calcium oxide</note> itself. Furthermore, I observed that mud is dissolved in corrosives and precipitated by common *mercury* in a highly refined and exalted form; I noted that this precipitate is "delighted" by *metals* and possesses the power of *ingress* <note>the ability of a substance to penetrate and transform a metal</note>. I have noted that stones are changed into mud by a certain extraction. At Amberg in the Upper Palatinate, I saw with my own eyes a great quantity of *iron ore* which, having been exposed to the air and not reduced into a metal body quickly enough (due to the lack of furnaces, which were destroyed in the German war <note>The Thirty Years' War, 1618–1648</note>), was changed in a short time into a pure mud, entirely devoid of *metal*. This occurrence strongly persuaded me that mud is the *foundation for metals*. *Tabernaemontanus* <note>Jacob Theodor von Bergzabern (c. 1522–1590), a famous physician and botanist</note> testifies that *gold has been changed into sealed earth* <note>original: "terra sigillata"; a medicinal clay</note>; and I noted above that a certain species of earth is so joined to *gold* that it can only be separated from it with the greatest difficulty, and not by common means. It is clearly evident in mines that a certain kind of earth, commonly called *bstig* <note>original: "bstig"; a German mining term "Besteg," referring to the clay or "gouge" lining a mineral vein</note> (of which I wrote in *Subterranean Physics* under the principle of sulfur), serves as the principle and nourishment for metals. In the town of *Blomberg* in the domain of *Fürstenberg* near the *Hercynian forest*, I saw *iron* being dug out just a few feet below the horizon of the earth. The vein is like *mud*, easily distinguishable from the rest of the earth, and about three feet thick. Below the vein, the earth is *sandy*, in which not a grain of metal is found; this is because the mud has ended, which acted as a receptacle for the subterranean sulfurous vapors. Observation <note>original: "autopsia"</note> makes it clear that various metals are generated according to the quality of the stones, earths, and clays. For in *raw* stones hardly anything grows, or if there is anything, it is meager. I categorize flints among the "earths" because they can be changed into *lime and sulfur*, yet it is within these that metals are most often generated. Hence, *Democritus* <note>Greek philosopher often cited in alchemical texts</note> was not incorrect to state that metals come *from lime and lye*; and *Aegidius Mauritanus* <note>An Alchemist often associated with the "Turba Philosophorum"</note> claims they are generated from ashes. This is because mud and stones can be changed by art into ashes, lime, and lye. Thus, when these substances are added outside of mines, *ores can be ripened and increased*, and even altered by infusion. Therefore, it is not without sufficient and pregnant reason that I have ascribed to mud—in this genesis of sulfur and refined earth—the quality of a metallic *nourishment*. I have thus attributed the completed *metallicity* to linseed oil and mud: to the linseed oil I attribute the metallic nature and malleability, and to the mud I attribute the color and fusion. But more on this later; now that this point is settled, I shall turn to the second question.

Namely, in this artificial genesis, what is the cause that makes it iron? In the previous question, I proposed the cause of *metallification* <note>the process of becoming a metal</note> in general; here, however, the specific reason for *iron-formation* <note>original: "ferreificationis"</note> must be explained. The *iron-forming* cause or form must be attributed either to the linseed oil, or to the mud, or to both. It is not the *linseed oil* alone, for I can provide a type of *mud* which, when treated with linseed oil, produces not iron, but another far more noble metal. Nor can it be assigned to the *mud* alone, for I will demonstrate a certain oil which, when poured over the same mud (from which iron is usually made in experiments with linseed oil), elicits not iron, but another metal. Therefore, the *form of iron must be assigned to both*.

### Chapter Three.

To help you understand this more clearly, I will illustrate this question with an example drawn from the kingdom of animal generation. If the seed of the male excels by its own virtue over that of the female, the offspring produced will resemble the parts of the male; the same is to be understood regarding the female seed. A good male seed corrects a faulty female seed, and a good female seed corrects a faulty male seed. However, if both are faulty, it is necessary and natural that a faulty fetus be produced: for as the seed is, so is the fruit. *Oil relates to the female, while mud relates to the male. Good oil produces something good even from impure mud; conversely, good mud draws something good out of faulty oil or <term>Mercury</term><note>Here, mercury refers to the philosophical principle of liquidity and volatility, not necessarily the liquid metal.</note>: for the goodness of one overcomes the faultiness of the other.* But if both should be *raw and imperfect*, it follows that a *raw and imperfect* metal will be produced from them. On the other hand, if both are good, it necessarily follows that a *perfect* metal will be generated.

You heard a little while ago <term>Geber's</term><note>original: "Gebri"; Geber is the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, an 8th-century figure considered the father of alchemy.</note> definition of iron: that it consists of unclean earthy *sulfur and mercury*. He continues in the cited chapter of his second book: *the dominance of fixed sulfur hinders the melting; for the more fixed sulfur the body has, the more slowly it flows.* He also calls it an *earthy, leaden body*. Furthermore, in Book One, Part Three, Chapter 27, he *defines <term>Mars</term><note>The alchemical name for iron, named after the Roman god of war due to its hardness and use in weaponry.</note> as being a metallic body that is very leaden, possessing an impure whiteness, not meltable by direct melting, and therefore of the hardest handling.* 

You see that he attributes this difficult melting to the *earthy sulfur of the mud*; because it has not been sufficiently *worked through* <note>original: "subactum"; meaning refined, kneaded, or brought into a subtle state</note> or mixed, and thus is not sufficiently *subtle* or refined. Just as in reality, all common mud and stone from which iron is made is raw and coarse; therefore, the fault lies in the mud. Next, he complains of the "leadenness" and earthiness of the *Mercury*. This fault must be ascribed to the oil, from which we demonstrated above that the mercurial nature proceeds. What wonder is it then? *If faulty parents produce faulty offspring.* 

Even though iron is as much a metal in its own species as any other, the iron produced in this manner is far more *perfect* than the natural kind; there is no doubt that by the purification of its principles, the nobility of *Mars* can be exalted to the highest degree. This is the reason why *iron* comes forth from this experiment. I could take this opportunity to add many more experiments on how *other metals are made*; but since all prudent men will gather this for themselves—*namely, that the whole business consists in the goodness of the oil and the mud, or the quicksilver and the sulfur, as well as the earth*—it would be superfluous to instruct them further on a matter they likely perceive as well as I do. For I am a disciple of all "Philochymists" <note>Lovers of chemistry/alchemy</note> rather than a teacher. 

Regarding the proportion of the *mixture*, you see nature working of its own accord, as the <term>Rosary</term><note>original: "Rosario"; refers to the 'Rosarium Philosophorum', a famous 16th-century alchemical text.</note> says: *Our water is the weight of wisdom; and heat helps nothing in this birth, except that it separates the remaining parts, mixes the suitable ones, and fixes them.* The *time* for this operation is completed in a few hours. For unless nature were forced to *collect* the principles of iron in this generation from those coarse envelopes of mud and oil, but instead joined them by art in a *collected, separated, and pure* state, this wonderful birth would surely occur in a moment, in greater quantity, and with higher perfection.

### CHAPTER IV.

# The Agreement of Authors.

Now that our opinion has been defended not only by a most clear experiment but also by the strongest reasons, it remains for us to demonstrate to the reader that many authors agree with us; thus, not only practice and theory, but also the authority of both ancient and modern authors stands on our side. We shall bring forward twelve witnesses: four of whom admit that the generation of minerals proceeds from the earth; four who testify that nature sometimes, in an extraordinary way, has produced metals even outside of mines in <term>meteors</term><note>In early modern science, "meteors" referred to any atmospheric or geological phenomena, not just shooting stars.</note>; and four who concede that this can be done through art.

*The first, who assigns the earth as the Mother of metals, is that sacred writer Ezra, who in book 4, chapter 8, verse 2, expressly admits that the earth indeed produces plenty of clay for molding earthenware, but produces only a little dust from which gold is made. Therefore, whether the word "little" denotes quantity—for it is certain that nature produces more iron than gold—or whether it signifies quality—that is, that the dust from which gold is made must be small, thin, refined, and subtle, and strongly mixed, as Albertus <note>referring to Albertus Magnus, a 13th-century polymath</note> says—he is nonetheless clear in this sense: that he establishes the earth as the principle of gold.*

*The second is that ancient Morienus <note>a legendary 7th-century alchemist</note>, whose following words are cited in the <term>Rosary</term><note>The "Rosarium Philosophorum," a famous 16th-century alchemical treatise.</note>: "O dearest one, understand this and you shall not err: the sperm of metals is living water, and the earth is the imperfect body. This earth is rightly called 'the Mother,' because she is the mother of all elements. Thus, when the sperm is joined with the earth of the body, it is dissolved into the water of the sperm, and it becomes one water without division; second is the conception, when the earth is dissolved into black powder and begins to retain a little of the mercury within itself; for then the Male acts upon the Female, that is, the <term>Azoth</term><note>original: "Azoth"; the universal solvent or essential mercurial principle in alchemy.</note> upon the earth." If you consider these words rightly, they point so directly to our artificial metallic generation that they require absolutely no further explanation.*

The third is Augustinus Pantheus, a Venetian philosopher, who in his art of metallic transmutation, in the <term>Voarchadumia</term><note>original: "Voarchadumia"; a term coined by Pantheus, likely meaning "Gold of Two Fires."</note>, explains a certain Hebrew word, <term>Dovorechad</term><note>A technical term used by Pantheus to link alchemy with Kabbalistic linguistic theories.</note>, which contributes much to <term>Alchemy</term>, as meaning common clay; in which explanation, as you have heard thus far, he is not mistaken.

The fourth is a certain anonymous philosopher hiding under the name of Philaletha <note>Eirenaeus Philalethes, a famous 17th-century alchemist</note>, whose short work recently became known to us through the care of Joannes Langius. However, Georgius Hornius, in the preface to Geber, judges this writing very unfavorably, writing: "There recently appeared an anonymous work, *The Open Entrance to the Closed Palace of the King* <note>original: "introitus apertus ad occlusum Regis palatium"</note>, which was sent to me many years ago as a manuscript from England; it is a plainly sophistical and fictitious work, as has been recognized through the experience of many who tested it exactly, to the loss of their time and expense." It would have been desirable if Hornius had edited Geber more correctly and left the labors of others untouched. Is that anonymous author "sophistical" simply because he wrote his work many years ago...

### CHAPTER FOUR.

...wrote; by the same reasoning, even **Horn's Geber** <note>Referring to Georg Horn, a historian who questioned the authenticity of Latin alchemical works attributed to Geber.</note>, which is much older, would be considered fraudulent. Nor will posterity look kindly on **Horn** for having deprived it of such a great treasure for so long. We owe more to **Lord Lange** <note>Likely Johann Lange, an editor of alchemical texts.</note>, who blessed us with it. Furthermore, why does he call it a "Sophistic" or fictitious writing? Because many, after a waste of time and expense, were unable to produce anything from it. By that name certainly, all the books of the Chemists—and especially those of **Geber**—would be "sophistic"; for it is certain that no common worker (among whom Horn should not even be counted, since he performed no practical work) ever drew any benefit from **Geber**. So much so that even **Count Bernard** <note>Bernard Trevisan, a famous 15th-century alchemist.</note> scarcely—hardly at all—refrains from declaring him fully a fraud. 

But let us return to our **Philalethes** <note>Eirenaeus Philalethes, the pseudonym for a famous 17th-century alchemist.</note>; whose writing, he himself warns in chapter 18, is not to be understood according to the literal word. For the rest, if there were nothing in the entire book except the second chapter on the component principles of **Sophic Mercury** <note>A purified, philosophical form of mercury used in the Great Work, distinct from common quicksilver.</note>, and the eleventh chapter on the discovery of the <term>magistery</term><note>The "mastery" or the successful completion of the alchemical process.</note>, all Alchemists would still be eternally indebted to this author, if they possess even the smallest spark of true light. For everything is so clearly set out and so corresponds to practice that I myself would not know how to present it otherwise. Let us produce from chapter 22 of that work what serves our purpose, namely the following:

> *“Some, led astray by lead, have worked with the greatest hope but the least fruit; but know that our lead is more worthy than any gold; it is the mud in which the soul of gold is joined with mercury, etc.”*

What else is this saying than that there is a subtle earthly substance, into which an unctuous moisture must be incorporated? How difficult this "mud" is to find, our Author confesses, by adding:

> *“Pray to God, brother, that He may deign to grant you this blessing, because it does not come from the one who runs, much less from the one who wills, but this blessing depends on the Father of Lights alone.”*

Whence the sacred text [Genesis 27:28] places among the formulas of blessing: *“May God give you of the dew of heaven, and the fatness of the earth”* <note>original: "pinguedine terræ"</note>; for indeed, that which is called the "fatness of the earth" is its very essence, namely the subtle terrestrial part—the **Matrix** <note>The womb or generative environment.</note>, the nurse, the Vessel, the **Lute of Wisdom** <note>original: "Sapientiæ lutum"; a paste used to seal alchemical vessels, here used metaphorically.</note>, the seal of Hermes, the Magnet, etc.

**The Fifth** witness, and the first among those who testify that nature produces metals even outside of mines, is **Gaston Claveus** <note>Gaston de Cloy, an apologist for alchemy.</note> in his *Apology against Erastus*, who notes the following: *“If it is true that iron is born in the clouds from that double exhalation condensed by cold and falls to the earth, how much more likely is it that metal is born beneath the earth from the same exhalation condensed by cold; and he testifies that this has happened.”*

Our **Sixth** witness is **Albertus Magnus**, who recounts from **Avicenna** <note>The Latinized name of the Persian polymath Ibn Sina.</note> that a mass of iron of a hundred pounds fell from the sky in a rain, from which sharp scimitars were forged; likewise, it is reported that such a mass fell from the sky at **Grimma** in **Meissen** that it could not be moved from its place.

The **Seventh** is **Petermann Etterlin**, who reveals in his *Swiss Chronicle* that during a great storm, with the falling of many stones, a mass of iron fell from the sky which was sixteen feet long, fifteen wide, and two feet thick. If we measure this mass geometrically as a cube, you will find it contains 480 square [cubic] feet. If you take each foot to weigh a hundredweight, this mass weighed 48,000 pounds. Since this was birthed in the clouds, what wonder is it if such a thing happens in the earth? I believe the Swiss would not be angry if such a piece of gold should ever fall from the sky; but I fear they would start a war over the ownership of the land.

### CHAPTER IV.

# The Agreement of Authors.

Now that our opinion has been defended not only by a most brilliant experiment but also by the firmest reasons, it remains for us to demonstrate to the reader that many authors agree with us. Thus, not only practice and theory, but also the authority of both ancient and modern writers stands on our side. We shall bring forward twelve witnesses; four of them admit that the generation of minerals proceeds from the earth; four testify that nature sometimes produces metals in an extraordinary way even outside of mines (such as in meteors); and four grant that this can be done through the Art <note>Referring to "The Art" of Alchemy.</note>.

The first, who assigns the earth as the Mother of metals, is that sacred writer **Esdras** <note>Referring to the apocryphal book 2 Esdras (or 4 Esdras), specifically 8:2.</note>, *who in Book 4, Chapter 8, Verse 2, expressly admits that the earth indeed produces abundant soil for shaping pottery, but produces only a little dust from which gold is made <note>original: "terram quidem copiofam humum pro fingendis fictilibus, parvum autem pulverem producere, unde aurum fit"</note>. Whether, therefore, by the word "little" he denotes quantity—for it is certain that nature produces more iron than gold—or whether he understands quality (that is, that the dust from which gold is made must be small, thin, refined, and subtle, and "strongly mixed," as **Albert** <note>Albertus Magnus, a 13th-century philosopher and theologian reputed to be an alchemist.</note> says), he is nonetheless clear in this sense: that he posits earth as the starting principle of gold.*

The second is the ancient **Morienes** <note>Morienus Romanus, a legendary 7th-century hermit and alchemist said to have taught the Ummayad prince Khalid ibn Yazid.</note>, *whose words are cited in the **Rosary** <note>The "Rosarium Philosophorum," a famous 16th-century alchemical treatise.</note> as follows: "O dearest one, understand these things and you will not err: the sperm of metals is living water; the earth is the imperfect body. This earth is deservedly called the Mother, because she is the mother of all elements. Thus, when the sperm is joined with the earth of the body, it is dissolved into the 'water of the sperm,' and they become one water without division. The second stage is the conception, when it is dissolved with the earth into a black powder and begins to retain a little of the mercury within itself; for then the Male acts upon the Female—that is, the **Azoth** <note>A term for the universal solvent or the essential mercury of the philosophers.</note> acts upon the earth." If you consider these words correctly, they point so clearly to our artificial metallic genesis that they require absolutely no explanation.*

The third is **Augustinus Pantheus** <note>Giovanni Agostino Pantheo, a Venetian priest and author of alchemical works in the early 1500s.</note>, a Venetian philosopher, *who in his art of metallic transmutation, titled **Voarchadumia** <note>A term coined by Pantheo, possibly meaning "gold of two rubies" or "the way of the two-fold craft."</note>, explains a certain Hebrew word **Dovorechad**—which contributes much to Alchemy—as meaning common clay. In this explanation, as you have heard thus far, he is not mistaken.*

The fourth is a certain anonymous Philosopher, hiding under the name **Philalethes** <note>Eirenaeus Philalethes, the "Peaceful Lover of Truth," a famous 17th-century alchemical pseudonym.</note>, whose small work has recently become known to us through the efforts of **Johann Lange**. Regarding this writing, however, **Georg Horn** <note>A 17th-century historian and critic of alchemy.</note>, in his preface to **Geber**, judges very unfavorably when he writes: "There recently appeared the anonymous *Open Entrance to the Closed Palace of the King*, sent to me many years ago from England in manuscript—a clearly sophisticated and fictitious work, as has been known by the experience of many who tested it exactly, with loss of time and expense." It would have been desirable if **Horn** had edited **Geber** more correctly and left the labors of others untouched. Is that anonymous writer "sophistic" <note>In this context, "sophistic" means fraudulent or deceptive.</note> simply because many years ago his work [was] writ-

...wrote; by the same reasoning, Hornius’s Geber <note>Referring to the works attributed to Geber (Jabir ibn Hayyan), the famous 8th-century alchemist. We owe more to Mr. Langius <note>Likely Johann Joachim Lange, who published alchemical collections.</note>, who blessed us with it. Furthermore, why does he call it a deceptive or fabricated writing? Simply because many, with a loss of time and expense, were unable to produce anything from it. By this logic, certainly all books of the chemists, and especially those of Geber, would be deceptive; for it is certain that no common laborer (among whom not even Hornius should be counted, since he performed no practical work) ever drew anything of use from Geber. Indeed, even Count Bernard <note>Bernard Trevisan, a 15th-century alchemist.</note> himself scarcely—and indeed not at all—refrains from pronouncing him a total deceiver. 

But let us return to our Philaletha <note>Eirenaeus Philalethes, the pseudonym for a famous 17th-century alchemist, likely George Starkey.</note>; he himself warns in chapter 18 that his writing is not to be understood according to the literal letter. For the rest, if there were nothing in the whole book except the second chapter on the component principles of **Sophic Mercury** <note>A specialized alchemical form of mercury, seen as the "seed" of metals.</note>, and the eleventh chapter on the discovery of the **mastery** <note>The "Magistery," or the process of achieving the Philosopher's Stone.</note>, all Alchemists would nonetheless be eternally indebted to this Author, if they possess even the smallest spark of true light. For everything is laid out so clearly, and so corresponds to practice, that I myself would not know how to hand it down any differently. But from chapter 22 of that same writing, let us produce what serves our purpose, namely the following:

> *Certain men, led astray by lead, have worked with the greatest hope but the least fruit; but know that our lead is worthier than any gold; it is the slime <note>original: "limus"</note> in which the soul of gold is joined with mercury, etc.*

What else is this to say than that there is a subtle terrestrial substance into which an oily moisture must be incorporated? How difficult this "slime" is to find, our Author confesses by adding:

> *Pray to God, brother, that He may deem you worthy of this blessing; because it is not of him that runneth, nor of him that willeth, but from the Father of Lights alone does this blessing depend.*

Wherefore the sacred text places this among the formulas of blessing: *May God give thee of the dew of heaven, and the fatness of the earth* <note>Genesis 27:28. original: "det tibi Deus de rore Cæli, & pinguedine terræ"</note>; for in truth, that which is called the "fatness of the earth" is its essence, namely the subtle terrestrial part, the **Matrix** <note>The "womb" or environment where minerals grow.</note>, the nurse, the Vessel, the clay of Wisdom, the seal of Hermes, the Magnet, etc.

The fifth witness, and the first among those who testify that nature produces metals even outside of mines, is **Gasto Claveus** <note>Gaston de Cloave, or Gaston "Dulco" Claveus, a 16th-century French physician and defender of alchemy.</note> in his **Apology against Erastus**, who notes the following: *If it is true that iron is born in the clouds from that double exhalation condensed by cold, and falls to the earth, how much more likely is it that metal is born beneath the earth from the same exhalation condensed by cold; and he testifies that this has indeed happened.*

Our sixth witness is **Albertus Magnus**, who recounts from **Avicenna** that a mass of iron of a hundred pounds fell from the sky during a rainstorm, from which sharp scimitars were forged; likewise at **Grimma** in **Meissen**, such a great mass is said to have fallen from the sky that it could not be moved from its place.

The seventh is **Petermannus Eterlin** <note>Petermann Etterlin, author of a famous Swiss chronicle published in 1507.</note>, who in his **Swiss Chronicle** reports that during a great storm, along with the casting down of many stones, a mass of iron fell from the sky which was sixteen feet in length, fifteen in width, and two feet in thickness. If we measure this mass geometrically according to its cube, you will find 480 square feet; if you take each foot for a hundredweight, this mass weighed 48,000 pounds. Since this was produced in the clouds, what wonder if such a thing happens in the earth? I believe the Swiss would not be angry if such a piece of gold should some day fall from the sky; but I fear that, because of the ownership of the land, they would start a war.

The eighth authority is Paul Merula <note>Paulus Merula (1558–1607) was a Dutch geographer and historian.</note>, who writes in his *Cosmographia* that six iron axes fell from the Sky. I do not actually think they were literal axes, but rather that they had the *shape* of axes; for even those stones that are commonly cast down from the Sky <note>The author is referring to meteorites or "ceraunia" (thunderstones), which were often mistaken for man-made tools in the early modern period.</note> possess such a figure, which is why in the German tongue they are called *Donneräxte* <note>original: "Donneräxte"; translated: "Thunder-axes." These were often prehistoric stone tools discovered in the earth and believed to have fallen during lightning strikes.</note>.

Now we shall proceed to those who profess that such a thing can be done by **art**; of whom the first, but in the general order of witnesses—

The ninth is well known: **St. John the Evangelist**, of whom the Roman Breviary <note>The liturgical book containing the public prayers of the Catholic Church.</note>—which certainly cannot err—sings the following on the day of St. John the Evangelist in the holy month of December. The author is Adam of St. Victor <note>A prolific 12th-century poet and composer of Latin hymns.</note>, beginning with: *Let us rejoice at the festival*, etc.

> ->*He brings forth an inexhaustible treasure*<-
> ->*who from twigs made gold*<-
> ->*And gems from stones.*<-
> <note>original: "Inexhaustum fert thesaurum / qui de virgis fecit aurum / Gemmas de lapidibus." This refers to a legend where St. John transformed stones and sticks into gold and jewels to demonstrate the power of God over worldly wealth.</note>

To make Gems from stones, whether natural or artificial, is not so absurd, since stones and gems are both categorized under the single genus of "stoniness." However, to make gold from twigs—a metal from a vegetable source—seems at first glance very difficult to accept. Indeed, for a long time I believed myself that the transmutation of one "kingdom" <note>The "Three Kingdoms of Nature": Animal, Vegetable, and Mineral.</note> into another was not possible. However, **a certain member of the Society of Jesus** <note>The Jesuits.</note>, acting with great confidence but fearing his superiors (since the rules of the Society prohibit Alchemy), gave me a small amount of powder which he testified was made from the vegetable kingdom. He asked me to reduce it into a solid body; I did so, and I found **gold**. He begged me by all the saints to remain silent, because he would incur the danger of imprisonment and persecution even unto death. This same **Jesuit** related for certain that around the tamarisk—that is, in the soil where the Tamarisk grows—some **gold** is always found. I could easily believe this, for the **tamarisk** usually grows near shores and in damp places where there is an alluvial wash of waters. Thus **Dr. Jonstonus** writes in Book 9, Chapter 5, Article 2, page 448 of his *Dendrographia* <note>John Jonston (1603–1675), a Polish naturalist of Scottish descent. *Dendrographia* is his treatise on trees.</note>: *The tamarisk grows near brooks and streams and in places that are inundated by them; by the Rhine near Breisach and Neuburg, along the Danube near Vienna, in sandy places adjacent to long bridges, in the county of Tyrol, in Italy, in Spain near the Ebro, and in Silesia, etc.* It is therefore credible that on the watery Island of Patmos, where **St. John** was in exile, the tamarisk was not lacking from which he might take twigs, since that wood is more "twiggy" than others; for the cited author says of it: *it has many fragile shoots divided into many branches.* By what method St. John made gold from these twigs is obvious to anyone who has properly understood my experiment concerning iron: beech wood placed with iron rods in a closed vessel for the space of a few hours, as soon as it experiences sufficient fire (yet not so much that it melts), changes that iron into the best steel; and thus by consequence, the same can happen to other things. Let it suffice that this making of gold from twigs by St. John is neither impossible nor repugnant to reason and experience. For I do not see why **St. John**, to whom the heavenly and most intimate secrets were communicated by God, should not have known the truth concerning earthly matters.

The tenth is **Michael Psellus, a Greek Philosopher**, cited in the preface of this supplement, who expressly confesses to the Patriarch of Constantinople, Xiphilinus, that he crushed certain stones and mixed certain herbs, and thus usefully and very pre-

The eleventh witness is **St. Thomas** <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the influential theologian who discussed the legitimacy of alchemical gold in his writings.</note>, who in the place cited above expressly admits that **Alchemists**, through the true art of <term>Alchemy</term> <note>The ancestral science of chemistry, focused on the transformation of matter.</note>, sometimes achieve a true generation of metals; elsewhere he writes that from sulfur and quicksilver <note>mercury</note>, art produces metals just as nature does.

The twelfth place is claimed by **Monsieur de Rochas, a French Chemist** <note>Henri de Rochas, a 17th-century physician and mineralogist.</note>, by proposing a marvelous experiment to the world in the following words: *"Having seen,"* he says, *"so many wonders of natural operation through the benefit of water, I desired to know what that same water could achieve with the help of art imitating nature. Therefore, taking water—which I knew well was not a compound, nor mixed with anything other than the <term>spirit of life</term> <note>spiritus vitae: a vitalizing essence believed by alchemists to permeate the universe</note> (of which he had spoken before)—and by applying an artificial, continuous, and proportioned heat by means of the aforementioned 'snail' of coagulation and fixation <note>likely a spiral-shaped glass vessel or a slow, winding chemical process</note>, I prepared and arranged it until it was turned into earth. This earth produced animals, vegetables, and minerals. I do not report here what species of animals, vegetables, and minerals those were, for that is reserved for another place; but the animals moved themselves, ate, etc. And by the aid of a proper anatomy I performed on them, I discovered them to be composed of much sulfur, a little mercury, and even less salt. The minerals began to grow and increase by turning one part of the earth prepared for that purpose into their own nature. They were solid and heavy; and by this truly demonstrative science, namely **Chemistry**, I found them to be composed of much salt, a little sulfur, and even less mercury."*

This experiment will seem a paradox to the **Aristotelians**, the **Peripatetics** <note>Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy, often criticized by early modern scientists for being too dogmatic.</note>, and other **Miso-chymics** <note>original: "Misohymicos"; literally "chemistry-haters."</note> and **Rolfincian Nonentists** <note>Followers of Werner Rolfinck, a professor who was skeptical of alchemical claims; "Nonentists" suggests they believed alchemical transformations were "non-entities" or imaginary.</note>, and it will exceed all belief. To me, however, it appears quite reasonable. If I wished, and if the narrowness of this space allowed, I could clearly demonstrate that it is just as true and possible as the experiment of **St. John** mentioned above, of making gold from twigs. For it is not surprising that in this operation of de Rochas, water was changed into earth; since **Van Helmont** and **Boyle** <note>Jan Baptist van Helmont and Robert Boyle, famous for experiments where plants seemed to grow from water alone, suggesting water could become solid matter.</note> produce many experiments of this kind, and it is an ancient opinion. From **Orpheus**, one of the ancients, namely **Athenagoras**, cites this testimony:
> From the water, slime was made.
> <note>original Greek: "Εϰ τυ ὑδατος ἰλυς ϰατεστη"</note>
To this, the Scholiast of **Apollonius**, a certain Greek author, adds:
> From the slime, the earth itself was produced.
> <note>original Greek: "Εξ ἰλιυ εβλαστησε χθων αυτη"</note>

**Thales, Homer, Zeno, Hesiod**, and many others subscribe to this opinion. That various animals and vegetables arose from this earth is not to be doubted, especially since it was impregnated with the spirit of life (of the world, which we discuss in the next chapter). For we see dried earth, devoid of all seed, when exposed for some time to the air and the rays of the stars, become impregnated with various seeds of vegetables and animals and rendered fertile. I have often proven this in the matter of **May Dew** <note>ros majalis: water collected from morning dew in May, believed by alchemists to be highly charged with celestial energy</note> alone, from which I produced earth and thereafter various animals and vegetables. This being granted, we now have metals ready at hand; for wherever there is something animal or vegetable, there also fat or oil is found. This book shows in the "iron-bearing experiment" <note>referring to a process for extracting or creating iron</note> that once oil and slime are obtained, metals can be produced. And that from the fatness of the earth and slime, in no sweeter or more natural way than in my experiment...

There is still living in Venice a singular friend of mine and diligent investigator of nature, *Don Marco Antonio de Castagnia, Supreme Prefect of Mines for the Venetian Republic and founder of the Panthetic Society* <note>A 17th-century scientific or alchemical society</note>, who will attest before anyone that it is possible by art, in any house or laboratory, to build a perpetual mineral in various ways, from which at set times true metal can be extracted, no differently than from a mine. Nor indeed is this a wonder if we consider what came before; namely, that <term>sulfur</term> <note>In alchemical theory, sulfur represented the principle of combustibility and color</note> is fixed in clay; from which foundation many ways are known to me of acquiring more from minerals, if treated by art rather than by the common way. 

In *Bruchsal*, not far from my homeland *Speyer*, under the jurisdiction of the *Most Reverend Prince Lothar, Bishop of Speyer* <note>Lothar Friedrich von Metternich-Burscheid (1617–1675)</note>, a supreme patron not only of the learned but of the *curious* <note>Meaning scientific investigators or virtuosos</note>, *my most Clement Lord*, there lived a Swiss man (if I am not mistaken) who worked at washing sand to select gold from the Rhine. Though unlearned, he knew how to give excellent reasons and experiences for his art.
