He demonstrated this by experiment, for *he exposed sand from which he had once separated the gold by washing to the sun*, and after some time, having washed it again, he found gold once more. He did this many times, so much so that he made various heaps of this sand, which he washed alternately and in turns, and thus he did not need to change locations so often for the sake of fresh sand. 

*There was a certain Jesuit* who had in his collection various glasses *full of sand and water*; asserting for a certainty that he washed gold from them at certain times; and if *one trusts Glauber's 'New Chemical Light'* <note>Johann Rudolph Glauber (1604–1670), a famous chemist who claimed gold was omnipresent in common soil and sand</note>, all sand is gold. From *snow, firefly wings, human blood*, and many other things, *gold and other metals were made*, as *Dr. Rapp, Chief Physician of Mainz*, once showed me. With which *Albertus Magnus* <note>A 13th-century Dominican friar and philosopher known for his work on minerals</note> agrees, writing expressly in his book on minerals: *"There is no thing composed of the four elements in which gold is not naturally found, in its ultimate refinement."*

From all these things it is therefore manifest that metals can be generated by art outside of mines in a short time from all things; and it is false that so much time is required for metallic generation, or that the planets must concur in their generation. Since also that which grows onto metals is homogeneous, nor does it need to be changed into dissimilar parts (as is necessary in animal and vegetable mixtures); there is no reason why, once the required principles are obtained, generation shouldn't happen in an instant. But to prepare the principles, purify them, separate them from their husks, exalt them, and perfect them, that is truly the *labor of the Philosopher* <note>The "Philosopher" here refers to the Alchemist or Hermetic scientist</note>. 

Meanwhile, it appears from all this that I wrote the truth in my *Underground Physics* <note>*Physica Subterranea*, Becher's most famous work</note>, page 88: *"The principles of metals are the earths which we daily tread upon with our feet, and it is an easy business, if God wishes to open someone's eyes, so that it can be prepared by art in the greatest abundance, so that what we have proven in small scale might be done in large scale."* And page 200: *"There is in such solvents a certain power and mineral potency, which has the greatest magnetism and similarity with metals, and to put a great secret and practice in few words..."*

# Supplement to Underground Physics
## CHAPTER V.
## Consequences.

And so, with our experiment candidly proposed and confirmed by physical reasons as well as the authority of authors, we shall at this point, as we hope, satisfy the reader, and with his kind permission, we might conclude. Yet, lest anyone object that I am sounding a trumpet for war <note>original: *classicum canere*; a Latin idiom for sounding the signal for battle</note> or renewing a "hard iron age" <note>A reference to Hesiod's Ages of Man; the Iron Age was the final, most degraded era</note> dedicated to Mars; or that I have wasted time and left the reader with no utility—echoing the words of Chrysostom <note>St. John Chrysostom, an early Church Father</note> regarding *foreign doctrine, boasting of many trifles, and detaining listeners with much wordiness, only to dismiss them empty-handed at last, having gained neither great nor small profit*—I wished to treat this matter a little more clearly. I do this not so much to answer such mocking objections (for who can ever satisfy them?), but to gratify the sons of doctrine and to remove every mask of envy, as anyone shall see. 

For I myself, weary of this present life—just as our friend Emericus Stahl, the retired Mining Official of the Harz <note>original: *Emeritus Herciinus*</note>, once wrote while dying in his little hut—do not envy the "golden ages" of others, even as the world envies my own "iron age." Therefore, so that the <term>Lovers of Chemistry</term> <note>original: *Philochymici*; those who pursue chemistry through an alchemical or philosophical lens</note> may grasp the consequence of all that has been said, I shall divide this chapter into two parts. In the first, I will demonstrate that there exists in nature a certain universal conservative entity, from which comes the spirit, force, and life of all bodies. In the second part, I shall explain how this entity may be acquired by art. In the final chapter, I will teach the power of this entity in Medicine and <term>Alchemy</term>. Meanwhile, you Lovers of Chemistry:

> *You who with unbroken heart have endured the winter times,*
> *And have been soaked by rainwater, smelling of soot,*
> *Blinded by smoke, burned by crackling flames,*
> *Endure; behold, the times of most lovely spring return,*
> *In which the earth will laugh, painted with various colors,*
> *The flowers of spring promise pregnant seeds.*

As for the first part of this chapter, that excellent Physician and Chemist, Bernard Penotus of Port-Sainte-Marie in Aquitaine, sets before our eyes the connection and necessary consequence of this proposed universality, most elegantly and learnedly in his book on medicines. Regarding him, Horstius <note>Gregor Horstius (1578–1636), a prominent German physician</note> skeptically remarked that he could observe nothing in this Penotus except "soul." But what sort of soul his was, you shall now hear from his deepest concepts; in which curious investigators of nature find more delight than in any gold, to which those thirsty "Horstian" quacks cling: those two-legged moles, always buried deep in the earth, as Palingenius <note>Marcellus Palingenius, author of the *Zodiacus Vitae*, a famous didactic poem</note> so well depicts them. But to come to the matter, our Penotus poses three general foundations for defending this universality; the first is, that God created nothing...

In Bruchsal, not far from my homeland of **Speyer**, under the jurisdiction of the **Most Reverend Prince Lothar, Bishop of Speyer**, a supreme patron not only of the learned but also of the curious, and my most clement Lord, there lived a man (a Swiss, if I am not mistaken) who occupied himself with washing sand to collect Rhine gold. There was a certain Jesuit who had in his museum various glass vessels full of **sand and water**; he asserted for a certainty that he **washed gold from them** at certain intervals; and if one puts faith in **Glauber’s *New Chemical Light*** <note>Johann Rudolph Glauber (1604–1670) was a famous chemist and apothecary</note>, every sand is golden. With these things **Albertus Magnus** <note>A 13th-century Dominican friar and philosopher known for his work in the natural sciences</note> agrees, writing expressly in his book on minerals: **"There is no thing composed of the four elements in which gold is not found naturally, in its ultimate refinement."** <note>original: *Non est ex quatuor elementis elementata, in qua non inveniatur aurum naturaliter, in ultima subtiliatione.*</note>

From all these things, therefore, it is manifest that metals can be generated by art outside of mines in a short time from all things; and it is false that so much time is required for metallic generation, or that the **planets** must concur in their generation. Since that which grows onto metals is also homogeneous, and does not need to be changed into dissimilar parts (as is necessary in animal and vegetable mixtures), there is no reason why, once the required principles are obtained, generation should not happen in an instant. But to prepare the principles, to purify them, to separate them from their coverings, to exalt and perfect them—that is truly the **Labor of the Philosopher**. Meanwhile, from all this it appears that I wrote the truth in my *Underground Physics*, page 88: **"The principles of metals are the earths which we daily tread under our feet,"** and it is an easy business, if God wishes to open someone's eyes, so that it can be prepared by art in the greatest abundance. Thus, what we have proven on a small scale might be done on a large scale. And on page 200: **"There is in such solvents a certain force and mineral power, which has the greatest magnetism and likeness to metals,"** and to put a great secret and practice in few words...

# Supplement to Underground Physics
## CHAPTER V.
### The Consequences.

And so, having candidly proposed our Experiment, confirmed by physical reasons as well as the *Authority of Authors*, we shall at this point, as we hope, satisfy the Reader, and with his kind permission we could conclude. Lest anyone should object that I am "sounding the alarm" <note>original Latin: *classicum canere*; a military metaphor for inciting conflict or making a grand, perhaps empty, proclamation</note> and renewing an iron age for the world, sacred to Mars; or that I have wasted time and left the Reader with no benefit, according to that saying of Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom, an early Church Father known for his eloquence</note>: "foreign doctrine, boasting many trifles, and detaining listeners with much talkativeness, finally dismisses them empty-handed, having gained neither great nor small advantage." I wished to treat this matter a little more clearly, not so much to answer such mocking objections (for who can satisfy them?), but to gratify the sons of doctrine <note>A traditional term for students or initiates of the alchemical arts</note>, with every mask of envy removed, as anyone shall see. For I, weary of this present life, as one dying in his little cottage—since our friend Emericus Stahl, the Retired Hercynian <note>meaning he was from the Harz Mountains region of Germany, famous for mining</note>, has written—do not envy others their golden ages, even as the world envies them their iron ones. 

So that the Lovers of Chemistry <term>Philochymici</term> may grasp the consequence of all that has been said, I will divide this chapter into two parts. In the first, I will demonstrate that there exists in nature a certain universal sustaining essence <term>ens conservativum</term> <note>a theoretical substance believed to maintain the life-force and physical integrity of all things</note>, from which comes the spirit, power, and life of all bodies. In the second part, I will explain how this essence may be acquired by art. In the final chapter, I will teach what the power of this essence is in Medicine and Alchemy <term>Alchymia</term>. Meanwhile, you Lovers of Chemistry,

> You who with unbroken heart have endured the winter times,
> And have been drenched with rain-water, smelling of soot,
> Blinded by smoke, scorched by crackling flames,
> Endure! For behold, the times of most pleasant spring return,
> In which the earth will smile, painted with various colors,
> And the flowers of spring promise pregnant seeds.

As for the first part of this chapter, that Excellent Physician and Chemist, Bernard Penotus of Port-Sainte-Marie in Aquitaine, places the connection and necessary consequence of this proposed universality elegantly and most learnedly before our eyes in his book on medicines. Regarding him, Horstius <note>Gregorius Horstius, a contemporary physician often skeptical of alchemical claims</note> skeptically remarked that he could observe nothing in this Penotus except his soul. What sort of soul it was, however, you shall now hear from his deepest concepts; in which the curious Investigators of nature take more delight than in any gold, to which those thirsty "Horstian" medical-pretenders cling—those two-legged moles, always buried deep in the earth, as Palingenius <note>Marcellus Palingenius, an author known for his philosophical and satirical poetry</note> so well depicts them. But to come to the matter at hand, our Penotus sets down three general foundations for defending universality; the first is, Nothing [that] God...

[He] created in truth above, without also creating some likeness of it below; so that through the likeness of what appears below, we might arrive at the truth of what exists above. *The second foundation is:* God created nothing invisibly in spirit, without also shadowing the same visibly in some body; so that through the body of the visible shadow, we might arrive at the truth of the hidden spirit. *He proposes a third foundation:* God created nothing dispersed invisibly in the infinite; without also creating the same collected visibly in some single finite thing, so that through this, which is finite and comprehensible in one, we might arrive at that which is infinite and incomprehensible in many. For God created all infinite things for Himself, who is infinite; but he created all finite things for man, who is finite: so that all things might have their beginning from Him from whom they are, and at the same time all things might testify to their end toward which they are. Having laid down these arguments, he proceeds to demonstrate the matter with the following example. All things whatsoever, come from <term>Heaven</term> <note>In alchemy, *Cœlum* or Heaven often refers to the "quintessence" or the celestial influence that gives life to matter</note>, and participate in the nature of heaven; for nothing is so natural as that the offspring should participate in the nature and substance of the Parent: since, therefore, the universal Parent of all lower things is Heaven; it is necessary that all lower things participate in the nature and substance of Heaven: and thus Heaven is hidden within all things internally, while it is manifested outside all things externally: and just as it is open most widely in its body on the surface of the world, so it is contracted most tightly in its spirit at the center of the world. Therefore, Heaven, the highest of all things in its body, is placed on high; and again, heaven is the *deepest* of all things: hidden in the spirituous depths; and just as it closes and rules all things with its body, so it penetrates and fills all things with its spirit. For Heaven is everywhere visibly in its form: and again, Heaven is in all things by its power: and just as nothing is more manifest than Heaven through all things, so again, nothing is more hidden than Heaven in all things. You, however, who always see Heaven outside of all things, should understand Heaven hidden in all things; and make this hidden Heaven reveal itself, then no power of the manifest Heaven will ever be hidden from you. *This Heaven, or the <term>Philosopher’s Stone</term>, is in all things, and passes through all things of the whole world, and is a certain life-giving, substantive, and essential spirit, bestowing life, substance, and essence upon all Creatures of this world, because from it, in it, and through it, they are, live, are nourished, grow, and all things are moved, and all things are full of its power, and nothing is empty of its essence and power.* Thus far <term>Penotus</term> <note>Bernard Georges Penot (c. 1519–1617), a French alchemist and physician</note>, whom <term>Gerhard Dorn</term> <note>A 16th-century Belgian philosopher and champion of Paracelsian chemistry</note>, <term>Nuyffement</term> <note>Jean de Nuisement, a French alchemical poet and official</note>, and many others follow. The substance of common fire is intangible but visible; the fire of the Philosophers <note>original: "ignis Philosophorum"; a term for the secret, life-giving energy used in alchemical transformations, distinct from the destructive fire in a hearth</note> is tangible and visible because it is a concentrated fire, just as common fire is a thinned or rarefied fire. The matter of the Philosophers causes growth, preserves, and perfects by entering and penetrating. In truth, that matter could be called **Brumazar** <note>A cryptic name used by some alchemists to refer to the "Universal Spirit" or the "Prima Materia" (First Matter)</note>, because it is arisen and generated by the perpetual circulation of the stars, acting as "sulfurs." In this way it ascends from the Earth to Heaven, and again descends from Heaven to Earth, and thus it receives the power of things above and things below into itself, as is more fully explained in the Emerald Tablet.* <note>The "Emerald Tablet" (Tabula Smaragdina) is a foundational text of Hermetic philosophy, famously summarizing the principles of alchemy and the "as above, so below" relationship.</note>

It is clear, then, that there is in nature a certain subtle, oily, terrestrial moisture, a warm innate "radical moisture," <term>radical moisture</term> <note>The "humidum radicale" was believed by pre-modern doctors and alchemists to be the fundamental life-fluid within an organism, which, when exhausted, led to old age and death</note> a vital and life-giving spirit of things. Its presence is life, and its absence is death; it preserves all things in the **microcosm** <note>the human being as a "little world"</note>; just as in the **macrocosm** <note>the universe as a "great world"</note> it matures and alters all things, for as Empedocles <note>A Greek Pre-Socratic philosopher who proposed the theory of the four elements</note> says:

> *We can assist nature with fire; besides this, we have no other help.*

This fire of nature is awakened by external fire, of which it is the offspring; from this comes that perpetual harmony, sympathy, and magnetism of things. In short, this moisture is the "head of the world," as we noted above. Hermes speaks most excellently of it:

> *Heaven, or the Stone, or that spirit, is the secret and life of each and every thing, and every person has need of it. This is the water which is the grain in wheat, the oil in the olive, the gum in peach trees, the fruit in all trees, and the principle of human generation. From it comes that living thing which does not die as long as the world exists, because it is the "head of the world"—that is, I say, the moisture in which the sulfurous and saline, fiery and watery influences of all the stars are joined in a sweet viscosity by the bond of the most subtle earthiness, and they are found everywhere. For as truly and as long as a certain body is preserved, so truly and so long does this essence excel; and as truly as the sun illuminates this world, so truly is this vital spirit the fountain and principle of life and of all generation. This is that spirit which, dwelling in the air, gives life even to all the insects of the earth, ferments the waters of the rivers (as you will hear later), moves and colors the blood in the veins, produces metals in the mines, grows into flowers and fruits in vegetables, and is all things to all in all things. It thunders in the clouds, rains, and snows; it grows, blooms, and sprouts in the lands; it gives life, alters, and matures in animals; it fumes, penetrates, and fixes in minerals. Applied by art, it preserves life, cures diseases, and transmutes metals; it is volatile in volatile things, fixed in fixed things, animal-like in animals, vegetable-like in vegetables, mineral-like in minerals—a Philosophical Chameleon, but in all things the most perfect nature, of the most penetrating property and the thinnest substance.*

According to the agreement of all Philosophy, they are composed of the four mixed elements, from which a body can be defined *as that which is a mixture of the four elements*. Therefore, that which is innermost or essential in this body is the most subtle part of that elementary mixture—that is, from the mixture, circulation, and alteration of the four elements, some fifth thing emerges, which Zalento <note>Likely an alchemical authority or a pseudonym used in Hermetic literature</note>, as I noted above, calls **Brumazar**. Whence it is called the **fifth essence** <note>original: "quinta essentia"; the quintessence, a refined substance beyond the four elements of earth, air, fire, and water</note>, because it is the purest fifth being of the four elements mixed in any body. Hence Scaliger <note>Julius Caesar Scaliger (1484–1558), a renowned Italian scholar and physician</note> in Exercise 307, Section 20, says: *Every form of each perfectly mixed thing, even if it is not a soul, is nevertheless a fifth nature, far different from the four elements.* Yet this universal being consists of the four elements, belongs to them, and is the fifth essence of whatever bodies are produced therefrom.

*The second sign is* that since it is proper to the essence of things to preserve its mixtures and bodies, it follows that every essence must be penetrative, subtle, and *spiritual*; otherwise, it could not perform these duties nor flow into all parts of the mixture. *Thirdly*, since the preservation of all mixed bodies consists in their not being deprived of internal moisture or their innate heat, the entire conservative power of this essence consists in **natural heat and moisture**; and so this essence will be hot in the moisture, fluid because of the moisture, and viscous because of the heat and oiliness—namely, an **oily moisture, supremely volatile, supremely penetrative.**

*Fourthly*, since no transition is given between two extremes unless a middle is interposed—that is, the spirit does not act on the body except through a certain bond; and it can be bound by nothing except a subtle earthy thing. Subtle, so that it may emulate the nature of the spirit; earthy, so that there may be access to the nature of the body. Therefore, we conclude from the aforementioned four points that this Universal Being is an **oily moisture strongly mixed with a subtle earthy substance, possessing preserving and penetrating properties, and of a hot and moist temperament.**

Lest you think these things are said or to be understood casually, know that by the word *oily*, one should not understand a buttery oiliness, but that of which Morienes <note>Morienus Romanus, a legendary hermit and alchemist said to have taught the Umayyad prince Khalid ibn Yazid</note> expressly writes: *Our sulfur is not common sulfur, but is fixed, and does not fly, and is of a mercurial and incombustible nature; for if you wished to say that common sulfur is the matter of metals, it would not be of a homogeneous nature, which is against all the sayings of the Philosophers.* Nor should you think that by "moisture" any other moisture is understood than that of Geber <note>Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan (c. 721–815), the "father of chemistry"</note>, concerning which he testifies: *We have tried all things and contemplated with great reason, but we have found nothing lasting in the battle [of the fire] except an oily moisture remaining permanent in the fire.* Nor should you believe that "strongly mixed subtle earthy substance" is common sifted earth; rather, it is that which, having been fanned many times, the wind carried in its womb, and which is *of the Sun and Moon, the Mother of all perfection*, as Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the mythical founder of alchemy</note> skillfully calls it. ### Chapter Five

In animals it brings life, in vegetables flowering, and in minerals the metallic nature. It is therefore the cause that preserves life, vegetation, and the process of becoming metal. Wherefore **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure to whom many foundational alchemical texts are attributed</note> rightly noted, as I mentioned above, *that it is the life of each and every thing: the grain in wheat, the oil in the olive, the gum in peach trees, the fruit in trees, the principle of human generation—because from this matter comes that living thing which does not die.* 

Next, by its "penetrating property," it should not be understood that it penetrates bodies like water soaks into paper or mercury into leather. Rather, it is a penetrating force, giving a body a power of penetration without increasing its weight—that is, an action related to reaction, as you will hear toward the end of this chapter. It is of a warm temperament, not actively but potentially; it is of the nature of fire from nature, not from artifice. In short, it is the **Philosophers' Mercury** <note>original: "mercurius Philosophorum"; not common quicksilver, but a refined, spiritual substance alchemists believed was the root of all metals</note>, *the only matter which they admire, and with which they alone occupy themselves as the kernel of things, leaving the husks to the common people.* 

They call it "Mercury" because, like the god Mercury, it changes into various shapes, and like **Proteus** <note>A shape-shifting sea god in Greek mythology</note>, it is found under various masks. I have therefore added this secondary definition so that the primary one may be more clearly understood: namely, the **Universal Being** <note>original: "ens universale"</note> *is an unctuous moisture, strongly mixed with subtle earth, preserving, penetrating, and warm-moist.* For you would have the same definition if you mixed common oil with common water and added quicklime <note>original: "calce viva"; calcium oxide, a caustic substance that reacts strongly with water</note>; for there would come forth an unctuous, moist mixture, strongly combined with subtle earth, preserving, penetrating, warm, and moist. Indeed, in truth, that Philosophical mixture is nothing other than *the oil, water, and quicklime of the Philosophers, mixed together.*

Having established this universal definition, it remains for us to demonstrate to the reader that thing which *is everywhere, yet is seen nowhere by the unwise,* specifically by showing it in certain subjects as examples. It might perhaps seem incredible that such a thing lies hidden in fire and even in the sun itself, were there not examples of this fact. It is evident through the natural process that the rays of the sun mix with vegetables and are fixed into a body, as I proved in the third part of my *Metallurgy* and in the chapter on fermentation in my *Underground Physics*. 

**Digby** <note>Sir Kenelm Digby (1603–1665), an English courtier and diplomat who was also a philosopher and experimental chemist</note> also testifies that this happens through *art* <note>meaning through human skill or experimental chemistry</note> in the first part of his treatise *On the Immortality of the Soul*, chapter 7, page 46, section 8 and following. On this occasion, there comes to mind the memory of a very rare experiment which a certain nobleman of most sincere faith—and one very closely joined to me in friendship—affirmed he had seen. Specifically, with the help of glass vessels made in a certain peculiar way and artfully arranged, the collected rays of the sun were precipitated into a powder of a brownish color, or a purple verging on red. No fraud could have been hidden in this operation, for nothing was contained in the vessels before they were arranged. It also had to be carried out in the warmer season of the year for such an effect to follow. Furthermore, by this operation, nearly two ounces could be collected in a few days. Its nature was wonderfully subtle, so that by its—so to speak—spiritual force, it could penetrate even gold itself, the heaviest and most solid of all bodies we deal with.

Indeed, that the flames of common fire mix with bodies and are reduced into a body is testified to by **Saffron of Mars** <note>original: "crocus martis"; a reddish-brown iron oxide used in alchemical preparations</note> and, among others, by **Mr. Tachenius** <note>Otto Tachenius (c. 1610–1680), a German physician and chemist known for his theory that all things are composed of acid and alkali</note> in his *Hippocrates Chymicus*. He says that the acid of flames is consumed and fixed by **iron**. I say nothing of the glowing fire of animals, fish, vegetables, and stones, which is nothing other than concentrated fire, or the **Philosophers' Moon** <note>original: "luna Philosophorum"; often referring to a refined silver or a specific stage of the alchemical process</note>. Whence **Aristotle** asserts in book 2 of *On the Generation of Animals*, chapter 3, that the seminal spirit of animals corresponds with the element of the stars. *There is*, he says, *in seeds a certain fertilizing power of the seed, or a spirit which is in...*

The aforementioned **Lord Digby** <note>Sir Kenelm Digby (1603–1665), an English courtier and natural philosopher</note> in his dissertation on the vegetation of plants, when making mention of the artificial nutrition of plants and a grain of barley so prepared that it produced 249 stalks and 18,000 grains, adds the following: *Do you truly think it is only saltpeter <note>original: "sal nitrum"; potassium nitrate, which was central to 17th-century theories of atmospheric vitality</note> which, when drawn into the seed or root, brings this fertility? In such air, which is greatly impregnated with this benign fire, we lead a healthy life; but in that which abounds with earthly exhalations and marine vapors, and contains little of the balsamic salt within itself, we lead an unhealthy life. **Cornelius Drebbel** <note>original: "Drebler"; Cornelius Drebbel (1572–1633), the Dutch inventor famous for building a navigable submarine</note>, having collected a great quantity of this salt into a certain narrow space, was able to refresh and revive his guests who were fainting in his narrow house under the water—after they had consumed all the balsam in the enclosed air in which they were shut up—by opening a certain vial which poured new spirits through that old, spoiled, and exhausted air. This spirit, therefore, which is in the air, is attracted as if by a certain magnet, through a saline liquid, etc. 

The experiments recently discovered in England by the extraction of air from various vessels correspond to this matter; among which they observed that air once breathed by a human is immediately deprived of this substance, so that it is of no value for further inhalations unless it is refilled with a new **spirit of the world** <note>original: "spiritu mundi"; the vital ether believed to permeate the cosmos</note>. ### Chapter Five

...the distillation of mud and the boiling of **red silt** <note>original: "rubri limi"; likely referring to iron-rich earth or ochre used in alchemical processes</note>, and the distillation of that boiled liquid teaches; for from there is drawn a **spirit that dissolves gold** <note>original: "spiritus aurum solvens"; a solvent like aqua regia</note>, possessing many medicinal virtues. Thus, this spirit lies hidden in all four elements. Now let us come to more **complex mixtures**, and indeed to **animals**; between whose **urine and gold** there is such a sympathy that without the former, gold is hardly dissolved. That long-lived animal, the **Deer**, carries a great abundance of this spirit in its horns, just as all animals do in their **hair** and other excrements. **Dr. Tachenius** <note>Otto Tachenius (c. 1610–1680), a German pharmacist and physician active in Venice, known for his theory that all things consist of acid and alkali</note> confessed to me in Venice that he had nourished **vipers** in glass for almost an entire year without any food, and could observe nothing else than that they live by the substance drawn from the **air**; whence also their flesh does so much to preserve a long life and to strengthen the vital spirits. It is well-known that the noble offspring of **pearls** comes forth from the union of **dew**. However, the great **restorative power** inherent in **pearls** cannot be told within the narrow limits of this paper. **Ambergris**, which the learned **Justus Fidus Klobius** <note>Author of "Ambrae Historiam" (1666)</note> testifies in his treatise on the subject to be the excrement of birds, swells so much with this noble essence that it fills the vital spirits even to the point of intoxication. Therefore, you Chief Physicians, for the sake of keeping your wealthy patrons in a long life and yourselves in an ample salary, should use no other restorative than the volatile salt of **Deer Horn** and **vipers**, dissolved in the spirits of **pearls and amber**, all made by themselves without addition, and kept for use; this noble medicine comes from the animal kingdom, and truly no nobler thing can be given for the restoration of the spirits. 

In **vegetables**, that noble **spirit of wine** is most full of this universal essence: many other highly fragrant spirits, or **volatile oils**, are the receptacles of this essence. The incorruptible **Mercury of wine**, of which **Ripley** <note>Sir George Ripley (c. 1415–1490), a famous English alchemist</note> wrote that he saw a **Red Toad** <note>A famous alchemical allegory representing the leaden or earthy matter being transformed by the "juice" of the vine</note> drink so much of the juice of grapes until its intestines burst; and it is not the juice of grapes alone that provides this, as you have perceived in our metalliferous experiment, that this mercurial essence lies hidden and is found in all oils. 

I proceed to the **mineral kingdom**, in which, according to the testimony of **Helmont** <note>Jan Baptist van Helmont (1580–1644), a pioneer of iatrochemistry who coined the term "gas"</note> on page 460, **there are Sulfurs which, once corrected, the whole cohort of diseases obeys**, inasmuch as their plurality is contracted into the unity of the **Archeus** <note>term: Archeus: In Helmontian medicine, the internal "vital programmer" or spiritual force that governs the functions of an organ or the body</note> as if into a fighting fist. In this way, combined in the very seat of the soul and the "duumvirate" <note>A Helmontian term for the stomach and spleen as the secondary seat of life</note>, we have seen **insanities, apoplexies, falling sickness <note>epilepsy</note>, paralysis, vertigo, asthma, wasting diseases, and immense defects** annihilated, while nature itself was surely amazed. I therefore urge students to learn how to strip the sulfurs of their poisonous nature, under whose guard the **vital fire** is hidden; they will lead the **archeus** most peacefully to the desired goals. 

The **substance of salts** is so full of this essence that the entire sea, being salty, has a mercurifying power and shines with the fire of the Philosophers, as you shall hear later. Experience teaches that even stones are not void of this essence, since they can be converted into alkali, which is the "steward and storekeeper" of this essence. **Metals and minerals** themselves owe their existence to this essence; for when it is present, they are metals; when it flies away, they are reduced to earth: when it is added in excessive quantity, **they become liquid and Mercury**. It is no different than if the earth of **stone** is added to metals, they are changed into glass; if the earth of **sulfur** comes upon them, they are changed into earth; for I have demonstrated enough and more in my *Subterranean Physics*, under the title "On Metallic Principles," that it is **impossible** for art, on account of the strongest mixing, to draw anything from metals that constitutes their simple principle: but whatever is granted to art in this business consists only in this, that principles be added onto metals, and...

...so metals, according to this or that principle, may be reduced by a new decomposition. This decomposition, especially of **quicksilver** <note>original: "Mercurii vivi"</note>, is denied to us by **Dr. Werner Rolfinck** <note>Guernerus Rolfincius (1599–1673), a German physician, chemist, and botanist at the University of Jena</note>, a Professor at **Jena**; in his recently published papers on the "non-existence of the Mercury of bodies." I do not know what phantoms <note>original: "larvae"; here implying delusions or misleading spirits</note> have incited this man—otherwise prudent, learned, and circumspect—to undertake the defense of this hateful subject; for which he will undoubtedly be mocked by the most skilled chemists and will disgrace himself. Although, due to the constraints of this space, it is not my purpose to refute the aforementioned papers, I cannot help but demonstrate their worthlessness to the reader in a few words. 

Every demonstration depends either on authorities, physical reasons, or experience. As for the authorities whom Dr. Rolfinck brings forward for the negative [view], we shall overcome them with a greater number of authorities who hold the affirmative. But as a representative of them all, let it be the very man to whom Dr. Rolfinck, despairing of his own followers, appealed, to whose decision he submitted himself, and whom he himself confesses in his preface to be beyond all praise and above all exception. And that is **Father Athanasius Kircher** <note>A famous Jesuit polymath (1602–1680) known for his works on magnetism and geology</note>, to whom he dedicated his papers; it is he himself, I say, who in his treatise on the physical magnetism of bodies, expressly confesses that **by salt water alone lead is turned into running Mercury, which is also true.** 

The Author's words are, in his book titled *The Magnetic Kingdom of Nature, dedicated to Alexander Fabianus, Rome, Printed by Ignatius de Lazzari, 1667,* in Latin, quarto, page 67, section 3, chapter 1, lines 15-16: **Lead, condemned to perpetual salty waters, is dissolved into quicksilver** <note>original: "hydrargyrum"</note>. What does Rolfinck say to this? Does he think Father Kircher will sing a retraction <note>original: "palinodiam canturum"; literally "sing a palinode"</note> for his sake? Not in the least, unless he wishes to be below rather than above praise. Or will he number Father Kircher—who establishes the existence of metallic Mercury—among the "Thrasonic <note>referring to Thraso, a boastful soldier in Roman comedy; meaning "braggart"</note> braggarts, show-offs, loud-mouths, and deceivers," as he calls all those who assert the Mercury of bodies (titles which we rightly hurl back at him)? What can you do here? Now that line from **Plautus** <note>Titus Maccius Plautus, Roman playwright</note> comes to mind: **Where shall I go or not go? What shall I say or not say?** See to what place you have appealed, you wretch; to a forum in which your cause was condemned before it was even proposed. You must have read very little of Kircher’s writings, since you did not notice these things, lest you stumble so badly. 

We shall now conclude: either the **Mercury of Saturn** <note>original: "Mercurius Saturni"; an alchemical term for mercury extracted from lead</note>, according to Father Kircher, is a true entity, or according to Rolfinck, a false entity. If the former, Rolfinck’s cause is condemned; if the latter, I do not see how Rolfinck can separate Kircher from the deceivers among whose number he has assigned him. But let these two see how they may agree with one another. With similar misfortune he cites **Tachenius**, forgetting that this author on page 48 and following of his *Chemical Hippocrates* establishes the entity of the **Mercury of the Moon** <note>original: "Mercurii lunae"; mercury extracted from silver</note>, and on page 229 sets down the signs and differences of metallic Mercury compared with the common sort. 

I now come to the second kind of demonstration, namely physical reasons, of which I find not even one in Rolfinck’s papers that proves the non-existence of the Mercury of bodies, or demonstrates that it is impossible for metals to become liquid through a Mercurial flow. # Chapter Five

...the distinction of virgin mercury from the common kind is that **gold** amalgamated with **Virgin Mercury** and exposed to fire causes the Mercury to be entirely removed, something common mercury cannot achieve. We thus see **quicksilver** <note>original: "Argentum vivum"</note> produced by nature; if it were not, one might rightly doubt the existence of such a marvelous subject and of the "water that does not wet the hands" <note>A classic alchemical riddle for mercury, which is liquid like water but does not soak into surfaces</note>. **Secondly**, we see that metals have such a sympathy with this Mercury that they join with it, take on a "running nature" <note>meaning they become fluid or liquid</note>, and finally pass through leather and fire together with the Mercury, keeping their bond in every necessity. **Thirdly**, we see metals brought into this mercurial flux of their own accord; therefore, there is no doubt that if an external fire acts to liquefy metallic bodies, an internal fire will act much more strongly to liquefy them. For so says **Paracelsus** of it: *My spirit (of Mercury) is hot, having the power to soften all the frozen members of my brothers.* **Fourthly**, we see that metals can be softened with little effort and reduced to a flux of **wax and metallic leaves**; if this is possible, why should we not conclude they can be softened entirely? **Dr. Rolfinck** himself, on page 8, asserts that this argument shines with its own light; yet, having conceded the premises, he denies the conclusion on page 16 against all reason, as if always forgetting himself. **There are therefore four very firm physical reasons for the existence and possibility of the Mercury of bodies**, against which Rolfinck cannot bring even one—namely, one that would prove it impossible for metals to be reduced to the fluidity of Mercury.

The third type of demonstration is **Experience**, of which **Rolfinck** brings some examples that are false and unsuccessful; I, however, shall bring him just as many that are successful. *What other* does he desire? Than that which is proposed by **Father Kircher** <note>Athanasius Kircher</note> in the place cited, whose **long** natural maceration <note>The process of softening or breaking down a substance by soaking it in liquid</note> of lead in salty waters I shorten by art in the space of a few hours with common salt. *What other?* Than that which is cited in **Dr. Tachenius’s** *Hippocrates Chymicus*, page 40. *What other, finally?* Than that which is communicated by **Beguin**. **Claveus**, speaking in his *Apologia* about certain experiments by which metallic Mercury can be fixed <note>To "fix" a substance in alchemy means to turn a volatile or liquid substance into a solid that can withstand fire</note> into nobler metals, adds that he spoke of **quicksilver drawn out of metals**; he argues that the common variety, because of its excessive coldness and moisture, is too resistant to "concoction" <note>The alchemical process of "ripening" or purifying a substance through heat</note>. For this operation, although he previously prescribed the **Mercuries of metallic bodies** in general, he especially commends Mercury extracted by art from silver. And elsewhere in the same book, he tells us that he himself experienced that, by simple cooking, **quicksilver drawn out of tin** could, by a certain efficient cause (as he calls it), be changed into **pure gold**. And the most experienced **Alexander von Suchten** tells us somewhere that in a certain way, which he hints at, **Mercury can be made from copper**—not one that is silvery in color like other Mercuries, but **green**. To this I shall add (says **Robert Boyle**, who notes these things in his *Sceptical Chymist*, pages 173 and 174) that an illustrious man, whose travels and learned writings have brought him fame (I suspect it is **Digby** <note>Sir Kenelm Digby (1603–1665), an English courtier, diplomat, and natural philosopher</note>), recently assured me that he had several times seen the **Mercury of lead** (which, regardless of what **authors** may promise, you will find very difficult to prepare, at least in any notable quantity) fixed into **perfect gold**; and when I asked him if any...

### Supplement to Subterranean Physics

...another Mercury underwent a similar change by the aid of the same operations, he maintained a negative result; thus far **Mr. Boyle** <note>Robert Boyle (1627–1691), a founding figure of modern chemistry who, despite his skepticism, remained deeply interested in alchemical transmutations</note>. I know that three years ago, in a very splendid city very close to Germany, "chemical gold" prepared from metallic Mercury was sold in a minting office or exchanged for 30,000 pistolettes <note>A gold coin used in various European countries</note>. When I asked his laborer or assistant <note>original: "Amanuensem"</note> what kind of Mercury it was, he replied: *of Antimony*. At the same time, he showed the vessels and a large apparatus for making such Mercury. We have the method of preparation in the ***Digbean Experiments*** <note>Referring to the works of Sir Kenelm Digby, a 17th-century philosopher and alchemist</note> on page 146; but so far I have only been able to extract a few grains in that way, which nevertheless were coagulated into ***gold*** within a few days.

**Glauber** <note>Johann Rudolf Glauber (1604–1670), a famous German-Dutch alchemist and apothecary</note>, in the fourth part of his *Spagyric Pharmacopoeia*, in the octavo edition, tells me on pages 44, 45, and 46 that he could never prepare the **Mercury of bodies** from so many thousands of processes, and thus always believed that whenever "metallic Mercury" was mentioned by the Philosophers, it should be understood metaphorically <note>original: "tropice"</note>; until he worked for a great Lord (*I believe it was the **Prince of Zulickoven***) to whom "Mercury of Saturn" <note>Mercury extracted from lead</note> was recommended by another Lord. Along with it, a sample <note>original: "signum"</note> of an ounce of said Mercury was sent, together with the method of fixation; when they took a proof of it, it was changed into the best gold. 

But that other Lord who had given the Mercury died; and **Glauber** with his own Lord could not prepare the same, even after exhausting two years of labor. Then Glauber's Lord also died; but **Glauber** always remained in hope of obtaining the **Mercury of Saturn**; which he finally confesses to have attained long afterward. He states that he communicated it to others on a small scale, who themselves confessed and openly attested to the truth of it. He sets down the process for small quantities in his treatise ***On the Three Principles***, under the title of ***Mercury***, on page 54 and following. I have tested some of these, but as I said, they only succeed on a small scale. **Rolfinck** would easily find the reasons why they do not succeed on a large scale, if the truth of natural things were closer to his heart than that desired **common gold-making** <note>original: "Plebeja aureitas"; literally "plebeian goldness," referring to the greedy pursuit of wealth rather than philosophical truth</note>. 

Furthermore, I know what the matter is: **Dr. Rolfinck** denies these experiences, and rightly so in a way, for they are not so arranged that they work themselves out spontaneously; for such results are what **Dr. Rolfinck** desires. Let him set his hands to the work, and he will see that these are not loose brooms, but joined ones that make up the rod with which those petulant **Chemistry-haters** <note>original: "Misochymici"</note> and resisters of truth are to be punished. 

**Dr. Rolfinck** observes a method plainly contrary to the laws of philosophy; for by censuring chemists, he wants to force them to teach the very method of preparing the ***mercuries of bodies***; whereas otherwise, this ought to be explored with prayers, studies, labors, and much expense, nor should it be revealed to anyone unless it be manifested to him by God. It is not that chemists, fearing censure, are unwilling to communicate this manual operation <note>original: "Enchirisin"</note> indiscriminately; but because all laws command us to hide the art. Hence **Mercurification** <note>The process of reducing a solid metal back into its essential liquid mercury</note>, as the key of the art, is to be hidden in every way, lest we incur the horrendous curse and excommunication of all the Philosophers. 

For it cannot be said how great a power—both ***medical*** and ***metallic***—the ***mercuries of perfected bodies*** possess. Common mercury, with its poisonous acids and its antimonial and arsenical earth (which is evident in its precipitation by itself), dissolves the whole human body; even in a very small quantity, it constricts the vital balsam, liquefies the entire fabric of the human body, and drives it into confusion. Conversely, the ***fixed Mercury of bodies*** does the opposite.

For indeed, taken internally in a small quantity, the "wandering acid," as Dr. Tachenius <note>Otto Tachenius (c. 1610–1699), a German pharmacist and physician known for his theory that all things consist of "acid and alkali"</note> says, absorbs it; it gently stills and brings to rest all the errors, furies, dissolutions, and liquefactions of the human body. To communicate this to you, Rolfinck <note>Werner Rolfinck (1599–1673), a German physician and chemist who was skeptical of many alchemical claims</note>, who despises it—and indeed to publish it for your benefit—would be a sacrilege <note>original: "piaculum"</note>. For as Helmont <note>Jan Baptist van Helmont (1580–1644), a Flemish pioneer of chemistry</note> says in his work *On Lithiasis* <note>A treatise on the "disease of the stone" or kidney stones</note>, chapter 3, section 5: "just as no sulfur is a metal, so every metallic Mercury is a true metal"; consequently, it cannot be changed into an arsenical, sulfurous, powdery, or heterogeneous precipitate. Gaston de Clave <note>Gaston "Claveus" Dulco, a 16th-century defender of alchemy</note> agrees with this in his *Apology against Erastus* <note>Thomas Erastus, a Swiss physician who famously attacked the theories of Paracelsus</note> on page 46 and following:

> *Nor indeed should it be thought that the "living silver" <note>original: "argentum vivum" (mercury)</note> which possesses the power of dissolving gold is that common variety which is sold openly by pharmacists or merchants; for since it must perform the dissolution of gold by means of a body that reflects gold in the likeness of its whole substance, and is of a hot and moist temperament: it cannot be denied that common living silver possesses that likeness, but it is certain that its temperament is extremely cold and most indefinite. But from elsewhere, by an ingenious art, we must draw out and lead forth a living silver from a body born to very few, which nature has cooked, which reflects gold in the likeness of its whole substance even more than common living silver does, and which—by no art, but by the first contact and friction—combines and mixes with gold no less than water mixes with water.*

Now contemplate more deeply what that body might be. On the occasion of this saying, I recall an experiment that I recently performed in Munich, in the presence of my friend Gerhard Gorifius of Rotterdam. I had a singular type of living Mercury, which I wished to amalgamate <note>To blend mercury with another metal, in this case gold</note> with gold in a glass dish. Upon the first contact with the gold, the Mercury became so hot and effervesced so much that there was a danger the glass dish might shatter; indeed, I had to move the hand with which I was holding it because of the heat. Furthermore, from this remarkable reaction arose a powerful scent of nutmeg, perfectly resembling its fragrance; it filled the entire heated room <note>original: "hypocaustum"</note> so much that we were all nearly intoxicated by the most penetrating vapor. At first I was afraid, remembering the story of Dr. Tachenius in his *Hippocrates* on page 213, where he recounts that he received a most sweet fragrance from arsenic but afterwards felt very ill; however, no harm followed from this Mercurial vapor, except that I was immediately relieved of a heavy head <note>original: "gravedine capitis" (meaning a headache or sinus congestion)</note> from which I was then suffering. Then I recalled the saying of Helmont regarding the reaction of Mercury in water that kills worms, where he says: "let the schools learn, even against their will, that certain agents act freely and with untiring strength without any suffering or reaction of the patients, and always maintaining their same weight." I observed this in this amalgam, which kept its weight, even though such a great abundance of spirits was emitted that I had presupposed the whole thing would have evaporated. ### Page 318

...precipitations, many claim that the "Philosophical Mercury" <note>A legendary alchemical substance, the "soul" of mercury, believed to be the key to transmutation</note> has been made; but they err, because they do not work within nature, which alone is refined within its own nature. Therefore, let them know that **our water** is composed of many things, yet it is a single thing made from diverse substances of one essence, grown together. Indeed, in our water, three things are required: first, fire; second, the "vegetable Saturnine liquor" <note>original: "liquor Saturniæ vegetabilis"; likely a reference to a solvent derived from lead or lead-acetate, often called "Sugar of Saturn"</note>; third, the bond of Mercury. 

The fire is of mineral sulfur, yet it is not strictly mineral, let alone metallic; rather, it is something intermediate between mineral and metal—neither one nor the other, but participating in both. It is a **chaos** or a spirit. For our **Fiery Dragon** <note>A common alchemical symbol for a volatile or corrosive substance</note>, which conquers all things, is nevertheless penetrated by the scent of the vegetable Saturnine liquor; its blood grows together with the juice of that Saturnine substance into one wonderful body. And yet, it is not a body, because it is entirely volatile; nor is it a spirit, because in fire it resembles a melted metal. It is, therefore, truly a **chaos**, which relates to all metals as a **Mother**; for from it I have learned to extract all things, even Gold <note>original: "Solem," literally "the Sun"</note> and Silver <note>original: "Lunam," literally "the Moon"</note>, without a transmuting elixir. He who has likewise seen this can attest to it. As the previously cited Anaxagoras of Clazomenae <note>A Pre-Socratic Greek philosopher</note> said:

> *Our Sun is red and burning; it is joined to a white soul and the nature of the moon by a middle spirit, although the whole thing is surely nothing other than the Mercury of the Philosophers.*

I do not say that much of this essence does not lie hidden in common mercury; but I admit it is very difficult to separate from it, due to the tenacity of the mixture. There are also those who, even if they see metallic mercury as living and true, pronounce it "sophistic" <note>meaning "fake" or "deceptive"</note>; but I have sufficiently refuted these people in my *Underground Physics* <note>original: "Physica subterranea"</note>, page 209 and following. 

Likewise, those people err who state that mercury produced from metals is a certain "principle" or part of the metal, as Helmont <note>Jan Baptist van Helmont (1580–1644), a Flemish chemist and physician</note> seems to do when he says in his treatise *On the Power of Medicines*, section 40:

> *I perceived that the crudity of Lead <note>original: "Saturni"</note> is soluble by the fatness of fixed salts, and thus the parts of the compound are divided, so that it permits the quicksilver <note>original: "argentum vivum"</note> to run.*

But I refuted this in Book 1, Section 3, Chapter 1 of my *Underground Physics*. Certainly, "running mercury"—whether common or made from metal—is not the "principle" <note>In alchemy, a "principle" is a fundamental building block of matter</note> of any metal. Rather, its *ens* <note>essence or being</note>, or that which makes metals "run" and gives them their "metallicity," is the true principle of all metals. Therefore, nothing in Lead is "crude" with respect to Mercury, since every metal and mineral is Mercury in its entire quantity; and if it were so made, a good metal could be made from it. It is no different than how a whole pound of copper is resolved into vitriol <note>A sulfate salt</note> by decomposition; which vitriol, when reduced, reveals an altered copper. See Geber’s and Claveus’s *Mercury of Jupiter* <note>Mercury derived from tin; Geber was a legendary 8th-century alchemist, and Gaston de Clave was a 17th-century French chemist</note>. 

In the process of "mercurification," there is no separation of parts, but rather an addition for the sake of decomposition. Just as the spirit of sulfur makes vitriol out of any metal—though that vitriol has different medicinal qualities depending on the variety of the metal—so the "Mercury of bodies" has different metallic qualities depending on the variety of its subject, as experience teaches. For **common Mercury**, and the **Mercury of Gold**, and the **Essence of Mercury** (or the decomposer of Mercury) are as different as Sun and Earth, medicine and poison, or sugar and acacia juice. One is changed by digestion into something *better*, the other into something *worse*; one into a medicine, the other into a poison; one degenerates into a golden *nepenthe* <note>A mythical medicine for chasing away sorrow</note>, the other into the cause of a lethal *hypercatharsis* <note>An excessive, violent purging of the bowels</note>, such as Hesling’s *Azoth* <note>A reference to a specific alchemical preparation by a chemist named Hesling</note> and similar things. 

But now, lest I be carried away by the wind of curiosity into the vast ocean of questions and experiments from the harbor of brief conciseness, I see—God is my witness—that I must pull in my sails, however unwillingly. I have already spoken as many things as words.

->### Chapter Five.<-

...as practitioners will observe; for in the second part of this chapter, I have so demonstrated the universal existence of the **philosophical essence** in all elements and all compounds or mixtures, that one would have to be a dullard not to understand these things. But I see that the reader desires the conclusion of this second part, namely the *preparation, acquisition, and treatment* of this essence; and although this has been sufficiently handed down and taught in the preceding sections, I will nevertheless explain it candidly and as far as is permitted in a few words for the beginners.

*Morienes* <note>Morienus, a legendary 7th-century alchemist and hermit, supposedly the teacher of the Umayyad prince Khalid ibn Yazid</note> says, *“Take this, which is trampled in its own dung; if you attempt to ascend without a ladder, you will fall on your head—that is, separate the essence, as much as possible, from the husks,”* understand by what reasoning this is done: First, *mortify and destroy any external form of whatever body; then reduce it to the form of universality, which is saline; from this salt, fish out the Philosophical Remora* <note>original: "Echeneidem"; refers to the remora or "ship-holder" fish, an alchemical metaphor for a substance that "stops" or fixes the volatile spirit</note>; *or: make from the bodies a volatile and fixed alkali, and you have the Philosophical Sea, in which is the horizontal line. Alternatively: take from any body, or from several bodies, a urinous, nitrous, acidic, saline, and sulfurous salt; when these five are joined, the philosophical chaos, or solvent, will arise, in which the magnetic metallic lime* <note>original: "calx"; the powdery residue left after heating a metal, now known as an oxide</note> *will easily attract the fifth essence, and it will become Mercury; from which you shall demand a tribute, and so that it may redeem its life, it will bless you with the liquor of pearls.* I have proved all these things not only many times through practice, but also theoretically with firm reasons throughout this entire discourse; nor do I lack the authority of the philosophers regarding this manual practice. Hear what that most ancient and equally learned French philosopher, *Gratianus*, contributes to our preceding practice (as cited by the *Rosary* <note>original: "Rosario"; likely the "Rosarium Philosophorum," a famous 16th-century alchemical compendium</note>), writing openly and proving the universal existence of the Mercurial being in the following words: *“From every thing, ash can be made; and from 그 ash, salt can be made; and from that salt, water is made; and from 그 water, Mercury is made; and from that Mercury, through various operations, the Sun* <note>Gold</note> *is made.”* For the things of nature, as we noted above from *Rhazes* <note>original: "Rhasi"; a 9th-century Persian polymath and alchemist</note>, are so bound together by a subtle artifice that in any thing, every other thing is present in potential, even if it is not seen in actuality. And *Albertus* <note>Albertus Magnus, a 13th-century Dominican friar and scholar</note> expressly confesses that, *“No compound thing is given in whose ultimate substance gold is not found;”* how much more so *Mercury*, seeing as gold cannot be made without it. *Van Helmont* says much in few words when he states, *“Sharp calcined things, when resolved with salt ammoniac and putrefied tartar, are sweetened, or rather, are turned into a Mercury that is not acidic and corrosive as common mercury is.”* The spirit of this Mercury is called the *star* and the *immature electrum*; and it is this of which we have treated until now. And we have explained it so clearly that we believe no mortal has ever done so before; nor could I write more clearly, unless it were my intention to cast pearls before swine—which may God forbid.

...I shall satisfy in this chapter. Let them know, therefore, that it is twofold: one for medicine, the other for the metallic, transmutatory art. As far as medicine is concerned, all the Philosophers testify that this entity is of such a nature that it preserves the human body in long-lasting health and cures any diseases whatsoever; furthermore, it also transmutates all metals into the most perfect gold. Both of these effects have always been most fiercely disputed and denied by the enemies of **Chemistry**; but in this place, we shall bring forward physical, true, and new reasons by which the truth of this twofold effect will be made most clearly evident to all who are powerful in reason and willing to use it. For we shall put forward nothing without natural causes, wherefore **St. Thomas** <note>Referring to a popular alchemical text falsely attributed to Thomas Aquinas, likely the 'Aurora Consurgens' or 'De Esse et Essentia Mineralium'</note> wrote to Brother **Reinaldus**: *do not care about the words of modern and ancient philosophers who differ concerning this science, since Alchemy has established its seat in the capacity of the intellect and in experimental demonstration.* 

The first difficulty regarding the existence of a **Panacea, or universal medicine**, arises from the fact that for different diseases, **different and often contrary** remedies must be sought; for some, dissolving agents are prescribed, for others, astringents; for some, hot remedies, and for others, cold. These diverse qualities cannot exist in one medicinal subject at the same time. And this is the opinion of the **pluralists, humorists, Galenists** <note>Followers of Galen, whose medical system relied on balancing the four humors: blood, phlegm, black bile, and yellow bile</note>, and the common **schools**, who believe this objection to be more tangled and unsolvable than any Gordian knot. But you will later see how they are deceived, if you hear a few preliminary things about the "factory" of man. 

For since it pleased Almighty God to produce an **animal mixture**, and specifically a human one, He did so according to the order He observed in all His creatures. As a foundation, He placed the **bones**; but because these could not move of their own accord, He added **nerves** to them, which had need of **movement and nourishment**. They needed movement so that the subtle spirit might penetrate and move them; and nourishment, lest they be dried out, contracted, or worn away by daily movement. Hence, He placed **muscles** beneath them and instilled **veins** into the muscles, so that they might be continuously moistened and nourished by blood. 

Lest this bloody fluid fail, there was a need for daily **drink and food**, and its transmutation and circulation into blood and spirits. Hence the necessity of the **intestines, stomach, liver, heart, and brain**. However, so that there would be something to alter and digest the daily nourishment into blood and spirit, the **Vital Fire** <note>original: "Ignis vitalis"; the innate heat believed by pre-modern scientists to drive metabolism</note> was instilled into man. By its help, food and drink are digested into blood, and blood into nervous, spermatic, and spiritual fluid. The vital fire itself, however, requires the perpetual refreshment of air, which is the workshop of the **lungs**. 

From this, it is obvious to anyone that the principal business of the human factory, and the observation of it, consists in the digestion or alteration of food into blood and spirits; for according to the **goodness or vice** of this alteration, humors are generated in the body, either upright or corrupt. Thus, that which is nourished by them must be either **healthy** or **diseased**. It is as certain and clear that the cause of this alteration flows solely from the **vital spirit** as it is that the **sun** alters and directs everything in the **macrocosm** <note>The universe or the world at large, as opposed to the "microcosm" of the human body</note>. And the **Galenists** err because they invent various different causes for these digestions, such as a chyle-making, blood-making, seed-making, or spirit-making **faculty** <note>original Greek: "ποιητικὴν" (poietiken), meaning 'creative' or 'productive' power</note>, as well as retentive, expulsive, and distributive faculties. These are trifles and metaphysical concepts; it is as if you were to say there is a "coal-ash-soot-making" faculty...

...and makes these various powers by reason of their origin; for it is certain that they all come from fire. In the same way, there is but one Sun that nourishes all things; it creates the root in the root, the stalk in the stalk, and the flowers in the flowers. Thus also in the human body—and in any animal—there is a fire or **vital spirit**, which digests food in the stomach and intestines, transforms it into blood in the liver, heart, and veins, and changes that blood in the brain, nerves, and reproductive vessels into a white, nervous, and spirited liquor. That spirit alone is the source and cause of digestion, excretion, retention, and the transformation of <term>Chyle</term> <note>The milky fluid produced during digestion</note> and <term>Chyme</term> <note>The pulpy acidic fluid passing from the stomach to the small intestine</note> into blood. 

Even **Sennert** <note>Daniel Sennert (1572–1637), a prominent physician who attempted to bridge the gap between traditional Galenic medicine and the new Alchemical or "Chymical" theories</note>, who was a friend to the **Chemists** only in their final struggles, is nevertheless compelled to confess the following regarding this universal spirit in Chapter 11 of his book *On the Agreement and Disagreement of the Chemists*:

*Actions said to come from the whole substance, as well as occult properties, are attributed to this spirit as its proper subject; it is the poisonous element in poisons, and the purging element in purgatives. For just as a kitchen fire cooks different meats and ripens or digests vegetables in a single pot, each according to its own quality, so in the entire human body this vital fire preserves all members and performs all digestions, each according to the requirements of the container and its contents.* 

And if it fails in one of these, an error in nature is immediately noticed. This is what we complain of in the plague: that this vital fire is so weakened that it can neither digest the poison nor drive it out. From this arise internal <term>apostemes</term> <note>deep-seated abscesses or swellings</note> and ulcers of the internal organs; from this comes the rawness of the blood, and from here so many diseases: <term>catarrh</term> <note>excessive mucus</note> in the brain, serum in the blood—sometimes bitter, sometimes too watery—and in the stomach and intestines, **Bradypepsia** <note>abnormally slow digestion</note>. As **Caspar Barlaeus** <note>A Dutch polymath and poet</note> learnedly expressed in his dedication to **Master Adrian Toll** <note>A professor of medicine at Leiden</note> regarding the *Golden Practice* of **Stocker**:

> *Whoever fixes your gaze upon the human body,*
> *Learn from that body how to die, even while you are yet healthy.*
> *We live; and we wretches are tortured by life itself,*
> *And pain kills us in more ways than one.*
> *Now the head is afflicted, now the ear rings sharply,*
> *Now cataracts press upon the eyes, now a lump constricts the throat.*
> *This man groans, that one coughs heavily from deep in his chest,*
> *That sick man carries about rotting waters within him.*
> *The tongue stammers for some, while for others their footsteps falter,*
> *This one is stiff with cold, this one burns with flames, that one trembles.*
> *Now nature labors broken from without, now from within,*
> *And every part of the master’s body is an enemy to its lord.*
> *We drag along a sluggish body, yet one so vulnerable to many diseases,*
> *And a different terror possesses every single limb.*
<note>Original Latin: "Quisquis in humano defigis corpore vultum / Sospes ab humano corpore disce mori... Corpus iners trahimus, sed tot cruciabile morbis, / Membraque diversus singula terror habet."</note>

But these diverse "Torturers" are rather the effects of one single torturer, who, when provoked, begins to rage through the entire body; not unlike a fire that, when agitated beyond measure, begins to act more strongly upon its flammable subject and consumes it more quickly. The logic is exactly the same with this vital fire; for it varies according to the nature of its fuel or nourishment. If you suffocate it, it is suppressed—as we see in **apoplexy**, strangulation, **Plethora** <note>an excess of blood</note>, **Pleurisy**, and other conditions. If you agitate it too much, it consumes itself—as in a hectic fever, <term>causone</term> <note>a violent, burning fever</note>, and other inflammations. If the nourishment is too easily thinned, thin, subtle, or oily, it will quickly be thinned, and...

Therefore, the quality of the **air** matters much—indeed, very much—for preserving this fire; since it can be revived or extinguished instantly by the mere smell of good or bad things, as I have often seen. The **wick** <note>original: *ellychnium*; the author uses the metaphor of a lamp where the blood's spirits act as the wick that draws up the fuel.</note> of this most subtle fire consists of the **spirits** of the blood; it is not at all fitting for these to be filled with gloomy, melancholic, or pestilential, contagious atoms, or by the various flare-ups of the passions of the mind; for according to its purity, the flame will also burn, just as when a common wick is changed, the flames can also be altered. The nourishment of this fire is the daily diet; what sort and how much it should be, the method of **diet** teaches, so much so that it would be superfluous and contrary to my intention to set it down here—for I promised the reader a supplement, not a medical textbook. Now, to pull in my sails and prove that a **universal medicine** can be granted, I say that two things must be considered regarding the human body: one which is the alterable, digestible nourishment; the other which is the **altering, digesting, and acting force.** The first is considered in the six, as they are called, **non-naturals** <note>In Galenic medicine, the "six non-naturals" were external factors that influenced health: air, food/drink, sleep/wake, motion/rest, excretion/retention, and passions of the soul.</note>; and in this, I admit the **dietary** method is very powerful, provided you correctly observe the quality and quantity of the thing to be altered. But this is not "curing" the body; it is merely preparing it so that it is curable. For unless you consider the second factor—that is, that universal **altering, digesting, and conserving force**—and look toward the vital fire, all your nutrition and medicine will be useless. On this point, Arnoldus <note>Arnaldus de Villa Nova (c. 1240–1311), a famous physician and alchemist.</note> says it best:

> *Certain ancient physicians did this: their sole intention was to invigorate nature, which, once relieved and invigorated, completes all things as is fitting.* <note>original: "Hoc egerunt quidam Veteres Medici eorum unica intentio fuit, vigorare naturam, quæ alleviata & vigorata, perficit omnia, ut expedit."</note>

For what use is medicine or food to a **dead man**, seeing as he is unalterable due to a lack of vital fire? Why do frequent sexual intercourse and bloodletting weaken the stomach and other internal organs? Because in these acts, much of the vital fire is lost. Why does medicine work quickly in some people and more slowly in others? Why do some people gain an excellent constitution from faulty and raw nourishment, while others gain the worst nourishment from the best food? Why are some wounded people healed and strengthened quickly, and others slowly? Why, I ask? Except that the vital fire is strong in some and weak in others. Do not look so much at the subject as at the object, and strengthen this vital fire, and reduce it from the plurality of your faculties, powers, and digestions into a unity, as Lullius <note>Ramon Llull (c. 1232–1315), a philosopher and polymath to whom many alchemical works were later attributed.</note> fatherly advises in the theory of his *Testament*, chapter 32 and following:

> *Blessed be the glorious, almighty God, who gave the human intellect the power to join and integrate the confused particulars of all medicine with a real universality, through which things will remain entirely rectified. And therefore, son, we advise you, if you desire to be a perfect physician, do not place your satisfaction in the particulars of medicine, because they are confused and not whole: for nature cannot endure them because of too much confusion. Instead, take pleasure in a single medicine, because there is only one that heals all malice, depravity, and infirmity, and strengthens the spiritual virtues.* <note>original: "Benedictus sit Deus gloriosus omnipotens, qui humano generi dedit intellectum..."</note>

And a little later:

> *He who knows how to reduce many and various particulars to universality will be better than others; for the virtues are found in the particulars...* <note>original: "qui multas & plures particularitates, sciet ad universalitatem reducere, inter alios erit melior ; in particularitatibus sunt virtutes"</note>

...confused, and in their universality, they are real virtues gathered and excited into one, as the course of all nature reveals. It is the medicine of medicines; he who possesses it has a gift from God, for it is an incomparable treasure—so much he [the previous author] said. 

You will admit, then, that when the **vital fire** is strengthened and kept safe, everything in the entire **human economy** <note>The author uses "economy" to describe the organized system of the body's functions and resources.</note> will be peaceful and secure; but if that fire is driven into a fury, everything rages. If it is strengthened, all digestions are well completed, pure humors are generated, obstructions are opened, and all members perform their duty. However, if it is altered or extinguished, what else is necessary and consequent but disease and death? 

For this vital spirit is diffused through the whole body—a center without a circumference, a fire without a hearth—though it is believable that the heart is the hearth of this fire, where it is first lit and where it remains until the very end. Since you are forced to admit that there is a single thing in the human body that acts upon all nourishment, humors, and medicines; and by this one thing all digestions, alterations, and transmutations that occur in the natural course of the human body are completed: by that same necessity, you must admit that a certain medicine can be given by which this vital fire may be purified, preserved, and strengthened. Once it is purified, preserved, and strengthened, all its actions in the human body must necessarily proceed correctly. 

It is necessary that this medicine be compatible with this spirit, or vital fire; otherwise, it would be a poison. For whatever opposes this fire is poison; whatever is like it is medicine. You see how a tiny dose of poison can agitate and finally extinguish this vital fire; why, then, do you doubt that even a small dose can revive and rekindle it even in the very extremities of life? If a few grains of "precipitated Mercury" <note>A chemical compound, likely mercuric oxide, used in early medicine</note> can dissolve the whole of nature into a salivation, why should the opposite of this precipitate not produce the opposite effect—restraining what is dissolved and reconciling what is wandering? 

I would have this understood regarding all poisons and their opposites. For nature has not fallen so far, as **Basil Valentine, the Benedictine Monk** writes, 

> Nature has not fallen so far, nor is she so cursed by God, that only evils must necessarily happen to her; rather, God has granted her solace and a remedy for every affliction of both soul and body.

I have said that such a medicine must be as similar to this fire as possible: namely, in its substance it should be airy, fiery, clear, spiritual, and penetrating. By its penetrating quality, this spirit opens all obstructions, flows into the nerves and limbs, and digests what must be digested; for all digestion and alteration occurs through penetration. Hence **the Philosopher** <note>Standard reference to Aristotle</note> requires alteration before mixing, and penetration before alteration. 

It must also be of a most equal temperament so that it resists putrefaction and corruption. In short, it should be an **innate, unctuous heat** <term>unctuosum calidum innatum: a term in alchemy and early medicine referring to the body's natural fuel or "oil"</term> by which the vital fire is preserved, and a **permanent, radical moisture** <note>original: *humidum radicale*; the vital fluid thought to sustain life, like oil in a lamp</note> so that it is not consumed by this fire. And this unctuous moisture is incorporated into a subtle earthiness, so that material may act upon material; since according to the **Galenists** <note>Followers of the ancient physician Galen, who focused on the balance of humors</note>, man is neither composed of nor preserved by metaphysical qualities, much less cured by them.

> And it should be known, he says, that the renewal and strengthening of the skin is achieved specifically with a drink of **the purest water of gold**: for it cures Hair Loss <note>original: *Alopecia*</note> and Tyria <note>A skin disease or form of leprosy mentioned in medieval texts</note>, and it transforms the human body, purifying and renewing...
