it is itself, and the power of many things approaches this operation, but it is this very thing which performs the aforementioned miracle. It is a substance that is not corrupted and is perfectly suited to the human **complexion** <note>In pre-modern medicine, "complexion" refers to the specific balance of the four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) within an individual.</note>. It neither heats nor cools, nor does it moisten or dry; rather, it is tempered by every temperament and exceeds every other thing in the balance and longevity it possesses. It also aids a cold stomach, makes the fearful bold, and comforts those with heart ailments. In its preparation lies the entire secret, which the wise have hidden out of envy.

*It strengthens and purifies the substance of the heart, and by the impression of its own purity, it casts out all impurity from it. Thus far, Arnald <note original: "Arnoldus">Arnald of Villanova (c. 1240–1311), a celebrated physician and alchemist whose works often bridge the gap between medicine and alchemy.</note>. However, the method of using this medicine is far different from what the common crowd of physicians believes. It can indeed *be taken at any time, for any condition, both as a cure and as a preventative, and at any age; it will always comfort the fire of nature—but only if you remove the obstacles to it, take away what is superfluous, and add what is necessary.* For the fire is that which nourishes, digests, and alters; it is not the thing which must be nourished, digested, or altered. Therefore, combine the subject with the object, and you will see that the Philosophers wrote the truth: namely, that there is *one great universal digestive.* 

So too, the common folk believe that this medicine alters metals without previous incorporation, or without the purging and preparation of the metals; but you shall hear later how they are deceived. Now I know everyone is ready and, according to that line of **Virgil** <note>The author quotes Aeneid 2.1: "Intentique ora tenebant," describing the rapt attention of an audience.</note>, *holds their faces intent* to hear how this medicine is prepared. But since I have placed its preparation in the preceding chapter, I did not wish to repeat it here. It is opposed to the **plague** <note>original: "pesti"</note>, a matter contrary to human nature in the **fourth way** <note>A scholastic classification of how things oppose one another; here meaning a total or essential opposition.</note>. Therefore, you will easily gather that this medicine is composed of its contrary—namely, a matter that is a friend to and similar to human nature in this same fourth way. 

The plague consists of corrupt aerial atoms, driven out of their proper temperament, extremely rare <note>In the sense of "thin" or "subtle," like a gas.</note>, which agitate and extinguish the vital spirits. The material of this medicine likewise consists of aerial atoms, but they are tempered and incorruptible, digested to the highest degree. Thus, whatever wanders furiously in error within the human body, this medicine moderately restrains and tempers. It is the closest possible food for the vital spirit, preserving it just as a flame of sulfur preserves wine. 

But, lest I become tedious to the reader with a longer description and exceed the limits of this compendium, I will end here concerning the *universal* medical power of our **Entity** <note original: "Entis">The "Ens," or the essential substance/being of the alchemical medicine.</note> in the human body. Let the **Galenists** <note>Followers of Galenic medicine who focused on balancing humors through herbs, often opposed by "chemical" physicians.</note> know from this that there are many and diverse bodies suitable for *nutrition and digestion* in the human body; there are also many medicines acting on the quantity and quality of nourishment. *However, there is only one universal digestive, one vital fire, and one preservative medicine given, without which all food and medicine tends toward vanity.* Now to the other part of this...

# Chapter Six. 325

I am moving forward to this part of the chapter; I will defend metallic transmutation, which occurs through this universal entity. For regarding that which happens through *reduction into principles by the first mixture*, I have already spoken sufficiently above regarding my *iron-bearing* experiment; I added such demonstrations that no prudent person could deny or disprove. But that some transmutation happens in an instant, by the mere projection of a very small amount of powder, is hard for many to believe and seems impossible to those who deny such a metallic panacea, just as they deny the medical one. But they will be convinced in the same way as before. However, two things occur that must be observed regarding this transmutation: first, the substance of the *tincture*, and then its *method* of acting or transmuting. You will hear of the substance later; but as a preliminary, I say that it is on one hand of a mercurial and sulfurous nature—most pure, most fixed, and astringent, that is, of a *fixing quality*. This is not unlike common clay <note>original: "limus"</note>, which, when joined to *mercury, arsenic, or cinnabar, or even volatile oils, fixes a part of them, or even eventually the whole. Even the "earth of vitriol" <note>The solid residue left after the distillation of sulfates.</note>, in the form of water or oil, when placed over any volatile or combustible bodies—even over distilled sulfur itself—fixes them so that they withstand the most intense fire and do not ignite.* Common *gold and silver* have the same power of fixing; for mercury, when cast into those liquids, is partially fixed by them. I know of a silver ore that gave no silver in a common trial <note>original: "proba"</note>, but if it was instead cast into melted common silver, it exhibited a good and large amount of silver. *Common mercury*, mixed with silver by a singular artifice and distilled, also remains even in the most intense fire; and *arsenic*, when properly mixed with silver, withstands the cupel <term>cineritium | a process of refining precious metals in a small, porous bowl made of bone ash, called a cupel</term> with it. It is dissolved by aqua fortis <note>nitric acid</note> just like *gold*, and is reduced into a heavy, *dark, lead-colored* body. When this is tested by itself in the cupel, it is absorbed by "Saturn" <note>The alchemical name for lead.</note>; but when remelted with silver, it resists it. This is a manifest sign that a fixing power lies hidden in these perfect bodies. *Gold* itself, when mixed with silver in a triple proportion, preserves it from aqua fortis, as all *assay-masters* <term>Docimastæ | historical experts who tested the purity and weight of metals</term> know. Who then will dare to deny this *fixing quality of the tincture*, since we are forced to grant it to common gold and silver, as well as to viler things? It cannot be called into doubt that this *fixing agent* exceeds its own quantity through its *multiplicative* quality. For since we see *four ounces of common sulfur coagulate sixteen ounces of mercury into a solid body (such as cinnabar); and we see four ounces of the same sulfur reduce a pound of oil to the consistency of liver; and one pound of oil restrain ten pounds of lye into the solidity of phlegm;* what is the difficulty if we also grant such a *multiplicative* fixing power to the *tincture*? You heard from the above-cited Count *Digby* <note>Sir Kenelm Digby (1603–1665), an English courtier and natural philosopher known for his "powder of sympathy" and alchemical interests.</note> that *one grain* of barley, after a certain soaking <note>original: "imbibitione"</note> was performed, was so increased in its seminal fertility that it brought forth 18,000 grains and had 249 stalks. This is still kept like a miracle in Paris among the Fathers of Christian Doctrine. Is it any wonder, then, if the metallic seed is so increased in its power that it later changes so many thousands of parts into its own nature? It is not, I say, a wonder, since metals are far more manageable regarding transmutation than *vegetables* <note>At this time, "vegetables" referred generally to the entire plant kingdom.</note> are. I will now demonstrate this clearly to the Philo-chemical reader by reviewing the process of true transmutation. This is twofold: for *one* concerns the generation and mixture of things, while the *other*...

...is observed concerning generated and mixed things. Regarding *the first point*, I spoke at the beginning of this book, namely that things can be easily altered and changed once their principles <note>In alchemy and early chemistry, "principles" refers to the fundamental building blocks of a substance, such as Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury.</note> are obtained. Since these principles can be purified, perfected, and changed through digestion, cleansing, and combination, they can produce a completely different body in a new composition, conjunction, and coupling. Therefore, *it is always easier to alter mixtures at the start of their mixing than to change those already fully composed in their own form.* 

This, to come to the second method of transmutation, seems almost impossible in certain bodies. This is because the mixing is completed during generation, and sometimes it changes into dissimilar parts, as happens in the mixture of animals and plants. *For who can change a human or a tree once it is already formed? In its mixing, the forming cause—or the doubled seed <note>original: "duplicatum semen." This refers to the early modern biological theory that both parents contribute a "seed" to create an offspring.</note>—has changed its growth into so many dissimilar parts; for it is impossible to reduce a human or a tree back into its seminal principles.* 

And this is the reason why defects which happen to occur during these primary mixings cling most stubbornly to the completed mixture, such as *all hereditary diseases.* Therefore, when Physicians saw that it was impossible to change the nature of a solid and mixed substance once the seed had already changed into a composite, they tried to see if they could alter and temper the defect of the seed through continuous *growth* <note>original: "accrementum." The author argues that even if you can't change the "blueprint," you can change the building materials added later.</note>—which a body requires to reach its proper proportion—*even outside of and after generation.* 

For this reason, Hippocrates (in Aphorisms, section 5, aphorism 7) pronounces those who suffer from the hereditary defect of their parents’ epilepsy to be incurable unless they are cured before their twenty-fifth year. Why? Because around that time, the greater part of growth is completed. This cause gave certain doctors the opportunity to change the *daily diet* in adults, from which blood and flesh are generated. From this, the *milk cure* <note>original: "cura lactis." A historical treatment where a patient lived almost exclusively on milk to "reset" the body’s humors.</note> recently came into use, not without success. Other doctors, seeing that the evil clung more deeply to the mixture, discovered the *transfusion of blood*, also not without success. *For it is certain that the whole mixture is altered according to the variety of the growth.* 

We see this clearly in plants: for wild fruits, when placed in garden soil, become domestic; and shoots grafted onto a tree of another species are notably altered. **All these things**, however, as I have said, only happen by reason of *altered growth*; because the doubled seed itself, once spread and congealed, cannot be reduced back into its primary matter and a homogeneous state. **But if that could be done, this transmutation would succeed far more happily.** We have an example of this in wine; for *because it is mixed somewhat homogeneously and consists of more similar parts,* it can be changed and transmuted in many ways in its entire nature during fermentation. 

*How much more, then, can this be done and succeed in metals, which are homogeneous and continuous, consisting of pure and similar parts?* Namely, so that they might be radically transmuted in their seed as well as in their growth. But before I come to the specific details and particularities of metallic transmutations themselves, I must first put forward the *object of metallic transmutation*, which no one will deny is a metallic body. Now, however, the *first question* arises: *which parts in a metallic body are to be transmuted?* I respond that if the transmutation is to be true and radical, the internal essential parts of the metallic body (both formal and material) must be altered. I think these are the parts that compose and specify the metal, and because of which a metal is not...

# Chapter Six

...it is not only a metal **in general**, but it is also this or that metal **specifically**. Above all, then—lest we err in the transmuting cause—we must direct that cause toward the *object* to be transformed; therefore, the metallic parts **to be transmuted** must be understood. Now, we have already said that these parts are those from which the matter and form of metals originate: namely, the essential parts constituting a metal, or to speak more clearly, the **principles of metals**. You have learned in the preceding chapters of this book, and indeed all **chemical** philosophy agrees, that these are three in number, calling them **Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury**. 

However, all Philosophers, when using these specific names, always protest that they do not mean common **salt, sulfur**, or **mercury** by these words. This is because common salt, sulfur, and mercury are "de-composed" <note>In this context, "de-composed" means complex substances made of many parts, rather than the "simple" or pure building blocks the alchemists sought.</note>, whereas the **Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury** of the Philosophers are the **simplest** principles. Why these simple metallic principles are designated and named after the common "de-composed" salt, sulfur, and mercury, there is no other reason than the rhetorical figure of "the container for the contained" <note>original: "continentis pro contento"</note> or "the whole for the part." For it cannot be denied that within these three common complex substances, the three primary principles of metals lie hidden. 

Truthfully, this naming convention has done more harm than good, because it greatly confuses both **novices** <note>original: "Tyrones," referring to beginners in the alchemical art.</note> and even experienced **veterans** of chemistry. Because of this terminology—which, as I said, arose from an internal **likeness**—they imagine and seek some agreement of the metallic principles with these common substances in their external **form**. Consequently, they waste their entire lives in the decomposition of various salts, sulfurs, and mercuries, losing both time and money. 

Since this is the first, greatest, and most dangerous obstacle in Alchemy, or the transmuting art, I cannot fail at this point to do a great service to all those who are wandering, by leading them back to the true path. He who is unwilling to follow may wander; for when one arrives at the **projection** <term>Projection: The final stage of the alchemical process where the "Philosopher's Stone" or "Tincture" is cast upon a base metal to transform it into gold or silver.</term>, all the speculations of the **Universalists** <note>These were alchemists who sought a "Universal Medicine" or agent that could fix all things at once, often through abstract or metaphysical theories.</note> cease, and only the **transmuting agent** and the **particular thing to be transmuted** meet face to face. 

What the transmuting agent ought to be, you shall hear later—provided you first understand the **essence and nature** of the metallic thing to be transmuted. For it is not enough for you to say, "The Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury of metals must be changed and perfected by changing them." This operation is **practical, and deals with materials materially**; therefore, all metaphysical concepts and "non-entities" <note>This is a jab at "armchair" alchemists who used philosophical abstractions rather than getting their hands dirty in a laboratory.</note> cease here. Accordingly, you must show what kind of **Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury** is to be transmuted. 

The **Tincture** <note>The "Tincture" is the active substance used to "color" or transform the base metal.</note> which performs the change must be **material**; therefore, the matter to be changed—namely the Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury—must also be material. When these principles are brought forward by chemists, good God! How ridiculous, how empty, how far from simple they are—they are "super-decomposed"! Here they will show **vitriol** <note>original: "vitriolum"; various sulfate minerals.</note> or **sugar of lead** <note>original: "saccharum saturni"; lead acetate, a sweet-tasting but toxic lead compound.</note> as their "Salt"; there they show any kind of **oil or arsenic** as their "Sulfur"; elsewhere they show nothing but a **volatile earth** as their "Mercury." Indeed, even if they have labored with great zeal to extract these from metals and have reduced them to "principles" according to their own ingenuity, they have operated so unsuccessfully that the original body refuses to take back its own principles, or the **principles** themselves—due to their heterogeneous decomposition—refuse to come together again to restore the former body. From all of this, it is clear how much **ignorance regarding the study of transmutation** occurs everywhere, whence also...

# Supplement to Subterranean Physics

...it follows that so few useful effects are seen regarding this in practice. However, so that I may strive for brevity in accordance with the summary of this supplement, I say that the **Philosophers** <note>In this context, "Philosophers" refers specifically to alchemists and natural philosophers.</note> deceive the world with nothing more than the variety of metallic principles. But he who wishes to be taught should use the **guiding star of nature** <note>original: "naturæ Cynosura"</note> which is observed in the generation and mixing of all things. That rule is this: **there must be an acting cause and a passive matter, and then nourishment or growth.**

**For example: in animals**, there is the male sperm, the female seed, and the menstrual blood flowing to the womb for the growth and nourishment of the fetus; or, the doubled seed of the parents and the blood that adds growth to that doubled seed. 

**In vegetables**, nature produces a **male seed** in every plant, which, when committed to the earth, attracts the juice of the earth as a **female** element, with rainwater and a portion of the earth acting as the nourishment and growth of the plant.

**In metallic bodies**, there is a **male seed** and a **female seed**. Both are a vapor, and both are sulfur: one is red, the other white. One is the active agent, the other is passive. Both are a "subtle earth," which when joined, creates an unctuous moisture that they call the **mercury of the Philosophers**, or **Brumazar** <term>Brumazar: A specialized alchemical term used by Becher and others to describe the "First Matter" or the essential root of mercury that forms the basis of all metals</term>. 

And that doubled seed, or doubled mercury, takes a certain earth as its nourishment for growth; when this is added, the mixture becomes what we call a metal. Just as the **animal** comes from the joined principles mentioned before, and the **vegetable** from vegetable principles—and just as if you provided an animal's doubled seed with something other than blood for growth, or a vegetable's doubled seed with something other than water, only a **monstrous** growth would occur—so certainly, if you provided the doubled mercury (the seed of metals) with anything other than the appropriate earth, nothing would be generated from it. 

This must also be understood: if you take either the male or female seed of one kingdom **alone, without the other, and apply it even to the correct nourishment**, nothing will arise from it. This is because the means of uniting the **seed with the nourishment** is missing; **this medium lies hidden in the male seed**. Thus, if only the **male sulfur** is applied to the genuine metallic earth, it does not grow, because the **Mercury** (acting as the female element) is missing. The medium that ought to grow would instead produce a shapeless mass or something else entirely. Nor could the nourishment by itself, without the **doupled seed**, ever be changed into any shaped and specific body.

You see, therefore, the necessity of this **Trinity of principles**; from this proceeds whatever is useful or curious produced by nature or art regarding the generation of things in the three kingdoms <note>The "three kingdoms" refers to the traditional classification of Nature into Animal, Vegetable, and Mineral.</note>. Therefore, a study of this **Trinity of principles** is necessary in every way. It would be impossible for **Farmers** to produce any plant if they were ignorant of the plant's seed, the earth, and the water. 

We should not, therefore, be seized with wonder as to why so few **Metal-workers** <term>Metallicole: A term for those who labor with metals, specifically alchemists or metallurgists</term> see the desired fruits of their labor. Most of them wish to sow in their brains through speculation alone that which must grow through material operation in the mines: namely, the doubled metallic seed joined to the metallic earth. Let the **Universalists** <note>Those seeking the "Universal Medicine" or the Philosopher's Stone that acts on all matter.</note> conceive whatever subtle speculations they wish; unless they consider the principles of metals, they will labor in vain. For they will never be able to apply a thing which is outside of matter to matter itself. 

Having now explained the necessity and the trinity of these principles, two things remain to be considered: **namely, how they operate, and what their proper names are.**

# Chapter Six

...[how these things] are held, or what they are materially, when considered specifically in themselves? *How they operate*, I have demonstrated more than enough in my *Subterranean Physics* <note>original: "Physica mea subterranea"; this was Becher's most influential work, first published in 1669, which laid the groundwork for the Phlogiston theory.</note>: namely, that *Almighty God* created in this Universe a universal mover and a movable thing; the mover being the Heavens, and the movable being the Earth. Or rather, that the heavens can be **rarefied** <note>Rarefaction is the process of a substance becoming less dense; Becher believed this expansion was the source of all motion.</note>, and through this expansion, perform all *Mechanical and Physical* motions. What I understand by those "Heavens," I have explained more fully at the beginning of that same work.

By "Earth" in the *act of creation*, I understand the **earth-water-air** globe, which I call the **triple earth**; namely, the opaque earth, the transparent water-earth, and the glowing air-earth. The more a body contains of the air-element, the more luminous it is. The more water-element it has, the more transparent it is; and the more earth-element, the more opaque. For I establish three created elements; since **fire** is only an element by *production*—specifically by rarefaction—which proceeds from the rarefied *earth-water-air* body. It is more truly an *act* than a stable element. Therefore, from these three "earths" and their various mixtures, all things that appear in this universe are composed.

It is not relevant here to discuss the *Harmony* of all the Orbs, spheres, and planets with our globe, nor what kind of motion occurs within our *earth-water-air* globe itself; since I explained all those things in my *Subterranean Physics*. I will only repeat from there, as is necessary for this context, that in this globe, all motions occur from the Center to the circumference *Physically*; just as then all motions occur from the circumference back to the center *Mechanically*. 

That is to say, in the **microcosm** <note>The human body, viewed as a miniature map of the universe.</note> or man, the *blood* is carried upward by *physical* motion <note>Driven by internal heat and vitality.</note>; but it is carried downward by mechanical motion—that is, by natural gravity. In the **macrocosm** <note>The universe or the Earth itself.</note>, which is our globe, *water* is carried upward from the Center of the earth to the circumference by physical motion; but it flows downward through rivers into the sea by its own gravity. In the *physical* motion, it is driven by internal heat; in the mechanical motion, it flows by external cold. 

From this principle, therefore, I have most solidly demonstrated in my physics that our globe always preserves the "idea" <note>In the sense of a blueprint or essential form.</note> of its first motion and location. For it was moved by the *spirit*, and was so positioned that the more subtle things were on the surface, and the thicker things were around the center. Thus, from the most subtle grades of earth, water, and air, the stars arose, then meteors, then animals. From the thicker portions, vegetables arose; then stones. From the thickest portions of earth, water, and air, the **metals** were born. In this way, the stars and meteors took their place in the highest realm, animals above the earth, vegetables on the surface of the earth, and metals took the deepest bowels of the earth as the place of their generation.

I say therefore, as a conclusion, if anyone has properly understood these preceding points—especially my *Subterranean Physics*—they will see that the *entire sea is still a certain remnant of that first **Chaos** or universal matter, containing within itself a significant mixture and influence of the opaque, transparent, and glowing earth (that is: earth, water, and air)*. 

Furthermore, I affirm that this seawater filters through the sea floor and drips into the concave center of the earth. There, as if in a large **distilling vessel** <note>Becher imagines the Earth’s core as a giant alchemical furnace (athanor) that distills seawater into minerals.</note>, its various components are separated and driven back toward the circumference of the earth through pores and cracks. These distillations are partly liquid, partly solid, partly airy, partly watery, and partly earthy; some are simple, some composite, and some doubly-composite, as I have explained most fully and specifically in *Subterranean Physics*. And indeed, by such a physical operation—and *not* by the influence of the stars or planetary circulation, as some believe—there arise among...

# Supplement to Subterranean Physics

### Page 330

Among other vapors of the earth, two were destined by God—the first orderer of things—for the generation of metals. These vapors, known as **brumazar** <note>original: "brumazar"; a term found in early modern chymistry to describe the "universal metallic vapor" or a specific mineral dew.</note>, consist of very thick air and subterranean water. One, by its aerial nature, is very hot and dry; the other, by its aqueous nature, is very cold and very moist. One plays the part of the male, the other the female; one is bright, the other transparent; one is red, the other white; one is active, the other passive.

When these two vapors meet, they seize each other most greedily and magnetically, and embrace one another, for dryness desires moisture and heat desires cold. From their mutual embrace and vaporous state—as if through some reaction—they are changed into a certain visible, semi-liquid and vaporous body, which the Philosophers call **living silver** <note>original: "argentum vivum"; more commonly known as quicksilver or mercury.</note>, **doubled mercury**, or the **doubled metallic seed**. 

This liquid vapor, which he calls **Brumazar** from the source Zalento <note>Possibly a reference to a specific alchemical author or a corrupted name from the alchemical tradition.</note>, penetrates even the thickest stones and earths because of its subtle power of penetration. Where it finds an earthy matrix <note>A "womb" or site of formation.</note>, or its suitable earthy growth, it subdues, penetrates, and prepares it, fixing itself within it like clay or a seal, and in this way produces metal. 

Let it suffice that I have presented these matters of my *Subterranean Physics* <note>Becher's "Physica Subterranea" was a foundational text for what would become the Phlogiston theory.</note> most succinctly and generally. From all this, I wish to clarify the second point: namely, that the principles of metals consist of aerial and aqueous vapors of a very thick, heavy, and fixed disposition. To these is added and mixed an "earth," serving as the growth-medium of the metals, designated by God for this purpose—a very thick species of earth indeed. 

From this it is clear that in metals, there is earth, water, and air; specifically in that disposition which suits them in their metallic nature. Thus, as is evident, the "mixture of metals" is best defined by Albert <note>Referring to Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a medieval scholar who wrote extensively on minerals.</note> as **an unctuous moisture incorporated into a strongly mixed earthy substance** <note>original: "unctuosum humidum terrestri fortiter commixto incorporatum"</note>, which is how it is defined by all the followers of Aristotle.

However, the Chemists go further and, as I noted above, they distinguish the principles of metals by the names of **salt, sulfur, and mercury**. By the name of **sulfur**, they mean the "male seed," which I have demonstrated above to be of an aerial and hot nature. The term **Mercury**, or **Menstruum** <note>A solvent or liquid medium.</note>, they improperly attribute to the female, since it is of an aqueous nature, moist and cold. When the male and female seeds are joined, they then call it **doubled mercury**, or their own **mercury** or **living silver**. 

By the name of **Salt**, they make mention of **their vessel**, **Lime**, the **Mud of Wisdom** <note>original: "luti Sapientiæ"; a special clay used to seal alchemical vessels.</note>, and the **Seal of Hermes**, which grows together with the doubled mineral vapor: namely, a certain species of earth, by the growth of which the mixture we call "metal" is made. 

And so, if anyone wishes to set aside these **chemical, nominal, and verbal masks**, they will more easily penetrate to the internal principles and hidden secrets of metals. I say, therefore, in truth, that for the generation of any metal, nothing else is required—either naturally or artificially—than that doubled subterranean vapor (aerial and aqueous, or sulfurous and mercurial) and the species of earth which receives and fixes both of these fumes. That is: Sulfur, Mercury, and Salt. 

But I also wish to set down the specific causes of the various metals, so that from this specific detail, the truth of what has been said may become clearer to everyone, as if through obvious examples. In general, however, this must be stated first as a universal axiom: that the metallic mixture itself arises and is determined according to the purity and perfection of the three principles. These are, according to the Aristotelians, the aerial vapor and the earth; and according to the Chemists, Sulfur, Mercury, and Salt. The purity and perfection of these metallic principles [rests] in...

# Chapter Six

The perfection of this process consists in this: the more hot and dry the active agent is, and the more cold and moist the passive element—namely, the earth capable of growth—the more it possesses homogeneity and stability. As **Albertus** <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a medieval scholar and bishop who wrote extensively on alchemy and minerals.</note> says, the more it *possesses the most of both*, the more perfectly it is formed. I say that the more strongly these principles are constituted, the more they desire each other, the more tenaciously they cling together, and the better they withstand fire, the hammer, corrosive substances, and weight. I will soon demonstrate this to you specifically and in detail through all the transformations of each individual metal. However, I wish to first set this down as an **axiom for everything that follows concerning the specific natures of metals.**

As is evident from experience and the "anatomy" of metallic bodies and mixtures, they consist—to speak in the language of Chemistry—of salt, sulfur, and mercury. That is to say, they are made from *sustenance, seed, male, and female* (or from earth and a doubled vapor, or from an oily moisture and a subtle earth). Furthermore, it is customary to ascribe the "fixing" cause <note>The "fixing" cause is the principle that makes a substance solid and resistant to being evaporated by heat.</note> to the **salt** (*clay, lime, stone, or earth*). **Basil Valentine**, a Benedictine monk, reveals much about the base of metals, their growth, earth, and lime in his *Last Testament* <note>original: "Basilius Valentin... in ultimo suo testamento"; Basil Valentine was a legendary alchemist, though scholars today often believe his works were written by various 16th-century authors.</note>. Even if this book is considered a forgery by the learned, it nevertheless contains many very true things. **Ripley** <note>George Ripley (c. 1415–1490), a famous English alchemist.</note> says in his *Gates*: *Every spirit is fixed with the limes of its own kind; if you notice this well, you will reap the fruit.* 

You will hear more later regarding the fixing power of the **Salt of Mars** <note>original: "salis Martis"; Mars is the alchemical symbol for Iron. His "salt" refers to iron vitriol or iron oxides.</note>. It is consistent with experience and reason that both "seeds" <note>Referring back to the male/sulfur and female/mercury vapors.</note> are incorporated and fixed by this sustenance. I recommend to you the power of fixing which resides in common clay, as is evident in experiments with iron. *Every salt can be changed into earth, and every earth into salt.* Therefore, do not allow yourselves to be deceived by the mask of "decomposition." There are, however, various types of earth, just as there are various decomposed substances that consist of them—namely various salts: alkaline, vitriolated, borax-like, aluminous, sulfurous, acidic, and urinous. There is *thick, coarse, red earth*; there is fusible earth that is sulfurous and easily turns into slag; and there is *lime, which resists melting.* For all earths, stones, clays, gravels, and sands turn either *into glass or into lime; that which gives glass does not give lime, and that which gives lime does not give glass*, as I have noted sufficiently in the final chapter of my *Subterranean Physics*.

For this reason, in the mines, **in the veins** <note>original German: "in den Gängen"</note>, you will find **a hard, coarse field-rock** <note>original German: "einen harten groben feld born-wacken"</note>; on the other hand, **a soft, gentle quartz or limestone** <note>original German: "einen zarten milden Quartz-oder Kalchstein"</note>; here **a fiercely tough, barren rock** <note>original German: "ein grimmig vestes daubes"</note>; and there **a yielding, soft, gentle mountain-ore** <note>original German: "gschnädigs, zartes lindes Gebirg"</note>. It is so evident that the matter of the place in which metals are generated contributes to the specific nature of the metal—in both quantity and quality—that it cannot be doubted. In this matter, experience and personal observation <note>original: "autopsia"; here meaning "seeing for oneself" rather than a medical autopsy.</note> resist all subtle speculations, no matter how they are produced to the contrary.

Therefore, I ascribe the most important part of the metallic mixture—not only its stability but also its color—to the principle of Salt; that is, to the *clay, earth, stone, lime*, or whatever matter the metals grow in (*for the word "Salt" must be retained, otherwise the Chemists would not understand me*). Regarding stability, **Maria, Sister of Moses** <note>original: "Maria Moysis Soror"; Mary the Jewess, an ancient alchemical authority often legendary identified as the sister of Moses.</note>, says: *Smoke embraces smoke, and the white herb on the hillocks [embraces] both heads.* What could be said more beautifully? What could be more true? Than that the sulfurous vapor seizes the mercurial—the *dry [seizes] the moist, the hot the cold, the active the passive—and the earth captures or "fixes" both?* Truly, I ask you, friends of Chemistry, for the sake of truth and yourselves: set aside those high speculations and work with the simplest method of nature, and you will see that you obtain all that nature is capable of giving. **Ripley**, as I cited before, says:

It is from this principle, as you will hear later, that all the defects of imperfect metals arise: they are simply **not mixed with their appropriate earth.** Because of this, some turn into slag, others into dross <note>original: "stomoma," a Greek term for hardened steel or the scales that fall from it during forging.</note>, some into glass, and many very easily turn into "crocus" <note>A "crocus" in alchemy refers to a fine, oxide-like powder, usually reddish or yellow, named for its resemblance to the saffron flower.</note>.

The chemical world will also marvel that I ascribe not only **fixity** but also **color** to this principle. Each of these is threefold, in positive, comparative, and superlative degrees. Specifically: **citrine, red, and dark; citrine in gold, red in copper, and dark in iron.** The white is also threefold: **dark, grey, and white. Dark in lead, grey in tin, and white in silver.** Now contemplate more deeply how these earths are named, and you will find the "salt of the philosophers," not only for changing any metal but also for generating it. Take this, I say, for **it is not commonly found by those traveling this path.**

Now, having moved from the matrix of metals, the vessel, and the subtle terrestrial growth—namely, the salt—I shall turn to the **doubled feminine principles**. In this metallic genesis, I rightly attribute the **form** to this principle. 

The metallic form consists in the **work of mixing**, specifically so that the metallic earth is best **mingled with the metallic water.** Yet this mixing must happen **by the mediation of metallic air**, because, as I have demonstrated in my *Underground Physics* <note>Referring to the author's primary work, *Physica Subterranea*, which laid the foundations for the Phlogiston theory.</note>, earth cannot be mixed with water except **by the instrument of air, as the subject of variability.** 

Hence the male seed—which, as you heard quoted from Aristotle above, is of an airy nature—holds the place of formation in every genesis, whether animal or vegetable. This you perceived with the clearest details in my *Underground Physics*, in the chapter on animal and vegetable mixtures. Therefore, metallic **mixture**—that is, the **subduing, preparation, and penetration of the metallic earth (whether already grown or yet to grow), and its mingling, glueing, incorporation, and compaction with the mercurial earth (the feminine seed)—is to be attributed to this principle as its form.** For it is the property of the **sperm** of any kingdom **to mix the feminine seed with the "menstruum" or nutrient** <note>The "menstruum" is a solvent or a nourishing fluid that allows for the growth of the seed.</note>, without which mixing neither form nor generation would occur. 

If, therefore, in the following discussions of metallic mixtures you hear that the nutrient does not adhere well to the feminine seed, or the salt to the Mercury, or the earth to the water, you should always conclude that **the defect lies in the form—namely, in the sulfur, the male, the sperm, or the air.** Therefore, I say **that all metallic conjunction, metallic entry, homogeneity, and metallic ductility consist in the essence of sulfur.**

Otherwise, it would be as easy to create a tincture for **essentially** dyeing metals as it is for anyone to dye common water with saffron.

**I now turn to the third principle, which is mercurial or feminine, namely metallic water; to this I ascribe "metalleity"** <note>The essential quality or state of being a metal.</note> **and weight, and to tell the truth, the more important form of the metallic mixture: for as much as a metallic body contains of this Mercury, so much can it be said to be a metal.** The remainder is an earthy accretion, mixed in and subordinated by nature for its subsistence, as you heard a little while ago. You see the appearance of this metallic water properly in common **quicksilver** <note>original: "argento vivo," literally "living silver."</note>; which is in truth the **feminine seed of metals, but corrupted by a vicious and arsenical masculine seed. From this, Mercury "fishes" for earth from **sulfur and salt, from which a compound of cinnabar and sublimates is made.** It mixes itself to some extent with these earths, because in these salts, the **masking earths** <note>original: "larvantes terrae," earths that hide or disguise the true metallic nature.</note> have been somewhat penetrated and subdued by the "entity of sulfur" lurking there, so that they can be mixed more easily with quicksilver than common earths can. Thus, **nature more easily receives nature,** even though the metallic mixture retains its own earth in the fire and leaves the "foreign guest" empty, since **everyone is closest to themselves.**

Having laid these foundations, I say that a metallic mixture is distinguished from all other created things by a very specific difference: it is earthy, homogeneous, heavy, malleable, able to endure fire, and fusible. For there are also stones that are earthy, homogeneous, heavy, and fusible, but they are not **malleable**. Therefore, these combined properties belong specifically to metals. Now, finally, we shall see how much of these properties each metal possesses; for the more a metal possesses these qualities, the more "metalleity" <note>The essential quality or state of being a metal</note> it has—that is, the closer it comes to perfect malleability. **Iron** <note>original: "ferrum"</note> occupies the first, yet lowest place, both in its physical quality and its political value. Many parts of a red, astringent, and difficult-to-melt earth essentially enter its mixture as "accreting matter." The oily principle, or forming cause, is indeed strong in iron, but small in quantity; nor is there a sufficient amount of metallic moisture in the mixture of iron. According to the **Chemists**, therefore, iron consists of much salt, little sulfur, and even less Mercury, as the learned French philosopher **De Rochas** <note>Henri de Rochas, a 17th-century physician and writer on mineralogy</note> notes in his well-known experiment. From this, I conclude that the metal produced there was indeed iron.

From this large portion of red astringent earth follows the crudity of iron, its hardness when melting, its fixedness, and its resistance in fire due to the lack of a sufficient mixing cause. This leads to a certain lack of uniformity in the mixture, as well as brittleness and hardness, because of the scarcity of quicksilver. It also results in a dark color, low metalleity, and meager weight. Hence, if a mixture of iron is pressed by fire, the mercurial moisture clings most tenaciously to the dry astringent earth and is easily changed back into earth—especially if a portion of earth is added from the flames or from solvents. For all moist substances easily adhere to the mixture of iron by a "natural magnetism," through which this mixture seeks from external sources what it lacks in itself; thus, it very easily turns into **crocus** <note>original: "crocum," an alchemical term for a fine metallic powder, usually an oxide</note> and rust.

By the addition of mercurial earth, I have seen iron changed into **lead**; this I observed to succeed in practice following the process of **Paracelsus** <note>The influential 16th-century Swiss-German physician and alchemist</note>. It is also certain that by the removal of the astringent earth, iron can attain a different proportion of temperament and mixture, and thus become another metal. It is worth noting that the earth which serves as an accretion in iron—and which is superabundant there—if separated from that mixture, purified, and subdued, and then penetrated by a suitable sulfur as a mixing cause, can then be projected onto mercurial metals to fix and **tinge** <note>To transform or "color" a base metal into a more noble one, like gold or silver</note> them. For this reason, *Basil* <note>Referring to Basil Valentine, a legendary figure in 15th-century alchemy known for his writings on antimony and the Three Principles</note> highly commends the oil of Venus <note>original: "oleum veneris"; Venus is the alchemical name for copper</note>, and various observations are made concerning the fire or element of *Venus*.

Gold <note>original: "Aurum"</note> possesses a very pure red earth, diluted and tending toward a citrus-yellow color, which is by its nature most "fixed" <note>stable in fire; not volatile</note>. This earth is united to a most pure and perfect Mercurial substance by means of the forming, mixing, subduing, penetrating, and fixing sulfur. Because this mixture is so strongly tempered and evenly combined, and arises from the excellent blending of these three principles, it produces the citrus color, the ringing sound, homogeneous fusibility, great weight, admirable ductility, and a pleasant softness. Silver <note>original: "Argentum"</note>, in regards to its mixture, is somewhat akin to iron. Yet it differs from iron in this: the earth entering the mixture of silver is white, more noble, better "subdued" <note>refined or processed by nature</note>, and finer; it adheres more strongly to the Mercurial substance because of the sulfur, which acts as a most perfect mixing cause. Therefore, if silver is to be changed into gold, the white earth must be tinged red, and either part of that earth must be removed or more Mercury must be added; otherwise, neither the color nor the weight of gold will be attained.

Tin <note>original: "Stannum"</note> contains much lime-like earth, very little Mercury, and an impure and imperfect sulfur, which has imperfectly mixed the earth with the moisture (namely, the Mercury). From this comes its crackling <note>original: "stridor"; refers to the "cry of tin," a distinct sound made when a bar of tin is bent</note>, its lightness, and its lack of uniformity. That small amount of moisture (its Mercurial nature) is swallowed up in the earth, which seizes it as if it were dry, so that it almost destroys its own mixture; upon reduction, it is hardly ever found in the original form of tin. However, because of the abundance of white, fixed earth it possesses—though it is not sufficiently refined—tin is nevertheless very akin to silver. It enters that mixture essentially, just as the earth of iron enters the mixture of gold. For this reason, the "salt of Jove" <note>Jupiter, the planetary association for tin</note> carries no small authority among the Chemists. The mixture of tin itself cannot be essentially changed except by correcting its sulfur as the forming cause and adding a great deal of Mercury.

From these aforementioned specific mixtures of metals (which, though they may appear new to some, nevertheless arise from practice), it is obvious to anyone that the *Transmutation Method is twofold; namely, aphæretic and prosthetic, being both particular and universal.* The aphæretic <note>from the Greek word for "taking away" or subtraction</note> and particular method occurs when a certain part, whether earthy or watery (*saline or mercurial*), is separated from the metallic mixtures; by this abstraction, the remaining mixture is essentially changed in its temperament. But because it is very difficult for anything to be separated from their principles due to the strong bonding of metals, the prosthetic <note>from the Greek word for "adding" or addition</note> method is not only more practical but also more universal: namely, adding to the metallic mixtures the appropriate metallic earth or water, by which addition the temperament of the whole mixture is radically altered. 

Now, no moisture is of use to (*mercurial*) metals unless earthiness has been introduced into its center, nor does any earthiness (*salt*) enter metals unless mercuriality has been introduced into its center—that is, unless it has been granted entry by mercury. Therefore, I say through experience that no earth can be radically joined to water except by the help of air; that is, no metallic earth radically adheres to quicksilver unless their conjunction is made by the help of sulfur: just as the body cannot be joined to the soul except by the medium of the spirit; and just as in the first mixture of the world, the earth was joined to the water by the help of the air or the "brooding spirit." 

All particular transmutations can therefore be reduced to a certain universal mixture; just as *Lullius* <note>Ramon Llull, a 13th-century philosopher and alchemist often cited for his "Universal Medicine"</note> previously urged that all particular medicines be concentrated into one. The parts of this mixture (*the tincture*) will be purified metallic earth and water, joined by the help of air—that is, join salt with Mercury by the help of sulfur, or join the humid to the subtle, oily, and earthy bodies. For by the help of Mercury, earth will have entry into metals; and by the help of earth, Mercury will withstand the fire; and by the intervention of sulfur, earth will be mixed with Mercury. 

And since no radical mixture (of the kind this philosophical work must be) can occur without penetration, the whole business consists principally in this: that the penetrating cause—which mixes and joins earth with water, or makes any metal "tincture-forming" <note>original: "tincturificans"; having the power to dye or transform</note> (that is, making it enter and dye)—be held at hand: *namely, the sulfur or air of the philosophers*. Once this is obtained, the "waxing" <note>original: "inceratio"; the process of softening a substance to a waxy consistency so it can be combined</note> of earth with quicksilver, and the entry of both into metals, follows naturally and by infallible consequence. So that you may more freely grant this, the other part of the tincture must be explained to you: namely, the manner of the tincture's action or transmutation, which consists solely in its penetration and subtlety. For if fixed things are intimately mixed with non-fixed things, they preserve them from the fire, and vice versa. This is indeed the reason why *gold mixed with silver in a small quan-*

## Chapter Six

[...quantity], it does not preserve it from *aqua fortis* <note>original: "aqua forti"; nitric acid</note>; whereas on the contrary, silver atoms, when more strongly penetrated by *aqua fortis* or another subtle water, not only resist the *aqua fortis* but also leave behind a good quantity of gold. In the same way, copper cannot be preserved from lead <note>original: "saturno"</note> in a cupel <note>term: "cupella"; a shallow porous vessel used in refining to separate precious metals from base metals like lead</note> by silver, because it cannot be sufficiently penetrated by the silver due to the physical density of both. We have an example of this in oil of roses: if mixed with water, even in a large quantity, and stirred, it communicates very little of its scent to the water; yet if that same oil is dissolved in alkali into a "soapy liquor," just a few drops mixed into water will infect it with such a most sweet fragrance as if the entire water were oil of roses. The cause of this is the alkali salt, which makes the oil penetrative and capable of mixing with water. By a similar reasoning, the spirit of urine <note>ammonia</note> exalts colors, as we noted at the end of our *Subterranean Physics* <note>original: "Physicæ nostræ subterraneæ"</note> citing Mr. Robert Boyle <note>original: "D. Boyleo"</note>, where the author noted that by the weight of a single grain of cochineal, 125,000 grains of water were tinted; this immense tinting is to be ascribed to nothing other than extension.

Therefore, substances that are intimately mixed preserve and alter one another; just as a metal, if it is pulverized and ground for a long time (as the Count of Wolffsegg, Vicegerent of the Upper Palatinate, now of blessed memory <note>original: "makarios"; Greek for "blessed," used for the deceased</note>, most curiously observed), and thus penetrated within itself, acquires various alterations both in color and substance. For example, the powder of lead found in hourglasses <note>original: "Clepsydris"</note> is so altered by its frequent and long-lasting flow that it can never afterward be reduced back into a metallic body by itself. The cause, therefore, of the extension and multiplicative expansion of the golden tincture is its own penetration and subtlety. Let silver be an example of this: in its solid body, it can never penetrate a copper coin of any thickness without losing its own form; but when dissolved in *aqua fortis* and precipitated with spirit of vitriol <note>sulfuric acid</note> or another salt, it becomes "horny" <note>term: "corneum"; likely referring to silver chloride, known as "horn silver" for its waxy appearance</note> and easily melted, penetrating like an oil. Indeed, if a copper coin is cast into it, it is so penetrated in a short time that it appears as silver both outside and within.

I am also aware of a method for making "oils" from metals; one or two drops of these cast into water will cover the entire wide surface of the water with a leaf of metal. Reason dictates that the "Golden Oil" of Sendivogius <note>Michael Sendivogius, a famous Polish alchemist</note> was not far from this goal of preparation; with it, he tinted one side of a silver Imperial coin into gold in the presence of Emperor Ferdinand II.

But why gold must be made penetrating, and why the entire artifice and effect consists in this penetration, is clear from the following experiment: we have observed that one part of a metal—or for better penetration, a *calx* <note>the powdery oxide left after heating a metal</note> or metallic powder—cast into five hundred parts of glass, tints it significantly. The reason is that glass in the fire is more porous and penetrable than metal. For there is no doubt that if liquefied metals were as penetrable as liquefied glass, they could also be tinted by such a small quantity of some metallic body. However, because this is impossible due to the weight and oily tenacity of Mercury, the Philosophers had to find another way: namely, the tincture had to be made more "subtle" <note>refined/diluted to a spirituous state</note> so that it could penetrate even the heaviest bodies.

Hence Democritus the Greek says:
> *The shadow of the dense body must be stripped away by the fiery medicine*; <note>original: "Pharmaco ignito spolianda densi est corporis umbra"</note>
by "shadow," he understands the corporeality and solidity of gold, which he commands must be stripped away—that is, thinned out by a fiery subject.

Hence the *Rosarius* <note>The "Rosary of the Philosophers," a famous alchemical text</note> says: *Our water is stronger than fire, because it makes a mere spirit out of the body of gold, which common fire cannot do, even if in li-*

...so that through liquefaction <note>The process of melting or making a solid substance liquid.</note> it penetrates the body of gold and softens it. You heard above that a powder made from the rays of the sun <note>original: "pulverem ex solis radiis factum"; likely referring to a chemically prepared "calx" of gold or a substance focused by a burning lens.</note> also achieves this; and singular experience teaches us that the "fire of nitre" <note>potassium nitrate or saltpeter</note> in a sub-liquid form has dissolved gold, and when in a closed vessel, it has coagulated with it into a dry and solid body. Regarding this, **Geber** <note>An influential 8th-century Arabic alchemist, known in Latin as Geber, whose writings formed the foundation of medieval alchemy.</note> writes most profoundly in Book 2, Part 1, Chapter 12: *We have proved, therefore, from my discourses, that spirits are more similar to and united with bodies through that which we see: they are more friendly to bodies than anything else in nature. For through this, it has been brought to us by true discovery that these spirits are the true medicine for the alteration of bodies. Therefore, we have exercised ourselves in every way of ingenuity possible, so that through them we may transform each one of the imperfect bodies, by a firm and true change, into a perfect lunar <note>silver</note> and solar <note>gold</note> body. For this reason, it necessarily happens that from the aforementioned spirits, diverse medicines are created according to the diverse intentions of those things to be altered.* 

And in Book 1, Part 2, Chapter 17, he detects the errors that can be committed regarding these spirits, and finally concludes: *If you wish to convert or transmute bodies, O sons of learning, then if it is possible for this to be done through any material, it must necessarily happen through spirits alone. But it is not possible for spirits that are not fixed to usefully adhere to or be joined with bodies, as we have said above.* Here, by "spirits not fixed," he understands those that are not currently fixed, though potentially able to be fixed. Hence all the Philosophers warn that we should make a spirit from the body, and a body from the spirit; and **Ripley** <note>George Ripley, a famous 15th-century English alchemist.</note> expressly confesses that *every spirit is fixed with the ashes <note>original: "calcibus"; the powdery remains left after a metal is heated.</note> of its own kind, and if this is well noted, the fruit will be returned.* 

Since, therefore, such great power of the "tincture" <note>A substance capable of transmuting or coloring a base metal into a noble one.</note> consists in gold being made subtle and penetrative, this gold is rightly distinguished from common gold; *for common gold is thick, compact, and solid, mixing itself with metals with difficulty and only superficially, like oil with water;* hence it is also easily separable from them again. The Gold of the Philosophers, on the other hand, is thinned by a certain spiritual matter, made extended and penetrative; whence it penetrates any bodies whatsoever with incredible depth, into the smallest atoms, and by this penetration it alters them, and introduces its own "fixing styptic power" <note>original: "vim stipticam figentem"; a power that contracts and stabilizes volatile substances.</note> (which we discussed above), without re-concentration or its own re-incorporation. 

*For you should know this: that this philosophical gold, on account of the admixture of the fixed spirit, can never again for all eternity be reduced into common gold, much less into a metallic body. Nor can this spirit by itself, without the gold, tint in any way when fixed; for that which tints is the gold, and that which makes the gold tint is our fixed spirit, giving to the gold its penetration and the faculty of tinting.* This is also to be understood regarding silver. For this fixed spirit is not the special cause of the red <note>gold-making</note> or white <note>silver-making</note> tincture; rather, the silver and the gold are the cause of the specification. For each of these, having been penetrated by this universal spirit, works according to the species of its own nature and the quality of the penetration. That is: *it tints because it has been penetrated, but it turns things into gold or silver because it is itself gold or silver.* 

Hence **Avicenna** <note>A Persian polymath whose medical and philosophical works were central to the Middle Ages.</note> says: *If I did not see gold and silver, I would say that the mastery <note>The alchemical process of the Great Work.</note> does not exist; but because I see them, I know the mastery is true.* And from this foundation also arises the "philosophical particular" <note>A process that transmutes only a portion of a metal rather than the whole.</note>; if, namely, by means of this spirit, you join gold to silver in such a way that the "Moon" <note>silver</note> is sufficiently penetrated by the "Sun" <note>gold</note> in its smallest parts, for in this way it will be graduated <note>refined or raised in quality</note>. Since nothing acts upon another which does not have the power of acting upon that other: but that power consists in penetration alone. Whence **Hermes** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of the hermetic and alchemical tradition.</note> rightly says: *You shall therefore drive away all darkness and blindness, for this strength snatches the palm <note>victory</note> from every other strength and power; for it [penetrates] every...*

# Chapter Six.

...which can penetrate and subdue both subtle and thick, as well as hard things; and in its preparation, it teaches *that the subtle and thin should be separated from the gross and thick, and indeed prudently, with modesty and wisdom.* Therefore, two things come to be considered in our mastery: *first, whether gold has an extensive quality—that is, whether it can be stretched; then, whether a matter is given that can extend it.*

I will demonstrate the first point with a mechanical example. *Melt two ducats <note>Gold coins used as a standard of purity.</note> with one mark of silver <note>A unit of weight, roughly 8 ounces.</note>, and on a touchstone <note>original: "lapide lydio"; a dark stone used to test the purity of precious metals by the color of the streak they leave.</note> you will observe not even the slightest hint of the color of the gold that was added;* on the contrary, let a round rod be made from a mark of fine silver, the length of a geometric foot, which is gilded with the two ducats. Afterward, let this rod be drawn, as is the custom, through various steel holes, each one narrower than the last—just as wire-drawers do. From this, you will draw approximately 100,000 feet of silver filaments, gilded on every side. 

I say now, the surface of this mark of silver is much more "tinted" <note>In alchemy, "tincture" refers to the coloring or transforming power of a substance.</note> than it was when those two ducats were cast into the melted silver; for then, their golden nature was not even visible. But now that this extension has been made, if you take a hundred filaments, join them tightly together, and cut this rope with pliers, you will find the gilded surface is everywhere, even inside. So much so that there is no doubt: if these gilded, stretched filaments could be melted and reduced back into a solid body—without losing the concentration and restriction of the stretched gilding—this body would be more than half gold. No one can deny this, just as anyone would be forced to admit *that all of this comes from extension.* Therefore, it is certain: *gold can be extended and multiplied in its tincture, and thus can tint more than when it was concentrated.*

The second question is: *is there something that can extend gold or silver by a physical means, without re-concentration, in the way I showed could be done somewhat mechanically?* 

I respond in the affirmative. For we see in the amalgamation of gold with Mercury <note>Quicksilver</note> that the mercury extends the gold very widely, which is the source of the gilding used by goldsmiths. Also, *gold mixed with the regulus of antimony <note>The metallic form of antimony.</note> and pulverized*, sprinkled like common glazing powder on earthenware, will gild ordinary pottery very widely as the antimony evaporates—a pleasant sight, if you proceed correctly. 

You heard above about the *leaves of concentrated rays* <note>Referring to the "sun powder" mentioned on the previous page.</note> and the singular penetrating power of *nitre <note>Saltpeter</note> and spirit of wine <note>Ethanol or high-proof alcohol.</note>*. I do not wish to hide from you that in common mercury there lies hidden such a penetrating force that, with the help of salts, it penetrates and tints even the thickest glass. *It rendered gold—the heaviest of all bodies we deal with—so subtle and penetrating that it passed through massive glass with the lightest heat, and the gold clung to the outside of the penetrated glass like leaves.* 

I know of a *metallic earth* which, when mixed with gold in flux <note>The state of being melted.</note> *and distilled from it several times*, penetrated it so thoroughly that it acquired a color *like the reddest blood*, without any increase in weight. When this gold was *cast upon silver, it tinted eight parts of it with the color of the best gold.* But because the penetrating cause was not yet fixed <note>In alchemy, "fixing" means making a volatile substance stable under heat so it does not evaporate.</note>, this golden nature was *re-concentrated in lead <note>original: "saturno"; Saturn is the alchemical name for lead.</note>*, even though it survived simple melting, antimony, and the "royal cement" <note>A refining process using salts and heat to purify gold by removing base metals.</note>. 

By the same logic, I have seen *running mercury* become very red; others claim this also happens with the *regulus of antimony*. But one must seek another being of a fixed disposition, which, as I said, is found in all things: *a most penetrating spirit, metallic in nature, and of a fixable disposition. For if common mercury [possesses] so much arsenical and antimonial metallic [earth]*...

...burdened and corrupted by a metallic quantity, yet it still penetrates gold in this way; what then do you think that substance would do which is the very essence of mercury, *and its purest spirit?* Therefore, use this to dissolve gold into the finest atoms, so that it may forever remain irreducible or incapable of being concentrated back into its old form (*on account of that fixed spirit introduced into the expanded pores of the dilated gold*); then coagulate it, and dissolve the coagulated mass again with new spirit, and recoagulate it—a process the Philosophers call "inceration" <note>Inceration is the process of softening a chemical substance to a wax-like consistency, usually by the gradual addition of a liquid.</note>. Do this many times until your gold is most subtly penetrated, subdued, and perfectly mixed with this fixed spirit. For then it will flow like wax *without smoke,* and whatever it touches, it will leave as perfected bodies, as the learned Palingenius <note>Marcellus Palingenius Stellatus, author of the 'Zodiacus Vitae,' a popular 16th-century didactic poem.</note> says. For it penetrates them like oil; and by its penetration, it achieves what I have told you so far. Let others speak of the change in metallic temperament which they ascribe to "tinctures" <note>A substance believed to have the power to change the color or nature of metals.</note>; I maintain that all this happens because of the entry and thinning out of the gold's penetration. All that you have heard so far is explained in an elegant process by *Nicholas Barnaud of Crista* <note>A 16th-century French physician and alchemist.</note> in his previously cited commentary, where he includes a memorable story:

*I remember it happened a little before I returned from Krakow to Prague—where I had been hosted for a year and a half by the most distinguished and learned Nobleman Thaddeus Hagecius <note>Tadeáš Hájek (1525–1600), a famous Czech astronomer and physician to Emperor Rudolf II.</note>, Doctor of Medicine and celebrated mathematician, and had been appointed physician to the most illustrious Lord William Ursinus of Rožmberk <note>Vilém z Rožmberka (1535–1592), a powerful Bohemian nobleman and supporter of alchemists.</note>, then Viceroy of the Kingdom of Bohemia, to look after his health—that by good fortune I encountered a Belgian man, a Doctor of Medicine named Anselm de Boodt <note>Anselmus de Boodt (1550–1632), a Flemish mineralogist and physician to Rudolf II.</note>. I formed a great familiarity with him, and I still enjoy and benefit from his friendship today. This good man, when he had arranged for a large collection of books from his deceased father's estate to be brought from Belgium to Prague, came across a small book which I eventually saw, written on ram's skin <note>Parchment.</note>, titled* The Golden Cymbal. *While he was thinking of recovering this with a new binding (for the boards it was bound in were broken), the Doctor removed a piece of the broken board. Quite unexpectedly, a hollow space appeared in the middle, covered with parchment, in which a small piece of paper was rolled up. On it was written the process for the Philosopher's Stone, together with a small portion of reddish powder, weighing about a grain <note>A very small unit of weight, roughly 65 milligrams.</note>, hidden away. At that time, Anselm was a most bitter hater of metallic philosophy <note>An alchemical skeptic.</note>, but moved by this sight, he performed an experiment upon mercury as the writing instructed. Throwing half of the powder into the fire upon the mercury, he saw the mercury turn into gold, not unlike natural gold. At first he was inflamed with excitement, then he was struck dumb; as he told it, his voice stuck in his throat. Afterward, he had a projection <note>The act of throwing the alchemical "stone" or powder onto a base metal to transmute it.</note> performed by a goldsmith with the same success. However, when the Doctor later attempted the written process to the letter, and many other experiments with Paul Grimmiller <note>The Supreme Examiner of mines in Bohemia.</note>, the chief inspector of His Imperial Majesty's mines in Bohemia, they were tried in vain. He threw down his shield, abandoned all chemical hope, and turned his mind elsewhere. Finally, he gave that process to me—which is not unlike the process found in Fernel's <note>Jean Fernel (1497–1558), an influential French physician.</note> book "On the Hidden Causes of Things"—and I now share it and make it public.* THE PROCESS. *Take two ounces of purest gold <note>original: "auri Obrizi"; gold of the highest refinement.</note>, and mix it with ten times as much mercury that has been prepared with great artistic skill; dissolve it with a gentle heat <note>original: "vulcano... languido"; literally "a sluggish Vulcan," referring to the god of fire.</note> until the mercury expires and the weight of the gold remains, reduced to a black powder. This powder, when melted, cannot be converted back into the former nature of gold. From this powder, using the heat of a water-vapor bath, draw out the mercury until the powder turns into a snow-white lime <note>original: "calcem"; calx, a powder produced by heating a metal.</note>. Sprinkle this seven times with the water that has been drawn off from it by evaporation, and work with every care so that by this frequent pushing and shaking, the substances may thin themselves out and emerge free from all filth and dross...*

### Chapter Six

...they yield the purest things, and receive the power of the superior and inferior things by descending into the earth and ascending again, as is read in the **Emerald Tablet of Hermes** <note>The 'Tabula Smaragdina,' a foundational text of Hermeticism which contains the famous phrase 'As above, so below.'</note>. This water is **Azoth** <term>Azoth: the universal solvent or "mercurial" spirit sought by alchemists</term>, the living spirit; the earth is the ferment; the water is the male, and the earth (or lime) is the female, from whose embrace the infant—the Stone—is born. 

But a woman does not conceive at just any time, but only when the womb has been prepared by nature for conception; therefore, putrefy the purified lime, or the **Sun of the Philosophers** <note>original: *solem Philoſophorum*; a common alchemical term for purified gold</note>, in a sealed vessel, or hide it away to digest for forty days until it thickens into a white and dense fluid. Into this, pour the water gradually at the proper daily intervals; this is the conjunction of the male and female, who are united in a marvelous way, and the female is entirely melted by her love for the male. This is the **solution**; leave it until it recovers its strength again, then let them come together once more, and do this so many times until the lime has drunk up all its water. Then let the "womb" be closed, lest anything escape, for then the infant grows solid, and from that frequent coagulation and solution, the Stone is solidified. 

All the Philosophers explain which colors arise during this; this powder shows these things to be true. Place this powder upon Mercury in a new crucible, yet in such a way that the Mercury has access to air; for two drachms <note>A unit of weight</note>, add a twelfth part of a grain, apply a strong fire, and afterward add borax. You will then have one drachm of gold. If you know the **multiplication** <note>The process of increasing the quantity and power of the alchemical medicine</note>, you will have no need of the Stone itself. You will find the entire process with me, if you are fortunate, with all its particulars; although this description suffices if you are diligent, for nothing is missing. Farewell, and you are unhappy indeed if you are pulled away from this work.

Thus far the Author. In his process, it should be noted that the basis is the frequent **inceration** <term>inceration: the process of softening a chemical substance to a wax-like consistency</term>, solution, and coagulation of gold with the spirit of Mercury. For in this way, the **tincture** <note>The transformative substance capable of transmuting metals</note> becomes penetrating and subtle, and thus the oily moisture is strongly mixed with the subtle earth. The reason he adds borax after the "projection" <note>The act of casting the tincture onto a base metal to transform it</note> is that he wishes to separate the dross <note>original: *scoreas*</note> of the Mercury from the gold in this manner. 

For just as a medicinal tincture in a person—as I noted at the beginning of this chapter—does not work in the human body unless the body is disposed by previous preparation, so also the metals to be tinted must be prepared and separated from foreign substances. Indeed, the gold itself, in its union with this spirit, casts off certain earthy impurities, as this process also notes. 

But above all, let the Philosopher and craftsman who approaches the preparation of this Mastery prepare **himself** as the primary object. Let him purge and free himself from the "dross" of greed, evil intent, and impiety. Next, let him diligently read **Geber** <note>Jabir ibn Hayyan, an 8th-century polymath considered the father of chemistry/alchemy</note>, book 1, chapters 3, 4, and 7, concerning the requirements of the craftsman. Then, let him speculate sufficiently in theory and leaf through approved authors, and, as **Basilius Valentinus** <note>A legendary 15th-century alchemist and monk</note> advises, let him look for the concordances (agreements) among different authors. 

"Do not, therefore," writes **Norton the Englishman** <note>Thomas Norton, author of the famous poem 'The Ordinal of Alchemy' (c. 1477)</note>, "trust the reading of a single book, but you must look to the works of many." 

"One book opens another," says the most learned **Arnaldus** <note>Arnaldus de Villa Nova (c. 1240–1311), a famous physician and alchemist</note>. **Anaxagoras** says the same about this work: "He who has been idle in reading books will not be able to be ready in preparing things." And **Bernard, Count of Treviso** <note>A 15th-century Italian alchemist known for his lifelong quest for the Stone</note>, expressly confesses that, after the grace of God, it was through the reading of good Philosophers, the collection of concordances among authors, and having held sufficient speculation upon them, that he possessed the true science perfectly in theory some years before he brought it into practice. 

It must be known, however, that the firmest theory of this science ought to be drawn not only from books, but also from the "hypotheses of nature"; all of which must be explored through practice. Otherwise, theoretical chemists are as useless as speculative physicians. For unless they move their hands to practice, they will work in vain.
