<meta>The previous page discussed the final stages of the alchemical process, specifically the solidification of the "Stone" through repeated solutions and coagulations. This page concludes the technical instruction with a call to practical experience and simplicity, ending with a prayer from the Hermetic tradition and the beginning of an author index.</meta>

# Supplement to *Subterranean Physics*, Chapter VI

...calls it, so Paracelsus in this place compels us toward practice; for he writes in the first chapter of his *Book on the Tincture of Philosophers*: *First, one must learn digestions, distillations, sublimations, reverberations, extractions, solutions, coagulations, fermentations, fixations, and everything required for this work; the instruments must be known through use, such as the glassware, cucurbits <term>cucurbit: a gourd-shaped chemical vessel used for distillation</term>, circulatory vessels, vessels of Hermes <note>original: vasa Hermetis; vessels sealed to be airtight</note>, baths, furnaces, coals, and others; only then will you be able to progress in Alchemy and medicine. However, as long as you cling to fictitious books through fantasy and opinion, you will be fit or predestined for none of these.* 

For in many things practice is contrary to theory; theories are usually subtle and multifaceted, while practices—if they imitate nature—are simple. This simplicity hinders many Artists <note>In this context, "Artist" refers to the skilled alchemist</note> from reaching the truth. Just as **Lull** <note>Raymond Lull (c. 1232–1315), a philosopher often associated with alchemical works</note>, as we cited at the beginning of this chapter, warned Physicians that they should *come from a plurality of recipients and medicines into unity*; so here I advise all Chemists to reduce the plurality of processes and chemical subjects into simplicity and unity. *For just as there is one universal, Catholic <note>original: *Catholica*; here used in its Greek sense of "universal" rather than referring to the Church</note>, harmonic, and primordial Religion of all religions; one language for all languages; one science for all sciences; so also there is one universal, Catholic, harmonic, and primordial matter for all matters, which they call Philosophical Matter.* One must aim for this, therefore, as the target and goal above all else, if one wishes to win the set prize. With this heartfelt warning, I conclude this little work and pray for the happy success of the efforts of all **Philochymists** <term>Philochymist: a lover of chemistry or alchemy</term>.

->Hermes near the end of the *Asclepius*<- <note>The *Asclepius* is a foundational Hermetic text attributed to Hermes Trismegistus</note>

> We give thanks to You, O Highest and Most Excellent. For by Your grace we have achieved such a light of Your knowledge; Your name is holy and to be honored, by which God alone is to be blessed with the religion of our fathers. For You deign to offer fatherly piety, religion, and love—and whatever efficacy is sweeter—to all, when You gift us with sense, reason, and intelligence. With sense, that we may know You; with reason, that we may track You through our wonder; with intelligence, that we, knowing You through knowledge, may rejoice and be made glad by Your divine power, through which You show Yourself entirely to us. We rejoice that You have deigned to consecrate us, while still situated in these bodies, to eternity. This is the only human thanksgiving: the knowledge of Your Majesty. We have known You, the Greatest Light, perceivable only by the intellect; we have understood You. O path of the true life! O fertile pregnancy of all natures! We have known You most fully by the conception of Your whole nature; we have known You, O eternal perseverance. In all this prayer, adoring the good of Your goodness, we ask only this: that You wish to keep us persevering in the love of Your knowledge, and never separate us from this kind of life.

# Register of Experiments recorded in this work.

*The Principal Experiment*, which this entire deduction discusses and for which the rest are brought forward, is the experiment of making *true and abundant iron* from common mud and *linseed* oil, in the space of a few hours, without the addition of any other material, and only with the help of fire. *Chapter Two.*

There follow other works of various authors related to this subject, as well as others by the author himself.

*The experiment of Michael Psellus the Greek*, to make gold by the crushing of certain stones and the mixing of certain herbs. *Preface.*

*The Experiment of Saint Thomas*, to bring about the true generation of metals by art. *Chapter I.* <note>Referring to Thomas Aquinas, to whom several alchemical treatises were falsely attributed in the medieval and early modern periods.</note>

*My own Experiment* to increase the fertile seminal quantity in vegetables. *In the same chapter.*

*On the generation and regeneration of metals*, experiments by various authors. *Chapter II.*

*The true reason why the magnet attracts iron.* *Chapter III.*

*The Experiment of a certain Englishman* for turning gold into Mercury, and that into a tincture. *In the same chapter.*

*Experiment* for making arsenic metallic.

*The Experiment of Saint John the Evangelist*, which the author most clearly and irrefutably proves to have occurred naturally, namely to make gold from twigs. *In the same chapter.* <note>This refers to a hagiographic legend where St. John transformed branches into gold and pebbles into gems to teach a lesson about the vanity of riches.</note>

*My own experiment*, to make Steel from iron with the help of twigs. *In the same [chapter].*

->Proving the Truth and Possibility of the transmutation of metals<-

# LEOPOLD. <note>Leopold I (1640–1705) was the Holy Roman Emperor and a significant patron of the sciences. Like many monarchs of his era, he maintained a keen interest in the potential of alchemy to bolster the imperial treasury.</note>

->AUGUSTINUS PETRAEUS’S PRAISE OF CHEMISTRY.<- <note>Augustinus Petraeus was a name associated with alchemical writings of the period; the name "Petraeus" (pertaining to rock or stone) is likely a symbolic reference to the Philosopher's Stone.</note>

The most noble art of Chemistry <note>original: "Chymiæ"</note> preserves a healthy person from diseases: it restores the sick to health: it relieves the poor from their poverty: it brings forth the hidden things of nature: it imbues the mind with solid knowledge: it does injury to no one: it benefits everyone: and finally leads to the knowledge of God <note>original: "DEI cognitionem"</note> himself.

# THE COLLECTION
## By the Archbishop Nicholas Melchior of Sibiu, Transylvania, formerly sent to Ladislaus, King of Hungary and Bohemia. <note>Nicholas Melchior of Sibiu (c. 1490–1531) was a Transylvanian priest and alchemist. He is famous for writing an alchemical mass, where the steps of the "Great Work" are paralleled with the liturgy of the Eucharist. King Ladislaus II Jagiello ruled Hungary and Bohemia until 1516.</note>

GOD, giver of all goodness, who especially at the end of time, by your goodness and wisdom alone, have inspired the light of the sacred Alchemical art <note>original: "sacræ artis Alchymicæ"</note> in your servant—not by his own preceding merits, but by your ineffable piety and preceding grace: grant, we beseech you, that what he has received as a gift from your Majesty may profit the health of his soul and body; and in him, mortify all vices and pour in the grace of virtue, so that he may faithfully employ this same sacred art solely for the praise and glory of your name and the propagation of the Christian faith, through our Lord Jesus Christ, Amen.

## The judgment of Abbot Trithemius of Sponheim on Alchemy. <note>Johannes Trithemius (1462–1516) was a Benedictine abbot, cryptographer, and polymath. While he was deeply learned in the occult sciences, he was often critical of those who sought alchemy for purely material gain.</note>

Chemistry <note>original: "Chymia"</note> is loved by many, and she is chaste; she has many familiar handmaidens who guard their Mistress with perpetual vigilance, and who substitute themselves in her name to preserve her from the advances of so many troublesome lovers, so that she remains untouched by such people for all eternity. Vanity, fraud, deceit, sophistry, greed, falsehood, over-confidence, lying, folly, poverty, despair, flight, banishment, and beggary are the attendants of Chemistry; feigning to be the Mistress herself so that they may keep her inviolate, they willingly prostitute themselves to lovers who are wealthy, avaricious, greedy, and arrogant.

<summary>This page contains a devotional prayer for the alchemist by Nicholas Melchior and a famous allegorical warning by Johannes Trithemius, which characterizes true Alchemy as a "chaste mistress" hidden behind a veil of vices that entrap the unworthy.</summary>

Having just finished the liturgical alchemical mass of Nicholas Melchior and the warnings of Trithemius, we now enter a formal "Preface to the Reader" written by the author (likely Becher himself or the compiler of this collection) to defend the inclusion of alchemical secrets in a book dedicated to the Emperor.</meta>

# Preface to the Reader.

Of three things I must give you an account, kind Reader, in this Preface; *First*, why I have undertaken to defend and vindicate Alchemy—a science hated by almost everyone, and indeed by the greatest men, suspected, ridiculed, and proscribed from all literary exchange, full of deceptions, frauds, buffoons, and impostures—before the whole world, and even in the sight of the *August Emperor Leopold* <note>Leopold I (1640–1705), Holy Roman Emperor, was a significant patron of the arts and sciences, including alchemy.</note>, not with words and testimonies, but with reasons and experiments? *Second*, why I have dedicated and inscribed this defense not to some private person, but to the Roman Emperor himself, and indeed in public print? *Third*, why I have brought forward such clear and transparent arguments and experiments in defense of Alchemy that I might seem to expose, profane, and prostitute the entire art before the worthy and unworthy alike? From these three points you will infer either that all the Alchemy-haters <note>original: "Misochymicos"</note>—that is, almost all the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle's philosophy, who dominated the universities and often argued that species (like metals) could not be changed.</note>—are mad for attacking Alchemy; or that I alone am mad for defending it. Furthermore, the demonstration that I undertake to defend before our most merciful Emperor will either fail to satisfy His Imperial Majesty, or it will succeed. If the former, I shall certainly incur the danger of public exposure and rashness before the whole world. If the latter—that is, if I prove the truth of Alchemy with my arguments—it is more than certain that a danger looms, and I will be close to being forced into a practical demonstration; since all Theory presupposes Practice <note>original: "Praxin"</note>. Third, you will infer that without the necessary demonstrations and arguments, the truth of Alchemy cannot be defended; but if these are published, the entire Art is made public. Thus, either I will not fulfill my promises regarding the demonstration, or if I do fulfill them, I will incur the curse <note>original: "anathema"</note> of all the Philosophers <note>In alchemical literature, "Philosophers" refers to the true masters of the art who swore to keep its secrets hidden from the "vulgar" or uninitiated.</note>. I shall respond briefly to each of these points in place of a preface, and I will inform the reader about everything as is proper.

-> I. <-

Regarding the first point or objection, I say: *The Art has no hater except the ignorant one.* <note>original: "Artem non habere osorem, nisi ignorantem." This was a common defensive motto among alchemists and artists of the Renaissance and Baroque periods.</note> No science is more hated and suspected by the world than *Jurisprudence* <note>The study of Law.</note>, inasmuch as more frauds, deceptions, rascals, and impostors are found within it, and it is more difficult to grasp and entangled in more contradictions. Yet it does not follow from this that Jurisprudence is not a science, that it should not be practiced, or that it should be outlawed from the public sphere. Because some people, beyond their calling, without order and without knowledge, rush into Chemistry, handle it badly, and—as they deserve—are impoverished by it, shall Alchemy therefore be a false science? Truly, he who undertakes to practice the art of glass-making and does not understand it should not wonder if he suffers loss, nor should he conclude that the art is impossible just because he himself is not skilled in it. And granted that some might truly be skilled in the Alchemical Art, yet in the meantime live very wickedly, it does not follow that the science is false. Most of the best painters live very extravagantly, but what does their poorly-mannered life have to do with the industrious pictures they paint? Thus, even if a luxurious buffoon, or even a heretic, produces true gold through the Chemical art, what does this man’s malice have to do with the quality of the gold? If it followed that "some Alchemists are rascals, therefore all Alchemists are rascals," then it would also follow that "some Theologians, Lawyers, and Politicians are Heretics and Atheists,"

# Preface

...[they are] Atheists, and without conscience; therefore all Theologians, Jurists, and Politicians are such. You see, therefore, that neither the ignorance nor the malice of **Alchemists** has any bearing on the truth or falsehood of the art of **Alchemy**; nor should **Alchemy** be held in such hatred just because it does not succeed for everyone who is "keeping a bad holiday" <note>original: "male feriatis" – a Latin idiom referring to the idle, the incompetent, or those who lack the proper devotion to the work.</note>. For how many are there who have spent their whole age and resources in the study of Jurisprudence <note>The science and philosophy of law.</note>; yet, not having attained its end, they are thus impoverished? By what right then would such people attribute their lost time and expenses to Jurisprudence? Certainly, I do not see by what right **Alchemy** ought to be pursued with hatred.

For just as a beautiful maiden is not the cause of someone looking at her and perishing miserably for love of her—since he could turn his face elsewhere—so **Alchemy** forces no one, nor does it harm any except the willing, since everyone is free either to cultivate or neglect it. Furthermore, **Alchemy** impoverishes men less than gambling, comedies, and hunting, which are nevertheless neither prohibited nor hated; indeed, **Alchemy** does not harm the Public Good <note>original: "Bono Publico"</note>, but intends to benefit it. For if procuring gold were an evil, then it would also be an evil to dig for gold at the risk of life and with uncertain costs. Yet, who is ignorant of the fact that metal mines are granted many privileges solely for the public good? Why then should it not be permitted to seek gold outside the mines—even if it were done at the same expense and risk—rather than only within the mines?

Moreover, if metal is not found in the mines, nothing else is found; but truly, even if the desired goal in **Alchemy** is not acquired, other sciences and experiments that are not to be despised are encountered. Thus, by the occasion of **Alchemy**, **gunpowder** <note>original: "pulvis pyrius"</note>, the **art of glassmaking**, **Enameling**, **Soap-making**, **Dyeing**, and many other crafts were discovered; I say nothing of **Medicines**, the growth of vegetables, and many other most curious secrets. An **Alchemist**, therefore, if he reaches the desired goal, can benefit his neighbor with both health and wealth; if he does not reach it, at least he harms no one else but himself: and not even to such an extent that he does not have the means to live honestly, provided he proceeds with moderation and does not spend money profusely on the art.

But, you will say, many are impoverished by seeking this art and scatter their goods on an uncertain thing. What then? Are not **Mining**, **Commerce**, and **farming the land** honest businesses? Yet meanwhile they are uncertain, since their end can never be certainly pledged. Should they therefore be abandoned? Should they therefore be prohibited? Even though it is certain that many are impoverished by them. Furthermore, you will object that it is most certain that very few, and scarcely one among a thousand, reach this art; therefore it is rash to hope for that fortune which scarcely happens to the thousandth man. To which I respond: it is certain by the words of our Savior himself that very few will enter the Kingdom of God; would it therefore follow that it is rash to aspire to the **Kingdom of Heaven** because it happens to so few to enter?

Finally, you will say that the word **Alchemy** sounds bad; but I reply that the words **Contribution**, **Impost**, **Excise**, **Interest**, **Tolls**, **Usury**, the **Treasury**, and such things sound worse, by which the goods of subjects are exhausted and burdened. Certainly, if the "sinews of affairs" <note>A common political metaphor: "nervus rerum," the essential strength or driving force of a state.</note>, according to the Politicians, is money—without which the Republic cannot be preserved, and for the sake of which a Prince may impose on his subjects almost whatever burdens come into his mind—then I would dare to say that no science, no proposition, and no estate is more honorable or useful for a Prince, nor more profitable for his subjects, than **Alchemy**: whatever that *Weber* <note>Likely referring to a contemporary critic or "Regular Canon" who wrote against alchemy; possibly Johann Georg Weber.</note>, that Regular Canon, writes against **Alchemy** in his *Principal Spirit*, the Prince...

# To the Reader

...and dissuades princes from it, with a style and doctrine surely less than Princely. For in **Alchemy** there is no shameful money-lending <term>original: "foeneratio" – the practice of lending money at interest, often used pejoratively here as usury</term>, no overtaxing of subjects, no sucking dry of another's purse; but rather the production of gold or silver, without prejudice to any Mortal. It is as if Most Holy Nature provided this, so that she who could not establish mines in every location might at least grant the art of maturing Metals outside of the mines, and of increasing and multiplying gold and silver without shameful usury. 

If, therefore, the Haters and Despisers of **Alchemy** would look more deeply into their own motives and behold **Alchemy** itself, they would surely find it commendable for the Public Good, for one's Neighbor, and for Oneself in every respect. For how many of the subjects' substances must be drained almost to the point of blood before the Treasury <term>original: "Fiscus"</term> acquires a thousand Ducats <note>A gold coin used as a standard currency throughout Europe.</note>; how many seas a Merchant must cross; how many shameful usuries must be established until he gains 50 for every 100; how many frauds must fill the arts and manufactures so that a gold coin may be obtained; and how many most learned and famous men must undergo shameful services just to earn a meager little salary! I say nothing of the prostitution of Justice—making it for sale—for the sake of some filthy and paltry gain! 

**Alchemy** cures all these things. For it removes the scarcity of things, greed, envy, filth, abject servitude, uncertainty, and the constant worry over one's means; it provides a true refuge and a constant companion <note>original: "vade mecum"</note> to the harbor of liberty. Therefore, I am not ashamed to defend this art, for almost nothing is more useful to the human race. Nor am I insane when I defend this art; rather, those are insane—indeed, they are slanderers—who, even when all their objections have been resolved, intend and proceed to tear it apart further with nothing but insults and calumnies. But for those whose habit it is to speak ill even of the Greatest Princes, they will speak ill of any science or thing according to the measure of their own character; for one must expect nothing but a croak from a crow, even if he betrays himself by that very song.

However, before I finish this point, an objection still occurs to me that must be dissolved. It was proposed by a certain Politician—whether subtle or dull—as if it were an insoluble Gordian knot <note>An ancient metaphor for an extremely complex problem, famously "solved" by Alexander the Great cutting it with a sword.</note>, with which he wonderfully flatters himself and thinks he has branded an inextinguishable stigma upon all of **Alchemy**. He argues thus:

Therefore, this Art was unknown to Solomon, and is thus non-existent and nothing.*

To which argument I respond by first granting the major premise <note>In formal logic, the "major premise" is the broad general statement that forms the basis of an argument.</note>; for I do not deny that Solomon had a knowledge of natural things infused by God. For he who understood the nature of vegetables from the Hyssop even to the Cedar <note>A reference to 1 Kings 4:33, describing Solomon’s vast biological knowledge.</note>, why would he not also have understood the nature of Minerals? However, I hardly believe that the general knowledge infused in Solomon extended so far into specifics that he knew every particular science. Hence, I would almost dare to assert that the art of preparing gunpowder, glass, paper, the printing press, and many other things were unknown to him. 

As for the minor premise <note>The specific claim that Solomon's actions prove he lacked alchemical knowledge.</note>, I deny it entirely. For let it be that Solomon favored trade by establishing voyages in Tyre and Sidon; that he extracted gold from Ophir; and that he demanded contributions from his subjects. It does not follow from this that the **Philosophers' Stone**...

<meta>This page continues the author’s response to a critic he calls the "Great Politician." The author is arguing that the possession of alchemical secrets does not lead a ruler to neglect his state duties, but rather provides a unique resource for the treasury.</meta>

->### Preface<-

...that the ancients did not possess the secret of the Philosophers. For granting—and may God bring it to pass—that our most August Emperor Leopold <note>Leopold I (1640–1705), Holy Roman Emperor, who was known to have a keen interest in alchemy.</note> should possess the **Philosophical Tincture** <term>Philosophical Tincture: a liquid form of the Philosopher's Stone used to transmute metals</term>; would that "Great Politician" then suggest that the Emperor should foster no commerce? That he should release his subjects from every contribution and tax, and thus from their devotion? Or indeed, that he should neglect all the gold and silver-bearing mines in Hungary and his own hereditary domains? Far be this from sound and political reasoning. *For public matters are not to be neglected on account of private ones.* <note>original: "Non enim publica negligenda sunt propter privata."</note>

And I would wish that politician to speculate a little more deeply: why did King Solomon establish a voyage to **Ophir** <note>A biblical port or region famous for its wealth; its actual location has been debated for centuries.</note> for the sake of gold? He will surely say: if Solomon could have made gold in his residence at Jerusalem, why was it necessary to cross such a great sea? To which I respond: it is not contradictory for Solomon to have had gold mines in **Ophir**, or to have known how to acquire it from there, and yet still have possessed the **Tincture** at home without abandoning his other sources. 

Furthermore, if he possessed the Stone, he might have chosen to prepare it in a distant place—which he called **Ophir**—rather than among his courtly family and neighbors, among whom no secret is safe. There, in that remote location, he could have transmuted base metal into gold and then brought it back by ship. Certainly, the best theologians and philosophers who have commented on Solomon estimate that **Ophir** was in the *East Indies*. But it is strange that no traces of such mines remain today; they surely ought to exist as notable pits or excavations, seeing as such a great abundance of gold and silver was dug out of them. For it is expressly written of Solomon *that he made gold and silver as common as stones on the ground.* <note>2 Chronicles 1:15.</note>

In truth, it is most certain that no silver mine exists in the **East Indies**. But if anyone says that Solomon established a voyage to *America*, I use the same foundation: no traces of Solomon’s mines exist there either. I pass over the fact that a voyage to such unknown and distant places would be equally uncertain, as it could not be completed without the use of the **Magnet** <note>original: "Magnetis"; the author refers here to the mariner's compass, which he correctly notes was unknown in Solomon's time.</note> which was unknown at that time. 

Or, if Solomon brought so much gold or silver from those parts by way of trade, it is not credible that those foreign peoples simply gave gold and silver to Solomon as a gift or offered it of their own accord. I ask you, what could be found in Judea, or in the whole of Solomon’s Empire, that would have been a fair and equivalent trade good to exchange for such a vast abundance of gold and silver? 

I also pass over the greatest argument: King Solomon’s son, **Rehoboam**, who was most greedy for gold, immediately neglected that gold-bearing voyage toward **Ophir** after his father’s death. Truly, I believe that he was ignorant of his father’s science <note>i.e., alchemy</note>. For he would not have so quickly forgotten or neglected his father’s enormous revenues—he who was certainly the first to greatly oppress his subjects due to a shortage of money. 

Furthermore, the gold brought from **Ophir**, according to the testimonies of writers, was much nobler than natural gold; it was of such quality and purity that even now nothing like it is found in either of the Indies. Therefore, it must be supposed that Solomon made gold by Art, and did so in a remote location, feigning a long voyage to hide the Secret. Otherwise, that most useful voyage would not have been lost or neglected so quickly after Solomon’s death, for gold mines could not have failed so suddenly. 

Whether, therefore, King Solomon practiced this science or did not, it does not mean that he did not know it; for we know many things that we do not put into practice. Or suppose he was entirely ignorant of this Art—which is not established—it does not follow that the Art of making gold is impossible simply because Solomon...

### To the Reader

...whether he knew it or not; whether he practiced it or not. As I have said, there is no universal rule stating that everything Solomon did not know is impossible. Indeed, more reasons stand in my favor—that Solomon did possess this knowledge—than against it. I conclude: *if the science of transmuting imperfect metals into gold is based upon natural and rational foundations, then it is certain that Solomon, if he possessed knowledge of all natural things, must have possessed this art as well, whether he exercised it or not.* The first part of this statement is true; therefore, the latter is also true, which has already been conceded to me in the thesis by that "Politician" <note>Referring back to the critic mentioned on the previous page.</note> who objects to my work. That the first part is true—namely, that this Art is founded upon and proven by natural principles—I shall demonstrate most abundantly and irrefutably in this, my Philosophical Demonstration, through this very book of mine. Therefore, it is clear and transparent that Solomon possessed this knowledge, and our Politician's objection is foolish, frivolous, and worthless. If, henceforth, our "Great Bartholus" <note>Likely a mocking reference to a contemporary polymath or "know-it-all," possibly referring to the legal scholar Bartolus de Saxoferrato as a placeholder for a pedant, or a specific contemporary encyclopedist like Bartholomaeus Keckermann.</note>, this Encyclopedist and "All-Wise" man, does not use firmer and more solid arguments and reasons in matters of politics, military affairs, finance, and the public state than he does in these Alchemical and Philosophical matters, then he will surely perform his profession much more unsuccessfully and unproductively than I do mine—namely, in vindicating the most noble art of Alchemy from trifles and slanders.

->II.<-

Regarding the second point: why I have dared to inscribe and dedicate these theses of mine to our **Most Invincible Emperor** <note>Leopold I (1640–1705), to whom this work is dedicated.</note>, and indeed to do so in public print before the entire literary and philosophical world, supported by reasons and arguments based on natural principles. To this I respond: it seemed to me entirely permissible. For if any buffoon is allowed to publicly mock Alchemy on the stage, in the Emperor's very residence—even in the face of the Court—and to expose it to the mockery, ridicule, and contempt of all (as was done during this recent **Bacchanalia** <note>The Carnival season before Lent, often celebrated with rowdy plays and satirical performances at the Habsburg court.</note>), why should it not also be permitted for a philosopher to defend, praise, and commend it in public writings with serious arguments and useful demonstrations before the learned and the **Friends of Chemistry** <term>Philochymicis: lovers or friends of chemistry/alchemy</term>? Furthermore, it is my duty to treat a serious matter seriously. For His Sacred Imperial Majesty gave me a commission to watch over and apply myself to these chemical matters. Since, therefore, things have reached the point where not only the science itself (the very subject of my commission) is regarded as a vain thing by the **Alchemy-haters** <term>Misochymicis: those who hate or have an aversion to alchemy</term>, but I myself am also attacked on its account and passed over for promotion in favor of others, I deemed it necessary to defend both the Art and myself. Primarily, I defend the one who gave me the commission: our most August Emperor. Although he once turned away from this Art, since he witnessed its truth with his own eyes and most sufficient experience two years ago, he has begun to respect it. When he was immediately marked with an unfair judgment by certain rigid censors—as if he were dealing with a playful and empty thing—I could not help but challenge them, and convict them of vanity and rashness. Let this Philosophical Demonstration cast a bit and a bridle upon those to whom Imperial Clemency has left the reins of blathering, so that they do not bray and kick without understanding like *horses and mules* <note>original: "equi & muli"; a biblical reference to Psalm 32:9.</note>, or even like common **Asses**. To silence them is, as I have already protested many times in this preface, the sole and primary goal of my writing.

### III.

To reach the final point of my preface: why have I undertaken the defense of this “besieged Sparta”? <note>The author uses the metaphor of "defending Sparta" to refer to taking up a difficult and often-attacked duty or province of knowledge.</note> This is partly clear from what has preceded, and partly, regarding the method of defense, it will be clear from what follows. For a Physician, it is no shame—indeed, it is necessary—to understand <term>Philosophy</term> <note>In the 17th century, "Philosophy" or "Natural Philosophy" referred to the study of nature and the physical universe, the precursor to modern science.</note>. Moreover, the greatest parts of Philosophy are <term>Physics</term> and <term>Mathematics</term>; my other writings will bear witness to what I have achieved in both.

Truly, a deep—indeed, a subterranean—branch of Physics is the knowledge and cultivation of metals. Therefore, no sane person would dare declare it unseemly or inappropriate for one who handles <term>Medicine</term> or <term>Cameralist affairs</term> <note>Cameralism (Cameralia) was the science of public administration and the management of the state's treasury and economy.</note> and the Prince’s treasury to cultivate this study. Yet let no one believe that the cultivation of metals can be fully and perfectly understood without <term>Alchemy</term>. Indeed, let him know for certain that if he shrinks from the name of Alchemy, he must also, by the same reasoning, either fail to understand or else neglect the cultivation of metals, coinage, and indeed the whole of <term>Metallurgy</term>—which is the principal part of his Prince's treasury. Thus, it is in no way contrary to my profession to write about this Art, to cultivate it, and to labor on experiments concerning it for its improvement.

I would not deny, of course, that those who spend their entire time trying to discover the <term>Philosophers’ Stone</term> <note>The legendary alchemical substance capable of turning base metals into gold and granting long life.</note> based on uncertain foundations perhaps do not benefit the Prince or fulfill their duty. Such a pursuit has been so far from my own practice that I have not only focused my primary aim on the useful processing, <term>maturation</term> <note>Alchemists believed metals "ripened" or matured into gold within the earth over long periods; the chemist sought to accelerate this natural process.</note>, and separation of metals and minerals, but I have also been able to secure many thousands <note>Original: "multa millia," likely referring to gold florins or thalers for the state budget.</note> annually for our Most August Emperor, far exceeding the common methods of handling metals and minerals. (Were it not for that <term>cacoëthes</term> <note>original: "cacoëthes," a Greek-derived term for a "bad habit" or "malignant custom."</note>—that wicked custom of admitting nothing new, however useful—which has established its unshakable seat in this Court just as it has in almost all other places). Indeed, I have also been occupied with the greatest labors regarding the useful introduction of commerce and other propositions, as very many official records testify concerning these activities of mine. I shall pass over the fact that in the few spare hours remaining to me, I have not ceased to benefit the <term>Republic of Letters</term> <note>original: "rei literariæ," the international community of scholars and intellectuals.</note> through various published writings, offering both counsel and aid.

Thus, there is a great difference between *cultivating Alchemy so that all other duties are abandoned*; *cultivating Alchemy solely for the sake of the Philosophers’ Stone*; and *cultivating Alchemy for the better processing of metals and minerals, which is more useful to the Prince and the Fatherland.*

To come to the second part of this point: I shall place this Philosophical Demonstration before your eyes with such clear arguments that even an envious eye shall not be clouded by them. In all my writings, I have always aimed *to write my own observations rather than those of others; to be clear rather than obscure; and to be succinct rather than long-winded.* For he who wishes to write what no one can understand would do a far better thing by remaining silent. Nevertheless, I am never unmindful of that well-worn proverb: *“The writer should always know more than his text.”* The gravity of the subject in this Demonstration required that I present my proofs visibly and write with the utmost clarity; yet from this very fact, the wise Reader will gather—and will not, I hope, think me entirely foolish—just how much still lies hidden, and how much I have kept silent regarding the practical application of the Art. For it is one thing to demonstrate that a route to the Indies exists, and quite another to sail to the Indies in person. *I wished to demonstrate the truth and possibility of the Art, but not to reveal and publish every hidden bolt and bar of the Art that is not necessary for this Demonstration.* You may object: *“How is it possible for one to show the way if he has not walked it himself?”* I respond:

A distinction must be made between Theory and Practice; it is one thing to know, and another to do. Mathematicians know and demonstrate the infallible distance of the Sun from the Moon; meanwhile, none of them has ever measured that distance with their own feet. Indeed, there would be few sciences in <term>Philosophy</term> <note>In this context, "Philosophy" refers to "Natural Philosophy," the study of the physical world and its laws.</note> unless they could be demonstrated more through Theory than through Practice. In Holland, there was a bookseller who perhaps never traveled outside the city where he lived; yet he delighted in <term>Hydrographic Maps</term> <note>Nautical charts used for sea navigation.</note>. With his compass, he discovered on those maps a much shorter and safer way of sailing to the East Indies than had been known before, even to the most skilled sea captains who had made the journey many times. This method was eventually embraced by the <term>East India Company</term> <note>original: "Societate Indiæ Orientalis"—The Dutch East India Company (VOC), the massive trading corporation that dominated 17th-century maritime commerce.</note> and has been practiced until now, not without a reward being given to that bookseller. Thus, it is no wonder if I too demonstrate a path, which it is neither established that I have reached the end of, nor would I wish it to be known if I had. 

Furthermore, I know there will be some to whom this Demonstration would be more pleasing if, following that saying of <note>original: "solve mihi hunc syllogismum"—Solve this syllogism for me.</note> **Arnold of Villanova** <note>A famous 13th-century physician and alchemist.</note>, I were to practically offer several pounds of the <term>Tincture</term> <note>The "Philosophers' Tincture" or "Stone," the substance believed to transform base metals into gold.</note> to His Majesty. I know, I say, that such people value money more than knowledge; but such people look more toward the money-changers than toward the Philosophers. *Happy indeed is he who possesses the effects of things, although the Poet proclaims only that man happy who is able to know the causes of things.* <note>A paraphrase of the Roman poet Virgil: "Felix, qui potuit rerum cognoscere causas."</note> 

His Most Sacred Majesty possesses a small amount of that powder, or the true Tincture of the Philosophers; he has seen its memorable effect, and the true <term>Transmutation</term> of metals into gold, as often as he wishes. But he does not know how to either prepare or multiply that powder; nor does the one who gave it know, for he found it by chance already prepared. Would it not be better to have discovered the science than merely the Art? 

Finally, I shall conclude: there are those who believe that this science, whether speculative or practical, will not be safe in the hands of powerful princes. What other Princes may do, or will do, with the possessors of this art, I do not know; but this I would dare to affirm: that however many philosophers, whether true or false, have come to this Imperial Court so far and proposed anything of this kind, they have always been most mercifully received and treated by His Imperial Majesty, even if they knew and performed nothing—indeed, even if they knowingly deceived him. I have often observed that he has almost committed an excess of Mercy. Far from the minds of good Princes and true Philosophers is that popular folly and greed: *"If I had this Art, I would start wars, I would crush my enemies, I would prepare an innumerable supply of gold and silver for myself, I would build I know not what magnificent works, I would give full rein to luxury and lust, and finally, I would omit nothing that would demonstrate to the World, through these charming arguments, that I possess the Tincture."* 

Thus think tyrants and fools, who measure the use of the Tincture according to the scale of their own perverse and humble minds. From this, they conclude that no Philosophers possess the true Tincture, provided they are not infected with the same insanity of ostentation and vain glory. If I am also convinced by this argument—that I know nothing of this art—I shall bear it with an even mind. My business is not with Politicians, but with Philosophers. To be defeated by these latter would be a mark of rashness and ignorance for me, since, as I said at the beginning of this point, I have undertaken to defend this "Sparta" <note>A reference to the Greek proverb "You have obtained Sparta, now adorn it," meaning to fulfill one's duty in a difficult province.</note>, and I hope I shall defend it manfully. 

But you, benevolent Reader, expect nothing more from me in the realm of Chemistry beyond my long-promised second book of *Subterranean Physics* and this Demonstration, which serves as a supplement to it. For no one, to finish with a quote from **Plautus**, shall come out from here: *"All the spectators (as far as practice goes) will finish the business inside."* <note>Original: "Spectatores omnes... intus conficient negotium." This is a play on a theatrical exit line, suggesting that the actual laboratory work (practice) remains private or "behind the scenes."</note> For I conclude with this most firm thesis:

->**He is an ass who speaks against Alchemy, but he is a fool and a scoundrel who**<-
->**offers it for sale in practice.**<-

## Preliminaries for a more easy understanding of my Philosophical Demonstration.

### I.

<margin>Transmutation is twofold: Essential and Accidental.</margin>
Transmutation is defined as the change or alteration of one body into another; *it is twofold, either essential*, where the internal form of the body is transmuted, such as when an egg is changed into a chick, a silkworm into a butterfly, or flesh into a maggot; *or accidental*, where the internal form remains, and only the *accidents* <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "accidents" are the non-essential properties of a thing, such as color, smell, or hardness, that can change without the thing becoming a different kind of substance.</note> are changed, as when sweet *wine* becomes *sour*, or unripe fruit *ripens*. *Essential transmutation of one form into another proceeds from generation and corruption <note>original: "generatione & corruptione" — The natural cycle of birth/creation and decay/destruction.</note>, but accidental transmutation of accidents proceeds from digestion and penetration. Indeed, Nature is occupied daily with both kinds of transmutation; and experience teaches, as much in the birth, mixture, and alteration of animals, plants, and minerals, that the art of Nature can be of great service in transmutations of this kind.*

### II.

<margin>The subject of transmutation into gold is every metallic body.</margin>
If, therefore, anything can be transmuted into *gold* by the Alchemical art, the question will then be whether such a transmutation occurs *either in the form or in the matter* of the subject being transmuted; and which subject is closer to this transmutation. To which I respond: those bodies are always more closely related to one another in transmutation, both essential and accidental, which most closely agree in weight; *for quantity is the first and principal accident of bodies.* Moreover, we see that no bodies are more similar to and consistent with gold in weight and all accidents than *metals*: hence we can conclude that metals, above all other subjects, are more easily transmutable into gold. Whether their form, or only the *accidents of their matter*, are transmuted into gold, is also necessary to know. I say that *all metals have only one and the same essential form* and matter, consisting in the cooking and perfection of <term>quicksilver</term> <note>original: "argenti vivi" — Mercury. Alchemists believed mercury was the "mother" or base matter of all metals.</note> as the matter of metals; and that the form of lead, tin, copper, iron, silver, etc., which appears *special and specific* to us, differs neither in form nor in matter, but only resides *in accidents* resulting *from the variety of cooking and purity* of the quicksilver. Hence, if such metallic matter—namely, quicksilver—should be *purest and most perfectly cooked*, pure and uniform, it then appears to us under the form of *gold*; but if it is *most imperfect*, then it appears as *iron*, and thus according to the degrees of cooking and purity of the quicksilver, it appears to us under the species of lead, tin, and the rest of the minerals. From these things it is clear that metals are not specified and diversified from one another *essentially*, but only *accidentally*, and thus *not an essential but only an accidental transmutation into gold is required, which consists solely in the purging and digestion of quicksilver, as the matter of metals.*

### III.

### III.

<margin>The transmuting Object, or Tincture</margin>
*The Object that transmutes metals into gold must be a certain material subject, of the substance of quicksilver <note>original: "argenti vivi" — mercury</note>, but of a quality contrary to common quicksilver. This subject is called the Tincture, or the Philosophers' Stone;* it is called a "tincture" because it "tints" or dyes metals into gold. Its preferred name, however, is derived from its common color, which serves as an accident <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, an "accident" is a property like color or smell that is visible to the eyes but does not define the essence of a thing.</note> perceptible to the sight. <margin>The Philosophers' Stone or stone of the Philosophers</margin> It is called the *Philosophers' Stone* because Chemical Philosophers <note>Alchemists</note> are occupied with preparing this Tincture; it is called a *Stone* because, to the outward eye, it resembles the appearance of a ruby, yet it is gold. Furthermore, this definition applies to the *Tincture* in every respect; for the *Tincture* must be something real, not something imaginary, nor something found in the "hollow of the Moon" <note>A reference to the sublunary sphere, often used to describe fantastical or unreachable things in old cosmology.</note>, nor some fantastical Peripatetic <note>Refers to the school of Aristotle.</note>, Aristotelian, or Galenic <note>Refers to the medical system of Galen.</note> faculty. Instead, it must be a real and material subject, just as the subject that must be transmuted is also a real, existing metal. Next, this *Object* or *Tincture* must be of the *substance of quicksilver*, that is, it must be metallic; otherwise, it would have no *entry* into the metals. For nothing essentially enters into metals, or mixes with them, that is not of *their own nature*. It has been taught previously that their nature is quicksilver; therefore, if the Tincture is to enter the metal, it is necessary that it be made of the substance of quicksilver. *For without entry, there is no contact; and without contact, there is no action; since no action occurs at a distance without the intervening medium being affected. Without action, truly, there is no mixing, alteration, or tempering.* Finally, the *Tincture* must be quicksilver in its substance, but contrary to common quicksilver in its qualities; otherwise, it could not *transmute* the quicksilver within the metals—namely, their metallic substance. This transmutation depends on the "temperament" <note>The specific balance of qualities like heat, cold, moisture, and dryness.</note>. But since the qualities of common quicksilver, and that which exists in imperfect metals, are clearly found to be crude, cold, volatile, impure, and heterogeneous <note>Composed of diverse, mismatched parts.</note>, it necessarily follows that the *Tincture, or that quicksilver which serves as the tincture, must be of a contrary temperament: namely, of qualities that are cooked, hot, fixed, pure, and homogeneous <note>Uniform and consistent in nature.</note>.* But such a subject, which is quicksilver in its substance and yet contrary to common quicksilver in its qualities, is found nowhere except in gold. Therefore, we rightly conclude that *gold is the true Object of the transmutatory art.*

### IV.

<margin>The Form, or its mode of acting through reconciliation</margin>
*I define the form of the Tincture as being of a subtle, permanent fixity,* a definition which I defend as follows. *SUBTLE:* for if imperfect metals are to be transmuted into gold by the Tincture, they must be altered in their temperament; but this alteration cannot happen except through the introduction of other qualities closer to gold. These qualities, however, cannot be introduced unless they reside within the subject to which they belong, namely gold. Therefore, gold must necessarily be mixed intimately with the metals; for without contact there is no mixing, and true contact...

<margin>

</margin>
Physicality consists in penetration, according to the Philosopher <note>Aristotle is often referred to simply as "The Philosopher" in Scholastic and Alchemical texts.</note>: *Every physical penetration is a true transmutation.* Gold, however, being a dense body, does not mix in its smallest parts with metals in such a way that it can imprint its powers and qualities upon them, nor can it be separated from them again without its powers being changed and without reaction. Therefore, it must be refined <note>original: "subtiliari" — to be made 'subtle' or fine, a process of breaking down a substance to its most essential, penetrative form.</note>, so that it may penetrate, alter, and temper the metals, which was the point to be proved.

**OF FIXITY.** <note>original: "FIXITATIS"</note> I have proved before that gold must be refined; this concerns the body—namely the substance of gold—not its qualities, which must remain unchanged; indeed, they must be exalted through this refining. Hence, any refining of gold that removes its qualities is to be rejected. The most powerful quality of gold, however, is its <term>fixity: the property of a substance to remain stable and solid when exposed to extreme heat, rather than evaporating</term>, by which gold is specifically distinguished from all other bodies by its very definition. Therefore, in the refining of gold, its fixity must be retained. Hence, the *Tincture* is well-defined by Geber <note>Geber is the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan (c. 721–815), a foundational figure in alchemy whose works were central to European science.</note>: namely, that it consists of a subtle fixity. And to be fixed is to be earthy; therefore, the absolute form of the Tincture will be earthy—namely, a fine powder, which is defined by Esdras as "a small powder from which gold is made." Where by "small," he means subtle and penetrating. For that which penetrates must not be large, but small. By "powder," he means a subtle earthy substance, as defined by Albertus Magnus <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280) was a German Dominican friar and philosopher who wrote extensively on the natural sciences and alchemy.</note>. But those bodies whose end-state is most fixed (that is, most earthy) must have a beginning that is most volatile (that is, most watery); for everything watery tends toward the earthy, just as every liquid tends toward the solid. Since the end-goal of the Tincture is a subtle earthy substance, its beginning must necessarily be a subtle watery or moist substance, an oily or incombustible oil that does not wet the hands. Such a moisture is quicksilver <note>original: "argentum vivum" — mercury</note>; therefore, the beginning of the Tincture, or the initial form of the Stone, will be the conversion of gold into quicksilver.

Now I say that no refining happens without the extension of the tiny particles; and no extension happens without the insertion of other tiny particles. Therefore, if gold is to be refined, then its particles or atoms <note>original: "atomi" — used here to describe the smallest constituent parts of matter.</note> must necessarily be expanded or stretched out; but such an expansion, so that no vacuum is created, cannot happen without the insertion of other particles. Indeed, all particles that could possibly be inserted would be of fire, air, water, or earth. Therefore, they must be earthy particles. But nothing from that class can be fundamentally united with gold, except for that which equals gold in weight, or at least comes very close to it; *for light things do not unite with heavy things, but float on top.* But no earthy body that is very heavy will also be subtle; rather it will be

hard, coarse, dense: therefore all stones, sands, earths, and minerals are to be rejected. But the common living silver of the masses is too humid, watery, cold, and indefinite for dissolving gold, which is the most fixed and hottest of all bodies; furthermore, on account of its indefinite humidity, it can never be coagulated into a fixed, meltable state by simple digestion alone. Therefore, there follows another "living silver," more digested, hot in its moisture, and proportioned for dissolving gold, establishing a reaction with the gold during the solution, and, through digestion alone, undergoing a fixed and meltable coagulation with it—namely, a permanent one that persists with the gold and preserves it from re-concentrating <note>The author means the gold remains in its refined, penetrative state rather than clumping back together into a solid, inert mass.</note>.

This living silver is indeed found in a mineral full of the hottest and most golden sulfur; such is iron. Its earthy golden part requires a most subtle moisture, such as is found in <term>antimony</term>. From these joined together, a subtle, earthy, and oily moisture arises, a living silver or <term>Mercury</term>; this is what the Philosophers call their own <note>original: "Mercurius Philosophorum," the secret starting material of the alchemical Great Work, distinct from the common mercury found in shops.</note>, having the power to permanently refine gold without it re-concentrating, which was the point to be demonstrated.

# THE GENERAL ARGUMENT OF ALL
## THESES.

God exists; from whom comes the life of all things; from which comes motion; from this, action and passion; hence, alteration; from which comes the transmutation of bodies, even of metals into gold. Metallic bodies are closest to this transmutation—not in their matter, which is "living silver," but in their form, namely differing by the degree of their <term>decoction: the process of 'cooking' or maturing a substance through steady heat</term>. Therefore, their matter can be perfected by decoction and can take on another form. 

This decoction of crude living silver occurs through a living silver that is more than perfectly cooked (namely, through the "concocting object," which is similar to common living silver in its substance for the sake of entry, but in its quality and temperament is contrary to it in the fourth degree for the sake of alteration). This subject is gold—not indeed in a coarse and solid substance, but in a refined and penetrative one. This refinement and penetration it acquires through the metallic spirit, which is living silver exalted and refined by art; by means of this, solid gold is resolved into a fluid and penetrating substance, and is coagulated by perfect fixation into a form that suits it according to its degree of refinement; this, they call the **Tincture**, the **Philosophers' Stone**, or the **Elixir**.

<margin>Of gold, which brings about the <term>Mercury of the Philosophers: a specialized, refined form of mercury believed by alchemists to be the essential "spirit" or "solvent" needed to dissolve gold and create the Philosopher's Stone.</term></margin>
Physical action is penetration, according to the Philosopher <note>original: "Physicus est penetratio, juxta Philosophum"; refers to Aristotle, whose theories of matter were central to alchemical thought.</note>: All physical penetration is a true transmutation. Gold, however, being a dense body, does not mix at the smallest microscopic level with other metals in such a way that it can impress its powers and qualities upon them; nor can it be separated from them again with its powers unchanged and without a counter-reaction. Therefore, it must be refined <note>original: "subtiliari"</note> so that it can penetrate, alter, and temper other metals—this is what was to be proven.

### OF <term>FIXITY: the property of a substance that allows it to remain stable and non-volatile when exposed to intense heat.</term>
I have proven before that gold must be refined. This concerns the "body"—namely the substance of the gold—and not its qualities, which must remain unchanged; indeed, they ought to be exalted through this refinement. Hence, any refinement of gold that removes its qualities is to be rejected. Now, the most powerful quality of gold is its fixity, by which gold is specifically distinguished from all other bodies by its very definition. Therefore, in the refinement of gold, its fixity must be retained. Thus, the <term>Tincture: in alchemy, a potent liquid or powder capable of transforming base metals into gold or acting as a universal medicine.</term> is well-defined by Geber <note>Geber is the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, the foundational figure of Arabic alchemy, though the text likely refers to "Pseudo-Geber," a 13th-century European author.</note> as being of a "subtle fixity." To be "fixed" is to be "earthy" in nature; therefore, the absolute form of the Tincture will be earthy. Specifically, it is a "fine powder" <note>original: "pulvisculus"</note>, which is defined by Ezra <note>Likely a reference to the apocryphal or alchemical texts attributed to the biblical prophet Ezra.</note> as being the small powder from which gold is made. By "small," he means subtle and penetrating. For that which penetrates must not be large, but small. By "powder," however, he means a subtle earthy substance, as defined by Albert the Great <note>original: "Alberto Magno"; a 13th-century bishop and philosopher rumored to have discovered the Philosopher's Stone.</note>. Yet, for those bodies whose end-state is most fixed (that is, most earthy), their beginning must be most volatile (that is, most watery). For everything watery tends toward the earthy, just as every liquid tends toward the solid. Since, therefore, the end of the Tincture is a subtle earthy state, its beginning will necessarily be a subtle watery or moist, oily substance—an <term>incombustible oil: a theoretical alchemical substance that remains liquid and oily but cannot be consumed by fire.</term> that does not wet the hands. Such a moisture is "living silver" <note>original: "argentum vivum"; common mercury.</note>. Therefore, the beginning of the Tincture, or the initial form of the Stone, will be the conversion of gold into living silver.

## OF FIXITY.
I have proven before that gold must be subtiliated; this concerns the body—namely, the substance of the gold—and not its qualities, which must remain unchanged; indeed, they ought to be exalted through subtiliation. Hence, any subtiliation of gold that removes its qualities is to be rejected. Therefore, in the subtiliation of gold, its fixity must be retained. By "powder," however, he understands a *subtle earthiness*, just as it is defined by Albertus Magnus <note>A 13th-century Dominican friar and philosopher known for his extensive writings on the natural sciences and alchemy.</note>. ...hard, thick, and dense: therefore all stones, sands, earths, and minerals are to be rejected <note>The author is narrowing down the "Subject of the Art," arguing that common solid minerals cannot be the key because they lack the necessary fluid or "subtle" properties.</note>. ### ANOTHER.

The author proves that through the course of nature, alterations, mutations, and transmutations of things necessarily arise; he then demonstrates that just as transmutations must be admitted in all bodies, it is likewise necessary to grant them to metals, insofar as they are of one genus and nature. And since nature always tends toward the more perfect, he proves that all metals aspire to the rank of gold; nor does he demonstrate this transmutation of imperfect metals into gold to be impossible or difficult, since metals are of one matter with gold; as for their species or form, however, they are diversified only by the purity and **cooking** <note>Original: "coctione." In alchemy, "coction" refers to the process of maturing or "ripening" a substance through heat, mimicking nature’s slow underground processes.</note> of their matter. He asserts that this diversification can be reduced to the identity of gold through purification and cooking. 

He proposes that the cause which digests and cooks the imperfect matter of metals into gold is, in its substance, a matter similar to the metals; but in its qualities, it is contrary to them—namely, thinned out and more than perfect and cooked. But regarding its mode of action, it must be of a **subtle** <note>In an alchemical context, "subtle" describes a substance that is refined, volatile, or capable of penetrating solid matter.</note> and penetrating **fixity** <note>Original: "fixitatis." Fixity is the quality of a substance that allows it to withstand the fire without evaporating.</note>; it must have fixity from its own substance, but it can acquire subtlety and penetration by art, through the most subtle and penetrating subject of the whole world, a thing to be wondered at: the **Philosophers' Mercury**, which the author teaches how to prepare.

## THE SUM OF ALCHEMY.

The end of Alchemy is Mercury, the middle is Mercury, the beginning is Mercury.

**The End**, namely the subject of Transmutation, is Mercury—either common mercury or the mercury of imperfect metals—which must be changed into gold. For if metals did not possess Mercury, or if there were no Mercury in the world, the transmutation into gold could not happen; because nothing can be changed into gold except Mercury. Nor do metals, in the moment of **projection**, <note>Projection is the final stage of the alchemical process, where the "Philosopher's Stone" or "Tincture" is cast upon molten base metal to transform it into gold.</note> yield more gold than the amount of Mercury they contain.

**The Middle**, that is the object or **Tincture**, <note>The Tincture is the transformative agent or "medicine" created by the alchemist.</note> is Mercury; specifically gold, which in its entire substance is Mercury, similar to common Mercury in its substance in all ways, but contrary to it in all its qualities: namely fixed, cooked, hot, dry, digested, and pure. Whence it possesses the quality and power of digesting, cooking, and altering common Mercury.

**The Beginning**, namely the mode of operating the Tincture, is Mercury; which dissolves, refines, and makes the gold penetrative so that it may be able to **tinge** <note>To "tinge" or "stain" was the alchemical term for the spiritual and physical transformation of a metal's color and nature.</note>; for the Tincture "aurifies" (makes into gold) because it is gold; but it extends its "gold-ness" in numerous multiplications because it has been refined and made penetrating. Such refinement, however, without reconcentration, cannot happen except through Mercury.

Therefore, whatever the Wise seek is in Mercury. Whence **Arnold of Villanova** <note>Arnold of Villanova (c. 1240–1311) was a famous physician and alchemist. This quote emphasizes that all metals are essentially "cooked mercury."</note> says:
> Let your whole intention be in the cooking of the Mercurial substance; for according to its dignity, the bodies shall also be signified, which are nothing else but Mercury cooked down by Nature.

->*Three wonders in Alchemy, unbelievable to the inexperienced.*<-
->*The most similar is the most dissimilar; the thickest is the most subtle; the heaviest is the lightest.*<-

THESIS I.

## On the necessity of Metallic transmutation and its connection with the universal course of nature.

God exists, from whom comes the life of all things; from life comes motion; from motion comes **action and passion** <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "action" refers to the act of doing or affecting, while "passion" refers to the state of being acted upon or receiving an impression.</note>; from these comes alteration; and from alteration comes the transmutation of all bodies and things—including metals.

### Defense of this Thesis.

<margin>1. God. 2. Life. 3. Motion.</margin>
That God exists, he who denies it should be convinced by the hand of an executioner rather than by the demonstration of a Philosopher; for all of nature and the universe is so bound to God that if you deny Him, you deny all things—indeed, you deny yourself. On the contrary, if you admit Him, you are forced to admit all the things I shall discuss here. Just as Plato says, *the nature of the soul cannot be known without the nature of the Universe*; so certainly the nature of the universe and universal things cannot be known without God. Once it is granted and settled that God exists, you will immediately and simultaneously admit life; for where there is God, there is life. For just as life is the source of heat, so God is the source of life. Hence God Himself calls Himself the living God, the God of the living, and the breather of life. Indeed, God is so much the life of all things that all things live in Him and through Him. Hence, the more things are in God, the more they live; Angels, souls, and minds live eternally. Much divine power is granted to the sun, whose rays are distributed to all bodies; giving them not only vegetative life, but even sensitive life: as we witness daily in worms and other insects and eggs, which are animated and gifted with life by heat alone. Now, if you admit life, by the same necessity you will grant Motion, for there is no life without motion; indeed, the heart is considered the principle of life for the very reason that motion begins there first. Therefore, where there is motion, there is life; and where there is life, there is motion. You will say: "Therefore the Sun lives, for it moves." I do not necessarily maintain that the Sun lives, though perhaps it would not be so absurd, since many attribute a soul to the world and life to nature. Yet this much is certain: the Sun is moved not by itself, but by some **motor** <note>Original: "motore." In medieval physics, a "motor" is the agent or force that initiates and sustains movement in an object.</note>, and this motor lives. To such an extent that I maintain nothing at all is moved that is not moved by another motor, and that such a motor is life.

You will object: "A clock moves, therefore it lives." I respond: the clock moves by means of a **spring** <note>Original: "elatere."</note> or a weight attempting to extend itself or tending toward the center of the earth. Therefore, you will say that the spring or weight, being the motors of the clock, must live. I respond: The spring and the weight are secondary motors; the primary motor of the weight, however, is the force impelling it toward the center of the earth, or the elastic force. That force is a certain intelligence: whether you call it magnetism or nature, it certainly flows from God, the first motor of all things. You see, therefore, that all things which

<margin>4. Action.</margin>
Now there is no motion that does not act; for it tends from one boundary to another, therefore it acts from one end to another: and while it does this, it affects the *medium* <note>In this context, the "medium" is the substance or space through which an action passes, like air for sound or water for ripples.</note>. For action at a distance is not possible without the medium being affected. Thus, *motion* both receives an impression and exerts an influence; it is acted upon by the end from which it departs, and acts toward the end toward which it tends. From this "passion" and "action" <note>The author uses "action and passion" in the classical sense: *action* is the doing, and *passion* is the being-done-to.</note>, different degrees arise; for the closer it is to the starting point, the more strongly it is acted upon: and the closer it is to the goal, the more strongly it acts. The *medium*, however, is an equal distance from one end to the other; namely reaction, or that which arises from being acted upon and acting. Furthermore, if you admit *motion*,

<margin>5. Reaction.</margin>
you will by the same reasoning also admit both *place and time*. For motion does not occur in a single *point*; but tends from one to another, and thus constitutes either a straight or circular line: the extremities of which constitute a different *place* by reason of distance. While *motion* tends from one place to another, a *period of time* must necessarily intervene; since, just as action at a distance is not granted without the *medium* being affected, so also it cannot be affected in an instant without *time*.

<margin>6. Alteration.</margin>
Now if you admit action and passion as results of motion, you will then confess that from this necessarily proceeds the *alteration* of things, or their "through-" or *transmutation*. For those things which are altered can rightly be called *changed*, indeed most excellently transmuted; especially if in their action, passion, and reaction, they reach from one end to the other. For while I come from Vienna to Rome and stand there; then I am certainly altered and translocated from the place of Vienna into the place of Rome.

<margin>7. Transmutation.</margin>
Thus if from a rich man I become poor, from a fool a teacher, from a subject a King, from sour sweet, from opaque transparent, from hard soft, from corruptible and mortal I become incorruptible and immortal; then I must necessarily be said to be altered and transmuted. Therefore, do not be stunned at the word *transmutation*. Since *transmutation* is nothing other than the *alteration of the previous essence* <note>original: "quidditatis" — 'quiddity' or the 'what-ness' of a thing</note>; and this proceeds from action and passion: the former from *motion*, the latter from *life*, and this from God. Hence, as we see as a completely natural thing every day, the *alteration of the stars, of minds, of kingdoms, of bodies*; which alteration encompasses translocation, transmigration, transmutation, transplantation, metempsychosis <note>The transmigration of souls into new bodies.</note>, palingenesis <note>Rebirth or recreation; in chemistry, the "regeneration" of a plant from its ashes.</note>, and all things by which alteration is caused. In the preceding pages you were forced to grant the transmutation of things in politics, morals, mechanics, metaphysics, astrology, and even in physics itself; both with experience herself as teacher, and indeed with reason itself urging: for since I have demonstrated that life cannot exist without motion; and that motion tends from one to another if it is not to stop: it follows most evidently that from such motions, especially *physical* ones, the alteration of bodies proceeds. For just as the subject of local motion is the *point*, from one to another, from which a line is made; so the subject of physical motion is the *body*, tending from liquid to solid or from moist to dry, from watery to earthy, from cold to hot and vice versa;

<margin>8. Of Animals.</margin>

<margin>9. Of Vegetables.</margin>

This occurs, of course, according to the quality of physical motion and the resulting action, reaction, or mixture. Therefore, if you admit these changes in bodies that are difficult to mix and composed of dissimilar parts—such as animals made of nerves, veins, muscles, and various organs, or vegetables made of various roots, stalks, herbs, flowers, fruits, and varying odors, colors, and flavors, where nature must look to the temperament of each part individually: 

<margin>10. Of Metals.</margin>
How much more easily will you concede transmutation and alteration in *metals*? These are composed of parts that are entirely similar and homogeneous; their temperament can therefore be adjusted by *melting* alone, just as water can be tempered with wine. You must either concede that the transmutation of metals occurs (and more easily than in other bodies), or you must altogether deny that the transmutation of vegetables and animals occurs. If that is denied, you will deny the action of physical motion, and with it the course of nature and its mover, God.

### THESIS II.

## On the Subject of Metallic Transmutation.

> *If the transmutation of metals is possible, it will occur toward a more perfect state, namely into gold. To this transmutation, metallic bodies are the closest substances, being like species of a single genus. They differ not in matter (which exists in quicksilver as the genus), but in form (which consists in the "coction" <note>original: "coctione." Specifically, only as much of a metal can be transmuted into gold as it contains quicksilver.*

# Chemical Thesis III.

### THESIS III.
## Concerning the Object of Metallic Transmutation.

> *Quicksilver, crude and imperfect within metals, cannot be changed except by mixing it with another quicksilver that has been "cooked" <note>original: *decocti*; refers to the alchemical idea that metals "ripen" through natural heat in the earth over time</note> by nature and is more than perfect. This [perfected quicksilver], in terms of its substance, is of the same nature as common quicksilver; but in terms of its temperament <note>original: *temperamentum*; the specific balance of the four qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry)</note>, it is contrary to common and metallic quicksilver in the fourth degree. Such a quicksilver is gold, serving as the object of the transmutative art.*

## Defense of this Thesis.

It is very clear from the preceding thesis that if any bodies can be transmuted into gold, those are the "near metals" <note>original: *proxime metalla*; substances that have already achieved a metallic state but are not yet gold</note>; and indeed, they are transmuted *only* in proportion to how much quicksilver they contain—that is, insofar as they are truly metals. For all other components are heterogeneous and foreign, which nature separates during transmutation, just as fermentation in grape must ejects everything that is not of the nature of wine. Now, it must also be explained whether and how common quicksilver, or the quicksilver of metals, *can be altered and transmuted*.

<margin>33. The accidents of metals are twofold.</margin>
It should be known beforehand that just as metals consist of matter (*quicksilver*) and form (the *cooking* or ripening of that quicksilver), so also they possess twofold "accidents" <term>accidents: in Aristotelian philosophy, these are properties of a thing (like color or weight) that can change without the thing itself ceasing to exist</term>, some arising from the matter and others from the form.

<margin>34. The accidents of metals and the accidents of metallic matter are the same.</margin>
Since, as I have demonstrated, all metals share one and the same matter—namely, quicksilver—it must necessarily follow that the accidents of metals that flow from their matter are one and the same: specifically *weight, malleability, and fusibility* <note>original: *gravitas, malleabilitas, fusio*; the ability to be melted</note>. For all metals enjoy these three properties (albeit to a greater or lesser degree), and by them, they are defined and distinguished from all other bodies in the world.

<margin>35. The accidents of the metallic form are various.</margin>
However, the accidents that come from the *form* of metals are various, diverse, and specific, according to the degrees of cooking and the purity of the quicksilver; these consist of *fixity, homogeneity, and color*. For those which are "cooked" to the ultimate end remain fixed <note>original: *fixa*; the ability to withstand the heat of fire without evaporating</note>; those which are pure in every way are homogeneous; and those which are sufficiently and long-cooked acquire *yellowness and redness*. From this, it clearly appears that metals can be altered in their form by "cooking" alone; for the prior form perishes or is changed whenever all its accidents are changed.

<margin>36. The form of metals is transmuted, not the matter.</margin>
Furthermore, experience teaches that the accidents of the metallic form can be changed; therefore, it follows that the form of metals can be transmuted while the *metallic matter* nonetheless remains. For just as the matter of a ripe and an unripe grape is one and the same—namely, *wine*—and the form of "unripe wine" is changed into "ripe wine" by the sun’s cooking alone while the matter of the grape remains: so the *form of metals* can be transmuted into the form of gold while the metallic matter remains. Indeed, it must retain this matter if a true metal is to be produced from such a transmutation.
