Hence the old saying: *Nature rejoices in nature, nature embraces nature, nature is not improved except in its own nature.* <note>original: "natura natura gaudet, natura naturam amplectitur, natura non emendatur nisi in propria natura"; a fundamental alchemical maxim suggesting that only related substances can truly combine or transform one another.</note> This we see in wine, which cannot be improved by oil, for oil is of a different nature <term>heterogeneous; consisting of different parts or natures</term>; thus it floats on top and does not mix with the wine. On the contrary, wine is easily improved by wine, because they mix essentially and fundamentally. Since, therefore, the essence or substance of metals is quicksilver <note>original: "argentum vivum"; literally "living silver," the common name for mercury</note>, it is necessarily concluded that the transmuting object must also be of the nature of quicksilver. For otherwise, it would have neither homogeneity, nor the ability to enter, nor a fundamental and physical contact with any metal, as we see in experience. For every tincture which cannot enter a substance neither dyes it nor alters it; but no tincture can enter into metals which is not of the nature of metals. That this substance is quicksilver, I have demonstrated above.

<margin>43. The transmuting object must be of the nature of quicksilver.</margin> Therefore it is clear that the *transmuting* object, which they call the tincture, must be of the substance of quicksilver; namely, it must be similar to the metals in terms of substance, but dissimilar in terms of qualities. For since the same or the similar does not act upon its own kind, the transmuting agent must necessarily be dissimilar in terms of its qualities or "accidents" <note>original: "accidentia"; in Aristotelian philosophy, these are non-essential qualities like color, hardness, or temperature that can change while the essence remains the same</note>—that is, it must possess contrary qualities and accidents to the thing being changed. But the subject to be changed is the *imperfect* quicksilver of the metals, which is of a cold, moist, liquid, crude, volatile, and impure nature. Therefore, if the transmuting object is to proportion itself to the subject being changed, it must necessarily be of contrary qualities and accidents: namely, of a *hot, dry, constricting, cooked, fixed, and pure* nature.

For if we did not see quicksilver "cooked" by nature into the form of *gold*, we would necessarily have to doubt whether art could reach that point. Furthermore, if we did not have gold, we would also lack the object which is quicksilver in substance, but in its qualities is contrary to common quicksilver and to the fourth degree of metals.

<margin>45. Why gold is the transmuting object?</margin> Without such an object, no tincture or transmutation could occur. Even if this were granted (though it is not conceded), it would not change the fact that certain particles of quicksilver perfectly cooked within gold could cook and perfect others more easily than those which are entirely raw in "imperfect" metals. Thus it follows that particles of quicksilver that are "more cooked" can temper those that are "less cooked." Experience teaches us that the particles of gold are more matured than all others. Therefore, I conclude that gold is the true object of the alchemical art of transformation.

### Chemical Thesis IV.

<margin>48. Only the mercurial substance in metals can be transmuted.</margin>
...in truth, nothing can be *transmuted into gold, except for their mercurial substance*: <note>original: "substantiam Mercurialem"</note> this can be tempered and altered by the mixing of some decocted and more-than-perfect quicksilver; and such quicksilver is *gold*. Now it remains for us to discuss the mixture; namely, the *means and manner* of gold acting upon a metal or upon common quicksilver.

<margin>49. Gold in its solid state does not act on a solid.</margin>
For you will object that even if gold flows with an imperfect metal, the metal is not altered by the gold, since it can be separated again by the art of separation down to the very grain. For example, let *one part of gold* flow together with *a thousand parts of silver*, and if a *thousandth part* of such silver is taken and tested, behold, you will find and separate that *thousandth part* of added gold. This is a sign that gold mixes intimately and flows with metals, yet they are not altered by the gold. To this I respond: **1.** *A solid body does not act upon a solid body*; yet metals are solid bodies, and gold is a solid body, therefore they cannot act upon one another.

<margin>50. A distinction must be made between juxtaposition and penetration.</margin>
**2.** A distinction must be made between *juxtaposition and penetration*; gold melted with silver adheres to it in no other way than by the mode of *juxtaposition* <note>the placing of things side by side without them becoming a new substance</note>, for each body is "closed" and perfect, and cannot exercise any action or passion upon the other. Hence, such bodies are separated with their substance and quality intact. However, melt one *part of tin* <note>original: "stanni"</note> with *many parts of silver or gold*, and you will see the entire mass rendered *friable* <note>brittle or easily crumbled</note>; whereas before the mixing, both metals—even the *tin* itself—were so malleable that they could be beaten and extended into leaves.

<margin>51. The effect of physical penetration.</margin>
The reason, therefore, for this third effect—namely, *friability*—stems from the *reaction of tin with gold*. Specifically, the impure, crude, and arsenical quicksilver of that tin, owing to its contrary qualities, acts upon the pure and decocted parts of the quicksilver of the gold, inducing an anomaly or dyscrasia <term>dyscrasia: a medical and alchemical term for an ill-mixture or imbalance of "humors" or qualities</term> contrary to the temperament of gold. And it does this because of the *porosity and open body* of the tin, by which it penetrates the gold in its smallest parts through its malignancy or dyscrasia; while the gold, because of its closed pores and solid body, does not react but is passive. If gold now possessed the same *penetrative power and porosity*, then it could certainly react upon *tin* or any other metal, penetrate it, and by penetrating, impress and diffuse its own tempered, golden qualities; that is, it could make friable bodies malleable. Just as tin made malleable metals friable. It is clear, therefore, that metals are altered not by juxtaposition, but by reaction.

<margin>52. Mechanical penetration.</margin>
Yet there can be no reaction where there is no penetration; *for every physical penetration, according to the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note>, is the principle of true transmutation*: which is also proven by experience, both mechanically and physically. Mechanically, indeed, where a *single ounce of gold, gilding a pound of silver*, is extended in the manner of a *rod*, drawn through holes into filaments several thousand fathoms <note>original: "orgyias"; an ancient unit of length based on the span of a man's arms</note> long; all these will be thoroughly gilded, that single ounce of gold having been extended *mechanically*. But if you melt that same amount in a flow with a pound of silver, you would not observe even the slightest golden color on a *touchstone* <note>original: "lapide lydio"; a dark stone used to test the purity of gold by the color of the streak it leaves</note>, whereas even half that amount of gold is otherwise hardly visible to the sight. It is clear, therefore, that gold tints more when it is extended, than [when it is melted...]

### Chemical Thesis IV.

...there you will find the same weight of silver you put in; but you will find the upper **copper hemisphere** so penetrated by the spirit of this volatile silver that, when tested, it reveals itself to be largely true and good **silver**. No other reason can be assigned for this transmutation of copper into silver except the penetrating power of the silver, which it received through the salt; without this salt, it is well known that nothing would happen. Furthermore, let silver be dissolved in **aqua fortis** <note>original: "aqua forti," literally "strong water," or nitric acid</note> or spirit of nitre, and let the solution be drawn off with gentle heat until it reaches the consistency of a **salt**. Afterward, let this be dissolved several times in **spirit of vinegar** <note>original: "spiritu aceti," acetic acid</note>, always drawing off the liquid and re-dissolving the residue. Finally, proceed in the same way with **spirit of wine** <note>original: "spiritu vini," or ethanol</note>, but at the last stage, leave the salt of silver in the spirit of wine without drawing it off. This spirit of wine, without any corrosion or violence, when dropped onto **common quicksilver** <note>original: "argento vivo communi," mercury</note>, fixes it almost in a moment and transmutes it into **silver**. And do not believe that no **more** silver is found than was originally in the spirit; certainly, if the trial is well-conducted and the weight properly examined, you will find that, beyond the weight of the original silver, a **notable quantity** of the quicksilver has been **changed into silver** and added to it. The reason for this transmutation must be ascribed solely to the **penetrating power** <note>original: "penetranitiæ"</note> of the silver. The same thing happens with **gold**; if you dissolve it in **aqua Regis** <note>original: "aqua Regis," "King's water," a mixture of nitric and hydrochloric acids</note> and add mercury, drawing off the liquor to the consistency of **salt**, then re-dissolving it in spirit of vinegar, filtering, purifying, and thickening it again to a consistency **that flows like wax**, it will **transmute any silver—even the thickness of thalers <note>large silver coins used in Europe</note>—into gold**, provided it is heated to a glow without melting; and this occurs with an **increase of gold**. I bring forward these experiments only so that it may be openly clear that gold or silver do not alter or transmute metals as long as they are in a state of **solidity**. Truly, as soon as they are **subtilized** <note>refined into a more fluid or spiritual state</note> so that they can penetrate, they immediately act upon metals according to the degree of their penetration, altering and transmuting them; and this is the reason for the actions of all those subtle waters which are commonly called **gradatory waters** <note>original: "gradatorias," liquids used to "graduate" or improve the quality and color of metals</note>.

### Chemical Thesis IV.

<margin>
69. 
Why quicksilver is the cause of the subtilization of gold.
</margin>
Things which are fixed, however, do not have a **weight** <note>original: *gravitatem*</note> appropriate for gold; much less the required subtlety and penetration, or a homogeneous mixture and fusion with gold. Therefore, one must necessarily take refuge in such a subject that excels in the aforementioned requirements. Such a thing is **quicksilver** <note>original: *argentum vivum*</note>; therefore, it is declared the adequate cause for subtilizing gold. I prove, moreover, that quicksilver is the **most subtle, heaviest, and of a fixable disposition** of all bodies, and thus friendly and homogeneous with gold. For it is well known that quicksilver evaporates in the form of a **most subtle** spirit, penetrating glass and any metals, even leather itself—which even the most subtle spirit of wine <note>An early term for distilled alcohol (ethanol).</note> cannot do. Secondly, in **weight**, it most closely equals gold, so much so that the most subtle thing is also the heaviest. Thirdly, quicksilver is an **incorruptible and incombustible** matter; for however it may be treated in the fire, it always gathers itself back together, and cannot be scorched, let alone burned or corrupted, but it is and always remains a homogeneous matter, preserving a spherical roundness like gold. Furthermore, if it is digested and fixed with gold or silver for some time, it admits a most fixed precipitation, which is a sign that it is of a **fixable** quality. Finally, because of these attributes, it has a great sympathy and agreement with gold; which we see in its amalgamation—that is, its digestion with gold: how greedily it seizes it, how intimately it is associated with it, how reluctantly it is torn away from it, how fluid it makes the gold, so that **when treated with it a few times, it flows like wax**, and penetrates and tints glass itself.

<margin>
70. 
Conclusion for the subtilization of gold by quicksilver.
</margin>
I conclude therefore: **gold must be subtilized and rendered penetrating; otherwise, it does not act upon metals, nor does it alter or transmute them; it cannot be subtilized, however, except through a subtilizing agent that is most penetrating, heaviest, and of a fixable golden disposition, or homogeneous with gold: but such qualities are found nowhere else except in quicksilver.** Therefore it follows necessarily that **gold must and can be subtilized by quicksilver**. Now we must further discuss the **form** of this subtilization, where I conclude absolutely: gold must be perfectly, essentially, and radically assimilated and reduced into the form of its subtilizing agent. But the form of the subtilizer is liquid, yet not wetting the hands; therefore gold must be reduced into a liquid form that does not wet the hands. Such a form is the form of **quicksilver**; therefore gold must be reduced into the form of quicksilver—that is, gold must become **quicksilver**.

<margin>
71. 
Gold must be assimilated to the form of the subtilizing agent.
</margin>
<margin>
72. 
The form of the gold's subtilization is Mercurial.
</margin>
And this is what the Philosophers <note>Alchemical authors often referred to themselves and their predecessors simply as "The Philosophers."</note> so often emphasize: **make Mercury by means of Mercury** <note>original: *fac Mercurium per Mercurium*</note>. For if it is certain, as I have sufficiently proved just before, that quicksilver is the most subtle and penetrating of all bodies, as well as the heaviest, and closest to gold regarding fixation and homogeneity, and thus most appropriate for the subtilization of it (gold); certainly it will be altogether necessary for gold to be totally converted into its nature. For unless this happened, a true subtilization would not occur, but the subtilizing agent would separate from the subtilized. Furthermore, no other form can be assigned to gold, if it is to be subtilized,

The multiplicative power of the tincture in quality and quantity.

The example of wine.

If this spirit is poured back into the wine from which it was distilled, it no longer re-composes the original wine—even though all the component parts of the wine are still present together—and this is due to the thinning of the spirit of wine, which is now greater than it was in the wine.

Common precipitated Mercury.

To this I *respond*: if gold can be reduced into quicksilver, then that quicksilver will either be coagulated during the process of digestion <note>slow heating</note> or it will not. If the latter, then no quicksilver in the mines or through art could ever be changed into metal; indeed, even less so, since raw quicksilver in the mines is much more impure and crude than that which is made from gold.

This is especially true *in quicksilver extracted from metals*, which is more "cooked" than the common kind, and which is fixed into metal in the space of a few days. ### Chemical Thesis V.

<margin>90. The nature of the absolute form of the Tincture.</margin>
...you should understand: Truly, if you desire the requirements that the Philosophers seek for their unique Mercury of bodies <note>original: "Mercurio corporum," referring to the metallic essence</note> destined for this effect—which you will perceive in the following thesis—you will surely cease to object on this point. For common Mercury is extremely cold and moist, very poor in internal fire, and therefore hardly capable of being coagulated into a perfect metal in an age; furthermore, it is infected with a livid, dark, leperous, and arsenical sulfur: hence it precipitates itself into a powdery, styptic <note>astringent or contracting</note>, false, and virulent form. On the contrary, the Mercury of the *Philosophers* or of *gold and silver* has its own perfect *warm* agent in a defined *moisture*; it possesses an absolute and fixed sulfur of permanent color, a molten substance that is not virulent or inducing salivation, but rather of a *diaphoretic medical quality* <note>a "diaphoretic" is a substance that induces sweating, used here to suggest a cleansing or transmuting medicinal power</note>.

### THESIS V.

->Concerning the acquisition of the penetrating and subtle nature of the transmuting object, namely gold; or concerning the initial form of the tincture—that is, the Mercury of gold—this thesis deals specifically with the object that "mercurifies" <note>converts into a mercurial or liquid state</note> gold, namely the Mercury of the Philosophers and its preparation.<-

*The object that mercurifies gold—or renders it subtle, penetrating, and capable of tinting—is running quicksilver <note>original: "argentum vivum currens"</note>, not the common kind, but the Philosophical. It is vegetated and animated by action and motion, by fire and the mineral archeus <note>the vital internal force or "spirit" of nature</note>, and by innate heat and radical moisture. It consists of a most pure, exalted metallic sulfur and salt of gold, extracted by art from steel and antimony. It revivifies metallic bodies, attracts them through sympathy, acts within them, grows hot through the reaction, carries them away with itself through the leather and the retort <note>standard tools for filtering and distilling chemicals</note>, unites with them in their smallest parts, and resolves and generates them into their first matter—namely, into quicksilver.*

### Defense of this Thesis.

<margin>
91. Division of this Thesis.
92. The mercurifying cause.
</margin>
So that the thesis may be properly understood and illuminated, two things must be explained: first, the specific nature of *Mercuries*, and second, that of *metals*. That is, how the matter of metals behaves in a free and running state, and secondly, how it behaves in a state coagulated or fixed from its form. Or, to speak more clearly: what is the cause that mercurifies and liquefies metallic matter, and what is the cause that *coagulates and fixes* mercurified matter. I shall set forth the former here, and the latter in the following thesis.

# Supplement II to Subterranean Physics

<margin>94. Definition of Quicksilver.</margin>
94. ...of incombustible sulfur or arsenic: or, *Mercury* is a mineral vapor—oily, viscous, and thick—congealed within the pores of the earth into a homogeneous liquid. These definitions are proven by experience, for *Mercury* is a liquid, as it flows; it is oily, and thus sulfurous, for it does not wet the hands; it is incombustible, for it is not burned away, even though it flees from the fire <note>Mercury evaporates at high temperatures, which alchemists described as "fleeing" the fire rather than being consumed by it</note>. From this it appears to be a vapor, and specifically a mineral one; for it is extremely heavy, very thick, and viscous, because it clings to itself in a homogeneous way like drops in a spherical roundness. It is otherwise called *oily moisture, subtle terrestrial matter, or water perfectly mixed with earth of its own kind.* Therefore, however it is taken, *Quicksilver* is a mixed matter, consisting of the four elements <note>Earth, Air, Fire, and Water</note> like all sublunary things; yet this is mixed far more strongly than the rest, for it is neither terminable nor dissolvable by fire or the other elements; although there are some who boast that they have found its *anatomy* <note>meaning they claim to have decomposed mercury into its constituent parts</note> in various parts: but these people are chiefly mistaken, because they either do not know the essence of quicksilver, which by natural accident in mines is [mixed] with *sulfur*...

<margin>95. Its dregs.</margin>
95. ...*arsenical, moist, acidic, or deceitfully by art*, it is adulterated and mixed with various things. Hence it can be called a *certain mineral metal, or a special compound and mixture.* Or, they do not realize that those substances which they added for the sake of "tearing apart" the Mercury often throw the *Mercury* back out under various masks,

<margin>96. Heterogeneous parts.</margin>
96. and are accustomed to deceive such careless "anatomists." It must be known, therefore, that certain heterogeneous small bodies enter into its essence which are not of its nature; these must therefore be drawn away, and in this place we consider only quicksilver in itself, purely considered, with all heterogeneous parts removed.

<margin>97. The error of those who suppose Mercury can be prepared from all things.</margin>
97. Furthermore, we must bypass those babblers who promise to elicit *Mercury* *from blood, herbs, water, and air*; which they will never achieve, unless they arrive there by chance and through error. For *Mercury* was destined by nature as the *radical moisture of metals* <note>original: "humido radicali metallorum"; alchemists believed metals possessed a fundamental liquid essence similar to the "humors" in a human body</note>; the nature of which metals requires an incombustible moisture, for it must endure the fire. Conversely, animals and vegetables, for their own being, enjoy a combustible moisture. Therefore, one must not confuse the order of nature,

<margin>98. Distinguishing between the radical moisture of things.</margin>
98. which associates light things with light, and heavy with heavy, in a most holy order; therefore, since *Mercury* is a very thick body, it is rightly attributed to minerals. I conclude, then, that *quicksilver* consists of earth and water—the heaviest and thickest of this world—excellently mixed and worked together, *designated by nature as the radical moisture of metals*; or if you prefer the chemical view, *quicksilver is the acetous salt of a mineral nature* <note>original: "sal acetoſum naturæ mineralis," a sharp, acidic mineral essence</note>, as defined by *Basil <note>Basil Valentine, a legendary alchemist</note> and Sendivogius <note>Michael Sendivogius, a famous Polish alchemist</note>*: or according to my own mind, from my *Subterranean Physics and its Supplement*, *quicksilver* consists of *earth of the third kind* <note>In Becher's theory, the "third earth" or "terra mercurialis" is the principle of liquidity and weight in metals</note>, namely from the *earth of acid salt*, from which it drinks in *urinous salt* <note>an ammonia-like salt</note>, and seizes all pestilential sulfur—as we see in the "venereal plague" <note>syphilis, which was treated with mercury</note>, the pestilence, and in sublimation

### Fifth Chemical Thesis

<margin>100. *Quicksilver in action.*</margin>
I call it **in action** <note>original: "in actu"</note> when quicksilver, while still in the mines, is impregnated and agitated by a certain sulfurous spirit—a mineral **archæus** <note>An 'archæus' is an invisible, animating vital force or spirit that alchemists believed governed physical processes</note>, an **internal fire**, or as **Basil** <note>Basil Valentine, a semi-legendary 15th-century alchemist often cited as an authority on antimony and mercury</note> calls it, the **first mover of metals**. In this state, it moves toward the coagulation of a metal; it is then properly called **living** (*vivum*), because it moves with a physical motion toward its final purpose, which is to become a metal.

<margin>101. *Quicksilver out of action.*</margin>
But quicksilver **out of action**, that is, outside of the mines, is dead. It is like blood shed from the body, which is immediately deprived of life, motion, and heat; therefore, unless its natural fire or mover is added back to it, it neither moves itself nor tends further toward the goal of becoming a metal. We have a clear example of this in common Mercury, which initiates no notable reaction with gold because it lacks this internal fire.

<margin>102. *The motion and reaction of quicksilver upon metals.*</margin>
However, as soon as it is distilled with **sulfurous** substances—for example, **vitriol** <note>a sulfate mineral</note> or **sulfurous metals**—and then joined to gold, it immediately attracts the gold with a sensible and mechanical motion. It dissolves the gold and, in the process of dissolving, reacts; through this reaction, it heats up significantly, much like **quicklime** <note>calcium oxide, which releases intense heat when it touches water</note> does.

<margin>103. *Its heating.*</margin>
Yet, if Mercury that has been "animated" in this way stands in the **air** for just a few days before it reacts with gold, it loses its heat, its fire, and its power to react. It then performs as poorly as **common Mercury**. From this, it is clearly evident that common Mercury is "out of action"; therefore, it is necessary that there exists a Mercury that is "in action." Thus, there are two kinds of Mercury: one active, the other inactive.

<margin>104. *The triple external form of quicksilver: Running, Cinnabar, Arsenic.*</margin>
Furthermore, Mercury—whether in or out of action—usually appears in three forms. It is found either in a **running** form in the mines, where it is called **virgin** Mercury (perhaps because it is unadulterated); or in the form of **cinnabar**, where it is naturally joined to sulfur (hence it is called **native cinnabar**); or in the form of **arsenic** or **realgar** <note>a bright red arsenic sulfide mineral</note>. Human **art** <note>meaning chemical technology or laboratory practice</note> also imitates these composite forms, preparing **artificial cinnabar** from Mercury and sulfur, and **artificial arsenic** (which they call **sublimate** <note>mercuric chloride</note>) from Mercury and salts. Thus, Mercury loves both **sulfur** and **salt**, which is not surprising. Even though these three appear different to our eyes, with a little effort, **common sulfur** can be prepared from **common salt**, and **running Mercury** can be prepared from sulfur. This is especially true of **arsenic**, so that the **arsenical sulfur of salt, common sulfur, and running Mercury** all flow from a single source, being of nearly the same nature.

<margin>105. *Mercury, cinnabar, and arsenic are convertible into one another.*</margin>
For **arsenic** is quicksilver that has been "cooked" <note>the Latin 'decoctum' refers to the alchemical process of maturation or ripening through heat</note> to some degree; **quicksilver** is fluid arsenic. Common sulfur participates in both; it is both arsenical and Mercurial. It is just as I said above regarding **sperm, female seed, and menstrual blood**: all are derived from the single source of blood, and are distinguished from one another only by the degree of "cooking." Although, as we shall hear later, I do not deny that in the mutation of Mercury into **cinnabar** or **arsenic**, some sulfur is mixed in (which can be separated again from the compound), it must nevertheless be established as certain that all sulfur—whether it be **phlogiston** <note>the substance of fire or "inflammable principle"</note> or **arsenical**—is Mercurial in nature. It proceeds from the source of Mercury and tends back toward it, as we shall hear further when discussing the coagulation of Mercuries. Now we shall hasten to the difference of Mercury regarding its **effect**, which is twofold: first...

These latter three effects demonstrate the perfect thinning and refinement of metals through Mercury, which is the sole object of desire and inquiry in this art.

Therefore, it is clear that an active force and life can be imprinted even upon common Mercury, so that it is animated and moved by a physical motion that tends from the liquid to the solid state.

### Thesis Chymica V.

<margin>110. Amalgamation assumes dissolution, which in turn assumes a reaction and heat.</margin>
...without dissolution, and no dissolution without reaction, no reaction without effervescence <note>original: "effervescentia"; here referring to the bubbling or internal motion during a chemical reaction</note>, and no effervescence without heat; therefore it is clear that any Mercury, even the common kind, grows warm during the amalgamation of gold, although it may be imperceptibly so to the touch. However, the stronger the Mercury is—and the more it is impregnated with metallic salt—the more powerfully it will resolve gold, and the stronger the reaction, its effervescence, and its heat will be; just as I demonstrated above regarding Mercury sharpened by <term>vitriol</term> <note>Vitriol refers to a class of chemical compounds, usually sulfates of metals like iron or copper, used as powerful acidic agents</note>. Furthermore, it is clear that *common arsenic* dissolves metals; and I have demonstrated above that common Mercury is *fluid arsenic*: therefore, it also dissolves metals. We see this clearly in *tin and lead*, especially if they are mixed, which are dissolved by Mercury even in the cold, and are Mercury-eaten and perforated. Therefore, it is clear that Mercury dissolves metals.

<margin>111. Mercury dissolves metals, and its dissolving power can be increased.</margin>
Now, what does it imply if it dissolves them? Why should it not be possible for it to be *exalted in its dissolving power*, as I have already shown it can be? For there are certain mineral and decomposed bodies, such as the <term>Regulus of antimony</term> <note>The "regulus" is the metallic form of antimony that settles at the bottom of a crucible during smelting</note>, which hardly take in Mercury during amalgamation; they reject it and do not allow themselves to be associated with or dissolved by it. Nevertheless, if they are moistened with <term>spirit of salt</term> <note>Historical name for hydrochloric acid</note> and *vitriol*, and treated with skillful grinding during amalgamation, the Mercury is so fortified that it overcomes these seemingly heterogeneous substances, dissolves them, and is amalgamated with them. This is an evident sign that Mercury can be exalted and aided in its amalgamating power, and therefore also in its dissolving quality.

<margin>112. Metals pass through leather along with Mercury.</margin>
3. Truly, it is not impossible that the Mercury of the Philosophers could so thin out *gold* that it passes through leather <note>original: "corium"; skins or chamois leather were used as filters to strain liquid mercury from solid amalgams</note> with it, provided it dissolves the gold more powerfully and intimately than *common* Mercury does. In the amalgamation of common Mercury, not only does the gold not pass through the leather, but it also retains a large part of the Mercury with it in the leather; this is a sign that *the gold acts more upon the Mercury by thickening it, than the Mercury acts upon the gold by dissolving it.*

<margin>113. An Experiment.</margin>
But let us remain with the example of common Mercury. If it is mixed in equal weight with *marcasite* <note>In this period, "marcasite" often referred to iron pyrites or sometimes bismuth or other metallic ores</note> and *molten lead*, and stirred with a rod until it cools, it will be so *increased in its dissolving power by the marcasite that it dissolves the lead in such a way that it not only does not remain solid in the cold, but its entire substance passes through linen and leather just like common Mercury.* What will you say to this? For it is certain that lead is a very heavy, tenacious, and thick body, and does not easily pass through leather; it is also certain that Mercury is coagulated more by the "odor" of lead than it is dissolved by it. Therefore, it is certain that the dissolving power proceeds in large part from the *marcasite*, for without this, the business does not succeed. Indeed, when *marcasite* is melted together with *antimony* and other metals, it unites all those things—even those that otherwise abhor the company of Mercury—with the Mercury itself, and produces a *most soft amalgam.* I said a moment ago that the dissolving power proceeds in part from the marcasite; because the lead itself contributes much to this solution, for *marcasite* alone without lead does not pass through the leather with Mercury, just as lead does not without marcasite; and what is more wonderful, where the leather [separates] all three (*Mercury, marcasite, and lead*)...

<margin>114. Mercury carries gold upward through the retort.</margin>
That the **Mercury of the Philosophers** <note>A refined, "living" form of mercury sought by alchemists, believed to have superior solvent powers compared to common mercury</note> carries gold with it through the **retort** <note>A glass vessel with a long, downward-curving neck used for distilling liquids or sublimating solids</note>, and is thus indivisibly mixed with it—that is, that it essentially softens the gold and truly mercurifies it—is no more surprising than that boiling water dissolves ice. For common Mercury—which is like cold water compared to the "heat" of Philosophical Mercury—can perform something similar if it is even slightly helped and sharpened; though it requires a greater quantity of itself, more time, and a laborious operation. 

For it is clear that with little effort, by means of Mercury and common sulfur, **cinnabar** <note>Mercury sulfide, a bright red mineral</note> can be prepared from all metals, even from gold itself. For in this way, Mercury is "exalted" and increased in its **volatilizing power** <note>The ability to turn a solid substance into a vapor so it can be moved or purified</note> by the sulfur, so that it raises even the heaviest bodies with itself during **sublimation** <note>The process where a substance is heated into a vapor and then solidifies again on a cooler surface</note>; especially if the bodies to be thus turned into cinnabar and raised are first prepared with corrosive and penetrating waters or salts so that they are raised more quickly. For in this way, they will mostly be sublimated with the Mercury and converted into cinnabar: and experience teaches that cinnabar can be **revivified** <note>Restored to its original metallic state</note> with little effort. 

Nor is there much need to protest about the volatilization of gold by Mercury; poor **Alchemists** often experience more than they would like that Mercury is a "thief" <note>A common alchemical joke: mercury "steals" the gold by dissolving it and carrying it away in vapors during heating</note>; but they do not know that if it is caught, it repays this theft with profit. If, therefore, as has been clear from what was said before, common Mercury can be brought to such a state that it performs the aforementioned essential effects of the Mercury of the Philosophers—albeit only partially—then there should be no doubt about the Mercury of the Philosophers itself: that it either does not exist or cannot produce such effects.

### Fifth Chemical Thesis

<margin>
115.
The logical leap from nature to art is invalid.
</margin>
Mercury has been found in mines which performs these tasks by its own power. To this I respond by first denying the logic of the argument: many manufactured things exist, such as soap, glass, <term>brass</term> <note>original: "orichalcum"; a golden-colored alloy of copper and zinc known since antiquity</note>, and so on, which are not produced by nature. Secondly, I deny the assumption that Mercury is not found "in action" <note>original: "in actu"; referring to a substance in its active, realized state rather than just its potential form</note> in nature; for if such were not the case, no metals would be produced at all. But the latter contradicts both experience and reason; therefore, the former must also be true.

<margin>
116.
The Mercury of the Philosophers is provided by nature.
</margin>
Even personal observation <note>original: "autopsia"; a term used by early scientists to denote seeing something with one's own eyes</note> confirms that the agent of metals in the mines is heat; for the caverns of the mines often glow with heat like baths. The stones themselves—even the most opaque, solid, and hardest—show that they have been penetrated by Mercury much more subtly than through leather: for, as I have said, personal observation shows that the finest gold is found in their midst. Furthermore, experience teaches that the mineral agent of Mercury dissolves and volatilizes metals, even **gold** itself, *within the mines*; so much so that where a metal existed a hundred years ago, none remains now; and where there was no metal, you will now find it.

<margin>
117.
But why is it rarely found in an active state?
</margin>
Just as you will find all the desired qualities of Mercury in the mines, I admit it happens very rarely that "running" Mercury <note>liquid, mobile mercury</note> is found there in an active state possessing these qualities. For when nature has brought Mercury to that point and equipped it with a **mineral soul**, she does not allow it to remain idle for long, but almost in an instant binds it into the nearest **metallic mass**. This is what the Philosophers call **second matter**, or the **chaos and rudiment of metals**, or **electrum**, or the **first metal**. From this, it later takes on various forms of metals until it reaches the final "cooking" of **gold**. Concerning this first metal, <term>Van Helmont</term> <note>Jan Baptista van Helmont (1580–1644), a pioneering chemist and physician who bridged the gap between alchemy and modern chemistry</note> says: *The first or masculine metal is necessarily clothed in metallic Mercury and sulfur.* But I will say more on this later when I deal with metals. At this point, I only wish to infer that it does not follow that in every mine where a metal is found, it is also necessary to find "running Mercury" or even "first metal." Rather, it is enough that something similar or **analogous** exists. Truly, in all mines, something mercurial, arsenical, antimonial, or sulfurous is found. Experience shows that from any or all of these, through the art of metals, the active agent—namely, **animated Mercury**—can be extracted.

<margin>
118.
The presence of nature's mineral fire perfects immature metals; in its absence, it leaves them in an imperfect state.
</margin>
You might object: if there were a certain active mineral force in these immature minerals, they would tend by their own nature and motion toward the goal of their perfection, namely the **state of gold**. However, it has been found that even with the help of art, and even with the longest digestion, they do not improve by a single grain. To this I respond: this proves nothing. Just as an unripe grape, plucked from the vine, does not ripen regardless of what heat is applied because it has been cut off from the vine and the trunk—from which the agent or fire of nature flows (specifically, a certain nutritious moisture that perfects and ripens the grape with the help of the sun’s heat)—so too a mineral taken from the mountain is cut off and deprived of all further Mercurial influx required for further maturation. Heat alone, unless it acts upon the proper moisture, is not sufficient for ripening: for heat alone is not enough to bring about maturation unless it works upon the required moisture. Thus it is no wonder that instrumental heat alone is not enough for the maturation of such a mineral *outside the mines*.

</margin>

4. That the **Mercury of the Philosophers carries gold with it through the retort**, and thus is mixed with it **indivisibly**; that is, that it **essentially** softens gold and truly mercurifies it: this is as little a wonder as that boiling water dissolves ice. Since **common Mercury**, like cold water in respect to **Philosophical Mercury** <note>Alchemists distinguished between "common mercury" found in shops and "Philosophical Mercury," a refined substance believed to be the true "seed" of metals</note>, if even slightly assisted and sharpened, performs something similar; but it requires a greater quantity of itself, more time, and a laborious operation. For it is clear that **with little effort, by means of Mercury and common sulfur, cinnabar can be prepared from all metals, even from gold itself.** <note>original: "cinabriam"; cinnabar is mercury sulfide, typically a bright red mineral</note> For thus Mercury is exalted and increased by sulfur in its power of making things volatile, so that it lifts even the heaviest bodies with it in sublimation; especially if the bodies to be so converted to cinnabar and lifted are first prepared with **corrosive** and penetrating waters or salts, so that they are more quickly lifted; for thus **they will for the most part be sublimated with the Mercury and converted into cinnabar:** indeed, experience teaches that **cinnabar** can be "revived" <note>returned to its metallic state</note> with little effort. Nor is there need to protest much over the making of gold volatile by Mercury; poor **Alchemists** often experience more than they would wish that Mercury is a **thief**; but they do not know that, **if it be caught**, it repays this theft with profit. If therefore, as has been clear from what was said before, **common Mercury** can be led into such a state that it performs the aforementioned **essential** effects of the Mercury of the Philosophers—albeit only in specific cases—then it must plainly not be doubted concerning the Mercury of the Philosophers itself, that either it cannot exist, or cannot produce such effects. You will object that the Mercury of the Philosophers is not produced by nature, therefore not by **art** <note>meaning "chemistry" or "technology" in this context</note>; but that it is **not produced by nature**, experience teaches, for never such...

He defends the existence and power of "Philosophical Mercury" by showing how common mercury can already perform similar feats when combined with sulfur or salts.</summary>

### Chemical Thesis V.

<margin>
115.
An inference from nature to art is not valid.
</margin>
It is argued that Mercury is found in the mines which performs these things of its own accord. To this I respond, first by denying the logical consequence: for many manufactured things exist, such as soap, glass, brass, and so on, which are not provided by nature. Secondly, I deny that "sublimed" <note>original: "sublimatum"; referring to a substance purified by heating it into a vapor that then solidifies</note> Mercury is not provided by nature in *act* <note>original: "in actu"; a philosophical term meaning a thing is currently in its fully realized or active state, rather than just having the potential to be so</note>; for if such were not provided, no metals would ever be produced. But the latter contradicts both experience and reason; therefore, so does the former.

<margin>
116.
The Mercury of the Philosophers is provided by nature.
</margin>
Furthermore, by <term>autopsy</term> <note>original: "autopsia"; here meaning "direct eye-witness observation" rather than a medical examination of a corpse</note> it is established that the active agent of metals in the mines is heat; for the caverns of the mines often glow with heat just like baths. The stones themselves—even the most opaque, solid, and hardest—teach us the same, for they are penetrated by Mercury much more subtly than through leather: for in the middle of them, *the finest gold* is found, as direct observation teaches. Then experience shows that this mineral Mercurial agent resolves and <term>volatilizes</term> <note>original: "volatilizare"; to turn a solid substance into a gas or vapor</note> the metals—even *gold itself—within the mines*; so much so, that where there was metal a hundred years ago, now there is none; and where there was no metal, you will now find metal.

<margin>
117.
But why is it rarely found in "act"?
</margin>
Thus you will find all the desired qualities of Mercury in the mines; but as for why "running" Mercury is so rarely found there in its active state, I admit this happens very seldom. For when nature has brought the Mercury to that place and equipped it with a mineral soul, she does not allow it to remain idle for long, but almost in a moment constrains it *into the immediate mass of metals, which the Philosophers call the "second matter," the "chaos," or the "rudiment of metals," and also "electrum" or the "first metal."* From this, it later takes on the various species of metals until it arrives at the "decoction" or ripening of gold. Regarding this first metal, <note>Jan Baptista van</note> Helmont says: *The first or male metal is necessarily clothed by a metallic Mercury and a metallic sulfur.* But more on this later when I deal with metals. At this point, I only wish to infer that it does not follow that in whatever mines a metal is found, running Mercury must also be found, nor even the "first metal"; it is enough that something similar or analogous is there. Namely, that in all mines something Mercurial, arsenical, antimonial, or sulfurous is found, from all or each of which—by the art of the metals—the active agent, namely "animated Mercury," can be drawn out, as experience teaches.

<margin>
118.
The presence of the fire of nature or the mineral fire leaves immature metals in an imperfect state.
</margin>
You might object: if there were some active mineral power in these immature minerals, then they would tend by their own nature and motion toward the end of their perfection, namely to the state of "gold-ness." But it is well known that neither by nature nor even assisted by art, nor by the longest digestion, is even a grain of them improved. To this I respond that this proves nothing. For just as an immature grape, once plucked from the vine, does not ripen no matter what heat it is digested in, because it has been *cut off* from the vine and the trunk—the source from which the agent or fire of nature flows (namely a certain nutritional moisture that perfects and ripens the grape, aided by the sun's heat)—so too a mineral taken out of the mountain is *cut off* and deprived of all further Mercurial influence required for further ripening. Hence it is no wonder that instrumental heat alone is not sufficient for the ripening of such a mineral *outside of the mines*.

119. An experiment for maturing metals.
</margin>
...ores, but there is also required a Mercurial humidity, that is, an active Mercury, endowed with its own heat. Nor, however, is the path of art entirely closed off from maturing such ores even outside of the mines, provided they employ the fire of nature. Certainly, using only common *sulfur and mercury,* I know how to mature all ores and metals—even those that have already undergone smelting—and to cook them further so that they leave behind a very notable quantity of silver and gold; and this in a short time, using sulfur and *mercury* that are neither purified nor well-joined, but applied, so to speak, in a crude manner. What then will the *Mercury of the Philosophers* accomplish, abounding as it does in so much *salt, so much sulfur, or so much moisture and so much fire?*

<margin>
120. From what does the Mercury of the Philosophers consist?
</margin>
But let us hasten to the end of this thesis, namely to the "mercurifying" object, or the *Mercury of the Philosophers,* which I have said consists of the *purest metallic salt and embryonic golden sulfur.* Let not those *Alchemists* be disturbed here who, under the name of *salt*, imagine for themselves the common *form of salt*; not noticing that the *salt of metals* appears *under the appearance of a true metal.*

<margin>
121. The salt of metals is metallic.
</margin>
Certainly, *antimony and marcasite* <note>original: "marcasita"; a term used historically for various shiny sulfide minerals, most often iron pyrites</note> are *bodies consisting entirely of metallic salt;* which is evident from their *resolving power and saline effect:* and yet they do not appear under the *form of salt,* which must also be understood regarding *metallic sulfur.* For just as *all Mercury of metals is true metal, so all metallic salt is true metal.* For *Mercury, salt, and sulfur* are the same in *substance,* but differ by reason of their *coction* <note>original: "coctio"; a term for "cooking" or "ripening" through heat, a central metaphor in early chemistry</note>, intensity, and conjunction.

<margin>
122. The salt and sulfur of metals are radical moisture and innate heat. Soul, spirit, body.
</margin>
*Sulfur is the innate heat of metals; salt is the radical moisture* <note>original: "humidum radicale"; the essential, life-sustaining fluid of a substance</note> *of metals; Mercury is the innate heat and radical moisture joined together: or, sulfur is the soul, salt is the spirit, and Mercury is the body and bond in which the soul and spirit dwell and are bound.*

<margin>
123. The difference between common Mercury and that of the Philosophers.
</margin>
You see, therefore, the composition of *sophic* <note>original: "sophici"; pertaining to the wise or the true philosophers (chemists)</note> Mercury, and in what it differs from *common Mercury;* namely, that the latter behaves like a *dead, soulless body, expiring or at least in its death-throes:* into which, for lack of a *vital spirit and soul,* any *malignant sulfur* breaks in: not unlike a *human body,* which as soon as it *begins to lack life, corruptive putrefaction enters.* However, just as if someone had the power of *bestowing a soul*, they could communicate it to and resuscitate no body more suitably than that from which it had expired a little while before, and which has already experienced the dispositions and operations of the soul; so indeed the *soul of metals* can be communicated to no subject more suitably than *common quicksilver, or the quicksilver in metals,* which has already experienced the power of this *mineral soul in its digestion, coction, and coagulation.* Hence the *quicksilver of metals* is always *more cooked and digested than common quicksilver;*

<margin>
124. The agent, soul, or mineral life, to which...
</margin>
I say nothing of the fact that through the *soul or mineral fire* resting in metals, the *life and spirit, as if coagulated and sealed, are resuscitated anew and set into motion.* But you will object: *this mineral fire is not given, or cannot be applied by art;* for it must either be sought in the ores, or outside the ores in minerals; but it can be found in none of these places, therefore it cannot be treated by art.

### Chemical Thesis V

<margin>
Is it more suited for resuscitating the body?
</margin>
You think you prove your minor premise when you say that this fire cannot be found in ores, much less outside of ores in metals. For if it were found only in ores, then all Philosophers would have been obliged to dig their material out of mines—indeed, they would have had to work within the mines and pits themselves—since this mineral fire would cease once removed from the mine. If it did not cease, minerals filled with this fire would continue to be perfected even outside the mines. However, the first point is absurd, and the second is refuted by experience; therefore, you argue, this fire can be found neither in the mines nor outside of them in a way that would serve the designated purpose: namely, of **revivifying** metals and bringing them into a state of maturation.

<margin>
125.
A distinction must be made between the inhabiting soul and the internal working soul.
</margin>
I respond that a distinction must be made between the *inhabiting* soul and the *working* soul. For a soul can inhabit a certain body without the operation of its faculties. For example, in an infant, the soul neither speaks, nor understands, nor reasons; in a deaf person it does not hear; in a blind person it does not see; in a paralyzed person it does not feel. This is due to the opposing instruments and materials by which the soul is hindered in its operation. Meanwhile, however, it cannot be denied that in the infant, the blind, the deaf, or the paralyzed, there dwells a soul just as perfect as in other bodies where the soul fully exercises its faculties. Likewise, in <term>common quicksilver</term><note>liquid mercury</note>, in **marcasite, antimony, lead, tin, copper, iron**, etc., there is just as much <term>mineral fire</term><note>the internal "soul" or energy that alchemists believed drove the growth of metals</note> as in the ores themselves. However, it is partly weak, partly hindered, and partly corrupted by the matter of the host body—such as by impure, immature, or imperfectly "cooked" **sulfur** or **arsenic**. In the mines, this defect would be overcome over a long period by the continuous *influence* of new fire; but when the metal is taken from the mine before its time, it remains stuck at that stage of <term>decoction</term><note>the natural "cooking" process of ripening metals in the earth</note> where the miner’s hand plucked it.

<margin>
126.
The soul or mineral fire lies and exists in many mineral subjects, but it is hindered in its action.
</margin>
It is no different than a grain of wheat in a granary, which contains its own fire, but a fire that is resting and no longer working. It is, as it were, sealed up until it is stirred, resuscitated, and revivified by the "fire of nature" that lies in the moisture of the earth, should the grain be committed to it. For then the internal, hidden fire of the wheat begins its action, grows warm, and sprouts into shoots—something it would never do without the resuscitation of its own fire.

<margin>
127.
Therefore it must be liberated and resuscitated.
</margin>
*If the fire of metals and minerals is manifested*, and if the impediments that hinder, constrain, and lull it to sleep are removed, the fire shows itself. Hence, skillful miners wisely distinguish all minerals and metals into two classes: they call one **a waking metal** <note>original: "ein wachend Metall"</note>, which is currently in the process of "cooking" or maturation; the other they call **a sleeping metal** <note>original: "ein schlaffend Metall"</note>, which is outside that process and is hindered.

<margin>
128.
Metals are distinguished into two classes.
</margin>
You will ask further: granted that the mineral fire can be drawn out of minerals and metals and brought into action, *in which metals would it primarily lie hidden*, or from which should it be extracted? I say that just as the perfection of a soul appears to us through its faculties which excel in the rest of the body, so also the intensity of the fire (or sulfur) and the subtlety of the water (or mineral salt) can be recognized from the mineral bodies and their **effects**, in which they exist more excellently than in the rest. But among all metals and minerals, none is found that is hotter, closer to "golden sulfur," and more universal than **iron**, which is evident...

# Supplement II to Subterranean Physics

<margin>129. The fiery agent in iron.</margin>
This fire is seen in the calcination of tartar with <term>martial regulus of Antimony</term><note>An alloy of antimony and iron; "martial" refers to Mars, the alchemical symbol for iron.</note> in a closed vessel, where it grows so hot that this very dry, powdered mass ignites and consumes every combustible thing without any visible flame. Likewise, it is evident from the reaction of iron with <term>aqua fortis</term><note>Nitric acid, a powerful solvent.</note>, from its combustion in fire, and its consumption if melted with gold. It is seen in the fiery sparks thrown off by friction, and from its affinity with gold and its ability to "exalt" it—for <note>original: "Solis & Martis domus communis aries"</note> **Aries is the common house of the Sun and Mars** <note>In astrology, Aries is the "exaltation" of the Sun (Gold) and the "domicile" of Mars (Iron), suggesting a deep cosmic sympathy between the two metals.</note>. This fire is further proved by the universal diffusion and "martial magnetism" throughout the entire world, from the North Pole to the South. Indeed, every bit of mud, stone, and gravel contains the potential <term>sulfur of iron</term><note>In alchemical theory, "sulfur" represents the principle of combustibility and "soul."</note>, as proven by the experiments in my *Supplement to Subterranean Physics*. Experiment proves that the sulfur of iron and gold are potentially one and the same; for the "sulfur of Mars" withstands all the tests for gold—specifically that which, through preliminary calcination and extraction, passes easily into perfect gold. These and many other shared properties of iron—with gold, with sulfur, with the magnet, and with heat—indicate that within <term>chalybs</term><note>Steel or hardened iron.</note> there hides the true mineral fire, the **first mover** of metals, or the embryonic golden sulfur which animates common Mercury and brings it into action.

<margin>130. The resolving salt in antimony.</margin>
Regarding the "resolving salt" of metals, or the <term>radical moisture</term><note>The essential liquid principle that allows metals to be dissolved and reborn.</note> of metals, I say that it excels in **antimony**. There is no mineral that resolves all mud, gravel, stone, and metals—even gold itself—as antimony does. None of all the metals and minerals flows as thinly—indeed, even thinner than <term>spirits of wine</term><note>Ethanol or high-proof alcohol.</note>—as antimony (which is why it is used by typesetters in the casting of printing letters).

<margin>131. The mixture of salt and metallic sulfur in the regulus of antimony.</margin>
Finally, there is no mineral so "hungry" for martial sulfur as antimony; hence it resolves it like water and creates a mixture which they call a <term>Regulus</term><note>The metallic button or mass that settles at the bottom of a crucible after smelting.</note>. Furthermore, nothing attracts iron except the magnet; yet that magnets, <term>magnesia</term><note>Here likely referring to manganese or a similar mineral used in glassmaking.</note>, arsenic, and antimony are of the same kind or produce similar effects is demonstrated in the whitening and clarifying of glass, as glassmakers well know. For it attracts to itself the "seed" and "sulfur" of iron which hides in flints or sand and is universally scattered—which is why glass is often tinted with an unpleasant color <note>Iron impurities in sand often turn glass green or brown.</note>, but is subsequently clarified by these arsenical substances. Lastly, there is nothing that purifies and exalts gold as much as antimony. Therefore, I finally conclude this article on the ingredients of the <term>Sophic Mercury</term><note>The "Philosophical Mercury," a refined substance capable of dissolving gold for the Great Work.</note>: namely, that the fire, sulfur, and innate heat of metals hide in **Mars** (iron), while their radical moisture and resolving salt are in **antimony**. These two are joined by a bond and incorporated into common quicksilver, and these two become one in Mercury.

<margin>132. The mixture of Philosophical Mercury.</note>
Such a Mercury becomes living, animated, resuscitating, and softening; it ultimately makes gold subtle, rendering it penetrative, dissolving it intimately, and leading it into the form of Mercury—that is, into the beginning stage of the **Stone**.

<header>Chemical Thesis VI.</header>

### THESIS VI.

## On the subject capable of being turned into mercury—namely gold and the remaining metals—and their preliminary preparation for the purpose of mercurification.

<note>"Mercurification" refers to the alchemical process of breaking a solid metal down into its "mercurial" or liquid essence, which was considered its primal, philosophical state.</note>

*The subject capable of being turned into mercury, or refined, is gold and silver; and on this occasion, any metal reducible to Mercury. Its coagulating force must be dissolved, which consists of either combustible sulfur, arsenical sulfur, or fixed sulfur. From this, there are three paths to Mercurification, or liquefaction, according to the three aforementioned degrees of metallic solidity. The first two paths are performed without [added] Mercury; however, the third degree can only be softened without Mercury with great difficulty. The first degree, namely of* **CONSISTENCY**, *is revived through the separation of combustible sulfur; the second degree, of* **COAGULATION**, *is revived through the resolution of arsenical sulfur; the third degree, of* **FIXATION**, *is revived through the softening of digested sulfur. 1. The separation of combustible sulfur is performed using subjects—whether metals, salts, or earths—that react against common sulfur. 2. The resolution of arsenical sulfur is performed by a certain salt that acts as a medium between fixed and volatile; this salt neither fixes nor volatilizes the arsenical sulfur, but by dissolving it, it sets free the mercury of the metal. Such a salt arises from the reaction of an alkali and a urinous salt <note>original: "salis urinosi"; likely ammonium carbonate derived from fermented urine, a common reagent in early chemistry</note>, from which reaction the fixed earth of the alkali is precipitated, and the urinous part is separated, joining together in a certain third salt that is a medium between the alkali and the urinous. This salt possesses the nature of both, being both saline and sulfurous—namely, soap-like <note>original: "saponatæ"</note>. Some call this "volatile alkali," or the "fixed fatness made volatile." The metals are to be joined to this medium salt or volatile alkali, and thus turned into mercury. By this method, the desired Mercury is also prepared from Iron <note>original: "Marte" (Mars)</note> and Antimony. 3. The softening of fixed sulfur is performed by using the Mercury of Iron and Antimony successively; however, gold made from this Mercury is softened more easily than common gold. This can indeed be facilitated and prepared for mercurial softening—to save time—by enabling easier amalgamation, sublimation, and melting.*

### Defense of this Thesis.

Up to this point, we have dealt with the Mercury of the Philosophers—that is, the **object** <note>In the philosophical logic of the time, the "object" is the active agent or tool used to work upon a material.</note> which turns gold and other metals into mercury, and the conditions required for it. Now it remains for us to discuss the **subject** capable of being turned into mercury—namely gold and the other metals. This involves two considerations: first, what constitutes the "coagulating force" of metals; and second, how that coagulating force may be weakened as much as possible so that it does not resist the mercurifying "object"—that is, so that the "subject" (the passive metal) is properly directed toward the "object" (the active agent). Since we have thus far discussed the object's...

Now that I have dealt with the nature and effect of the active subject—namely, the <term>Mercury of the Philosophers<note>A purified, "living" form of mercury believed by alchemists to be the universal solvent and the key to the Philosopher's Stone.</note></term>—and the intensification and strengthening of its "mercurifying" quality, I must also necessarily put forward some points regarding the nature and effect of the **passive subject**—namely, the metals—as well as the loosening and weakening of their "coagulating" quality. For just as it is not enough to strengthen or, as they say, "arm" a magnet so that it is made more ready to attract and its pulling power is increased;

<margin>133. The disposition of the passive toward the active is required—namely, the metal to be turned into mercury must be prepared for its mercurification.</margin>

unless in the meantime you also free and loosen an iron or steel nail fixed in a wall in such a way that it can follow the attracting magnet; so too it is not enough to animate the Mercury and increase its mercurifying power, unless you also free the metals (as subjects capable of being turned into mercury) from their "coagulating" and "fixing" cause. Only then can they obey the mercurifying object and freely pass into its nature. I know that right at the start of this discussion you will interrupt and **object** that metals can be reduced to Mercury without the use of [external] Mercury, and therefore Mercury is not needed for "mercurification." I shall respond to this objection once I have first set forth some points regarding the coagulation of metals.

<margin>134. The cause of the coagulation of metals arises from the sulfur of the quicksilver.</margin>

You should know, therefore, that all metals *consist of quicksilver* <note>original: "argento vivo"</note>, as I demonstrated in the preceding second thesis; if a metal contains anything more, that is **heterogeneous** <note>Meaning "foreign" or "not belonging to the true essence."</note>, such as stones, grit, and other things. Indeed, that **quicksilver of the metals** contains within itself its own "coagulating" cause—namely fire or <term>sulfur<note>In alchemical theory, "sulfur" was the principle of combustion and solidity, while "mercury" was the principle of liquidity and volatility.</note></term>—which is moved and excited by the external motion of the elements. In this way, that which contains the quicksilver itself perfects and "coagulates" <note>Solidifies.</note> it, without any other substance or thing.

This is clearly taught by Bernard, Count of Trevisan, a most excellent philosopher, when he writes:

> *Let us see how metals are naturally made, composed of the four elements, like Mercury. If these elements are moved, they heat the Mercury, and through this motion, the Mercury receives natural heat. Thus the fire which is within the Mercury is moved along with the air and is gradually excited—because these are elements more worthy than water or earth—yet moisture dominates in the Mercury, and it catches the motion of fire and heat.*

Geber, the prince of philosophers, agrees with this when he says:

> *In the depths of Mercury is sulfur, which cooks it and brings it to perfection through a long delay in the veins of the earth's mines:*

And regarding the active Mercury, or that of the Philosophers, Morienes confirms the following:

> *In our Mercury there is a fixed and incombustible sulfur, which brings our work to perfection without any other substance or thing. For our quicksilver has in its depths its own fixed and incombustible mercurial sulfur; through that sulfur various metallic colors are produced (namely, according to the degrees of "digestion"), and when that sulfur is excited, it then cooks and tempers the moist and cold qualities, ruling over them with perpetual constancy.*

<margin>135. Quicksilver tends from liquidity—</margin>

Therefore, to come to the point, I say that the physical motion of nature in every act of generation tends from the liquid to the solid. Thus fish are generated in the sea; every seed of animals tends from the liquid to the solid; all rainwater committed to the earth turns from a liquid into a

138. Coagulation of quicksilver in imperfect metals.

From these aforementioned points, it is easily apparent that the method of mercurifying metals and minerals is not one and the same, but threefold, according to the triple degree of solidity, namely: consistency, coagulation, and fixity.

### Supplement II to the Underground Physics

<margin>142. Axioms of the method of mercurification.</margin> Those things which have been constricted through the simple positioning of sulfur alongside them are to be freed through simple separation; those which have been coagulated by arsenical sulfur are to be freed through the resolution and separation of that sulfur; but those which have been fixed by "decoction" <note>A process of prolonged heating or "cooking" to mature a substance.</note> must be liberated and revived through the softening and **re-incrudation** <note>original: *redincrudatio*; the alchemical process of returning a "ripe" or fixed metal to its "crude" or raw state.</note> of that fixation and decoction. For indeed, softening is the opposite of hardening, re-incrudation is the opposite of decoction, resolution is the opposite of coagulation, and separation is the opposite of juxtaposition.

<margin>143. Revivification of cinnabar.</margin> Hence we see that, according to this method, mercurification succeeds best in practice: and indeed, first in the revivification of **cinnabar** <note>Mercury sulfide, the most common ore of mercury.</note>, whether native or artificial, the **Mercury** is immediately revived as soon as the combustible sulfur is separated from it. This happens through all those substances which retain sulfur and release the **Mercury**, such as **quicklime**, **salt of tartar** <note>Potassium carbonate.</note> or **lye**, **vinegar**, **lead**, **silver**, and the **regulus of antimony** <note>The metallic form of antimony.</note>. For when cinnabar is mixed with these, it deposits its sulfur into these subjects and releases the **Mercury** in liquid form.

<margin>144. Revivification of sublimate.</margin> Secondly, we see that **Salts** adhere more strongly to **Mercury** in **sublimate** <note>Mercury(II) chloride, often called corrosive sublimate.</note> than sulfurs do in **cinnabar**; hence they are separated with greater difficulty. However, separation occurs through such substances upon which the **Salts** act, and by that reaction they release the living **Mercury**; such substances include **oil of tartar**, **filings of lead**, **iron**, **silver**, and **regulus of antimony**, by which the mixture of the sublimate can be divided and the mercurial part liberated.

<margin>145. Revivification of arsenic.</margin> Moreover, I have demonstrated elsewhere, and will demonstrate hereafter in the preparation of the **arsenic of silver** and **lead**, that all **Salts**, especially **common salt** and **salt of vitriol**, are **arsenical** in nature. Therefore, the more fixed and metallic these sulfurs are, the more tenaciously they adhere to quicksilver—both common quicksilver and that of metals—so that they clearly withstand the fire of fusion, as we see in the imperfect metals, lead, copper, etc., as well as in **marcasite** and **antimony**:

<margin>146. Arsenical sulfur tenaciously adheres to metals.</margin> These consist for the most part of **Arsenic**, so that their form in the sublimation of **flowers** <note>A powdery vapor produced by sublimation.</note> represents a white and natural **arsenic**. In the meantime, however, they withstand fusion and behave like molten metal, fleeing from the fire with great difficulty and only successively, as their arsenic evaporates along with the **Mercury**. This collects near the chambers or the mouths of the furnaces in the form of **saline** and **crystalline arsenic**, in which experience teaches that quicksilver is present. It is therefore clearly evident that **arsenical sulfur**, according to its disposition, coagulates, fixes, and volatilizes mercury, and is torn away from the Mercurial substance only with the greatest difficulty.

<margin>147. Arsenic of the moon.</margin> We have an example of this in common fixed silver, which, when dissolved in *aqua fortis* <note>Nitric acid.</note> and precipitated with common salt, seizes the **arsenical** sulfur so tenaciously that it forms a mixture from then on (which they call **horn silver** <note>original: *lunam cornuam*; silver chloride.</note>) which can be freed from this **arsenical sulfur** by no washing or sweetening, without the greater part of the silver flying away with it in the fire. And if it is captured during sublimation, it represents perfect **arsenic**; which, however much you might cook, extract, or precipitate it, you will surely reduce your silver back to its former state only with great difficulty and no small expense. From these things I infer this: that the coagulation of Mercury by **arsenical sulfur** is much stronger than in **cinnabar** by **combustible sulfur**, and therefore...

### Supplement II. on Subterranean Physics

<margin>155. Arsenical sulfur should be resolved, not coagulated; hence fixed and volatile substances are to be avoided.</margin>
...it is to be stripped. [Liquid], for liquids work more easily upon solids; [it should be] resolving, for the resolution <note>The process of breaking a substance down into its constituent parts.</note> of **arsenical sulfur** <note>original: *sulphuris arsenicalis*</note> is opposed to its coagulation <note>Hardening or solidifying.</note>, leaving the **Mercury** in a free state, specifically so that it is not "fixed" <note>In alchemy, "fixing" means making a volatile substance solid or resistant to fire.</note>. From this it is certain that **arsenical sulfur** likewise should neither be fixed nor made volatile, but should be left in its own state; for if it were fixed, it would then also fix **its own Mercury**: if it were made volatile, then the Mercury would also ascend <note>Rise as vapor or gas.</note> at the same time, which we clearly see in **antimony**. For if that is dissolved or melted by an alkaline salt, then the **arsenic** and the **Mercury of antimony** are fixed together with that alkali, and remain fixed; but if it is sublimated <note>The process of heating a substance to a vapor so it collects as a solid elsewhere.</note> by salt or vitriol—or even sublimated by itself—then both the **arsenic** and the **Mercury of antimony** ascend together. Thus, however the **analysis of antimony** is performed, you will always find the **arsenic** and the **Mercury of antimony** *together*.

<margin>156. What quality the object that resolves arsenical sulfur ought to possess.</margin>
For what they call the **golden sulfur of antimony** <note>original: *sulphur auratum antimonii*; a chemical compound of sulfur and antimony, often used medicinally.</note>, if you melt and reduce this, it will be the same **antimony**, namely **arsenic** and **Mercury of antimony**; and what they call **Mercury of life** <note>original: *Mercurium vitae*; also known as Pulvis Algarothi, a white powder derived from antimony.</note> is nothing other than sublimated **arsenic** and **Mercury of antimony**, with the **combustible sulfur** having been separated. However, it also remains to be considered what kind of liquid **arsenical** subject acts upon **arsenic** and does not alter the **Mercury**, but rather frees it from the **arsenic** and makes it volatile. It is clear from the nature of **arsenic** that it is of a soapy nature; namely, **saline and sulfurous**.

<margin>157. Arsenical sulfur is to be left in a free state.</margin>
It is of a **saline** nature because it is dissolved in common water, and in a molten state <note>original: *in fluxu*</note> it dissolves metals just like **saltpeter** <note>original: *nitrum*</note> does; whence it is not undeservedly called by some a "coagulated **strong water** <note>original: *aqua fortis*; nitric acid, a powerful corrosive.</note> of nature." But it is of a **sulfurous** nature, for it is accustomed to behave like sulfur, and, like **orpiment** <note>original: *auripigmentum*; a deep yellow arsenic sulfide mineral.</note> or **realgar** <note>original: *realgar*; a ruby-red arsenic sulfide mineral.</note>, it is ignited and catches fire: it is also dissolved by oil, which only sulfur does. From this it is concluded that the proper solvent of **arsenic** must be of both natures—namely, **saline and sulfurous**.

<margin>158. Experiment regarding antimony.</margin>
For just as soap is most mildly dissolved by soapy water, so **arsenic** is congruently dissolved by liquid **arsenic**. I have demonstrated, moreover, that **arsenic** is of a **saline and sulfurous** substance; therefore the solvent must be of the same dual nature.

<margin>159. What is golden sulfur?</margin>
