### Chemical Thesis VI.

...perhaps more [on these matters], when I shall have treated of **arsenical sulfur** <note>original: *sulphure arsenicali*; in alchemy, this refers to the combustible, often toxic component that "binds" a metal's true essence.</note>.

For the specific medicinal power and virtue of metals resides in these types of extracted, resolving, and corrected **arsenical sulfurs**; **Helmont** <note>Jan Baptista van Helmont (1580–1644), a foundational chemist and physician.</note> seems to point toward their correction when he writes that it ought to be:

<margin>163. But of a liquid and resolving nature.</margin>
> I therefore urge novices to learn to strip sulfurs of their foreign and virulent power toward nature, for surely under its custody the vital fire is hidden. There are certain saline sulfurs which, once corrected and perfected, the whole army of diseases obeys, becoming like soaps. In this way, we have seen madness, apoplexy, the "falling sickness" <note>Epilepsy.</note>, paralyses, vertigos, asthma, dropsy, wasting diseases, and monstrous defects annihilated, while nature itself stood amazed.

<margin>164. Of a resolving alkali. Their nature is contrary to arsenical resolution.</margin>
Furthermore, you may object that there is no "middle ground" between a **fixed salt** and a **volatile salt**; and that **Helmont** in clear words commends both fixed and volatile salt for **Mercurification** <note>The process of extracting the "philosopher's mercury" or the metallic essence from a mineral.</note> when he says: *I sensed the crudity (the arsenical sulfur) of **Saturn** <note>The alchemical name for Lead.</note> was soluble in the "fatness" of fixed alkaline salts, and thus the parts of the compound are divided, allowing the quicksilver and the urinous parts to run; and elsewhere, the sharpest calcined substances are sweetened by resolved **sal ammoniac** <note>Ammonium chloride.</note> and putrefied **tartar**.*

<margin>165. An agent is provided without the change of the solute.</margin>
I respond: 1. Experience testifies that there are "middle salts" which are neither volatile nor fixed; for no one will deny that the **tartar of wine** is a salt, yet this salt is neither volatile nor fixed, although it can become either. As for **Helmont** commending fixed salt in the **Mercurification of lead**, this is wrongly attributed to Helmont; he does not commend fixed salts themselves, but the *fatness* of fixed salts—that is, a certain fatty liquor resulting from fixed salts after the "fixing" quicklime of the salts has been separated, which hinders all Mercurification.

<margin>166. The medicinal power of metals [is found] in corrected arsenical sulfurs.</margin>
Or, to speak more clearly, **Helmont** understands salts to be **volatilized alkalis**, as he hints in another place when he writes (in *The Power of Medicines § 65*): *If fixed alkalis are volatilized, they equal the powers of the great drugs; for by the power of incision, resolution, and cleansing, their power is carried even to the threshold of the "fourth digestion" <note>The final stage of metabolic processing in Helmontian medicine, where nutrients become part of the living tissue.</note>, and they fundamentally remove the tenacity of things coagulated in the vessels:* and elsewhere (in *The Passive Deception of the Schools of the Humorists, Chapter 1. § 89*):

<margin>167. Helmont’s opinion on the middle salt, or volatile alkalis.</margin>
> *But if something more stubborn and hidden remains in the deeper recesses, then **volatile alkalis** must be taken, which like soap wipe everything away; it is truly a wonder what the unique volatile **salt of tartar** can achieve, for it cleanses all dregs from the veins and disperses the stubbornness of obstructions and the gathered assemblies of abscesses.* Regarding this volatile salt, that saying of **Paracelsus** <note>The famous 16th-century Swiss-German physician and alchemist.</note> is true: that wherever it does not reach, scarcely anything more powerful will arrive.

<margin>168. Volatile salt of tartar.</margin>
Therefore, whatever resolving power **Helmont** attributes to volatile alkali for the more stubborn obstructions in the human body, he certainly would not deny this to **metallic coagulation**; for it requires it even more than other obstructions due to the tenacity of the adhering sulfur. Especially since in another place **Helmont** says that by means of the **circular salt** <note>original: *salis circulari*; a universal solvent or highly refined salt.</note>, or the volatile salt of tartar, he distilled **gold** through a retort in the form of a pomegranate-red oil; and elsewhere, following **Paracelsus**, he notes that **spirit of wine** does not dissolve gold unless the circular salt is present within it.

<margin>169. The Circulatum of Paracelsus.</margin>
This is the reason why the whole crowd of Chymists strives so anxiously in the preparation of the **volatile alkali salt**; which is certainly as difficult as the **Mercury of the Philosophers**, yet this is the clearest way to its preparation, without which one could scarcely reach it.

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of chemical salts from the previous page. Having established that metallic virtues are locked within "arsenical sulfurs," the author now moves to explain how these "fixed" salts (alkalis) are formed through fire and why researchers seek to turn them back into a volatile state (gas or vapor) to increase their medicinal and chemical power.</meta>

# Supplement II to the Subterranean Physics

<margin>170. The volatilization of fixed salts is difficult.</margin>
To explain the **volatilization** <term>the process of turning a solid substance into a gas or vapor</term> of fixed salts or **alkali** <term>basic, non-acidic substances usually derived from plant ashes</term> in a few words, the composition or texture of alkali must first be properly explained. It works like this: in no plant is there actual alkali, whether volatile or fixed; rather, it is first created by fire. For in every plant (taking **tartar** <note>original: *tartarum*; the crust found in wine barrels, used as a primary chemical source</note> as the supreme example) there is a certain earth—I call it **lime** <note>original: *calcem*; here meaning the powdery residue of combustion, not necessarily calcium</note>, though you may name it what you wish; then there is a certain fatness. Chemists call the earth "salt" and the fatness "sulfur," to the extent that all things consist of salt and sulfur.

<margin>171. Account of the production of fixed salt resulting from combustion.</margin>
When, therefore, a certain plant (for example, *tartar*) is burned or distilled, the subtler fatness and earth—or sulfur and salt—exhale. If they are captured in water, oil, or a subtle salt-like consistency, they dissolve and solidify. In this combustion, however, while a violent separation of the textures of these small bodies occurs, the **volatile sulfur** joins with the **volatile salt**—which is the source of the urinous and smoky smell and taste. Meanwhile, a portion of the fatness is "fixed" with the earth by this combustion and a kind of roasting; or, sulfur is fixed with salt, and they take on the nature of a salt which they call **alkali** or **fixed salt**.

<margin>172. Soot, a volatile urinous salt, is a volatile alkali salt.</margin>
You see, therefore, that "whatever is above is like that which is below" <note>A famous Hermetic maxim suggesting that the qualities of volatile vapors correspond to the qualities of the solid residues</note>. Specifically, **volatile urinous salt** consists of salt and sulfur (or fatness and earth) just as much as the **fixed salt** found in the bottom or the ashes. The latter consists of salt and sulfur (or earth and fatness); there is no difference except that one is fixed and the other volatile. Hence, one is "lixivial" <note>related to lye</note> and the other "urinous," yet they share a single root, origin, and effect.

<margin>173. Fixed alkali salt.</margin>
For **lye** <note>original: *lixivium*</note> performs all the same functions as urinous salt, and vice versa—namely, in the dissolving and precipitating of things. Therefore, you might object that there is no need for the volatilization of fixed salt if urinous salt is already a true **volatile alkali**.

<margin>174. The affinity between urinous and fixed salt.</margin>
I respond that this does not stand in the way. In the meantime, the volatilization of alkali or fixed salt is still desired because the fatness (or sulfur) in combustion has been rendered more "digested," fixed, fiery, and solvent by its passage through the earth. Thus, if it is made subtle through volatilization, it is more penetrating than that which exists in volatile urinous salt, which flew away immediately at the start of combustion and did not endure the penetration of the fire.

<margin>175. The difference between them.</margin>
Just as I said in the *Fourth Thesis*, that which is made subtle, if it is then fixed, necessarily acquires a subtler "fixity" according to the form and degree of its refinement; so I say here: *Every fiery fixed substance, if it is refined and volatilized, acquires greater power and penetration than if it had never been fixed, or if no hot qualities had been introduced into it.*

<margin>176. Fixed alkali salt becomes fiery in combustion; if volatilized by art, it is more [penetrating]...</margin>
We can see the nature of this concentration of "fieriness" in combustion even from coals alone, which through such concentration become extremely dry and hot—an exceeding quality they never would have received without combustion. We also see the remarkable **caustic** <term>burning or corrosive</term> power of lye-salts and their potent ability to dissolve, especially that lye prepared from tartar by the **regulus of Mars** <note>original: *regulum Martis*; a metallic form of antimony reduced with iron</note>, which is so strong it dissolves even metals themselves when they are in flux. There is no doubt, therefore, that through combustion the sulfur (or fatness) of vegetables is altered and fixed, acquiring fiery, caustic, and solvent qualities; and these, if refined by volatilization, are rendered more penetrating,

### Chemical Thesis VI.

<margin>...is [more powerful] than common volatile salt.</margin>
...than if they had never been fixed and concentrated: just as we see in the penetrating and urinous volatile salts <note>original: *salibus volatilibus penetrans & urinesis*; these are nitrogen-rich salts like ammonia that have a sharp, urine-like smell</note> that exhale or distill at the beginning of combustion, having never endured the force of the fire; these act very little or not at all in relation to alkalis.

<margin>
177. 
The method 
of volatilizing 
alkali.
</margin>
This, therefore, is the reason why the Philosophers and Helmont <note>Jean Baptiste van Helmont (1580–1644), a foundational Flemish chemist and physician</note> seek **volatilized alkali salt** <note>original: *sal alcali volatilifatum*; a salt that has been "freed" from its solid state to become a vapor</note>; however, it is better to know what the **method** for this volatilization is. From the preceding pages, you have heard what the structure, texture, or composition of alkali is: namely, that it consists of a fixed earth, like **quicklime** <note>original: *calcis vivæ*; a caustic substance produced by heating limestone</note>, which has attracted the "fatness" or oil of the vegetable herb during combustion for its own preservation. It preserves this fatness all the way until it becomes ashes; when these ashes are leached <term>the process of washing minerals out of a solid</term>, they provide as much **lixivial salt** <note>original: *salis lixivialis*; salt obtained from wood ash lye</note> as the earth was able to "clothe" and defend with that fatness.

<margin>
178. 
What is 
the "Dead 
Head"?
</margin>
For the rest of the material is reduced **into tasteless earth**, or as they call it, the **dead head** <note>original: *mortuam* or *caput mortuum*; the useless residue left after a chemical reaction or distillation</note>. This fixed salt does not yet have sufficient fatness, which is why it attracts from all other bodies what it lost of its own.

<margin>
179. 
Experiment.
</margin>
Hence, a small amount of **alkali** dissolved in a large quantity of **acidic** or harsh **wine** attracts the **acidic tartar** <note>original: *tartarum acidum*; the potassium bitartrate crystals found in wine barrels</note> from the wine with a violent reaction. It becomes tartar once again, and thus the **harsh wine** becomes pleasant, mild, and **is sweetened**. This is the fundamental principle of the **art of soap-making**; for they use a lye which attracts added fatness, from which a compound arises that they call **soap** <note>original: *smegma*</note>. If, therefore, you wish to **volatilize** alkali (that is, the fatness which is within the alkali, and which Helmont calls the **fatness of fixed salts**, which dissolves the **rawness of Saturn** <note>Saturn is the alchemical name for Lead; "rawness" refers to its base, unrefined state</note> so that it **allows quicksilver to run** <note>allows mercury to be extracted or move freely</note>), it is necessary that you remove the fixed earth from it. Yet, this bond between the fixed earth and the fatness in the texture of alkali is so strong—having endured the "torture of the fire" without breaking—that it cannot be dissolved by any force without changing the entire composition and its qualities (**for it finally turns into glass**).

<margin>
180. 
Violence 
must be 
avoided.
</margin>
Therefore, one must abstain from violence and approach the business through a "contrary texture" and decomposition.

<margin>
181. 
The texture 
of sal 
ammoniac.
</margin>
Before I explain this, the nature of its opposite, a volatile alkali, must be explained—for example, **the texture of common salt and the texture of sal ammoniac** <note>original: *salis armeniaci*; ammonium chloride</note>. The latter, as is known, consists of a urinous volatile salt and common salt. You have already learned what alkali salt and urinous salt are; however, I have not yet explained what **common salt** is. At this point, where it is relevant, I say it is a **middle salt** <note>original: *sal medium*</note>: it is neither alkali nor urinous, neither fixed nor volatile, neither salty nor sulfurous, but **both**, and it is disposed toward either state. Hence, by the help of **common salt alone**, metals can be "mercurified" <term>turned into a liquid, mercury-like state</term> and converted into a tincture; although this does not happen as easily or quickly as when **fixed alkali** is brought into such a state.

<margin>
182. 
Analysis 
of soap.
</margin>
Even **common salt** is greatly desired by alkali and is attracted to it as if by magnetism, as we see in the **analysis of soap**. When soap is dissolved in water and a little common salt is sprinkled in, the **alkali is immediately attracted** to the salt. It immediately deserts the fatness or **grease** <note>original: *axungia*</note> which it previously loved so much and with which it had joined to form the soap; it casts the grease to the surface, having found a better and more acceptable guest in the salt.

### Supplement II. on Subterranean Physics

<margin>Common salt tends toward the state of both volatile and fixed salts.</margin>
...reaches **common salt** <note>original: *sal commune*; sodium chloride</note>, it mixes with it and is sublimated into a compound that we call **sal ammoniac** <note>original: *sal armeniacum*; ammonium chloride, historically used in dyeing and metallurgy</note>. From this double decomposition, it is clear that **common salt** tends toward the state of both fixed and volatile salts; and therefore, it exists as a **medium** <term>a middle-ground or bridge between two chemical states</term> of nature between those two, obeying whichever is more powerful.

<margin>184. Analysis of alkali.</margin>
Now I shall come to the **analysis of alkali salt**. Take whichever fixed alkali you please; let it be dissolved either by itself or in common water into a lye; on the other hand, let **sal ammoniac** also be dissolved in water. Having filtered both well and purged them of all dross, pour them together gradually; and <margin>185. Reaction of alkali.</margin> you will observe a marvelous reaction, a union, and a dissolution of both compounds (the **alkali** and the **sal ammoniac**). For the alkali—or rather the **fatness** <note>original: *pinguedo*; in 17th-century chemistry, this referred to an oily or flammable principle within a substance</note> that is in the alkali—will attract and associate with itself the **common salt** which is in the sal ammoniac. From this association, two **separations** will follow: <margin>186. A new decomposition of alkali.</margin> one in the alkali, which will cast its **fixed earth** <term>the solid, inert mineral residue</term> to the bottom; the other in the sal ammoniac which, being despoiled of its common salt, commands the **urinous spirit** <note>original: *spiritum urinosum*; ammonia gas, characterized by its sharp, urine-like odor</note> to depart, which will immediately strike the nostrils. Therefore, let all the liquor be filtered, and the fixed, dead earth that previously bound the "fatness" of the alkali will remain in the filter; let the filtered liquor be distilled, and you will have the **urinous spirit** that was in the sal ammoniac. Let the remaining liquor be drawn off to the consistency of salt, or by two-thirds, and it will yield pleasant crystals, neither lye-like nor urinous in nature, but of some third nature, <margin>187. Hitherto unknown to the world.</margin> **unknown** to the world until now, or at least little known in terms of its effects. This salt <margin>188. Having the power of resolving.</margin> has a wonderful power of **resolving** <term>breaking down or dissolving a substance into its components</term>, especially if, in the preparation of the sal ammoniac, you use vitriol or **spirit or oil of vitriol** <note>original: *spiritum vel oleum vitrioli*; sulfuric acid</note> instead of common salt. <margin>189. A shorter process.</margin> A salt of this kind is also prepared in a shorter way if you mix **oil of tartar** <note>original: *oleum tartari*; a concentrated solution of potassium carbonate</note> with alum dissolved in water; for then both the quicklime of the alum and the lime of the salt of tartar fall away. The remainder is filtered and thickened to the consistency of salt by distilling and preserving the **spirit** that proceeds from the reaction and evaporation; where also, with continued fire, you will acquire the **volatile salt** itself. <margin>190. Method of making volatile salt from oil of vitriol.</margin> This succeeds by the same method with vitriol (or **spirit or oil of vitriol**) and **oil of tartar**, or **borax**. Furthermore, if you gradually cast **powdered tartar** into **oil of tartar** (or common lye) and apply a modest digestion in a closed vessel; and when the reaction or the fermentation of bubbles is finished, you distill the liquid matter, you will by a similar reasoning acquire a powerful **urinous spirit**. You will find that all fixed alkali salt has taken on a middle nature with the tartar, <margin>191. Salt of tartar takes on a middle nature.</margin> and is of the same quality as the salts mentioned above arising from previous reactions. <margin>
213.
The third class of bodies to be converted into mercury, namely the fixed bodies, gold and silver.
</margin>
...by warm water, through which its pores are penetrated; in plainly the same manner, gold is dissolved in the *quicksilver of the Philosophers*, which is warm, liquid, and subtle. For this reason, *Democritus the Greek* commands that the *shadow* <note>original: *umbram*; here meaning the physical solidity</note> of the dense body (gold) must be stripped away by a *fiery medicine* <note>original: *pharmaco ignito*</note>. Furthermore, in the *Rosary concerning the Mercury of the Philosophers* <term>The *Rosarium Philosophorum* is a famous 16th-century alchemical series of illustrations and texts</term> it is read: *Our water, or our Mercury, is stronger than fire, because it makes a pure spirit out of the body of gold, which common fire cannot do.* And *Paracelsus* says of this spirit: *My spirit is a warm spirit, for it has the power of heating all the congealed limbs of its brothers* (namely the metals). In his book *The Vexations of the Alchemists*, when he describes a specific philosophical operation, he speaks as follows (however, I shall add a commentary in parentheses according to my own mind and experience):

<margin>
214.
Explanation of Paracelsus's process for converting into mercury via the Mercury of antimony.
</margin>
*If you lead the Sphere or heaven of Saturn* (antimony) *with the life of the earth* (Mercury) *into a* [Mercurial] *course (that is, if you make Mercury out of antimony), then add to it the imperfect metals in the proper weight: Jupiter* (tin), *Mars* (iron), *Venus* (copper), *and a small amount of the Moon* (silver, to further sharpen the Mercury). *Allow it to run with the heaven for so long (amalgamate and distill the amalgam with the Mercury of antimony) until the heaven of Saturn has totally vanished (namely, until the Mercury of antimony has extracted all the Mercury from the added metals and carried it through the retort with itself). Then the metals alone remain consistent; they are dead with their old corruptible bodies (meaning their dead earth and arsenical sulfur remain in the retort), and they have taken on a new, perfect, incorruptible body (namely that substance which passes through the retort with the Mercury of antimony). This body is also the spirit of heaven (namely spiritual gold lurking in such Mercury) from which planets are revivified and re-embodied (namely in the digestion and fixation of such an animal Mercury, either by itself or with a perfect body). Separate this new body from life and from earth (namely, separate the superfluous Mercury, precipitate and fix the rest, and from this fixed earthy precipitate, extract gold through some solvent; the rest, which does not allow extraction, is earthy dregs to be rejected, as it prevents the entry of the purer substance) and keep the remainder, for it is gold and silver.*

Thus far the passage of *Paracelsus*, upon which not a few—especially *Glauber* <note>Johann Rudolf Glauber (1604–1670), a famous chemist known for "Glauber's Salt"</note>—have commented, thinking that this whole operation refers to re-fixation through saltpeter, or in a cupel within a furnace. But they are mistaken; for by that kind of re-fixation, no more gold or silver is separated from the metals than was already physically present in them—a task for a laborer, not a Philosopher. Truly, the very words, the sense, and the operation most clearly teach that *Paracelsus* means the conversion of imperfect metals into mercury by means of the *Mercury of antimony*, just as I have noted in the parentheses. *Paracelsus* also explains himself clearly regarding this step in Book 1 of *On the Nature of Things*: *Regeneration,* he says, *and the renewal of metals occurs just as a human returns to the earth from which they were first taken, and so will be regenerated again on the last day; so also metals [again]...*

### Chemical Thesis VI.

[Metals] can return into the Mercury from which they were first born, and be dissolved with it, and become Mercury, and again be reborn and clarified through fire—which will also judge the world. In this way, he says, the specific tinctures of silver and gold are generated. Let one read what Suchtenius <note>Alexander von Suchten, a 16th-century chemist who wrote extensively on the secrets of antimony</note> writes concerning the dissolving power of the Mercury of antimony, and how gold is separated from Mars <term>Mars: the alchemical name for iron</term> by it, and how this gold is coagulated into a body by the spirit of Venus <term>Venus: the alchemical name for copper</term>. Likewise, in the process of Barnaud <note>Nicolas Barnaud, a French physician and alchemical author</note> cited toward the end of my supplement to my *Underground Physics*, where he <margin>215. The dissolving power of Mercury.</margin> commands gold to be turned into a black powder by the Mercury of the Philosophers—a powder which can no longer be reduced into gold—and all things will agree most clearly: that the Mercury of the Philosophers has the greatest power to dissolve not only all metals, but even silver and gold themselves, as I proved more extensively in the preceding thesis.

<margin>216. Preparing gold for easier conversion into mercury.</margin>
Now indeed in this thesis, by way of conclusion, some points must be touched upon regarding the "habilitation" <note>original: *habilitationem*; here meaning the preparation or making ready of the metal</note> of gold or silver; specifically so that they may become more prone to mercurification <term>Mercurification: the process of reducing a solid metal back into its essential liquid state</term> and more willingly obey the Mercury of the Philosophers. Philalethes <note>Eirenaeus Philalethes, a famous 17th-century alchemist</note> seems to be mindful of this preparation when he says in his *Entrance* <note>referring to his work *Open Entrance to the Closed Palace of the King*</note>, chapter 18: *Undo the bolts of common gold, which is called the first preparation, by which the enchantment of its body is dissolved, without which it cannot complete the work of the husband <note>The "husband" represents the masculine principle, or gold, in the alchemical marriage</note>.* <margin>217. Philalethes's doctrine on these matters.</margin> *Then you must implore the aid of scorched Vulcan <term>Vulcan: the god of fire, representing alchemical heat</term>: elsewhere, if you have worked with common Sun <term>Sun (Sol): the alchemical name for gold</term>, the materials must be sublimated and boiled, so that afterwards you may be able to unite them with the Virgin’s Milk <note>a term for a white mercurial solvent</note>; and elsewhere, take one part of well-purified common Sun and three parts of our most clear Mercury, join them, and place them on the fire, giving enough heat for it to boil and sweat; let its sweat circulate, and do this day and night for 90 days and nights, and you will see that this Mercury has dispersed all the elements of common Sun and joined them together again; afterwards boil it for another 50 days, and you will see the common Sun converted by our Mercury into OUR SUN, which is a medicine of the first order. And elsewhere: "Truly now, if you apply the regimen of the Stone to the decoction of common Sun (however pure) with our Mercury, you are certainly on the path of error. Therefore, if you have worked with common Sun, you need a strong decoction and proportioned fire, but afterwards proceed with a most gentle fire." And elsewhere: "If you have begun the process in the work of common Sun, then action and passion occur in the rebina <note>likely a variant of 'rebis', the dual-natured matter</note>." And elsewhere: "In the Mercury I have described, and in the most pure common Sun, if you work with the proper fire, you will find our Sun within seven or nine months at most, and our Moon <term>Moon (Luna): the alchemical name for silver</term> within five months."*

<margin>218. Notes on Philalethes's opinion.</margin>
From these sayings, three things must be considered: 1. That another mercurification can be given besides that of common gold and silver. 2. That common gold joined with the Mercury of the Philosophers is not dissolved instantly, but requires a certain amount of time. 3. That the management of the fire in the mercurification of common gold with the Mercury of the Philosophers is different than in the boiling of philosophical gold, or resolved gold. Philalethes confirms the first point in the clearest words in chapter 18, writing the following: *Know that our Mercury gives gold from itself; if you do not know this, which is our secret subject, you must sell it as common gold, and in every test it is true gold and therefore salable—that is, it can be sold to anyone without hesitation; our Sun is therefore salable to the public, but not to be bought by the public, because for it to be ours, our art is required.*

# Supplement II to Underground Physics

*...you could find our Sun <term>Sun: the alchemical name for gold</term> and Moon <term>Moon: the alchemical name for silver</term> in the common sun and moon. I myself have sought it in them and found it, but the work is not easy. It is far easier to make the Stone itself than to find the immediate material of the Stone in gold bought from a merchant. Therefore, our gold is the immediate material of our Stone; the gold of the common people is near; [base] metals are remote; and those things which are not metallic bodies are most remote, or rather, foreign. The common gold is that whose soul, in order to be safe from the tyranny of Vulcan <note>original: "Vulcanityrannide"; Vulcan refers to the god of fire, representing the destructive heat of the furnace</note>, has retreated into a locked fortress. But if you seek our gold in a middle state, look between the perfect and the imperfect, and you shall find it. And elsewhere: Having obtained this sulphur (namely, gold), do not believe you have the Stone and its material, which you might seek and find in an imperfect thing within a week. And elsewhere: Some speak of the gold and silver of the common people and speak the truth, while others deny the same and also speak the truth. And elsewhere: Our Stone is in every metal and mineral, because the common sun can be extracted from them, from which our "near sun" can be sought. In all common metals, our sun is contained, but in gold and silver, it is held more closely. Therefore, Flamel <note>Nicolas Flamel, the legendary 14th-century French scrivener and alchemist</note> says: some worked in Jupiter <term>Jupiter: tin</term>, some in Saturn <term>Saturn: lead</term>, but I worked in the Sun and found it. There is, however, one thing in the metallic kingdom of wondrous origin, in which our sun is closer than in the common sun and moon—if you seek it in the hour of its birth—which melts in our Mercury like ice in warm water, and yet in a way resembles gold. However, you will not find this immediately in common gold; but from that, by digesting it with our Mercury for 150 days, you will find this same true material, which is our gold, sought by a longer way, and not yet as powerful as that which nature has left ready at hand. And yet, by rotating the wheel a third time, you will find the same in both, though with this difference: in the former, it takes seven months; in the latter, a year and a half.*

<margin>
219. The Mercury of the Philosophers is matured into gold by digestion alone.
</margin>
*These and similar words of Philalethes <note>Eirenaeus Philalethes, a 17th-century alchemist, likely George Starkey</note> can be easily understood if one considers what I wrote in the preceding thesis regarding the Mercury of Mars <term>Mars: iron</term> and antimony: namely, that it is a metallic agent and a mineral fire in motion. Therefore, it will perfect itself into gold, and it is matured into gold by digestion <note>the process of maintaining a gentle, steady heat over a long period</note> alone; and that Mercury is of a golden substance, and bestows a golden hue.*

<margin>
220. An Experiment.
</margin>
*For the Regulus of Mars <note>the purified metallic part of the ore</note>, when ground and mixed with cinnabar <note>mercury sulfide</note> and distilled, casts down a "regulus of the regulus" which, when tested by blast or cupellation <note>refining processes used to separate precious metals from lead or base metals</note>, yields gold of good quality. Therefore, it must be of a golden nature; and much more so the Mercury derived from it.*

<margin>
221. What is Horizontal Gold?
</margin>
*It should be known that the precipitated Mercury of Mars and antimony is called "Horizontal Gold" and "Philosophical Sulphur." This precipitate, when it is fixed <note>made resistant to the action of fire</note>, is very easily dissolved into a new Mercury of its own kind under the appearance of a powder, and thus fixity is always introduced more and more into the Mercury. For when Mercury passes into the solidity of a precipitated powder, it then passes from the nature of Mercury into the nature of Sulphur; just as blood is cooked into the nature of seed <note>original: "spermatis"; here referring to the biological refinement of vital fluids</note>.*

<margin>
222. Easily resolvable through Mercury.
</margin>
*But this specific fixed sulphur, when resolved in its own Mercury, necessarily introduces a greater form of fixity into its Mercury. Indeed, Mercury makes [the substance] more subtle by dissolving this specific sulphur. From this, the exaltation of the tincture, the shortening of the process, and the introduction of a subtle form necessarily follows. Hence Lullius <note>Ramon Llull, a 13th-century Majorcan philosopher and alchemist</note> speaks best in chapter 32: "We remember having said in our Testament, that no quicksilver..."*

Exaltation of the tincture.

It should be known, however, that if this precipitated powder is reduced into a body, its ability to dissolve in its Mercury largely perishes because it has acquired a thicker body; although it remains more soluble than common gold, as witnessed by *Alexander von Suchten* <note>A 16th-century German physician and alchemist known for his influential work on the medicinal and transmutative properties of antimony.</note> in the second book of his treatise on *Antimony*, where he recounts the example of silver and gold made from Regulus <term>Regulus: the metallic button or mass that settles at the bottom of a crucible after smelting an ore, particularly antimony.</term> through the Mercury of antimony and reduced back into Mercury, which common gold does not do.

<margin>
225.
Cohobation of Mercury over its own Mercury.

Therefore, the *Author* rejects that gold and silver; but at the same time he plays with the reader, as if this gold or Moon <term>Moon: the alchemical name for silver (Luna).</term> made from antimony were worthless, namely to deter the reader from it, even though the shortening of the work consists in it.

<margin>
226.
The reduction of philosophical gold into a metallic body harms the art.
</margin>
Furthermore, what *Philalethes* <note>Eirenaeus Philalethes, a famous 17th-century alchemist, often identified with the American George Starkey.</note> says about the silver of the Philosophers is not to be understood as if silver were the "form" of silver; but before the Mercury of antimony reaches the decoction of gold, it necessarily attains the degree of the Moon (silver): so that, even if the tincture was made from corporal gold, if its reduction was truly performed, it will first tinge silver before gold, since it is in the state of whiteness. Therefore, when the Philosophers speak of the silver of the Philosophers, or of the tincture for white, they mean the Mercury of gold, boiled down to the degree of silver. And this is the reason why *Philalethes* sets nine months for the work of gold, but only five months for silver; for the less perfect requires a shorter time for boiling than the more perfect.

<margin>
227.
Difference between philosophical gold and common gold.
</margin>
Secondly, from the aforementioned, it is clear that common gold is not dissolved immediately even by the Mercury of the Philosophers, but successively; namely, preceded by calcination in Mercury, which others improperly call putrefaction. This calcination behaves like the preparation of <term>bynes: malt (grain that has been sprouted and then dried, used in brewing).</term>, where wheat, unless it is moistened and roasted, heated and sprouted, is not resolved so that it can communicate its substance to the water; thus, unless gold is mixed with Mercury, moistened, heated, and grows into little trees <note>This refers to the "Philosophical Tree" or "Diana's Tree," an alchemical experiment where a metallic amalgam forms branching, tree-like structures.</note>, fixed and precipitated, it will not be resolved so that its Mercurial substance can be extracted from it.

The fallacy of Alexander von Suchten.
</margin>
Then we see that all bodies which have great fixity, solidity, hardness, and dryness, are not resolved and liquefied except by the passage of time and successive moistening, or as they call it, cohobation <note>Cohobation: the alchemical process of repeatedly pouring a distilled liquid back onto its solid residue and re-distilling it to concentrate its power.</note>:

<margin>
229.
The tincture for white does not require a sulfur different from gold.
</margin>
Thus also gold is not resolved in one go by Mercury, especially common Mercury, because of its excessive moisture and thickness, and because the structure of gold is too thick, dry, tenacious, and tight; but rather by frequent moistening and cohobation. This we see by clear experience; for gold or silver, when amalgamated with Mercury, if it loses the Mercury through distillation and is amalgamated with it again, and this operation is repeated several times, the gold or silver is rendered so fusible that like wax in—

It is therefore one thing to *prepare the matter, and another to shape the prepared matter.*

### Chymical Thesis VI.

<margin>
237.
Two in one.
</margin>
...the actual golden qualities will call forth the potential golden qualities of Mercury, and the entire business will be completed more easily and briefly. However, it may not "tinge" <note>original: "tingat"; in alchemy, "tingeing" refers to the transformative power of the Philosopher's Stone to change the color and nature of base metals into gold.</note> so many thousands [of parts], since actual gold can only with difficulty be reduced to such a level of refinement <term>Subtlety (subtilitas): the state of being refined into extremely small, mobile particles, which alchemists believed was necessary for one substance to penetrate another.</term> as that which exists in its "flesh" (which is potential gold) if it is fixed; for coagulation *directs itself according to refinement.* Meanwhile, it must not be denied that the work can be greatly accelerated,
<margin>
238.
False and empty operations.
</margin>
namely according to the *refining of the gold*; since this refining varies, the operation, its subtlety, time, and effect will also vary. I admit that the method which Philaletha <note>Eirenaeus Philalethes (1628–1665) was a highly influential, anonymous alchemist whose works, like "The Open Entrance to the Closed Palace of the King," were standard texts for the era.</note> describes with common gold—by simple boiling with Mercury—is tedious and long, because the gold is not prepared. Truly, if before
<margin>
239.
The philosophical intention of Alchemy.
</margin>
it is joined to Mercury, it is made fit for "mercurification" <term>Mercurification: the process of turning a solid metal back into its "first matter" or a liquid, metallic state resembling mercury.</term> and refined, the business will succeed much more briefly and easily. Both reason and experience teach that such a refinement and *preparation of gold* exists, so that it may be mercurified *more easily* with Mercury. You will object that I rejected, in the preceding fourth thesis, every refinement of gold that is not done by Mercury. To this I respond by making a distinction:
<margin>
240.
Only the Mercury of the Philosophers passes into the tincture.
</margin>
I rejected the refinement of gold through *solvents—namely aqueous, fiery, and earthy ones, and all others*—which are not of the nature of Mercury, *in regard to the actual mercurification of the gold*; but I did not reject them in regard to making the gold fit or preparing it beforehand for that mercurification. We see an example in antimony: both *raw and powdered gold* are dissolved *not at all* in *spirit of turpentine*; but when
<margin>
241.
Example.
</margin>
it is sublimated by itself into "flowers" <note>original: "flores"; in chemistry, "flowers" are the fine powder or crystals formed by sublimation (turning a solid directly into vapor and back).</note> and refined, it is immediately dissolved in the aforementioned spirit. Yet the sublimation of antimony into flowers is not the [actual] solution of antimony in the spirit of turpentine; meanwhile, it leads to it and prepares the antimony for it. So
<margin>
242.
The variation of operation and time consists in the degrees of refinement of gold.
</margin>
raw gold is dissolved in Mercury with difficulty; but gold refined through solvents is dissolved very easily. Not that these refinements or *solvents* are the *mercurifying* subjects themselves, or the actual act of mercurification; but they *prepare* the gold so that it is rendered more fit for mercurification. Let us see, therefore, what is required for this making-fit, or the easing of mercurification. There will be *three things: namely, amalgamation, sublimation, and revivification.* Regarding amalgamation, you will say it is a marvel that I bring it forward as a difficulty,
<margin>
243.
Refined gold [leads] more easily and briefly to the tincture.

# Supplement II to Subterranean Physics

<margin>

Since these are of the nature of volatile salts—namely "urinous" salts (meaning they contain much of the "earth of the third kind" which mercurifies or fluidifies, as I showed in my *Subterranean Physics* regarding principles)—they therefore make gold and silver fusible and "sweet." <note>"Sweet" (dulce) in alchemy often refers to a substance being non-corrosive or in a softened, receptive state.</note> To be soft and fusible is the first step toward mercurification; therefore, this preparation is useful, as we see clearly in the "spirit of sal armoniac" <term>Spirit of sal armoniac: a solution of ammonium chloride, used as a powerful solvent in early chemistry.</term> mixed with "spirit of wine" <note>original: "spiritu vini"; ethanol or high-proof alcohol.</note>. For gold, once melted and poured into this doubled liquor, is greatly sweetened so that it becomes soft like lead. If this melting and infusion are repeated several times, the gold will flow even with the slightest heat.

<margin>

An Example.
</margin>
I know of a method, using a certain *urinous spirit*, to make *gold* and *silver*—and indeed every metal—extremely fluid and sweet, so that it flows like wax and may be easily amalgamated with Mercury, passing into its liquid state.

<margin>

Three requirements for easier preparation for mercurification.

I say, therefore, that such an amalgamation is a true preparation of gold or silver (and every metal) for undergoing both amalgamation and mercurification. For the more easily and intimately bodies unite, the more willingly and strongly they are mixed and penetrated. As I demonstrated above, *every passive penetration of nature is the foundation of intimate transmutation*; therefore, if gold or silver is so prepared and made fusible that Mercury can penetrate it *more intimately* than in common amalgamation, it will necessarily attract and fluidify it more fundamentally.

Amalgamation.
</margin>

### Chemical Thesis VI.

<margin>271. First.</margin>
...[many opinions] are put forward; but I have demonstrated above how much these authors err. For **quicksilver** <note>original: "Argentum vivum"; common mercury</note> is a compound, consisting of metallic matter and a **mercurifying earth**; as I have demonstrated in my *Underground Physics* <note>original: "physica mea subterranea"; Becher's most famous work, published in 1669</note>. Metallic matter is found nowhere except in the mineral kingdom; however, **mercurifying earth**—namely, a **volatile alkaline salt**, or to speak more clearly, a certain **white arsenical sulfur**—is found in every thing in this world, so widely is its substance diffused. This is true despite what **Morhof** <note>Daniel Georg Morhof (1639–1691), a German scholar who wrote on alchemical history</note> denies in his *Letter on the Transmutation of Metals to Langelott* on page 82, where he professes that he cannot understand how **linseed oil** could contribute to a metallic nature. But he will easily become capable of understanding if it is observed by experiment that in every oil and fat—especially that of **tartar** <note>potassium bitartrate deposits from wine</note> and **urine**—there lies a sulfur that is mercurifying, even capable of **whitening gold** and bringing about **fixation** <note>the process of making a volatile substance resist fire</note> with it. **Glauber** <note>Johann Rudolf Glauber (1604–1670), a famous chemist known for "Glauber's salt"</note> recounts certain experiments of this kind in his *Animal Stone*. There are, therefore, some who not ineptly state that the **universal mercurifying cause** exists and lies hidden in every thing, especially in substances containing urine; however, such people mistake the efficient cause for the effect when they say that **Mercury** itself lies hidden in all things. It is no different than if I were to say that **vitriol of Venus** <note>original: "vitriolum Veneris"; copper sulfate</note> lies hidden in all sulfur, simply because all sulfur can create vitriol from **Venus** <note>copper</note>.

---

<margin>272. Second.</margin>
Secondly, just as the former group supposes quicksilver to be in every thing, at least potentially; so on the other hand, some are found who deny that quicksilver can be prepared in any way even from metals. Examples include the **Author of the Non-entities** and **Rolfinck** <note>Werner Rolfinck (1599–1673), a German physician and chemist</note>; but I have publicly censured and refuted the latter, both with reasons and with experiments, in the chapter on liquefaction in my *Underground Physics* and in the first supplement, chapter five. For even if it is not agreed upon among Chemists regarding the cause and method of **mercurification**, and even if **Rolfinck** cannot grasp these things, one must not, in the meantime, cry out against a manifest experiment. For let him prepare **vitriol** from **Mars** <note>iron</note> or **Venus** <note>copper</note> in the common manner; let him dissolve this in

### Supplement II to *Underground Physics* ###

...urine, let him digest it slowly for several days, filter it: let him keep the **white earth** in the filter until he recognizes it and thanks me; but let the filtered liquor be gently distilled through an **alembic** <note>a chemical apparatus consisting of two vessels connected by a tube, used for distillation</note>, applying the **fire of sublimation** <note>a high heat used to vaporize a substance, which then cools back into a solid or condensed liquid</note> toward the end. Behold an experiment clearer than the midday sun, against which there is no objection. There is no time now to recount the causes of these operations, for they are clear from what has come before.

<margin>
273.
Third.
</margin>
**Thirdly**, there are some among the Mercurialists who are, as it were, neutral; they neither prove nor deny the **mercurification** <note>the process of turning a metal into mercury or extracting mercury from it</note> from metals, but they maintain that common **mercury can be animated** <note>given "life" or chemical activity</note> so that it performs everything that **quicksilver** <note>original: "argentum vivum"</note> extracted from metals does. This is achieved through the addition of **salts and sulfurs**. By this method, mercury is prepared which **dissolves and extracts gold**, establishing a reaction and heating with it. Here it must be noted that nothing "sharpens" common mercury unless it is of a **sulfurous nature**; but experience teaches that the perfection of sulfurs consists in their **subtlety** <note>refinement or fineness of particles</note>, and that this is acquired through salts. Thus, the sulfur found in **nitre** <note>saltpeter or potassium nitrate</note>, common salt, or **urine** possesses great power. Experience teaches that sulfur exists in these salts which has an analogy and sympathy with metals, and even with mercury itself, as I have demonstrated more extensively in my ***Underground Physics*** <note>original: "Physica mea subterranea"</note> on pages 88 and 89. Read and understand those two passages, and you will not regret your study.

<margin>
274.
Fourth.
</margin>
**Fourthly**, there are those who maintain that metals can be mercurified, but not without the use of mercury; a view held by **Theophrastus** <note>Theophrastus von Hohenheim, better known as Paracelsus (1493–1541)</note>, **Alexander von Suchten** <note>c. 1520–1575; a chemist who specialized in the properties of antimony</note>, **Tackenius** <note>Otto Tachenius (c. 1610–1680), a German chemist known for his theory that all things consist of acid and alkali</note>, and many others...

### Chemical Thesis VI ###

...others confirm this. For they say that just as fire is the **principle** <note>the fundamental source or essential nature</note> of heating, so **Mercury** is the principle of **mercurification** <note>the process of turning a solid metal into a liquid, mercury-like state</note>. **Paracelsus** <note>Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim (1493–1541), a foundational figure in Swiss-German medicine and alchemy</note> records this method—quite faithfully for once, contrary to his usual habit—in the sixth book of his *On the Resuscitation of Natural Things* <note>original: "de resuscitatione rerum naturalium"</note>, on page 897, at marginal letter **b**. However, near the end, while dissolving the **analogous acid of mercury** <note>original: "acidum Mercurii analogum"; a substance acting like mercury's acidic essence</note>, he omits the fact that he extracts **quicksilver** <note>original: "argentum vivum"; liquid mercury</note> from the **fluid lime** <note>original: "fluida calce"; here referring to a metallic powder or residue in a liquid state</note>.

*This is truly a wonderful operation;* for when common Mercury is added, the whole amount is later separated out again in its exact weight. Yet, in the meantime, it enables and prepares the **lime** for mercurification, while the **powers of the quicksilver remain intact.** This is what **Helmont** <note>Jan Baptist van Helmont (1580–1644), a chemist and physician known for his work on gases and catalysts</note> says of it: *“Thus let the schools learn, even against their will, that certain agents act freely and with tireless strength, without any suffering or reaction from the subjects they act upon, and always remaining at the same weight.”* Indeed, one pound of common quicksilver could convert I-know-not-how-many thousand pounds of silver or gold into Mercury, while the original pound remains unchanged in both quantity and quality; *just as light kindles light, or as leaven starts a ferment.* Truly, if I had not seen this with my own eyes and performed it with my own hands, I would have been just as unable to grasp it as the reader perhaps is.

---

<margin>275. Fifth.</margin>
**Fifthly**, there are those who maintain that metals can be mercurified without the use of Mercury, but they claim that the result is then *not true quicksilver,* but *either an analogy or a sophisticated imitation.* **Ludovicus de Comitibus** <note>a 17th-century alchemist known for his writings on the "Alkahest"</note> holds such an opinion in his practical disputation. But from this, I have gathered that this author is neither a true Philosopher nor possesses the **Alkahest** <note>the hypothetical "universal solvent" capable of dissolving every substance</note> about which he writes so much. I refuted him in my *Underground Physics* <note>original: "Physicæ meæ subterraneæ"; the author’s own major work on chemistry and mineralogy</note> in the chapter on liquefaction, page 105 and following.

---

**Sixthly**, there are those who maintain that metals can be mercurified without Mercury; namely, that they can be **revivified** <note>restored to a metallic or liquid state</note> by **resuscitative salts**, once their **arsenical sulfur** <note>original: "sulphure arsenicali"; in alchemical theory, the brittle or "combustible" component of a metal that prevents it from being liquid mercury</note> has been softened,

->BY JOHANN JOACHIM BECHER,<-
->Doctor of Medicine and Counselor to His Sacred Imperial Majesty.<- <note>original: "Sacr. Cæs. Maj. Consil."; Becher served as an economic and scientific advisor to the Holy Roman Emperor.</note>

# A NEW AND CURIOUS EXPERIMENT CONCERNING THE
# PERPETUAL SAND-MINE.

## OR A Preliminary History, OR

->The Proposal prepared by the Author and presented to the Lords of the States of Holland,<- <note>The "States of Holland" refers to the governing body of the County of Holland during the Dutch Republic.</note> ->concerning the extraction of gold by means of coastal sand, through the method of a perpetual mine or a great and profitable smelting operation.<-

### Serving as the THIRD SUPPLEMENT to his Subterranean Physics.

---

## FOREWARNING.

LEST the Reader, right at the very entrance, stumble over the difficult term <term>Artificial Perpetual Mine</term> <note>original: "Mineræ Artificialis Perpetuæ"; a concept in alchemy and early chemistry referring to a source of mineral or a chemical process that continuously replenishes itself or operates without end.</note> and be deterred from further reading, they must be forewarned; this term is not so unknown and foreign, but was well-known to the most illustrious writers of this century. For they mentioned the *artificial perpetual mine* in their writings and taught its composition: that subtle Majorcan, *Ramon Llull* <note>original: "Raimundus Lullius"; a 13th-century philosopher and polymath often associated with alchemical works.</note> in his *Clavicula* <note>original: "Little Key"</note>, who is not unknown to the English. So too that great *Francis Bacon of Verulam*, the Englishman; and *Caneparius* <note>Pietro Maria Canepari, a 17th-century Venetian physician.</note>, a Venetian Professor, in his treatise *On Inks* <note>original: "de Atramentis"</note>. *Marcantonio de Castagna*, the supreme Overseer of Mines for the Republic of Venice and author of the *Panctetic Society*. *Gaston Claveus* <note>Gaston Dulco Claveus, a French lawyer and alchemist.</note> the Frenchman, writing against *Erastus*, concerning the perpetual animation, augmentation, and fixation of Mercury. *Martin Schmuck* the German, in his *Small Treasury on creating a perpetual mine of Saltpeter*. *Johann Rudolf Glauber* <note>A famous German-Dutch alchemist and chemist known as one of the founders of modern chemical engineering.</note> in his treatise *On the Secret Fire*, and on creating a *perpetual mine of Saturn* <note>original: "Minera perpetua Saturni"; in alchemical terminology, Saturn refers to the metal Lead.</note>. *Cornelis Drebbel's* <note>original: "Cornelii Trebbellii"; Drebbel was a famous Dutch inventor who built the first navigable submarine.</note> perpetual mine, by means of sulfurous vapor. *Montanus's History of Copper* treated in a similar fashion. *William of Rosenberg* <note>Vilém z Rožmberka (1535–1592), a powerful Bohemian nobleman and patron of alchemists.</note>, Knight of the Golden Fleece and Privy Counselor to the Imperial Majesty, formerly the supreme [governor] of the Kingdom of Bohemia...

->To the Most Illustrious and Most Potent<-
# HOLLAND AND WEST FRIESLAND
->The States, his most<-
## GRACIOUS LORDS,
->J. J. BECHER, Dr., offers his services.<-

To you who have suffered the evils of Mars <note>Mars here refers to war; the Dutch were frequently engaged in naval and land conflicts in the late 17th century.</note>, I offer a remedy of Mars, taken from Neptune <note>Neptune refers to the sea. Becher is poetically suggesting that his "remedy" for the state's war-torn finances comes from the sea (specifically, sea sand).</note>, who is always favorable to you. I have prepared it with long labor and offered it with much study; it was received by you with great affection. However, what has hitherto restrained or deterred you from the use of it, I do not know. I am well aware that those medicines are usually suspect whose preparation is unknown, whose experience is unfamiliar, and which "smell of Chemistry." First, in this writing, I set forth as much as is permitted to be publicly communicated. Since you hesitate for the experiment to be risked in your own Country, I shall perform it in a foreign place and bring the testimony to you.

As for Alchemy: he who deems it irrational is himself irrational. Whoever deters you from it, or judges it unworthy for your Republic to devote effort to such a Science, plays the role of Diocletian <note>The Roman Emperor Diocletian.</note> who, according to the testimony of <term>Suidas</term> <note>A 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia; it records that Diocletian burned alchemical books to prevent the Egyptians from gaining the wealth to rebel.</note>, ordered the chemical books of the Egyptians to be burned, lest they become wealthy and powerful.

Therefore, if you wish to consider Honor, Reason, and Utility regarding this matter, you will observe that it is in the interest of your Republic: **Honor**, that you keep your word given to me by obligation and entice others to your service; **Reason**, that you believe this proposition is not a paradox, but consistent with Nature and all Philosophy; **Utility**, that you do not deprive your Republic of such an inexhaustible and incorruptible treasure, but embrace it for the public good and the safety of the people. Namely, that you may enjoy your own goods, hitherto unknown to you, without prejudice to anyone. 

As for me, whatever you shall do matters little, since in the end I have suffered almost more disgrace and loss in Holland because of this proposal than I can expect glory and reward there. Nevertheless, I shall bear all things with a calm mind, hoping for better things, and that next summer, if it pleases God and You, I shall see Holland again—especially if you demonstrate protection, means of subsistence, and further affection toward the art. May God keep your Republic and its inhabitants safe.

London, the Calends of March, <note>March 1st.</note>
1680.

### PREFACE TO THE READER
### Concerning the Occasion of this Discovery and Proposal.

**W**hen, in the year 1669, I was writing down my thoughts and experiments on the nature of minerals and other subterranean bodies and published them for the public good under the title *Subterranean Physics* <note>original: "Physicæ Subterraneæ"; Becher’s most influential work, which laid the groundwork for the later Phlogiston theory.</note>, I nurtured—among other things—an opinion on the generation of metals that seemed new to some. This opinion was that the "Principles" <note>In 17th-century chemistry, "Principles" refers to the fundamental building blocks or elements of a substance.</note> of metals were earthy, and consisted of a threefold earth. This proposition began to be studied deeply among the curious and the learned, and many desired to know its foundation more profoundly, as is testified by letters written to me from various parts of the world. 

Even though this opinion of mine is not entirely new, but rather very ancient—as Geber <note>Geber is the Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, an 8th-century polymath; Becher is appealing to ancient authority to validate his "new" ideas.</note> admits right at the start of his book, stating *that the principles of metals cannot unite unless they become earthy*—I nevertheless thought it wise to once again strip the mask from this ancient doctrine, which has hitherto been disguised as common Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury. I sought to defend it with certain new experiments and uncommon reasons, restoring it to truth and simplicity. To this end, in the year 1671, I published the first Supplement to my *Subterranean Physics*, in which I showed, primarily through a notable experiment, that metals are generated from Earths. 

I demonstrated that common Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury are actually composite bodies made of earth, and therefore cannot be considered fundamental principles. This demonstration was so evident that it was embraced by many and gave rise to many other speculations—especially since I demonstrated the "Universality of Metallic Principles" (namely, the Mineral Earths) in things where one might not even suspect them to be present. Specifically, I showed that iron is generated in all common clay or mud. Morhof <note>Daniel Georg Morhof (1639–1691), a famous German scholar and polymath who corresponded with many scientists of the era.</note> argued with me that iron is *present* in common mud but not *generated* there; however, he does nothing but grant me exactly what I want: namely, that iron exists "potentially" in every bit of mud, and is brought into "actuality" by my operation. 

Not content with iron, I also claim that Gold is contained there. I maintained in that same work that gold lies hidden potentially not just in any mud, but in *any* sand, and that it can be brought into actuality through a certain operation. I also explained at length how in all fat, urine, and common salt, there lies hidden the "Principle of Mercury"—or the <term>mercurifying</term> and <term>whitening earth</term>. When this is joined to either mud or sand, the full number of metallic principles is completed, and a true metal is produced. Here you have the philosophical origin and occasion for extracting gold from mud and sand. At that time, I published this for the sake of curiosity, possibility, and truth, rather than for utility or civil use; nevertheless, by the curious and by those who [seek] to mix <note>The Latin text breaks off at "mi-", likely "miscent" (they mix).</note> the sweet with the useful—namely, gainful experiments <note>original: "Experimenta lucrifera"; a term popularized by Francis Bacon referring to experiments designed to produce wealth.</note> with enlightening ones <note>original: "Experimenta lucifera"; Baconian term for experiments designed to shed light on the laws of nature.</note>—

...this proposal of mine was also brought into civil consideration, and the question was raised: whether anything useful and profitable could be established from coastal sand, river sand, hill sand, or from silt—either concerning the improvement <note>original: "meliorationes"</note> or melting <note>original: "fusiones"</note> of minerals and metals, or concerning the artificial production and augmentation of metals. To that end, I had instituted two notable and great trials <note>original: "Probas"; refers to experimental demonstrations or assays.</note> in **Vienna, Austria** with excellent success. The first of these concerned the fixation of volatile minerals <note>In alchemy, "fixation" is the process of turning a substance that easily evaporates (volatile) into a solid state that can withstand heat.</note>; the second concerned the melting and extraction of **Danube** sand. This can be seen in the attached Document **marked D.** 

However, since in Vienna whatever savors of ingenuity or any novelty—especially **Alchemical** novelty—is valued at nothing (as usually happens in almost all **Courts**), but is rather suppressed more than it is encouraged, nothing further was done regarding this experience of mine made there, even though it would have been most profitable for the Emperor. Furthermore, terrified by the recent example of others, I did not wish to studiously deserve further hatred and persecution from the Court by doing good. 

In the meantime, it happened that **Baron d'Isola**, the Emperor’s Envoy at **The Hague**, sent a certain Dutchman named **Liffrinc** (the son of the Secretary of the West India Company) to **Vienna** with a certain new invention for washing gold out of sand. When I perceived the vanity and weakness of this invention, I revealed it to the Most Serene Prince **Hermann, Margrave of Baden**, who was staying in **Vienna** at the time and was my greatest **Patron**. I also showed him how I dared to perform far greater things with my own invention without the need for washing, of which I had also shown a trial. This Prince wrote back to **Lord d'Isola** as his most trusted friend, who was the first to think of proposing this invention to the Dutch, as they were in a place most abundantly supplied with sand and all other requirements. He therefore negotiated with the **Lord Pensionary of the States** <note>The Grand Pensionary was the most powerful political official in the Dutch Republic.</note> regarding this proposal, and when he received the desired resolution, he wrote back to me. *You have the other part of the story:*

> *Namely, by what means and on what occasion this proposal reached the Dutch. That I did not intrude myself, how coldly I held myself back, and how little I solicited, will be easily apparent from this: that although in the year 1671 the Lords of the States resolved upon this business and gave their resolution in writing, I nevertheless delayed for nearly eight years, until finally in the year 1678 I first repeated the matter and contracted anew with the Lords of the States, as is clear from their obligation under letter (O). Nor even then or afterward did I bind myself to the Lords of the States by any word or writing, but have always kept my freedom intact and secure <note>original: "sartam tectamque"; a Latin legal idiom meaning "in good repair."</note> until now. For it is one thing to propose and demonstrate a matter, and another to work out the demonstration as a craft. A reward is due for the former, but a salary for the latter work; there was a contract for the former, but never a word spoken in Holland about the latter.*

So, while I was undertaking the work and performing a trial in **Amsterdam** before the appointed Lords **Commissioners**, as can be seen from **Letter K**, the same Lords **Commissioners** (without me, as I was staying in Amsterdam at the time) instituted another trial on behalf of **The Hague** and found it in agreement with my Amsterdam trial. From this, they made a report to the **Lords of the States**, who [issued] two resolutions, also...

<meta>This page continues Becher's account of his stay in the Netherlands. ->( 421 )<-

In the usual manner, they published these resolutions in print. In the first, they admit that the Preliminary Trial <note>original: "Anti-Proba"; a small-scale initial test to prove a concept.</note> succeeded, and therefore that they should proceed to the Great Trial <note>original: "magna Proba"</note> of one hundred marks <note>A mark was a traditional unit of weight for precious metals, roughly 250 grams.</note>. To this end, they gave orders to the Lord Commissioners to prepare the silver and all necessary materials to promote the Great Trial (see Document **M**). The second of the resolutions stipulates that once the Great Trial was completed and successful according to their wishes, ten thousand florins <note>A significant sum of gold or silver currency.</note> would be paid to me as a reduction of the stipulated reward (see Document **N**).

These two resolutions were made known to me, and I was summoned to **The Hague**. Arriving there, ready to begin the Great Trial, I found neither a location nor any apparatus prepared. Instead of starting the Great Trial, the discussion turned to entering into and repeating small trials <note>original: "parvis Probis"</note>; this was done for reasons I shall explain later. Thus, in a location that was not at all convenient, and with people designated for the task who were more occupied with other matters than these, the better part of the year—namely the entire summer—was consumed. Although I frequently protested that such small trials were superfluous operations and disproportionate to the great operation, and that according to the resolution of the Lords of the States we should proceed to the Great Trial, I obtained nothing. I was not even permitted to attempt the Great Trial for the sake of my own curiosity and satisfaction. 

And yet, after I performed it anyway at my own expense, the place for further progress—namely the Glassworks <note>original: "Officina Vitraria"</note>—was forbidden to me. Even though a private trial with two hundred marks was carried out with the best success and admiration in the presence of many men—including certain Lords of the States, the Pensionary <note>A high-ranking legal and political official in the Dutch Republic.</note>, various Residents, and many Nobles—nevertheless, that most notorious compiler of newsletters from **Utrecht**, *Broer Appellaer*, saw fit to write the opposite in his news-sheets and disparage the work. He was a bribed actor, acting under whose impulse he himself knows best. 

Certainly, **Van Nispern**, the General Master of the Mints at **The Hague**, spoke so foolishly, contemptuously, and passionately about this work that he was not ashamed to go out into the public courtyard, gather a crowd, and in their midst thrust his passions and opinions against this work upon the bystanders. He even took up another person’s legal case in **The Hague**, which did not concern him at all, out of pure hatred for me. 

Finally, as I was always calling for the Great Trial, it was permitted a second time, but again on the condition that I should undertake it in my own name and in a private place. Therefore, a furnace having been built at the house of a certain **French barber**, the location was afterwards found to be unsuitable due to the intensity of the fire. Consequently, whatever had been started there had to be abandoned, and another place in the public foundry <note>original: "Officina publica fusoria"</note> had to be sought, which nevertheless could not be obtained. Meanwhile, that brawling barber went about all of **The Hague** with furies and curses because I did not wish to continue the work at his house—or rather, because he could not spy on every little thing and secretly report it to others who had hired him for that purpose. 

And so, it has not been possible to reach the Great Trial, which ought to have been done for the Lords of the States according to their resolution. This was certainly not through my fault, for I spent the entire summer of the past year for that purpose; but it happened chiefly, to profess the honest truth in conclusion, for the following reasons. *First*, there were those who weighed and esteemed this proposition according to its immense utility, as appears from Document **K**, and these people, seeing...

<meta>This page continues the author’s account of his alchemical and metallurgical proposal to the Dutch States General. Following the previous page’s discussion of the successful preliminary tests, the author now describes the political and social opposition he faced from skeptical or jealous rivals.</meta>

( 422 )

Those who perceived the current condition of the Republic <note>original: "Reipubl."; referring to the Dutch Republic.</note> proclaimed that such a proposal would be useful. In view of their consideration, the proposal was accepted and it was concluded that it should be put into effect. However, others who were ignorant and malevolent resisted; they neither strived to serve the public good themselves, nor could they tolerate others doing so. These people brought forward whatever sinister and contemptuous remarks they could regarding this resolution of the Lords of the States <note>original: "D. D. Statuum"; the States General, the governing body of the Netherlands.</note>. Specifically, they claimed my proposal smelled of some "alchemical deception" through which the Lords of the States were being strangely disgraced by a useless waste of money. Thus, slander joined with envy, and aided by ignorance, it provided an occasion for distrust and a stinginess regarding expenses. From this it happened that this business was never handled skillfully, publicly, and boldly, or with a liberal hand, but was always suppressed and undertaken as if it were a desperate and failed work. Hence came such coldness, so many delays, so many precautions, and so many thousands of difficulties and mercantile sordidness <note>The author is complaining that the government treated his scientific endeavor like a petty commercial transaction rather than a great state project.</note>, that even the most stout-hearted man would have been weary of further dealings.

Therefore, having lost the summer with small trials, I did not wish to spend the winter uselessly as well. I returned to my private affairs, though I am ready to return to the Great Trial <note>original: "magna Proba"; the large-scale test of his gold-extraction process.</note> as soon as I perceive in Holland a more eager spirit, the required means, silence and protection, as well as a better estimation of the work. For to serve the unwilling, or those who do not value one's service, is the same as doing a kindness for the unworthy. 

Meanwhile, as many people were watching and longing for the progress and success of the work—and noticing it was being delayed, though they perhaps did not see or know the preceding causes—a "Camarina" <note>A classical reference to a stagnant marsh that was dangerous to disturb; here it refers to a "quagmire" of legal troubles.</note> of certain creditors seized an opportunity. Even though it was for a small and partially unjust sum, they obtained a writ from the magistrates through underhanded means <note>original: "sub & obreptitie"; a legal term for obtaining something by concealing the truth or making a false statement.</note> to pursue me. They hoped to obtain from me something that was not in my private power to give. Since at that time my private cause was mixed with public business and unknown to the Lords of the States—nor could it be exposed for recognition during that "fermentation," or perhaps if exposed, they would not have wanted to recognize or settle it—it was better to follow Cardan’s Counsel <note>referring to the Italian polymath Girolamo Cardano.</note>: *Absence and time will give what presence and reason have denied.* For one can negotiate more freely in the field than in closed fortresses. For there is required:

# INTRODUCTION.

## I.

Since Man was created primarily to serve God and his neighbor in this world, I too have strived to do so, as far as was possible for me. What I have done in the former case <note>i.e., service to God.</note> concerns me and is known to God alone, to whom I must also give an account. However, what I have performed in the latter case <note>i.e., service to his neighbor.</note>, as much as

<meta>catchword: piata (principles)</meta>

As I was permitted, my various writings—specifically my *Soul-Wisdom* <note>original: "Psycho-Sophia"; Becher’s work on psychology and ethics.</note> and my *Balance of Human Fortune and Misfortune*—show that I have strived to reconcile the soul of my neighbor to God, to adorn his mind with virtues, to imbue his intellect with all kinds of necessary knowledge, and to provide for the health, sustenance, and care of the body. Because in all these matters I have aimed only at what is most necessary, simple, concise, and consistent, I still considered it my duty, in this final section on sustenance, to reveal my thoughts and experience regarding the care of the mind somewhat more deeply and clearly.

### II.

Therefore, no method of sustaining life seemed better to me, more concise, more useful to one's neighbor, or involving less harm than the cultivation of mines—especially gold and silver—after agriculture and the crafts <note>original: "Agriculturam & Opificia"; the fundamental industries of the 17th century.</note> (which are indeed tedious). However, since these mines cannot be found everywhere on earth, and cultivating them is laborious—and thus not everyone is suited for this task—I applied myself to see whether such metals could also be obtained above the ground and in the open air in all, or at least most, places with easier effort and light expense. In this way, profitable <term>mines and smelting works</term> <note>original: "Fodinæ, & Uſtrinæ"</note> could be established in many locations.

### III.

The cause for falling into such thoughts (which seem miraculous at first glance) was provided to me by the inquiry and investigation into the nature of minerals. Through long study and labor, a knowledge eventually followed, as my *Subterranean Physics* <note>original: "Physica Subterranea"; Becher's most famous work (1669), which laid the foundations for the phlogiston theory.</note> with its two Supplements testifies. There, I demonstrated that metals—indeed, gold and silver themselves—are bodies composed and mixed from earthy particles. These earthy particles, before their mixture, are not as precious in civil use as they are when mixed and already made into a perfect metal. In the same way, the individual wheels of a <term>watch</term> <note>original: "Horologii"; Becher uses the mechanical watch—the high technology of his era—as a metaphor for chemical composition.</note> are not valued as highly as when they are assembled to constitute a perfect watch, complete in all its parts.

### IV.

Furthermore, experience gave me further confidence in this matter. I was taught by experience that metals can be reduced back into such earthy particles, and that all kinds of common earth, sand, and gravel can enter into metals, take on a metallic nature therein, and be able to increase them.

### V.

To these things I have perceived that Nature generates metals above the ground as well; therefore, it is necessary that the principles of such earth are also found there. Indeed, to further corroborate my opinion and to rest upon a certain foundation in this philosophy, I learned by experiment how to extract iron and gold from every kind of clay <note>original: "Argilla"; Becher famously claimed he could transform common clay into precious metals through specific additives.</note> (marked A). I have written a specific deduction on this matter, as can be seen in my first Supplement. This extraction of iron from mud <note>original: "Limo"</note> should cause the reader no wonder, nor should it seem impossible, because I can prove by certain experiments that the <term>principles</term> <note>original: "Principiata"; the fundamental building blocks of matter in alchemical theory.</note> exist in all elements, especially in coal, soot, fat, wool, hair, tartar, salt, urine, and other things of that kind.
