### VIII.

However, because my opinion is certainly contrary and foreign to a certain well-known and formidable sect of **Theosophists** <note>Early modern mystical philosophers; the author likely refers to followers of Jacob Böhme or similar rivals who held more spiritualistic views of nature than his own mechanical chemistry.</note>, or rather philosophers—as much in their scholastic affairs as in their political, critical, physical, and mathematical ones—I could not escape their hostilities. In all the courts and residences of the illustrious where they have managed to insert their servants and gain authority, they have opposed my efforts. This happened even though my efforts would have been of the greatest use and could have been put into effect very easily, indeed showing the greatest evidence of success. They intended nothing else than to destroy all performance of useful duties and thereby block the resulting merits and my promotion. I was therefore induced, and persuaded by others, to take my intentions to a certain free Republic. I chose to select the *Dutch* <note>original: "Hollandicam"</note> Republic, as it is greedy, industrious, and attentive to profit. There, one would know himself to be free from the fear of the aforementioned sect; there, sand and the materials or principles required for it are available as abundantly and at as low a price as anywhere; there also, enough money would be ready to promote the matter, and a prize not to be despised could be had, and what was promised could be certainly expected. Indeed, their protection would keep one safe from the persecutions of foreigners. Before I undertook this proposal in *Holland* with the help of *Prince Hermann, Margrave of Baden*, and *Baron Lisola*, the Imperial Resident, the following four questions under the letters F, G, H, I were more than sufficiently examined and discussed both physically and politically, so that I did not enter the field with empty husks <note>A metaphor for coming prepared with substance rather than just talk.</note>.

### X.

The error was committed not in the physical treatment, but in the political one; however, this can be corrected at any hour by the aforementioned Lords of the States. ->VIII.<-

But because my opinion is certainly contrary and foreign to a certain well-known and formidable <term>sect of Theosophers<note>Likely referring to his intellectual rivals or specific mystical-philosophical groups at court who combined religious and scientific thought in ways Becher found obstructive.</note></term>, or rather Philosophers, in their Scholastic as well as Political, Critical, Physical, and Mathematical matters—and for that reason I could not escape their animosity—they opposed my efforts in all the courts and residences of the Illustrious, wherever they have insinuated their servants and gained authority. They intended nothing else than to obstruct all performance of useful duties and thus block my subsequent merits and promotion. I was therefore induced and persuaded by others to bring my intention to a certain free Republic, where I chose to select *Holland*. It is a place greedy, industrious, and attentive to profit, where one knows oneself to be free from the fear of the aforementioned Sect; where sand, and the materials or principles required for it, are found as copiously and cheaply as anywhere else; where there was also enough money ready to promote the matter; and where a reward not to be despised could be had, and what was promised could be surely expected. Indeed, the protection of the same would keep one safe from the persecutions of foreigners. But before I undertook this proposal of mine in *Holland* with the help of Prince *Hermann*, Marquis of *Baden*, and Baron *Lisola*, the Imperial Resident, the following four questions under letters F. G. H. I. were more than sufficiently examined and debated both physically and politically, so that I did not descend onto the floor <note>A metaphor for entering an arena or starting work.</note> with empty husks.

# Now follow the Documents Required for this.

## SECTION A.

### Demonstration that Iron and Gold are present in all Clay from which Bricks are usually baked.

Take common clay and form it into balls with linseed oil, in the manner of musket balls <note>original: "sphærularum sclopetorum"</note>. Distill them from a glass vessel with a retort neck <note>A "retort" is a classic alchemical glass vessel with a long, downward-pointing neck used for distilling liquids or gases under high heat.</note> using a fierce fire. You will see blackish-gray globes; remove these from the vessel, then crush, sift, and wash them. You will find a heavy black sediment remains, from which, by means of a magnet, it is possible to extract iron that contains much gold within itself.

*N. B. N. B. If, therefore, instead of the common materials mentioned first, mud and oil of a Metallic Nature were known to you—which can be obtained in many places on Earth, but most especially in Holland, England, Sweden, and Poland in abundance and at a low price—and you knew how to unite them, you would discover that in place of Iron, Silver and Gold would truly be produced. This is what I reported regarding the profit of 2 percent to be made every single week.*

## SECTION B.

### Demonstration that Gold lies hidden in all transparent, fusible Sand.

Take clear, fusible sand and vitrify it <note>To "vitrify" means to turn a substance into glass by heating it to extremely high temperatures.</note>. Melt silver with this glass and hold it in a state of flux for some time; you will perceive that as much gold has been added to the silver as I have claimed.

*N. B. N. B. If you are now able to vitrify metals by means of sand and then reduce them back to their metallic state, you will see a notable improvement in them, so that in this way perpetual mines and <term>smelting-houses<note>original: "ustrinæ"</note></term> can be established.*

## SECTION C.

### Demonstration that all kinds of Earth and Stones are of a metallic nature and can take it on; conversely, that Metals enjoy an earthy nature and can be converted into earth.

Take sand, clay, emery, hematite, garnets, talc, calamine, and other things of that kind. Melt each one—though separately, whichever you wish—with a due quantity of antimony. Then these species of earth will enter into the mixture and emerge metallic, and they will partly form a <term>regulus<note>In early chemistry, the "regulus" is the heavy, metallic button that settles at the bottom of a crucible after an ore has been melted and purified.</note></term>.

## SECTION D. <note>original: "LIT. D."</note>

### Demonstration that at Vienna I extracted twelve times more from the Ore than it otherwise contained, and that common Danube Sand contains five times more than washed Hungarian ore.

IN THE YEAR 1676, on the 9th of September <note>original: "V. Idus Septembr."</note>, I presented the following specimen in the Emperor’s public smelting house <note>original: "Ustrina"</note> in Vienna.

One hundredweight <note>original: "Centenarii"</note> of Danube Sand, unwashed, just as it is found mixed with double the amount of mud and limestone, yielded 1 hundredweight and 50 lbs of slag when liquefied and fused. The sum of the whole is 3 lbs minus 1/2 dram of silver. Therefore, the pure, simple sand of the Danube—which is raw, unwashed, and not even mined—contains five times as much as the washed Hungarian ore commonly called *grinding-sludge* <note>original: "Schleiffer Schlamſchlich"; a technical German term for the fine, muddy residue left after ore is crushed and washed.</note> from Kremnica <note>original: "Crembnicenſis"; a major mining town in modern-day Slovakia.</note>. That ore must be dug out, crushed, washed, and roasted with great labor, yet a hundredweight of it yields no more than 2 drams; whereas, on the contrary, one hundredweight of Danube Sand contains 12 drams. For this reason, smelting houses could be erected in every location along the Danube river.

### Demonstration that Iron and Gold are present in every Clay from which Bricks are usually fired.

->LIT. E.<-

# History and Series of the Seven Perpetual Artificial Minerals Known to the World Until Now.

The first and most natural, as it most closely approaches and imitates nature, is the practice of Rocha the Frenchman and *Marco Antonio de Castagnia of Venice*, where clay, sand, and stones of a certain kind are mixed, and once prepared fumes and metallic vapors penetrate and scent them, minerals and metals are produced. This is also imitated by skilled metallurgists who fill up metal mines that have already been excavated and cut out—yet are still swollen with mineral vapors—with mud, sand, stones, slag, and other earthy materials. They seal them, and after several years they open them and find newly produced metal, just as certain lead mines that were exhausted became metallic again after a few years. That most sagacious investigator of nature, the most illustrious Mr. *Boyle* <note>Robert Boyle (1627–1691), a foundational figure in modern chemistry and member of the Royal Society</note>, here in LONDON while I was writing this, related to me that certain industrious tin miners in England separate the metallic stones from the rest, and those separated stones, which contain little or no metal, are gathered in a heap in the open air; from these, after a year or two, they again extract a plentiful tin of good quality.

Not far from London by the Thames in the town of *Deptford*, led by curiosity, I personally inspected a memorable preparation of Vitriol of Mars <note>Iron sulfate, traditionally called "green vitriol" or "copperas"</note>, which they make in great quantity, such that they dissolve twenty or more hundredweights of Mars <term>Mars</term> <note>The alchemical name for iron</note> in a single lead vat. They do this in an acid liquor which is brought there from a type of marcasite <note>Iron pyrite or "fool's gold"</note> and exposed to the air in heaps, where it turns to salt; then, in positioned tunnels or trenches, it is leached when it rains. The liquid runs through all the trenches into a larger pit destined for that purpose, from where it is removed again and channeled into a lead vat. Then the iron is placed in it and dissolved; once dissolved, it is then thickened in the common manner into the concretion of greenish vitriol. Here two things worthy of note in physics occur: First, that this acid liquor from the pyrite or marcasite is not yet vitriolated, nor mineral, but is that universal decomposing acid of which I made mention in my *Physica subterranea*, by the help of which various compounds can be made, which I reviewed in that place. This solvent, generated through the air in the pyrite, is to be numbered among the Universal Principles of Metals, whence *Rupecissa* <note>Jean de Roquetaillade (c. 1310–1366), a Franciscan friar and alchemist famous for his work on the "quintessence"</note> not without merit writes:

> *Vitriol or Salt (meaning this one) is the first matter of metals, or their remote principle*, <note>original: "Vitriolum seu Sal (puta hoc) est prima Metallorum Materia, seu illorum Principium remotum"</note>

hence, whatever the philosophers write about their Salt and sweet Vitriol, which is generated from the Air and Earth—namely, about their Magnet attracting the Astral Salt—I judge should be understood as referring to this liquor and salt rather than any other. A specific book could be written about this liquor and salt, or white vitriol, for it is not...

...so corrosive and astringent as the common sort, but sweet; and rightly so, for it is free from all actual metal. Therefore, it is not a "decomposed" <note>In 17th-century chemistry, "decomposed" often referred to complex substances that could be broken down further, whereas "simple" meant more fundamental or primary mixtures</note> substance, but a simple composite, consisting of sulfurous earth and astral salt, of which the former is its magnet. Thus, *Caneparius* <note>Pietro Maria Canepari, an Italian physician and author of the 1619 treatise *De Atramentis* (On Inks)</note> in his treatise on inks does not wrongly call pyrite, or marcasite <note>A common iron sulfide mineral often mistaken for gold or silver ore</note>, the first rough form and matter of metals and minerals. This marcasite is transported from the Isle of *Wight* <note>original: "Vectis"</note> to the aforementioned place; and the inhabitants say that even if it is carried away, it is always regenerated there. This is another point worthy of note, and it is specifically why I wanted to bring this up here. 

I took some quantity of this pyrite as well as the liquor with me out of curiosity, for it is difficult to find a subject in which the "universal decomposing acid" exists that has not already turned into a "decomposed" form—namely alum, borax, sulfur, or vitriol. Once these are "decomposed," they are difficult to tear apart and reduce back to their first simple mixture without requiring the great violence of fire. Under the "torture" <note>A common alchemical term for the intense heat and pressure of the furnace</note> of fire, even the earthy particles are made volatile, resulting in the intense corrosive heat of such spirits, which is not found in this "Philosophical Oil of Vitriol" <note>A refined, highly concentrated sulfuric acid sought by alchemists for its purity</note>. 

Even Vitriol of Venus <note>Copper sulfate</note> can indeed be freed from copper particles by means of iron, which dissolves in it, but then it becomes Vitriol of Mars <note>Iron sulfate</note>; and those particles can be precipitated with zinc, becoming Vitriol of Zinc. Thus, if you wish to avoid one inconvenience, you fall into another. Finally, if you wish to precipitate vitriol with a strong lye <note>original: "Lixivio"</note> without metal, you disturb the whole mixture and create a new "decomposed" substance; you will never obtain that celebrated "Virgin Astral Sulfurous Salt" or Universal Decomposing Acid. Many more specific details about this remarkable liquor and the perpetual pyrite-bearing mine are known to the *most illustrious Mr. Boyle* <note>Robert Boyle (1627–1691), the famous English natural philosopher and chemist</note>, who had better opportunity, more time, and a more subtle genius for investigating such things.

### SECOND SPECIES OF MINERAL

This is also simple, yet very natural. Sand, from which gold has been washed, is flooded with water and exposed to the heat of the sun; thus, more gold is gradually generated inside it, especially if it is sprinkled with salty water and rain. Others have imitated this, mixing sand with mud, limestone, or chalk; they dissolved metals in non-corrosive solvents <note>original: "menstruis"</note> and sprinkled the earth with these solutions. After exposing them to the sun and leaching <note>original: "elixarunt"</note> them at the end of summer, they reduced the extract and found the metal produced and increased. 

I know some who have reduced metals back into "ores" (through a rather easy manipulation); they ground these and saturated them with alkali or mixed the metals with other salts and noticed a significant effect. However, when they occasionally erred in their Art, they found the metal transmuted into running mercury <note>Liquid quicksilver</note>, following the observation of *P. Kircher* <note>Athanasius Kircher (1602–1680), a Jesuit polymath who wrote on the "subterranean world"</note> cited by me in the first supplement to my *Physica Subterranea* <note>Becher's major work, "Subterranean Physics," foundational to early chemical theory</note> against the "non-existence of mercury in bodies" argued by *Rolfinck* <note>Werner Rolfinck (1599–1673), a German physician and chemist</note>:

> *Lead, soaked for a long time in salt waters, is dissolved into Mercury.*

Others, imitating this, took excavated ores—whether poor, immature, or volatile—and mixed them with mud and lime. They soaked them with a certain kind of lye and exposed them for a certain time to the rays of the sun and moon. Afterward, they smelted them and found a not insignificant increase...

At this point, I could demonstrate a certain singular **Lye** <note>original: "Lixivium"; a solution of alkaline salts often used in early chemistry for leaching metals</note> of admirable operation, but I do not wish to treat the unworthy equally with the worthy; rather, *I wish to give hay to the Ox, and sugar to the Parrot.* <note>A Latin idiom meaning to provide each person with what is appropriate for their station or capacity</note> There are many certain Minerals which, because of their poverty <note>Low yield of precious metal</note>, or immaturity, or their volatility and the irregular melting that results from them, cannot be processed; yet all of these could be conveniently cultivated with the help of this medium.

The third species of perpetual Minerals consists in the extraction of various sands and Earths by means of some base solvent, about which **Glauber** <note>Johann Rudolf Glauber (1604–1670), a famous German-Dutch alchemist known for his work in manufacturing salts and acids</note> wrote entire treatises to the point of satiety, and almost even to nausea. Yet he has had few followers, for the world today is lazy and does not gladly delight in complexities; it seeks true Gold in large masses through tedious labors, and not in tiny atoms. However, if the Lords of Provinces and Kingdoms knew and considered what such washings and extractions perform collectively and annually—since there is hardly a stream whose sandy atom, and not even its smallest Flint, does not contain some Metal—they would look more deeply. Hence, even the mud and filth of the Streets is often rich in Gold, as I could cite a memorable example here concerning a certain significant City in the World, if I wished to serve the ungrateful as well as the grateful. For these and other reasons, I say, the Rulers of affairs ought to compel their subjects to apply their efforts to this study (for it would be better to collect this filth or mud than to gather broken glass and old iron); for every little bit collected helps, as Esdras rightly says, *the Earth gives a little dust, from which Gold is made.* <note>A reference to 2 Esdras 8:2 in the Apocrypha: "The earth giveth much mould whereof earthen vessels are made, but little dust that gold cometh of."</note> I know a certain great Monarch who sometimes does not have as much Gold in his **Purse** as his Peasants or washers hide in their washing cloths as **Gold-Spangles** <note>original: "Bifetta Auri"</note> and steal from him; from which it can be gathered how much the *business of washing* brings in.

The fourth species of perpetual Minerals indeed emulates the first species, but it is more artificial; for instead of simple or mineral Earth, Metals are taken and, with great skill, are continuously inflamed and digested by **Sulfurous vapor**, with the addition of a moderate degree of fire. This labor is very natural and useful. I have experienced wonders regarding **Lead** treated in such a way, and certainly **Glauber** does not write empty things about this matter in his book on the ***Secret Fire***, where he expressly demonstrates that the first mobile agent, or maturer of Metals, is **Sulfurous Acid**, which he demonstrates by no negligible experiments. He especially teaches how to construct a **perpetual Mineral**, which I saw with my own eyes thus constructed at **Vienna** by a certain **Friend of Chemistry** <note>original: "Philo Chymicum"</note> named **Hoffmuller**, which was heavy with many hundreds of pounds of Metal. Elsewhere I have also seen imperfect Minerals, such as Arsenic, Orpiment, Antimony, Cobalt, and Marcasite fixed in this way. Here it is to be noted—and it is a beautiful sight—that even silver itself, mixed in due proportion with Sulfur, roasted, and treated with the requisite precise degree of Fire, can cause the Metallic mass to grow over some span of time, with a sufficiently strong fire, into beautiful **Massive little trees**, <note>The author is describing the formation of "dendrites" or crystal growths that resemble trees, which alchemists saw as proof of the "life" of metals</note> just as sometimes happens in Mines. This method is the basis for that celebrated transplantation of **Wilhelm von Rosenberg**, which I mentioned in the preface: **Montanus on the Flame of Sulfur reacting upon molten Copper for some time**...

matter, as **Morhof** <note>Daniel Georg Morhof (1639–1691), a German scholar and historian of literature and science</note> alleges in a letter to **Langelott** <note>Joel Langelott (1617–1680), physician to the Duke of Holstein and an alchemist</note>, he recounts a memorable story. Another and far more memorable history, with a practical method attached, is known to me and is in writings at hand from a very ancient Codex—a source deserving of truth—whereby the continuous, skillful application of a **Sulfurous Flame** converts **Moon** <note>original: "Luna"; the alchemical name for Silver</note>, or **Silver**, into Glass and a tincture, with observations that are far from common. The associates and relatives of **Cornelius Drebbel** <note>Cornelius Drebbel (1572–1633), the famous Dutch inventor of the first navigable submarine and a pioneer in chemical technology</note> admit that he possessed a certain chemical **particular** <note>original: "particulare"; in alchemy, a process that achieves a partial transmutation or works on a specific metal rather than the "Universal" elixir</note>, though they know nothing more of the matter than what they remember: that they continually smelled the odor of a sulfurous flame in his house because sulfur was always burning. Experience demonstrates what even common flames can achieve—if they lick **Lead**, **Tin**, **Iron**, or **Copper** at a certain and continuous degree—converting them into impalpable powders. Regarding their perfection and transmutation, metals so **calcined** <note>reduced to powder by heat</note> and extracted can no longer be converted back into their original substance, but instead take on another nature. Hence, the most sagacious **Verulam** <note>Francis Bacon, Baron Verulam (1561–1626), the influential English philosopher who promoted the experimental method</note> sensed that if metals were held in a continuous flux and treated with the required altering agents, they must be changed and perfected. He wrote on this matter and proposed a method in the fourth century <note>a "century" refers to a division of 100 observations or experiments</note> of his *Natural History*, by which it seemed possible to him to change a baser metal into Gold. After he reviewed the requirements for this work, he finally ordered the matter to be instituted as follows in number 327:

### Verulam’s Artificial Mineral.

> *Let a narrow furnace be prepared and a temperate heat be excited; indeed, such a heat as keeps the metal perpetually molten, not more 
vehement, which is of the greatest importance for the matter. Let the material be silver, the metal most symbolizing gold, with which a tenth part of **quicksilver** <note>original: "Mercurii vivi"</note> is added, and a twelfth of **nitre** <note>saltpeter</note> of the correct weight, which serve to vegetate and open the body of the metal. I would wish the operation to be continued for at least six months, and that oily substances be injected at times—such as those used in recovering gold that has been made difficult to separate by cannons <note>likely referring to the refining of gold from scrap or contaminated sources</note>—to the end that the parts may be disposed more tightly or loosely. This is of great importance to the design, for gold, as is well known, is the most compact and heaviest of all metals, and the most flexible and extensible. Thus far, Bacon of Verulam.*

I know there will be many who turn up their noses because I seem to agree with Bacon's method, which appears utterly absurd. For who has ever seen or heard of Silver being melted with Mercury for six continuous months without the Mercury immediately flying away at the first moment in the melting fire? Therefore, its addition and mixing with Silver would be useless. To these I respond that one must look more to Bacon’s intention than to his literal words. For I know of someone who held silver in flux for a long time and repeatedly injected quicksilver, but captured the evaporating mercury through a specific receptacle, and he did not perform a vain labor. Truly, as to what Verulam means by the "oiliness" to be injected frequently, which workers use in the reduction of the **calx of gold** <note>the powdery residue left after gold is heated or treated with acids</note>, first...

Therefore, by industry, we have gathered that it is highly advantageous to have a crucible carved from a **millstone** <note>likely a hard sandstone or quartzite</note> rather than a soft one; I have often known these to resist the fire for a very long time, even for a year. When these things are done, it will be proper that we hasten to the act of establishing the mineral. But where there is the choice to establish a perpetual mine, it is necessary to continue the fire without any intermission, and when thirty days have passed from the beginning, you shall begin on the following first day to draw out one ounce of **molten metal** from the crucible, for it will be **pure gold**, in whose place an ounce of **Silver** must be supplied into the crucible itself. It is necessary to work diligently so that it melts with the others in turn; soon the prepared **red vitriol** should be added on top, and thereafter the **cinnabar**. Afterward, the work requires the crucible to be covered and the fire to be zealously guarded, and after each twenty-fourth hour has passed, it is profitable to do the same: first by taking from the crucible one ounce of that which will be molten, and in its place supplying an ounce of **Silver** to be melted; after it is liquefied, let the **red lizard** be put in, and subsequently the **prepared cinnabar**. Soon the vessel is covered, and so every twenty-fourth hour the same order is restored, even unto infinity. Two things, however, it will be right to notice: one, namely, do not let one [ingredient] be placed before the others, but let the rule assigned above be followed. The other is to put an iron rod into the crucible with which the hard skin is broken—this occurs from the metals in the likeness of a crust. Therefore, four or six times, if necessary, between day and night, let the crust be broken every day with the iron rod so that it melts and is mixed, for in this way it will happen according to your wish.

Thus far **Caneparius**; whose obscurity of style, terms, and manipulation—following his custom—is encountered by everyone throughout this process, so much so that this process would require an entire commentary. I could supply this if I believed it were my duty to correct the labors of others, to amend what is poorly placed, to supply what is omitted, and to explain what is obscure. They have a base, yet the same and certain effect can never be guaranteed; for there are **Vitriols** <note>original: "Vitriola"; sulfates of metals, highly prized in alchemy for their acidic properties</note> whose oil already contains actual **Gold** <note>original: "Aurum"</note> within itself, as can be demonstrated, especially in the *Hungarian* variety. In this *Forgatschian Process* <note>named after the Hungarian noble family Forgách, known for their interest in alchemy</note>, therefore, *Hungarian Vitriol* is taken and calcined to redness; vinegar is poured over it three or four times, and the *Essence of Vitriol* is extracted by distillation. The extraction is decanted, filtered, and evaporated to the consistency of a red syrup. Of this, three ounces are taken, along with five ounces of **cinnabar** <note>mercury sulfide</note>; once well mixed, they are moistened and slowly dried with the water of **sal ammoniac** <note>ammonium chloride</note>. This is repeated three or four times. Then it is mixed with an equal weight of *lime of the Moon* <note>original: "calcis Lunae"; silver that has been reduced to a powder or "calx"</note> and distilled through a *Retort*. That which remains is "fulminated" <note>refined at high heat</note> in a *Cupel* <note>a shallow porous vessel used in assaying</note> by means of *Saturn* <note>Lead</note>, and is separated in *aqua fortis* <note>original: "aqua forti"; nitric acid, used to separate silver from gold</note>. This *Mass of Vitriol and Cinnabar* can also be injected successively into molten silver; the same effect follows, but the **Mercury** <note>original: "Mercurius"</note> is lost, which, from this labor, is not to be despised.

The same work succeeds differently if you take the *Pyrrmieson stone, or the Stone of Three Smokes* <note>original: "lapidem Pyrrmieson seu lapidem de Tribus fumis"; a cryptic alchemical substance, possibly a sulfurous or arsenical mineral</note>, and pulverize it. Take one ounce of this powder and three ounces of *Saffron of Venus* <note>original: "Croci Veneris"; copper oxide</note>, and grind them very well, soaking them with *Oil of Vitriol* <note>sulfuric acid</note>; repeat this three times and dry it. Then melt fine **Silver** <note>original: "Lunam"</note> and successively inject this powder until the **Silver** becomes entirely brittle and pulverizable (which usually happens with an equal weight of the aforesaid powder). Detonate this pulverized **Silver** twice with an equal weight of a flux prepared from eight parts **Niter** <note>saltpeter</note>, four parts **sulfur**, and two parts **Tartar**. Then melt this detonated **Silver** with a flux of **Niter** and **Tartar** in equal parts for three hours over a strong fire. Pour it into a *Cone* <note>a conical casting mold</note> and the **Silver** will fall into a *Regulus like a Marcasite* <note>original: "Regulum instar Marchasitae"; "Regulus" refers to the metallic button found at the bottom of the crucible; marcasite here refers to its crystalline, metallic appearance</note>. To this, add an equal part of **Gold** <note>original: "Auri"</note>, and let it flow again with the flux of **Niter** and **Tartar**; you will again acquire a *Regulus*. Mix this with an equal weight of **Antimony**, and refine this *Regulus* with the salt from detonated **Niter** and **Tartar**. For this salt absorbs the **Antimony** and the remaining crudity of the **Silver**. If, after one attempt, the *Regulus* does not become malleable, repeat the labor until the mass is malleable. If it is not sufficiently tinged with a golden color, melt it with the *Red Gradatory Glass of Venus* <note>a chemical preparation of copper used to "grade" or improve the color of metals</note>; if the color becomes too reddish in this, then melt the mass once more in the ordinary way through **Antimony**, and it will acquire a most pleasing color. This process can also be set up so that the *Pyrrmieson Stone*, fixed with *Saffron of Venus and Oil of Vitriol* and reduced to powder, is injected successively into molten silver to which some **Gold** has been added. This labor is repeated continuously until the **Silver** is sufficiently brittle; then, by the injection of **Niter** alone in the same vessel, it can be refined by flux and fire. This refining should continue until the **Niter** is no longer tinged; then the slag should be removed and the work repeated anew with the *Pyrrmieson* stone and refined with **Niter** as was said. You will find this method of refining described more at length in *Glauber* <note>Johann Rudolf Glauber, 1604–1670, a famous chemist and apothecary</note>, in his explanation of the *Miracle of the World* <note>original: "Miraculi Mundi"</note>, who also wished to create a "perpetual ore" for merchants out of the *Martial Regulus of Antimony* <note>an alloy of antimony and iron</note>. But the good man was deceived in this, as many are, because he sought corporal gold in the *Regulus of Mars* <note>iron</note>, which is only to be found in its slags, as it lies hidden in the *Regulus* only spiritually, and cannot be drawn out except in a Philosophical manner. On the contrary, I would not have denied him the construction of the "perpetual ore" if he had injected the properly prepared slags of either *Mars* <note>Iron</note> or *Venus* <note>Copper</note>, whether separately or joined, into the influence of the **Silver** <note>original: "Lunae"</note>, and had drawn them out again and refined them by means of **Niter**. And this is the reason why *Alexander van Suchten* <note>c. 1520–1575, a Paracelsian chemist</note> commands that the first slags in the preparation of the *Regulus of Mars* be reserved, and to them the MYSTERY

As for what now pertains to the **Second Operation**, namely in the sulfurous grading liquids <note>liquids used to "grade" or improve the quality and color of a metal toward the appearance of gold</note>, one may read what **Claveus** <note>Gaston "Claveus" Dulco, a French alchemist who defended the art against critics</note> writes in his *Apology against Erastus* concerning **Silver** <note>original: "Luna"</note> transmuted into **Gold**, in these words: *“Let a most sharp and tingeing water <note>original: "aqua acerrima & tingens"; a strong acid, likely nitric acid or a similar solvent</note> be distilled, which many are familiar with; it must be distilled several times until no dregs remain at the bottom of the vessel after distillation. For it is of great importance that all things be purged of impure dross and thickness. Common **quicksilver** <note>original: "argentum vivum"; mercury</note> must also be purified by many repeated sublimations until it is clear, and then revived. Let two ounces of the purest silver be dissolved separately in the distilled sharp water. In the same water, let four ounces of the purest quicksilver be dissolved separately, and let the dissolved portions be mixed. Let the water be distilled first with a weak fire until it has all dripped over. From here, let the degree of heat be increased so that the quicksilver also expires <note>is driven off as vapor</note> through distillation; then let the glass vessel be broken. In the bottom of the vessel, you will see a silver mass colored partly gray and partly a dark, obscure red. Finally, reduce this back into a solid body. This silver, though it has not yet changed its color nor is it yet gold, is nonetheless purer and more solid than natural silver, and its moisture is more defined. Therefore, in the test of gold—namely through cementing—it is separated only with great difficulty and only after frequent repetitions. Indeed, when it is dissolved by the sharp water of separation <note>nitric acid</note>, you will see certain filings of pure gold remain. By this sign, you shall judge that the entire mass of silver can be changed into gold, since the nature of the whole is the same as the nature of the part. This work of maturation bears a certain hope of fruit. For as soon as grapes ripen, you will see some grains suffused with a black color, while the others are without any change in color; yet when the maturation is finished by preceding and continued heat, they are all black. Thus, if the same Silver is dissolved more often by the same sharp water, and the dissolved quicksilver is mixed with it, and the water is distilled, and the quicksilver expires, and the mass settling at the bottom is reduced into a body, the whole will be changed into gold. By reiterating the cooking, it will eventually acquire various colors, until at last a red, splendid, fixed, and unchangeable color appears, which is the sign of perfect concoction. But great diligence must be applied in the reduction into a body, lest it lose too much weight; otherwise, almost all the silver will vanish into vapor in the spirits of the sharp waters during the repetition of the work. No other danger is to be feared in this experiment. Ingenious men will be able to avoid this impediment, nor does reason suggest pouring everything out to the common crowd.”* To these things which **Claveus** writes, that most celebrated poet of Rimini, **Augurellus** <note>Giovanni Aurelio Augurello, author of the 1515 poem "Chrysopoeia," which framed alchemy in Virgil-style verse</note>, seems to harmonize in his poem on **Gold-making** <note>original: "Chrysopœia"</note>, in the following verses:

> I have seen one who properly scattered thin plates of silver,
> And the powder of crushed brick, and to this alone
> Ordered green scales of copper, and snowy flakes of burnt salt
> To be crushed and joined;
> Piling up dusty heaps from other things,
> Which both reason and the art itself forbid to be recounted,
> Lest it become cheapened for the uses of the filthy commoner,
> And so that the art does not reveal to anyone what must be hidden.
> Soon, with the plates thus arranged in a narrow box,
> He subjected the enclosed items to flames under a chalky arch,
> Such as I would believe the springs are scorched in the Underworld <note>original: "Tartara"</note>
> Or where the Air presses upon dreadful places in sulfurous caves.

But what need is there for subtle and enigmatic descriptions of this kind? Convert **Sulfur** into **fixed Earth**, and resolve this into water; you will have the best grading liquor <note>original: "liquorem gradatorium"; a solution used to increase the "grade" or purity and color of a metal</note>, indeed almost a transmuting one. Read what **Glauber** <note>Johann Rudolf Glauber (1604–1670), a significant chemist whose work bridged alchemy and modern chemistry</note> writes in his book *On the Three Principles*, in the section on Sulfur, near the end regarding its fixation and conversion into a liquor; where he says: *that **Lead** <note>original: "Saturnum"</note> digested in it, in the space of fourteen days, was half changed into **Silver** <note>original: "argentum"</note>.* Since, however, he confesses that the reduction of fixed Sulfur into a liquor is very difficult, he slips into another invention, which he also calls the **Perpetual Mineral**. It consists of mixing common ashes with this fixed Sulfur, forming cupels <note>small shallow bowls used in assaying gold or silver</note> and ash-vessels from them, refining **Lead** <note>original: "Saturnum"</note> with **Silver** <note>original: "Luna"</note> upon them, and then reducing the refined material. But this labor relates rather to my 7th Mineral and the **Grillian Process** <note>likely a reference to a specific procedure by an alchemist named Grill or Grillus</note>, and it is much more difficult than the former.

For by a simple method and perpetual increase, I know how to convert common Sulfur into a **fixed earth**—much like the **Dead Head** <note>original: "capitis mortui"; the useless residue left after distillation</note> of **Vitriol** <note>sulfuric acid or metallic sulfates</note>—and how to reduce this fixed and tasteless earth back into an aqueous liquor or oil by perpetual increase. This is not unlike the **Oil of Vitriol**, which is a true **liquid Earth**, and perhaps not undeservedly called by some the **Oil of the Philosophers**. Let this seem strange, impossible, or contrary to reason to no one: for since it is clearly established that Earth can be made from water, it should not be doubted that Earth can also be reduced into water, or that Earth is condensed water, and water is fluid Earth. These changes, through the rarefaction and condensation of prudent distillation or chemical operation, can be demonstrated to anyone's eyes. There, too, wonderful effects are to be seen which arise from solvents in which rarefied earthy atoms are present. 

But because these mysteries, for other reasons, are not to be scattered among the common people, I rightly abstain, and only recommend the use of the **Spirit of Nitre** <note>Nitric acid</note>, provided it is properly prepared; relying on the testimony of those who know the truth of my words. For I say that such a Spirit returns much more profit to its possessor from the conversion of **Silver** <note>original: "Luna"</note> into **gold** than the **Bank** or that famous **Amsterdam Exchange** <note>original: "Argentaria Amstelodamensis"</note> returns annually in interest for a hundred to its depositors. From this, that liquor obtained the name **THE TRIBUTARY PEASANT** <note>original: "RUSTICI TRIBUTARIUS"; suggesting a substance so productive it pays its "taxes" or "tribute" in gold</note> among certain people.

*Let a most sharp and staining water be distilled, which many know; it must be distilled, and repeatedly, until no dross remains at the bottom of the vessel after distillation. For it is of great importance that all things be purged of impure dross and thickness. Common **quicksilver** <note>original: "argentum vivum"; mercury</note> must also be purged by several repeated sublimations, until it becomes transparent, and from this it is revived. Let two ounces of the purest silver be dissolved separately by the sharp distilled water. By the same water, let four ounces of the purest quicksilver be dissolved separately; let the dissolved substances be mixed. Let the water be distilled first with a weak fire, until it has all dripped over. Then let the degree of heat be increased, so that the quicksilver also exhales through distillation; then let the glass vessel be broken. In the bottom of the vessel, you will see a silver mass tinted partly with an ash-colored and partly with a dark-red color. Finally, reduce this into a metal body. Although this silver has not yet changed its color, nor is it gold, it is nevertheless purer and more solid than natural silver, and its moisture is more defined. Therefore, in the trial of gold—namely by cementing—it is separated only with the greatest difficulty, and only after frequent repetitions. Indeed, even when it has been dissolved by the sharp water of separation, you will see certain filings of pure gold settle at the bottom. By this sign, you shall judge that the entire mass of silver can be changed into gold, since the nature of the whole is the same as the part. This work bears a certain resemblance to the ripening of fruits. For as soon as grapes begin to ripen, you will see some grains suffused with a black color, while the others remain without any change of color; yet when the ripening is completed by the preceding and continued heat, they are all black. Thus, if the same silver is frequently dissolved by the same sharp water, and dissolved quicksilver is mixed with it, and the water is distilled, and the quicksilver has exhaled, and the mass settling at the bottom is reduced into a metal body, the whole will be changed into gold. By reiterating the "digestions" <note>original: "coctiones"; literally "cookings"</note>, it will also contract various colors from time to time, until finally a red, brilliant, fixed, and unchangeable color appears, which is the sign of perfect digestion. The ingenious will be able to avoid this impediment, nor does reason persuade one to pour out all secrets to the common crowd.*

The **Perpetual Philosophical Mine** <term>Minera Philosophica perpetua: a theoretical alchemical process where a small amount of gold acts as a "seed" to produce more gold indefinitely</term> is so called, and it consists in this: that **Gold** <note>original: Aurum</note> is resolved through a certain kind of **quicksilver** <note>original: Argenti vivi</note> into a **Mercury**, which passes through both leather and a retort, and which, when fixed, exhibits Corporal Gold. From this, the term **Philosophical Particular** <term>Particulare Philosoph.: a "particular" work is a lesser alchemical success that transmutes a specific amount of metal, rather than the "Universal" medicine or Stone</term> arose; namely, if a particle of this fixed powder is reduced in the fire into gold and sold for civil use. But the remaining particle of the powder is mixed again with three parts of **suitable** Mercury and placed for fixation. Thus, approximately every month, you will be able to take out half and reduce it into Gold, while perpetually increasing the remainder. For you possess the **perpetual ferment**, which they call **Physical** or **Philosophical Gold**, provided you do not lack that which is growable and fermentable—namely, our required **quicksilver**, which is nothing other than entirely fluid Gold, that is, potential **Gold**. 

Where it is also a curious sight that silver, or **Gold**, amalgamated with **Mercury**, whether by the liquid or dry path, grows out into the most beautiful little trees, unchangeable by any goldsmith, which even show their own fruits, all arranged in a wonderful manner; whence such an outgrowth is usually called the **Philosophers' Tree** <term>Arbor Philosophorum: a crystalline growth of silver or gold in a solution, often involving mercury, which resembles a miniature tree</term>. I could suggest many things here, not only curious but also useful, but since God created this Mine only for **Philosophers**, it would be a sin and a crime to bring it into political <note>In this context, "political" refers to common, public, or profane commercial use.</note> use. 

Nevertheless, what **Claveus** <note>Gaston "Claveus" Dulco (c. 1530–1591), a French physician and alchemical writer who defended the art against critics.</note> wrote concerning this **perpetual Mine** and its eternal Increase—namely, concerning the properties of the suitable **Mercury**—is true, and consistent with reason and practice; for he who has seen it can likewise testify. Therefore, I wished to subjoin his words here, so that those who think the conditions of this **Philosophical Mine** are so irrational, impossible, and difficult may be convinced to the contrary by reason and experience. I am commanded to remain silent here for the sake of the unworthy; otherwise, I could open the eyes of the whole world in a few lines and fulfill the prophecy concerning this **eightieth** year <note>Likely 1680, a year associated with several alchemical and chiliastic prophecies in the late 17th century.</note>. But since evils are not to be done out of contempt and for the revenge of a few (lest hatred and loss spring from it, and the curse of all Philosophers), it shall suffice to have added the following words of **Claveus** and to have commended this Homogeneous **Mercury**.

    But since **Claveus** explains all these things at great length and breadth, I do not wish to fill these papers of mine with the writings of others against my custom, but rather to reduce them to a compendium. Therefore, I will offer the reader a very brief extract, excerpted by me from **Claveus** with great study, which is as follows:

    After the Author had most learnedly and profoundly explained the whole history of mixture and accretion <note>Accretion: the process by which metals "grow" or increase in weight/purity in alchemical theory.</note>, especially proper to metals, and solidly demonstrated that nothing can grow onto Gold which cannot first be intimately united with it; and that such a union cannot happen except through a radical solution <term>radical solution: a process where a substance is dissolved back into its most fundamental, "root" components</term>; and that from such a solution, a radical coagulation and fixation must necessarily follow according to the course of Nature.

❃ ( 438 ) ❃

The **Perpetual Philosophical Mine** <note>original: Minera Philosophica perpetua</note> is so named because it consists of this: that **Gold** <note>original: Aurum</note> is resolved into **Mercury** <note>original: Mercurium</note> by a certain kind of **quicksilver** <note>original: Argenti vivi</note>. This Mercury passes through both leather <note>Alchemists often squeezed mercury through chamois leather to filter out impurities</note> and the retort <note>a glass vessel with a long, downward-pointing neck used for distillation</note>, and when fixed, it yields "Corporal Gold." From this arises the term **Philosophical Particular** <note>original: Particulare Philosoph.</note>; for if a small portion of this fixed powder is reduced in the fire into gold, it may be sold for common use. But the remaining portion of the powder is mixed again with three parts of suitable Mercury and set for fixation. In this way, approximately every month, you can remove half and reduce it to Gold, while perpetually increasing the remainder. For you possess a **perpetual ferment**, which they call **physical gold** or **philosophical gold**, provided you do not lack the "growable" and "fermentable" substance—namely, our required **quicksilver**, which is nothing other than fluid gold in its entirety, that is, **potential gold**. 

It is also a curious sight to see how silver or gold, when amalgamated with Mercury, whether by the liquid or dry path, grows into most beautiful little trees. These cannot be imitated by any goldsmith, as they even display their own "fruits," all arranged in a wondrously elegant manner; hence such an outgrowth is usually called the **Tree of the Philosophers** <note>original: Arbor Philosophorum; a dendritic growth of silver or gold crystals, often called "Diana’s Tree"</note>. I could suggest many things here, not only curious but also useful; however, since God created this "Mine" only for **Philosophers**, it would be a divine offense and a sin to bring it into common political use. Nevertheless, what **Claveus** <note>Gaston "Claveus" Dulco, a 16th-century alchemist and defender of the craft</note> wrote concerning this perpetual mine and its eternal increase—specifically regarding the properties of the "suitable Mercury"—is true, and consistent with both reason and practice. For he who has seen it can likewise testify to it. Therefore, I wished to subjoin his words here, so that those who think the conditions of this **Philosophical Mine** are irrational, impossible, or too difficult, may be convinced otherwise by reason and experience. I am commanded to remain silent here for the sake of the unworthy; otherwise, in a few lines, I could open the eyes of the whole world and fulfill the prophecy concerning this **Year Eighty** <note>original: Anno hoc octuagesimo; likely referring to the year 1680, a year of great apocalyptic and alchemical expectation</note>. But since evil things should not be done out of contempt or for the sake of a few people's revenge (lest hatred and loss spring from it, along with the curse of all Philosophers), it shall suffice to have added the following from **Claveus** and to have recommended this **Homogeneous Mercury**.

But since **Claveus** explains all these things copiously and at length, I do not wish to fill these pages of mine with another man’s writings against my custom. Instead, I will reduce them into a compendium. I will therefore offer the reader a very brief extract, excerpted by me from **Claveus** with great study, which is as follows:

After the Author has most learnedly and profoundly explained the whole history of mixing and growth (which is characteristic of metals above all else) and has solidly demonstrated that nothing can grow onto Gold which cannot first be intimately united with it; and that such a union cannot happen except through a radical solution <note>a "radical solution" refers to dissolving a substance back to its "root" or primary matter</note>; and that from such a solution, according to the course of Nature, a radical coagulation and fixation must necessarily follow.

Although our author has handed down the Art clearly and faithfully enough, many things will nevertheless prove difficult for the reader in practice; for the Chemical Philosophers, however faithfully they have acted with readers, have never wished to be bound to their own words, any more than politicians. For in every writing, one must look rather to the meaning and the matter than to the manner of writing and the letter: for no less in Hermetic Philosophy than in Jurisprudence, circumstances change the law. Thus if our author seems to vary in this—that now he takes two, now three parts of animated Mercury, now commends animated common Mercury, now prefers the "Mercury of the bodies," now orders Gold and Silver to be passed through leather by **Amalgamation** <term>the process of mixing mercury with another metal to form an alloy</term>, and to be distilled through a **Retort** <term>a glass vessel with a long neck used for distilling liquids</term>, and yet it does not succeed in practice—then it must be known that the Author explains himself in other places, or wishes to be understood according to the spirit and not the letter. 

For example, when he varies in weight, he explains himself: *Therefore, there is one ounce of golden lime, and three of animated quicksilver; yet if more were mixed with three ounces of animated quicksilver, even up to five, there would be no danger; for the "seed" would dissolve faster, but would thicken and coagulate more slowly.* Item: *For quicksilver is drawn forth from tin, lead, and brass with the greatest art, and is mixed with silver or golden lime, as was handed down above, is cooked together, and is reduced into a silver or golden body.* 

But no quicksilver from all metallic bodies, when mixed with golden lime, is changed more quickly and perfectly than that which is drawn forth by art from pure silver. Item: *I have said that the efficient cause draws forth quicksilver from tin, lead, brass, and iron.* For they themselves are not the **proximate** matter <note>the immediate or direct substance needed for a reaction</note> to Silver and Gold, but only near matter; therefore, by a simple dissolution, the proximate matter must be separated from their matter, which is quicksilver. 

Nor does it matter whether that quicksilver was fluid or not; as long as it has been purged of all filth and substance foreign to the nature of quicksilver: indeed, the more perfectly it is cooked, the closer a "subject" it will be. For if we must define silver and gold by their matter, surely both will be nothing else than pure quicksilver, purified from all foreign substance and defined and cooked according to the degree of each. For gold is purer and far more decocted <note>original: decoctum; highly refined or "cooked" by nature's heat</note> even to the extreme of metallic nature, while silver is less so. 

That these things are so is clear from the mutual embrace of quicksilver, gold, and silver, and truly from the similarity in certain of their own properties mentioned above, and also because by Art, gold is almost dissolved into fluid quicksilver. <meta>This page continues the discussion of the "Mercury of the bodies" versus common quicksilver, specifically focusing on the temperature required to unite the "moist" and "dry" principles to achieve "fixation"—the process of turning a liquid or volatile substance into a stable solid.</meta>

The goal is to unite the moist with the dry, and to fix both with a firm and solid fixation <term>fixation: the alchemical process of making a volatile substance stable in fire</term>. Hence, in the observation of each external degree of heat, this shall be the **Law**: that the Heat be equal and tempered, such that it can alter both seeds when mixed, and not rarefy them into vapor. If, therefore, common animated silver <note>original: "Argentum vulgare animatum"; here referring to treated quicksilver</note> is mixed with gold, the degree of heat must be sent forth gently; for at the beginning of the Work, it is more indefinite and volatile. But if quicksilver polished by art <note>quicksilver extracted from other metals through chemical processes</note> is mixed with the same Gold, a slightly more intense degree of Heat must be applied. For quicksilver of this kind, since it is thicker and more decocted <term>decoction: a process of long-term heating to achieve "ripeness" or purity</term> by nature, tolerates a greater force of fire, nor does it easily fly off into smoke from the heat of the fire, as common quicksilver does. Furthermore, we have learned from the **Doctrine of Aristotle** <note>Referring to Aristotle’s *Meteorologica*, which explains the formation of minerals from "vapors" and "exhalations" within the earth</note> that the cause of solidification is partly the dryness of the Earth, which is present in the moisture of the gold and constrains it, and partly the external cold and dryness, which thicken and drive together the vapors (which are the nearest matter of Metals) within the rocks. Therefore, internal moisture, and external moisture and heat, shall be the efficient causes of the solution <note>dissolving</note> of gold into a moist substance. Now, this external moisture must be of the same nature as the moisture of the gold, such as the moisture of quicksilver, so that it can dissolve the dryness of the gold by its own quantity. But the less this moisture of quicksilver possesses a cold quality, the more readily it dissolves gold. Therefore, I would not wish to disapprove of the opinion of those who are accustomed to draw forth quicksilver from lead, tin, bismuth, or antimony; for it is less cold than common quicksilver, and is a little more digested and defined. And I hear many use these for the solution of gold, and from the mixture of both, they have perfected the work as if with the true seed. Regarding all these aforementioned things, though they recommend the *Mercury of the Bodies* <note>mercury extracted from "perfect" metals like lead or tin</note>, our Author seems to sound the **Signal** <note>original: "Classicium canere"; a trumpet call to battle or a definitive proclamation</note> with one breath in the following words, when he expressly recommends common **Mercury** above all others. The words of the Author are these:

> But I am not to be disapproved of if I say that common quicksilver is the other part of the seed, provided that it has first been mixed and truly united with a small portion of Gold; for then it is called, by a transfer of terms, animated quicksilver—not because it has a soul, for it is inanimate, but because just as the soul makes an animal warm as long as it is in the body, so Gold wards off and tempers the coldness of quicksilver when it is truly mixed with it. For of the Philosophical Stone, or the gold-making salt (which is nothing other than gold decocted far more than natural gold), the smallest portion redeems and tempers infinite parts of quicksilver from excessive coldness. One must insist upon this animated quicksilver rather than that which is drawn from metals by art. For that is not brought out from metals except by great ingenuity of art, and much labor and expense. But we have a vast supply of common quicksilver, and it can easily be purified and mixed with gold, and united to it, as I shall soon say. Therefore, to put an end to this question: quicksilver drawn by art from lead, or tin, or antimony, or common quicksilver prepared and animated (let it be permitted now and hereafter to use the terms of the art, so that all things may be said more significantly) is the other part of the seed of our gold-making **Salt**, so that both mixed together are its true seed.

Wherein I wish the Reader to be advised to notice why **Claveus** <note>Gaston "Claveus" Duclo, a 16th-century alchemist known for defending the possibility of transmutation</note> prefers common Mercury: namely, because it can be had in vast supply, easily purified, and can be mixed and united with gold. But with what Gold? Namely, such gold that can, in its smallest portion, redeem, heat, animate, and temper infinite parts from the coldness of quicksilver. He himself indicates that this is not common gold, but gold decocted far more than natural gold, which is the Gold of the Philosophers, and Physical Gold, in which the *Mercury of the Bodies* abounds; common Mercury, however, must extract this from other bodies with much study and labor.

...so much so that for one who knows the easy **Extraction of Mercury** <term>mercurificatio: the alchemical process of extracting the "essential" or "philosophical" mercury from a solid metal</term> from *Bodies* [metals], that method is rightly to be preferred over the animation of common quicksilver; and for one who knows the latter by an *easy* method, it should, on the contrary, be preferred over the extraction of mercury from bodies. Thus, these contradictions can be reconciled, for they agree on this one point: that what animates the *Mercury* and makes it uniform is the *internal fire*, namely the *soul, or Physical Gold.* <note>original: "Aurum Physicum"; this refers to a spiritual or essential form of gold, not the common metal.</note> Again, *Claveus* <note>Gaston Duclo, known as Claveus, a 16th-century French alchemist and defender of the art.</note> seems to contradict himself regarding the preparation of the Mercury of the Bodies. For in one place he says: *Now, that quicksilver exists within metallic bodies is judged by this: that when melted and liquefied by fire, they all appear as fluid quicksilver. Indeed, I have seen and known how to extract fluid quicksilver from all Metals with the help of common quicksilver. For by washing and macerating it perfectly, whatever is impure and foreign to the nature of quicksilver goes into the dregs; what remains is dissolved by the heat of a vapor bath.* Then, elsewhere, regarding the preparation of Mercuries from *Lead, Tin, and the Regulus of Antimony* <note>original: "Regulo Stibii"; the metallic form of antimony produced after smelting.</note>, he wants them to be carried upward by the force of an intense fire until a certain dry vapor ascends, thickens on the sides of the vessel in the cold, and congeals. He wants this to be soaked in Oil of Tartar, ground, and thus reduced into the fluid substance of quicksilver, redeemed from earthly dregs. In this latter method of extraction, he followed *Geber* <note>The Latinized name of Jabir ibn Hayyan, the most famous early authority on alchemy, whose works defined medieval chemical practice.</note>, but in the former, he followed *Alexander von Suchten* (whose process wanders through the world today under various disguises). I distinguish this contradiction thus: metals that are not easily vaporized but are more easily *amalgamated* <term>amalgamation: the process of dissolving a metal into quicksilver</term> are more easily "mercurified" with *living* [common] Mercury. But those, especially *Minerals* like *Antimony*, which can be vaporized more easily than they can be amalgamated, can also be more easily "mercurified" by that path of vaporization; this can also apply to *lead*, so that both methods of extraction may apply to it. For lead is both *amalgamated and vaporized* easily, but one way is longer and the other shorter; one more productive, the other thinner. The former is known to many, while the latter—due to a lack of proper tools and the misunderstood vaporization methods of *Geber*—is known to

Nevertheless, the good man had an excellent concept, but he could not remove the smallest obstacle encountered on his path because he was ignorant of common studies, and especially of *Geber’s philosophy*. He separated things that were joined and mixed things that were separated, like a wretched *Sisyphus* <note>A figure from Greek mythology condemned to roll a boulder up a hill for eternity; used here to describe futile, repetitive labor.</note> pushing his stone. Since Geber establishes his sublimations for the sake of separation and purification, using a furnace and a manner certainly known to few, it is of such a kind that it is easier to discover it for oneself (and one may call upon Geber at least as a witness to the discovery). Moreover, both paths of extraction require the skilled hand of an Artist; neither common Mercury alone, without the prior sharpening of its central Salt—namely, the *increase of its dissolving power*—can do it; nor can the sublimation of Bodies alone, without the separation of the *arsenical* Earth, achieve it. But let the Reader know that such **revived** Mercury does not serve for the gilding of Goldsmiths; for it is highly dissolving, **making gold volatile and piercing** the silver that is to be gilded.

2. 3. ...can even be fixed by itself. I once knew a person who, from two **drachms** <note>A unit of weight; one drachm is roughly 3.9 grams.</note> of such Mercury, obtained **one drachm** of the best gold through the process of fixation. 5. This Mercury ought to occupy **less space** and yet **weigh more** than common Mercury; this is a clear sign that it is more compressed. It passes, moreover, from twelve degrees to **Six** at most. 6. From this it follows that such Mercury must also be thicker and denser than common Mercury; and though it may pass through leather or a **retort**, <note>A glass vessel used for distillation.</note> it is of such a consistency that when cut with a knife, it no longer flows back together, but behaves like **lard**; <note>original: "axungiae"; refers to the consistency of animal fat or grease.</note> behaving differently when dissolved in **strong water**. <note>original: "Aquae fortis"; Nitric Acid.</note> 7. And finally, it must be perfectly homogeneous, which will be apparent during **digestion**, <note>A process of gentle, continuous heating in a sealed vessel.</note> if it ejects no more black powder—or, if the black powder it does eject is **gold**, or if gold itself, when digested with such Mercury, is converted into a black powder that can no longer be **converted back into its old form of gold**. On this, read the *Process of Barnaud* <note>Nicolas Barnaud, a 16th-century French physician and alchemist.</note> and *Fernel's On the Hidden Causes of Things*. <note>Jean Fernel (1497–1558) was a prominent French physician; his work explored the "occult" or hidden forces in nature and medicine.</note> 

From these seven properties of homogeneous Mercury, there follows the multiplicative introduction of the golden form into metals, which is the "tincture"; yet our author here desires only an <term>anatic</term> <note>From the Greek 'ana,' meaning 'of equal parts.' In alchemy, this refers to a process where gold and mercury are combined in equal proportions to increase the quantity of the gold.</note> **accretion**. This can hardly be denied to him, but rather easily granted, if those who have prepared this homogeneous Mercury with no small amount of labor, care, and time are so foolish as to not know how to advance it further into a tincture, but are instead forced to "fix" it to Gold and reduce it to Gold. Many, perhaps not content with the value of the gold alone in respect to their labors, have ceased this perpetual augmentation, even though the added part is nobler than the base material. Hence our <term>Claveus</term> <note>Gaston Duclo, known as Claveus, a 16th-century defender of alchemy.</note> wisely says:

> *But if one were permitted to proceed further, I would dare to affirm that Quicksilver so "animated" is nothing other than raw and undefined Silver and Gold, which, once defined by the efficient cause, immediately transforms into them.*

But just as the genius of man is of such a nature that it always desires to investigate, overcome, and reconcile high, difficult, and impossible things, so in our times people have been found who investigated the "sharpening" and animation of Quicksilver by a lighter and shorter path. They did this not for the ultimate **Philosophic Work**, nor even for the preceding Philosophic "particular" or augmentation, but only incidentally, for the purpose of separating that **Gold** which exists within imperfect metals. This gold is so hidden beneath their **arsenical** dross that it does not come to light through common separation, but clings most tenaciously to the innermost atoms themselves. 

These men, seeing and having truly proven that **all metals are nothing other than gold surrounded by heterogeneous earthly particles** (as the most learned Claudius Berigardus, the Paduan philosopher, demonstrates in his *Pisan Circle*), <note>Claude Guillermet de Bérigard (1592–1663), an advocate of atomism who taught at Pisa and Padua.</note> and observing that once the contrary particles are removed, the remaining ones cling more strongly to each other, they wished to test the **spagyric** <note>The alchemical art of "separating and recombining" elements to achieve a purer state.</note> name in this task. They established a **Philosophic separation**; they foresaw that nothing in the world, by reason of weight, had a greater affinity with metals than **Mercury**. They judged that since bodies in the world **do not differ essentially more than they do by reason of their quantity**, Mercury would be the best "separator." It would, in the fullness of time, extricate the smallest atoms, resolve them, eject the lighter ones, and retain and unite the heavier ones—especially since they observed in Mercury not only a certain separating faculty, but also a **collecting** faculty, by means of which...

...to give entry and a metallic support or dwelling-place to those things which were otherwise exiled from the Mineral kingdom. Therefore, they took subjects in which the **Sulphur of Gold** is contained in quantity. They prepared and joined these by means of two other mercurial subjects, making them suitable for **Amalgamation**. They then mixed, digested, and dissolved them with a quantity of **Mercury**. In this way, they **whitened two walls with one bucket** <note>original: "una fidelia duos parietes dealbarunt"; a Latin idiom similar to "killing two birds with one stone," implying they achieved two alchemical goals simultaneously.</note>: namely, they freed the **common gold** that was impacted within these bodies in its smallest parts, and simultaneously separated the heterogeneous earth. Once that was separated, the remainder of the body was reduced into Mercury, and was thus impregnated with this spiritual, embryonic, and potential **Golden Sulphur**, or **Physical Gold**. This they obtained freely, with an increase in both quality and quantity, whether for the Philosophical Work or for the Philosophical Ore. The costs and expenses of the entire operation were paid for by the dissolving of the earthy dross and the corporal gold produced from it—as I could provide more than sufficient testimony regarding this experiment, which has been performed by certain great and honest men. Thus, this secondary operation can serve as the **Ore** and root of the preceding *Clavean* philosophy <note>Referring to the work of Gaston Claveus, a 16th-century alchemist.</note>, and that is enough said of it.

## The Lullian Perpetual Physical Ore of the Moon and Sun. <note>Referring to the alchemy of Silver (the Moon) and Gold (the Sun).</note>

It appears that our author, Claveus, derived and refined the preceding "Ore" from the most subtle **Ramon Lull**, <note>Ramon Lull (c. 1232–1315), a famous Majorcan philosopher; many influential alchemical texts were attributed to him in the centuries following his death.</note> the Majorcan philosopher not unknown to the English. Therefore, I hope it will not be unwelcome to the chemical-loving reader if I lead them to the very foundations and roots of this Ore; for truly, as the saying goes, *waters are drunk more purely from the source itself*. In no other philosopher is the term **perpetual physical ore** found more frequently or solemnly than here in the works of **Lull**. Nowhere did he write more clearly or faithfully than in this, his *Clavicula* <note>Latin for "Little Key."</note>, which he therefore also calls the *Apertorium* <note>The "Opener."</note>. It has pleased me, then, to place a few things from it before the reader's eyes—only a few, and only those pertaining to the matter at hand. Thus Lull begins:

We have called this work of ours the **Little Key**, because without this present book, no one can understand what we have written in our other books, in which we have completed the entire art—though in words somewhat obscure for the ignorant. I have written many and lengthy books divided into sections, and those are obscure, as appears in our *Testament*, where we treated the **Natural Principles**. There, everything pertaining to the art is set down, yet it is **under the hammer** <note>original: "sub martello"; likely a metaphor meaning the truth is "forged" or hidden within the difficult text, requiring hard work to uncover.</note> in the first text of Philosophy; likewise in our chapter on the **Living Mercury of the Philosophers**, and in the second part of the *Testament* concerning the **PHYSICAL EXUBERANCE OF ORES**, and in our book on the **Fifth Essence** <note>The "Quintessence," the purest or fifth element believed to be the life-force of matter.</note>: specifically, the first book on the fifth essence of gold and silver. Then, in other books made by me, where the entire art is complete: but we have hidden the **Secret** as much as possible. However, because without this Secret no one can enter the ores of the **Philosophers**, nor do anything else that might benefit them, therefore, with the help of the Most High, to whom it has pleased to [reveal] this...

Therefore, sons, I ask that you walk in the light with open eyes, and do not fall like the blind into the pit of destruction.

## On the Difference between Common Quicksilver and Physical Quicksilver.

We say that common quicksilver cannot be the Quicksilver of the Philosophers, by whatever craft it is prepared, because the common kind cannot be held in the fire except by another corporeal quicksilver that is *hot and dry* and more digested <note>In alchemy, "digestion" refers to the slow heating of a substance to bring it to maturity or purity</note>. Therefore, I say our Physical [mercury] is of a more fixed and hotter nature than the common kind. And this is because *our* corporeal quicksilver has been converted into a running quicksilver that does not stain the fingers; and when it is mixed with the common kind, they are joined and embrace each other with a bond of love, so that they are never separated from one another, just like water mixed with water, because such is the pleasure of nature. For *our* quicksilver enters and is actually mixed with the other common kind, drying up its phlegmatic moisture and removing the coldness from the body, turning it as black as coal, which it afterwards converts into *powder.* Note, therefore, that common quicksilver cannot perform such operations as *our Physical* [mercury] can, which in all its qualities possesses the heat of a truly tempered nature; and therefore the common kind is turned into its own tempered nature. Indeed, it even does something else, for after its transmutation it converts into pure Metal—that is, into the Sun or the Moon, depending on how it is extended, or from the Sun and Moon, as is shown in the second part of our practice. Furthermore, it possesses something greater, for it changes and converts *common* Mercury into a medicine that can transmute imperfect metals into perfect ones. Moreover, it turns the common kind into true Gold and Silver, better than that from a Mine. Note again that one ounce of *our* Physical Mercury can make a hundred Marks <note>A traditional European unit of weight for precious metals, often equal to 8 ounces</note> and so on to infinity with common quicksilver, without the ORE EVER FAILING. Furthermore, another...
