## LETTER H.

# Whether the Author's proposal can be profitably carried out and practiced in Holland?

After reading, hearing, and considering what has been brought forward thus far, some who are willing to set aside their passions and use free reason are indeed forced to admit the well-founded truth of the Proposition in nature. However, although they concede the *substance* of the proposal, they nevertheless speculate upon and object to serious <term>accidents</term> <note>original: "accidentia"; in the philosophy of the time, "substance" is the essence of a thing, while "accidents" are the external circumstances or non-essential qualities like cost or location</note> by which they seem to subvert the entire practice and the resulting utility.

1. For they object that many things can be proven *in Theory* which nevertheless have no place *in practice*.
2. That many things and operations succeed on a small scale, but not on a large scale.
3. That the expenses in operations of this kind usually exceed the returns.
4. That usually more of the substance of the silver is lost than the value of the gold added to it increases.
5. That the wages of workers in Holland, by reason of high rent and the price of food, far exceed those in Germany; and that such instruments, furnaces, and smelting operations require many men and cause various complications and confusion.
6. That fire and coal in Holland are of a much higher price compared to Germany, and that this is the sole reason why, even if minerals were found in Holland, they could not be treated with fruit and profit.
7. That the subjects, materials, and instruments necessary for this work, and other requirements, ought to be obtainable in quantity and at a good price; and that this work should and can only be carried out in forests and near the mines themselves in poor regions, but not in Holland, which is rich in commerce and wealth.

These and other reasons, since they seem to have some weight, deservedly merit a resolution. I respond therefore to the *first* point: It is true that some things are conceived in Theory that do not succeed in Practice, but this also cannot be denied: many things succeed more easily in practice than the cause and reason for their success can be assigned in Theory. We have an example in the <term>Magnet</term> <note>the lodestone or magnetic compass</note>, and its radiation and direction toward the Pole. Truly, any blacksmith can make a magnetic needle, yet even the most subtle philosopher can scarcely explain the cause of its motion and declination theoretically. Rather, therefore, things succeed in practice when Theory proceeds from Practice; *for every truly founded Theory must arise from some practice, and every true Practice must lean upon Theoretical precepts.* I say, therefore, that a Theory will not succeed in Practice if it has no practical principles; but that Theory will infallibly succeed in Practice which has taken its principles from that very practice. This is the true Method of all real Theory and Practice: namely, that one arises from the other and one confirms the other. It will be clear from what has gone before that the *Theory concerning the extraction of Gold from Sand is not a <term>chimera</term> <note>an impossible or idle fancy</note>, but rests upon much Practice, so much so that it is more practical than it is Theoretical.*

*Regarding the second,* it is true that many things succeed on a small scale which do not on a large scale. However, it also cannot be denied that many things can only be practiced on a large scale and not on a small one. We have an example of this regarding reduction in the furnaces they call *Stichofen* <note>original: "Stichofen"; a German term for a blast furnace or "tap-furnace" where molten material is periodically drained</note>, where it is certain that slag, ashes, stones, minerals, and other substances cannot be liquefied or reduced over a small fire in a tiny furnace. This must also be understood regarding bells and cannons, whose casting always succeeds better on a large scale than on a small one. This was my specific complaint throughout the entire summer at *The Hague* <note>original: "Hagæ Comitis"</note> and my protest to my Lords Commissioners: that it is impossible to demonstrate a small-scale trial regarding the smelting of Sand <note>original: "Arenæ"</note> by the same method that must be established on a large scale. Since the business is impossible on a small scale and does not succeed, I offered, on the contrary, to smelt and complete—within the space of 24 hours on a large scale, if work were required and demanded—ten thousand pounds of metallic glass made from sand, with the help of only three persons and *the measure of one fathom of wood* <note>original: "unius orgyiæ ligni mensura"; an "orgia" or fathom was a standard measurement for stacked firewood</note>. Although this experiment would have cost very little, I could never obtain permission, nor was even a place granted for it. It is certain, therefore, that the processing of Sand succeeds more easily on a large scale than on a small one.

*Regarding the Third,* processes that require many ingredients, operations, and time are indeed expensive, and it cannot be denied that the results sometimes do not compensate for the expenses. But in my work with sand, all things are most simple. Indeed, I require no more than three materials, no more than *three* operations, no more than *three furnaces*, and no more than *three men*. These are sufficient for *processing twenty thousand marks every day*. This labor is easily continued for an entire year. These claims will deserve some measure of belief and possibility if we consider the great smeltings of ores at the metal mines—how much labor and work they finish in the course of a day. This labor is well known to me, especially since it is known that for this very reason I maintained a glass furnace in Vienna for an entire year, day and night, at no small expense.

*Regarding the Fourth,* the general Assay-master <term>Docimasta</term> <note>A specialist in the testing and assaying of metals to determine their purity</note> of Holland, *Braunsteinius*, as well as *Keerwolf* of Amsterdam and my clerk *Farnerius*, will testify that the silver applied to this work not only lost nothing of its weight after use, but rather something was added to it. For from one mark of Silver—namely, 16 loth <note>original: "lothonibus"; a "loth" was a unit of weight equal to about half an ounce</note>—we sometimes acquired 17 loth of the highest quality silver. The reason for this increase is easily apparent to anyone slightly experienced in Chemistry.

*Regarding the Fifth,* I do not believe there is any part of the world in which the price of grain and human ingenuity drive men to labor more than in Holland, nor where a greater abundance of workers can be had, nor where the matter of salary is debated more accurately, nor where common men live more sparingly. This is certainly not the case in Germany. I can further add that if those very high taxes upon food and drink did not exist in Holland, there would be no place in Europe where one could live at a lower price than there, and the salary of the workers would be of the lowest cost. But what need is there for such shortcuts, when this processing of sand brings in so much profit that the workers can be honorably paid from it? Nor is there a need *to muzzle the mouth of the ox that treads the grain* <note>A biblical reference to Deuteronomy 25:4, implying that those who do the work deserve to share in the fruits of the labor</note>. **First**, I conclude: the author's sand-work is easier to practice on a large scale than on a small one.

**Second**, it is more useful, requiring less labor, lower expense, and less equipment than ordinary metal mines.

**Third**, the silver or gold applied to this work is not deteriorated or diminished, but is increased and improved.

**Fourth**, the equipment, location, wages, workmen, fuel, instruments, materials, and everything required for this work are available in Holland in such quantity and at such a good price as in any other part of the world.

From these points, no prudent person will find a just reason to decide that this operation is impracticable in Holland; on the contrary, those Hollanders who judge otherwise do a great injury to themselves and their own Fatherland while they pronounce it incapable of such a great benefit—of which, as has been said, it is more capable than all other parts of the world.

## LETTER L.

### Attestation regarding the Preliminary Proof.

I, the undersigned, a publicly appointed Assayer of Amsterdam, by the tenor of this document attest that I received from Dr. Johannes Joachim Becher, Councilor of the Imperial Chamber, two ounces of Silver, free of gold. I melted these with a certain **melting glass** <note>original: *vitro fusorio*; a flux or chemical compound used to facilitate the melting and reaction of metals</note> of equal weight for 3 hours, and nothing of the weight of the Silver was lost. Separating it in **strong water**, <note>original: *Aqua forti*; nitric acid, used to dissolve silver and leave gold behind</note> I found 1 1/2 **as** of gold, and a Mark yields 6 **asses**. I myself made the aforementioned glass from sand according to the instruction of the aforementioned Dr. Becher, and I can affirm that no gold was added. I applied my hands to the work alone. Done at Amsterdam on the 16th day before the Calends of March [February 14th], 1679.

The Equestrian Order, the Nobles, and the Cities of the Provinces of Holland and West Friesland, representing the States of those Provinces, having heard the report of the Noble and High and Mighty Lords Commissioners, and adhering to the committee’s decision made on **March 25th** <note>original: *D. IIX. Calend. April.* (8 days before the Calends of April)</note>, and intending to execute the proposal which **Mr. Johann Joachim Becher**, Imperial Councilor, made to the Noble and High and Mighty States some time ago; which proposal consisted of the aforementioned **Mr. Becher** offering to provide and reveal a certain method by which a significant sum of money—specifically a million Imperial thalers <note>original: *centum Myriades Imperialium*</note>—could easily be obtained every year without any burden being placed on persons, goods, or estates; and consequently, it would not consist of any personal or property tax, but rather in a **Sovereign Right** <note>original: *Jure Regali*; income derived from state monopolies or natural resources belonging to the crown or state</note> which the **Noble and High and Mighty States** could claim for themselves, from

# C O N C L U S I O N.

### How the matter turned out at The Hague, and why Dr. Becher departed.

IN public Republics, promises are indeed sometimes better kept than in the courts of Monarchs, but on the other hand, the things to be dispatched are protracted for a much longer time, and there is less gratitude present. For since no single succession takes place there, but everything is carried out through many Nobles, it usually happens that, **"What belongs to everyone is neglected by each individual"** <note>original: *Quæ ad omnes pertinent, a singulis negligantur*—a common legal and political proverb</note>; there are as many opinions as there are heads. From this, votes are split into opposing sides and factions arise; some understand the business and promote it, while others do not understand it and therefore hinder it. Moreover, in such a large multitude, hardly anything can be kept secret, and the common people enjoy too much freedom of speaking and judging. I do not say that the **Dutch Republic** <note>original: *Batavorum Rempublicam*</note> labors under such vices, but I will say only this: that in my own case, I experienced the two following things to my great loss.

**First**, the greatest part of the Proposal and my own person were unknown to the people, and therefore, out of the innate and customary Dutch freedom of speaking—or rather of **slandering**—they judged it so absurdly and falsely that I ought to have been ashamed, and it would have affected me with the greatest grief, had I not seen that they also directed similar taunts against their leaders, and indeed their own magis—

...I heard them blathering while spread out [on the ground], meanwhile the rumor is dispersed, and takes root here—
->Slander boldly, something always sticks.<-
<note>original: *Calumniare audacter, semper aliquid hæret.* A famous Latin proverb suggesting that even false accusations leave a lasting stain on a reputation.</note>

Second, the **Assayers** <term>Docimastæ: specialists who test the purity and weight of precious metals</term> in Holland can hardly tolerate that anyone else, especially a German, should have any knowledge in the **Metallic Sciences** <note>Metallurgy and mining</note> besides themselves. Indeed, I have heard that to one or two Belgian Assayers, who admire only their own nation, all Hungarian and German miners and laborers have become so contemptible that compared to the Belgians they seem like **fools and children** <note>original: *Stulti, & pueri*</note>. Yet those very men, even their General Assayers, are so ignorant in **smelting** <note>original: *liquefacido*</note> that they cannot even properly conduct an **Ore Assay** <term>Proba: a small-scale trial or test to determine the metal content of an ore sample</term>, nor do they know how a **vitrifying dish** <term>patella vitrificatoria: also known as a scorifier, a shallow ceramic vessel used in the assaying process to separate precious metals from impurities</term> should be used, or how the types of minerals on it are to be imbued with lead and vitrified. 

How slanderously the General Commissioner of Mints, **de Nissern**, and the General Assayer **Braunstein** spoke of my work in **The Hague** <note>original: *Hagæ Comitis*</note> is manifest; and how one can make progress with such men is easy to gather. In such a manner, the General Assayer at The Hague consumed the entire summer with useless questions and contradicted himself. I, for my part, was forced by him to spend several hundred **Imperial Thalers** <note>original: *Imperialium*</note>, and finally, due to a lack of the means required for living, to prepare my departure. For in this commission, a daily allowance was established for him, and it mattered little to him how long it lasted; conversely, I stayed in an Inn, where I not only paid several hundred Imperial Thalers but also fell into debt, for which I was harassed. 

This occurred even though ten times as much is owed to me in Holland as I owe to others. Because equity was not administered in paying the debts owed to me, but they even wanted to force me to pay the uncertain debts of others contracted outside the Province, I cannot satisfy my creditors in any other way than the same manner of payment [i.e., by being paid what I am owed first]. They have themselves to blame if they are not paid, as they drive me out and prevent me from paying them. Not a little was contributed to this by the fact that in **Zeeland** <note>original: *Selandia*</note>, led and deceived by lies from the aforementioned malicious people, I suffered a loss of six thousand Imperial Thalers, and in Holland an even **greater sum** <note>original: *majoris ſummæ jacturam fecerim*</note>. 

This is to say nothing of the many parasites and adversaries who, under the pretext of friendship and offering services, were a harm to me. Meanwhile, in **Amsterdam** <note>original: *Amſtelodami*</note>, I experienced another stroke of my fortune's malice, when a burning, malignant, and contagious **fever** invaded my family, which carried off seven people from our midst, so that I could not go there to arrange my affairs. Although I entreated the Lord Commissioners that money be repaid to me and implored their protection, neither of these followed; instead, I was much more driven by persecution from others through suborned agents. Finally, having fallen into illness myself, I could no longer endure the Dutch food nor the **heaviness of the climate** <note>literally "gravity of the sky"; a common 17th-century belief that the damp, thick air of the Low Countries caused bodily imbalances and disease</note> any longer. 

I was necessarily forced to change my climate; indeed, the event showed that as soon as this was done, I began to feel better, whereas without a doubt I would otherwise have contracted a most grave illness. Meanwhile, from all my expectations and labors in The Hague, I could promise myself nothing other than continuous criticism from both adults and youths, disputes with Assayers, and pronouncements of no weight; and on the other hand, the disclosure and sharing of my knowledge...

...[making my] communication for nothing, while several foreigners were burning with desire for it, to the Ministers. As for why I moved to England, I was moved by the **healthfulness of the climate**, different food and drink, a different spirit of the People, learned, noble, and curious men, every kind of sand and **Minerals**, and the opportunity of performing—with all prejudice removed—a **Proof** <term>Proba: a technical test or assay to determine the value or success of a chemical/metallurgical process</term> of my **Art of smelting Sand** <note>Becher famously claimed he could extract gold from sea sand through a specific smelting process</note>, and of obtaining a testimony upon it, the better to persuade the **States of Holland** <note>The governing body of the Dutch Republic</note> to pursue the work in the coming Spring, when I intend to return—provided I am certain of the terms regarding Secrecy, Protection, and subsistence, as well as the great Proof to be undertaken, for which I have petitioned. However, before I departed from Holland for England, I observed and performed these *four* things:

1. *I delivered a certain small preliminary assay to the Commissioners of Amsterdam*, who then, in my absence and without my knowledge, arranged for a **Counter-assay** to be made by the **General Assayer** <term>Docimasta: a specialist in testing the purity of metals</term> of The Hague; and the Counter-assay from The Hague agreed with the one from Amsterdam, and was consistent with my Proposition. Once this was done, the Lords of the States decreed that a large Proof should be made, and if it succeeded well, a **myriad of Florins** <note>10,000 guilders</note> was to be paid to me as a deduction from my stipulated Reward.

2. *I performed a Great Proof of two hundred Marks in a Glass-works at The Hague, according to my wish, in the presence of many Illustrious and Distinguished Men*; the effect of which I can still demonstrate. Then, according to the mandate of the Noble and Most Powerful Lords of the States, I requested that a large Counter-assay also be established. However, I could not obtain my wish; instead, they wanted everything to be done under my name. Whether they feared that the Assay would succeed prosperously (in which case ten thousand Florins would have to be paid to me), or whether it was thought that it could be done without my labor once I had departed, remains unknown to me.

3. *I demonstrated and showed by the thing itself that all requirements for this work exist in Holland*, especially vessels that withstand fire, and that fuel itself can be obtained as cheaply as at the mines and **smelting houses** <note>original: *Ustrinas*</note> in Germany—indeed, cheaper than coals cost in the middle of a Forest—a fact which alone is worthy of remuneration.

4. *Before my Departure, I delivered to the Commissioners in writing a Description and Process of the whole work, in small and in Large scale*, as far as was possible, faithfully recorded with all its circumstances. By following this practice, if they do not desire my labor, they may meanwhile carry it into effect; though perhaps they will perceive that they have withdrawn themselves from the Master's instruction sooner than was right, the **instruction fee** <term>Didactrum: a fee paid for teaching a secret art or science</term> having not yet been paid.

Whether, after considering all these things performed, *I have acted foolishly and without counsel—because I was no longer willing to perish for the delight of my Adversaries (both native and foreign), to waste the Winter as I did the Summer uselessly, to prostitute my Knowledge, and to further neglect and lose my entire Well-being, Health, and Family—I leave to be judged by the Reader whose mind is uncorrupted by Partisanship.*

# *Final Warning.*

**J** *ust as we entered this Sand Mine* <note>original: "Minera arenaria"; Becher uses this as a metaphor for his specific project of extracting gold from sea sand</note> *not without a Forewarning, so it is only right that we depart with a Final Warning.* This consists of two points.

*First*, let the Reader not imagine that anything in this treatise has been written or handed down without sufficient prior Theory and Practice—as is abundantly demonstrated by my *Commentary on Secret Tunnels* <term>Cunicularius: A work by Becher regarding mining and chemical secrets</term>, which I have reserved for my Friends and shared with only a few, containing as it does a great and inexhaustible gold mine of various Secrets. I offer only this single piece of advice to all my Friends and the Possessors of Secrets—learned from my own many damaging experiences: never sell any Secret for money. To do so is not **Philosophical** <note>In this context, "Philosophical" refers to the ethical code of Alchemists and Natural Philosophers, who believed sacred knowledge should not be commodified</note>; it brings a divine curse upon the Work, it prostituted and spreads science among the unworthy, and it carries a most certain punishment. For it is ridiculous to litigate in a civil court over the sale of Sciences, nor can a secular judge decide such a dispute without gaining knowledge of the Secret himself and thus making it public. For this reason, the Seller, abhorring such a prospect, will choose to drop the case if he is wise; the Buyer, however, will deny the debt all the more stubbornly, easily manufacturing various excuses: either that he already knew the Art before, or that others were already skilled in it, or that they found it published in print, or that it did not succeed for him—claiming the fault lies in the Vessels, or the Materials, or here, or there, or on a small scale, or on a large one. Furthermore, since no one is willing to pay until they have first learned and tested the art, the Secret of the matter must be handed over to them like a certain pledge; meanwhile, the Seller holds only a signed piece of paper as a useless "antidote," from which nothing of value comes, except that he can certainly expect insults and mistreatment from the buyer in place of gratitude. And lest the Reader think I write these things without Experience, I shall show him the highly-secured original contracts entered into with the **Dutch** regarding various kinds of Secrets, valued at two hundred thousand **Florins** <term>Florenos: a gold or silver currency used throughout Europe</term>. I fulfilled all of these on my part; but from the other side of the contracting parties, I received not a single penny besides insults and curses. Moreover, by reason of the expenses regarding the Demonstrations and the delay of time, I lost several thousand from my own pocket. Thus, that line from **Ovid** <note>The Roman poet Ovid, specifically from his work *Tristia* (Sorrows)</note> applies to me with merit:

> *If I, who now give this warning, had been warned myself of these things beforehand,*
> *I might perhaps still be in the city where I ought to reside.*
> <note>original: "Hæc ego si monitor monitus prius ipse fuissem, / In qua deberem forsitan urbe forem."</note>

*Second*, I have learned enough from **Court Practice** <term>Praxi Aulica: the experience of serving as an advisor or official in a royal or princely court</term> to know that Truth is always confused there, no less than elsewhere, with lies—purity with clouds, the internal with the external, the essential with the accidental. Since there is always more falsehood in men than truth, falsehood predominates; although, for my own consolation, it does not escape me that even if Truth appears small, it is stronger and always eventually triumphs over falsehood. However, Truth is troublesome to its followers for this one reason: it comes out into the light for its own defense slowly, and is thereafter perceived by only a few, while in the meantime

<meta>catchword: Accessit</meta>

Falsehood resounds through entire regions and Royal Courts with vain and abundant Rumor, and it has already preoccupied the minds of very many people. I write this from my own Experience; for what fables did they once spread about me in Munich regarding Religion, the nullity of which was later revealed by the outcome? What manner of Treason <term>Crimen læsæ Majestatis: A crime of "injured majesty," or high treason against the sovereign</term> was sycophantically imputed to me in Vienna, even though I had served the Roman Empire most excellently? This is testified by the letters written to me by the Emperor himself, the Vice-Chancellor of the Empire, and many Electors and Princes, in which they commend and praise the services I rendered. Now, it does not escape my notice that when this writing reaches Holland, it will find the minds of everyone turned against me—namely, because I have eluded the attempts and snares of Malicious men; because they despise an Art of which they are ignorant; and because Merchants, accustomed to growing rich solely through swindling <note>original: "æruscationibus"</note> and exactions, dread healthier counsel and remedies. Hence, they transform a serious matter into a joke, producing it upon the stage and in public plays, so that it is already "known to every bleary-eyed man and barber" <note>This is a Latin idiom (lippis et tonsoribus) derived from Horace, meaning something is common street gossip known to everyone</note>. Other grave men, however, use ignorance of this matter as a pretext; others are ashamed of it, or find it tedious. I would therefore dare to assert that, amidst such a variety of temperaments and false preoccupations, there will be very few—and those only true Philosophers—who will understand and value this writing, receive it most gratefully, read it most avidly, and through experience, recognize and defend the truth.

> *These men are few, but with the few I can be happy,*
> *For surely God brings forth few of the best things on Earth.*
> *Go to these men with reverence, and display our Wares to them;*
> *If they praise them, it is enough. Whatever the rest of the*
> *Crowd may say, care little, and laugh at the insults of the common folk.*
> *Foolish things please fools; everyone seeks the food*
> *Worthy of their own palate, and one pleasure does not suit all.*
> *But the learned and the good listen to those things which are*
> *Truly good and honorable, and they read avidly and learn willingly.*
> *This is their food, this is the consolation of the mind;*
> *Therefore, to such Men—unless my premonitions fail me—*
> *This labor will be pleasing.*

And so much for the warnings regarding the handling of Alchemy, both Physically and Politically.

### The Author’s Added Index of Books both published by him and still to be published.

The method of measuring time is indeed very ancient (for Holy Scripture testifies that <term>Sciaterica: The science of telling time by shadows, as with a sundial</term> already existed in the time of Hezekiah <note>This refers to the biblical "Sundial of Ahaz" mentioned in 2 Kings 20:11</note>; and for how many years before the birth of Christ the first sundial was brought to Rome and refined, one may read Mr. Zulichem <note>Christiaan Huygens (1629–1695), the Lord of Zulichem, who invented the pendulum clock</note> in the preface of his *Pendulum Clock* addressed to the Lords of the States of Holland). Yet, because of its necessary and great use—both in Astronomy and in finding degrees of Longitude, as well as in civil and public affairs (hence the proverb in the German language: "An accurately running clock in the tower is the external sign of a well-constituted Republic")—it has always been under consideration and improvement, and consequently has always been varied and manifold.

The most well-known and ancient method of measuring time was indeed by the rays and shadow of the sun, namely through <term>Gnomonics: The art of using a gnomon (a pin or rod) to tell time by shadows</term> and shadow-clocks, about which Father Kircher <note>Athanasius Kircher (1602–1680), a celebrated Jesuit polymath</note> wrote extensively in his *Great Art of Light and Shadow*. Time is also customarily measured by the fire of torches and candles in civil dwellings and during criminal tortures; thus Campanella <note>Tommaso Campanella (1568–1639), a philosopher who was imprisoned and tortured by the Inquisition</note>, during the Spanish Inquisition in Naples, counted 48 candles consumed, for he was stretched upon the <term>Fidiculae: A torture device using thin cords or strings to stretch the victim</term> for that many hours. Various <term>Automata: Self-moving mechanical devices</term> have also been constructed with the help of air and bellows <note>original: "folium"</note>, but these are less perfect; it should be noted, however, that in certain places and at certain hours the wind is observed, as is common at the Paderborn fountain and in seafaring navigation. <term>Thermoscopes: Early versions of the thermometer that showed changes in temperature through the expansion and contraction of air</term> are driven by the movement of air, and they demonstrate the rarity and density of the air.

After the sundials, <term>Clepsydras: Clocks that measure time by the flow of a substance, such as water or sand</term> held the next place in use among the ancients, filled with either water or sand. I cannot wonder enough that Father Kircher, Schott <note>Gaspar Schott (1608–1666), a scientist and student of Kircher</note>, and many others, when measuring weights successively so that they might not require wheels, place them above a basin filled with sand, in the bottom of which is a hole from which the sand runs out successively, and with it the intended weight is lowered. 

In this, I have noted that if the two glasses of a sand-clock—namely the upper and the lower—are open, or if they have a hole, the sand will by no means run through the diaphragm and its hole, even if it were made twice as large, but it will stop itself and stand still. The cause is that air must always pass from the lower glass through the middle hole to ventilate and move the sand; hence both glasses must be properly sealed. The upper one must be closed so that air does not enter, but as the sand flows down into the lower glass, for fear of a vacuum in the upper glass, air is drawn from the lower glass through the hole in the diaphragm. The lower glass must be closed so that the sand flowing in from the upper glass causes a compression of the air; then, for fear of the "penetration of bodies" <note>An old physics concept that two objects cannot occupy the same space at the same time</note>, the air is driven through the hole of the diaphragm into the upper glass. Thus, the upper glass draws air and the lower glass expels it, resulting in a continuous ventilation of the sand around the hole of the diaphragm, without which the sand would immediately stop and block itself. If, therefore, a basin is used instead of the upper glass, and it is open above and below for moving the machines—as Father Kircher and many others arrange them—it will be impossible for the sand to flow down. From this it is clear that such authors have not tested even such light matters in practice, upon which they nevertheless found such impressive machines. As for hydraulic water-clocks, everyone sees that they are most imperfect, for the flow and movement of water is unequal in individual parts of the day, due either to its rarity or densi-

...due to density, or quantity, or quality, or height, or many other causes, it <note>original: "peccat" — literally "sins," but here meaning to fail or err in accuracy</note> fails; wherefore I cannot wonder enough that Father Maria Rheita, in his optical treatise to which he gave the title *The Eye of Enoch and Elijah* <note>original: "Oculus Enoch & Eliæ" — a famous work on optics and astronomy published in 1645</note>, would construct a machine that exactly exhibits the "Planetologium," or the motions of the planets, yet places the entire foundation of this motion upon a certain hydraulic wheel. He writes: "Assuming, therefore, that the first wheel with its buckets turns once in every <term>first scruple: a minute</term>," etc. But the good man did not consider that this supposition, being the primary one, would be most uncertain. Nevertheless, I shall add, at the end of this deduction, a method I have invented for moving clocks most accurately by means of water; for it is certain that, until now, the construction of accurate water-clocks has remained unknown to the world.

Ancient astronomers, because they could not see <term>second scruples: seconds</term> on their sundials <note>original: "Sciatericis"</note>, and because mechanical clocks <note>original: "automata"</note> were not yet in use, measured the time of eclipses by the vibrations of pendulums swung by hand. One may see Father Riccioli <note>Giambattista Riccioli (1598–1671), a Jesuit astronomer known for his work on pendulums</note> regarding these vibrations. But after mechanical clocks were invented, they turned to those. Who the first inventor of them might be is unknown, nor can it even be known, because the motion of the mechanical clock was discovered through multiple and successive inventions. There is such an extravagance of genius that in modern times, people err more through the variety and multiplicity of clocks than those clocks serve for actual use.

For we now have mechanical clocks that strike whole hours and quarters, wake the sleeping, light, trim, and extinguish candles at a set time, and most accurately play songs on bells, strings, and pipes. They move statues, images, dances, hunts, skirmishes, and theatrical presentations; they play with balls and spheres, pour water, and exhibit a thousand other things. Well known is the machine of our ingenious Nuremberg citizen, Hautsch <note>Hans Hautsch (1595–1670), a famous mechanician from Nuremberg</note>, by which, at the command of the King of the French, he exhibited for the <term>Dauphin: the heir to the French throne</term> an entire army in combat; just as he skillfully displayed the movements of almost all craftsmen, and also constructed a carriage that could proceed without horses. These and other similar curiosities may be seen in the works of Polydore Vergil and Simone Majolo. Known too is the machine of Cornelius Drebbel exhibited to the Emperor Rudolf; and antiquity testifies that Archytas of Tarentum lived there, who made a wooden flying dove.

However, although various types of motion can be exhibited through machines (just as instruments have now been invented by which one man can weave twelve ribbons, and I know of a machine by which three men can finish a hundred <term>ells: a traditional unit of measurement, roughly the length of a man's arm</term> of cloth in a day’s time—not to mention various types of mills, and that English knitting instrument by which stockings are woven), nevertheless, the following four things seem to me impossible for a machine to perform:

**First**, to imitate the human step. For a man walks on only one foot and stands on two. Because this walking motion not only always changes the equilibrium from one side to the other, but also requires a propelling force, it is impossible to imitate by art. Clockmakers do indeed make statues and running beasts, but they do not move their feet; rather, they only roll upon wheels.

**Second**, it is equally impossible to imitate the human voice. For although in Amsterdam, in the church near the court, they exhibit a certain sound in the larger organ which they call the "human voice," it is rather an inarticulate murmur imitating a full song. Hence, what [is said] concerning the machine of Albertus Magnus <note>A 13th-century scholar rumored to have built a brass talking head or "android"</note> which emulated a man and advanced its step, and to the Saint...

However, what I have attempted regarding these four paradoxes, and how far I have progressed, I shall indicate elsewhere; meanwhile, I leave these four "knots" to be untied by sagacious minds, and I approach more closely the autonomous structure and condition of clocks <note>original: "horologiorum"</note>. I establish, therefore:

That no measure of time can be made without motion; for it could not be observed even in sundials <note>original: "Sciatericis horologiis"</note> unless the Sun moved, or if you prefer, the Earth. This being supposed, it must be known that no motion occurs except in the air—that is, without the air being moved; the air is therefore the **Mobile** <term>Mobile: the object or medium being moved</term>, or the object of all motion. Therefore, according to the alteration and change of the air—namely, of its Atmosphere—every motion will also be altered and vary. The **Object** (the Mobile) of all automata or clocks is therefore the Atmosphere of the air, which is struck back by the **remora** <term>remora: literally a "delay," here referring to the fan-fly or governor that regulates a clock's speed through air resistance</term> or the fan of the clock. The **Subject** (the moving cause or motor) in a clock will be the weight or the spring <note>original: "elateribus"</note>, acting upon the wheels and the fan-governor. Or, if you wish to define a clock differently: its **Object** is the air (the Mobile), its **Subject** is the weight or spring (the moving cause), and the **Medium** or connecting term by which the motor acts upon the mobile (the weight upon the air) is the fan-governor of the clock. From this it is clear that the equality of time measurement consists in the equality of motion, and this principally depends on whether the Atmosphere of the air impresses an unequal motion upon the fan-governor, or vice versa. We shall explain generally how this happens, or how to prevent it: first, by reason of the Atmosphere of the air surrounding the clock. Since air is subject to heat and cold, and thus to rarefaction and density, it will resist the motion and percussion of the clock's fan-governor sometimes more and sometimes less; it will be moved by it sometimes more strongly and sometimes more weakly. Hence it has been observed that all clocks proceed faster in the summer time than in the winter <note>Becher correctly identifies that air density affects the "fly" regulator, though modern physics would also note the expansion of metal parts due to heat.</note>. From this, an unequal motion will necessarily be caused according to the variety of the year, the season, the day, the heat and cold, and also the subsequent humidity and dryness. However, these accidents of the air are only external, just like wind and other impediments which can be met; but rarefaction and density are internal and inevitable accidents of the air, which cannot be hindered except by a singular remedy, about which more later. Second, by reason of the fan-governor of the clock and its structure, a great variety and inequality can also exist, being more or less obnoxious, subject to, or dominating the Atmosphere; a small fan causes a small impetus, a large one a large impetus, but it is also more strongly <margin>is seized</margin> by the Atmosphere...

is snatched away; Next, one must consider this: that the intended purpose for which **restraints** <note>original: "remorae." In early horology, these are the components like the fly-wheel or the balance that "restrain" the clock from running down all at once.</note> were invented be achieved—namely, that they might beat back and compress the air, and by doing so, delay the time; hence they are called "restraints." For if these were removed from clocks, the weight would immediately drop with a great clatter of wheels, which otherwise, by the help of the restraint, would have lasted an entire day. Therefore, the more the restraint struggles with and compresses the air, the more time it uses up. Hence, it is better that the **blades** <note>original: "labra," literally "lips" or "vanes"</note> which are attached to each side at the end of the restraint be positioned vertically rather than horizontally, and be larger rather than smaller; for in this way they compress the air more, whereas otherwise they merely slice through it. I observed this here in London in the automatic machines that move roasting meats <note>The "roasting jack," a clockwork spit used in kitchens.</note>, where the **fans** <note>original: "ventilabra"</note> are placed horizontally; they would press the air much more strongly and use up more time if they were upright and vertical.

Thirdly, some restraints move circularly, and some are carried by a **retrograde** <note>back-and-forth or oscillating</note> motion. Circular motion runs down far too quickly and uses up little time; but retrograde motion, because of the intervals—specifically when the restraint returns—impresses a gap or pause upon the indicator. For this reason, in such clocks, not even seconds <note>original: "scrupuli secundi"</note> can be reliably observed, let alone thirds <note>original: "scrupuli tertii," a division of time equal to 1/60th of a second</note>.

Finally, in certain clocks, the weight and the wheels absolutely dominate the restraint, which happens in circular and horizontal types; but in others, the restraint and its momentum and vibration dominate the wheels and the weight, as in the **pendulum**. The pendulum, even with a weight attached, does not move into motion unless an initial impetus is applied to it, so that the weight is not sufficient to lead the pendulum into motion, but only to maintain that motion once it has begun. This does not happen with other restraints, whose motion depends absolutely on the weight and the wheels. Furthermore, it affects the restraints commonly used until now quite significantly that they all move with a continuous motion, and thus, being driven into momentum by even the slightest change in the **atmosphere**, they are carried away by it for a long time until they return to their proper balance, which can be perceived by sight and sound in small clocks.

But having sent forth these general remarks concerning restraints, we shall specifically consider their types, of which there are four:

The first is the **restraint which is carried circularly**, whether positioned vertically or horizontally. This is no longer in use in clocks, because it is too much snatched away by and dependent on the atmosphere; it runs down quickly and uses up little time. It is used, however, for ringing bells, automatic roasting spits, and other things of that kind. It is called in German a <term>Windfang</term> <note>literally "wind-catcher"</note> and in Latin a <term>Ventilabrum</term> <note>a fan or vane</note>, as if it catches the air and moves it so that it appears to complete a circle before one's eyes. Indeed, in small clocks driven by springs <note>original: "elateribus"</note>, when they strike the hours, this fan moves so forcefully that it entirely escapes the sight and stirs up a sound in the ears because the air is moved so much. This motion is also applied to machines that move a great mass, require a heavy weight, and desire an equal motion, such as in the drums that strike bells or cymbals, or in the cutting instruments with which teeth are cut into iron wheels; hence such fans are called in German <term>Schwungrader</term> <note>flywheels or "swing-wheels"</note> and in Latin <term>Rotæ vibratoriæ</term> <note>vibrating wheels</note>.

The second type of restraint is **retrograde and horizontal**, following the common manner used until now. It depends immediately on the wheels and the weight, and is subject to all the inconveniences I reviewed above. It is so strongly snatched by the atmosphere of the air that at every beat, the restraint appears to move the pointed wheel <note>The "escape wheel" or "crown wheel," whose teeth are often shaped like points or cusps.</note> backward, as both sight and hear-

The third type of restraint is the **balance** <note>original: "bilanx." A T-shaped or scale-like regulator.</note>, or the previous type positioned vertically; I do not recall ever seeing this in a large-scale clock, except in Amsterdam in the great clock of the Court tower. The fourth type of restraint, accepted for use in our own time, consists of restraints situated perpendicularly, which is why such clocks are called **Pendulum Clocks** <note>original: "Horologia Pendula."</note>. Their use has increased beyond all others because they are found to be more accurate. However, I myself find more success using a **Triangular Pendulum**, and one weighing two pounds at that, as it is less subject to the variations of a common plumb line. See the Figure, according to which I personally oversaw the construction of such a clock in practice in London. 

**Christiaan Huygens van Zulichem** <note>original: "Hugenius a Zulichem," the Dutch physicist and astronomer who patented the first pendulum clock in 1657.</note>, a Dutchman, claims the invention and introduction of these for himself, having published a treatise on the structure and reasoning of such clocks for the Lords of the States of Holland, from whom he obtained a patent; later he presented it to the King of France, from whom he earns a stipend. However, **Count Magalotti** <note>Lorenzo Magalotti, a diplomat and scientist.</note>, the Resident of the Grand Duke of Tuscany at the Imperial Court, contradicts him. He recounted the entire history of this clock to me by word of mouth, just as about three years ago in **Augsburg** <note>original: "Augustæ Vindelicorum."</note>, a clockmaker named **Treffler** <note>Christoph Treffler, who worked for the Medici family.</note>, who served the late Grand Duke of Tuscany (the father of the current one), told me a similar story. He confessed that, by order of the Grand Duke and at the instigation of his mathematician **Galileo Galilei**, he had constructed the first pendulum clock in Florence, a model of which later reached Holland. 

Furthermore, **Caspar Doms**, a Fleming by birth and a mathematician to the late Elector of Mainz, Johann Philipp von Schönborn, told me when he was an old man that in Prague, during the time of Emperor Rudolf, he had seen a "vibrating clock" made by the Emperor's most celebrated mechanic and clockmaker, **Jost Bürgi** <note>original: "Justo Borgen." Bürgi was a Swiss clockmaker and mathematician who developed highly accurate experimental clocks for astronomical use.</note>, which the great mathematician **Tycho Brahe** used in his astronomical observations. This is indeed clear from Father **Riccioli** <note>Giovanni Battista Riccioli, a Jesuit astronomer.</note> and others: that the use of vibrations, oscillations, or pendulums was employed for more accurate astronomical observations. Why it was not applied to clocks and brought into daily use until our own times, we shall hear later.

The pendulum restraint behaves like the others regarding the drag of the atmospheric air and its immediate connection with the wheels. It also shares the divided and **retrograde** <note>back-and-forth</note> motion with the common clocks and restraints reviewed so far. However, it differs from common clocks in that the restraint, with its own weight and momentum, dominates the wheels and their primary driving weight. Unlike other restraints, it does not move immediately when the weight is hung, but must acquire an external momentum <note>i.e., it must be started by hand.</note>, which is then preserved by means of the Atmosphere; thus, the main weight serves more to continue the vibrations than to initiate them. 

Huygens van Zulichem supposes that measuring time through the vibrations of this pendulum is the most accurate method of all—so much so that he wished to find degrees of **Longitude** <note>Determining longitude at sea was the "great problem" of the age, requiring a clock that remained accurate on a moving ship.</note> by this means. He relied on two foundations: first, that the vibrations of pendulums, whether they be long or short, fast or slow, are always equal; second, that the momentum of the pendulum overcomes the wheels and their inequality, and especially the primary weight...

...so that the main weight attached to them predominates, in such a way that a little or a lot of weight can be added to the wheels without a notable change to the pendulum. He argues that even if the teeth of the wheels are unequal—trying to push the pendulum either more forcefully or more weakly, or more slowly or more quickly—they are nonetheless moderated by the pendulum’s **vibratory motion** <note>This refers to the oscillation or swinging of the pendulum.</note>, so that excessive force and speed are halted, while slowness and weakness are promoted. He denies, moreover, that the motion of the pendulum depends immediately on the wheels, because between the final **pointed wheel** <note>original: "rotam cuspidatam." This is the escape wheel, which has sharp teeth to catch the regulator.</note> and the lips of the pendulum rod, he provides a small geared wheel. This allows for a loose freedom, so that although the vibrating motion of the pendulum may complete its period either widely or narrowly, it cannot impress a notable change upon the pointed wheel or the hand that moves to show the **seconds** <note>original: "scrupulos secundos." Early terminology for the second division of the hour.</note>. Finally, the rarity and density of the air is suspected by him; however, he professes—or rather calculates in his imagination—how little that can harm the vibrations of the pendulum over the space of a year, namely throughout winter and summer. 

But now we shall weigh, one by one, how all these things stand in relation to the fundamental laws. The first and main foundation for measuring time equally is placed, not undeservedly, by **Mr. Zulichem** <note>Christiaan Huygens van Zulichem, the Dutch scientist.</note> in the equal motion of the vibrations. He demonstrates their equality from the fact that vibrations, though they may be small and make a short arc, compensate for their slowness by their period when compared to longer, faster-moving vibrations. He relies here on the old estimation of the **Astronomers**, although he also tries to demonstrate this laboriously and ingeniously according to the **Laws of Statics**. 

But the following will demonstrate how much this supposition errs in practice. Let a pendulum be made from an iron or wooden rod ten feet long; let a weight of three pounds be placed at its end; let it be suspended and raised to a fourth part of its arc. And—lest inequality be attributed to the hand—let it be balanced by a certain **latch** <note>original: "repagulo." A mechanical trigger used to ensure a consistent release.</note>, and afterward let all its vibrations be counted until it comes to rest perpendicularly. Then, let this movement be repeated two or three times; you will observe that it always completes more or fewer vibrations before it rests. 

Construct yet another pendulum of the same proportion and weight, and place it next to the first; release them with the same latch, and you will see the vibrations of the plummets immediately vary and alter among themselves, and they will not agree. Furthermore, if the vibrations successively failing from the first impulse nonetheless constituted an equal time—namely, the shorter **oscillations** <note>The back-and-forth swings.</note> with the longer ones—then they ought to do so by a certain proportion and always maintain it. But apply a straight rule to the top of the pendulum with a tooth near the end, and make it so that this rule always moves a toothed wheel in one period. Then you will observe that this small wheel will not be moved by any adequate proportion; it will soon catch three teeth, even in a machine most skillfully constructed. These are evident signs that the vibrations are unequal not only in their circuit, but even in their motion, and that the thirtieth or fortieth vibration does not constitute the same time as the first or third. For it is certain that a longer arc of vibration disturbs the **Atmosphere** <note>The author uses this term to refer to the resistance of the air.</note> more forcefully than a short one; therefore, they vary not only in measure, but also in motion and time.

Even granted, but not conceded, that such successive vibrations from the first impulse complete an equal time, Mr. Zulichem nevertheless speaks of the successive vibrations of a free plummet and, as he pleases, of their mutual (even if diverse)...

forming an arc) equal as far as the first vibration is concerned, one ought not to argue concerning a **plumb-line** <note>original: "perpendiculum." In this context, it refers to the pendulum rod and weight.</note> tied and subjected to the wheels and the weight leaning upon it, and forced to complete individual vibrations at a single distance, such as the pendulum of his Clock is; nor do I believe Mr. Zulichem would assert this: that the vibration of the pendulum applied and impulsed in his Clock completes the same time whether it fulfills a period of one foot or three feet, assuming one and the same impelling weight and the same wheels. Indeed, it can be observed that his pendulum—though it be exactly applied to the Clock—does not constitute equal arcs in its vibrations when a goal <note>A marker or physical limit used to measure the swing.</note> is placed on either side of the vibration; it will always touch them unequally, oscillating now beyond and now within the goals. This equality certainly does not arise from the vibrations of the plumb-line itself, which (unlike the previously mentioned **free vibrations** <note>Oscillations of a pendulum swinging freely without being attached to a clock mechanism.</note>) have no successive relation or proportion to each other or to the first impetus. This is because individual vibrations receive their impulse and impression from the Clock’s wheels and weight—otherwise they would suddenly come to rest. Therefore, this inequality must necessarily arise either from the wheels, or from the **Atmosphere**, or from both causes. Since the vibration of pendulums is much more active and swifter than the common **regulators** <note>original: "remoris." Likely referring to the foliot or balance bar used in older clocks, which moved horizontally and more slowly.</note> moved horizontally, it is necessary that the error of inequality in such a swift vibration fails even more frequently and strongly, being seized by the Atmosphere (as we shall demonstrate later). From this I rightly conclude that, although the vibrations in a free **Astronomical pendulum** constitute an equal time through the inequality of their period, this has no consequence for the vibrations of a Clock pendulum constrained by wheels and impulse.

Secondly, Mr. Zulichem certainly supposes that his pendulum so predominates over the wheels that the progress of all of them depends on and is moderated by the pendulum’s motion. If this were so absolutely true, it would prove, in turn, that all the inequalities of the pendulum's vibrations would overflow back into the wheels. We demonstrated a little while ago that these inequalities are not few. If anyone wishes (as I have) to conduct an experiment and multiply the indicator wheels until they designate **thirds** <note>original: "scrupulos tertios." A "third" is a 60th of a second, just as a second is a 60th of a minute.</note>, he will see clearly on that index of thirds how unequally and how inconsistently the hand is carried. This certainly proceeds from nothing other than the unequal vibrations of the pendulum, which impress such fluctuations upon the Clock’s wheels and drivers.

Furthermore, regarding Mr. Zulichem's claim that the small weight of the pendulum predominates and outweighs the larger weight of the wheels: while I might not deny this, I will not concede (as he indeed thinks) that the larger weight can be increased or diminished by half without any alteration, acceleration, or deceleration of the pendulum. He is certainly mistaken in this, since the motion of a plumb-line is so delicate, sensible, and subtle that it is altered or stopped even by a slight cause. This must also be understood regarding the wheels and **drums** <note>The barrels or cylinders around which the weight-cord is wound.</note>, which, unless they are exactly positioned in such a Clock, will stop the motion of the plumb-line by a slight hindrance—more easily, in fact, than common regulators. Pendulums also require more teeth for Clocks because of the faster vibrations of the pendulum, and consequently a greater weight than common Clocks. Finally, as to what Mr. Zulichem says about the rarity and density of the air, and how little he observed it to have hindered the motion of the pendulum over the space of a year, let the credit for that remain with the author; but he will never lead me to his opinion, since practice...

...might teach the contrary. For first, it must not be denied, as it is established by daily observation from **Thermoscopes** <note>Early instruments for measuring temperature and air density, precursors to the thermometer.</note>, how great a difference there is on any given day or night—from twelve to twelve, and from the month of January to July—regarding the rarity and density of the air. Secondly, it is evident that air moves more easily perpendicularly than horizontally; for this reason, the air is moved more strongly by the vibrations of a **plumb-line** <note>The pendulum rod and weight.</note> than by a horizontal delay, indeed in a long and continuous line. This is clear from the fact that if three or four pendulum Clocks are arranged horizontally so that their pendulums stand in a straight line, and then each individual Clock is set in motion, their pendulums will move unequally at first—each according to its own impulse—but a little while later they will all agree in a single motion. Some have wished to cite this at first glance as an argument for the perfectly equal motion of pendulums, but upon deeper inspection, it was found that the layer of the **Atmosphere** <note>The body of air surrounding the mechanisms.</note> in which the pendulums are placed moves all its pendulums according to the vibration of that pendulum which has the greater force. From this it is certainly clear how widely the Atmosphere is moved by a single vibration of a pendulum; and since the motion of a pendulum is continuous, it necessarily follows that once a pendulum is caught up by the Atmosphere, it depends entirely upon it. It has no support by which it might free itself from the force of the Atmosphere and reclaim its original freedom of its own motion. And so much for the fourth kind of **Hindrances** <note>original: "Remorarum." Factors that slow down or interfere with the clock's timing.</note>, namely, perpendicular hindrances.

Now that the four kinds of Hindrances have been completed and specifically examined, we shall proceed to consider the third disadvantage of Clocks: namely, the structure of the **Wheels**, **Pinions** <note>original: "Tympanorum," often referring to lantern gears or drums in early clockwork.</note>, **Teeth**, and **axles**. However diligently these may be fashioned, they can still err, either by a fault of manufacture, or by their novelty (the wheels and pinions not yet being worn into one another), or by age (being too worn down), or by various external accidents interfering with the structure of the wheels. These include various atoms <note>Tiny particles of matter.</note>, dust, bits of straw, chaff, hair, wool, feathers, and six hundred other things. I say nothing of the fact that the wheels, axles, and pinions of Clocks do not proceed well without **oil**, and that such oil, when smeared on, over the course of time and through heat and cold, solidifies, becomes sluggish, and undergoes various changes. Thus there is need for frequent repair, for even among so many axles and teeth, the smallest thing is easily worn, broken, or goes astray. I pass over how often the teeth of the wheels enter and exit the rods of the pinion—that is, they complete the top and bottom of a single tooth—and that these always cause a double motion: a stronger one at the top and a weaker one at the base of the tooth. Who now will manufacture all the wheels so precisely, in terms of their dimension, weight, and other requirements, that either nothing is lacking in the making, or that nothing of perfection is lost from those well-made through daily use? 

The fourth and last thing that comes to be considered in Clocks is the **moving cause**, whether it consists of a weight or a spring. Weights are preferred over springs for their equality, while springs are preferred over weights for their convenience. However, the elastic motion in Clocks is uncertain and not safe; for its beginning is stronger than its end, and over the passage of time, the elastic force also weakens. Clockmakers busily try to correct these two disadvantages: the first by a **spiral line** <note>A "fusee," a cone-shaped pulley that compensates for the weakening of a mainspring as it unwinds.</note> starting from the smallest periphery and ending at a larger circumference, so that in this way, that which is stronger in the elastic motion near the beginning is balanced by the brevity of the circumference...

circumference, and so that what is weaker toward the end is tightened by the size of the periphery; truly, the weights alter the elastic force, which gradually diminishes via a **spiral** <note>Latin: *helyce*; likely referring to a spiral spring or a fusee, a conical pulley used to equalize the pull of a mainspring.</note>. Weights, which I have said proceed more correctly, are more commonly used in Clocks; for we have found that a weight suspended in a perpendicular line, whether high up or low down, does not weigh more or less, except for the added mass of the cord—an issue which, as we will show later, can easily be remedied. And let these words suffice concerning the four general properties of all Clocks used up to now, as well as their condition and structure.

But now we shall hasten to the remedies—namely, my Clock, the corrective and **panacea** <note>A "cure-all" or universal remedy.</note> for all the others. It consists of four means, according to the observations noted in the preceding sections:

**First**, that the **aerial Atmosphere** <note>The surrounding air.</note> (in which the Clock operates and against which the **regulator** <note>Latin: *remora*; literally a "delay" or "hindrance," here referring to the pendulum or balance mechanism that regulates the speed.</note> continually struggles) does not affect the regulator in any way, whether by its rarity or density; and if it should happen to affect it, the Clock should provide a remedy of proportion for the regulator itself.

**Second**, that the regulator is never drawn into synchronization with the movement of the Atmosphere, but instead pushes against the Atmosphere with a most equal period and motion, never more slowly nor more quickly, more strongly nor more weakly, more nor less.

**Third**, that wheels, drums, and teeth are not applied to the regulator, but rather the regulator moves without their help—or, if one chooses to use them, that it moves in such a way that it does not feel the defects of the Clock. Thus, any **automatic machine** <note>Latin: *automatum*.</note>, even the most imperfect one built for turning bellows, could be applied to this use without any error in the regulator. For the fewer the wheels, the more perfect the Clock; if no wheels at all are needed, or if those used communicate none of their own flaws to the regulator, so much the better.

**Fourth**, that the primary driving weight be subject to the weight of the regulator, and that the regulator and its **vibration** <note>The oscillation of the pendulum.</note> do not depend immediately upon that primary weight.

Thus, the entire correction of Clocks and the structure of my machine consist of four points:
1. That the alteration and commotion of the aerial Atmosphere does not affect the regulator.
2. That the vibration of the regulator does not push the Atmosphere unequally.
3. That wheels, drums, and teeth are not required, or if required, cannot alter the regulator.
4. That the primary moving weight does not prevail over the regulator-weight, but rather the latter dominates the former.

The preceding demonstrations show that once these four requirements are brought into practice and due perfection, the most perfect Clock that can exist in this sublunary world will arise therefrom. And so much for the indicated remedies according to the indicated causes; now we shall hasten to the material of those indications—namely, the structure of such a Clock. For it is not enough to detect the cause of a disease and indicate the medicine; one must also prepare it and administer the prepared remedy, lest we seem to thrust upon the reader a game or trial of subtle wit rather than a possible practice.

To arrive at the first point, then—the correction of the properties of the aerial Atmosphere in which the Clock (especially the regulator) is situated—I have found these properties to be twofold: namely, **external** and **internal**. The external ones are weather, wind, physical shocks, dust, atoms, rain, humidity, and others, all of which can be avoided rather than corrected. Specifically, they are avoided when the compartment for the regulator is protected by a glass and metal case, so that the air contained within is immune and safe from external harm, as is commonly done with **assay scales** <note>Latin: *bilancibus docimasticis*; highly sensitive scales used by goldsmiths and chemists.</note>. But as for the internal properties of the aerial Atmosphere, which are intrinsically its own...

Rrr 2

Namely, the rarity and density of the air cannot be avoided as easily as external factors, for they are innate <note>Latin: *connaturalia*; existing as a natural part of the environment.</note> to the system. I will not philosophize here on what it means to be "rare" or "dense," or how something can occupy a larger or smaller space without a change in its quantity or weight; for that, one may look at what I wrote in my **Subterranean Physics** <note>Latin: *Physica subterranea*; the author’s major work on chemistry and natural philosophy.</note> near the very beginning concerning the Heavens and the Hyperphysical Element. Certainly, the **Aristotelians** <note>Followers of the traditional philosophy of Aristotle, which the author frequently critiques.</note> do not satisfy me with their definitions, namely: "quantity is that by which something is said to be *how much*"; "rare is that which occupies more space, and dense that which occupies less"; likewise, "a weight on a balance scale weighs more the further it is removed from its axis." But I would like to know *why* it weighs more the further it is removed from the axis.

However, putting these matters aside as they belong more to Philosophy than to Mathematics, we must return to the rarity and density of the air. For the **Mechanical Reader** who is perhaps unskilled in such things, we shall indicate only this: air swells with heat—or rather, a certain nature lies hidden in the air which causes it to swell with heat and occupy a larger space. **Natural Philosophers** <note>Latin: *Physici*; refers to those who study the physical world.</note> call this **rarefaction** <note>The process of air becoming thinner or less dense.</note>. Conversely, when air contracts with cold and occupies less space, they call this **condensation** <note>The process of air becoming thicker or more dense.</note>; hence the terms *Rarefaction* and *Condensation*. 

It is established by experience and reason that the air is thin and difficult to traverse <note>Latin: *ægre prævium*; likely a typo for *pervium* (permeable), or suggesting that the thinness of air presents its own subtle resistance to movement.</note>. Now, since it cannot be denied that the heat of the Sun varies greatly between day and night, summer and winter, it is necessary that the entire aerial atmosphere heats up and cools down according to those degrees. Consequently, it must rarefy and condense, just as these degrees of rarefaction and condensation can be accurately observed in **Thermoscopes** <note>Latin: *Thermoscopia*; early versions of the thermometer that showed changes in temperature without a standardized numerical scale.</note> invented for that purpose. Thus, no one can deny that the motions of **regulators** <note>Latin: *remorarum*; the parts of the clock that regulate speed, such as the escapement.</note> and pendulums are necessarily accelerated or slowed according to these aforementioned degrees. 

Therefore, to remedy this inevitable inconvenience and, as it were, "original evil" which we cannot avoid—for no place in the world is immune to rarity and density (see what **Claude Bérigard** <note>Latin: *Claudius Berigardus*; a 17th-century philosopher and physicist.</note> writes in the *Pisan Circle* regarding locations and chambers situated under water)—let us endure it wisely, but in such a way that we find a medicine from the evil itself. Since we cannot moderate the changes of the air to suit the requirements of Pendulums and regulators, we must take the opposite approach: the motions of the regulators and Pendulums must be directed according to the degrees of the air's rarity and density. 

At first glance, this will certainly seem difficult, if not entirely impossible. For who would adjust the Clock’s Pendulum to the thermometer's degrees at almost every moment? And although small weights attached to common pendulums can be raised or lowered for that purpose, and the pendulums themselves can be adjusted, the cause and the method of doing so are still debated. 

**Cornelius Drebbel** of Alkmaar <note>A famous Dutch inventor (1572–1633) known for his "perpetual motion" machines and early submarines.</note> is said to have been the first inventor of the **Thermoscope**. He not only taught its use in showing and designating degrees of rarity and density (as common thermometers are now everywhere seen and sold), but he also understood its static and mechanical use. This is demonstrated by that celebrated machine of his, called a **Perpetual Motion** machine, which he presented with a variety of different scenes to Emperor **Rudolph II**, as can be read in the *Mathematical Recreative Hours* of **Schwenter** and **Harsdörffer** <note>A popular 17th-century collection of mechanical and mathematical wonders.</note>. After him, as far as I know, no one applied a Thermoscope to mechanical motions, except for myself in the year 1656, when I presented a glass image to Emperor **Ferdinand III**, showing itself under a clear sun from artificially made clouds...

Further developing the study of wind, in the year 1660 in Holland, I saw to it that an **engraving** <note>Latin: *Iconismum*; a technical illustration or diagram, often printed from a copper plate.</note> was cut into a folio sheet, where I further explained the application and use of **Thermoscopes** <note>An early instrument for indicating changes in temperature, the precursor to the thermometer.</note> for Static, Mechanical, and **Wonder-working** <note>Latin: *Tavmaturgicas*; refers to "thaumaturgy," or the creation of marvelous mechanical effects that seem like magic.</note> matters. I even brought the matter to the point that it would be useful for Chemists in constructing an **Athanor** <note>A self-feeding furnace used by alchemists designed to maintain a steady heat over long periods.</note> that always provides heat very evenly. Specifically, the Thermoscope is placed into the digestion vessel itself along with the other glass vessels to be heated; the desired degree of heat is noted on it, and then the required little machine is applied so that the furnace is properly refilled with coals every 24 hours. Then, if the fire increases too much, the Thermoscope will close the opening of the chimney; if the heat begins to fail, it will open the same opening, whereby the heat will be increased. Thus, the Thermoscope applied in this way is always occupied in regulating the heat. From this, I observed that a furnace arranged in such a way did not deviate even slightly in its degree of heat for the space of a month, whereas otherwise it would be impossible by the touch of hands alone to regulate the fire so evenly day and night—truly a great aid in those operations which require an exact degree of **digestion** <note>In alchemy and early chemistry, "digestion" is the process of exposing a substance to gentle, continuous heat.</note>.

With this invention already published by me in the year 1660, I wonder that a short time ago—say a year or two—a certain Frenchman brought forward some things about the mechanical use of Thermoscopes, though they are tasteless, impractical, and inaccurate. It is just as when **Father Kircher** <note>Athanasius Kircher (1602–1680), a famous Jesuit polymath known for his massive, though sometimes disorganized, scholarly works.</note>, nearly two decades later, sold his "art of languages" to the world, although it was undigested and difficult, as Kircher’s own student **Father Schott**, and **Erasmus Francisci** in his *Oriental* works, and **Professor Sturm** of Altdorf admit.

But returning to our intent, and by the application of the thermometer <note>The author uses *thermometri* and *thermoscopii* somewhat interchangeably here.</note> to regulate and direct the motion of the **pendulum** according to the requirements of the degrees of rarity and density of the air: I say that if the air is **rare** <note>Thin or less dense, providing less resistance.</note>, the pendulum's motion will become faster; hence it must be made heavier. This can happen by the lowering of the ordinary attached small weight; namely, with the small weight moving further away from the center of the pendulum's radius, it adds more gravity. On the contrary, if the air is **dense**, the pendulum's motion will be slowed, therefore it must be accelerated. This is done by lightening the pendulum, which happens through the attraction and closer approach of the small weight to the axis of the pendulum. Therefore, the entire regulation of the pendulum according to the degrees of rarity and density consists in the raising and lowering of the pendulum's small weight. My method of making and applying the Thermoscope performs this most excellently and accurately of all. So much so, that if the air varied in rarity and density every minute or hour from one extreme to the other—namely from one to twelve degrees—and the motion of the pendulum during that time always continued without interruption, nonetheless, by the application and help of my Thermoscope, without an interval of motion—

The structure of my **Thermoscope** for this purpose is as follows: since there are two kinds of Thermoscopes—some allowing for the rarefaction and condensation of air in a bulb or vial at the top, and some at the bottom, and thus either drawing in or releasing the contained liquid by heat or cold—one must choose one of these types. When these are combined in this way, it will happen that—according to the degrees of the air's rarity and density—the quicksilver will either rise or fall, driven by the air’s compression or the "fear of a vacuum" <note>Latin: *loci vacui metu*; a reference to the Aristotelian concept that nature abhors a vacuum, here used to explain fluid displacement.</note>. Now we shall hasten to the second remedy, which consists of correcting errors in the **regulator** <note>Latin: *remora*; literally a "delay." The third, if with each vibration the motion is either stopped or broken—each of which will be made more fully clear from the structure and the attached diagram.

The third remedy is that the wheels and weights moving the regulator should not act upon it directly, but through such an interval and medium that their error or defect is never felt in the regulator. Specifically, the primary weight and wheels of the Clock should not drive the secondary weight of the regulator, but only wind it back up. In this way, even the most defective **automata** <note>Mechanical devices or "engines."</note>—even those intended for **turning roasts** <note>Latin: *ad assaturas vertendas*; mechanical meat spits used in kitchens, which were notoriously irregular in their motion.</note>—can most perfectly revolve the regulators of any clocks whatsoever and measure time with extreme accuracy. # From this mathematical demonstration of mine, four
## new inventions result.

->I.<-

The structure of **thermoscopes** <note>Early instruments used to detect changes in temperature, the precursors to modern thermometers.</note>, by which the weight of the pendulum is self-moderated and directed according to the rarity and density of the air.

->II.<-

A circular pendulum motion, yet one that is alternating, which nonetheless prevails over the atmosphere and the primary driving weight.

->III.<-

That the wheels and the primary weight do not act directly upon the **escapement** <note>original: *remora*; literally a "delay" or "hindrance," referring here to the mechanical component that regulates the release of the clock's energy.</note>; therefore, their flaws are not felt within it, no matter how great they might be. From this, a perfect clock can be constructed even from a common **air-blast machine** <note>original: *asslatura*; likely referring to a simple bellows or wind-driven mechanism.</note>.

->IV.<-

That a most exact clock can be built at very little expense and in a very short time without any wheels at all, moving and revolving itself for as long as the material lasts, and thus representing a **perpetual motion machine**.

## Corollaries are added.

->I.<-

To regulate the degrees of fire in chemical <note>original: *chymicorum*; referring to the practice of alchemy or early chemistry.</note> furnaces with the utmost consistency by the aid of thermoscopes.

->II.<-

The motion of a **triangular pendulum** of two units <note>original: *bilibris*; weighing two pounds or having a dual-balance.</note>.

->III.<-

To manufacture very exact **hydraulic clocks** <term>water-clocks</term> at the lowest cost.

->IV.<-

An instrument for generating a massive force of vibrations, which by a new method contributes significantly to the demonstration of artificial perpetual motion.
