->If these and similar things please the Reader, the following will be added.<-

->I.<-

My observations concerning the **elastic force** <note>original: *vim elasticam*; here referring to the tension or potential energy stored in a material.</note> of the nerves in animals and of metallic springs in **wonder-working machines** <note>original: *Taumaturgicis*; referring to "thaumaturgy," the design of mechanical marvels, automata, or "magic" tricks using engineering.</note>, where it is proven that—just as the force or impulse of the atmosphere through a fan <note>likely referring back to the "air-blast machine" on the previous page.</note> brings the possibility of demonstrating artificial perpetual motion—so in this place the **elastic force** brings the possibility of artificial flight. Specifically, I show that anything which can move many times more, and exert its power more, than its own bodily mass weighs, possesses what I call "elastic force." I demonstrate how this force can be strengthened twenty times more in human nerves, and how much they can exceed their own bodily mass. On this occasion, I digress into the history, trials, and requirements of the **art of flying** <note>original: *arte volandi*.</note>. Finally, I conclude by considering birds, their feathers, and their wonderful structure and movement (which has been understood by few until now), an art which is scarcely, or rather not at all, imitable by human craft.

On the compression and pressure of lines in water: a **mathematical demonstration** against the common structure of hydraulic compression machines and the false assumptions of certain mathematicians.

A physical history of the **Art of Dyeing** <note>original: *Artis Tinctoriæ*.</note>, concerning the coloring of liquids, hair, wool, silk, linen, **cotton** <note>original: *Xylino*.</note>, leather, bones, horns, feathers, wood, straw, paper, wax, shells, stones, glass, and metals.

The **Perpetual Sand-Mine** <note>original: *Minera Arenaria perpetua*.</note>, or a precursor to the history or proposal made by the Author to the **States of Holland** <note>The governing body of the Dutch Republic.</note> regarding the extraction of gold from coastal sand, by means of a "perpetual mine" or a great smelting operation conducted with profit.

## GEORG ERNST STAHL, M.D.
->Public Professor at Halle and Fellow of the Academy of Nature’s Seekers.<- <note>The "Academy of Nature’s Seekers" refers to the *Academia Naturae Curiosorum*, now known as the Leopoldina, one of the world's oldest scientific societies.</note>

## PREFACE.

When I was not only asked to review Johann Joachim Becher’s *Subterranean Physics* <note>original: "Physicam Subterraneam"; Becher's most famous work, which laid the groundwork for the Phlogiston theory</note> for a new edition, but was also ready to listen to the request to provide whatever help or advice I might have—not just regarding the printing process, but even more so for the better use of the book—I judged, given the character of the book itself, the nature of the writing, and indeed the condition of the whole subject, that it would be most useful not to cling to the words or to follow and interpret the author's assertions point by point. Instead, since he thinks practically about practical matters and does not so much "speculate" (as they say) as demonstrate and bring things before the senses, I decided to follow the author’s own style of illustration. Using this method, I aim to show those things that can lead to a simpler presentation or deduction of his claims. There is an old complaint about the Author's writings—and one shared by my own recent, modest works—that the style is intricate and obscure. Yet, this very claim is itself intricate and obscure, and therefore requires explanation. Namely, this fault lies either in the words, the subject matter under discussion, or the treatment and method by which such discussions are conducted. Regarding words, there is again a twofold obscurity: one is simple and grammatical, occurring when words fail to grasp through their own meaning what they ought to express and define. Instead, they speak of things either too coldly and generally, or in a fleeting and ambiguous way, when a proper and exact determination—a definition free from all confusion—ought to have been provided. The other is rheto- <note>The word is cut off and continues on the next page as "rhetorical."</note>

<summary>This page serves as the title page and opening preface for Georg Ernst Stahl's "Specimen Beccherianum," where he defends Becher’s scientific style and outlines his editorial approach to the "Subterranean Physics." Stahl argues that perceived "obscurity" in chemical writing often stems from the difficulty of the subject matter rather than poor writing alone.</summary>
<keywords>Georg Ernst Stahl, Johann Joachim Becher, Subterranean Physics, chemical composition, scientific method, early modern chemistry, Phlogiston theory foundations, Halle University</keywords>

...rhetorical, of humble and ignoble origin, since they cannot claim for themselves a pedigree's dignity or ancestral splendor—not from *Arpinum* <note>original: "Arpis"; Arpinum was the birthplace of the great Roman orator Cicero</note>, from *Cicero’s* family, or from the titles of *Caesar* (amidst the extravagance of civil bloodshed and the oppression of the fatherland, even his name threatening empire) with such follies. And so, by Censors worthy of such a magistrate, amidst the hatred and wailing of boys, they are convicted of barbarism and slavishly beaten with rods—the magistrate himself wielding the bundles of rods <note>term: "fasces"; a bundle of rods with an axe, symbolizing magisterial power in ancient Rome</note> because public slaves are lacking. If anyone dares to accuse our Author or myself of the former obscurity <note>meaning the "humble origin" of their prose style</note>, I will immediately provide sureties. On behalf of the latter [the charge of barbarism], I respond with nothing else except that it were to be wished that *Germany* had contracted no vice from nations whose speech is barbaric, rather than from words troublesome to *Cicero*. We—for I rightly join myself with the Author in this regard—do not write for the schools, or for their Masters, nor indeed for those fellow Germans who work so ambitiously to rub the marks of their own servitude <note>a metaphor for those who obsess over following rigid, foreign rules of style</note>. Instead, we write for those who understand the force of things rather than words, and who deem no outward polish or useless selection worthy of any price. 

That the obscurity of the subjects is very great, we grant with both hands; but only to the unskilled, and those entirely ignorant of the nature and scope of *Becher’s Physics*. It never entered our minds to describe processes, to walk in buskins <note>term: "cothurno"; high-heeled boots worn by ancient tragic actors, implying a grand or pompous style</note>, to indulge in promises—in a word, to equip either a laboratory or a kitchen, whether chemical or pharmaceutical. Those whom such things trouble can go to *Schröder*, *Hartmann*, and their like—and their interpreters—who, where those others (with an older German fidelity) blushed to wander too high, have condemned useless modesty and measure everything in superlatives. The Author, about to bring forth the reasons for things, presupposed a proper knowledge of them. But as for the new things he proposed, he preferred to name them from manifest circumstances—even in the immediate manner of their becoming and acting—rather than to indulge in those high-sounding terms (if the things are even to be grasped) like "first, second, third element," or their mutual birth from friction, collision, conflict, effort, "Symbolisms," "magnetisms," "elasticities," and so on, using things obscure in themselves for the purpose of illustration.

->Therefore, as for the obscurity of the things themselves, in that order in which we both use them,<-
namely for immediate explanations and applications, we boldly take it upon ourselves to say there is none; indeed, we gladly defer the judgment to those skilled in the subject. But of the *Method*, there is certainly a primary obscurity and a completely varied entanglement; but again, only for those sorts of intellects that are soft from leisure, impatient with all diligence, and indeed unequal to it. Those people only interpret a style as perfectly clear when one page mentions perhaps one thing, and with repeated tautologies—to the nausea of men with little leisure—it tires and exhausts them, not otherwise than a dog does a hare. The Author rightly asserted that he wrote as many things as he did words; and truly, if he had treated those things which our Author handled—that is, not just naming them, but indicating the "nerve" <note>the essential core or strength</note> which ought to be seen and attended to in them—yet this very thing...

...contented himself with doing so from time to time; such things, I say, if they had to be called back to those buskins <note>original: "cothurnos"; the high-soled boots worn by ancient tragic actors, here a metaphor for a pretentious or overly lofty rhetorical style</note> from which words sprout for such censors even out of nothing, this little book would have provided volumes, and this work—the first of its kind from every side—would have had to be divided into many books. However, for those who work with a good and honest mind, but who perhaps suffer from some slowness of intellect or a lack of the usual studies, it should not be a burden to reread what they have read; they must not look at these things in passing, but read them through, for these ideas must certainly harmonize and be joined together. In this way, they will most surely understand the meaning—indeed, the practical use—not only of the words and style, but truly of the matters themselves. It is a strange thing, if you ignore the causes, why those who are accustomed to understanding, doing, and writing about real things are always to be accused of writing obscurely. I would dare to associate Becher and myself (at least in this third category) with a man who is, in all other respects, the most highly regarded I know: **Daniel Ludovici** <note>A prominent 17th-century German physician known for his work on pharmacy and medicine</note>. Who will rescue his writings from the greatest obscurity? Yet he wrote more brilliantly on **Materia medica** <term>Materia medica: The study of the origin and properties of substances used for healing</term> than anyone else who had even thought of the subject up to that day. 

For this specific purpose, I judged that there could be no better way to assist the somewhat tangled method of Becher’s treatment (where he follows such a great number of things without ever breaking the thread) than if these matters were placed before the eyes in a shorter and simpler order—indeed, in a more general summary. I have done this in the present specimen. In this work, as if by a certain example, I have set my mind to present the **Becherian Subterranean Physical Philosophy** <note>original: "Philosophiam Physicam subterraneam"; refers to Becher's foundational work on mineralogy and early chemistry</note> through shorter porisms <note>term: "porisms"; here used as derived propositions or secondary insights that follow from a primary theory</note>, whether of Becher’s doctrine or his opinions, forming arguments or documents from them, and finally putting forward experiments. 

Time did not permit me to use actual citations of Becher’s words or specific passages, nor did my respect for him require it; I judged it unnecessary to adhere absolutely "foot by foot" <note>original: "κατὰ πόδα" (kata poda); a Greek idiom meaning to follow someone's footsteps exactly</note> to the Author's words or examples. I did this all the more to avoid any conspicuous difference in how things were excepted, proved, demonstrated, or operated—differences that might seem to have been added by me to the Author rather than proceeding directly from him. This was not because I feared, again and again, those false accusations of seeking vain glory—for a mind conscious of its own rectitude laughs at the lies of rumor—but rather so that I might make our shared matters solid, as they truly are. Indeed, it is something more: my own contributions are not so much to be compared with Becher’s as they are to be referred back to him. They are "Becherian," I say, the things I bring forward; they have always been most highly valued by me because of his solid method of experimenting and explaining, and they were born for me as well. I follow all good men who desire to serve the republic of letters well—not to mention those who have mastered it—with all veneration, and I truly venerate even their ashes. But it is impossible for me to allow everyone to command my obedience or to squeeze lies from me on their behalf. However, that decree of the supreme judges, **Minos** and **Rhadamanthus** <note>In Greek mythology, the judges of the dead in the underworld</note>, is just and fair:

### OF THE BECHERIAN SPECIMEN,
# PRINCIPLES
## For demonstrating Subterranean Mixing, <note>original: "Mixtionis Subterraneæ"; this refers to the chemical composition and formation of minerals and metals within the earth</note>
## PART ONE.
### SECTION I.
## THE FOUNDATIONS OF THE BECHERIAN THEORY.

---

### SECT. I.
### Member I.
## The Foundations of the Becherian Theory.

As I set out to illustrate Becher’s *Subterranean Physics* <note>original: "Physicam Subterraneam"; the title of Johann Joachim Becher's 1669 foundational work on alchemy and mineralogy</note>, I believe that, before all else, some actual distinctions should be set forth. This Author [Becher] assumes these as a foundation, so that his mind and his concept of such matters—as well as the truth of the things themselves—may be successfully understood. It will also show that his concepts correspond entirely to this truth and are grounded in the Truth of Experience.

Just as it is an eternal truth in human affairs that nothing is blessed in every respect; and in this regard, even our Author himself seems to have "suffered something human" <note>original: "aliquid humani passus"; a Latin idiom meaning to make a mistake or show human fallibility</note> once or twice, yet no more than we ourselves might experience in our own lives. Thus, we will indeed present our Author’s views and place them in view in a proper sequence and connection. However, according to our own understanding and concept, we will soon point out where he himself seems to have turned away from the true nature of things, or at the very least, where we harbor a different opinion on the matters. We will carry this out in such a way that we give an account for our judgment or our differing opinion, and thus leave it free to the prudent and skillful reader to choose or follow what they wish.

(I.) First of all, it must be known that the Author did not properly intend to establish his treatise on the nature, character, and constitution of Natural Bodies *in general*; rather, he speaks solely, or at least chiefly, of Subterranean things.

Therefore, the things he has mixed in concerning the constitution of *Plants* and *Animals*—and indeed with some length—should not be understood otherwise than that in these...

### SPECIMEN OF BECHER, PART I, SECTION I.

...he wished to show by examples some *analogy* of the *principles* which *materially* constitute these different species, as he himself professes and declares. Or, as it appears to me, he rather wished—or certainly was able—to exhibit only some notable *alterations* or *changes* of those Principles which are common to *Vegetables* and *Animals* as well as subterranean things; changes which draw their origin partly from the mixing of *water* and partly from the admission of *air*.

## (II)
Of this Subject, Subterranean Matters, he undertook to consider not just any conditions or—as they commonly say—qualities and properties; but only their *Matter*, or their *material principles*, from whose union or *Mixture* they are born, consist, and subsist.

For this reason, he did not need to concern himself much with the various behaviors of these subterranean bodies regarding solutions, combustions, mutual mixtures, and compositions—nor even the simple separations of various products that break out from them (especially by the help of Fire) under various forms, even if they did not pre-exist in those same consistencies within these Mixtures, and so on. Instead, he was rightly content to mention only those from the great number of common chemical operations that seemed to fit the demonstration of the *principles of the simpler Mixtures*.

This is the reason why those wander "by the whole heaven" <note>original: "toto cœlo"; a Latin idiom meaning to be completely wrong or far apart</note> who, interpreting this *Subterranean Physics* as a common *System of Chemistry*, look for those sculleries and "Sephasiarian" <note>original: "Sephasiarias"; likely referring to low-level, manual, or "sooty" alchemy associated with trade secrets rather than philosophy</note> kitchens of trivial pharmacists and quacks <note>original: "Medicastrorum"; a derogatory term for poorly trained doctors</note>; or at the very least, they think that deductions for all so-called *chemical processes* ought to be made here. When they see their hopes are not satisfied in every respect, they become indignant as if at a crippled and useless collection of scraps.

I say, our Author did not have it at heart to investigate all compositions and resolutions, but only those *Mixtures* which are, as it were, the *first*, most intimate, and firmest. With this in view, he especially produced those operations and experiments which he judged could serve to achieve this goal.

## (III)
One must therefore note and always keep in mind Becher’s Distinction, by which he discerns Mixtures (*Mixta*), Compounds (*Composita*), Decompounds (*Decomposita*), and even Super-decompounds (*Superdecomposita*). <note>This hierarchy describes the complexity of matter: Mixtures are the most basic combination of elements, while Super-decompounds are complex substances like ores or salts.</note>

## (IV)
He interprets Mixtures to be *Concretes* <note>original: "Concreta"; solid masses or combined substances</note> of that kind which are fused together from different ingredients (as they say). Yet those ingredients, considering each one separately, are—as far as we humans can grasp—purely homogeneous, of the simplest essence, and not yet fused from several others that are different in species.

From several *different species*, I say. For it can indeed happen that such a constitutive part—or to use a common term, an *ingredient*—might be a small body or molecule consisting of several small bodies of the same species closely adhering to one another. It can happen that such a molecule, *homogeneous in species* but plural in *number* (consisting of many in number), enters a Mixture along with others that are also different in species:

<meta>catchword: rentibus : (completing the word "cohaerentibus" or "adhering")</meta>

### SECTION I.
#### Article I.
### The Foundations of the Becherian Theory.

As I set out to illustrate Becher’s *Subterranean Physics* <note>original: "Physica Subterranea," Becher’s most famous work on the composition of the earth and minerals</note>, I believe that first of all, certain real distinctions must be put forward which this Author assumes as a foundation. Just as it is an eternal truth in human affairs that nothing is blessed in every respect; and in this regard, even our Author himself seems once or twice to have "suffered something human" <note>original: "aliquid humani passus"; a common Latin idiom meaning to make a mistake or show human frailty</note>—though not more than we ourselves might experience in our own work. Thus, we will indeed present our Author’s views and arrange them for view in a proper sequence and connection. However, we will soon point out, according to our own understanding and concept, where he himself seems to have drifted from the nature of the things themselves, or at least where we harbor another opinion about the matters. We will execute this in such a way that we give an account of our judgment or differing opinion, leaving it free for the prudent and skillful reader to choose or follow what they wish.

...[he] wished to show through examples some analogy of the principles that *materially* constitute these various species, as he himself declares and maintains. Or, as it appears to me, he rather wished—or certainly was able—to exhibit only some notable alterations or changes of those principles which *Vegetables* and *Animals* indeed have in common with subterranean things <note>i.e., minerals and metals</note>, which derive their origin partly from the mixing of *water* and partly from the admission of *air*.

(II) Regarding this subject of Subterranean Things, he undertook to consider not just any conditions or—as they commonly say—qualities and properties; but only their *Matter*, or their *Material principles*, from whose gathering or Mixture they are born, consist, and endure.

For this reason, he had little need to labor over the various behaviors of these subterranean bodies regarding solutions, combustions, mutual mixings and compositions, or even the bare separations of various products which break forth from them (especially by the help of Fire) under various forms—even though these do not pre-exist in these Mixtures in that same consistency, etc. Instead, he was rightly content to mention only those from the great number of common chemical operations which seemed to fit the demonstration of the *principles of the simpler mixtures*.

This is the reason why those who interpret this *Subterranean Physics* <note>original: "Physicam hanc Subterraneam"</note> as a *System of common Chemistry* wander as far as the heavens are wide <note>original: "toto coelo aberrant"; a Latin idiom meaning to be completely mistaken</note>. They look there for those "kitchens" <note>original: "culinas," a derogatory term used by theorists to describe the practical, messy work of experimentalists</note> and apothecary shops of trivial pharmacists and medical quacks; or at the very least, they think that deductions of all "chemical processes" (as they call them) ought to have been made here. When they see that their hope is not satisfied in every respect, they become indignant, treating the work as a maimed and useless Rhapsody.

It was not, I say, all compositions and resolutions that our Author had at heart to investigate, but only those which are the *primary*, most intimate, and firmest Mixtures. With this view, he primarily produced those operations and experiments which he judged could serve to achieve this goal.

(III) Therefore, one must note and always keep in mind that distinction of Becher's, by which he discerns Mixtures, Compounds, Decompounds, and even Super-decompounds. <term>Mixta, Composita, Decomposita, Superdecomposita: This is Becher's hierarchy of matter. "Mixtures" are the primary combination of elements; "Compounds" are made of Mixtures; "Decompounds" are made of Compounds, and so on.</term>

(IV.) From several *different species*, I say. For it can indeed happen that such a constitutive part or—to use the common term—ingredient, may be a tiny body or molecule <note>original: "corpusculum seu molecula"</note> consisting of many particles in number, yet all of the same species and bound tightly together. It can happen that such a molecule, homogeneous in species but plural in number, enters into a Mixture along with others that also differ in species;

<header>SPECIMEN OF BECHER. PART I. SECTION I.</header>

...[for another] kind of mixing, there is also required a small body of the aforementioned ingredient, which is also simpler in *number*, or rather the simplest: namely, one. Thus, homogeneity, purity, and simplicity in the business of Mixture—regarding the principles that materially constitute the Mixture—must be understood primarily and, as it were, absolutely, in terms of the homogeneity of essence or species. Secondarily and relatively, it sometimes also applies to numerical simplicity—that is, that such a principle in a certain mixture is required to be pure and simple in both species and number, and one in its essence.

This distinction has its primary place in the mixing of subterranean things—or the most strictly defined *earthy* particles—and their degrees of *rarity* and *density*, which are to be traced back to mechanical principles. This should be noted and impressed upon the mind all the more carefully because our Author himself, through neglect of this consideration, struggled greatly (not to say stumbled <note>original: "cespitavit"</note>) regarding the *degree of rarity* of earths. He allowed himself to imagine almost new *species* for every principle, distinguished by an innate or created degree of rarity. There is certainly no need for these laborious suppositions if one understands that rarity depends on *numerical simplicity*, while density depends on *numerical plurality*—with the only addition in this latter case being a "complication," or as they commonly say, a "cohesion," that is exquisite and very firm among several such particles of the same species. There will be an opportunity to say more about this matter in its proper place.

(V.) By **Composites** he understands those things which have finally been born and grown together from the cohesion and mutual connection of Mixtures.

This classification can indeed be illustrated and explained much more easily with examples, since most materials handled in common *chemical* operations are either composites of this kind or are made into such by those very operations.

For thus, not only are all *minerals*—as they are taken from subterranean places—composites of this kind, since they consist of mixtures of *Sulfur* (sometimes also *Arsenic*, *antimony*, *realgar* <note>a bright red arsenic sulfide mineral</note>) and *metal*; but rather, if we wish to speak more precisely, these minerals are *de-composites* <note>meaning "doubly composed" or mixtures of mixtures</note>. This is because sulfur itself can already be judged a *composite* rather than a simple *mixture*. For this same reason, at the very least, the following are composites: *Cinnabar* (both artificial and native), *sublimated mercury*, *precipitated mercury*, *Butter of antimony* <note>antimony trichloride, a chemical compound with a butter-like consistency</note>, *Vitriols* <note>sulfate minerals, often called "copperas"</note>, various *solutions*, and the precipitates of dissolved things that retain something of their solvents, such as *Luna cornua* <note>literally "horny moon," an old name for silver chloride</note>, *Aurum fulminans* <note>fulminating gold, a highly unstable and explosive compound</note>, and so on. Every single one of these consists of two or more mixtures grown together into this third thing.

Regarding *Super-decomposites*, it should be noted that our Author does not use this word quite so precisely according to its etymology. For what he calls *super-decomposition* does not happen as commonly to composites as it does to mixtures. In a word, "super-decomposition," as the Author more formally accepts it, denotes nothing other than when something is still connected to a complete mixture or composite—whether it be something simple (and thus belonging to the tally of the principles themselves) or whether it reflects a more *mixed* nature. Indeed, this word is most familiar to the Author when he wants to indicate that even a *pure Principle* is added to some mixture in an overabundant quantity: Namely, a larger...

# FUNDAMENTALS OF BECHER’S THEORY

...namely, than what would be required for some simpler mixture (as if of a positive degree).

VI. The Author certainly understands **Mixture** to mean a **Combination** of corpuscles <note>Small, physical particles of matter.</note> of such a kind that, although they are indeed intricately folded together and held in a firm society by a mutual bond or cohesion—as if they stood exquisitely as one—nevertheless, each of them retains its ancient and proper **Essence** even under this bond.

In this, our Author most rightly agrees and harmonizes with the sound **Mechanical-Corpuscular Theory**. This theory correctly understands that any combinations whatsoever are achieved in no other way than through close apposition, an exact *joining*, and sometimes even an *interweaving* (of twisted, hooked, barbed, or spiral-shaped) corpuscles.

For from this foundation, the separation of combinations into their constitutive principles succeeds; these principles once again exhibit their ancient, *proper, and essential constitution and qualities* <note>original: "crasin & affectiones"</note>. Indeed, they behave in such a way that they can either be collected separately and led out from that bond as *pure* substances, or they may be transferred into another mixture.

An example of this might be, for instance, *Cinnabar* <note>A bright red mineral consisting of mercury sulfide, the primary ore of mercury.</note>; from it, both *sulfur* and *running mercury* <note>Liquid quicksilver.</note> can be separated with their powers unharmed. Indeed, they can be joined together again and once more reduced into Cinnabar, and this may be repeated as often as one pleases. Likewise, sulfur can be stripped of its flammable part through ignition, and its acidic portion can be retained, having been similarly set aside. By adding a new flammable substance of that kind (for example, from charcoal) to this acidity, Sulfur is immediately produced, mixed, or combined once again.

The Ancients, unskilled in more sincere artificial resolutions <note>Chemical analysis or breaking substances down.</note> and combinations, nurtured a strange concept regarding mixture and that "form" which, as it were, *penetrates* the mixture. For they wanted it to be understood as if that mixture brought about such a deep mutual penetration of principles that if such a Mixed body were divided even into mathematical points—as if unto infinity—every single one of those "smallest of smalls" would nonetheless remain mixed, or participate in that mixture which had previously existed in that physically-indivisible minimum.

This opinion, evidently, proceeded in lockstep from that "golden phantom" of Aristotle concerning the mathematical divisibility of Physical Bodies—that is, that physical points (which certainly have dimension) can be divided into mathematical points, which are devoid of all quantity.

Our Author is far removed from this kind of insanity; for this reason, he did not recognize such a "penetrative confusion" of principles into an absolute, single chaos. Since the properties of the principles would be utterly destroyed by such a confusion—which is contrary to Experience—our Author, being taught otherwise by Experience, could not admit it.

Furthermore, the idea that the properties of principles are destroyed by mixture is suggested—indeed, urged—by that solemn assertion that the introduction of a new form, constituting a new mixture,

### SPECIMEN OF BECHER'S WORK, PART I, SECTION I.

...presupposes the **Privation** <note>In the Aristotelian tradition, "privation" is the absence of a form or quality that a thing should naturally possess.</note> of the former form: but from privation back to a state of being <note>original: "habitum"</note>, no return is granted. These are mere flourishes of this philosophy—unless you would rather call them mushrooms growing from the philosophical brain.

VII. **Mixture**, however, excels **Composition** in this: that in a mixture, the cohesion of the principles <note>The basic constituent parts or elements.</note> is far firmer against the force of dissolution than in a composition; the latter’s constitutive parts are more loosely joined and are therefore more readily dissolved again.

At this point, if wishes had any power, one might long for that energy of "dividing" which so flourished in the brain of **Aristotle** that, in his leisure, he could tear apart the smallest natural bodies into infinity. However, if this energy were so unbridled that it recklessly ripped a body to be divided into any dimension whatsoever, it would surely be useless to us. For indeed, unless the division proceeds along the physical **line of the joint** <note>original: "lineam commissurae"</note> of the combined corpuscles, it would wander in vain through countless other mathematical lines.

Indeed, those who wish to divide natural bodies not by idle fantasy in the brain, but by actual effect, must know for certain that they cannot establish or perform this division immediately through mere thought or imagination. Rather, they will understand that they have need of **instruments** with which they may either grasp those corpuscles and tear them away from their mutual bond, or work upon the joint itself, as it were, and split it with wedges, etc.

Thus, they easily recognize that a proportion is necessary here between the subject being divided and the dividing instrument. Consequently, they understand that in their **physical** subjects—whether mixed or combined—there cannot and should not be that senseless ripping into "parts outside of parts" <note>A philosophical term referring to the way matter occupies space, with one part distinct from the next.</note> in every dimension across mathematical lines **into infinity**. Instead, there must be a **separation** <note>original: "dimotio"</note> through and according to those very **seams** and **joints** by which those corpuscles that constitute the mixture cling to one another and are contained among themselves. This must be done with the caution that no more corpuscles in **number** are expected to come out than joined together to constitute that mixture in the first place: for that number is by no means infinite, but is instead strictly defined.

To be sure, it is not our purpose to examine all the games of every idle mind. Otherwise, one would rightly have to touch upon that "most solid solidity" and "most impenetrable impenetrability" which is a necessary supposition of our more recent thinkers (lest, for instance, a motion falling upon one corpuscle from elsewhere might move everything into infinity by penetrating through all the rest). And yet, despite this, such corpuscles easily undergo **abrasion** and a **shaving down** into countless smaller bits—indeed, the smallest possible bits—without end.

For those who acknowledge real truth, and tend toward learning and collecting things that actually happen rather than those things that can only be *thought* to happen: for them, I say, it remains certain and firm that the division of natural corpuscles in any combination never occurs in any other way than through simple tearing away or pushing apart from that seam and joint where, until now, they had been tightly folded together or held fast by mutual pressure.

# THE FUNDAMENTALS OF BECHER’S THEORY

Just as, from this perspective, those corpuscles which are absolutely unique in number and kind are by that very fact necessarily smaller in size than others which arise from the combination <note>original: "complicatione"</note> of several of these same parts; so it is entirely consistent with reason that those bodies which must be employed as *instruments* for *grasping these smallest of all things*, and for drawing them apart from their mutual connection, must also necessarily be by far the most subtle.

Furthermore, just as division is properly a *moving apart* <note>original: "dimotio"</note>, and the act of division is necessarily a *motion*; so it follows with the same evidence from this consideration that the *motion* which must be applied to the division of the most tender and absolutely smallest physical corpuscles ought not be *rough* or *coarse*—that is, breaking in by means of *coarse and rustic instruments*. Instead, it must be equally matched to them by means of very *delicate* instruments; indeed, instruments which are not unequal in proportion to those very corpuscles which are to be divided and torn apart.

(What we have just said concerning physical minima indicates that those primordial, entirely simple corpuscles, which we commonly call principles, are those *impenetrable* and truly *solid* things which can admit no further resolution of themselves, nor *undergo that famous extension of Aristotle and Descartes*—which, as is well known, *allows for parts outside of parts in a physical sense*. <note>The author is attacking the idea that matter is infinitely divisible. He argues that while you can imagine dividing something forever (mathematically), physically there is a solid limit—the atom or "principle."</note> For Aristotle is truly ridiculous with his rustic confusion of mathematical dimension or *distinction* and *physical division*, a matter we deal with in the *Halle Observations*, Vol. VII. <note>The "Observationes Hallenses" refers to a scholarly journal associated with Georg Ernst Stahl and the University of Halle.</note>

For it is clearly one thing to be *able to be described, distinguished, and discerned mathematically, as it were, into various dimensions* by mathematical lines *directed* according to breadth and depth. It is quite another thing, *by real effect* and with the penetration of bodily solidity, to be *split apart* <note>original: "diffindi"</note> and thus *physically moved aside*. For those mathematical distinctions, made according to the various terms of a mathematical line distinguishing or running through from the periphery of the universe through the center of a minimum, differ as much from that *physical* splitting which locally moves things apart, as a thought differs from the mass of this entire universe, if the latter were nothing other than a pure, solid, stony globe, etc.)

Regarding that subject—namely, the *respect and proportion of the dividing instrument to the body to be divided*—I have already given some warning in the *Treatise on Zymotechnia* <note>J.J. Becher’s *Zymotechnia Fundamentalis* (1667), a foundational text on the chemistry of fermentation and the "fermentative" motion of particles.</note>. There, I especially emphasized this: that from a certain coarse moving force, which does not run into another body through *a single line (a physical one, however) but through many joined together at once—that is, through a physical surface*—there follows the shoving and local movement of the whole body far more certainly than the <unclear>division</unclear> of any single particle from the many that constitute that body. This warning, being absolutely fundamental, I recommend again and again.

From this practical theory flows a clear enough reason why that division of *Mixts* <term>Mixta: In early modern chemistry, these are the primary combinations of elements (like salts or metals) which are very difficult to break apart.</term> is so difficult, while the division or resolution of *Compounds* <term>Composita: Secondary combinations—aggregates of "mixts"—which are more easily separated into their constituent parts.</term> is far easier. This is because the corpuscles that constitute Mixts are not only the most subtle and *smallest* in mass, but they also close together into a *junction* and *structure* so tight that

### VIII.

Our Author <note>The author refers to Johann Joachim Becher (1635–1682), the German physician and alchemist whose theories are being discussed.</note> also warns that the principles of mixed bodies <note>original: "mixtorum"</note> can hardly ever be separated from one another in a pure state. They cannot be collected or shown by themselves in their naked simplicity and sameness. Instead, this is usually done by a process of transfer <note>original: "transsumptionis"</note> from an earlier mixture into another; namely, so that one mixture is dissolved [to create the next].

The ancient thesis—*The destruction of one thing is the birth of another* <note>original: "Unius corruptio est alterius generatio." This is a fundamental principle of Aristotelian physics adopted by alchemists to describe how matter changes form.</note>—may have grown out of coarse observations, yet its truth is found to be far more universal. Indeed, as much as our weak ability to experiment allows, it seems to be an absolute rule. So much so that, regarding mixtures, we see a perpetual birth of a new mixture from the destruction of the old one. This fact is so obvious to the senses that it does not need a long explanation, as it shows itself everywhere in practical examples. However, we need a slightly deeper theory to understand the *manner* in which this happens.

To build this theory, we must pay attention to the **twofold mechanism** by which the instruments used for dissolving mixtures can produce their effect. This happens in two ways:
1.  The instrument might grab the tiny body it is meant to separate by applying itself deeply or tangling with it, pulling it into its own motion and tearing it away from its companions. 
2.  Or, it might simply penetrate the physical **seam** <note>original: "commissurae"</note> of the body like a wedge or a lever, attempting a simple displacement.

In the first way, instruments produce their effect by **material collision** <note>original: "materiali concursu"</note>, as they say in the Schools. In the second way, they act **merely formally**. In the first, they achieve their effect through *constant contact and internal motion*; in the second, through *temporary contact and outward motion*.

<margin>Observed motions</margin>
Now, if we look at the reality of things and actual practice, we find this **first** type of motion is so common in every dissolution of mixtures and compounds that we see almost no trace of the second. The only exception is found in the traditions and stories told about the **Liquor Alcahest** <note>The Alcahest was a legendary universal solvent sought by alchemists, said to be capable of reducing any solid matter into its primary liquid form without being changed itself.</note>. But while there are many mentions of this substance, there are no confirmations that we can safely rely upon—at least from witnesses who are not biased. Therefore, it is necessary to be cautious. However, if the thing actually works as reported, no other way of thinking would fit it better than the mechanical mode just mentioned. Meanwhile, this theory can be read in the *Inaugural Dissertation on the Liquor Alcahest* held at Jena some time ago by my now-deceased friend, the doctoral candidate Mr. **Wedekind** <note>Rudolf Wedekind, who defended a thesis on the Alcahest at the University of Jena in the late 17th century.</note>; where the rest of the matter, which even...

Neither, however, are these the only two ways <note>Referring to the methods of penetration mentioned on the previous page.</note>, as if no third way could be given by which the striking apart and thrusting down of tiny particles <term>corpusculorum</term>—which are joined closely together—might probably be achieved. This is so that a probable reason can be given as to which of such effects—and when and why—have either an easy or a difficult success in carrying out the dissolution of mixtures.

Since, however, to a significant number of readers this deduction might seem too speculative and therefore cause them boredom, I will refer them instead to the *Halle Observations* <note>original: "Observationes Hallenses"; likely referring to the *Observationes selectae ad rem litterariam spectantes*, a scholarly journal from the University of Halle.</note>, Volume VII.

### X.

Experience confirms this almost as an absolute rule: that **mixtures are not resolved except by the sole transfer of principles** <note>original: "transumptione principiorum"</note> **immediately into another mixture.**

As this matter is confirmed by many examples, so if we inquire theoretically into the reasons for it, it becomes most likely to our understanding that resolution is ordinarily performed not by the method of a wedge, nor by the method of striking a single particle to be separated on its own; but rather **by the method of "apprehension"** <note>The word "apprehensio" here suggests a physical grasping or taking hold.</note> **or close application to that very particle which, by such a method, comes to be torn away or plucked out from the others.**

For if the division were made in the two former ways (by "formal influence" <note>original: "formali influxu"; a technical term from Scholastic philosophy meaning a change that affects the form of a thing without necessarily sharing its substance.</note> alone, as the Schools say), those particles so separated ought to be obtained in their **homogeneous** state. But since no such thing happens, and instead a very stubborn alteration follows, whether in the **solvent** or in the **substance being dissolved** <note>original: "solvente" and "solvendo"</note>—that is, something of the principles of the mixture coalesces intimately with the solvent, or something of the solvent's substance grows most stubbornly onto the mixture—it is therefore most agreeable to reason that such effects happen by a closer union of the solvent with the substance being dissolved, rather than by a bare and simple formal, instrumental division.

This rule holds true, as has been said, primarily regarding **mixtures** <note>Mixtures here refer to chemically bonded substances.</note> and their resolution. In **Composites** <note>Composites refer to looser physical groupings of matter.</note>, however, or at least in many of them, such apprehension is more uncertain, or certainly far more sluggish,

On the other hand, since ***Compounds*** consist of somewhat larger molecules, the reason is clear why these molecules can be grasped quite readily by other physical instruments—as if by bodily hands—and their seams weakened or even dissolved.

VIII. Our Author further warns that the principles of mixtures <term>mixtorum; substances made of chemically bonded principles</term> can hardly ever be separated from each other in a pure state. They can neither be collected nor displayed separately in their naked, simple, and uniform state. Rather, this is only conveniently done through "transsumption" <note>The transfer of a substance from one combination directly into another.</note> from a prior mixture into a new one—namely, by dissolving one mixture so that its parts may form another.

Although that thesis of the ancients—***The corruption of one is the generation of another*** <note>original: "Unius corruptio est alterius generatio"; an Aristotelian principle suggesting that matter is never lost, only changed from one form to another.</note>—may have sprung from coarse examples and observations, its truth is found to be far more universal. Indeed, as far as our limited ability to experiment allows, it is found to be most universal of all. So much so that, if we look at the nature of mixing, we observe a perpetual generation of a new mixture arising from the corruption of the old. This fact strikes the senses so evidently that it does not require a long-winded explanation, especially since it manifests itself everywhere in practical examples. Thus, it is enough to have proposed it here as a simple thesis. However, regarding the *way* this happens and how we should conceive of it, we need a slightly deeper theory.

To form this theory, we must necessarily attend to that **dual mechanism** by which the instruments used for the dissolution of mixtures can produce their effect. Specifically: either they seize that tiny body <term>corpusculum</term> (which they must separate or tear away from others) by a more intimate application or entanglement, pulling it into their own motion and thus snatching it away from the others with which it had previously clung; or they simply penetrate the physical line of the **seam** like a wedge or a lever, thus attempting a simple displacement.

In the first way, they produce their effect through a **material** encounter (as they say in the Schools); in the second, they act merely **formally**. In the former, they achieve their effect through **perpetual contact and inherent motion**; in the latter, through **transitory contact and emanating motion.**

<margin>the more common motion</margin>
Now, if we look at the reality of things and at practice itself, that **former motion** occurs so familiarly and almost universally in every dissolution of mixtures and compounds that scarcely any trace of the latter is observed—excepting those traditions and accounts usually brought forward regarding the ***Alkahest Liquor*** <note>The "universal solvent" of the alchemists, legendary for its supposed ability to reduce any body to its first matter without being changed itself.</note>. For this reason, it is necessary to **suspend judgment** <note>original: "ἐπέχειν" (epéchein); a term from Greek Skepticism meaning to withhold assent until more evidence is found.</note>. However, if the matter itself truly behaves as reported, certainly no other mode than the one described would fit for conceiving it. For a third method can indeed be conceived, which I spoke of in the cited ***Zymotechnia*** <note>Johann Joachim Becher's 1667 work on fermentation and chemical physics.</note>. This occurs if a body set in exceptional motion should, through a single physical line of contact, strike a single particle (out of many combined together) along such a path and dimension relative to the common center of gravity <term>centrum gravitatis</term> that the motion it imparts to that single corpuscle introduces no convergence toward that center. Otherwise—that is, if such convergence toward the center of gravity is introduced to all these united particles together—the removal of one from the rest will not follow. Instead, there would be a movement of all of them together as a single unit, according to one common center of gravity; thus, it would be a simple forward movement of the whole, but no actual separation of one particle, as a part, from the others.

Just as these points concerning mechanical powers can not only be conceived this way but are entirely true—provided a proper reciprocal proportion exists between the moving force and the object to be moved—so it would be all the more just, and indeed necessary, to include that uniquely necessary proportion at the same time. This is so that a probable reason can be given as to why such effects might meet with either easy or difficult success in carrying out the dissolution of mixtures.

However, since this deduction might seem too speculative to a significant number of readers and thus cause them boredom, I will refer them instead to the ***Halle Observations*** <note>original: "Observationes Hallenses"; likely referring to the *Observationum selectarum ad rem litterariam spectantium*, a scholarly journal from Halle.</note>, Volume 7.

**X. Experience also confirms this almost absolutely: that mixtures are not resolved except through the "transumption" <term>transumptio; the direct transfer of chemical components from one state to another</term> of principles immediately into another mixture.**

This matter is confirmed by many examples. Furthermore, if we investigate the reasons theoretically, it becomes highly probable that dissolution is ordinarily carried out not by the method of a wedge, nor by striking a single particle to be separated on its own, but rather by way of **apprehension** <term>apprehensio; a "grasping" or bonding action</term>—that is, a close application to that very particle which is to be torn away or plucked out from the others by such means.

For if the division were made in the two previous ways (by "formal influence" <note>original: "formali influxu"; a Scholastic term referring to an external cause acting on the form of an object.</note> alone, as the Scholastic philosophers say), those separated particles ought to be obtained in their own "homogeneous" or pure state. But since nothing of the sort happens—and instead a very stubborn alteration follows, whether in the **solvent** <term>solvente</term> or in the **substance being dissolved** <term>solvendo</term>—it is clear that something from the principles of the mixture bonds intimately with the solvent, or something from the substance of the solvent clings most tenaciously to the mixture. Therefore, it is most consistent with reason that such effects occur through a tighter union of the solvent with the substance, rather than by a naked and simple mechanical division.

This principle applies, as has been said, primarily to ***mixtures*** and their dissolution. In ***Compounds***, however—at least in many of them—such apprehension is more uncertain, or certainly far more sluggish.

### SPECIMEN OF BECHER’S THEORY. PART I. SECTION I.

...hension <note>Original: *apprehensio*. This word completes the sentence from the previous page.</note>, and through the mode of apprehension, division and separation occur: Since those instruments of dissolution <note>solvents</note> carry away the dissolved material so very promptly again, any probability of a firmer bond might seem to waver considerably.

Examples of this can be: *Extractions of resins by spirit of wine <term>Spiritus Vini; high-proof alcohol</term>; of salts by water; indeed of gold and silver by quicksilver <term>Argentum vivum; mercury</term>, etc.* Since solvents of this kind are so very easily separated from those dissolved substances—resins by the pouring in of water; salts by an evaporation that is almost spontaneous in the open air without any force of fire; *quicksilver* by heat and all means that can agitate and scatter it even when pure and connected to nothing else—it seems very likely that the foundation of such solutions and what we call "extractions" (or more simply, separations) consists in the pushing down of these types of small bodies, followed by the bare, confused agitation of these fluids without any significant bond.

Meanwhile, if we examine and weigh the experience concerning each and every one of these things more circumspectly, that Thesis remains firm and unshaken: that this tearing away occurs much more—indeed, immensely more commonly—by way of *apprehension* <note>a "grasping" or bonding action</note> or tenacious cohesion, even in compounds themselves, than by the mode of some other transitory and (as they call it) merely *formal act* emanating from one body into another as if from an instrument.

For we shall remain silent on the fact that it could be denied, or at least called into doubt, whether in the cited examples those same resinous, saline, or pure metallic particles were actually held in a true bond of composition or mixture <term>mixtio; a deep chemical union</term> with the remaining things from which they are, as it were, washed out by the said solvents. Rather, they were perhaps at least *interspersed and confused* with them, as in a certain heap, more than they were *connected* with them. (For surely where a more certain and intimate bond of composition or mixture is present, a separation cannot be obtained so easily by these types of instruments or solvents; nor, if anything is obtained at all, is it then so loosely and superficially joined with such solvents that it can be separated from them again with the same readiness.) Thus, a great certainty—that these cited dissolutions occur not only *formally* but more so *materially*—seems to be brought in by the circumstance that even in these very examples, a clearly real *kinship of matter* <term>cognatio materiae; the principle that "like dissolves like"</term> exists between the solvents and the things to be dissolved. For instance, *burning spirit* <note>alcohol</note> attacks materials participating in the "burning principle" <note>oils or sulfurs</note>; *water* dissolves such materials in which water is implanted and bound by a more intimate connection; *mercury* admits only substances coinciding with it in various *essential qualities*, and so on. Regarding this matter, express mention must be made in what follows.

XI. Meanwhile, the motion of dissolution does not always succeed in a single, simple, prompt, and hasty progress everywhere. It occurs only where a more manifest embrace of the divider with the thing to be divided promptly finds a place, and moreover, where the body to be divided is of a *composite* rather than a *mixed* nature <note>Becher distinguishes between "composite" things (loosely gathered) and "mixed" things (chemically unified at a fundamental level).</note>.

Indeed, Langelotus <note>Joel Langelott (1617–1680), a physician and chemist who advocated for extended "digestion" or heating to break down substances.</note> complains with good reason that long-lasting, diligent *digestion* <term>Digestio; the process of exposing a substance to gentle, continuous heat</term> is to be numbered among those things which common Chemistry <note>Original: *Chymia*</note> tends to overlook, neglect, and ignore.

<summary>Becher argues that chemical dissolution is not merely a mechanical breaking of parts but requires a "kinship of matter" where the solvent and solute share similar properties. He distinguishes between loose physical mixtures and intimate chemical bonds, noting that the latter require much more effort (such as long digestion) to separate.</summary>

...to yield. For just as, according to the proverb, *A drop hollows the stone, not by force, but by falling often*; that is, not by one single strike, but by striking more often and in various ways: So, among the extremely numerous strikes, which are to be counted by *myriads of myriads*, at last, at some time, by chance, one hits that line, meets that face, or concurs in that position which responds to the desired displacement. Although in some other, or indeed in other similar small bodies of the same mass, this very thing might happen elsewhere by a single strike—a thousandth, or perhaps a hundredth—by striking, rubbing, or wearing away, and might there achieve an effect of this kind. For in a business of this sort, nothing is absolutely necessary regarding the ratio of time, but the entire ratio of time here is a matter of *merely accidental event*, and it can easily be recognized to be so.

Fermentation itself provides a primary and completely clear example of this thing; especially *Vinous* fermentation, and whatever participates more in a saline substance, of a sweet substance turning sour. For in this way, the must <note>Original: *mustum*; unfermented grape juice</note> continues its heat for ten, twelve, or fifteen weeks; before all the particles floating in its broad domain—of a saline-sulfureous-earthy composition—not only undergo motion, but finally, by the multiple strikes of motions, mutual meeting, collision, and rubbing, also obtain their divisions, separations, and translocations.

So also in metallic fusions, those who are able to somewhat grasp physical points of time in their minds will easily conceive that, for a human, the numbers of motions that happen to the individual small bodies of that mass through the space of a quarter of an hour, in the vigorous flow of metal, are innumerable. Meanwhile, not only in dissolving, but also afterwards in combining various metallic principles of this kind, there is often an absolute need for a long continuation of such a flow, under which—no differently than under fermentation—in the fluid-moist state, among innumerable strikes and meetings, collisions, and rubbings, that dimension might at last be reached once which, whether by displacing or by tearing away, rightly meets and satisfies one such small body here and there.

This is entirely the reason why, from those experiments which come about through the performance of *fusion*, such varied success is noted from time to time; indeed, those who are able to measure in their minds neither the nature of thin fusion, nor the convenient shape of the vessels, nor the proper ratio of time, commonly fail in the whole truth and every success of the experiment. One could cite some examples of this matter, as much from that Becherian *Sand-Ore* <note>Original: *Minera arenaria*; Becher claimed to extract gold from common sand</note> and similar so-called *Grading Glasses* <term>Vitra gradatoria; vessels or substances used to "grade" or increase the purity of metals</term>; as from the Isaac-Hollandish <note>Referring to the works of Isaac Hollandus, a 15th-century alchemist</note> *fusion and reduction of lead*, providing something of a better metal as often as it occurs: But since the thread of the discussion suggests reserving such things for other places, it is pleasing to bring forward at the minimum, as an example, the separation of *Gold* from silver through fusion, or, as they commonly say, *dry* separation. Where certainly, unless the consideration of time, the flow of proper thinness, and to some extent (at least for a better operation) the nature and consideration of the *vessels* also concur, more than one experimenter has experienced that what both could and should have happened does not occur.

Hence indeed, just as anyone would be considered a fool who expected common good wine from his good must within **24** hours, or one or another day, or, if this were not succeeding...

### SPECIMEN BECHERIANUM PART I. SECTION I.

...grasping <note>Original: *apprehensio*</note>, and by the mode of grasping, division and separation: Since they [the particles] very quickly desert the instruments of dissolution once dissolved, so that every probability of any firmer bond seems to waver.

Examples may include: *Extractions of resins by spirit of wine <note>Original: *spiritum Vini*; ethanol</note>; of salts by water: even of Gold and silver by quicksilver <note>Original: *argentum vivum*; mercury</note>, etc.* Since solvents of this kind are separated again from these dissolved substances very easily: resins by the pouring in of water; salts by evaporation <note>Original: *exhalationem*</note> even spontaneously in the open air without any fire; *quicksilver* by heat, and all means that can agitate and pull apart the quicksilver itself even when pure and not connected to anything else. From this it seems most likely that the foundation of such solutions—which we call extractions, or rather, separations—consists in the dislodging of these tiny bodies, followed by a confused agitation of these fluids without any significant bond.

Meanwhile, if we examine and weigh Experience regarding all these things individually and more carefully, the thesis remains firm and unshaken: that far more commonly—infinitely so—that tearing away occurs by the mode of *grasping or tenacious cohesion*, even in compounds themselves, rather than by a transitory and (as they call it) merely *formal* act emanating from one body into another as if by an instrument.

For we should not stay silent on the fact—which can be denied, or at least doubted—whether in the examples provided, those *purely resinous, saline, or metallic* particles were ever held in a true bond of composition or mixture <note>Becher distinguishes between a "composition," which is a loose physical arrangement, and a "mixture," which implies a deeper chemical union</note> with the remaining substances from which they are washed out by the solvents. Rather, they were perhaps interspersed like a heap, confused rather than bonded with them. (*Indeed, where there is a certain presence of a deeper composite or mixed bond, there separation cannot be obtained so easily by such instruments or solvents; nor, if anything is obtained, is it then joined so loosely and superficially with those solvents that it can be separated from them again with the same readiness.*) Thus, great certainty seems to be inferred (that these cited dissolutions occur not only formally but rather materially) by the circumstance that even in these examples, a clear material kinship exists between the solvents and the substances to be dissolved. For instance, *burning spirit* <note>alcohol</note> attacks substances sharing in the burning principle <note>likely referring to sulfur or the "inflammable earth"</note>; *Water* dissolves those substances in which water is implanted and bound by a deeper connection; *Mercury* admits only substances coinciding with it in various *essential* properties, etc. This will be explicitly mentioned in the following sections.

XI. Meanwhile, the *motion of dissolution* does not always proceed in one simple, prompt, and hasty manner; but only where a more manifest embrace of the divider with the thing to be divided occurs readily, and where the body to be divided is of a composite rather than a mixed nature.

Indeed, *Langelottus* <note>Joel Langelott (1617–1680), a German physician and chemist known for his work on "digestion" and mechanical chemistry</note> complains not without cause that long-term, diligent *Digestion* <note>The process of exposing a substance to gentle heat over a long period to encourage chemical change</note> is to be numbered among those things which *common chemistry* overlooks, neglects, and fails to heed...

...to fall <note>The text continues a sentence from the previous page</note>. For just as, according to the Proverb, *A drop hollows the stone, not by force, but by falling often* <note>Original Latin: *Gutta cavat lapidem non vi, sed sæpe cadendo*</note>; that is, not by one single strike, but by striking more often and in various ways: So, among the most numerous assaults—to be counted in *myriads upon myriads*—one strike eventually happens by chance upon that line, meets that face, or concurs in that position, which corresponds to the desired displacement. Although in some other particle of the same mass, or indeed in others of similar tiny bodies, this very thing might happen elsewhere by a simple thousandth, or perhaps a hundredth strike, rub, or friction, and thus achieve its effect there. For in this kind of business, nothing is absolutely necessary regarding time, but the entire calculation of time here is a *matter of mere fortuitous event*, and can easily be recognized as such.

*Fermentation* itself provides a primary and thoroughly clear example of this; especially *Vinous* fermentation, and whatever participates more in the Saline substance by turning from sweet to sour. For in this way, the must <note>unfermented grape juice</note> continues its bubbling heat <note>Original: *fervorem*</note> for ten, twelve, or fifteen weeks before all the particles of a Salt-Sulfur-Earthy composition floating in its broad domain not only undergo motion, but finally, through the manifold assault of motions, mutual meeting, collision, and friction, they also attain their divisions, separations, and relocations.

So too in *metallic fusions*, those who are able to grasp "physical points of time" <note>infinitesimally small moments</note> somewhat in their minds will easily conceive that for a man, there are innumerable counts of motion that happen to the individual small bodies of that mass during the space of a quarter of an hour in the vigorous flow of metal. Meanwhile, not only in dissolving but also afterward in combining different metallic principles of this kind, there is often an absolute need for a long continuation of such a flow. Under this flow—no differently than under fermentation—within the liquid-fluid state, among countless assaults and meetings, collisions, and frictions, that dimension might finally be reached once, which—either by displacing or tearing away—properly meets and satisfies one such small body here or there.

This is entirely the reason why, from those experiments which are carried out by *fusion*, such varied success is occasionally noted; indeed, those who cannot estimate in their minds either the nature of *thin* <note>low viscosity; a "watery" melt</note> fusion, nor the convenient shape of the vessels, nor the proper calculation of time, commonly miss the whole truth and every success of the experiment. In this case, unless the calculation and consideration of time, and of a flow of the right thinness, and to some extent (at least for better operation) of the vessels also concur, more than one experimenter has experienced that what could and should have happened did not.

<header>SPECIMEN OF BECHER, PART I, SECTION I.</header>

...[were to cease] <note>The text continues a sentence from the previous page</note>, he would despair of the whole truth of the transformation of must into wine. Just so, I do not know how much consideration can be given to anyone who hopes to obtain the effect of any other most subtle *Resolutions* <term>Resolution: the chemical process of breaking a substance down into its component parts</term>, especially in a larger quantity of material, so prematurely and in a minimum span of time, or otherwise does not fear to judge poorly and pronounce falsely about the entire truth of the experiment.

In this business, certainly, is founded that difference of truly great importance: that *certain metallic operations, in a small quantity of material, exhibit some special effects; yet in larger weights, they frustrate expectation.* For however much ignorance of that greatest difference often lies beneath—namely, the difference between melting in Vessels <note>crucible melting</note> and *melting by contact and material mixing of Coals*—even if fusions are performed on a large scale in Vessels, without the entry and mixing of coals, that immense diversity causes very different outcomes. This is due to the difference between the mutual thinness of the flow and the measure of time in a small versus a large vessel, and the narrow or spread-out scope and vast domain <note>Original Latin: *latifundio*</note> of the material, which creates the disparity between the effects or products of small and large quantities.

### XII. Mixture happens in an instant.

We have spoken up to now of the contrary regarding the *Dissolution* of a mixture, and we hope the reason for this matter can become all the clearer from what was said before, if one attends to that remarkable difference between the absolute necessity of *Instruments* <note>physical agents like heat, acids, or tools</note> to carry out a dissolution; and, on the other hand, the energy of *Motion* alone for the joining of combinable Bodies.

Truly, we think it is far easier to conceive that tiny bodies <note>Original Latin: *corpuscula*</note> can be joined, folded together, and rest upon each other by a single mutual encounter, than that they can be torn apart again from such a manifold layering, closing together, reciprocal embrace, and constant simultaneous pressure. It is harder still to keep them in such a torn-apart state so that they can actually be found divided, separated, and scattered from one another.

Indeed, this is even the reason *from experience* <note>Original Latin: *a posteriori*</note> why it is absolutely impossible to find the *principles* <note>the fundamental building blocks or elements</note> of mixtures *pure and unmixed* anywhere outside of the actual state of mutual combination. To such an extent that, through the things said above, even the separation itself—whether spontaneous and natural or artificial—cannot be carried out except either by way of a new *snatching* and transfer or seizure; or at the very least, through the immediate occurrence of a new coalescence of those very particles which had been moved out of some preceding mixture, but now immediately coalesce and fold together among themselves once more.

Hence, since for mixture or the mutual *bringing together* of tiny bodies, nothing is required but simple and naked *motion*; while for the *division* of mixed things, there is a need for *Instruments* that produce this effect by a thoroughly *material*, and not only *formal* <note>In this context, "formal" refers to the conceptual arrangement or "essence" of a thing, while "material" refers to physical substance and energy</note>, concurrence. The difference in general is therefore easily understood, as is the reason for the unequal ease or difficulty of success *in specific cases*.

<meta>This page continues the theoretical exploration of motion and matter, specifically addressing how the physical properties of the "Geocosmos" (the earthly realm) favor the aggregation of particles into solid masses, and how "rest" is actually a result of active motion.</meta>

<header>FUNDAMENTALS OF BECHER’S THEORY</header>

To this matter is added the fact that new combinations, gatherings, and retentions are promoted all the more—and are all the more stubbornly fostered and supported—by the concurrence and protection of things that are increasingly alien to the activity of *motion*. This is most common in our Geocosmos <term>Geocosmos: the Earth as a physical, geological system</term> (in things that are earthy, dense, rigid, cold, and aggregated into large and thick masses).

For however much *Plato*—if we trust the reports—is said to have carried in his Seal as a motto: *It is easier to move what is at rest than to bring motion to rest* <note>Original Latin: *Facilius esse movere quietum, quam quietare motum*</note>; yet in truth, if we examine the matter correctly, this assertion is not valid except regarding the coarser aggregates and masses of bodies. From these, a great force of motion passes far more impetuously into something else that was previously at rest (and thus impels it) than that resting body can resist it—as people commonly trifle—unless it resists according to the activity of opposite motions by which such a body remains held and contained even under the contact of this new assault.

But the matter behaves far differently in the motion of *minimal corpuscles* <note>The smallest possible particles or "atoms" of matter</note>; where the opposite is observed: namely, that everything is driven and compelled from a state of simplicity or singular motion into *aggregation*, accumulation, and a compact mass.

Indeed, since even removal, dispelling, and division do not bring about a naked, pure, and absolute motion, but rather a plainly *determined*, most specific, and strictly directed motion: it cannot be a wonder if instead a naked, general, and indeterminate motion sweeps corpuscles into accidental mutual encounters, drives them into mutual concurrence, and thus compresses and binds them into a mutual rest among themselves. Consequently, this proceeds more toward the production of compositions—and indeed aggregations—than it achieves divisions along certain and exquisite lines, sides, and surfaces.

By this reasoning, that which we call *Rest* is produced by nothing other than perennial motion itself: it is the forcing together, binding, and compression of many corpuscles into one single mass. It is properly a certain active contention or compression, made and sustained by motion itself. Meanwhile, for this entire business, a proportion of the particles in terms of their mutual shape is certainly required, so that this compression finds its place according to the nature of the subject, and the subject fits correctly for such an act. However, the plan of our current work does not permit us to treat this matter more at length in this place.

### XIII. *Mixed, or rather composite things, do not fall under our senses, except in aggregation.*

It cannot be said how much damage has been brought upon the theoretical resolution of the chemical art by the neglect of this Truth. Indeed, why do I speak only of *Chemical Theory*? The whole of *Physics*—whatever it had to say about *mixture, composition, principles, combination, union, contiguity, and continuity*—will never explain them clearly as long as it neglects to correctly grasp this axiom from practice itself. Certainly, our entire common Physics, from the age of *Aristotle* even to the present day, remains stuck in this mud: it confuses the *qualities of aggregation* with the properties of the *individual* corpuscles of each species.
