# EXAMPLES OF BECHER’S THEORY. PART I. SECTION I.

See [Georg Ernst] Stahl’s *Introduction to Physical-Chemical Causality*, Jena, published by Bielke, 1683—my youthful aspirations <note>Original Latin: *desideria juvenilia mea*. Stahl is reflecting on his early work and his intellectual journey.</note>.

I recall that I once reproached a certain champion of Aristotle <note>Original: *Aristotelis Promacho*. A "promachos" is a defender or front-line warrior for a cause.</note> with a polite complaint: that Aristotle had left us nothing regarding substances mixed according to their specific types. This man excused that greatest of philosophers, saying that countless—and perhaps the most precious—of his monuments of writing had perished. Certainly, from those that remain, enough examples exist to show what kind of things he might have written on these matters as a professional. But there is no reason for us to dwell on him; if we listen to those closer to our time, such as Digby <note>Sir Kenelm Digby (1603–1665), an English natural philosopher and courtier</note> in the passage where he discusses the difference between *the contiguous and the continuous* (in his treatise *On the Immortality of the Soul*), what miserable fluctuations we find there between the distinctions of *the contiguous and the continuous in a small branch*. These stem from nothing other than a confusion between a *fragment and a whole*, a *twig and the wood*, an aggregate *in general* and something *structured*—not to mention the difference between an aggregate *made of many* parts versus the *single unit* composed of those many.

To hide nothing, one cannot ignore how this same difficulty led our Author <note>Referring to Johann Joachim Becher, whose work Stahl is commenting on.</note> astray. This is clear if one notices how, in explaining the reasoning behind *generation, growth, and formation*, he introduces a very specific convergence of *specific gravity* <term>Specific gravity: the density of a substance compared to a reference, used here to describe an inherent weight-force in particles.</term>, which he considers to be created along with the *corpuscles* <note>Small particles or "atoms" of matter</note> as individuals. Thus, he confusingly applies the property of *one* corpuscle not only to certain necessary conditions resulting from an *aggregate* of such corpuscles, but plainly to the necessity of a very specific *structure*—as if that *structure* follows such a form, and no other, out of the *pure necessity of the matter*.

Therefore, it is all the more necessary that this business be scrutinized exquisitely and kept perpetually in mind: those *corpuscles* of which it is said they are *mixed* or *composite* are of such *delicate* size that they escape all the senses; and yet, even so, every such *corpuscle* consists of *many* parts.

From this consideration, we must learn and weigh carefully that it is necessary to speculate soberly about the conditions of such things and to abstain from crude concepts. Specifically, we must recognize that the nature of the *instruments* used for separation as well as combination must certainly have some proportion to subjects equipped with such *extremely tiny shapes, dimensions, and joints*.

If we join these thoughts to what we said a little earlier regarding the more formal mode of separation and combination—namely, that it occurs by way of *grasping, application, and adhesion*—it can become even clearer: the *instruments* as well as the subjects must display an extraordinary subtlety and *thinness*. Thus, in Theory, no place at all can be left for crude concepts, and in Practice, none for crude materials and operations.

I have dealt with this matter briefly in words, but at length (if one considers the substance of it) in the *Halle Observations, Volume V, regarding the difference between Mixed, Woven, Individual, and Structured Aggregates*.

What flows from this consideration into Chemical Practice are primarily these two conditions: I. (That one should not assume or intend, especially for mixtures,

That no other modes or instruments of mixing operations should be adopted than those which can correspond to very fine particles, to be moved, proportionally, in the most refined way. Under these latter modes, primarily *long digestions* <note>Slow heating of a substance in a flask, often for weeks or months</note> (*if the materials are fluid or completely volatile*), *extremely refined* and *long-lasting fusions* (*if the materials are fixed and meltable*), very delicate *precipitations*, repeated cohobations <term>cohobation: the process of repeatedly distilling a liquid from its solid residue to increase its potency</term>, soakings, *solutions* and *coagulations* (*if the materials are soluble*), and vaporous mixtures (*if the materials can be resolved into vapors*) are useful. And this is solely on the basis that since *mixed substances* are of such great fineness that they escape the senses, the things to be mixed must be so prepared in their own fineness that they can be grasped by the mind rather than by the senses.

### XIV. Like things fit with like; even more so in aggregation.

It is commonly said: *Like rejoices in like* <note>Original Latin: *Simile simili gaudet*</note>. It can be more truly said of inanimate things that they *fit* together: that is, those things which have the same dimension correspond to each other.

It is not my intention to wander too far into general suppositions here—such as how one or another kind of shapes might correspond to each other from all sides, or might not correspond but rather differ. For although a probability can be drawn from such a theory—that the *shapes of simpler natural bodies* seem to relate more to angular planes than to *curved lines and paths*—I do not wish to designate this matter with more than a word.

Meanwhile, for practical application rather than mere explanation, this can serve: that the rational Chemist should remember that he can neither *dissolve* nor set up or construct mixtures more easily and surely than if he employs materials of whose *conspicuous similarity* he is clearly certain.

However, since it is impossible to investigate or recognize these things *a priori* <note>from first principles or before experience</note>, it is necessary to begin here *a posteriori* <note>from observations and results</note>: Namely, either from direct, certain *Experience*, that such things, by nature or art, *tend* to grow together; or from a slightly more reflective consideration of this kind, namely that from *actions* or *passions that are entirely similar*, such things appear to testify to and exhibit the very same lineage.

For example, the craftsman can learn and understand from Experience that *native Cinnabar* <note>The bright red ore of mercury</note> consists of *sulfur* and *quicksilver* <note>mercury</note>; and other things fit so well with sulfur as to seize it even *more readily*, so that they can grow together with it into one body similar in external appearance to Cinnabar. Such a substance is *Antimony*. Therefore, for the purpose of dissolving it according to this method, the composition of Cinnabar adds the *Regulus of Antimony* <term>regulus of antimony: the metallic form of antimony, separated from its stony ore</term> to it, and by this means it resolves the Mercury from its bond with the Sulfur. Meanwhile, it reduces this same sulfur, together with the regulus, back into *Antimony*, etc.

From reason, however, one could gather this: since *sulfur catches fire and flame*, there is *inflammable matter* <note>This "inflammable matter" is the precursor to what Stahl would later call "phlogiston"</note> in sulfur; and since sulfur yields *acid* from itself without any suspected solid change, such an *acid* is certainly present in it. And so...

In this way, one can also quite clearly understand the similarity of oils with resins and with sulfur from this consideration.

However much this *Axiom* <note>The principle that "like fits with like" discussed on the previous page</note> is not yet placed so far beyond all doubt that it may be used and applied absolutely in every case, it certainly offers some hope that, in time, perhaps whatever still remains hidden in mystery can be more deeply understood from it.

For instance, the *Spirit of Nitre* <note>original: "Spiritus Nitri"; nitric acid</note>, in which there is undoubtedly some of the *inflammable* principle, dissolves, or at least attacks, those metals in which the inflammable substance abounds, such as *iron, zinc, tin, antimony <note>original: "regulum"</note>, copper, and lead*. Yet it also dissolves *silver and mercury* <note>original: "argentum vivum"</note>, in which it is not possible to demonstrate any inflammable principle. However, it attacks *earths* not by reason of inflammability, but because of their saline principle.

But why does it not dissolve *charcoal*? Why not common *sulfur*? Why not *resins*? Reasons are not lacking, but this is not the appropriate place for them.

That the *Spirit of Nitre* dissolves these metals by reason of their inflammable principle is clear from the fact that it does not touch these metals at all when they have been stripped of their inflammable part, no matter how simply. This can be seen in *Saffron of Mars* <note>original: "Croco Martis"; a reddish-brown iron oxide</note>, *Ashes of Tin* <note>original: "Cineribus Stanni"; tin oxide</note>, *Calx of Antimony* <note>original: "Antimonii calce"; the residue of antimony after heating</note>, and *Diaphoretic Antimony* <note>original: "Antimonio Diaphoretico"; a medicinal chemical prepared from antimony and saltpeter</note>.

This matter also has an exceptional use in the *Instruments* themselves <note>Here, "instruments" refers to the agents or methods used in chemical reactions</note> to be applied in a new mixture and the preceding dissolution; indeed, it is used repeatedly in these formal "leaves," as it were, which act as instruments or organized systems. For example, *Igneous motion* <note>The movement of heat or fire</note> is most highly suited for snatching away the inflammable matter from some mixture, but it can very rarely be applied except through *actual fire*—that is, a similarly inflammable matter that has been set into igneous motion. I said "very rarely" so as to except *Phosphorus and Fulminating Gold* <note>original: "Aurum fulminans"; an explosive gold compound</note>, which can be ignited even by mere friction.

This fact, when correctly understood, gave *Becher* the occasion to assert that various *super-decompositions* <note>Becher’s term for adding extra components to a substance already considered a mixture</note>, as he calls them, arise from the abundant growth of a single principle, as if added to the side of small bodies of the same kind already stuck in some mixture. For example, he interprets the *mercurification* <term>mercurification: the process of turning a solid metal into a liquid state resembling mercury</term> of metals in this way: that it happens by means of such growth. While such *mercurial particles* are already mixed into metals (insofar as they are metals), it is because of them that the metal—with its bright consistency, its ductile softness, and especially its similarity to *flowing in fire*—seems to correspond to running mercury. If, however, more particles of the same kind unite with these particles that already work together in a proportionate quantity to form the metal, the result is that the metal increases in all these qualities; it becomes very bright, very soft, and fluid even outside of fire—namely, it is rendered into running Mercury.

# FOUNDATIONS OF BECHER'S THEORY

Nor is it truly necessary to appeal to these kinds of deeper, most tenacious combinations, since various such examples occur even in more superficial combinations—provided they are truly *such* (and not mere jumbles). Examples of this kind include amalgamation <note>The process of combining mercury with another metal</note>; the joining of sulfur with a large quantity of alkali salt <note>original: "sale alkali"</note> so that it flows in fire—even if it does not bond so immediately with the alkali salt as it does with the remaining, smaller quantity of *sulfur* that is already connected to the alkali. This same principle also applies to the water that mixes itself into crystals of vitriol <note>Iron or copper sulfates</note>, alum, and borax, in a quantity immensely greater than would be required by the method of *mixture* <note>original: "mixtionis"; here referring to a specific chemical proportion</note> with the acidic vitriolic salt to constitute spirit of vitriol <note>original: "spiritum vitrioli"; sulfuric acid</note>, and so on.

### XV. The four commonly named elements are not the components of mixtures, but only their storehouses; yet they may well be called the instruments of mixtures—and indeed, of dissolutions.

In the four so-called *elements* <note>Earth, Air, Fire, and Water</note>, one must consider both their specific *matter* and—as people say today—the *mode* or *form* of this matter. This "form" is, most evidently, a certain *motion* of such matter.

Thus, for example, the *ice* immediately demonstrates that the *matter* of water does not bring about "fluidity" from its absolute essence. Unless a certain degree of *heat* concurs, ice will never be, nor become, water. But if that heat *stirs* <note>original: "commoveat"</note> the ice, only then is it, and is it called, water. Similarly, *fire* is not some absolute thing, but is a collection of tiny particles <note>original: "corpusculorum"</note> affected by a most violent *vortex-like motion* <note>original: "verticillari motu"</note>. Therefore, as long as those particles are not agitated by this *motion*, they are not Fire, nor can Fire exist without them. But just as motion leads ice into water, so *motion* reduces fatty particles (or those which are the foundation of fatness <note>A reference to the "inflammable principle" or early ideas of phlogiston</note>) into Fire.

Nor should these *elemental matters* and—as the Schools <note>The traditional university philosophers</note> call them—*forms* be distinguished from one another without a significant and evident cause. For although the more scrupulous Scholastics may consider that *form* to be *immanent* <note>Inherent and inseparable</note> and inseparable—remaining, for instance, so implanted and ingrained in individual *watery* particles that through this form these particles are, always and everywhere, fit and ready for the motion of fluidity, moisture, and vaporous expansion—these speculators nonetheless lose all concept, let alone knowledge, of the formal conditions and properties of these particles when considered in this way: separately, individually, and outside the state of aggregation. Thus, they lose all consideration of them *a priori* <note>From the cause/theoretical beginning</note>—namely, how and to what extent they deserve to be called *elements*, what kind of specific disposition they exhibit (in the individual particle, not the cluster), or how they behave and conduct themselves regarding a mixture or composition, or within the state of mixture itself.

Meanwhile, that state which these so-called elements display in their state of *aggregation* <note>Physical collection or mass</note> is so far from being something that can or should be neglected, that rather this very state—the state, I say, of their *aggregation*—deserves exceptional consideration in two respects. The *first* respect is that in that bare state of aggregation (outside of a manifest *mixture*), these so-called

But why does it not dissolve *charcoal*? Why not *common sulfur*? Why not *resins*? There is no lack of reasons, but this is not the appropriate place for them.

That *Spirit of Nitre* dissolves these metals by reason of their *inflammable* principle becomes clear from the fact that it does not affect these metals at all when they are simply stripped of their *inflammable* part: as may be seen in *Saffron of Mars* <note>original: "Croco Martis"; iron oxide</note>, *Ashes of Tin* <note>original: "Cineribus Stanni"; tin oxide</note>, *Lime of Antimony* <note>original: "Antimonii calce"</note>, and *Diaphoretic Antimony* <note>original: "Antimonio Diaphoretico"; a medicinal salt of antimony</note>.

Indeed, this matter also has an excellent use in the *Instruments* themselves to be employed for new mixtures and preceding dissolutions—indeed, sometimes even in such formal instruments or *organisms* alone. For thus, for example, *igneous motion* <note>The movement of heat or fire</note> is most highly suited to snatching away the *inflammable* matter from some mixture, but it can rarely be applied except through *actual Fire, that is, matter* that is likewise inflammable and has been brought into igneous motion. I said "rarely" so as to exclude *Phosphorus and Fulminating Gold* <note>original: "Aurum fulminans"; an explosive gold compound</note>, which can be ignited even by mere friction.

This matter, when rightly understood, provided the occasion for *Becher* to assert that various *super-decompositions* (as he calls them) arise from the abundant accretion of a single principle, as if to the side of corpuscles *of the same kind* already clinging within some mixture. For example, he interprets the "mercurification" of metals in this way: that it happens by means of such an accretion. For while in metals, insofar as they are metals, such *mercurial corpuscles* are already mixed in—by virtue of which the metal seems to correspond to running mercury in its *shining* consistency, its *ductile softness*, and especially its similarity to *liquidity in fire* <note>original: "fluoris in igne"</note>—if more particles *of the same kind* should join with these particles that meet in a proportionate quantity to constitute the metal, it follows that the metal increases in all these qualities, becoming highly shining, very soft, and fluid even outside of fire: namely, it is rendered into Running Mercury.

### XV.
The four elements, as they are commonly called, are not the materials of mixtures, but only their **storehouses** <note>original: "penuaria"; literally a pantry or larder</note>; however, they may rightly be called the instruments of mixtures, and indeed, of dissolutions.

In the so-called **four elements**, one must consider both their specific matter and—as people say today—the "mode" or **form** of this matter, which is most evidently **a certain motion of such matter**.

For example, **ice** demonstrates immediately that the *matter* of water does not imply **fluidity** by its absolute essence. For unless a certain degree of **heat** <note>original: "caloris"</note> concurs, ice will never be, or become, water. But if that heat **agitates** <note>original: "commoveat"</note> the ice, only then is it, and is it called, water. Similarly, **fire** <note>original: "ignis"</note> is not some absolute thing, but is a mass of little bodies affected by a most violent, whirling **motion**. Hence, as long as those little bodies are not agitated by this **motion**, they are not Fire, nor can Fire exist without them. But just as **motion** leads ice into the state of water, so **motion** reduces fatty little bodies (or those which are the foundation of fatness <note>original: "pinguedinis fundamentum"; a reference to Becher's *terra pinguis*, the principle of inflammability later known as phlogiston</note>) into Fire.

There is no compelling or evident reason to distinguish these elementary **matters** and—as the Schools <note>The "Schools" refers to the traditional Scholastic philosophers who followed Aristotle</note> call them—**forms** from one another. For although the more scrupulous Scholastics might consider that **form** as something internal and inseparable (staying so ingrained in each **watery** particle that, through this form, these particles are always and everywhere ready and fit **for the motion of fluidity, moisture, and vaporous expansion**), such theorists lose all conceptual grasp, let alone knowledge, of the formal conditions and properties of these little bodies when they are considered separately, individually, and outside of a state of **aggregation**. Thus, they lose all consideration of them *from the beginning* <note>original: "a priori"</note>: how and to what extent they deserve to be called **elements**, what kind of specific disposition they exhibit (in the individual particle rather than the mass), or how they behave during the state of mixture or composition.

Meanwhile, the state that these so-called elements display in their state of **aggregation** <note>The physical clustering of particles, as in a liquid or solid mass</note> is so far from being something that can or should be neglected, that this very state of their **aggregation** deserves extraordinary consideration in two respects. The **first** respect is that, in that bare state of aggregation (aside from any manifest mixture), these so-called...

the said elementary bodies can be better considered as **pure and simple**; thus, their properties in that state are recognized as simpler and more unadulterated. The second consideration is that, especially in this state of simple aggregation—without manifest mixing—they uniquely concur by **their own motion** not only toward combination or mixture, but also toward dissolution.

I say that by this **motion** of theirs, they are the **instruments** of mixture and dissolution; or, that this **motion** of theirs is the **instrument** of mixture and dissolution—while their remaining substance exists rather as the **matter** of the mixture.

It is especially in this respect that we speak here of these immense **motions** of the **elements**, so to speak: of the **airy** spacious aggregate and expanse; of the **watery** mass, from a single drop, even from mere moisture, up to the Ocean; of a **spark** or a lamp flame, up to fire-vomiting mountains <note>original: "montes ignivomos"; a reference to volcanoes</note>; of a **dusty particle of earth**, up to the entire **Geocosm** <note><term>Geocosm</term> (original: "Geocosmum"); Becher’s term for the Earth viewed as a single, complex, and integrated physical system or machine</note>.

For by their own **motion**, **fire, water, and air** serve these ends; indeed, through the transfer of motion, **earth** itself serves for commotions, removals, bringings-together, and conjunctions.

Whence, certainly, unless we attend most exquisitely to the nature of these things, we will be able to understand none of those things which can and must be achieved by this energy alone—I mean by their **motion**.

And this consideration is truly of such great moment for establishing a provident and solid estimation of things of this nature and power—for combining or dissolving, that is, for **moving**—that if these are neglected, nothing remains but to invent those wretched internal and "con-created" **strivings** <note>original: "nisus"; Becher is criticizing the old Scholastic idea that matter has internal "desires" or "strivings" to move, arguing instead for mechanical motion</note> for each and every particle of the things to be mixed, in order to outline some sort of shadow of spontaneous combinations (that is, of mutual movings-toward).

Indeed, since these things—Fire, Air, Water, Earth—must be the **primary instruments of the chemist**, upon which he must build his entire art, it would be contrary to reason to neglect or be ignorant of them. Therefore, I all the more earnestly commend this consideration: how, through these elements commonly and strictly so called—Fire, Air, Water, Earth—not only must the **Chemical Artist** labor at and carry out mixtures and dissolutions by art, but **Nature herself** uses these things in that way we have indicated, or rather by **motion**: by **fiery motion**, **watery motion**, **airy motion**, and **earthy motion** (which people commonly call **rest**).

All the more so because our **Thesis** emphasizes that in the business of **Dissolutions**, account must be taken of these elementary **motions**; since there, they sometimes seem to act more absolutely **formally** <note>In the language of the time, "formally" refers to the "form" or essential character and active power of a substance, as opposed to its raw "matter"</note>, and thus **longer and more vigorously**. Whereas on the contrary, in the business of **mixture**, not only does the whole **matter** of these elements coalesce into the mixtures, but even this very **specific motion of theirs** of which we speak soon ceases, or is mingled into the **common** motion of that whole concrete body, to which the matter—which that **specific motion** previously possessed—has been added and joined.

Thus, those elementary bodies commonly so-called concur toward **mixture or dissolution**, formally indeed, by those motions which, as if they were still purer, in large [aggregates...]

in their aggregations. However, they concur **materially** by their own substance, or rather through a reciprocal rest with those things to which they are mutually applied. Thus, they always provide the **first act** through a certain aggregative abundance and mass; however, **individual particles**, or at least **as individuals**, undergo the **effect** of growth and cohesion.

I say, as individuals. For although I warned above that even corpuscles of the **same species**—not just single ones, but several—can concur to constitute a single **mixed** corpuscle <note>Becher distinguishes between a "mixed" body (chemically combined) and a "composite" or "aggregate" body (mechanically joined).</note> in number, nonetheless, an immediate union or **immediate contact** with the others of a different species does not occur except on one side of **one** particle, or certainly on **only one side** of each individual among several. Therefore, cohesion is **either of all as one, or of each individual as one**.

XVI. The material principles of mixture are primarily Earth, Water, and Fire, in their substance and by individually numbered corpuscles. Air, as far as we certainly know, does not enter into mixtures, but rather only into aggregations <note>Becher believed air was too "volatile" or "spacious" to chemically bond with solid matter, serving only as a medium or a loose collection.</note>.

How many disturbances and conflicts have arisen for some decades now between the followers of Aristotle <note>Aristotelians believed in the four elements (Earth, Water, Air, Fire) and their associated qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry).</note> and Epicurus <note>Followers of Epicurus, or Atomists, believed the world was composed of indivisible atoms and void.</note> concerning the tradition of the four elements! This is so well known that it would rather disgust any sensible person to see those empty—if compared to the truth of things—**word-battles** <note>original: "λογομαχίαν"; a dispute over words rather than reality</note>.

For who today can be unaware that those **qualities** attributed to the **elements as their own** do not immediately imply or make necessary a **single, most specific species**? That is, they are not absolutely, in the most specific sense, **one** homogenous, pure, elementary **water**; rather, there could be many and **diverse** species of "wateriness." There is not absolutely **one** single most specific **species of Fire**, but there could also be diverse **species of Fire**. There is not **one** absolute species of **Earth**, nor indeed must one necessarily be supposed for air itself. Meanwhile, under those highest genera of **Water, Fire, Air, and Earth**, diverse species could also be recognized which possess those generic qualities they call "elementary," but which differ from one another as species by some most specific difference.

Just as it is hardly unknown to anyone from mathematical-arithmetic foundations that a huge number of transpositions can be formed from a few **principles in number**, so too if we look to the beginnings of natural species and diligently distinguish **mixtures** (made from principles) from **compositions** (made from things already mixed). Moreover, let us separate both of these even more from **Aggregates**. We will undoubtedly find such a number of **species** that even a fairly small **number of principles** can **correspond** to and satisfy it.

So much so, that from this **reasoning from causes** <note>original: "a priori"</note> alone it can become clear that there is no need for some immense number of corpuscles, each of which possesses a special new shape, constant and immutable, from which—as from so many species of principles—innumerable species of mixtures would be generated. For since by this reasoning the **species** of mixtures as well as compositions would have to increase to infinity, experience itself immediately refutes this opinion, rendering utterly useless 
that 
<meta>catchword: that (original: "illam")</meta>

...that conclusion, since it provides us with so small a number of diverse mixtures.

Clearly, that warning has a place here as well, which constitutes the most profound foundation of **Physical Theory**: that it is not fitting to speculate on what *could be done*, but rather on ***what is actually done***. If we follow this guiding star <note>original: "cynosuram," referring to the North Star used for navigation.</note>, we certainly discover by the reality of the matter that so small a number of **true mixtures** is offered to us in the vast estate of Nature, that not only can a quite small number of **principles** satisfy them, but even such principles as we are able to call by some other more familiar, specific name. This is better than wandering immediately into those general, fixed shapes that can never be grasped by the mind—those most absolute of hidden qualities.

For instance, if it is said of the mixture of **Salt** in general that it consists of one (or more than one) **earthy** particle, and one (or more than one) **watery** particle, I obtain through this a real concept. I know what is meant by "**water**" and what is meant by "**earth**." At the same time, I become certain that if I wish to extract salt from somewhere, earth and water must certainly be present there. Furthermore, such a mixture finally can and must fall apart and be resolved back into water and earth.

On the contrary, if I say salt consists of **sharp, angular** particles, longer than they are wide, and so on—if someone then orders me to seek Salt from somewhere, I certainly could not find it based on these qualities. Nor could I be taught by anyone, based on such evidence, where a "**sharp, angular, oblong thing**" might be encountered or found; whereas, by contrast, there is hardly a person who could not instruct me on where Salt is found.

Thus, it would indeed serve **Mathematical Theory** if we were able to measure **what kinds of shapes, angles, and points Salts have**, so that the proportion of their application, entanglement, and cohesion along lines could be understood. But we do not yet possess the knowledge of where, *after the fact* <note>original: "a posteriore"</note>, such specifically conditioned little bodies can be sought or expected.

Indeed, even those who are not entirely foolish in this matter candidly despair that it will ever happen that the true shapes of these particles may be clearly seen or investigated. Thus, that most general reasoning—that individual corpuscles are endowed with a **certain** shape—has become almost everywhere worthless. It provides an occasion for grammatical confusion, fallacies, or certainly a suspicion of frivolous and willful deception. For the cited formula, according to **grammar**, only wishes to say this: "Each individual corpuscle is certainly endowed with *some* shape." It does not mean a **certain** shape (understood, by the force of grammar and the legitimate use of the word, as a shape **certain to us**). 

Therefore, this most general physical-mathematical **aetiology** <note>The study of causes or origins.</note> is certainly far more sterile here than that physical-grammatical expression: "These corpuscles are of an **earthy, watery, fiery, or airy nature; or glassy, salty, sulfurous, or elastic; fixed, volatile, dense, fluid, inflammable, etc.**" For all these things are certain and known, and are also closer to the natural order, while those uncertain shapes—hidden in their appearance and purely absolute—remain remote and nothing more than **most general** abstractions.

# FOUNDATIONS OF BECHER'S THEORY

Truly, if we consider the business of *mixture* <note>The term "mixtio" refers to the chemical combination of elements into a compound, rather than a simple physical mixing.</note> and the nature of *Principles* with such insight—even if it is not absolutely and purely demonstrative—the ancient opinion concerning those commonly called the four *Elements* is far more solid than those wandering concepts about the innumerable species of simple shapes exhibited by so many numerous types of tiny bodies, which are supposedly primary, simplest, indivisible, and immutable.

For this is most certain: it is far easier and more immediate to demonstrate from mixtures those tiny bodies that constitute the mixture—which are of a *fiery, watery, or earthy* disposition—than it is to derive anything from them to which a specific, determined shape can be truly and demonstrably assigned.

Thus, we judge our Author <note>The "Author" refers to Johann Joachim Becher (1635–1682), whose theories this text explains.</note> to be supported by a much better foundation, because he establishes *Earth* (specifically of *three different types*) <note>Becher proposed three types of earth: "vitrifiable" (stony), "inflammable" (oily), and "mercurial" (fluid).</note> as the principle of subterranean things; while for things above the earth, he assigns *Water*, and in his own sense, *Air* and *Fire* as well. Although these last two deserve to be regarded not so much as *material* components but rather as *instrumental* ones.

Regarding *Fire*, it must be noted here that it should not be conceived as some kind of absolute matter which, from its own simple, pure, and naked nature, constitutes what we call *fire* or *flame*. Not at all. Rather, for *burning, glowing, flaming fire* to be formed, it is necessary that this matter first combine with others; only in their company does it become subject to that motion which we call *fiery, flaming, hot, or burning*. However, there is a direct cause: even in this association with others, the substance that primarily and directly makes that whole structure capable of fiery motion is uniquely this principle. Therefore, because of this direct effect, we are compelled to call it "elementary fire," or rather the *Element* or *principle of fire*, working *from the effect back to the cause* <note>original: "a posteriori"; reasoning from observed consequences back to their origins.</note>—from its remarkable and chief effect—since *from the cause to the effect* <note>original: "a priori"; reasoning from theoretical principles before observation.</note> we find no other occasion or method for conceiving, reasoning, or naming it.

Now, what we said—that fire plays the part of an *instrument* rather than *matter* in mixtures above the earth—must be understood as fire already brought into *action*. That is, the principle of making-fire is united with other particles in such a way that, within this structure, it can undergo the motion we call *fiery*. However, we cannot conceive of such a thing separately if it were left to itself, naked and pure; or at least, we have no foundation for such a thing.

Briefly, for the *act* of mixing, fire that is *flaming, burning, and hot* joins in and is most effective as an *instrument*. But for the *substance* of the mixture itself, as an ingredient (in common parlance) and as a *material principle and a constitutive part of the whole compound*, what joins in is the *matter and principle of fire*, not fire itself. I have begun to call this ***Phlogiston*** <note>This is a landmark moment in chemical history where Georg Ernst Stahl names the "inflammable principle" derived from Becher's work.</note>. Specifically: *the first ignitable, inflammable Principle, uniquely and eminently capable of receiving and fostering Heat*—provided it joins with other principles in some mixture. Truly, we must speak of this substance (as well as others) *from the effect back to the cause* <note>original: "a posteriori"</note>, since *from the cause to the effect* <note>original: "a priori"</note> we can achieve absolutely no concept, n—

Namely, there is a place here for that warning which constitutes the deepest foundation of **Physical Theory**: that it is not appropriate to speculate on what *could* happen, but rather what *actually happens in fact*. If we follow this guiding star, we surely discover in the reality of things that so small a number of **true mixtures** <term>mixtorum: chemical compounds where the ingredients are intimately combined, not just a physical heap</term> is offered to us in the broad fields of Nature, that not only can a quite small number of principles satisfy them, but even such principles as we can call by some other more familiar, specific name. This is far better than wandering off immediately into those general **FIXED figures** that can never be grasped by the mind—that is, into those most absolute "hidden qualities."

For instance, if it is said of Salt, as a general mixture, that it consists of one (or more) **earthy** particles and one (or more) **watery** particles, I certainly gain a real concept from this, since I know what is meant by "water" and what is meant by "earth." And at the same time, I become certain that if I wish to extract salt from somewhere, water and earth must surely be present there; and that such a mixture finally can and must fall apart and be resolved back into water and earth.

On the other hand, if I say that salt consists of *sharp, angular* particles, longer than they are wide, and so on: if someone then orders me to seek Salt somewhere, I certainly could not find it under those qualities. Nor could I be taught by anyone, based on these indicators, where a *sharp, angular, oblong* thing might be met with or found. In contrast, there is hardly a man who could not instruct me as to where Salt may be found.

Hence, it would indeed benefit Mathematical Theory if we were able to measure what sort of *figures, angles, and points* salts have, so that from there we might understand the proportion of their application, entanglement, and cohesion along certain lines. However, we would still lack the knowledge of where, *from experience* <note>original: "a posteriore"</note>, such conditioned little bodies could be sought or expected.

But since even those who are not completely foolish in this matter candidly despair that it will ever happen that we might see or investigate the true shapes of these particles, that most general reasoning—that individual tiny bodies are endowed with a **certain shape**—has become cheapened almost everywhere. This grammatical confusion provides an opening for fallacies, or at least for the suspicion of a frivolous and willful deception. For the cited formula, according to the rules of **grammar**, only wants to say: "Individual tiny bodies are certainly endowed with *some* shape." It does not mean a **certain** shape (understood, by grammatical force and the legitimate use of the word, as a shape *certain to us*). <note>The author is playing on the Latin word "certus," which can mean both "fixed/definite" and "some/a particular." He argues that saying an atom has a "certain shape" is a linguistic trick that sounds scientific but explains nothing.</note> 

For this reason, this most general physical-mathematical etiology <note>The study of causes.</note> is certainly far more sterile than that "physical-grammatical" expression: "These tiny bodies are of an **earthy, watery, fiery, or airy nature; glassy, saline, sulfurous, or elastic; fixed, volatile, dense, fluid, or flammable,** etc." For all these things are certain and known, and are closer to us in the order of things, whereas those uncertain shapes remain absolutely hidden in appearance, remote, and nothing more than generalities.

->### THEORETICAL FOUNDATIONS OF BECHER<-

Truly, if we consider the business of **mixture** <term>mixtio: in this context, the chemical union of elements into a compound</term> and the nature of the **Principles** with such a perspective, the ancient opinion regarding those commonly named four **Elements** is far more solid than those wandering concepts about the innumerable types of simple shapes supposedly displayed by so many countless types of corpuscles <note>original: "corpusculorum" — refers to the "corpuscular philosophy" of the 17th century which sought to explain chemistry through the geometric shapes of atoms</note>, which are likewise claimed to be primary, most simple, indivisible, and immutable.

For this is by far most certain: that such corpuscles which constitute a mixture—being of a *fiery, watery,* or *earthy* disposition—can be demonstrated from those mixtures far more easily, and much more directly and closely, than anything can be derived from those theories to which any specific shape can be assigned truly and with certain proof.

For this reason, we judge our Author <note>Referring to Johann Joachim Becher</note> to be supported by a much better foundation because he establishes **Earth** as the principle of **Subterranean** things, but specifically of three different types; while to **Superterranean** things he further attributes **Water**, and in his own sense also **Air** and **Fire**. Although these latter two deserve to be considered not so much as **material** parts, but rather as **instrumental** ones.

Regarding **Fire**, it must be noted in this place that it should not be conceived as some most absolute matter which, from its own simple, pure, and naked nature, constitutes that which we call **fire** or **flame**. By no means. Rather, for the purpose of establishing a **burning, glowing, or flaming fire**, it is necessary that this matter finally combine with others, in whose company it at last becomes subject to that motion which we call **fiery, flaming, hot, or fervent**. However, this occurs under such a direct cause that, even in this association with others, that substance which **primarily** and **directly** renders that whole structure fit for fiery motion is uniquely this principle. Therefore, from this direct effect of its own, we are compelled to call it elementary fire, or rather the **Element or principle of fire**, *after the fact* <note>original: "a posteriori" — reasoning from observed effects to their causes</note> based on its remarkable and chief effect; whereas *beforehand* <note>original: "a priori" — reasoning from theoretical principles to effects</note> we find no other occasion or method for either conceiving of it or naming it with reason.

Moreover, what we have said—that fire has the role of an **instrument** rather than **matter** in superterranean mixture—is to be understood as fire already brought into **action**. That is, it refers to the principle of igniting when it is so united with other particles that, within this structure, it can undergo that motion which we name **fiery**. Yet, we are unable to conceive of such a thing separately if it were left to itself, naked and pure, or certainly we have no foundation for such a thing.

Briefly: for the **act** of mixing, flaming, fervent, hot fire concurs and is most powerful as an **instrument**. For the **substance** of the mixture itself, as an ingredient (in the common phrase) or as a **material** principle and a constitutive part of the whole compound, there concurs the **matter and principle of fire**, not fire itself. I have begun to call this **Phlogiston** <note>This is a pivotal moment in the history of chemistry where Georg Ernst Stahl (the likely author) names the principle of inflammability "Phlogiston," which would dominate chemical theory for a century.</note>; namely, the first **ignitable**, inflammable Principle, directly and eminently capable of receiving and fostering Heat, provided that it concurs in some mixture with other principles. For indeed, we must speak of this substance as well as others *after the fact* <note>original: "a Posteriori"</note> because *beforehand* <note>original: "a priori"</note> we can achieve absolutely no concept, ne—

->### SPECIMEN BECHERIANUM PART I. SECTION I.<-

...nor regarding the rest of their constitution, nor any of their arrangements, or their tendency toward actions or passions.

The matter is different with *air*, concerning which it is not so precisely certain whether it actually enters into *mixtures or compositions* <term>mixtio: in this period, a "mixture" refers to a true chemical compound where ingredients lose their individual identity, as opposed to a simple physical aggregation</term>. It is most evident, however, that it joins in various aggregations. Yet, two distinct aspects of this matter deserve to be considered. For we must distinguish any *active* participation—whether preceding, accompanying, or cooperating—from a participation that is essentially *purely passive*, following as a result, and depending on the preceding internal constitution of the remaining structure in such a way that it is merely *permitted* by that structure, rather than being *equally assumed or required*.

Thus, for example, **to form a flame**, *air* is absolutely necessary, or at minimum, a vapor and watery *blast* <note>original: "flatu"; a stream of air or gas</note> expanded elastically like air. However, no experiment that I can recall has proved that air is required by any necessity for a glowing ignition or a simple heating. **For crystallizations**, there is a need for water or certainly some humid fluid that surrounds and intervenes; so much so, that it is certain that by its very fluid *motion*, acting as a mechanical tool, it absolutely cooperates in some way toward the *crystallization*. Yet, for a **simple coagulation**, air has no *active* efficacy, etc.

On the other hand, in looser (aggregative) concretions, where those tiny parts constituting the aggregate do not touch one another along precise lines on every side, but leave some *gaping* little spaces, it is certainly *consequent* that the air idly occupies this space left abandoned. However, one cannot argue from this that the air contributed anything beforehand to joining the aggregate, nor does it exist as necessary or even useful for holding or sustaining that same thing after the fact.

Although I said a little earlier that experiments are not equally available to rely upon to confirm that air enters into *mixtures as a constituent part*, I have not forgotten those experiments performed in an evacuated Receiver <note>The "evacuated receiver" refers to the glass chamber of an air pump, used by scientists like Robert Boyle to study vacuums</note> with metallic solutions, which might seem relevant here. Namely, if a small tube—visible with suspended mercury (following the Baroscopic Method <note>Using a barometer to measure pressure</note>)—is placed in the Receiver, and at the same time a glass vessel is placed in the same receiver with a quantity of *nitric acid* <note>original: "aqua forti"; literally 'strong water,' a common name for nitric acid</note> into which a piece of *copper* has been put: the *air* is then drawn out by the pump until the level where the mercury in the tube settles is noted. It then happens that the bubbling produced by the nitric acid with the copper during its dissolution gradually supplies enough aerial expansion again that the mercury in the tube rises higher and higher once more, and even maintains this durable progress and position. But truly, this experiment cannot prove that this *aerial* expanded vapor was "stuck" in the *mixture* of the copper; rather, at most, it was in its aggregation, or it is owed to the participation of the solvent itself. This is clear enough from the fact that in such a solution, the copper is certainly present, constantly endowed and equipped with its own entire and inviolate mixture, and it can easily be separated from it again in various ways, pure and unsullied.

Certainly, if an argument for air being entangled in a *mixture* appears anywhere, it seems to show itself in **Nitre** <note>Potassium nitrate, or saltpeter</note>; seeing as this, with sulfurous materials, undergoes such a violent expan-

However, since no experiments are yet available to show how far and how long such an expansion spreads—and thus presents and establishes the true *nature of air*—there is indeed a significant argument to the contrary. Specifically, *Nitre* <note>original: "Nitrum"; saltpeter, often studied for its explosive release of "air" or gas</note> mixed with such sulfurous substances <note>In this context, "sulfurous" refers to the principle of inflammability (fatty earth), not just the chemical element sulfur</note> refuses to show this vigorous expansion in an evacuated receiver <note>original: "Recipiente evacuato"; a vacuum chamber, likely a reference to Robert Boyle's pneumatic experiments</note>. Rightly, therefore, we have declared in our Thesis that the *material Elements—earth and water*—and even fire (in this sense) are the material Elements or Principles of *mixtures* <term>mixtorum: chemical compounds where the ingredients are transformed into a new substance</term>. *Air*, however, fulfills the role of an *instrument or an extraneous participant*.

XVII. The Three Kingdoms <note>The traditional division of nature into Mineral, Vegetable, and Animal</note> do not differ except by a different mixture of wateriness and, consequently, saltiness, and especially by their texture and aggregate structure. This structure regards gravity least of all, but rather a destined distribution and arrangement.

This reason for the diversity between the *principles of mineral mixtures and those of vegetables and animals* kept our Author <note>Johann Joachim Beccher</note> greatly perplexed. Indeed, he frequently looked toward earths of many kinds, which differ from one another by very specific *innate* differences. At last, most probably, he referred the whole matter to a different *degree* of rarity and density.

But that the matter is entirely so—that is, I say, that *Vegetables* as well as *Animals* consist of no other principles than those of *mineral* lineage and subterranean nature, and that no new species of matter or very specific purpose underlies these different Kingdoms—seems to me to shine through most clearly from this: *Vegetables* certainly obtain their entire solid *nutriment* from nowhere else but *the earth*; *Animals* are either nourished immediately by *Vegetables* grown from the *Earth*, or at least mediately, since even *Carnivorous Animals* take more delight in *grain-eaters* and *grass-eaters* than in other *carnivores*. This reality seems to show us with exquisite certainty that the same nutritive and constitutive *Earths* of the *Subterranean realm* are employed for the nutrition and mixing of both *Vegetables* and *Animals*, and not some other absolutely different substances.

However, that which constitutes the true and real foundation of the whole difference is the more intimate and formal mixing of *Wateriness*, and the concurrence of *fieriness*, which is now more disposed toward action.

I say *fieriness disposed toward action*. For I noted in the preceding Thesis that the *igneous Principle* does not easily undergo that motion which we call fire, except in some composition or continuity with others. Now, reason itself suggests that those corpuscles with which this *Phlogiston* <note>original: "Phlogiston"; from the Greek for "inflammable." This is a landmark introduction of the term that would dominate chemistry for a century, referring to the substance of fire contained within combustible bodies</note> (as it may be called from now on) is joined—the principle that properly permits fiery motion—those corpuscles, I say, ought not to be of a more *immobile* nature or prone to denser aggregations.

<meta>This page continues the discussion from the previous section regarding the composition of the three kingdoms of nature. It moves from the general principles of minerals to the specific "watery-ignescent" (watery-fire) composition of the Vegetable and Animal kingdoms, explaining why they are more prone to heat and oiliness than the Mineral kingdom.</meta>

### SPECIMENS OF BECHER, PART I, SECTION I.

For since that which we humans recognize as fire, flame, and heat always, and by a certain necessity of its essence, presupposes *aggregation* <note>the gathering together of particles into a mass</note>; and especially since flame exists as an absolute aggregate—the thinnest and most noble kind—reason itself suggests that whatever is suited to produce or induce a dense and *thick* aggregation would be most unfit for forming a flame.

Therefore, the more the *inflammable disposition* in that principle <note>original: "principio"; referring to the principle of inflammability or Phlogiston</note> must be brought into *action*, the more it must be united and blended with those things which, when they coalesce with it (when a great number of such particles come together into an aggregate), can nonetheless give rise to an *aggregate mass* that is very thin, open, and obedient to the freest local motion, and which can persist as such.

Nor is our discussion here about mere possibility, but about the ease and readiness with which a substance undergoes igneous motion <note>the movement associated with fire</note>. For indeed, all things—even those less mobile than this first and direct igniting *Principle*—can be driven into igneous motion, not so much by the "concourse" <note>harmonious meeting</note> but by the *incursion* <note>violent assault</note> of this Principle. However, there is no substance that responds to this principle more promptly, easily, and with almost a natural aptitude for undertaking *igneous motion* than this. Hence, our present aim is uniquely directed toward the conclusion that the joining and meeting of other remarkably mobile corpuscles <term>corpusculorum: "little bodies" or particles of matter</term> with the *Phlogiston* principle is required, so that an igneous, flaming, and eminently hot motion may be induced with less labor and more readily embraced.

Accordingly, these sorts of *Corpuscles* are watery, with very fine *earthy* parts intervening throughout. And these *watery-ignescent Corpuscles*, established in such a state—existing, I say, in such a concrete union or society—contribute primarily to the *Composition* (rather than a simple mixture) of the *vegetable* as well as the *animal* kingdoms.

And for this reason, there occurs not only a rich abundance of *Oils, Fats, and Resins* throughout the vast territory of these two kingdoms; but it is also evident (which is well worth noting) that there is a greater instrumental cooperation of *heat*. This heat affects that matter—which is already fit or becoming fit for igneous motion—more and more, and not only agitates it within itself, but *distributes* it as something mobile, or renders it fit for distribution.

Hence, it is no wonder that both during the *production* and the elaboration or upbringing of *Vegetables* and *Animals*, the *motion of heat* is applied from the beginning and always follows afterward. Indeed, this heat is proper to the more specific Matter of these entire Kingdoms: I mean the *Watery-Phlogiston* matter, coupled with another very fine earth.

Nor is this *watery-ignescent* matter, clinging together by mutual union, more proper to *Vegetables* and *Animals* than to *Subterranean* or *Mineral* things solely for that reason; but there also lies beneath it yet another combination of this kind, growing more intimately with *water*—namely, a fine earthy substance from which *saltiness* <note>original: "salsedo"</note> is born.

# FUNDAMENTALS OF BECHER’S THEORY

### THE FUNDAMENTALS OF BECHER’S THEORY
<note>This refers to Johann Joachim Becher (1635–1682), a German physician and chemist best known for his "earth" theory that led to the development of the Phlogiston theory.</note>

Through these two types of water-mixing—acting as a sort of primary product or "mixture" <note>original: *mixto*; in 17th-century chemistry, a *mixt* was a substance where components were chemically combined, not just physically mixed</note> and as a principle for further composition—plants and animals differ primarily from **subterranean** things. It is observed that this specific character of mixture is not equally present, or at the very least, is familiar only in a very few species of minerals. Nevertheless, various arguments—both from theory and observation—make it highly probable that the method of subterranean mixing proceeds in a similar way.

However, the thing by which Plants and Animals differ from **subterranean things** "by a whole heaven" <note>original: *toto coelo*; a Latin idiom meaning "entirely" or "diametrically opposed"</note> is the absolute necessity of **aggregation**, and indeed a most precisely **ordered** aggregation, namely, a **structure**. For since the entire **animal** Body is absolutely organic—(*we understand nothing of Plants and their ultimate purpose* <note>The author admits a lack of biological understanding regarding the "teleology" or final goals of plants compared to the obvious functions of animal organs</note>)—it required a coarser structure and thus a more abundant aggregation of matter. In Subterranean things, however, the entire species considered in a single individual is a unique thing in its very number; it is of such subtlety that it truly has no "integral parts" <note>parts that can be physically separated while remaining the same substance</note>, meaning parts that are physically divisible. Instead, it has only "Constituents." When these are pulled apart from one another, the substance is not resolved into **parts** like a **whole** (where integral parts are distinguished from the components of the whole), but solely into **simple elements**, as a **mixture** is resolved into its basics.

In the meantime, it must be especially noted that our Author <note>Becher</note> does not observe this distinction very scrupulously. In this, he shares a common trait with all theorists up to this day: they prefer to derive the logic of structure in Plants and Animals from the necessity of the matter itself (which our author seeks in **specific gravity**) rather than from a certain direction <note>a guiding force or "Vitalism"</note> that might arrange matter toward a specific **use and end**, matter which is otherwise bound by no strict necessity. For I believe no man would seriously assert that the necessity of matter is so great that it would absolutely require a distinction between **right and left** in any given subject being formed.

Therefore, although these kinds of combinations <note>original: *σύγκλίσεις* (synclises); a Greek term for "leanings together" or "conjunctions" of atoms/parts</note> also occur in our Author's work, he seems to argue from the chemical mixture to the physical structure, or rather to confuse the two. Yet, it would be most unfair to blame him specifically for this. In this matter, he was carried away by the common opinion of Physicists, just as the stars are carried by the first motion of the heavens. He can be forgiven all the more easily because in the rest of his argument regarding the **nature of Subterranean things**, he walks a far different path; his most useful diligence easily earns him a pardon for these stumbles into foreign topics. This is especially true since those who are unfit even to understand—let alone build—solid science are the ones who arrogantly and indignantly criticize him for this.

Therefore, what we have noted so far to illustrate our Author’s mind on this business must be understood primarily regarding plant and animal mixtures. In this, he most correctly establishes that even in the plant and animal kingdoms, the mixtures of these realms are completed by principles that are the same, at least in a general sense, as the principles of **Subterranean things**. He also points out that there is a far more familiar (indeed, almost perpetual) gathering of **Water**, as a **material principle**, toward the vegetable and...

In this, however, it appears he <note>Referring to Becher</note> deviates: he believes that these earths of the Vegetable and Animal Kingdoms do not originate from the Mineral Kingdom, nor can they be reduced back to it. Instead, he considers them to be an absolute and *most specific species* of earths, neither related to nor intended for any other kingdom than the animal and vegetable. We find no reason to follow him in this opinion. This would be easy to demonstrate if the nature of our current project allowed us to wander too far from *Subterraneans to Subterraneans* <note>original: *Subterraneis ad Subterranea*; a play on words suggesting a detour from one mineral topic to another</note>. Therefore, it will suffice to have touched upon these matters here; they may perhaps be demonstrated more precisely elsewhere or at another time.

XVIII. Certainly, the principles of most major subterranean things are earthy in character; they form without the material involvement of Water, though water is involved "formally" <note>In Aristotelian terms, a "formal" cause provides the shape or nature of a thing, whereas a "material" cause provides the actual physical substance.</note>. However, the mixture of vegetables and animals requires a primary involvement of water, which is just as much a material component as it is a formal or instrumental one.

I have named the primary and most common mineral mixtures. Truly, if *mixtures* <note>original: *mixta*; in 17th-century chemistry, this referred to substances where elements were chemically unified, as opposed to "composites" which were mere physical groupings.</note> are understood in the strict sense—and not as *composites*, or what our Author calls *super-decomposites*—I would not hesitate to decree that *all subterranean mixtures lack the material involvement of water*, with the sole exception of the mixture of the original mineral *Acid*. Those further subterranean species produced by the intervention of this acid are composites rather than true mixtures: namely, all volatile, inflammable, and saline substances, and solid formations <note>original: *concrementa*</note>.

In the meantime, it appears that this *acid* itself is not absolutely *indifferent* <note>meaning "neutral" or "unbiased"</note> toward all *three* Kingdoms; it stands, at the very least, at an equal distance between the mineral and the vegetable, serving both in a *material* and *formal* capacity.

It certainly serves the *Vegetable* Kingdom to such an extent that no vegetation or vegetable *mixture*, from its very first beginnings, displays anything more clearly than the involvement of a *saline* substance. In this *saline* form, earthy matter is supplied for the texture of the plant's structure in an extremely thin consistency. Through the *igneous* principle <note>the principle of "fire" or heat</note>—which flows abundantly from both the air and the depths of the earth itself—this matter is brought to a state of separation. Once the *saline* mixture is cast off, the matter recovers its *earthy* consistency. Thus, as the matter is gradually accumulated into a large mass and skillfully distributed, the process of mixing proceeds with all the fecundity we see in the growth of various kinds of plants.

Finally, regarding *Animal* mixture, although it is not perceived that this Acid involves itself *materially* in any way, it clearly provides the primary *instrument* of preparation. This is evident from the *fermentation* of food in the stomachs and the souring nature of *milk* itself—though this is certainly more pronounced in *grass-eating* animals <note>original: *graminivoris*; herbivores</note> than in any others.

Furthermore, that Water involves itself as a material Principle in the mixture of both Vegetables and Animals becomes clear from the *aqueous-saline* as well as the *fatty-oily* substances of these kingdoms. These are found not only in the fluids, as...

in the primary parts of both kingdoms <note>The Vegetable and Animal kingdoms</note>, it manifests itself, but it is also found to cling within the very internal structure of solid substance so firmly that it cannot be driven out except by a true, internal analysis.

How, in turn, the fiery substance—specifically the "fiery principle"—returns most intimately and promptly into a mineral mixture, no one (as far as I know) has demonstrated earlier or more simply than I have myself. I did so both in my *Experiment of Producing Sulfur by Art* in July 1697, and in my *Dissertation on the Foundations of Metallurgy and Pyrotechnic Assaying* <note>original: *Docimasiæ Pyrotechnicæ*; the art of testing chemicals and metals using heat</note>. There, I explained the actual practice by which base metals have been, and are to be, brought back to this solid consistency throughout so many centuries: namely, through the substance of the Fiery Principle supplied to them by the immediate contact of coals. (A clear and simple example of this is the reduction of glassy lead slags *through the tapping-furnace* <note>original German: *durch den Stich-Ofen*; a furnace where molten metal is released by piercing a clay plug</note>). Furthermore, by providing the most ready method of operation, I demonstrated that mineral sulfur actually consists of this **Phlogiston** <note>The hypothetical substance of fire that 17th-century chemists believed was released during combustion</note> matter and that subterranean acid; it is resolved into these components, and from them, it is instantly restored by art.

Nor should we pass over in silence the inseparable mixing of Vegetable Earth (when reduced to glass) with the glasses of mineral earths, and its various mutual combinations with the metals themselves. For not only does this Vegetable Earth coincide purely with Subterranean Earths in a general way regarding its glass-making consistency, but it also offers us an even more specific similarity—indeed, an "identity," as they say—through these aforementioned mutual alterations.

However, that formal or instrumental cooperation of both "aqueousness" and "fieriness" regarding the continuation of mineral mixtures requires the greatest attention.

We mentioned earlier in a specific place that *mixing occurs through the smallest particles* <note>original: *mixtio fiat per minima*; a core concept in early chemistry suggesting that substances only react when broken down into their smallest components</note>, which are of such great delicacy that they escape all our senses. Simple reason suggests that these smallest particles must be placed in a state of free movement, so that they may freely encounter one another, and freely run together and be joined. Truly, such a free state can be nothing other than one of fluidity: *whether it be a watery moisture; or an airy, breath-like vapor; or a fiery-flaming, soot-like, molten state.*

Now, since the species of subterranean things do not strike our senses except in a "Mass" or "Aggregate"—and indeed they occur everywhere as completed masses—a state where the principles are in a solid aggregate would be absolutely unfit for such a massive mixing. From this results the necessity of the opposite state: one that is fluid and delicate.

This is exactly how our Author <note>Becher</note> must be understood when he asserts that the principles of metals and minerals are accustomed to "wear a mask" and wander about, now in the form of air or vapor, now in the form of water. In this, he certainly should not be understood as speaking of pure, uniform principles—as if a pure earthy principle could ever be found in a fluid aggregate of water, identical in consistency but participating in nothing of "Water" strictly defined. Rather, it must be understood as a true watery substance, abundantly impregnated with those earthy particles.

which, when they encounter the principles of other categories under such a *freely mobile* state of aggregation, are so much more ready to undergo a mixture <note>original: *mixtionem*; the chemical combination of different substances</note>.

It seems, moreover, that this work is supported all the more by that truth known *from experience* <note>original: *a posteriori*; knowledge derived from observation rather than theory</note>: namely, that in any deeper mineral site, water and the perpetual presence of vapors are found together. At the same time, these deeper places are always found to be more fertile in metals and minerals. For although—as we shall soon add—the minerals found distributed through veins or tracts are observed today neither to be "born" nor "reborn" in that same way, Experience nonetheless confirms that even for those minerals growing *outside the direct distribution*—indeed, even those being renewed—the deeper, humid, and vaporous places are more fertile than those closer to the surface of the earth. This is so much the case that even portions of mineral-metallic tracts connected to the surface, or those rising above the surrounding plain in hills or mounds, are very frequently found "orphaned" and stripped of their mineral-metallic mixture. This occurs with all the more certainty the more they are deprived of the help of watery humidity, while the rest of the rocky structure, due to its softness and porosity, has lain exposed to the energy of aerial-fiery movements <note>The actions of the atmosphere and heat at the surface</note>.

Otherwise, these are surely the only and unique aids or *Instruments* of the Art: that by the help of watery, vaporous, and fiery commotion—which move through the smallest parts—one may establish and carry out artificial mixtures. In this business, craftsmen proceed more successfully the more they rightly understand this causal reasoning: namely, that the "sinew" <note>The essential core or strength</note> of the matter consists in the most subtle and thin motion, meeting, and convergence of the most internal, tiny particles. Thus, we must disregard those who, in the manner of *crude, unlearned folk*, sweat to grind mixtures together, and when they retain nothing but "bran" <note>Metaphorical "husks" or useless residue</note>, they curse the truth. Those, however, who use such means in the way that a just *proportion* requires for the end goal, are never deprived of a result that bears witness to the Truth of Nature.

From this, indeed, we find that solutions, digestion, cohobation <note>term: <term>cohobation</term> — the process of repeatedly distilling a liquid over the solid matter from which it was just drawn to extract more "virtue"</note>, deliquescence <note>The process of a solid turning into a liquid by absorbing moisture from the air</note>, the precipitation of dissolved substances, amalgamations, cementations <note>term: <term>cementation</term> — a process of heating a solid in a powder to change its properties, often used in refining gold</note>, long-lasting and very thin fusions, the *exclusion of untimely air*, reductions, and deflagrations or detonations, are the *Instruments* by which we constantly experience—through Art and the skilled guidance of directing reason—that old mixtures are dissolved and new ones are established.

*This is the work, this is the labor* <note>A famous quote from Virgil’s *Aeneid*: "Hoc opus, hic labor est," referring to the difficulty of returning from the underworld</note>: to rightly distinguish these things, and not to use these Instruments *backwardly* under such an arrangement that they might satisfy a *material* use rather than a purely *formal* one; or, in the reverse order, to use them in a state more suited for bare *instrumental* efficiency when they ought to have been applied to a *material* mixture.

But neither this place, nor perhaps our own strengths, would allow us to speak worthily of this matter; we shall therefore leave the business to those who write of themselves as Chemists. They will certainly have an excellent opportunity here to demonstrate that they understand something more than merely arranging pharmaceutical formulas with superlatives.

# BECHER’S FUNDAMENTAL THEORIES

**XIX.** Regarding subterranean mixed substances <note>minerals and ores</note>, we must distinguish their "aggregative disposition" (how they cluster together) and, even more importantly, their distribution throughout our Earthly world [*Geocosmum*], from their simple numerical condition <note>the quantity of individual particles</note>.

We touched upon this matter previously in Thesis XIII, but it truly deserves careful consideration in any theory of inanimate species. The "individuals" <note>the smallest particles or atoms</note> of these species are so tiny that they escape all the senses. Therefore, it must be accepted as beyond all controversy that in every "molecule" that is actually visible [*sensibili*]—or at least perceptible to the senses—there exists an aggregation of many particles into a single structure. If even such tiny masses are already aggregates, how much more so are those large masses and fragments found swollen with metal in the subterranean tracts.

Although these aggregates and fragments themselves possess various properties that come to them not from the direct nature of their chemical mixture, but from the character of their "social" gathering or grouping, there is another consideration of far greater importance. This is the very specific **distribution** by which these mineral-metallic clusters are found throughout the globe. They are not found scattered randomly, nor gathered here and there by the chance meeting and "embrace" of chemical principles; rather, they are seen to be placed with such a **highly specific** and exquisite order, position, and sequence, that nothing can be judged as accidental or attributed to the mere flow and meeting of secondary causes.

I have discussed this matter more at length and by design in the Program prefixed to the *Dissertation on the Foundations of Metallurgy and Assaying* <note>original: *Metallurgia & Docimasia Fundamentis*</note>, specifically in the section on the *Origin of Metallic Veins*. I declared my view that I recognize metallic veins and their ordered fragments—**veins, fissures, rubble, and seams, which have their proper horizontal direction, upper and lower walls, dip and outcrop, host rock and border** <note>original German: *Gänge, Klüffte, Geschübe, Flötze, die ihr richtiges streichen, hangend und liegendes, fallen und ausgeben, Gestein und Salband, haben*</note>; which, I say, keep their "hour" <note>original: *ihre Stunde*; a mining term referring to the compass direction of a vein</note> even when rising or falling—I recognize these vast tracts stretched and distributed through the bowels of the Earth as "Treasuries" [*Gazophylaciis*] for such species. They were fixed and implanted into the globe during its first production by the direct will, intention, direction, and distribution of the Almighty Creator.

Indeed, I could never conceive of the order and sequence of these metallic inflows as purely accidental. In a purely accidental model, only the external rocks of various kinds (which wrap around the vein like a solid **envelope** and form its case) would arise first, and the mineral-metallic matter would then fall into their center, or rather into an exquisitely empty space "cut out" for it. Instead, this process happens with such specific directional positioning that, in an almost infinite progression, it maintains a line corresponding to the **points of the horizon** <note>original: *Cardinibus Horizontis*; the cardinal directions of a compass</note>. As the saying goes, **"the vein holds its hour into eternal depth"** <note>original German: *daß der Gang seine Stunde hält, in ewige teuffe*</note>. Furthermore, the position of the rocks "ruling" the vein (not according to the length, but the **width of the vein**) also shows a very specific orientation: **the dip and outcrop of the rock carries its own direction, perpetually forming equal angles of intersection with the line of length.** Moreover...
