->### SAMPLES OF BECHER, PART I, SECTION I.<-

...does not surround and enclose the vein itself from every side, but only from two sides, opposite to one another, while in the meantime the other two sides, coming between these on both sides, are almost entirely devoid of that protection, and touch the rock or foundation of the mountain or ground as if by naked contact.

These circumstances, which no worker in the mines is ignorant of, I do not know how they escaped our Author <note>Becher</note>, so that he labors so anxiously to describe how minerals and metals are generated in the earth by way of vapors, propelled upward from the center of the earth (or rather from a vast fiery abyss, which in his mind occupies the interior of the globe) and collected in suitable Matrices <note>The "mother" rock or cavities where ore forms</note>.

Since, however, this consideration is somewhat removed from his direct aim—which was to discuss *chemical mixture, rather than the physical clustering, dissemination, or distribution* of a great quantity of Minerals through certain tracts—I would dare to defend him from all reproach with even better right; especially since no one before him, if you look at the etiology <note>the study of causes</note>, has brought forward anything more solid on this matter. Rather, he followed the common path of all those before him, and thus he should not have to pay for a common error alone.

Hence, indeed, in this Treatise of ours, only that question comes to be examined: *from what principles mixed minerals consist, into which they can be broken down, or from which they can be restored and fused together, as they usually are; as much by Nature* (setting aside that perfect distribution into veins, but looking instead at *clays, cracks, and "nests"* as it were, in <term>Letten</term> <note>clay-like mining soil</note>, <term>Thamm</term> or <term>Thon-Erde</term> <note>loam or clay-earth</note>, <term>Küfften</term> <note>clefts or cavities</note>, and <term>Nestern</term> <note>pockets of ore</note>, whether sprinkled into the mountain, fermented out, flowed out, grown, or forced out like flowers or a river, etc.) *as by Art* <note>Human skill, such as chemistry and smelting</note>.

In this, the principal role of Art <note>Human skill</note> lies in again variously destroying both mineral and metallic mixtures and compounds; yet Nature itself is not poor in these outcomes. Spontaneous disturbances of minerals also occur, where a good metallic mixture is lost and the whole vein degenerates into some inert and sterile mineral. The city of <note>original: "Schneeberga"</note> Schneeberg can testify to this, where once-rich veins of silver now vomit forth almost nothing more than bare <term>Cobalt</term> or <term>Arsenic</term>. Here and there, one even finds traces or remains of metal-bearing veins that have decayed, such as <term>Mulm</term> <note>loose, earthy ore</note>, <term>Faulen</term> <note>rotten, decomposed rock</note>, <term>lääres Nest</term> <note>an empty pocket</note>, or <term>taube Gilben</term> <note>sterile yellow earth</note>, etc.

Indeed, a well-known rule in the study of mineral tracts serves our consideration exceptionally well: at the *extremities*, where they are closer to the surface of the earth (especially the more recent and drier surface), the minerals suffer from a lighter, more volatile, cruder, and less noble temperament. On the contrary, the *deeper* they go, even if the metal is not of a higher quality, they nevertheless carry and offer a greater quantity of their own metal.

The reason for this can be sought partly in the *exhalations* of certain parts of the mixture, known as <term>Auswitterungen</term> <note>weathering out</note> or <term>Ausbränden</term> <note>burning out</note>. Partly, and with no less likelihood, it can be attributed to the *intermixing* of many particles of Water and "Fiery Matter," which provides the foundations of a *Salino-Sulphureous, arsenical, volatile, and combustible* nature.

# FOUNDATIONS OF BECHER'S THEORY
Page 29
Aaa a 2
<meta>catchword: To here</meta>

There is one matter regarding the intersections of mineral *tracts* which is most worthy of notice—indeed, of observation, examination, and scrutiny—far beyond the knowledge of unrefined miners, and perhaps it would not fail to be worth the effort. It is specifically that which the metal-workers express as: *A meager, poor, or even "dead" <note>original: "tauber"; in mining, this refers to rock that contains no useful metal</note> vein ennobles itself through accidental encounters <note>original: "zufällige Geschicke"; here referring to the chance intersection of geological paths</note>.* That is to say, a *poor or even sterile vein (hitherto showing only mineral matter without metal)* takes on a more noble character and provides good and plentiful metal from the *intersection of some other vein*.

In this matter, our attention is increased all the more because sometimes even the intersection of two *poor* veins produces a *noble* lineage; and this is so much the case that sometimes this change for the better (or at least into something else) does not extend far beyond that point of commingling or mutual intersection of the *veins*.

Truly, here some hope seems to shine through for looking a little deeper into the families and affinities that metals and minerals have with one another: indeed, for divining something of the state of the metallic *principles* <note>The fundamental "elements" or "seeds" of metals in Becher's chemistry</note> within various species of *minerals*. One might see where this or that principle perhaps abounds, or where it is held by a less strict bond and is more ready to join with others; and in which other kind of *mineral* such a *sympathetic* <term>symbolisa</term> <note>referring to substances that share "symbols" or qualities, allowing them to communicate or combine easily</note> communication is felt, so that one confers and contributes to the other. From their intersection and *union*, something else is born than what had existed before. But it is proper to expect these insights only from God and time; meanwhile, it will not hurt to be reminded of things that do not commonly come to mind.

XX. Regarding primordial mixture, we have nothing probable; but regarding subsequent mixture, and even more so regarding the breakdown and corruption of substances, we have much: both by nature's own power and by art <note>referring to "Ars," the skill of the chemist or alchemist</note>.

I wish to introduce this Thesis, although it does not depart much from the preceding one, so that we may more purposefully inspect that remarkable difference between those massive *aggregations* and the exquisite *distributions* of *underground veins*, and the truly *special or specific* constitution of the individual *Minima* <note>The smallest possible physical particles of matter</note> that make up these masses.

Next, it will not be inconvenient to introduce something regarding the true nature of the difference that exists between the powers of *Nature* and *Art* <note>Chemistry</note>, as this seems to be handled less precisely by the common sort.

As for the first point, we have already said various things pertaining to it in the preceding Thesis. But it is almost necessary to emphasize again and again the true concept of *Mixture*: namely, that it is a *cohesion* of a great many *Physical Minima*—indeed, physically and in fact *Indivisible* corpuscles. This is a *cohesion, a fitting-together, and a weaving-together* so exquisite that, because of this exactness of union, the separation of those parts from one another is most difficult; further, because of the extreme smallness of the *Whole* corpuscle thus mixed, as well as the superlative tininess of the *individual* parts making it up, our instruments for separation fail us.

To this point, we must certainly refer the Thesis mentioned above in number XIII, so that it may be understood just how meager in mass (since it escapes all the senses) is a **single numerical unit**—or a **single individual**, as it is most rightly called—of that species. In this unit, however, a true and firm mixture—namely, that aforementioned most firm entwining of Principles—is truly present and remains within.

These points must be emphasized so strongly because the common opinion and concept of **mixture** considers nothing other than a sort of crass **confusion within a gathered mass**. It is as if various types of tiny bodies were merely driven together, swept up, shaken, and tossed about, and that the "mixture" resulted from this (which, in this sense, is actually nothing but bare Confusion)—indeed, as if the mixture consisted properly in these mutual collisions.

But in truth, a certain and true consideration of **mixture** does not consist in the **aggregation** of many things of any kind (even of one and the same species); rather, it consists in the **coupling of several different species into a single tiny body of insensible smallness.** This consideration, I say, leads us all the better to weigh the **manner** in which (at least in general) even those great, indeed immense, masses—which are gathered from such "minima" <note>The "minima" or "atoms" are the smallest possible particles of matter in 17th-century physics</note>—were originally made with respect to the **individual** parts of which they consist. It also shows us what face and consistency their prior or primary matter necessarily bore and possessed.

It is entirely possible to derive this **mode of matter** (as they say today) from this consideration. However, as for the determined **motion**—to what place and for what reason so many masses and such an immense quantity of such matter were **distributed** only in **certain directions**—we must still suspend our judgment.

The most probable suspicion of all would perhaps be that our earthly globe was able to develop great and monstrous **cracks** at some first, most ancient time; that these **cracks, at the time of the Flood**, were filled with a thin mud; and that other, most subtle **vapors** from the depths of the earth were able to penetrate this mud. Thus, it would appear that the generation of such a great quantity of minerals followed in this way.

Our Author <note>Referring to Johann Joachim Becher (1635–1682), the German alchemist and physician</note> also leans toward this consideration. But I do not approve of it, owing to certain principal circumstances which render the business not so much perplexed as it is futile. They are as follows:

First of all, one would certainly have to suppose that this **conception of cracks or fissuring of the Earthly Globe** happened **before the Flood**; that the filling of them with that most porous **mud** happened **during the Flood**; and the **generation of minerals happened after the Flood.**

Secondly, even if this supposition about the Flood-mud did not seem necessary, and these **fissures** were assigned to any other pre-Flood causes, reasons would still have to be given both for this occurrence and for the **filling up** of **only** these fissures.

Now, as to the first point, exceptional and even insuperable difficulties stand in the way. 1.) **From prior reasoning**, Holy Scripture records that not only **metals**, but even the very working of metals, was already known to the descendants of Cain. <note>Genesis 4:22 mentions Tubal-Cain as an instructor of every artificer in brass and iron</note> 2.) **From posterior reasoning**, there are **great**, indeed often immense, **fragments** to be found within the hollows of mountains or around valleys at the feet of mountains, which they commonly call **Föze** <note>A German mining term (often "Föze" or "Fötze") referring to "float" or fragments of ore and rock broken off from a main vein and moved by water</note> (namely, fragments broken off from the veins by the flow and impetus of the Flood and tumbled elsewhere). How, I ask, did these fragments reach such places in such mass...

In these very **subterranean things**, which are to be altered, masked, or diverted by another composition in various ways, **Art** has **greater** efficacy than Nature herself. The ratio of **Instruments** is so different that Nature usually uses more general and more **immediate** ones, and those fewer in number and kind: while Art has more at its disposal, by which sometimes directly, sometimes through roundabouts <note>indirect methods or complex processes</note>, with a secondary result, it performs what does not usually proceed in the natural order, and sometimes also cannot.

For art has certain instruments which it fashions for itself—namely those to be produced and prepared by Art itself. For example: **Fire**, **ardent spirits** <note>Alcohols or strong distillates</note>, **fixed Alkalis**, **composite salts** commonly called **Armoniac** <note>original: "Armeniacalia"; Sal ammoniac or ammonium chloride</note>, **vinegar**, etc., with which it can work various things that would never occur spontaneously in that way.

The chief thing in which art **differs** from nature, however, is the measure of **time**, and the intensity of acting within time, as also the destination of the action toward a specific, chosen end or goal.

For certainly concerning natural mixtures, as such, one can hardly doubt that today everything happens as if by chance, if you look at the time. For just as those things which are done deliberately and destined for a certain end—with all actions properly directed toward it—I say, those things are opposed to **things made by chance**: but those things are understood to happen by chance which emerge correctly and in order from a concourse of efficient causes, but nevertheless...

### FUNDAMENTALS OF BECHER'S THEORY

...without purpose or intention that they should happen; without a certain and determined regard for the time in which they occur. Indeed, [they happen] under other unforeseen *coinciding* circumstances. Thus, no one, I think, will doubt that the generation of metals and minerals which still happens *today outside of Veins* <note>original: "extra Venas"; refers to the belief that ores could grow in soil or outside traditional mining lodes</note> belongs to these latter causes.

On the other hand, the *Artisan* <note>meaning the chemist or alchemist</note>, at whatever *time* is convenient for him, takes in hand *selected materials* that are suitable, joins them correctly and using *proper instruments*, and being conscious and knowledgeable of these *proportions*, he produces a hoped-for effect *deliberately* and *on purpose*, just as he had planned in his mind. Thus, the Artisan can undertake such a thing at whatever time and place he pleases; whereas with *spontaneous* production, such a thing hardly ever happens even over the longest period of time. Namely, it occurs only through the more *accidental* gatherings of more universal causes, both in the external alteration of the air and the internal alteration of the terrestrial globe. Here *clouds, winds, rains, torrents, stagnant waters, earthquakes, forest fires*, the stripping of hills and mountains that have been subject to *forest shade* for many years, *new fissures in the earth, etc.*, can provide the occasion for various alterations regarding the eruptions or *collections of exhalations and vapors*.

Truly, however, even if we wish to seek the truth in fact, there is no such notable production of these things that it could supply a great history <note>In the 17th-century sense, a "history" is a systematic collection of observations or data</note>. A far greater frequency occurs of *breakdowns* and *corruptions* that are also *spontaneous*, especially in *metals* exposed to the weather by human industry.

But it is not pleasing to discuss these matters at greater length, since from what has been said it is easy to gather what relationship *art has to nature*, and how for the most part the former depends on the latter. We shall proceed rather to those things which still remain to be known for a better understanding of *Becher’s Theory*.

**XXI. The instrument common to Nature and Art is the *fluid-vaporous* mode.**

It has been decided to include in a specific Thesis the consideration of *that method* by which it is necessary, *a priori* <note>from first principles or theoretical necessity</note>, that *minerals and metals were generated, and are still generated today*.

Where, however, it should be noted right from the start: that although we have so far spoken mostly of *minerals and metals*, the consideration should by no means stop there, or be restricted by these boundaries. Instead, it should be extended to all subterranean things, so that it also encompasses the entire family of *rocks and earths*. For since the question of when and how <term>mineral Veins</term> <note>original: "Venae minerales"; the cracks or fissures in rock filled with ore</note> arose can seem complex, I think it would be even more obscure [to ask] from where and how all and every *rock, and the entire mass of the Earth*, had its origin, and whether it has *always* existed in the *state* in which it is now; or whether it was also at some time in another condition, from which it finally passed into this present one.

Indeed, if this matter is weighed as it truly is, namely, that in *all* of this...

# SPECIMEN BECHERIANUM PART I. SECTION I.

...between <note>original: "Inter"; matching the catchword from the previous page</note> this globe of the Earth, there is no bit of matter—not even the smallest that can be seen—which does not consist of a great number of even smaller parts. Each of these individual little bodies <term>corpuscles: Becher uses the term "corpuscula" to describe the fundamental building blocks of matter, similar to modern atoms or molecules</term> eludes all our senses due to their extreme thinness. Furthermore, this *division* into such "minima" <note>the smallest possible units</note> is not a matter of *mathematical* power—that is, it is not possible to divide them from any point along any line. Instead, division occurs only along those lines which form the *seams* <note>original: "commissuram"</note> where these little bodies join together. Beyond these lines, those little bodies are *impenetrable* and cannot be physically split into any other dimension, but can only be mathematically measured or distinguished. 

From this consideration of the matter as it truly is, there necessarily follows the supposition *that these little bodies were once in a discontinuous state, removed from one another and separated by other intervening things; thus, they were visible in a state other than their present solid, hard, and dense aggregation.*

However much we may lack knowledge about *that time* or *that exact state* which befell these things before they were struck together into this solid aggregation, *Holy Scripture* nevertheless hints in a general way at the *separation of the dry from the moist*. By this very fact, it implies that the *dry was so thoroughly mixed with the moist that it eventually had to be separated from it.*

Indeed, there is a certain *mutual agitation*—however confused—of *drying corpuscles with moist ones*. I speak of such corpuscles which, by *aggregating into density*, come together into a solid, and their joining with such others that *form a fluid aggregation*. The meeting of these two, I say, represents a *fluid-drying* state, which we call *steamy or vaporous* <note>original: "halituosum aut vaporosum"</note>. In this state, the smallest particles—being simple and individually distinct—are carried and driven so freely *outside of a crowded or firm aggregation* that they cannot come together into a *homogeneous aggregation* <note>a cluster of the same kind of matter</note> except by separating from the foreign particles running between them. Nor can they simply take on a *deeper mixture* with those *foreign* particles, but only with those that are *proportioned* <note>chemically compatible or "fitting" in size and nature</note> to them.

Furthermore, since the mixing or *numerical union* of even *proportioned little bodies (of different species)* must happen through *each individual minimum* (of those two, three, or four species), a specific state is required for these aggregates. Wherever a great number of them are present, regardless of what stands between them, they must be kept distinct from one another so that they do not gather together randomly. Instead, they must remain as individual units so they can admit the growth <note>original: "concretionem"</note> of other proportioned particles.

We call such a *discontinuous state* "humidity, fluidity, or vapor." This kind of constitution must be introduced to those things which one intends to mix together—that is, to combine through their tiniest parts. Since *moist fluidity essentially requires heat*, or at least is far better prepared for both combinations and resolutions through the presence of heat, we must speak of this highly important circumstance with the dignity it deserves.

# FOUNDATIONS OF BECHER'S THEORY

Among <note>original: "Inter"; matching the catchword from the previous page</note> the various levels by which aggregated masses, possessing motion, depend upon one another, the highest level of all is due to the *motion of heat*, since the motion of the *fluidity of water* depends most immediately upon it. Indirectly, the motion of other *moist* fluids also depends on it, insofar as they partake of water, such as *oils* and *saline spirits* <note>original: "Spirituum salinorum"; acidic or alkaline solutions derived from salts</note>. Indeed, the movements of *air* and *quicksilver* <note>original: "argenti vivi"; mercury</note> themselves depend remarkably on the impulse of heat.

For just as simpler water, if heat were absolutely lacking, would coalesce into hard, firm, dense, dry ice; and thus, having lost its *fluidity*, we would by necessary consequence be deprived of all those motions which are carried out through water acting as an instrument. So too, since water constitutes and completes a great part of *oily* fluidity, and uniquely provides *saline* fluidity: I say, therefore, that if the motion of heat which impels water is largely absent in such oily and saline fluids, very little *commotion* <note>internal movement or agitation of particles</note> is observed in all these fluids. Thus, their immense dependence on heat becomes clearly apparent to the senses. This is all the more true since these fluids acquire a most evident and powerful *increase* of motion from applied heat, which is very well known in all *solutions*—whether they be *sulfureous-resinous*, *earthy-saline*, mineral, or metallic—and even in *amalgamation* <term>amalgamation: the process of mixing mercury with other metals to form an alloy</term> itself.

Regarding those most volatile materials themselves, which appear to be moved strongly enough by the bare air even without an evident sense of *heat*, nevertheless, when slightly more careful observations are made, it is discovered that the efficacy of *Heat* is just as great as that of *cold* regarding their movements.

For just as it is manifest that they can be greatly impelled by *heat*, it is also a consequence that their motion can be diminished by *cold*. An example of this was shown to me by *Volatile Sulfurous Spirit of Vitriol, rectified* <note>original: "Spiritus vitrioli volatilis Sulphureus rectificatus"; likely a fuming or concentrated sulfuric acid solution, or sulfur dioxide gas</note>, which usually dissipates far and wide into the bare air. For when this was congealed into ice by intense cold, it even broke the glass container; and although the fragments of glass fell away from it, leaving the substance bare, not only did none of it evaporate into the air, but while it was in that state of ice, it did not even give off any significant *odor*. Yet, it did so most intensely as soon as it flowed again from a gentle heat.

Indeed, even in those motions which appear to be *agitated* by the bare *air*, this must be noted regarding the *air* itself: we do not truly keep in mind how much the *aerial motion* depends on heat. So much so, that it is certainly very likely that if absolutely no motion of heat occurred or flourished, then the air itself would reach a certain degree of solidity, *rigidity, and density*, and thus would be most unfit for performing any degree of *motion* as an instrument.

I hope the reason can become clear from this why I have made no mention of the *heat* of other things in the Thesis. Namely, because all other types of fluid and vaporous motions are so encompassed under *heat* that they depend on it remarkably—indeed, if you look at motion in general, they depend on it almost uniquely. Furthermore, we act here with all the better right by treating *heat* separately, since in the preceding Thesis we have already discussed *fluid*, both *moist* and *vaporous motion*. Meanwhile, it is certainly appropriate to note that point in this place.

<meta>This page continues Becher's exploration of the microscopic structure of matter. Having previously discussed how fluids like water and mercury respond to heat, he now moves into a theoretical explanation of "corpuscles"—the tiny, indivisible building blocks of the physical world—and how they must be separated into a "vaporous" state to combine into new substances.</meta>

# FOUNDATIONS OF BECHER'S THEORY

In this globe of Earth, there is no tiny particle—even the smallest that can be seen—which does not consist of a great number of still smaller ones. Individually, these **little bodies** <note>original: "corpuscula"; the tiny, indivisible building blocks of matter in Becher’s theory, similar to the modern concept of atoms or molecules</note> are so fine that they elude all our senses. Furthermore, this division into such **minima** <note>the smallest possible units of a physical substance</note> is not a matter of mathematical potential—that is, it does not happen at any arbitrary point along any line—but occurs only along those lines which form the seams or joints where these corpuscles meet. Beyond these lines, those corpuscles are impenetrable and cannot be physically split into any other dimension, but can only be measured or distinguished mathematically. From this consideration of the matter as it truly is, the necessary conclusion is that these corpuscles were once in a **discontinuous state**, separated from one another and spread out by other intervening things; thus, they were visible in a state other than their current solid, hard, and dense aggregation.

However, although we have no direct knowledge of that time or of the exact state that these things possessed before they were compressed into this solid aggregation, **Holy Scripture** <note>a reference to the creation story in the Book of Genesis</note> generally hints at the "separation of the dry from the moist." By this very fact, it implies that the dry was once so thoroughly mixed with the moist that it eventually had to be set apart from it by separation.

Indeed, the mutual agitation—no matter how confused—of the "drying" corpuscles with the "moist" ones represents a "fluid-drying" state which we call **halituous** <note>breath-like or gaseous</note> or **vaporous**. I am speaking of the joining of corpuscles that form solid density with those that form a fluid aggregation. In this state, the smallest particles are carried and driven about as if they were simple and singular individuals, outside of any bulky or firm aggregation. They cannot come together into a uniform mass except by being separated from the **different** <note>original: "heterogeneis"; substances of a different kind that prevent the "like" particles from touching</note> particles running between them. Nor can they achieve a more intimate mixing with those different particles, but only with those that are **proportionate** <note>compatible or of a similar nature, capable of bonding together</note>.

Furthermore, since the mixing or **numerical union** <note>the joining of particles one-by-one in specific ratios</note> of proportionate corpuscles of different species (whether of two, three, or four types) must happen through each individual minimum particle, there is a direct requirement for a specific state within the mass. Wherever a great number of them are present, no matter what other substance is between them, they must be held apart from each other so that they do not clump together at random, but can individually admit the union of other proportionate particles.

We call such a discontinuous state **humidity**, **fluidity**, or **vapor**. This kind of constitution must be introduced into those things which we intend to mix together—that is, to combine at the level of the most minute parts. Since moist fluidity absolutely requires heat, or at least its cooperation, to be far better prepared for both **combinations** and **resolutions** <note>the chemical process of breaking substances down into their component parts</note>, we must speak of this circumstance of such great importance with the dignity it deserves.

### XXII. Heat is the primary common instrument of nature and art; Fire is more specific to art <note>In the 17th century, "Art" referred to human technology, specifically alchemy and chemistry</note>.

<summary>Becher explains that all matter is composed of tiny, impenetrable "corpuscles" that were once separated in a vaporous state. He argues that to combine different substances, they must be returned to this fluid or vaporous state using heat, which he identifies as the primary tool of both nature and chemistry.</summary>

# FOUNDATIONS OF BECHER'S THEORY

### Page 35
#### FUNDAMENTALS OF BECHER'S THEORY

Among the various degrees by which aggregated masses <note>collections of particles forming a solid or liquid body</note> that enjoy motion depend on one another, the highest degree is entirely owed to the **motion of heat**. From this, the motion of **watery fluidity** depends more immediately; indirectly, it also governs other **humid fluids** <note>original: "fluorum humidorum"; liquid substances</note> insofar as they contain water, such as **oils and saline Spirits** <note>acidic or alkaline solutions</note>. Indeed, the **motion of air** and **quicksilver** <note>mercury</note> themselves depend remarkably on the **impulse of heat**.

For just as simple water, if heat were absolutely lacking, would solidify into hard, firm, dense, dry ice; and thus, having lost its **fluidity**, we would by necessary consequence be deprived of all those **motions** that come to be performed **through water** as an instrument. In the same way, since water constitutes and completes a large part of **oily** fluidity, and uniquely provides **saline** fluidity as well; so, I say, if the motion of **heat** driving the water also fails significantly in such **oily** and **saline** fluids, then **scant disturbances** <note>minimal movement or chemical activity</note> are observed in all these fluids. This makes their great dependence on **heat** clearly evident to the senses. This is all the more true because these fluids acquire a very evident and strong increase in motion from applied heat, which is most well known in all **solutions**, whether **sulfurous-resinous**, **earthy-saline**, mineral, or metallic—even in **amalgamation** <note>the process of alloying mercury with other metals</note> itself.

Regarding even those most **volatile materials** themselves, which appear to be stirred strongly enough by bare air even without an evident sense of **heat**, nevertheless, after conducting slightly more attentive observations, it is discovered that the efficacy of **Heat**, as well as of **cold**, is immense regarding their movements.

For just as it is manifest that they can be greatly driven by heat, it is also a consequence that their motion can be diminished by **cold**. An example of this was shown to me by **Rectified Volatile Sulfurous Spirit of Vitriol** <note>likely a solution of sulfur dioxide or concentrated sulfuric acid derivatives</note>, which usually dissipates far and wide in the open air alone. For when this was congealed into ice by intense **cold**, it even shattered the glass; yet when the fragments fell away from it, leaving the substance bare, not only did nothing evaporate into the air, but even while fixed in ice, it did not even scatter any notable **odor**. However, it did so most intensely as soon as it flowed again from a mild heat.

Indeed, even in these types of motions that appear to be agitated by the bare **air**, this must be noted about the **air** itself: we do not truly keep in mind how much the **aerial motion** depends on heat. So much so, that it is certainly very likely that if **absolutely no motion of heat** occurred or flourished, then even the air itself would reach a certain degree of solidity, rigidity, and density, and thus would be most unfit to provide any degree of **motion** as an instrument.

I hope the reason can become clear from this why I have made no mention of other things besides **heat** in the Thesis. Namely, because all other types of fluid and vaporous motions are so encompassed under **heat** that they depend on it remarkably—indeed, if you look at motion in general, they depend on it almost exclusively. Above all, we deal with **heat** here separately with even better justification because, in the preceding Thesis, we already discussed **fluid** motion, both **humid** and **vaporous**. Meanwhile, it is certainly fitting to note at this point—

It happens, and should be kept in a mindful memory for the future, that all **mixtures**, by absolute necessity, must be made through **singular tiny particles** <note>original: "minima singularia"; the smallest individual components or corpuscles of matter</note>. Therefore, whenever these must be made in a larger number or quantity (that is, they are carried out **under a certain aggregation** <note>as a collective mass</note>), these smallest particles must be arranged in such a mode of aggregation where the free state and motion of each individual particle is not only unhindered; but indeed, the **penetration** of one kind of particle into those of another kind is not interrupted at all. Rather, both mutual access and mutual **embrace** <note>original: "complexus"; the binding or interlocking of particles</note> can be most freely carried out by that free **motion**, and even by impulse, within that consistent mass.

From this, the energy and universal utility we have designated for **Heat**, and for both **humid** and **vaporous fluidity** <note>original: "fluoris"; the flowing state of liquids or gases</note>, is truly immense for performing **mixtures** as well as **resolutions** <note>the decomposition or breaking down of substances into their constituent parts</note>. However, an excellent difference exists regarding the diverse power of nature and art <note>here "Art" refers to the skill of the chemist or alchemist</note>: in the **macrocosm** <note>the natural world at large</note>, Heat has its places and **times** more fixed or determined. If by some fortune the **matter** happens to be present that obeys such a degree of heat, then—at that specific time and place—resolutions or mixtures occur. On the contrary, the artisan, at the time he intends to establish mixtures or resolutions, can not only seek out **materials** that rightly fit his purpose (pure and, as much as possible, homogeneous); but also, most aptly and at a convenient **time**, with a success that is as free as possible and moderated by his own judgment, can pursue the whole business above all with a **suitable degree of heat** (as the primary **Motion**). This is done in a way that is consistent with the **intellect** that is knowledgeable and skilled in these things *a priori* <note>reasoning from theoretical principles or causes to effects</note>, as well as with the will, the intention, and the purpose or end to be legitimately obtained. Thus, whatever in natural effects is more **fortuitous** <note>accidental or left to chance</note> and uncertain—such as the requirement that the prepared matter be available precisely at the time and place where heat happens to arise—can be most conveniently arranged by the artisan's choice. In this way, not only are all the mutually necessary circumstances collected and prepared at one and the same time and place, but they are also fitted to one another, so that both **matter** and **motion** are immediately applied to each other in the proper order.

Just as today, wherever either new **mixtures** or **resolutions** are made in subterranean places <note>such as mines or deep within the earth's crust</note>, there a consistency always clearly presents itself that is either **humid**, aqueous-saline, **oily**, or **slimy-viscous**; or, especially in the case of **resolutions**, a **vaporous** or **steamy** appearance occurs. So much more so in artificial experiments of these kinds: not only does a **fluid** consistency serve (through various thinnings) for the mixtures and resolutions intended, but this very state, as well as a **vaporous** temperature, is sustained, promoted, and intensified by heat.

From this, art truly enjoys a great advantage in this type of **instrumental equipment** over Nature itself; while, conversely, Nature possesses the greatest advantage over art because it is supplied with a larger storehouse of **matter**, which Art must absolutely borrow from it.

Meanwhile, we must not remain silent about a point that remains highly debatable: whether Nature only finally *produces* suitable materials at the end of a process, or whether she releases them from other mixtures to apply them to new ones. Or rather, has she been so equipped from a most abundant storehouse—ever since the first distributions of this **Geocosmos** <term>Geocosmos: a 17th-century term for the Earth viewed as a complex, living physical system</term>—that only the most delicate and mobile species of principles are carried here and there, driven about, snatched away in one place, and entangled in another? Whereas those that are **more consistent** (meaning those that provide the primary earthy solidity to the whole mixture) remain scattered or distributed in abundance here and there. This indeed is the most likely of all; so much so that **Art** <note>the skill of the chemist or alchemist</note> itself can draw a significant medley from those storehouses, *which are always and continually enclosed there*. 

A clear example is found in the **loamy** and **muddy** earths of various kinds, which almost always and everywhere contain a certain type of very fine "earthiness" interspersed within them. This earthiness might undergo a more fixed mixing of some metal if those other more mobile and subtle principles are joined to it. Or, depending on the diversity of the operation, it can be led into a more volatile state, seized, and carried away. Evidence for this includes Becher’s **Iron-bearing** experiment <note>original: "Ferriferum"; a process where Becher claimed to produce iron from non-metallic earths</note>; the fixations of volatile minerals through earths performed by **Schellenberg** and similar men; and conversely, the burning and melting of *such things with an added weight of the most mobile principles, as used in the sublimation of Geber* <note>original: "sublimatione Gebriana"; referring to the techniques of Jabir ibn Hayyan, an 8th-century polymath</note>, etc.

So it seems by far the most probable that in the natural succession of things, principles of every kind are not just aimlessly wandering in a *state, or rather motion*, where they would constantly meet, entwine, and coalesce, and thus produce the abundant mineral and metallic mixtures we see today. Or certainly—whatever the case may be, as experience testifies—it is more a matter of that nature which shows an abundant **influx** of those **most mobile** principles, rather than confirming a sparse meeting of **all** principles (and especially the **more solid** principle among the rest). This makes us more certain that **all** principles of every kind are today in the power of Nature, so that she can use them for new subterranean mixtures with an equal energy of movements, transferring them from here and applying them there.

An example is sand of every kind. Surely, through each of its grains, it is a somewhat pure homogeneous aggregate—if not absolutely and uniquely of that **first** principle (according to Becher’s numbering <note>Becher proposed three types of "earth": the stony/glassy, the fatty/inflammable, and the fluid/mercurial</note>), then at least containing a great deal of it. This is proven by the effect arising even from superficial contact; I mean, the **surface** of the **corpuscles** <term>corpuscles: the tiny, invisible particles that make up all matter</term> making up each grain. For by such bare surface contact, when interspersed with quicklime, it coalesces with it into a total stony hardness. Whereas lime without sand would remain perpetually **soft, brittle, and powdery**.

It is of the same kind that those metalliferous experiments, such as Becher’s **iron-bearing** one, succeed far more readily and abundantly with loam or oven clay (**Ofen-Leimen**) <note>original: "Ofen-Leimen"; a heat-resistant clay used for furnace linings</note> than with potter's clay (**Töpffer-Thon**) <note>original: "Töpffer-Thon"; common clay used for ceramics</note>. For that **loam** is truly of a refined **sandy** lineage; hence it **turns to glass** <note>original: "vitrescit"; the process of vitrification</note>. Which the blacksmiths...

Consequently, whatever is more *accidental* and uncertain in natural effects—such as the right matter being ready at the specific time and place that heat happens to arise—can be most conveniently arranged by the chemist’s choice. Not only are all the necessary circumstances gathered in one time and place, but they are fitted together so that both *matter* and *motion* are immediately applied to each other in the correct order.

These very states, as well as the *vaporous* temperament, are sustained, promoted, and intensified by heat.

Thus, art enjoys a much greater advantage in this type of *instrumental apparatus* compared to **Nature** itself. Conversely, Nature possesses the greatest advantage over Art because it is equipped with a more abundant *storehouse of matter*, which Art absolutely must borrow from her.

### XXIII. *Nature is less capable than Art when it comes to the motion of fire.*

It is exactly so; in her ordinary course, the "igneous motion" <note>the movement or energy caused by fire</note> is unknown to Nature. However, it is most well-known and commonly used in Art. From this depend various artificial productions that Nature can absolutely never bring to such a state; some she cannot even achieve or imitate. Or at the very least, she can neither provide nor obtain them with such **readiness** or **purity**.

Various examples of this occur. The primary one is the **purification, separation, and homogeneous** collection of many minerals as well as metals. Such things never occur in the ordinary course of nature to the extent that, even if a piece of more **homogeneous** mineral or metal is occasionally found—what they call **native** <note>original: "gediegen"; metal found in nature in its metallic form rather than as an ore</note>—it absolutely never occurs so completely pure from other differing species. Instead, it remains difficult to work with and resistant, especially to metallic ductility, and is never rendered free of all foreign mixture except by **the help of Art**, to the desired degree. The sole exception is **virgin mercury**, which is found in its ore in a notable quantity, so pure and flowing (see the *Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society* <note>original: "Act. Anglic. Philos."; the world's first scientific journal, published in London</note> for the year 1669, and Supplement I of our author [Becher]) that no heterogeneous matter is felt to be mixed in with it. At the very least, it enjoys such an abundance of its own "flow" or fluidifying principle that it can carry even the most compact gold upward with it, or even eventually dissolve it internally—if one believes those who reported this energy of mercury to Becher. Regarding this matter, as we lack such true Mercury, no experiment is available to us.

As for our statement that the strictly-defined "igneous motion" is unknown to Nature in her ordinary course, that is entirely the case. For although those immense examples of fire in burning mountains <note>volcanoes</note> are well known and visible—indeed, even here and there, forest fires are known to arise by chance or misfortune—

...as even in nearby Meissen near **Zwickau** <note>original: "Zwiccaivam"</note>, whether by chance or human error, a vein of **stone-coal** <note>original: "lithanthracum," an early term for pit-coal or mineral coal</note> caught fire and burns to this day. Indeed, this is rather the reason why so many **inflammable** as well as other **volatile** heterogeneous substances are found clinging to **metallic** mixtures. They are found not only in such quantity that they would be easily dissipated by even the smallest degree of **fiery** heat, but also with such qualities that they could not possibly be retained if they had truly been exposed to the occurrence of **fiery** motion.

For while it is not far from the truth that mineral vapors—breaths easily prepared from more mobile principles—can flow into metallic mixtures that have already reached their perfection, and thereafter be entwined with them by an intimate adhesion so that the mixture we are speaking of results (namely, that of **minerals with metals**); nevertheless, one cannot overlook the careful consideration that these same **minerals** occur elsewhere without such metals, or without such a large confluence, as if in their own more homogeneous ore. Furthermore, they still possess the same **consistency** which they display when united with the metallic ores themselves. Indeed, they quite frequently present themselves in such great abundance, and in that very specific distribution of **certain tracts** or veins—and are only finally reached by the accidental meeting of metal-bearing or metal-forming **conduits**—that it cannot be believed otherwise than that these **minerals** were born there at the **very first** moment of their origin and emergence, rather than appearing as a later **secondary formation** <note>original: "ἐπιγένεσιν" (epigenesis), a Greek term referring to a substance formed later upon a pre-existing one</note> brought in over time.

Indeed, the very **position** of the groupings found in subterranean places is too orderly—even for those concretions that are otherwise most suited to receiving **fiery** motions—and shows clearly enough that they did not come together into such an order by being shaken by that **violent** and rapid fiery motion. Instead, they were fitted together by a far more peaceful process. For example, where the ore of **sulfur** is seen gathered into cubic or slightly **rhomboid** shapes. Indeed, those crystalline growths of glass-like density—even of greater hardness than glass—which are so strangely familiar to metallic ores and which are commonly called **Drusen** <term>Drusen: A German mining term (druses) for a cavity or "vug" in a rock lined with crystals</term>, just as they hardly yield to violent **fire**, so it surpasses all belief—and fits not a single observed phenomenon—that they were brought into such a state by any **fiery** motion rather than a **fluid-moist** one.

### SPECIMEN OF BECHER, PART I, SECTION I. ###

Art <note>Ars: In this context, "Art" refers to alchemy or chemistry—the human skill of manipulating natural substances.</note>, however—both in the simple distinction of the diverse natures of mineral materials from their confused gathering, and in the resolution of the inner bonds of their composition, or rather their **mixture**—performs by **the help of fire** those things which are almost absolutely impossible in the natural order. For example, it can take the most subtle **volatiles** and extremely **clear oils**, and in an instant, reduce them to a **dry, dark** powder, diametrically opposed to their clear transparency and rendered incapable of being turned into vapor by any heat. Nothing of this kind occurs in the whole nature of things, except perhaps in accidental and violent fires.

In the meantime, it certainly deserves due consideration to note that huge quantity of such artificial (or, with respect to Nature, violent) products which are scattered into our world or geocosmic **atmosphere** in innumerable quantities from the fiery consumption of directly **combustible** materials.

For it is most evidently well-known that if a room, **capable of holding ten paces in length, width, and height**, could be so exquisitely sealed that it could have no commerce with the free external air, it is most certain that the air enclosed in such a space could scarcely receive as many **phlogistic** corpuscles <note>phlogistorum: from "phlogiston," the historical chemical theory that a fire-like element is contained within combustible bodies and released during burning.</note> **as could proceed from a portion of a wax candle weighing half an ounce**. Now, if we calculate how much of such material is sent into the air every winter day and night from one populous city—from the flames of furnaces and kitchens, and even from candles and lamps—it will be observed that the space filled by it is without doubt **immensely** greater than anyone has perhaps thought until now. Consequently—which amounts to the same thing—an immensely greater quantity and number of similar corpuscles are thrust into the **atmosphere** from such material and by such motion than anyone could ever persuade the common people to believe.

However, even greater—and in a way that Nature could never imitate—is that power of Art, by which it can not only set other bodies in most subtle motion by **fiery motion**, but can also, under that same motion, instantly and intimately intermix them with the **matter of fire**, the **Phlogiston** <note>original: "τὸ Φλογιστὸν" (to Phlogiston). Becher was the primary architect of the Phlogiston theory.</note>, I say, as a principle. This very thing is almost the absolute foundation of the **art of smelting** <note>artis fusoriae: the craft of melting and casting metals.</note>, and certainly of the **reduction** <note>reductionis: the chemical process of returning a metal to its pure form from an ore or oxide.</note> of the base metals. This has also been exposed to the light of day in other experiments previously rendered by me through **customary etiology** <note>solita etiologia: a systematic explanation of causes.</note>, such as the **artificial production of sulfur, its genesis, the volatile spirit of vitriol, even the volatile spirit of sulfur itself, and the destruction and reduction of reguli** <note>reguli: the metallic heart or "little king" of an ore; the pure metal that sinks to the bottom during smelting.</note> **of tin, etc.**

Furthermore, just as **fire** is the tool of the artist for performing various purely **artificial** things, which are as if unknown to nature—both in the business of **mixture** and of **resolution**—it is nevertheless also necessary to note that the imprudent administration of fire often hinders the artist. It may prevent him from imitating nature successfully enough in material things, and from being able to separate her **untainted** products one from another.

# FOUNDATIONS OF BECHER'S THEORY #

We shall not speak at length about that necessary distinction between **Pyrotechny** <note>original: *Pyrotechnia*; the chemistry of fire and metallurgy</note>, **Halotechny** <note>original: *Halotechnia*; the chemistry of salts</note>, and **Zymotechny** <note>original: *Zymotechnia*; the chemistry of fermentation</note>, and their very different effectiveness in separating various substances—whether mixed and composite or merely blended together—with or without a notable alteration of their substance. It will suffice to briefly point out how even artificial fire can remain closely related to the heats of nature. In this way, its productions can be handled and kept **untainted**, and partly even imitated, provided the craftsman remembers to apply fire under the same regulations that one experiences and observes in the circumscribed **natural** heat of the earth.

These regulations are: 1) **degree**, 2) **mode**, and 3) **place**, all of which are familiar to natural heat. Regarding **degree**, it is well known that natural heat never reaches a **boiling heat** <note>original: *fervorem*; a state of intense agitation</note> that could even slightly approach that of **boiling** water. Regarding the **mode**, experience proves that nature everywhere uses a heat that is **moist** rather than **dry**; that is, it acts either truly in **fluid form** or at least in a **moist vapor**.

The **place** which nature uses (we are speaking here of the subterranean world), and in which it holds the energy of its heat confined, is an **enclosed space** in which no room is granted for a **flaming** fire. One can immediately observe how much difference this makes even in **artificial** operations by looking at **sulfur** and **imperfect metals** <note>original: *metallis imperfectis*; base metals like iron or lead that react with air, as opposed to "noble" metals like gold</note>. Although *sulfur* is a material with a very weak mixture <note>i.e., its components are not tightly bound</note>, when it is in an **enclosed** space where there is no room for the agitation of a flame, it preserves and retains its mixture untainted. Even if it is strongly moved by the fire, nothing is removed, **resolved**, or displaced.

So also **iron, tin, copper, and lead**, when agitated in an **open, flaming** fire, experience a separation of their essential parts so that they waste away into powder; in this state, they truly cease to be a real metal. On the contrary, in an **enclosed** place where commerce with the air is blocked, nothing is weakened.

From these observations, we believe it is possible to comfortably understand—not only for **theory** and historical knowledge, but also for **practical** use and direction—what difference lies between **subtle fire** and that most powerful or rapid motion <note>i.e., open flame</note>, which is unknown to nature but very well known, and indeed familiar, to Art.

**XXIV.** Subterranean things consist of principles coalescing into a solid dry aggregate or into vapors that are becoming dry. Custom dictates that we call this consistency "earthy" or "powdery."

We correctly put forward this method of naming so that no dispute arises over words—something which is known to have happened to our Author <note>Becher</note> at times. Just as it is easy for prudent men to plead this cause and rely on that single wise rule of **Galen** <note>Galen was an influential Roman physician and philosopher</note>: *let us be easy with words, provided we agree on the matter*. Yet this matter seems to require a more solid confirmation under that name, lest **water from a pumice stone** <note>original: *aqua ex pumice*; a Latin proverb meaning to attempt the impossible or get something from a dry source</note> be expected from metallic and other **dry** minerals. Lest it be thought that this is a groundless fear or a random scenario, the matter occurs exactly in these terms in the writer

...he was even considered quite skilled in chemical matters—namely, **Gerhard Dorn** <note>Gerhard Dorn (c. 1530–1584) was a prominent philosopher and translator of Paracelsus; here, Becher critiques his understanding of metallurgy</note>, who held it as a certainty that metals could be **distilled**. This was based on an observation that was not necessarily bad, but certainly poorly understood: that those who smelt metals with a **vivid flame** and a free flow of air—such as the casters of bells and military cannons—often suffer a significant loss of their metallic weight if they urge their metal with **that flame** (and especially with an immoderate rush of **air**) longer than is proper. This good observer therefore attributed this to the **exhalation of metals**, as if in a watery form, and so he trusted that by skillfully applying instruments to such furnaces, the metal could be **captured or distilled**.

Truly, as pertains to those properties by which **earth** may be described, and which deserve to be ascribed to earth, we must repeat whatever we advised above regarding **elemental qualities**. In short, there is no knowledge available there other than those qualities which such substances possess in their aggregate state. Hence, concerning the **affections of earth**, we are able to comprehend nothing else except how it behaves within **aggregations** <note>In 17th-century chemistry, an "aggregation" refers to the gathering of individual particles into a solid mass or compound</note> and how it presents itself within them.

From such a perspective, that which undergoes and forms dry, solid, dense aggregations—even in a **purely homogeneous** state (meeting with no other small bodies than those of its **own single species**)—is called **earthy**.

Of such a nature are the **subterranean** bodies; absolutely the **metallic** ones and the **intermediate minerals**, but especially the mixed **saline, sulfurous, and bituminous** ones. Of these, **Metals** are certainly so plainly and absolutely dry and (with the sole exception of **quicksilver** <note>original: *argento vivo*</note>) solid, that they constitute a true model of these qualities and, in every way, most solidly represent and exhibit the **earthy nature**.

That single circumstance—that they **flow** in fire and are **flexible and malleable**—cannot detract from their **earthy** nature. For every kind of **vitrifiable earth** <note>original: *terra vitrescibilis*; earth or sand capable of being turned into glass</note> likewise **flows** in the fire and is flexible and **malleable** as long as it glows; yet, for that reason, no one would doubt its earthy lineage.

Above all, the solidly earthy nature of **metals** is proven by the fact that no **moisture** can be drawn out or demonstrated from them by any artifice, with the exception of **mercury**. Likewise, **minerals** (with the exception of salt, bitumen, and sulfur), however much they may otherwise be **mobile and volatile**, are nonetheless always found to be dry and suited for **solidifying** aggregations.

Hence, I do not think there is cause for us to offer more **in general** regarding the **earthy** constitution of **minerals**. As for what concerns **salts** in particular, which we asserted should be regarded as primarily of an **earthy** nature: certainly, their own consistency when they have solidified with **earthy substances**, their readiness to so solidify, and finally their intimate connection—indeed, their **intermixing and reduction** into earth—all testify to such an earthy lineage of salts.

-># FOUNDATIONS OF BECHER'S THEORY #<-

This can be demonstrated with an example that I am surprised did not occur to our author: **Borax**. If anyone were to deny that this solid substance is saline, they would truly not deserve an answer. However, that it is a **composite** rather than a pure **mixture**—which **Becher** himself established—is certainly easier to say than to prove. The presence of the substance of **water** is shown by its bubbling <note>Referring to the way borax expands and "boils" as it loses its water of crystallization when heated</note> and its solubility in water. Finally, the test of its **earthy** nature is demonstrated by its reduction into pure, clear **glass**.

From this specimen, I believe one can easily judge what should be thought about this **origin of salts**, which others imagine is formed from the meeting of **water and ether**. I recall a charming story about this. When a question arose regarding the **principles of salts**, one person offered the opinion that salts consist of **water and earth**. Another immediately disagreed: "Can you make salt out of **water and earth**?" When the first remained silent, the second argued at length that salts, being such subtle, agile, and penetrating substances, could not have something as coarse as **earth** as a principle. He substituted **ether and water** instead, as principles worthy of such a superlatively subtle thing. But the first man—either because he didn't believe it or because he longed to know such a subtle demonstration—immediately took up the other's objection: "But can *you* produce salt from **ether and water**?" Caught by this unexpected question, the proponent of **ether** also fell silent. Thus, both remaining fixed in their own opinions, left the practical demonstrations of their hypotheses to those more skilled, by the law of retaliation <note>original: *jure talionis*; meaning "an eye for an eye," or here, returning an unanswerable challenge with another</note>.

In this story, a distinction should have been applied between **demonstration *a priori*** and ***a posteriori*** <note>*A priori* refers to reasoning from theoretical principles, while *a posteriori* refers to reasoning from observed effects or experimental evidence</note>. For certainly, as our affairs go, it is very often absurd to argue from the inability of art to prove something *a priori* to the negation of things that are clearly evident *a posteriori*—especially in questions that lie more simply beneath us, namely, in assigning causal relationships to **experience** itself. For example, who has not known for a very long time that something exists in base metals that can be consumed by **ignition**? Who in all the metal-working shops has not been able to see, for just as long, that violent melting and the **immediate contact with coals** brings such burnt-out metals back to their metallic consistency? Who has not experienced the same thing very often with that assaying powder commonly called **the black flux** <note>original: *den schwartzen Flaß*; a chemical mixture used by metallurgists to reduce metallic ores back to their pure state</note>? Yet who among all these people has formed any rational thesis to show how a certain **material**—and indeed a most simple **inflammable principle** <note>This "inflammable principle" is the precursor to the Phlogiston theory, suggesting that fire is a physical substance that can be added back into a metal</note>—materially grows into these metallic ashes from the **charcoal** and the carbonaceous substance of **tartar**? Indeed, I say more: who has at least seriously acknowledged that in that incinerating ignition, something is truly **materially** lost from these metals, which must therefore be replaced with a similar material? From these and six hundred other things, it is easy to see how reckless that argument is which goes from a lack of an obvious practical demonstration *a priori* to the negation of the thing itself.

From these considerations, it can be sufficiently known what should be thought about the arguments for establishing an earthy nature, and how those arguments [serve] to stabilize our assertion...

# SPECIMEN OF BECHER, PART I, SECTION I #

...be sufficient; we shall not dwell on this matter at greater length: especially since some aspects of it will need to be revisited later in our author’s applications and proofs. Therefore, for the time being, we rest content with what has been said on this subject.

**XXV.** These **earthy principles** are of three species. The **first**, which is fundamental, is earthy in the strict sense <note>This is Becher's *terra lapidea* or "stony earth," providing solidity and coldness</note>; the **second**, named for its secondary effect, is the **foundation of inflammability** <note>Becher's *terra pinguis* or "fatty earth," the precursor to the later concept of Phlogiston</note>; the **third** is the principle of the most refined mobility, the **mercurial** kind <note>Becher's *terra mercurialis*, which provides weight and volatility</note>, and is otherwise of a subtle, airy-volatile nature.

In that place where our Author intends to treat of **Subterranean** things <note>referring to Becher's famous work *Physica Subterranea*</note>, it was certainly appropriate for him to be concerned—indeed, primarily concerned—with nothing other than the true nature of these solid compositions.

Since most of these substances, the more they belong to this class of natural things, are of a **dry earthy** mixture: for that reason, he spoke even more decisively regarding their principles, stating that they are **earthy**. However, he also noted the involvement of **water** in the mixtures and compositions of **salts, and those things resting on a saline foundation, as well as bitumens and sulfurs.**

Certainly, by reason of their location, no one could find fault with including water itself among the "subterraneans," if the **porous and cavernous structure of the earth** is considered; and if one simultaneously observes the evidence of preceding experience, which finds that **all the deeper subterranean places are entirely stuffed with water.** For otherwise, if the nature of the earth in relation to water were considered purely by reason of **weight** <note>meaning density</note>, without considering the **porosity of the accumulated mass**, the earth would surely be lower; it would settle at the bottom, while the waters would take their place upon its surface.

Yet this very constitution of the earth, which receives **water** so intimately into its bosom, offers at the very least this advantage for correctly performing mixtures: that the **instrumental concurrence of the fluidity of water** can exert its effect, even if it contributes nothing more intimately through a **material** concurrence to the mixture in an absolute sense.

In few words, we must entirely admit that the nature of water itself is not yet sufficiently understood—specifically, how it can concur to form even a **dry earthy** mixture. That it is capable of uniting into a **solid, dense, hard, and dry** state is demonstrated by its own simpler freezing into **ice**. That it can pass into dryness and hardness through the interposition of other drying agents, besides various kinds of **salts**, is suggested by experiments—some pointed out long ago by **Glauber** <note>Johann Rudolf Glauber (1604–1670), a famous chemist known for "Glauber's Salt"</note>, and some promoted by more recent experiment or report, **concerning a great mass of water converted into a very hard crystal by adding a tiny weight of some additive.** Certainly, such an experiment would yield to no other attempts at **metallic transmutation** <term>transmutation: the alchemical process of changing base metals into gold or changing one substance's fundamental nature</term> in terms of either curiosity or significant utility. Indeed, our Author also reports elsewhere from an account that a certain man in **England**, aware of this experience, was so confident it could be put into effect with such quantity and ease that he even promised the King **to provide squared stones from sea water and coastal sand in great abundance.**

Thus, our Author arranges those ***primordial earths*** so that, in the first place, as the true ***basis*** and the receptacle of all others—the ***womb*** and ***receiver***—he places that which, through its aggregations, forms and constitutes what is most solemnly and by the preeminent meaning of the word called ***earth and earthy***. This is the ***matter*** which, by its most abundant predominance, forms and constitutes all ***stones*** (especially transparent ones), right down to ***sand and gravel***. Experience testifies that this principle is most fundamentally suited for closer concretion—even ***aggregative*** concretion. By a very just classification, he also recognizes it as the ***first foundation of the first concretion*** for the ***mixture*** itself: since reason itself dictates that this very mixture is achieved in no other way than through this mode of ***combination***.

The second ***earthy principle***, in his view, is that which subsequently serves the composition of ***Inflammability*** <note>original: "Ignescentiæ"</note>, and thus of mixed and composite things that form and nourish ***fire***. This, I say, he places in the second position. This is primarily because it forms a copious union with most subterranean things, as well as a notable enough union with nearly ***all*** of them. In this respect, he uses a more theoretical designation, naming this substance the second principle. But in practical terms, speaking of minerals, he calls it the ***sulfurous*** principle <note>Becher's *terra pinguis* or "fatty earth," which was later renamed Phlogiston by his student Stahl</note>, because in sulfur it constitutes, as it were, the absolute whole form of such a solid body. However, in reality—which our Author, like many others, appears to have overlooked—it concurs in the base metals (***iron, tin, copper, lead, regulus of antimony, zinc, bismuth***) with no less ***essential*** necessity than it does in constituting ***sulfur*** itself. By this very fact, it abundantly marks and demonstrates its mineral, ***subterranean earth-spirit*** <note>original: "Geodem"</note> nature.

The business concerning that ***third*** principle in our Author’s count seems more perplexed than all the others; he calls it the specific matter for metals, namely of a ***strictly-speaking mercurial*** nature. In truth, however, this perplexity involves—and I believe will involve—***practice*** much more (in imitating the product of this mixture) than it does that ***theory*** of which we speak here: namely, whether it can be recognized as true that even that principle which gives metals their ***mercurial*** nature and proportionate ***softness***...

...conciliates [softness], is of an *earthy* nature and deserves to be called so? For certainly, regarding this consideration, a clear enough example of this matter is provided by *running Mercury* itself <note>original: "Mercurii currentis"; refers to liquid quicksilver</note> (in which this principle abounds), which possesses a true and strictly defined dryness. Even more so, the metals—most absolutely free of humidity—certainly possess a unique and, as it were, intrinsic nature that is utterly alien to moisture. I believe no one will deny that dryness, especially in a solid or at least heavy and ponderous aggregation, is a property of *earth* rather than any other elemental disposition.

Furthermore, this third principle <note>The "mercurial earth," which Becher believed gave metals their weight and liquidity</note>, by its exquisite *fineness*, among the other principles of similar general properties (by which *earthiness* is judged), comes very close to *watery tenderness*. This can be inferred from its effect of *fluidity*, as well as from the tradition upheld with one voice by the proponents of the *Alkahest* <note>The hypothetical "universal solvent" sought by alchemists to break substances down to their primary matter</note> liquor—or rather, as if from a single mouth—that this liquor is finally so subdued by water, as its equal, that it refuses to be separated from it any longer.

Whether this principle should be sought more in water than in fire is a question not yet suitable for the present discussion. Our Author [Becher] sought it, or rather found it, in *salt*. He perceived, or judged more and more, that it lies hidden not so much in the *saline* part, but in a certain *sulphurous* part of the salt (perhaps not without reason so named), which he therefore thinks should be called the *sulfur of salt* <note>original: "sulphur salis"</note>. With the same view, if we are not mistaken, he attributes far more to volatile salts—of *urine, soot, vinegar*, etc.—wherever he presents more *practical* matters on this subject, than to pure and bare *common salt*.

In the ignoble and more imperfectly mixed metals, one might not know how to distinguish the yield or the consistency within the mixture itself, as well as the various outcomes—such as ductility <note>The ability of a metal to be drawn into wire or hammered thin</note>, which depends solely on the addition of this principle—from the substance of the *second principle, the sulphurous phlogiston* <term>phlogiston: the hypothetical principle of fire or inflammability</term>, so that they do not seem to be either one and the same thing, or at least, by our current techniques, something inseparable. But about these things, we shall speak in another place.

->XXVI. Water now enters degraded minerals, or renders them degraded.<-

We call "degraded" <note>original: "degenera"; here meaning changed from its original mineral genus or diverged into a different form</note> minerals like *salt, bitumen*, and even *sulfur* itself. This is mostly because *salt* occurs in the mineral kingdom in only one or at most two types, whereas in the *vegetable and animal* kingdoms, it admits various differences. And yet, beyond all controversy, it is transferred into these two kingdoms from the *earthy* subterranean realm; thus, as we said, it migrates or "degrades" from a mineral nature into a vegetable and animal one.

Certainly, since *salts*, in this consistency by which they retain their *mixture* with water, do not enter the composition of any other subterranean species (except for *bitumen, sulfur, and arsenic*), yet they enter into almost any of the most delicate and specific compositions of *vegetables*—and hence *animals*—and are clearly *essentially* required for them: we assert with the best right that *Salt*, insofar as it is such and must *remain* so, is more suited to other kinds of mixtures than to the mineral realm alone.

### THE FOUNDATIONS OF BECHER'S THEORY

Meanwhile, it is consistent with reason and well-known through common experience that earths—and especially that very first mineral earth <note>Becher's "stony earth" or *terra lapidea*, the principle of solidity</note>—can pass from a saline mixture and form (which they may have entered with water) into more purely earthy underground mixtures. For although I do not recall reading a sufficiently distinct note in any chemist, nor even in our author [Becher] himself, on how *salts* are *reduced into earth* by daily experiment; nevertheless, the experiment is in fact *most simple* (as often happens more than once in such matters), as we shall demonstrate in its proper place. Meanwhile, anyone wishing to remember this can do so by recalling the event where vegetable salts <note>original: "vegetabilia salia"; refers to alkalis like potash derived from plant matter</note> crumble into bare and simple earth, returning by this very act to that principle from which we asserted they drew their origin: namely, bare earth.

Whenever the *primordial earths of minerals* also advance toward subterranean mixtures by means of a saline mixture, they must then lose the saline mixture again and release their *watery* portion. Since water can never coalesce into a saline mixture with earths of this kind unless they are well refined and reduced from their aggregations to a *numerical simplicity* <note>original: "simplicitatem numericam"; a technical term in 17th-century chemistry referring to the most basic, indivisible units or "atoms" of matter</note>, it happens by this very fact that under such simplicity—by which they were able to undergo mixture with water—they become all the more fit to undertake other mixtures again. Indeed, a state disposed toward mixture involves *numerical simplicity*, as was mentioned above.

There is no small proof of this very thing in the fact that salts so readily establish a meeting and a cohesion of some kind with other corpuscles of a more purely earthy nature, associating and fixing themselves to them. Indeed, the prompt meeting, intertwining, and cohesion of salts with *earths* does not occur because of the *watery* portion of the salts (as it seems easy to believe according to a superficial concept). This is shown by the *dulling* of the taste and of all *sharp* activity when they have grown together with earths. For just as no one would easily attribute the sharpness of salts to their wateriness; so indeed, if the earths that usually grow onto salts were to coalesce directly with their *watery* portion, that other portion—which is the author of the penetrating *acrimony* <note>original: "acrimoniæ"; the biting, corrosive quality of salts and acids</note>—ought to remain unimpaired. But since this is not the case, the direct conclusion is easy.

This becomes all the more evident from the fact that not only do earths joined to salts dull their remaining taste and sharpness (for it could be supposed that an earthy molecule, placed upon the watery portion of the salts, might so entangle and hinder this wateriness that it could only affect that other part—namely, its original *saline* portion—with much slower movement); but an equal effect occurs even when *caustic salts*—I mean the sharpest <term>alkalis</term> <note>Strong bases that react with acids</note>—are joined with the most violent corrosive acids, as is well known. In this way, unless the remaining substance of the salts itself (aside from the *watery* part), coalescing together, were to entangle and weigh itself down,
