...it would blunt it; indeed, the water ought to retain that caustic sharpness at least on one side or the other: none of which, however, happens.

Furthermore, as to the specific reason and method by which this might succeed more easily or successfully—so that the bond between earth and water (which we assert the salt mixture provides) may be severed again—although we do not yet judge it timely to present a full explanation of that business here; we can nevertheless demonstrate in general that, even in the mineral kingdom, this appears to occur primarily through the association of sulfurous or **inflammable matter**.

Certainly, that experiment deserves closer consideration, in which I have shown at greater length that mineral sulfur can be both destroyed and restored by art <note>The author, Georg Ernst Stahl, refers here to his own chemical experiments proving that sulfur is a compound of sulfuric acid and "phlogiston."</note>, partly in *Zymotechnia* page 117, and partly in my own treatise in the *Monthly Sketches for July 1697*. For in this act of mixing, the **inflammable principle** joined to the acid mineral salt immediately causes this salt to spurn any commerce with water, and to mix itself with metals and other earthy bodies in a far different manner than it could previously under its bare saline form. For it is known to everyone that common sulfur, which is formed from such a salt in this way, admits no commerce with water. Various experiments likewise testify how easily—indeed, how most intimately—it joins with all metals, and even with gold more than with any other (if we except *tin* and the *Regulus of Antimony* <note>original: "Regulum Antimonii"; refers to the pure metallic form of antimony</note>), to such an extent that some of these are notably altered even by bare contact when cold; meanwhile, that salt from which the sulfur was thus constructed could hardly touch even the smallest part of them.

From these circumstances it clearly becomes evident how the sulfurous principle, through this bare and hurried combination, not only largely alienates the earthy substance of the mineral salt from that inclined fellowship with water, but also, on the contrary, renders it all the more fit for a readier application to other substances of an earthy nature, the more it has shaken off the predominance of water from it.

It is a matter of another chapter how [the sulfurous principle] also breaks up this same earthy substance of the mineral salt, or blunts it by its interposition (*that is, according to mechanical concepts, it either affects or occupies and envelops its sides and angles with an unequal, curved, or rounder figure*) so that it loses not only all saline taste and all corrosiveness (which it previously displayed as entirely caustic), but also now barely clings even in passing to a fixed alkali salt, with which it had previously entered into an intimate fellowship—separable again by hardly any other art except this single reduction into sulfur.

However much this ***phlogiston*** <note>The "fire principle" or inflammable substance hypothesized by Stahl to explain combustion and calcination.</note> or sulfurous principle embraces the earthy element of salt so as to greatly diminish its familiarity with water by that very act, it does not, however, remove the entire watery mixture with the salt all at once: for the mixture of that mineral salt remains intact within the mixture of sulfur itself.

# FUNDAMENTALS OF BECHER'S THEORY
<meta>catchword: Sulphur-</meta>

We cite this account for this reason alone: so that it becomes clear, at the very least, how that *phlogiston principle* <note>original: "principium Φλογίστος"; the "inflammable principle" hypothesized to be the essence of fire and combustion</note>, by its very first union with this salt, traps the watery part of the salt within such narrow bounds that it is no longer permitted any commerce with other small bodies of its own kind—that is, with watery aggregates. From this, the conclusion is all the more justified that this principle, through its further intervention and stirred-up action, will eventually cast out water from the entire mixture. Experience confirms this exactly, in accordance with this reasoning.

Just as this very principle, by its gathering together, can exert force upon the *mixture* of water with the *first-order earth* <note>original: "terra primo prima"; in Becher's system, this is "terra lapidea" or stony earth, the principle of solidity and vitrification</note>; so, meanwhile, it is fitting to marvel at that "Circle," the symbol of the Eternity of Motions, by which all things revolve from the same source, through a circuit, back into the same.

For in this way, this very *watery mixture*, once it has reduced that *first-order earth into salt*, proceeds by the usual progress of nature into even further *compositions*, or at the very least, *mixtures*. From this is formed both that saline substance of *vegetables* which they commonly call *essential* salts—which in some places is of a *nitrous* <note>related to saltpeter</note> nature and in others a *muriatic* <note>related to sea salt or brine</note> nature—as well as *nitre* itself, and *marine* or common kitchen salt. Under these forms, it proceeds further to even more subtle *saline-oily* mixtures: some somewhat *fixed*, as in the *tartar of wine and vinegar*; some *intermediate*, as in the substance of wine and vinegar (especially in *distilled vinegar*); and finally, *volatile* forms. Such are found in *urinous* volatile substances <note>likely referring to ammonia-based salts derived from organic matter</note>, as well as in *fats, resins, and distillable oils*. From these things, at last, it returns to its ancient simplicity; from the watery mixture—from the saline consistency, I say—it returns to a terrestrial simplicity, so much so that it yields not only *earth*, but even, depending on the variety of circumstances, *manifest sand*. This will be deduced at greater length below.

But for our present treatment, it will suffice to have shown how water causes mineral earth to change its nature <note>original: "degenerare," literally to deviate from its type or degenerate</note> into a substance materially suited for other kingdoms. Indeed, if the scope of our project permitted it, we could explain by the same effort how the *saline* structure serves as the primary material not only for *vegetables* but also for *animals*. From this structure, through the mediation of *sulfurous* substance, the earthy consistency is again freed from its *bond* with wateriness, providing these bodies with their entire "hypostasis" <note>original: "Hypostasin"; the underlying substance or essential foundation</note>—which is found joined together in the bodies of immense trees and the bodies of *elephants and whales*, forming masses that are more like mountains than mere bulks.

For just as I established the thesis above—departing from our Author <note>Becher</note> himself, though not without pregnant reasons—that the essential *earths* of *vegetables* and *animals* derive their origin from *earth strictly so-called* <note>mineral earth</note>, together with their *subterranean* mother; and they are distinguished from that mineral earth more by the *rearrangements* <note>original: "μεταχηματισμοῖς" (metaschēmatismois); transformations or changes in outward form/structure</note> of their mixtures than by any difference in their own absolute essence (as if they were something different, unfit for *subterranean* mixture and destined only for those other kingdoms). This is proven all the more by the reduction of those mixtures back into simple *earths*, which, being sometimes of a *glassy* and sometimes of a *limy* nature, are equal to minerals. Indeed, when their substance catches fire, immediately and directly, they pro—

# SPECIMEN OF BECHER, PART I, SECTION I.
<meta>catchword: [princi]-ple</meta>

...for constructing mineral sulfur, or for restoring *metals* to their whole state, they provide an absolutely suitable material; that is, of the kind that is appropriate for *subterranean* mixing.

Hence, in truth, the reduction of this *first earth* <note>original: "primæ... terræ"; in Becher's system, this is "terra lapidea" or stony earth, which provides substances with their solidity and ability to melt into glass</note>, strictly speaking—from a degenerate saline mixture back into its own proper terrestrial nature—is somewhat more laborious and not so easily seen by everyone. Certainly, it does not strike them as if by itself, even though in fact it exists as the foundation of immense daily use and the object of the most common practice. Rather, it is neglected, and consequently, its true method—and the clear demonstration resulting from it—is not understood. On the other hand, the reduction of the *second earth* (the predominant one) or the *inflammable* Principle <note>original: "Principio ignescibilis"; Becher's "terra pinguis" or fatty earth, which Stahl famously renamed <term>phlogiston</term></note> is far more obvious. This involves taking it from this degenerate watery mixture and returning it to a state that is immediately suitable again for mineral mixing. Indeed, from any highly volatile distilled oil, the *wateriness mixed in until now* is driven out in the blink of an eye, so that the oil is seen reduced into a dry, very fixed earth, which at that same moment most readily enters into the *mixture* of either *sulfur* or one of the baser *metals*. Even though this *matter of the second Principle* can pass immediately from its fluid consistency into a metallic mixture, it does so not only as a dry substance, but specifically (in its more absolute and simple nature) by immediately applying it, at least in the form of a pure fluid fatness, as it is at hand.

Here, certainly—unless men were ashamed of such things—there would be room to note with most justified contempt those who accuse me of a pursuit of empty glory because I may have said at some point that I was perhaps the first to apply my mind to these matters. I say this because, even today, I am not aware of anyone else who can be seen to have done so. Yet, if you look at the core of <term>Physico-Chemical</term> <note>Stahl's term for a science that combines physical laws of matter with the experimental observations of chemistry</note> demonstrations, this matter surely ought to have been more frequently discussed. Meanwhile, whatever grief this causes their hearts, the judgment of good men will surely remain for some time as to whether it is true or not that I was the first, or certainly among the first, to note and record the truth of this matter: namely, how and in what way principles from the other two kingdoms <note>the vegetable and animal kingdoms, as opposed to the mineral kingdom</note> are reduced to a mineral character, and most readily of all, that <term>phlogiston</term> of which we have just spoken.

But even if neither glory nor profit should return to me from this, nevertheless, until *someone else is pointed out as having said it before me*, I shall certainly be the first for the time being to have stated the things pertaining to this: Namely: 
1.) That the terrestrial inflammable substance, which together with a watery mixture constitutes the most volatile oils, can be separated from that mixture and presented and collected in a moment in a dry, solid, and fixed consistency. 
2.) That it can immediately thereafter be reduced into a mineral and metallic mixture. 
3.) Indeed, that it can be directly taken from its own mixture and transformed into a metallic state. 
4.) And that the experiments proving these things, though very common, have nonetheless been *properly understood and explained* by no one until now. 
5.) Least of all by those who set out to treat and demonstrate these things scientifically. 
6.) That salts, too, from their mixture with water, are reduced to earth.

# FUNDAMENTALS OF BECHER'S THEORY

...especially the sulfurous or inflammable principle; and 8.) In which most common manuals this occurs every day.

From these foundations, I have explained in the Dissertation held on this subject how most operations of both *fire-based metallurgy* and *metallic assaying* <note>The art of testing ores and metals to determine their composition and purity.</note> arise. Whether I did this before or after others, or whether I demanded that these be considered my own great inventions—worthy of special praise—I leave freely to be judged by all truthful and honest men.

But whether these matters (by whomever they are brought forth) are not only suitable but *necessary* for scientific development and theoretical demonstrations, as well as for practical uses, is not a judgment that can or should belong to just anyone. It is fitting to entrust that decision to the judgment of upright, skilled, and learned men—provided these facts are arranged rightly and in order, under their proper connections, and with the supporting evidence of joint experiments and their effects. From such theories, practical uses can be promptly and skillfully gathered and practiced with certainty of results.

### XXVIII. 

The nature of the third principle <note>original: "Tertii principii"; in Becher's system, this is the *terra mercurialis* or "mercurial earth," which was thought to give metals their weight, shine, and ability to be hammered (malleability).</note> is more obscure. This is due to a justified concealment—indeed, a difficulty—of sufficient artificial experiments, and a scarcity, or rather a total lack, of natural ones.

I wish to plead this lengthy case in a few words. *I blame the scarcity of natural observations* because the yield of mercury throughout the entire world is the rarest and most meager compared to any other metals. I argue there is a *lack* [of information] because those who could perhaps investigate these things more curiously, or who would certainly wish to try, seem to have always hesitated to travel to those places where mercury is born. They hesitate to spend their lives there, to devote time to this matter, and to be freely admitted to more skilled and deeper scrutinies. I do not know if they even considered the effort worthwhile, perhaps due to significant public or private reasons; I remember nothing worthy of mention being attempted or noted by anyone concerning this business. Therefore, since the resources for curious investigation are failing, I believe much must certainly be attributed here [to theoretical reasoning].

As for the fact that artificial experiments are difficult, I can bring forward witnesses: men famously accustomed to experiments—not merely in the mind, but in the laboratory—trained and skilled, such as *Glauber* <note>Johann Rudolf Glauber (1604–1670), a famous German-Dutch alchemist and apothecary known for "Glauber's salt."</note>, *Kunckel* <note>Johann von Löwenstern-Kunckel (1630–1703), a chemist who worked on glass-making and phosphorus.</note>, and *Cassius* <note>Andreas Cassius (1605–1673), known for "Purple of Cassius," a pigment made from gold.</note> *(in his treatise on gold)*, as well as other learned and literate men who have also professed the doctrine of all *chemistry*. The former group speaks much of the difficulty of such experiments. The latter group declares them so difficult that they pronounce them absolutely null and false, asserting they are naked impostures, *boastful vauntings, and lies* <note>original: "thrasonicas gloriationes, & mendacia esse"; "Thrasonic" refers to Thraso, a boastful soldier in Roman comedy.</note>.

But indeed, no one would deny that there is a justified concealment even of those experiments of this kind that remain, if they were to admit—at least for a moment and only by hypothesis—that mercury, once drawn out from the more imperfect metals, can soon pass into a more noble metal. Just as it is right to acknowledge from first principles, rather than by simple faith, that certainly, if any reduction of base metals into a *mercurial* state is granted...

...it must, more certainly than certain, either expel, or blunt, soften, and soothe their styptic <term>styptic: astringent or contracting, here referring to the harsh, brittle nature of unrefined minerals</term>, inflammable, and quickly vitrifying <note>The tendency of minerals to turn into glass or slag during smelting rather than remaining metallic.</note> earths. We also predict he will be accused of hatred, idleness, trifling occupations, and sterile intentions and inventions. Nay, we even fear for the peril of his entire reputation, honesty, liberty, noble character, body, life, and—may God forbid—his very soul. We urge him to take care, lest these misfortunes seem to have befallen him with any shadow of justice.

### OF THE BECHERIAN SPECIMEN

### PART I.

### SECT. II.

### THE EVIDENCE FOR THE BECHERIAN THEORY.

Although in the preceding section I have already produced various points—and perhaps even the majority—that might serve to establish the foundations of Becher’s *Subterranean Physics*, it does not seem foreign to our purpose, nor will it be troublesome to you, the reader and lover of sound philosophy, if those matters that were perhaps already touched upon are revisited under a different framework of application. Indeed, it is even more important that those elements which have not yet been brought in to support our argument should likewise be put to use.

For it must certainly be noted—and firmly assumed regarding our author’s <note>Johann Joachim Becher (1635–1682), the German physician and alchemist whose theories Stahl is expanding upon.</note> labors—that his intention was to organize a "Subterranean Physics." By this, he meant a scientific explanation <note>original: "evolutionem," here meaning an unfolding or detailed explanation.</note> of those things which are found partly by natural occurrence in the underground kingdom, and partly performed through artificial experiments and practical work upon materials of this category.

For a study is only truly scientific if the circumstances of subterranean things—the materials from which they bond together, the manner and movement of that bonding, and their various respective properties regarding both their formation <term>concretion: the process of substances growing together or solidifying into a mass</term> and their breaking down <term>dissolution: the process of a solid substance dissolving or being decomposed into its parts</term>—are sought from their most direct, real, and true foundations, and through experiments that correspond to practical experience. These things must be deduced in order: from simplicity to mixtures and compositions, and conversely, from these back to their basic components <note>original: "resolutiones," the chemical process of reducing a compound to its constituent parts.</note>.

### SPECIMEN OF THE BECHERIAN THEORY, PART I. SECTION II.

...progress into a simpler state might be revealed; and finally, that the various uses of these things and operations—both everyday and more specialized—might be demonstrated.

Various experiments have certainly lain not only before our eyes, but almost here and there under our very feet—both in *mining workshops* and *laboratories*, as they are called by the chemists; indeed, even in the workshops of artists and various *craftsmen* who use *subterranean* products to refine their works. But what *scientific arrangement* <note>original: "syntaxis scientifica," referring to a systematic, theoretical framework</note> has been drawn from them so far? Who has demonstrated anything from this? To what further use—physical, metallurgical, civil, or even chemical—have such older experiments been adapted? I would rather ask this question than answer it.

Indeed, the prior age has seen, and the future will see, various—nay, almost all—chemical experiments arising from the handling of subterranean materials being claimed for *Medicine*. They are celebrated through every superlative and hyperbole of *admirable virtue and stupending efficacy*, and with <unclear>mysterious silences</unclear> <note>original: "ἀποσιώπησες" (aposiopeses), a rhetorical device where one stops speaking suddenly; here suggesting alchemical secrecy.</note> regarding their secret effects. I, in my own order, gave my opinion in the preface of December, and there were those who followed it completely. But truly, no man, unless he is entirely ignorant, can fail to know that no benefit for *chemical and physical science* flows from such commentaries or recommendations. *Those who dare to boast about the arts do not make them great, but rather those who can discover what is really in each of them.* <note>original Greek: "Οὐ μεγάλας ποιεῖσι τὰς τέχνας οἱ τολμῶντες ἀλαζονεύεσθαι περὶ αὐτῶν, ἀλλ᾽ οἵτινες ἂν ὅσον ἔνεσιν ἐν ἑκάστῃ, τοῦτο ἐξευρεῖν δύνανται."</note> Isocrates, *Against the Sophists*. Quite right.

Lest this whole preface of ours be thought similar to a "battle of the Andabatae" <note>Gladiators who fought with closed helmets, essentially fighting blind.</note>, where one fights against shadows with blind effort and exertion, I shall illustrate the matter with an example.

I described in my *Treatise on the Foundations of Fermentation* <note>original: "tract. de Zymotechniæ fundamentis," published by Stahl in 1697.</note> (page 117) an experiment showing how true sulfur, such as is found in the bowels of the earth, can be produced *by art* <note>i.e., through human chemical intervention rather than natural geological processes.</note>. I thought the matter, as it is indeed most simply simple, was so plain that it would be exposed more to contempt (such is the pride of men) than to controversy. Yet a controversy was stirred. I shall say nothing of the manner in which it was stirred. However, *three* principal propositions came into dispute. *First*, that I was not the first to say this; *Second*, that the whole business does not proceed from the materials that I require and assume; *Third*, that the sulfur produced in this way is by no means true sulfur, homogeneous with the mineral kind.

The *first* assertion was confirmed by the fact that a certain famous man <note>likely a reference to older chemists like Robert Boyle or Johann Glauber</note>, already ten years ago in some noted treatise, had said that sulfur consists of an acid and a fatty matter.

The *second* was proved from the fact that even pure alkali—namely, *potash* <note>original: "cineres clavellati," literally "clubbed ashes," a high-grade potassium carbonate used in glass and soap making.</note>—assumes a similar color, smell, and taste, whereby that *acid* which I assume would have no need or use.

The *third* was given a plausible appearance because the sulfur thus born or produced: 1.) does not precipitate in the form of *milk of sulfur* <note>a fine, white powder of sulfur produced by precipitation from a solution.</note>. 2.) does not burn. 3.) does not smell or breathe out an acid like true sulfur. 4.) does not blacken silver.

<meta>This page continues Georg Ernst Stahl’s defense of Johann Joachim Becher’s chemical theories. ->### DOCUMENTATION OF BECHERIAN THEORY<-

The month of July reveals how I publicly responded to all these objections, as they were being made publicly. First and foremost, the allegation that someone else had already said the same thing many years ago was completely unfounded. For when the specific passage was inspected, nothing else appeared there except a citation of **Boyle**, who demonstrated by experiment (using Oil of Vitriol and turpentine <note>original: "Oleo vitrioli & terebinthinae." Oil of Vitriol is concentrated sulfuric acid.</note>) that sulfur consists of an acid and a fatty substance <note>original: "pingui," referring to the combustible principle later known as phlogiston</note>. I myself had also cited this same experiment of **Boyle’s** with equal faithfulness. But this was not *that experiment of mine* over which the controversy had been raised. Indeed, even country folk have believed since time immemorial that in sulfur there is an *acid*, obvious to *smell and taste*, and an *inflammable matter*, obvious to *sight and touch*—and even to *hearing* in the case of explosions—and thus its principles are to be grasped by all five senses.

Now, if this whole doubt could have been investigated properly and in order, it certainly should have been framed this way: *Has this experiment—of producing true sulfur so very promptly from the simplest materials proposed by me—already been handed down by anyone else, in these terms, from these materials, and in this way of proceeding? Does it succeed? Is it true sulfur? Does it burn? Does it blacken silver? Does it contain an acid?* No one could doubt these things, since they all ought to be discovered not by debate, but by the help of experiment. Hence, even when the experiments did not succeed through their own attempts (due to some defect I know not what), I myself finally settled the whole dispute regarding the truth of the fact by demonstrating with my own hands: 1.) that from the acid of vitriol, joined with alkaline salt and charcoal, there is born what they call <term>Hepar sulphuris</term> <note>literally "Liver of Sulfur"; a mixture of potassium polysulfides named for its liver-like color</note>; 2.) that this, dissolved in water into the consistency of a *yellow liquor*, is precipitated through a narrow space into <term>lac sulphuris</term> <note>literally "Milk of Sulfur"; a fine, white precipitated sulfur</note>; 3.) that this *Liver*, when nitre <note>saltpeter</note> is added, flashes, and is therefore *truly burning* sulfur; 4.) that when brought into contact with silver, it *immediately and deeply blackens it*; 5.) that while commercial potash <note>original: "cineres clavellati"</note> does this same thing, it does not do so because of its *alkaline* part; 6.) since *calcined tartar, fresh salt of tartar, extemporaneous salt of tartar* (prepared with nitre), and even nitre fixed with charcoal itself, achieve none of these things—which was thrust before their eyes by experiments performed on the spot.

Thus, so much labor was truly necessary so that even those who objected that these experiments had already been handed down and worn out years ago might finally (after contentious, not to say scandalous, methods of contradicting me, since this entire matter absolutely did not concern them) have it thrust upon their senses: how, and to what extent, these experiments are both true and depend upon one another, and how they reciprocally agree. From these experiments, when mutually subordinated in the proper order, there results a true and certain scientific demonstration: that is, it establishes the underlying reasons for the experiments.

I shall add yet another example of this kind. In the month of April, 1598 <note>This date is likely a typographical error for 1698, as Stahl was active in the late 17th century</note>, I brought forward an experiment showing how, by means of common commercial sulfur joined with potash, raw and pure gold is *not only dissolved in an instant into a lime* <note>original: "calcem," a powder or metallic oxide</note>; but also a good part of it is so intimately and subtly joined to the sulfur that *it is not only dissolved with the sulfur in water, but also passes through a filter, and falls to the bottom with it through precipitation*. And not only this, but it is also altered in its color by the now-bare sulfur and tends toward blackness.

# SPECIMEN BECHERIANUM PART I. SECTION II.

I would like to be shown—for no other reason than pure and simple curiosity—any chemical writer who has not only handed down but actually *believed* this proposition, or rather these propositions, in these exact terms. On the contrary, one could hardly be called a novice in chemistry who does not know that all chemists, with one voice, absolutely exclude gold from any interaction or attack by common sulfur. <note>In traditional alchemy, gold was considered a "noble" metal that resisted the corrosive effects of common sulfur, which usually only tainted base metals.</note>

Truly, after I had proposed this publicly, the same proposition was published shortly thereafter: that common sulfur dissolves gold in flux, provided it is first bound by an alkali so that it can tolerate the fire for a time; and it was added that this is done according to the "most well-known method" of **Monschnider** and **Glauber**. <note>Johann Rudolf Glauber (1604–1670) was one of the most famous chemists of the 17th century, known for his "sal mirabile" or Glauber’s Salt.</note>

To adapt the matter to our purpose, the question must be: who, in the terms of my proposition and this repeated one, has ever not only proposed this experiment, but also explained, deduced, and emphasized the way of doing and making it—I will not say merely hinted that they knew and understood it—but simply *believed* it?

Here it is called the *most well-known method*. Therefore, all chemists must have been most ignorant, for they never paid attention to a "most well-known" thing before it was forced upon them—especially since it has not been possible, until now, to find this theory or practice (which is now, by a favorable wind, becoming common and well-known) in a single one of them.

However, lest I stir up ill will while I charge chemists with being ignorant of "most well-known" things, my conscience compels me to count myself among them in sincere good faith. For just as in all my life I have never heard of a certain **Monschnider** by report, much less heard or seen if he wrote anything similar, so I never believed—and cannot bring myself to believe today until it is shown to my eyes (which I can demand by the law of retaliation <note>original: "jure talionis," the principle of "an eye for an eye," implying a fair demand for proof in exchange for his own work.</note>)—that this method could be known, let alone "most well-known," from **Glauber**.

Indeed, I certainly know that **Glauber** taught—or rather, almost unwillingly betrayed—how to calcine <term>To reduce a metal to a powder (oxide) by heating it.</term> and dissolve gold using *sal mirabile* <term>Sodium sulfate, still known as Glauber’s Salt.</term> and charcoal (though he hides it everywhere under the fugitive silence <note>original: "ἀποσιώπησι" (aposiopesis), a rhetorical device where one stops speaking to leave a thought unfinished, often used to imply a "secret" in alchemical texts.</note> of a "great secret"). But it is impossible that this "most well-known" method of **Glauber** is the one by which sulfur is fixed and gold is then calcined through it. Indeed, I can produce letters signed by his own hand which profess that the sulfur produced by my and **Glauber's** method is so unknown that they reject it and refuse to recognize it, even concluding with these words: *"I would consider the author of such an elegant and [most ...?] experiment to be held in high regard by the entire learned world if, by this (our) art, I could establish a true, burning, acid-breathing sulfur that blackens silver."* I rejected this sterile praise and sent it back to its source, commending only Experience—which was so far from knowing or being able to do this thing (now supposedly "most well-known") that it finally required my own manual labor to demonstrate it to their eyes.

As for the rest, if **Monte-Snyder** <note>Johannes de Monte-Snyder, a 17th-century alchemist known for his work on the transmutation of metals.</note>—cited by me with my usual and, until now, solid faith—is supposed to be that **Mon-** or whatever-**Snyder**, I would certainly [continue]...

### THEORETICAL DOCUMENTATION OF BECHER

Even among the most ignorant, I would have known from all of his printed papers this *most well-known* method of his: calcining pure and naked gold using sulfur fixed with alkali. <note>Calcination refers to the process of heating a substance to high temperatures in air to change its chemical state, often turning a metal into a powdery oxide.</note> For just as he—who is not "lunatic" <note>A play on the word *lunaticus*, suggesting someone influenced by the moon, often used to mean mad or foolish.</note> but a "man of the mountain," **Snyder** <note>Johannes de Monte-Snyder (c. 1625–1670) was a famous alchemist. Stahl is punning on his name: "Monte" (Mountain) and "Snyder" (Tailor). The German text calls him "an ill-fated... called Schneider’s Mountain."</note>—wants to appear wiser in much higher matters than these well-known things: so too, those experienced in the craft not only know, but must truly understand, that his tradition in this simple genus frustrates all good hope. This is evident to anyone who has perceived even the lightest foundations of practical chemistry; for this reason, he *necessarily ensures that it does not succeed*. Indeed, following Monte-Snyder’s mind and will, the *solution of gold is, as he supposes, so intimately, absolutely vain and false*; this can be demonstrated immediately, not with words, but with *facts and reasons* that become very clear after the fact.

From these examples—setting aside all moral respect for what might drive me to repeatedly claim my little works as my own, since they belong to no one else—it can become clear what the difference is between a bare and crude practical knowledge of an experiment (even the skill of performing it) and the true understanding of it, which relies on many other experiments, observations, and *rational comparisons*. To be sure, learning experiments—or even bringing them to actual effect, which is quite rare—is something; but it is more a work of *memory* than of any *judgment*. However, to collect and understand what happens more intimately beneath those things from many such experiments is absolutely an object of *judgment*. Because we have the documents at hand to approach and establish this, we shall give documentation of this matter as well.

Among the *imperfect* metallic bodies <note>In alchemy, "imperfect" metals were base metals like iron, lead, and tin, as opposed to "perfect" metals like gold and silver.</note>, when fire *and air* run together freely, something is burned away, so that they collapse, as it were, into ashes. Ordinary *blacksmiths, coppersmiths, and tinsmiths* complain of this, as do those craftsmen of tin buttons for fastening clothes—*the button-makers*. From this comes *iron scale* <note>original: "Hammerschlag"</note>; *copper ash* <note>original: "Kupffer-Asche"</note>; and *tin ash* <note>original: "Zinn-Asche"</note>; as well as *lead ash*, as known by the *shot-casters* <note>original: "Schrot Giessern," makers of lead pellets or shot.</note>.

All who deal even slightly with these metals know this fact. But as to where it originates, *what it is and of what kind*, what it is that thus *departs* from the metals, and how it is to be either prevented from happening or restored—this is so far from being established by the judgment of craftsmen (excepting, however, those more skilled with some judgment), that not even among the *learned* is there agreement on these considerations. Consequently, some wander from the truth and diversity of the experiments themselves while they confuse ores with metals already restored to their own homogeneity. Others recognize common sulfur even in pure and workable metals; they argue its acidity is either produced by fire, or changed into acidity by fire (for here they vary again), or introduced by fire as an acid, fixed in the pores of the metal, which then pulls it apart or holds it back until it is saturated now by an alkaline salt, now by a "cinerary earth," <note>An earthy residue or ash used in chemical separation.</note> or simply until its sharp points are blunted by "fatness," <note>A reference to "phlogiston" or the "inflammable principle" which Becher and Stahl championed as a "fatty earth" (terra pinguis).</note> so that the metal can again come together in its consistency. Meanwhile, this opinion, which might occur to a simpler judgment in one or two experiments inspected in passing, is restrained by more...

### SECTION II.
## CHAPTER I.
### PROPOSITION I.
# UNDERGROUND MATTERS ARE OF AN EARTHY NATURE.
->Proofs of the earthy nature of underground things.<-

Various proofs are available to show that no kind of subterranean body exists that does not participate greatly in the nature of earth. Among these, the first that deserves to be mentioned is that very *true and real distinction between earths and waters, by reason of their entire location and site*, about which we have already put forward some points above. *For thus:*

(1.) If *earths were condensed by the more solid aggregations that were more proper to them, water would certainly be absolutely excluded from the category of subterranean things. For indeed, earth would occupy the lower position so absolutely, and water the upper, that nothing would be subterranean at all.* <note>Becher is arguing that if earth and water were perfectly separated by density, water would only exist above ground, and the "subterranean" world would be entirely solid earth.</note>

# THE FUNDAMENTALS OF BECHER'S THEORY

(2.) Furthermore, since all **subterranean** materials (and for the most part, **absolutely** so) are not only **dry**, but also **dense, solid, and hard** in their physical aggregation—properties which properly define an **earthy nature**—it becomes even more evident from this that **subterranean** things belong to the **earthy tribe**, as they share this same nature.

(3.) Their **dry** nature is not diminished by (α) **softness**, which leans toward fluidity; nor by **fluidity** itself, which most things acquire through the agitation of fire. This fluidity is even visible without **fire**, indeed in the midst of **cold**, in one specific substance: **quicksilver** <note>original: "argento vivo"; mercury</note>. Nor is it diminished by (β) that type of **adhesion** that mimics **moisture**, by which **molten glass** or **molten sulfur** stick to various harder objects. **Quicksilver**, however, does not attach itself to anything except certain bodies—specifically metals—in the same way that water is accustomed to attach to **all** bodies. In this same way, **tin** fixes itself to **iron and copper**; even **gold and silver** attach themselves to that same **copper**. The entire difference is resolved by the distinction between **fluid** and **moist** <term>fluid vs. moist</term> <note>The author distinguishes between "fluids" (things that flow, like molten metal or mercury) and "moist" things (liquids like water that wet and penetrate surfaces).</note>.

(4.) Indeed, although water itself—whose most **essential** property is **moisture**, or **moist penetration** and **adhesion**—appears to be brought into this state by heat, it should rather be called **dry** than **moist** when heat is absent. **Ice** provides the evidence for this. Thus, it is permissible to interpret that there is no **specific** difference between **water and earths**, or those **soft and mobile subterranean** materials, but only a **gradual** one. Nevertheless, according to the accepted **usage** of speech in these matters based on prior **naming**, those things ought to be called **dry** (α) which are not brought to that subtle penetration we call **wetting** <note>original: "madefactionem"</note> except by intense **fiery** motion. On the other hand, those things are called **moist** which reach this effect with lighter heat—indeed, heat that is scarcely noticeable to us. Furthermore, (β) those things which, under the lightest or even no usual heat, nonetheless imitate wetting, are distinguished from truly **moist** things by the fact that they only perform this with a very few things related to themselves. Conversely, things called **moist** in a more **absolute** sense do this with all other things. Thus, in the first sense, all **metals and glasses**, and even for the most part **sulfur** itself, are excluded from "moisture" strictly defined. In the latter respect, **running mercury or quicksilver** is also excluded.

(5.) Just as **calcareous earths**, **loam and clay** <note>original: "Lutum Letten und Thon"</note>, **quicklime, tin ashes, burnt alum, gypsum, red ochre, hematite, asbestos, etc.** provide the primary example of an earthy nature through **dryness, fixity, hardness**, or **solid** aggregation above all others; nonetheless, evidence of a certain softness, or conversion, or at least an inclination toward fluidity and a partnership (if not a kinship) with water, is found in these earths when they are committed to waters.

(6.) For it is very well known how sudden and deep is the mixing of **quicklime** with water, so that it combines with it into a semi-fluid, pulpy consistency. Indeed, in some part, it undergoes a true **mixture** with it. But just as it is one thing to be moved by a fluid rather than by moisture, and another to be fluid or moist oneself, so too lime dissolved by water into a pulp is nonetheless still solid in its own substance.

# SECTION II.
## PART I.
### THESIS I.
### SUBTERRANEAN THINGS ARE OF AN EARTHY NATURE.

->Evidence of the earthy nature of subterranean things.<-

There are various pieces of evidence to show that no kind of *subterranean* body exists that does not participate heavily in the nature of *earth*. Among these, the first to be mentioned is that true and real separation of *earths from waters*, based on the logic of their entire *location* and *position*, about which we have already said something above. For in this way:

(1.) If *earths were condensed into the more solid groupings* <note>meaning solid mineral formations</note> that are more characteristic of them, water would certainly have to be excluded from the tally of *subterranean* things. Indeed, earth would so absolutely occupy the lower position, and water the *upper* position, that only the earth would be considered *subterranean*.

### FOUNDATIONS OF BECHER'S THEORY

(2.) Furthermore, since all **subterranean substances** <note>original: "Subterranea"; referring to minerals, metals, and earths found underground.</note> are—for the most part and in an absolute sense—not only **dry**, but also **dense, solid, and hard** in their clumping <term>aggregation</term> <note>How the individual particles of a substance stick together.</note>; and since these properties are precisely what define an **earthy** nature: it becomes all the more clear that subterranean substances belong to the earthy class, as they share this same nature.

(3.) Their **dry** nature is not diminished by (α) **softness**, which tends toward fluidity; nor by **fluidity** itself, which most of these substances acquire through the agitation of **fire**. This fluidity is even visible without fire—indeed, in the midst of cold—in one substance: **quicksilver** <note>original: "argentum vivum"; mercury.</note>. Nor is their dryness diminished by (β) that type of **adhesion** that mimics wetness, by which molten glass or molten sulfur sticks to various harder things. **Quicksilver**, however, does not attach itself to anything except **certain** things (namely metallic bodies), unlike water, which usually attaches to **all** bodies. In the same way, **tin** attaches to **iron and copper**; indeed, **gold and silver** attach themselves to that same **copper**. This entire difference is resolved by the distinction between **fluid** and **humid** <note>In early modern science, "fluid" meant a substance that flows, while "humid" meant a substance that "wets" or sticks to the surface of what it touches.</note>.

(4.) Indeed, even **water** itself—whose most **essential** property is **humidity** (that is, a wet soaking and sticking)—seems to be brought into this liquid state by **heat**. Without the presence of heat, water ought to be called **dry** rather than **humid**; **ice** provides the proof of this. Thus, one might interpret the difference between **water and earths** (or those soft and mobile subterranean substances) as not being a difference in **kind**, but only a difference in **degree**. Nevertheless, following the accepted way of speaking, we should call **dry** (α) those things that are only brought to that subtle soaking we call **wetting** <note>original: "madefactionem"</note> by **intense fiery motion**; whereas we call **humid** those things that achieve this effect through **lighter** heat (which we hardly even call "heat" in an absolute sense). Furthermore, (β) those substances that mimic **wetting** under very slight or even no heat (in the common sense) are distinguished from truly **humid** things by the fact that they only do this with a **very few** things related to them. In contrast, those things called **humid** in a more absolute sense do this with **all** other things. In the first sense, all **metals, glasses**, and for the most part **sulfur** itself, are excluded from "humidity" strictly defined. In the second sense, **running mercury** or **quicksilver** is excluded.

(5.) Just as the **calcareous earths** <note>Lime-based earths.</note> provide the primary example of an earthy nature through their **dryness, fixity, and hardness** (or solid aggregation) above all others—such as **Loam, Potter's Earth, and Clay** <note>original: "Lutum Letten und Thon"</note>; **quicklime, tin ashes, burnt alum, gypsum, red ochre, hematite, asbestos**, etc.—so too, a proof of some degree of softness, or conversion, or at least an inclination toward fluidity and a **partnership** (if not a kinship) with water, is found in these earths when they are combined with water.

(6.) For example, that sudden and quite deep mixing of **quicklime** with water is very well known; they combine into a semi-fluid, paste-like consistency. Indeed, in some part, it undergoes a true **mixture** with the water. But just as it is one thing to be moved by a fluid rather than being a fluid oneself, so too **lime**, even when dissolved by water into a paste, remains nonetheless solid in its substance...

...and **dry**, no one would doubt: since, on the contrary, it draws water itself toward a state of **dryness**, as is evident in lime mortars.

(7.) An even more evident proof of this matter is found in **Gypsum** <note>original: "Gypso"; Plaster of Paris.</note>; for if this is properly "cooked" <note>Heating gypsum to dehydrate it into plaster.</note>, it **hardens** (that is, prevents from flowing) and dries out water within a few moments. In this hardening, the **density** deserves to be noted; for even when it is just about to set and still looks damp to the eye, **gypsum rings** <note>original: "tinniat"; it makes a metallic or clear clinking sound when struck.</note>, which is entirely foreign to the nature of **water and ice**.

(8.) Furthermore, a final argument for the **earthy** consistency of minerals is that they can reach a **weight** <note>original: "pondus"; referring to specific gravity.</note> far greater than even the most sincere and pure water. For just as anything that everyone immediately recognizes as **earthy** is **heavier** than anything commonly agreed to be **aqueous**: so too must we assume that such compounds and mixtures—which not only **equal** common earths in weight but exceed them—do so because of an eminent earthy nature rather than any suspicion of containing water.

(9.) However, it is true that not absolutely **all** minerals or subterranean things exceed water in **weight**; for even **bitumens** <note>original: "bitumina"; natural petroleum or tars.</note> as such, and those **oils** flowing from subterranean springs, can float upon water, as seen in the example of the **Dead Sea**. Nevertheless, our assertion is true not only of all other subterranean things, but it also applies to the dry and earthy part of these mixtures; for in the blink of an eye, petroleum turns into a **dry, fixed** powder, which, when properly immersed in water, seeks the bottom, and thus demonstrates the superiority of its **gravity** over the liquid.

(10.) Regarding the various types of **rocks, stones, flints, and sands**, there is perhaps less doubt that they are earthy in nature. Regarding **metals**, however, and **salts, bitumens, and sulfur**, there will perhaps be more ambiguity. But indeed, that **metals** were also of an **earthy** nature is demonstrated by the very obvious agreement of the four **base metals** <note>original: "ignobiliorum"; literally "less noble," referring to lead, tin, copper, and iron.</note> with earths: partly in their **glassy flow** <note>original: "vitrescente fluxu"; their ability to be turned into slag or glass.</note>, partly in the **limy-earthy** dryness of **tin**, and finally in their **dissolution** by **corrosive salts**.

(11.) **Salts** demonstrate their earthy nature when, through the help of sulfur and earth, they are separated from their partnership with water and resolved into **fixed and spiritless earths** <note>original: "terras fixas atque fatuas"; refers to the "dead" residue or 'caput mortuum' left after chemical processing.</note>. **Bitumens** exhibit their **earthy** part in a moment, even from their thinnest, volatile, oily purity.

(12.) It is also characteristic of the earthy nature of subterranean things (with the sole exception of running **mercury**—for I do not count **Niter** <note>original: "Nitrum"; saltpeter.</note> among subterranean things, nor acid salt, as it is clearly a compound with water) that they lack **elasticity** <term>elasticitas</term> <note>In the 17th century, this referred to the "springy" power of air or water vapor to expand and contract.</note> in **fire**, which is inseparable from both air and water. For although **molten** metals—and indeed, as in the case of iron, even those that are merely glowing—occupy more space (which is why balls cast from lead or tin, which showed a perfect roundness as long as the metal was flowing, form a small pit <note>original: "scrobiculum"; a shrinkage cavity or 'pipe' formed as cooling metal contracts.</note> once cooled), this is not **elasticity**, but a simple displacement arising from a closer clumping and an extremely tight positioning of parts. ...expansion of the collective group, the latter occurs by the expansion of individual *particles* <note>original: "individuorum"; referring to the smallest distinct units of a substance.</note>. On the other hand, a collective expansion can happen even without any internal change to the *particles* themselves, simply by moving them out of a cramped arrangement. Farmers know this when measuring grain—or perhaps they know it through trickery—when they avoid shaking the bushel-measure with great care, so the grains don't pack into a tighter space and demand more to fill it. This is a very well-known fact regarding pumice stone <note>Pumice is highly porous, appearing large in volume but having very little actual "earthy" matter.</note>.

(13.) Nor indeed is *combustibility* (as it is commonly called) of most metallic bodies—or their *evaporation into the breezes*—contrary to their *earthy* nature. For just as no one would deny that the greatest part of *wood ash* is *earthy* (from which it thickens into *glass*, a solid and very dense thing), women themselves know this well enough: that if the ashes are not removed from the remaining flame and the heat of the coals in time, they truly *exhale into the air* from hour to hour, so that nothing remains proportional to the original amount. Indeed, from a pile about six feet <note>original: "orgyiam"; a classical unit of length roughly equal to a fathom.</note> or about three yards <note>original: "ulnas"; an "ell" or yard.</note> high and wide in a kitchen hearth, it can easily happen that scarcely a cubic span <note>original: "spithama cubica"; a span is the distance from the thumb to the little finger.</note> of ash remains, provided they are constantly mixed back into the glowing coals beneath the flaming wood. This process is even more clearly visible if volatile soot from pitch—*pine soot* <note>original: "Kienruß"</note>—is burned in a strictly closed vessel; for once burned this way, even with *repeated* burnings in the closed container, it loses absolutely nothing of its weight or remaining substance. However, when it is lit *in the open air*, it then glows like a coal and vanishes entirely into the breezes, so that from its great bulk, barely a small amount of ashen substance remains. Something similar is true of charcoal itself, if burned so that it can flame with air moving beneath it: where very little remains of its former weight.

(14.) Before their breakdown into an earthy, more fixed, and tasteless dryness, salts also demonstrate an earthy nature. They do this because they not only combine so readily with earths, but through this very union, they place their *saline properties (strictly speaking)* under the "yoke" of the earthy elements. Thus, they exchange their *flavor*, *corrosive sharpness*, *volatility*, and *misty-damp* constitution for a tasteless, dull, fixed, and dry state—leaving behind only the character of *fluid, damp solubility*.

(15.) Finally, *Location* itself provides testimony of an earthy nature, acting as the natural or *native* place in which the subjects under discussion—namely *minerals*—are generated. For minerals are not only found among rocks, stones, flint, mud, and slime, but they are also found dispersed *within the very substance of the rocks*, in the heart—or rather the vast expanse—of earths, flints, and stones. And since they are observed to be thoroughly woven into these "earthy concretes" (more directly and strictly speaking), it is even more certain that those minerals have been granted an affinity with the earths themselves. From this evidence, their earthy nature is quite conveniently inferred.

### SECTION II
### THESIS II

# SUBTERRANEAN SUBSTANCES ADMIT AN AQUEOUS MIXTURE.

## Evidence of the aqueous nature of certain subterranean substances.

**A**lthough in the study of mixtures, evidence and experiments are not always equally available from both the synthetic and analytic methods to resolve all difficulties with clarity and simplicity, it is sufficient that experience matches at least one side. That is, in some cases it offers *manifest evidence through combination* <note>original: "syncris"; the alchemical process of joining elements together to form a compound.</note>, and in others it demonstrates through *separation* <note>original: "diacris"; the process of breaking a substance down into its basic components.</note> what can serve as scientific proof. For:

(1.) **SALTS**, and especially that more *primordial* salt which—being common in mineral veins—provides the *underlying substance* <note>original: "hypostasin"; the essential foundation or "body" of a substance.</note> for the *origin of sulfur* <note>original: "sulphuris genesi"; in 17th-century chemistry, "sulfur" was often viewed as a "fatty earth" principle responsible for flammability.</note>, are shown *from the start* <note>original: "a priori"; based on theoretical deduction rather than observation of effects.</note> to share in an aqueous substance. This is shown not only by (α) their *moist-vaporous* or even *moist-fluid* consistency, (β) but also by their very ready inclination to merge with *moist fluids*.

(2.) This goes so far that they even reconcile various *dry earths* with water—earths which, by their own nature, had tolerated no intimate connection with *water* at all. Thus, together with the salts, these earths undergo and admit *solution or fluidity*, which in this case is *moist* in nature.

(3.) Furthermore, the *aqueous mixture of salts* is taught *from the results* <note>original: "a posteriori"; reasoning from observed effects back to causes.</note> by their reduction into earth, which hereafter rejects direct contact with *water*. Indeed, when these substances become *fixed in fire, dry, or turn entirely into dense glass*, it provides sufficient evidence that the substance which—in its previous state as salt—had produced so many examples of *moisture, fluidity, and solidifying* (or at least of very ready *merging*) with *waters*, was truly of *aqueous* lineage. Just as, on the other hand, this remaining portion—*dry, fixed, glassy, or lime-like*—which constitutes the other part of the salt mixture, easily proves its *earthy nature* by these properties.

(4.) Truly, the most perfect evidence of a water-earth mixture is that native, subterranean mineral from which *commercial borax* is extracted through purifying and preparation. The *taste* and *vapor* testify that it is an *aqueous mixture*, while the *glass* produced so abundantly from it <note>When heated, borax swells and eventually melts into a clear, bead-like glass, a property still used in "borax bead" chemistry tests today.</note> is evidence of its very solid earthy nature.

(5.) In this way, it is also well known that **fixed alkali** <note>original: "alcali fixum"; a stable alkaline salt like potash or soda that does not evaporate when heated.</note>, when combined with **glass**, eventually turns for the most part into glass itself. Just as a gentle **calcination** <note>original: "calcinatio"; the process of heating a substance to high temperatures in the presence of air to change its properties.</note> of this same alkali, or even just a long-term **digestion** <note>original: "digestio"; the process of exposing a substance to gentle, continuous heat, similar to how food is broken down in the stomach.</note> above a furnace (following the observation of **Blessed Ludwig**) <note>Refers to Daniel Ludwig (1625–1680), a respected German physician and chemist.</note>, reduces it more and more into a **tasteless and insoluble earthy** consistency. (However much in that Ludwigian method there often remains not so much an earth as a firm, **acid-alkaline consistency**). And even a spontaneous **liquefaction** <note>original: "deliquatio"; the process where a salt absorbs enough moisture from the air to turn into a liquid.</note> accomplishes more here than solutions made with water—specifically with hot or **boiling** water.

(6.) Furthermore, do not the various differences among **glasses** themselves provide a shining proof of their subterranean tendency to enter into a partnership with **aqueous** substances? For those glasses are very well known which are corroded by **corrosive liquids**, such as **strong water** <note>original: "aqua forti"; nitric acid.</note>, hardly less easily than marble. Or, if they do not admit this so readily, they are **nonetheless affected by corrosives over time**. On this account, I have not yet seen a glass, **white or very clear**, that did not eventually yield to the long-term attack of **strong water, spirit of salt** <note>original: "spiritus salis"; hydrochloric acid.</note>, **fresh and well-saturated antimony wash** <note>original: "clysti antimonii"; a liquid chemical preparation of antimony.</note>, and even a **solution or decoction of sal ammoniac** <note>original: "salis armeniaci"; ammonium chloride.</note> (which is often more effective than the others), causing the glass to break apart into many large cracks and nearly infinite small ones. Indeed, there are glasses at hand—**pure, bright, hard, and dense**—which, by the **infusion of wine alone**, are gradually turned into **flakes and cracks**. Surely this happens by no other action than that of **moisture** or its reconciliation.

(7.) Nor is it demonstrated only by evidence **after the fact** <note>original: "a posteriori"; reasoning from observed effects to their causes.</note> that subterranean things are suited for **aqueous** mixtures. Examples also exist **from first principles** <note>original: "a priori"; reasoning from causes to effects.</note> and by way of **synthesis** <note>original: "syncriseos"; the chemical process of joining substances together.</note>, which confirm the combination of earthy particles with **waters** and the resulting properties of a **composite** nature. For instance, from the works of **Becher**, a fact truly worthy of note is the reduction of **flints**, and even **crystal**, into **salt, a fatty oily substance, and a mucous subtlety** (**which is close to a saline thinness and a more intimate mixture**), with nothing else contributing **materially** except water alone.

(8.) Lest we seek evidence from too far away, or burden ourselves with more laborious manuals of this kind, **quicklime** <note>original: "calx viva"; calcium oxide, produced by burning limestone.</note> can serve as our proof. In this substance, the following clear circumstances serve to confirm our **thesis**:
(α) **Limestone shows no immediate reaction with water**; and thus **it provides no evidence of any actual salt existing within it.** 
(β) **No matter how much this stone has already been burnt into quicklime, there is nothing in it that flees the fire.** For it is, in a sense, born in the fire, and by a more vehement or long-lasting fire, it is finally rendered most correctly both fixed and subtle at the same time.
(γ) **Nor does it, under this constitution, show evidence of any truly saline nature**, but rather only a subtle—indeed, most subtle—earthy nature.
(δ) **Even when it is not rightly and properly combined with water, it barely shows any just or evident traces of saltiness.** 
(ε) **If, however, it is correctly worked with water, it joins itself with the water into a saline consistency**, namely, melting into a clear solution in the water.
(ζ) **Its corrosiveness, equally effective on sulfur, fats, membranes, etc., reveals itself further**, as does its immediate taste.
(η) **The predominance of the mixed-in wateriness...**

<meta>This page continues Becher’s chemical argument that water is not merely a solvent, but a "fixable" element that becomes a structural part of solid minerals. ...if the water is expelled, they immediately lose all their hardness and return to dust. Meanwhile, second, lest it be believed that this is merely a bare **roasting** <note>original: "ustulatio"</note> of the lime substance itself—by which it is simply made more porous without the expulsion of anything (namely, its "wateriness")—this very effect of repeated burning teaches us the opposite: that through that burning, the lime **revives** again. That is, once the old wateriness is expelled, it admits new water again. With this new water, just as the first time, it is made fit for a hardening bonding with sand, as well as for those other saline effects praised above. However, it does not perform this with the same quality through repeated cycles, because in truth, that which had already taken on a more intimate saline texture during the first mixing with water, when fire is applied again, evaporates into the air right along with its wateriness. What remains is a coarser, more earthy substance, which is neither exquisitely "alive" nor capable of reviving.

(14.) A mineral growth of a **Gypsum-Lime** nature is found here and there, but especially around the city of Jena, where entire mountains are composed of this substance. It has a **stony texture**, consisting of pure, shining threads, almost like **silver filaments**. It appears similar to **Asbestos**, but the threads of this substance are thicker than those of Asbestos; they are also harder and not at all flexible, yet they can be very easily crushed with one's own fingers. Indeed, the common people use it there for the drying of recent writing, <gloss>using it as strewing-sand <note>original: "Strau-Sand"; a powder (pounce) used to dry ink on a page before the invention of blotting paper.</note></gloss>. If this substance is finely powdered and then slightly moistened—without any other preparation—into the form of a thin paste, it hardens of its own accord and quickly. It comes together into a far firmer aggregation—even a dense hardness—than it had been before. Since it later preserves this same consistency unshaken, there is no doubt that this deserves to be ascribed to an intimate bonding with the water. Indeed, no reason can be given why this powdery substance (as it was before the meeting with water) would not crumble back into that same scattered state if the water truly evaporated from it purely and simply.

(15.) We perceive a new proof of this kind in that salt which is called **Enixum** <note>original: "sal Enixo"; a "neutral" salt, typically potassium sulfate, formed during the production of nitric acid.</note>, or "middle salt," which grows together from the **acid of Vitriol** <note>original: "acidum Vitrioli"; sulfuric acid.</note> and a **fixed alkali salt** <note>such as potash.</note>. (α) Concerning that acid, when it is purer, it is certainly known that it is dissipated by hardly any heat except an intense, almost glowing heat; this is well known regarding **oil of vitriol**. (β) Concerning **fixed alkaline salts**, it escapes no one that they are not quickly destroyed by fire, water, or air. (γ) However much even the vitriolic acid and the fixed alkali, when diluted with copious water, may evaporate significantly. (δ) Nevertheless, in such a mutual embrace and union, one might believe that their united strength would be stronger. (ε) And just as such a "neutral" salt strongly resists fire and easily maintains that double fixity in this trial, (ζ) so it deserves all the more consideration because of the directly opposite diversity which this salt exhibits when combined with water. (η) For although in this type of salt it has the peculiarity of not being dissolved in water very promptly, (θ) even though both those bodies from which it grew would most promptly take on a watery consistency, (ι) yet when it is once dissolved with sufficient water and exposed to evaporation, it then commonly evaporates in a far greater quantity along with the bare watery vapor than either the **spirit of vitriol** separately or, much less, the alkali salt itself would have done.

A mineral formation of a **Gypsum-Lime** <note>original: "Gypseo-Calcariae"</note> nature is found here and there; especially, however, around the city of **Jena**, whole mountains are underlaid with this formation. It has a **stony** texture, consisting of pure, shining threads, like silver filaments. It appears similar to **asbestos** <note>original: "Asbesto"</note>, but the threads of this are thicker than those of asbestos; they are also harder and not at all flexible. If this substance is finely powdered and lightly moistened without any other preparation into the form of a somewhat thick paste, it **hardens** from there spontaneously and quickly, and comes together into a far firmer aggregation—indeed, a dense hardness—than it had been before. And since it afterwards preserves this same consistency unshaken, there is no doubt that this deserves to be ascribed to some more intimate union of water. Indeed, no reason can be given why this powdery substance, such as it was before the meeting with water, *would not collapse again into the same state of dissipation* if the water truly evaporated from it again purely and simply.

(15.) We catch sight of a new proof of this kind in that salt, as they call it, **Enixum** <note>original: "Enixo," usually referring to Potassium Sulfate, a "neutral" salt</note>, or neutral salt, which is formed from **acid of vitriol** <note>original: "acido Vitrioli," sulfuric acid</note> and **fixed alkali salt** <note>original: "sale alcali fixo," such as potash</note>. (**α**) Concerning that acid, when it is purer, it is certainly known that it is scarcely dissipated except by a more intense, indeed nearly glowing, **heat** <note>original: "astu"</note> of warmth, which is sufficiently known regarding **oil of vitriol** <note>original: "oleo vitrioli," concentrated sulfuric acid</note>. (**β**) Concerning fixed alkaline salts, it escapes no one that they are not so quickly snatched away by **fire**, nor water, nor air. (**γ**) Even though both the vitriolic acid and the fixed alkali, when diluted with copious **water**, evaporate quite a bit. (**δ**) However, in such a mutual embrace and union, one might believe that their united force would be stronger. (**ε**) And just as such an *enixum* salt strongly resists **fire** and, in this trial indeed, easily maintains that double **fixity** <note>original: "fixitatem"</note> of its. (**ζ**) So it deserves to be considered all the more, as this diversity which this salt exhibits when joined with **water** is almost directly opposite. (**η**) For although in this type too, it has this peculiarity, that it is not very quickly **dissolved** in water; (**ϑ**) since, however, both those bodies from which it grew together most quickly underwent an aqueous consistency, (**ι**) when it is once dissolved in sufficient water and exposed to evaporation, then it commonly evaporates in a far greater quantity with a bare aqueous breath, which neither the vitriolic **spirit** separately, nor much less the **alkali salt** itself, would have done.

(16.) Truly, how tight this union of wateriness is with these earthy, dry, saline corpuscles, the author of that *Discourse on the Immortal* liquor *Alkahest* seems to have admired plainly. (17.) There remains a piece of evidence for the disposition of underground substances to receive an aqueous mixture, which is as rich as it is evident. From this, one can easily learn how abundantly waters coalesce with earthy corpuscles, lead them into a saline state, and adapt them for various subtle fluid motions. Thus, by that very fact, they confirm in many ways and with immense abundance what is stated in our Thesis: namely, that underground substances admit an aqueous mixture.

they might, if they remembered that *the affirmation of one is not the removal of the other* <note>original: *unius positio non sit alterius sublatio*; a logical maxim meaning that establishing one fact doesn't necessarily negate another</note>; and for that reason, we do not wish to snatch away from them the numerous *types of shapes* <note>original: *species figurarum*</note> of different kinds in establishing various types of *Composites*, provided they fulfill the following conditions for us: 1. that they show that a *larger* shape cannot be made from *smaller ones joined together*, 2. that all those shapes supposed by them are *absolute* and *materially* unique in number—that is, they cannot be formed from several *material* parts joined into one—3. and therefore, which sounds like the same thing, that they are absolutely *simple and primordial*.

*But I think I can bring forward far more brilliant evidence that not so many, but indeed very few, principles seem to be required; if only we attend to that number—certainly not a large one—of such species which, by their firm and intimate cohesion, can testify that the principles from which they grew together are not only moved apart from each other with the greatest difficulty because of their extreme smallness; but also because of the true physical indivisibility of those final principles, or, in a sound sense, their impenetrability.*

It is not pleasing to repeat in this place those things which we said above (though they are by no means to be neglected) concerning the disagreement of our moderns from the ancients in mere words; and yet their agreement with them in actual things: and indeed, what is worst, an agreement even with those ancients who felt the opposite. For the moderns disagree with the ancients in that the latter posited *primary* qualities—those which are not truly *intrinsic* to bodies, but only *relative* and matters of comparative *respect*—such as *dryness, humidity, heat, and cold*. In place of these, the moderns substitute *size, shape, and solidity*. And they have done rightly so far, except that these are actually more words than things as soon as they are transferred from the *general class* to the *specific types*. They agree with the ancients, however, in that the ancients established their *elements* as *immutable* or *unconvertible*: which the moderns also perpetually hammer home with superlatives, saying they are not just *solid*, but *most solid*, not *impenetrable*, but *most impenetrable*. But since there were also some among the ancients who leaned toward the opposite opinion—namely, that elements can be *transmuted* or *converted* into each other—certain of the moderns certainly subscribe to this, supposing those *abrasive* grindings <note>original: *attritorias comminutiones*; the idea that particles can be worn down or broken into smaller bits through friction</note> of their simplest corpuscles, notwithstanding that superlative *solidity and impenetrability*.

We, if we must sacrifice to the naked and pure truth, say that all these crowds and entanglements have as their foundation a lack of both sufficient *experiments* and a proper *comparison* of them. Once this double defect is certainly overcome, it will more easily appear that there is nowhere a need for such a grand apparatus and such a hodgepodge; but that in truth nature *is content with a few things*, and, like an excellent *arithmetician* <note>Becher uses the metaphor of nature as a mathematician who creates complex results from a few simple numbers</note>, can compute a proportionate number of *mixtures* from a few *simpler* parts: and from this number, finally, a vast number of *compositions*.

Therefore, following nature through experience, we shall insist upon *our three Becherian earthy principles* <note>Johann Joachim Becher proposed that all solid matter consisted of three "earths": *terra lapidea* (stony), *terra pinguis* (fatty/inflammable), and *terra fluida* (mercurial). This was the precursor to the Phlogiston theory</note>; not even disguising that they lead indeed *more toward a duality*...

It does not please me to repeat in this place those things which we said above (though they are by no means to be neglected) concerning the disagreement of our more recent thinkers from the ancients in mere *words*, while they nevertheless agree with them in *reality*: and indeed, what is worst, they even agree with those ancients who hold contrary opinions. And they have done rightly thus far, except that these are really more words than things as soon as they are transferred from the general category to specific types. The moderns also perpetually insist upon this with superlatives: that elements exist not merely as *solid*, but *most solid*; not *impenetrable*, but *most impenetrable*. If we must offer a sacrifice to the bare and pure truth, we say that all these crowds of confusion and intricacies have as their foundation a *lack* both of sufficient *experiments* and of a proper *comparison* of them. Certainly, once this double defect is overcome, it will more easily appear that there is nowhere a need for such a grand apparatus and such a hodgepodge of theories. Rather, nature is in reality content with *few things*, and like an excellent *arithmetician* <note>original: *arithmeticus*; Becher uses the metaphor of a mathematician to describe how Nature calculates complex results from simple starting points</note>, she is able to compute a *proportionate number of mixtures* from a few simple numbers; and from this number of mixtures, she can finally compute a vast *number of compositions*.

He now moves into empirical "documents" or proofs to support his theory of the three primary "earths."</meta>
