### SPECIMEN OF BECHER, PART I, SECTION II.

...not to the matter itself, but only toward the triplicity of numerical consistency, let us incline. Thus, the evidence:

(1.) Experience confirms by the following example that the principles from which subterranean mixtures coalesce are diverse. From most of the more clearly *mixed* bodies <note>original: *mixtis*; Becher uses "mixture" to refer to what we would call chemical compounds</note> found underground, substances of different kinds can be separated. That these are indeed of different kinds is clear from the fact that they do not obey the same solvent <note>original: *menstruo*; a liquid used to dissolve a solid</note> or instrument of separation; rather, in various other ways—both of composition <note>original: *syncriseos*; the joining of parts</note> and of separation <note>original: *diacriseos*; the breaking down of parts</note>—they always display such a different nature that they can never be absolutely converted into one another, nor can their entire substance be reduced back into one single kind. In truth, by using the term "more clearly *mixed*," we wish to avoid the necessity of a long-winded distinction between those subterranean things that should be classed as *less certainly mixed* and those that are *more certainly* so. However, we use the name "mixture" here in a broader sense, namely by including compounds as well, primarily because there are certain *true earthy mixtures* in which it is not so easy to demonstrate such things strictly by means of separation. Meanwhile, what can less easily be achieved through separation can almost always be achieved through *combination*. Let *silver* <note>original: *argentum*</note> be the proof. Resolving this into its different principles is indeed a difficult task. But to *produce it, or to mix it by combination*, from things that are not *silver*—not just once, but again and again—is certainly not difficult for the skilled. Yet, let those "Arcadian sheep" <note>original: *Arcadiæ illa pecora*; a classical idiom for fools or the lazy</note> stay away, who expect *masses and heaps* to come from this: let them remember that "like lettuce is eaten by like lips" <note>original: *similes labris esitare lactucas*; a proverb meaning that crude things suit crude people, or that fools deserve their own folly</note>. We speak and offer our work not to laziness, but to art; not to greed, but to science. In this matter, Robert Boyle <note>original: *Boylæus*</note>—despite his usual sharpness—seems rightly to have been less than fully practiced when, in his *Sceptical Chymist* <note>original: *Chymista suo sceptico*; published in 1661, this famous book attacked the idea of the "three principles"</note>, he denies that those *three principles* exist in various things, and therefore concludes that they are not the principles of all things. For certainly there exist *simpler things* in which not everything is present; there exist very *simple things* in which none of the others are present in any *notable quantity*. There are also *mixed things* from which it is not so easy to set aside something *different* as our simple labors might wish. There are true, and even lightly or casually *compounded things*, which are neither dissolved by any superficial labor, nor immediately perceived by a judgment sharpened by vessels and other things—various arguments could be brought forward here if it were our purpose to investigate further rather than to positively produce evidence.

(2.) By no means, however, should we touch so briefly or pass over "with a dry foot" <note>original: *sicco pede*; a Latin idiom for passing over something without paying much attention</note> that method by which, conversely, it is proved through *synthesis* <note>the process of building up a substance</note> what cannot be proved purely and nakedly through *analysis* <note>the process of breaking a substance down</note>. Truly, one must insist here on the better-known things, for unknown things do not provide evidence; hence I do not care if it is objected that I always dwell on the same things. We are not speaking here of many new experiments, but of arguments and evidence. Certainly, others should be believed when they claim they could bring forward new things, even when they have given no evidence of it yet; I can rightfully demand that I be believed that I could perhaps bring forward other things as well, since I have already produced some which—if they cannot be called "unheard of"—may at least be called "unseen." Thus, the introduction of that *phlogiston* matter <note>original: *phlogistæ*; Becher's "inflammable earth" (Terra Pinguis), the substance he believed was responsible for fire and combustion</note> into various other mineral mixtures provides a proof of the utility of this synthetic method...

<summary>Becher argues that the composition of minerals is best proven through "synthesis" (rebuilding substances) when "analysis" (breaking them down) is too difficult. He defends his theory of three principles against Robert Boyle's criticisms and introduces the concept of phlogiston as a key component of mineral mixtures.</summary>

<header>DOCUMENTATION OF BECHER'S THEORY</header>

...of mixture. Thus *Becher* himself was eager to offer the palm of victory to the younger *Helmont* <note>Jan Baptist van Helmont (1580–1644) or his son Franciscus Mercurius van Helmont, famous pioneering chemists</note>, if he were willing to share that experiment with the public by which *iron* might be produced from simple mud and *sulfur*. And yet, surely this experiment, in terms of scientific knowledge, would still have been as worthless as an empty nut; for it would not yet have removed the doubt as to by what specific means, or by which of its material principles, sulfur concurs in the production of iron. However, after *Becher* himself learned to perform the same feat with a far more noble proof and experiment—using *linseed oil*, a *matter* entirely foreign to any mineral nature (according to *his* own opinion and that of others)—he established an unheard-of type of demonstration, believed by no man before, through such a *synthesis* <note>original: *synthesi*; the process of "putting together" components to create a compound</note>. Certainly, this was in many ways more enlightening than all the *analyses* <note>original: *analyses*; the process of "breaking down" a substance into its parts</note> that had been offered since the world was born, or at least since it became civilized. 

Indeed, to briefly clarify the proof cited in the previous section—here where we are discussing the *three earths* <note>Becher's theory that all solids are made of three types of "earth": the stony (terra lapidea), the oily (terra pinguis), and the fluid (terra mercurialis)</note>, the primordials of minerals—I assert: *if that earth which Becher calls the "First" can be joined with lead and introduced into it in an intimate way; and if his "Second" earth can then be worked in (which craftsmen call "waxing" <note>original: *incerare*; to soften a substance to a waxy consistency so it can be mixed with others</note>) and intimately bound with the lead: then by this method the lead can truly be converted into silver.* And although this true theory of *synthesis* may seem difficult and abstruse, the thing itself in *practice* is not only very easy, but not even unknown. 

That *lead* may thus pass away into *silver* is proven by the fact that absolutely nothing metallic is added except pure and simple lead; yet in each operation, a grain of silver is obtained *larger by ten pounds than would be found in an entire hundredweight of lead left to itself, even when the same fire-assay <note>original: *docimasia*; the standard method for testing the purity of metals</note> is used for both.* And this happens as many times, from one and the same portion of lead, as it is treated over and over again with the same labor, without any other metallic addition. I repeat, this experiment *is not unknown*; indeed, it was hammered home by *Becher* himself until he was hoarse. But I will maintain that this theory of his, or his solid reasons, have been understood by no one until now (excepting *Becher* in some part), until the contrary is proven. But our discourse is about proofs, theories, and *physical science*: not about bare, wandering experiments which are better known to laborers (as this very one is) than to those *Doctors* <note>meaning university-educated scholars or physicians</note> who can scarcely be taught enough by any arguments to see this difference.

(3.) The longer the deduction suggested in the preceding section was, the shorter the proof can be for admitting *Becher’s First Earth* into the status of the primary principle of subterranean things. Our author established this principle as the *matter of every strictly defined earthy consistency: dryness, solidity, density, hardness, even thickness, weight, glassy flow, or the fixity of lime.* Now, since almost all subterranean things enjoy these properties to a greater or lesser degree, it is clear as day that such a principle cannot be denied to them.

(4.) But this question can be raised: Is there truly some *material* principle that confers these properties substantially <note>original: *ὑποστατικῶς* (hypostatikōs); meaning "as an underlying essence"</note> to subterranean things? Or is it at least some Peripatetic <note>Aristotelian philosophy</note> *form* or *formal mixture*? In favor of the former member of the question—namely, that there is a certain material principle that preserves these properties in a mixture—

This can be proven (1.) *from the outset* <note>original: *a priori*</note>, because the greatest part of the entire subterranean mass is more immediately, and as if by universal confession, undoubtedly *earthy, dry, solid, dense, hard, glass-forming, powdery, and fixed.* (2.) Because all other species of subterranean materials are embraced, involved, surrounded, and indeed contained within the very marrow of these **more absolutely earthy** concretions, such as rocks, flints, silts, and clays <note>original: *boli*; refers to bole, a type of medicinal or fatty clay</note>. (3.) Because various subterranean *mixtures*, once their components of a different nature are separated, soon clearly crumble into a consistency that is glassy or lime-like—in short, more analogous to *pure earth*. (4.) Just as, conversely, from such a *glassy-earthy* consistency, they are restored to their metallic integrity when materials of the nature they had lost are supplied to them. Namely, if other suitable materials are added to that glassy matter present: the experiment of this thing is very well known, though performed without *theory*, in the *reduction* <note>original: *reductio*; the chemical process of returning a metal from its oxide or "glass" back to its metallic state</note> of *lead glass* into the metal of lead, and of the *glass of antimony* into its metallic heart <note>original: *regulum*; the pure metal that settles at the bottom of a crucible</note>. Indeed, since *common furnace-clay* <note>original: *limus communis, furnarius*, or *Ofen-Leimen*</note> turns by itself into a dull *glass*, a significant portion of it is turned into iron when fatty substances <note>original: *pinguedinibus*; likely referring to carbon-rich oils or fats used as reducing agents</note> are applied, according to the First Supplement of the *Subterranean Physics*.

(5.) Truly, that a *glass-forming* <note>original: *vitrescens*</note> principle lies within such mineral and metallic bodies as *antimony* and *lead*, and even *iron, copper*, etc., is sufficiently and conveniently proven by their *calcination* <note>original: *calcinatio*; heating a substance to high temperatures in air to turn it into a powder or oxide</note>. For both *antimony* and *lead* can be burned, without any additive and by the moderate control of *fire* alone, so that they do not differ much from the temperament of common *pure sand-glass*; indeed, they testify more than is necessary to their purely *glassy-earthy* nature by their resistance to *melting* <note>original: *fusionis*</note>, their total lack of color, and the difficulty of their *reduction*.

(6.) Indeed, it is certainly the fault of this nature that, for example, *pure lead*, even when *burned*, as well as *lead ashes* and *litharge* <note>original: *lithargyrium*; lead oxide</note>, never recover their original weight during *reduction*, but fall much too short. For although *litharge, minium* <note>red lead</note>, and *lead ashes* acquire a *greater weight* during their calcination than the first quantity of lead assumed had shown; nevertheless, in the *reduction*, not only does that "supernumerary" portion perish, but a notable weight of the entire first assumed gravity also vanishes. It does not perish so absolutely, however, that the whole of it exhales purely and nakedly into the breezes (though it does this in part), but a truly not insignificant portion of it is converted into *glassy dross* <note>original: *scorias vitreas*</note> of a more purely glassy sort, which no longer returns to a metallic nature. As an example, an experiment can be set up with simple glass made from naked lead, turned into glass in a vitrifying dish: *Litharge-glass* <note>original: *Glett-Glaß*</note>, made on a *refining-dish* <note>original: *Trieb-Scherbel*; a cupel or shallow ceramic vessel used in assaying</note> from pure lead, without sand, flint, or any other glass-forming substance added; this is never reduced in its total quantity back into lead, but some of it remains in glassy form. This happens much more abundantly, however, if the lead has been reduced to *ash*—which flows with great difficulty—by a long-lasting, *gentle roasting*.

(7.) In a word, quite clear proofs are given of *Becher’s First Earth*, which fixes, hardens, and coagulates. Thus, it would be superfluous in this place to touch at length upon those "waxings" <note>original: *incerationes*; an alchemical process of softening a substance</note> of alkaline salts which *Isaac Hollandus* <note>a legendary 15th-century alchemist</note> insists upon, or the efficacy of the *lime of eggs* praised by him in various ways; especially since things of this kind...

these matters are so little to the heart of the "curious" seekers of the modern fashion that they prefer to speak of a thousand little bodies, particles, figures, angles, and points, rather than recall to mind a single experiment that is somewhat more laborious or truly requires diligence and time. Hence, such experiments are almost entirely dismissed as fables, regardless of what **Boyle** (in his treatise *On the Parts of Nitre* <note>original: *tr. de Nitri partibus*; refers to Robert Boyle's work on saltpeter</note>) may suggest to the contrary.

(8.) But regarding those remaining **earths** named by **Becher**, the business is necessarily more intricate, because no one, before or besides **Becher**, brought forth any monument, much less a **documented proof**, of this matter. For who ever dared to profess that it had entered his mind that the matter of fire is a substance to be likened to the nature, mixture, and composition of **earth**? To be sure, since the time of Aristotle, the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle's philosophy</note> have asserted that fire *formally, as fire*, is the material principle of all mixtures. But since they had no concept of the **matter** of fire insofar as it is distinguished from its formal definition—indeed, they understood so little of that **formal** nature of fire that they could have no regard for its **matter**—it followed that they did indeed recognize that in various mixtures and compounds there is something that can be stirred by fiery motion, or even **transformed** into fire; yet they conceived of nothing distinct regarding this **motion**.

(9.) However, a consideration that is real, solid, and corresponds to a clearer understanding is this: that in the constitution of very many mixtures, there is indeed present such a **matter** which, under certain circumstances, can truly become the immediate **subject of fire**; or rather, in a strictly philosophical sense, it becomes the **matter of fire**, which, without any other internal material concurrence, becomes fire formally through a certain **formal** act, **first and primarily**; or rather it makes, **forms**, and constitutes fire. Nevertheless, as far as we are able to understand even today, this substance—naked, alone, and **by itself**—hardly forms **fire** or **heat** without other materials and the joint concurrence of other matters. Meanwhile, just as it exists as the Author and first element, **subject**, and **instrument** of fiery **motion** (which is the swiftest of all motions we understand in the universe, and indeed **luminous**), so too, with whatever other matters it is joined—even those disposed toward coarser and denser aggregations—it always produces this effect in them: it bestows upon them a certain appearance of subtlety, whether by reason of union or by reason of mobility.

(10.) A manifest proof of this thing is provided by ($\alpha$) the effects of this phlogistic principle in **imperfect metals** <note>Metals that "burn" or rust when heated, such as lead, tin, or antimony, as opposed to "noble" metals like gold</note>. Where the remaining substance of those metals—dense, very hard, and certainly among the coarser aggregates of this kind—forms powders or **Glasses** (where indeed I believe anyone will easily remember that glasses are far harder than iron); there, this phlogistic matter, interspersed and intimately mixed with them, renders them tender, soft, fusible, and even volatile. A most ready proof of this matter is shown by the **regulus of antimony** <note>The metallic form of antimony</note>. If this is stripped of its inflammable substance by means of **nitre** <note>saltpeter</note>, so that it passes into that white powder which some call **ceruse of the regulus** (but it is the same as **diaphoretic antimony** <note>A medicinal powder made from antimony</note>), and if this powder is heated on charcoal by the fire of a lamp using a goldsmith’s soldering tube (**blowpipe** <note>original: *Löth-Röhrchen*</note>), it smokes not at all, or indeed scarcely any; as soon as

...indeed, in that part where it touches the pit of the charcoal, and thus the charcoal directly, it revives into a **regulus** <note>original: "regulum"; a small mass of purified metal found at the bottom of a crucible</note>, where it is seen to smoke quickly and copiously, and is entirely resolved into the air in the form of **flowers** <note>original: "florum"; in early chemistry, "flowers" refers to a fine, flakey powder produced by sublimation—solidifying from a vapor</note>: which even **lead** itself, with the right handling, accomplishes by the same reasoning, though with a somewhat slower success. So too in **iron**, although the rest of its substance is of a thick and coarse nature, the following circumstances teach that this **phlogiston** matter is the author of all thinness and **softness** <note>original: "mollitiei"</note> in every way. 

($\alpha$) **Crocus** of Mars <note>original: "Crocus martis"; literally "Saffron of Mars," a traditional name for reddish iron oxide or rust</note>, as it is commonly called, is by itself so difficult to melt into **glass** that there have perhaps been few who believed it could be done; especially if it has been exquisitely burned out by the labor of many days. 

($\beta$) But when this principle of phlogiston is restored to it, so that it returns to its metallic face and true iron, although this too is difficult to melt, it nevertheless melts. 

($\gamma$) Indeed, an even more immediate proof shines forth from the fact that common sulfur, mixed with fresh, non-rusty **iron** filings, if cast into a glowing crucible (indeed, it need barely be **glowing**) and covered with a small brick so that an entry for the **bellows** <note>original: "follis"</note> remains open, by which the flame of the sulfur can be reflected back into the mass itself; it happens most promptly that the iron **melts together** into a mass. 

($\delta$) This also happens promptly in copper plates without any bellows, but with a more vividly glowing crucible, if a piece of sulfur is added to them and the flame is pushed down somewhat by the mere breath of the mouth: by which method a **small mass** of copper weighing even half an ounce easily flows together to the bottom, melted into a liquid, which certainly is known to experts what degree of fire it requires otherwise. In truth, no one who pays attention would be ignorant that this is the effect of **sulfur**, and specifically of its more **phlogisticated** part, in experiments; because the **acid** part of sulfur rather greatly hinders fluidity, as appears in **vitriol** <note>original: "vitriolo"; a term for metal sulfates, often appearing as glassy crystals</note>; which not only rejects all fusion before the **acid** has been expelled from the metal, but even after its final expulsion, leaves the metal very difficult to **melt**: even though this metal, even in its whole, **meltable** substance, had combined to form the vitriol.

(11.) But I believe another, and according to common opinion until now, a much more difficult and greater proof will be expected from us: namely, that this **phlogiston** matter deserves to be reckoned as being of an **earthy** nature. Concerning which matter, so that the **understanding**, or true acceptance of both words and things, may first be established, we advise that just as the property of common **air** and **water** is elastic expansion; so the **common affection** of **earth** and our igniting principle is exquisite dryness and a **lack** of elasticity strictly speaking. Just as water, therefore, seems very much related to air, and plays, meets, and cooperates with it in various ways: so our **phlogiston** principle, in view of this **common** property with earth, is not only easily and greatly, but also firmly coupled with **earths**, etc. Regarding which matter we consider some things in the *Halle Observations* <note>original: "Observat. Hallens."; likely referring to the academic journals published by Georg Ernst Stahl and his colleagues at the University of Halle</note>, namely that we ought to attribute the fiery effect to this principle, not as the only, first, and perhaps chief effect: but only because we are thus far ignorant of others, perhaps even purer effects proper to it.

<meta>This page continues the technical investigation into phlogiston, the hypothetical substance of fire. Having established that phlogiston is a physical material rather than just an abstract "form," the author now explores whether this substance originates from the atmosphere or the depths of the earth, settling on the latter.</meta>

# THEORETICAL DOCUMENTS OF BECHER

...and the order of succession: does this matter flow more from the things above the earth into the subterranean regions, or the opposite? I do not know whether the primary origin of this matter should rather appear to be attributed to the **subterranean**; or at the very least, by a most universal distribution, it is imparted to the entirety of our sublunary system <note>The "sublunary system" refers to the Earth and its atmosphere, which in pre-modern science was everything below the orbit of the moon.</note> for its chief and almost supreme uses. For certainly, outside the underground, it is perceptibly found nowhere else than in vegetable resins and animal fats: from which things it is finally introduced into *nitrous acid* <note>original: "nitrosum acidum"</note>. On the contrary, in the subterranean kingdom, it is present in all **metals**; not only most clearly in the more "imperfect" ones <note>Metals like lead, tin, or iron that were thought to "corrode" or lose their metallic nature easily.</note>, but by the argument of these, also in the noble ones: since it appears to be the most direct cause and author of **metallicity** <note>original: "metalleitatis"; the quality that makes a substance a metal.</note> in the imperfect ones. It is present, furthermore, in sulfur; it is in **bitumen**, both the purest, **petroleum**: and the most impure, **coal** <note>original: "lithanthracum"; literally "stone-coal."</note>. Indeed, there is no doubt that it is present in all opaque solid bodies; the only question is in which it exists more **immediately**, and in which it exists **mediately** <note>That is, whether it is a primary ingredient or secondary addition.</note>.

(13.) Furthermore, it is not right to overlook that this matter adheres to waters themselves; not only terrestrial waters—the sea, springs, and stagnant well water (whence comes the bituminous or bitter-salty taste of the sea, and the foul putrefaction of other waters)—but also in the water evaporating from these and rising into the atmosphere. This explains the foul scent of mists, and the immense vegetative fertility of rain and dew. It is quite probable that these waters, and especially the sea waters as well as the dew itself, acquire a substance of this kind from the earth, or from the subterranean kingdom.

(14.) Thus indeed it may be likely *a priori* <note>based on theoretical reasoning</note> that this matter—our principle, I say, **phlogiston**—not only agrees perfectly with an earthy nature, but also has its seat, in large quantity, **under the earth**: where it celebrates its marriage or most extensive mixture with the remaining earthy principles. But a clear proof *a posteriori* <note>based on observation and experiment</note>, and one all the more commendable and evident for its simplicity, is shown to us by those experiments in which this matter is restored—even from most exquisitely subtle mixtures, namely from extremely thin and volatile oils that are fluid, moist, and highly elastic—in the blink of an eye into a **solid, dry, dense, fixed substance**. And it is not only **earthy** in appearance and properties, but also readily miscible with the most solid earthy mixtures: namely with **metals**, as well as with **glass**, as **glassmakers** <note>original: "hyalurgi"; from the Greek for "glass-workers."</note> know best. And in truth, it has been a source of wonder more than once how this most simple, yet at the same time most clear experiment, escaped the memory of our Author; or rather how the application of judgment and observation was missed by others through the mere cleverness of modern philosophy. They have more than once raised a joke—though certainly not a crude one—with this problem, when high-sounding talk turned to chemical curiosities, proposing: *How, without any material addition, any most pure and volatile distilled oil can be converted in the blink of an eye into a dry, fixed, earthy powder, and thus ether (for they call oils "ethereal"), or as the common proverb regarding exquisite opposites has it, how **heaven can be changed into earth**.*

->SPECIMEN OF BECHER, PART I, SECTION II.<-

Indeed, it is certain and true everywhere that the highest simplicity escapes and leaves behind the affected wisdom of **inexperienced** <note>original Greek: "ἀπειρίστων" (apeiristōn); referring to those who lack practical skill or experimental trial.</note> men. For this very matter provides a most brilliant proof of the difference between those "panoplies of a frolicking memory"—I mean that hodgepodge of merely *memorized* numerous experiments and superficial comparisons, involving not only the coarsest shared habits and effects but also a flawed and deceptive consideration and determination of them—and **deeper attention** and observation of the true circumstances of even a single, most simple, and obvious experiment. In such a case, it is a matter of reason to understand and recognize that almost any of the *simplest* experiments and products are the true, *solid*, and indeed *only* **principles** in this kind of knowledge. Just as products are more useful and pave the way for various and manifold compositions—either for putting them together or reducing them back to simplicity—the simpler they are.

(15.) This very experiment truly serves as a significant proof of the disposition and tendency of this principle, which has a far greater affinity for **subterranean** than **above-ground mixing**; since, because of its intimate *fiery bond*, it is most readily reduced into a solid state by this method. This state is not only *earthy*, but immediately suitable for the intimate earthy mixture of *sulfur and metals*. Conversely, we have no experiment yet available to show how this substance can actually be raised from an earthy state into that delicate *aqueous fluid*, with one single exception. However, that exception must be taken or understood not with a *grain*, as they say, but with a *globule of salt* <note>A play on the phrase "cum grano salis" (with a grain of salt), suggesting the evidence is even smaller or requires more scrutiny.</note>, since the substance is not actually led from an earthy state into a *fluid* as our problem requires, but only from a most fluid *natural* state into a slightly more fluid or thinner *artificial* one. This indeed seems to be the only—though certainly most laborious—way that this thinning, or the transfer of our matter into a *fluid* state, can be achieved from its *earthy* mixture and character, and its not only most ready but also most firm embrace.

(16.) These points could suffice **by way of a formal argument** <note>original Greek: "κατὰ θέσιν" (kata thesin); a proposition or thesis.</note> as proof, not only direct but also most simple, regarding the earthy nature of *that principle* which we call **phlogiston** <term>Phlogiston: From the Greek for "burnt up." 17th-century chemists believed this was a physical substance trapped in combustible materials (like wood or metals) that was released as fire during burning.</term>, named for its more powerful and better-known effect. But as an example of how much *bare memory* and *judgment* concerning experiments differ, it will be worthwhile to examine those fabrications and arguments which do not quite agree that this principle, phlogiston, exists in metals as something pure and simple. Instead, they think and teach—attacking those with opposing views—that the *mixture of mineral sulfur* itself is what resides in them. These people propose that the sulfur which exists in metals is burned away by fire, so that once its flammable part has been sent out, the **acid** <note>In early chemistry, "acid" was often thought to be the "stony" or "salty" residue left over after the fire-principle left a substance.</note> alone remains firmly with the metal. *Others*, or the same people elsewhere, say that this sulfur in metals is merely changed into *acid* by fire. *Still others* want the flame itself to be acidic; thus, they believe the metal is reduced to powder <note>The "powder" refers to "calx," the ashy residue left after a metal is burned or rusted, which we now know as an oxide.</note> not by the taking away of any constituent substance from the metal, but by the action and the material **addition** <note>original Greek: "prosthesei" (προσθέσει); a technical term for adding material to a mixture.</note> of the flame. Such is their philosophy *regarding the former*. Regarding *the latter*, a new mixing—

mixture in the *reduction* <note>In historical chemistry, "reduction" refers to the process of restoring a metallic "calx" (oxide) back to its solid, usable metallic form.</note> of metal, relying on those positions of theirs, they say: that the *reduction* of such burnt metals can be carried out by *fixed alkali salt*, just as well as by charcoal. They therefore provide, according to their own Reason, such an etiology <note>A detailed explanation of causes.</note> of this supposed effect: that the *reduction* of such metals into a shiny, malleable consistency, meltable by metallic flow, consists solely in either the *removal* or the *saturation* of that acid which had previously reduced the metal to a calx <note>A powder or "ash" produced by heating a metal in air; what we now call an oxide.</note>. But certain difficulties are not removed by such an explanation, which it is impossible to pass over; and not only this, but rather new ones are introduced and formed, which it would be impossible to untangle. Above all, that *experiment* which is assumed as the soul of this entire etiology—*that simple and pure fixed alkali reduces imperfect metals and such metallic bodies as regulus <note>The pure, metallic form of a mineral, often referring here to antimony.</note> and Bismuth, when calcined by burning*—is absolutely **unproven** <note>original Greek: "ἄπειρον" (apeiron); meaning without trial, experimental basis, or experience.</note>. From this, certainly, to wish to infer through experiments things directly contrary to experience is a beginning that tends toward the opposite of the rules of good philosophers. Secondly, the chief difficulty is what then becomes of that *inflammability* of these metals; where, indeed, I fear that with far greater certainty than is imputed to me, metaphysical difficulties must be thought to lie beneath. Namely, that the state of fire does not depend on any kind of *matter*, but is only a naked *quality*, or rather—lest we cause offense with words—a naked *mode of matter*, which is modified differently by fire, and indeed *more by addition than by subtraction*. But truly, there is a new difficulty: how not only fire, but *nitre* <note>Also known as saltpeter (potassium nitrate), a key ingredient in gunpowder and a powerful oxidizing agent.</note> as well, not only snatches away inflammability from metals, but—what is of the greatest consideration—by means of a *brilliant flame*. Since, however, it is established by no experiment that nitre *burns into a flame* except with things that are *materially*, by their own nature, inflammable. But truly, it must yet be demonstrated how this *inflammability*—I mean the matter which, when nitre is added again and again, forms a flame or passes into a flame—could be restored *by the subtraction alone* of some material. That *fixed alkali* does not reduce metallic ashes can be proven by direct experiments. We are speaking chemically, however, of true ashes, or exquisitely burnt-through calxes, not those only partially, cursorily, and superficially scorched, such as *Antimony* moderately burnt, and the thicker *iron scales* <note>original: "battitura ferri"; the flakes of iron oxide that fall off during smithing.</note> which even a magnet still attracts. For nothing is ever reduced from such ashes with alkali unless charcoal has fallen into it. But the business becomes even more manifest *from the result* <note>original: "a posteriori".</note>, while *alkali salt destroys even the whole regulus of antimony* into a powder; it is so far from being able to restore the same to its meltable, shiny, metallic consistency. But again, *nitre* produces the chief difficulty. For if alkali ought to restore the metal to its flow and consistency by destroying that effect of whatever kind, and of whatever origin of acidity; what should that caustic and *most penetrating alkali* not do—certainly most fit for saturating and blunting acid—which is produced when the regulus of antimony is burned with nitre? But it is so far from any reduction following therefrom, that instead the whole mass remains most stubbornly dry; or if it is melted at all, it is reduced into a consistency similar to glass. Most absolutely, it never returns from this constitution into a metallic form through alkali: which, on the contrary, happens most readily...

(17.) Meanwhile, it becomes clearer than the midday sun from this example that not only do bare experiments fail to satisfy the requirements of reason—I mean, the physical science to be constructed regarding these matters—but also that a deficiency or ignorance of the experiments themselves lies at the foundation. And these are not perhaps difficult, abstruse, or secret experiments, but the *simplest* ones lying right before our feet. For our purpose, we must certainly defend our thesis, or this positive assertion: that phlogiston, or that fire-producing matter, is truly something *corporeal* <note>meaning it has a physical "body" or substance</note>; and that it *effectively* enters into the mixture of minerals and the metals themselves. Therefore, for the understanding not only of the *principles* of mixtures, but also of the mixtures themselves, the instruments, and the methods of mixing, these experiments—and their agreement and true, rational comparison—must not only be known and evident and established, but without this, one may never hope to reach even a shadow of a scientific concept regarding these affairs. When, on the contrary, with experiments and reasons correctly collected and connected with each other, everything becomes clear and transparent. For there, when acid is joined with alkali, all *inflammability* is certainly far away; and who could have introduced it here with any absorbent, or by something directly and simply dulling the acid? Especially since fixed alkali, when joined with the whole flammable sulfur itself, is so far from increasing its inflammability that it instead notably entangles or retains it. On the contrary, the acid, which constitutes almost the entire body or weight of the sulfur, cannot prevent that phlogistic substance from burning much more vigorously there than in **charcoal**, where it is not bound by such an acid. Indeed; since in this simple and clear experiment, the *opposite* of all these things occurs, while the acid itself is rather the most manifest *receptacle* of that flammable substance; this flammable thing, however, exists truly not as some *mode of matter*, an accident, or a metaphysical quality, but entirely as a certain true and visible *matter*. It is manifest in that state and in that subject from which it is taken into our new mixture as something *flammable*. It remains, moreover, even under this new combination, just as *flammable*, and it places, introduces, and produces the entire effect of inflammability even in this new mixture. Furthermore, by its own proper mode and motion of inflammation, it can be driven out from this same mixture again whenever one pleases, and again—

# SAMPLES OF BECHER, PART 1, SECTION II

Becher seems to have noticed in many places that these principles follow the body from the very beginning, like a shadow follows a form. Perhaps the most prominent examples are those where, in common salt, he recognizes, identifies, and distinguishes not only the *arsenical* principle of *volatility* and *elasticity*, but also the *mercurial* principle of *metallicity*. Furthermore, he describes the *tight bond between them*, and notes that it is no more difficult to discern them than it is to actually divide and physically segregate them. Most of all, he groups these materials as if under one genus, calling them *sulphurs*: the *arsenical sulphur of salt* and the *mercurial sulphur of salt*. Moreover, he himself notes and recommends this very point—as if it were a common error—to both critics and to those who are more prudent and curious about experiments. I will open my own mind regarding this business in three words. I have always warned that our principle of *igniting* <note>The author is referring to the "principle of inflammability," which would later be famously known in the 18th century as phlogiston.</note> is not of such a nature—that is, it is not "fiery" or "igniting" itself—except when it is combined with other materials. Indeed, I said more about this matter in *Section One*: that true *ignition* and *inflammability*—which must not be deprived of *elasticity*—is finally acquired only from the marriage of *elastic principles* within a <term>salt-bound wateriness</term> <note>original: *sub falsedine hærentis aquositatis*. This refers to a specific chemical state where moisture is held or trapped within a saline substance.</note>. If, from this subject we are discussing—this *principle of inflammability*—one could subtract that which causes these irregular commotions in imperfect compounds (while leaving the rest of its substance intact); and if this principle, restored to its purity in this way, were joined with other pure "earthy-metallic" principles, it is impossible that a product of exact proportions would not be born from it: *not only metallic in a general sense, but surely an absolute and perfect metal in its most specific form.*

(28.) Significant evidence for this is provided by certain traditions that should certainly not be entirely despised. As far as I know, no one has praised or emphasized these since *Isaac Hollandus* <note>A legendary alchemical figure, likely 15th-century, whose writings on the "Stone" and the nature of metals were highly regarded by later chemists.</note>, except for *Cramer in his Dissertation on the Transmutation of Metals* and *Kunckel*. This evidence concerns the <term>calcination</term> <note>The process of heating a metal or mineral in air to reduce it to a powder or "calx."</note> of all metals, even the noble ones, through a long-term, moderate heating. Just as this <term>experimental process</term> <note>original: *enchirifis* (enchiresis). A term used for the manual or practical handling of chemical materials.</note> is not without value for base metals that are more susceptible to fire, it might be worth the effort to see what it can achieve even in the noble metals. Although I would not rashly guarantee the promises that Isaac Hollandus builds upon this assertion—if taken according to the naked letter or a crude understanding—I believe there is more hidden in this foundation than the external appearance promises, for anyone who has undertaken to believe anything regarding these universal matters.

(29.) I have already declared my mind above concerning this business: namely, that I do not think the principle of *igniting* and the principle of *making mercury* (or *making metals*) differ in kind or species; it is more likely they differ only in number <note>In the logic of the time, this means they are essentially the same substance, differing only as individual instances or by degrees of purity/density.</note>. For the time being, while there is little room for anything more than rational *conjectures*, this shall suffice. If anyone is able to speculate more sharply or, better yet, to prove these matters, I promise in good faith to not only grant them their deserved praise but also to honor them as much as is in my power.

And truly, how this might benefit both the private individual and the public—and even more so both together—I would hope to see for myself under the most favorable of omens. However, the tracks of those who came before me frighten me, lest I rashly venture onto such a path; as I professed, not without foundation, in the conclusion of the preceding first Section.

(30.) The *Evidence* <note>original: *Documenta*</note> which *Becher* brought forward in support of this opinion—namely, regarding the *earthy nature* <note>original: *terrestreitate*</note> of this *mercurial* substance—is drawn not only from metals, but also from the *constant dryness* of *mercury* itself. He points to the tendency of *mercury* toward a *powdered* state, which is quite different from its usual fluid nature. (Though in truth, I would rather leave that experiment untouched than try to imitate it—namely, the act of precipitating running mercury into a powder using heat alone.) He also draws evidence from the easy *solidification* <note>original: *concretione*</note> of mercury into a solid *dryness when combined with salts*. These are compounds that, when separate, are not only fluid but entirely liquid in their makeup. Furthermore, he preferred to attribute the great volatility and elasticity of common running mercury to its "crudeness" (that is, the *heterogeneity* or "un-mixedness" of its other material principles) rather than deriving it directly from the *nature of the mercurial principle* itself. Indeed, he views the *mercurial* compound as something *metallically homogeneous*. For those curious about such matters, his suggestions are not to be overlooked; he hints not only that certain *homogeneous metallic-mercurial subjects* can exist that do not take a liquid form, but also declares that *mercuries* created from metals do not coagulate into *powder* (much less remain forever fluid), but soon grow together into a *consistent metallic mass*. Since these matters are somewhat obscure, it is enough to have recounted them on the authority of our Author, and of *Van Helmont* <note>Jan Baptist van Helmont (1580–1644), a foundational chemist and physician.</note> whom he cites, and perhaps also *Suchten* <note>Alexander von Suchten (c. 1520–1575), an alchemist known for his work on the secrets of antimony.</note>.

(31.) We add only this one point. If indeed the reports concerning the *Chinese* and the *Japanese* are true—though they are certainly not beyond all doubt—it is said that they know how to reduce not only *gold*, but even *iron*, to such a state of *softness* that they can stamp anything they wish upon it as if it were *lead* (those who exaggerate prefer to say "as if it were *wax*"). Once this is done, they can restore the metal to its original *hardness* while preserving the entire engraving. If this were true, I say, it would certainly be worth the great effort to discover the craftsmanship behind it. Otherwise (even if it lacks the latter part, namely the *restoration to its original state*), we would truly owe more thanks to our *Becher* if he had more faithfully described the method by which he claims to have experienced *iron being changed into lead*, literally following the tradition of *Paracelsus* <note>Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim (1493–1541), the Swiss physician and alchemist.</note>. For since *Paracelsus*, in that passage, recommends nothing more than a *good melting powder*, it seems entirely consistent with his wisdom—unrefined as it was regarding all philosophical or scientific *chemistry* <note>original: *chymiæ*</note>—that he used some powder containing <term>litharge</term> <note>Lead oxide, often produced during the refining of silver; it can easily be "reduced" or turned back into metallic lead when heated with a carbon source.</note> under the general idea of a "good melting powder." From this, a *reduction of lead* could occur during the smelting. It seems harsh to attribute such a thing to *Becher*, though it leaves room for some suspicion, because in his *Subterranean Physics* <note>original: *Physica Subterranea*, Becher's most famous work (1669), which laid the groundwork for the phlogiston theory.</note>, he spoke less about the entire business of the *reduction* of metals than the matter itself appears to demand; but

### SECTION IV.

## THESIS IV.

# SUBTERRANEAN SUBSTANCES TEND TOWARD METALLICITY; METALS TEND TOWARD PERFECTION.

This is an assertion pointed out here and there by our Author [Becher]. Just as the entire *antiquity of Alchemists* gives this idea its full approval <note>original: *pollicem premit*, literally "presses the thumb," a Roman expression for favor</note>, so we, being unable to agree any more than *truth* itself does, must offer certain warnings for the sake of the true sense—not only of the phrasing, but also of a sound understanding of the concept. 

To be sure, regarding the word or phrase that these materials "tend" toward another state: it is not to be understood as if such materials possess a *natural love, some propensity, or a sort of desire*, as in the fictions of the Peripatetic <note>Aristotelian</note> Scholastics. Nor should we follow some modern philosophers who believe matter possesses an innate, restless *striving* <note>original: *nisum*</note>, through the *activity* of which they might seek and desire their own change into something further, or indeed something better—which would be the common way of speaking. 

Nor is this assertion to be taken in the sense that such *actual* progress is anything more than a potential or a suitability; rather, it is often wrongly treated as if it were an effect actually led into being. These are the idle tales <note>original: *naeniae*</note> of the vainer *mineralogical and metallogical* speculators, especially if they are imbued with an alchemical "tincture." Such people always have these formulas in their mouths: *That nature in the mines can scarcely perfect in a thousand years or more—such as "cooking" tin or lead into silver, or copper and iron into gold, or mercury into one or the other—what art can accomplish in a few months by shortening the process.* 

In this, they suppose that the "ignoble" <note>Base</note> metals, ordinarily in the bowels of the earth, are accustomed—or rather, are destined—to be converted into "noble" <note>Precious</note> metals. And I almost fear for our Author, that by indulging here and there in these received formulas (not just of speaking, but of thinking), he might be suspected of a similar opinion. However, one must attend to the whole scope of his entire new system. There, he teaches and contends with all his might and through the very essence of his Physics, that nothing is achieved in these matters by bare, absolute "cooking" <note>original: *coctione*, the process of metaphorical maturation through heat</note> without a new physical addition and intermixture of materials.

Therefore, this position should instead be understood only in this way: that these aforementioned materials are suited to be brought over partly from their *simplicity* into a *greater composition*, and partly from *looser compositions* into a *weaker mixture*. That is to say, this occurs if such materials and such *motions* of mixing happen to coincide—whether spontaneously (though we have indicated above how accidental this is in subterranean places, and not to be attributed to or assigned to any destined directions) or whether these things are sought out by art and fitted together with one another by right and convenient instrumental methods, modes, and motions.

Hence, there is no danger, either for our *Germans* or for nations further north, that their *iron* riches and the most abundant fertility of this metal will someday randomly degenerate into *gold*. They are rendered all the more secure from this fear because they have never heard it said, even from the most ancient times of their ancestors, that even one *small fissure* <note>original: *rimula*, referring to a minor mineral vein</note> of these veins has been "ripened" <note>The alchemical theory that metals "grow" or "cook" in the earth, eventually becoming gold.</note> into that *softness* <note>Alchemists often described gold as a "soft" or "ripe" metal compared to the "harshness" of iron.</note> which is unfit for stern and serious uses. Yet, if it were a matter of necessity, this certainly ought to happen; specifically, a vein of small thickness, or as the miners call it, a *small fissure*, ought to be "cooked through" in a shorter time than a wider stretch or a *thick vein*. But whatever they may babble about the "fat" <note>In this period, "fatness" (*pinguedo*) was a chemical quality associated with sulfur and flammability.</note> small fissure of some vein, "regarding the fatty fissures" <note>original German: *von denen Schmeer-Klüfftigen*</note>: they do not find a foreign offspring there, but rather one that is genuine and of the same lineage as the rest of the vein—certainly not gold. As the saying goes, "For they don't get it quite that rich" <note>original German: *Dann so fett kommts ihnen nicht*. An idiom suggesting things are not as profitable as one hopes.</note>.

Indeed, that Geographo-Geocosmic observation deserves more consideration—one which has truly been recalled to mind by no one yet, not even in passing, let alone with the dignity it deserves: why are *certain regions of the world found to be supplied with certain metals*, while others are destitute? Truly, it is not without most deserved wonder that the supply of *quicksilver* <note>original: *mercurii vivi*, literally "living mercury"</note> occurs in so few places throughout our known world that it is worthy of mention. But the narrowness of our time does not allow us to wander more widely into business of this kind; it will suffice to have injected a mention of them and to have wished that those equipped not only with better leisure, but also with better resources, would above all compile a history of these matters worthy of reading—if indeed they should judge that reaching some of the causes at the same time (in which we would most easily agree with them) is still a matter of too deep an investigation.

Meanwhile, to arrive at our purpose, I say we shall satisfy the *documents*—that is, the evidence that our thesis truly corresponds to experience—from the mind of our Author [Becher] in the following manner.

(1.) However, it rightly wearies and disgusts one to "cook, chew, crumble, and cram" <note>original: *coquere, mandere, interere atque ingerere*. A reference to a German idiom about spoon-feeding information to the unwilling.</note> such matters for idle and malicious minds through one's own industry, labor, expense, and waste of time—and indeed, through hatred and envy, as the Germans say. ...For if it were done by this method of experimenting, which is possible, through honest gain rather than through many idle tales, there would be room for both solid utility and solid curiosity. (2.) To be able to understand, unfold, and derive these correctly would be a task far more worthwhile for restoring the splendor of *physical doctrine* than many other showy trifles. For the simplest experiments cited there teach, by *perfect demonstration*, both parts of our thesis: namely, partly that *subterranean things readily join themselves to a metallic nature, or, so to speak, pass into it*; and partly that *baser metals transmigrate into better ones*.

(3.) Docimasy is the technical art of testing and assaying ores to determine the amount of precious metal they contain.</note>, whatever our thesis contains. This is necessary because today's philosophical experimenters, even if they hear about, see, or perhaps imitate some experiment in general, are usually satisfied with only the external surface, the first, coarsest, and most obvious appearance, which suffices for them to praise "admirable and stupendous things." ...if these things are carried out correctly, perfect metals emerge, not only gold, which our Author <note>Johann Joachim Becher (1635–1682)</note> hints at, but also silver.

(4.) Thus these are the proofs: 1.) that subterranean substances tend toward metalleity <note>Metalleity refers to the essential quality or potential of a substance to become a metal.</note>. For the subterranean substances recommended there, which are neither metal nor contain actual metal, produce metal through this treatment. Now, this metal was neither in the substances themselves nor in those other additives: therefore, it is manifest that it has finally emerged from the meeting of both. (2.) Nor is there any trace or vestige of a better metal in those metallic bodies recommended there, before their meeting with these sterile subterranean substances (which are prescribed in that experiment we intend); but finally, after the meeting of those things with such a metal, that better metal is born. Therefore, this genesis of a better metal arises certainly from the meeting of both, but nevertheless chiefly from the metal itself—by its progress, I say, to a more perfect state. Since (3) if those subterranean substances are treated separately by such a method, and if such a metal is also treated separately by such a method: in neither way is anything produced similar to the products of the other method. Indeed, a metal is more easily ruined into a more ignoble <note>In alchemy, "ignoble" or "base" metals are those that oxidize or corrode, like lead or copper, as opposed to "noble" metals like gold.</note> and plainly degenerate state than it is promoted into a better one. This should be noted.

(5.) Indeed, what increases the wonder is that even those very simple subterranean substances, which are here transformed into a metallic consistency, generate silver and gold far more easily than any other more ignoble metal. And, the conversion of one ignoble metal into another ignoble one is far more difficult and less known than the individual improvement of each into a perfect one.

# SPECIMEN OF BECHER PART I. SECTION II.

Not only can no silver or gold be found in those assumed materials through the most exquisite <term>assay|The process of testing a metal or ore to determine its ingredients and quality</term> ever instituted; but that improvement, with regard to the *metal* assumed, can be *repeated* so many times with the same metal—which was used in that way the first or second time—until any of the metal still remains. Truly, from those other *earthy* principles (in the <term>Becherian sense|Referring to Johann Joachim Becher's theory that all solid matter is composed of three types of "earths": stony, fatty/inflammable, and fluid/mercurial</term>) which are employed, absolutely nothing *metallic* can be demonstrated by any assay; it always remains at least ambiguous whether it was produced by the *operation* itself rather than simply *extracted* or *separated*. 

But indeed, this settles the whole dispute: even if a common assay shows some metallic trace, by this deeper method of ours, such a vastly different quantity is produced that no one skilled in assaying would deny that such a grain as is gathered by a proper operation (for example, from half an ounce of those earths, one easily gets two grains of silver, which also yields a conspicuous proof of gold) could by no means have either escaped a common assay or been so hidden in an operation skillfully performed, because they would present themselves immediately in the very first act of proper melting.

(8.) Truly, it would be an eternal disgrace to those who have ever wished to be called **Chemists**, if so much silver remained in such materials and they had never yet called this matter to mind, and had kept silent about such a great benefit to the public utility during such a great public shortage of silver. For certainly, it can be seen with one's eyes at any hour that at least one *mark* <note>A traditional unit of weight for precious metals, roughly 230 grams</note> of silver remains in a civil hundredweight of this material (though according to us, materially speaking, it is to be *prepared* through this one method rather than *separated*). 

Indeed, to remove this objection regarding our obligation toward the public from ourselves, let me whisper three words in the ear of such doubters. We, who profess the name of **Philosophy**, must also study these things. What if this operation succeeded in *small tests* (in which the instruments for mixing can be used with due effectiveness), but in large quantities, and in smelting houses and refineries, it refused to comply with those superficial labors? Let others raise a laugh in their usual way and call the art *useless*; I believe the whole argument regarding civil use—and indeed that these things happen rightly and in order so that *like lips have like lettuce* <note>original: "similia habeant labra lactucas" — a Latin proverb meaning "like treats like," or that things are appropriately matched to their recipients</note>—is the work of divine providence. Those who look at **practical Philosophy** will not value this argument highly; those who understand **theoretical Philosophy** will certainly value it most. For it enriches them not with silver and gold, but with *science*, which they prefer to seek first rather than to claim for themselves.

(9.) This matter is certainly another huge and most exquisite proof of the difference between the bare, crude memory of an experiment and the understanding of it, along with its proper interpretation—I mean both its scientific explanation and its application. The *experiment in smelting houses and refineries* is a daily occurrence; it establishes a certain right not only for the refiners, but also for the **Owners of the Mining Company** <note>original: "Gewerksschafft" — a traditional Germanic mining collective or guild</note> who possess the entire fruit of the ores. And this is true not only from the smelting house and the refining hearth, but from the assaying furnace itself. # BECHER’S THEORETICAL DOCUMENTATION

Our moderate debaters—and they judge nothing else besides their own kind to be worthy of their estimation—do not understand this. However, those who actually live among metals understand a little better that because matter is often sterile, one should not despise small yields.

(10.) Thus, not without cause have I explained this matter at length. Since it would be superfluous, in my judgment, to bring forth well-known things over and over again, if any perhaps still ignore this *most famous* experiment, they can at least go to the authors and draw the richest instruction from them. But let them beware of one thing: that they do not allow themselves to be repelled by the excuse that these assertions of ours are nothing but <term>chimerical|Imaginary, fantastic, or impossible, named after the Chimera of Greek mythology.</term> concepts and ideas. I will supply a most peaceful solution to such arguments for our curious questioners: namely, that in the face of all those harsh excuses, they should persist in the *thesis* <note>The formal proposition or specific point of the argument.</note> and ask that the question be answered directly: can the critics demonstrate this *most famous* experiment, and the very clear results included within it, or not? If they can, then they should certainly not speak ill of others for asserting that so many and such solid scientific demonstrations are found in this experiment. If, however, they cannot demonstrate it, our questioners should respond nothing to all those insults, but silently leave these people behind. They should seek these things out for themselves around metallurgical and <term>docimastic|The art of assaying, or testing the purity and composition of metals and ores.</term> workshops regarding the experiment itself, and weigh the evidence with sound reason so that they may understand the documentation.

# Evidence that these things truly are so and happen thus, spontaneously, in the macrocosm, and by art.

The next step is to move from providing documentation to proceeding with experiments. From this, I will further refine this thesis by gathering those experimental documents which have, until now, been cited somewhat sporadically, and collecting them into one place. This is done so that it might become clear, again and again, how a simple experiment or observation differs from the *use* of that experiment—that is, its scientific connection, its reasoning, explanation, and application. However, by the very nature of these things, such applications are themselves produced in every way as experiments and, properly speaking, deserve to be called such. 

Thus, for example, the fact that *glass of antimony and lead*, as well as the *calces* <note>original: "calces"; these are metal oxides produced by heating, appearing as powders.</note> *of antimony, lead, tin, and bismuth*, can be restored to their metallic consistency using *charcoal*, are all individual experiments; even though the general principle behind the experiment is but *one*. Meanwhile, a "document" differs from a "strict experiment" in that for the former goal, a bare allegation is sufficient; for the latter goal, however, an express prescription of manual circumstances is required. This includes, for example, the *selection of materials, weight, preparation for better processing, and the specific type of operation to be used*—whether the business succeeds better by *distilling, sublimating, dissolving and drawing off, dissolving and precipitating, cementing, or melting*.

Therefore, according to this method, we shall consider in this section (in the manner of documentation) those experiments which our Author produces from daily and skillful observation, as well as those supplied by the rest of experience.

(1.) Many and varied experiments and observations demonstrate that from these earths—namely the *sandy, gravelly, glass-making, flammable, dry substance*—and finally that most subtle *metallizing* matter, there come forth *glasses of various tints; calces* (that is, earthy concretions of various compositions); *metallic mutations; the destruction of metals from their own mixture and their restitution or reduction back into it; the volatilization of fixed things; and the fixation of volatile things (or at least their binding)* by means of a firmer connection in a *dry, earthy form*. All of these things are demonstrated most clearly and manifest by *art* <note>In this context, "art" refers to the skilled practice of chemistry or alchemy.</note> itself. Yet, a good portion also happens *spontaneously*, even in the hidden depths of the underground, as shown by observations already cited here and there (and thus to be briefly repeated here), while others are shown by various practices and observations still to be found if one pays attention. 

For instance, regarding *natural compositions*, it is well known from various experiments that *very red earths, hematite, red ochre, and garnets* contain within themselves a substance very close to an *iron mixture*. This is supported by what the Author brings forward in Book 1, Section 3, Chapter 5, Number 12: how *red ochre* <note>original: "rubrica"; a red iron ore used as a pigment.</note>, solely by extraction through <term>spirit of salt|Now known as hydrochloric acid.</term>, is so exhausted of that composition which penetrates every part of its substance (down to the smallest individual grain of its consistency), that once this matter is removed, nothing remains but *white slime* <note>original: "albus limus".</note>. # BECHER’S THEORETICAL DOCUMENTS
<meta>Catchword: (4.) Where</meta>

...that substance which imparts color to them can be separated, and partly compressed into a *metallic-like regulus* <note>The term "regulus" refers to the pure metallic button or mass that settles at the bottom of a crucible after smelting.</note>; and partly collected and separated again from such a body, like a kind of dye. Where, just as with that very incorporation—by which something from these types of stones works its way into a metallic-like consistency (which even chalk does not escape)—it becomes clear from this that for these substances of a more *earthy* nature, a readiness for metallic mixing is easily approached, if not fully undergone.

(2.) Indeed, what greater evidence can we bring forward than *Cadmia* <note>original: "Cadmia"; here referring to calamine or zinc ore.</note> itself? Since no one until now has dared to remove it from the category of *earthy-stony* solids. Meanwhile, it is well known how large a portion of it combines with copper so that it not only reflects a metallic appearance but even maintains an exquisite malleability, such that it can be reduced into those gilded leaves known as *false gold-leaf* or *beaten metal-leaf* <note>original: "falsche Gold-Blätter, oder geschlagene Metall-Blätter"</note>. And yet—what might seem worthy of wonder—even under this very mixing with the metal (the copper), it is and remains a pure and simple *earthy substance*. By its own solitary nature, it is not only entirely alien to that bright, dense, and firm aggregation seen in metals, but especially regarding malleability—it cannot be compared even in a dream; it is rather the exact opposite. 

Just as that substance can be separated from the copper again without the slightest effort of alteration or new change, through the simplest naked *separation*, in the form of a very fine dry powder. This is done by skillfully amalgamating the filings of *brass* <note>original: "orichalci"</note> with quicksilver <note>mercury</note>, adding only plain water; by this means, the powdery substance (which the mercury wipes away from the metal) can be washed out. It happens in another even more immediate, indeed momentary act, when the brass (thinned into those leaves) is mostly driven off into the air by way of a visible *fiery* or *glowing consumption*. This occurs when such a leaf is moved toward a *candle flame* at any side or corner: from there, in a moment, the glow creeps across it, and as far as it reaches, it leaves behind a copper leaf that looks more like copper ash.

(3.) Certainly similar things happen in *lead*, as well as in *tin*, and even in *iron* itself—namely, that such diverse substances (which are more *earthy* than the truly *homogeneous* nature of any metal) still cling tenaciously to them. This is evidenced not only by the different workability of *iron*, both when *hot* under the hammer and when *cold* (specifically its flexibility), but also by that abundant actual separation of *glassy slag* <note>original: "vitreæ scoriæ"</note> when the cruder *iron* substance of the first smelting is melted again. In this process, the *phlogiston* <note>original: "Phlogistos"; in Becher's theory, this is the "inflammable earth" or principle of fire found in charcoal.</note> from the charcoal works its way into the finest part of the iron, forcing the coarser earthy part to separate of its own accord. In *lead*, it is not entirely likely that all that *zinc* <note>original: "Zinki"</note> substance is removed so perfectly that absolutely nothing remains within the metal. Truly, more than one experiment has shown us that *tin*, which is used especially by the makers of pewter beads—the *button casters* or *pewter button makers* <note>original: "die Knopffgiesser oder zinnern Knopffmacher"</note>—is adulterated with an arsenical metallic substance.

### SPECIMENS OF BECHER, PART I, SECTION II

(4.) Indeed, since we have happened upon the mention of **arsenic**, it can also be noted how it unites with copper with such great readiness into a metallic, shiny, and workable body. This is remarkable because, by its own natural character, arsenic exists as nothing more than a substance of **regulus-like** <note>original: "regulinae"; a "regulus" is a brittle, semi-metallic substance that settles at the bottom of a crucible during smelting.</note> consistency. For this reason, it can be separated from copper that has been whitened in this way by a simple manual process—just like **calamine** <note>original: "Cadmia"</note>—namely through a bare amalgamation and separation using mercury <note>original: "argentum vivum"</note>. The same thing happens with the **regulus of antimony** among metals undergoing amalgamation, and with **zinc**, in the case of that brass-like alloy which they call **Prince’s Metal** <note>original: "Printzmetall"; a type of brass consisting of copper and zinc, named after Prince Rupert of the Rhine.</note> today, where the zinc is separated in the form of a powder.

(5.) Furthermore, most exquisite evidence of how, conversely, **metals approach an earthy nature** is surely provided by the **reduction into glass** <note>original: "deductio in vitrum"; the process of vitrification.</note> of the "imperfect" metals—**lead, copper, iron**, and also **regulus** of antimony—even without the addition of other earths. In the case of **tin**, however, this requires the addition of **glass-making earths**. 

Just as conversion into **glass** belongs primarily and immediately to those **earths which are worthy of this name by common consent—silt, gravel, sands, flints, rocks, and crystals**—and is most directly their own property: so too is it a remarkable effect when **ductile metals (which are far removed from transparency and share much in common with mercury) turn into glass (a substance that is exquisitely brittle, the direct opposite of ductility, transparent, and entirely alienated from intimate contact with mercury)**. This effect brings metals as close as possible to **earths**; indeed, it thoroughly proves and convinces us of the **earthy** nature of metals. 

Lest I allow a "prejudicial question" (as they say) to interfere with the worth of this testimony, there is no need to look for an argument for the degenerating metallic nature—and its descent toward the earthy—in the fact that vitrified metals so deeply reject any interaction with mercury. It is also seen in how they turn away from their own former metallic body, refusing any intimate contact with it. Hence, **glass of lead** <note>original: "vitrum Saturni"; "Saturn" was the alchemical name for lead.</note>, prepared without any additives, neither enters into the lead itself, nor does the lead (while still whole and true metal) receive the glass into its company. Instead, the glass floats upon the metal, and they touch each other only at their outermost surfaces. This same behavior is observed in other **glasses**, such as that of **antimony**, not only with its own **regulus**, but with all other **metals** in exactly the same way. 

By this example, I do not see how any greater proof could be brought forward—not only a positive proof of the metal's agreement with **earthy** properties, but also a negative proof of its abandonment and **degeneration** from a texture that was, moments before, entirely similar to itself. Indeed, at this very time, the metal is no longer similar to itself in its glass-like consistency, except perhaps in its total mass or weight. For another such metal can be brought into the same state with only a very small loss of weight; once it has acquired that same glassy consistency, it merges intimately and thoroughly with the previously vitrified quantity.

(6.) Becher calls the **reduction of metals into earth** the **Great Secret** <note>original: "Magnum arcanum"</note>. He believes that anyone who knows how to reduce metals into **earth** in this way must excel in Chemistry. For my part, I have willingly left the discovery and publication of this craftsmanship to those who excel in Chemistry. Meanwhile, if anyone should find the delay tedious, since even—

...called, namely the better *reguline* <note>original: regulina — refers to the pure metallic state of a substance, often the "button" found at the bottom of a crucible after smelting</note> part of *antimony*, when deflagrated with an equal quantity of *niter* <note>original: nitri — saltpeter or potassium nitrate</note>, exhibits and presents a substance of a completely *glassy* consistency. This is *soft, brittle, meltable, volatile*, clearly dark and unapparent <note>original: $\alpha\phi\alpha\nu\eta s$ (aphanes) — indistinct, invisible, or lacking a clear form</note>. If a half-weight of niter is mixed into this material (both being well pulverized) and a detonation is triggered in a lightly glowing crucible, the nitrous spirit <note>original: spiritus nitrosus — nitric acid vapors</note> smokes away; the alkali of the niter, however, joins with the acid of sulfur that had remained in that glassy mass to form "enix salt" <note>original: sal enixum — an archaic term for potassium bisulfate</note>. If this salt is separated from the remaining powder by hot water and then coagulated and melted with charcoal, it exhibits sulfur once again. Indeed, at least when it is crystallized from solution, it produces crystals identical to vitriolated tartar <note>original: tartaro vitriolato — potassium sulfate</note>. Thus, it demonstrates that the *acid of sulfur* remains within that glassy body.

(12.) Whether this *acid* is specifically what causes the metal to *vitrify* <note>turn into glass</note> is another question, which we have already largely examined above. Certainly, in the *regulus* <note>the metallic heart of the ore</note>, there is no *acid of sulfur*, yet it still vitrifies, and does so with a caustic *alkali* concurring and interwoven within it, as shown by that *amber-colored dross* mentioned in the same place. Regarding lead turning into *glass* with *niter*, there is that well-known procedure <note>original: enchirisis — a Greek term for a practical manual or technique</note> produced long ago by *Glauber* <note>Johann Rudolf Glauber (1604–1670), a famous German-Dutch alchemist and chemist</note> for refining metals using *lead* and *niter* in a crucible. Truly, the remaining *inflammable* substance not only reduces the *regulus* and other metals (when present in sufficient quantity) into their clearly metallic consistency, but also tints and darkens their glasses as long as it still stubbornly adheres to them. Not only does it tint them, but it also makes them *meltable* and *soft*. This is proven by the removal <note>original: aphæresis — a Greek term for taking away or withdrawal</note> of that substance from the regulus; either by a sufficient quantity of the same *niter*, or even by simple *prolonged* heating in the open air. For just as with a large quantity of *niter*, the powder becomes *white and very delicate*, and very *fixed* <note>stable under heat</note> when enclosed; so too under prolonged heating, even from bare Antimony—and even more so from the regulus—a very white calx <note>original: calx — the crumbly oxide residue left after a metal is burned</note> is produced. In both ways, the material is not only extremely resistant to melting, but is also endowed with a very pale color. In short, conversely, the paler the color of the reguline and metallic glass, the more difficult it is to melt this same glass. Furthermore, what sooty smoke can do, even in common *sand-based glasses*, is experienced and witnessed not only by glass-blowers using *damp* or *resinous woods*; they are also unable to prepare pure and clear glasses using fossil coals in open vessels, because the sooty vapors enter the glass and blacken it.

(13.) Not without cause have we indulged a little more extensively in describing these artificial matters, so that these things may be examined in full at a convenient time, place, and quantity. These veins—by their perfectly *friable* porosity and their entire consistency, which is *not stony, not muddy, not slimy, and not purely sandy*, but unusual in color, texture, and indeed in whatever mixture still adheres to them—provide sufficient proof that they once contained something *metallic* or *sulfurous*.
