(14.) Moreover, specimens of this kind occur here and there in mountainous tracts; just as in the mountains around the city of *Jena*, countless such veined channels appear. These, while mimicking the constitution of a perfect vein, meanwhile contain nothing but a *powdery, purple-blackish* <note>original: fabulosam purpureo-nigricantem — "fabulosa" here likely refers to "sabulo" or sandy/powdery earth, common in descriptions of mineral "mulm"</note> marrow, which can be crushed with the fingers. These are enclosed above and below by *greenish mud* and held within a *stony fortification*. Furthermore, in the very mines that are fertile in ores, such sterile and corrupt passages are often encountered. There, either in the *veins* themselves, or in certain *branches* or *fissures* of them, such exhausted, sapless, and even "sucked-out" spaces are found, as if eaten away and consumed by decay or rot. The miners call these *Mulm* <note>German: loose, earthy, or decayed mineral matter</note> and *Faulen* <note>German: rot or decay</note>. These areas are either stripped of all mineral—especially *metal*—or are at the very least volatile, styptic, inert, and very dry concretions. However, that such *decayed*, *soft*, and seemingly eaten-away structures sometimes occur in which *silver* <note>original: argentum</note> is nonetheless present, is both attested by experience and not contrary to reason. For just as it is not found that *silver* is so readily dissolved, so on the contrary, it is not at all inconsistent with the nature of these things that other more corruptible *minerals*, which had remained mixed with the silver, have meanwhile been resolved into a vapor and dissipated, leaving the *silver* behind.

(15.) Indeed, that this is the particular fate of certain *more corruptible* minerals and ores is also shown by the fact that this kind of "lifelessness" of metals is more rarely encountered deep in the *profundity* of a vein’s position, where it is perfectly beset by waters; rather, it occurs more often, or entirely, where there is contact and deeper penetration of freer *air*, or at most in such subterranean spaces where the constitution is more *vaporous-humid* than immersed in absolute fluid.

(16.) Furthermore, the *breaking open* of such *vaults* <note>original: cryptarum — referring to natural underground cavities or pockets</note> often demonstrates what has occurred within them; for when they suddenly pour out the most piercing and foul vapors, they suffocate unwary miners. Or, in a slightly more tolerable eruption, they emerge from the fissures of the tunnels like fermenting beer, with the appearance of *smoky dregs*; hence they are called *Guhr* <note>German: a mineral deposit that is still liquid or pasty</note> and *ausgaehren* <note>German: fermenting out</note> by the metal-workers. Just as higher up at the surface of the earth, such vapors and smoky exhalations—by scorching, consuming, and suffocating grass and trees in the manner of lightning—have earned the names *Witterungen* <note>German: weathering or noxious mineral vapors</note> and *Ausbrande* <note>German: burn-outs or scorched spots</note>.

(17.) It is surely from this foundation that the common saying of the miners flows—a saying also cited once or twice by *Becher*—when, in the meeting of such *sterile* tracts, they complain that they have come too late and found an *empty nest*, the birds having flown. For in truth, it is immensely easier and more common for it to happen this way: that ores truly imbued with metal are again stripped of it; and that the metal, reduced into vapors or a *humid* dissolution, is either snatched away far and wide by the *exhalation* from that veined tract, or is carried off mixed into the surrounding waters. ...mountains, or metallic tunnels—*on paths, galleries, lengths, and adits* <note>original: auf Zügen, Strecken, Lengen, Stollen — these are specific German mining terms for the orientation and type of underground passages</note>. In the former, through distilling and gathering, and in the latter, by flowing forth, they often break out in no small quantity, indeed even with violence. They provide waters of this kind, either exquisitely *vitriolated* <note>original: vitriolatas — saturated with sulfates, often green or blue in color</note>, such as those from *Spiš* <note>original: Scepusienses — a region in modern-day Slovakia</note>, not far from *Kremnica* <note>original: Cremnitio — a famous mining town in Upper Hungary</note>, which contain the purest copper. There are also various acidulated waters, or at the very least, waters so notably imbued with such vitriolic material that they are unfit, even harmful, for use by men and cattle. These are eminently worthy of the name *wild mountain-water* <note>original: wild Berg-Wasser</note>, or "ferine" <note>wild or beast-like</note> waters.

(18) Of this same *dissolution* and *diffusion* of such minerals through waters into the most widespread tracts of land—which show no orderly *direction* of veins, but rather lie open as if in immense expanses—the effects are primarily those most abundant and inexhaustible heaps of *earths*. These are imbued with metallic *colors*, or rather *solutions*, appearing in various shades of *green*, *yellow*, and *red*. A massive example and proof of this nature is the *Goslar Ochre* <note>original: Ochra Goslariensis — a famous iron-oxide deposit in the Harz mountains</note>, which springs up in an inexhaustible supply. It is entirely the offspring of *mineral earth*. We do not believe this mixture happened at its very birth; rather, these *vitriolic* waters, while passing through these earths, corrode the subtle earth and *wash away* <note>original: abstergendo</note> the metal they contain, reducing these earths to this state. Therefore, although other common assayers <note>technicians who test ores for metal content</note> usually find nothing of value, such as copper, to be separated from *Ochre*; if it is treated according to *Becher’s* experiment—by adding *linseed oil* <note>original: oleo lini</note>—and only then is that heavier sediment subjected to assaying, the presence of copper becomes quite conspicuous. As *Cramer* <note>Johann Andreas Cramer, a renowned 18th-century metallurgist</note> has already noted in his *Dissertation on the Transmutation of Metals*. Indeed, this *vitriolic* washing and separation in *Ochre* is also proven by its effectiveness in the *distillation of mineral spirits, niter, and common salt.*

(19) However, just as this *resolution* and *destruction* of minerals—and even of *metals*—into a degenerate earthy nature is prompt, so, on the contrary, the production and *new generation* of similar metals or minerals is quite rare. Regarding *veined tracts*, we have already stated our opinion above, which we repeat in a word: nothing of the sort is usually regenerated today. Whatever exists of these things was placed there immediately during the first production and distribution of the *Geocosmos* <note>original: Geocosmi — Becher's term for the Earth as a chemical and physical system created by God</note>. Yet, we are so far from denying that a certain *regeneration* took place in other locations after that *primary* production—and can still happen today, though in a purer form—that we rather recognize no small *proof* of it in the filling-up of fragments and carcasses of both *animals* and *vegetables* found here and there. These are found preserved in their original shape, but filled with such subtle *metallic ore* in place of their original matter. Various specimens of this occur, but nowhere more abundantly than what was once discovered in the county of *Mansfeld* in *shale* <note>original: fissili lapide, Schieffer</note>. There, the bodies of *fish* of various kinds were frequently found, so exquisitely transmuted into such ore that nothing could surpass them. Likewise, in the Princely County of *Henneberg*, not far from the city of *Ilmenau*, such stones of a fissile nature—but actually of *muddy* origin—were found not so deep down. In these were fragments of not only *algae* but especially *ferns*, to be distinguished most exquisitely, bitu- <note>catchword for next page: bituminosa (bituminous)</note>

This is enclosed above and below by a **greenish** mud and contained within a rocky fortification. Furthermore, in the mines themselves, even those fertile with minerals, such sterile and corrupted passages are frequently encountered. In these places—either in the veins themselves or in certain *branches* or *fissures*—these exhausted, juice-less, or rather "sucked-out" spaces are found, as if eaten away and consumed by decay or rot. Miners call these *Mulm* and *Faulen* <note>original: Mulm und Faulen — German mining terms; "Mulm" refers to pulverized, earthy ore, and "Faulen" to decayed or "rotten" rock</note>. However, experience testifies—and reason does not oppose it—that such decayed, soft, and seemingly gnawed-away constitutions sometimes occur in which **silver** nonetheless remains. For just as it is not found that **silver** resolves so readily, so on the contrary, it is not at all inconsistent with the nature of these things that other more corruptible *minerals*, which had remained mixed with the silver, have meanwhile been resolved into a breath and **dissipated**, leaving the **silver** behind.

(15.) ### EXAMPLES FROM BECHER, PART I, SECTION II

...voluminous mineral matter, substituted in place of the former substance <note>original: "minosa-minerali materia, in locum antiquæ substantiæ substituta"; the first word "voluminosa" began on the previous page</note>. For however many people there are who lean toward the idea that those shapes of fish have no such simple origin, but were instead formed by a **"game of nature"** <term>game of nature: (Latin: lusus naturae) a historical term used to describe fossils or unusual natural formations that seemed to mimic living things but were thought to be "jokes" or accidents of the earth</term>, as they call it; yet, has any evidence of such a "playful nature" ever actually been found? 

On the contrary, among matters however obscure, one particular explanation fits far better than the other: namely, that even after the time of the Flood—indeed, even after Christ was not only born but worshipped—high floods occurred. These floods, or other violent causes, produced the collapse of mountains or hills, which in turn created plains. In that very process, they filled lakes and lagoons, and animals, humans, corpses, and various movable goods were either immediately enveloped or carried there by the settling of the watery dregs. All these things, I say, are certainly more probable to reason than those supposed "games" of a mind that is too credulous and shrinks from complex or unusual events, attributing them to "nature" or some "spirit" intent on the humorous mixing and structuring of minerals.

(20) Indeed, much more worthy of consideration is that assertion we briefly indicated above, which applies a difficult but brilliant proof to these matters: namely, that a primary fertile principle, **Phlogiston** <note>original Greek: Φλογιστόν; the substance of fire and inflammability in Becher’s chemistry</note>, is of the greatest use in reducing saline-earthy vapors or flows into a dry mixture. For since this principle—especially in its most subtle state and delicate, watery mixture (from which it returns to an earthy state through the series and order of combinations and resolutions in the universe)—abounds in such vegetables and animals, it associates itself in various ways with the other principles of the saline-earthy constitution, following that most worthy **experiment of Becher** <note>referring to Johann Joachim Becher, 1635–1682, the chemist whose theories this text defends</note>. In this way, it produces metals. It therefore follows from these good consequences that the condition of these things in these fossil examples could not have been otherwise than it actually was.

(21.) These theories are supported by the fact that the **metal** usually found in such figures is, most frequently of all, **Copper** <note>original: Cuprum</note>; indeed, we have not yet been able to see any other metal in such shapes. This exquisitely demonstrates the abundance of that **Phlogiston** principle, because copper is not only dissolved by **acids**, as other metals are, but also by **alkalis** and **fats** (oils). Even in an open **fire**, it is reduced to ash more readily than any of the other metals. From this, the champions of chemical science have used the clumsy argument that acidity must be present in oils because they dissolve copper; however, the opposite can be deduced from the same foundation: that oils are alkalis, because they dissolve copper just as an **alkali** does. Indeed, this is true not just in a grammatical sense, but in a physical sense—it acts in the same manner and proportion as an alkali: namely, **delicately, thinly, and sparingly**, quite unlike acids.

(22.) Thus, these are also proofs, according to our thesis, that the **earthy** mixtures—consisting of the first, second, and even the third principles—are found both in the **bowels of the earth (the macrocosm)** and by art in the **laboratories and workshops of the microcosm** <term>macrocosm and microcosm: the "great world" (the universe/earth) and the "little world" (man or the laboratory), reflecting the alchemical belief that the same laws govern both</term>...

### BECHER’S THEORETICAL DOCUMENTS

...in producing as well as in reducing, generations and mixtures are brought about. Moreover, from this same foundation flows that concern of prudent **miners**, which was not without cause not only noted but also praised by our Author <note>The "Author" refers to Johann Joachim Becher, the 17th-century chemist and physician</note>: the practice of throwing fragments of rocky, slimy, or earthy veins back into the **shafts** <note>original: "Schächte"</note> that necessity forces them to abandon. This is done in the hope that such wandering mineral-metallic vapors might, over some stretch of time, work their way into them again. The Author also advises and urges this; however, as for his command to also add **slags** <note>original: "scorias"; the stony waste matter separated from metals during smelting</note> from the melt to these shafts, I either do not grasp his meaning or I do not follow it. This aggregation <note>the slag</note> is too firm and intimate for any mixing—or even simple access, let alone deep entry—to find a place there.

(23.) For although I agree as much as possible that not every glassy state excludes all mixing or composite infiltration, a great difference nevertheless exists between **glassy slags**, which are very dense and firm, and **tender glasses**. The latter are not only still provided with the **Phlogiston** <note>original Greek: Φλογισῷ; the 17th-century principle of inflammability and fire</note> principle, but are also thoroughly imbued with sulfurous acid. Smelters know well enough, almost all of them, how much difference lies between **tender and tough, hard slags** <note>original German: "Unter weichen, und harten strengen Schlacken"</note>. Some also know the reason for that difference, and what **soft slags** <note>original German: "weiche Schlacken"</note> actually are compared to the tough, thick ones. Indeed, the disposition of "tender" glassy compositions is even more ready—and thus entirely different in this category—for mixtures. This can be illustrated by examples of glass: 1.) **antimonial**, 2.) **saturnine** <note>"Saturnine" refers to lead; Saturn was the alchemical name for the metal lead</note>, and 3.) **common** window glass.

It is very well known that **antimonial glass** is affected by water alone, and even more so by salty liquids. This is shown by its famous emetic power <note>The "emetic cup" was made of antimonial glass; wine kept in it became a powerful medicine to induce vomiting</note>, which it grants to infusions of such liquids. Today, hardly anyone would still doubt that this happens not through "mere irradiation" or the "mere mode of matter" (an "act of formal emanation," as the Schools <note>Scholastic philosophers who favored abstract explanations over material ones</note> say), but surely through a **material communication** <note>meaning actual particles of the substance pass into the liquid</note>.

As for **saturnine glass**—prepared, for example, from three parts of any glass-forming **lead calx** <note>lead oxide</note> and one part flint or very white sand—it is a joy to behold its momentary change when powdered. The powder changes from its white or yellowish color to a dark brown or blackish hue if a dish half-full of a solution of common or antimonial sulfur is placed next to this powder (spread out on paper), and the precipitation of this solution is triggered with vinegar. For by that volatile sulfurous vapor alone flowing toward it, the entire surface of this spread-out powder quickly **turns black**. This happens throughout its entire extent if the lower parts are periodically brought to the top by stirring.

It is no less curious to see how such **discoloration** occurs on those glazed dishes—the **pottery-porcelain** <note>original: "Töpffer-porcellain"</note> of Holland, Berlin, and Frankfurt. The white part of the glass is not equally affected or altered, nor is the blue portion affected so strongly; it is primarily those streaks of **black glass** drawn around the figures. Around these, a wide blackness, almost like a **purple pigment** <note>original: "purpurissum"</note>, is quickly induced. And indeed, this is not merely superficial so that it could be wiped or washed away, but is entirely constant and lasting. It is a common phenomenon, though certainly of this nature, how a "saccharine" <note>sweet-tasting; likely referring to "Sugar of Lead" or lead acetate</note> solution of this glass or of **litharge** <note>lead oxide</note> reacts with such sulfur or a solution...

### SPECIMEN BECHERIANUM PART I SECTION II

...it is known even to children, in the case of **sympathetic ink** <note>A type of invisible ink that becomes visible through chemical reaction or heat</note>, that it is blackened by the vapor of **orpiment** <note>original: "auripigmenti"; a deep yellow arsenic sulfide mineral</note>. Women also notice that **common** window glass is altered, and indeed so deeply that it can no longer be wiped clean, if the windows are washed with **lye** <note>original: "lixivio"; a strong alkaline solution</note>—especially the dark kind made from coals—and then immediately exposed to the heat of the sun. However, there might also be a contribution here from **wooden** dyes from the square wooden frame surrounding the window, as the saline lye spreads sulfurous portions of this wood into the glass. The result is, of course, a permanent clouding of the glass. But these effects are far removed, not only from the **slags** <note>original: "scoriis"; stony waste matter from smelting</note> of the smelting houses, but also from any deeper penetration and mixture.

(24.) In preference to **slags**—which are certainly and absolutely useless for such a purpose—I would prefer that **silt** <note>original: "limum"</note> which comes from a certain silty, fissile rock <note>original German: "Schiefer, die das blosse Wetter bebt, daß sie geschlemmt werden können"; Shale, which the mere weather breaks down so that they can be washed</note> found in various places, either without roasting or at most after a light roasting, where the cooperation of **rain and air** alone allows it to dissolve into silt. I am certain that such silts, if collected more abundantly by fitting pits under a stream or by simply diverting the stream into a broad plain, would be immensely more suitable for these purposes. Furthermore, **silts** of this nature promise even greater hope for a new impregnation because they frequently exhibit the fertility of that principal **separative** principle, the **sulfurous-flammable** <note>A reference to the phlogiston theory, the 17th-century idea of a fire-element within combustible materials</note>. Indeed, when ignited in large heaps, they burn or glow continuously for a vast amount of time—for three months, more or less—while giving off a stench that is far more **bituminous** <note>Like coal or tar</note> than purely sulfurous. There is little doubt that a **bituminous** disposition can provide the instrument for at least the genesis and mixture of **copper**; just as a more indefinite **inflammable** principle, or one mixed with water, can serve both instrumentally and materially in the generation of such metallic mixtures. With this very view in mind, I would prefer that any **fatty** materials—**stems, stalks, roots, leaves, twigs, and clippings**—be associated, joined, and worked into those silts by whatever means. However, this space is too narrow to test that theory which suggests it is likely that the **carcasses of aquatic animals** might be of **greater** use and disposition in aiding, or even entering into and constituting, a mineral mixture than those of animals living in the air and utilizing thinner waters.

(24.) I may be permitted to put forward a certain speculation, which a slight observation has raised in me, concerning rivers that show **gold flakes** <note>original: "auri ramenta"</note>. Regarding those rivers which provide such things in great abundance, I would by no means doubt or deny that they carry true fragments from **gold-bearing veins or channels** <note>original: "venarum auriferarum"</note>, having rolled them down from the mountains where they originate, or having seized them by scouring and scraping from such channels hidden in the narrows that confine them; especially if that circumstance which has caused me doubt is absent. Yet, thus far it has not failed to be observed that rivers upon which a great quantity of **fatty, resinous wood—fir, pine, and pitch-wood**—is carried and floated every year <note>original German: "Flüsse, worauff Brand- und Bau-Holtz geflæsset wird"; Rivers upon which fuel-wood and construction timber are floated</note> often prove fertile in gold. During this floating, these woods lose not a little of their resinous substance...

...that [vapors] are drawn away is hardly unknown to any man, let alone a matter of doubt. However, we have indicated thus far what this might contribute to the metallic genesis.

(26.) I might perhaps be criticized for having brought forth too little regarding the **mercurifying principle** <note>original: "mercurificante principio"; the theoretical chemical agent or process believed by alchemists to give metals their liquid, "mercury-like" quality or to transform them into quicksilver</note>, since our Author [Becher] is so very long-winded here and there regarding that artifice. I, however, would rather dare to allege this very fact as my excuse, which might otherwise be brought against me as an argument: namely, that precisely because the Author was so prolix in this matter, it does not seem to me that there is any place or reason to expand further on this subject. 

Added to this is the fact that hardly anyone would expect anything from me except from a purely **practical** perspective: that is, there will be few who desire to hear the **science** of these things, the **theory**, or scientific **documents** from me. Instead, they seek the **practice** itself and **raw experiments**. Since I have every right to excuse myself from this request—at least here, where the discussion concerns **documents**—the entire sum of the **experiments** proposed by the author simply comes down to this: in those subjects that are taken up, there must surely be present that which afterward exerts itself in the effect. 

Since the product is dry, the **material which effects this must also be of a drying nature**. But when the product is brought from a solid state into a **fluid**, and indeed a most subtle one, the cause of such great thinning must certainly be remarkably **subtle**. By that very fact, it is not conspicuous for any great mass or weight; for the effect of **thinning** <note>original: "subtiliationis"; the process of making a substance less dense or more volatile</note> seems not to admit, let alone require, these rather **coarse** properties. Furthermore, the **earthy** nature of this principle is all the more established by the fact that—specifically for the mercurial effect—it ought only to be united with **earths (for the purpose of metallizing)** or with **metals themselves (for the purpose of mercurifying)**, etc. 

These things, I say, being involved with little difficulty, I promise myself a ready and easy pardon if I abstain from all long-windedness in this matter. To state the matter in the briefest possible way: there is such a great fog surrounding the exquisite distinction of the **specific properties of the product, mercury**, that we absolutely admire nothing but those general circumstances: **fluidity, volatility, extreme subtlety, etc.** Therefore, it will be all the less feasible for us to philosophize at length about the **direct cause of such a constitution**. And, since **metallicity** <note>original: "metalleitas"; the essential quality that makes a substance a metal</note> itself exists as something very special, it is even more so with the **mercurial flow** <note>original: "mercurialis fluor"</note>, to which nothing similar is found in the entire remaining treasury of nature. Consequently, the **effect** of this principle in other mixtures cannot be easily reduced to a true and solid concept that has any relation of similarity to that **effect** which completes **metallicity or mercuriality**.

(27.) However, I will not allow those who are indeed waiting with great expectation for revelations of this kind to be stirred up against me with unfair suspicion—as if I were laboring to hide these secrets from them, not out of caution (which no one with a clear conscience fears), but out of **envy**. Rather, I will candidly profess that, of those processes which render metallic bodies **fluid without mercury**, I can follow no other with the testimony of my own experience except: 1.) that which is prepared with **salt of tartar and vinegar** <note>Potassium carbonate and acetic acid</note> (according to the prescription of **Isaac Hollandus**, **Basil Valentine**, and his commentator, **Kerckring**), and specifically from the **regulus of Antimony** <note>The pure, metallic form of antimony that settles at the bottom of a crucible during smelting</note>.

2.) *To bear witness that from a good regulus of antimony* <note>The "regulus" refers to the purified metallic form of antimony, separated from its ore.</note>, *without any other addition, through a proportionately long digestion, running mercury arises. (28) Moreover, from those processes which are performed with mercury, I can recommend those which are carried out *with a well-prepared regulus*: But certainly not *those empty grindings on marble, and washings with water*, which *Zwölffer* <note>Matthias Zwölffer (1605–1668), a prominent chemist and physician.</note> indeed hands down, but surely with no credibility; and another person attributes them as a fraud to *Philalethes* <note>Eirenaeus Philalethes, a famous and mysterious 17th-century alchemist.</note>; but I do not know by what reasoning, since he—whoever else he might have been—never, as far as we know, advised such crude labors. Instead, he recommended work *after more diligent amalgamation, by suitable digestions and finally at last by instituted washing and distillation: And by repetitions of these things, no less numerous than laborious.* Certainly, however, both the *treatments of silver with sublimated mercury and with live mercury*, when skillfully instituted, are not without curious effects. Just as finally that method which the Author recommends from *Paracelsus* and confirms with his own calculation—by *repeated amalgamations and abstractions*—certainly deserves greater consideration than its external appearance suggests. Our Author still desires a *mercurial solvent* <term>Menstruum mercuriale: A liquid substance used in alchemy to dissolve or "open" metals, specifically mercury.</term> near the end; Which, whether it be supplied by well-rectified *oil of vitriol* <note>Concentrated sulfuric acid.</note> with much *common salt*: or by the common method of sublimation with *vitriol, nitre, and salt*: or by *sublimated mercury* <note>Mercury(II) chloride.</note> itself, it will eventually be easier to understand what truth lies beneath both the tradition of *Paracelsus* and the *commentary of our Author.* Meanwhile, I know this for certain, and I predict it therefore from well-known experience, that I am confident no more effect will be obtained by all these observations and additions than if I had not uttered a word. And this is mostly for the reason that those processes which are required for experiments in *mercurification* <note>The alchemical process of extracting "mercury" or "quicksilver" from a base metal.</note> require a far different *precision* <note>original Greek: ἀκρίβειαν (akribeian)</note> than *ordinary kitchen cooking* allows: And they require a far different *circumspection*, demand a far different *patience and assiduity*, requiring a far greater time and *repeated cohobations* <note>The process of repeatedly distilling a liquid off the solid residue it was just distilled from.</note>, *grindings, long-lasting boilings, and sufficient but careful digestions, and in some cases even quite peculiar manual techniques for drying and subliming.*

He once came to me, as a student of our art (as he knew I was also fond of chemical things): he offered for inspection a weight of nearly half a pound of *live and vivid mercury* <note>original: "vivi atque vividi mercurii"; liquid, metallic quicksilver.</note>, floating among those well-known flowers: and he hinted that this was that *mercury of antimony*, produced at last with light labor, but prepared with a rich yield. Indeed, regarding the **materials**, I ordered him to consider whether something unusual had been added. He constantly denied all these things; he even alleged some kind of exposures of the mixture to the open air for "imbibition" <note>The process of a solid absorbing a liquid, often used in alchemy to "nourish" a substance.</note>, and similar things. Even today I do not doubt that these were not made up, but were reported in good faith and performed by him with good hope. When I had repeatedly advised him to compare this current method of proceeding with those he was otherwise accustomed to use—for he often prepared such things and sold them to physicians throughout the province—where he had achieved nothing similar, I urged him above all to soon repeat this experiment again, exquisitely in the same way. Before all else, he should treat the **materials**, especially the **antimony**, bought both from the merchant he had just used and from another merchant, with comparative experiments; for certainly the yield of **mercury** would have been very much worth the effort.

When I had injected a doubt into the man regarding the sincerity of his experiment by these serious and constant arguments and admonitions, he returned home. Shaking out his memory, he finally remembered that the **antimony** used for this operation had been a piece of a certain **cake** <note>original: "placenta"; a flat, solid mass of material cooled in the bottom of a vessel.</note>, shaped like a **plano-convex** mass, weighing about two pounds, which he had bought from a certain apothecary at a very low price. He returned to me, reporting this circumstance, and now spontaneously offering an explanation. 

Indeed, it was easy now to guess that this **antimony** had been the residue from that common "kitchen" <note>A metaphorical term for a standard chemical process or laboratory setup.</note> of **Butter** <term>Butter of Antimony: antimony trichloride, a heavy, oily liquid</term> and **Cinnabar of antimony** <term>Cinnabar: mercury sulfide. In the preparation of "Butter of Antimony," mercury was often used, and its residue would naturally contain mercury.</term>; in which, if the fire is gentler at the beginning, a huge part of the cinnabar remains involved at the end, not expiring so quickly or being sublimated by the fire that makes the antimony flow. I therefore persuaded him that—not despising the travel and the effort—he should seek out that **dead head** <note>original: "caput mortuum"; the useless solid residue remaining after distillation or sublimation.</note> **of Butter** of antimony from apothecaries everywhere, and destine the mercury revived from it for whatever better use he could. Thus the "most clever invention" had perished <note>The author realized the experimenter hadn't discovered a new way to make mercury, but was simply accidentally recovering mercury that was already present in the apothecary's industrial waste.</note>.

(32.) I might be warned with a better appearance of reason that up to this point, speaking perpetually of nothing but **earthy concretions** and **earthy natures**, I am clearly forgetting the **saline** mixtures, in which our Author [Becher] was so extensive. Especially while he insists once and again that **metallic** mixtures can be formed from mere **salts**. 

I truly, if the matter is rightly estimated, think that I—especially in Section I—have put forth more regarding **theory**, if not quite as extensively, than perhaps our Author himself. With this only excepted: that I did not value **nitre** <note>original: "nitrum"; saltpeter or potassium nitrate.</note> as much as our Author does. Rather, I have indicated that the **second principle** <note>In Becher's system, the "second principle" is "mercurial earth" (terra fluida), which gives metals their shine and fluidity.</note> is not only much closer and readier for mixture, but also much more promptly obedient to the **operation** in such subjects and methods. This principle fits and satisfies the foundations and documents of theory as much as the experiments of practice, with a far more expedited success, a larger yield, and in a more manifest way. Lest I seem to have failed in this matter, I will bring to this place also what I have written dispersedly elsewhere, especially under the months of **July, August, September, and December 1697, and January, February, and part of March and April 1698.**

BECHER'S THEORETICAL DOCUMENTS.

# SECTION VI.
## THESIS VI.
### MINERAL SALTS ARE GENERATED BY THE 
### MIXTURE OF MINERAL EARTHS 
### WITH WATER.

#### Evidence of the terraqueous <note>Meaning a mixture of earth and water.</note> nature of mineral salts.

Mineral salts are usually called *Vitriol* <note>original: "Vitriolum"; metal sulfates like iron or copper sulfate</note>, *Alum* <note>original: "Alumen"</note>, *Saltpeter* <note>original: "Nitrum"</note>, *Native Saltpeter* <note>original: "Halonitrum"</note>, *Rock Salt* <note>original: "Sal gemmae"</note>, and common salt. To these should rightly be added that solidified substance from which *Borax* is prepared, and that salt which greatly favors *mineral springs* <note>original: "acidulis"; naturally occurring acidic or carbonated waters</note>, having a composite rather than purely acidic-sulfurous or vitriolic nature. Meanwhile, there is no doubt that there are other tasteless saline solidifications which nevertheless share the nature of these things, as far as their truly saline portion is concerned. Just as, for example, cobalt melts for the most part in liquids, as does *arsenic*, etc.

Therefore, the plan of our work urges us to produce evidence of their terraqueous nature and mixture, partly *from theoretical principles* <note>original: "a priori"</note> and partly *from observation* <note>original: "a posteriori"</note>. Just as it will be necessary to cite certain things about the nature of others—whether arising further from these by nature or by art—through the power and method of teaching itself; so by that very fact, their nature can be illustrated even more clearly, and thus the character of both can be conveniently investigated. Of those *salts*, some are native; while others are artificial. Native salts are not only those which coalesce into a crystalline consistency and form from the juices of vegetables or their gently evaporated decoctions—commonly called *Essential* salts—but also those which, lying hidden in large quantities beneath the remaining decoction, make not only the whole remaining soft, *pumice-like* <note>original: "subpumicidam"</note> matter, but especially the resinous-fatty material, soluble with water.

A significant example of this is provided by, for instance, a decoction of the *small field daisy* <note>original: "Bellidis minoris arvensis"</note>. This is indeed flavorful and, if examined with a salt-gauge or <term>Salt-Probe</term> <note>original: "Saltz-Probe"; a hydrometer or scale used to test the density or salt content of a liquid</note>, is soon seen to have a notable thickness or weight of solidifying matter; but it is very colorless, appearing watery. It continues this apparent clarity until it reaches a notable degree of thickening, where it suddenly turns dark and soon thickens into a blackish-green mass. It takes on a nature that becomes increasingly dense, thick, and dry; nevertheless, especially if that first thickening was done gently, it can immediately be reduced back to that clearer, thin state by adding more water. And there are many other examples of this character in vegetable extracts which demonstrate the saltiness dominating in them; just as—to provide one more example of this—the decoction of Guaiacum wood <note>original: "ligni Guajaci"; a medicinal wood used in the early modern period to treat various ailments</note> provides evidence. # SECTION VI.
## THESIS VI.
### MINERAL SALTS ARE GENERATED BY THE MIXTURE OF MINERAL EARTHS WITH WATER.

->Evidence of the terraqueous <note>Meaning composed of both earth and water</note> nature of mineral salts.<-

**M**ineral salts are commonly called *Vitriol <note>A historical term for metallic sulfates, like copper or iron sulfate</note>, Alum, Nitre, Halonitre <note>A form of saltpeter or mineral soda</note>, Rock salt, and common salt.* To these should be added, by the highest right, that solid from which *Borax* is prepared; and that salt which is very favorable to acidic mineral waters, being of a composite nature rather than purely acidic-sulfurous or vitriolic. Meanwhile, no one doubts that other tasteless saline deposits also exist which share the nature of these things, at least regarding their truly saline portion. Just as, for example, *cobalt* melts for the most part in liquids; so too does *arsenic*, and so on.

The plan of our undertaking, therefore, prompts us to produce evidence of the terraqueous nature and mixture of these salts, partly *a priori* <note>from theoretical reasoning</note> and partly *a posteriori* <note>from observation and experience</note>. However, just as it will be necessary to cite certain things about the nature of other salts—whether arising further from these by nature or by art—through the very force and method of teaching; so by that very act, the nature of those salts can be illustrated all the more clearly, and thus the character of both can be conveniently investigated. Furthermore, some of those salts are natural, while others are artificial. Natural salts are not only those which coalesce into a crystalline consistency and form from the juices of vegetables or from their gently evaporated decoctions (which are commonly called *Essential salts*); but also such things which, hiding abundantly within the rest of the decoction, render not only the remaining soft and somewhat moldy matter, but especially the resinous-oily matter, soluble in water. A significant example of this is provided, for instance, by a decoction of the *common field daisy* <note>original Latin: Bellidis minoris arvensis</note>. This is indeed flavorful, and if it is tested with a salt-gauge <note>original German: Saltz-Probe; a device or method for measuring salt content or density</note>, it is soon conspicuous by the remarkable thickness or weight of the solidifying material. Yet it is very colorless, or watery in appearance. It continues this, as it were, transparency even until a significant progress in thickening occurs, where, as if unexpectedly, it joins into a dark state, and soon entirely into a black-green thickness. It takes on an increasingly dense, coarse, and drying nature; from which, nevertheless, it can be reduced again into such a transparent thinness by adding more water, especially if that first thickening was performed quite gently. There are also several other examples of this character in the extracts of vegetables, which demonstrate a saltiness also dominating in them. To produce one more example of this matter, evidence is provided by the decoction of *Guaiacum wood* <note>A hard wood from the Caribbean used historically to treat various ailments</note>. For when from the whole *Guaiacum* wood by distillation, or otherwise immediately...

It is certainly noteworthy, not only in general but specifically for our task, that from a *decoction* <note>original: "decoctu"; an extract made by boiling</note> of this wood—whether it is thickened or extracted—not only the same amount, but nearly more of this salt is drawn out, provided everything is performed correctly. Furthermore, those *acids* and *sour-harsh* substances are *natural*, as are all the *sweet* things that present themselves to us in fruits, stems, leaves, buds, twigs, and stalks; and indeed, the bitter things should be counted not least among them. For just as all things that become sweet are, in their very beginnings (a state we call *immaturity*), *sour-harsh* and *bitter*, so too do these sweet things themselves—through *fermentation*—rush into *acidity*. This often happens with headlong force; if we do not wish to dismiss as fiction what is told of *sugar juice*—that it may fall into a notable *sourness* in a single night—the same is true of *wine*, or more accurately *must* <note>Unfermented or fermenting grape juice</note>, from the vines. This acidity is not only *vinous*, but the very well-known *acetic* <note>vinegar-like</note> quality.

*Artificial salts* include not only the greater part of *tartar of wine* <note>original: "tartari vini"; potassium bitartrate</note>, but especially *wine* itself, *vinegar*, and both *fixed* and *volatile alkalis*. From these, further elaborate *ammoniacal* compounds are produced, and even to this day, through various methods and ingenuity, *wonderful salts* <note>likely a reference to "sal mirabile" or Glauber's salt</note> are created. Among these, one must certainly not rank in the last place that *spirit not only of sulfur, but also of volatile vitriol* <note>original: "spiritus ille non solum sulphuris: sed etiam vitrioli volatilis"; forms of sulfuric or sulfurous acid</note>, which we have discussed partly in the *Halle Observations, Volume I*, and more fully in the month of *August*. We shall, therefore, proceed to the matter itself.

( 1. ) *Mineral salts strictly speaking* are, above all, that native mineral origin of *Borax*, or *crude Borax*, called by some of our countrymen *rock alum* <note>original: "alume di rocca" or "alumen rupeum"</note>; and that *acid* which, in *sulfur* and *vitriol*, makes up by far the largest part of the whole compound in the former, and a much smaller part in the latter. Elsewhere it is also found under another texture of mineral composition, as *Becher* <note>Johann Joachim Becher (1635–1682), a famous alchemist and physician</note> records regarding that which constitutes the *vitriolic* ore of the Isle of *Wight*, and as *Grimm* <note>likely Hermann Nicolaus Grimm</note> mentions in the *Acts of the Nature Curiosi* concerning a certain ore of *sulfur* (Decade II, Year 1, observation 170). This is unless both of these fossils are the same, or at least very similar to our German *solar iron ore* <note>original: "minera martis solaris"; likely iron pyrites</note>, or the *sulfurous-iron vitriolic ore* from Hesse. Indeed, quite a few of our *aluminous ores* similarly gape open spontaneously in damp air, betraying and bringing into action that *sulfurous acidity* inherent within them.

( 2. ) *How these mineral salts are generated*—specifically regarding *Borax* (which could be shown by various arguments and evidence to be the *Baurach* of the Arabs rather than our *Nitre* <note>Saltpeter</note>; and that *Salt of the rock* is rather some other stony, native, fossilized thing than our *manufactured nitre*)—is still entirely obscure. For not only do we have an insufficiently exact history of this mineral, but we also know well enough that its refinement is not fully understood. We have found that it is largely prepared through a very *caustic alkali*. It is well known that the *mineral solid* itself, from which it is so prepared, has hitherto been sought primarily from the East Indies. It seems hard to believe that it is not found throughout the rest of the world; but that the *Venetians* never prepared *Borax* from some *fissile* <note>easily split</note> or *specular stone* <note>original: "speculari lapide"; a transparent or reflective mineral like mica or selenite</note> of Europe...

(3.) I can truly assert in good faith that back when I was still a novice in chemistry <note>original: "chymiæ tyroni"</note>, I once obtained true *borax* from a certain task involving *antimony*: specifically, from *Crocus of Antimony* <note>original: "Croco antimonii"; a yellowish-orange powder produced by heating antimony ore with salts</note> prepared *by means of alkalis*, which was exposed to the open air for some time. Because of this exposure, it began to crumble into a fine *dust* <note>original: "pollinem"</note>, sprinkled with many white, flour-like particles. After I poured a little water onto this powder—thinking those floury specks had sprouted from the alkaline salt still intimately trapped within—but then neglected this infusion for several days through forgetfulness, I finally observed in it several crystals the size of a small pea, shaped like a slightly slanted square <note>original: "quadratæ leviter rhomboidis"; a rhomboid shape</note>. When removed and dried in the sun, they turned white on the surface, just like *borax*; otherwise, they were solid and hard, again like *borax*. The taste was that of *borax*, though a little milder, specifically not quite as remarkably *urinous* <note>A term used by early chemists to describe the sharp, pungent taste or smell associated with ammonia or alkaline salts</note>. When it was held to a candle flame, it underwent the bubbling typical of *borax* in the most exquisite way; and when I took up a blowpipe <note>original: "fistula cæmentatoria"; a tool used to direct a flame for melting or soldering</note>, it quickly melted into a very pure *glass*. Thus, I discovered it to be true *borax* in all its properties.

(4.) Nor does the *theory* differ in any way. For surely no one is unaware that the substance of antimony—whatever part of it turns into *crocus*—is not only of a *glass-forming* <note>original: "vitrescentis"</note> nature, but is also quite clearly *fusible* <note>capable of being melted</note>. It is no less celebrated that this same substance, when *fixed*, is used for medical effects, such as the purification of the blood, even in its coarser powdery consistency. Furthermore, it is commonly known that pharmaceutical effects similar to those of *borax* are attributed to it. Thus, nothing complicates the other considerations: (1.) *from the outset* <note>original: "a priori"</note>, that other *native* mineral from which borax is known to be prepared; and (2.) *from the result* <note>original: "a posteriori"</note>, that peculiar *method* of performing this—if I may say—*conversion* into a salty state by means of a *fixed alkali*. For not only common opinion but also the opinion of our *Author* <note>Referring to Johann Joachim Becher (1635–1682), a famous chemist and physician</note> holds that *borax is a fine, glass-forming earth, dissolved by an acid salt.*

(5.) However, a curious man, skilled in the *refining* or preparation of borax from its ore, convinced me for certain that no *acid* salt is present; rather, he asserted that a certain *caustic alkali* is used. Moreover, those experiments seem to support this, in which a floury corrosion arises from common soluble glasses and, for example, spirit of vitriol <note>sulfuric acid</note>; this corrosion actually becomes far more resistant to melting into glass than any bare fragment of the same glass—far from increasing its melting, which is the primary characteristic of *borax*, which vitrifies most readily. This matter is made most clear by the fact that nothing is precipitated from it by *alkalis*.

(6.) Meanwhile, as far as our present theory is concerned, there are far more manifest and ready proofs that *borax* is an *earth-watery* mixture than in any other salt. For we are accustomed to measure its *saline* nature by its very ready mixing into water, or *aqueous solubility*, which *borax* admits most readily; and by its *taste*, which *borax* likewise exhibits as *urinous-earthy*. It demonstrates its *earthy* nature, however, by that ready melting into *glass*—delicate, to be sure, but nonetheless sufficiently dense, dry, and stable.

### SAMPLES OF BECHER. PART I. SECTION II.

(7.) However, just as the occurrence of this solid substance—whether natural or artificial—is quite rare, so on the other hand is the mixture of that **sulfur-vitriolic** salt very common. It provides the base for the creation of *sulfur* and *vitriol* <note>original: "vitrioli"; a historical term for metal sulfates, such as copper or iron sulfate</note>, and even constitutes *alum* from its truly saline portion. This same salt resides especially in *sulfur*; hence one hardly ever encounters a mineral that yields vitriol or alum (either spontaneously or by art) without it also yielding sulfur through a far more immediate and simpler trial. So, for example, that Hessian iron ore <note>original: "minera martialis Hassiaca"; "Martial" refers to Mars, the alchemical symbol for iron</note> which they commonly call *solar iron ore*: if it is treated with fire while very fresh, it pours out an abundance of *sulfur*. When, however, it has lain for several weeks in damp, shaded places, it completely crumbles into a vitriolic saltiness, having lost all its true flammable *sulfurous* property.

(8.) To be sure, *sulfur* remixed with bare and pure *iron* does not undergo this dissolution or reaction into iron by the concurrent energy of either air or moisture. For although that phenomenon is certainly worthy of more attentive consideration—wherein common *sulfur*, even if somewhat coarsely powdered, when mixed with fresh *iron filings* <note>original: "limatura martis"</note> and moistened, conceives an intense *heat* after a few hours; indeed, it so penetrates the filings themselves that after the whole mass has dried spontaneously (which usually happens if the vessel is left open), it is rendered almost *entirely brittle*—nevertheless, the *sulfur* does not undergo a true dissolution of its mixture in this way, nor does the **phlogiston** <note>The theoretical principle of fire and inflammability used by 17th and 18th-century chemists</note> principle release its *acidity* unless ignition follows.

(9.) Just as this ignition (which I mentioned) can be quickly sparked by applying a candle as long as the material is still hot and semi-dry—by which intervention a far more prompt and larger yield of *vitriol* arises all at once than by the common immediate calcination <note>A process of heating a substance to high temperatures to change its physical or chemical state</note> of iron with sulfur—so too it often happens that this ignition occurs spontaneously. This happens when iron is dissolved by a sulfurated salt, the solution is liquefied again in water, and the salt thus resolved is separated; the powder, namely the sulfurated iron, is then placed on blotting paper. There, not infrequently, a new spontaneous heating of this material follows, even unto *spontaneous combustion*, and under this calcination, it soon supplies *vitriol*. Meanwhile, neither of these experiments succeeds conveniently unless a good quantity, at least *half a pound* <note>original: "libræ semis"</note> of material, is used.

(10.) However, proof that this substance resides not only in *sulfur*, but wanders about diffused in the air itself, is provided by the reduction of a fixed alkali salt into a neutral salt <note>original: "enixum"; refers to a neutral salt formed by the combination of an acid and an alkali</note> solely by the benefit of the free air. For thus, if the common alkaline salt of ashes (**potash** <note>original: "cineres clavellati"; literally "clubbed ashes," referring to the wood used in the process</note>) is submerged in a little water and placed in some room in an open vessel, solid, firm, and bitter crystals successively grow, identical to *vitriolated tartar* <note>original: "tartaro vitriolato"; an old name for potassium sulfate</note>. This happens even faster if linens soaked in a saturated alkaline lye are left to the free air in a place not entirely inaccessible to the winds, until they offer a consistency that is not only dry but also downy-saline.

(11.) Just as the most abundant quantity of this acid is ready at hand in *sulfur* underground and, as said before, is hardly ever detected more familiarly than when imbued with a *sulfurous* mixture; so too in the sulfurous mixture itself, even then, that saline, acidic consistency...

...that it was present, I say, in such a constitution to concur in the generation of the **sulfur** mixture, is proven by a most certain piece of evidence: that it can soon be liberated again from its other partner principle by art, and thus stand separately in its acidic nature; but also, in this acidic form, when combined with flammable matter, it can once again produce sulfur.

(12.) It seems all the more probable that this **acid** is born from a refined earthy substance, especially since in those places where sulfur is found, a kind of subtle **glassy-earthy** consistency is almost inseparable. For this reason, not only **sulfur**, but no other **minerals**, and least of all **metals**, ever arise except in **earths, muds**, or **stones** suitable for or related to glassy flow <note>original: "vitreo fluxui"; refers to substances that can melt into glass, acting as a flux in smelting</note>. ~ The closer such a subterranean earthy substance is to a **crystalline** tenderness (being subtle and therefore suited to transparent aggregation), the closer it is, above all, to the birth of **sulfur**, and commonly also of **metals**. We have already indicated several times that a mixture of saline acidity is presupposed beneath sulfur.

(13.) Indeed, a twofold experience provides clear evidence of the sulfurous nature of those **crystalline** earthy-stony growths (known as *druses, flows, and flowers* <note>original: "der Druſen, Flüſſe, und Blumen"; German mining terms for different types of mineral formations and crystal clusters</note>): (1.) that such **crystalline** bodies, when coarsely powdered and exposed to a light, dim heat, are affected more by a very subtle light than by a flame; hence **Baldwin’s phosphorus**, which he called **Hesperus** <note>Christian Adolph Balduin discovered a phosphorescent substance (calcium nitrate) in 1674; "Hesperus" refers to the evening star</note>: (2.) Even in medium-sized pieces, these **crystalline** growths, **encrusted with mud**, when placed in a gentle heat and quickly removed, if lightly moistened after cooling with their muddy crust, give off a powerful stench of **sulfur**. We shall explain more broadly in the appropriate places that no mineral **sulfur** exists without a mixture of the most abundant **acidic salt**, which constitutes the greatest part, indeed its entire mass.

(14.) It would be unnecessary to repeat at length here what was said above in *section II of this part concerning the crystalline-sandy substance of sand*, and how it forms that stony hardness with **quicklime** <term>quicklime (calx viva): calcium oxide, produced by heating limestone, which reacts strongly with water</term>—certainly in no other than a **saline** way and character; likewise regarding **quicklime** itself, how it combines with water into a saline mixture, etc. It is sufficient simply to have cited them. However, what we touched upon regarding **gypsum** <note>original: "Gypſo"; calcium sulfate dihydrate</note>—how this solid, too, undergoes a kind of intimate saline mixing and deeper soaking with water—were the more significant, or rather better known, points brought forward for our purpose. I am pleased to include here **Glauber’s assay** <note>Johann Rudolph Glauber was a major 17th-century chemist known for his work on salts</note>: that in **limestones and gypsums**, there is already a certain immediate **salty** disposition, as when he orders these stones to be dissolved with **nitrous spirit** <note>nitric acid</note> and the solution, with fixed alkali salt, to be reduced into a saline body. From this, a greater weight of physical salt is obtained than emerges from an equal weight of the same spirit joined separately with an equal quantity of alkali salt. But indeed, just as care is needed because not all limestones absolutely show an equal assay by this method, so too is it a matter of similar difficulty to expect a purely and truly **nitrous salt** from it; instead, it is more generally something such as a **vitriolic-aluminous-sulfurous** salt <note>original: "vitriolico - aluminoſo - ſulphureum"; a salt sharing the properties of vitriol (sulfates), alum, and sulfur</note>. # EXCERPTS FROM BECHER. PART I. SECTION II.

->SPECIMEN BECHERIANUM PART I. SECTION II.<-

...not without cause, he mutters here and there about a salt which he interprets as **nitrous** <note>original: "nitroso"; likely referring to a precursor of saltpeter or a general "fiery" salt principle</note>, not yet burning, or flashing with other inflammable things: Which is indeed nothing else than this **more universal acid** we are speaking of, which is as yet less specified or determined.

(15.) Moreover, we advise—as a clearer piece of evidence *a priori*—that one should better examine that **resolution of flints by fire and water**, to which **Becher**, not without cause, appeals more than once. For certainly, if that observation is true which **Gassendi** brings forward in the *Life of Peiresc* <note>referring to Pierre Gassendi's biography of the scholar Nicolas-Claude Fabri de Peiresc (1580–1637)</note>, namely that this skillful investigator, from his adult years when he used to wash and exercise his body in rivers, observed flints being born from a **mucous matter**, which at first exists as **soft** and manageable, like a rival to a certain gelatin: This agrees remarkably with that experiment of **Becher’s**, in which he asserts that **Crystal**, by fire and water alone, returned into a gelatinous-waxy or viscous consistency of this kind. And just as a **slimy** <note>original: "mucida"</note> consistency is the closest step from a saline delicacy; so it would certainly be obvious to reason from such an observation that the concept is far more accessible: that a slimy consistency can either arise from a saline thinness as it gradually loses its watery mixture, or even return to that saline thinness from this slimy state, as if to something more closely related. This is more plausible than the idea that it passes from a slimy softness and delicacy into that density, hardness, and most firm structure which is often observed in the hardest flints—those found in water, suited for striking against steel to produce sparks.

(16.) But truly, this matter—namely the original softness of flints—can be rendered all the more plausible by a fact not unknown to skilled craftsmen: the compacting of **Gypsum through mucous substances**, as well as **quicklime**, into a very firm hardness. For just as the firm hardening is well known which is granted to **quicklime by egg whites** for the purpose of gluing cracks in glass vessels, so too the **hardening of quicklime and related species through dairy products** does not belong solely to "joking" experiments. **Becher** extols this to such a height that he asserts somewhere that he observed a stony consistency generated from quicklime and **cheese**, which did not yield much to the hardness of a **diamond**. At the very least, in the case of that artificial **Marble** which is cast from **Gypsum** with the aid of mucous additives, a hardness is often obtained that does not differ much from the firmness of **Porphyry** or even **Jasper**; provided that good and well-prepared Gypsum is at hand, and the manipulation <note>original: "enchirisis"; from the Greek for "hand-work" or "process"</note> of the mixture is performed with the proper dexterity. For by untimely and improper agitation beyond the required time, even the best mass of this kind can be made looser and more fragile.

(17.) However, just as a **saline mixture** may rightly be sought from the concretion of **earth** with water, so a great distinction must be made between absolute saltiness and that which is already determined, which is to be distinguished by the names of **acid, alkali, volatile, and fixed**. These names form and encompass such specific differences. In this sense, it is fitting to accept whatever **Becher** comments, often and at length, regarding the **acid of vitriol and sulfur** <note>vitriol refers to sulfate minerals or sulfuric acid; sulfur refers to the flammable principle</note> and their fixative power <note>their ability to turn substances solid or "fix" them</note> over other bodies. I, proceeding from that principle of which I have already spoken elsewhere—that the **sulfurous principle is properly a separator of the Earthy-Sa-**

# THEORETICAL DOCUMENTS OF BECHER

...substances from a watery mixture, I would almost dare to attribute more in such cases to the mixture of sulfur itself; for it is evident from observable phenomena that sulfur not only joins more readily, but also forms a firmer bond with other metallic-earths. Indeed, it is very well known—especially after the observations I shared in **April 1698**—that common sulfur merges most easily with all metals. However, the nature of **vitriolic acid** <note>original: "Acidi vero vitriolici"; known today as sulfuric acid</note> is not at all the same, at least in the case of gold. Moreover, when this acid does merge with metals, it is commonly separated from them again by a relatively light roasting with fire; sulfur does not do this with equal ease.

(18.) This is demonstrated by an experiment that **Becher** cites time and again regarding this firm connection of sulfur with various metals; namely, when it is joined with, for example, **copper, iron, lead, or the regulus of Antimony** <note>original: "regulo Antimonii"; the metallic form of antimony separated from its ore</note>. Regarding this document cited by **Becher**, I cannot help but attach a small observation, which may help one understand how great the <term>oversights</term> <note>original Greek: ὑπεροράματα; refers to errors or things overlooked</note> can be that are committed in such matters. I have in my hands today a copy of **Becher’s Tripod** <note>original: "Tripodis Beccheriani"; likely referring to Becher’s *Tripus Hermeticus Fatidicus* (1689)</note>, which was previously owned by someone highly skilled in physical-mechanical matters, as well as exceptionally expert in medical-anatomical and pharmaceutical-chemical practices. However, he had been trained by his teachers more toward **Skepticism** than toward practical application. In his own hand, at this passage, he added a little commentary or note—or rather, a witty bit of skepticism. The passage is in *Becher’s Tripod*, page 94, the bottom five lines:

> Among other rare, curious, and even useful experiments, a certain experiment regarding sulfur is known to me; how it may be **burned, and yet not burned**, which likewise always succeeds: Namely, let it be done (\*) by a certain common [way], and in the space of one hour it can be turned back into that same **burning** sulfur. Thus art plays with nature, and **nature with art**.

(\*) To these words, our commentator attached those asterisks which I have inserted in their places; and following these, he added the following remarks. Specifically, at the first asterisk, regarding the words: *let it be done by a certain common... etc.* he adds:

> <margin>Why do you fail here? You who pretend you are about to speak: for the printer seems hardly to be blamed.</margin> <note>The critic is accusing Becher of being intentionally vague about the "common way" to perform the experiment, suspecting him of hiding a secret or being a fraud.</note>

At the words *nature (plays) with art*, he adds:

> <margin>And perhaps fraud plays with credulity.</margin>

Thus he casts upon the author a suspicion not only of deceptive concealment, but also of a fraudulent mind. Yet, regarding the **first** doubt, it is most obvious that—whether through the ignorance of the scribes or the printer—"it be done for a common way" <note>original: "fiat pro via vulgari"; the author argues the Latin was just a typo</note> was what was intended. Regarding the **latter** doubt, any person even moderately well-versed in Chemistry should have been able to solve this problem of his own accord. Indeed, by paying only slight attention, he could have read the explanation laid out even more extensively than necessary on pages 146 and 147. Thus, those who might actually be feared for their skill are exposed to a thousand such daily insults; they are slandered even when they recommend a <term>theoretical principle</term> <note>original Greek: τὸ θεωρητὸν; the object of contemplation or theory</note> from such obvious things. Meanwhile, while they strive to be brief so as not to be accused of useless wordiness in trivial matters, they are burdened with the suspicion of not only concealment, but of fraud and lies as well. That is to say, to speak of the matter itself: those who know these experiments (and many more) well by memory, but are unable to grasp the theory behind them, react this way if such a theoretical problem is proposed to them as the true **use** of even common experiments.

...they are so far from understanding such matters that they do not hesitate to hold and declare—indeed, to proclaim—his questions to be mere sophistry or wordplay, his assertions to be vain boasting, and his citations to be frauds. Yet when the proofs and experiments that contain that theoretical power are finally revealed, they immediately accept the result itself. However, they excuse their own ignorance—their inability to understand without an interpreter—by blaming the obscurity of his reasoning or application and his difficult style. Then, at the very next opportunity, they are not ashamed to look down upon the matter as trivial, or as something already well-worn even by the common people. Indeed, **imprudence** and **impudence**, differing by only a single letter, are easily joined in marriage, especially since the former is masculine and the latter feminine. <note>The author is making a pun on the Latin words "imprudentia" and "impudentia," noting their linguistic similarity.</note>

(19.) One may discover noteworthy **proofs** <note>original: "documenta"</note> of that **original acid** <note>original: "acidi illius primigenii"</note>—which tends toward, or rather returns to, an **earthy** nature—in those experiments where our Author [Becher] suggests reducing and "fixing" sulfur into an **earth that melts on its own** <note>original: "terram sponte deliquescentem"; referring to deliquescence, where a substance absorbs moisture from the air until it dissolves into a liquid</note> in various places. He advises elsewhere to perform this through digestion and distillation with **oil of vitriol** <note>original: "oleo vitrioli"; what we now call sulfuric acid</note>. Another proof of our entire assertion—that such an earthy disposition exists in vitriolic oil or acid, and that the sulfurous principle is shielded from its dissolution by a watery mixture—is shown by that experiment already commended by the highly experienced **Kunckel** <note>Johann Kunckel (1630–1703), a famous German chemist and glassmaker</note>. In it, from **concentrated oil of vitriol** and **pure oil of turpentine**, a residue is obtained that is not only dry, fixed, and earthy, but also of a remarkable, stony density.

(20.) Nor should we, in this business of ours, deprive the following experiment of its status as a proof: the creation of **glass** <note>original: "vitrum"</note> through the joint fusion of **sulfur and alkaline salt**. For certainly, if **alkaline salt**—even if it is somewhat ashen or earthy (like common **potash**) <note>original: "cineres clavellati"; potassium carbonate derived from wood ashes</note>—is melted by itself, no such **glassy** solid can be readily expected or obtained. However, if that same **alkali** is melted with an equal part, or **three-fourths**, or even less of common **sulfur**, using a sufficiently vigorous fire in a crucible covered only by overlying coals, then after some continued melting, a significant portion of glass is produced—and not just glass, but a **colored, blackish** glass. Without the involvement of sulfur, hardly anything glassy would come together, let alone anything with such a conspicuous color.

(21.) Before we consider the nature and origins of **alkaline salt**, we shall briefly contemplate those other two **mineral** salts: **niter and common salt**. We have already suggested above that **niter** <note>original: "nitrum"; saltpeter or potassium nitrate</note> can only be called a mineral in the broader sense. The nature of **culinary or common salt** <note>original: "salis communis"</note>, however, is quite different. For this not only bursts forth from the depths of the earth in **salt springs**, but the entire sea and even **great lakes** here and there in the middle of inland regions teem with it. We have a clearly noteworthy example of this nearby at the Castle of **Seeburg** <note>A town in Saxony-Anhalt, Germany, known for its lakes</note>; there, two large lakes, separated by a dike that is not very thick, are of such completely different natures that one teems with **fresh** lake water, while the other is **salty**, and indeed tastes as such immediately. Not only this, but fishermen observe that in just a few years, this **saltiness** <note>original: "salsedo"</note> has increased so much that the water has become entirely unfit for drinking; whereas previously, when busy on the lake during the summer heat, they did not hesitate to quench their thirst with it. Moreover, an unusual [mortality] of the older fish...

...a certain depletion <note>original: "strages"; literally a slaughter or ruin. In this context, it refers to the exhaustion of a mineral deposit, reflecting the 17th-century belief that minerals "grew" in the earth like living things</note> has been observed over the last year or two: *but a far sparser yield of the younger ones.* Furthermore, it is likely that this contributes not a little to both the flowing **springs** and such **lakes**; for this **salt** is found in a solid, truly **mineral** and fossilized accumulation, just as mountains filled with inexhaustible abundance are reported in **Poland**, in the **Tyrolean salt-works** <note>original: "Tyrolensibus Halis"; referring to the famous salt mines at Hall in Tirol</note>, and also in the **Hungarian** provinces. These sources supply what is commonly called dry, fossilized, or rock-like salt: **gem salt** <note>original: "sal gemmeum," known today as rock salt or halite</note>.

(22.) In truth, however, this underground product deserves no less consideration than various others regarding the very specific **station**, as it were, of this mineral salt in the not-so-many places of the entire known world. Reason suggests us to recognize that there is something entirely special required for the **genesis** <note>the origin or formation process</note> of this salt, which does not exist so abundantly in just any soil or earthy mixtures.

(23.) In common salt, however, there are **two** things worthy of consideration, both referring to its **saline** nature and composition. **First**, namely, the **acidic** portion of this salt; which indeed, in the strictest and almost **specific** sense, sustains and encompasses the **character** and nature of this salt. But then there is also the **other** part of it, which supplies that **acid** with a consistency, or a dry and dense—even crystalline—bodily structure, and restrains and tempers its simple **acrimony** <note>sharpness or corrosive quality</note>. Various properties and conditions make it manifest that this very part is not only of a **saline** nature, but furthermore of a certain special character.

(24.) People commonly call this substance—which allows the **acid** of common salt to be both tempered and coagulated—**alkaline**; and it cannot be denied that it belongs, in general, to this lineage. For not only does it effervesce with **acids**, saturating, dulling, breaking, and coagulating them (**which earths also do**), but it also dissolves spontaneously and promptly in water, indeed **by deliquescence** <note>original: "per deliquium"; the process where a salt absorbs enough atmospheric moisture to turn into a liquid solution</note>: which constitutes a common trait of other *salts*. Moreover, it dissolves common **sulfur** when melted, and other **fatty substances** in solutions, which is characteristic of *alkalis*. However, it differs from other, artificial *alkalis* in that it neither enjoys such great *acrimony*, nor does it pass into a similar solid when combined with *acids* as those *alkalis* do. Proof of this is provided by the union of this **earthy-alkaline** substance from **common salt** with **oil of vitriol** <note>original: "acido vitrioli"; what we now call sulfuric acid</note>. For while that **common alkaline salt**, when joined to that **vitriolic** acid, dulls it completely so that nothing remains except a bitter taste with no power of dissolving; on the contrary, the marriage of this **saline-alkaline solid** (to be sought from **common salt**) with that same acid provides a certain composite salt that is still able to **dissolve** metals to some extent. Furthermore, while that "strenuous" salt <note>original: "enixum illud sal"; likely referring to potassium bisulfate</note> which is born from **common alkali and the acid of vitriol** rejects all melting: this product, a **third salt** <note>original: "sal tertium"; a neutral salt formed by the reaction of an acid and a base</note> from the substance of common salt and the acid of vitriol, melts easily and promptly. (25.) Indeed, in its own union with common salt itself, it has this peculiarity: that by simple repeated dissolution, coagulation, and toward the end, strong boiling <note>original: "concoctione"</note> and a degree of heating to redness <note>original: "candefactione"</note>—by repeating these operations several times, I say—it breaks down into a tasteless earth which can no longer be dissolved in water, nor does it melt in fire with the same ease as before. It is as if the acidic portion of the salt vanishes, or the entire salt compound degenerates into this earthy state.

(26.) Another proof and specimen of the more specific nature of this saline subject—and not the least important one—is provided by what is commonly called **glass gall** <note>original: "fel vitri"; also known as sandiver, this is the layer of saline scum that floats on top of molten glass during its manufacture</note>. This is surely a certain saline-earthy mixture that mimics the taste of common salt; however, its consistency is indeed a looser glass-like form, yet much firmer than salt. It imitates the saline-earthy dross <note>original: "scoriæ"</note> that usually forms from the union of nitre and the metal of antimony <note>original: "regulo"</note>. I am speaking here of its simple consistency. However much the origin of this growth might be attributed to the glass itself—suggesting that its consistency, being closer to an earthy nature, proceeds from the glass, and that the salty portion from the common salt used in the mass merely melts into it—one must primarily consider the intimate connection of this salty portion with the earthy-glassy part. They cannot be entirely separated from one another but cling together firmly.

(27.) Those who are more skilled in the art of glassmaking will not find fault with me for speaking of common salt here, even though it is not customary to use common salt in making glass. But they will remember that the **soda** <note>original: "soda"; here referring to sodium carbonate or barilla</note> which craftsmen use to prepare glass more perfectly is certainly not common salt, yet it is much less a pure alkali. It contains far more saline substance than any of our alkalis. Indeed, the genuine origin of alkaline salt holds true here: it comes from that fatty, succulent, maritime herb, **Kali** <note>original: "Kali"; saltwort (Salsola kali)</note>, whose juice is salty even to the coarse senses. Hence, in our region, it grows only near salt lakes and ditches carrying brine (as it does in those salty ponds near **Lützen** <note>A town in Saxony, Germany</note>), and it provides an exquisitely salty taste. Alkali prepared from such a plant differs greatly from any other simple salt, especially from nitre-based alkali, both in taste and in its other characteristics, sharing in the nature of common salt.

(28.) Let no one expect me to laboriously track every specific detail of the nature of common salt here, or how it differs from the more universal "sulfurous-vitriolic" acid or from the "nitrous" acid. That it is of an earthy-aqueous mixture must be taught through our thesis. This is proven not only *a priori* <note>from theory or cause</note>, because it is certainly a salt, but also *a posteriori* <note>from observation or effect</note>, because it degrades and breaks down into a tasteless earth. Whoever is led by further curiosity may investigate with due **precision** <note>original Greek: "ἀκριβείᾳ" (akribeia)</note> what those fixed parts are and where they come from which remain behind whenever the proper sublimation of **Mercury** <note>original: "Mercurii"; likely referring to the preparation of corrosive sublimate (mercury chloride)</note> is repeated. Similarly, that experiment performed with corrosive sublimate over iron plates can provide an opportunity for curious but more attentive observations. And...
