### THEORETICAL DOCUMENTS OF BECHER

These points may indeed suffice, in a general sense, regarding the earthy nature of this material. However, as for that specific earthiness of it, by which it might primarily serve a **mercurial** <note>original: "Mercuriali"; referring to substances containing or resembling mercury or "quicksilver"</note> mixture, we shall leave that untouched for now, in accordance with the mind of our *Author* <note>Referring to Johann Joachim Becher, the influential 17th-century chemist/alchemist</note>. And truly, so that nothing is imputed to me as if I were panting for some small scrap of glory, I would rather leave this field open to anyone who wishes to run this course of study and—by such a new demonstration, rather than just an argument—deserve the very best from the public. I myself do not refuse to subscribe to it, provided he brings forth certain and solid evidence: I grow old while always learning many things <note>original Greek: "γηράσκω μὲν αἰεὶ πολλὰ διδασκόμενος"</note>.

(29.) It will not be out of place, in this very section, to recall a certain tradition resting on historical testimony. In my youth, I remember reading in one or two of those wandering little books—which bring forth stories now about gems, stones, and minerals, now about animals, primarily from the works of **Albertus Magnus** <note>Albert the Great (c. 1200–1280), a medieval scholar famous for his writings on the natural sciences</note> (among which perhaps some **Fallopian** <note>original: "fallopiana"; likely referring to the works or pseudo-works of the 16th-century anatomist Gabriele Falloppio, who also wrote on minerals</note> works might be counted)—that *quicksilver* <note>original: "argentum vivum"; mercury</note> is sometimes found in marshy pools, especially those that are salty. For my part, I always looked upon the matter with disdain rather than following it with any belief. At last, it happened that a young man about to begin the study of *Medicine* requested my guidance while I was still living in *Jena*. He was a native of *Schwäbisch Hall* <note>original: "Hala Suevorum"</note>; otherwise, he was imbued with a tolerable knowledge of polite literature, but was ignorant of specialized *Physics* and all medical matters. When once, returning from a *botanical* walk, the conversation happened to turn to minerals and metals (on the occasion of seeing certain vein-like tracks or paths in those mountains), he hesitated at the name of **quicksilver** <note>original: "mercurii vivi"</note> as if it were an unknown thing. Since he could recall it neither by its German name nor by experience from the practice of Goldsmiths, I gave a description of it based on its likeness to flowing lead, which our subject mimics perpetually even when cold. Thereupon he interrupted, as if the thing were now easily recognized, yet hesitating because of the unworthiness of his birthplace: saying that perhaps it was not this *mercury* that is sometimes found in the puddles of the streets after rains; though it displayed that same total likeness of flowing lead. To my questioning—and indeed while I was smiling—as to where he had read or heard this: he denied both, but appealed to his own *eyewitness observation* <note>original: "autopiam"; the act of seeing something for oneself</note> so constantly that, while I expressed my incredulity with various questions, he meanwhile appeared to be restrained only by his modesty from marvelling at my own ignorance regarding a thing that occurred so commonly. But truly, I share this skepticism with a great crowd of curious seekers; and just as it is unusual in the rest of the world for it to rain *quicksilver*, so too is that city—in whose soil there is such a free yield of this substance that it even floats in the mud of the puddles—unfortunate in that it ignores its own good fortune. But the things which are recorded ought to be true.

### SPECIMEN OF BECHER, PART I, SECTION II.

...it also forces coals to burn far more steadily, until they are fully consumed, than they are usually inclined to do on their own. Not only this; but by this very act, the *salt* itself is resolved into a conspicuous white smoke; which, if it is captured in any collection vessel, resembles white saline flowers: which white soot soon adheres to any earthenware or metallic vessels placed over it, and presents itself to the eyes.

(31.) It is well known how *Glauber* <note>Johann Rudolf Glauber (1604–1670), a renowned chemist and alchemist famous for "Glauber's Salt"</note> commands *spirit of salt* <note>hydrochloric acid</note> to be distilled in abundance; but without vitriol or alum, it is in vain. When a friend once tested the truth of the matter and placed coals—which had been soaked in a solution of salt for a long time and were not sufficiently dried—into a furnace that was not yet properly heated, these coals, though mixed with other pure ones, refused to ignite at first for many hours. But when they finally caught fire, with the slightest ventilation admitted, they glowed so continuously and steadily that their ignition lasted for about 12 hours, more or less; as a result, not only the furnace but the entire room became exceedingly hot. However, that expected spirit did not follow, but only a useless phlegm <note>a watery, inactive byproduct of distillation</note> was produced.

(32.) It is also known that from the distillation of *spirit of salt* through *spirit of nitre* <note>nitric acid</note> or *aqua fortis* <note>literally "strong water," also nitric acid</note>, a most foul-smelling *oil* came forth, floating on top; just as I have collected an oil or empyreumatic <note>referring to the "burnt" smell of organic matter distilled at high heat</note> fat from the simple distillation of salt with that common Bohemian bole <note>a type of medicinal clay or earth</note>. But it is established by *Glauber's* experiment that *spirit of wine* <note>alcohol/ethanol</note> itself, under the proper circumstances, can be reduced into an oily nature with *spirit or oil of salt*. *Basilius Valentinus* <note>A legendary, possibly pseudonymous, 15th-century alchemical author</note> and others promise that something similar can be obtained with *oil of vitriol* <note>sulfuric acid</note> as well, but I cannot yet cite my own experience. Furthermore, how much this contributes to the generation of *volatile urinous salts* <note>ammonium salts</note> is especially apparent from the fact that *animal* matters are observed to be seized by a *salty* sourness before they fully pass into putrefaction—the primary midwife of those salts. Moreover, the fertility of urine for generating *volatile salt* is very well known: based on no other foundation than that it abounds in *salt*, a rival to *common salt*. Hence, it is not a useless experiment to add *salt* to those very substances while they are rotting, for a greater yield of *volatile salt*. *Vigani* <note>John Francis Vigani (c. 1650–1712), the first professor of chemistry at the University of Cambridge</note> recommends this for obtaining a greater quantity of *volatile salt of amber* <note>succinic acid</note>. As for what happens in producing *sal ammoniac* <note>ammonium chloride</note> from *raw salt*, *urine*, and soot, let those curious about these matters investigate; for this time, we are excluded by the shortage of time, as the *publisher* <note>original: "Bibliopola," literally bookseller, who acted as publisher</note> is pressing us because of the trade fair <note>referring to the major book fairs in Frankfurt or Leipzig, which dictated publishing deadlines</note>.

(33.) It will be necessary to be far less long-winded regarding *nitre* <note>saltpeter or potassium nitrate</note>, since I have already considered its nature and the various circumstances and reasons for its properties in the months of February and March 1698. It will therefore suffice for the present place only to transfer the main points of the matters themselves. It is known that *nitre* is generated in the earth; especially in *muddy* earth, which I have proven by the effect of the distillation of spirits to be imbued with mineral acid. However, it is born in such earth only when something *putrefying* is mixed with it and actually undergoes *putrefaction* within it. Hence the walls of latrines, built of baked brick, abound with this product; as do *manure piles and stables*, especially *sheepfolds*. The *walls* of rustic huts, built of *dirt, mud, slime, and much straw*, also produce it; and indeed, these walls do so no deeper than the rains can penetrate them. Indeed, all... <note>catchword: pites</note>

### Mmm m

...heads, grasses, weeds, dug-up earth, and above all the dung of grass-eating animals, and the urine of everyone.

(34.) The creation of matter is completed by the subtle mixing of the fiery-luminous substance, or <term>Phlogiston</term> <note>original: Φλογιστᾶ; in early chemistry, this was the hypothetical "substance of fire" contained within all combustible bodies</note>, into that primordial acid; by this very act, the acid is likewise refined. The resulting product is an acid salt that is highly volatile, colored, and subtle, and prone to catching fire—provided, of course, that it can be strengthened by a secondary addition of another flammable substance to shake loose the bond of the earthy-saline principle.

(35.) For this reason, I did not hesitate to demonstrate from a common experiment something that had previously occurred to no one: namely, that by this very deflagration of nitre <note>saltpeter</note>, not only is the mixture of this salt dissolved, but its nature is revealed through the physical-mechanical actions and effects of both the ignition and the fiery swelling, or <term>spring</term> <note>original: elateris; 17th-century scientists used this term to describe the expansive, elastic pressure of gases</note>. These are direct proofs of the character of this very mixture.

(36.) The daily demands to finish—or rather, to break off—increasingly dictate my limit, because these pages must be enriched for the Frankfurt fairs <note>the Frankfurt Book Fair was a major deadline for scholars and publishers in the 17th century</note> ten days from today. Therefore, I would indeed conclude these considerations here, were I not afraid that those who take pleasure in our studies might bear it with impatience (perhaps with some blame on my part) if I omitted a proof I touched upon above. In this business, it easily takes the prize over various others: namely, the **reduction of salts into earth**, and thus their dissolution from their watery mixture, and their <term>palingenesis</term> <note>chemical "rebirth" or restoration to an original mineral state</note> back to their mineral origin.

(37.) To explain this consideration more correctly, I recall to memory those things I warned about earlier regarding this business: namely, that not only do vegetables obtain their origin and primary matter from the earth, and animals are nourished immediately or mediately by vegetables; but also that the matter of nutrition, in its first forms, has a saline-slimy consistency. From this state, it is cast down and restored to that earthy-slimy constitution, especially through the intervention of the sulfurous or <term>phlogiston principle</term>, acting now as a tool and now as the material itself.

(38.) A proof of this can be seen in that harshness and acidity which fills the substance of flavorful, succulent fruits from their tiniest size until they reach their proper growth and ripeness. Experiments confirm that their acidic and harsh saltiness does not ferment or produce anything subtly "burning" <note>spiritous or alcoholic</note>, but is merely overtaken and corrupted by its position. However, after this acidic-bitter substance is not only increasingly tempered by a greater addition of oily fatness, but is also driven by the agitation of heat to subdue that saline substance, it subdues it as it enters or joins itself more intimately with it; the coarser particles are cast out to generate the remaining pulp. Thus, it offers a **sweet**, namely a **smooth** and **entirely blunted taste of acidity**. I usually recommend a sample of this in the tasting of vinegar; if pure vinegar is tasted against vinegar altered with common salt, the latter will actually be perceived to taste somewhat sweeter. That this sweetness is truly introduced by a fatty substance blunting the acid, I show...

### BECHER’S SPECIMENS. PART I. SECTION II.

...proof of this is that remarkable *spirituous inflammability*, which produces and sustains "burning spirit" <note>original: spiritum ardentem; this refers to alcohol or ethanol produced during fermentation</note> through the process of fermentation. Just as this spirituous quality in this specific substance takes its origin directly from that sweet salinity, it is confirmed by the evidence that the sweeter the must <note>unfermented grape juice</note> has become by the grace of the weather, the more spirituous or "generous" the resulting wine will be.

(39.) To come closer to our *theory* and establish our proofs—namely, that those salts born from the earth are not merely lightly and superficially coated by a fatty substance, but are also gradually released again from their mixture—we can cite in the very first place *fermentation* itself, and its efficacy in generating wine from the sweetness of the must. For as we see there, through *fermentation*, a certain *separation* of parts is soon formed from the must, which was previously clear, transparent, and of a uniform consistency. Indeed, these are *earthy-fatty* parts, such as the *dregs* <note>original: faeces; the sediment or lees of the wine</note>, which separate by both rising to the top and sinking to the bottom. Thus, as this hidden act of fermentation is intensified and prevails, a greater quantity of that *salinity* is shaken out and reduced back into an *earthy, dry, powdery, opaque consistency*. For this reason, winemakers desire to restrain the fury of the fermentative boiling in every way, just as the <term>brewers</term> <note>original: Zythopœi; from the Greek 'zythos' (beer) and 'poiein' (to make)</note> themselves likewise condemn that violent heat: *when the must, or beer, rages itself out.* <note>original German: wann der Moſt, oder Bier, ſich abtobet; referring to the end of the violent phase of fermentation</note> The *effect* in both subjects (and all similar ones) is a copious production of dregs, while the remaining liquid—because the saline parts have been more abundantly resolved and separated into an earthy form—acquires a *flat* taste and a vapid *thinness*, or a slimy slipperiness beneath that watery thinness. All these are the consequences, observable both before and after the fact, of salt decaying into earth.

(40.) However, let this business not be attributed to any other "chimeras" rather than to this *simplest* progress, method, and motion of nature (as is the habit of our wretched common *theories*, which always "savor of high things" <note>original: altum sapientes; a play on words suggesting they try to be profound while ignoring the obvious</note> but do not see what is right before their feet). It is better to follow the matter closely and insist upon it to its innermost conclusion so that, by reading the very tracks of the process, the path of this entire success cannot deceive us. Therefore, to finally give our absolute thesis indicated above—that this *conversion* of salts from their aqueous mixture into pure and naked earth is a matter of daily use and occurrence, and far more familiar than men might wish—I bid you to contemplate the *putrefaction* <note>in 17th-century chemistry, "putrefaction" often referred to any biological breakdown or secondary fermentation</note> of saline and vegetable things; the best specimens of this are <term>tartar</term> <note>the crystalline crust (potassium bitartrate) that forms in wine vats</note>, wine, and vinegar.

(41.) We shall first inspect *wine left to itself*. *Wine*, without any other addition, first of all turns into *vinegar*. Under this act, just as under the first *vinous fermentation* or the generation of wine from must, there arises a conspicuous *separation* of earthy matter. This manifests partly by covering the surface of the liquid like a *film* <note>original: cuticula; literally "little skin," referring to the "mother of vinegar"</note>, testifying to its *fatty* texture, and partly by soon sinking to the bottom, demonstrating its *earthy* nature. In truth, this entire yield of earthy substance can be regarded as a naked *separation*; for clearly that *acid*, which was once made dull and slippery by "fatness," but was altogether *saturated* with a certain absorbed and dissolved *earth*, gradually releases this earth again. I do not greatly [regard] this matter...

# BECHER’S THEORETICAL DOCUMENTS.

I shall strive to resist; but concerning the manner of *withdrawal* alone, due to the brief passage of time, I will commend to your mindful spirit that the leader, torch, author, and companion of this entire *separation* is entirely (*materially*) *phlogiston* <note>original: phlogistos; the hypothetical principle of fire and inflammability</note>, the substance commonly called *sulfurous* or *fatty*.

(42.) But truly, what shall be said of the *putrefaction of vinegar*? Someone might gather that something *earthy* still resides in vinegar from its *tartar* <note>the sediment or crust formed in wine/vinegar vessels</note>, and from the drying of some portion of vinegar into a *salt-moldy-fatty* consistency. Yet that portion is minimal, and moreover, it is very different from its *acidic* part, since the latter can be drawn off from that more solid residue by distillation alone. Indeed, if nothing else happened during *putrefaction* except the liberation of the *acid* within the vinegar through that copious sequestration of *earthy* sediment, then the *vinegar itself* ought to emerge stronger and more *acidic* from this process. But the opposite happens, such that this compound loses not only its *acidity*, but all of its *consistency* entirely, and is converted instead into *simple, insipid, and thin water*.

(43.) Meanwhile, during this act of *putrefaction*, a copious, thick, drying, and powdery matter separates, forming an *earthy sediment*. What is this, and from where is it produced? Various signs certainly testify that a *sulfurous-fatty* matter is present in it: the color, the odor, its inflammability, the *charcoal blackness* <note>original: carbonaria nigredo</note> that follows its burning, and indeed an *actual fatness* manifesting as an empyreumatic <note>burnt-smelling</note> oil, a *volatile salt*, and so on. But there is little of this—in fact, a very small amount—in proportion to the dry, solid residue. Indeed, *from the cause* <note>original: a priori</note>, the acidic substance of the vinegar was substantial; where did it go? No one would say it was converted into *fatness*. Few would believe it was converted into this *earth*; certainly, until now, no one has believed it, at least *theoretically* and cautiously. For *practically*, anyone could not help but acknowledge it, since even housewives <note>original: foeminae matresfamilias</note> daily detest this loss when their vinegar spoils.

(44.) We shall add to this deduction several further *practical* documents. That saline *acid* is reduced into *earth* by this method is confirmed by the fact that this entire operation is promoted *by earthy substances*. I cited an example for this demonstration—certainly not one to be rejected—in the month of *October* 1697, regarding either the preservation or, conversely, the sudden *corruption of wine* and concentrated *vinegar* by the addition of soluble earths. For just as *must* <note>unfermented grape juice</note>, or any fermenting liquor whatsoever, becomes more insipid the more it is *diluted* with water and casts down more *earthy dregs* from the start <note>original: a priori</note>; so *afterward* <note>original: a posteriori</note>, even such concentrated *saline-sulfurous* liquors, if they are aided by some *earthy* body, the *earthy-saline* portion gains dominance and shakes off the *watery mixture* in a headlong divorce. This is magnificently favored and aided by that *sulfurous* principle, which loathes and spurns water in many ways.

(45.) Truly, here again we owe something to the attention of experimental *Chemists*. However, I do not designate by this name those who merely hawk themselves under this title. Here, that distinction once uttered by a sophisticated <term>Empirical Chemist</term> <note>an "empirical" chemist at this time was one who focused on practical laboratory work rather than just philosophy</note> holds true: the difference between *Oven-heaters* and *Oven-sitters*; between *Coal-blowers* and *Ear-blowers* <note>original: Ofenhitzer und Ofensitzer: Kohlenbläser und Ohrenbläser; a play on words comparing those who work hard at the furnace with those who merely sit by it or whisper empty theories into people's ears</note>. I mean those who are skilled, attentive, diligent, and curious in their operations. From their ranks comes *Kunckel* <note>Johann von Löwenstern-Kunckel (1630–1703), a famous German chemist known for his work on phosphorus and glass</note>, who quite skillfully...

# SPECIMEN OF BECHER’S THEORY. PART I. SECTION II.

[He] noted, or certainly alleged, that artificial mode of **putrefaction** <note>In 17th-century chemistry, "putrefaction" referred to a controlled process of decomposition or fermentation used to break substances down into their primary elements</note>, or rather the management of its outcome, by which that appearing **earthy, slimy, powdery, and dreggy separation** might be driven, even when mature, **into an aggregation** that is most subtly **solid, dense, and firm**; provided, of course, that a moderate heat is applied seasonably during the **putrefaction**. By this aid, that material—which otherwise settles in the form of a fine powder—can even be gathered into **hard sand**, and thus can exhibit the **ultimate proof of an earthy nature**.

(46.) Indeed, unless time were to fail us, various other effects of **putrefactions** instituted in different ways could still be examined. Here, one might also deserve to consider the **secretion** of the more inward **false-earthy** heterogeneities <note>impurities or different substances mixed within a liquid</note> obtained from the waters themselves through repeated putrid fermentations. So too could the efficacy of our **sulfurous** principle <note>original: sulphurei; here referring to the 'principle of inflammability' or phlogiston</note> be taught for expediting these separations, showing by a certain easy experiment how **rain water** both **putrefies** and **does not putrefy**. But the sails must be furled, with the gods of the sea being all the more favorable now that we have been permitted to reach land from the salt sea, and to cast anchor in the solid, sandy slime.

In this way, we have indeed brought these **DOCUMENTS OF BECHER’S THEORY**—namely, the accounts of the experiments which strengthen and establish this theory—to an end. More could have been said, but scarcely more of importance; it could have been said better, but I do not know if better things could have been produced by me. I believe that the **foundations** of any art, and the **evidence** of those foundations, are the soul of various imitations, trials, and manifold experiments and theories alike. The title itself proclaims that **these are Becher’s**; if they are argued not to be his, they shall be mine. But if anyone else should wish to claim something from them for himself or others, provided he does not wound good faith, let him easily have it for himself: so long as there is nothing against **truth**; nothing against **good morals**; and nothing against a **good and fair reputation**. Whoever, then, shall uprightly and candidly favor the facts rather than the persons, for him we pray that, from the weighing of these contemplations, he may attain

### THE BECHERIAN SPECIMEN
### P A R T II.
### EXPERIMENTS OF THE BECHERIAN
### THEORY.

Just as all *human science*, in the order of understanding, must be *Analytical*, namely *a posteriori* <note>original: "a posteriori"; reasoning from observed effects back to their causes</note>, proceeding from the circumstances of things themselves toward their *number, connection, order, method* of coming together, and the *proportion* by which they may be joined, and so forth; so, for the attainment of this *science*, I say, it is absolutely necessary that *experience* precedes, or, at minimum, *runs alongside at a steady pace*. Through this, the *simple knowledge* and *history* <note>in this context, "history" refers to a systematic account of natural phenomena rather than a timeline of events</note> of things and effects—as well as the *character of those aforementioned things, both individual and shared—can be perceived in and from them as the true object of theory and the subject of science.*

But so that these individual steps may be done correctly and proceed in order, it is entirely necessary that those *experiments* themselves be *as simple as possible*; or by pursuing them to the point of simplicity, they are thereby freed from all *complicated considerations*. This is so that opinion, stumbling somewhere and *wandering from the very foundations*, does not *recede further and further from the truth as the number of various considerations grows, eventually extending and spreading that error into many other objects.*

It is truly and rightly to be lamented in this place that *human reason*, even in this business, holds onto its *primordial stain*—*pride* and *arrogance*—as a *stumbling block and the foundation of its fall*; *while loathing simplicity, it affects nothing but the showy, the laborious, the convoluted, and the abstruse: meanwhile, it despises the more well-known, the easier, and the unique: striving for the summit in a perverse order, it is either completely shaken off from there and [falls] into emptiness* <note>The text ends mid-word "decidit" (falls), completed by the catchword below.</note>

<page-num>120</page-num>
<header>SPECIMEN OF BECHER, PART II.</header>

...hidden or finding everything there closed and sealed, and finding it impossible to penetrate the interior, the mind imagines for itself certain powers based on the waves of more obvious phenomena. It imagines *material* powers with great difficulty, but *immaterial* ones most readily. Among these, those modern concepts hold the first place: *innate and concreated impulses and motions*, *internal matter*, and whatever faculty possesses and completes them. These are essentially what was *called "nature" by the ancients*, the *innate and absolutely proper principles of motion and rest*, and also an *internal and immanent principle*. This is what our Germans express most sincerely in their own vernacular: *It just has its own way of being.* <note>original: "Es habe seine Art also"; a common phrase suggesting an inherent, inexplicable nature or character.</note>

Meanwhile, since even when proceeding by the clearest path, there is and remains a huge, twofold difference: (1.) Between *experience itself*—that is, the bare knowledge of it, the systematic account <note>original: "historia"; in a scientific context, this means a detailed description of natural phenomena.</note>, or even the habit of perceiving such experience—and *variations of experiences*, which involve the *consideration and understanding* of its causes and relations. (2.) Between *some sort of preservation of these causes*, whether general or partial, adhering only to one or another specific aspect; and an *exquisite, fundamental* preservation that proceeds and penetrates to the *simple elements*—both material and formal, *individual and shared*, *absolute and relative circumstances*. Indeed, the former leads to nothing but errors in both theory and practice, and introduces not only solid ignorance but the *phantoms of false opinions*. *The latter alone—just as truth is one—provides both science and* (in suitable subjects) *art*; that is, the habit of acting according to right reason. *Therefore, it is highly advantageous, not only in general, to follow this latter path—namely the <unclear>path</unclear> of solid science and well-founded art—but also to recognize the trails and paths aiming toward a single goal.* *Above all, one must have a very clear direction of these toward the goal, under a firm guiding star* <note>original: "cynosura"; literally the constellation Ursa Minor, used here to mean a reliable guiding principle.</note>, *lest we wander from the goal and leave it behind us, rather than reaching that simple and single goal with a steady step.*

Such, therefore, must be the *scientific treatment of the chemistry of subterranean things, so that it is not and does not remain merely empirical and confusedly artisanal* <note>original: "fabrilis"; referring to the work of a common laborer or craftsman who works by rote without understanding the underlying principles.</note>. *Instead, it should subject experiments to reason and, through proper comparisons, attain the causes of effects and events.* *Since this can be done in no other way than by the help of simpler properties and facts (or observations and operations), any such simple experiences—even those often placed before our very feet—must be valued all the more in this field.* Yet, they are often judged unworthy of consideration or not even admitted into the mind, which is a most backward approach. *For this reason, in this Part, we will consider it our most vital duty to seek out every simple fact exposed to observation or operation with all the more zeal, because they uniquely constitute and provide not only the matter or subject, but also the form or object of the connections, both theoretical and practical.*

# PART II.
## SECTION I.
# EXPERIMENTS ON SALTS.
## CHAPTER I.
# ALKALINE SUBSTANCES.
### Observation.

ALKALIS, according to common usage, are understood to be both *saline* <note>original: "salina"</note> substances—which, through spontaneous solutions (both active and passive) in a watery or their own fluid form, readily unite with acid salts and *sulfurous-fatty* <note>original: "sulphureo-pinguibus"; referring to oily or combustible substances</note> concretions—and *earthy* substances, which primarily undergo the former process, namely the most rapid bonding with acids. From this shared nature, and the common understanding built upon it, there arises that *fundamental* experimental observation which serves as the guide for the experimental operations themselves. This observation provides the *Basis* <note>original: "Lemma"</note> of our alkaline experiments, namely:

->**ALKALIS ARE REFINED EARTHS.**<-
<note>original: "ALCALIA SUNT TERRÆ SUBTILIATÆ." Becher’s core theory was that alkalis are not a separate category of matter, but simply "earths" that have been broken down into finer particles through heat.</note>

Experiment I. All *earths* <note>here meaning minerals or solid matter</note> that, through frequent heating until glowing <note>original: "ignitione"</note> and quenching, are reduced to a state where they can be readily joined with acid salts.
II. Those commonly called *calcareous* <note>original: "calcariæ"; such as limestone or chalk</note>, which reach this state through heating alone, without needing to be quenched.
III. Such are all *limestones* known from the former method.
IV. From the latter method, it is known that all stones *refusing to melt into glass* <note>original: "vitream fusionem abnuentes"</note> fall into this category.
V. Also all *solid, dry marine* objects that show no signs of intricate plant life: *Shells, Corals, etc.*
VI. Indeed, even those *earthy* materials that do melt into glass when treated with the proper heat.
VII. Thus the *ashes of vegetables*, as long as they are soft and have not yet been semi-liquefied by a more violent fire, are dissolved by acids.
VIII. In fact, they are reduced into a formal *alkali* through the continued, subtle, and gentle action of heating, or a moderate *reverberatory fire* <note>a furnace that reflects heat back onto the substance</note>.
IX. This happens especially when a *flaming fire* is used; specifically, when the flame physically strikes those ashes.
X. Yet these same ashes, if subjected to a stronger fire, melt into *glass* <note>original: "vitrum"</note>.
XI. In this intimate, firmer, and dense state of aggregation, they will hereafter strongly resist acids.

<header>EXAMPLES FROM BECHER’S SECOND PART, SECTION I.</header>

XII. Afterwards, however, the substance must again be restored to that state of fineness, so that it might once more be open to and obey those acids.

XIII. *The principal non-vitrifying <note>Original "non vitrescentes," meaning they do not easily turn into glass.</note> earths are Chalks, marls, the marrow of stones <note>original: "saxorum medullæ"; likely referring to lithomarge or kaolin</note>, various Boles, various clays, and "Letten" <note>A German term for a specific type of stiff clay</note>:* But this is especially true of their purer parts, for these are primarily dissolved by acids.

XIV. However, the more compact parts, which have already attained a glassy or sandy density, are either clearly *not* dissolved in this state:

XV. Or they are dissolved weakly at best, and only after long periods of time.

XVI. This also occurs in *sandy* glasses, which often only submit to acids after a long duration:

XVII. Nor does this happen *equally* throughout the substance, but only through certain *cracks*, where the structure has been loosened here and there.

XVIII. Some substances, however, do dissolve *equally, so that they crumble into a fine powder.*

XIX. This is primarily what happens to **glasses melted together from sand or river-pebbles <note>original: "filicibus aquatilibus"; refers to flint stones found in water</note> with alkaline salts.**

XX. But these very glasses do not immediately dissolve or unite intimately and subtly with acids for that reason alone:

XXI. Instead, by crumbling only into a *fine powder*, they allow for the dissolution of only the most refined parts remaining from the rest.

XXII. *Flint-based glasses, and the flints themselves*, are delicately broken down by melting them with *fixed alkaline salt.*

XXIII. By a reciprocal action, the glassy structure of these flints is thinned out into a fineness nearly equal to that of salt:

XXIV. And in turn, the alkaline salt is woven into the glassy density and transparency.

XXV. Here indeed is an experiment that is both curious in practice and worthy of deeper consideration, which *Baldwin* <note>Christian Adolph Balduin (1632–1682), a chemist famous for discovering a phosphorescent substance</note> mentions by title alone as *The Hermetic Encaustic* <note>A type of fused coating or paint</note>: but *Glauber* <note>Johann Rudolf Glauber (1604–1670), a pioneering chemist known for "Glauber's salt"</note> long ago provided the actual practice. It is: *A clear liquor, which, by the spontaneous evaporation of its moisture, reveals a crystal.*

XXVI. Truly, one must take note of that entire difference which alkaline salt displays when melted with *flints*, as opposed to when it is melted with *glass already prepared from flints.*

XXVII. Just as its effect also differs when it is melted with *its own vegetable ashes*, compared to when it is melted with *glass already prepared from them.*

XXVIII. Fixed alkaline *salt, strictly so-called*, is prepared solely by artifice from *vegetables* through the operation of fire.

XXIX. Native alkali is found nowhere except in *common salt*: namely, the matter which provides the "body" for it.

XXX. This is demonstrated if common salt is mixed with *good spirit of vitriol or nitre* <note>original: "spiritu bono vitrioli aut nitri"; Sulfuric or Nitric acid</note>. From both, "spirit of salt" <note>Hydrochloric acid</note> is produced; the residue in the retort <note>A glass vessel used for distillation</note> is a new salt, fused from the acid of vitriol or nitre and this *fixed body.*

<meta>catchword: XXXI.</meta>

<summary>Becher discusses the chemical relationship between earths, flints, and alkaline salts, specifically how they can be fused into glass or dissolved back into powders. He notes that "fixed" alkaline salts are artificial products of fire, except for a core component found in common salt.</summary>

<header>BECHER’S THEORETICAL EXPERIMENTS</header>

XXXI. Thus, if that acid of vitriol <note>original: "acidum vitrioli"; sulfuric acid</note> or of nitre <note>original: "nitri"; nitric acid</note> is torn away from this body once again, an alkaline saline body remains.

XXXII. This coincides with purely artificial alkali in that:
(α) it may be dissolved in water and by deliquescence <note>The process where a salt absorbs moisture from the air until it dissolves into a liquid.</note>;
(β) it also flows readily in fire;
(γ) it dissolves mineral sulfur, both in a state of fire-induced flow <note>original: "igneo fluore"; molten state</note>
(δ) as well as in a watery flow;
(ε) and it dissolves other fats in a similar manner.

XXXIII. *It differs from that artificial alkali* in that:
(α) it is native <note>found naturally occurring rather than manufactured</note>;
(β) when combined with acids, it produces a different shape of crystals;
(γ) it has a different solubility in water;
(δ) and it introduces a different behavior regarding *fusion in fire.*

XXXIV. *Artificial alkaline salt*, in the strictest sense of the name, is prepared from the herb *Kali* <note>glasswort or saltwort plants</note>, or rather from other salty maritime plants. This is the *Spanish* Soda of the glassmakers.

XXXV. From this, it partly follows the nature of *common salt*: in its taste; in its fusion with *glass*; and in experiments with *acids.*

XXXVI. With glass, it primarily generates *glass gall* <note>original: "fel vitri"; a salty scum or "sandiver" that floats on top of molten glass during the manufacturing process</note>; clearly salty under various circumstances.

XXXVII. However, it leaves behind purer glasses; whereas simple vegetable alkalis *bring about a greater greenness and softness* in them.

XXXVIII. *Caustic alkali* of a simpler nature is prepared from vegetables that are provided with a more *nitrous* salt.

XXXIX. It is indeed a refined earthy substance; first through *inflammable matter* <note>referring to Becher's "terra pinguis" or the precursor to the phlogiston theory</note>: then, by means of this, *through fire.* Thus, the first state of matter exhibiting alkali is *Charcoal* <note>original: "Carbo"</note>:

XL. Namely, a fine earthy material, most deeply penetrated by an inflammable fatness.

XLI. This excludes all ready and deep entry of *water and acids*: hence *charcoal is altered neither by water nor by acids.*

XLII. *But by fire and open air*, once that inflammable substance is burned away, the remaining earthy substance is highly refined, and therefore mixes itself with water through its affinity for a saline nature.

XLIII. It also associates itself with *acid* salts, or is dissolved by them readily and skillfully, in the manner of even less refined earths:

XLIV. *Charcoal* does not mix with glass—at least not intimately, deeply, or in large quantities.

XLV. This is done readily by *ash*, even when it has not yet been fully freed from its inflammable components.

XLVI. Even the *alkaline salt* itself, now purer, has a great deal of interaction with glasses.

XLVII. Indeed, with sand and flints, it first boils or forms an effervescence.

XLVIII. From which *Glauber* <note>Johann Rudolf Glauber (1604–1670), a contemporary chemist famous for his work on salts</note> *also observes the breathing out of acidity.*

XLIX. And it boils in this way, especially when still pregnant with some charcoal-like fatness or inflammable matter. *Though it does so even without that being prominent.*

<header>SPECIMEN BECHERIANUM PART II. SECTION I.</header>

L. Truly, it performs all these things through fusion in fire, or melting.

LI. Which caustic and strongly saline alkali undergoes readily; the *less caustic* kind, being of a somewhat thicker and earthier nature, does so *more slowly.*

LII. Indeed, *alkaline salt* liquefies [deliquesces] even by the moisture of the air alone.

LIII. Through *repeated* instances of such liquefaction and coagulation, it is reduced to a state of extreme flowability:

LIV. In fact, it eventually reaches such thinness that it can hardly admit *coagulation* <note>The process of becoming solid or thick again.</note> anymore:

LV. Instead, it seeps into the pores of the containing vessels; it melts solid things. *Boyle makes some mention of this matter in general in his treatise on the parts of nitre.* <note>Robert Boyle (1627–1691), a foundational figure in modern chemistry. The "parts of nitre" refers to his work on potassium nitrate.</note>

LVI. *Alkali becomes caustic* when married with its own proper earth—that is, rich ash. If ashes from nitrous woods—for example, *Birch*—are lightly moistened and burned again in a flaming fire, the salt may then be boiled out <note>original: "elixetur"; extracted by boiling</note> and coagulated.

LVII. Just as it also occurs with *quicklime* <note>original: "calce viva"; calcium oxide</note>, by boiling the alkaline lye with it, decanting the liquid, and thickening it.

LVIII. Such alkali dissolves all tough substances into a slime, such as *feathers, hair, nails, bones, and horns*; it turns fats into *soap*; and transforms *Sulfurs* into a red liquor.

LIX. The most caustic form performs such things even while *cold, in the form of lye*: the weaker form requires being heated or *boiled.*

LX. After it dissolves *common sulfur*, it spreads a most foul, penetrating, and volatile *odor*. Consequently, all silver objects in the vicinity are blackened. With fats, it also forms a certain heavy-smelling stench, following the example of *soap*: indeed, it spontaneously exhales a urine-like and nauseating odor, especially if it is pregnant with the smoky [empyreumatic] fat of charcoal.

LXI. Alkali is *fixed* against burning and even fusion; that is, it does not easily lose any of its weight:

LXII. However, it does so more easily through long burning or fusion in the *open air* than by fusion or burning in a *closed vessel.*

LXIII. When *boiled* with much water while exposed to the open air, it *exhales* into the breezes along with the water: yet it does so without any taste, odor, or any conspicuous corrosive or even saline power.

LXIV. *But in a closed vessel, it does not do the same*: or at least it does so with an immensely unequal readiness.

LXV. Alkali *unites with acids* of every kind, promptly and intimately.

LXVI. When diluted, it *effervesces* with diluted acids; but when both are in a thicker [more concentrated] state, this does not occur.

LXVII. There is no *contrariety* <note>A common 17th-century theory that acids and bases reacted because they were "enemies" or opposites; Becher argues here for a "subtle embrace" or attraction instead.</note> here, but an intimate and most subtle embrace of both: hence the *cohesion* of alkali with any acid is firmer than that of any other soluble thing.

LXVIII. On this basis, fixed alkali also *precipitates* <note>Causes a solid to fall out of a solution.</note> any species that have been dissolved by acids.

LXIX. That there is still some thicker *inflammable* matter present in fixed alkali is indicated by

# BECHER’S THEORETICAL EXPERIMENTS

...its color becomes black, and again like coal, if, when saturated with distilled vinegar, it is fired once more.

LXX. Fixed alkali <note>original: "Alcali fixum"; likely potassium carbonate or sodium carbonate</note> promptly dissolves *thicker and slightly slimy fats*, such as *animal fats*, *vegetable resins*, and *mineral sulfur*.

LXXI. However, it does not [easily] dissolve *subtle fats* or *distilled oils*.

LXXII. Yet it can dissolve them quickly and in large quantities if the proper manipulation <note>original: "enchirifi," likely a corruption of the Greek term "encheirisis" meaning manual procedure or method</note> is applied.

LXXIII. Without that method, it happens only with the greatest slowness and in a special consistency that yields only to fresh water. For example: one ounce of juniper oil was poured into eight ounces of an alkaline solution prepared with the "phlegm" of spirit of wine <note>The watery byproduct left over from the distillation of alcohol.</note>. This mixture sat for perhaps a year with no other effect than the oil slightly thickening and turning a reddish hue. The oil was then poured off, with only a tiny amount remaining. After several weeks, a certain rim or film <note>original: "limbus"</note> clung to the glass, corresponding to the level where the oil had floated upon the liquid. When that lye-like liquid was shaken, this film was not altered. But when the liquid was poured out and a little fresh water was poured in, the film immediately dissolved into a milky, soapy consistency, with a sharp and bitter taste that still recalled the nature of juniper rather than expressing it fully.

LXXIV. To this class of experiments belongs that final entry among *Digby’s Chemistry* <note>original: "Chymica Digbaeana"; referring to the works of Sir Kenelm Digby (1603–1665), a famous natural philosopher and privateer.</note> for the preparation of *Matthews’ pills* <note>A popular 17th-century medicinal pill containing soap, oils, and often opium.</note>.

LXXV. In this case, one night of *deliquium* <note>The process of a substance absorbing moisture from the air until it dissolves into a liquid.</note> achieves more than a month spent using other methods.

LXXVI. Alkali does not dissolve in *spirit of wine* <note>Alcohol</note>, except very sparingly, even when it is quite caustic. *Animal fat* behaves the same way. And yet *soap*, which consists of these two substances together, dissolves in it in significant amounts.

LXLVII. <note>The original text misnumbers this as 97 instead of 77.</note> For this reason, *distilled oils* are more easily joined to alkalis if they are already imbued with a somewhat thick, resinous body.

LXXVIII. But even when these pure oils are properly associated with pure alkali, while they partly enter the mixture and connect, they also partly remain floating on top. In the former case, they produce a *milky consistency*; in the latter, they take on a *reddish*—indeed, a tawny—color.

LXXIX. *Spirit of wine* also takes on a *blood-red* color from caustic alkali, especially when it is *oily*.

LXXX. Similarly, *sulfur*, when dissolved by a very caustic alkali or by its cold liquid form, mimics the *color of a garnet*.

LXXXI. In the flow of fire [fusion], the alkali both dissolves the sulfur and holds it in the fire so that it does not *fly away* <note>original: "evolet"; i.e., evaporate or sublime.</note>.

LXXXII. Nor does it burn, so long as free air is absent; but when air is present, it burns.

LXXXIII. Indeed, some part of the sulfur is "fixed" by the alkali so that it settles in the form of a *black powder* when a solution is made with water—though this powder turns white upon drying.

LXXXIV. Another part of it is mixed with the alkaline salt as it *gradually turns into glass*, tinting the glass a *dark color*.

LXXXV. The alkali does not bond firmly with the sulfur; for the sulfur is separated from it again by any acid, even the weakest.

# SPECIMEN OF BECHER, PART II, SECTION I.

LXXXVI. The same occurs with **fats**: from which soap is immediately resolved into floating fat <note>Becher is describing "salting out" or the decomposition of soap, where the fatty component separates and floats to the top.</note>.

LXXXVII. In the case of **alkalis**, however, when they are worked more intimately with **distilled oils**, this separation does not occur.

LXXXVIII. Alkali salt does not take up the **flammable part** <note>This refers to phlogiston, the theoretical substance of fire and inflammability.</note> from coals, in its naked and pure state, in an equally coarse or sensible manner;

LXXXIX. But it is worked well with a certain coarser, slimy substance: for example, **vegetable juices** combined with alkali; and the so-called **black fluxes** <note>A mixture of tartar and nitre used in smelting to help metals melt and to prevent oxidation.</note>.

XC. Yet the **flammable substance**, when more subtly mixed with the alkali salt with the appropriate aid of air, imparts **volatility** to it.

XCI. This happens partly by the addition of coals and proper melting; partly with **crude tartar** or suitable vegetable juices, skillfully joined with alkali. The former is in the manner of **Geber** <note>An influential medieval alchemist (Pseudo-Geber) known for his works on metallurgy.</note>; the latter in the manner of **Langelott** <note>Joel Langelott (1617–1680), a German physician and chemist known for his mechanical improvements to chemical apparatus.</note>.

XCII. Just as alkali clings weakly to **sulfur**, so that it can be separated from it by the lightest other acid; so it clings most firmly with the **acid of sulfur**, once separated from its flammable part. Namely, if such alkali is melted with an equal weight of sulfur and then burned off with a gentle, glowing fire; not only does the excess quantity of sulfur burn away, but even that which clung more intimately to the alkaline salt remains most firmly remixed with the alkali in the form of a salt-acid, its flammable part having been burned away.

XCIII. For it cannot be separated from the alkali, neither by fire, nor air, nor water, nor by any other salt, nor by any earthy additive, nor by any metallic means.

XCIV. It is separated only by that **phlogiston** <note>original: "phlogisto"</note> itself, mixed in intimately once again; namely by coals heaped upon it. Thus reduced back into sulfur, it clings only loosely and casually to the alkali; to be driven out by any very light acid salt.

XCV. Indeed, the alkali salt loses through this bond with that acid all its (α) **burning power** <note>original: "καῦσιν" (kausin)</note> (β) **fluidity**, whether by water <note>original: "p. d.", likely *per deliquium* (dissolving by absorbing moisture)</note> or (γ) by fire: (δ) all reaction toward other acids; (ε) and toward mineral sulfur, (ζ) or any fats whatsoever.

XCVI. Although it neither flows nor smokes in the fire, it is nevertheless dissolved by water, though sluggishly, with the help of boiling, and only with a large quantity of water:

XCVII. While boiling with water, with the help of free air, it evaporates abundantly into the breezes.

XCVIII. With no taste or smell, or only the slightest, which nevertheless grows stronger with repetition.

XCIX. Alkali also combines with all other **acids**; such as with **nitrous acid**, into nitre <note>Potassium nitrate, or saltpeter.</note>; with **culinary acid**, into a salt rivaling common salt <note>Common table salt (sodium chloride).</note>; with **vinegar** and the acid of **tartar** itself, into a certain third thing, a rival of tartar; and with volatile sulfur, into a kind of salty concretion.

C. From these compositions it is displaced again, always by the addition of a new, stronger acid; the highest and ultimate of which is the **acid of vitriol** or **sulfur** <note>Sulfuric acid, considered the "strongest" acid in early modern chemistry.</note>.

He explains that while sulfur and alkali bond loosely, the "acid" of sulfur (sulfate) bonds so tightly to alkali that only the addition of phlogiston (via charcoal) can break the bond.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the technical chemical observations of Johann Joachim Becher, focusing on how fixed caustic alkalis (such as potassium carbonate) interact with various metals and organic spirits. It builds on the previous discussion regarding the "flammable principle" (phlogiston) and the corrosive power of alkalis.</meta>

<page-num>127</page-num>
->### BECHER’S THEORETICAL EXPERIMENTS<-

CI. From **metallic compounds**, it dissolves, by itself: **lead, copper, tin, regulus of antimony, and iron.** <note>The "it" refers to the caustic alkali discussed in previous sections.</note>

CII. **Lead** is dissolved if caustic alkali is cooked with shavings or with **calx of lead**. <term>Calx: An oxide produced by roasting a metal in air; the "ashes" of a metal.</term>

CIII. **Copper**, by the infusion of **caustic lye**, with fine shavings, filings, or calx (precipitated by iron from vitriol or any other solution) or even with **verdigris**. <note>original: "viridi aeris"; verdigris is the green pigment/crust that forms on copper, typically copper acetate.</note>

CIV. **Tin**, partly by a similar infusion, and partly by **fusion** <note>melting together at high heat</note>.

CV. **Regulus of antimony, by fusion**: if caustic alkali is melted with the regulus, it resolves it into **saffron-colored crocus**; but with a very strong fire, it turns into a **transparent, glass-like** thinness, amber in color. <term>Regulus: The pure, metallic form of a mineral (in this case, antimony) that has settled at the bottom of a crucible after smelting.</term>

CVI. **Iron**, by the proper combustion of iron with **nitre** <note>saltpeter</note>; from which the remaining **caustic** alkali salt of nitre dissolves a portion of the iron such that it carries it through a filter with a clear **amethyst-purple** color.

CVII. Joined with **sulfur**, it subtly dissolves **antimony** into "golden sulfur"; **tin**, so that almost all of it melts away in water, and once filtered, passes through as a dark brownish-black liquid; and finally **gold** itself, so that it flows through the filter with the consistency of a sulfurous solution.

CVIII. It also alters various substances, metallic ones especially, by **precipitation** from acid solutions: so that afterwards they are **no longer** dissolved by acids. Or they are not dissolved by the same ones, but by different ones: as occurs with **precipitated mercury**, which is later soluble in vinegar.

CIX. It grants a dry consistency to **volatile urinous spirits**, or at least leaves them so; which **lime** and **earthy** substances do not do as effectively: for these induce a liquid form in those salts. <term>Volatile urinous spirits: Ammonia-based solutions derived from biological sources like urine.</term>

<note>The numbering in the original text skips CX and proceeds directly from CIX to CXI.</note>

CXI. It separates, however, both from these salts and from the **burning spirits** <note>alcohols</note> themselves, the **superfluous and superficial oiliness.**

CXII. From this it **turns reddish**: Indeed, when caustic alkali is reduced with **spirit of wine** <note>ethanol</note> into a more saturated alkaline tincture, if this spirit is allowed to evaporate gently in the open air (without added heat), there eventually remains a watery-alkaline liquid of a **dark blood-red** color: a tincture you would suspect neither in the **spirit**, nor in the **salt**, nor in the combination of the two.

CXIII. Oils treated with spirit of wine in this "tartarized" manner increase the wonder; among these, oil of anise takes on the most saturated tincture.

CXIV. Just as alkalis are made from **earth**, refined by the **flammable principle**, by **burning**, and by the long penetration of fire: so **quicklime** is a refined **earth** of a saline disposition—or indeed a "mixture" according to some—thinned out by the penetration of fire.

CXV. It is certain that something **moist** is present in limestone; for it smokes while it is burned. That something of **phlogiston** lies beneath it is suggested by the fact that it also smells oily during burning. <term>Phlogiston: A theoretical substance once believed to be the essence of fire and released during combustion.</term>

CXVI. Certainly those **marine** shells <note>original: "ostracodermata"</note> are provided with a certain scorched fatness: but when burned, they yield **quicklime**.

While the previous page focused on how caustic alkalis dissolve metals like lead and iron, this page shifts to comparing the properties of quicklime (calcium oxide) with those of alkaline salts (potassium carbonate). It details the chemical behavior of lime in mortar, its reaction with acids, and its role in preventing glass from forming.</meta>

<page-num>128</page-num>
->### BECHER’S SAMPLES, PART II, SECTION I.<-

CXVII. To these belong, in some measure, **egg shells** as well.

CXVIII. **Quicklime** <note>original: "calx viva"; calcium oxide</note> differs from **alkaline salt** in several ways: ($\alpha$) it does not melt in fire; ($\beta$) when dissolved in water, it evaporates very clearly into the air; ($\gamma$) it does not possess a notable **taste**, let alone a **caustic** one <note>Becher likely refers to the sharp, salty, or "soapy" taste of potash compared to the dry, stony taste of lime</note>; ($\delta$) it coagulates **acids** not into a dry or crystalline consistency, but into a **liquid** one; ($\epsilon$) by itself it never reaches a liquid solution; ($\zeta$) with **sulfur** it turns into a dry consistency **mimicking crystals**, which alkali does not do; ($\eta$) with **sand** it grows together into a hard mass; ($\vartheta$) it does the same even with **mucilage, egg white, and milk curds**, which alkaline salt would instead liquefy; ($\iota$) it fixes **sulfurs** more effectively.

CXIX. It agrees with alkali in that: ($\alpha$) it **saturates acids**, ($\beta$) and holds them firmly; ($\gamma$) and thus also **precipitates** <note>causes a solid to fall out of a liquid solution</note> other things dissolved by them; ($\delta$) and alters them, though not with the same property as alkali; ($\epsilon$) it dissolves **sulfur and fats**; ($\zeta$) and especially **mucilaginous** substances.

CXX. Its **special** efficacy is that it "fixes" more—that is, it reduces substances to an earthy nature—more than **alkaline salt** does.

CXXI. Just as the aforementioned sulfur of **antimony** is reduced to a fixed earthy substance by a single long boiling.

CXXII. It also alters **other metals** in various ways when combined with sulfur and volatile minerals.

CXXIII. **Lime** never turns into glass; rather, it **prevents** vitrification <note>the process of turning into glass</note> when added in large amounts. If a very small amount is added, it gives the glass a powdery, milky **opacity** <note>original: "aphaneitate"; a lack of transparency</note>.

CXXIV. By roasting and the force of fire, nothing of the lime flies away; however, when it has undergone mixing **with water**, whatever part of it is so mixed turns to vapor and exhales.

CXXV. The combinations of **quicklime** with various acids have not yet been sufficiently examined—for example, with **tartar**, with **raw vinegar**, with **distilled vinegar**, with **spirit of nitre** <note>nitric acid</note>, **spirit of vitriol** <note>sulfuric acid</note>, **spirit of tartar**, or **spirit of wood**. Only its combination with the acid of **salt** <note>hydrochloric acid</note> is better known, though barely in passing; they call it **fixed sal ammoniac** <term>Fixed sal ammoniac: Historically, this refers to calcium chloride, produced by reacting lime with ammonium chloride or hydrochloric acid.</term>.

CXXVI. **Quicklime heats up** when mixed with water; however, it does so more greatly and far more strongly when **whole and in large pieces than when crushed**.

CXXVII. It makes the saline alkali quite **caustic**; but only when "married" with earthy-dry bodies, such as **regulus of iron** <note>original: "regulo martiali"; the metallic form of iron</note> or **cadmia** <note>typically zinc ore or furnace soot used in alchemical processes</note>.

CXXVIII. When **exposed to the air** alone, if it is humid, the lime **gradually crumbles**; it does not heat up perceptibly, nor does it expand as greatly or dissolve as finely as it does when **slaked with water**.

CXXIX. Most importantly, when crumbling under the air alone in this way, it **does not harden** afterward when mixed with sand.

CXXX. **Quicklime**, no matter how thoroughly slaked, **does not harden by itself**.

CXXXI. Even if it is dried for a **very long time**, it remains good, retaining its **ability to harden**.

CXXXII. It **hardens**, however, within hours or at most a few days, when mixed **with river sand**.

<meta>This page continues the comparison between the properties of alkaline salts (such as potash) and quicklime (calcium oxide). In the previous section, the author established the basic differences in how these substances react with acids and heat. Here, Becher explores their roles as "fluxes" in metallurgy and glassmaking, their behavior in open air, and cites historical accounts of salt production in Asia to illustrate chemical transformations.</meta>

<page-num>129</page-num>
->### BECHER’S THEORETICAL EXPERIMENTS<-

CXXXIII. **Alkaline salt promotes the melting of metals and glass more "positively,"** by adding substance and increasing the power of the furnace: **quicklime** <note>original: "calx viva"; calcium oxide</note> barely does so, except "privatively," by taming and suppressing foreign impurities like sulfur and arsenic.

CXXXIV. **Alkaline salt, when left in the open air, turns into a salty or neutral salt:** of a **vitriolic-alkaline** nature <note>Becher refers to the salt absorbing moisture and carbon dioxide or sulfur from the air to form potassium sulfate or carbonate</note>.

CXXXV. **It does not become common sea salt or muriatic salt, according to Kunkel** <note>Johann von Löwenstern-Kunckel, a famous 17th-century chemist</note>; nor does it become **nitrous salt, according to Balduin** <note>Christian Adolph Balduin, known for discovering a type of phosphorescent salt</note>.

CXXXVI. Unless, of course, it is changed by additives, or kept in air filled with specific vapors, or under a certain internal disposition.

CXXXVII. **Thus Tavernier** <note>Jean-Baptiste Tavernier, a 17th-century French gem merchant and traveler</note> **relates regarding the inhabitants of the Kingdom of Assam, that from the leaves of a tree which they call "Adam's Fig"** <note>The banana tree, *Musa paradisiaca*</note>—**which has been brought to Europe—they prepare a caustic alkaline lye used to bleach yellow silk into white. Since they lack common table salt, they prepare for themselves an edible salt from this same lye, which corresponds to common salt, by this method: they stir and whirl this lye in an open tub or vat under the open sky with brooms for twelve continuous hours; afterward, they boil it down until it coagulates or granulates. In this way, they obtain a muriatic salt.**

CXXXVIII. **A significant difference between alkaline salts is their degree of causticity:** and by extension, their "fluxibility" <note>the ease with which they melt</note>, both when moisture is added and through fire. Nevertheless, they remain alkalis. The best is that which is most caustic, melting most quickly and deeply, and flowing readily and subtly.

CXXXIX. **We have said that alkalis become caustic when mixed with quicklime.** We add that this is even more effective with **fresh** and truly "live" lime. However, it also works for a long time with lime that has been properly **slaked** <note>lime treated with water</note>. Indeed, it works quite notably, though not to the same degree, with lime that has **crumbled spontaneously** and turned to powder slowly in the open air.

CXL. **However, such an alkali** <note>one mixed with lime</note> **stains glass:** it is also not as suitable for making melts more fluid as a **simple, gentle alkaline salt.** Indeed, it should not be used indiscriminately for any operations if a certain <term>ἀκρίβεια</term> <note>original Greek: *akribeia*; meaning "precision" or "exactness"</note> is desired.

CXLI. There is also a different relationship between alkaline salt and fresh urine, compared to quicklime and urine. **Urine yields much less volatile salt** <note>ammonia</note> when treated with the former than it does with lime.

CXLII. **Quicklime, in large quantities, "fixes" and kills volatile salts, which saline alkali does not do.**

CXLIII. **In "fixing" greedy minerals** <note>corrosive or reactive minerals like arsenic or sulfur</note>, **lime acts more strongly than alkali.**

CXLIV. **Neither lime nor alkaline salt can "reduce"** <note>return a metal from its oxide state back to a metallic state</note> **the "calces" of base metals, unless they were produced from acid solutions.**

CXLV. **But if they were produced by fire (as ashes), they cannot be reduced at all:** although alkali works well if **crude tartar or charcoal** is added; in these cases, the power of these flammable substances is the primary cause.

CXLVI. **Regarding what Kunkel promises concerning "mercurification"** <note>the process of turning a solid metal into a liquid, "mercurial" state</note> **using caustic alkalis that are easily melted and purified of all solid foreign matter, one may read his own account in his *Observations*.**

CXLVII. Various authors praise what they [alkaline salts] can achieve here when combined with **fats**, in **soap** <note>original: "smegmate"; referring to the saponification process where alkali reacts with fat</note>, and in those **oily salts** cited above; when joined with soot, they also demonstrate a potency that should not be overlooked.

CXLVIII. Indeed, with such substances, they are prepared for a state of **volatility**: a great example of which is the **volatile salt of wine dregs** <note>original: "sal volatile fæcum vini"; an early term for ammonium carbonate or similar nitrogenous compounds derived from organic matter</note>.

CXLIX. Let that substance which arises from the deflagration of **tartar and niter** <note>potassium bitartrate and saltpeter</note> be compared—provided it is done skillfully—by **rectifying** it <note>purifying through repeated distillation or sublimation</note>.

CL. Alkali, when combined with **glass-making materials** <note>original: "vitris"; likely referring to silica or sand</note>, or by any more ready method, **is reduced into an earth insoluble in water and becomes glass.**

CLI. Glass has a remarkable analogy with earths and metals: **yet it is more "sandy" than "ashy."** <note>Becher distinguishes between the silica-based part of glass and the plant-ash alkali part</note>

CLII. Glass made from ashes flows with greater difficulty the further they [the ashes] **are still removed from an alkaline saline substance or tenderness.** <note>The "tenderness" likely refers to the fluxing ability of the salt to lower the melting point</note>

CLIII. Sandy glasses turn out clearer; Ash-based glasses turn out green.

CLIV. Glasses promote the **melting of refractory metals, iron and copper: but even more so if phlogistic substances** <note>original: "substantiæ phlogistæ"; substances containing "phlogiston," the theoretical principle of fire and inflammability proposed by Becher</note> **are present.**

CLV. Molten glasses are stained by **soot flowing into them by chance.**

CLVI. Experts strongly assert the difference between **fixed niter** <note>potassium carbonate produced by burning saltpeter with charcoal</note> and common **ash-based alkalis**, noting a purer effect when used with glass.

CLVII. The prerogative of **salt of tartar** <note>potassium carbonate derived from wine lees</note> over any ash-based alkali is its subtler purity.

CLVIII. This purity should also not be denied to that alkali which **results from niter and tartar.** <note>Known as "white flux" in metallurgy</note>

CLIX. Tartar suggests examples of the **reduction of things into alkaline salt**; for (α) when lightly burned, it is charcoal, exhibiting a **terrestrial** nature in various ways. (β) When that **inflammable** part is burned away and the salt extracted, there remains an **earth**, which is not soluble in water, but is soluble in acids. (γ) Meanwhile, this earthy substance, through the skillful application of burning, for the most part vanishes into the air: (δ) especially if **crystals of tartar** are used, which are free from the thicker, truly earthy **muddy** substance.

CLX. Meanwhile, even **wood ashes**, when repeatedly moved back into the coals and flames, are gradually consumed entirely.

CLXI. **Vegetable earth** approaches a mineral nature more closely if it has been predisposed through **putrefaction**.

CLXII. Unless this [earth] also draws the parts of animals away **from their lime-like dryness and from an alienation from a glass-like state**, it could hardly achieve anything else.

CLXIII. It deserves observation what alteration the detonation of **bones and animal coals** with niter might bring about.

CLXIV. But when mixed into **melting** vessels <note>crucibles</note>, these **animal earths** render the vessels most consistently enduring of glass-making heats; provided the rest of the clay consistency is kept free from cracks.

<header>EXPERIMENTS AND THEORIES OF BECHER</header>

CLXV. *Indeed, land animals give evidence of their alkaline nature through the abundant yield of volatile alkaline salt.*

CLVI. *However, shellfish, eggshells, and carapaces are of a more **calcareous** <note>lime-like</note> nature than a salty one.*

CLXVII. *Fresh animal urine is not to be attributed to an alkaline nature in the same way; but once thoroughly putrefied, it is: hence the effects of the two are different.*

CLXVIII. *It would be incorrect to count acid-earth solutions—such as spirits of salt <note>hydrochloric acid</note> with quicklime, or spirits of nitre <note>nitric acid</note> with the same—as alkalis.*

CLXIX. *But the products of these mineral salts, when burned for a long time with lime, are of a different character.*

CLXX. *Furthermore, nitre <note>saltpeter</note>, without any additive, if melted for a longer time in an open vessel, exerts its caustic-alkaline part more as its more volatile parts are expelled.*

CLXXI. *The same thing happens to common salt; thus, fused salt **deliquesces** <note>absorbs moisture from the air until it dissolves</note> more easily.*

CLXXII. *Especially if it lies upon planks or wooden tables: where salt, even if otherwise not so prone to melting, does so promptly.*

CLXXIII. *It is worth investigating through experience how alkaline salts, when fused for a long time with nitre and then separated from it again, behave toward glass in terms of color.*

CLXXIV. *It is certain that alkalis bubble and foam more when combined with nitre.*

CLXXV. *Common salt does not do this; rather, it melts calmly with the alkali.*

CLXXVI. *However, nitre also foams of its own accord when melted by a more intense flame.*

CLXXVII. *But most intensely when liquefied together with **Borax**.*

CLXXVIII. *Least of all, however, with common salt.*

CLXXIX. *Alkali also boils with charcoal: gently with their powder, but more strongly with chunks, due to the fault of their porosity.*

CLXXX. Regarding **manipulations** <note>original: "Enchirises"; manual laboratory procedures</note>, caution is required lest a chunk of alkali, however slightly damp, be thrown into another molten substance: where, through the expansion of the moisture, it causes the rest to foam up and overflow; or, with the moisture first driven from the edges to the center and then expanding more violently, it causes the chunk to rupture with a sound and scatter. Certainly, we have seen these **violent outbreaks** <note>original: "παροξύσματα" (paroxysmata); sudden, intense reactions or "fits"</note> often cause damage.

CLXXXI. Just as the contact of molten common salt with a drop of water produces a dangerous explosion with scattering, often hazardous to the unwary operator.

CLXXXII. So also by adding nitre to alkaline salt with molten mineral sulfur, that loud crash with scattering is often produced, just as happens in **thundering powder** (Knall- oder Schlag-Pulver) <note>original German: "Bang- or Strike-powder"; an early explosive mixture similar to flash powder</note>. These are minor things, but neglect and forgetfulness often bring about losses.

CLXXXIII. The purification of alkaline salts from foreign substances is best carried out through spontaneous **deliquescence** <note>the process of a salt turning into liquid by absorbing moisture from the air</note>.

CLXXXIV. The mixture of *common salt* is excepted; from which it is better freed by...

CLXXXV. From *nitre* <note>saltpeter</note>, by pouring over charcoal, or the metallic part <note>original: regulo</note> of antimony.

CLXXXVI. An alkali becomes very caustic if it is baked <note>original: cementetur; a process of heating a solid in a powder without melting it</note> with the metal of Mars <note>iron</note> for a long time, rather than being melted.

CLXXXVII. This also happens if equal parts of nitre are detonated with that metal and burned for a longer time in such a vigorous fire without melting. The metal of Jove <note>tin</note> does the same; both are clearly more caustic than the *simple* alkali.

CLXXXVIII. With *iron* or *tin* alone, detonating nitre becomes sufficiently caustic in its alkaline part, its acidic parts having been destroyed.

<margin>so that it even boils up with water.</margin>
CLXXXIX. Such a salt, especially prepared with those metallic parts, is rendered so caustic:

CXC. This <term>burning quality <note>original: καῦσις (kausis)</note></term> is lost if that metal is precipitated out of it by charcoal.

CXCI. A prime example of a *mineral* nature appearing from a vegetable source is the proper burning of tartar <note>a deposit from fermented grapes</note>; through this, it shows traces of *mineral sulfur* without any other additive.

CXCII. Reason suggests that alkali dissolved *by moisture* <note>original: per deliquium - the process where a salt absorbs water from the air until it turns into a liquid</note> undergoes specific changes from the air depending on its condition. Thus, it has been noted that such a solution can take on the scent or fragrance of *roses*.

CXCIII. But it completely destroys other scents—for example, those of *distilled oils*—if it bonds too closely with them.

CXCIV. Hence even *oil of cinnamon*, when one or two drops are joined to a sharp alkaline tincture, changes or loses its flavor remarkably.

CXCV. For the same reason, it reverses and breaks down the corrosive tastes of *acids*, as well as the sharpest *smells*, such as the *volatile spirit of sulfur*.

CXCVI. If *vinegar* is saturated with alkaline salt, and the greater part of its water is allowed to gently evaporate, and finally *spirit* or *oil of vitriol* <note>sulfuric acid</note> is added drop by drop, the vinegar is regenerated in a fortified or concentrated state, according to what was said above.

CXCVII. It is of the same class if *crude tartar* is combined with *salt of tartar* <note>potassium carbonate</note>, the solution filtered, and evaporated very gently to the consistency of a fine beer. When *acid of vitriol* is added drop by drop, the *tartar* falls out as a very pure and white powder.

CXCVIII. Salt of tartar, when mixed with *wine dregs*, crude *tartar*, or crude *vinegar*, aided by acidic substances, undergoes putrefaction and partly becomes volatile, while partly *crumbling into earth*.

CXCIX. Indeed, even when united with the acid of vitriol itself, it does not refuse such changes under those conditions.

CC. Just as when it is heavily overwhelmed by the *bitter* parts of vegetables or the *moldy* parts of animals.

CCI. *Acidic tartar*, imbued with oily fatness, turning into *fixed alkali* with every trace of acidity leaving it, is a matter for Theory.

CCII. Similarly, all woods will fail to produce alkaline salt unless they first exhibit signs of acidity.

I have chosen to present a sample of these experiments to show how every new perspective, as many new operations and observations, deserves to be not only noted but also considered and compared with others. Thus, anyone wishing to pursue these matters deeper into theory may remember from this circumstance that our <term>Becher <note>Johann Joachim Becher (1635–1682), a German physician and chemist whose "Physical Education" laid the groundwork for the Phlogiston theory</note></term> derived *alkali and acid* from a single root. ## SECTION II.
# ACIDS.

In the preceding Section, we dealt with the experimental *phenomena* of alkalis; we mixed in some points there concerning *calcareous* <note>Lime-like or chalky.</note> earths as well as *glasses*. We noted at the same time that some diversity is observed even regarding the glasses themselves, so that the condition of *vegetable* glasses is different from that of other *earthy* glasses. Since it pleases us not at all to mix in theories here in any way, we shall say only this one thing (referring more to *experience* than theory): whereas in the previous Section we mentioned glasses insofar as they approach *alkalis*, in this place we shall hand down some facts about them insofar as they also favor *acids*. So that anyone wishing to pursue these matters deeper into theory may recall from this very circumstance that our Becher, not without sound reasons, derived *alkali and acid* from a single root; and he traced *earthy* things—not only *calcareous* or <term>vitrifying <note>original: vitrescente; the property of turning into glass when heated.</note></term> ones—ultimately back to this *vitrifying earth*, as if to the simplest and final one. Nevertheless, it will be permitted for us in this very place to subject the acidic salts also to a kind of <term>trial <note>original: docimasiae; the chemical testing or assaying of a substance.</note></term> of a certain axiom, which is as follows:
