### BECHER’S THEORETICAL EXPERIMENTS

XXXI. A not inelegant assay <term>docimasia; the art of testing metals for purity</term>, of a more specific arrangement regarding a certain species of metallic nature, is the color produced from such earths, intensified either in certain solvents or within glasses.

XXXII. In this way, that purple-colored precipitation made with tin reveals "solar" <note>original: *solares*; referring to gold</note>, yet perfect extractions or solutions; for it exhibits such a conspicuous change even in the smallest quantity. <note>This refers to the "Purple of Cassius," a pigment formed by the reaction of gold salts with tin chloride, still used today to color glass.</note>

XXXIII. Evidence of a "lunar" <note>original: *Argenteæ*; referring to silver</note> but complete nature becomes visible through an experiment with *mercury* or copper.

XXXIV. The presence of physical copper is detected either by *urinous spirit* <note>original: *spiritu urinoso*; an early term for ammonia, traditionally derived from fermented urine</note>, which intensifies the smallest quantity into a saturated cyan-blue color; or by substituting *iron* in the place of the dissolved copper. This latter method is most effective if the copper happens to be "white copper," <note>Likely an alloy of copper and arsenic or nickel</note> and thus cannot be recognized by the color change triggered by urinous substances.

XXXV. I would not deny that **Becher** relies somewhat on the foundation of experience when he attributes to *antimony* at least some capacity for the easier "reduction" <term>the process of returning a metal from an ore or salt back to its solid, metallic state</term> into a complete metallic nature, as cited in the aforementioned place; this is clear not only from *metallic slags*:

XXXVI. But also from that experiment which **Becher** asserts notably elsewhere: That the *regulus* <note>original: *regulus*; the metallic heart or "little king" that settles at the bottom of a crucible during smelting</note> imbibes every styptic <note>original: *stipticam*; refers to astringent, metallic-tasting earths like vitriol or alum</note> earth, re-embodies it, and facilitates its entry into the "sun" and "moon" <note>gold and silver</note>.

XXXVII. Otherwise, for such inward preparations of these kinds of earthy extracts, skillful reciprocal precipitations of solutions can also serve. An example of this matter (I speak here of the experiment and the manual procedure, not of the remaining alchemical promises) can be the solution of *gold* in *royal water* <note>original: *aqua regis*; a mixture of nitric and hydrochloric acids</note> precipitated with a solution of *silver* in *strong water* <note>original: *aqua forti*; nitric acid</note>. In this case, while the *acid of salt* <note>hydrochloric acid</note> or the *sal ammoniac* <note>ammonium chloride</note> of the *aqua regia* joins with the dissolved silver, the silver is lost [precipitates]; meanwhile, the *nitrous acid* <note>nitric acid</note> cannot hold the gold. They therefore fall [precipitate] together in a sufficiently fine and close mixture.

XXXVIII. Thus, even vitrification itself, by reducing truly earthy parts into a purer glass, makes the gathering and incorporation with their own kind much easier for those parts which have already moved beyond a simple consistency toward a state of metallic mixture. Hence, all glasses that are notably colored from colored earths, when *fused for a long time and thinly* with silver, provide a clear proof of *gold*.

XXXIX. To this point belongs, as if to its proper place, that experiment—or rather multiple experiments under one heading—which the author has regarding "sandy ore" <note>original: *mineræ arenariæ*</note> Letter C, and indeed Letter B.

XL. Glass-forming earths, the more readily they flow <note>i.e., melt</note>, the more they promote the fusion of metals.

# SPECIMENS OF BECHER’S WORK, PART II

XLI. *Indeed, they mix even more easily with metals that melt thinly and into a glassy fusion. For this reason, lead, when it breaks down into glass, most readily dissolves even these types of earths. Thus, while they would scarcely flow on their own, they flow most readily once the lead becomes glassy in this manner.*

XLII. In this way, powdered flints do not melt together into glass except by the most vehement fire; yet with lead, they are quickly and readily reduced into a very thin, liquid-transparent glass by a very light fire.

XLIII. From these tinted glasses themselves, it is also possible from time to time to draw out a diverse substance—one that is colored and therefore colors the solvents <term>menstrua; liquids used to dissolve or extract substances</term>. Indeed, when these solvents are removed, the substance remains in various colored consistencies. Useful here are solvents that are *semi-sulfurous*, *acetic*, and even those corrosive liquids *semi-sweetened* by fatty substances. <note>In 17th-century chemistry, "fatty" or "oily" substances often referred to the "terra pinguis," Becher’s principle of inflammability later known as phlogiston.</note>

XLIV. *This is all the more true since even these fatty substances, more immediately, resolve the connection of this matter from its simpler earthy substance, leading it actually into a metallic state, according to that famous Becherian experiment.*

XLV. What various solid earths can achieve even within the perfect metals themselves is attested by the alterations of gold by pumice; and of silver by bricks, asbestos <gloss>feather alum</gloss>, hematite, and processes of cementation. <note>Cementation was a high-heat refining process where gold or silver was packed with dry materials like brick dust or salts to remove impurities.</note>

XLVI. For the distillation of saline mineral concretions, earths and stones serve equally well. For instance, **Viganus** <note>Giovanni Francesco Vigani (c. 1650–1712), the first professor of chemistry at Cambridge University</note> prepares a very reddish spirit from nitre <note>saltpeter</note> and flints, just as the ordinary spirits of these substances are distilled from bolary <gloss>clay-like</gloss> earths combined with nitre and salt.

XLVII. *Indeed, the most subtle dissolution of flints through mere heating and quenching <note>original: "ignitionem & extinctionem"; the process of heating a stone to redness and plunging it into liquid to shatter its structure</note>, according to Becher in "Physica Subterranea" (Section 3, Chapter 2, Number 12), is an experiment truly worthy of consideration.*

XLVIII. *Just as the diversity of solubility in different earths must be observed; for flints and mountain crystal <note>clear quartz</note>, however much they appear to be hard bodies, are dissolved by moderate acids, whereas sands and various other earths are not affected by them at all.*

XLIX. *These same powdered flints, when mixed with a good alkaline salt, are melted so that the salt plainly dissolves them and they intimately penetrate one another—an effect that does not occur similarly with most other earths.*

L. *However, to satisfy our author’s assertion that antimony—not simply by reason of its sulfur, but also by its metallic <gloss>regulus</gloss> part—absorbs and resolves earths and stones, let an experiment be conducted with sulfurated alkali (and in abundance). This will reveal how much more is dissolved by the antimony or by simple sulfur prepared in such a way.*

LI. Notable is the recommendation of the calcination <term>heating a substance to a high temperature to change its properties or reduce it to powder</term> of earths and precious stones with sulfur; but it is also certain, and equally known to the skilled, that commonly, in its raw state, sulfur effects nothing.

### EXPERIMENTS IN BECHER’S THEORY

...he may accomplish. If anything is to be attempted here, or rather, if it is to be achieved, it would be better to proceed by this method, using sulfur and alkali.

LII. The power of **lean earths** <note>original: *macrarum terrarum*; mineral earths that are "poor" or low in combustible "fatty" matter</note> is especially effective in absorbing, transforming, and subduing saline-sulfurous and arsenical materials. For this reason, they are conveniently applied in processes of **cementation** <term>cementatio; a process of heating a solid metal with powdered chemical reagents to change its properties</term>.

LIII. A significant example of this can be found in the propositions of Schellenberg, which can be seen in the *Chemical Concordance*, section XII.

LIV. Indeed, the inventor's intention is to be praised: that he uses not only these lean earths, but also those that are **vitrifiable** <note>glass-making</note>, sandy, or muddy—or rather silty—**not clayey, but loamy** <note>original: *nicht thonicht, sondern leimicht*</note>. He does this so that whatever remains after the volatile part has been fixed may acquire what they call "actual entry," namely, **fusibility**.

LV. Truly, just as many ores cause much trouble for smelters because of their hard and stubborn flow, so too can **furnace mud** <note>original: *limus furnarius*; the residue or lining of a furnace</note>, sandy earths, and **fusible flints** bring them no small convenience and benefit—provided they are not just mixed haphazardly with the ores, but are first lightly roasted together before being exposed to final smelting and roasting. There is certainly a great difference between these methods. Indeed, even simple piles of such earthy and mineral mixtures often show how they react together, as they bond into a dense mass. Certain lead-like <note>original: *plumbagineæ*</note> ores do this when mixed with sandy or clay-like earths. Another example is found in that softer **cobalt glass** <note>smalt, a blue pigment made from cobalt ore and silica</note> used by **pottery painters**; when tempered with sand and kept more or less moist in closed barrels, it bonds with the sand into a stone-like hardness.

LVI. This is not the place, nor is there time, to discuss at length the behavior of different earths toward different acids. It will suffice to advise that a careful selection is necessary, especially if the earthy substance itself, or something mixed within it, is to be treated. The Author has discussed this quite aptly more than once, specifically regarding "sandy ore" and the extraction of **golden sulfur** <note>original: *sulphuris aurei*; likely antimony trisulfide or a similar vibrant precipitate</note> (under "martial sandy ore," section I).

LVII. It will be useful to keep this consideration in mind: most **solvents** do not attack even the **metallic calces** <term>calx; the powdery residue left after a metal is roasted, now known as an oxide</term>—much less these earthy substances which are even further removed from a metallic state—unless an **inflammable mixture** <note>referring to Becher's theory that "fatty earth" or inflammability must be added to turn a powder back into a metal</note> is restored to them. Therefore, one must carefully weigh what benefit can be obtained in such earths by applying **Becher's method** (according to Supplement I) before they are treated with solvents.

LVIII. Finally, one must not neglect the careful smelting and, especially, the **reduction** of earthy glasses or **slags** <note>original: *scoriarum*</note> remaining from old, perhaps superficial, treatments. An excellent example of this is recorded in Albinus’s *Chronicle of Schneeberg*...

### SPECIMENS OF BECHER’S THEORY, PART II.

...There, when the smelters were besieged by the worst weather for several days, so that access for mineral transport was cut off by shifting floods, out of boredom as much as the lack of earned wages, they re-melted old heaps of **slag** <term>scoria; the stony waste matter separated from metals during smelting</term>, from which they obtained a great quantity of silver.

LIX. This is especially true in the softer **leady slag** <note>original: *plumbagineis scoriis*; German: *weichen Schlacken*</note>, in which lead not infrequently still remains. This lead would not be worth the effort through simple **reduction** <term>the chemical process of extracting a metal from its ore or slag</term>; however, by combining such slag with very fresh lead-rich materials and melting them all at once with a vigorous fire in a reduction furnace, a profit will hardly ever be lacking. This is true even if such a business is undertaken by design, as Becher rightly advises.

LX. Indeed, although I do not clearly see what that notable expression means in the *Chemical Concordance*, Part XII, no. 187: "**Therefore making lead is my first foundation**" <note>original: *Derhalben ist Bley machen mein erstes Fundament*</note>. While it would certainly be no small art to be able to **produce** lead (meaning from cheaper and everywhere abundant materials), I think these themes are also derived from **Schellenberg** <note>Johann Jacob Schellenberg, a chemist and contemporary often cited by Becher</note>. They correspond to the earlier sections, specifically the last deduction of number 1: "**Now follows — in the mining towns —**" <note>original: *Nun folget ----- in denen Berg-Stätten ----*</note>. There, under the fourth division, he speaks of **lead-antimony** ores; those who do not know how to precipitate these metals are forced to buy lead from **Poland**.

LXI. Meanwhile, whatever the case may be, the report transcribed at **Paris** on August 27, 1667, is certainly unworthy of being forgotten (referenced in *Prætorius in the Pot of Luck*, p. 464). It states that a certain man proposed and offered to the Council there to smelt **copper** and **tin** from coals and earths, of the same absolute quality as that imported from **England** into France. It is mentioned that at that time, such metals were usually imported from foreign regions for a price of 150,000 pounds (50,000 Thalers) annually.

LXII. Just as also that melting of the **sand of the Danube**, which our author mentions in *Ores of the Sand* [Miner. Arenar.] at letter D, rightly belongs to the present account.

LXIII. Furthermore, the palm of victory for proving the demonstrations of this class goes entirely to that experiment which I presented more fully in Part IV; it is the simplest of this group, as stated there—indeed, it was also mentioned at length a little earlier.

LXIV. For this reason, it seems to me that our author himself, in *Ores of the Sand*, viewed that **Grillian process** <note>likely referring to a process by the chemist Grill</note> from a far different angle than he really ought to have. Indeed, had he followed his own much simpler advice, he would certainly have managed this business better. But "**sometimes even the good Homer nods**" <note>original: *quandoque bonus dormitat Homerus*; a Latin idiom meaning even the most skilled experts can make mistakes</note> (cited in letter B).

LXV. Those who desire to contemplate some experimental specimen of the **entry of extracted styptic earths** <note>original: *terreorum extractorum stipticorum*; "styptic" here refers to mineral substances with astringent or binding properties</note> into metallic mixtures can consider that Becherian warning which he tosses in several times, sometimes **directly**, sometimes **indirectly**, concerning the **extract** of

LXVI. LXVII. For the rest, the effectiveness of black earth—or charcoal ash derived from **tartar** <term>the potassium-rich sediment left in wine barrels</term>—or other ashes not thoroughly burned to whiteness, does not belong equally to this present chapter. These substances can impart a certain whiteness to both copper and gold itself, if they are melted together after a long period of **cementation** <term>a process of heating a metal in contact with a powdered reagent</term>.

These points may suffice for the experimental consideration of earthy bodies. I may seem to have strayed somewhat from my plan toward the theoretical recommendation of these matters in this section; but I testify that I have done so quite deliberately, because I had to break off due to the pressures of the work. In this view, I preferred to at least point out things which time and place do not allow me to fully execute. Indeed, I would conclude the entire treatise even here, were I not still bound by the sequence of my deduction to add something through experiments concerning the effectiveness of the **inflammable principle** <note>a reference to the "sulfur" or "phlogiston" thought to be the source of fire and color in minerals</note> in the mineral and metallic kingdom, which I shall accomplish as briefly as possible.

## PART IV.

# SULFUROUS SUBSTANCES.

Experiments regarding the sulfurous nature and its effectiveness in the subterranean kingdom are so far from being neglected in a physical and scientific treatment of minerals, that I instead believe for certain that the most powerful effects—both in mixing and penetrating, as well as in materially entering and constituting—must be ascribed to that species of terrestrial matter. For certainly that assertion of mine—considered so subtle and perhaps "purely intellectual"—which I proposed at the end of my teachings, stands firm: *That this sulfurous principle is, as it were, the supreme and final **crown** <note>original: *Colophon*; a finishing touch or peak of achievement</note> of the mixing agency and the completion of the material constitution in the artificial synthesis of noble metals.* This assertion, I say, exists so sensibly and, as it were, tangibly in the actual fact and experiment, that I would not hesitate to deem anyone who dared to doubt it unworthy of a response. For while all other principles fail to bring that generation to a complete effect—indeed, demonstrating their insufficiency by a clearly unequal result—this principle of ours, as soon as it arrives, [brings] the whole matter (namely a perfect one, and indeed within our arts...)

...of a *dissolvable mixture*, it brings about the act and effect almost in an instant. Indeed, as the discussion here concerns experiments, I will use suitable arguments and cite this experiment: that if that matter which, by the benefit of our *sulphureous principle* <term>the "fatty earth" or inflammable principle in Becher’s system, later associated with phlogiston</term>, produces and brings forth a noble metal in just a few moments; even if it were joined and worked with silver or gold for a long time by **cementation** <term>heating a metal with powdered reagents</term>, smelting, or whatever superior method, it nevertheless provides no increase to the metal itself. This would be impossible if that metal were already physically present in that mass, and was not rather brought to sight by *production* <note>meaning the actual creation of the metallic form</note> rather than mere simple extraction through the meeting of our *sulphureous principle*.

Indeed, so that the evidence of our assertion—and the true logic of the whole experiment—may be more apparent, I add this: if those materials (from which silver is produced by the meeting of the *sulphureous principle*), no matter how well united they are, are reduced to the clearest glass by the power of a suitable fire, not only does no speck of better metal settle or separate from this; but also the *color* of that glass so produced shows not the slightest alteration that might suggest an interwoven noble metal. Yet neither gold nor silver, however small the quantity, allow themselves to be mixed into *glasses* without settling; or certainly, they would inevitably alter or cloud the *color of the glass*. None of this happens here.

Meanwhile, just as this experiment itself is truly very *simple* as an experiment, as I have repeatedly warned; so certainly it hardly occurs even to those well-versed and skilled in it that such subtle *theoretico-practical* effects lie beneath it. But what is *true* is indeed simple; and just as *truth* always encompasses evidence for the sake of knowing, so it is wrong to wonder that truth presents itself here even in simple things and aspects. Since this entire class of experiments consists of very plain and simple operations, we can fulfill them all the more conveniently by applying only this preliminary axiom:

->THE SULPHUREOUS PRINCIPLE ENTERS<-
->MINERAL AND METALLIC MIXTURES<-
->MOST PROMPTLY, MOST SIMPLY,<-
->AND MOST DEEPLY.<-

### EXPERIMENTS.

**I.** *The four ignoble metals* <term>base metals: lead, tin, copper, and iron</term> *contain an inflammable substance; which, partly escaping into the air by an open flame, leaves the metal crumbling into ash; and partly can be burned with nitre* <term>saltpeter</term> *so that it forms a flame with it.*

# EXPERIMENTS ON BECHER’S THEORY

<page-num>157</page-num>

II. *Copper* is most readily consumed by fire; even by simple heating, which produces the **copper-ash** <note>original: *Kupffer-Asche*</note> used by goldsmiths whenever they heat their plates:

III. As well as by urging it with a more vehement open fire, where it exhales entirely into the **air**, as occurs in a **docimastic furnace** <term>an assaying furnace used to determine the purity of ores and metals</term>.

IV. Likewise, when it is thinned by **spirit of vinegar** <note>acetic acid</note> and finally joined with **spirit of wine** <note>ethanol</note> and soaked into paper, it is also entirely scattered into the air, as noted by the Author.

V. Next to **copper**, **iron** is burned most quickly; after **iron**, **steel**:

VI. After these, **tin**: and last of all, **lead**:

VII. Indeed, both of these [tin and lead] are burned most quickly and abundantly when **joined together** and exposed to the open air under a vigorous fire.

VIII. Above all these, the **regulus of antimony** <term>the metallic form of antimony, as opposed to its ore</term> is reduced to ashes most rapidly, and indeed by a gentle glowing fire.

IX. **Iron** especially, but also **regulus of antimony**, **copper**, and **lead** (provided nothing is present with which they might turn into glass), do not burn when in a strictly closed environment.

X. Not even **tin** burns in a strictly closed and full vessel, in whose cavity—even if empty of metal—the air cannot prevail.

XI. All these metals are also burned very quickly with **nitre** <term>saltpeter or potassium nitrate</term>, with a flame breaking forth, provided the metal has been **reduced to powder**.

XII. This is done most intensely by **tin, iron, and regulus of antimony**; it occurs more mildly, and without a significant flame, with **lead and copper**.

XIII. Thus **lead**, if remixed with an equal part of nitre and brought to a gentle glow while the nitre is flowing, and stirred with an iron rod, breaks down entirely into the consistency of **litharge** <term>lead monoxide, a secondary mineral form of lead</term>. This, once the salt is washed away and it is further heated gently, turns into a stable, glass-forming **calx** <term>the powdery remains left after a metal has been burned; an oxide</term>.

XIV. If, however, the **nitre** is melted with the **lead** so that they flow as a liquid, the nitre seizes some portion of the lead, though small; once its inflammable part is more perfectly burned away, it reduces it to a **white powder**, which is to be collected after the salt has been dissolved and washed away.

XV. The **deflagration of iron with nitre** <note>a rapid, forceful burning</note> succeeds most readily of all if two parts of **nitre** are added to three parts of iron; or indeed, one part of **nitre** to two parts of iron.

XVI. Each and every one of these metals is burned more readily when fused with **regulus of antimony** and then burned with nitre in the form of a powder.

XVII. The burning of **copper** in this class is a curious thing: for example, when one part of **copper** is mixed with several parts of **silver** and about three parts of **regulus of antimony** (relative to the weight of the copper), they are separated by the successive injection of nitre under a vigorous fire. From this, the first **slags** <term>the stony waste matter separated from metals during smelting</term> (which must be removed in stages) are white or slightly yellowish; but the **very last** are clearly red. These, when purified, result in **clear glasses**,

XVIII. Once these metals have been so thoroughly burnt <note>original: *combustis*; here meaning oxidized or calcined</note>, they are not permitted to return to their metallic appearance through any other experiment or additive, except one that can again communicate and instill in them such **inflammable matter** <term>this refers to 'terra pinguis' or phlogiston, the substance Becher believed was responsible for fire and metallicity</term>. Indeed, once this is applied, they most readily regain their former complete mixture, metallic fusion, **ductility, solubility**, and mutual convergence or liquid **blending**. They had been deprived of each and every one of these properties until now by the **subtraction** of that same inflammable principle.

XIX. This is achieved by simple melting with charcoal; in the case of lead and the regulus of antimony, it happens immediately without any other additive, provided that their **calces** <note>original: *calces*; the powdery metallic ash or oxide</note> produced by burning are first melted into a glass and then charcoal is thrown upon it.

XX. For other metals, however, salts are conveniently used to ensure at least a subtle friction and penetration: **alkali or fixed nitre, and common salt**, with pulverized charcoal thrown on top. Or **tartar** may be used, since it penetrates these salts more deeply than charcoal does; it is from this that the composition of **black flux** <term>a mixture of potassium carbonate and carbon used in smelting to transform ores back into metal</term> took its origin.

XXI. Since copper flows with greater difficulty when alone, this experiment can be conducted with the regulus of antimony; namely, two parts of **regulus of antimony** and one part of **copper** are melted together, pulverized, and burnt into a powder using one and a half times the total weight of **nitre** <note>saltpeter</note>, or more. Thus, if a small particle is taken and the salt is washed away, it provides a powder born from those metals. If, however, **charcoal** is perpetually supplied to the remaining mass under a vigorous melting flame until the charcoal finally floats idly upon the surface of the dross, not only the **regulus** is reduced in the meantime, but also the **copper** itself, which had previously been burnt into that tender powder.

XXII. If **tin** is held in a large iron spoon and melted to a gentle glow, it gradually acquires a dark skin or film across the surface, which, when stirred with a poker, stands as a powdery substance. When a certain amount of this material has been produced, it is sufficient to throw on small pieces of **tallow** <note>animal fat</note> or even **pitch**, and stir the material vigorously. Thus, all at once, all that ashen powder returns and melts into a shining liquid and true **tin**.

XXIII. Likewise, the immediate effectiveness of **oily substances** <note>original: *pinguium*; fats or oils</note> upon colored earths of this sort is known from **Becher’s iron-bearing experiment** (found in *Supplement I*) using brick-clay, furnace-mud, and linseed oil.

XXIV. Cramer <note>Johann Andreas Cramer (1710–1777), a famous metallurgist and chemist</note> has already noted that **copper** can be restored from **ochre** in the same manner.

XXV. Furthermore, the fact that an abundant mixing or, more importantly, an intimate working-in of this **inflammable** matter with these metallic substances brings about **volatility** in them, is demonstrated to the eye by melting them with copious amounts of charcoal; or rather, **fusion through the midst of coals**, especially when a rush of free air is applied. Thus they are dissolved...

<meta>This page continues the experimental proofs of Becher's theory. The preceding text discussed the reduction of metals and the role of the inflammable principle (terra pinguis) in restoring metallic properties. This page transitions from metallic "flowers" to the synthesis of sulfur.</meta>

-> EXPERIMENTAL PROOFS OF BECHER’S THEORY <-

<page-num>159</page-num>
<header>EXPERIMENTAL PROOFS OF BECHER'S THEORY</header>
<sig>Rrr 3</sig>

...as much minerals as metals of that kind, simple ones; and all the more so for those treated with sulfur, glasses, crocus powders <note>original: *croci*; referring to metallic oxides, often iron or antimony, named for their saffron color</note>, etc. [They are reduced] into the finest **flowers** <note>original: *flores*; a term for the fine powder or sublimation product formed in a furnace</note>.

XXVI. Nay, indeed, the very ignition of such metals with nitre <note>original: *nitro*; potassium nitrate or saltpeter</note> reduces some of these into flowers: most likely on this same basis, that while certain inflammable portions are resolved into flame, they snatch away some other portions—agitated and refined by that same incomplete action or motion—from the remaining thicker parts.

XXVII. What might be achieved by this method through the **regulus of antimony** <term>the pure metallic form of antimony</term> remixed with metals, or the saline-arsenical substance mixed with horn-like precipitates <note>original: *corneis præcipitatis*; likely referring to silver chloride, known as "luna cornea" or horn silver</note>, and various other semi-volatile preparations of metallic bodies for greater volatilization: this must be left to careful experience.

XXVIII. It remains to say something about mineral sulfur itself: from which, however, we shall pluck only the more important points pertaining to our specimen. Sulfur, once stripped of its inflammable part, is an acid salt, famous under the name of **spirit or oil of sulfur** <note>original: *spiritus aut olei sulphuris*; sulfuric acid produced by burning sulfur</note>: indeed, it is the spirit or oil of vitriol.

XXIX. If this acid is in any way subtly worked and intimately mixed with the inflammable substance from charcoal, or with any very fine soot burnt (in a closed vessel), it becomes sulfur again.

XXX. It is an observation of Boyle’s: *Oil of vitriol <term>concentrated sulfuric acid</term> digested with oil of turpentine, when finally driven by heat—at first gently, then strongly when nothing more follows from gentleness—passes over as sulfur.* Various difficulties, however, underlie the manual operation <note>original: *enchiriseω*; a Greek term for the practical handling or "hand-work" of an experiment</note>.

XXXI. The same is done more conveniently if opium is made into a paste with oil of vitriol, or some similar succulent, fatty matter. And let the distillation *be conducted with such a proportionate succession of impulses* that a similar sulfurous concretion finally comes forth.

XXXII. Most exquisitely, with no wasted cost, no superfluous labor, no confusion of products, and with the clearest reasons for the whole process of making and producing, the entire business is completed by the method I have described at length in *Zymotechnia* and *The Month of July* <note>Two works by Georg Ernst Stahl, who edited and championed Becher's theories</note>. Namely, through this acid fixed with any alkali; take half an ounce of the resulting neutral salt <note>original: *enixi salis*; literally "strained salt," referring to a neutral salt like potassium sulfate</note> and mix it with an equal part <note>original: *p. æ.*, abbreviation for *partes æquales*</note> of raw alkali, or even common salt, and expose it to a melting fire. When the alkali or common salt softens (for that compound salt resists melting), let charcoal, coarsely pulverized, be supplied: in this way, the whole mass will flow like liquid. By throwing onto this more of that neutral salt—that is, *acid fixed by alkali*—many pounds, indeed almost an infinite amount, can be melted together, provided charcoal is always supplied. In this way, **Liver of Sulfur** <term>potassium polysulfide, named for its liver-brown color</term> is made; that is, sulfur joined to an alkaline salt. *For the alkali was used to bind the acid; and this acid, with the inflammable principle from the charcoal, turns into sulfur.* Thus Liver of Sulfur is formed: from this, by means of vinegar, true sulfur is precipitated in the form of a **milky powder**, which by gentle melting over the fire flows together into common sulfur. It becomes and remains absolutely true common sulfur, fully equipped and visible with all the actions and properties familiar to the native variety.

<meta>catchword: XXXIII.</meta>

<summary>This page discusses the volatilization of metals into "flowers" and provides experimental proofs for the composition of sulfur. Stahl explains how sulfur can be synthesized by combining its "acid" (sulfuric acid) with an inflammable principle derived from charcoal or oils.</summary>

<keywords>antimony, nitre, flowers of sulfur, oil of vitriol, Robert Boyle, Zymotechnia, Liver of Sulfur, alkali, phlogiston theory, synthesis of sulfur</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of sulfur and its chemical principles. While the previous page focused on the physical reduction of metals into "flowers" and the composition of sulfur, this page addresses the historical context of these experiments—specifically Johann Rudolf Glauber’s "miraculous salt"—and provides a detailed list of how sulfur, when bound with an alkali, interacts with various metals.</meta>

-> SPECIMEN OF BECHER, PART II <-

<page-num>160</page-num>
<header>SPECIMEN OF BECHER, PART II</header>

XXXIII. Through a different experiment regarding one ingredient, but based on the absolute same foundation, **Glauber**—the first among those with deep insight—performed this same feat nearly half a century ago **with his miraculous salt** <note>original: *salis mirabilis*; now known as sodium sulfate</note>. Specifically, he used **vitriolic sulfuric acid** joined with the **alkaline substance of common salt**. This differs from our own salt in two ways: (1) **Fusibility**, which Glauber’s salt possesses without any additive, whereas ours does not; (2) **The cost of preparation**, which in his case is measured in many **groschen** <note>original: *grossorum*; a silver coin of significant value</note>, or even more, while in ours it is measured in **pennies** <note>original: *nummorum*; small, common coins</note>.

However, **Glauber** had no **theory** for this experiment, expressing only **wonderment**, from which he gave it the name **"miraculous salt."** Nor did anyone after him provide a theory; instead, the **contrary** was always assumed—as if the **product** were not **true sulfur**, but merely **something analogous** to it.

XXXIV. We must add an experiment that is **playful in its operation**, yet **profoundly philosophical in its consideration**. This occurs when this **inflammable matter** <term>original: *phlogistos*; the principle of fire or flammability</term> is introduced into a **compound of extremely subtle oils**, with which it seems most intimately joined, only to be separated from them again **in a moment**. It changes from a subtle fluid into a **solid form**, and from a volatile state into a **fixed** one (by burning it in closed vessels). Specifically, that **inflammable** substance is reduced into **soot** <note>original: *fuliginem*</note>.

XXXV. This **subtle inflammable matter** does not have an **immediate** entry into **gold**; rather, it enters **mediately** <note>indirectly, through an intermediate step</note> under the compound form of **sulfur**. Thus, the **Glauberian** experiment showed this long ago by the very truth of the matter; but because it was **understood** neither by the author nor by anyone else, it always remained "miraculous." Finally, however, it has been shown that all this efficacy belongs to **common sulfur**, without any need for miracles. This is certainly due to its **inflammable** part. For if this were the effect of the **acid** part, other **weaker**—even the **weakest**—substances would not be able to drive out such an **acid**; just as it could not be separated from it again by simple **inflammation**.

XXXVI. In the final place, it is pleasing to set down the efficacy of **sulfur**, thus bound by **alkali**, upon **metals**:

I. It dissolves **all metals** (except **mercury**, which flies away) as well as **intermediate minerals** and finally **soluble earthy** substances.

II. It dissolves **gold, tin, and the regulus of antimony** <term>the pure metallic form of antimony</term> so finely that (by repeating the process) it **carries them with it through a filter**, either entirely or nearly so.

III. It does not resolve **copper** in the same way, yet it appears to dissolve it, as the **sulfur** precipitated from that solution takes on not a **milky color**, but a **reddish-yellow color**, and leaves something behind after **burning away**, etc.

IV. With **silver, iron, and lead**, it sinks to the bottom as if separated from the **alkali** itself.

V. Whatever among all these things is not so intimately united with the **sulfur** as to pass through the filter soon settles to the bottom in the form of an extremely fine powder or **calx** <term>a metallic oxide or residue left after heating</term>.

VI. And **any such metal**, even **gold** itself, is dissolved into the **most tender powder** by this momentary labor. **I treated this subject in the month of April, 1698.**

<summary>Becher explains the chemical theory behind Glauber’s "miraculous salt," arguing it is a form of sulfur acting through its inflammable principle (phlogistos). He also details how sulfur combined with alkali can dissolve or reduce various metals into fine powders.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes the series of experiments and theoretical observations regarding the principles of minerals and sulfur discussed in the preceding pages. While the previous page contrasted Becher’s findings with those of Johann Rudolf Glauber, this page serves as a philosophical and moral postscript to the work.</meta>

<page-num>161</page-num>
<header>BECHER’S THEORETICAL EXPERIMENTS</header>

Many more *operations*, or experiments, as well as observations or proofs, could still be produced: were it not for the fact that the inevitable constraint of time <note>original: *fatalis temporis ratio*; likely referring to the publication deadline or the author's own life circumstances</note> commanded us to bring this to an end. Thus, we leave many more things to the skill of the reader. This much is certain: whoever—either before us or through us—is able to exquisitely grasp and understand these matters which have been presented here both *theoretically and practically* through various perspectives, will require no further instruction in this genre, as they will be able to attain the rest of their own accord. 

However, we caution that no one should hope for "lofty wisdom" <note>original: *altum sapere*; a warning against intellectual pride or over-reaching beyond one's station</note> from this; rather, let them remember the words of that comic poet: *To flee, but not beyond the house.* <note>original: *Ita fugere, ut ne, præter casam*; a proverb from the Roman playwright Terence, meaning to avoid a mistake without running into a worse one, or not to overreach in one's efforts.</note> We have sealed all these works of ours under the title of *Subterranean Physics*; not *Chemistry*, much less *Alchemy*; and we have appealed from *greed* <term>original: *concupiscentia*; Becher uses this to describe the "lust for gold" that motivated many alchemists</term> to *Science*. 

For those preparing better things, the field is open and free. They will not suffer envy, provided they bring none themselves: by carping or slandering against *science*, against the facts and their connections, against the *evidence*, against the authors of these works, or against *prudence* and various true moral and personal considerations. In this way, everything will either succeed well, or at least turn out well; either for the *advancement of science*, or at least not to its *detriment*. Indeed, most of all, let it be for the **Glory of Divine Wisdom**, which remains our perpetual goal and most desired end.

->GLORY TO GOD ALONE!<-
